DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Termination of pregnancy may be offered when chromosomal aberrations and syndromes are present. Fetoscopic endoluminal tracheal occlusion (FETO) with a balloon, particularly for fetuses considered otherwise unviable, has yielded survival rates approaching 50%. Gestation should be prolonged until near term if possible; maternal corticosteroids have also been proposed. In newborns, pre- and post-ductal percutaneous oxygen saturation measurements may assess the pulmonary function. Spontaneous ventilation or high frequency, low pressure ventilation (<20-25 cm H2O), no relaxation, alkalinization and adoption of modest gasometric goals (pre-ductal saturation of 80-95%, PaO2 60 mm Hg, hypercapnia <60 mm Hg) are now the standard. Extra-corporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) has also been used. Inotropic drugs (eg: dobutamine, dopamine) may be used to treat cardiac anomalies. Surgical repair of the hernia, undertaken only after cardio-respiratory functions are stable, replaces viscera into the abdomen and closes the diaphragmatic defect; a prosthetic patch may be necessary to repair the defect. Some surgeons perform this operation by video-assisted thoracoscopy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Considering prenatal and preoperative fatalities, mortality is 50-60%. Post-operative survival rate is 70-80%, up to 90% in certain institutions, particularly in non-syndromic CDH. Right-sided hernias seem to have a worse prognosis and may require more ECMO support. After surgical repair, pleural effusions and chronic respiratory tract disease are frequent, along with gastroesophageal reflux. Neurodevelopmental deficits are a risk following bouts of cerebral hypoxia. Neurosensorial deafness has been reported in a small proportion of patients.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pallister-Hall syndrome (PHS), a pleiotropic autosomal dominant malformative disorder, is characterized by hypothalamic hamartoma, pituitary dysfunction, bifid epiglottis, polydactyly, and, more rarely, renal abnormalities and genitourinary malformations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Approximately 100 patients have been reported to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most patients with PHS present at birth with skeletal polydactyly of the third or fourth digit or postaxial polydactyly; either may be accompanied by cutaneous syndactyly and nail dysplasia. Facial features may include a short nose, flat nasal bridge, and low-set, posteriorly angled ears. Cleft palate, cleft uvula and multiple buccal frenula have been reported in some patients. An asymptomatic bifid epiglottis is nearly pathognomonic, however, some patients present with more severe posterior laryngeal clefts leading to potentially fatal respiratory insufficiency. Hypothalamic hamartoma is often asymptomatic, however, it may be associated with panhypopituitarism. Acute primary adrenal insufficiency may also occur in severe cases, as well as milder forms of adrenal insufficiency. Precocious puberty manifests in some cases. Neurological involvement can include gelastic epilepsy (seizures that manifest as facial grimacing, smiling or laughter) or other seizure types. Renal agenesis or dysplasia as well as other genitourinary anomalies have been reported, including vaginal atresia or hydrometrocolpos, microphallus, or cryptorchidism. Other findings may include intrauterine growth retardation, abnormal lung lobation, generalized skeletal dysplasia with mesomelic shortening and radial bowing of limbs, imperforate anus and congenital heart defects.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: PHS is due to mutations of the GLI3 gene (7p13) that encodes a transcription factor activated by the sonic hedgehog pathway. Mutations lead to alterations in gene expression during development.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Clinical diagnostic criteria of patients with at least one family member with PHS require two findings: hypothalamic hamartoma, visualized on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) as a non-enhancing, midline hypothalamic mass that is isointense to gray matter on all pulse sequences, and mesoaxial polydactyly. This may be confirmed by full sequence analysis of GLI3.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include oral-facial-digital syndrome type 6, Holzgreve-Wagner-Rehder syndrome, McKusick-Kaufman syndrome, Holt-Oram syndrome, Bardet-Biedl syndrome, Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, as well as craniopharyngioma, Greig cephalopolysyndactyly syndrome Ellis Van Creveld syndrome and congenital hypothalamic hamartoma syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal genetic testing may be considered in families harboring a known PHS causative mutation of GLI3 and fetal MRI can exclude hypothalamic hamartoma. However, familial occurrences of PHS are generally milder than sporadic ones.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: PHS is autosomal dominant, passed on to 50% of offspring, but expression is highly variable and many cases are sporadic, due to de novo mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic. Medical imaging should include MRI to assess the hypothalamic hamartoma, X-rays of hands and feet and a full-skeletal survey as well as renal ultrasound. Laboratory assessment including a full endocrinological function and cholesterol synthesis analysis should be performed. At birth, breathing of patients with polydactyly should be monitored and indirect laryngoscopy should be performed. Tracheotomy may be necessary. If present, surgical intervention for imperforate anus must be undertaken. Multiple lifelong hormone replacement therapies may be required.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis should be assumed to be excellent until proven otherwise. However, in its most severe forms, panhypopituitarism and severe airway malformations can be lethal; imperforate anus may also be lethal if not recognized. Intellectual deficits and behavioral alterations have not been directly correlated with the syndrome.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A very rare genetic multisystemic disorder characterized by progressive neurological, ophthalmologic and endocrine manifestations leading to severe handicap.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The neurological manifestations include peripheral neuropathy, spastic paraplegia and cerebellar ataxia. The symptoms progressively worsen for patients over time. The ophthalmologic manifestations are caused by chorioretinal dystrophy presenting widespread chorioretinal atrophy (thinning of the retina, loss of retinal architecture and choroid vessels) under fundus observation. The onset of visual impairment ranges widely from 1 year old to 60 years old. Hypogenitalism is present at birth due to hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism with primary amenorrhea, small penis and testes, or absence of pubic hair/breast development. Related growth delay during adolescence can also occur.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Likely pathogenic or pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 gene have been identified in patients with Laurence-Moon syndrome (LMS). The PNPLA6 gene codes for the patatin-like phospholipase domain-containing protein 6, also called neuropathy target esterase (NTE), a 1375 amino acids long protein (UniProt accession number: Q8IY17). The protein is composed of 5 domains including a single pass transmembrane domain (N-terminus), 3 cyclic nucleotide-binding domains (cNMP) and a NEST domain (NTE-esterase domain) at the C-terminus. The protein is a serine hydrolase that functions as a phospholipase B by catalyzing the deacylation of glycerophospholipids. It has also been shown to have a strong lysophospholipase activity. Altogether it plays a major role in phospholipid homeostasis, membrane trafficking, and axonal integrity in cells. Previously, the terms Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome or Laurence-Moon-Bardet-Biedl syndrome were used for this disease. However, the association Laurence-Moon/Bardet-Bield is no longer relevant given the different underlying gene mechanisms. It should be underlined that this condition is now clearly considered as part of the continuous spectrum of PNPLA6-related disorders linked to NTE activity. Recent evidence seems to inversely correlate the level of NTE activity with disease severity and tissue onset.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected on clinical presentation and confirmed by genetic testing including sequencing of the PNPLA6 gene (by direct Sanger sequencing or panel/exome next generation sequencing).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses are the other PNPLA6-related disorders such as autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia type 39, cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome, ataxia-hypogonadism-choroidal dystrophy syndrome and trichomegaly-retina pigmentary degeneration-dwarfism syndrome that share all or a subset of the clinical manifestations, sometimes with a different age of onset.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible where the pathogenic variant(s) have previously been identified in an affected family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is only symptomatic and depends on the severity of the neurological manifestations. Optical aids can be provided to manage visual impairment.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Data on prognosis is limited for patients with PNPLA6-related disorders but recent evidence has shown a highly dependent relation between the NTE activity and severity of the disease and/or tissue onset.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare developmental defect during embryogenesis characterized by abnormal development and enlargement of the cerebellum, and an increased intracranial pressure. The tumors can be characterized by the abnormal growth of ganglion cells that regulate activities in the cerebellum.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Dysplastic gangliocytoma of the cerebellum; LDD

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Approximately 230 cases of Lhermitte-Duclos disease (LDD) have been reported in literature to date, there is no sex or race preference. It typically presents between ages of 30-50, although it may occur in infants and adults over age of 60.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: It manifests, most commonly in the third and fourth decades of life, with headache, nausea, cerebellar dysfunction, occlusive hydrocephalus, ataxia, visual disturbances and other cranial nerve palsies. Various associated abnormalities may be present (megalencephaly, microgyria, hydromyelia, polydactyly, partial gigantism, macroglossia). Co-existing conditions include Cowden syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is uncertain; germline mutations in tumor suppressor gene PTEN have been identified in some patients with LDD.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of LDD is confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and genetic testing for germline PTEN pathogenic variant.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis include Cowden syndrome as LDD can co-manifest along with Cowden syndrome features.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible if the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in the family, but was never described in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: This is an autosomal dominant condition which may occur sporadically or in a familial form. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk family members to inform them of the 50% risk of transmission for each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management includes decompressive surgical intervention.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: There is no data regarding the prognosis of this disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A partial autosomal trisomy characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, generalized hypotonia, postnatal growth retardation, variable brain and heart anomalies and dysmorphic features, including frontal bossing, round face, full cheeks, low-set ears, broad nasal bridge, short nose with anteverted nares, long philtrum, thin upper lip vermilion, and everted, thick lower lip. Unspecific associated congenital anomalies have also been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Somatic-type malignancy (STM) can occur infrequently within a primary or metastatic testicular germ cell tumor (TGCT) and is associated with dismal prognosis and survival. STM with chondrosarcomatous features is exceedingly rare and head and neck involvement has not been previously documented. A 39-year-old white man presented with nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Imaging disclosed a 6.9-cm expansile tumor involving the nasal cavity and skull base with intraorbital and intracranial extension. The histopathologic properties of the tumor were compatible with chondrosarcoma, grade II-III. Immunohistochemically, malignant cells were strongly and diffusely positive for S100 and epithelial markers, and showed loss of SMARCB1 expression. IDH1/2 mutations were not detected. Following whole-body PET scan, a 7.0-cm left testicular mass was discovered and diagnosed as seminoma with... [PMC10796880, PMC1016136]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: A balanced complex chromosome rearrangement (CCR) in a parent, even if apparently balanced, can lead to different types of aneuploid germ cells. This can result in liveborn children with multiple congenital anomalies and unbalanced karyotypes, such as partial trisomy for 5q and partial monosomy for 12p. The specific case described involved a mother with a balanced CCR across four chromosomes, leading to an unbalanced karyotype in her child. [PMC1016136]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurocutaneous syndrome characterized by the association of cerebellum (rhombencephalosynapsis), cranial nerves (trigeminal anesthesia), and scalp (alopecia) abnormalities. Other features observed in patients were craniosynostosis, midfacial hypoplasia, bilateral corneal opacities, low-set ears, short stature, moderate intellectual impairment and ataxia. Hyperactivity, depression, self-injurious behaviour and bipolar disorder have also been reported.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Cerebellotrigeminal-dermal dysplasia syndrome; Craniosynostosis-alopecia-brain defect syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Gómez-López-Hernández syndrome (GLHS) was first described in 1979. To date, 57 patients with GLHS have been reported in the literature. The etiology of this syndrome remains unknown. Based on the limited number of described cases, GLHS appears to be a very rare condition. [PMC8988015]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Gómez-López-Hernández syndrome (GLHS) is characterized by a triad of cerebello-trigemino-dermal dysplasia. Key features include rhombencephalosynapsis (RES), alopecia, trigeminal anesthesia, and brachyturricephaly. RES involves the fusion of cerebellar hemispheres with agenesis of the cerebellar vermis, and mild dilation of the lateral ventricles may be present. Alopecia is typically bilateral parieto-temporal, and brachyturricephaly presents as a broad skull shape with tower-like elongation. Other findings can include low-set posteriorly retracted ears, strabismus, hypotonia, and ataxia. While trigeminal anesthesia is a characteristic, it may not be present in all cases. GLHS is considered part of the spectrum of RES-associated conditions and can co-occur with Autism Spectrum Disorder. [PMC8527131, PMC8988015, PMC6119670]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Despite its first description in 1979, the etiology of Gómez-López-Hernández syndrome remains unknown. While one case report noted prenatal exposure to misoprostol, this does not establish a definitive cause for the syndrome. [PMC8988015]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Gómez-López-Hernández syndrome is characterized by a triad of cerebello-trigemino-dermal dysplasia. Diagnosis relies on a distinctive phenotype, including rhombencephalosynapsis, alopecia (often bilateral parieto-temporal), trigeminal anesthesia, and brachyturricephaly. Rhombencephalosynapsis can be confirmed by MRI, which may also show mild dilation of the lateral ventricles. The presence of brachyturricephaly, rhombencephalosynapsis, and bilateral alopecia is considered sufficient for diagnosis. Other findings may include low-set ears, strabismus, hypotonia, and ataxia. [PMC8527131, PMC8988015, PMC6119670]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Gómez-López-Hernández syndrome (GLHS) is characterized by rhombencephalosynapsis (RES), alopecia, trigeminal anesthesia, and a distinctive phenotype including brachyturricephaly. It has been suggested that GLHS should be considered as part of the spectrum of RES-associated conditions that also feature alopecia, trigeminal anesthesia, and craniofacial anomalies, rather than being viewed as a distinct entity. [PMC8988015]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The etiology of Gómez-López-Hernández syndrome remains unknown. While one case was molecularly evaluated and had prenatal exposure to misoprostol, no specific genetic cause or inheritance pattern has been identified. One reported case involved an only child born to non-consanguineous parents with no similar cases in the family or among close relatives, suggesting a sporadic occurrence in that instance. However, there is insufficient information to provide specific genetic counseling regarding recurrence risk or inheritance. [PMC8988015, PMC6119670]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: on Gomez-Lopez-Hernandez syndrome (GLHS) in a Caucasian patient, Georgian, 36 months, male, only child born to non-consanguineous parents. There were no similar cases in the family and among close relatives. MRI study confirmed rhombencephalosynapsis (fusion of cerebellar hemispheres in combination with the agenesis of cerebellar vermis) and mild dilation of the lateral ventricles. Other main findings are bilateral parieto-temporal alopecia and brachiturricephaly (broad skull shape and tower-like elongation of the cranium in the vertical axis), low-set posteriorly retracted ears, strabismus (in the right eye), hypotonia (Beighton scale score - 6) and ataxia (trouble maintaining balance). Patient has no signs of trigeminal anesthesia, no recurrent, painless eye infections, corneal opacities and ulcerated wounds on the facial skin and buccal mucosa were observed. Based on the scientific... [PMC6119670]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Carey-Fineman-Ziter (CFZ) syndrome is a rare condition characterized by the association of hypotonia, Moebius sequence (bilateral congenital facial palsy with impairment of ocular abduction), Pierre-Robin sequence (micrognathia, glossoptosis, and high-arched or cleft palate), unusual face, and growth delay.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Less than 20 cases have been reported the literature, including two pairs of sibs.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most patients had non-specific peripheral (myopathy) or central (brain anomaly) causes of hypotonia. Some had a non-specific myopathy, with consequent severe scoliosis. Other features, reported in one or two patients with CFZ, included brain anomalies (ventriculomegaly, reduced white matter, neuronal heterotopias, small foci of necrosis with microcalcifications, small pons and brainstem with enlarged pre-pontine and pontocerebellar cisterns), absence of the pectoralis major muscle with an ulnar deviation of the hand (Poland sequence), laryngostenosis, unexplained intermittent arterial hypertension with facial flushing and sweating, hydronephrosis, glanular hypospadias, and talipes equinovarus. Intelligence may be normal but mental disability has been reported. One patient also presented with a gastrointestinal disturbance with biopsy-proven villous atrophy.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis can be made on the basis of clinical features, but magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is necessary to detect the brain anomalies.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Although CFZ syndrome has been reported in two pairs of sibs, suggesting an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance, the recurrence risk does not seem to be as high as 25%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Scoliosis necessitated rod placement in one patient during adolescence, and in another case induced restrictive lung disease and death from pneumonia at 37 years of age.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Horstick et al. (2013) previously reported a homozygous p.Trp284Ser variant in STAC3 as the cause of Native American myopathy (NAM) in 5 Lumbee Native American families with congenital hypotonia and weakness, cleft palate, short stature, ptosis, kyphoscoliosis, talipes deformities, and susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia (MH). Here two non-Native American families, who were found to have STAC3 pathogenic variants. The first proband and her affected older sister are from a consanguineous Qatari family with a suspected clinical diagnosis of Carey-Fineman-Ziter syndrome (CFZS) based on features of hypotonia, myopathic facies with generalized weakness, ptosis, normal extraocular movements, cleft palate, growth delay, and kyphoscoliosis. We identified the homozygous c.851G>C;p.Trp284Ser variant in STAC3 in both sisters. The second proband and his affected sister are from a... [PMC5843189]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Carey-Fineman-Ziter syndrome (CFZS) exhibits phenotypic overlap with other conditions, notably Moebius syndrome (MBS) and Native American myopathy (NAM). Patients with CFZS often present with hypotonia, myopathic facies with generalized weakness, ptosis, normal extraocular movements, cleft palate, growth delay, and kyphoscoliosis. NAM should be considered in the differential for individuals with facial and generalized weakness, normal or mildly abnormal extraocular movement, hypotonia, cleft palate, and scoliosis, particularly if there is a history of malignant hyperthermia. Similarly, MBS may present with facial and generalized weakness, minimal limitation of horizontal gaze, cleft palate, and hypotonia. [PMC5843189]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic or acquired, cerebral malformation characterized by an intracerebral fluid-filled cyst or cavity with or without communication between the ventricle and subarachnoid space. Clinical manifestations depend on location and severity and may include hemiparesis, seizures, intellectual disability, and dystonia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Point prevalence of acquired and genetic forms is unknown. However, birth prevalence of porencephaly is estimated at 1/19,000 in Japan and 1/28,500 in the USA.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Porencephaly may manifest before or after birth. The cysts or cavities can be located anywhere within the cerebral parenchyma and are typically lined by smooth walls and surrounded by an atrophic cortex. The clinical picture is highly variable, even within affected families, with severe cases presenting major disability to mild cases with only slight, or even undetected, neurological involvement. The main clinical manifestations include hypotonia, microcephaly, spastic hemiparesis or quadriparesis, seizures, and global developmental delay. Intellectual disability is also a common finding and ranges from very mild to severe.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Prenatal- and postnatally-acquired cysts (acquired porencephaly) may be due to a number of causes including hemorrhage, local damage from ischemia or traumatic brain injury. Mutations in the COL4A1 (13q34) and COL4A2 (13q34) genes have been identified in familial (Familial porencephaly) and de novo cases. In these genetic cases, porencephaly results from antenatal or perinatal hemorrhage and is often associated with other brain abnormalities (bilateral white matter changes, calcifications, microbleeds) and ocular involvement (congenital cataract, retinal arterial tortuosity).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is suspected based on the clinical manifestations and is confirmed radiologically by computed tomography (CT), magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), or ultrasonography showing characteristic intracerebral lesions. Cysts or cavities are well demarcated, contain cerebrospinal fluid and do not show contrast enhancement.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include arachnoid cyst, schizencephaly, ependymal cyst, encephalomalacia, hydranencephaly, and other COL4A1 or COL4A2 related diseases, including childhood stroke, CADASIL and retinal vasculopathy with cerebral leukodystrophy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Ultrasonography may detect porencephaly prenatally after the 30th week of gestation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance for familial porencephaly is autosomal dominant. Genetic counseling should inform parents of the 50% risk of transmission for future offspring. Occasionally, genetic cases arise de novo.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: No specific treatment is available for porencephaly. Treatment is therefore symptomatic and supportive and may include physical therapy, speech therapy, and anticonvulsant medication to treat seizures.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable and depends on the site and extent of the lesion.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A hookworm infection caused primarily by the species Ancylostoma duodenale or Necator americanus, usually acquired through penetration of the skin, (often asymptomatic but that can also manifest with an allergic reaction at the site of skin penetration), followed by the migration of larva through the bloodstream to the lungs (causing asymptomatic pneumonitis, eosinophilia) and finally reaching and colonizing the small intestines where they cause blood extravasation leading to diarrhea, abdominal pain, and when untreated, melena, iron-deficiency anemia and protein malnutrition.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Ankylostomiasis, or hookworm infection, is a major public health concern, particularly in rural areas of tropical and subtropical countries, where almost 472 million people are infected. The primary human pathogens include Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale, and Ancylostoma ceylanicum, typically acquired through percutaneous invasion of larvae from contaminated soil. While rare, vertical transmission can occur in infants. Zoonotic hookworms like Ancylostoma caninum and Ancylostoma braziliense cause cutaneous larva migrans, acquired through direct contact with soil contaminated by animal feces. Cases are reported globally, including endemic regions like China and the Peruvian Amazon, with emerging reports of cutaneous larva migrans in developed countries like the UK. [PMC11884172, PMC12032795, PMC12089704, PMC7871578, PMC7839857]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Ankylostomiasis, or human hookworm infection, is primarily caused by the nematodes Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale, and Ancylostoma ceylanicum. Humans typically acquire the infection through direct percutaneous invasion of infective larvae from contaminated soil. Animal hookworms, such as Ancylostoma caninum and Ancylostoma braziliense, can also cause human disease, including cutaneous larva migrans and, less commonly, enteric infections. In infants, transmission can occur vertically through transplacental routes or breastfeeding. [PMC11884172, PMC12032795, PMC12089704, PMC7871578, PMC7839857]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Hookworm infection remains of considerable importance to public health. However, because critical cases caused by hookworm infection are rarely observed in China, accurate and prompt diagnoses are difficult to achieve in clinical practice. In , how we combined morphological and molecular approaches to achieve the clinical diagnosis of hookworm infection. A 75-year-old Chinese woman who presented with dizziness, poor appetite, poor sleep, and weakness in her limbs was diagnosed with chronic atrophic gastritis and was positive for Helicobacter pylori, iron deficiency anemia with a hemoglobin concentration of 35 g/L, and left atrial enlargement. However, after symptomatic treatment, the patient did not improve. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed the presence of live nematodes in the descending portion of the patient's duodenum. Fecal examination via saturated brine flotation... [PMC11884172, PMC12032795, PMC7871578, PMC6924899, PMC6777378]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Ankylostomiasis should be considered in the differential diagnosis for several conditions. In infants and children, it presents with abdominal symptoms, vomit, weight loss, anemia, and unexplained persistent eosinophilia, and can lead to malnutrition, retarded growth, and impaired cognitive development. For adults, hookworm infection is a rare cause of acute major gastrointestinal bleeding, particularly in patients on anticoagulant therapy, and should be considered in cases of obscure gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Furthermore, it can be a leading cause of anemia, especially when conventional treatments are ineffective, and may manifest with symptoms like chest tightness, shortness of breath, and edema. In developing countries, hookworms are also a potential cause of non-traumatic small bowel perforation, alongside conditions such as typhoid, HIV, and tuberculosis. [PMC7871578, PMC5882382, PMC5594724, PMC4977793, PMC2408541]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Ankylostomiasis is primarily managed with anthelmintic treatment. Albendazole has been successfully used for infections caused by Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale, and hookworm-related cutaneous larva migrans, leading to resolution of anemia, cessation of gastrointestinal bleeding, and overall recovery. Mebendazole has also proven successful in treating Ancylostoma duodenale infection in infants. Supportive measures for associated conditions, such as anemia, are also important. While treatment in infants shows potential benefit, further studies are needed to define the best clinical management. Early recognition and efficient access to therapy are vital for effective treatment. [PMC11884172, PMC7871578, PMC7839857, PMC5882382, PMC5594724]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, congenital cardiac anomaly characterized by a common atrioventricular junction with a common AV valve, an interatrial communication just above the common AV valve (ostium primum defect), a posterior interventricular communication (inlet VSD), that results in shunting at both the atrial and ventricular level. Morphologically, the common atrioventricular valve has 4 or 5 leaflets including superior and inferior bridging leaflets with a single annulus.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CAVC; Complete atrioventricular canal defect; Complete AVSD; Complete atrioventricular canal; Complete atrioventricular septal defect with atrial and ventricular components

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence at birth of complete atrioventricular septal defect (CAVSD) is suggested to be 1/5,000 in Europe. Both sexes are equally affected.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Infants typically present within the first year of life with symptoms of congestive heart failure which may include feeding difficulties, excessive sweating, tachycardia, tachypnea, mild wheezing, failure to thrive, and poor peripheral blood perfusion. If untreated, affected individuals develop irreversible pulmonary hypertension which improves signs of congestive heart failure but worsens tolerance to effort and results in cyanosis and Eisenmenger syndrome. Recurrent pulmonary infections are common. Morphologically, the ventricles may be equal or nearly equal in size (balanced) or one of the ventricles may be significantly larger than the other (unbalanced). The balanced form is typically observed in Down syndrome. Unbalanced ventricles are associated with varying degrees of malalignment of the common atrioventricular valve over the hypoplastic ventricle and hypoplasia of the arterial valve above. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is observed in 5-10% of CAVSD.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CAVSD is strongly associated with Down syndrome and heterotaxy. Cilia gene mutations could be involved in isolated AVSD. A small fraction of CAVSD cases have been associated with NR2F2 (15q26.2), GATA4 (8p23.1), GATA6 (18q11.2) and CRELD1 (3p25.3) mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Echocardiography is used for postnatal diagnosis. Typical findings include a left and superior QRS axis in the frontal plane and counterclockwise depolarization. Chest X-ray may show ventricular enlargement and a greater anterior position of the left atrioventricular valve due to the inlet septal defect, which gives a ''goose neck'' appearance to le left ventricular outflow tract.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other congenital cardiac anomalies that result in early heart failure including partial atrioventricular canal, atrial septal defects and large ventricular septal defects.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: CAVSD can be detected with fetal echocardiography; the detection rate is approximately 67%.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Atrioventricular septal defects (AVSD) can occur in the offspring of mothers with CAVSD.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Digoxin, diuretics and angiotensin-converting enzymes may be used to treat congestive heart failure prior to surgery. Surgical repair is advised at 3 months of age and is typically performed between 3 and 6 months of age. The three classical techniques are single patch technique, two patch technique (most frequent), and the modified single patch technique. To avoid surgically induced AV block, the position of the AV node and bundle of His must be considered, with the AV node positioned more posteriorly and inferiorly, the non-branching bundle running slightly on the left side of the septal crest with the branching bundle being exposed. Pulmonary artery banding can be proposed before 3 months in very ill patients despite optimal medical therapy. Combined repair of other cardiac anomalies is often performed with desirable results. In case of associated tetralogy of Fallot, complete repair is usually delayed up until 1 year of age. Lifelong follow-up every 2 to 3 years is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Without surgery, many of the affected individuals will die in infancy. Prognosis after surgical repair is good; however, patients who weigh less the 3 kg or are less than 2.5 years old have a higher risk of mortality during surgery. Pregnancy increases the risk of developing left AVV regurgitation, arrhythmias, deterioration of heart failure, and is not recommended for women with severe pulmonary hypertension.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1 (CMT1) is a group of autosomal dominant demyelinating peripheral neuropathies characterized by distal weakness and atrophy, sensory loss, foot deformities, and slow nerve conduction velocity.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Autosomal dominant demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease; CMT1; Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy type 1; Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 1

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of CMT1 is estimated to be between 1/7,000 and 1/5,000, with CMT1A representing 70% of cases.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Age of onset of CMT1 varies widely and ranges from infancy to the fourth or subsequent decades of life. Typically, patients become symptomatic between the first and the second decade of life; however, the full clinical picture may appear later. Clinical severity is variable, ranging from extremely mild disease, which goes unrecognized, to considerable weakness and disability. Affected individuals typically develop distal weakness, symmetric atrophy of muscles (mainly peroneal), and reduced-to-absent tendon reflexes. Sensory deficits of position, vibration, and pain/temperature commonly occur in the feet and later in the hands. Pes cavus (or planus) with hammer toes is often present since childhood. Variable scoliosis may develop during adolescence.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CMT1A can be caused by 1.4 Mb duplications or by point mutations in the PMP22 gene (17p12). CMT1E is caused by point mutations in the PMP22 gene (17p12). CMT1B is associated with MPZ (1q22) gene mutations. CMT1C, CMT1D and CMT1F are associated with pathogenic variants in LITAF (16p13.3), EGR2 (10q21.1) and NEFL (8p21.2), respectively.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of CMT1 is based on progressive peripheral motor and sensory neuropathy; slow nerve conduction velocity (NCV) with motor NCV <38 m/s in upper limbs; and positive family history (however, sporadic presentations may occur, due to de novo mutations). Genetic testing is the gold standard for diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other genetic neuropathies, especially X-linked CMT, autosomal dominant CMT2, CMT4, and hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies. CMT1 identification may be challenging when there is no family history and acquired demyelinating neuropathies must also be taken into account.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Preimplantation genetic diagnosis may be an option for families in which the pathogenic variant has been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant with complete penetrance and genetic counseling is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is multidisciplinary and includes use of special shoes, inserts and/or ankle foot orthoses; forearm crutches, canes, and wheelchairs for the most severe cases, as needed for mobility; surgery for severe pes cavus, as needed; exercise for muscle strengthening, as tolerated; stretching to prevent Achilles' tendon shortening; and regular foot examination for pressure sores. Occupational therapy focused on strategies/tools to help patients with daily living activities is useful, especially for those with hand weakness.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: CMT1 is slowly progressive and affected individuals experience long plateau periods without obvious deterioration. Most patients remain ambulatory throughout life and have a normal lifespan.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare osteochondrodysplasia characterized by shortened limbs, normal sized head, short stature with short extremities (final adult height is 120cm +/- 20cm), spinal deformities and joint malformations leading to multiple joint contractures (principally involving the shoulders, elbows, interphalangeal joints and hips). The name indicates the ''twisted'' appearance of the spine and limbs in severe forms that is peculiar of this condition.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Although the exact prevalence of diastrophic dysplasia is unknown, it is estimated at approximately 1:100,000. This condition is more common in Finland, where prevalence is about 1:33,000. The disorder affects both genders.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical features of diastrophic dysplasia include short stature with limb shortening, contractures of large joints, spinal deformities including cervical kyphosis in newborns and children and kyphoscoliosis, cleft palate, bilateral clubfoot and gap between the first and second toes. Typical deformities of the hands include brachydactyly, ''hitchhiker'' thumb, and ulnar deviation of fingers. Radiographic findings include shortened long bones with metaphyseal flaring, flat epiphyses, cervical kyphosis in newborns and children and kyphoscoliosis, and bowed radius and tibia. The severity of the clinical manifestations is variable, ranging from very severe to moderate forms. Limb shortness, contractures of large joints, early onset osteoarthritis and scoliosis cause significant physical difficulties affecting the patients' quality of life.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Diastrophic dysplasia is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. It is caused by mutations in the SLC26A2 (also known as diastrophic dysplasia sulfate transporter) gene which is located on chromosome 5 (5q31-q34). It encodes a widely distributed sulfate transporter of the plasma membrane. Mutations in SLC26A2 cause a family of skeletal dysplasias ranging from lethal conditions such as achondrogenesis type 1B and atelosteogenesis type II to non-lethal conditions such as diastrophic dysplasia (severe) and multiple epiphyseal dysplasia type 4 (mild). Heterozygous carriers are asymptomatic.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on characteristic clinical and radiological findings and/or biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC26A2 identified by molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis for diastrophic dysplasia should include chondrodysplasia with joint dislocations, gPAPP type, Desbuquois syndrome, arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, otopalatodigital spectrum disorder, Larsen syndrome, atelosteogenesis type I, and omodysplasia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound examination may identify short fetal limbs, clubfoot, polyhydramnios, and/or small thorax, in a fetus not known to be at risk raising the possibility of diastrophic dysplasia. The finding of radially deviated thumbs ("hitchhiker thumbs") might suggest diastrophic dysplasia. Once the SLC26A2 pathogenic variants have been identified in an affected family member, carrier testing for at risk relatives and prenatal genetic testing are possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder. The parents of an affected child are heterozygous carriers and they are usually asymptomatic with normal stature. At-risk couples have a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Patients with diastrophic dysplasia are mainly treated with physiotherapy. Corrective orthopedic surgery might be required to treat the cervical kyphosis, scoliosis, and clubfoot, but it should be considered cautiously since deformities tend to recur. Total arthroplasty of hips and knees might be necessary in individuals with early onset degenerative arthritis.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: In the absence of severe complications associated with spinal malformations, most patients with diastrophic dysplasia live into adulthood. However physical difficulties due to skeletal deformities affect the patients' quality of life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A new leukoencephalopathy, the CACH syndrome (Childhood Ataxia with Central nervous system Hypomyelination) or VWM (Vanishing White Matter) was identified on clinical and MRI criteria. Classically, this disease is characterized by (1) an onset between 2 and 5 years of age, with a cerebello-spastic syndrome exacerbated by episodes of fever or head trauma leading to death after 5 to 10 years of disease evolution, (2) a diffuse involvement of the white matter on cerebral MRI with a CSF-like signal intensity (cavitation), (3) a recessive autosomal mode of inheritance, (4) neuropathologic findings consistent with a cavitating orthochromatic leukodystrophy with increased number of oligodendrocytes with sometimes ``foamy'' aspect.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Childhood ataxia with diffuse central nervous system hypomyelination; Leukoencephalopathy with vanishing white matter; Myelinosis centralis diffusa

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: A total of 148 cases have been reported so far. Prevalence of this disease remains unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical symptoms are variable, from fatal infantile forms (Cree leukoencephalopathy) and congenital forms associated with extra-neurological affections, to juvenile and adult forms (ovarioleukodystrophy) characterized by cognitive and behavioural dysfunctions and by a slow progression of the disease, leading to the term of eIF2B-related leukoencephalopathies.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: This disease is linked to mutations in the five EIF2B genes encoding the five subunits of the eukaryotic initiation factor 2B (eIF2B), involved in the protein synthesis and its regulation under cellular stress. The patho-physiology of the disease would involve a deficiency in astrocytes maturation leading to an increased susceptibility of the white matter to cellular stress.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on the detection of eIF2B mutations, predominantly affecting the EIF2B5 gene. A decrease in the intrinsic activity of the eIF2B factor (the guanine exchange activity, GEF) in lymphoblasts from patients seems to have a diagnostic value.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: No specific treatment exists besides the ``prevention'' of cellular stress. Corticosteroids sometimes proved to be useful in acute phases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis seems to be correlated with the age of onset, the earliest forms being more severe.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A subtype of autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy characterized by childhood onset of progressive proximal weakness of the shoulder and pelvic girdle muscles, resulting in difficulty walking, scapular winging, calf hypertrophy and contractures of the Achilles tendon, which lead to a tiptoe gait pattern. Cardiac and respiratory involvement is rare.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Alpha-sarcoglycanopathy; LGMD2D; Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy due to alpha-sarcoglycan deficiency; Autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2D; Alpha-sarcoglycan-related LGMD R3; LGMD type 2D; LGMD due to alpha-sarcoglycan deficiency; Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2D

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Alpha-sarcoglycan-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R3 (LGMDR3) exhibits varying ages of onset. Among patients who experience loss of ambulation (LOA), early childhood-onset is predominant, accounting for 74% of LGMDR3-6 cases. Adult-onset disease is uncommon in this group, representing only 14%. For those with early childhood-onset LGMDR3-6, the mean time to loss of ambulation is approximately 12.3 years. [PMC9398075]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Alpha-sarcoglycan-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R3 (LGMDR3-6) cases that progress to loss of ambulation primarily have an early childhood-onset (74%), while adult-onset disease is uncommon (14%). For patients with early childhood-onset LGMDR3-6, the mean time to loss of ambulation is 12.3 years. Generally, early childhood-onset disease tends to have faster progression to loss of ambulation compared to late childhood- or adult-onset disease. [PMC9398075]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Alpha-sarcoglycan-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R3, also known as limb-girdle muscular dystrophy 2D (LGMD2D), is caused by mutations in the α-sarcoglycan gene (SGCA). These mutations can include missense mutations and partial heterozygous deletions. Such genetic alterations lead to the reduction or complete absence of α-sarcoglycan and other sarcoglycan proteins, as the loss of any single sarcoglycan protein can cause a reduction or absence of the other three. [PMC6850699]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis cannot be made solely on clinical symptoms or conventional immunohistochemical staining due to a lack of specificity. While the disease is caused by mutations in the α-sarcoglycan gene (SGCA), the loss of any sarcoglycan protein can lead to the reduction or absence of the other three. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is crucial for identifying specific SGCA mutations, such as missense mutations or partial heterozygous deletions, to establish a definitive diagnosis. [PMC6850699]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis of alpha-sarcoglycan-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R3 (LGMD2D) is challenging due to the lack of specificity in clinical symptoms and conventional immunohistochemical staining. The loss of any single sarcoglycan protein (α, β, γ, or δ) can lead to the reduction or absence of the other three, making it difficult to distinguish LGMD2D from other sarcoglycanopathies solely based on protein expression patterns. For instance, absent α- and γ-sarcoglycans on biopsy can be observed in beta-sarcoglycanopathy. Therefore, definitive diagnosis relies on molecular genetic testing, such as next-generation sequencing, to identify specific mutations or deletions in the SGCA gene. Careful re-evaluation of NGS data is important, as intragenic deletions might be missed in initial screenings. [PMC6850699, PMC4879147]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Alpha-sarcoglycan-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R3 (LGMDR3), also known as LGMD2D, is an autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in the SGCA gene. Genetic testing, such as Next Generation Sequencing, can identify specific mutations, including missense mutations and partial heterozygous deletions. Clinical symptoms and conventional immunohistochemical staining are not sufficient for diagnosis, as the loss of one sarcoglycan protein can lead to the reduction or absence of others. For LGMDR3-6, early childhood-onset is common among patients who experience loss of ambulation, with a mean time to loss of ambulation of 12.3 years, indicating faster progression compared to later onset forms. [PMC9398075, PMC6850699]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: There is no specific curative therapy or management strategy detailed in the provided abstract. However, severe cardiomyopathy has been observed in patients with sarcoglycan deficiencies, leading to early mortality. Therefore, it is suggested that cardiac function in limb-girdle muscular dystrophy patients with defective sarcoglycan expression should be monitored to anticipate and manage potential cardiac complications. [PMC1734518]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Progression to loss of ambulation (LOA) in Alpha-sarcoglycan-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R3 (LGMDR3-6) is primarily observed in cases with early childhood-onset disease. Among LGMDR3-6 patients who experienced LOA, 74% had an early childhood onset. The mean time to LOA for patients with early childhood-onset LGMDR3-6 was 12.3 years (SD 10.7, n=56). Generally, early childhood-onset disease tends to lead to faster progression to LOA compared to late childhood- or adult-onset disease. [PMC9398075]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic macular dystrophy disorder characterized by the presence of small yellow-white accumulations of extracellular material under the retinal pigment epithelium in the ocular posterior pole, and affecting multiple members of a family. The disease has a variable clinical presentation ranging from asymptomatic patients to progressive loss of vision and scotomas, possibly associated with subfoveal choroidal neovascularization, extensive pigmentary changes, geographic atrophy and/or subretinal hemorrhage.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): DHRD; Dominant drusen; Dominant radial drusen; Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy; Malattia leventinese

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Familial drusen, specifically Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy (DHRD) and malattia leventinese (ML), is described as a rare allelic condition. It is characterized by massive drusen in the posterior fundus and is associated with EFEMP1 gene mutations. The condition is observed in families, with reports including a Chinese family and a mother-daughter pair, highlighting its inherited nature. [PMC6292057, PMC3002954, PMC2734481, PMC1311550]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Familial drusen, also known as Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy (DHRD) or malattia leventinese (MLVT), is a rare condition characterized by massive drusen in the posterior fundus. Patients typically present with decreased or impaired vision, often bilaterally, which can be attributed to macular atrophy or active choroidal neovascular membranes. Drusen are distributed along vascular arcades in a radiating pattern, in the central macula, and peripapillary region. Associated findings include pigmented scarring, exudation, and retinal pigment epithelial atrophy. Multimodal imaging reveals sub-retinal pigment epithelium deposits, separation of the RPE and Bruch's membrane, and disruption of photoreceptor layers. The clinical phenotype, including age of presentation and vision function, can be variable. [PMC7852973, PMC6292057, PMC2734481]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Familial drusen, often manifesting as Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy (DHRD) or malattia leventinese (ML/MLVT), is an autosomal dominant condition primarily caused by mutations in the EFEMP1 gene. Specific heterozygous mutations, such as c.1033C > T leading to p.R345W, have been identified. These genetic alterations result in the accumulation of sub-retinal pigment epithelium material and massive drusen in the posterior fundus, which are associated with disrupted photoreceptor integrity. [PMC6327555, PMC6292057, PMC3002954, PMC2734481, PMC1311550]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of familial drusen relies on pattern recognition and multimodal imaging. Fundus photography, autofluorescence, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and angiography (fluorescein and indocyanine green) are used to identify drusen, their characteristic distribution (e.g., along arcades, peripapillary), RPE atrophy, subretinal deposits, and fluid. OCT can reveal sub-RPE deposits, RPE/Bruch's membrane separation, and photoreceptor disruption. Functional assessments include Goldmann perimetry, full-field and multifocal electroretinogram, dark adaptation, and color vision testing. Genetic sequencing for EFEMP1 gene mutations, such as c.1033C > T (p.R345W), confirms the diagnosis of conditions like Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy/malattia leventinese. [PMC7852973, PMC6292057, PMC3002954, PMC2734481]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Familial drusen should be differentiated from other hereditary macular dystrophies. Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy (DHRD) and malattia leventinese (ML/MLVT), caused by EFEMP1 gene mutations, are characterized by massive drusen, often distributed along vascular arcades and peripapillary regions, and involve sub-retinal pigment epithelium deposits. North Carolina Macular Dystrophy (NCMD) presents with drusen-like yellowish lesions, but these differ from true drusen by the absence of material accumulation between the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch's membrane. Pseudoinflammatory macular dystrophy (PMD), a dominantly inherited condition, also requires differentiation, particularly from dominant drusen of Bruch's membrane, and other hereditary causes of subretinal neovascularization such as angioid streaks, vitelliform dystrophy, optic nerve drusen, and myopia. [PMC7852973, PMC6292057, PMC3002954, PMC2734481, PMC1311550]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Familial drusen and related macular dystrophies are hereditary conditions with distinct genetic bases. Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy/malattia leventinese (DHRD/ML) is an allelic condition caused by heterozygous mutations in the EFEMP1 gene, such as c.1033C > T (p.R345W), identifiable through gene sequencing. North Carolina Macular Dystrophy (NCMD) is an autosomal dominant macular dystrophy linked to a locus on chromosome 5p13-p15, observed across multiple generations. Pseudoinflammatory macular dystrophy (PMD) is also dominantly inherited. These conditions demonstrate familial transmission, with variable phenotypes possible even among affected relatives, highlighting the importance of genetic analysis for family members. [PMC6292057, PMC3002954, PMC2734481, PMC1311550]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management strategies for familial drusen, such as Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy, include addressing complications like choroidal neovascular membranes with anti-vascular endothelial growth factor injections. Additionally, subthreshold nanopulse laser treatment has been reported to improve visual acuity and retinal function, with observed benefits in both treated and untreated eyes, suggesting a potential systemic effect. Multimodal imaging and pattern recognition are crucial for accurate diagnosis and guiding the management of associated complications. [PMC7852973, PMC6327555]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Familial drusen, including Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy and pseudoinflammatory macular dystrophy, can lead to decreased visual acuity, particularly when macular lesions are present. Complications such as macular atrophy, pigmented scarring, exudation, and choroidal neovascular membranes contribute to vision loss. Untreated pseudoinflammatory macular dystrophy can result in legal blindness. While overall treatment efficiency is often unsatisfactory, specific interventions like nanopulse subthreshold laser treatment have shown short-term improvements in visual acuity and retinal function in some Doyne honeycomb retinal dystrophy patients. Early obliteration of subretinal neovascularization with photocoagulation is suggested for pseudoinflammatory macular dystrophy to prevent severe vision loss. [PMC7852973, PMC6327555, PMC6292057, PMC1311550]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare degenerative inflammatory disorder of skeletal muscles characterized by late onset weakness, starting in either the quadriceps or finger flexors and slowly progressing to include other groups of limb muscles. Distinctive histopathological features include inflammatory and degenerative features.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): IBM; Sporadic inclusion body myositis; sIBM

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Inclusion body myositis (IBM) has a highly variable prevalence according to geographic, ethnic and age criteria. Prevalence in the general population ranges from 1/14,000-1,000,000 but a three-fold increase is observed when considering only a population over 50 years. Underdiagnosis may be an explanation for the high ethno-geographic variation. Male-to-female ratio is 2:1 on average (but varies between 0.5 to 6.5:1).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: IBM onset is over 50 years but the disease may also occur earlier, in the 4th decade. Compared to other idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, the clinical phenotype is characteristic with distal and asymmetrical muscle involvement, amyotrophy, and no extramuscular manifestations. First signs are weakness or even atrophy of the quadriceps or of the finger flexors, leading to difficulties in rising from chairs or ground, climbing stairs, gripping, lifting and using tools, and thereby provoking falls. Flexor digitorum profundus and flexor pollicis longus are more severely involved than the forearm extensor muscles, especially during early stages of the disease. With disease progression, other groups of muscles are also involved, such as the elbow flexors, the hip, knee or neck flexors, and the ankle dorsiflexors, leading to footdrop. Patients frequently have a mild weakness of facial muscles, except for the extraocular muscles. Dysphagia may occur in approximately 66% of patients in advanced stages of the disease and can be severe in some cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Etiology of IBM is poorly understood. No causal gene has been identified but genes encoding the major histocompatibility complex (MHC), HLA-DR3 and 8.1 ancestral haplotypes (HLA-A1, B8, DRB1*0301), have been shown to correlate with IBM susceptibility. Ageing and environmental factors are also surmised to play a triggering role. Whether IBM is primarily an immuno-inflammatory disorder leading to muscle degeneration or a degenerative disorder leading to muscle inflammation is still under debate. The pathogenic role of anti-cN1A, which is detected in 30-50% of patients, is also debated as it is not specific to IBM and may be found in patients with other autoimmune diseases as well as in healthy controls.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on physical examination (especially the detection of finger flexor weakness), age of presentation and a duration of symptoms over 6 months. Muscle biopsy identifies the inflammatory (diffuse MHC class I sarcolemmal overexpression, endomysial inflammatory infiltrates including CD8+ T cells, T cell invasion of non-necrotic muscle fibers) and degenerative features (rimmed vacuoles, P62 and/or TDP43 aggregates and, occasionally, an abnormally elevated number of COX-negative fibers). Laboratory findings are not specific as serum creatine kinase is only slightly raised in some cases. Electromyography only helps in confirming the myopathic origin of the weakness or atrophy. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) helps delineating the characteristic pattern of muscle involvement.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis may include other idiopathic inflammatory myopathies and, in early stages of the disease, arthritis or any motor neuron disease.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative treatment for IBM, and patients usually do not respond to anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressant therapies. The standard of care involves symptomatic treatments including exercise therapy, ergotherapy, and orthotic appliance. However, clinical trials are ongoing for new therapeutic strategies, of note for sirolimus, an inhibitor of mTOR.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: No change in mean life expectancy has been observed. IBM patients present a progressive and continuous loss of muscle strength between 3.5-16.8% per year. There is a major impact of the disease on the daily activity. After 5 years, most patients require a walking aid and after 10, a wheelchair.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:181

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, also known as Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome, is a rare inherited monogenic disorder. It is the most common type among the over 192 distinct ectodermal dysplasia disorders. The most prevalent method of transmission is X-linked recessive, manifesting fully in men and only partially in female carrier heterozygotes. [PMC11930058, PMC3918636]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, also known as Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome or anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, is a hereditary disorder characterized by developmental defects in ectodermal derivatives. It presents with a classic triad of anhidrosis (inability to sweat), dysodontia (abnormal or missing teeth), and hypotrichiasis (sparse hair). Anhidrosis can lead to life-threatening hyperthermia. Dental manifestations are striking, often including anodontia or hypodontia in both deciduous and permanent dentition, which can result in lack of alveolar development and lip protrusion. The X-linked recessive inheritance pattern means it manifests fully in men and partially in female carriers. Rare characteristics like atrophic rhinitis and nasal myiasis have also been reported. [PMC11930058, PMC3918636, PMC3448356]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, also known as Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome, is an inherited monogenic disorder and the most common type of ectodermal dysplasia, characterized by developmental defects in ectodermal derivatives. The most prevalent transmission method is X-linked recessive, fully manifesting in males and partially in female carriers. Genetic causes include mutations in the EDA, EDAR, EDARADD, and WNT10A genes. EDA mutations are the most frequent, with identified types including missense and nonframeshift deletion mutations. Patients with EDA missense mutations have a higher frequency of hypohidrosis. [PMC11930058, PMC7010634, PMC3918636, PMC3448356]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia, also known as Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome, is primarily based on a characteristic clinical triad of anhidrosis (inability to sweat), dysodontia/hypodontia (abnormal or missing teeth), and hypotrichiasis (sparse hair). Dentists are often the first to diagnose cases due to the prominent dental manifestations. Genetic diagnosis is established using whole-exome sequencing (WES) to screen for HED-related genes, followed by confirmatory Sanger sequencing. This approach identifies pathogenic mutations, particularly in the EDA gene, and provides a foundation for genetic diagnosis and counseling. Genotype-phenotype correlations, such as EDA missense mutations being associated with a higher frequency of hypohidrosis, can also be considered. [PMC11930058, PMC7010634, PMC3918636, PMC3448356]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Ectodermal dysplasia (ED) refers to a group of inherited diseases that have developmental defects in at least two major structures derived from the ectoderm, that is, hair, teeth, nails and sweat glands. Although more than 192 distinct disorders have been described, the most common is X-linked recessive hypohidrotic ED (Christ-Siemens-Touraine syndrome). Since such patients usually presents with missing teeth, dentists are usually the first person to diagnose such cases. Diagnosis of such cases is important because absence of sweat glands can lead to hyperthermia which can be life-threatening if proper care is not taken. Through this manuscript, a case of anhidrotic ED affecting deciduous and permanent dentition, which is rare. [PMC3918636]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: investigate the genetic causes of hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia (HED) in two families and elucidate the molecular pathogenesis of HED in Chinese Han patients. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was used to screen HED-related genes in two family members, followed by confirmatory Sanger sequencing. Bioinformatics analysis was performed for the mutations. We reviewed HED-related articles in PubMed. χ 2 - and Fisher's tests were used to analyze the genotype-phenotype correlations. (1) WES identified EDA missense mutations [c.1127 C > T (p.T376M; NM_001005609)] in family 1 and an EDA nonframeshift deletion mutation [c.648_683delACCTGGTCCTCCAGGTCCTCCTGGTCCTCAAGGACC (p.216_228delPPGPPGPPGPQGP; NM_001005609)] in family 2. Sanger sequencing validated the . ANNOVAR (ANNOtate VARiation) annotation indicated that c.1127 c > T was a deleterious mutation. (2) The review of published papers revealed 68... [PMC7010634]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is an inherited monogenic disorder with a prevalent X-linked recessive transmission. The condition manifests fully in men, while female carrier heterozygotes typically show partial manifestations. Genetic diagnosis and counseling are supported by identifying pathogenic mutations, primarily in the EDA gene, using such as whole-exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing. Genotype-phenotype correlations have been noted, with EDA missense mutations, for example, linked to a higher frequency of hypohidrosis. This genetic information provides a foundation for diagnosis and counseling. [PMC11930058, PMC7010634]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management primarily addresses specific manifestations. For dental issues such as anodontia or hypodontia, prosthodontic interventions, including removable partial and complete dentures, are utilized to improve psychological development and stomatognathic system function. Other complications, such as atrophic rhinitis and nasal myiasis, have been managed conservatively. [PMC11930058, PMC3448356]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for X-linked hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia is significantly influenced by the absence of sweat glands. This condition can lead to hyperthermia, which is a life-threatening complication if proper care is not taken. Therefore, careful management is essential to mitigate the risks associated with this aspect of the disease. [PMC3918636]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare chondral and ectodermal dysplasia characterized by short ribs, polydactyly, growth retardation, and ectodermal and heart defects.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It is a rare disease with approximately 150 cases reported worldwide. The exact prevalence is unknown, but the syndrome seems more common among the Amish community.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Prenatal abnormalities (that may be detected by ultrasound examination) include narrow thorax, shortening of long bones, hexadactyly and cardiac defects. After birth, cardinal features are short stature, short ribs, polydactyly, and dysplastic fingernails and teeth. Heart defects, especially abnormalities of atrial septation, occur in about 60% of cases. Cognitive and motor development is normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Mutations of the EVC and EVC2 genes, located in a head to head configuration on chromosome 4p16, have been identified as causative.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: EVC belongs to the short rib-polydactyly group (SRP) and these SRPs, especially type III (Verma-Naumoff syndrome), are discussed in the prenatal differential diagnosis. Postnatally, the essential differential diagnoses include Jeune dystrophy, McKusick-Kaufman syndrome and Weyers syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: This rare condition is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait with variable expression.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The management of EVC is multidisciplinary. Management during the neonatal period is mostly symptomatic, involving treatment of the respiratory distress due to narrow chest and heart failure. Orthopedic follow-up is required to manage the bones deformities. Professional dental care should be considered for management of the oral manifestations.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is linked to the respiratory difficulties in the first months of life due to thoracic narrowness and possible heart defects. Prognosis of the final body height is difficult to predict.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of Ellis-van Creveld syndrome is possible, particularly when fetal ultrasound reveals anomalies such as a narrow thorax, short limbs, postaxial polydactyly, cardiac malformations, or renal pelvis separation. Genetic testing, including whole exome sequencing and targeted sequencing, can identify pathogenic variants in EVC or EVC2 genes in fetuses with such ultrasound findings. Prenatal findings are considered good predictors of disease outcome. Genetic counseling, especially for families with consanguineous marriages, can help identify at-risk individuals and facilitate earlier detection through careful prenatal care. [PMC10568384, PMC8958661, PMC8491797, PMC4976583]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Bonnemann-Meinecke-Reich syndrome is a syndrome of multiple congenital anomalies characterized by an encephalopathy which predominantly occurs in the first year of life and presenting as psychomotor delay. Additional features of the disease include moderate dysmorphia, craniosynostosis, dwarfism (due to growth hormone deficiency), intellectual disability, spasticity, ataxia, retinal degeneration, and adrenal and uterine hypoplasia. The disease has been described in only two families, with each family having two affected siblings. An autosomal recessive inheritance has been suggested. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1991.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Bonnemann-Meinecke-Reich syndrome is characterized by an encephalopathy, including intracerebral calcification and white matter lesions. The onset of the disease typically occurs during the first year of life with retardation of motor development. Later manifestations include dwarfism due to growth hormone deficiency, microcephaly, mental retardation, spasticity, ataxia, and retinal degeneration. This condition is considered a form of connatal leucodystrophy. [PMC1017060]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Two sibs with an encephalopathy, including intracerebral calcification and white matter lesions, dwarfism owing to growth hormone deficiency, and retinal degeneration are reported. The onset of the disease in both patients occurred with retardation of motor development during the first year of life. Later, dwarfism, mental retardation, spasticity, ataxia, and retinal degeneration became apparent. These cases probably represent some form of connatal leucodystrophy. The differential diagnosis is discussed. [PMC1017060]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Two sibs with an encephalopathy, including intracerebral calcification and white matter lesions, dwarfism owing to growth hormone deficiency, and retinal degeneration are reported. The onset of the disease in both patients occurred with retardation of motor development during the first year of life. Later, dwarfism, mental retardation, spasticity, ataxia, and retinal degeneration became apparent. These cases probably represent some form of connatal leucodystrophy. The differential diagnosis is discussed. [PMC1017060]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Two sibs with an encephalopathy, including intracerebral calcification and white matter lesions, dwarfism owing to growth hormone deficiency, and retinal degeneration are reported. The onset of the disease in both patients occurred with retardation of motor development during the first year of life. Later, dwarfism, mental retardation, spasticity, ataxia, and retinal degeneration became apparent. These cases probably represent some form of connatal leucodystrophy. The differential diagnosis is discussed. [PMC1017060]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The condition has been reported in two siblings, indicating a familial occurrence. This observation suggests a genetic basis for the encephalopathy, intracerebral calcification, white matter lesions, growth hormone deficiency, microcephaly, and retinal degeneration. Genetic counseling would therefore be relevant for families with affected individuals to discuss the implications of this familial pattern. [PMC1017060]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The disease typically manifests in the first year of life with retardation of motor development. Over time, patients develop dwarfism due to growth hormone deficiency, mental retardation, spasticity, ataxia, and retinal degeneration. The condition is characterized by encephalopathy, intracerebral calcification, and white matter lesions, suggesting a progressive connatal leucodystrophy. [PMC1017060]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: TARP syndrome is a rare developmental defect during embryogenesis syndrome characterized by Robin sequence (micrognathia, glossoptosis, and cleft palate), atrial septal defect, persistence of the left superior vena cava, and talipes equinovarus. The phenotype is variable, some patients present with further dysmorphic characteristics (e.g. hypertelorism, ear abnormalities) while others do not have any key findings. Additional features, such as syndactyly, polydactyly, or brain anomalies (e.g. cerebellar hypoplasia), have also been reported. The syndrome is almost invariably lethal with affected males either dying prenatally or living just a few months.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Pierre Robin sequence-congenital heart defect-talipes syndrome; Pierre Robin syndrome-congenital heart defect-talipes syndrome; Talipes equinovarus-atrial septal defect-Robin sequence-persistence of the left superior vena cava syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: TARP syndrome is a rare X-linked genetic disorder with low prevalence, caused by mutations in the RBM10 gene. Historically, it was considered to be universally fatal in the early neonatal period, often leading to pre- or postnatal lethality in affected males. However, recent case reports have expanded the phenotypic spectrum, describing patients surviving beyond infancy, including into childhood and adulthood. Maternal mosaicism and de novo mutations have also been observed as causes of the condition. [PMC10032413, PMC9691016, PMC8149317, PMC6587983, PMC5455125]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: TARP syndrome is an X-linked disorder caused by RBM10 gene mutations, classically defined by talipes equinovarus, atrial septal defect, Robin sequence (micrognathia, glossoptosis, cleft palate), and persistent left superior vena cava. However, the phenotypic spectrum exhibits high clinical variability, with patients often missing cardinal features or presenting with additional traits. Reported associated findings include intellectual disability, scoliosis, renal malformations, optic nerve atrophy, multiple hemivertebrae, imperforate anus, aplasia of thumbs and first toes, and abnormal liver function tests. Although previously considered universally fatal in the early neonatal period, recent cases demonstrate survival into childhood and adulthood, expanding the known prognosis and clinical course. [PMC10032413, PMC9691016, PMC8149317, PMC6587983, PMC5455125]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: TARP syndrome is a rare X-linked disorder caused by mutations in the RBM10 gene, located on the human X-chromosome. These mutations, which include splicing variants, frameshifts, and deletions, lead to developmental defects during embryogenesis and can result in truncated or decayed RBM10 transcripts. While initially considered a lethal syndrome, patients with milder symptoms and longer survival have been described, expanding the phenotypic spectrum. The condition exhibits high clinical variability, with patients sometimes lacking cardinal features or presenting with additional traits, and de novo mutations and maternal mosaicism have been observed. [PMC10032413, PMC9691016, PMC8149317, PMC6587983, PMC5455125]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of TARP syndrome primarily relies on genetic testing, often initiated by clinical suspicion based on characteristic features such as talipes equinovarus, atrial septal defect, Robin sequence, and persistent left superior vena cava. Exome sequencing, including diagnostic exome sequencing, is a key method used to identify pathogenic variants in the RBM10 gene. Direct sequencing and massively parallel sequencing are also employed to detect RBM10 mutations. Molecular and cellular analyses, such as RNA analyses, Western blotting, and immunofluorescence staining, may be used to verify the pathogenicity of identified variants. Additionally, carrier testing for RBM10 mutations is recommended for mothers and sisters of affected individuals. [PMC10032413, PMC9691016, PMC8149317, PMC6587983, PMC5455125]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: TARP syndrome should be considered as a possible diagnosis in males presenting with severe or profound intellectual disability. This is particularly relevant when combined with a septal heart defect, and additional features such as Robin sequence, micrognathia, or cleft palate. The phenotypic spectrum can be broad, as evidenced by an adult patient presenting with intellectual disability, scoliosis, and other findings, alongside novel features like a prominent nose, esotropia, and small teeth. [PMC6587983]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of TARP syndrome can involve the prenatal detection of associated anomalies such as intrauterine growth restriction, persistent left superior vena cava, interatrial communication, and horseshoe kidney. However, traditional prenatal testing, including chromosome analysis and microarray, may not identify the underlying cause of multiple congenital anomalies. While molecular diagnosis via exome sequencing has been utilized to establish a genetic diagnosis, this was described as a postnatal method in one reported case. [PMC8149317, PMC5455125]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: TARP syndrome is an X-linked condition caused by mutations in the RBM10 gene, often resulting in pre- or postnatal lethality in affected males, though milder phenotypes and adult survival have been reported.
