The phenotypic spectrum shows high clinical variability, making genotype-phenotype correlation essential for counseling. Genetic counseling is crucial due to the X-linked inheritance, with observed de novo mutations and maternal mosaicism. Diagnostic exome sequencing can aid in diagnosis and inform future reproductive options. It is recommended that sisters of affected males undergo carrier testing before family planning, even if the mother has been tested, due to the possibility of maternal mosaicism. Accurate diagnosis and counseling are important for families. [PMC9691016, PMC6587983, PMC5455125, PMC4443488, PMC3183328]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for TARP syndrome is supportive, addressing specific complications. One reported patient required nocturnal ventilator support for chronic lung disease and was fed exclusively through a gastro-jejunal tube. Sensorineural hearing loss was managed with a hearing aid, and atrial flutter necessitated recurrent ablation of intra-atrial re-entry pathways. [PMC3183328]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: TARP syndrome was historically considered a lethal X-linked disorder, often resulting in pre- or postnatal lethality, with a high rate of mortality in the neonatal stage. However, recent case reports have expanded the phenotypic spectrum, describing patients surviving beyond early infancy, into childhood, and even adulthood. This improved survival is noted in patients with milder symptoms or specific genetic variations, such as certain splicing mutations or exon skipping. Despite extended survival, affected individuals can experience severe complications, including chronic lung disease, ventilator dependence, feeding difficulties, sensorineural hearing loss, optic atrophy, cortical visual impairment, and severe intellectual disability. The prognosis shows significant variability, influenced by genotype and phenotype. [PMC10032413, PMC9691016, PMC8149317, PMC6587983, PMC5455125]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Familial acute necrotizing encephalopathy or ADANE is a potentially fatal neurological disease characterised by neuropathological lesions principally involving the brainstem, thalamus and putamen.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It has been described in 11 members of one family.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset occurs during early childhood, typically a few days after a febrile illness. Manifestations include vomiting, seizures, spasticity, language regression, rigidity and abnormal posturing of the head. Residual neurologic impairment (muscle weakness, speech disturbance, intellectual deficit and mood disorders) persists in some patients. The disease is chronic in one out of two cases.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The mode of transmission appears to be autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 9 syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 9 is a uniparental disomy of maternal origin that most likely does not have any phenotypic expression except from cases of homozygosity for a recessive disease mutation for which only mother is a carrier.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 9, specifically segmental disomy, has been linked to inherited CARD9 deficiency. This genetic alteration can predispose individuals to severe fungal diseases, such as disseminated Exophiala dermatitidis infection. Patients with this condition may appear otherwise healthy prior to developing these invasive fungal infections. [PMC10582337, PMC4447834]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Maternal uniparental disomy (UPD) of chromosome 9 involves inheriting both homologous chromosomes from only the mother. This condition has been shown to arise after the postzygotic loss of the paternal chromosome 9 from a trisomic cell line. In some cases of mosaic trisomy 9 syndrome, a maternally derived pericentric inversion of the heterochromatic area of chromosome 9 has been observed in duplicate in the trisomic cell line. Genetic analysis, such as chromosomal microarray, has revealed homozygous regions involving the whole chromosome 9 in patients with UPD 9. Replication-based mechanisms, including microhomology-mediated break-induced replication, are also proposed to induce genomic rearrangements and segmental uniparental disomy. [PMC10582337, PMC4266739, PMC1016137]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 9 syndrome involve a combination of prenatal screening and definitive genetic testing. Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) can identify pregnancies at high risk for trisomy 9, with a positive predictive value of 42.86% in high-risk cases. Second-trimester maternal serum screening, particularly with abnormal levels of biochemical markers like human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) and unconjugated estriol, may also indicate a high risk for trisomy 9 mosaicism. Confirmatory invasive prenatal diagnosis typically involves amniotic fluid karyotype analysis and SNP-array chip detection. For definitive diagnosis and to determine the origin of uniparental disomy, genetic testing such as chromosomal microarray (CMA), UPDtool, methylation-specific multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MS-MLPA), whole-exome sequencing (WES), and whole-genome oligonucleotide single-nucleotide polymorphism (oligo-SNP) arrays are employed, alongside cytogenetic and molecular analysis. [PMC12276342, PMC11424189, PMC10582337, PMC4266739, PMC1016137]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis for maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 9 syndrome includes other rare autosomal trisomies (RATs), particularly trisomy 15, 16, and 10, which show relatively high positive predictive values in non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) and are associated with poor pregnancy outcomes. Trisomy 18 should also be considered, as abnormal maternal serum markers such as high alpha-fetoprotein and low unconjugated estriol, human chorionic gonadotropin, and inhibin A can indicate a high risk for both trisomy 9 and trisomy 18. Trisomy 9 mosaicism is also a related condition, as maternal uniparental disomy for chromosome 9 can arise from the postzygotic loss of a paternal chromosome 9 from a trisomic cell line. [PMC12276342, PMC11424189, PMC5278532, PMC1016137]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 9 syndrome involves several considerations. Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) can indicate a high risk for trisomy 9, showing a relatively high positive predictive value of 42.86%. Abnormal maternal serum markers, such as high alpha-fetoprotein and low unconjugated estriol and human chorionic gonadotropin, may also suggest chromosomal abnormalities like trisomy 9. Confirmation of the diagnosis and origin of uniparental disomy (UPD) using genetic testing, such as chromosomal microarray, is crucial. Counseling should be individualized, adopting different prenatal diagnostic measures and discussing potential pregnancy outcomes, as high levels of mosaic trisomy 9 can significantly affect the fetus and may lead to pregnancy termination. The presence of a maternally derived pericentric inversion of chromosome 9 in trisomic cell lines may also have implications for counseling. Expanding detailed phenotypes and genotypes provides effective guidance for molecular testing and genetic counseling. [PMC12276342, PMC11424189, PMC10582337, PMC1016137]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: To investigate the prenatal diagnostic value and pregnancy outcomes of rare autosomal trisomies (RATs) as indicated by non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), and to contribute to good childbearing. This was a retrospective and cross-sectional analysis of 83,842 pregnant women who received NIPT in our hospital. Amniotic fluid karyotype analysis and SNP-array chip detection were used to evaluate the prenatal diagnostic value and pregnancy outcomes of pregnant women at high-risk of RATs. In 83,842 pregnant women, 331 were identified to be at high-risk of RATs; the positive screening rate was 0.39% (331/83,842). Among the 331 women at high risk of RATs, 245 received invasive prenatal diagnosis, and the referral reasons for NIPT were advanced maternal age (≥ 35 years), serological borderline risk, and single serological marker median (MoM) abnormality, with the constituent ratios of 27.35%... [PMC12276342, PMC11424189, PMC10582337, PMC5278532, PMC4447834]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: To investigate the prenatal diagnostic value and pregnancy outcomes of rare autosomal trisomies (RATs) as indicated by non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), and to contribute to good childbearing. This was a retrospective and cross-sectional analysis of 83,842 pregnant women who received NIPT in our hospital. Amniotic fluid karyotype analysis and SNP-array chip detection were used to evaluate the prenatal diagnostic value and pregnancy outcomes of pregnant women at high-risk of RATs. In 83,842 pregnant women, 331 were identified to be at high-risk of RATs; the positive screening rate was 0.39% (331/83,842). Among the 331 women at high risk of RATs, 245 received invasive prenatal diagnosis, and the referral reasons for NIPT were advanced maternal age (≥ 35 years), serological borderline risk, and single serological marker median (MoM) abnormality, with the constituent ratios of 27.35%... [PMC12276342, PMC11424189, PMC10582337, PMC5278532]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by pre- and postnatal overgrowth, distinctive craniofacial features, variable congenital malformations, organomegaly and an increased tumor risk.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): DGSX; Golabi-Rosen syndrome; SDYS; SGBS; SGBS1; Simpson dysmorphia syndrome; Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome type 1; X-linked dysplasia gigantism syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The birth prevalence is unknown. Approximately 250 cases have been reported to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome (SGBS) manifests a broad clinical picture with varying degrees of severity. It is characterized by pre- and postnatal overgrowth with macrosomia, distinctive craniofacial features (macrocephaly with coarse face, macroglossia, hypertelorism, dental malocclusion, palatal abnormalities), supernumerary nipples, congenital heart defects and arrhythmias, vertebral segmental defects, abdominal visceromegaly (renal dysplasia/nephromegaly, splenomegaly and hepatomegaly), diaphragmatic hernia, diastasis recti/umbilical hernia, limb anomalies (polydactyly/brachydactyly of the hands, cutaneous syndactyly, nail hypoplasia), and genital involvement (cryptorchidism, hypospadias). Involvement of central nervous system presents with variable degrees of intellectual disability, motor delay and speech delay. Patients with SGBS are at increased risk for embryonal tumors (Wilms tumor), hepatoblastoma, adrenal neuroblastoma, gonadoblastoma, hepatocellular carcinoma.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: SGBS is due to loss-of-function mutations in the GPC3 gene (Xq26), encoding Glypican-3 (GPC3), a cell surface heparin sulfate proteoglycan which acts as a negative regulator of Hedgehog (Hh) signaling during development. Mutations in GPC3 result in the hyperactivation of Hh signaling, that ultimately leads to overgrowth and cancer.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical findings, family history, genetic testing for GPC3 mutations, and array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) analysis of genomic imbalance in Xq26. Imaging techniques help to detect skeletal anomalies and central nervous system involvement. Screening for embryonic tumors is performed by imaging (serial abdominal ultrasonogram and chest X rays), serial measurement of tumor markers and catecholamine metabolites in urine. Kidney function is monitored in cases of kidney involvement.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis include overgrowth syndromes such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome and Sotos syndrome, and additional disorders such as fragile X syndrome, Bannayan-Zonana syndrome, PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome, Marshall syndrome, Nevo syndrome, mosaic trisomy 8 and Pallister-Killian syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis and/or pre-implantation genetic testing are possible for at-risk pregnancies when a mutation has previously been identified in the family. Prenatal ultrasound examination can detect disproportionate fetal overgrowth, while elevated maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels may also be useful to suspect SGBS.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: SGBS follows an X-linked recessive pattern of transmission. In the offspring of an affected male, daughters are heterozygous and sons are unaffected. For each pregnancy, a heterozygous female has a 25% risk of having an affected son and a 25% risk of having a carrier daughter (usually not affected or showing minimal clinical findings due to lyonization). SGBS may also result from de novo mutations (20-30% of cases).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management requires a multidisciplinary approach with pediatric cardiologists, neurologists, orthopedics, and speech therapists. Congenital malformations may require surgery. Special attention should be paid to cardiac abnormalities that are responsible for the increased perinatal and infant mortality. Tumor management and follow-up should be performed.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of the disease; in the most severe cases, SGBS is life-threatening before birth or in infancy, whereas in milder cases patients often live into adulthood.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A form of portosinusoidal vascular disease characterized histologically by varying degrees of phlebosclerosis, primarily involving the small and medium branches of the portal vein with heterogeneous distribution, in the absence of cirrhosis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: a case of hepatoportal sclerosis (HPS) identified in an 81-year-old woman taking a traditional Chinese herbal supplementation, Cordyceps . The patient presented with splenomegaly and weight loss. After an extensive evaluation, liver biopsy confirmed loss of the small portal veins with characteristics of obstruction at the level of the small and large portal veins, suggestive of HPS. After a comprehensive history and exclusion of other etiological factors, patient's HPS was attributed to Cordyceps use. Ultimately, the patient's features of HPS improved with the cessation of Cordyceps . [PMC10686585]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hepatoportal sclerosis can present with symptoms such as splenomegaly and weight loss. Diagnosis is confirmed by liver biopsy, which reveals a loss of small portal veins and characteristics of obstruction at both small and large portal vein levels. In some cases, the condition may be attributed to specific factors, such as the use of Cordyceps, and improvement in features can be observed upon cessation of the causative agent. [PMC10686585]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hepatoportal sclerosis has been attributed to specific etiological factors in reported cases. One instance linked the condition to the use of the traditional Chinese herbal supplement, Cordyceps, where symptoms improved upon cessation of the supplement. Additionally, POEMS syndrome has been observed to manifest with portal hypertension, initially presenting as noncirrhotic portal hypertension of unknown etiology, suggesting a potential association. [PMC11300253, PMC10686585]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of hepatoportal sclerosis (HPS) involves an extensive evaluation, including a comprehensive history and the exclusion of other etiological factors. Liver biopsy is a key diagnostic method, confirming HPS by revealing the loss of small portal veins and characteristics of obstruction at the level of small and large portal veins. Pathological biopsy can also confirm noncirrhotic portal hypertension. [PMC11300253, PMC10686585]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: When portal hypertension is a main manifestation, conditions such as cirrhosis may initially be considered. However, noncirrhotic portal hypertension of unknown etiology can also be a diagnosis. POEMS syndrome should be included in the differential diagnosis, as it can present with portal hypertension as a primary symptom, which may lead to diagnostic delays if not recognized. [PMC11300253]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: In a reported case, hepatoportal sclerosis was attributed to the use of a traditional Chinese herbal supplement, Cordyceps. The patient's features of hepatoportal sclerosis improved with the cessation of Cordyceps, suggesting that identifying and removing the causative agent can be an effective management strategy. [PMC10686585]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: In a reported case of hepatoportal sclerosis attributed to Cordyceps use, the patient's features of the disease improved following the cessation of the traditional Chinese herbal supplementation. This suggests that in cases where an etiological factor like Cordyceps can be identified and removed, a favorable outcome with improvement in HPS features is possible. [PMC10686585]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is characterized by disseminated intra-peritoneal mucinous tumors and mucinous ascites in the abdomen and pelvis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence is estimated at 1/1,000,000 with female predominance.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease is usually diagnosed after the age of 40. In 30 to 50% of cases, patients present with progressive abdominal distension (so-called ``jelly belly''). Diagnosis may follow discovery of an ovarian mass in women or recent development of inguinal hernia, appendicitis or intestinal occlusion. Other less common signs include abdominal pain, weight loss, urinary symptoms, constipation, vomiting, and dyspnea.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In 90% of cases, the primary lesion is an appendiceal mucinous tumor, but ovarian mucinous tumors have been reported (7%) and, more rarely, mucinous tumors of the colon, stomach, pancreas, and urachus.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on chest-abdominal-pelvic computed tomography (CAP-CT) findings (revealing the characteristic compartmentalized distribution pattern of mucinous ascites) and on pathology (performed by two experts), while tumor markers (carcinoembryonic antigen and CA19-9) are relatively non-specific.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes secondary peritoneal carcinomatoses and other rare peritoneal tumors.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment strategies require a multidisciplinary approach and must be discussed by a panel of physicians in a specialized center. There are currently no validated recommendations on clinical management and no cytotoxic agents have been granted a European Marketing Authorization (MA) in this indication. Nonetheless, the best curative option appears to be complete cytoreductive surgery (visceral resections and peritonectomy procedures) combined with hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) (off-label use), sometimes followed by intravenous chemotherapy (off-label use) which can only be considered in young patients with good general status.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is slowly progressive but recurrence after complete tumor removal may occur. Following combined treatment (complete cytoreductive surgery and HIPEC), the 5-year survival rate reaches 70% for non-aggressive peritoneal pseudomyxoma in patients treated in a specialized center.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Pseudomyxoma peritonei is an infrequent condition with a global annual incidence of only one to two cases per million people. Mucinous neoplasms, widespread intraperitoneal implants, and mucinous ascites characterize it. Currently, most clinicians misdiagnose this condition, which leads to delayed management. A 44-year-old North Indian female presented with a 1.5-month history of an abdominal lump. Physical examination revealed a sizeable abdominopelvic mass at 36 weeks. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography showed a massive multiloculated right ovarian cystic mass measuring 28 × 23 × 13 cm with mild ascites and elevated carcinoembryonic antigen levels (113.75 ng/ml). A provisional diagnosis of ovarian mucinous neoplasm was made, for which the patient underwent laparotomy. Intraoperatively, there were gross mucinous ascites, along with a large, circumscribed, ruptured right ovarian... [PMC11212264]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Patients with low-grade appendiceal mucinous carcinomas (LAMNs) treated with cytoreductive surgery (CRS) and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC) have a favorable prognosis. However, a subgroup of patients presents a clinically aggressive course with disease progression despite receiving treatment. The purpose of is to report the experience of clinically aggressive LAMN patients treated by the same team, and to present a review of the literature. The cases of four patients with clinically aggressive LAMNs were reviewed. Clinical and histopathological characteristics were re-examined. Recurrences and the time of recurrence, as well as the survival time, were recorded. These patients were four men with clinically aggressive LAMNs treated with CRS plus HIPEC. One of them underwent CC-0 surgery, two underwent CC-1 surgery, and one underwent CC-3 surgery. All patients received... [PMC10670747, PMC9088063]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Hypercoagulability syndrome due to glycosylphosphatidylinositol deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital disorder of glycosylation characterized by cerebral and portal vein thrombosis, portal hypertension, macrocephaly, and persistent absence seizures. Additional reported features include mild to moderate global developmental delay and intellectual disability, as well as thrombocytopenia. Brain imaging may show variable stages of infarction and cerebral and cerebellar atrophy.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Congenital disorder of glycosylation due to PIGM deficiency; PIGM-CDG

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hypercoagulability syndrome due to glycosylphosphatidylinositol deficiency, specifically PIGM deficiency, presents with a heterogeneous phenotype. Key clinical features include thrombotic events such as cerebral and portal vein thrombosis, and infantile-onset cerebrovascular thrombotic events. Patients also experience neurological manifestations like atypical or persistent absence seizures. Macrocephaly has been observed as part of the expanded phenotypic spectrum. [PMC10569059]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hypercoagulability syndrome due to glycosylphosphatidylinositol deficiency stems from defects in the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) biosynthesis pathway, an emerging subgroup of congenital disorders of glycosylation. A specific etiology involves a mutation in the promoter of the PIGM gene, which in a syndrome characterized by features such as portal vein thrombosis, persistent absence seizures, macrocephaly, and infantile-onset cerebrovascular thrombotic events. [PMC10569059]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for glycosylphosphatidylinositol deficiency due to a PIGM promoter mutation involve molecular delineation to identify the specific genetic defect. This is crucial for confirming the diagnosis in patients presenting with the characteristic clinical phenotype, which includes cerebral and portal vein thrombosis, macrocephaly, and atypical absence seizures. Additionally, prenatal diagnosis of PIGM deficiency has been successfully performed, allowing for early characterization of the disease's natural history. [PMC10569059]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: The first prenatal diagnosis of PIGM deficiency has been described. This allowed for the characterization of the natural history of the disease from birth. [PMC10569059]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Hypercoagulability syndrome due to glycosylphosphatidylinositol deficiency is a genetic disorder arising from defects in the GPI biosynthesis pathway, specifically linked to mutations in the PIGM promoter. This condition has been identified in multiple patients across unrelated families, suggesting a familial inheritance pattern. The first prenatal diagnosis of PIGM deficiency has been described, which allows for early characterization of the disease's natural history from birth and provides a critical tool for genetic counseling. [PMC10569059]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Insights regarding targeted treatment for this rare disorder, characterized by defects in the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) biosynthesis pathway and associated with thrombotic events, have been offered. Specifically, sodium phenylbutyrate is suggested as a potential therapeutic approach for this condition. [PMC10569059]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Defects of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) biosynthesis pathway constitute an emerging subgroup of congenital disorders of glycosylation with heterogeneous phenotypes. A mutation in the promoter of PIGM, resulting in a syndrome with portal vein thrombosis and persistent absence seizures, was previously described in three patients. We now report four additional patients in two unrelated families, with further clinical, biochemical and molecular delineation of this unique entity. We also describe the first prenatal diagnosis of PIGM deficiency, allowing characterization of the natural history of the disease from birth. The patients described herein expand the phenotypic spectrum of PIGM deficiency to include macrocephaly and infantile-onset cerebrovascular thrombotic events. Finally, we offer insights regarding targeted treatment of this rare disorder with sodium phenylbutyrate. [PMC10569059]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Myoclonus-dystonia syndrome (MDS) is a rare movement disorder characterized by mild to moderate dystonia along with 'lightning-like' myoclonic jerks.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Alcohol-responsive dystonia; Hereditary essential myoclonus; Myoclonic dystonia

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated prevalence of MDS in Europe is 1/500,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset usually occurs in the first or second decade of life. Myoclonus is usually the presenting manifestation and is described as swift ''lightning-like'' jerks that can rarely appear at rest but that are usually triggered by complex motor tasks such as drawing and writing. These movements mainly affect the neck, arms and trunk but can also rarely be seen in the legs or the larynx. In two thirds of cases, dystonia is also experienced in the form of focal or cervical dystonia, which may be only mild and does not exacerbate with time. Postural and other forms of tremor have sometimes been reported. MDS is often associated with depression, anxiety, panic attacks, obsessive-compulsive behavior and personality disorders and alcohol abuse. Isolated torticollis is seen in extremely rare cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The only known causative gene of MDS is the epsilon-sarcoglycan (SGCE) gene (7q21.3), encoding a transmembrane protein that is part of the dystrophin-associated glycoprotein complex found in skeletal and cardiac muscle. The epsilon-sarcoglycan protein is also abundant in monoaminergic neurons, cerebellar Purkinje cells, the cortex and the hippocampus of the brain. In one family with MDS, linkage to chromosome 18p has been reported (named DYT15), but the gene has not yet been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the presence of characteristic clinical symptoms. Neuroimaging studies are normal. Genetic molecular testing of SGCE can confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes cervical dystonia, Dopa-responsive dystonia, Tourette syndrome, familial cortical myoclonus, Wilson disease, spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3) and type 14 (SCA14), ataxia with vitamin E deficiency, genetic disorders with myoclonus as a major component (e.g. Unverricht-Lundborg disease, Lafora disease) and other secondary forms of dystonia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal testing is possible in families where a disease-causing mutation is identified.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: MDS is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. However, the SGCE gene is maternally imprinted, therefore in most cases (95%) a patient who inherits the mutation from their mother will remain healthy and only those that inherit the mutation from their father will develop MDS. De novo mutations also occur. Genetic counseling is recommended in those with a known mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment plans are individualized to a patient's presenting symptoms. Benzodiazepines (clonazepam) and antiepileptic drugs (valproate, levetiracetam) are effective in relieving myoclonus and tremor, but patients should be carefully monitored. Similarly, alcohol frequently improves symptoms temporarily, but its long term use is not recommended. Injections of botulinum toxin can relieve focal and cervical dystonia. If these treatments fail or are insufficient, bilateral deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the internal globus pallidum (Gpi) and the central intermediate nucleus (VIM) of the thalamus have shown positive results in providing lasting relief from both myoclonus and dystonia. Gpi stimulation is often sufficient in treating MDS, and may be favored over VIM stimulation, which generally has very little effect on dystonia. In a staged surgical procedure, quadruple stimulation (VIM and Gpi) may also be considered in selected cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Patients with MDS have normal life-expectancy, but quality of life can be severely affected.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Deafness is the most frequent form of sensorial deficit. In the vast majority of cases, the deafness is termed nonsyndromic or isolated and the hearing loss is the only clinical anomaly reported. In developed counties, 60-80% of cases of early-onset hearing loss are of genetic origin.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Isolated genetic deafness; Isolated genetic hearing loss; Non-syndromic genetic hearing loss
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Between 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 700 children were born with profound or severe hearing loss.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The majority of cases presenting at birth concern perceptive deafness (with a neurosensory origin associated with the inner ear) rather than conductive deafness (anomalies in the amplification of sound waves between the middle ear - tympanum and auditory ossicles - and the outer ear). Autosomal dominant forms are characterised by very early onset and bilateral hearing loss with varying degrees of severity (ranging from mild to profound). No malformations of the inner ear can be detected by CT scan. Mutations in the PDS gene are responsible for 7% of cases of childhood deafness. In these cases, the deafness is marked by early-onset, usually bilateral (but sometimes asymmetric) hearing loss with autosomal recessive transmission. This form of deafness is always associated with malformations of the inner ear that can be detected by CT scan. In rare cases, thyroid gland disease may also be present. For the autosomal dominant forms of deafness, mutations in the COCH gene result in progressive postlingual deafness associated with severe attacks of vertigo and subjective tinnitus. This form of deafness should be distinguished from Meniere's disease. Autosomal dominant mutations in the WFS1 gene cause either a form of hearing loss affecting mainly low frequency sounds or deafness associated with optic atrophy.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: To date, 86 causative genes for sensorineural deafness have been identified and localised and 37 of these genes have been cloned. Eleven of these genes have been implicated in both isolated and syndromic forms of deafness. Mutations in the gene encoding connexin 26 appear to be responsible for the majority of cases of childhood perceptive deafness.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Hearing loss can be evaluated by audiogram and grouped as either mild (loss between 20 and 40 dB), moderate (loss between 41 and 70 dB), severe (loss between 71 and 90 dB), profound (loss between 91 and 120 dB) or as cophosis (loss beyond 120 dB).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In 85% of cases, the deafness is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait (DFNB type). Autosomal dominant inheritance accounts for between 10 and 15% of cases (DFNA type), whereas only 1% of cases are inherited as an X-linked trait (DFN type).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management should be multidisciplinary (involving a paediatrician, general practitioner, ORL specialist, speech therapist and hearing aid specialist). Hearing aids (either implanted or external) generally provide the only management option for improving hearing loss, although surgical treatment may sometimes be proposed for some forms of conductive hearing loss.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare chromosomal anomaly characterized by the presence of extra chromosome 13 material and manifesting with severe intellectual disability and multiple congenital anomalies including holoprosencephaly, microcephaly, microphthalmia, scalp defect, cleft lip/palate, congenital heart defects, and postaxial polydactyly. Neurological involvement may lead to seizures and hypotonia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence at birth is between 1/3500 and 1/5000. In 1st trimester diagnosis, the rate is 1/1,500 in the Danish register. Risk increases with maternal age.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In utero death occurs in over 95% of affected fetuses. Median survival is 7-10 days, and less than 30% survives beyond 1 year. Intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) is common. Neurological manifestations are severe and present as hypotonia and hyporeactivity with an apparent lack of awareness of surroundings. Holoprosencephaly (resulting from a defect in the division of the brain into two hemispheres) is present in 70% of cases and can be observed as variable degrees of hemisphere fusion on MRI. Facial anomalies are variable and may range in severity from hypotelorism and premaxillary agenesis (80% of cases) to cyclopia. Cleft lip/palate (50-80%), micro- or anophthalmia (40%) eye coloboma, areas of cutaneous aplasia of the vertex (30%), postaxial polydactyly (50%), congenital heart defect (CHD) (80% of cases) and renal malformations (40%) may also be present.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Free trisomy 13 (T13) is found in around 75% of cases. In 20% of cases, T13 is associated with a Robertsonian translocation in which the supernumerary chromosome 13 becomes attached to another acrocentric chromosome (chromosomes 13, 14, 15, 21 or 22). In rare cases, the syndrome is caused by reciprocal translocation between chromosome 13 and a non-acrocentric chromosome. Mosaic T13 (in which there is both trisomic and normal cell types) has been reported in a few patients with a clinical picture that varies between a normal phenotype and that of classical T13 according to the number of trisomic cells present in the tissues.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: T13 must be confirmed by conventional karyotyping. Chromosomal microarray will show T13 but may not discriminate free from translocation T13.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes trisomy 18, Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, CHARGE Syndrome, Meckel syndrome and, in a minority of cases, other ciliopathies like Joubert syndrome and Bardet-Biedl syndrome (which may present with renal anomalies, polydactyly, brain anomalies).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Analysis of fetal DNA in maternal blood (non-invasive prenatal testing; NIPT) has high sensitivity (> 97%). Maternal serum screening based on blood markers and nuchal translucency ultrasound scan may detect a proportion of T13 fetuses. Most T13 fetuses can be detected by routine fetal ultrasound scan (holoprosencephaly, polydactyly). Invasive prenatal testing like amniocentesis or chorionic villi sampling (CVS) will confirm any suspicion raised by prenatal screening.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The risk of recurrence of trisomy (21, 13 or 18) in families of an index case with T13 is around 1%. However, in families in which T13 is associated with translocation (Robertsonian or balanced) the risk of recurrence is higher if one of the parents is a carrier of a balanced translocation.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is supportive/palliative only. Follow-up is needed for cardiac, respiratory, neurological, genitourinary, abdominal, otolaryngologic, and orthopedic complications.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Surgical treatment of the malformations does little to improve the poor prognosis associated with this syndrome: half of the infants born alive die within the first month of life, 70% die before 1 year of age from cardiac, renal or neurologic complications, and 10% more die before 5 years of age. Prolonged survival (in some cases into adulthood) has been reported and is more common in cases of mosaic or partial trisomy and in the absence of severe brain malformations. In general, non-mosaic patients develop only limited autonomy (absence of speech and ambulation).

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:88637

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Hypomyelination-hypogonadotropic hypogonadism-hypodontia syndrome (4H leukodystrophy) is a rare, progressive, autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder. It is described as a rare hereditary brain white matter disease. For a specific common POLR3B mutation, only two patients had been described, with another patient later reported. Cerebellar hypoplasia with endosteal sclerosis (CHES syndrome), which is considered a severe form of 4H-leukodystrophy, has only five described patients. The condition is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, with cases reported in siblings and from consanguineous parents. [PMC11923466, PMC9410618, PMC7318643, PMC5883641, PMC5567146]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hypomyelination-hypogonadotropic hypogonadism-hypodontia syndrome (4H syndrome) is a rare, progressive, hypomyelinating leukodystrophy caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in POLR3A, POLR3B, POLR1C, or POLR3K genes. The classic features include hypomyelination, hypodontia, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Patients often present with neurodevelopmental delay or regression, ataxia, dystonia, nystagmus, and intellectual disability. MRI shows characteristic hypomyelination, sometimes with cerebellar atrophy, thin corpus callosum, or polymicrogyria. Dental abnormalities include delayed dentition, persistent milk teeth, and hypoplastic crowns. Endocrine dysfunction can be progressive, encompassing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency, central hypocortisolism, hypoprolactinemia, and rarely, type 1 diabetes mellitus or Hashimoto’s thyroiditis. Other features may include epilepsy, myopia, optic atrophy, and neurogenic bladder. Phenotypes can vary significantly, even with the same genotype. [PMC11923466, PMC9410618, PMC7318643, PMC5883641, PMC5567146]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hypomyelination-hypogonadotropic hypogonadism-hypodontia syndrome (4H syndrome) is a rare, hereditary, autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder. It is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in genes encoding subunits of RNA polymerase III (Pol III). Specifically, mutations in POLR3A, POLR3B, POLR1C, and POLR3K genes have been identified as the genetic causes of this condition, also known as POLR3-related leukodystrophy. These mutations can be homozygous or compound heterozygous. [PMC11923466, PMC9410618, PMC8527611, PMC7318643, PMC5883641]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: 4H syndrome is a rare, progressive, hypomyelinating leukodystrophy. Hypomyelination, hypodontia, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism are the three classic features of 4H syndrome. Biallelic pathogenic variants in POLR3A, POLR3B, POLR1C , and POLR3K gene cause 4H leukodystrophy. Herein, clinical features in two siblings with 4H syndrome. The first patient (16 years) presented with hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, euthyroid Hashimoto’s thyroiditis and type 1 diabetes mellitus (DM). The second patient (13.5 years) showed normal physical, biochemical and hormonal examination at presentation. The second patient was followed up for epilepsy between the ages of 6 months and 6 years, when his epilepsy medication was discontinued, and he did not have seizure again. T2-weighted magnetic resonance images showed increased signal intensity secondary to hypomyelination in both. They were subsequently... [PMC11923466, PMC9410618, PMC8527611, PMC5883641, PMC5487884]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis for hypomyelination-hypogonadotropic hypogonadism-hypodontia syndrome (4H-leukodystrophy) includes other POLR3-related disorders and conditions with overlapping features. Cerebellar hypoplasia with endosteal sclerosis (CHES) syndrome is highly reminiscent of 4H-leukodystrophy, sharing hypomyelination, hypogonadism, and hypodontia, and is considered a severe form of 4H-leukodystrophy, also linked to POLR3B variants. Demyelinating Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease, particularly forms caused by POLR3B variants, should also be considered, although these may present without the characteristic hypodontia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Furthermore, unexplained chronic bladder dysfunction or endocrine abnormalities like growth failure and absent sexual development may precede a 4H diagnosis, requiring careful evaluation to distinguish from other causes. [PMC8527611, PMC5567146, PMC4351912]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: 4H leukodystrophy, one of POLR3-related leukodystrophy, is a rare hereditary brain white matter disease caused by the pathogenic biallelic variations in POLR3A, POLR3B, or POLR1C. Hypomyelination, hypodontia, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is mainly presented in patients with 4H leukodystrophy. Patient concerns: Here, we reported the brother and the sister with new compound heterozygous (c.1615G>T and c.165-167del) with various degrees of phenotypes including dysbasia, myopia, dental abnormal, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. Diagnosis: The brother and sister were diagnosed with 4H leukodystrophy. Interventions: Gonadotrophins treatment of the brother could significantly improve the development of secondary sexual characteristics and genitalia. Outcomes: showed that the same genotype of POLR3B may have variable clinical phenotypes in the brother and sister. The exploration of... [PMC9410618, PMC7318643, PMC5883641]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: 4H syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in POLR3A, POLR3B, POLR1C, and POLR3K genes. Genetic counseling is crucial for families, providing anticipatory guidance about the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern and recurrence risk. The same genotype can lead to variable clinical phenotypes, and the disease spectrum may expand, making comprehensive counseling important. Genetic confirmation is necessary for diagnosis, and reporting cases helps determine appropriate genotype-phenotype correlations. De novo variants have also been reported, further delineating the phenotype. [PMC11923466, PMC9410618, PMC8527611, PMC7318643, PMC5883641]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Hypomyelination-hypogonadotropic hypogonadism-hypodontia syndrome involves both targeted and supportive interventions. Gonadotrophins treatment has been shown to significantly improve the development of secondary sexual characteristics and genitalia in affected individuals. Supportive care includes physiotherapy, developmental therapy, speech therapy, and the provision of hearing aids. Additionally, genetic counseling and anticipatory guidance are crucial for families, addressing the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern and recurrence risk. [PMC9410618, PMC5883641]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: 4H syndrome is a progressive hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, with neurological deterioration often worsening over time, including motor performance, cerebellar involvement, ataxia, and moderate to severe intellectual and language difficulties. Endocrine dysfunctions, such as hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, growth hormone deficiency, and central hypocortisolism, can also be progressive or manifest over time, with some cases presenting with type 1 diabetes mellitus. While some individuals may have a remarkably mild clinical course, others exhibit a severe phenotype with neonatal onset, severe psychomotor delay, and chronic issues like bladder dysfunction preceding later neurological decline. The progression of symptoms can vary, with some patients experiencing an initial period of stability followed by significant worsening. [PMC11923466, PMC7318643, PMC5567146, PMC4557838, PMC4351912]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A desmoid tumor (DT) is a benign, locally invasive soft tissue tumor associated with a high recurrence rate but with no metastatic potential.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: DTs account for < 3% of soft tissue tumors. Their annual incidence is estimated to range between 1/250,000-1/500,000. They predominantly affect women and can occur between the ages of 15-60 years, but frequently during early adolescence and with a peak age of about 30 years.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In principle, DTs can occur in any part of the body: extra-abdominally (neck, shoulders, upper limbs, gluteal region), abdominally (originating from muscle fascia or the abdominal/chest wall), and more rarely intra-abdominally in the mesentery or retroperitoneum. Usually, they are firm and smooth palpable masses upon discovery. Depending on the location of the tumor, symptoms may include pain, fever, and functional impairment or loss of function of the organ involved. DTs may appear after surgical resections, typically after caesarian section. Intra-abdominal DTs are often observed in patients with an association of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) or Gardner syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: DTs result from the proliferation of well-differentiated myofibroblasts. The exact etiopathogenetic mechanism is still unknown, but they seem to have a multi-factorial origin with hormonal and genetic factors being involved. Somatic mutations in the CTNNB1 gene (3q21) encoding beta-catenin have been found in about 85 % of sporadic cases. In cases with FAP, DTs have been associated with mutations in the tumor suppressor gene APC (5q21-q22) encoding the adenomatous polyposis coli protein.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Initial diagnosis is based on imaging techniques (computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging) revealing the presence of an infiltrative growing mass. Diagnosis is confirmed by tumor biopsy showing abundant collagen surrounding elongated spindle-shaped cells containing small and regular nuclei and pale cytoplasm. Immunohistological examination shows expression of muscle cell markers (e.g. actin, desmin, vimentine) and absence of CD34. Moreover, diagnosis can be confirmed by screening for mutations of CTNNB1.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis is broad with fibrosarcomas on the one extreme and myofibroblastic processes such as nodular fasciitis and even hypertrophic scars and keloids on the other. The differential diagnosis of intra-abdominal DTs includes gastrointestinal stromal tumors, solitary fibrous tumors, inflammatory myofibroblastic tumors, sclerosing mesenteritis and retroperitoneal fibrosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Most cases are sporadic. Familial cases (5-10 %) are associated with FAP.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Complete surgical resection remains the therapeutic mainstay of DTs. For unresectable tumors or those not amenable to surgical resection with R0 (microscopic tumor clearance) intent or accompanied by an unacceptable function loss, non-surgical treatments comprise radiotherapy, anti-estrogen therapy, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents, chemotherapy (e.g. methotrexate, vinblastine/vinorelbine, pegylated liposomal doxorubicin) and/or tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g. imatinib, sorafenib). As DTs have a variable and often unpredictable clinical course, a period of watchful waiting is advisable for asymptomatic patients. As DTs often recur, a surveillance strategy every 3-6 months is essential.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Local recurrence occurs in around 70 % of cases. Prognosis depends on the type of tumor. Life expectancy is normal for abdominal and extra-abdominal tumors. However, it is lower in cases of intra-abdominal DTs due to complications such as intestinal obstruction, hydronephrosis or sepsis. Repeated surgical resections are associated with a greater risk of morbidity.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare dendritic cell tumor characterized by an aggressive, high-grade neoplasm derived from Langerhans cells, most commonly extranodal and multifocal, involving the skin and underlying soft tissue, as well as lung, liver, spleen, and bone. Primary nodal involvement is seen in a minority of patients. Immune-phenotyping and the presence of Birbeck granules on ultrastructural examination reveal the Langerhans cell derivation of the neoplastic cells. Prognosis is generally poor.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Langerhans cell sarcoma (LCS) is a rare malignant neoplasm originating from Langerhans cells. Proposed etiological factors include immunosuppression, virus infection (such as Epstein-Barr virus), and prior hematological disease. LCS can arise de novo or from antecedent conditions like Langerhans cell histiocytosis, low-grade follicular lymphoma, or acute B-lymphoblastic leukemia, often through transdifferentiation. Genetic alterations are frequently observed, including mutations in CDKN2A, TP53, and KRAS (e.g., p.G13D), as well as copy number loss of CDKN2A, CDKN2B, and FOXA1. MAPK pathway mutations are enriched, and a high tumor mutational burden is characteristic. Clonal relationships between antecedent hematological malignancies and LCS support transdifferentiation. [PMC12319524, PMC8803631, PMC8265357, PMC6417513, PMC6190545]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Langerhans cell sarcoma is a rare malignancy for which an optimal treatment strategy has not yet been identified. Polychemotherapy is a common modality, with various regimens reported, including ABVD, ESHAP, E-CHOP, EPOCH, and CHOP. Radiotherapy and surgical resection are also utilized. Outcomes are variable, ranging from partial response and recurrence to successful treatment, continuous remission, or fatal progression. Molecular testing for targetable genomic alterations, such as MAPK pathway mutations and KRAS mutations, holds potential for personalized therapeutic options. Allogeneic peripheral blood stem cell transplant has also been reported to achieve remission in one case. [PMC11217968, PMC8265357, PMC6417513, PMC6190545, PMC6407472]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Langerhans cell sarcoma (LCS) is an aggressive, high-grade malignancy typically associated with a poor or dismal prognosis. It is characterized by overtly malignant cytological features and often involves multiple organs. Fatal outcomes due to disease progression and metastasis have been reported, with some patients dying within months or less than a year after diagnosis despite treatment. Recurrence is also observed, even after chemotherapy. While some specific cases, such as primary cutaneous forms or those treated with allogeneic stem cell transplant, have shown periods of remission or no recurrence, the overall clinical behavior is aggressive. [PMC12319524, PMC11217968, PMC6417513, PMC6407472, PMC5413838]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A benign congenital skin disease characterised by progressive dilation of the subepidermal skin vessels manifesting as purple punctate lesions usually appearing on the lower limbs and buttocks and following the lines of Blaschko.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Not applicable, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The disease occurs almost exclusively in females.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: A mutation in the Xp11.3-Xq12 region has been identified in one of the reported families. However, in this family the AS was associated with oesophageal papillomatosis leading to the suggestion that this case of familial AS represents a mild form of focal dermal hypoplasia.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The majority of cases are sporadic. Only a few familial cases have been reported in the literature so far and transmission may be autosomal dominant or X-linked.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Angioma serpiginosum is a rare, benign nevoid disorder or vascular anomaly affecting the small vessels of the upper dermis. It typically presents during childhood with the onset of vascular reddish macules and papules, often in a monolateral, linear, or serpiginous pattern. While usually unilateral, symmetrical or congenital presentations have been reported, with lesions potentially extending during puberty. Lesions can be deep-red and asymptomatic, appearing on various body parts including the abdomen (rarely zosteriform), soles, and palms, sometimes with soft tissue hypertrophy. Extracutaneous findings are rare. Histopathology reveals clusters of dilated, thickened capillaries in the upper dermis, and immunohistochemistry may show WT-1 positivity, suggesting a vascular proliferation. [PMC12306886, PMC10389151, PMC8077343, PMC6487031, PMC4540500]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Angioma serpiginosum is confirmed through dermoscopy and light microscopy. Dermoscopy reveals characteristic features such as an erythematous parallel ridge pattern with double rows of irregular dots and globules, which can aid in diagnosis, especially in specific skin areas. Light microscopy typically shows clusters of dilated, thickened, and PAS+ capillaries in the upper dermis. Additionally, immunohistochemistry may demonstrate positive WT-1 staining. Genetic analysis using next-generation sequencing has not detected mutations in reported cases. [PMC6487031, PMC4540500]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Angioma serpiginosum, especially with acral volar skin involvement, must be included in the differential diagnosis of acral vascular lesions. Dermoscopic features, such as an erythematous parallel ridge pattern with double rows of irregular dots and globules, may aid in its diagnosis in these specific skin areas. [PMC4540500]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Angioma serpiginosum is described as a rare, benign nevoid disorder. It is rarely associated with extracutaneous findings, suggesting a localized condition. While typically presenting in childhood, the vascular macules and papules can extend, with cases reporting further extension during puberty. The condition is considered a vascular proliferation. [PMC8077343, PMC6487031]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare myotonic dystrophy of juvenile or adult-onset characterized by mild and fluctuating myotonia, muscle weakness, and rarely cardiac conduction disorders.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Myotonic dystrophy type 2; Proximal myotonic dystrophy; Ricker disease; Ricker syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence estimates of around 1/100,000 in Germany and 1/600,000 in the United Kingdom have been suggested. Most cases have been reported in individuals of European origin (mainly in Eastern Europe with a founder effect).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical presentation is marked by significant variability as is the age of onset (juvenile to late adulthood). The primary manifestations include muscle weakness (with early involvement of neck flexors or finger flexors, later involving hip girdle muscles), myotonia, and possibly severe fluctuating or episodic muscle pain, and stiffness. Cataracts, hypogonadism or testicular failure in males, insulin insensitivity, excessive sweating, cognitive abnormalities are rare features. Cardiac disorders are rare and may include conduction abnormalities (atrioventricular and bundle branch block) and cardiac arrhythmias. Gastrointestinal complications are common and can include constipation, dysphagia, and abdominal pain. Increased risk of cancer involving colon, brain and pancreas has been reported. The phenotype may be particularly mild in a large number of affected individuals.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by a CCTG expansion in the first intron of the cellular nucleic acid binding protein gene (CNBP; 3q21). Mutant alleles have 75 to 11,000 uninterrupted CCTG repeats. The pathogenesis is poorly understood.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: There may be considerable difficulty and delay in the diagnosis due to the wide clinical spectrum and non-specific manifestations. The diagnosis is based on molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: There are several overlapping features with Steinert myotonic dystrophy; whilst the diseases are similar, they are genetically distinct and have different courses and management requirements. The main difference is the absence of congenital form, which is seen in Steinert myotonic dystrophy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible in affected families with an index patient.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant. Genetic counselling should be provided to affected families. There is a 50% risk of disease transmission to offspring from an affected parent. A parent with intermediate CCTG repeat expansion is considered to have a premutation and thus there is a risk of transmitting the disorder to their offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management primarily involves monitoring of cataracts, insulin metabolism, and cardiac conduction.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is generally good with no impact on life expectancy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare endocrine disease characterized by an excessive or uncontrolled insulin secretion and recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia that can result in neurological sequelae if left untreated. There are two forms according to the response to first line treatment: diazoxide-sensitive and diazoxide-resistant hyperinsulinism; and three histopathological forms: focal, diffuse and atypical forms. Focal forms are only observed in early-onset cases of diazoxide unresponsive patients.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): PHHI; Persistent hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia of infancy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Isolated Congenital hyperinsulinism (CHI) is the most frequent cause of severe and persistent hypoglycemia in the neonatal period and early infancy. The average birth prevalence is 1/27,000 worldwide, but it may be as high as 1/2,500 in communities with substantial consanguinity.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: CHI can present from birth through early adulthood according to the severity of hypoglycemia. Neonatal onset is the most frequent; newborns, often macrosomic, present with poor feeding, intolerance to fasting and persistent hypoglycemia. Hypoglycemic episodes range from mild (lethargy, hypotonia and irritability) to severe (apnea, seizures or coma) that lead to neurologic sequelae. Patients who present later have recurrent, typical hypoglycemia (pallor, profuse sweating and tachycardia).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Nine genes are associated to CHI; the most common variants involve ABCC8 (11p15.1) and KCNJ11 (11p15.1), the genes encoding the ATP-sensitive potassium channel in pancreatic beta cell.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Detectable serum insulin/C-peptide, low ketone bodies and suppressed fatty acids during hypoglycemic episodes are diagnostic of hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia. Requirement of continuous glucose above the physiological rate of liver glucose production is pathognomonic of hyperinsulinism (HI). Later onset CHI may require provocative testing. The congenital (genetic) form should be established via family history consistent with HI or monogenic diabetes, abnormal biochemical features (hyperammonemia in association with GDH variants, or high plasma C4-OH and urine 3OH-glutarate with HADH variants), and genetic testing. Lastly, in cases unresponsive to diazoxide urgent genetic testing for ABCC8 / KCNJ11 variants and, when necessary, 18F-DOPA-Positron emission tomography (PET) imaging is indicated in order to differentiate the focal and diffuse forms.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis include all the other causes of recurrent hypoglycemia: for HI observed from birth these include transient neonatal HI as well as syndromic CHI (more than 30 syndromes feature HI at birth, the most frequent are Beckwith-Wiedemann, Kabuki and Turner syndrome); later in life, these may include insulinoma, post bariatric surgery HI, drug-induced HI, and auto-immune syndromes (HI due to anti-insulin antibodies) etc.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal genetic testing is possible when the molecular etiology has been identified in a proband.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder can be autosomal dominant or recessive, and thus genetic counseling will depend on the variants responsible (de novo, germline or somatic mutations). Genetic testing may be offered to affected families when the molecular etiology has been identified in a proband.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Normoglycemia must be rapidly recovered and maintained to prevent irreversible brain damage, especially in neonates. At birth, severe hypoglycemia might require continuous glucose infusion and glucagon injection. Diazoxide is the first line of medical therapy and octreotide is added as an adjunct in diazoxide unresponsive patients. Partial pancreatic resection is curative for focal HI. For patients with diffuse disease, a conservative treatment is proposed when safely possible; for patients resistant to diet and medical management, near-total pancreatectomy may be necessary.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: For neonatal-onset CHI, the main concern is the cognitive outcome, which might be impaired in up to 30 to 50% of patients, especially in those who suffered from prolonged and severe hypoglycemia. The spontaneous evolution of glycemia varies: in children the disease severity reduces with time, and sometimes might even resolve, while in others it persists through adulthood. When resolved, a life-long follow-up is advised due to a risk of diabetes. In cases of subtotal pancreatectomy, glucose intolerance and diabetes mellitus requiring insulin is inevitable, occurring within 15 years after the surgery.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, congenital muscular dystrophy due to dystroglycanopathy characterized by early onset muscular dystrophy, severe muscular hypotonia, severe intellectual disability and typical brain and eye malformations including pachygyria, polymicrogyria, agyria, brainstem and cerebellar structural anomalies, severe myopia, glaucoma, optic nerve and retinal hypoplasia. A broad clinical spectrum is observed with variable involvement of each organ system.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): MEB syndrome; Muscle-eye-brain syndrome; Santavuori congenital muscular dystrophy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown but it is very rare among other congenital muscular dystrophies. It is more frequently observed in Northern European countries (Scandinavian region) due to a founder mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients carrying the Finish founder mutation present with marked hypotonia and global developmental delay from birth. They have generalized muscle weakness, including facial and neck muscles. Severe eye disease is often present and includes congenital myopia, pachygyria, polymicrogyria, agyria, cerebellar and brainstem hypoplasia, cerebellar cysts, congenital glaucoma, pallor of the optic discs, and /or retinal hypoplasia. Adults have severe intellectual and motor disability, extremely limited communication skills, visual impairment, epilepsy, and spine and joint deformities. Many patients have associated behavioral difficulties (bruxism, autism, temper tantrums, self-mutilation). Creatine kinase (CK) levels are increased, and the biopsy shows abnormal alpha-dystroglycan expression. Brain MRI may reveal cortical neuronal migration disorder, with type II lissencephaly in the most severe cases, white matter abnormalities, flat brainstem, cerebellar hypoplasia, and hydrocephalus. Electroencephalograms are abnormal and often show paroxysmal tracing. Patients with other mutations present with a broad clinical spectrum ranging from severe (prenatal death, and brain and posterior fossa malformations) to mild muscular dystrophies (with or without eye or brain structural abnormalities, constant speech and cognitive delay, but possible acquired walking). Almost all develop seizures, such as myoclonic jerks or refractory partial/generalized epilepsy.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Muscle-eye-brain disease (MEB) is caused by mutations in the POMGnT1 gene (Chr 1p32-34), encoding protein O-linked mannose b1,2-N-acetylglucosaminyltransferase 1 (POMGnT1). Other gene variants have been identified in a small number of patients.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected on clinical presentation, characteristic neuroimaging and electromyography findings, muscle biopsy results, and molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other dystroglycanopathies and muscular dystrophies with brain and/or cognitive impairment. Patients presenting with MEB symptoms would be diagnosed with Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy (FCMD) in Japan. Therefore, there is an increasing tendency to use the global term MEB/FCMD syndrome. Other dystroglycanopathies include CMD due to FKRP, ISPD with brain involvement or cognitive delay, Walker-Warbourg Syndrome, laminin subunit alpha 2-related congenital muscular dystrophy, Duchenne muscular dystrophy with cognitive involvement, CDG-syndromes, and chromosomal disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Genetic prenatal diagnosis is possible where the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management includes physiotherapy, treatment of orthopedic, respiratory and cardiac complications, respiratory aid, and medical or surgical treatment for spinal or joint contractures, nutritional and gastrointestinal problems. Control of seizures requires antiepileptic drugs. Surveillance includes monitoring for respiratory and cardiac function. Severe intellectual disability and behavior disturbances may require specific care and management in specialized centers.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends mainly on the severity of neurologic, cardiac or respiratory complications. Patients may remain ambulant into adulthood.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, acrokeratoderma disease characterized by multiple, symmetrical, asymptomatic, skin-colored (rarely, brownish), flat-topped, wart-like papules located on the dorsal aspects of the hands and feet (occasionally found on other parts of the body, such as knees, elbows and forearms), typically associated with palmoplantar punctate keratosis and variable nail involvement (including leukonychia, thickening, ridging, longitudinal striations and splitting). Histology reveals undulating hyperkeratosis, papillomatosis, hypergranulosis, and acanthosis, creating a characteristic 'church spire' appearance, with no acantholysis nor dyskeratosis associated.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf (AVH) is described as a rare dermatological disorder. While it can manifest in nonfamilial cases, its rarity and diagnostic challenges, stemming from its resemblance to other conditions such as seborrheic keratosis, lichen planus, and Darier disease, necessitate increased awareness among dermatologists. This vigilance is essential for accurate and early recognition, particularly in nonfamilial presentations, to prevent misdiagnosis and facilitate effective management. [PMC12007786]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf (AVH) is a rare dermatological disorder characterized by keratotic lesions, often described as wart-like, primarily on the dorsal surfaces of the hands and feet, and sometimes on the neck. Patients may also present with nail dystrophy, such as a V-shaped notch on the nails. Histopathological examination typically reveals marked hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, papillomatosis, and church spire-like epidermal elevations. Diagnosis can be challenging due to its clinical similarity to other conditions, including seborrheic keratosis, lichen planus, and Darier disease. [PMC12007786]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf (AVH) is a rare dermatological disorder. It is caused by a missense mutation in the ATP2A2 gene. This genetic alteration leads to the characteristic keratotic lesions observed primarily on the dorsal surfaces of the hands and feet. [PMC12007786]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf (AVH) relies on thorough clinical and histopathological evaluations. Clinically, patients present with keratotic, wart-like lesions primarily on the dorsal surfaces of the hands and feet, often accompanied by V-shaped nail notches indicating dystrophy. Histopathological examination of a skin biopsy reveals characteristic features such as marked hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, papillomatosis, and church spire-like epidermal elevations, which confirm the diagnosis. AVH is caused by a missense mutation in the ATP2A2 gene, suggesting genetic testing as a diagnostic tool, though resource limitations may preclude it. Diagnostic challenges arise due to its similarity to conditions like seborrheic keratosis, lichen planus, and Darier disease. [PMC12007786]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf (AVH) presents diagnostic challenges due to its clinical similarity to other dermatological conditions. Key differential diagnoses include seborrheic keratosis, lichen planus, and Darier disease. Darier disease, like AVH, is caused by mutations in the ATP2A2 gene and is characterized by reddish-brown keratotic papules and plaques, which can lead to confusion. Thorough clinical and histopathological evaluations are crucial for accurate diagnosis to distinguish AVH from these conditions. [PMC12007786, PMC12023721]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Acrokeratosis verruciformis of Hopf (AVH) is a rare dermatological disorder associated with keratotic lesions primarily on the dorsal surfaces of the hands and feet, caused by a missense mutation in the ATP2A2 gene. Here, the case of a 24-year-old woman presenting with multiple wart-like lesions on the hands, feet, and neck over four years. A V-shaped notch on the nails indicated nail dystrophy. The patient had no family history of similar symptoms and an unremarkable medical history. The histopathological examination of a skin biopsy revealed marked hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, papillomatosis, and church spire-like epidermal elevations, confirming the diagnosis of AVH. AVH poses diagnostic challenges due to its similarity to other conditions, such as seborrheic keratosis, lichen planus, and Darier disease. Despite resource limitations precluding genetic testing, thorough clinical and... [PMC12007786]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autoinflammatory disorder characterized by recurrent attacks of fever and sterile abscesses.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Aseptic abscesses syndrome; Aseptic systemic abscesses; Disseminated aseptic abscesses; Corticosteroid-sensitive aseptic abscess syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It is a rare disease with approximately 150 patients documented to date, among which 85 cases are in the French aseptic abscess syndrome register.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: It affects mainly young adults and is characterized by recurrent attacks of fever and abscess-like collections, most frequently localized in the abdomen. Blood markers of inflammation and polymorphonuclear neutrophil levels are elevated. Aseptic abscesses may be either isolated or associated with an underlying condition (60% of patients) such as inflammatory bowel disease or relapsing polychondritis. The abscesses usually precede the diagnosis of inflammatory bowel disease, possibly by several years. A neutrophilic dermatosis, like pyoderma gangrenosum, may also be observed.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is unknown: all searches for a pathogen, including those using PCR with universal and specific probes, remain negative.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: On pathologic examination, aseptic abscesses consist of a core of altered polymorphonuclear leukocytes surrounded by palisading histiocytes and sometimes giant cells.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Aseptic abscess syndrome is a diagnosis of exclusion. The non-exhaustive list of etiologies to be considered and ruled out includes infectious abscesses (primarily pyogenic, as well as Chlamydia, Bartonella, and Tropheryma whipplei), mycobacterial infection, neoplasia (particularly lymphoma), chronic septic granulomatosis, splenic infarction, and inflammatory conditions (such as sarcoidosis, Wegener's disease, or rheumatoid nodules).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Antibiotics fail to cure the patients, but dramatic improvements are seen with corticosteroids and immunosuppressive drugs, including biologics.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: In the short term, once the diagnosis is established, patients undergo a significant transformation following the initiation of treatment, marked by a rapid resolution of fever. In the longer term, aseptic abscess syndrome is characterized by a high frequency of relapses (60% of patients), with the possibility of multiple relapses. Clinicians have at their disposal numerous treatment options, including biologics. Colchicine, typically used in combination with other treatments, has been described as a protective factor against relapse. There has been no recorded death directly related to aseptic abscess syndrome to date.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare soft tissue sarcoma characterized by palpable, slow-growing, deep-seated swellings, with or without pain or tenderness, affecting mostly children and young adults. Patients may have pain or joint contractures that precede swelling. Contrary to its name, lesions do not originate from intra-articular synovium, but from primitive mesenchymal cells. Majority of the lesions arise in the extremities, predominantly in the lower extremity, however can also occur in the head and neck region, trunk, lungs and pleura. Metastasis to the lungs, bone and regional lymph nodes can be observed. Increasing size, age and tumor grade are reported as negative predictive factors for both local disease recurrence and metastasis.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Synovial sarcoma is a rare malignant mesenchymal neoplasm. Primary pericardial synovial sarcoma, a rare and aggressive form, arises from pluripotent mesenchymal cells of the pericardium. The pathognomonic genetic hallmark is the chromosomal translocation t(X;18)(p11;q11), which in the SS18-SSX fusion oncogene. This fusion oncogene disrupts transcription regulation and chromatin remodeling, ultimately leading to carcinogenesis. [PMC12142290, PMC12293661]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of synovial sarcoma is often challenging due to its indolent growth, atypical presentations, and non-specific clinical and radiological signs, frequently leading to misdiagnosis as common joint disorders, tuberculosis, hematoma, or benign lesions. Imaging studies like CT, MRI, and flexible nasofibrolaryngoscopy are used to define tumor location and extent, but their findings are often non-specific and can be misleading. Accurate diagnosis primarily relies on pathological and histopathological examination, often requiring biopsy. Immunohistochemistry analysis plays a crucial role in confirming the diagnosis and identifying histological subtypes. While molecular testing, such as fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for the SS18-SSX fusion oncogene, can confirm the diagnosis, it is not always necessary when clinical, histological, and immunohistochemical findings are conclusive. A high index of suspicion and thorough pathological assessment are essential for timely and accurate diagnosis. [PMC12211441, PMC11729148, PMC12313373, PMC11743864, PMC12088537]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Somatostatinoma (SSoma) is an extremely rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor or duodenal endocrine tumor that originates either in the pancreas (50%) or the gastrointestinal tract (50%) and mainly presents with non-specific symptoms of abdominal pain, weight loss, jaundice and diarrhea but, in approximately 20% of pancreatic cases, leads to a somatostatin hypersecretion syndrome (somatostatinoma syndrome) characterized by diabetes mellitus, cholelithiasis, steatorrhea and hypochlorhydria.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated incidence is of 1/40,000,000. Approximately 80 cases of pancreatic SSoma have been reported to date but this is probably an underestimate.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: SSomas usually range in size from 3-11cm. Most SSomas present with non-specific symptoms of abdominal pain, weight loss, painless obstructive jaundice and diarrhea. Somatostatinoma syndrome occurs in those with a functioning pancreatic SSoma with manifestations including diabetes mellitus, cholelithiasis, diarrhea, weight loss, steatorrhea and hypochlorhydria. More than half of all SSomas are malignant and they have often metastasized at the time of diagnosis. Duodenal somatostatinoma is often associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Some SSomas are components of familial endocrine tumor syndromes. The cause of sporadic SSomas is not clear. SSoma hypersecretes stomatostatin, which inhibits the secretion of numerous gastrointestinal hormones (such as gastrin, secretin, insulin, glucagon, and cholecystokinin), resulting in somatostatinoma syndrome
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Somatostatinomas are generally associated with a poor prognosis, often presenting as malignant, large lesions frequently accompanied by metastases. For pancreatic somatostatinomas, the overall survival was reported as 47.74 months, with metastatic disease being associated with worse survival. Despite this, aggressive surgical approaches, including resection of the primary tumor and hepatic metastases, have been shown to result in long-term survival, even in patients with metastatic disease. While metastasectomy for pancreatic somatostatinomas did not demonstrate a survival benefit in a small study, aggressive surgery is generally preferred to improve survival. [PMC10611615, PMC7811659, PMC6340528, PMC3365451, PMC2801086]
