DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A disorder of glyoxylate metabolism characterized by an excess of oxalate resulting in kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis and ultimately renal failure and systemic oxalosis. There are 3 types of PH, types 1-3, all caused by liver-specific enzyme defects.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Primary Hyperoxalurias (PH) prevalence ranges from 1-3/1 000 000 and the estimated incidence is between 1-2/10 000 000 per year with no differences between sexes. There are higher rates reported in isolated populations, especially in the Middle East and North Africa. A significant proportion of patients are diagnosed at adulthood which implies an important underdetection of patients. PH1 accounts for 85% of patients, PH2 8-10% and PH3 5-7%.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Hyperoxaluria may lead to kidney stones, nephrocalcinosis and ultimately renal failure and systemic oxalosis. Symptoms can appear at any age and may vary from infantile failure to thrive and cortical nephrocalcinosis with renal failure to hematuria, medullary nephrocalcinosis or sporadic stone disease, even within one family. PH1 is the most severe form; overall, more than 70% of PH1 patients develop end-stage kidney disease over time; this may even occur in patients with sporadic stone disease. Storage of oxalate occurs in severe renal failure and may affect bone, eyes, heart, arteries and peripheral nerves (systemic oxalosis). PH2 has a more benign course; no infantile oxalosis has been described and end-stage kidney disease occurs at relatively late age in about 20% of patients. PH3 is most benign with so far only a few reports of renal impairment and no end-stage kidney disease.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: PH type 1 is caused by mutations of the AGXT gene causing dysfunction of the liver-specific peroxisomal enzyme alanine glyoxylate aminotransferase (AGT). Over 50 different mutations have been found, leading to either absence or dysfunction of AGT. Two common Western mutations (G170A, Phe152Ile) lead to a mitochondrial mistargeting of AGT. Type 2 is caused by mutations of GHRPR gene causing dysfunction of the cytosolic enzyme glyoxylate/hydroxypyruvate reductase, type 3 by mutations in HOGA1 causing dysfunction of the mitochondrial enzyme 4-hydroxy-2- oxoglutarate aldolase.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis methods consist of an analysis of urine collection for 24h (at least 2 consecutive assessments) on oxalate, creatinine, glycolate (PH1), citrate (decreased in PH1), L-glycerate (PH2) and HOGA (PH3). Mutation analysis on AGTX gene can be done in case of hyperoxaluria. If negative or in case of high l-glycerate or HOGA mutation analysis on GRHPR or HOGA1 genes are realized. Assessment for systemic oxalosis in case of high plasma-oxalate and /or eGFR<40: fundoscopy, US heart, bone assessment.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes hypercalciuria, hypocitraturia, cystinuria.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: If eGFR>30 ml/min/1.73m2: the patient needs first high fluid intake (>3 liter/day/m2 body surface). Then pyridoxine challenge in PH1 starting dose 5 mg/kg/day, increase to max 20; reduction urine oxalate >30% = positive response (about 30% of patients in Europe). In third potassium-citrate 0,5 mmol/kg/day. If eGFR<30 ml/min/1.73m2 it is consider to direct combined liver-kidney transplantation, sequential liver-kidney transplantation in case of severe systemic oxalosis or kidney transplantation in B6 responsive PH1 patients. Dietary oxalate restriction is probably of limited use.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Severe infantile oxalosis has a poor prognosis quoad vitam. The prognosis for other PH1 B6 unresponsive patients is poor with respect to renal function (> 80% renal failure over time), better for B6 responsive patients, if timely diagnosed and treated. End-stage kidney disease has been found in 20% of PH2 patients, so far not in PH3.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Sneddon's syndrome (SS) is a rare non-inflammatory thrombotic vasculopathy characterized by the combination of cerebrovascular disease with livedo racemosa.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Ehrmann-Sneddon syndrome; Livedo racemosa-cerebrovascular accident syndrome; Livedo reticularis-cerebrovascular accident syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: SS has an estimated annual incidence of approximately 1/250,000. The disease predominantly affects women in young adulthood.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The mean age of onset of neurological symptoms is 39 years, though the livedo is generally observed up to 10 years earlier and sometimes since childhood. Livedo racemosa is a persistent net-like violaceous-cyanotic, mottled discoloration of the skin affecting primarily the legs and arms, but also involving the buttocks and the trunk, and that is exacerbated by cold or pregnancy. Livedo reticularis, that is limited to the extremities and is visible only in the cold, has also been observed in some cases. Neurological manifestations include recurrent transient ischemic attacks (TIAs) and infarcts, often of the middle cerebral artery territory resulting in contralateral hemiparesis, aphasia, and/or visual field defects. Rarely, spinal strokes or intracranial or subarachnoid hemorrhages occur. Headache and vertigo may precede the onset of livedo racemosa and cerebrovascular manifestations by several years. In the course of the disease, memory disturbances, personality changes, and cognitive decline leading to dementia occur frequently. Rare neurologic symptoms include seizures, chorea, or myelopathies. Secondary hypertension is common, as are valvular heart disease, ocular and kidney involvement.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: While about 50% of cases are idiopathic, SS can be associated with autoimmune diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus, antiphospholipid syndrome, Behçet disease, and mixed connective tissue disease. The manifestations of SS are caused by a progressive, non-inflammatory arteriopathy, usually of the small to medium arteries, leading to occlusion of these arteries by excessive endothelial proliferation with impaired blood flow and clotting. Genetic factors may play a role in the pathogenesis of SS. Loss-of-function mutations in cat eye syndrome chromosome region candidate 1 CECR1 (22q11.2) encoding adenosine deaminase 2 have been found.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: SS is suspected on the basis of the clinical picture. It has to be considered in cases of unexplained stroke at a young age, cognitive decline without stroke, and assumed autoimmune-related vasculitis in which immunosuppressive therapy has proven ineffective. Skin biopsy may confirm the diagnosis, revealing occlusion of arterioles by intimal proliferation. MRI typically reveals white matter changes, infarcts, microbleeds or atrophy, and is more sensitive than CT. Laboratory testing for antiphospholipid antibodies may be positive in about 60% of cases.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, MELAS syndrome, cerebrovascular dementia, migraine, the autoimmune diseases with which SS can be associated, and cerebral angiitis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Most cases are sporadic but some familial cases with an autosomal dominant inheritance have been reported. In these cases, a genetic susceptibility is likely.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The most widely accepted treatment is anticoagulation with warfarin. Some suggest that aPL-negative patients should follow a less aggressive approach consisting of antiplatelet therapy with aspirin, while others recommend warfarin with a higher international normalized ratio (coagulation index) target. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors have been suggested to reduce endothelial proliferation, and prostaglandin to improve microvascular perfusion. Successful intravenous systemic fibrinolysis with tissue plasminogen activator (tpA) has been reported in acute ischemic stroke. While the use of immunosuppressive therapy (azathioprine, cyclophosphamide) doesn't seem effective, there are data indicating that rituximab may be effective in aPL-positive patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: SS is a chronic, intermittent or progressive disease leading to major morbidity. Dementia occurs in 50% of patients resulting in early retirement.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A benign, inherited liver disorder characterized by chronic, predominantly conjugated, nonhemolytic hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver histology.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Rotor syndrome (RT) is a very rare disorder: the exact prevalence is unknown but over 50 cases have been reported in literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: It is usually diagnosed in children or adolescents, but mild jaundice is often noted from birth. The main symptom consists of mild-to-moderate, recurrent jaundice without pruritus. Attacks of abdominal pain and low-grade fever can occur but are rare. Total serum bilirubin (mainly in the conjugated form: 50-80%) is elevated, usually between 2 and 5 mg/dl. Hematologic tests (including measurements of liver enzyme activities) and liver histology are normal. However, absolute and relative concentrations of urinary coproporphyrin I are elevated. Hemolysis is not a feature of the syndrome; however, coinheritance of hemolytic disorders, such as G-6-PD deficiency and beta thalassemia, has been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Analysis of the retention of the cholephilic dyes indicates that RT results from a defect in hepatic storage capacity of conjugated bilirubin and other organic cholephilic anions.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: As the genetic basis remains unknown and the clinical, biochemical and histological features are non-specific, RT syndrome remains a diagnosis of exclusion. RT should be considered in all patients exhibiting predominantly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with no concomitant change in liver enzyme activities (i.e. aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase) and in the absence of any septic condition, ultrasound anomaly of the liver or interfering drug. In this context, elevated (250 to 500% higher than controls) urinary concentrations of both total coproporphyrins and coproporphyrin I are very suggestive, but not completely specific for RT. Taken together with these findings, normal liver histology generally allows the diagnosis to be confirmed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The principle differential diagnosis is Dubin-Johnson syndrome (DJS). DJS and RT can be distinguished on the basis of measurements of urinary coproporphyrin excretion (total coproporphyrin excretion levels are normal in DJS) and liver histology (black-brown liver cell pigmentation is specific to DJS). If liver biopsy is not feasible or is refused, 99mTc-HIDA cholescintigraphy (revealing prominent kidney excretion in RT) or molecular analysis (detection of ABCC2 gene mutations in DJS patients) can be useful for distinguishing between RT and DJS.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: RT appears to be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, with the parents and siblings of affected individuals showing a pattern of urinary coproporphyrin excretion that is intermediate between that of RT patients and controls.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: As RT is a benign condition, no specific treatment is recommended or generally required. Affected individuals are advised to avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis for RT patients is good, highlighting the need for correct diagnosis to avoid unnecessary diagnostic procedures, treatment and follow-up. Unless there is a concomitant chronic liver disease, progression to liver failure, cirrhosis or hepatic fibrosis is not observed.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: X-linked intellectual disability-cubitus valgus-dysmorphism syndrome is characterised by moderate intellectual deficit, marked cubitus valgus, mild microcephaly, a short philtrum, deep-set eyes, downslanting palpebral fissures and multiple nevi. Less than ten individuals have been described so far. Transmission is thought to be X-linked recessive.

Curry-Jones syndrome is a form of syndromic craniosynostosis characterized by unilateral coronal craniosynostosis or multiple suture synostosis associated with complete or partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, preaxial polysyndactyly and syndactyly of hands and/or feet, along with anomalies of the skin (characteristic pearly white areas that become scarred and atrophic, abnormal hair growth around the eyes and/or cheeks, and on the limbs), eyes (iris colobomas, microphthalmia,) and intestine (congenital short gut, malrotation, dysmotility, chronic constipation, bleeding and myofibromas). Developmental delay and variable degrees of intellectual disability may also be observed. Multiple intra-abdominal smooth muscle hamartomas, trichoblastoma of the skin, occipital meningoceles and development of desmoplastic medulloblastoma have been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Happle-Tinschert syndrome (HTS) and Curry-Jones syndrome (CJS; OMIM 601707) are rare, sporadic, multisystem disorders characterized by hypo- and hyperpigmented skin patches following Blaschko's lines, plus acral skeletal and other abnormalities. The blaschkoid pattern implies mosaicism, and indeed CJS was found in 2016 to be caused by a recurrent postzygotic mutation in a gene of the hedgehog signalling pathway, namely SMO, c.1234C>T, p.Leu412Phe. More recently the original case of HTS was found to carry the same somatic mutation. Despite this genetic and phenotypic overlap, two significant differences remained between the two syndromes. The histological hallmark of HTS, basaloid follicular hamartomas, is not a feature of CJS. Meanwhile, the severe gastrointestinal manifestations regularly reported in CJS had not been described in HTS. a patient whose phenotype was entirely consistent... [PMC6972552]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Curry-Jones syndrome (CJS) is a rare, sporadic, multisystem disorder characterized by a pattern of malformation. Key features include hypo- and hyperpigmented skin patches following Blaschko's lines, acral skeletal abnormalities, craniosynostosis, pre-axial polysyndactyly, and agenesis of the corpus callosum. Severe gastrointestinal manifestations are regularly reported, including structural malformations (such as intestinal malrotation or duplication), motility disorders, upper GI bleeding, and abdominal obstruction, often due to smooth muscle hamartomas in the bowel. CJS can also overlap phenotypically with basal cell naevus syndrome, potentially including early-onset medulloblastoma. [PMC6972552, PMC5933242]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Curry-Jones syndrome (CJS) is caused by a recurrent postzygotic, or somatic, mutation in the SMO gene, specifically c.1234C>T, p.Leu412Phe. This gene is a component of the hedgehog signaling pathway. The blaschkoid pattern of skin lesions implies mosaicism, and molecular analysis has demonstrated the SMO mutation in varying amounts in affected tissues, such as skin and intestinal hamartomas. This somatic mutation in SMO likely accounts for the characteristic structural malformations and the predisposition to form bowel hamartomas and myofibromas. [PMC6972552, PMC5933242]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Curry-Jones syndrome is clinically diagnosed based on a pattern of malformation that includes craniosynostosis, pre-axial polysyndactyly, and characteristic cutaneous findings such as hypo- and hyperpigmented skin patches following Blaschko's lines. The blaschkoid pattern implies mosaicism. Genetic diagnosis confirms the condition by identifying a recurrent, mosaic postzygotic mutation in the SMO gene, specifically c.1234C>T, p.Leu412Phe. Molecular analysis can detect this somatic mutation in varying amounts in affected tissues like skin or intestinal hamartoma. [PMC6972552, PMC5933242]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Curry-Jones syndrome (CJS) shows significant phenotypic and genetic overlap with Happle-Tinschert syndrome (HTS) and segmental basal cell naevus syndrome (BCNS), all categorized within the 'mosaic hedgehog spectrum'. These rare, sporadic, multisystem disorders share features such as blaschkoid hypo- and hyperpigmented skin patches and acral skeletal abnormalities. CJS and HTS are both caused by recurrent somatic mutations in SMO. Key distinctions include severe gastrointestinal manifestations, like intractable constipation, in CJS, which are not typically seen in HTS. Conversely, HTS is characterized by basaloid follicular hamartomas, a feature absent in CJS. Segmental BCNS, caused by somatic mutations in hedgehog signalling genes like PTCH1, also shares overlapping features with CJS and HTS. [PMC6972552]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Curry-Jones syndrome is caused by a recurrent, postzygotic, somatic mutation in the SMO gene, specifically c.1234C>T, p.Leu412Phe. This genetic basis in a mosaic pattern, with the mutation detected in varying amounts in affected tissues such as skin and intestinal hamartomas. The condition is described as a rare, sporadic disorder, indicating that it arises de novo rather than being inherited. Therefore, genetic counseling would emphasize the sporadic nature and the mosaic distribution of the SMO mutation. [PMC6972552, PMC5933242]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Gastrointestinal complications, including structural malformations, motility disorders, and upper GI bleeding, are major causes of morbidity in Curry-Jones syndrome. Abdominal obstruction, often due to intestinal malrotation or smooth muscle hamartomas, typically requires surgical intervention. For instance, an infant with intestinal malrotation underwent a Ladd procedure. Surgical management is a recognized approach for these specific gastrointestinal features. [PMC5933242]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Curry-Jones syndrome is associated with significant morbidity, primarily due to severe gastrointestinal manifestations. These regularly reported complications include structural malformations, motility disorders, intractable constipation, and upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Abdominal obstruction, often requiring surgical intervention for issues like intestinal malrotation, is common, frequently linked to smooth muscle hamartomas. Additionally, early-onset medulloblastoma has been observed in a patient with classic features of the syndrome. [PMC6972552, PMC5933242]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic multisystemic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by a distinct facial appearance, cardiac anomalies (most frequently supravalvular aortic stenosis), cognitive and developmental abnormalities, and connective tissue abnormalities (e.g., joint laxity). Facial dysmorphism is characterized by a broad forehead, bitemporal narrowing, periorbital fullness, stellate and/or lacy iris pattern, short upturned nose with bulbous tip, long philtrum, wide mouth, full lips and mild micrognathia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is approximately 1/7,500. There is no difference between the sexes.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: All individuals have facial dysmorphism; in addition to the characteristic features, young children have epicanthal folds, full cheeks, a flat profile and small, widely spaced teeth. Older children and adults often have a narrow face and long neck. The majority of patients (80%) suffer from cardiovascular disease, primarily stenosis of the medium and large arteries (supravalvular aortic stenosis (70%), hypertension (50%), and degeneration of aortic and/or mitral-valve leaflets). Developmental milestones are delayed. A relative strength in language and verbal short-term memory, and a significant weakness in visuospatial construction is characteristic. Intellectual disability is common (75%), and a characteristic cognitive profile with an overly friendly and social personality with enjoyment of music but hypersensitivity to sound is characteristic (90%). Emotional dysregulation is common and many patients (50%) require pharmacologic treatment for anxiety and/or attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. Endocrine abnormalities include hypercalcemia (15-45%), impaired glucose tolerance/type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM), obesity in adolescents/adults, subclinical hypothyroidism (15-30%), and osteopenia or osteoporosis (50%). Other problems include axial hypotonia, peripheral hypertonia with increased deep tendon reflexes in the lower extremities, ataxia and tremor. Growth in children is approximately 75% of normal growth rate. Young children have joint laxity; joint contractures occur in older children/adults leading to an awkward gait. Lordosis, kyphosis and scoliosis are common. Other common problems include ocular, auditory and dental anomalies, sleep disorders, feeding difficulties, gastrointestinal problems, bladder diverticula, urinary tract malformation, urinary infection and enuresis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Williams syndrome (WS) is caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 7q11.23, a region containing 26 to 28 genes including ELN.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on phenotype and genetic testing (fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) or chromosome microarray).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The primary differential diagnosis is familial supravalvular aortic stenosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counselling should be provided to affected families. Most cases arise de novo, and thus the recurrence risk is low (<1%). Affected individuals have a 50% risk of transmitting the deletion to offspring. A specific inversion polymorphism in the area may increase the risk of having a child with WS.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: A lifelong multidisciplinary approach involving medical monitoring, anticipatory guidance, direct therapies, pharmacotherapy, surgery, and adaptive changes is necessary. Close cardiac follow-up during the first year of life, and close monitoring of serum calcium during the first 2 years of life is recommended, as well as careful pre- and postoperative planning due to increased risk of cardiovascular complications during surgery. Children should be referred to an early intervention program for physical, occupational and speech therapy. Information, education and support groups are recommended for affected patients, families and caregivers.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: A formal assessment of life expectancy is lacking. Cardiovascular complications are the major cause of death. Cardiovascular stenoses may progress, especially during the first 5 years of life. Peripheral pulmonary stenoses often resolves spontaneously. Most individuals will require lifelong supervision at both their home and their workplace.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hepatic disease characterized by acute onset of severe liver dysfunction without evidence of underlying chronic liver disease. Patients present with nonspecific symptoms like jaundice, upper right abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, pruritus, fatigue, and fever. The condition may rapidly progress to hepatic encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and life-threatening multiorgan failure. Liver biopsy typically shows massive hepatic necrosis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Acute hepatic failure; Fulminant hepatic failure

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Coloboma of macula-brachydactyly type B syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital malformation syndrome characterized by the combination of bilateral coloboma of macula with horizontal pendular nystagmus and severe visual loss, and brachydactyly type B. The hand and feet defects comprise of shortening of the middle and terminal phalanges of the second to fifth digits, hypoplastic or absent nails (congenital anonychia), broad or bifid thumbs and halluces, syndactyly and flexion deformities of the joints of some digits.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Sorsby syndrome is a dominantly inherited combination of bilateral macular colobomas and apical dystrophy of the hands and feet (brachydactyly type B). on a further three affected members of the family originally described by Sorsby. Two of these have a single kidney, two have hearing loss, and one has a uterine anomaly. [PMC1050457]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Sorsby syndrome is a dominantly inherited condition characterized by bilateral macular colobomas and apical dystrophy of the hands and feet, specifically brachydactyly type B. Affected individuals may also present with additional anomalies, including a single kidney, hearing loss, and uterine anomalies, as observed in some family members. [PMC1050457]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Coloboma of macula-brachydactyly type B syndrome, also known as Sorsby syndrome, is a dominantly inherited condition. It is characterized by a combination of bilateral macular colobomas and apical dystrophy of the hands and feet, which is brachydactyly type B. Associated features can include a single kidney, hearing loss, and uterine anomalies. [PMC1050457]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Coloboma of macula-brachydactyly type B syndrome, also known as Sorsby syndrome, is based on the recognition of its characteristic clinical features. It is identified by a dominantly inherited combination of bilateral macular colobomas and apical dystrophy of the hands and feet, specifically brachydactyly type B. Associated findings that may also be present include a single kidney, hearing loss, and uterine anomalies. [PMC1050457]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Sorsby syndrome is a dominantly inherited combination of bilateral macular colobomas and apical dystrophy of the hands and feet (brachydactyly type B). on a further three affected members of the family originally described by Sorsby. Two of these have a single kidney, two have hearing loss, and one has a uterine anomaly. [PMC1050457]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Coloboma of macula-brachydactyly type B syndrome, also known as Sorsby syndrome, is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Affected individuals typically present with bilateral macular colobomas and apical dystrophy of the hands and feet (brachydactyly type B). Variable features have been observed within affected families, including single kidney, hearing loss, and uterine anomalies. [PMC1050457]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Sorsby syndrome is a dominantly inherited combination of bilateral macular colobomas and apical dystrophy of the hands and feet (brachydactyly type B). on a further three affected members of the family originally described by Sorsby. Two of these have a single kidney, two have hearing loss, and one has a uterine anomaly. [PMC1050457]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Gaucher disease type 2 is the acute neurological form of Gaucher disease (GD). It is characterized by early-onset and severe neurological involvement of the brainstem, associated with an organomegaly and generally leading to death before the age of 2.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Acute neuronopathic Gaucher disease; Infantile cerebral Gaucher disease

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The annual incidence of GD in the general population is around 1/60,000 and the prevalence is approximately 1/100,000. GD type 2 is very rare, with an incidence of approximately 5% of all GD patients and has a prevalence of virtually zero, taking into account its severity and early death.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease usually presents in infants aged 3 to 6 months with systemic manifestations of hepatosplenomegaly and an early onset and severe neurological syndrome. The first signs are oculomotor paralysis or bilateral fixed strabismus associated with bulbar signs, in particular severe swallowing difficulties, progressive spasticity and dystonic movements. Seizures occur later and manifest as myoclonic epilepsy that is refractory to treatment with antiepileptics.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: GD type 2 is a lysosomal storage disease caused by a mutation in the GBA gene (1q21) that codes for the lysosomal enzyme, glucocerebrosidase. The deficiency in glucocerebrosidase leads to the accumulation of glucosylceramidase (or beta-glucocerebrosidase) deposits in the cells of the reticuloendothelial system of the liver, of the spleen and the bone marrow (Gaucher cells).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: A definite diagnosis requires the demonstration of a deficit in the enzymatic activity of glucocerebrosidase.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Biochemical prenatal diagnosis can be proposed to couples who have already had a child with GD type 2. It can be carried out by measuring the enzyme activity in chorionic villus samples at 10-12 weeks of pregnancy or in amniocytes in culture towards 16 weeks of pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The treatment does not seem to have an effect on neurological manifestations and is therefore not indicated for patients with GD type 2.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor with most patients dying before the age of 2.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal trisomy 2p is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from the partial duplication of the short arm of chromosome 2, with a highly variable phenotype principally characterized by pre- and post-natal growth failure, global developmental delay, facial dysmorphism (incl. high forehead/frontal bossing, abnormal ear shape and/or position, hypertelorism/telecanthus, broad/depressed nasal bridge) and ocular anomalies (e.g. exophthalmos, retinal hypopigmentation, optic nerve and foveal hypoplasia). Other reported anomalies include generalized hypotonia, pectus excavatum, long fingers and toes, syndactyly, congenital heart (e.g. ventricular and atrial septal defects) and neural tube defects, seizures, pulmonary hypoplasia, diaphragmatic hernia and urogenital anomalies.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Distal duplication 2p syndrome is associated with a range of clinical features. These include arachnodactyly and agenesis of the lung, with one case specifically reporting agenesis of the left lung. A significant finding is the association with neuroblastoma; germline duplication of chromosome 2p, potentially involving the N-myc proto-oncogene, may predispose individuals to its development. [PMC1734504, PMC1051129, PMC1885927]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal duplication 2p syndrome is characterized by a duplication of the distal part of the short arm of chromosome 2. One reported case involved a germline duplication of chromosome 2p (p23-pter) on chromosome 13 (q34), including the N-myc proto-oncogene, which may predispose to neuroblastoma. Another patient presented with a duplication of the distal part of the upper arm of chromosome 2 (46,XX,2p+) associated with agenesis of the left lung. These findings indicate a genetic etiology, with specific chromosomal duplications leading to varied clinical features. [PMC1051129, PMC1885927]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of distal duplication 2p syndrome involves cytogenetic analysis, as evidenced by a reported case with a karyotype of 46,XY,der(13)t(2;13)(p23;q34). Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) studies are used to confirm the duplication, specifically showing chromosome 2p (p23-pter) duplicated on chromosome 13 (q34). [PMC1051129]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for distal duplication 2p syndrome should address the increased risk of neuroblastoma, as germline duplication of chromosome 2p, potentially involving the N-myc proto-oncogene, has been associated with its development. Additionally, agenesis of the lung has been observed in patients with distal 2p duplication, and familial cases of lung agenesis suggest a need for further understanding of its genetic aspects. [PMC11611621, PMC1051129, PMC1885927]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Wilms tumors are commonly associated with predisposition syndromes, many but not all of which include overgrowth. Several of these syndromes also include a risk of other embryonal malignancies-particularly hepatoblastoma. Guidelines for surveillance in this population were published in 2017, and recently, members of the American Association for Cancer Research Pediatric Cancer Working Group met to update those guidelines with a review of more recently published evidence and risk estimates. This perspective serves to update pediatric oncologists, geneticists, radiologists, counselors, and other health care professionals on revised diagnostic criteria; review previously published surveillance guidelines; and harmonize updated surveillance recommendations in the North American and Australian contexts for patients with overgrowth syndromes and other syndromes associated with Wilms tumor... [PMC11611621]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for individuals with distal duplication 2p syndrome can be severe, as evidenced by reported cases. One child with germline duplication of chromosome 2p developed a fatal neuroblastoma, with two other cases of neuroblastoma also described, suggesting a predisposition to this life-threatening condition, possibly linked to the N-myc proto-oncogene. Another patient presented with agenesis of the lung, indicating other significant developmental anomalies. These findings highlight serious health complications and potentially fatal outcomes associated with the syndrome. [PMC1051129, PMC1885927]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: T-cell large granular lymphocyte leukemia (T-cell LGL leukemia) is a lymphoproliferative malignancy that arises from the mature T-cell (CD3+) lineage.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Proliferation of large granular lymphocytes; T-LGL; T-cell LGL leukemia

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: T-cell large granular lymphocyte leukemia (T-LGLL) is a rare, chronic lymphoproliferative disorder characterized by persistent clonal expansion of mature T-cells, often with an indolent course. The median age of diagnosis is 59 years, and most patients (76.7%) report disease-related symptoms. Common clinical features include neutropenia, anemia, and thrombocytopenia, with disease-related deaths mainly due to recurrent infections linked to severe neutropenia. T-LGLL is frequently associated with various autoimmune conditions, particularly rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren syndrome, immune thrombocytopenia, and autoimmune neutropenia. Renal involvement, such as crescentic glomerulonephritis or endocapillary glomerulopathy, and cutaneous manifestations like livedoid eruption or infiltration, are rare. While generally having a favorable prognosis (5-year OS 82.2%, 10-year OS 63.8%), a small proportion of patients face shorter survival, especially with an ECOG performance status over two or a platelet count below 100 x 10^9/L. Progression to aggressive T-cell lymphoma is also possible. [PMC12237350, PMC11694120, PMC12025433, PMC11532115, PMC11011145]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: T-cell large granular lymphocyte leukemia (T-LGLL) generally has a favorable prognosis and an indolent course. The median overall survival is often not reached, with 5-year and 10-year overall survival rates reported at 82.2% and 63.8%, respectively. However, a small proportion of patients face a relatively short survival time, with disease-related deaths mainly due to recurrent infections linked to severe neutropenia. Factors associated with worse overall survival include an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status over two and a platelet count below 100 × 10^9/L. While immunosuppressive therapy may allow for long-term survival, it often does not eradicate the leukemic clone, and conventional treatment can be unsatisfactory for high-risk patients. Transformation into aggressive T-cell lymphoma has also been reported. [PMC12237350, PMC11694120, PMC11011145, PMC10561584, PMC9657804]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A genetic condition characterized by optic nerve dysplasia and renal hypodysplasia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Coloboma of optic nerve with renal disease; Papillo-renal syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence and prevalence at birth are not known. 177 mutation-positive cases (90 different families) have been reported. The number of mutation-negative individuals with clinical findings of Renal coloboma syndrome (RCS) is not known. There is no ethnic predilection.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: RCS is characterized primarily by ocular signs (77%) and renal manifestations (92%). Eye anomalies consist of a wide and sometimes excavated dysplastic optic disc with emergence of the retinal vessels from the disc periphery, frequently called optic nerve coloboma or ''morning glory'' anomaly. Associated findings may include a small corneal diameter, retinal coloboma, scleral staphyloma, reduced corneal diameter, optic nerve cyst, microphthalmia, foveal hypoplasia and pigmentary macular dysplasia. Nystagmus and myopia have also been reported. Consequences include decreased visual acuity, blindness, and retinal detachment. Renal malformations and/or insufficiency are frequently the presenting feature and consist of small and abnormally formed kidneys known as renal hypodysplasia. Histologically, kidneys exhibit fewer than normal enlarged glomeruli (oligomeganephronia). Other renal findings include multicystic dysplastic kidney and horseshoe kidney. Consequences include hypertension, proteinuria, vesicoureteral reflux, and renal insufficiency that frequently progresses to end-stage renal disease (ESRD). ESRD may present prenatally with severely hypoplastic or dysplastic kidneys and oligohydramnios resulting in fetal loss due to Potter sequence. Patients can progress to stage 5 chronic kidney disease at any age. High frequency (HF) hearing loss is reported in 7% of patients.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Mutations in thePAX2gene (10q24) have been identified in about 1/2 of patients with renal hypodysplasia and abnormalities of the optic nerve. PAX2 mutations have been identified in about 9% of unselected individuals presenting with renal hypoplasia. The genetic basis of the remaining cases is not known.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Formal diagnostic criteria have not been established. However, the disorder should be suspected in patients who have the classical findings of optic nerve dysplasia or coloboma and renal hypodysplasia. Oligomeganephronia is a common histologic finding in renal hypodysplasia but it is not pathognomonic for RCS.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes conditions where colobomas and renal anomalies have been identified such as CHARGE syndrome and Joubert syndrome with oculorenal defect. However these disorders generally have other characteristic findings not found in RCS.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis or pre-implantation genetic testing is possible if a clearly pathogenic PAX2 mutation has been identified in a family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: RCS is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern, though this is complicated by de novo cases, variable expression, incomplete clinical penetrance, and maternal and paternal gonosomal mosaicism.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management involves care for the renal and ophthalmologic manifestations. Patient evaluation should include renal function testing, renal ultrasound, urinalysis (proteinuria), blood pressure measurements and evaluation for vesicouretal reflux if clinically indicated. Long-term follow-up by a nephrologist and ophthalmologist are recommended. Low vision experts may also be called upon if needed. Audiologic evaluation for HF hearing loss is indicated as it may affect verbal communication.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends primarily on appropriate specialized treatment. Renal failure can occur at any age requiring dialysis and renal transplantation. Formal longitudinal studies of visual prognosis have not been carried out. However, decreased visual acuity over time has been reported.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Leprechaunism is a congenital form of extreme insulin resistance (a group of syndromes that also includes Rabson-Mensenhall syndrome, type A insulin-resistance syndrome, and acquired type B insulin-resistance syndrome) characterized by intrauterine and mainly postnatal severe growth retardation.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It is a very rare condition with less than 1 case in every million births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Leprechaunism is associated with a characteristic dysmorphic facies (resembling that of the 'leprechauns' in Irish folk traditions), atrophic subcutaneous adipose tissue (lipoatrophy) and muscular hypotrophy. Signs of virilization are often observed in young girls. Biologically, episodes of hypo- and hyperglycemia are observed along with marked hyperinsulinemia due to an extreme resistance to insulin.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is associated with homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the insulin receptor gene (INSR; 19p13.3-p13.2).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: A positive diagnosis requires identification of one mutation in each allele of this gene.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include the other forms of extreme insulin resistance.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment with recombinant insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1) may be considered. A combination treatment with insulin-like growth factor binding protein 3 (IGF-BP3) resulted in an increased lifespan in one case.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is uncertain, growth is severely affected and life expectancy rarely exceeds a few months.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Genetic diagnosis of Donohue syndrome can be performed through sequencing of the INSR gene. This technique permits antenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling for subsequent pregnancies, particularly in families with a known risk or history of the condition. [PMC4753905]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A frequent form of acrocephalosyndactyly, a group of inherited congenital malformation disorders, characterized by craniosynostosis, midface hypoplasia, and finger and toe anomalies and/or syndactyly.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated incidence of Apert syndrome is reported to be 1/100,000 to 1/160,000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients generally have extensive structural and functional impairments related to cranial and limb deformities. Craniosynostosis can lead to acrobrachycephaly or turribrachycephaly with delayed closure of fontanels and a possible impact on brain growth and neurological development. Macrocephaly is also found. Limb malformations mainly consist of soft tissue and bony syndactyly of fingers and toes (involving variable numbers of digits), occasional rhizomelic shortening, and elbow ankylosis, with functional impairments and restriction of mobility. Facial findings include midface hypoplasia that is generally moderate to severe with hypoplasia of the maxilla, shallow orbits, strabismus, hypertelorism, down-slanting palpebral fissures, and proptosis, as well as depressed nasal bridge and deviated nasal septum. Dental findings include delayed eruption, impaction, crowding, thick gingival swelling, and missing teeth, along with a high risk of caries. Unilateral and bilateral posterior crossbites are frequent. Common associated complications include chronic otitis media, hearing loss, and increased ocular pressure that can cause blindness. Moderate to severe intellectual disability and variable developmental delay are also common in AS (more than 50% of cases). Some patients are also reported to have agenesis of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, hydrocephalus, fused cervical vertebrae (usually C5-C6), and occasionally, cardiac and gastrointestinal defects, radiohumeral synostosis, or cleft velum.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: A mutation in the FGFR2 gene (10q25.3-10q26) involved in cell signaling during embryonic development is causative in Apert syndrome. Advanced paternal age has been associated with de novo mutations, which are found in most cases.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the clinical findings at birth. Some cases may be identified prenatally. The diagnosis can be confirmed by molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other syndromic craniosynostosis syndromes, such as Pfeiffer, Crouzon, Saethre-Chotzen, Muenke, and Jackson-Weiss syndromes.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal MRI or molecular genetic testing can be used to diagnose suspected cases.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Apert syndrome is autosomal dominant, with complete penetrance. In healthy parents of an affected child, the recurrence risk in their children is low, but in affected patients, the risk of transmitting the disease to their offspring is 50%. Genetic counseling should be provided to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: A multidisciplinary approach to care is necessary with life-long monitoring. Treatment primarily involves craniosynostosis release, followed by surgical advancement or distraction for midface hypoplasia, and reparative or cosmetic treatment of other malformations. Successful treatment can improve aesthetics and functional performance (breathing, mastication, oral and ocular health). In patients with mitten-glove syndactyly, surgical separation of the digits generally provides little functional improvement. The psychosocial aspects of the syndrome should also be taken into account.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is guarded. Many individuals have life-threatening complications, including airway and central nervous system compromise. Others can do relatively well with proper medical and surgical management, but intellectual limitations are still very common. Life expectancy varies among patients with AS due to variable clinical severity and treatment success.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder of pyrimidine metabolism characterized by a variable phenotype ranging from absence of symptoms to severe neurological involvement with developmental delay, intellectual disability, and seizures. Additional signs and symptoms may include hypotonia, microcephaly, ocular abnormalities (such as microphthalmia, nystagmus, and strabismus), and autistic behavior, among others. Analysis of urine typically shows high levels of uracil and thymine. Patients are at risk of suffering from severe toxicity after the administration of the anti-neoplastic agent 5-fluorouracil.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder, with a wide clinical spectrum ranging from asymptomatic to severely affected individuals. While complete enzyme deficiency is uncommon, partial deficiency is more frequently observed among DPD deficient patients. This condition is a significant risk factor for severe fluoropyrimidine-associated toxicity. DPYD gene variants causing DPD deficiency are found across diverse ethnic groups, including European, African American, East Asian, Latin American, Middle Eastern, and South Asian populations, though the prominence of specific variants may differ geographically. [PMC10962175, PMC11300675, PMC7816174, PMC3891063, PMC442471]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder with a wide clinical spectrum, ranging from asymptomatic individuals to severely affected patients. Clinical manifestations can include intellectual disability, motor retardation, developmental delay, and seizures. A critical aspect of DPD deficiency is the high risk of severe, and potentially fatal, toxicity upon exposure to fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutic agents like 5-fluorouracil, capecitabine, or doxifluridine. These severe adverse events can manifest as gastrointestinal disorders, including severe diarrhea, fever, hematochezia, mucosal shedding, bleeding throughout the gastrointestinal tract, and ileitis, leading to persistent nutritional management issues. Other toxicities include mucositis, febrile neutropenia, and severe neurotoxicity. Such severe reactions can occur even in individuals who are otherwise asymptomatic or have partial DPD deficiency. [PMC10962175, PMC9449621, PMC3992533, PMC2911560, PMC3891063]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by deleterious variants in the DPYD gene, which encodes the initial and rate-limiting DPD enzyme in pyrimidine catabolism. These causative genetic variants in DPYD can include polymorphisms, abnormalities, and large intragenic deletions, such as those eliminating exons 9 and 10. The deficiency can manifest as complete or partial enzyme activity loss. In some instances, a double DPYD and UTG1A1 gene mutation has been identified. [PMC10962175, PMC11300675, PMC7816174, PMC3992533, PMC2911560]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) deficiency include genetic testing and biochemical assays. Pre-treatment DPYD screening, mandated in some regions, involves genotyping for specific DPYD gene variants, such as four common European variants, though extending screening to include variants in non-European ancestries is suggested. Genetic investigations can involve clinical exome sequencing, MLPA, and Sanger sequencing to identify causative DPYD gene variants, including intragenic deletions. Biochemical testing includes DPD deficiency testing based on uracilemia, which requires careful interpretation in patients with renal impairment, potentially needing reassessment or post-dialysis sampling. DPD activity levels in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and DPD mRNA levels are also used to confirm deficiency, especially in patients experiencing severe fluoropyrimidine toxicity. [PMC10962175, PMC11300675, PMC10265596, PMC9449621, PMC7816174]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Renal impairment significantly impacts dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) phenotyping, potentially leading to misdiagnosis. Patients with renal impairment or those undergoing dialysis may exhibit elevated uracilemia, increasing the risk of being incorrectly classified as DPD deficient. This confounding effect is observed independently of hepatic function, with the rate of DPD deficiency classification decreasing dramatically after dialysis or restoration of renal function. Therefore, renal impairment should be considered in the differential interpretation of DPD deficiency testing, and uracilemia should be reassessed or measured after dialysis to avoid misleading . [PMC10265596]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase (DPD) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by deleterious variants in the DPYD gene. Affected individuals exhibit a wide clinical spectrum, ranging from asymptomatic to severe presentations including intellectual disability, motor retardation, developmental delay, and seizures. Critically, individuals with complete or partial DPD deficiency, including heterozygous carriers, face a high risk of severe and potentially fatal fluoropyrimidine-associated toxicity, even if clinically asymptomatic. Pre-treatment DPYD genetic screening is recommended by agencies like the European Medicines Agency to identify at-risk patients, allowing for reduced 5-FU dosing or alternative therapies. Current screening panels, often focused on common European variants, may miss other significant variants, such as large intragenic deletions or those prevalent in non-European ancestries, highlighting the need for expanded genetic testing to improve patient safety and reduce health inequalities. [PMC10962175, PMC11300675, PMC7816174, PMC3891063, PMC442471]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Dihydropyrimidine dehydrogenase deficiency presents with a wide clinical spectrum, ranging from asymptomatic individuals to those severely affected by intellectual disability, motor retardation, developmental delay, and seizures. A critical prognostic factor is exposure to fluoropyrimidine chemotherapy. Patients with complete or partial DPD deficiency, even if asymptomatic, face a high risk of severe and potentially fatal toxicity from agents like 5-fluorouracil or capecitabine. Such toxicities can include severe gastrointestinal disorders with persistent nutritional issues, severe mucositis, febrile neutropenia, and neurotoxicity, with total DPD deficiency leading to lethal outcomes. However, pre-treatment DPYD screening, reduced dosing, or alternative systemic therapies can significantly improve patient outcomes and prevent severe or fatal adverse events. [PMC10962175, PMC11300675, PMC9449621, PMC7816174, PMC3992533]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A chronic and rare endocrine disorder due to autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex and resulting in a glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency. Properly speaking, it designates autoimmune adrenalitis, but it is a term commonly used to describe any form of chronic primary adrenal insufficiency (CPAI).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Primary Addison disease; Autoimmune adrenalitis; Classic Addison disease; Autoimmune Addison disease; Primary adrenal insufficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of AD is 1/9,000-1/6,900 in the developed countries.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset peaks around 40 but it can occur at any age. It presents insidiously with nonspecific symptoms that can be mistaken for other more prevalent conditions. Common manifestations include fatigue, loss of energy, malaise, weight loss, nausea, anorexia (failure to thrive in children), muscle and joint pain. Pigmentation of skin and mucous membranes (darkening of the skin especially in the palmar creases, knuckles, scars, oral mucosa and sites of friction) is a cardinal sign of AD. Symptoms of postural hypotension and hypoglycemia are late manifestations. Patients may also crave salt. Vitiligo and alopecia areata are often present. AD also causes dehydroepiandrosterone deficiency causing additional symptoms seen only in women (loss of axillary/pubic hair, absence of pubarch in children, reduced libido and dry skin). Acute primary adrenal insufficiency (AAI), also called an adrenal crisis, can occur if treatment is not followed or during precipitating illnesses and is a life threatening medical emergency.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: AD results from autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex and can be isolated or seen as part of an autoimmune disorder (autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1, 2 or 4).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Biochemical tests are needed to diagnose AD. Early morning serum cortisol and plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) levels are measured. Plasma ACTH is much higher in individuals with AD (>22 pmol/L) and morning serum cortisol levels are usually low (<83nmol/L) but can fluctuate. A stimulation test observing the cortisol response to exogenous ACTH is a useful tool in confirming a diagnosis. In healthy subjects serum cortisol concentrations increase (>500 nmol/L) after exogenous ACTH administration but no increase is seen in AD patients. Raised plasma ACTH levels confirm AD diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Secondary adrenal insufficiency needs to be eliminated. Causes include pituitary tumors, lymphatic hypophystitis, pituitary tuberculosis and sarcoidosis, all of which are differential diagnoses. Infiltrative disorders and other causes of CPAI should be excluded and include tuberculosis, fungal infections and AIDS-associated opportunistic infections. Genetic disorders, tumors, and treatment with certain drugs are other less common causes of CPAI.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is life-long and requires a multidisciplinary team. Glucocorticoid replacement with oral hydrocortisone (10-25 mg daily taken in 2-3 doses) is given to mimic physiological cortisol secretion patterns. Oral fludrocortisone is given to replace mineralocorticoid hormones. Dehydroepiandrosterone replacement is optional. Glucocorticoid levels can be adjusted during times of stress to prevent AAI. The dose of hydrocortisone is maintained on the basis of clinical assessment and responses, taking into account a patient's well-being and presence of signs of over-replacement or under-replacement. An assessment of plasma renin activity is helpful in optimizing the dose of fludrocortisone. Growth and development in children must be monitored. Patients should carry a ready to inject hydrocortisone preparation and carry a medical alert card, in case of adrenal crisis.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: There is no cure for AD but with proper treatment and care taken to prevent AAI there is no decrease in life expectancy. AD is only life threatening when ignored.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Autoimmune Addison's Disease (AAD) is by far the most common cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in developed countries, occurring more commonly in women compared with men. The condition is associated with a spectrum of disorders affecting fertility and reproductive health. Premature ovarian insufficiency (POI) is a clinical condition defined by cessation of menstrual cycles and menopausal range gonadotrophins before the age of 40 years. This occurs with a prevalence of 1-2% in the general population, but has been estimated at 6-10% for women with AAD. One registry study demonstrated that one-third of those with AAD who develop POI, do so before the age of thirty. The onset of POI precedes or is contemporaneous with the diagnosis of AAD in the majority. It has also been demonstrated that women with AAD are more likely to use hormone replacement therapy. The pathophysiology of POI in... [PMC12216664, PMC11152880]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for Addison disease is complex due to its genetic heterogeneity and overlap with other conditions. Conditions like X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD), caused by ABCD1 gene variations, can initially present as Addison's disease, necessitating genetic testing, especially with neurological symptoms. Familial glucocorticoid deficiency, linked to MC2R and MRAP gene variants, also presents with adrenal insufficiency, with some variants showing founder effects in specific populations. Furthermore, Xp21 contiguous gene deletion syndrome, which can be maternally inherited, involves genes associated with adrenal hypoplasia. Therefore, comprehensive genetic investigations are crucial for accurate diagnosis, differentiating underlying genetic causes, and informing family risk. [PMC11218101, PMC11319056, PMC10115399]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare primary bone dysplasia characterized by multiple enchondromas (benign cartilage-forming tumors). The lesions are generally unilateral or asymmetrically distributed. The most common affected site is the appendicular skeleton.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Multiple Enchondromatosis type I; Enchondromatosis Spranger type I; Multiple Enchondromatosis, Ollier type

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of Ollier disease (OD) is estimated at 1/100,000, but mild presentations without skeletal deformities may be underdiagnosed. OD is approximately evenly represented in both sexes.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical expression of the disease is variable, it can involve a single bone segment or multiple limbs. The lesions develop during childhood and adolescence (median age of 13), but presentation in adulthood is also possible. It usually manifests with painless bony masses, which mostly occur in an asymmetric bilateral fashion, albeit symmetrical distribution has been described. The most frequently affected sites are the bones of the appendicular skeleton, in particular the hands (phalanges and metacarpals) and the metaphyses and diaphyses of the long tubular bones (i.e. femur, tibia, humerus). Rarely, spine, ribs, sternum, and skull can be involved. Pelvis involvement can lead to scoliosis. Patients present with multiple swelling, leading to apparent morphological abnormalities. Rarely, bone shortening can be the only presenting feature. Deformity around the joints, angular deformity, genu valgus, cubitus varus, joint mobility limitation, leg-length discrepancy, pathological fractures, facial asymmetry, and cranial nerve palsy can also be associated. OD is associated with an increased risk of malignancies compared to the general population such as chondrosarcoma (variably estimated but as high as 50% in some studies), central nervous system tumors, and occasionally gliomas, acute myeloid leukemia, and juvenile granulosa cell tumors.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is due to somatic variants in IDH1 (2q34), IDH2 (15q26.1) and, more rarely, PTH1R (3p21.31), coding for isocitrate dehydrogenase 1, 2 and parathyroid hormone 1 receptor, respectively. Mutations are limited to the involved tissues. No familial case has been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis relies on clinical features and imaging findings, in particular conventional radiological evaluation. Enchondromas appear as slow growing, radiolucent defects that originate in the metaphyses. Both CT and MRI are useful for monitoring the disease, with MRI allowing evaluation of intraosseous and soft tissue involvement.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnoses include multiple hereditary exostosis (also known as multiple osteochondromas), osteitis fibrosa cystica, chondroma and chondrosarcoma.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: No specific therapy exists for OD. The management is usually conservative, but surgical approach can be proposed and is at present the only option when complications (e.g. pathological fractures) occur. Because of the risk of malignant transformation, annual monitoring of patients is recommended. Scintigraphy, ultrasound or biopsy for histological examination can be indicated for surveillance of lesions that become symptomatic (pain, increase in size) or suspected of malignant transformation. No specific guideline is available for the surveillance of other cancers risk due to the small number of patients reported and the limited data about the real incidence of other neoplasms in OD.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is difficult to assess due to the wide clinical expression and variability of the disease. Depending on the extent of skeletal involvement, OD may result in severe deformities with functional and quality of life repercussions. Negative predictors are early onset, gross asymmetrical distribution, with severe shortening or deformity of the skeletal segment involved (e.g. limb asymmetry or phalangeal deformity) and malignant transformation (which is the most serious complication, potentially affecting the life span).

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic skin disease characterized by childhood onset of follicular keratotic papules slowly progressing to characteristic ''honeycomb'' atrophy on the cheeks, preauricular area, and forehead. Less frequently, the condition may affect also the upper lip, ears, or limbs. Additional features include facial erythema, milia, and follicular plugs.

Gorlin-Chaudhry-Moss (GCM) syndrome is a multiple congenital anomaly syndrome characterized by craniofacial dysostosis, facial dysmorphism, conductive hearing loss, generalized hypertrichosis, and extremity, ocular and dental anomalies.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Craniofacial dysostosis-genital, dental, cardiac anomalies syndrome; Cranofacial dysostosis-hypertrichosis-hypoplasia of labia majora syndrome; Dental and eye anomalies-patent ductus arteriosus-normal intelligence syndrome; GCM syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, 7 cases of GCM have been described in the world literature and all patients are female with no known parental consanguinity.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: GCM is a congenital disorder in which patients present with a stocky body build, normal intelligence, coronal craniosynostosis, facial dysmorphism (brachy/turricephaly, low anterior and posterior hairline, coarse hair, synophrys, depressed supraorbital ridges, short and downslanted or upslanted palpebral fissures, ectropion of lower eyelid, underdeveloped ala nasi, prominent columella, midface hypoplasia, and underdeveloped small ears with increased posterior angulation), conductive hearing loss, ocular (coloboma of the eyelid, hyperopia, microphthalmia) and oro-dental (microdontia, irregularly shaped widely spaced teeth, oligodontia, narrow, and high arched narrow palate with medial cleft) anomalies and generalized hypertrichosis. Anomalies of the extremities (hypoplastic distal phalanges, small/aplastic nails, cutaneous syndactyly, absent flexion crease of the thumbs, single transverse palmar creases), umbilical hernia, and hypoplasia of labia majora are also observed. Other additional features that may be observed include congenital laryngomalacia and heart disease (patent arterial duct). Progeroid syndrome, Petty type and Saethre-Chotzen syndrome have overlapping features with GCM syndrome and should be considered in the differential diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is still unknown and, to date, no causative gene has been implicated in the physiopathology of GCM.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: GCM is considered to be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. However, the lack of consanguinity combined with the fact that all affected patients are female could suggest a de novo X-linked dominant disorder with male lethality.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Gorlin-Chaudhry-Moss syndrome (GCMS), now reclassified as Fontaine progeroid syndrome (FPS), is characterized by typical clinical features including craniofacial dysostosis, hypertrichosis, underdeveloped genitalia, ocular and dental anomalies, generalized loose skin, and growth retardation. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic analysis, specifically identifying mutations in the solute carrier family 25 member 24 (SLC25A24) gene. For individuals already diagnosed with GCMS/FPS, screening for aortic pathology is recommended to aid early detection of complications. [PMC7453031, PMC6882017]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Gorlin-Chaudhry-Moss syndrome (GCMS) is closely related to Fontaine syndrome, also known as Fontaine-Farriaux syndrome (FFS), as both share similar clinical manifestations. A common genetic basis, specifically de novo missense mutations in the SLC25A24 gene, led to their recent reclassification and integration into a single disorder named Fontaine progeroid syndrome (FPS). Therefore, FPS represents a key consideration in the differential diagnosis, encompassing the features previously attributed to GCMS and FFS. [PMC7453031, PMC6882017]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for Gorlin-Chaudhry-Moss syndrome (GCMS) includes screening for aortic pathology. This recommendation is crucial for patients previously diagnosed with GCMS/Fontaine progeroid syndrome to aid in early detection of aortic disease and prevent acute presentations, such as aortic dissection. [PMC7453031]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Patients with Gorlin-Chaudhry-Moss syndrome (reclassified as Fontaine progeroid syndrome) experience prenatal and postnatal growth retardation, leading to short stature throughout childhood. While developmental outcomes can be nearly normal, there is a significant risk of severe complications in adulthood. Acute aortic dissection has been reported in patients as old as 45 years, prompting recommendations for screening for aortic pathology to facilitate early detection and prevent acute presentations. [PMC7453031, PMC6882017]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A benign non-epithelial bone cavity that is asymptomatic and that is found most commonly in the second decade of life by chance. The long bones are most often affected, but cases involving the jaw bone have been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Solitary bone cysts (SBCs) are benign, fluid-filled bone lesions typically affecting the long bones of children and adolescents. They are generally asymptomatic and often detected incidentally. While usually solitary, multifocal SBCs are exceptionally rare. SBCs comprise 1% of all cysts affecting the jaws, and cystic lesions of the carpal bones, including SBCs, are rare entities. SBCs can be associated with acquired generalized lipodystrophy or, rarely, with florid cemento-osseous dysplasia. In the latter association, patients are predominantly women of African origin with a mean age of 41, and this association may be underdiagnosed. Familial cases suggest a potential genetic predisposition. [PMC11843777, PMC12395575, PMC6900696, PMC4656962, PMC4120036]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: BACKGROUND Simple (unicameral) bone cysts (SBCs) are benign, fluid-filled bone lesions that are typically solitary and can be unicameral (single chamber) or septated. Most commonly affecting the long bones of children and adolescents, SBCs can be asymptomatic or associated with pain or fractures. Multifocal SBCs, featuring multiple cysts across different bones, are exceptionally rare and pose unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Here, an exceptional case of a 20-year-old woman with multifocal SBCs affecting 9 known anatomical sites and discuss the unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. CASE REPORT A 20-year-old woman presented with right proximal tibia pain after a fall. Radiographs and MRI revealed radiolucent lesions in the proximal tibia, distal tibia, and fibula, with additional lesions identified on whole-body scintigraphy in the left proximal and distal tibia, left... [PMC11843777, PMC12395575, PMC11092003, PMC6047714, PMC5114264]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiology of solitary bone cysts may involve genetic factors, as suggested by cases of siblings presenting with the same condition. Additionally, unicameral bone cysts can be an important manifestation of acquired generalized lipodystrophy. In patients with acquired generalized lipodystrophy, intramedullary adipose tissue loss may be a predisposing factor for the development of these bone lesions. [PMC4656962, PMC2853647]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of solitary bone cysts (SBCs) typically involves a combination of imaging and histological examination. Radiological assessment, including X-rays, MRI, CT, CBCT, and whole-body scintigraphy, often reveals characteristic radiolucent or marrow-replacing lesions. However, definitive diagnosis frequently requires a biopsy, as initial biopsies can be inconclusive. Surgical biopsy and subsequent histological evaluation confirm SBCs, demonstrating features such as cyst walls, cholesterol clefts, and fibrin-like deposits. A multidisciplinary approach involving radiologists and pathologists is crucial, especially given that SBCs can be misdiagnosed or present with similar clinical and radiographic features to other conditions. Extended diagnostics are often necessary, particularly in cases of pathologic fractures. [PMC11843777, PMC12395575, PMC11092003, PMC11619725, PMC6900696]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Solitary bone cysts (SBCs), also known as unicameral bone cysts, present a varied differential diagnosis depending on their location and presentation. In some cases, SBCs can be associated with and misdiagnosed as part of florid cemento-osseous dysplasia. When occurring as cystic lesions in carpal bones like the scaphoid, other considerations include intraosseous ganglia, aneurysmal bone cysts, and primary hydatid cysts. Furthermore, multiple unicameral bone cysts, particularly in the skull and cervical spine, may initially raise concern for malignant processes such as metastatic disease or multiple myeloma. [PMC12395575, PMC6900696, PMC6047714]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Beginning the study of benign tumors of the bone in children and adolescents, a group of diseases that have in common the clinical aspects, evolution, and surgical treatment, genetic theory in the etiology of the solitary bone cyst, can be sustained by some cases of siblings with the same disease. presents the particular case of two brothers, treated in our clinic for the same condition: solitary bone cyst of the proximal humerus. The two brothers were admitted with the same symptoms, the localization was the same. Because of the genetic studies regarding this condition, we think that it is an interesting aspect of this pathology. also tried to find the most appropriate approach in the treatment of these tumors. [PMC4656962]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of solitary bone cysts frequently involves surgical intervention, such as curettage, often combined with bone grafting or intramedullary decompression. Adjuvant therapies like doxycycline sclerotherapy or argon beam may also be employed. Minimally invasive techniques, including trepanation guided by 3D-printed surgical guides, can facilitate precise access and promote bone healing. For cysts presenting with fractures, open reduction and internal fixation may be performed concurrently with cyst treatment, with arthroscopically assisted repair considered for intra-articular fractures. While many cases demonstrate complete resolution and healing, recurrence can occur. Some lesions, particularly in the skull or cervical spine, may be managed with surveillance imaging without active therapy. A multidisciplinary approach is recommended for multifocal presentations. [PMC11843777, PMC12395575, PMC11092003, PMC6900696, PMC6047714]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Solitary bone cysts generally show a favorable prognosis following treatment, with many cases achieving complete or near-complete resolution and bone healing. Follow-up periods of 6 months to 2 years have demonstrated complete reossification and resolution of lesions, with patients remaining asymptomatic. Clinical improvement is common after treatment, often resulting in full wrist range of motion without pain. However, recurrence is a known complication, reported in some cases, with instances occurring several years after initial treatment. [PMC11843777, PMC12395575, PMC11092003, PMC6900696, PMC5114264]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Spina bifida and other spinal dysraphisms
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A group of rare neural tube defect disorders characterized by improper closure of the spinal column during embryonal development that is usually not associated with other major congenital malformations but may include ventriculomegaly. The extent of the closure defect may vary, ranging from spina bifida occulta, in which the site of the lesion is not exposed (e.g. an isolated posterior vertebral arch defect), to spina bifida aperta, in which the lesion may be conformed of proturding spinal cord and meninges (myelomeningocele) or meninges exposure only (meningocele), with or without a proturding sac at the site of the lesion, to the most severe defect which includes total exposure of the spinal cord along its full length (rachischisis). Depending on the type, size and site of the defect, severe morbidity, typically inlcuding motor, sensory and sphincter dysfunction, and mortality may be associated. Spina bifida occulta may be asymptomatic.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Isolated spina bifida; Isolated spinal dysraphism

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: The aim of is to present and discuss atypical instances of spina bifida (SB) within a Nigerian paediatric cohort, highlighting their distinctive clinicoradiological features. Additionally, a brief literature review is provided to contextualise these congenital anomalies. This series comprises eight rare cases of SB managed in a Nigerian neurosurgical facility. Additionally, a brief literature review is provided to contextualise these congenital anomalies. This case series comprises eight rare cases of SB managed in a Nigerian neurosurgical facility. Amongst these, four cases exhibited segmental spinal dysgenesis (SSD; one thoracolumbar, one lumbar, and two sacral). Each of these cases demonstrated diverse associated musculoskeletal, cutaneous, and perineal anomalies, accompanied by varying degrees of neurological dysfunction. Other cases included lipomyelomeningocele (LMMC), human tail... [PMC11676024]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Spina bifida is a congenital neural tube defect, often characterized by incomplete fusion of vertebral elements, such as the spinous process and lamina. Spinal dysraphisms, including congenital dermal sinus, result from aberrant development of ectodermal, mesodermal, and neuroectodermal tissues, forming persistent epithelial-lined tracts. Atypical forms of spina bifida encompass segmental spinal dysgenesis, lipomyelomeningocele, human tail, membranous meningocele, and myeloschisis, which present with diverse vertebral, musculoskeletal, cutaneous, and perineal anomalies. Neural tube defects are also observed in rachipagus conjoined twins, involving spinal fusion and absent posterior vertebral elements. Furthermore, spina bifida myelomeningocele can be a component of complex birth disorders like the omphalocele-exstrophy-imperforate anus-spinal defects (OEIS) complex. Spinal arteriovenous malformations, caused by abnormal anastomoses, may also be associated with congenital dermal sinuses. [PMC12297412, PMC12178146, PMC11981514, PMC11812443, PMC11676024]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Deafness-infertility syndrome (DIS) is a very rare syndrome associating sensorineural deafness and male infertility.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It has been reported in fewer than 5 families.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Male infertility is caused by abnormal spermatozoid morphology and motility. DIS is due to a contiguous gene deletion at chromosome 15q15.3 including 2 genes CATSPER2 and STRC, and is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner: affected males are homozygous for the deletion, parents are asymptomatic carriers and homozygous females are deaf but not infertile.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Deafness-infertility syndrome encompasses conditions characterized by hearing loss and infertility. Perrault syndrome, a heterogeneous disorder, typically presents with sensory neuronal hearing loss in both sexes and premature ovarian failure or infertility in females. Associated features can include neurological findings like spastic limbs, muscle weakness, and ataxia, as well as delayed puberty and irregular menstrual cycles. CEP78 variants are linked to cone-rod dystrophy with hearing loss and reduced male fertility due to sperm abnormalities. HSD17B4-deficiency can also manifest with ovarian dysgenesis, hearing loss, ataxia, peripheral neuropathy, and azoospermia, often with evidence of peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation dysfunction. [PMC7187288, PMC5198008, PMC4015298]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of deafness-infertility syndromes primarily relies on genetic testing. include chromosomal microarray (CMA) for detecting deletions, with allele-specific PCR used for refining breakpoints.
