Genome-wide homozygosity mapping via SNP microarray analysis, followed by candidate gene Sanger sequencing, identifies specific gene mutations such as in CLPP or CEP78. Targeted exome sequencing can detect single nucleotide variants, small insertions/deletions, and infer copy number variants (CNVs) using computational algorithms, as demonstrated for HSD17B4. Functional characterization in patient fibroblasts and assessment of cilia assembly may also support diagnosis. Additionally, biochemical findings, such as elevated pristanic:phytanic acid and arachidonic:docosahexaenoic acid ratios, can be indicative. [PMC7187288, PMC6687617, PMC5198008, PMC4015298]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for conditions presenting with deafness and infertility include Perrault syndrome (PRLTS), a heterogeneous disorder characterized by sensory neuronal hearing loss in both sexes and premature ovarian failure or infertility in females. PRLTS is associated with mutations in genes such as HSD17B4, HARS2, CLPP, LARS2, and C10orf2. HSD17B4-deficiency can also present with hearing loss and infertility, including azoospermia in males or ovarian dysgenesis in females, and may overlap with Perrault syndrome. Cone-rod dystrophy with hearing loss (CRDHL), caused by CEP78 variants, is another distinct phenotype that can include reduced male fertility. CEP78 loss-of-function variants may also be misdiagnosed as Usher syndrome. [PMC7187288, PMC5198008, PMC4015298]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Prenatal diagnosis of genetic deletions associated with deafness-infertility syndrome is possible. Clinical chromosomal microarray (CMA) testing can detect compound heterozygous deletions, such as those at chromosome 15q15.3, which may include genes like CATSPER2, linked to male infertility. However, CMA's resolution can be limited, making it unclear if neighboring genes, such as STRC for hearing loss, are affected. In such cases, novel molecular strategies, like allele-specific PCR, can be developed to refine deletion breakpoints and clarify gene involvement. [PMC6687617]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Deafness-infertility syndrome is genetically heterogeneous, primarily inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, with compound heterozygous mutations commonly identified in genes such as CEP78, STRC, CATSPER2, HSD17B4, CLPP, HARS2, LARS2, C10orf2, and SECISBP2. Maternal uniparental disomy has also been reported. Founder effects for specific variants, like a missense allele in CEP78, are observed in certain populations. Genetic counseling should address the complex inheritance patterns, the need for comprehensive genetic testing including copy number variant detection, and the potential for differential diagnosis with conditions such as Usher syndrome. Prenatal detection of deletions, requiring high-resolution molecular techniques to refine breakpoints, has been demonstrated. [PMC7187288, PMC6687617, PMC5397338, PMC5198008, PMC4015298]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Perrault syndrome symptoms, including neurological and hearing loss, typically appear early in life, while female infertility cannot be detected before puberty. The clinical course is variable; some individuals with CLPP mutations may present with a milder phenotype lacking neurological findings. While D-bifunctional protein deficiency, caused by HSD17B4 mutations, is a severe infantile-onset disorder with few patients surviving past two years, other presentations of HSD17B4-related Perrault syndrome can manifest in adolescence or adulthood, suggesting a broader prognostic spectrum. [PMC5198008, PMC4015298]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Terminal osseous dysplasia-pigmentary defects syndrome is characterised by malformation of the hands and feet, pigmentary skin lesions on the face and scalp and digital fibromatosis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It has been described in 18 females, six of whom came from four different generations of the same family.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Phenotypic expression is very heterogeneous. In the majority of patients, the bone dysplasia is limited to the hands and feet but shortening and/or bowing of the bones of the arms and legs has been reported in severe cases. The pigmentary lesions and digital fibromatosis appear a few months after birth.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The causative gene remains unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The syndrome is transmitted as an in utero male-lethal X-linked dominant trait, explaining the large number of miscarriages reported in the affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Terminal osseous dysplasia-pigmentary defects syndrome (TODPD) is based on characteristic clinical features, including distal limb anomalies, brachydactyly, digital fibromatosis, and pigmentary skin defects, often described as punched-out abnormalities over the face and scalp. Other features may include dysmorphic facial features, hypertelorism, and iris colobomas. Skeletal surveys can reveal generalized skeletal involvement. Genetic testing identifies pathogenic variants in the FLNA gene, such as the recurrent c.5217G>A or novel c.5217+5G>C variants. Detection of mis-spliced FLNA transcripts and X-inactivation analyses may also support the diagnosis. [PMC9292317, PMC2909110]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Straddling or overriding tricuspid valve is a rare, congenital, tricuspid valve malformation characterized by the tricuspid valve that overrides the ventricular septum and communicates with both ventricles, as part of the tension apparatus of the valve crosses the ventricular septal defect and is attached in the left ventricle. The anomaly occurs with other congenital heart defects (transposition of great vessels, left ventricle outflow tract obstruction, double outlet right ventricle, hypoplastic right ventricle), which determine the main clinical manifestation.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: A case report describes a four-year-old girl who had a straddling tricuspid valve, indicating that the condition can be present and identified in early childhood. [PMC1216767]

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Straddling or overriding tricuspid valve is an anomaly where the valve connects to both the right and left ventricles, often with two orifices. In some cases, valve tissue may attach to the crest of the ventricular septum, sealing off an expected interventricular communication, as observed in a patient with pulmonary atresia. This condition can also manifest as right atrial outlet atresia with a straddling left atrioventricular valve, which is considered a form of double outlet atrium. Accurate characterization of the right ventricular chamber's morphology and its connections is crucial for diagnosis and differentiation from other complex congenital heart defects. [PMC1216767, PMC482528]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of straddling or overriding tricuspid valve may be possible clinically if the anomaly is considered, requiring differentiation from conditions like common atrioventricular canal with atrial outlet atresia. Characterization of the right ventricular chamber, including its morphology and connections, is crucial, though it can be difficult. Echocardiography can reveal complex congenital heart conditions. For comprehensive assessment and surgical planning, especially with complex associated anomalies, CT angiography is crucial. [PMC11963316, PMC482528]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differentiation from common atrioventricular canal with atrial outlet atresia is important, as total repair may be feasible for the latter but not for cases with straddling atrioventricular valves. For semantic and practical reasons, atrial outlet atresia is preferred over tricuspid or mitral atresia in these cases. Classifications of tricuspid atresia may need to be enlarged to include cases with double outlet from either ventricular chamber or anatomically corrected malposition, suggesting a need to distinguish these conditions. [PMC482528]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Surgical correction has been performed for straddling tricuspid valve, with satisfactory outcomes reported in some instances. However, the feasibility of total repair varies depending on associated anomalies; for example, it may not be feasible in cases of right atrial outlet atresia with straddling left atrioventricular valve. Accurate diagnosis, often aided by CT angiography, is crucial for comprehensive assessment and guiding treatment decisions, particularly in complex cases where optimal surgical strategies are still being explored. [PMC11963316, PMC1216767, PMC482528]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Prognosis varies significantly depending on the specific anatomical presentation and associated anomalies. In one reported case of a straddling tricuspid valve without a ventricular septal defect but with pulmonary atresia, surgical correction led to a satisfactory outcome. However, for cases involving right atrial outlet atresia with a straddling left atrioventricular valve, total repair does not appear feasible. [PMC1216767, PMC482528]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare acquired dermis elastic tissue disorder with increased elastic tissue characterized by focal dermal elastosis and transepidermal elimination of abnormal elastic fibers, presenting as small keratotic papules or plaques arranged in groups in serpiginous or annular patterns on the neck, face, and arms, while other areas are less frequently affected. Although spontaneous regression is possible, the lesions often persist over longer periods of time. The condition typically occurs during childhood or early adulthood and is more frequent in men than in women.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) is a rare and uncommon dermatological condition, primarily documented through case reports. It is frequently drug-induced, with D-penicillamine being a notable cause, and is associated with Wilson's disease. EPS has also been observed in patients with Down Syndrome, where a mean prevalence of 0.5% has been reported across multiple studies. [PMC10337497, PMC10334906, PMC6464679, PMC4680324, PMC1000997]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) is a rare and uncommon dermatological condition affecting the papillary dermal tissue fibers of the skin. It is a classical perforating dermatosis, characterized by the transepidermal elimination of dermal material, specifically elastic fibers. EPS is commonly drug-induced, with D-penicillamine being a notable cause, and has been reported as a rare side effect in patients with Wilson's disease and rheumatoid arthritis. It is also associated with Down syndrome, where it has a reported prevalence of 0.5%. [PMC10337497, PMC10334906, PMC6464679, PMC5324979, PMC4680324]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) is commonly drug-induced, with D-penicillamine being a reported cause. It frequently occurs along with Wilson's disease. Additionally, EPS has an increased prevalence in patients with Down Syndrome, where it is considered among the associated cutaneous disorders. [PMC10337497, PMC10334906, PMC6464679, PMC4680324, PMC1000997]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Perforating dermatoses are a group of skin diseases characterized by transepidermal elimination of dermal material. The disease is divided into two groups: the primary group and the secondary group. The classical or primary perforating dermatoses are subdivided into four types according to the eliminated dermal materials: Kyrle disease, perforating reactive collagenosis, elastosis perforans serpiginosa, and perforating folliculitis. The secondary form is known as acquired perforating dermatosis. The term was proposed in 1989 by Rapini to designate the perforating dermatoses affecting adult patients with systemic disease, regardless of the dermal materials eliminated. describes a case of the disease with elimination of collagen and elastic fibers in a patient with chronic renal failure. [PMC5324979]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Elastosis perforans serpiginosa (EPS) is classified as a classical perforating dermatosis. Other conditions within this group, which should be considered in the differential diagnosis, include Kyrle disease, perforating reactive collagenosis, and perforating folliculitis. Acquired perforating dermatosis, a secondary form affecting adults with systemic disease, also falls under the broader category of perforating dermatoses. EPS can be drug-induced, notably by D-penicillamine, and has been reported in conjunction with D-penicillamine-induced pseudo-pseudoxanthoma elasticum. [PMC10337497, PMC10334906, PMC6464679, PMC5324979, PMC4680324]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Isotretinoin therapy has shown sustained improvement in elastosis perforans serpiginosa. Acitretin has also demonstrated an excellent rapid response in cases of D-penicillamine-induced elastosis perforans serpiginosa. The effectiveness of isotretinoin has been noted in other reports as well. [PMC10950559, PMC6464679]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for elastosis perforans serpiginosa can be favorable with specific treatments. Sustained improvement has been observed following isotretinoin therapy. Additionally, an excellent rapid response to acitretin has been reported, particularly in D-penicillamine-induced cases. However, it is noted that most previously used treatment modalities have shown suboptimal responses, indicating that outcomes may vary depending on the therapeutic approach. [PMC10950559, PMC6464679]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare cardiac disease characterized by thickening of the endocardium due to deposition of collagen and elastic fibers and leading to dilated cardiomyopathy-like phenotypes more often than to restrictive forms. It predominantly occurs in infants and children and may be observed as an isolated disorder or in association with congenital heart conditions.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Primary endocardial fibroelastosis (pEFE) is a rare neonatal cardiomyopathy, affecting 1/5000 live births and accounting for 25% of all pediatric dilated cardiomyopathy. Fetal cardiac involvement, including isolated EFE or EFE combined with arrhythmia, is strongly associated with maternal immune diseases, particularly in the presence of anti-SSA and anti-SSB antibodies. In one study, EFE was observed in 65% of fetuses with cardiac manifestations due to maternal immune diseases. Genetic contributions to pEFE include recessive ciliopathy mutations, such as those in the ALMS1 gene, which have been linked to Alstrom syndrome. [PMC12206730, PMC8541947]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Endocardial fibroelastosis (EFE) can present as an isolated fetal cardiac manifestation or co-occur with bradyarrhythmias, including sinus bradycardia and atrioventricular block. These fetal cardiac abnormalities are strongly associated with maternal immune diseases, particularly in cases with positive anti-SSA and/or anti-SSB antibodies, and can be detected by prenatal ultrasound. Primary EFE (pEFE) is a rare and severe neonatal cardiomyopathy, affecting 1/5000 live births and accounting for 25% of pediatric dilated cardiomyopathy, with a devastating course and grave prognosis. Pathologically, pEFE has unique features and can be linked to recessive ciliopathy mutations, such as a novel ALMS1 variant implicated in Alstrom syndrome, which affects cellular signaling and function. [PMC12206730, PMC8541947]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Endocardial fibroelastosis (EFE) is associated with maternal immune diseases, where fetal cardiac involvement can manifest as isolated EFE or EFE combined with arrhythmia. A strong association exists between maternal autoimmune diseases, particularly those with anti-SSA and anti-SSB antibodies, and fetal EFE. Furthermore, primary EFE has been linked to genetic factors, with integrative genomic analysis identifying recessive ciliopathy mutations. A novel homozygous variant in the ALMS1 gene, implicated in Alstrom syndrome, suggests ciliopathy as a potential underlying mechanism for this form of neonatal cardiomyopathy. [PMC12206730, PMC8541947]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for endocardial fibroelastosis (EFE) include prenatal ultrasound and echocardiography, which can identify fetal cardiac involvement. Given the strong association between maternal autoimmune diseases and fetal cardiac abnormalities like EFE, prenatal ultrasound findings should prompt screening for maternal autoimmune antibodies, such as anti-SSA and anti-SSB. For confirmed primary EFE, pathological diagnosis is noted. Additionally, integrative genomic analysis, including whole exome sequencing, has been utilized to investigate genetic contributions in specific cases, identifying mutations like a novel homozygous variant in ALMS1. [PMC12206730, PMC8541947]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Endocardial fibroelastosis (EFE) should be considered among neonatal cardiomyopathies, particularly in relation to pediatric dilated cardiomyopathy, from which it has unique pathological features. Fetal cardiac involvement due to maternal immune diseases, which can present as isolated EFE or EFE combined with arrhythmias (such as bradyarrhythmias), warrants screening for maternal autoimmune antibodies. Furthermore, rare recessive ciliopathies like Alstrom syndrome, known to be associated with cardiomyopathy, have been suggested as a potential underlying mechanism for primary EFE. [PMC12206730, PMC8541947]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of endocardial fibroelastosis (EFE) can be made through prenatal ultrasound, which may reveal isolated EFE or EFE co-occurring with bradyarrhythmias. Such fetal cardiac abnormalities, including EFE, are strongly associated with maternal autoimmune diseases. Therefore, prenatal ultrasound findings of EFE should raise suspicion for maternal immune disorders, prompting a recommendation for screening maternal autoimmune antibodies. [PMC12206730]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Primary endocardial fibroelastosis (pEFE) can have a genetic basis, with integrative genomic analysis revealing parent-transmitted homozygous mutations in genes involved in cilia function. Specifically, a novel homozygous variant in ALMS1, a gene implicated in Alstrom syndrome (AS), a rare recessive ciliopathy, was identified in a case of pEFE. This suggests an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern for this form of the disease, where both parents are carriers of the mutation. Genetic counseling would involve discussing the implications of such recessive mutations, the potential association with Alstrom syndrome, and the recurrence risk for future offspring. [PMC8541947]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: To analyze the clinical characteristics, echocardiographic features, and prognosis of fetuses with maternal immune diseases. We retrospectively evaluated 20 fetuses with cardiac manifestations due to maternal immune diseases from our center between 2019 and 2023 in China. Clinical and echocardiographic data of fetuses and maternal sero-immunity were collected. The pregnancy outcomes were followed up. The cardiac manifestations seen in 20 fetuses were categorized into three types: type I: isolated-arrhythmia: seven cases (35%); type II: isolated endocardial fibroelastosis (EFE): four cases (20%); and type III: both arrhythmia and EFE: nine cases (45%). The arrhythmias in all cases were bradyarrhythmia, including sinus bradycardia and atrioventricular block. The of maternal antibody test showed the following three types: (1) five cases were positive for anti-SSA antibody alone; (2) 10... [PMC12206730]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inborn error of metabolism characterized by increased concentrations of sarcosine in plasma and urine due to sarcosine dehydrogenase deficiency. The condition is considered benign and not associated with any specific clinical phenotype. Mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Sarcosinemia, resulting from a mutation of the mitochondrial SARDH gene, leads to formaldehyde deficiency. This deficiency in endogenous formaldehyde, which is normally generated by mitochondrial sarcosine dehydrogenase (SARDH), is associated with cognitive deficits in affected children. Endogenous formaldehyde regulates learning and memory via the NMDA receptor, and its deficiency in sarcosinemia contributes to these observed impairments. [PMC6884489]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Sarcosinemia is caused by a mutation of the mitochondrial sarcosine dehydrogenase (SARDH) gene. This genetic alteration leads to a deficiency of endogenous formaldehyde, a molecule that regulates learning and memory via the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor. The formaldehyde deficiency observed in children with sarcosinemia is linked to cognitive deficits. [PMC6884489]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Gaseous formaldehyde is an organic small molecule formed in the early stages of earth's evolution. Although toxic in high concentrations, formaldehyde plays an important role in cellular metabolism and, unexpectedly, is found even in the healthy brain. However, its pathophysiological functions in the brain are unknown. Here, that under physiological conditions, spatial learning activity elicits rapid formaldehyde generation from mitochondrial sarcosine dehydrogenase (SARDH). We find that elevated formaldehyde levels facilitate spatial memory formation by enhancing N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) currents, but that high formaldehyde concentrations gradually inactivate the NMDA receptor by cross-linking NR1 subunits to NR2B via the C232 residue. We also report that in mice with aldehyde dehydrogenase-2 ( ALDH2 ) knockout, formaldehyde accumulation due to hypofunctional ALDH2 impairs memory,... [PMC6884489]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Sarcosinemia, caused by a mutation of the mitochondrial SARDH gene, leads to formaldehyde deficiency. This deficiency in cognitive deficits, as endogenous formaldehyde regulates learning and memory via the NMDA receptor. [PMC6884489]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare teratogenic disease due to embryo/fetal exposure to valproic acid (VPA) and subsequently characterized by a distinct facial dysmorphism, congenital anomalies and developmental delay (especially in language and communication).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Fetal valproic acid syndrome; Valproic acid embryopathy; Fetal valproate syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of fetal valproate syndrome (FVS) is unknown. An incidence of neural tube defects (NTDs) of 1-2% has been associated with the use of VPA during the first trimester of pregnancy (10-20 times the rate seen in the general population) while the incidence of congenital heart disease, neurodevelopmental delay and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are estimated to be around 4 to 5 times higher than in the general population.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The majority of infants exposed to VPA in utero are born healthy. Intrauterine growth retardation is present in 10% of cases but postnatal growth is usually normal and general health is good. Characteristic facial features of FVS are many of the following: high/broad forehead with bifrontal narrowing, metopic craniosynostosis, epicanthal folds, medial deficiency of eyebrows, infraorbital groove, small/broad upturned nose, long and shallow philtrum, long upper lip with thin vermillion borders, thick lower lip and downturned angles of mouth. Congenital anomalies associated with FVS include neural tube defects (e.g. spina bifida aperta), congenital heart defects (e.g. ventricular septal defect), oral clefts, genital abnormalities (e.g. hypospadias with undescended testicles) and limb defects, and less commonly, inguinal and umbilical hernia, tracheomalacia, supernumerary nipples, bifid ribs and pre-axial defects of the feet. Children exposed to VPA have a higher risk of developmental problems such a decreased cognitive function (especially in verbal intelligence), attention deficit disorder, learning difficulties and often the communication problems of ASD.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FVS is caused by the exposure during pregnancy to VPA (valproate), a mood stabilizer and broad-spectrum antiepileptic drug (AED. Primarily metabolized in the liver, VPA readily crosses the placenta, where concentrations are higher than in the mother. Embryos and fetuses exposed to VPA during the 1st trimester (especially to doses exceeding 600 mg/day but lower doses may also be teratogenic) have a higher risk of developing FVS, as this is the principal period of structural development.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the presence of the well-recognized cluster of clinical findings in infants born to mothers who took VPA during pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other types of AED-related embryofetopathies (e.g. fetal hydantoin syndrome) and possibly fetal alcohol spectrum disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible by the detection of anomalies such as NTDs, cardiac and other organ anomalies by ultrasonographic examination and estimation of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (with a history of antenatal valproate intake).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: VPA should be avoided (if possible) during pregnancy and high dose folic acid (4-5 mg/day) should be started 6 weeks before conception and continued through the first trimester. In pregnant women with no effective alternative, VPA should be administered in slow release form at the lowest possible divided dosage and preferably as a monotherapy along with high dose folic acid. Surveillance of the newborn should include searching for dysmorphic facial features, congenital malformations and withdrawal symptoms at birth. Long-term follow-up of the child should include early diagnosis and management of any potential behavioral or neurodevelopmental effect and educational and psychosocial support, whenever needed. Management of congenital anomalies should follow standard treatment protocols. Children with ASD should receive the regular treatment offered to children with communication disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis of newborns is highly variable and depends on the clinical and behavioral symptoms, timing of exposure and the dosage of VPA taken by the mother. Life expectancy may be decreased in those with multiple congenital anomalies (in particular of the cardiovascular system and NTD) or with significant intellectual disability.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Fetal valproate spectrum disorder is caused by prenatal exposure to valproic acid (VPA), a known teratogen that induces congenital malformations, including neural tube defects, cardiac anomalies, and skeletal malformations, in about 10% of cases. It also increases the prevalence of neurodevelopmental problems such as reduced cognitive abilities, language impairment, autism, and ADHD. Teratogenic effects are dose-related, with daily doses below 600 mg having limited potential. Preconceptional counseling is crucial, especially for epileptic women, to discuss risks and potential medication adjustments. High doses of folic acid administered prior to and during pregnancy might alleviate some teratogenic effects of VPA, and periconception folic acid/multivitamin supplementation has shown efficacy in reducing congenital abnormalities in offspring of epileptic mothers. While VPA crosses the placenta, nursing is permitted due to low concentrations in milk. [PMC10779436, PMC5094134, PMC4110861]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) comprises a group of neurodegenerative disorders, characterized by progressive changes in behavior, executive dysfunction and language impairment, as a result of degeneration of the medial prefrontal and frontoinsular cortices. Four clinical subtypes have been identified: semantic dementia, progressive non-fluent aphasia, behavioral variant FTD and right temporal lobar atrophy.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are linked by shared genetic mutations and overlapping clinical features, forming a clinical spectrum. This systematic review and meta-analysis analysed 97 studies, including 3212 patients with key ALS/FTD gene mutations, to identify gene-specific behavioural profiles. Chromosome 9 open reading frame 72 ( C9orf72 ) mutations were strongly associated with psychotic symptoms and aggression, while superoxide dismutase 1 ( SOD1 ) mutations had minimal cognitive effects. Progranulin ( PGRN ) mutations correlated with apathy and hallucinations, microtubule-associated protein tau ( MAPT ) mutations with disinhibition, and charged multivesicular body protein 2B ( CHMP2B ) with social impairments. Fused in sarcoma ( FUS ) mutations caused early sleep disturbances, TANK-binding kinase 1 ( TBK1 ) led to disinhibition, and... [PMC12250155, PMC12270496, PMC11538089, PMC10422061]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Frontotemporal dementia (FTD) exhibits significant genetic heterogeneity, with various mutations identified as causative factors or associated with the disease. Key genes include GRN, MAPT, TBK1, C9orf72, CHMP2B, TARDBP, FUS, PSEN1/2, SOD1, and ErbB4. Many of these mutations, such as those in TBK1, MAPT, and CHMP2B, follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, with some observed across multiple generations. Genetic testing is crucial for confirming diagnoses and evaluating atypical presentations, especially given the clinical heterogeneity and overlapping features with conditions like ALS. Understanding gene-specific behavioral and cognitive profiles can inform tailored care strategies and improve patient and family support, necessitating refined guidelines that integrate genetic information. [PMC12337398, PMC12291237, PMC11889931, PMC12082706, PMC12250155]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Frontotemporal dementia is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, with symptoms that can advance gradually or rapidly depending on genetic factors. Patients experience progressive decline in functional communication, behavioral changes, and cognitive abilities, including speech difficulties, language impairments, and executive dysfunction. Motor symptoms, such as unstable walking and tremors, can also progress. Pathologically, the disease involves accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau, neurite degeneration, and synaptic loss, which are associated with behavioral abnormalities. Specific genetic mutations, such as in TBK1 or MAPT, are linked to rapid deterioration, while others like TARDBP I383V or GRN and ErbB4 mutations may lead to a slower progression. [PMC12337398, PMC12291237, PMC12250155, PMC11802456, PMC11253250]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Severe combined immunodeficiency due to adenosine deaminase deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) due to adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency is a form of SCID characterized by profound lymphopenia and very low immunoglobulin levels of all isotypes resulting in severe and recurrent opportunistic infections.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): ADA deficiency; SCID due to adenosine deaminase deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: SCID due to ADA deficiency accounts for 10-15% of all cases of SCID. Its annual incidence is estimated to be between 1/200,000 and 1/1,000,000 live births. Both males and females are affected.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: SCID due to ADA deficiency has a variable clinical presentation. The most common form presents in infancy with severe and recurrent opportunistic infections (including respiratory tract infections and candidiasis), failure to thrive, and usually results in early death. Ten to 15% of patients have a delayed clinical onset by age 6-24 months, and a smaller percentage have a partial form of ADA deficiency with later onset between ages 4 years and adulthood, both types showing less severe infections and gradual immunologic deterioration. Patients may also present with extraimmune manifestations (including neurodevelopmental deficits, behavioral disorders, sensorineural deafness, and skeletal and hepatic abnormalities) as a result of the systemic nature of ADA expression.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: SCID due to ADA deficiency is caused by mutations in the ADA gene (20q13.11). The extraimmune manifestations are caused by toxic levels of purine metabolites that result from the deficiency of ADA.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on evidence of low or undetectable ADA activity in erythrocytes in combination with evidence of a marked reduction of T, B and NK cell counts when compared to age-matched healthy controls. Diagnosis can be confirmed by raised levels of dATP and reduced S-adenosyl homocysteine hydrolase (SAHH) activity in red cells and elevated amounts of deoxyadenosine in urine.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes all forms of SCID.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis can be carried out through mutation analysis or measurement of enzyme activity in trophoblasts cultured from chorionic villus sampling or in cultured amniocytes.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is based on allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), enzyme replacement therapy with pegylated adenosine deaminase enzyme or gene therapy by infusion of CD34+ marrow cells that have been transduced with an ADA-containing vector.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of the disease. Without treatment, SCID due to ADA deficiency that presents in infancy usually results in early death. Survival rates after allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or gene therapy are high.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Idiopathic camptocormia is a postural disease characterized by an anterior flexion of the torso (during walking or standing) that resolves in the supine position and that is caused by weakness of the lumbar paraspinal muscles (spinal extensors), due to massive fatty infiltrations of posterior spinal muscles, without an identifiable etiology.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Idiopathic camptocormism; Idiopathic progressive lumbar kyphosis

DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Camptocormia, a disabling forward bending of the trunk, has heterogeneous etiologies requiring a broad diagnostic approach. It is frequently encountered in movement disorders such as Parkinson's disease, atypical parkinsonism, multiple system atrophy, and dystonia. Myopathies are also common causes, including sporadic late-onset nemaline myopathy, glycogen storage disease type 5 (McArdle disease), late-onset multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency, myotonic dystrophy, and inflammatory myopathies like polymyositis or scleroderma-polymyositis overlap syndrome. Other potential causes include degenerative joint disease, drug-induced parkinsonism (e.g., from dopamine receptor blockers), motor neuron disease, POLG1 gene mutations, and delayed postirradiation complications. Comprehensive work-up is mandatory to ascertain the individual diagnosis, especially for treatable conditions. [PMC12303437, PMC11460110, PMC11002662, PMC6868766, PMC6377804]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurologic disease characterized by bilateral cataract, Dandy-Walker malformation, and childhood onset of distal spinal muscular atrophy. Patients present with progressively deteriorating symmetrical distal muscle weakness and atrophy of the lower limbs (and, to a much lesser degree, also the upper limbs) and decreased tendon reflexes in the lower and upper limbs.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Spinal muscular atrophy, Dandy-Walker complex, and cataracts in two siblings: a new entity? [PMC1739742]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Spinal muscular atrophy, Dandy-Walker complex, and cataracts in two siblings: a new entity? [PMC1739742]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Spinal muscular atrophy, Dandy-Walker complex, and cataracts in two siblings: a new entity? [PMC1739742]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Spinal muscular atrophy, Dandy-Walker complex, and cataracts in two siblings: a new entity? [PMC1739742]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Spinal muscular atrophy, Dandy-Walker complex, and cataracts in two siblings: a new entity? [PMC1739742]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare non-malignant adnexal neoplasm that originates from the apocrine or eccrine sweat glands and is characterized histologically by cystic, papillary, and ductal invaginations into the dermis lined by double-layered outer cuboidal and luminal high columnar epithelium and connected to the epidermis. Dilated capillaries and a dense infiltrate of plasma cells are characteristic. Clinically, lesions are asymptomatic with a heterogeneous, non-distinctive appearance ranging from skin-colored to pink papules or plaques, occurring most commonly in the head and neck area.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Papillary syringocystadenoma; Fistulous vegetative verrucous hydradenoma; Naevus syringocystadenomatosus papilliferus; SCAP; Syringadenoma papilliferum

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, approximately 730 cases have been reported in the literature. The condition has been reported worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Syringocystadenoma papilliferum (SCAP) may be present at birth (50% of cases) or develop around puberty (15-30% of cases). SCAP typically presents as slow developing, non-specific, smooth, skin-colored to pink papule, verruca or nodule, which may be exudative. It may also be seen as hairless plaques, smooth or raised, usually less than 4 cm in diameter, skin-colored to brown. It is rarely pigmented. In the majority of cases, it is asymptomatic, but it may grow progressively and has been occasionally associated with pruritus, pain, and/or bleeding. Three clinical types have been described: the plaque type, the linear type and the solitary nodular type. The plaque type usually presents as an alopecia plaque on the scalp which may increase in size at puberty and often transforms to nodular or verrucous lesions. The linear type consists of multiple pink to reddish, firm papules or umbilicated nodules, 1-10 mm in diameter, and is extremely rare. The solitary type includes dome-shaped, pedunculated nodules, 5-10 mm in diameter, with a predilection for the trunk, shoulder and axillae. Rarely, segmental variants are found. In 75% of cases, SCAP is located on the head or cervical region and less frequent in other regions, or on a postoperative scar. SCAP develops in existing nevus sebaceous in about one-third of cases, 10% of which are associated with he development of basal cell carcinoma and more rarely other carcinomas. SCAP can also be associated with other benign lesions. Transition to malignancy is rare but, possible. Syringocystadenocarcinoma papilliferum is the malignant counterpart to this lesion and may develop in a long-standing case of SCAP.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of SCAP has not been elucidated. It seems to arise from the pluripotent cells with the potential to exhibit either apocrine or eccrine lineage, although apocrine differentiation is more common. The pathogenesis of SCAP remains unclear although, both in sporadic cases and lesions arising in nevus sebaceous, the human papillomavirus (HPV) DNA and mutations in the RAS/mitogen-activated protein kinase signaling pathway have been detected. BRAF V600E mutation or activating mutations in HRAS (or in one case KRAS) have been reported in sporadic forms.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected on clinical presentation of non-distinctive lesions and confirmed on biopsy showing the characteristic histology. Immunohistochemically, the tumor cells stains positively for carcinoembryonic antigen. Dermatoscopy is not diagnostic.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis is broad, requiring histological confirmation of cases. The main diagnostic issue is the distinction of SCAP from hidradenoma papilliferum. Other conditions to be considered include basal cell carcinoma, cutaneous lymphoma, factitious dermatitis, viral warts, subcutaneous fungal infection, linear verrucous nevus, pyogenic granuloma, warty dyskeratoma, inverted follicular keratosis, as well as eccrine nevus, nevus comedonicus, cylindroma, and basaloid follicular hamartoma.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment involves complete surgical excision. However, recurrence is common. Carbon dioxide laser treatment can be useful for lesions in anatomic areas not favorable for excision and grafting. SCAP has also been successfully treated with Mohs micrograhic surgery.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The condition is mostly benign but extensive lesions may have an impact on quality of life and transformation to malignancy cannot be ruled out.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Ectopic Syringocystadenoma Papilliferum on the Arm in a Patient with Noonan Syndrome. [PMC10043701]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic motor neuron disease characterized by a peripheral and cranial neuropathy, neuronal loss in anterior horns and atrophy of spinal sensory tracts, causing muscle weakness, sensory loss, diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory insufficiency, and multiple cranial nerve deficits such as sensorineural hearing loss, bulbar symptoms, and loss of vision due to optic atrophy. Depending on the transporter affected, Riboflavin transporter deficiency 2 (RFVT2) and Riboflavin transporter deficiency 3 (RFVT3) are distinguished.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Riboflavin transporter deficiency (RTD) has been reported in more than 100 genetically diagnosed cases to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset may occur from early infancy until adulthood, with a more severe presentation at a younger age. The most frequent presenting symptoms are cranial neuropathy, sensory ataxia, muscle weakness and respiratory insufficiency due to diaphragmatic paralysis. The cranial neuropathy leads to sensorineural hearing loss, loss of vision due to optic atrophy, dysarthria, dysphagia, feeding problems, facial weakness and eye movement impairments. Peripheral neuropathy in combination with anterior horn cell dysfunction and atrophy of the sensory tracts in the spinal cord causes muscle weakness with atrophy and (sensory) ataxia. Diaphragmatic paralysis in combination with general muscle weakness may rapidly lead to respiratory insufficiency, especially in infants and young children. Often, feeding through a nasogastric tube or gastrostomy device and artificial ventilation and tracheotomy are required. Sensory ataxia and optic atrophy seem more prevalent in RFVT2 than RFVT3 deficient patients.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Pathogenic biallelic mutations in the genes SLC52A2 and SLC52A3 that encode riboflavin transporter 2 and 3 cause RTD2 and RTD3, respectively. Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) is a water-soluble vitamin that is essential for normal metabolism. The loss of function of the riboflavin transporter results in cellular flavin deficiency in different tissues. As flavins play an important role in mitochondrial function, mitochondrial dysfunction might act as a pathomechanism contributing to neurodegeneration in RTD.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is only possible through mutational analysis of all genes coding for riboflavin transporters. Biochemical tests can show abnormalities such as abnormal (MADD-like) plasma acylcarnitine profiles, abnormal urine organic acids and decreased plasma flavin levels; however, approximately 50% of patients have normal results. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is normal in the large majority of RTD patients. Electrophysiological testing (EMG) can show findings consistent with a sensorimotor axonal neuropathy with signs of anterior horn cell dysfunction, but normal results can also be observed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis include neuromuscular diseases, in particular congenital or mitochondrial myopath and rapidly progressive neuropathies.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible if family mutations in the SLC52A2 or SLC52A3 genes are known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Riboflavin supplementations is lifesaving and daily administration of a high dose oral riboflavin supplementation should be started immediately upon suspicion of RTD; treatment is lifelong. In cases with early onset, assisted ventilation, tracheostomy, and maintenance of nutrition via gastrostomy may be required. Regular clinical evaluation is required and includes neurological examination as well as evaluation of hearing and vision, respiratory function and skeletal deformities like scoliosis. Depending on the symptoms, physical and speech therapy should be initiated. Cochlear implants have proven highly successful for hearing loss in RTD.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: If untreated, RTD is progressive and often fatal, with respiratory insufficiency as the main cause of death. However, severity and rate of progression vary between patients. When treated with high doses of riboflavin, the majority of patients show improvement over time and early treatment may even result in full recovery and normal development. In contrast, patients with irreversible damage may show stabilization but no improvement of symptoms. No deaths have been reported in riboflavin-treated patients.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is a clinically heterogeneous, neurocutaneous genetic disorder characterized by café-au-lait spots, iris Lisch nodules, axillary and inguinal freckling, and multiple neurofibromas.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Nonmosaic neurofibromatosis type 1; Von Recklinghausen disease; Nonmosaic NF1

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is reported to be 1/3,000 live births. NF1 is reported in many ethnic groups and affects males and females equally.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical features are highly variable, even within the same family. Multiple café-au-lait macules are found in almost all patients (some at birth and most before the first year). Intertriginous freckling develops starting at 5 years of age. Multiple cutaneous and subcutaneous neurofibromas develop in adults. In older patients, they continue to increase in number and size. Cutaneous neurofibromas do not become malignant. Plexiform neurofibromas (growing along the nerve and its branches) may cause disfigurement, pain, and functional problems and are usually present at birth and may become malignant later in life. Ocular manifestations include optic pathway gliomas and iris hamartomas (Lisch nodules). Optic pathway gliomas usually develop before age 6 years, and rarely progress thereafter. Osteopenia, osteoporosis, bone overgrowth, short stature, macrocephaly, scoliosis, skeletal dysplasia (sphenoid wing, vertebral), and pseudoarthrosis may be present. Other features include hypertension, vasculopathy, intracranial tumors, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumor (MPNST), and occasionally seizures or hydrocephalus. Intellectual development is usually not severely affected but cognitive deficits and learning difficulties are frequent (50%-75%). The overall cancer risk is higher than the general population (lifetime risk of 10-12% for MPNST, mostly between 20-40 years; increased risk of breast cancer before age 50). Familial spinal and segmental forms of NF1 have been described. Watson syndrome forms part of the NF1 spectrum. Neurofibromatosis-Noonan syndrome is a variant of NF1 in 99% of cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: NF1 is caused by mutations in the tumor suppressor neurofibromin 1 NF1 gene (17q11.2) and rarely by 17q11 microdeletion (only 5%).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Formal diagnostic criteria have been established. 2 or more of the following are diagnostic: more than 5 café-au-lait macules, 2 or more neurofibromas or one plexiform neurofibroma, optic glioma, freckling, 2 or more Lisch nodules, specific bone dysplasias, first-degree relative. Magnetic resonance imaging can determine the extent of plexiform neurofibromas. Molecular genetic testing can be requested but is mostly not needed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Legius syndrome is often clinically indistinguishable from NF1 and is seen in about 2% of people fulfilling NF1 diagnostic criteria. There are however a small number of individuals with NF1 who like Legius syndrome patients do not develop non-pigmentary manifestations. Constitutional mismatch repair deficiency syndrome should be considered. Other differential diagnoses include McCune-Albright syndrome, Noonan syndrome with lentigines and Proteus syndrome. Most cases of multiple non-ossifying fibromatosis are cases of NF1.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing for at-risk pregnancies is possible
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The mode of inheritance is autosomal dominant. 1 in 2 cases is caused by de novo NF1 mutations. Penetrance is 100% but disease manifestations vary widely, complicating genetic counseling.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Specific cardiovascular, ocular, neurological and orthopedic manifestations should be treated by corresponding specialists. Cutaneous or subcutaneous neurofibromas can be removed surgically. Plexiform neurofibromas are far more difficult to treat.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Overall prognosis is good but significant morbidity is common. MPNST generally has a poor prognosis. Malignancy and vascular disease are the most common causes of early demise.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Short-limb skeletal dysplasia with severe combined immunodeficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An extremely rare type of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) characterized by the classical signs of T-B- SCID (severe and recurrent infections, diarrhea, failure to thrive, absence of T and B lymphocytes), associated with skeletal anomalies like short stature, bowing of the long bones and metaphyseal abnormalities of variable degree of severity.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Achondroplasia-SCID syndrome; Achondroplasia-Swiss type agammaglobulinemia syndrome; Achondroplasia-severe combined immunodeficiency syndrome; Immunodeficiency-short limb dwarfism syndrome; Short limb skeletal dysplasia with SCID

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: This is a rare condition, with a limited number of reported cases. The current report describes two patients. A review of previously published cases with severe combined immunodeficiency and documented skeletal findings identified eight patients with prenatal onset of bowing and shortening of extremities and metaphyseal abnormalities, including two sib pairs. An additional four published cases with associated adenosine deaminase deficiency were also noted. [PMC1016741]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Short-limb skeletal dysplasia with severe combined immunodeficiency is characterized by short stature, short-limbed dwarfism, and severe immune system dysfunction. Skeletal manifestations include rhizomelic shortening of the extremities, bowing of the femora, and sometimes spondylo-acrodysplasia, joint dislocations, or a small, malformed chest. Metaphyseal abnormalities can be present, though some cases show mild or no significant metaphyseal changes. Bone histopathology may reveal grossly irregular costochondral junctions. Clinical signs of severe combined immunodeficiency can develop early, leading to severe failure to thrive and early lethality in some patients. Late-onset aplastic anaemia has also been reported, and the presentation of immune dysfunction is variable. [PMC1735290, PMC1051096, PMC1016741]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Short-limb skeletal dysplasia with severe combined immunodeficiency, which also presents with bowing and late-onset aplastic anemia, is caused by novel mutations in the RMPR gene. [PMC1735290]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis is based on the characteristic clinical presentation, which includes short-limbed dwarfism, often with prenatal onset of bowing and shortening of the extremities, and severe combined immunodeficiency. Immune function tests, such as assessment of immunoglobulins, lymphocyte subpopulations, and lymphocyte function, are used to support the diagnosis of severe combined immunodeficiency, although can be variable. Bone histopathology may reveal grossly irregular costochondral junctions. Necropsy findings have also contributed to diagnosis. Furthermore, the identification of novel mutations in the RMPR gene indicates a genetic basis for the condition. [PMC1735290, PMC1051096, PMC1016741]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for short-limb skeletal dysplasia with severe combined immunodeficiency includes other immuno-osseous dysplasias. Conditions such as Schimke dysplasia, adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency with osseous changes, and Omenn phenotype with short limbed dwarfism should be considered. Notably, ADA deficiency cases may present with only mild metaphyseal abnormalities. A distinct spondylo-mesomelic-acrodysplasia with joint dislocations and severe combined immunodeficiency has also been recognized. Furthermore, Swiss-type agammaglobulinaemia combined with achondroplasia represents another reported association to differentiate. [PMC1051096, PMC1016741, PMC1944378]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Severe prenatal shortening and bowing of the extremities, along with a small, malformed chest, have been observed in affected individuals. Review of previously published cases also indicates prenatal onset of bowing and shortening of the extremities and metaphyseal abnormalities in some patients. [PMC1016741]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The condition is caused by novel mutations in the RMPR gene. Review of previously published cases, including two sib pairs concordant for skeletal changes, suggests an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. This implies a 25% recurrence risk for future offspring of carrier parents. [PMC1735290, PMC1016741]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for short-limb skeletal dysplasia with severe combined immunodeficiency is poor, often leading to early lethality. Two reported cases illustrate this, with one patient dying at 21 months and another at 5 months of age, both after developing severe combined immunodeficiency symptoms. The condition is characterized as an early lethal type 1 skeletal dysplasia. Some cases with associated adenosine deaminase deficiency also showed no linear growth. [PMC1016741]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare ectodermal dysplasia syndrome characterized by ectrodactyly, syndactyly, mammary hypoplasia, and excessive freckling as well as other typical ectodermal defects such as hypodontia, lacrimal duct anomalies, hypotrichosis, and onychodysplasia.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: ADULT syndrome is a TP63 gene disorder, often considered part of a broader ELA syndrome that includes EEC and LMS syndromes, all sharing similar features. Clinical manifestations observed in a patient diagnosed with ELA syndrome included ectrodactyly affecting the hands and feet, syndactyly of the feet, and abnormalities in tooth shape. [PMC7598809]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: ADULT syndrome is caused by a disorder of the TP63 gene. It shares similar features with EEC syndrome and limb-mammary syndrome, which are also TP63-related. A specific R319H mutation, identified as a heterozygous G>A transition at cDNA position 956 of the TP63 gene, was reported in a patient diagnosed with ELA syndrome, a combined entity encompassing ADULT syndrome. [PMC7598809]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of ADULT syndrome, often considered part of the broader ELA (EEC/LM/ADULT) syndrome, is established through a combination of clinical features and genetic analysis. Clinical presentation may include ectrodactyly, syndactyly, and tooth shape abnormalities. Definitive diagnosis involves mutation analysis of the TP63 gene, typically performed on peripheral blood samples, to identify specific mutations such as a heterozygous G>A transition at cDNA position 956. [PMC7598809]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: ADULT syndrome is closely related to Ectrodactyly ectodermal dysplasia-cleft lip/palate (EEC) syndrome and limb-mammary syndrome (LMS), as all three are caused by TP63 gene disorders and present with similar features. The concept of ELA syndrome, which unifies EEC, LMS, and ADULT syndromes into a single clinical entity, is useful for clinicians to better understand these TP63-related conditions and improve their differential diagnosis. [PMC7598809]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Rationale: Ectrodactyly ectodermal dysplasia-cleft lip/palate (EEC) syndrome, limb-mammary syndrome (LMS), and acro-dermato-ungual-lacrimal-tooth (ADULT) syndrome are caused by a TP63 gene disorder and have similar features. In the present article, a R319H mutation in TP63 is reported, and the correlation between genotype and phenotype is discussed based on the current case and previous literature. The patient was diagnosed with ELA (EEC/LM/ADULT) syndrome based on his clinical features and mutation analysis . Interventions: The patient underwent surgery to... [PMC7598809]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for ADULT syndrome, as described in a case report, involved surgical interventions to correct specific malformations. A patient underwent surgery for a left foot malformation at 1 year of age and for right foot syndactyly at 11 years of age. These operations were successful, with no complications reported, and allowed the patient to walk comfortably. No additional interventions were planned, but continued follow-up was maintained. [PMC7598809]
