Additionally, a left ventricular apical thrombus can mimic hypertrabeculation, which itself is a feature that needs careful differentiation from non-compaction. [PMC12233010, PMC11767094, PMC8355401]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of left ventricular noncompaction (LVNC) is possible, with cases of ventricular noncompaction (VNC) being managed in utero. VNC is defined by the presence of prominent ventricular trabeculations and deep intertrabecular recesses within the endomyocardium. The detection of ventricular tachycardia and complete heart block in utero may raise suspicion for conditions like Long QT syndrome, which can be associated with VNC. A suspected cardiomyopathy identified during the fetal period might also be misdiagnosed as LV non-compaction. [PMC12233010, PMC8116813]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for Left Ventricular Noncompaction (LVNC) is crucial due to its highly heterogeneous inheritance, most commonly autosomal dominant. Familial forms are important for risk prediction and counseling of relatives. Genetic testing is recommended for accurate diagnosis and care, with various genes implicated, including TTN, MYH7, DSG2, TBX20, DES, MTUS1, TPM1, ERBB2, SLC22A5, and FHOD3. However, not all LVNC cases have a genetic predisposition, as reversible forms without identified genetic variants exist. Some genetic variants may also require additional factors for clinical manifestation. Genetic counseling is also relevant for pregnancy planning in affected women. [PMC11854591, PMC12145837, PMC11641563, PMC10969955, PMC10646383]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Ring chromosome 7 syndrome is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, with highly variable phenotype, principally characterized by growth failure, short stature, intellectual disability, dermatological abnormalities (nevus flammeus, dark pigmented nevi, café-au-lait spots), microcephaly and facial dysmorphism (incl. facial asymmetry, small ears, abnormal palpebral fissures, ptosis, epicanthic folds, hyper/hypotelorism). Additional reported features include convulsions, cleft lip and palate, clinodactyly, kyphoscoliosis and genital anomalies (i.e. cryptorchidism, hypospadias, micropenis).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Ring chromosome 7 syndrome is a rare condition, with early reports describing a limited number of cases. In 1990, clinical findings were compared with five other reported cases of ring chromosome 7. By 2011, at least 19 cases of complete ring chromosome 7 mosaicism had been reported, including the first survived case with mosaic supernumerary ring 7 without a normal karyotype detected in peripheral lymphocytes. Specific cases have been documented in a newborn girl, a 22-year-old man, and a 39-year-old man. [PMC9351601, PMC3045371, PMC1017186]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Ring chromosome 7 syndrome is characterized by multiple congenital anomalies and developmental delay or mental retardation. Patients often exhibit prenatal onset growth deficiency, bone anomalies, and various dysmorphic features, including facial dysmorphism. Skin manifestations are common, presenting as pigmentary or vascular changes, an increased incidence of hemangiomas, café-au-lait spots, and melanocytic nevi. Some melanocytic nevi, such as desmoplastic Spitz nevi, may harbor BRAF fusions, potentially due to the instability of the ring chromosome. Ocular and genital anomalies are also reported. [PMC9351601, PMC3045371, PMC1017186]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Ring chromosome 7 syndrome is characterized by the presence of a ring chromosome 7, which can be unstable. In one reported case of de novo mosaic ring chromosome 7, the distal arm of chromosome 7p (at least 255 kb from the telomere) was part of an extra ring chromosome 7, and the distal arm of 7q (at least 8 kb from the telomere) was missing. The instability of the ring chromosome 7 may increase the likelihood of BRAF fusions, which can contribute to an increased incidence of melanocytic nevi in affected individuals. [PMC9351601, PMC3045371, PMC1017186]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of ring chromosome 7 syndrome primarily relies on cytogenetic and molecular cytogenetic investigations. Karyotyping and conventional cytogenetics are employed to identify chromosomal abnormalities, including the presence of a ring chromosome. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a crucial technique, used to characterize supernumerary ring marker chromosomes, determine their origin, and investigate the size of fragments lost at the distal ends of chromosome 7. Multicolour banding can further rule out structural rearrangements within the ring chromosome, and chromosome painting with chromosome-specific libraries confirms the involvement of specific chromosomes. While routine chromosome banding analysis may be insufficient for definitive identification, these advanced provide detailed characterization. Phenotypic evaluation also contributes to assessing developmental status. [PMC9351601, PMC3702848, PMC3777464, PMC3045371, PMC1682354]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: A 13 year old girl was referred with congenital microcephaly, developmental delay, a prominent nose, highly arched palate, and an apparently low set left ear. She was found to have a pericentric inversion of one chromosome 7 and a ring chromosome 8, 46,XX,inv(7) (pter----p22::q11.23----p22::q11.23----qter), r(8) (p23q24.3). The concurrence of these two abnormalities is a rare event and has not been reported previously. [PMC1015827]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for ring chromosome 7 syndrome addresses its diverse clinical manifestations and origin. Patients may present with prenatal onset growth deficiency, bone anomalies, pigmentary or vascular skin changes, and ocular and genital anomalies. An increased incidence of hemangiomas, café-au-lait spots, and melanocytic nevi has also been observed, possibly due to BRAF fusions arising from the instability of the ring chromosome 7. Molecular cytogenetic analysis can identify the chromosomal abnormality, with some cases, such as mosaic supernumerary ring chromosome 7, reported as de novo, indicating a sporadic occurrence. [PMC9351601, PMC3045371, PMC1017186]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Patients with ring chromosome 7 syndrome can survive into adulthood, with reported cases of individuals living to 22 and 39 years of age. However, the condition is associated with significant challenges, including prenatal onset growth deficiency, developmental delay, mental retardation, and multiple congenital anomalies such as bone, ocular, and genital anomalies, as well as pigmentary or vascular skin changes and facial dysmorphism. Survival can be precarious, as evidenced by a reported case being the first to survive with mosaic supernumerary ring chromosome 7 without a normal karyotype in peripheral lymphocytes. Furthermore, in the context of acute myeloid leukemia, the presence of deletion 7q along with a ring chromosome is considered a high cytogenetic-risk factor with a poor prognosis. [PMC9351601, PMC3702848, PMC3045371, PMC1017186]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Malakoplakia is a chronic multisystem granulomatous inflammatory disease characterized by the presence of single or multiple soft plaques on various organs of the body.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown but more than 700 cases have been described in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Malakoplakia can occur in all ages, with a mean age at diagnosis of 50 years old and a female predominance. Pediatric cases are rare. It is most common in immunodeficient patients with a history of diabetes, transplantation, lymphoma, steroid therapy or alcoholism. In the majority of cases (60-80%), malakoplakia affects the urinary tract (bladder, kidney, and ureters) and cases of locoregional extension have been reported (retroperitoneal region and lymph nodes). Other organs can also be involved, with the gastrointestinal system (left colon, sigmoid, rectum, stomach) being the second most common site (15%). Other sites include the genital tract, skin, neck, tongue, lungs, and central nervous system. Patients are either asymptomatic or present with clinical symptoms that are non specific (fever, pain) and that vary depending on the organ involved. In case of urinary tract involvement, patients generally present with chronic urinary tract infections and symptoms such as urinary urgency, hesitancy, intermittent dysuria, hematuria, and proteinuria. In case of gastrointestinal involvement, patients can present with symptoms such as recurrent diarrhea, dyspepsia, abdominal pain, and hemorrhage. In case of malakoplakia of the female genital tract, patients usually present with vaginal bleeding. Cutaneous malakoplakia presents as papules or ulcerations on various locations (abdomen, face, perianal region) associated with rash and itching. Malakoplakia can also be associated with other granulomatous diseases such as sarcoidosis and tuberculosis, and with carcinomas (prostate and colorectal carcinomas).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Malakoplakia seems to be due to an impaired response to bacterial infection. Macrophages and monocytes show a defective phagolysosomal activity: they phagocytose bacteria but are unable to digest them completely. Partially digested bacteria accumulate in the cytoplasm and lead to a granulomatous reaction of the immune cells. It has been suggested that the defective phagolysosomal activity could be due to a decrease in the concentration of intracellular cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of malakoplakia is difficult due to the absence of specific clinical symptoms and no specific characterization in imaging. Diagnosis is based on endoscopy which reveals the presence of vascularized yellowish or white polypoid nodules or plaques. The diagnosis is confirmed by biopsy of the affected tissue. Histological examination reveals the presence of von Hansemann cells (histiocytes with small nuclei and granular acidophilic cytoplasm) with Michaelis-Gutmann bodies (periodic acid-Schiff and von Kossa positive calcific inclusions). This lesion is pathognomonic for malakoplakia. Michaelis-Gutmann bodies probably correspond to partially digested calcified bacterial inclusions.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Depending on the organ involved, differential diagnoses include primary or metastatic malignancies, inflammatory diseases (sarcoidosis, Crohn's disease), infections (tuberculosis, Whipple disease), and cutaneous fungal infections.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment consists in antibiotherapy that uses intracellular molecules (fluoroquinolones, trimethroprim-sulfametoxazol). Currently, the duration of therapy is still not standardized. In pseudo-tumoral cases, surgical removal of the lesions is required.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is usually good. However, recurrences and complications may occur over the years such as renal failure in case of urinary tract involvement.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Malakoplakia is a rare condition characterized by inflammatory masses with specific histological characteristics. These soft tissue masses can mimic tumors and tend to develop in association with chronic or recurrent infections, typically of the urinary tract. A specific defect in innate immunity has been described. In the absence of randomized controlled trials, management is based on an understanding of the biology and on case reports. Here a case of presacral malakoplakia in a British Indian woman in her late 30s, presenting with complex unilateral foot drop. Four years earlier, she had suffered a protracted episode of intrapelvic sepsis following a caesarean delivery. Resection of her presacral soft tissue mass was not possible. She received empiric antibiotics, a cholinergic agonist, and ascorbic acid. She responded well to medical management both when first treated and following a... [PMC10080903]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by growth retardation, alopecia, pseudoanodontia and ocular manifestations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Approximately 60 patients with GAPO syndrome have been reported in literature since the first description in 1947.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients have a short stature, growth retardation and a typical facies with high and bossing forehead, hypertelorism, puffy eyelids, midfacial hypoplasia, depressed nasal bridge, anteverted wide nostrils, thick and everted lower lip, micrognathia, protruding, low-set and folded ears, and premature aging appearance mainly due to redundant hyperelastic skin with unusual wrinkles. Scalp hair may be primarily present but disappears after the first months of life resulting in complete or partial alopecia. Eyebrows and/or eyelashes are sparse or in some cases absent. Primary and permanent teeth are formed but fail to erupt. Ocular manifestations may include progressive optic atrophy, glaucoma, strabismus, photophobia, megalocornea, myelinated retinal nerve fiber layer, bilateral keratoconus, nystagmus and ptosis. Otorhinolaryngological features are choanal atresia, deafness and presence of flaccid and pulsatile masses with an audible murmur in the mastoid area associated with dilated and tortuous scalp veins. Patients have a mild intellectual deficit. Some patients have also been reported with umbilical hernia, hyperextensible joints, osseous anomalies (congenital dislocation of hips or delayed bone age) and cutaneous manifestations (hemangioma or depigmented areas). Other manifestations include intracranial hypertension in infancy, hypothyroidism, mitral valve dysfunction or cardiomyopathy, pulmonary diseases, headache, hepatomegaly, renal impairment and altered gonadal functions (irregular periods or amenorrhea, oligoasthenospermia). Cryptorchidism, ankyloglossia and hearing loss is also reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Homozygous nonsense or splicing mutations in the ANTXR1 gene (2p13.3), encoding anthrax toxin receptor 1, also known as tumor endothelial marker 8 (TEM8) causes GAPO Syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis mostly relies on physical and ophtamologic examination. Additionally skin biopsy, cerebral angiography and magnetic resonance imaging contribute to more specific diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes cerebral alterations and cutaneous manifestations such as prominent cortical veins, occluded or absent left transverse sinus and left sigmoid sinus, agenesis of left jugular vein, prominent scalp veins, dermis anomalies including amorphous hyaline substance, and pyoderma vegetans.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is not possible from fetal ultrasound (US). In utero growth retardation may be observed on US but is not specific.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them of that the risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy is 25%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative treatment. Management mostly relies on ophthalmologic surveillance and symptomatic treatment of the multiple health problems.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: GAPO patients are reported to have a reduced lifespan (until the fourth to sixth decade of life).

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic multisystem disorder characterized by progressive pancytopenia with bone marrow failure, variable congenital malformations and predisposition to develop hematological or solid tumors.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The expected prevalence at birth is at least 1/160,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The first signs of Fanconi anemia (FA) are typically non-hematological features. Limb anomalies typically affect the extremities, are unilateral or (usually asymmetric) bilateral. Minor anomalies can also be present such as low birth length and weight, microcephaly and/or microphthalmia. Skin pigmentation abnormalities (café-au-lait spots) and hypoplastic thenar eminence are frequent. Almost 20% of patients have ear malformations with or without hearing loss. Congenital malformations may involve other organ systems and vary within families. Short stature is syndromic and/or associated to endocrinopathies. Fertility is frequently impaired in males, and is highly disturbed in half of females. When congenital malformations are not prominent, diagnosis may be delayed until the onset of hematological anomalies. Bone marrow failure (BMF) occurs at a median age of 7 years, developing in 90% of patients by 40 years of age. The first manifestations are macrocytosis (very early) and thrombocytopenia. In patients with somatic mosaïcism, blood counts may stay normal until occurrence of hematological malignancy. In general, patients are highly predisposed to solid tumors (most frequently head and neck or anogenital regions).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FA is genetically heterogeneous and the implicated variants are involved in DNA repair and genomic stability. More than 90% of patients have mutations within FANCA, FANCC, FANCG or FANCD2 genes. Mutations in genes with an upstream role in the FA-core complex are associated with classic FA. Some of ''Downstream'' variants (e.g.BRCA2) are associated with a very high risk of solid tumors in infancy and early childhood.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on the evaluation of chromosomal breakage induced by diepoxybutane (DEB) or mitomycin C (MMC). This test may be normal in patients with somatic mosaicism; in which case, tests should be performed on fibroblasts.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: FA clinical manifestations overlap with many malformation syndromes (Dubowitz, Seckel, Holt-Oram, Baller-Gerold, thrombocytopenia-absent radius, Nijmegen breakage syndromes, VACTERL association, dyskeratosis congenital, Blackfan-Diamond anemia) and diagnosis of FA is often delayed until a patient develops BMF or malignancies. FA should be considered in the differential diagnosis of all young patients with BMF of unknown etiology, and in other cancer predisposition syndromes (Bloom, Rothmund-Thomson or Werner syndromes) or syndromes with either constitutional or acquired BMF.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is feasible with a chromosomal breakage assay on fetal blood or, when the mutation is known, by genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is usually autosomal recessive. Very rarely, X-linked (FANCB, < 1%) or autosomal dominant (FANCR, <1%) transmission may occur. If the variant is known, medical assisted reproduction should be offered to parents.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Supportive care includes transfusions of packed red blood cells (RBC) or leucodepleted platelets but if regular transfusion is required, hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) should be considered. Currently, the only curative treatment for hematologic manifestations is HSCT. Symptomatic treatment includes oral androgen administration, which improves blood counts in most patients but is associated with severe liver toxicity and does not suppress the leukemic risk. Administration of G-CSF, best after bone marrow aspirate, should be considered in patients with acute severe infections. Regular screening for hematological malignancies is recommended during childhood in non-transplanted patients; with the exception of 1q anomalies, identification of a clonal event should lead to transplantation. Screening for solid tumors should start in adolescence, especially in the post-transplant setting; risk may be higher in patients with chronic GVHD. Any suspect lesion should be biopsied. When malignancies develop, treatment is complicated by the sensitivity to radiation and chemotherapy of FA patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: HSCT efficiently treats BMF. Solid tumors prevention and treatment are the main challenge for transplanted patients.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome is a very rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the combination of progressive cerebellar ataxia with onset from early childhood to the fourth decade, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (delayed puberty and lack of secondary sex characteristics). Cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome belongs to a clinical continuum of neurodegenerative disorders along with clinically overlapping disorders such as ataxia-hypogonadism-choroidal dystrophy syndrome.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Gordon-Holmes syndrome; Luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone deficiency with ataxia

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome, also known as Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome, is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the PNPLA6 gene. It is considered a distinct pleiotropic single gene disorder. The syndrome is still poorly recognized, with few cases reported in the literature, including familial cases and those from consanguineous families. Its autosomal recessive inheritance pattern has been observed in multiple affected families. [PMC8859865, PMC6070386, PMC1051065, PMC1083171, PMC1048753]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome, also known as Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome (BNHS), is a rare autosomal recessive disorder primarily characterized by chorioretinal dystrophy (or retinal pigmentary degeneration), hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and cerebellar dysfunction, ataxia, and atrophy. Patients often present with progressive night blindness, primary amenorrhea, and undeveloped secondary sexual characteristics, with neurological deterioration and progressive cerebellar atrophy noted over time. The hypogonadism stems from pituitary gonadotrophin deficiency or hypothalamic LHRH deficiency. While commonly associated with biallelic pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 gene, genetic heterogeneity exists, with some cases linked to de novo HK1 gene variants. Other reported features include short stature, hypersegmented neutrophils, mental retardation, hearing loss, and ectodermal abnormalities. [PMC12176038, PMC8859865, PMC8485629, PMC1735249, PMC1051065]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome, also known as Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome (BNHS), is a rare pleiotropic single gene disorder with an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. It is primarily caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 gene. Genetic heterogeneity has been observed, with a de novo variant in the HK1 gene also identified in an individual presenting with a BNHS-consistent phenotype. The hypogonadism associated with the syndrome can stem from either pituitary gonadotrophin deficiency or a primary hypothalamic disturbance. [PMC12176038, PMC8859865, PMC8485629, PMC1735249, PMC1051065]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome, including Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome, involves clinical evaluation, genetic testing, and endocrinological assessment. Clinically, the syndrome is characterized by cerebellar ataxia, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and often chorioretinal dystrophy, with other features like night blindness, impaired vision, and primary amenorrhea. Gene sequencing, particularly whole-exome sequencing, is the primary diagnostic method to identify pathogenic variants in genes such as PNPLA6, HK1, or SQSTM1, with Sanger sequencing for confirmation and RNA-sequencing for expression analysis. Endocrinological evaluation includes measuring plasma gonadotrophin levels and performing LHRH and TRH stimulation tests to assess for pituitary or hypothalamic dysfunction. Imaging, such as CT scans, may reveal cerebellar and brain stem atrophy. [PMC12176038, PMC8859865, PMC8485629, PMC6070386, PMC1051065]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome includes several conditions where ataxia is associated with hypogonadism. Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome (BNHS) is a key consideration, characterized by chorioretinal dystrophy, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and cerebellar dysfunction and atrophy, and is associated with PNPLA6 or HK1 gene variants. Other entities presenting with ataxia and hypogonadism include Gordon-Holmes syndrome, Marinesco-Sjögren syndrome, and Perrault syndrome. Rare conditions like mitochondrial disorders and Woodhouse-Sakati syndrome may also present with hypogonadism alongside other movement disorders. Additionally, a distinct syndrome involving olivopontocerebellar degeneration, hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism, short stature, and ectodermal features should be considered. [PMC12176038, PMC8859865, PMC8485629, PMC1735249, PMC1051065]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome, particularly Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome, is primarily inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, often caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 gene. However, genetic heterogeneity exists, as de novo variants in the HK1 gene can also present with a similar phenotype, including hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and cerebellar atrophy. Gene sequencing is the primary diagnostic method for identifying these genetic causes. For individuals with HK1 variants, evaluation for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is recommended, as it may be amenable to treatment. The autosomal recessive inheritance pattern implies that unaffected parents of an affected individual are typically carriers. [PMC12176038, PMC8859865, PMC1051065, PMC1083171, PMC1048753]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Individuals with variants in HK1, presenting with cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome, should undergo evaluation for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, as this specific component of the syndrome is potentially amenable to treatment. [PMC12176038]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Longitudinal follow-up of individuals with Cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome (Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome) indicates neurological deterioration, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and progressive cerebellar atrophy. While hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is a feature that may be amenable to treatment, the overall neurological course is one of decline. [PMC12176038]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Monosomy 21 is a chromosomal anomaly characterized by the loss of variable portions of a segment of the long arm of chromosome 21 that leads to an increased risk of birth defects, developmental delay and intellectual deficit.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Monosomy 21 is a very rare condition with less than 50 cases described in the literature. Full monosomy 21 is probably not compatible with life.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The severity of the phenotype depends on the location and size of the deleted area. In general, proximal and distal deletions lead to a milder phenotype (e.g. few dysmorphic features or congenital anomalies, and mild to moderate intellectual deficit), whereas deletions involving band 21q22 have a more severe effect on the phenotype. In the later case, the most common clinical features include intrauterine and postnatal growth retardation, microcephaly, prominent occiput, and facial dysmorphism characterized by up or down-slanted small palpebral fissures, prominent nasal bridge with a broad nose, and large ears. Multiple malformations including structural brain malformations (e.g. cerebral atrophy, cortical dysplasia, and corpus callosum dysgenesis) and heart defects (e.g. patent ductus arteriosus, septal defects) are also frequently observed. Severe intellectual deficit is common. Joints may be stiff and held in an unusual position. Abnormal muscle tone, respiratory infections and seizures are usual. Specific blood disorders (e.g. thrombocytopenia, myelodysplasia) have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is due to the loss of variable portions of the long arm of chromosome 21. Partial 21q deletions are interstitial or terminal. They occur de novo or as the result of a parental rearrangement. Monosomy due to malsegregation of a parental rearrangement is usually associated with another imbalance that could complicate the phenotype. Some cases result from formation of a ring chromosome 21.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical findings that lead to chromosomal analysis. Depending on their size, partial 21q deletions may be diagnosed by classical or molecular karyotyping. Molecular techniques are necessary for the genetic characterization of the deletion.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis of 21q deletion is possible by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling and cytogenetic analysis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The risk of having another affected child is higher if a chromosomal rearrangement is present in one of the parents.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is multi-disciplinary and requires evaluation and treatment by a general pediatrician, and relevant specialists. Children will benefit from early assessment and access to the major developmental therapies. Physiotherapy may be important to improve both the muscle tone and the joints flexibility.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the size and location of the deletion. It is severe if band 21q22 is involved, with vital prognosis depending on the severity of congenital malformations.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: 21q deletion syndrome can mimic hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) in newborns, presenting with similar features such as severe hypotonia, respiratory and feeding difficulties, intractable seizures, and radiologic findings of ischemic encephalopathy, which can lead to initial misdiagnosis. Neonatal encephalopathy, caused by metabolic disorders, congenital infections, or other genetic abnormalities, can also present with HIE-like features. Therefore, careful evaluation of clinical course and multidisciplinary assessment, including genetic testing, are crucial to differentiate 21q deletion syndrome from these conditions. [PMC10529320]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal anomaly characterized by variable clinical features, including early growth retardation and short stature, microcephaly, developmental delay, some degree of intellectual disability, facial dysmorphism and café-au-lait spots. In some cases, congenital heart disease and endocrine abnormalities have been reported.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): RC11; r(11) syndrome; Ring chromosome 11; Ring 11

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Ring chromosome 11 syndrome is characterized by mental retardation, microcephaly, and short stature. In one reported case, a Wilm's tumour developed at 8 months of age. Cytogenetic analysis in reported cases showed karyotypes such as 46,XX,r(11)(p15 X 4q2 X 5) or 46,XY,r(11)(p15q25), with some cases demonstrating minimal chromosome deletion. [PMC1049155]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Ring chromosome 11 syndrome is characterized by the presence of a ring chromosome 11, which represents a complex structural rearrangement. Cytogenetic analyses, including G banding, Q banding, and FISH, are used to identify this chromosomal abnormality. While some cases show no visible loss of chromatin, others present with minimal chromosome deletion. This condition has been reported in individuals with developmental features such as mental retardation, microcephaly, and short stature, and can also be associated with acute myeloid leukemia or Wilm's tumour. [PMC9881703, PMC1049155]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of ring chromosome 11 involves cytogenetic analysis. Classical and molecular cytogenetic analyses, utilizing techniques such as GTG banding, high resolution G banding, Q banding, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), are employed to identify and characterize the presence of ring chromosome 11. These can reveal complex structural rearrangements and minimal chromosome deletions. Molecular cytogenetic analysis is suitable for better identification and characterization of these chromosomal rearrangements. [PMC9881703, PMC1049155]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Two cases of ring chromosome 11 are reported. Both had mental retardation, microcephaly, and short stature. High resolution G banding in case 1 showed no visible loss of chromatin, the karyotype being assessed as 46,XX,r(11) (p15 X 4q2 X 5). In case 2, a Wilm's tumour developed at 8 months and the child died at 18 months. Cytogenetic analysis by Q banding demonstrated minimal chromosome deletion and the karyotype was considered to be 46,XY,r(11) (p15q25). [PMC1049155]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Context: Complex karyotypes in acute myeloid leukemia (AML) are characterized by an overall low response rate with frequent relapses after clinical treatment. Here, the case of a 61-year-old obese female with clinically diagnosed AML who presented a complex karyotype involving an uncommon abnormality: ring chromosome 11. Immunophenotypic analysis confirmed the diagnosis. Classical and molecular cytogenetic analyses, using GTG banding and FISH (fluorescence in situ hybridization), revealed the presence of complex structural rearrangement involving r(11), add(12)(p13), der(5) and der(13). Molecular cytogenetic analysis is suitable for better identification and characterization of chromosomal rearrangements in AML. Case reports like this, as well as population-based studies, are necessary for understanding the karyotypic changes that occur in humans. [PMC9881703]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for individuals with ring chromosome 11 syndrome can be severe. Reported cases include features such as mental retardation, microcephaly, and short stature. A serious complication observed was the development of a Wilm's tumour, which led to death at 18 months in one patient. Furthermore, ring chromosome 11 can be part of complex karyotypes in acute myeloid leukemia, which are characterized by an overall low response rate and frequent relapses after clinical treatment. [PMC9881703, PMC1049155]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A group of hematologic diseases characterized by impaired late-stage erythropoiesis and abnormal erythroid precursors, leading to chronic anemia of variable severity.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The global prevalence of congenital dyserythropoietic anemia (CDA) is unknown. Between 1967 and 2024, >300 CDA I, >400 CDA II, and 60 CDA III clinically suspected cases were reported worldwide. About 11 cases of CDA type IV and 10 cases of thrombocytopenia with CDA (XLTDA) have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease severity ranges from hydrops fetalis or severe transfusion dependency in infancy or childhood to minimal or no anemia in adulthood. Onset typically occurs in childhood or early adulthood, though signs may occasionally appear neonatally. Patients present with chronic anemia of variable severity, relative reticulocytopenia, cholelithiasis, jaundice, and often splenomegaly and/or hepatomegaly. Symptoms include fatigue, poor growth in infants, headache, dizziness, leg cramps, tachycardia, and insomnia. Most patients develop secondary hemochromatosis due to ineffective erythropoiesis, worsened by transfusions and hemolysis. CDAs are classically divided into three subtypes (CDA I, II, III) based on bone marrow morphology, though additional variants exist (notably CDA IV and XLTDA). Erythropoiesis is always impaired, with erythroblast anomalies and erythroid hyperplasia. Except for XLTDA, nonerythroid lineages are generally unaffected.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CDA I is caused by mutations in CDAN1, encoding a histone chaperone-interacting protein, or in CDIN1, encoding an endonuclease putatively involved in DNA replication or chromatin assembly. CDA II results from mutations in SEC23B, encoding a COPII vesicle component essential for endoplasmic reticulum-Golgi trafficking. Dominant CDA III is linked to KIF23, encoding a centralspindlin kinesin subunit regulating cytokinesis, while the recessive form involves RACGAP1, encoding a Rac GTPase-activating protein that dimerizes with KIF23. CDA IV and XLTDA result from mutations in the erythroid transcription factors genes KLF1 and GATA1.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis involves three lines of investigation. First, hematochemical parameters, hemolysis markers, iron balance, and personal/family history are assessed. Second, biochemical tests and especially bone marrow smear analysis are performed. While all CDA subtypes show erythroid hyperplasia and bi-/multi-nucleated precursors, each has specific features (see dedicated pages). Third, genetic testing is conducted, mainly using multi-gene panels.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: CDAs have traditionally been classified by bone marrow morphological abnormalities, but these are often nonspecific, reflecting underlying defective erythropoiesis. Similar erythroid changes can appear in other hereditary red cell disorders, such as thalassemias or enzyme deficiencies. Misdiagnoses are common, particularly between CDA I and hereditary stomatocytosis, and between CDA II and hereditary spherocytosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible where the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: CDA I and CDA II follow an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, while CDA III can be inherited in either a dominant or recessive manner. CDA IV is inherited as an autosomal dominant condition. Thrombocytopenia with CDA shows an X-linked inheritance. Genetic counseling is available for all CDA types.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management typically involves monitoring of complete blood count and iron status. In cases of severe anemia, transfusions remain the mainstay of treatment. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may be considered in severe forms. Iron overload is managed with iron chelation therapy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The overall prognosis is good, with normal life expectancy. However, quality of life may be impacted by complications related to iron overload.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital progressive muscular dystrophy often characterized by brain malformation (cobblestone lissencephaly), dystrophic changes in skeletal muscle, severe intellectual deficit, epilepsy and motor impairment.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): FCMD; Fukuyama congenital muscular dystrophy; FKTN-related congenital muscular dystrophy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The disease has a high prevalence in the Japanese population due to an ancestral mutation, and is extremely uncommon elsewhere. The prevalence of Fukuyama type muscular dystrophy (FCMD) in Japan is estimated at 1/25,000-50,000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset typically occurs in early infancy. Initial symptoms include a poor suck, weak cry, floppiness and developmental delay. Symmetrical generalized muscle weakness and hypotonia are present. With time, patients develop retractile phenotype and show contractures of the hips, knees and interphalangeal joints. Later features include myopathic facial appearance, pseudohypertrophy of the calves and forearms, and ophthalmologic abnormalities (visual impairment and retinal dysplasia). Progressive cardiac involvement, respiratory failure and swallowing and feeding disturbances (leading to recurrent aspiration pneumonia and death) occur in infants with severe FCMD and in patients over ten years of age. Seizures (generalized tonic-clonic convulsions, complex partial seizures and partial seizures with secondary generalization, infantile spasms, tonic seizures and myoclonic seizures) occur in over 50% of affected individuals (median age of seizure onset 1-3 years of age). All patients with the Japanese ancestral mutation show severe intellectual deficit and the intelligence quotient (IQ) is usually between 30 and 60.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: It is caused by mutations in the fukutin gene (FKTN; 9q31-q33). Of note, FKTN variants are responsible for a clinical spectrum ranging from CMD without brain involvement to isolated, dilated cardiomyopathy.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on the clinical picture, characteristic neuroimaging and electromyography findings, muscle biopsy results, and molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophies, and other muscular dystrophies associating a type II lissencephaly (known as dystroglycanopathies). Brain, cerebellar and ocular abnormalities observed in most FCMD patients are similar to and would be diagnosed out of Japan as MEB syndrome. Therefore, there is an increasing tendency to use the global term MEB/FCMD syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible where the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management includes physiotherapy, treatment of orthopedic, respiratory and cardiac complications, respiratory aid, and medical or surgical treatment for nutritional and gastrointestinal problems. Control of seizures requires antiepileptic drugs. Surveillance includes monitoring for respiratory and cardiac function.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of complications, mainly neurologic, cardiac or respiratory.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Early infantile developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A severe form of age-related epileptic encephalopathies characterized by the onset of tonic spasms within the first 3 months of life that can be generalized or lateralized, independent of the sleep cycle, and that can occur hundreds of times per day, leading to psychomotor impairment and death.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Early infantile epileptic encephalopathy with suppression-bursts; Ohtahara syndrome; EIDEE
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Incidence has been estimated at 1/100 000 births in Japan and 1/50,000 births in the U.K.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset of EIEE occurs within the first 3 months of life but some present within the first few weeks after birth. Neonates have poor suckling reflexes, hypotonia and manifest with generalized and symmetrical tonic spasms that can appear in clusters or singly and can last for up to 10 seconds. The pattern of these spasms remains unchanged during wakefulness and sleep and they can occur hundreds of times per day. Other seizure types, including generalized tonic-clonic seizures, focal motor seizures and hemiconvulsions, are seen in 1/3 of cases. Those who live past the age of 2 years manifest with severe psychomotor deficits. In some, EIEE can transition into West syndrome (between 2-6 months of age) and later into Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Certain genetic variants manifest with additional signs such as dyskinetic movements and an atypical Rett-syndrome phenotype. Death is often due to pneumonia or other complications of a complex disability.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: EIEE may be the result of different etiologies. Many cases have been associated with structural brain abnormalities. Some cases are due to metabolic disorders (cytochrome C oxidase deficiency, carnitine palmitoyl transferase II deficiency) or brain malformations (such as porencephaly, hemimegalencephaly) that may or not be genetic in origin. Genetic variants of EIEE have been associated with mutations in certain genes such as ARX (Xp22.13) , CDKL5 (Xp22) , SL25A22 (11p15.5) and STXBP1 (9q34.1), among others. The genetic abnormalities are thought to lead to EIEE as they are related to neuronal dysfunction or brain dysgenesis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical and electroencephalographic findings. The characteristic electroencephalogram (EEG) displays a suppression burst pattern (which appears with the onset of spasms) that is comprised of bursts of high amplitude spikes and polyspikes that alternate with periods of low voltage basic rhythm (suppression). This EEG pattern is continuous and remains unchanged during both waking and sleeping states. Structural abnormalities can often be seen on cranial MRI.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other epileptic encephalopathies such as early myoclonic encephalopathy, West syndrome and other early onset epileptic encephalopathies.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible in families with a known genetic etiology.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Autosomal recessive inheritance has been reported, but most cases of EIEE are sporadic (de novo mutations). Genetic counseling is therefore very valuable to inform parents that their risk of having further children with EIEE is low.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for EIEE and patients require constant supervision and care. Antiepileptic drugs such as benzodiazepines, valproate, levetiracetam, zonisamide and phenobarbital have shown limited success in controlling seizures as has pyridoxine. A ketogenic diet has been reported to show some success in seizure control. In those with associated metabolic disorders, once these conditions have been treated there can be an improvement in the course of EIEE. Similarly, EIEE patients with certain structural abnormalities have benefited from surgical intervention, if unilateral.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor with death usually occurring in infancy (50% before age of 2). Survivors have severe psychomotor impairments with continuing seizures.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect (PA-VSD) is a rare cyanotic congenital heart malformation characterized by underdevelopment of the right ventricular outflow tract and atresia of the pulmonary valve, ventricular septal defect (VSD) and pulmonary collateral vessels. Clinical features depend on the anatomic variability of the lesion and patients may be minimally symptomatic, severely cyanotic or may develop congestive heart failure. PA-VSD may represent a severe form of Tetralogy of Fallot.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect, particularly with coronary-to-pulmonary artery fistula (CPF), is a rare disease. A review of 69 cases from 42 studies revealed an equal male-to-female ratio. Only 3% of these patients exhibited 22q11.2 microdeletion syndrome. Diagnosis of CPF in this population occurred at 0 years of age in 39% of patients, with 10% diagnosed in adulthood. [PMC9867298]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect (PA/VSD) presents with a wide variety of pulmonary and coronary artery abnormalities. These include coronary-to-pulmonary artery fistula (CPAF), which can be diagnosed prenatally or in adulthood, and unilateral or discontinuous pulmonary arteries, where origins may vary (e.g., right pulmonary artery from the right coronary artery, left pulmonary artery from the ductus arteriosus or left subclavian artery). Other associated features can include major aortopulmonary collateral arteries, double aortic arch, or right aortic arch. While rare, 22q11.2 microdeletion syndrome and Takotsubo cardiomyopathy in toddlers have been reported. Adult patients, particularly those who missed early corrective surgery, are prone to progressive aortic dilation, aneurysm, or dissection, and may experience cardiac dysfunction due to myocardial ischemia. Some individuals with unrepaired PA/VSD can survive into adulthood. [PMC11734237, PMC9867298, PMC9260803, PMC9226865, PMC8019495]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect (PAVSD) is associated with various anatomical malformations. The 22q11.2 microdeletion syndrome has been identified in a small percentage of patients. Other associated anomalies include coronary-to-pulmonary artery fistulas, often originating from the left coronary artery, and other major aortopulmonary collateral arteries. Patients may also present with pulmonary ductal coarctation, unilateral or discontinuous pulmonary arteries, where one or both pulmonary arteries may arise from alternative sources like the ductus arteriosus, subclavian artery, or coronary arteries. A double aortic arch can also be associated with PAVSD. [PMC9867298, PMC9291456, PMC8019495, PMC5062698, PMC1524706]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect includes other complex congenital heart defects. Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) is a key consideration, often presenting with inadequate pulmonary blood flow and major aortopulmonary collateral arteries (MAPCA) or an aorto-pulmonary window. Dextro-transposition of the great arteries (D-TGA) with a ventricular septal defect and pulmonary atresia is another related conotruncal abnormality. Other conditions include double outlet right ventricle with pulmonary atresia, and pulmonary atresia with intact ventricular septum (PAIVS), which can cause left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. [PMC11743443, PMC8787576, PMC9291456, PMC8218086, PMC4521333]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Prenatal diagnosis of pulmonary atresia with ventricular septect defect (PA/VSD) is possible, primarily through fetal echocardiography. This condition presents with a wide range of pulmonary and coronary artery abnormalities, including rare manifestations like coronary-to-pulmonary artery fistula (CPAF) and unilateral pulmonary artery discontinuity. While CPAF is seldom detected during pregnancy, its prenatal diagnosis can facilitate better postnatal therapeutic strategies. Unilateral pulmonary artery discontinuity, especially when co-occurring with other cardiac abnormalities, may be missed or delayed on prenatal echocardiography. Therefore, clinicians should carefully assess the origin of both pulmonary arteries during fetal evaluation. [PMC9226865, PMC8019495]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The existence of a coronary-to-pulmonary artery fistula (CPF) in pulmonary atresia with ventricular septal defect (PAVSD) potentially affects treatment; however, its clinical features have not been comprehensively described due to the disease's rarity. We reviewed 69 cases from 42 studies to reveal the clinical overview of patients with CPF and PAVSD. Among the included patients, the male-to-female ratio was exactly 1:1, and only two patients (3%) exhibited the 22q11.2 microdeletion syndrome. Regarding anatomical features, CPFs originated from the left coronary artery in 65% of patients, and 62% had other major aortopulmonary collateral arteries. Thirty-nine percent of patients had a definitive CPF diagnosis at 0 years of age, whereas 10% were diagnosed in adulthood. Seventy percent underwent catheter angiography to obtain a definitive CPF diagnosis. Ninety-five percent of patients... [PMC9867298]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurocutaneous disorder characterized by multisystem hamartomas, most commonly involving the skin, brain, kidneys, lungs, eye, and heart, and associated with neuropsychiatric disorders.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Whilst prevalence has been historically estimated at 1/10,000, more recent data from the UK and Taiwan estimates prevalence at 1/20-25,000 and 1/100,000, respectively. However, current estimates are likely an underestimate given the variability in phenotypic expression, severity and age of onset.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Skin involvement is almost constantly present, beginning as hypomelanotic macules in the first years of life and evolving to facial angiofibromas by 3-4 years, followed by ungual fibromas, cephalic and lumbar (shagreen patch) fibrous plaques, and ''confetti'' skin lesions appearing in childhood to early adolescence. Brain involvement includes cortical dysplasias (tubers), subependymal nodules, and/or subependymal giant cell astrocytoma (SEGA), and is seen in almost all cases. SEGA affects 10 to 20% of tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC) patients, almost exclusively children and young adults. Early-onset epilepsy (focal seizures and/or infantile spasms) is present in 85% of patients. TSC-Associated Neuropsychiatric Disorders (TAND) include intellectual disability, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorders (ASD), psychiatric disorders, neuropsychological deficits, as well as school and occupational difficulties. Renal angiomyolipomas (AML) develop during childhood with a higher risk of growth during adolescence and adulthood and manifest by pain, hematuria/retroperitoneal hemorrhage, abdominal masses, hypertension and renal failure. Lymphangioleiomyomatosis, multifocal micronodular pneumocyte hyperplasia and pulmonary cysts develop during adulthood and manifest with dyspnea, pneumothorax, or chylothorax. Cardiac rhabdomyomas appear during the fetal period, are rarely symptomatic, and tend to decrease in size in early childhood. Additional features include retinal and liver hamartomas, dental enamel pitting, intraoral fibromas, skeletal dysplasia, and rarely neuroendocrine tumors.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: TSC is due to mutations in either TSC1 (9q34) or TSC2 (16p13.3) which encode proteins that indirectly inhibit the mTOR pathway. In excess, mTOR causes increased cell growth and proliferation, as well as disproportionate glutamate activity leading to disrupted synaptic plasticity. Expressivity of TSC is variable due to mosaicism and to genetic-epigenetic modifiers.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: A definite diagnosis is defined as presence of ≥ 2 major features or 1 major and ≥ 2 minor features. Possible TSC is considered in the presence of 1 major or ≥ 2 minor features. The identification of a pathogenic variant, confirms the diagnosis regardless of the clinical findings.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease type 1 with tuberous sclerosis is seen in up to 5% of patients presenting with TSC and should be excluded. Other differential diagnoses include vitiligo, Ito hypomelanosis, acne, skin rash, cardiac myxoma, isolated brain tumors, pulmonary emphysema, and kidney cysts.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is made in two situations: familial cases with genetic diagnosis (amniocentesis, chorionic villus sampling) or de novo cases with the discovery of cardiac rhabdomyoma or less frequently brain abnormalities on routine pregnancy exams.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is autosomal dominant; however, two thirds of cases are the result of a de novo pathogenic variant. In one third of cases, TSC is inherited from one of the parents and, in such cases, genetic counseling is recommended to inform the parents that the risk of having an affected child is 50% for each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is multidisciplinary and includes frequent clinical follow-up as well as treatment of epilepsy, tumors, and TAND. Early referral to a specialized pediatric epilepsy center is strongly recommended. Epilepsy treatment includes the use of vigabatrin (GABA transaminase inhibitor) for infantile spasms and early onset focal seizures. For pre-symptomatic infants, video electroencephalogram monitoring is recommended to identify subtle or electrographic seizures. If vigabatrin fails, other antiseizure medicine, ketogenic diet, vagal nerve stimulation, or mTOR pathway inhibitor (everolimus) might be helpful. Early identification of candidates for epilepsy surgery is highly recommended. The developing tumors require frequent follow-up and can be treated with mTOR inhibitors or surgery.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: TSC is a chronic, life-long condition. As patients transition into adulthood, seizures may persist; renal and/or pulmonary issues may become more frequent and clinically significant.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Fried syndrome is a rare X-linked mental retardation (XLMR) syndrome characterized by psychomotor delay, intellectual deficit, hydrocephalus, and mild facial anomalies.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown, but the syndrome was originally described in a large Scottish family.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Mutations in the AP1S2 gene (Xp22), coding for a subunit of the clathrin-associated adaptor protein complex involved in intracellular protein trafficking and synaptic vesicle recycling, have been identified in seven families.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The presence of basal ganglia calcifications, detectable by CT scan, and elevated CSF protein levels are characteristic features of Fried syndrome and should prompt genetic analysis when found in individuals with XLMR.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Beyond the management of hydrocephalus and follow-up of psychomotor development, no specific treatment is available.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Fried syndrome is a rare X-linked mental retardation syndrome, first described in 1972. Its distinctive phenotype includes mental retardation, which can be severe, along with hydrocephalus or ventricular dilatation, and mild facial dysmorphism. A key diagnostic feature is the presence of marked calcifications of the basal ganglia, which is considered an essential parameter for recognizing this syndromic disorder. Affected individuals may also develop spastic diplegia. The condition is associated with mutations in the AP1S2 gene. [PMC2752185, PMC1050991]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Fried syndrome, an X-linked mental retardation, shares phenotypic similarities with MASA syndrome, which is caused by mutations in the L1CAM gene in Xq28. However, linkage to Xq28 markers has been excluded for Fried syndrome, indicating it is not allelic with MASA syndrome and is a distinct disorder. The evolving phenotype of Fried syndrome includes severe mental retardation, spastic diplegia, ventricular dilatation, and distinctive calcifications of the basal ganglia. The presence of marked basal ganglia calcifications is considered an essential parameter to recognize Fried syndrome and may help identify families with X-linked mental retardation for AP1S2 mutation screening. [PMC2752185, PMC1050991]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Fried syndrome is an X-linked mental retardation syndrome caused by mutations in the AP1S2 gene, located at Xp22.2. Genetic counseling should emphasize the X-linked inheritance pattern, where affected males present with severe mental retardation, hydrocephalus, and distinctive calcifications of the basal ganglia. The presence of these basal ganglia calcifications is considered an essential diagnostic feature and can guide the identification of families for targeted screening of AP1S2 mutations. Specific mutations, such as an intron 3 mutation leading to exon 3 skipping or a p.Gln66X nonsense mutation, have been identified in affected families. [PMC2752185, PMC1050991]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The phenotype of Fried syndrome evolves into a distinctive and severe clinical picture. Affected individuals develop severe mental retardation, spastic diplegia, ventricular dilatation, and calcification of the basal ganglia. These features represent the long-term outcome of the condition in surviving affected subjects. [PMC1050991]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare pediatric rheumatological disease characterized by the variable occurrence of chronic arthritis, intermittent high spiking fever, maculopapular rash during fever episodes, hepatomegaly and/or splenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and serositis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is one of the most common pediatric chronic diseases, with a yearly incidence between 1.6 and 23 new cases per 100,000 children. Systemic-onset JIA accounts for roughly 10-20% of all JIA patients, with incidence estimated at 1/166,000 and prevalence at 1/32,000 in the prediatric population. Frequency is higher in some countries; for example in parts of Asia, sytemic-onset JIA may account for up to 30-40% of all JIA cases.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset usually occurs between 3 and 5 years of age. The clinical signs include fever with oscillating temperatures over a 24-hour period and peaks of over 39°C or more. The fever peaks are associated with the transient occurrence of an evanescent macular rash. Any joint, small or large, may be affected at disease onset, and involvement is nearly symmetrical and may be oligo- or polyarticular. Arthritis tends to increase in severity over time, and thus may not appear until later in the disease course. The course of the disease varies between individuals, ranging from a monocyclic disease course, to recurrent predominantly systemic disease course, to a progressive polyarthritis that could lead to severe and destructive joint disease.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Whilst the underlying mechanisms and triggering factors are not fully understood, IL-1 and IL-6 play a major role in the pathogenesis of the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical and biological findings in a child under the age of 16 presenting with fever for at least 3 consecutive days and 2 major criteria (arthritis and evanescent rash) or 1 major and 2 minor criteria ((1) generalized lymph node enlargement and/or hepatomegaly or splenomegaly (2) serositis (3) arthralgias lasting 2 weeks or longer (4) leukocytosis > 15.000/mm3 with neutrophilia) A confirmed diagnosis requires exclusion of other causes of the symptoms.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnoses is extensive and includes bacterial infections (including occult bacterial infection, brucellosis, Lyme disease, cat scratch disease, tuberculosis, and infectious mononucleosis), malaria, malignancies (such as leukemia, lymphoma, and neuroblastoma), viral infections, hereditary recurrent fever syndromes, other inflammatory diseases (such as systemic lupus erythematosus, systemic vasculitis, Kawasaki disease, Behçet disease, inflammatory bowel disease, Sweet syndrome, PFAPA, Takayasu arteritis, Castleman syndrome, rheumatic fever, and polyarteritis nodosa), connective tissue diseases, and periodic fever syndromes.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management by a specialized multidisciplinary team is required. Treatment is typically first with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and, if the inflammation is not controlled, followed by high dose corticosteroids. Treatment with cytokine inhibitors (anakinra, canakinumab, and tocilizumab) has shown to be highly effective. Furthermore, these drugs can help mitigate damage caused by the inflammatory process. Generally, complications such as macrophage activation syndrome, limitations in functional outcome by arthritis and long-term damage from chronic inflammation continue to be a major issue in patients' care, but have decreased since the use of biological treatment.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The disease course is long with major impact on quality of life. The risk of complications due to the illness or medication has been significantly reduced by the early use of biological treatment. Nowadays, osteopenia and osteoporosis, growth impairment, erosive arthritis, and secondary or reactive amyloidosis have almost disappeared. Currently, therapeutic strategies using anakinra (a recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist), JAK inhibitors, and IL-6 inhibitors are also being studied. In severe case, where these is no response to these treatments or to high-dose corticosteroid therapy, intensive care becomes quickly necessary.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Systemic-onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis (SJIA) has been associated with genetic factors. Many previous studies have revealed that common heterozygous or homozygous mutations in the MEFV gene are linked to SJIA. For example, a heterozygous E148Q mutation in the MEFV gene has been identified in patients with the condition. [PMC5429510]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare bone dysplasia characterized by short stature, short hands and feet, mild facial dysmorphism, and characteristic X-ray abnormalities of the hands.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown. Fewer than 60 patients with this condition have been reported to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Length is usually normal at birth but postnatal height falls progressively below the normal percentiles. The mean adult height is 130 cm (133 cm in males, 129 cm in females). The hands, feet, and limbs are short and occipitofrontal circumference is normal. There is no intellectual deficit. Mild dysmorphic features have been noted, including a round face, narrow palpebral fissures, well-defined eyebrows, long eyelashes, a bulbous nose with anteverted nostrils, a long and prominent philtrum, and thick lips with a small mouth. Other features include well-developed muscles, a hoarse voice, generalized joint limitations in some patients, frequent ear, tracheal, and respiratory complications, and spine abnormalities. Long-term follow-up shows that facial dysmorphism becomes less obvious in adults and that carpal tunnel syndrome is frequent in older patients. The entity known as Moore-Federman syndrome characterized by short stature (with disproportionately short legs), joint stiffness, ocular abnormalities (hypermetropia, glaucoma) and thickened skin on the forearms, is believed to represent a variable clinical expression of acromicric dysplasia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by heterozygous mutations in the FBN1 gene. Mutations are all located in exon 41-42, encoding TGFβ binding protein-like domain 5.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of acromicric dysplasia can be suspected on association of severe postnatal short stature, short hands and feet, normal intelligence and mild facial dysmorphism. X-rays show delayed carpal bone age, cone shaped epiphyses, short metacarpals and phalanges with an internal notch of the second metacarpal, an external notch of the fifth metacarpal, as well as an internal notch of the femoral heads. Notches of the hands disappear in adulthood.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Overlapping syndromes include geleophysic dysplasia, Weill-Marchesani syndrome, and Myhre syndrome. Geleophysic dysplasia can be distinguished from acromicric dysplasia by the presence of cardiac abnormalities (e.g. cardiac valvular thickening), Weill-Marchesani syndrome by the presence of microspherophakia, and Myhre syndrome by the presence of prognathism, deafness, developmental delay, and a thick calvarium.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant. Affected individuals have a 50% risk of transmitting the disease to their offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Orthopedic management may be needed for hip dysplasia during childhood and for carpal tunnel syndrome in older patients. Physical therapy is required to prevent progressive joint limitation. In a few cases, children have been treated with growth hormone therapy. Regular multidisciplinary follow-up is required, especially for respiratory abnormalities.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis for affected individuals is usually good with a normal life expectancy. However, complications may occur, such as respiratory disorders, which may worsen the prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal anomaly characterized by variable clinical features, most commonly including global developmental delay, hypotonia, growth retardation with microcephaly, intellectual disability with severe speech delay, seizures or abnormal EEG, autistic spectrum disorder and other behavioral characteristics.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Ring chromosome 22 syndrome presents with a range of clinical features, commonly including severe global neurodevelopmental delay, mental retardation, and significant speech abnormalities, such as severe delay or absence of expressive speech. Patients may exhibit autistic behavior, facial dysmorphism, and various skin anomalies like urticarial rashes, café-au-lait macules, or pigmentary changes distributed in the lines of Blaschko. Unilateral or asymmetrical features, such as hemiatrophy, have also been reported. Neurological manifestations can include bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria. There is an increased risk of tumor development, including atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors of the central nervous system, unilateral vestibular schwannomas, and multifocal meningiomas. Some patients also present with features consistent with Phelan-McDermid syndrome or, less commonly, Cat Eye Syndrome. [PMC5869459, PMC5999866, PMC3119894, PMC2758865, PMC1734329]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Ring chromosome 22 syndrome can be associated with or mimic other conditions. Phelan-McDermid syndrome (22q13.3 deletion syndrome), caused by SHANK3 haploinsufficiency, is closely related, as ring chromosome 22 can lead to the characteristic deletions. Cat Eye Syndrome (CES), associated with duplication of 22q11.2 or small supernumerary marker chromosomes derived from chromosome 22, may present with overlapping features, sometimes due to mosaicism for a dicentric double ring chromosome 22. Furthermore, Metachromatic leucodystrophy (MLD) can occur in patients with a ring chromosome 22 that includes a deletion of the arylsulphatase A gene. [PMC7880375, PMC5869459, PMC3119894, PMC1734329, PMC1051701]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Small supernumerary marker chromosomes cannot be accurately identified by G-banding, and the related phenotypes vary greatly. It is essential to specify the origin, size, and gene content of marker chromosomes using molecular cytogenetic techniques. Herein, three fetuses with de novo marker chromosomes were initially identified by G-banding. Single nucleotide polymorphism array and fluorescence in situ hybridization were performed to characterize the origins of the marker chromosomes. The karyotypes of the three fetuses were 47,XY,+mar, 46,X,+mar[32]/45,X[68], and 45,X[62]/46,X,+mar[9]. In case 1, the karyotype was confirmed as 47,XY,+ idic(22)(q11.2). Therefore, the sSMC originated from chromosome 22 and was associated with cat eye syndrome. In case 2, the marker chromosome derived from ring chromosome X, and the karyotype was interpreted as 45,X[68]/46,X,+r(X)(p11.1q21.31)[32].... [PMC7880375]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for ring chromosome 22 syndrome is complex, necessitating detailed characterization of marker chromosomes through combined cytogenetic and molecular genetic techniques, including FISH and array CGH. This comprehensive approach is vital for accurate prognostic assessments and informed decision-making, particularly in prenatal diagnosis and cases involving infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss. The presence of mosaicism can complicate diagnosis, sometimes requiring repeated investigations or skin biopsies. Parental carrier status and de novo events have implications for recurrence risk within families. Additionally, patients with ring chromosome 22 should be monitored for NF2-related tumors starting in adolescence. [PMC7880375, PMC7376793, PMC2758865, PMC1051701, PMC1050079]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of ring chromosome 22 syndrome involves accurate diagnosis to facilitate informed decision-making, including prenatal options such as continuation or elective termination of pregnancy, and to provide proper prognostic assessments. Patients should be monitored for NF2-related tumors, with surveillance recommended to begin in adolescence. Detailed characterization of marker chromosomes is essential for personalized support, particularly for individuals experiencing infertility. Additionally, diagnosis enables accurate genetic counseling to address recurrence risk and provide comprehensive information to families. [PMC7880375, PMC7376793, PMC2758865, PMC1051701, PMC1050079]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for individuals with ring chromosome 22 syndrome includes an increased risk of developing specific tumors due to the inherent instability of the ring chromosome. This instability can lead to chromosomal loss, acting as a first hit in oncogenesis. Patients are at risk for highly malignant atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumors (AT/RT) of the central nervous system, where ring chromosome instability can lead to SMARCB1 inactivation. Additionally, there is a risk of NF2-related tumors, such as vestibular schwannoma, which can arise from the loss of the ring chromosome and a second hit in the NF2 gene. Therefore, monitoring for NF2-related tumors is recommended starting in adolescence. [PMC7880375, PMC5999866, PMC2758865]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pituitary dermoid and epidermoid cysts is a rare, acquired pituitary hormone deficiency characterized by the presence of rare, benign tumor in the sellar region. Clinical presentation is either acute or insidious, and is variable according to the cyst location, size and potential rupture. Most commonly patients present with headache, visual disturbances, and pituitary dysfunction.

Cranioectodermal dysplasia (CED) is a rare developmental disorder characterized by congenital skeletal and ectodermal defects associated with dysmorphic features, nephronophthisis, hepatic fibrosis and ocular anomalies (mainly retinitis pigmentosa).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, 20 cases have been reported in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: CED is primarily characterized by an abnormal development of bones (i.e. craniosynostosis/dolichocephaly, narrow thorax, pectus excavatum, rhizomelic micromelia, brachydactyly, syndactyly, clinodactyly, hyperextensible joints), and ectodermal defects such as dental anomalies (reduced enamel thickness, hypodontia, microdontia, taurodontism, malformations of the cusps), sparse hair, and abnormal finger and toe nails. Dysmorphic features are observed such as epicanthic folds, hypotelorism, anteverted nares, and everted lower lip. Patients frequently develop chronic renal failure due to nephronophthisis, usually between the ages of 2 and 6. Liver involvement (hepatic fibrosis) can also be observed. Recurrent lung infections, heart defects and ocular anomalies (nystagmus, myopia, retinal dystrophy, and particularly retinitis pigmentosa) are also possible in the course of the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CED is a heterogenous condition belonging to the ciliopathy group of diseases and is due to mutations in the IFT122, IFT43, WDR19 and WDR35 genes involved in intraflagellar transport (IFT). This genetic background explains the pleiotropic phenotype of CED that includes manifestations of several ciliopathies.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical examination. Imagery (ultrasonography), laboratory findings (urine analysis, serum electrolytes, and lipid profile), histological examination and liver and renal function tests allow detection of potential renal and liver anomalies. Ocular anomalies can be detected by eye fundus and electroretinography.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis of CED includes Jeune syndrome from which it can be distinguished by the presence of craniosynostosis, and skin and dental dysplasia. CED also overlaps with Ellis van Creveld syndrome which also shows ectodermal defects and narrow thorax.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In most cases, transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: In many cases, renal function rapidly deteriorates, requiring treatment of metabolic acidosis, oral sodium chloride supplementation, then dialysis or renal transplantation in case of end-stage renal failure.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on renal, heart and lung defects which can be life threatening.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inherited subacute encephalopathy characterized by the variable association of basal ganglia calcification, leukodystrophy, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) lymphocytosis and evidence of enhanced type I interferon signaling in blood and CSF.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Encephalopathy with basal ganglia calcification; Encephalopathy with intracranial calcification and chronic lymphocytosis of cerebrospinal fluid

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: More than 500 cases of Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS) have been reported in the literature to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The majority of affected infants are born at full term with normal growth parameters. In its classic form, onset occurs within the first few days or months of life with severe, subacute encephalopathy (feeding problems, irritability and psychomotor regression or delay) associated with epilepsy, chilblain skin lesions on the extremities and episodes of aseptic febrile illness. These features can continue over several weeks/months (with the development of microcephaly and pyramidal signs) before the disease apparently stabilizes. Less severe forms have been described with onset after 1 year of age, and relative preservation of communication skills, cognitive function and head circumference. The phenotype can manifest with marked inter- and intrafamilial variation. Less frequently still, mutations in AGS-related genes can be associated with other distinct phenotypes, including bilateral striatal necrosis, non-syndromic spastic paraparesis of the lower limbs with normal intellect and neuroradiology, cerebrovascular disease similar to Moyamoya, and even complete clinical non-penetrance.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Since 2006, causative mutations have been identified in nine genes encoding: (i) the 3'->5' exonuclease TREX1; (ii) the three components of the RNase H2 endonuclease complex (RNASEH2A, RNASEH2B and RNASEH2C), (iii) SAMHD1, which functions as a deoxynucleoside triphosphate triphosphohydrolase; (iv) ADAR1, which catalyzes the hydrolytic deamination of adenosine to inosine in RNA; (v) MDA5, (encoded by IFIH1) a cytosolic double stranded RNA sensor; and (vi) two components of the histone pre-mRNA processing complex (RNU7-1 and LSM11). Mutations in TREX1, RNASEH2C and RNASEH2A are more often associated with severe neurological problems, whereas mutations in RNASEH2B, SAMHD1, IFIH1 and ADAR1 can be associated with a relative preservation of skills. The phenotype associated with mutations in LSM11 and RNU7-1 have yet to be fully determined.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Calcification (involving the basal ganglia and white matter), cystic leukodystrophy (predominantly frontotemporal in very early onset cases) and cortical-subcortical atrophy are cardinal features of typical AGS, sometimes associated with atrophy of the corpus callosum, the brain stem and cerebellum. Elevated IFN-alpha activity and lymphocytosis in the CSF are frequent but not constant findings in the initial stage of the disease, but tend to normalize or resolve within a few years.
