According to the data gained by different molecular cytogenetic techniques, such as fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) with whole and partial chromosome painting probes, yeast artificial chromosome (YAC) probes, and comparative genomic hybridisation (CGH), the derivative chromosome 9 can be described as dup(9)(pter-->q22. 1::q31.1-->q22.1::q31.1--> q22.1::q31.1-->qter). Four breakpoint spanning YACs have been identified (y806f02,... [PMC1734635, PMC1013295]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal duplication 9q syndrome is caused by partial trisomy 9q, a rare chromosomal aberration involving a duplication on the long arm of chromosome 9. Molecular cytogenetic analysis has characterized the chromosomal breakpoints, with one case showing a derivative chromosome 9 described as dup(9)(pter-->q22.1::q31.1-->q22.1::q31.1-->q22.1::q31.1-->qter). Breakpoint spanning YACs have been identified for the proximal breakpoint. The critical region for associated features, such as pyloric stenosis, is narrowed to subbands 9q22.1-q31.1, resulting from partial trisomy of genes in this region or a gene disrupted in 9q31. [PMC1734635, PMC1013295]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of partial trisomy 9q involves molecular cytogenetic techniques. These , including fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with whole and partial chromosome painting probes, yeast artificial chromosome (YAC) probes, and comparative genomic hybridization (CGH), are utilized to determine the size of the duplication and characterize chromosomal breakpoints. For example, breakpoint spanning YACs can be identified to define the affected region. [PMC1734635]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: A male infant is presented with an extra derivate chromosome No. 9 resulting from a 3:1 meiotic segregation of a maternal balanced translocation involving the long arms of chromosomes No. 7 and 9. The patient is trisomic for the short arm and secondary constriction of the long arm of No. 9 and for the telomeric end of the long arm of No. 7. In addition to the features of the 9p trisomy syndrome he presents marked congenital myopia and extreme hypoplasia of the penis. [PMC1013295]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Partial trisomy 9q, a chromosomal aberration, has been detected prenatally. A case report describes a 1-year-old female patient with dysmorphic features and pyloric stenosis, where partial trisomy 9q was identified before birth. This indicates that distal duplication 9q syndrome can be diagnosed antenatally. [PMC1734635]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The syndrome can result from unbalanced segregation of a parental balanced translocation. For instance, a male infant was presented with an extra derivative chromosome No. 9 due to 3:1 meiotic segregation of a maternal balanced translocation involving the long arms of chromosomes No. 7 and 9. This indicates that parents carrying balanced translocations may be at risk of having offspring with partial trisomy. [PMC1013295]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic multi-system disorder characterized by a wide range of muscle-related manifestations (muscle weakness, myotonia, early onset cataracts (before age 50) and systemic manifestations (cerebral, endocrine, cardiac, gastrointestinal tract, uterus, skin and immunologic involvement) that vary depending on the age of onset. The very wide clinical spectrum ranges from lethal presentations in infancy to mild, late-onset disease.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset: Adolescent, Adult, Antenatal, Childhood, Infancy, Neonatal

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It is the most frequent adult muscular dystrophy and has an estimated prevalence ranging from 1/215,000 in Taiwan to 1/5,500 in Croatia. It appears to be more prevalent in the Saguenay-Lac-St-Jean region-Quebec, Canada (1/600), suggesting a founder effect. The disease occurs worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The age of onset is highly variable, from prenatal to adulthood. The clinical manifestations also cover a wide range and may differ within and between affected families. Five forms are currently recognized: congenital, early childhood, juvenile, adult-onset and late-onset. Congenital disease (15% of cases) is the most severe form and includes severe generalized weakness at birth with respiratory distress, hypotonia, and feeding difficulty. Patients subsequently develop delayed cognitive and motor milestones intellectual disability, and autism spectrum disorder. The course may be fatal in congenital cases (30-40%). In childhood onset cases (with the age of onset between 1 and 10 years of age), the main clinical manifestations involve muscle weakness (including both proximal and distal muscle group, facial weakness, respiratory and gastrointestinal complications such as respiratory distress, aspiration, dysphagia, constipation and speech disturbances), myotonia, sleep breathing disorders, recurrent infections, cognitive impairment, psychiatric disorders (phobia, depression, anxiety, attention deficit-hyperactivity). The juvenile form with the age of onset between 11 and 20 years of age, is characterized by scholar and behavioral problems and is often under recognized. The classic adult form (75% of cases), which develops between 20 and 40 years of age, is characterized by progressive distal muscle weakness, pain, myotonia and multiorgan involvement (irritable bowel disease, conduction and other cardiac disorders, cataracts, ophthalmoplegia, diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism, hypotestosteronism, and thyroid dysfunction). Intellectual deficit is also present in adult cases. Balding may occur in affected males and females and infertility may be present. Late-onset disease after 40 years of age involves mild myotonia and weakness, daytime sleepiness, and cataracts. A higher cancer risk has been reported in affected patients.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is due to abnormal CTG expansion in the non-translating region of the DMPKgene (19q13.3). Disease severity generally correlates with the number of DNA repeats. More than 2000 CTG repeats may be found. The expansion is unstable, which may explain the clinical variability.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected on the characteristic clinical manifestations and a consistent family history, and confirmed by molecular genetic testing of the causative gene expansion. Muscle biopsy is not anymore necessary for the diagnosis and is has been replaced by genetic testing, which represents the gold standard.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: There are several overlapping features with myotonic dystrophy type 2; however, the diseases are distinct genetically and have different courses and management requirements.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Early-onset cases may be identified prenatally with polyhydramnios and reduced fetal movements.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant. Genetic counselling should be provided to affected families. Whilst there is a 50% risk of disease transmission from an affected parent to their offspring, the disease shows variable penetrance.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: No specific targeted treatment is currently available. Management primarily includes monitoring for complications and supportive care (assistive devices, hormone therapy, pain medication).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Some cases are severe and may have an impact on life expectancy, particularly early-onset cases caused by massive gene expansions. The prognosis in adult-onset cases is mainly dependent on the severity of cardiac manifestations. Causes of death include respiratory failure, cardiovascular disease, arrhythmia, and neoplasms.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare progressive autosomal recessive tapetoretinal degeneration disease, occurring in the third decade of life, characterized by small sparkling crystalline deposits in the posterior retina and corneal limbus in addition to sclerosis of the choroidal vessels and manifesting as nightblindness, decreased vision, paracentral scotoma, and, in the end stages of the disease, legal blindness.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): BCD; Bietti crystalline corneoretinal dystrophy; Bietti crystalline retinopathy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Bietti crystalline dystrophy (BCD) is a rare, genetically determined chorioretinal dystrophy. Visual impairment commonly occurs between the second and third decades of life, potentially leading to legal blindness by the fifth or sixth decade. The disease has been reported in Oriental populations, including Chinese and Japanese individuals. In a study of 92 unrelated Chinese probands, the c.802_810del17insGC mutation was identified as the most prevalent, with an allele frequency of 52.7%. [PMC10046287, PMC4287718, PMC1311548]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Bietti crystalline dystrophy, characterized by crystalline retinal deposits, requires differentiation from other conditions presenting with similar features. Cystinosis, for instance, should be considered and can be ruled out by blood testing. The presence of optic nerve head drusen, which may be associated with Bietti crystalline dystrophy, should also be noted when evaluating patients with progressive vision loss, blurry optic nerve head margins, and retinal pigment epithelium atrophy. [PMC9628052]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Bietti crystalline dystrophy is a rare inherited chorioretinal dystrophy caused by mutations in the CYP4V2 gene, with over 100 variants identified. The disease is genetically determined, with cases of homozygosity and compound heterozygosity reported, indicating an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. While some observations suggest certain homozygous variants may be associated with more severe disease, and less severe forms may relate to milder mutations, a clear genotype-phenotype correlation has generally not been established, with phenotypic variations observed even within the same genotype. Visual impairment typically begins in the second to third decades of life, potentially leading to legal blindness by the fifth or sixth decade due to progressive chorioretinal atrophy. [PMC11916969, PMC10046287, PMC8151499, PMC6208130, PMC4287718]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Bietti crystalline dystrophy primarily focuses on addressing complications. For choroidal neovascularization (CNV) or choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM), intravitreal injections of Bevacizumab or ranibizumab have been used, leading to restoration or stabilization of visual acuity and scarring of the membrane. Cystoid macular oedema has been successfully treated with oral acetazolamide, resulting in oedema resolution and improved visual function. In one case, no surgical treatment was recommended for an asymptomatic full-thickness macular hole. [PMC10046287, PMC9249107, PMC6208130, PMC5149010, PMC3958638]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Bietti crystalline dystrophy is a progressive retinal disease, with visual impairment commonly commencing between the second and third decades of life. Vision loss can become severe, potentially leading to legal blindness by the fifth or sixth decade. Over time, retinal crystalline deposits are gradually replaced by progressive atrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium and choroid, leading to a decline in visual acuity, function, and constriction of visual fields. While crystal area may decrease in some retinal regions over a two-year period, this likely reflects the progression to atrophy. The disease course and severity vary significantly, with some genotypes associated with more severe phenotypes, including complications like macular hole formation and retinal detachment. However, genotype-phenotype correlation is not always clear, and phenotypic variations can occur even within the same genotype, suggesting the existence of less severe forms. [PMC11916969, PMC10046287, PMC9628052, PMC9249107, PMC8151499]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by sustained peripheral blood neutrophilia, bone marrow hypercellularity due to neutrophilic granulocyte proliferation, and hepatosplenomegaly. Other organs may be infiltrated in addition. Microscopically, the bone marrow shows an increase in proportion of myelocytes and mature neutrophils, but no significant dysplasia in any of the cell lineages. Peripheral blood neutrophils are mostly segmented, although band forms may also be substantially increased. Cytogenetic abnormalities are absent in most cases. The disease is slowly progressive with progredient neutrophilia followed by anemia and thrombocytopenia. Transformation to acute myeloid leukemia may occur.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Chronic neutrophilic leukemia (CNL) is a rare and life-threatening myeloproliferative neoplasm with a poor prognosis. Historically, less than 40 cases were reported or clinically suspected meeting 2008 WHO diagnostic criteria. It is frequently associated with plasma cell dyscrasias, such as monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and less commonly with lymphoma or autoimmune hemolytic anemia. The median age of diagnosis for monoclonal gammopathy-associated CNL is 69 years, with reported cases ranging from 28 to 73 years. The presence of CSF3R mutations is a key diagnostic criterion. [PMC11763460, PMC11512872, PMC10220385, PMC8993655, PMC9048254]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Chronic neutrophilic leukemia (CNL) is a rare, life-threatening BCR/ABL-negative myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by persistent mature neutrophilia, bone marrow hypercellularity, and often splenomegaly. Clinical presentation varies from asymptomatic to highly symptomatic, with constitutional symptoms. Diagnosis relies on specific genetic mutations, particularly in the CSF3R gene (e.g., T618I), which is a key diagnostic criterion, along with the absence of other myeloproliferative neoplasm markers. The disease has a poor prognosis, with patients often succumbing to complications or transforming to acute myeloid leukemia or mixed phenotype acute leukemia. It can also be associated with autoimmune hemolytic anemia, plasma cell dyscrasias like monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, or lymphoma. Co-occurring mutations like ASXL1 and SETBP1, or features like bone marrow fibrosis and dysplasia, may indicate a worse prognosis. [PMC11763460, PMC11512872, PMC10220385, PMC8870680, PMC8993655]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Allogeneic stem cell transplantation is considered the only curative option for chronic neutrophilic leukemia, though it carries high rates of treatment-related mortality. Current management strategies emphasize JAK inhibitors, such as ruxolitinib, which have shown significant responses but may face resistance. Other treatments include cytoreductive agents, hydroxyurea, and various chemotherapy regimens, with early intervention potentially delaying disease progression. Despite ongoing research, management remains suboptimal, highlighting challenges like therapeutic resistance and the need for a personalized medicine approach. [PMC11763460, PMC11512872, PMC10220385, PMC9825857, PMC8870680]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic multisystem disorder characterized by the variable association of retinal dystrophy, obesity, polydactyly, genitourinary and kidney anomalies, learning disability and hypogonadism, with a wide spectrum of other minor manifestations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: In the USA, the prevalence is estimated at 1/100,000. Whilst epidemiological data is limited in Europe, a prevalence of 1/59,000 has been estimated in Denmark and 1/45,000-66,000 in the Reunion Island, France (due to a founder effect).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical manifestations are highly variable, even within affected families. Post-axial polydactyly, sometimes associated with brachydactyly and/or syndactyly, is a common congenital feature. Other manifestations develop gradually over the first decade of life. Rapid weight gain is often described in early childhood, with obesity/overweight present in over 90% of individuals after 5 years of age; it is often difficult to treat and is associated with the metabolic syndrome in adults. Rod-cone or choroidal dystrophy causes decreased visual acuity, night blindness, photophobia and loss of central and color vision by late childhood/early adulthood. Other ocular manifestations include strabismus, cataracts, and astigmatism. Kidney and urinary tract abnormalities are common and may lead a progressive decline of kidney function: stage II-V chronic kidney disease (CKD) is described in 30 to over 40% of affected individuals. Developmental delay, cognitive deficit and behavioral disorders (autism, psychosis) are frequent features. Hypogonadism is often reported, especially in males. Minor signs include diabetes mellitus, heart (valvular stenoses, patent ductus arteriosus, cardiomyopathy), gastrointestinal tract (Hirschsprung disease), central nervous system (clumsiness, ataxia), liver (fibrosis, biliary cirrhosis, portal hypertension), and dentition (dental crowding, hypodontia, malocclusion, enamel hypoplasia) abnormalities. Subtle and inconsistent dysmorphic features (brachycephaly, macrocephaly, hypertelorism, midface hypoplasia, retrognathia) have also been reported. Anosmia or hyposmia may also be found as well as bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS) is a ciliopathy associated with abnormalities in proteins involved in the development and function of primary cilia. Pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in at least 24 different genes have been associated with BBS to date. Depending on the population origin, BBS1 (11q13.2) and BBS10 (12q21.2) are the most frequent genes, respectively accounting for ~23% and 15% of genotyped BBS patients.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of BBS is based on the clinical manifestations (at least four major clinical signs or 3 major and 2 minor clinical signs) and can be confirmed by molecular genetic testing of the causative genes in more than 80% of patients. Visual manifestations are often the first sign leading to diagnosis in patients with no polydactyly; polydactyly and kidney anomalies (hyperechoic or multicystic kidneys) can be antenatal presenting signs.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Main differential diagnoses include Alström syndrome, McKusick-Kaufman syndrome, Joubert syndrome, Jeune syndrome, Sensenbrenner syndrome and Senior-Løken syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Genetic prenatal testing for BBS is possible in families with an identified gene mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: BBS is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Oligogenic inheritance has also been reported is some affected families. Genetic counseling should be provided to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Multidisciplinary management and treatment is required. Most manifestations are treated following standard practice for the general population (obesity, learning disability, kidney anomalies). Setmelanotide was approved for hunger control in genetically confirmed Bardet-Biedl syndrome patients. Genital abnormalities and polydactyly may be treated with surgery.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Chronic kidney disease is considered the main cause of morbidity and mortality; its severity varies among patients but may potentially lead to end-stage kidney disease requiring dialysis or transplantation. Progressive vision loss due to retinal dystrophy, together with moderate intellectual deficit (when present), behavioral anomalies, hypomimia and obesity will affect the social life of these patients.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, systemic amyloidosis characterized by a triad of ophthalmologic, neurologic and dermatologic findings due to the deposition of gelsolin amyloid fibrils in these tissues. Clinical manifestations include corneal lattice dystrophy, cranial neuropathy, especially affecting the facial nerve, bulbar signs, cutis laxa, increased skin fragility, and less commonly peripheral neuropathy and renal failure.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Familial amyloid polyneuropathy type IV; Familial amyloidosis, Finnish type; Gelsolin amyloidosis; Hereditary amyloidosis, Finnish type

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: AGel amyloidosis, also known as Familial amyloidosis of the Finnish type (FAF) or hereditary gelsolin amyloidosis (HGA), is a rare, autosomal dominant hereditary disorder. It is primarily reported in Finland, where it is considered prevalent. However, cases have also been identified in other countries, including Portugal, the United States (in a family with a gelsolin mutation not found in Finland), the United Kingdom (first reported case), and Korea (first reported family). The identification of initial cases or families in these diverse regions suggests that early diagnosis can be challenging and that the condition may be underrecognized globally. [PMC9668035, PMC5494018, PMC4773268, PMC1723421]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: AGel amyloidosis is a rare, inherited multisystemic disorder typically presenting with a triad of ophthalmic, neurological, and dermatological findings. Ophthalmic manifestations commonly include corneal lattice dystrophy, corneal amyloid deposits, and occasionally bilateral optic neuropathy. Neurological symptoms feature progressive bilateral facial neuropathy, cranial neuropathy, peripheral neuropathy, and may involve bulbar motor neuropathy, epileptic seizures, or brain lesions. Dermatological features include loose skin or cutis laxa, and heart arrhythmia has also been reported. While some patients experience subjective hearing difficulties, objective audiometry has not shown peripheral or central hearing impairment in those up to 60 years. Early diagnosis can be challenging, and the condition should be considered in the differential diagnosis of progressive bilateral facial neuropathy. [PMC9668035, PMC7865823, PMC8543933, PMC7195602, PMC6305910]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: AGel amyloidosis, also known as familial amyloidosis of the Finnish type (FAF) or hereditary gelsolin amyloidosis (HGA), is an autosomal dominant hereditary disorder caused by pathogenic mutations in the gelsolin (GSN) gene. These mutations lead to an internal abnormal degradation of a gelsolin variant. The most frequently associated pathogenic variant is p.Asp214Asn (also referred to as p.D214Y or Asn-187), but other identified mutations include c.640G>A, p.Glu580Lys, p.Met544Arg (c.1631T>G), and a heterozygous G duplicate in exon1 (c.100dupG) causing a frameshift. These variants are predicted to affect gelsolin function or stability, with some substitutions located in critical protein domains. [PMC10314070, PMC9668035, PMC7865823, PMC7195602, PMC6305910]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Gelsolin amyloidosis typically presents with corneal lattice dystrophy and is most frequently associated with pathogenic GSN variant p.Asp214Asn. Here clinical and histopathological features of gelsolin amyloidosis associated with a novel GSN variant p.Glu580Lys. We studied DNA samples of seven members of a two-generation family. Exome sequencing was performed in the proband, and targeted Sanger sequencing in the others. The heterozygous GSN variant p.Glu580Lys was identified in six patients. The patients exhibited corneal dystrophy (5/6), loose skin (5/6) and/or heart arrhythmia (3/6) and one presented with bilateral optic neuropathy. The impact of the mutation on the protein structure was evaluated in silico. The substitution is located in the fifth domain of gelsolin protein, homologous to the second domain harboring the most common pathogenic variant p.Asp214Asn. Structural... [PMC7865823]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic disorder characterized by split-hand/split-foot malformation (SHFM), facial anomalies, cleft lip/palate, congenital heart defect (CHD), genital anomalies, and intellectual deficit.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): ACFS; CCGE syndrome; Cleft palate-cardiac defect-genital anomalies-ectrodactyly syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence of ACFS has not been determined due to the low number of reported cases (9 to date). A similar occurrence among genders is expected.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The spectrum of defects occurring in ACFS is wide, and both interindividual variability and clinical differences among sibs have been reported. Bilateral or unilateral cleft hand is a constant feature. Cleft foot and cutaneous finger and toe syndactyly have been reported in some cases. Congenital heart defects of varying types have been detected in two thirds of patients. Facial anomalies are not specific for the syndrome, and clinical expression appears to be variable. Male patients manifest different genital anomalies, ranging from micropenis to cryptorchidism and hypospadias. Growth retardation is a common prenatal and postnatal finding. The frequency of intellectual deficit in ACFS is at present unknown due to the early death of most patients. Neurological anomalies such as hypotonia, hypertonia, and seizures have been reported in the first days and months of life.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The genetic mechanism underlying ACFS is still unknown. Isolated or syndromic SHFM has been linked to different loci or genes. Mutations in the p63 gene, responsible for ectrodactyly - ectodermal dysplasia - cleft lip palate (EEC) syndrome and related disorders with SHFM, have been excluded in a patient with ACFS.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based solely on clinical characteristics. The major diagnostic criteria include SHFM and CHD. Cleft lip/palate and genital anomalies are less common features. Although facial anomalies are not specific to this disorder, low-set dysmorphic ears appear to be a constant feature.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other ectrodactyly syndromes and clefting conditions associated with genital anomalies. However, EEC syndrome, Rapp-Hodgkin syndrome and ectrodactyly-cleft lip/palate-hand/foot deformities-intellectual deficit can be ruled out based on lack of ectodermal involvement. Malpuech syndrome can also be excluded based on distinct facial features and absent limb defects. CHD, cleft palate, and genital anomalies are features of genito-palato-cardiac syndrome, but none of the reported cases had ectrodactyly.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: The major features of ACFS can be detected prenatally by ultrasonography. A second trimester scan, including echocardiography and upper/lower limb evaluation, is recommended for monitoring pregnancies when parents have had a child with the disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: ACFS follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. The risk of transmitting the disease for the parents of an affected child seems to be up to 1 in 4.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Patients are at high risk of death in the first months of age. Cardiac and respiratory problems should be treated by specialists. A nutrition specialist should be consulted for feeding problems. Surviving patients will benefit from physical therapy, which should start in the first months of life in babies manifesting hypotonia/hypertonia and motor delays. In surviving patients, neuropsychological assessment should be performed every year to check for developmental and cognitive delay.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy is very low. Most reported patients survived only a few hours or months. Cardiopulmonary complications were the main cause of death.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked syndromic intellectual disability considered to be a severe variant of dyskeratosis congenita characterized by intrauterine growth retardation, microcephaly, cerebellar hypoplasia, progressive combined immune deficiency and aplastic anemia.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Hoyeraal-Hreidarsson syndrome (HHS) prevalence is unknown. The syndrome may be underdiagnosed due to high mortality rates.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease generally presents in early childhood and primarily affects males. Growth retardation is usually of prenatal onset. Other clinical manifestations include microcephaly, mucocutaneous lesions (hyperpigmentation, nail dystrophy, premalignant leukoplakia affecting oral and gastrointestinal mucosa), early onset bone marrow failure, immunodeficiency and pancytopenia. Cancer predisposition is also reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: HSS is caused by mutations in the DKC1 gene (Xq28), encoding the nucleolar protein dyskerin which interacts with the human telomerase RNA complex. Mutations in other genes (TERT, RTEL1 or TINF2, ACD, PARN) involved in telomere maintenance may be associated with this disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The disorder diagnosis is based on neuroimaging. Molecular genetic testing is needed to confirm diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include dyskeratosis congenita, Revesz-Debuse syndrome, Pseudo-TORCH syndrome, Fanconi anemia and Nijmegen breakage syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Intrauterine growth failure and cerebellar hypoplasia can be detected by prenatal imaging (ultrasounds, MRI). If the familial mutation is known, prenatal genetic testing can be proposed.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: HHS follows an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance. The disorder is very rarely inherited as an autosomal recessive form.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The aplastic anemia and immunodeficiency can be treated by bone marrow transplantation. Supportive treatment for gastrointestinal complications and infections is required.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is poor as the disease follows a very severe course and premature death in childhood can occur due to bone marrow failure, but survival into adulthood is possible.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: C syndrome is a rare multiple congenital anomaly/intellectual disability syndrome characterized by trigonocephaly and metopic suture synostosis, dysmorphic facial features, short neck, skeletal anomalies, and variable intellectual disability.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): OTCS; Opitz C trigonocephaly; Opitz trigonocephaly C syndrome; Opitz trigonocephaly syndrome; Trigonocephaly C syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence has been estimated to be between 1/800,000 and 1/1,000,000. Less than 60 cases have been reported so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: C syndrome is a congenital disorder characterized by trigonocephaly, dysmorphic craniofacial features that include upslanting palpebral fissures, thick epicanthic folds, strabismus, depressed nasal bridge with short/thick nasal septum and columella, flat philtrum, thin vermilion borders, micrognathia, highly arched palate, buccal-gingival frenula, and multiple minor ear anomalies along with frontal midline capillary hemangioma. Cleft palate is an occasional finding. The neck is apparently short, but this appears to be related to residual nuchal lymphedema, which may be generalized. Skeletal defects include short rhizo- and acromelic limb segments, hypermobile elbows with crepitus, polydactyly (usually postaxial), syndactyly of toes, sacral dimple and deformed chest. Intellectual disability may be severe, but normal intelligence quotient (IQ) has also been described in a few patients. Seizures and neonatal hypotonia have also been reported. Additional anomalies may include congenital heart malformations (50% of cases, and include interauricular communication, ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot, Eisenmenger syndrome), hernia (in particular diaphragmatic hernia), renal malformations (unilateral renal agenesis, multicystic dysplastic kidney or horseshoe kidney), genital anomalies (enlarged clitoris, small penis), and anal stenosis. Perinatal mortality rate appears to be around 50%.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of C syndrome is still unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Although most of the reported patients are sporadic, rare cases of familial occurrence have been described. Reports of recurrence in sibs with unaffected parents suggest that familial cases may be caused by germinal mosaicism. As recurrence in siblings has been reported, subsequent pregnancies in affected families should be monitored.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of C syndrome is based on characteristic clinical features including trigonocephaly, unusual facies, psychomotor retardation, redundant skin, joint and limb abnormalities, and visceral anomalies. Genetic analysis can identify specific causes, such as a missense mutation in the CD96 gene, which has been found in patients with C-like syndrome. Chromosomal abnormalities, including a balanced translocation t(3;18)(q13.13;q12.1) disrupting the CD96 gene, or deletions at 9q34.3, have also been associated with features of the syndrome. [PMC2227933, PMC1736036]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The C syndrome is characterized by trigonocephaly and associated anomalies, such as unusual facies, psychomotor retardation, redundant skin, joint and limb abnormalities, and visceral anomalies. In an individual with the C syndrome who harbors a balanced chromosomal translocation, t(3;18)(q13.13;q12.1), we discovered that the TACTILE gene for CD96, a member of the immunoglobulin superfamily, was disrupted at the 3q13.3 breakpoint. In mutation analysis of nine karyotypically normal patients given diagnoses of the C or C-like syndrome, we identified a missense mutation (839C-->T, T280M) in exon 6 of the CD96 gene in one patient with the C-like syndrome. The missense mutation was not found among 420 unaffected Japanese individuals. Cells with mutated CD96 protein (T280M) lost adhesion and growth activities in vitro. These findings indicate that CD96 mutations may cause a form of the C... [PMC2227933, PMC1736036]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inborn error of metabolism characterized by a deficiency in erythrocyte catalase, an enzyme responsible for the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide. The disorder is usually asymptomatic but may be associated with oral ulcerations and gangrene, or diabetes mellitus and atherosclerosis in certain populations.

DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Biologic, morphologic, and biochemical investigations performed in 2 patients demonstrate multiple peroxisomal deficiencies in the cerebrohepatorenal syndrome of Zellweger (CHRS) and neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy (NALD). Very long chain fatty acids, abnormal bile acids, including bile acid precursors (di- and trihydroxycoprostanoic acids), and C29-dicarboxylic acid accumulated in plasma in both patients. Generalized hyperaminoaciduria was also present. Peroxisomes could not be detected in CHRS liver and kidney; however, in the NALD patient, small and sparse cytoplasmic bodies resembling altered peroxisomes were found in hepatocytes. Hepatocellular and Kupffer cell lysosomes were engorged with ferritin and contained clefts and trilaminar structures believed to represent very long chain fatty acids. Enzymatic deficiencies reflected the peroxisomal defects. Hepatic glycolate oxidase and... [PMC1888479]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Zellweger cerebrohepatorenal syndrome (CHRS) should be considered in the differential diagnosis, as patients with CHRS exhibit a deficiency of particle-bound catalase in cultured fibroblasts. CHRS is a peroxisomal disorder characterized by multiple peroxisomal enzymatic deficiencies, including deficient hepatic glycolate oxidase and palmitoyl-CoA oxidase activities. Other distinguishing features include the accumulation of very long chain fatty acids, abnormal bile acids, and generalized hyperaminoaciduria, with peroxisomes often undetectable in liver and kidney. [PMC1888479]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare immunologic pulmonary disorder caused by hypersensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus, clinically manifesting with poorly controlled asthma and recurrent pulmonary infiltrates.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of ABPA in the general population is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: ABPA is most commonly diagnosed in adults although it is increasingly being diagnosed in children. Although affected individuals can occasionally be asymptomatic, most of them present with wheezing, bronchial hyperreactivity, hemoptysis, productive cough, low-grade fever, malaise, weight loss, and/or worsening symptoms of asthma and cystic fibrosis, the two underlying diseases of most of the ABPA patients (about 2% of patients with asthma and 1 to 15% of patients with cystic fibrosis develop ABPA).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: ABPA is an immunologic disorder due to a predominant T-helper 2 lymphocyte response to Aspergillus fumigatus infection without tissue invasion. The resulting lung inflammation induces mucus production, airway hyperactivity and, finally, bronchiectasis. Its increased frequency in patients with asthma or cystic fibrosis is consistent with a genetic susceptibility to ABPA.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnostic findings of ABPA include immediate cutaneous hyperreactivity to A. fumigatus antigen, elevated A. fumigatus specific IgE levels and total serum IgE levels over 1,000 IU/mL. High levels of A. fumigatus-specific IgG antibodies and eosinophils can also be observed. Chest radiographs and thoracic high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) can reveal fleeting pulmonary parenchymal opacities, central bronchiectasis, high attenuation mucus, air trapping and centrilobular nodules. Pulmonary function tests may detect airflow obstruction. According to laboratory and imaging findings, five stages of the disease have been defined: acute, remission, recurrent exacerbation (with presence of pulmonary infiltrates, elevation of total serum IgE), corticosteroid-dependent asthma (severe wheezing resulting from discontinuation of the treatment) and fibrotic (irreversible pulmonary function abnormalities). However, the disease usually does not progress through these successive stages.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes severe asthma with fungal sensitization, newly diagnosed cystic fibrosis, tuberculosis, infectious pneumonia (especially during exacerbations) and other causes of eosinophilic pneumonia like Churg-Strauss syndrome, and bronchocentric granulomatosis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The best treatment approach is not currently established. Therapeutic options include oral corticosteroids (e.g: prednisolone, prednisone) and antifungal agents (like itraconazole, voriconazole or posaconazole). Other treatments that have been tried include pulse doses of methylprednisolone, and nebulized amphotericin B and omalizumab (antifungal agents). The duration of corticosteroid therapy ranges from several weeks to several months after an acute episode but corticosteroid-dependent asthma patients are very difficult to wean off steroids. The duration of the antifungal therapy has yet to be established. However, if tolerated, it can be used for years.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The clinical course of ABPA is variable. Many ABPA patients can be stabilized for long periods when treated. However, long-lasting remissions are seen in only 50% of patients and many patients require recurrent courses of therapy. Central bronchiectasis, high-attenuation mucus and concomitant aspergilloma at diagnosis identify a patient with a propensity for recurrent relapses and chronicity, which requires close monitoring.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism characterized by increased urinary excretion of dicarboxylic amino acids, glutamate and aspartate, that can be associated with kidney stones and neuropsychiatric manifestations.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Dicarboxylic aciduria can be a manifestation of primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency, a clinically and genetically heterogeneous disorder. In a reported case, a patient presenting with dicarboxylic aciduria, severe lactic acidosis, and hepatic insufficiency harbored a homozygous c.545T>G, p.(Met182Arg) alteration in the COQ2 gene. This gene is involved in coenzyme Q10 biosynthesis, and the defect was confirmed in fibroblasts, where it could be rescued by supplementing the culture medium with coenzyme Q10. [PMC4430297]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Coenzyme Q10 deficiency is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous disorder, with manifestations that may range from fatal neonatal multisystem failure, to adult-onset encephalopathy. a patient who presented at birth with severe lactic acidosis, proteinuria, dicarboxylic aciduria, and hepatic insufficiency. She also had dilation of left ventricle on echocardiography. Her neurological condition rapidly worsened and despite aggressive care she died at 23 h of life. Muscle histology displayed lipid accumulation. Electron microscopy showed markedly swollen mitochondria with fragmented cristae. Respiratory-chain enzymatic assays showed a reduction of combined activities of complex I+III and II+III with normal activities of isolated complexes. The defect was confirmed in fibroblasts, where it could be rescued by supplementing the culture medium with 10 μM coenzyme Q10. Coenzyme Q10 levels... [PMC4430297]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Coenzyme Q10 deficiency is an important consideration in the differential diagnosis, as it can manifest with dicarboxylic aciduria. This disorder is clinically and genetically heterogeneous, with presentations varying from fatal neonatal multisystem failure to adult-onset encephalopathy. A case of primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency presented neonatally with severe lactic acidosis, proteinuria, dicarboxylic aciduria, and hepatic insufficiency, alongside cardiac dilation and rapid neurological worsening. Biochemical and morphological features, such as lipid accumulation and swollen mitochondria, were crucial for directing the diagnosis. [PMC4430297]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The disorder is genetically heterogeneous, with one reported case linked to a homozygous mutation in COQ2, suggesting an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. For families with an affected child, there is a potentially high recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancies. Early CoQ10 supplementation should be considered for newborn siblings, even before a definitive biochemical or genetic diagnosis is established, due to the importance of timely intervention. [PMC4430297]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: In a severe neonatal case presenting with dicarboxylic aciduria due to primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency, aggressive care was provided, but the patient died. In vitro, the defect in fibroblasts was rescued by coenzyme Q10 supplementation. Given the importance of early CoQ10 supplementation for CoQ10 deficiency, clinicians should consider CoQ10 treatment for siblings of affected patients, even prior to genetic diagnosis. [PMC4430297]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Coenzyme Q10 deficiency is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous disorder, with manifestations that may range from fatal neonatal multisystem failure, to adult-onset encephalopathy. a patient who presented at birth with severe lactic acidosis, proteinuria, dicarboxylic aciduria, and hepatic insufficiency. She also had dilation of left ventricle on echocardiography. Her neurological condition rapidly worsened and despite aggressive care she died at 23 h of life. Muscle histology displayed lipid accumulation. Electron microscopy showed markedly swollen mitochondria with fragmented cristae. Respiratory-chain enzymatic assays showed a reduction of combined activities of complex I+III and II+III with normal activities of isolated complexes. The defect was confirmed in fibroblasts, where it could be rescued by supplementing the culture medium with 10 μM coenzyme Q10. Coenzyme Q10 levels... [PMC4430297]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Familial hyperthyroidism due to mutations in TSH receptor
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hyperthyroidism characterized by mild to severe hyperthyroidism, presence of goiter, absence of features of autoimmunity, frequent relapses while on treatment and a positive family history.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Familial non-immune hyperthyroidism; Resistance to thyroid stimulating hormone

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Familial nonautoimmune hyperthyroidism (NAH) is a rare, autosomal dominant disorder caused by constitutively active germline mutations in the TSH receptor gene. Neonatal hyperthyroidism, including the nonautoimmune form, is also a rare disorder. While hereditary nonautoimmune overt hyperthyroidism is considered very rare, TSHR activating mutations causing subclinical hyperthyroidism may be more common, particularly in familial contexts. Activating TSHR mutations are rare in neonates and the pediatric population, typically occurring in the germline either inherited or de novo. As of 2010, 55 activating TSHR gene mutations have been documented, with 14 described as sporadic germline cases. [PMC11408929, PMC3005687, PMC2974847, PMC2858372, PMC5800789]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Familial hyperthyroidism due to TSHR mutations is a nonautoimmune condition, often autosomal dominant, presenting with a wide spectrum of clinical consequences. It can manifest as severe hyperthyroidism in the neonatal period, potentially complicated by respiratory compromise. In adults, affected family members may exhibit varied levels of hyperthyroid features, including fluctuations between euthyroid and subclinical hyperthyroidism, mild hyperthyroidism, or overt hyperthyroidism, even with the same pathogenic variant. Subclinical hyperthyroidism, which may be associated with a thyroid nodule, can remain stable for years without progression to overt disease or thyroid enlargement. [PMC11408929, PMC3005687, PMC2974847, PMC5800789]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Activating somatic mutations in the thyrotropin (TSH) receptor have been identified as a cause of hyperfunctioning thyroid adenomas, and germline mutations have been found in familial nonautoimmune hyperthyroidism and sporadic congenital hyperthyroidism. All mutations reported to date have been located in the transmembrane domain. We now report an example of an activating mutation in the extracellular, TSH-binding domain, found in a male infant with congenital hyperthyroidism due to a toxic adenoma. The pregnancy was remarkable for fetal tachycardia. Scintigraphic studies demonstrated a large nodule in the right lobe, and a hemithyroidectomy was performed at the age of 2 yr. Direct sequencing of the TSH receptor gene revealed a mutation in one allele resulting in a substitution of serine281 by isoleucine (Ser281--> Ile) in the extracellular domain. The mutation was restricted to the... [PMC508345]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Familial nonautoimmune hyperthyroidism is an autosomal dominant condition caused by constitutively active germline mutations in the TSHR gene. Affected family members can present with varied levels of hyperthyroid features, even with the same pathogenic variant. A family history of TRAb-negative hyperthyroidism is important for identification before TSHR genetic testing, and TSHR activating mutations should be considered in familial subclinical hyperthyroidism. While most TSHR mutations are associated with benign thyroid conditions, clinicians should be cautious about the possibility of locally invasive thyroid malignancy with certain mutations, such as TSHR I568T, especially when associated with suspicious cytopathology. Sporadic cases due to de novo germline mutations have also been reported, where parents do not carry the mutation. [PMC11408929, PMC9002183, PMC3005687, PMC2974847, PMC5800789]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: For familial nonautoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by constitutively active TSHR gene variants, total thyroidectomy followed by radioiodine therapy is generally recommended for long-term management. However, ablative therapy may not be necessary for late-onset mild hyperthyroidism without coexisting diseases. In cases of subclinical hyperthyroidism, the condition may remain stable without therapy. Fractionated radioiodine therapy alone has also been shown effective in controlling thyroid function and reducing goiter size in some patients. [PMC11408929, PMC10580448, PMC2974847, PMC2858372, PMC508345]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis of familial hyperthyroidism due to TSH receptor mutations varies, with affected individuals presenting diverse thyroid dysfunctions, even with the same pathogenic variant. Some adult family members with late-onset mild hyperthyroidism without coexisting diseases may show no progression of hyperthyroidism or thyroid enlargement, and ablative therapy might not be necessary. For individuals with subclinical hyperthyroidism, the clinical condition can remain unchanged for over three years without developing overt hyperthyroidism, even without therapy. With appropriate management, such as fractionated radioiodine therapy, long-term control of thyroid function can be achieved, goiter size can be significantly reduced, and relapse of hyperthyroidism can be avoided. Low TSH levels during treatment are not indicative of subclinical hyperthyroidism or a risk of relapse. [PMC11408929, PMC10580448, PMC2974847]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare corneal disorder characterized by non-inflammatory, non-progressive, bilateral ingrowth of vascularized, opaque scleral tissue into the peripheral cornea, obliterating the corneoscleral limbus and scleral sulcus. The condition is not associated with other ocular abnormalities.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Sclerocornea is consistently described as a congenital disorder or pathology, characterized by corneal opacification and scleralization present at birth. While the condition itself is congenital, diagnosis of associated syndromes or initiation of treatment may occur later in early childhood, such as at 2 years of age or in a 12-year-old boy with multiple congenital anomalies. The condition is static and present from birth. [PMC6875196, PMC5072933, PMC2831198]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Sclerocornea is a rare congenital disorder characterized with the opacification of the cornea. Here, a nonconsanguineous Chinese family with multiple peripheral sclerocornea patients spanning across three generations inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. This is a retrospective case series of a peripheral sclerocornea pedigree. Comprehensive ophthalmic examinations were conducted and assessed on 14 pedigree members. Whole-exome sequencing was used to identify the genetic alterations in the affected pedigree members. Lymphoblastoid cell lines (LCLs) were established using blood samples from the family members. Functional tests were performed with these cell lines. Six affected and eight unaffected members of a family with peripheral sclerocornea were examined. All affected individuals showed features of scleralization over the peripheral cornea of both eyes. Mean horizontal and... [PMC6875196, PMC2831198]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Isolated congenital sclerocornea is a rare, static congenital disorder characterized by opacification and scleralization of the cornea, causing it to resemble the sclera. This condition is often bilateral, presenting with decreased horizontal and vertical corneal diameters, and can involve vascularization of the peripheral cornea. Affected individuals may exhibit significantly increased apex pachymetry and smaller corneal size, leading to poor visual acuity. Associated ocular findings can include descemetocele, microophthalmos, iridocorneal adhesions, and severe anterior segment dysgenesis. The ophthalmic parameters of sclerocornea do not resemble those of cornea plana. [PMC6875196, PMC5072933, PMC2831198]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Isolated congenital sclerocornea is a rare congenital disorder with diverse etiologies. It can be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, with a RAD21 C1348T variant identified as cosegregating with peripheral sclerocornea, suggesting RAD21 functions are involved in its pathogenesis. Sclerocornea is also associated with the chromosome 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, indicating a genetic locus at 22q11.2 may play a role in anterior segment embryogenesis. Furthermore, sclerocornea can be found in some cases of PHACES syndrome. [PMC6875196, PMC5072933, PMC2831198]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of sclerocornea relies on comprehensive ophthalmic examinations, which identify characteristic features such as peripheral corneal scleralization, decreased corneal diameter, and altered apex pachymetry. The cornea appears opaque and vascularized, resembling the sclera, and may present with descemetocele, microophthalmos, or anterior segment dysgenesis. Genetic testing, including whole-exome sequencing, can identify associated variants like RAD21. For children with sclerocornea and systemic findings suggestive of 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is used to confirm the microdeletion, and genetic referral is recommended. [PMC6875196, PMC2831198]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Sclerocornea can be a manifestation of various systemic conditions, necessitating a comprehensive differential diagnosis. It has been observed in cases of PHACES syndrome, which includes posterior fossa malformations, hemangiomas, arterial anomalies, cardiac defects, eye abnormalities, sternal cleft, and supraumbilical raphe. Additionally, sclerocornea is associated with the chromosome 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, encompassing phenotypes such as DiGeorge, velocardiofacial, and Takao syndromes. While some forms of peripheral sclerocornea have been noted to have no association with cornea plana, this condition may still be considered in the diagnostic process. [PMC6875196, PMC5072933, PMC2831198]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Reported ocular findings in the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome (which encompasses the phenotypes of DiGeorge, velocardiofacial, and Takao (conotruncal-anomaly-face) syndromes) have included posterior embryotoxon (prominent, anteriorly displaced Schwalbe's line at the corneal limbus or edge), retinal vascular tortuosity, eyelid hooding, strabismus, and astigmatism. seven 22q11.2 patients from multiple centers with sclerocornea, an eye finding previously unreported in the literature. Four boys and three girls were identified with sclerocornea, systemic DGS/VCFS findings, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH)-confirmed microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2. FISH diagnosis was perinatal in six patients but at 2 years of age in one child. Sclerocornea was bilateral in five patients. Findings included descemetocele (five eyes), microophthalmos (one eye), iridocorneal adhesions (one bilateral... [PMC2831198]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Sclerocornea can be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, as observed in a family with peripheral sclerocornea spanning three generations linked to a RAD21 variant. It is also associated with the chromosome 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, where a microdeletion at 22q11.2 was confirmed in patients presenting with sclerocornea and systemic findings. This suggests a genetic locus at 22q11.2 may be involved in anterior segment embryogenesis. Therefore, ophthalmologists diagnosing sclerocornea in children with systemic findings suggestive of 22q11.2 deletion should ensure appropriate genetic referral. [PMC6875196, PMC2831198]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Surgical intervention, specifically penetrating keratoplasty (PKP), is a primary management strategy for sclerocornea. Corneal transplantation has been performed, including bilateral procedures, with successful outcomes reported. One method for PKP involves preserving the limbus through lamellar dissection and posterior recession, which has demonstrated long-term corneal clarity and useful vision. Concomitant procedures such as lens aspiration and release of peripheral anterior synechia may also be performed during surgery. Successful stabilization of the corneal surface post-PKP is achievable, particularly when the limbus is preserved. [PMC5072933, PMC2831198]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Sclerocornea is a static congenital condition. The prognosis following penetrating keratoplasty (PKP) can be influenced by several factors, with poor outcomes correlated to the presence of vascularization in the peripheral cornea and a smaller diameter of the recipient cornea. However, stabilization of the corneal surface is possible after PKP, particularly if the limbus is preserved during the operation and the epithelium maintains a corneal phenotype, preventing pannus growth. In one reported case, a patient maintained useful vision of 20/400 after 6 years post-PKP, with the cornea remaining clear and free from inflammation or conjunctivalization. [PMC5072933, PMC2831198]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder of the anterior segment of the eye, characterized by a severe recurrent allergic reaction affecting the cornea and the conjunctiva. It presents with red eyes, ocular itching, photophobia, foreign body sensation, mucous discharge, blepharospasm, and blurring of vision. The symptoms are typically bilateral but may be asymmetric. Characteristic signs include conjunctival injection, giant papillae mostly on the upper tarsal conjunctiva (cobblestone appearance), limbal gelatinous infiltrates (Horner-Trantas dots), and variable corneal signs. The condition is more prevalent in hot climates and most commonly affects young boys.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is a chronic, recurrent, and severe allergic ocular condition predominantly impacting children and adolescents in tropical and subtropical areas. It has been reported in patients with HIV, where a Th1-Th2 immune shift and decreasing CD4 counts may contribute to its initiation and worsening. While often considered a type I allergic disorder, with significantly increased tear IgE levels observed in a majority of patients (63.5% in an Israeli cohort), a notable subset (29%) presents with normal to low IgE levels, suggesting potential non-IgE mediated causes. [PMC12110089, PMC6032743, PMC1039732]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) is a chronic, recurrent, and severe allergic ocular condition characterized by an inflammatory-allergic reaction of the cornea and conjunctiva. It is often considered a type I allergic eye disorder. Immunological findings indicate that some patients exhibit strikingly elevated IgE levels in serum and tears, with specific IgE antibodies to allergens and marked eosinophilic reactions. However, other cases present with normal IgE levels and no IgE antibodies or eosinophilic reactions, suggesting non-IgE mediated causes. A T-helper 1-T-helper 2 shift in the immune response, particularly in progressive HIV patients with decreasing CD4 counts, is also identified as a probable cause for the initiation and worsening of VKC. [PMC12110089, PMC10021954, PMC6032743, PMC1040191, PMC1039732]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is based on characteristic clinical manifestations, including severe itching, photophobia, lacrimation, and a viscous mucoid discharge. Ocular examination, often via slit-lamp, reveals signs such as conjunctival hyperemia, papillary hypertrophy, giant papillae, limbal thickening, shield ulcers, Horner-Trantas dots, or hypertrophic limbal mass lesions. Imaging techniques like anterior segment optical coherence tomography (AS-OCT) and in vivo confocal microscopy enhance diagnostic accuracy. Histopathological examination of lesions may show eosinophils, lymphocytes, and fibroblasts, with specific T and B lymphocyte infiltration. While some patients present with elevated serum and tear IgE levels and eosinophilic reactions in conjunctival scrapings, these immunological findings are not consistently observed across all cases. [PMC12110089, PMC10021954, PMC8961886, PMC8917557, PMC2629892]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) should be considered in the differential diagnosis for patients with Down syndrome, especially when keratoconus, a frequent eye pathology in this population, is observed, as it can be secondary to unrecognized VKC. Furthermore, VKC can be distinguished from giant papillary conjunctivitis by the absence of associated factors such as sutures or contact lenses. [PMC10021954, PMC4244347]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis in twins: case report and literature review. [PMC8196533]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Vernal Keratoconjunctivitis (VKC) involves a multi-faceted approach. Pharmacological treatments include mast cell stabilizers, antihistamines, and corticosteroids, which can be administered topically, orally, or via supratarsal injection. Immunomodulators such as topical or oral cyclosporine and tacrolimus are utilized, particularly for refractory cases, with novel biologics targeting interleukin pathways showing potential. Surgical interventions address complications like limbal mass lesions, giant papillae, and advanced keratoconus, often involving keratoplasty (e.g., penetrating, lamellar) and amniotic membrane transplantation for vision restoration. Other therapies include scleral lens prosthetic devices and patient education on avoiding eye rubbing. A comprehensive approach combining immunosuppression, surgical therapy, and prosthetic devices can effectively manage chronic VKC. [PMC12110089, PMC10021954, PMC8961886, PMC8785578, PMC8917557]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis is a chronic, recurrent, and severe allergic ocular condition that profoundly affects quality of life and can lead to vision-threatening effects. Complications include shield ulcers, corneal leukoma, punctate epithelial keratitis, corneal neovascularization, advanced keratoconus, and limbal stem cell deficiency. Long-standing cases may also develop conjunctival inclusion cysts. While the disease poses considerable diagnostic and treatment difficulties, comprehensive and long-term management, including immunosuppression, surgical interventions like keratoplasty, and prosthetic devices, can achieve favorable visual outcomes and a stable ocular surface, even in severe, chronic cases over many years. Some manifestations can resolve completely with appropriate treatment. [PMC12110089, PMC10021954, PMC8785578, PMC8917557, PMC6032743]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis of the anterior tibial tubercle described in active adolescents and characterized by gradual onset of pain and swelling of the anterior knee causing limping that usually disappears at the end of growth.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Aseptic necrosis of the tibial tubercle; Osteochondrosis of the tibial tubercle

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a common cause of anterior knee pain in adolescents. While symptoms often resolve with rest or physiotherapy, resolution can take several years. A significant proportion of affected teenagers are prevented from participating in sports for extended periods, and some may experience persistent knee pain into adulthood. [PMC4330449]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a common cause of anterior knee pain in adolescents. In many cases, the pain is relieved by stopping sport, sometimes in conjunction with physiotherapy, though symptom resolution may take several years. A proportion of teenagers are prevented from participating in sport for prolonged periods, and some experience persisting knee pain into adulthood. The condition can be severe enough to prevent participation in competitive sports for a year. [PMC4330449]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Osgood-Schlatter disease often involves stopping sport, sometimes in conjunction with physiotherapy, which can relieve pain, though resolution may take several years. For refractory cases, a surgical option like percutaneous fixation of the tibial tuberosity has shown complete symptom resolution, allowing a return to competitive sport. In one reported case, symptoms recurred upon screw removal but resolved again after replacement. [PMC4330449]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Osgood-Schlatter disease is a common cause of anterior knee pain in adolescents. In a good proportion of cases, symptoms are relieved by stopping sport alone or in conjunction with physiotherapy. However, resolution of symptoms may take several years. A proportion of teenagers are prevented from participating in sport for a prolonged period, and some experience persisting knee pain into adulthood. Even in refractory cases treated surgically, symptoms may return upon resuming sport. [PMC4330449]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A toxic embryofetopathy characterized by a group of symptoms with unspecific neurologic involvement that may be observed in a foetus or newborn when the mother was exposed during pregnancy to excessive amounts of methylmercury.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Prenatal methylmercury poisoning; Congenital Minamata disease; Intrauterine methylmercury poisoning; Fetal methylmercury poisoning

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Severe methylmercury poisoning cases were reported in the context of two large epidemics: in the Minamata area, in Japan, and in Iraq, both affecting hundreds of people. The Japanese cases resulted from local seafood consumption and sea mercury pollution by a local industrial installation. Iraqi cases resulted from contaminated flour consumption. Large cohort studies in New-Zealand, the Faroe Islands and the Seychelles have documented a risk of less severe prenatal (and/or postnatal) methylmercury poisoning associated with frequent fish consumption (more than 2 or 3 times a week) in thousands of individuals.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In severe cases, the clinical picture of prenatal methylmercury poisoning is one of unspecific infantile cerebral palsy, with ataxic motor disturbances, psychomotor retardation and seizures. In populations with high fish consumption, the only manifestations of methylmercury encephalopathy are impaired psychomotor and cognitive performances. They are associated with increased risks of preterm delivery, lower birth weight, and impaired postnatal growth.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Methylmercury is absorbed from the intestinal tract, through the skin and by inhalation. Most of the human exposure is through food ingestion. In blood, methylmercury being lipophilic is mostly in red cells. It is transported through the placenta to the fetus and accumulated in fetal brain. In cells, methylmercury is partly demethylated into inorganic mercury which is mostly distributed in the liver and kidneys. Elimination is mainly through the fecal route; about 10 % of the amount excreted is in the urine, in the form of inorganic mercury. Methylmercury is also excreted in milk (where its concentration is about 5 % of the concentration in the maternal blood).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The best biomarkers of methylmercury exposure and internal dose are mercury concentrations in hair and whole-blood. In most individuals from the general population, they are under 2 µg/g and 8 µg/L, respectively.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The clinical picture in prenatal or postnatal severe methylmercury poisoning is one of unspecific encephalopathy. The responsibility of methylmercury should be considered when a high fish consumption is characterized.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Since exposure to methylmercury is primarily through fish consumption, it is recommended to consume not more than 2 portions of fish per week, especially for children and women of childbearing age. Fish consumption should be reduced in individuals with hair or whole-blood mercury levels of more than 2.5 µg/g or 10 µg/L, and without delay, when these levels exceed 10 µg/g or 40 µg/L, respectively. Biomonitoring and search for neurodevelopmental disorders are recommended for children with hair or whole-blood mercury levels above 10 µg/g or 40 µg/L, respectively or born from mothers who exceeded these levels during pregnancy. Mercury chelation should be considered only in those cases where severe neurological complications are possible.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Methylmercury-induced cognitive and psychomotor impairments are not always completely corrected by the decrease of internal methylmercury dose. However, a correct diet, a careful surveillance of neurodevelopment with attentive learning stimulations, can counterbalance the effects of this neurotoxic substance.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for fetal methylmercury syndrome should address the neurodevelopmental effects of environmental contaminants on the fetus, particularly for mothers planning future pregnancies who have a child with learning difficulties potentially linked to such exposures. Counseling should include advice on identifying and limiting exposure to mercury and other persistent organic pollutants, especially concerning dietary sources like fish and wild game, to mitigate risks for future children. [PMC113803]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Infantile Refsum disease (IRD) is the mildest variant of the peroxisome biogenesis disorders, Zellweger syndrome spectrum (PBD- ZSS), characterized by hypotonia, retinitis pigmentosa, developmental delay, sensorineural hearing loss and liver dysfunction. Phenotypic overlap is seen between IRD and neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy (NALD).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): IRD; Mild peroxisome biogenesis disorder-Zellweger spectrum disorder; Mild PBD-ZSD

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The birth prevalence of PBD-ZSS is estimated to be around 1/50,000 in North America and 1/500,000 in Japan. More than ½ of patients with PBD-ZSS have the NALD-IRD forms.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: IRD has an onset at birth or early infancy but manifestations may be subtle enough that diagnosis is not until adulthood. In infancy, symptoms may include nystagmus, hypotonia, sensorineural hearing loss, growth retardation, mild facial dysmorphism, and hepatomegaly. Hepatic dysfunction is first displayed in infants with jaundice and later in some with episodes of intracranial bleeding due to coagulopathy. In childhood, progressive retinitis pigmentosa, developmental deficits and hypotonia are seen. Most achieve motor milestones, though delayed, and communicate in a few words or signs. Osteoporosis and fractures can occur in the less mobile. Adrenal insufficiency and renal calcium oxalate stones can present in older children. Leukodystrophy with loss of previously acquired skills can occur at any age and may stabilize, or progress and be fatal. Atypical presentations (visual and hearing loss with preservation of intellect and cerebellar ataxia with/without peripheral neuropathy) have been described.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: PBD-ZSS is caused by mutations in one of 13 PEX genes encoding peroxins. Mutations in these genes lead to abnormal peroxisome biogenesis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: IRD is suspected on physical exam and definitively confirmed with biochemical evaluation. Plasma very-long-chain fatty acid (VLCFA) levels indicate defects in peroxisomal fatty acid metabolism with elevated plasma concentrations of C26:0 and C26:1 and elevated ratios of C24/C22 and C26/C22. Erythrocyte membrane concentrations of plasmalogens C16 and C18 are usually reduced, but can be normal. Plasma pipecolic acid levels and bile acid intermediates (THCH and DHCA) are increased. Occasionally, VLCFA levels and enzymatic assays in fibroblasts can be within the normal range, requiring additional assessment in expert laboratories. Sequence analysis of the 13 PEX genes can be performed. MRI can be used to identify myelin changes.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses include Usher syndrome I and II, other PBD-ZSS disorders, single enzyme defects in peroxisome fatty acid beta-oxidation, and disorders that feature severe hypotonia, neonatal seizures, liver dysfunction or leukodystrophy. IRD should not be confused with adult Refsum disease.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal screening of cultured amniocytes and chorionic villus sampling for VLCFA and plasmalogen synthesis is possible. If both disease causing alleles in parents have been identified, prenatal diagnosis can be performed as well as preimplantation genetic diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: IRD is inherited autosomal recessively, so genetic counseling is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for IRD. Cataracts should be removed in early infancy and glasses used. Hearing aids should be provided to those with hearing impairment and cochlear implants considered when hearing loss is profound. Hepatic coagulopathy can be treated with vitamin K supplementation and liver function may improve with primary bile acid therapy. A gastrostomy tube may be necessary to allow for adequate calorie intake. Foods rich in phytanic acid (such as cow's milk) should be restricted. Standard epileptic drugs are used for seizures. Lifelong follow up monitors changes in hearing, vision and liver function.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Great variation is seen with respect to life expectancy, medical complications and preservation of neurological function. Many patients survive childhood, and survival to adulthood is possible.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare lysosomal storage disease characterized clinically by severe global development delay due to neuronal dysmyelination, hypotonia which gradually progresses to spasticity during childhood, speech deficits, progressive visual impairment (due to corneal clouding, retinal degeneration and optic atrophy), achlorhydria, with increased gastrin secretion and iron deficiency anemia, and kidney disease and failure, all in the absence of dysmorphic features.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Mucolipidosis type IV (MLIV) is rare in the general population but is more prevalent among Ashkenazi Jews, among whom the prevalence at birth is 1/40 000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical spectrum of MLIV can range from severe to mild. MLIV patients typically have severe cognitive impairment, ocular abnormalities and achlorhydria with iron deficiency anemia. The most common presentation is of severe global developmental delay by the end of the first year of life and a progressive visual impairment during the first decade of life secondary to bilateral corneal opacities and retinal degeneration and resulting in blindness by adolescence. Development is usually limited to few or no words and poor hand use, and most patients do not achieve independent walking. Neurologic deficits (dys-/anarthria, slow chewing, eating and swallowing, spastic di- or quadriplegia, and hyperreflexive hypotonia) usually remain static during the first three decades of life, but in up to 15% neurologic deterioration may be observed. Brain MRI typically shows hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, signal abnormalities in the white matter, increased ferritin deposition in the thalamus and basal ganglia and (later in life) atrophy of the cerebellum. Progressive renal failure develops in the third decade of life. Strabismus and iron deficiency are present in about 50% of the patients. Milder manifestations or disproportionate affection of one of the organ systems may be observed. All of the MLIV patients have (asymptomatic) constitutive achlorhydria.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MLIV is caused by biallelic mutations in the MCOLN1 (19p13.2) gene coding for mucolipin-1 protein, a nonselective cation channel which is distributed in the membranes of late endosomes and lysosomes in all tissues, with the highest expression in brain, kidney, liver, spleen, and heart. The exact pathophysiological mechanism is unknown, but is hypothesized that abnormal flux of calcium is probably the most important, resulting in disruption in sorting and/or transport of late endosomes/lysosomes. Two variants, c.406-2A>G and 6.4 kb del, account for 95% of pathogenic variants in individuals of Ashkenazi Jewish heritage.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: MLIV is suspected in the individuals with typical clinical findings and elevated plasma gastrin levels or polymorphic lysosomal inclusions in skin or conjunctival biopsy. Identification of biallelic pathogenic variants in MCOLN1 (19p13.2) confirms the diagnosis. Periodic Acid-Schiff staining of conjunctival cells reveals autofluorescent amorphous inclusions. Urine mucopolysaccharides, oligosaccharides and plasma lysosomal hydrolase assays are normal.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Corneal clouding may initially lead to suspicion of mucolipidoses and mucopolysaccharidoses but MLIV is distinguished by absence of dysmorphism. The developmental profile is different to GM1 gangliosidosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is done by molecular testing.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: MLIV is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait. Parents of an affected child bear a 25% risk of disease recurrence among the future offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: No specific treatment exists, and management is symptomatic and targeted towards the visual manifestations and the neurological problems (cognitive delay, spasticity and speech deficit). Physical therapy with special focus on spasticity and ataxia can improve motor function. A speech therapist can advise patients with swallowing problems. Iron supplementation is used to treat iron deficiency. Cataract or strabismus surgery is often necessary.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Compared to other mucolipidoses (I and II), MLIV patients have a prolonged survival.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A partial autosomal monosomy characterized by variable combination of developmental delay, intellectual disability, ectodermal, genitourinary and minor cardiac anomalies, and specific dysmorphic features (prominent forehead and low-set ears). Specific combination depends on the size and breakpoints of deleted regions.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Non-distal deletion 12q syndrome is characterized as a multiple malformation syndrome. Clinical features include cleft lip and palate, in addition to cardiac abnormalities. This syndrome is caused by an interstitial deletion of chromosome 12q. [PMC1049959]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The syndrome is caused by an interstitial deletion of chromosome 12q. This genetic anomaly leads to a multiple malformation syndrome, which can manifest with features such as cleft lip and palate and cardiac abnormalities. [PMC1049959]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Multiple malformation syndrome including cleft lip and palate and cardiac abnormalities due to an interstitial deletion of chromosome 12q. [PMC1049959]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Multiple malformation syndrome including cleft lip and palate and cardiac abnormalities due to an interstitial deletion of chromosome 12q. [PMC1049959]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) is a biliary tract cancer (BTC) originating in the epithelium of the biliary tree, either intra or extra hepatic.
