DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Costello syndrome (CS) estimated number of patients worldwide is 300. Estimated birth prevalence has been reported to be 1/300,000 to 1/1 250 000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients have above-average birth weight from mild hydrops and usually present with severe postnatal feeding difficulties and failure to thrive. The severe feeding difficulties typically necessitate the placement of a feeding tube. Developmental delay with short stature and mild to moderate intellectual disability are present in most cases. Features include relative macrocephaly, coarse facial features (epicanthal folds, full cheeks, low set and prominent ears, upturned nasal nasal tip, large mouth with prominent lips), curly or sparse, fine hair, loose soft skin with deep palmar and plantar creases, and papillomata (torso, extremities, perinasal and/or perianal region generally during childhood). Musculoskeletal features include joint laxity and ulnar deviation of wrists and fingers, hip dysplasia, and kyphoscoliosis in older individuals. Cardiovascular manifestations include valvular pulmonary stenosis, arrhythmia (ectopic or multifocal atrial tachycardia), hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and rarely aortic dilation. The reported neurological signs are hydrocephalus, seizures, Arnold-Chiari malformation type I, syringomyelia, and tethered spinal cord. In later childhood, patients often develop tight Achilles tendons that may require surgical correction. Puberty is often delayed or disordered. The disorder progresses with age and patients often show signs of premature ageing, osteoporosis and osteopenia. An increased risk of about 10-15% for solid malignant tumors (embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, neuroblastoma in early childhood and transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder in adolescence) is reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CS is caused by heterozygous germline mutations in the proto-oncogene HRAS (11p15.5) involved in controlling cell growth and division in multiple organ systems. The most common variant results in the p.Gly12Ser amino acid substitution, present in about 80% of patients.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the constellation of clinical findings, although no single feature is characteristic of the disorder. Diagnosis can be confirmed by molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Costello syndrome shows significant clinical overlap with Noonan syndrome and cardiofaciocutaneous syndrome, which are also RASopathies. Other disorders to consider include Beckwith-Wiedemann, Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines (formerly known as LEOPARD syndrome) and Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndromes.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible if the disease-causing mutation has been identified in an affected family member, or if the diagnosis of CS is suspected prenatally and HRAS sequence analysis is performed.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: An autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance may be found, typically due to de novo dominant mutations. Genetic counseling should be proposed to individuals having the disease-causing mutation informing them that there is 50% risk of passing the mutation to offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Failure to thrive and cardiac manifestations should be treated with standard measures. Specific educational and intervention strategies may be required for intellectual development and developmental delay. Facial papillomata may require removal with cryotherapy or electrocoagulation. Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound examinations can be considered to screen for embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma and neuroblastoma until 8-10 years of age. Neoplastic complications are treated with standard approaches. Tethered cord may be screened by imaging. Hip dysplasia should be evaluated by an orthopedist.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The risk of neoplasia and severe hypertrophic cardiomyopathy negatively affects the prognosis. The prognosis varies by the specific missense mutations, with neonatal lethal phenotypes and attenuated phenotypes reported.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Nemaline myopathy (NM) encompasses a large spectrum of myopathies characterized by hypotonia, weakness and depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes, with pathologic evidence of nemaline bodies (rods) on muscle biopsy.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence has been estimated at 1/50,000 live births in a Finnish study but the disease is more common in the Amish community.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The age of onset varies from birth to adulthood. The main clinical manifestations include weakness (usually most severe in the face, the neck flexors and the proximal limb muscles), hypotonia and depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes. Facial weakness may lead to sucking, swallowing and speech difficulties. Respiratory muscles are frequently involved. NM is divided into 6 clinically overlapping subtypes depending on the age at onset and the severity of motor and respiratory involvement. Typical NM (approximately 50% of patients) is a moderate form of the disease with onset in the neonatal period. Most patients are able to live an independent, active life. Severe congenital NM (10-20% of patients) is characterized by severe hypotonia and little spontaneous movement. Survival after infancy is rare. Intermediate NM (20% of patients) is characterized by slow achievement of gross motor milestones, and loss of ambulation and/or independent respiration by age 11 years. Adult-onset NM is usually sporadic (<5% of patients). Onset is between 20 and 50 years of age. This form is characterized by rapid progression. Mild NM or childhood onset NM (10-15% of patients) is characterized by the development of symmetric weakness of ankle dorsiflexion and foot drop around 10 years of age. Weakness is slowly progressive. An Amish NM has been observed in several families. It has a neonatal onset and life expectancy rarely exceeds 2 years.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Seven genes involved in muscle thin filament structure and function, have been linked to NM: NEB (2q22), TPM2 (9p13), TPM3 (1q21.2), ACTA1 (1q42.13), TNNT1 (19q13.4), CFL2 (14q12) and KBTBD13 (15q22.31). Clear genotype/phenotype correlations have not been established.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical examination and histopathological findings on muscle biopsy, which may reveal a change in fiber type proportion and size and, if combined with the Gomori trichrome staining method, show rod-shaped structures (nemaline bodies) in the sarcolemma and more rarely in the nucleus. Muscle imaging studies such as ultrasonography, computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), may help selecting muscles to biopsy and can guide genetic testing. Muscle enzymes are generally normal or mildly increased. Molecular genetic testing may confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other neuromuscular diseases displaying nemaline bodies: dermatomyositis, myotonic dystrophy type 1 and mitochondrial myopathy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is feasible since genetic tests are available to detect mutations in ACTA1, NEB, TPM3, TPM2,TNNT1, CFL2 and KBTBD13. It requires prior identification of the familial causative mutation(s).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: A multidisciplinary approach is needed to handle respiratory insufficiency (permanent or intermittent use of mechanical ventilation and treatment of lower respiratory tract infections) and feeding difficulties (feeding techniques and calorie-enriched diets). Scoliosis, joint contractures or speech anomalies must be managed as usual. Cardiac function must be monitored.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the NM type, and life expectancy ranges from few months to a near-normal lifespan.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for nemaline myopathy (NM) is complex due to its genetic heterogeneity, with at least eleven causative genes and predominantly autosomal recessive inheritance patterns, involving biallelic, homozygous, or compound heterozygous variants. While some genotype-phenotype correlations exist, particularly regarding neonatal findings and long-term outcomes, the overall correlation with clinical severity remains poor, posing challenges for prognostic counseling. Genetic confirmation is imperative for accurate management and counseling, especially given the severity of some forms. For instance, KLHL40-related NEM8, a severe autosomal recessive disorder, warrants prenatal genetic counseling and diagnosis, particularly in Chinese populations where specific founder mutations like c.1516A>C are prevalent. Expanded carrier screening panels are suggested for these populations due to the condition's severity and relatively high incidence. [PMC12368771, PMC12258819, PMC11906229, PMC11385988, PMC8981653]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasia characterized by short-limbed short stature (due to severe metaphyseal changes that are often discovered in childhood by imaging), waddling gait, bowed legs, contracture deformities of the joints, short hands with clubbed fingers, clinodactyly, prominent upper face and small mandible, as well as chronic parathyroid hormone-independent hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, and mild hypophosphatemia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (JMC) is consistently described as a rare disorder, a rare skeletal dysplasia, and a rare autosomal dominant condition. It is caused by activating mutations in the PTH/PTH-related peptide receptor (PTHR1), with five different mutations reported. Research cohorts, such as one assessing 24 patients and studies of individual families, further indicate its rarity. [PMC6486824, PMC5095231, PMC2630869]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (JMC) is a rare autosomal dominant skeletal dysplasia characterized by severe growth plate abnormalities, abnormal endochondral bone formation, and short-limbed dwarfism. It from activating mutations in the PTH/PTHrP receptor (PTHR1/PTH1R), causing constitutive receptor activity. Clinically, patients typically exhibit PTH-independent hypercalcemia, often severe in childhood (11.8 ± 1.37 mg/dL) but tending to normalize in adulthood, though overt hypercalcemia is not universally present. Hypophosphatemia, consistently elevated hypercalciuria, and markedly elevated serum FGF23 levels are also characteristic. Most patients experience significant growth impairment, with adult heights well below the 3rd percentile, except for those with the T410R mutation. Nephrocalcinosis is common, sometimes progressing to chronic kidney disease, and orthopedic surgical procedures are frequently required. [PMC6486824, PMC5095231, PMC2630869]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (JMC) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by heterozygous activating mutations in the PTH/PTH-related peptide receptor (PTHR1 or PTH1R). Five different mutations, affecting three distinct amino acid residues, have been identified as causative. These include H223R, T410P, I458R, I458K, and T410R, with H223R being the most frequently reported. These mutations lead to ligand-independent, constitutive activation of the receptor, resulting in varying degrees of cAMP signaling activity and abnormal endochondral bone formation. [PMC6486824, PMC5095231, PMC2630869]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (JMC) is established through a combination of clinical, radiographic, and biochemical findings, confirmed by genetic testing. Patients typically exhibit severe growth plate abnormalities, short-limbed dwarfism, and other characteristic skeletal abnormalities, with radiographic evidence being crucial for early diagnosis in infants and toddlers. Biochemical markers include PTH-independent hypercalcemia, which can be severe but may be absent in some cases or normalize in adulthood. Hypophosphatemia, low or undetectable PTH/PTHrP levels, consistently elevated urinary calcium/creatinine, and markedly elevated serum FGF23 concentrations are also characteristic. Definitive diagnosis involves identifying activating heterozygous mutations in the PTH/PTHrP receptor (PTHR1/PTH1R) using such as Sanger sequencing. [PMC6486824, PMC5095231, PMC2630869]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Metaphyseal dysostosis type Schmid. [PMC2211607]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia (JMC) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by heterozygous activating mutations in the PTH/PTH-related peptide receptor (PTHR1 or PTH1R). Five different activating mutations have been reported, including H223R (the most frequent), T410P, I458R, I458K, and T410R, which has been observed in a father and his two sons. Establishing a diagnosis can be challenging, especially in infancy or early childhood, and in the absence of a family history or overt hypercalcemia. For instance, individuals with the H223R mutation may not always present with overt hypercalcemia, making early diagnosis difficult without genetic confirmation. [PMC6486824, PMC5095231, PMC2630869]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia commonly includes orthopedic surgical procedures, which most patients have undergone. The disease is also associated with complications such as nephrocalcinosis and, in some cases, advanced chronic kidney disease, necessitating their management. While an inverse agonist ligand has demonstrated the ability to reduce PTH-independent cAMP formation in vitro, suggesting a potential future therapeutic approach, this remains an investigational path rather than an established treatment. [PMC6486824]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Patients with Jansen metaphyseal chondrodysplasia experience severe growth plate abnormalities and significant growth impairment, with adult heights typically well below the 3rd percentile, except for those with the T410R mutation. Hypercalcemia is common in childhood (0.15-10 years) but tends to normalize in adulthood, though hypercalciuria persists. Most patients require orthopedic surgical procedures and develop nephrocalcinosis, with some progressing to advanced chronic kidney disease. The severity of growth impairment and mineral ion abnormalities is largely similar across different PTHR1 mutations, excluding T410R. [PMC6486824]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital malformation characterized by the absence of calvarial bones, dura mater and associated muscles while skull base, facial bones and brain structures are normal. Central nervous system is usually unaffected, however some neuropathological abnormalities such as holoprosencephaly, hydrocephalus, micropolygyria and gyration anomalies can be present. Prenatal diagnosis by ultrasonography is usually confirmed by magnetic resonance imaging as it can be confused with anencephaly or encephalocele.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Acalvaria is an exceptionally rare congenital disorder, with reported cases in the literature being infrequent. This condition often leads to fatalities in newborns, though a few cases of prolonged survival have been documented. It is characterized by the absence of flat bones of the cranial vault, dura mater, and associated muscles. Amniotic band syndrome is identified as an etiological factor for acalvaria, which presents with highly variable manifestations, as no two cases are the same. [PMC11556999, PMC1721025]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Acalvaria is an exceptionally rare congenital disorder characterized by the absence of the flat bones of the cranial vault, dura mater, and associated muscles, while the facial bones and base of the skull remain intact. Newborns may present with an excessively soft skull, and maternal polyhydramnios can be noted. Although the central nervous system is typically unaffected, cases can show foci of hemorrhage or, in the context of acrania with amniotic band syndrome, disorganized cerebral hemispheres. The condition can be associated with other anomalies, such as absent clavicles, or a spectrum of craniofacial and visceral defects when linked to amniotic band syndrome. Acalvaria often in fatalities with short life expectancies, though some cases of prolonged survival have been documented, and the overall prognosis remains poor. [PMC11556999, PMC1721025]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: While no exact mechanism is fully demonstrated for acalvaria, disturbances in mesenchymal migration during the fourth week of development are the most documented. Amniotic band syndrome (ABS) is also recognized as an etiological factor. ABS encompasses a spectrum of non-genetic anomalies that can result in major craniofacial defects, including acalvaria. [PMC11146448, PMC1721025]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Acalvaria can be diagnosed antenatally, with early detection being essential, typically after 11 weeks of gestation. 2D/3D ultrasound is a primary diagnostic tool, revealing key sonographic features such as absent calvaria and a dorsally bulging brain, sometimes described as a 'Mickey Mouse head' sign. Postnatally, diagnosis is confirmed through imaging modalities like head ultrasound, X-rays, and CT scans. These verify the absence of skull vault bones and allow for assessment of brain structures, including the presence of hemorrhage. [PMC11556999, PMC11146448]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Acalvaria, characterized by the absence of the dome-like superior portion of the cranium and dura mater with normal skull base and facial bones, can be distinguished from other conditions. Acrania is a fetal malformation defined by the complete or partial absence of the calvaria above the orbits and supraciliary ridge, often presenting with an absent calvaria and dorsally bulging brain. Both acalvaria and acrania have been reported in the presence of amniotic bands, as Amniotic Band Syndrome (ABS) is an etiological factor for acalvaria and can include major craniofacial defects. Aplasia cutis congenita, a congenital disorder with absence of skin, muscle, and/or bone, usually affecting the scalp, may also present with large scalp and skull defects, as observed in cases of Adams-Oliver syndrome. [PMC11146448, PMC9874222, PMC1721025]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Early antenatal diagnosis of acalvaria is essential and can be established after 11 weeks of gestation. Key sonographic features include an absent calvaria and a dorsally bulging brain, sometimes described as a 'Mickey Mouse head.' Diagnosis can be made using 2D/3D ultrasound, as demonstrated by a case diagnosed at 17 weeks of gestation. Following prenatal diagnosis, appropriate counseling for affected families is necessary. [PMC11556999, PMC11146448, PMC1721025]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for acalvaria must consider its diverse etiologies. While some cases, particularly those linked to amniotic band syndrome, are described as non-genetic anomalies, other presentations, such as a case involving first-cousin parents, may suggest a genetic component. Appropriate counseling for affected families is essential following prenatal diagnosis. This includes informing families about the extremely poor prognosis and discussing management options, such as elective termination of pregnancy. [PMC11556999, PMC11146448, PMC1721025]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for acalvaria depends on the timing of diagnosis. Following prenatal diagnosis, elective termination of pregnancy is considered the treatment of choice due to the extremely poor prognosis. For live-born infants, supportive care is the primary management approach, focusing on stabilization and monitoring, often provided in a neonatal intensive care unit. Early antenatal diagnosis is essential for appropriate family counseling and management decisions. [PMC11556999, PMC11146448, PMC1721025]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for acalvaria is generally poor, often resulting in fatalities with newborns typically having short life expectancies. The condition is considered to have an extremely poor prognosis, leading to elective termination of pregnancy as a treatment choice. Despite this, a few documented cases of prolonged survival exist. For example, one patient showed normal feeding and function after three weeks in the neonatal intensive care unit, though the overall prognosis remained poor. [PMC11556999, PMC11146448]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder characterised by a slowly progressive pure cerebellar ataxia associated with dysarthria. It has been described in 53 individuals from 26 families of Canadian origin. The mode of transmission is autosomal recessive. Positional cloning has led to the identification of several gene mutations.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): SCAR8; ARCA1; Autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia type 1

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Autosomal recessive ataxia, Beauce type (SCAR8; ARCA-1) is a neurological disorder associated with SYNE1 variants, characterized primarily by cerebellar ataxia of variable onset. Patients can present with a complex multisystemic phenotype, including highly elevated creatine kinase levels and lower-leg muscle atrophy. Electromyography and muscle magnetic resonance imaging often reveal a neurogenic pattern of muscle involvement. Muscle histology may show COX-negative fibers and mtDNA deletions, which can initially mimic mitochondrial disease. More proximal homozygous SYNE1 variants are typically linked to this recessive cerebellar ataxia. [PMC11476505, PMC10743207, PMC6016514, PMC5255944]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Autosomal recessive ataxia, Beauce type, is primarily caused by pathogenic variants in the SYNE1 gene, which encodes nesprin-1 isoforms. These isoforms are crucial for cytoskeletal, nuclear, and vesicle anchoring in striated muscle and neurons. Identified genetic mechanisms include novel pathogenic variants, compound heterozygous variants (such as nonsense mutations and large intragenic deletions), and homozygous nonsense mutations. More proximal homozygous SYNE1 variants are specifically linked to recessive cerebellar ataxia (SCAR8; ARCA-1). While variants in the DYSF gene have been observed, their role as modifiers rather than primary causative agents has been suggested. [PMC11476505, PMC10743207, PMC5255944]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis primarily relies on genetic testing, with whole-exome sequencing (WES) being a key method to identify pathogenic variants in the SYNE1 gene. This can be supplemented by high-resolution array comparative genomic hybridization (array-CGH) to detect copy number variations, including large intragenic deletions. A pangenomic approach is valuable for heterogeneous neuromuscular presentations. Electromyography and muscle magnetic resonance imaging can indicate a neurogenic pattern of muscle involvement. Segregation analysis of identified variants helps confirm pathogenicity and exclude other conditions. mRNA analysis may also be used to assess mutant transcript expression. While initial findings like COX-negative fibers on muscle histology might suggest mitochondrial disease, genetic identification of SYNE1 variants confirms the diagnosis. [PMC11476505, PMC10743207, PMC5255944]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Autosomal recessive ataxia, Beauce type, associated with SYNE1 deficiency (ARCA1/SCAR8), can present with a complex multisystemic phenotype, including elevated creatine kinase levels and lower-leg muscle atrophy, necessitating differentiation from DYSF-associated muscular dystrophy. The condition may also mimic mitochondrial disorders, particularly when patients exhibit cerebellar ataxia, COX-negative fibers, and mtDNA deletions, highlighting the importance of comprehensive genetic investigations. Furthermore, early progressive cerebellar dysfunction, a hallmark of SYNE1-associated ataxia, can lead to misdiagnosis as other neurodegenerative disorders, such as Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker disease (GSS) with the P102L PRNP mutation. [PMC11476505, PMC10743207, PMC6016514]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Autosomal recessive ataxia, Beauce type, is caused by pathogenic variants in the SYNE1 gene, with both homozygous and compound heterozygous variants reported. Genetic counseling should emphasize the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Diagnosis can be challenging due to the clinical and genetic heterogeneity, often mimicking other conditions like mitochondrial disease, necessitating the identification of causative pathogenic variants. Whole exome sequencing, supplemented by high-resolution array comparative genomic hybridization and pangenomic investigations, is valuable for diagnosis, including the detection of rare copy number variations. Segregation analysis of identified variants is crucial. A genotype-phenotype correlation exists, where more proximal SYNE1 variants typically cause recessive cerebellar ataxia (SCAR8; ARCA-1), while distal truncating variants may lead to congenital muscular weakness with distal arthrogryposis. [PMC11476505, PMC10743207, PMC5255944]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Gerstmann-Sträussler-Scheinker disease (GSS) with the P102L mutation in PRNP gene is characterized with progressive cerebellar dysfunction clinically and PrP Sc plaques neurologically. Due to the cerebellar ataxia in the early stage, GSS P102L is often misdiagnosed as other neurodegenerative disorders. We presented here a 49-year-old female patient with proven P102L PRNP mutation, and three heterologous mutations in hereditary ataxias associated gene SYNE1, including p.V3643L, p.M3376V and p.T2860A. The patient appeared progressive unsteady gait in early stage and developed the Creutzfeldt-Jacob disease (CJD) - associated clinical manifestations, including progressive dementia, myoclonus, pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs. She is still alive but with akinetic mutism 21 months after onset. Observation of intense signal changes in cortical regions (cortical ribboning) in diffusion... [PMC6016514]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome (ARS) is a generic term used to designate overlapping genetic disorders, in which the major physical condition is anterior segment dysgenesis of the eye. Patients with ARS may also present with multiple variable congenital anomalies.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The syndrome has an estimated prevalence of 1/200,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical manifestations of ARS are highly variable. Features can be divided into ocular and non-ocular findings. Ocular abnormalities mainly affect the iris: hypoplasia, corectopia or hole formation in the iris mimicking polycoria; cornea: prominent and anteriorly displaced Schwalbe's line (posterior embryotoxon); and the chamber angle: iris strands bridging the iridocorneal angle to the trabecular meshwork. Eye dysgenesis in ARS may cause increased ocular pressure (IOP) leading to glaucoma. Glaucoma can develop in infancy, but usually occurs in adolescence or early adulthood, occasionally after middle age. The most characteristic non-ocular findings are mild craniofacial dysmorphism, dental anomalies and redundant periumblical skin. Mid-face abnormalities include hypertelorism, telecanthus, maxillary hypoplasia with flattening of the mid-face, prominent forehead, and broad, flat nasal bridge. Dental abnormalities may include microdontia or hypodontia. Hypospadias in males, anal stenosis, pituitary abnormalities and growth retardation may also be observed.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Patients with ARS have been found to have mutations in the transcription factor genes PITX2 (4q25) and FOXC1 (6p25). A large number of different mutations have been identified but there is no clear genotype-phenotype relationship. However, PITX2 mutations are mainly detected in ARS patients with non-ocular changes. The underlying genetic defect is unknown in 60% of cases, and at least two more loci have been associated with ARS.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: ARS is diagnosed by ophthalmologic and clinical examination. Associated systemic findings are supportive of diagnosis. Genetic testing can be used to confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include iris hypoplasia (IH), primary congenital glaucoma (PCG) and Peters anomaly. Absence of other corneal abnormalities, such as megalocornea, sclerocornea and corneal opacity are useful in distinguishing ARS from other anterior segment disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: If the disease-causing mutation has been identified in a family, prenatal testing for at-risk pregnancies is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorders that comprise the ARS spectrum are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with high penetrance. Genetic counseling can be offered to patients and their families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: An annual slit lamp examination should be performed, along with gonioscopy, IOP measurements and funduscopy to assess the retinal nerve fiber layer and optic nerve head involvement due to possible glaucoma. Autoperimetry (automated measurements of the visual fields) is necessary whenever glaucoma is suspected. Should glaucoma develop, drug therapy is recommended before surgery. In case of glaucoma, the goal of treatment is to reach low IOP. Surgery is performed if eye drops are not sufficient in lowering IOP. Medications that decrease aqueous output (beta-blockers, alpha-agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors) are more beneficial than those affecting outflow. However, alpha-agonists should be used with caution in young children because of possible CNS depression. If surgery is necessary, the procedure of choice is trabeculectomy with the adjunctive use of antimetabolites. If photophobia is present in patients with corectopia and polycoria, contact lenses may be used to cover the holes in the iris.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is good, particularly in the absence of glaucoma.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Crisponi syndrome (CS) is a severe disorder characterized by muscular contractions at birth, intermittent hyperthermia, facial abnormalities and camptodactyly.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Since the first description of the disease in 1996, it has been described in less than 30 patients from 13 Italian (mainly Sardinian) families.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Extensive paroxysmal muscular contractions in the face (resembling neonatal tetanus) develop after minimal stimuli. Frequent contractions of the oropharyngeal muscles associated with absence of the swallowing reflex lead to major feeding and respiratory difficulties. All patients described to date displayed facial anomalies, including a large face, chubby cheeks, a broad nose with anteverted nostrils and long philtrum, and bilateral camptodactyly. Hypertonia is frequent. Early in the neonatal period, CS patients develop continuous hyperthermia (unrelated to infectious agents), dyspnea, spells of apnea, and cyanosis during crying. Abnormal central control of respiration may be present at birth, increasing the risk of sudden death. Febrile episodes disappear after the first year of life, whereas feeding difficulties persist. Paradoxal sweating after exposure to low ambient temperatures has been observed in some adolescents.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Mutations in the CRLF1 gene are causative.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: CS belongs to a group of conditions with overlapping features, including cold-induced sweating syndromes and Stüve-Wiedemann syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disease is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Surviving patients usually develop severe progressive kyphoscoliosis that requires corset therapy or corrective surgery. Marked feeding difficulties require nasogastric tube feeding.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Characteristic hyperthermic crises frequently lead to death within the first months of life.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Crisponi syndrome is diagnosed through genetic , primarily by identifying pathogenic variants in the CRLF1 and KLHL7 genes. Homozygosity mapping using high-density single-nucleotide polymorphism arrays can identify critical chromosomal regions, leading to the detection of CRLF1 mutations. Whole-exome sequencing and targeted Sanger sequencing are employed to identify bi-allelic mutations in KLHL7 or homozygous/compound heterozygous mutations in CRLF1. Additionally, real-time quantitative polymerase chain reaction can reveal a significant decrease in CRLF1 mRNA expression in patient fibroblasts. [PMC6386622, PMC5005468, PMC1852730, PMC1852726]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, syndromic renal disease characterized by the entrapment of left renal vein (LRV) between the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) and the abdominal aorta, resulting in increased luminal pressure, renal hilar varices, hematuria and, at the microscopic level, rupture of thin-walled veins into the collecting system in renal fornices.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Left renal vein entrapment syndrome; RNS

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact prevalence is not known. Most cases have been reported from the Far-East. Women are more commonly affected than men.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients with renal nutcracker syndrome (NCS) are usually asthenic, tall and thin. Many patients remain asymptomatic and are incidentally discovered during radiological imaging for other causes. Symptomatic cases present mostly in second/third decade of life with urological or gynecological symptoms. Urological manifestations include left loin/abdominal pain, left-sided macroscopic or microscopic hematuria (on endoscopy, varicocele, or lower limb varices. Gynecological symptoms resemble pelvic congestion syndrome and include symptoms of dysmenorrhea, dyspareunia, post-coital ache, lower abdominal pain, dysuria, pelvic/vulvar/gluteal/gonadal or thigh varices, and emotional disturbances. Three types of renal nutcracker syndrome have been defined, according to the site of LRV compression: anterior nutcracker syndrome, posterior nutcracker syndrome and combined nutcracker syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Normally SMA separates from the abdominal aorta (AA) at a 90-degree angle. The LRV lies anterior to the aorta in the fork between the SMA and AA. In anterior NCS, the SMA arises from the aorta at an acute angle, compressing the LRV causing left renal venous hypertension. In posterior NCS, the LRV courses posterior to the AA and is compressed between the aorta and the vertebral column. In combined NCS, the anterior branch of the duplicated LRV is compressed between the aorta and the SMA, while the posterior is sandwiched between the aorta and the vertebral column.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis should be suspected upon presentation with left-sided loin pain and hematuria. Diagnostic tests include urine analysis, ultrasound scan, color Doppler scan, CT or MR angiography, and left renal vein phlebography and manometry. Doppler sonography is usually the first imaging tool, which can detect collateral veins around LRV, whose presence sustains venous hypertension and are a radiological criterion for NCS. The ''gold standard'' for diagnosis remain phlebography, intravascular pressure measurement and intravascular ultrasound through which the venous pressure gradient between LRV and inferior vena cava and the renal vein diameter can be measured. Patients usually show an LRV/inferior vena cava pressure gradient >1 mmHg. Computed tomography venography and magnetic resonance venography are noninvasive evaluation tools which provide good definition of LRV compression and grade of involvement of other organs.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Compression of LRV leading to loin pain and hematuria can be seen in pancreatic neoplasms, paraortic lymphoadenopathy, retroperitoneal masses, overarching testicular artery, lordosis, reduced retroperitoneal and mesenteric fat or too much fibrolymphatic tissue between SMA and AA.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Surveillance is appropriate in pubertal patients, who may undergo spontaneous remission with physical development and weight gain, and in patients with insignificant symptoms and microscopic hematuria, or intermittent painless gross hematuria with a normal hemogram. Open surgery procedures with good outcomes include vascular transpositions and renal auto transplantation. Extra-vascular stenting can be performed through open or laparoscopic surgery. Intravascular stenting is a treatment option in which a self-expanding metallic stent is deployed in the stenotic region of the LRV.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: As this is a benign condition, overall prognosis is excellent. In highly symptomatic patients, with severe pain, frank/recurrent hematuria requiring blood transfusion, active intervention needs to be considered. Prognosis following intervention is excellent.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, life threatening rare neurologic disease characterized by a sudden rupture of an intracranial aneurysm into the subarachnoid space. It usually presents with a sudden, severe, excruciating headache accompanied by nausea, vomiting and syncope. Other features may include focal neurological signs, third and sixth nerve palsies, seizures and cardiac failure. Early complications include rebleeding, hydrocephalus, and seizures.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: A 67-year-old male presented with sudden headache and decreased consciousness, diagnosed as spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Imaging revealed an anterior communicating artery (ACoA) aneurysm and congenital absence of the left internal carotid artery (ICA), confirmed by the absence of the carotid canal. The aneurysm was surgically clipped. Postoperative angiography demonstrated that the left anterior and middle cerebral arteries were perfused via collateral flow from the posterior circulation. The patient made a full recovery. Congenital ICA absence is rare but significantly alters cerebral hemodynamics, especially within the circle of Willis, predisposing patients to aneurysm formation. This case underlines the importance of vascular imaging in patients with SAH and highlights the need for urgent diagnosis and intervention in the presence of congenital vascular anomalies.... [PMC12279337, PMC12126640, PMC12014724, PMC12202963, PMC12254079]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder of multiple-pathway glycosylation characterised by psychomotor delay, seizures, failure to thrive, cardiomyopathy, and ichthyosis-like cutaneous anomalies.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CDG syndrome type If; CDG-If; CDG1F; Carbohydrate deficient glycoprotein syndrome type If; Congenital disorder of glycosylation type 1f; Congenital disorder of glycosylation type If

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: MPDU1-CDG, also known as CDG-If, is a congenital disorder of glycosylation. Patients present with severe psychomotor retardation, seizures, failure to thrive, dry skin and scaling with erythroderma, and impaired vision. This condition is caused by a defect in the MPDU1 gene, which affects the use of donor substrates for lipid-linked oligosaccharides, resulting in the synthesis of incomplete and poorly transferred precursor oligosaccharides lacking both mannose and glucose residues. [PMC200991]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: MPDU1-CDG, also known as CDG-If, is caused by a defect in the MPDU1 gene, which is the human homologue of hamster Lec35. This disorder is characterized by a homozygous point mutation (221T-->C, L74S) in a semiconserved amino acid of MPDU1. The defect impairs the use of donor substrates for lipid-linked oligosaccharides, rather than their biosynthesis. This leads to the synthesis of incomplete and poorly transferred precursor oligosaccharides that lack both mannose and glucose residues, specifically those donated by Glc-P-Dol and Man-P-Dol. [PMC200991]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of MPDU1-CDG, also known as CDG-If, is established by identifying a defect in the MPDU1 gene. A homozygous point mutation (221T-->C, L74S) in MPDU1 has been identified as causative. This genetic defect in the synthesis of incomplete and poorly transferred precursor oligosaccharides that lack both mannose and glucose residues, which can be detected. Functional studies using cell lines transfected with the patient's MPDU1 allele demonstrate only weak restoration of normal glycosylation, confirming the pathogenic effect of the mutation. [PMC200991]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: MPDU1-CDG, or CDG-If, is caused by a defect in the MPDU1 gene. The reported patient presented with a homozygous point mutation (221T-->C, L74S) in this gene, indicating an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. This implies that both parents are likely carriers of the mutation. Genetic counseling would involve explaining the implications of this inheritance, including the risk of recurrence in future offspring and the importance of carrier testing for family members. The defect leads to the synthesis of incomplete and poorly transferred precursor oligosaccharides, lacking both mannose and glucose residues. [PMC200991]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: a new congenital disorder of glycosylation, CDG-If. The patient has severe psychomotor retardation, seizures, failure to thrive, dry skin and scaling with erythroderma, and impaired vision. CDG-If is caused by a defect in the gene MPDU1, the human homologue of hamster Lec35, and is the first disorder to affect the use, rather than the biosynthesis, of donor substrates for lipid-linked oligosaccharides. This leads to the synthesis of incomplete and poorly transferred precursor oligosaccharides lacking both mannose and glucose residues. The patient has a homozygous point mutation (221T-->C, L74S) in a semiconserved amino acid of MPDU1. Chinese hamster ovary Lec35 cells lack a functional Lec35 gene and synthesize truncated lipid-linked oligosaccharides similar to the patient's. They lack glucose and mannose residues donated by Glc-P-Dol and Man-P-Dol. Transfection with the normal human... [PMC200991]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Respiratory bronchiolitis - interstitial lung disease is a mild inflammatory pulmonary disorder developed by cigarette smokers and characterized by shortness of breath and cough, pulmonary function abnormalities of mixed restrictive and obstructive lung disease and high resolution CT scanning showing centrilobular micronodules, ground glass opacities and peribronchiolar thickening.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease (RB-ILD) is a recently described clinicopathological entity. It occurs almost exclusively in current heavy cigarette smokers, with cigarette smoking identified as the commonest cause. However, other exposures, such as biomass combustion from burning sage, have also been reported to cause RB-ILD, even in never-smokers. Few cases of this condition have been reported in the literature, highlighting the need for an extensive occupational or exposure history in respiratory medicine. [PMC12226064, PMC1746837]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease (RB-ILD) is a recently described clinicopathological entity. Patients typically present with symptoms such as worsening breathlessness, and the presentation can be acute. While it occurs almost exclusively in current heavy cigarette smokers, cases have also been identified in never-smokers with exposure to biomass combustion, such as sage burning. Diagnosis involves radiological evidence of RB-ILD and histological confirmation. In one case, bronchoscopic lavage demonstrated striking green pigmented macrophages, presumed to be chlorophyll uptake. An extensive occupational or exposure history is crucial for diagnosis. [PMC12226064, PMC1746837]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Respiratory bronchiolitis-interstitial lung disease (RB-ILD) is most commonly and almost exclusively associated with current heavy cigarette smoking. Beyond smoking, biomass combustion is also identified as a high risk factor for causing respiratory disease. A case report described RB-ILD in a never-smoker linked to burning sage and oils for spiritual work, with cessation of exposure leading to a positive outcome. This highlights the importance of an extensive occupational or exposure history in identifying potential etiologies. [PMC12226064, PMC1746837]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of respiratory bronchiolitis-interstitial lung disease (RB-ILD) involves several . Radiological evidence is crucial, with findings that may include diffuse micronodular patterns, although these can mimic other conditions. Histopathological assessment is frequently required for definitive diagnosis, as RB-ILD can be histologically proven. Bronchoscopic lavage may reveal specific features, such as striking green pigmented macrophages, which can aid in diagnosis. An extensive occupational or exposure history, combined with clinical and ancillary radiological findings, is also important for refining the differential diagnosis. [PMC12226064, PMC7903078, PMC1746837]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Organising pneumonia (OP), particularly its rare diffuse micronodular manifestation (MNOP), should be considered in the differential diagnosis, as MNOP can mimic respiratory bronchiolitis on imaging. Other conditions that are part of the imaging differential diagnosis for MNOP, and thus potentially relevant, include endobronchial infections such as tuberculosis, and hypersensitivity pneumonitis. Histopathological assessment is often required to distinguish these conditions due to implications for treatment and prognosis. [PMC7903078]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management primarily involves the cessation of exposure to causative agents, such as cigarette smoking or biomass combustion (e.g., sage burning), which has been shown to lead to positive outcomes. While smoking cessation alone can be effective, corticosteroids may be combined with cessation therapy, particularly in cases where cessation alone is insufficient or for acute presentations. Currently, there are no formal studies on the effect of treatment, with management strategies largely based on clinical experience. [PMC12226064, PMC1746837]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Cigarette smoking remains the commonest cause of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and respiratory bronchiolitis-associated interstitial lung disease (RB-ILD). Biomass combustion remains a high risk for causing respiratory disease. Method: a case of a 41-year-old woman and never-smoker with worsening breathlessness. It was identified that she made fire pits burning sage and oils for spiritual work, but beyond this had no respiratory risk factors. Radiological evidence of RB-ILD was identified and a bronchoscopic lavage demonstrated the presence of striking green pigmented macrophages, presumed to be chlorophyll uptake. Cessation of burning sage exposure has resulted in a positive outcome. This case highlights the need for an extensive occupational or exposure history in respiratory medicine and describes histological features of interstitial lung disease not previously... [PMC12226064, PMC1746837]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:91357
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Esophageal duplication cysts are congenital anomalies, originating from aberrant embryonic foregut development during the 5th to 8th week of embryonic life. While most are diagnosed prenatally or in early childhood, they can manifest across the lifespan. Prenatal detection has been reported in the third trimester, and symptoms like respiratory distress can appear shortly after birth or in infancy (e.g., at 6, 10, 16 months, or 2-3 years of age). Although predominantly found in children, these cysts are also identified in adults, with cases reported in individuals aged 18, 32, 35, 52, and 64 years. In adults, they may present with symptoms like dysphagia or be incidentally discovered as asymptomatic lesions. [PMC11423446, PMC7187343, PMC6641662, PMC5704793, PMC4955461]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Esophageal duplication cysts (EDCs) are rare congenital anomalies, representing 10-15% of all alimentary tract duplication cysts. Prevalence estimates vary, with reports ranging from approximately 1/22,500 to 1/8200 live births. While some sources state the true prevalence remains unknown, it is suggested that many asymptomatic cases may go undetected, and improved diagnostic modalities could reveal them to be less rare than currently thought. Most EDCs are diagnosed prenatally or in early childhood. They can occur anywhere along the esophagus, predominantly in the thoracic segment or mediastinum, with cervical and abdominal locations being very rare. [PMC11423446, PMC5008520, PMC4543962, PMC3309918, PMC3128727]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Esophageal duplication cysts (EDCs) are often diagnosed prenatally or in early childhood. While antenatal detection, particularly for cervical cysts, is fairly uncommon, cases have been diagnosed prenatally, such as in the third trimester. Raising awareness of ultrasonographic features is important for improving the rate of prenatal diagnosis. Early diagnosis is crucial for timely treatment before symptoms and complications arise. [PMC11423446, PMC5008520]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Duplication of the esophagus is a rare congenital anomaly. While antenatal detection is uncommon, prenatal diagnosis allows for proper counseling of parents regarding the prognosis and the necessity of a multidisciplinary approach after birth. [PMC11423446]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for esophageal duplication cysts is generally favorable, especially with timely surgical intervention. Symptomatic cysts, which can cause respiratory distress, dysphagia, or pulmonary infection, often resolve completely after excision, with patients recovering well and experiencing uneventful postoperative courses. Early diagnosis and treatment, even in the neonatal period, are emphasized for safe and effective outcomes, preventing complications. Asymptomatic cysts may remain undetected and require no intervention. However, untreated symptomatic cysts can be life-threatening due to airway compression, and complications like bleeding or infection can occur. Tubular esophageal duplication carries a risk of malignant transformation, which can be reduced by oesophagectomy. Complete excision of the cyst mucosa is crucial to prevent recurrence. [PMC11423446, PMC7187343, PMC6641662, PMC5704793, PMC5008520]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Benign occipital epilepsy is a rare, genetic neurological disorder characterized by visual seizures and occipital epileptiform paroxysms reactive to ocular opening which present in infancy to mid-adolescence. Vomiting, tonic eye deviation and impairment of consciousness are typically associated with the Panayiotopoulos type, while visual hallucinations, ictal blindness and post-ictal headache are commonly observed in the Gastaut type. Electroencephalographic findings in both types are similar and include bilateral, synchronous, high voltage spike-wave complexes in a normal background activity located predominantly in the occipital lobes.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Self-limited childhood occipital epilepsy is a benign epilepsy syndrome that appears in childhood, with an age of onset typically ranging from 3 1/4 to 10 years. It encompasses distinct types such as Panayiotopoulos syndrome (PS) and idiopathic childhood occipital epilepsy of Gastaut (ICOE-G). The condition is generally considered self-limiting, with seizures usually not continuing into adulthood, and a benign clinical course. However, diagnosis can be tricky, and atypical evolution or refractoriness to treatment may occur, particularly with ICOE-G. Some cases of PS have been observed to evolve into juvenile myoclonic epilepsy in adolescence, suggesting that longer-term follow-up may be warranted. [PMC7744758, PMC3841599, PMC488932, PMC1292962, PMC1292380]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Self-limited childhood occipital epilepsy includes syndromes such as Panayiotopoulos syndrome (PS) and idiopathic childhood occipital epilepsy of Gastaut (ICOE-G). PS is a self-limited focal epilepsy appearing in childhood, often characterized by predominant autonomic symptoms, though presentations can be varied and unusual, sometimes mimicking conditions like septic shock. Seizures in these syndromes can be challenging to diagnose as visual symptoms are not always the presenting feature. Some cases of benign occipital epilepsy may have a stormy onset with prolonged loss of consciousness, tonic aversion of eyes or head, partial or generalized convulsions, headache, and vomiting, typically with an age at onset from 3.25 to 10 years. While generally considered to have a good prognosis and be self-limiting, some cases, particularly ICOE-G, can show atypical evolution or refractoriness to treatment. Rarely, PS may evolve into juvenile myoclonic epilepsy in adolescence. [PMC7744758, PMC5540684, PMC4922291, PMC3841599, PMC488932]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Self-limited childhood occipital epilepsy is considered age-dependent and is presumably genetic, with family studies supporting a familial component. Its etiology involves a complex interplay between brain maturation processes and genes that confer susceptibility. Epileptogenesis in such idiopathic focal childhood epilepsies may stem from a sleep-related epileptic transformation of normal neurological networks, specifically a derailment of NREM sleep-related homeostatic plasticity. [PMC7491282, PMC5540684, PMC1292962, PMC1292380]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of self-limited childhood occipital epilepsy is based on clinical history and electroencephalography (EEG). Clinical presentation can be challenging, as visual symptoms are not always the initial feature, and visual hallucinations may be difficult to elicit. Seizures can manifest with prolonged loss of consciousness, tonic aversion of the eyes or head, partial or generalized convulsions, headache, or vomiting. Interictal EEGs consistently show occipital paroxysms or discharges typical of the condition. [PMC7491282, PMC5540684, PMC3841599, PMC488932]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Self-limited childhood occipital epilepsy falls under benign occipital seizure syndromes, which include Panayiotopoulos syndrome (PS) and idiopathic childhood occipital epilepsy of Gastaut (ICOE-G). PS, a self-limited focal epilepsy with predominant autonomic symptoms, can present atypically, even mimicking septic shock. Other childhood epilepsies to consider include benign epilepsy with centro-temporal spikes (BECTS), which is the most common focal epilepsy in children and part of a spectrum that includes atypical benign focal epilepsy and Landau-Kleffner syndrome. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) and absence epilepsy (AE) are also relevant, as PS can evolve into JME. Structural lesions like dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors (DNTs), which can cause partial seizures in the occipital lobe, should also be differentiated. The stormy onset of benign occipital epilepsy, characterized by prolonged loss of consciousness and focal features, may initially suggest an acute cerebral insult. [PMC7744758, PMC7491282, PMC5540684, PMC4922291, PMC3841599]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Childhood epileptic syndromes, including benign focal epilepsies, are considered to be presumably genetic, involving genes that confer susceptibility. Family studies on benign occipital epilepsy of childhood further support a familial or genetic component. While specific inheritance patterns or genes are not detailed, the condition is understood to have a genetic basis. [PMC5540684, PMC1292962, PMC1292380]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Self-limited childhood occipital epilepsy, including Panayiotopoulos syndrome, is generally considered benign and self-limiting, often with a good prognosis even without medical treatment. Anticonvulsant therapy may be employed, and in some cases, treatment can be successfully discontinued. While seizures typically respond well to treatment, atypical evolution and refractoriness can occur, particularly with idiopathic childhood occipital epilepsy of Gastaut. Although long-term observation is often deemed unnecessary, longer-term follow-up may be warranted for Panayiotopoulos syndrome due to the potential for evolution to other epilepsy types. Medical treatment might also be considered if neuropsychological deficits are present. [PMC7744758, PMC5540684, PMC4922291, PMC3841599, PMC488932]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Self-limited childhood occipital epilepsy, including Panayiotopoulos syndrome (PS) and benign occipital epilepsy, is generally considered benign with a good prognosis, and seizures often do not continue into adulthood. Many cases show a complete recovery, and seizures may respond well to treatment, sometimes allowing for discontinuation of anticonvulsants. However, atypical evolutions can occur. PS, for instance, may rarely evolve into juvenile myoclonic epilepsy in adolescence, warranting longer-term follow-up. Similarly, while traditionally benign, conditions like benign epilepsy with centro-temporal spikes can be associated with neuropsychological deficits, including linguistic, cognitive, and behavioral impairments, and should only be considered benign in their absence or mildness. Idiopathic childhood occipital epilepsy of Gastaut may also show refractoriness to treatment. [PMC7744758, PMC5540684, PMC4922291, PMC3841599, PMC488932]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare brain inflammatory disease characterized by acute or subacute encephalitis with involvement of the midbrain and basal ganglia occurring in children as well as adults. Initial symptoms are pharyngitis and fever, followed by progressive lethargy, sleep disturbances, extrapyramidal symptoms (parkinsonism, chorea, dystonia), neuropsychiatric manifestations (obsessive-compulsive behavior, mutism, catatonia), and ocular features (oculogyric crises). Autoantibodies against human basal ganglia are often positive. Survivors may develop post-encephalitic syndromes, most prominently parkinsonism.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Encephalitis lethargica is historically associated with the 1918 influenza pandemic. While the diagnosis of post-encephalitic Parkinsonism is rarely considered today, recent cases conforming to encephalitis lethargica have been reported, with eight patients discussed, six of whom presented in the last 20 years. There is growing concern about a possible new wave of neurological complications following the worldwide spread of SARS-CoV-2, drawing parallels to the development of neurological disorders like encephalitis lethargica after the 1918 influenza. [PMC8059684, PMC491086]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Encephalitis lethargica presents with distinct clinical features, including malignant catatonia. The disorder is also associated with post-encephalitic Parkinsonism, which is a defining characteristic used for diagnosis. While the diagnosis of post-encephalitic Parkinsonism is rarely considered today, recent patients have conformed to the diagnosis of encephalitis lethargica based on these clinical presentations. [PMC1737107, PMC491086]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Encephalitis lethargica has been historically associated with respiratory virus infections, notably following the 1918 influenza pandemic. However, herpes simplex virus antigen has been found to be absent in the brain in cases of encephalitis lethargica. The condition is sometimes referenced when considering neurological complications of other viral infections, such as SARS-CoV-2, which can trigger encephalitis with prominent parkinsonism, potentially through an immune-mediated mechanism. [PMC8059684, PMC1028018]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Considering the similarities with other pandemics due to respiratory virus infections and subsequent development of neurological disorders (e.g. encephalitis lethargica after the 1918 influenza), there is growing concern about a possible new wave of neurological complications following the worldwide spread of SARS-CoV-2. However, data on COVID-19-related encephalitis and movement disorders are still limited. Herein, the clinical and neuroimaging (FDG-PET/CT, MRI and DaT-SPECT) findings of two patients with COVID-19-related encephalopathy who developed prominent parkinsonism. None of the patients had previous history of parkinsonian signs/symptoms, and none had prodromal features of Parkinson's disease (hyposmia or RBD). Both developed a rapidly progressive form of atypical parkinsonism along with distinctive features suggestive of encephalitis. A possible immune-mediated etiology was... [PMC8059684, PMC1028018, PMC491086]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for encephalitis lethargica include conditions presenting with similar neurological features. SARS-CoV-2-related encephalitis, particularly with prominent parkinsonism, is a consideration, given its resemblance to post-encephalitic parkinsonism and historical parallels to encephalitis lethargica following the 1918 influenza. Additionally, herpes simplex virus encephalitis might be considered, though studies have shown an absence of herpes simplex virus antigen in the brain in encephalitis lethargica, helping to differentiate it. [PMC8059684, PMC1028018]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Considering the similarities with other pandemics due to respiratory virus infections and subsequent development of neurological disorders (e.g. encephalitis lethargica after the 1918 influenza), there is growing concern about a possible new wave of neurological complications following the worldwide spread of SARS-CoV-2. However, data on COVID-19-related encephalitis and movement disorders are still limited. Herein, the clinical and neuroimaging (FDG-PET/CT, MRI and DaT-SPECT) findings of two patients with COVID-19-related encephalopathy who developed prominent parkinsonism. None of the patients had previous history of parkinsonian signs/symptoms, and none had prodromal features of Parkinson's disease (hyposmia or RBD). Both developed a rapidly progressive form of atypical parkinsonism along with distinctive features suggestive of encephalitis. A possible immune-mediated etiology was... [PMC8059684]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Encephalitis lethargica can lead to severe outcomes, including malignant catatonia. A significant long-term sequela is post-encephalitic Parkinsonism, a diagnosis that, while rarely entertained today, has been observed in recent patients conforming to encephalitis lethargica. [PMC1737107, PMC491086]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic skeletal dysplasia marked by disproportionate short stature and the characteristic Madelung wrist deformity.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of Léri-Weill dyschondrosteosis (LWD) is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The characteristics of mesomelic disproportion of the limbs and Madelung deformity may develop over time, presenting anywhere from birth to adolescence. The wrist deformity is bilateral and is characterized by shortened and bowed radii and ulnae leading to dorsal dislocation of the distal ulna and limited mobility of the wrist and elbow. Expression is variable but the clinical features are generally more severe in females. Male patients show an athletic body habitus due to muscular hypertrophy, without any underlying muscle disorder. Intelligence is normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In around 70% of cases, LWD is caused by haploinsufficiency of the short stature homeobox (SHOX) gene, which maps to the pseudoautosomal region 1 (PAR1) of the sexual chromosomes (Xp22.33 and Yp11.32). Haploinsufficiency results from heterozygous mutations and deletions of SHOX, or of the enhancer regions located upstream and downstream of SHOX, in the PAR1. The molecular defect remains unknown in the remaining 30% of LWD cases. SHOX-associated LWD is part of a spectrum of disorders (ranging from the most severe Langer mesomelic dysplasia (LMD) to LWD to short stature, all associated with SHOX/PAR1 anomalies. The prevalence of SHOX/PAR1 mutations is estimated at 1/1000.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of LWD may be suspected on the basis of the clinical and radiologic findings and can be confirmed by molecular analysis (preferably multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification for PAR1 deletions and DNA sequencing for point mutations, small deletions and insertions of SHOX).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses should include the other SHOX-related haploinsufficiency disorders and related conditions such as Turner syndrome and distal monosomy Xp.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal genetic testing is available; however, requests for testing for these disorders are uncommon but are more frequent for LMD. LWD may be suspected by ultrasound at 20 weeks of gestation on presentation of short limbs.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: LWD is inherited in a pseudoautosomal dominant manner with each child of an affected individual having a 50% risk of inheriting the mutation. If both parents have LWD, the offspring will have a 50% risk of having LWD, a 25% risk of having LMD, and a 25% risk of having neither condition.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management should include regular surveillance with biannual height evaluations and annual wrist radiographs. Treatment options include administration of recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) to improve final adult height; or concurrent use of rhGH and gonadotrophin-releasing hormone agonist (GnRHa) to prevent the blunted pubertal growth spurt caused by the presence of estrogen. Molecular genetic testing of at-risk family members ensures early treatment with rhGH therapy to improve growth. Wrist splints, supports and ergonomic devices may reduce wrist discomfort. In some cases, surgical intervention (physiolysis of the ulnar aspect of the distal radius and excision of the Vickers ligament) is required in mid-to-late childhood and may decrease pain and restore wrist function.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The quality of life is good for individuals with LWD. Pain may worsen with age due to arthritis in the joint. Individuals with LMD have problems associated with their severe short stature and severely shortened arms.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autoimmune coagulation disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia (a platelet count <100,000/microL), in the absence of any underlying disorder that may be associated with thrombocytopenia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The annual incidence is estimated at between 1/25,600-37,000 in Europe, with a female to male ratio of 1.3:1. Although immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) can occur at any age, incidence shows an age-specific bimodal distribution for men with two incidence peaks observed in boys (under 18 years old) and among those older than 60 years of age.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: ITP exposes to a risk of bleeding. It is defined as severe when the presence of bleeding symptoms at presentation is sufficient to warrant treatment or when the occurrence of new bleeding symptoms requires additional therapeutic intervention. It is asymptomatic in one-third of cases. Mucocutaneous hemorrhage with purpura is the most frequent clinical manifestation, usually occurring when the platelet count is below 30,000/microL. Severe visceral bleeding (hematuria, gastrointestinal hemorrhage or cerebromeningeal bleeding) is mainly observed when thrombocytopenia is below 10,000/microL and is rare, occurring mainly in elderly with comorbidities or in children in whom the disease is often self-limited; however, most children do not have severe bleeding problems despite very low platelet counts. Depending on the disease duration, ITP is classified into newly diagnosed, persistent (duration of 3-12 months) and chronic (duration of more than 12 months). Persistence or chronicity occurs in about 30 % of children compared with about 70% of adults.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is unknown. However, the disease origin is not genetic as familial cases are exceptional. Platelet destruction, mediated by autoantibodies mainly in the spleen, is associated both with impaired platelet production and with T-cell-mediated effects.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: A presumptive diagnosis is made when the history, physical examination, complete blood count and examination of the peripheral blood smear do not suggest other etiologies for the thrombocytopenia. There is no `gold standard' test that can reliably establish the diagnosis. A positive response to intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) and/or steroids is supportive of the diagnosis. In ITP the bone marrow is normal, and bone marrow aspiration is indicated mainly in patients over 60 years' of age, in case of anomalies of other cell lines, when thrombocytopenia is refractory to first-line treatments, or when other diagnoses are suspected such as myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). In addition to the morphologic assessment, cytogenetic testing should be considered if an MDS is suspected.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include causes of secondary ITP (drug-induced), autoimmune diseases (such as systemic lupus erythematosus), HIV infection and hepatitis C. In elderly patients, MDS should be ruled out. In children, inherited thrombocytopenias are often misdiagnosed with ITP. ITP can be associated with genetic immunodeficiency syndromes (typically common variable immunodeficiency) and is observed mainly in children and young adults.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The therapeutic strategy should be adapted both to the severity of the disease and to the patient's age. At diagnosis, children with mild or even moderate bleeding can be managed with monitoring. Treatment is rarely indicated in adults with platelet counts above 20 to 30x10exp9/L in the absence of bleeding. Corticosteroids (oral prednisone or short course of dexamethasone) are the standard first-line treatment. Use of intravenous immunoglobulins should be reserved for patients with severe bleeding (bleeding score could be used to help the physicians for IVIg indication) who are unresponsive to prednisone or for the rare patients with contra-indications to steroids. In case of chronic severe ITP, splenectomy has been used as the reference treatment for a long time. However, biologics (such as rituximab, eltrombopag, romiplostim) and even immunosuppressants (such as mycophenolate mofetil) can now be considered as an alternative to splenectomy as second-line treatment for patients refractory to first-line treatments. The respective place between these different second-line therapeutic options is still debated; ultimately, treatment should be personalized according to the patient's characteristics.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The mortality rate is generally below 2%, but may exceed 10% in the rare patients refractory to first- and second-line treatments (including splenectomy).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) can be associated with underlying genetic factors. For instance, ITP has been reported in patients with X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA), an X-linked primary immunodeficiency. Furthermore, some patients presenting with isolated thrombocytopenia may carry bone marrow failure-related germline variants (ITGV-BMFs). These germline variants are linked to an earlier age of onset and a significant risk of progression to conditions like aplastic anemia or myelodysplastic syndrome. While whole-exome sequencing can identify these variants, elevated mean corpuscular volume and reticulocyte counts may indicate ITGV-BMFs, allowing for earlier diagnosis and intervention. Genetic counseling may be considered to assess these underlying genetic risks and their implications for prognosis and family members. [PMC12019708, PMC12203705]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: GTP-cyclohydrolase I deficiency, an autosomal recessive genetic disorder, is one of the causes of malignant hyperphenylalaninemia due to tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency. Not only does tetrahydrobiopterin deficiency cause hyperphenylalaninemia, it is also responsible for defective neurotransmission of monoamines because of malfunctioning tyrosine and tryptophan hydroxylases, both tetrahydrobiopterin-dependent hydroxylases.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): GTPCH deficiency; Hyperphenylalaninemia due to GTP cyclohydrolase deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: When left untreated, the deficiency causes neurological signs at age 4 or 5 months, although clinical signs are often obvious from birth. The principal symptoms include: psychomotor retardation, tonicity disorders, convulsions, drowsiness, irritability, abnormal movements, hyperthermia, hypersalivation, and difficulty swallowing.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: GTP-cyclohydrolase I deficiency should be suspected in all infants with a positive neonatal screening test for phenylketonuria, especially when hyperphenylalaninemia is moderate. The most effective way to diagnose the disorder is to measure pteridine levels in urine and to confirm the result by measuring neurotransmitters (5-hydroxyindolacetic acid, homovanillic acid) in cerebrospinal fluid and with an oral tetrahydrobiopterin-loading test (20 mg/kg).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The treatment attempts to bring phenylalaninemia levels back to normal (diet with restricted phenylalanine intake or prescription of tetrahydrobiopterin) and to restore normal monoaminergic neurotransmission by administering precursors (L-dopa/carbidopa and 5-hydroxytryptophane).
DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency is an extremely rare inborn error of tetrahydrobiopterin synthesis, with the recessive form being an ultrarare and poorly characterized disorder. A systematic review of the recessive form presented data on only 45 patients, highlighting its rarity. Diagnosis can be challenging, particularly in countries without universal newborn screening programs, which may lead to under-recognition or delayed detection. The first reported case in a South Asian child further emphasizes its rarity and the importance of considering GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency in patients with unexplained neurological and autonomic symptoms. [PMC11452796, PMC6570886]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency is caused by mutations in the GCH1 gene, which encodes the enzyme guanosine triphosphate cyclohydrolase I (GTPCH). This enzyme catalyzes the rate-limiting step in the biosynthesis of tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), a critical cofactor for the production of monoamine neurotransmitters and for phenylalanine homeostasis. The disorder exists in both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive forms. The dominant form is a common cause of dopa-responsive dystonia, while the recessive form is an ultrarare disorder with earlier, more complex presentations, potentially disrupting neurodevelopment. Biochemical findings often include a BH4 defect, reduced neopterin, and low cerebrospinal fluid levels of monoamine metabolites. Hyperphenylalaninemia can also be observed in some cases, and the clinical spectrum is characterized by a gradient of BH4 defect and genetic variant severity. [PMC11452796, PMC6570886, PMC4005918, PMC3116226, PMC1736164]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency should be considered in the differential diagnosis of DOPA-responsive dystonia, which can manifest in both recessive and dominant forms. It is an extremely rare inborn error of BH4 synthesis, and the recessive form can also present with malignant hyperphenylalaninemia, recurrent hyperthermia, and progressive neurological and autonomic dysfunction. Patients with unexplained neurological and autonomic symptoms, especially those with hyperphenylalaninemia, warrant testing for GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency. Furthermore, any patient with dystonia of unclear etiology should receive a trial of levodopa, given the condition's responsiveness. Initial genetic screening may be negative, necessitating follow-up biochemical evaluation. [PMC9985884, PMC8840640, PMC6570886, PMC1736164]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency is caused by GCH1 gene mutations and can present in both autosomal dominant and recessive forms. The recessive form is ultrarare, exhibiting a broad phenotypic spectrum from early-infantile encephalopathy to late-onset dopa-responsive dystonia, with genotype and biochemical alterations potentially predicting clinical severity and guiding early, critical treatment. The dominant form typically presents as dopa-responsive dystonia, though intrafamilial variability in clinical phenotype can occur. Diagnosis can be challenging, sometimes requiring reanalysis of exome sequencing and biochemical evaluation, especially for patients with unexplained neurological and autonomic symptoms. [PMC11452796, PMC8840640, PMC6570886, PMC4005918, PMC1736164]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis of GTP cyclohydrolase I deficiency is highly variable, influenced by the specific phenotype and timing of intervention. Recessive forms present a spectrum from early-infantile encephalopathy with profound disability to dystonia-parkinsonism with developmental stagnation, and a late-onset dopa-responsive dystonia phenotype. Early pharmacological treatment is critical, particularly for severe presentations, to prevent disabling neurodevelopmental outcomes, though residual neurological dysfunction may persist. Hyperphenylalaninemia is associated with a higher likelihood of intellectual disability. The dominant form also shows intrafamilial variability, ranging from mild, completely levodopa-responsive cases to severe dystonia with progressive contractures and only partial responsiveness. Overall, treatment with agents like levodopa, sapropterin, and 5-hydroxytryptophan can lead to significant improvement in motor symptoms, depression, and function. Genotype and biochemical alterations may help predict clinical severity. [PMC11452796, PMC6570886, PMC4005918, PMC3116226, PMC1736164]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Zebra body myopathy is a benign congenital myopathy, characterised by congenital hypotonia and weakness. Prevalence is unknown. Less than ten patients have been described so far. Muscle biopsy shows zebra bodies and other myopathic changes. Mutations of the alpha-skeletal actin (ACTA1) gene may be involved.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Zebra bodies, observed as osmophilic accumulations via electron microscopy in the myocardium, are consistent with Fabry disease. Fabry disease is posited to lead to end-stage kidney disease, which can alter calcium phosphate metabolism. This alteration is a proposed mechanism for conditions like caseous calcification of the mitral annulus. The presence of zebra bodies is therefore indicative of underlying Fabry disease, which can contribute to multifactorial cardiac issues. [PMC11801426]
