DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Electron microscopy (EM) is a diagnostic method used to identify myeloid/zebra bodies, which appear as osmophilic accumulations. These accumulations can also be detected in myocardium through Toluidine blue staining. The presence of myeloid/zebra bodies is consistent with conditions such as Fabry disease. [PMC11801426]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Fabry disease should be considered in the differential diagnosis for conditions presenting with zebra bodies. Electron microscopy can reveal myeloid/zebra bodies, which are consistent with Fabry disease, as demonstrated in a case where these findings were noted in myocardial tissue. [PMC11801426]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Caseous calcification of the mitral annulus (CCMA) is a rare variant of mitral annular calcification (MAC) usually described as an antemortem finding. a case of sudden cardiac arrest in a 39-year-old male with end-stage renal disease undergoing hemodialysis with a history of Fabry disease by kidney biopsy. Autopsy revealed significant circumferential annular calcification in both mitral and aortic valves with a caseous gross appearance. Histologically, these areas consisted of amorphous basophilic material accompanied by a surrounding granulomatous-appearing infiltrate. Von Kossa staining on non-decalcified tissue revealed strong positive staining, confirming CCMA diagnosis. While identifiable, the atrioventricular node was displaced and distorted by caseous deposits. Toluidine blue staining of myocardium showed osmophilic accumulations, and electron microscopy (EM) showed myeloid/zebra... [PMC11801426]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Microvillus inclusion disease (MVID) is a very rare and severe intestinal disease characterized by intractable neonatal secretory diarrhea persisting at bowel rest and specific histological features of the intestinal epithelium.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Congenital microvillous atrophy; Congenital microvillus atrophy; MVID; Microvillous inclusion disease

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence data are not available. Less than 200 cases have been reported to date. There is a male predominance, with a sex ratio of 1.5:1.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Two clinical forms of MVID have been described: an early-onset form, developing within hours or days of birth, and a late-onset form, occurring in the first months of life. In both, intractable, watery diarrhea is profuse and leads to severe metabolic acidosis, dehydration, malabsorption and failure to thrive. Total parenteral nutrition is necessary, however, in some later-onset cases, partial oral absorption has been described. The intestinal insufficiency is progressively life-threatening in the absence of rapid, appropriate hydroelectrolytic and nutritional compensation. Developmental delays may be present and rare associated anomalies (e.g. inguinal hernia, renal dysplasia) have been reported. Long-term parenteral nutrition may be complicated with specific liver cholestasis. Atypical forms of MVID, without detectable microvillus inclusions and less severe course, have been described.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MVID is caused by mutations in the MYO5B gene (18q) resulting in perturbation of intestinal epithelial cell apical polarity. Disorganized microvilli impair the absorptive capacity of the enterocytes. A variant of the disorder, without microvillous inclusion vesicles, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the syntaxin 3 (STX3) gene (11q12.1), and when associated with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, can also be caused by mutation of STXBP2 (19p13.2) gene. Some patients do not display mutations in any identified gene.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is suspected based on clinical manifestations and is confirmed by histological analysis of small bowel biopsies showing villous atrophy and abnormal periodic acid-Schiff stain (PAS)-positive inclusion material in intestinal epithelium, without crypt hyperplasia. Electronic microscopy reveals microvillous atrophy and in most cases, microvillous inclusion vesicles in the cytoplasm of enterocytes. Molecular genetic testing has become essential to confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes rare congenital enteropathies such as autoimmune enteropathy, chloride diarrhea, congenital sodium diarrhea, and congenital tufting enteropathy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: As MVID is a rare disease with no specific and systematic prenatal signs. Prenatal diagnosis is possible only if the specific gene mutation has been identified in an affected member of the family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The inheritance pattern of MVID is autosomal recessive (parents of an affected individual have a probability of 25 % to transmit the causal mutation to their offspring). Genetic counseling should be offered to affected families in order to provide more information about this genetic condition, its risk of recurrence and the necessity/availability of prenatal diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: To date, there is no curative therapy for MVID. Treatment involves total parenteral nutrition, intestinal transplantation (when long-term parenteral nutrition is no longer possible) and, when required, associated liver transplantation.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Due to the severity and precocity of the symptoms, as well as the long-term parenteral nutrition's complications, prognosis for MVID is generally poor. Causes of death include severe dehydration and metabolic imbalance, malnutrition, and sepsis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Microcephaly-cardiomyopathy syndrome is characterised by severe intellectual deficit, microcephaly and dilated cardiomyopathy. Hand and foot anomalies have also been reported. The syndrome has been described in three individuals. Transmission is autosomal recessive.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Microcephaly-cardiomyopathy syndrome is a rare condition, with only a few cases reported in the literature. It was initially observed in two siblings, and a second reported case confirmed the phenotype. The syndrome is believed to be a new autosomal recessive disorder, suggested by its occurrence in siblings. [PMC1734265, PMC1015794]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Microcephaly-cardiomyopathy syndrome, initially described as a new autosomal recessive phenotype, is associated with diverse etiologies. Genetic causes include biallelic pathogenic variants in the PARS2 gene and compound heterozygous mutations in the VARS2 gene. Homozygous null mutations in the ITPA gene can lead to a Martsolf-like syndrome featuring microcephaly and dilated cardiomyopathy. De novo heterozygous spliced mutations in the ERCC8 gene are linked to Cockayne syndrome with microcephaly and cardiac anomalies. Furthermore, a de novo unbalanced chromosome translocation resulting in monosomy for proximal 14q and distal 4p has been identified. Congenital Zika syndrome, caused by Zika virus infection, also presents with severe microcephaly and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. [PMC10767575, PMC7543855, PMC7216809, PMC6968568, PMC6428344]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of microcephaly-cardiomyopathy syndrome often involves a combination of genetic, imaging, and clinical assessments. Genetic investigations, including whole exome sequencing, whole-genome sequencing, RNA sequencing, karyotyping, and molecular refinement, are used to identify pathogenic variants or chromosomal abnormalities in genes such as PARS2, ERCC8, VARS2, ITPA, or TREX1. Imaging techniques like prenatal sonography, MRI, echocardiography, and hip ultrasound are crucial for detecting microcephaly, cardiomyopathy, and other structural anomalies. Electrographic features, such as those from prolonged sleep EEG, and biochemical analyses, including lactic acidemia or TORCH IgM titres, may also be employed. For infectious causes like Zika, real-time PCR is used. A multidisciplinary approach is recommended for comprehensive evaluation. [PMC10767575, PMC9806047, PMC7543855, PMC7216809, PMC6968568]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for microcephaly-cardiomyopathy syndrome encompasses several genetic and congenital conditions. Biallelic pathogenic variants in PARS2 are associated with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, microcephaly, and cardiomyopathy. Congenital Zika Syndrome presents with severe microcephaly and mild hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Cockayne syndrome can include microcephaly and, atypically, cardiac anomalies such as dilated cardiomyopathy. VARS2 gene variants are linked to epileptic encephalopathy, microcephaly, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. ITPase deficiency causes a Martsolf-like syndrome with postnatal microcephaly and lethal infantile dilated cardiomyopathy. Additionally, chromosomal abnormalities like Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome with monosomy for proximal 14q and distal 4p can manifest with microcephaly and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. [PMC10767575, PMC9806047, PMC7543855, PMC7216809, PMC6968568]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of conditions involving microcephaly and cardiomyopathy can be achieved through prenatal sonographic examination. At 27 weeks of gestation, sonography has revealed intrauterine growth retardation, microcephaly, cardiomegaly with arrhythmia, and asymmetry of the upper limbs. Fetal cardiomyopathy has also been identified during pregnancy. Genetic amniocentesis can further confirm an abnormal karyotype, such as a de novo unbalanced chromosome translocation, providing a definitive diagnosis. [PMC9806047, PMC7543855, PMC1051524]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Microcephaly-cardiomyopathy syndrome is genetically heterogeneous. Biallelic or compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in genes such as PARS2, VARS2, and ITPA have been identified as causes, typically indicating an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. The general microcephaly-cardiomyopathy phenotype has also been observed in siblings, suggesting autosomal recessive inheritance. Furthermore, de novo unbalanced chromosomal translocations, such as monosomy for proximal 14q and distal 4p, can also lead to this syndrome. Genetic counseling should address these diverse genetic etiologies, their associated inheritance patterns, and the implications for recurrence risk and family planning, noting potential phenotypic variability. [PMC10767575, PMC6968568, PMC6428344, PMC1734265, PMC1051524]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS) induces innate immune activation. It can present with cerebral calcifications and hepatosplenomegaly mimicking congenital infections. The present case report discusses the diagnosis and treatment of a case of fetal cardiomyopathy whose postnatal symptoms resembled TORCH (toxoplasmosis, other agents, rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes and syphilis) infection. The mother had a history of two lost pregnancies due to fetal cardiomyopathy and the same was identified in the current pregnancy. At 34 weeks of gestation, the mother delivered a late preterm male neonate due to intrauterine growth restriction weighing 1590 g with respiratory distress and cardiomyopathy at birth. The neonate had cerebral calcifications, hepatosplenomegaly and thrombocytopenia. As the infant's TORCH IgM titre was negative, pseudo-TORCH syndrome similar to AGS was suspected. Clinical... [PMC9806047, PMC7543855, PMC7216809]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for microcephaly-cardiomyopathy syndrome is often severe, with many affected individuals not surviving beyond 10 years, particularly in cases linked to PARS2 variants. Early death due to malignant arrhythmia has been reported in VARS2-related disorders, and ITPA deficiency is associated with a lethal infantile dilated cardiomyopathy. However, some cases of microcephaly-cardiomyopathy syndrome present with a self-limiting dilated cardiomyopathy, as observed in a 9-year-old girl and two siblings, indicating variability in cardiac outcomes. Genetic modifiers may also contribute to disease variability and longer survival in certain instances. [PMC10767575, PMC6968568, PMC6428344, PMC1734265, PMC1015794]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare metabolic disorder belonging to the neutral aminoacidurias, mainly characterized by skin photosensitivity, ocular and neuropsychiatric features, due to abnormal renal and gastrointestinal transport of neutral amino acids (tryptophan, alanine, asparagine, glutamine, histidine, isoleucine, leucine, phenylalanine, serine, threonine, tyrosine and valine).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated prevalence is approximately 1 in 30,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most subjects who fulfil the biochemical diagnostic criteria (mostly detected by newborn screening programs) remain asymptomatic. In the few symptomatic subjects, clinical symptoms usually appear in childhood (3-9 years of age), but sometimes manifest as early as 10 days after birth, or as late as early adulthood. Symptomatic subjects usually present with skin photosensitivity (pellagra-like skin eruption), neurological symptoms (intermittent cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, delayed motor development, trembling, headaches, and hypotonia), and psychiatric symptoms (anxiety, emotional instability, delusions, and hallucinations). Ocular manifestations may occur (double vision, nystagmus, photophobia, and strabismus). Intellectual deficit and short stature have been described in a few patients. Exacerbations are seen most frequently in the spring or early summer after sunlight exposure. Symptoms may also be triggered by fever, drugs, and emotional or physical stress. They progress over several days and last for 1-4 weeks before spontaneous remission occurs.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Hartnup disease is caused by mutations in SLC6A19 gene (5p15.33), encoding the sodium-dependent and chloride-independent neutral amino acid transporter B(0)AT1, expressed predominately in proximal renal tubules and intestinal epithelium.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Neutral hyperaminoaciduria (determined by urine chromatography) is the diagnostic hallmark. Diagnostic confirmation relies upon the mutation analysis of the SLCA19 gene (broad allelic heterogeneity).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Pellagra is the main differential diagnosis. Blue diaper syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia, hydroa vacciniforme, pityriasis alba, and xeroderma pigmentosum should be excluded.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Symptomatic subjects benefit from a high-protein diet, sunlight protection, and avoidance of photosensitizing drugs. Treatment includes nicotinamide supplements (40 to 200 mg per day). Some patients may respond to a tryptophan-rich diet. Patients with severe central nervous system involvement require neurologic and psychiatric treatment.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The presentation of the disorder is commonly benign. Hartnup disease probably does not adversely affect pregnancy and would be harmless to the fetus.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Epidermal nevus syndrome (ENS) is a rare congenitally acquired syndrome, characterized by the presence of epidermal nevi in association with various developmental abnormalities of the skin, eyes, nervous, skeletal, cardiovascular and urogenital systems.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Epidermal nevi are developmental disorders characterized by hyperplasia of epidermal structures in a circumscribed area of the skin. Most are present at birth, occur sporadically and affect both sexes. All well-defined ENS are lethal gene syndromes, except nevus comedonicus syndrome. About 50% of the patients have neurological abnormalities that include mental retardation and epilepsy, spastic paresis, cerebral vascular malformations, cortical atrophy, lateral ventricle enlargement. About one third of the patients may have ocular abnormalities such as colobomas of the eyelid, iris and retina, conjuctival lipodermoids and choristomas, cortical blindness, micro-, macro- or anophthalmia, corneal opacities and cataracts. Skeletal abnormalities and many other non-cutaneous abnormalities may be present.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: No ideal medical therapy for the cutaneous lesions of ENS exists. The skin lesions may be amenable to surgery. The inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevus (ILVEN) sometimes responds to Erbium-YAG laser or vitamin D analogues. Salicylic acid, topical and systemic retinoids, emollients, shave dermabrasion and cryotherapy have been tried. The concomitant skeletal and ocular defects can be surgically repaired. Epilepsy should be treated appropriately.
DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Epidermal nevus syndrome, encompassing variants such as Schimmelpenning, linear nevus sebaceous, nevus sebaceous, and nevus comedonicus syndromes, is consistently described as a rare neurocutaneous disorder. Specific presentations, like those involving PTCH1 gene mutations and cerebral infarction, are noted as exceptionally rare. While individual case reports describe patients across various ages and sexes, the provided abstracts do not offer specific prevalence rates or broader demographic trends for the syndrome. [PMC11509802, PMC9520847, PMC8163158, PMC8234150, PMC8630880]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Epidermal nevus syndrome, also known as Schimmelpenning syndrome, is a group of congenital neuroectodermal and/or mesodermal disorders. Its etiology is primarily linked to genetic mosaicism, often resulting from postzygotic, somatic single nucleotide mutations. Common mutations occur in RAS family proto-oncogenes, including HRAS and KRAS, with specific variants like codon 146 KRAS and c.35G > T (p.Gly12Val) KRAS identified. Other implicated genes include PTCH1 (c.109G > T mutation), NEK9 (c.1755_1757del), FGFR3, and PIK3CA. These genetic changes are found in affected tissues like epidermal nevi, brain, and other associated lesions, but are typically absent in peripheral blood leukocytes. [PMC11509802, PMC9520847, PMC8999796, PMC8234150, PMC8630880]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of epidermal nevus syndrome is primarily based on characteristic clinical findings, including epidermal nevi and associated systemic abnormalities affecting the central nervous system, eyes, skeleton, cardiovascular, and renal systems. Dermatological examination reveals hyperpigmented verrucous plaques, often arranged along lines of Blaschko. Histological analysis of skin lesions typically shows hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and papillomatosis. Further diagnostic evaluation includes radiological imaging, such as brain MRI, to identify intracranial tumors, cortical malformations, cerebral infarction, or aneurysms. Electroencephalography may be used for neurological symptoms like seizures. Molecular genetic testing of affected tissues is crucial, often identifying somatic mutations in genes such as HRAS, KRAS, PTCH1, or NEK9, with targeted gene sequencing panels being useful for increasing detection. [PMC11509802, PMC9520847, PMC8999796, PMC8411292, PMC8234150]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Epidermal nevus syndrome (ENS) is part of a continuum of mosaic neurocutaneous RASopathies, a group of syndromes with high phenotypical variability. Postzygotic KRAS variants have been described in ENS, oculoectodermal syndrome (OES), and encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis (ECCL), with phenotypic overlap noted between ECCL and OES. ENS also shares features with other neurocutaneous syndromes, such as neurofibromatosis type 1 and encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis. [PMC12146159, PMC8999796, PMC7976813]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Epidermal nevus syndrome is characterized by genetic mosaicism, often resulting from postzygotic single nucleotide mutations in proto-oncogenes. Common mutations include those in the RAS family, such as HRAS and KRAS, with specific variants like c.35G > T (p.Gly12Val), c.35G > A (p.Gly12Asp), and codon 146 KRAS variants identified in various forms of the syndrome, including isolated epidermal nevus, nevus sebaceous syndrome, and oculoectodermal syndrome. Other implicated genes include PTCH1 (c.109G > T) and NEK9 (c.1755_1757del). The mosaic nature of these mutations means they may not be detectable in peripheral blood leukocytes, highlighting the utility of targeted gene sequencing panels for molecular genetic testing, especially for newly identified hot spots like codon 146 KRAS variants. [PMC11509802, PMC9520847, PMC8999796, PMC8234150, PMC8630880]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Epidermal Nevus Syndrome is highly variable due to its heterogeneous nature. While some systemic manifestations, such as hypophosphatemic rickets in cutaneous-skeletal hypophosphatemia syndrome, can show significant improvement in growth, physical function, and bone pain with targeted therapies like burosumab, other bone lesions may still show partial progression. Intracranial tumors, such as astrocytomas, can be successfully managed with surgery, often without neurological sequelae. Epilepsy, a common neurological feature, frequently responds well to surgical intervention, leading to seizure freedom and cognitive improvement. However, renal involvement in linear nevus sebaceous syndrome can significantly impact long-term prognosis, and skin lesions may not always respond to treatment, requiring ongoing monitoring for potential malignant transformation. [PMC12146159, PMC11509802, PMC9120998, PMC8411292, PMC8163158]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Isolated congenital megalocornea is a genetic, non-syndromic developmental defect of the anterior eye segment characterized by bilateral enlargement of the corneal diameter (>12.5 mm) and a deep anterior eye chamber, without an elevation in intraocular pressure. It can manifest with mild to moderate myopia as well as photophobia and iridodonesis (due to iris hypoplasia). Associated complications include lens dislocation, retinal detachment, presenile cataract development, and secondary glaucoma.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Isolated congenital megalocornea is a congenital disorder, with onset at birth. While it usually presents early in life, with some patients diagnosed between 4 and 10 years of age, it can be almost asymptomatic in young patients and may be overlooked. Consequently, adult presentations are also noted, with cases reported at ages 29, 40, 47, and 51 years. Late-onset adult presentation is described as common in non-familial anterior megalophthalmos. [PMC8515447, PMC8406643, PMC6707321, PMC5627800, PMC3519131]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Isolated congenital megalocornea, also known as anterior megalophthalmos, is described as a rare, congenital, and hereditary disorder. While it usually presents early in life, atypical and late-onset adult presentations, particularly in non-familial cases, have been reported. The condition can affect males, with one case series describing four male patients with a mean age of 6.5 years. Despite its apparent nature, it can remain undiagnosed during previous examinations. [PMC8515447, PMC6707321, PMC5627800]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Isolated congenital megalocornea, also known as anterior megalophthalmos, is a rare, bilateral, nonprogressive, hereditary, congenital disorder characterized by the enlargement of all anterior segment structures. It typically presents early in life, though adult-onset cases are noted. Characteristic findings include megalocornea (mean horizontal diameter ~13.8 mm), a deep anterior chamber (mean depth ~3.8 mm), iridodonesis, iris atrophy, and zonular abnormalities. Common complications involve premature cataract formation, pigmentary glaucoma, and elevated intraocular pressure. The disorder can also extend to the posterior segment, leading to posterior lens dislocation, vitreous degeneration, and rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. [PMC8515447, PMC6707321, PMC5627800, PMC3519131]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Isolated congenital megalocornea, as a feature of anterior megalophthalmos, is described as a rare, bilateral, nonprogressive, hereditary, congenital disorder. It typically presents early in life and is commonly associated with a positive family history. However, non-familial cases have been observed where the family history is negative, sometimes presenting with atypical features or a variant phenotype, including late-onset adult presentation. [PMC8515447, PMC5627800]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of anterior megalophthalmos relies on a comprehensive ocular evaluation, including clinical history, slit lamp examination, and dilated fundus examination. Characteristic findings include bilateral megalocornea, a deep anterior chamber, and often iridodonesis, iris atrophy, or zonular abnormalities. Scheimpflug imaging, such as with Pentacam-HR, is a valuable tool for demonstrating corneal and anterior segment pathological changes, providing measurements like horizontal corneal diameter, central corneal thickness, keratometry, and anterior chamber depth. Other diagnostic indicators can include cataract, phacodonesis, raised intraocular pressure, and vitreous degeneration. While typically presenting early, atypical adult presentations with varied phenotypes and absent iris involvement are possible, and the condition may be overlooked despite apparent signs. [PMC8515447, PMC6707321, PMC5627800, PMC3519131]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for isolated congenital megalocornea includes anterior megalophthalmos, which typically presents with megalocornea, a deep anterior chamber, iris atrophy, and zonular abnormalities, often accompanied by glaucoma and cataract. Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome is another consideration, characterized by megalocornea, Haab's striae, and posterior embryotoxon. Additionally, congenital keratoglobus, sometimes associated with Marshall/Stickler phenotype, involves globular corneas with diffuse thinning and blue sclera. These conditions share features of corneal enlargement or shape abnormalities, necessitating careful differentiation. [PMC8515447, PMC7380832, PMC6707321, PMC5627800, PMC5200994]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Isolated congenital megalocornea is described as a hereditary, congenital disorder. While it usually presents with a positive family history, indicating a familial component, non-familial forms also exist. In these non-familial cases, the family history is negative, and presentations may be atypical or manifest later in adulthood. [PMC8515447, PMC5627800]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of isolated congenital megalocornea focuses on addressing its associated complications. Cataracts can be successfully treated with standard phacoemulsification and posterior chamber intraocular lens (PCIOL) implantation, though care is needed due to potential zonular abnormalities. For eyes with inadequate capsular support, intrascleral haptic fixation of intraocular lenses may be employed, with novel techniques developed to accommodate large corneal diameters. Pigment dispersion glaucoma can be managed with topical anti-glaucoma medication. Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment, a potential complication, may require vitrectomy with silicone oil tamponade for successful reattachment. Ophthalmologists should recognize and manage these associations and complications. [PMC11994171, PMC6707321, PMC5627800, PMC3519131]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Isolated congenital megalocornea is a nonprogressive disorder, though it can lead to various ocular complications over time. While young patients may be largely asymptomatic, blurred vision due to corneal astigmatism is common. Later complications include premature cataract formation, pigmentary glaucoma, raised intraocular pressure, and glaucomatous optic nerve damage. More severe issues can involve posterior dislocation of the crystalline lens, vitreous degeneration, and rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. Visual acuity can range significantly, but successful visual rehabilitation is possible through interventions like cataract surgery and retinal reattachment procedures. Care is advised during cataract surgery due to potential zonular abnormalities and lens enlargement. [PMC8515447, PMC6707321, PMC5627800, PMC3519131]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Rheumatic fever (RF) is a multisystem inflammatory disease occurring as a post-infectious, nonsuppurative sequela of untreated streptococcus pyogenes (Group A streptococcus [GAS]) pharyngitis, and mainly occurs in individuals aged 5 to 15 years. The most common presenting signs are fever, migratory polyarthritis and carditis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence of RF in industrialized countries, due to sporadic outbreaks, is typically less than 1/20, 000 individuals. In the developing world, the annual incidence is at least 100 times higher with some reports of > 1/200 individuals in select subpopulations, such as Australian Aboriginals. RF remains a major cause of acquired cardiac morbidity and mortality among people under 50 years of age.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: RF usually initially occurs between 5 and 15 years of age, and involves the heart, large joints and skin and is a delayed sequela of untreated GAS pharyngitis. The major diagnostic criteria include migratory polyarthritis (46-66% of cases), most commonly in the knee, ankle, elbow and wrists; carditis (53-68% clinical and additional ''subclinical'' diagnosed by echocardiogram), which is typically inflammation of the mitral (90%) or aortic valve (10%) in isolation, but any combination of all 4 valves have been reported; Sydenham chorea (8-15%); erythema marginatum (1-11%); and subcutaneous nodules on the flexor surfaces (1-8%). Minor criteria include fever (35-75% of cases), arthralgia (35-56%), first degree heart block (prolonged PR interval) (20-29%) and elevated inflammatory markers (53-91%). There is not always a prior clinically apparent GAS infection.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: There are proposed associations with certain HLA types (most frequently HLA-DR7), but numerous types have been implicated and are not always consistent among different populations. Immunological cross-reactivity is believed to occur through molecular mimicry and has been attributed to the M-protein in the GAS cell membrane. Tumor necrosis factor α and mannose-binding lectin may also be upregulated in individuals with increased RF susceptibility.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The revised Jones criteria require the presence of two major or one major and two minor criteria, as well as evidence of a prior GAS infection. Diagnostic tests include an antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) or C reactive protein (CRP), electrocardiogram to detect first degree heart block, and echocardiogram to diagnose valvulitis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other causes of febrile polyarthritis in children: juvenile idiopathic arthritis, Lyme disease, mixed connective tissue disease, reactive arthritis, sickle cell anemia, systemic lupus erythematosus, and septic arthritis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment of RF includes: 1) treatment of pharyngitis to eradicate GAS, with penicillin as first line therapy, 2) anti-inflammatory treatment, usually aspirin in the acute phase, although the use of corticosteroids is sometimes suggested, especially with severe carditis, and 3) secondary antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrence of RF, usually with benzathine penicillin every 3 to 4 weeks.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is generally good after initial episode of RF and all of the symptoms usually resolve completely with the exception of cardiac valve damage, which can progress over time, especially with subsequent episodes of RF, and require chronic medical management for heart failure and eventual surgical valve replacement.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An X-linked syndromic intellectual disability characterized by congenital ataxia and generalized hypotonia, global developmental delay with intellectual disability, myoclonic encephalopathy, progressive neurological deterioration, macular degeneration, and recurrent bronchopulmonary infections.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Mutations in the MTM1 gene cause X-linked myotubular myopathy (XLMTM), characterized by neonatal hypotonia and respiratory failure, and are responsible for a premature mortality in affected males. Female carriers are usually asymptomatic but they may present with muscular weakness because of a hypothesized skewed pattern of X-chromosome inactivation. By combining next generation sequencing (NGS) and CGH array approaches, we have investigated the role of MTM1 variants in a large cohort of undiagnosed patients with a wide spectrum of myopathies. Seven novel XLMTM patients have been identified, including two girls with an unremarkable family history for myotubular myopathy. Moreover, we have detected and finely mapped a large deletion causing a myotubular myopathy with abnormal genital development. Our data confirm that the severe neonatal onset of the disease in male infants is sufficient... [PMC4862961]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of X-linked myotubular myopathy (XLMTM) involves molecular testing of the MTM1 gene. Next-generation sequencing (NGS) is a primary diagnostic approach, capable of identifying pathogenic variants, including novel intronic variants that interfere with normal splicing and lead to abnormal transcripts. Sequencing of intron-exon boundaries is important for comprehensive analysis. CGH array approaches can also be utilized. The severe neonatal onset of the disease in male infants is a sufficient clinical indicator to direct molecular testing towards the MTM1 gene, and MTM1 variants may also be investigated in symptomatic female carriers. [PMC9499315, PMC4862961]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for X-linked neurodegenerative syndrome, Bertini type, include X-linked myotubular myopathy (XLMTM), caused by MTM1 gene mutations, which presents with generalized weakness, respiratory insufficiency, and neonatal hypotonia. Other considerations are AIFM1-related disorders, such as severe infantile encephalopathy with combined oxidative phosphorylation deficiency, and X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMTX4) characterized by axonal sensorimotor neuropathy, deafness, and cognitive impairment. AIFM1 mutations can also lead to early-onset mitochondrial encephalopathy with cortical and motor neuron involvement. All these conditions are X-linked and involve significant neurological or neuromuscular manifestations. [PMC9499315, PMC4862961, PMC4755377]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: This X-linked neurodegenerative syndrome is caused by mutations in the MTM1 gene. Affected males typically present with severe neonatal hypotonia and respiratory failure, often leading to premature mortality. Female carriers are usually asymptomatic, but some may develop muscular weakness due to skewed X-chromosome inactivation, and the number of symptomatic female carriers is likely underestimated. Direct molecular testing of the MTM1 gene is indicated for male infants with severe neonatal onset. [PMC4862961]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Mutations in the MTM1 gene cause X-linked myotubular myopathy (XLMTM), characterized by neonatal hypotonia and respiratory failure, and are responsible for a premature mortality in affected males. Female carriers are usually asymptomatic but they may present with muscular weakness because of a hypothesized skewed pattern of X-chromosome inactivation. By combining next generation sequencing (NGS) and CGH array approaches, we have investigated the role of MTM1 variants in a large cohort of undiagnosed patients with a wide spectrum of myopathies. Seven novel XLMTM patients have been identified, including two girls with an unremarkable family history for myotubular myopathy. Moreover, we have detected and finely mapped a large deletion causing a myotubular myopathy with abnormal genital development. Our data confirm that the severe neonatal onset of the disease in male infants is sufficient... [PMC4862961]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A cerebrohepatopathy and a rare and severe form of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) depletion syndrome characterized by the triad of progressive developmental regression, intractable seizures, and hepatic failure.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Alpers progressive sclerosing poliodystrophy; Alpers syndrome; Progressive neuronal degeneration of childhood with liver disease

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence of AHS is estimated to be between 1/100,000 and 1/250,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Development is usually normal until disease onset and presentations are highly variable. The most common age of onset is between 2-4 years (ranges from 3 months to 36 years). Seizures (mainly partial, secondary generalized tonic-clonic, or myoclonic) are often the presenting feature, evolving into focal status epilepticus, epilepsia partialis continua, and/or multifocal myoclonic epilepsy. Seizures may respond to treatment initially but usually become intractable. Headaches, visual disturbances and movement disorders (e.g. myoclonus and choreoathetosis) are also common. Cerebellar ataxia develops in most patients. Peripheral neuropathy develops in many and becomes increasingly common in older children and young adults. Loss of cognitive function progresses with varying rates (rapid regression seen during infectious diseases) with manifestations including somnolence, irritability, loss of concentration, loss of language skills and memory deficits, ending in dementia and visual loss. Gastrointestinal involvement (i.e. swallowing dysfunction, intestinal dysmotility) is also noted. Liver disease may be indolent for years before the first acute exacerbation, but may be the first presenting symptom in some children. The clinical course of both brain and liver abnormalities is often episodic with acute exacerbations followed by periods of partial recovery.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: AHS is due to mutations in the polymerase gamma (POLG) gene (15q24). This gene encodes DNA polymerase subunit gamma-1, which is involved in the replication and repair of mtDNA. Ecogenetic and epigenetic stressors, including incidental infections and drugs like valproic acid, can accelerate the onset of symptoms and modify how the phenotype unfolds.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical and laboratory findings. Electroencephalogram findings include explosive seizures with asymmetric occipital lobe predominance of epileptiform discharges, evolving into epilepsia partialis continua or status epilepticus. Neuroimaging may show neuronal loss/gliosis and generalized brain atrophy. Mitochondrial respiratory chain deficiencies and low levels of mtDNA are noted in the liver and muscle as the disease progresses. Molecular genetic testing revealing a POLG mutation confirms diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses are numerous with some examples being disease phenocopies caused by mutations in the C10ORF2 gene (10q24), which can cause autosomal dominant progressive external ophthalmoplegia (adPEO) as well as recessive mutations that can lead to other phenotypes that may overlap with AHS. Others disorders include infantile neuronal ceroid-lipofuscinosis, late-infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, MERRF and MELAS. Other POLG-related disorders include recessive mitochondrial ataxia syndrome (MIRAS), ataxia neuropathy spectrum (ANS), and autosomal recessive PEO.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible in families with a known disease-causing mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: AHS is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Genetic counseling is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for AHS and treatment is symptomatic and palliative. Anticonvulsive therapy is prescribed for the management of epileptic seizures but is not always successful. As valproic acid may trigger or worsen liver disease, it is contraindicated. Occupational, physical, and/or speech therapy may be offered to maintain neurologic function as long as possible. Tracheostomy placement, artificial ventilation and placement of a gastric feeding tube may all be necessary as the disease progresses.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is severe with life-expectancy in patients ranging from 3 months to 12 years, after disease onset.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Griscelli syndrome (GS) is a rare cutaneous disease characterized by a silvery-gray sheen of the hair and hypopigmentation of the skin, which can be associated to primary neurological impairment (type 1), immunologic impairment (type 2) or be isolated (type 3).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Chédiak-Higashi-like syndrome; Griscelli-Pruniéras syndrome; Partial albinism-immunodeficiency syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, approximately 150 cases have been reported, predominantly in Turkish and Mediterranean populations. GS type 2 appears to be the most common of the three known types, while GS type 3 is the least common.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: GS occurs in infancy to childhood. In addition to the silvery-gray sheen of the hair and the light-colored skin, GS type 1 patients present with delayed motor development, intellectual disability and hypotonia. GS type 2 patients have the same hypopigmentation features but in association with immune pathology. Patients exhibit a lymphocyte cytotoxic defect resulting in an uncontrolled T-lymphocyte and macrophage-activation syndrome, also known as hemophagocytic syndrome (HLH), in which activated T cells and macrophages infiltrate the lymph nodes and other organs (including the brain), producing hemophagocytosis. Patients with GS type 2 can present neurological symptoms due to brain infiltration by the activated hematopoietic cells. In GS type 3 patients, hypopigmentation of the skin and hair is the only feature.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: GS type 1 is caused by a mutation in the myosin Va (MYO5A) gene located on chromosome 15q21 and likely corresponds to Elejalde disease. GS type 2 is caused by mutations in the RAB27A encoding gene. Myosin-5a and RAB27A genes have been localized to the same chromosomal 15q21 region and encode for proteins which are key effectors of intracellular vesicular transport. Myosin Va regulates organelle transport in both melanocytes and neuronal cells, whereas RAB27A, regulates exocytic pathways, especially the cytotoxic granule exocytosis. The cytotoxic defect caused by RAB27A mutations is responsible for the hemophagocytic syndrome observed. GS type 3 is due to mutations in the MLPH gene, a gene encoding melanophilin, which forms a protein complex with Rab 27a and myosin Va, and participates in melanosome transport in melanocytes.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of the three types of GS can be established by the clinical signs and light microscopic examination, evidencing large clumps of pigment in hair shafts and the accumulation of mature melanosomes in melanocytes. A decrease in T and NK lymphocyte degranulation and cytotoxicity characterize GS type 2. No immunological or cytotoxic defects have been observed in GS type 1 or 3. Thus, based on the patient's clinical and biological features, sequencing of the corresponding causative gene allows confirmation of the type of GS.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: GS can be distinguished from Chediak-Higashi syndrome by the lack of giant granules in granulocytes of GS patients. The differential diagnosis of GS type 1 also includes Elejalde disease.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis of GS type 1 and 2 can be performed through chorionic villus sampling by the sequencing of the MYO5A or RAB27A gene, respectively.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: GS is an autosomal recessive disorder and genetic counseling informing affected couples of a 25% risk of having an affected child is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment for GS type 1 is only symptomatic. In GS type 2, the hemophagocytic syndrome is often fatal and the only cure is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Currently there is no specific management for GS type 3.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: If not treated by HSCT, the prognosis for long-term survival in GS type 2 is relatively poor, with many patients not surviving the first decade. The prognosis of GS type 1 is good. GS type 3 should be better considered as a pigmentation phenotype rather than a pathology with a prognosis similar to the control population.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Body skin hyperlaxity due to vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic skin disease characterized by severe skin laxity affecting the trunk and limbs.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: The condition presents with an overlapping pseudoxanthoma elasticum and cutis laxa-like phenotype, characterized by loose and sagging skin with loss of recoil. Patients exhibit characteristic calcification of elastic structures in the mid dermis and moderate-to-severe angioid streaks. This phenotype is associated with mutations in the GGCX gene, which encodes γ-glutamyl carboxylase, an enzyme essential for the activation of vitamin K-dependent blood coagulation factors. Consequently, GGCX mutations can lead to these skin manifestations in conjunction with multiple vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor deficiency. [PMC8935359]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Body skin hyperlaxity, often presenting with pseudoxanthoma elasticum (PXE)-like features, in association with vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor deficiency, is primarily caused by mutations in the GGCX gene. The GGCX gene encodes γ-glutamyl carboxylase, an enzyme essential for the activation of both blood coagulation factors and matrix gla protein. Mutations in GGCX lead to reduced carboxylase activity. This reduction impairs the carboxylation of matrix gla protein, which in its fully carboxylated form prevents ectopic mineralization, thereby allowing peripheral mineralization to occur. The impaired carboxylase activity also directly contributes to the deficiency of vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors. Mutations in VKORC1 are also implicated in vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor deficiency. [PMC8935359, PMC2630561]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves genetic analysis, primarily mutation analysis of the GGCX gene, which can be performed using next-generation sequencing panels. Affected individuals often present with characteristic skin features, including loose, redundant skin and calcification of elastic structures in the mid dermis, consistent with pseudoxanthoma elasticum/cutis laxa overlap. Skin analysis by specific antibodies may demonstrate predominantly undercarboxylated matrix gla protein associated with mineralized areas. While the condition is linked to vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor deficiency, some patients with GGCX mutations may not exhibit coagulation abnormalities. [PMC8935359, PMC2630561]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for body skin hyperlaxity due to vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor deficiency includes conditions with overlapping cutaneous and systemic manifestations. Pseudoxanthoma Elasticum (PXE), typically caused by ABCC6 gene mutations, is characterized by ectopic mineralization affecting the skin, eyes, and cardiovascular system. However, PXE-like clinical findings, often presenting with loose and sagging skin characteristic of Cutis Laxa (CL), can also arise from GGCX gene mutations. These GGCX mutations are known to cause such overlapping skin phenotypes, with or without associated vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor deficiency. Furthermore, vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor deficiency itself can be caused by mutations in either the GGCX or VKORC1 genes, underscoring the genetic and phenotypic complexity. [PMC12296144, PMC8935359, PMC2630561]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The condition is an autosomal recessive disorder, primarily linked to mutations in the GGCX gene. Affected individuals typically present with compound heterozygosity for GGCX mutations, leading to reduced γ-glutamyl carboxylase activity. This enzyme is crucial for activating blood coagulation factors and matrix gla protein, which prevents ectopic mineralization. Genetic counseling should address the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, the implications for family members, and the potential for carrier status. [PMC8935359, PMC2630561]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A very rare genetic gastroenterological disease characterized by severe malabsorptive diarrhea (requiring parenteral nutrition and disappearing at fasting) due to a lack of intestinal enteroendocrine cells. It is associated with early-onset (within the first weeks of life) dehydration, metabolic acidosis and diabetes mellitus (that can develop until late childhood). Patient may display various degrees of pancreatic insufficiency that does not explain diarrhea, as it is not reduced with pancreatic enzyme supplementation. Central hypogonadism (developing in the second decade), as well as an association with celiac disease have been reported.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Congenital malabsorptive diarrhea due to paucity of enteroendocrine cells

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Severe congenital diarrhea occurs in approximately half of patients with Aristaless-Related Homeobox (ARX) null mutations. The cause of this diarrhea is unknown. In a mouse model of intestinal Arx deficiency, the prevalence of a subset of enteroendocrine cells is altered, leading to diarrhea. Because polyalanine expansions within the ARX protein are the most common mutations found in ARX-related disorders, to characterize the enteroendocrine population in human tissue of an ARX mutation and in a mouse model of the corresponding polyalanine expansion (Arx). Immunohistochemistry and quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction were the primary modalities used to characterize the enteroendocrine populations. Daily weights were determined for the growth curves, and Oil-Red-O staining on stool and tissue identified neutral fats. An expansion of 7 alanines in the first polyalanine tract... [PMC4308495]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Enteric anendocrinosis is characterized by severe congenital or neonatal malabsorptive diarrhea, which can be accompanied by metabolic acidosis. Patients with PCSK1 deficiency may also exhibit early-onset obesity, rapid weight gain with total parenteral nutrition, high proinsulin levels, and low adrenocorticotropin. Despite neonatal malabsorptive diarrhea, small intestine morphology can appear normal. Mutations in ARX, particularly polyalanine expansions, alter enteroendocrine differentiation, leading to reduced populations of cholecystokinin, glucagon-like peptide 1, and somatostatin cells. ARX is required for the specification of a subset of enteroendocrine cells. [PMC8151971, PMC4308495]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Enteric anendocrinosis can arise from distinct genetic etiologies. Loss-of-function mutations in the PCSK1 gene, encoding Proprotein convertase 1/3 (PC1/3), cause a recessive complex endocrinopathy characterized by malabsorptive diarrhea due to impaired processing of key protein precursors. Additionally, mutations in the Aristaless-Related Homeobox (ARX) gene, including null mutations or polyalanine expansions, are implicated. ARX is essential for the specification of a subset of enteroendocrine cells, and its mutations lead to dysgenesis or altered differentiation of these cells, resulting in severe congenital diarrhea and changes in specific hormone populations such as cholecystokinin and glucagon-like peptide 1. [PMC8151971, PMC4308495]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for enteric anendocrinosis primarily involve genomic analysis, including whole genome sequencing, to identify specific gene mutations such as those in PCSK1 or ARX. Statistical genetics approaches help prioritize disease genes based on de novo recurrence and compound heterozygosity. Immunohistochemistry and quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction are also used to characterize enteroendocrine cell populations, revealing altered differentiation or reduced levels of hormones like cholecystokinin, glucagon-like peptide 1, and somatostatin. In vitro analysis can further assess the functional impact of identified mutations. [PMC12328722, PMC8151971, PMC4308495]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Conditions presenting with congenital or neonatal malabsorptive diarrhea and enteroendocrine dysfunction should be considered. Loss-of-function mutations in the PCSK1 gene cause a recessive complex endocrinopathy with malabsorptive diarrhea, early-onset obesity, high proinsulin, and low adrenocorticotropin. Additionally, Aristaless-Related Homeobox (ARX) null mutations or polyalanine expansions within the ARX protein lead to severe congenital diarrhea due to dysgenesis of enteroendocrine cells, characterized by altered populations of cholecystokinin, glucagon-like peptide 1, and somatostatin. [PMC8151971, PMC4308495]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Enteric anendocrinosis can be caused by mutations in specific genes, such as PCSK1 and ARX. Loss-of-function mutations in PCSK1 are associated with a recessive complex endocrinopathy, with homozygous mutations identified in affected individuals. ARX null mutations and polyalanine expansions are also linked to severe congenital diarrhea. Genomic analysis, including whole genome sequencing, is a valuable tool for diagnosing ultra-rare monogenic presentations, enabling the identification of disease genes and specific mutations, including those with de novo recurrence or compound heterozygosity. [PMC12328722, PMC8151971, PMC4308495]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Total parenteral nutrition is a reported management strategy. It has been observed to facilitate rapid weight gain in infants presenting with congenital malabsorptive diarrhea and metabolic acidosis. [PMC8151971]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Proprotein convertase 1/3 (PC1/3), encoded by the PCSK1 gene, is expressed in neuronal and (entero)endocrine cell types, where it cleaves and hence activates a number of protein precursors that play a key role in energy homeostasis. Loss-of-function mutations in PCSK1 cause a recessive complex endocrinopathy characterized by malabsorptive diarrhea and early-onset obesity. Despite the fact that neonatal malabsorptive diarrhea is observed in all patients, it has remained understudied. The aim of was to investigate the enteroendocrine pathologies in a male patient with congenital PCSK1 deficiency carrying the novel homozygous c.1034A>C (p.E345A) mutation. This patient developed malabsorptive diarrhea and metabolic acidosis within the first week of life, but rapid weight gain was observed after total parenteral nutrition, and he displayed high proinsulin levels and low adrenocorticotropin.... [PMC8151971]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Mosaic trisomy 2 is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, with a highly variable phenotype, principally characterized by intrauterine growth restriction, growth and motor delay, craniofacial dysmorphism (e.g. microcephaly, hypertelorism, micro/anophthalmia, midface hypoplasia, cleft lip/palate), congenital heart and neural tube defects, as well as various skeletal (e.g. scoliosis, radioulnar hypoplasia, preaxial polydactyly) and gastrointestinal (e.g. intestinal malrotation, Hirschsprung disease) anomalies. Central nervous system malformations (including ventriculomegaly, thin corpus callosum, spina bifida) have also been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Mosaic trisomy 2 syndrome is associated with variable clinical presentations, often detected prenatally. Observed features include increased chorion and placental thickness, fetal growth retardation (intrauterine growth restriction or small-for-gestational-age), hyperechoic bowel, challenging visualization of kidneys, dolichocephaly, ventriculomegaly, and pronounced oligohydramnios. Pathological examination of affected fetuses has revealed internal hydrocephalus, atrophy of brain structure, and craniofacial dysmorphism. Pregnancies with NIPT-indicated trisomy 2 carry elevated risks of fetal loss. While some cases with confined placental mosaicism may result in intrauterine growth restriction with good postnatal catchup growth, low-level true fetal mosaicism can be associated with severe abnormalities. [PMC12404953, PMC10965300, PMC10138005]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Mosaic trisomy 2 syndrome is characterized by the presence of a trisomic clone of chromosome 2 in a mosaic pattern. This can manifest as confined placental mosaicism, where the trisomy is predominantly found in placental tissues, or as true fetal mosaicism, where a low frequency of trisomy 2 cells may be present in fetal tissues. Uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 (UPD2) can be associated with confined placental mosaicism for trisomy 2, and the mechanisms giving rise to UPD2 are explored. UPD2 itself can lead to homozygosity for pathogenic variants in genes located on chromosome 2. [PMC10965300, PMC10138005]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Prenatal detection of trisomy 2 or mosaicism can be indicated by non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), particularly whole-genome sequencing-based NIPT, although targeted NIPT may show low risk. NIPT for rare chromosomal abnormalities has a low positive predictive value, necessitating further invasive prenatal diagnosis. Confirmatory include conventional cytogenetic analysis (karyotyping), chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA or aCGH), and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), performed on samples such as placental biopsy, amniotic fluid cells, or fetal blood. These techniques are crucial for distinguishing true fetal mosaicism from placental-confined mosaicism and for determining mosaic levels. Karyotype analysis, CMA, and FISH each have distinct advantages and limitations, and their combined use provides a more rigorous and accurate diagnosis, mitigating culture-related bias. [PMC12404953, PMC10138005, PMC10568385, PMC8238360, PMC7755766]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for mosaic trisomy 2 syndrome, particularly in prenatal settings, primarily involves distinguishing true fetal mosaicism from confined placental mosaicism (CPM). CPM for trisomy 2 can be associated with intrauterine growth restriction but may lead to good postnatal catch-up growth, necessitating cytogenetic analysis of amniotic fluid or fetal blood for confirmation. Additionally, uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 (UPD2) should be considered, as it can arise from trisomy rescue. UPD2 may lead to autosomal recessive disorders if homozygous pathogenic variants are present on chromosome 2, such as sepiapterin reductase deficiency or a neurodevelopmental disorder associated with ZNF142. However, UPD2 can also be an incidental finding with a normal phenotype. [PMC10965300, PMC10138005]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of mosaic trisomy 2 syndrome often begins with non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), which can indicate rare chromosomal abnormalities, though it has a low positive predictive value. Whole-genome sequencing-based NIPT is preferred for trisomy 2. Ultrasound findings such as increased chorion thickness, fetal growth retardation, and oligohydramnios may also suggest the condition. Confirmation requires invasive prenatal diagnosis, utilizing techniques like karyotyping, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). These have varying strengths in detecting mosaicism and determining mosaic proportions, with CMA sometimes revealing trisomic mosaicism not detected by karyotyping or showing higher mosaic levels. It is crucial to distinguish true fetal mosaicism from placental-confined mosaicism, often necessitating cytogenetic analysis of amniotic fluid cells or fetal blood. The combined use of these genetic analysis techniques provides a more rigorous and accurate diagnosis. [PMC12404953, PMC10138005, PMC10568385, PMC8238360, PMC7755766]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for mosaic trisomy 2 syndrome involves navigating complex prenatal diagnostic findings. Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) for rare chromosomal abnormalities like trisomy 2 has a low positive predictive value but indicates elevated risks such as fetal loss, small-for-gestational-age, and uniparental disomy (UPD). Whole-genome sequencing-based NIPT is preferred for at-risk pregnancies. Confirmatory invasive testing, including cytogenetic analysis of amniotic fluid cells or fetal blood, is crucial to distinguish true fetal mosaicism from confined placental mosaicism. Techniques like karyotyping, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), and FISH have different strengths for detecting mosaicism, and their combined use, potentially with like SD-QF-PCR, provides a more rigorous diagnosis and helps determine mosaic proportions. Confined placental mosaicism for trisomy 2 can lead to UPD2, which may be associated with intrauterine growth restriction or autosomal recessive disorders if pathogenic variants are present on chromosome 2. Despite the low PPV of NIPT for RCAs, these findings are clinically significant for risk stratification and pregnancy management. [PMC12404953, PMC10965300, PMC10138005, PMC10568385, PMC8238360]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) has demonstrated robust performance in detecting common trisomies and copy number variations. However, its clinical utility for rare chromosomal abnormalities (RCAs) remains controversial due to low positive predictive value (PPV). retrospectively analyzed the data of 94,125 cases that underwent NIPT at Ganzhou Maternal and Child Health Hospital in China. This dataset was used to evaluate NIPT performance in RCAs detection and track pregnancy outcomes of positive cases. In the cohort of 94,125 pregnancies undergoing NIPT, 336 cases (0.36%) were found to carry RCAs. Among them, 102 cases underwent validation through karyotyping and/or chromosome microarray analysis. Of the 102 validated cases, seven were true positives (PPV = 6.86%). Additionally, 3 cases exhibited uniparental disomy consistent with the NIPT-reported chromosomal anomalies. Of 268... [PMC12404953, PMC10965300, PMC10138005]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for mosaic trisomy 2 syndrome is highly variable, depending on the extent of true fetal mosaicism versus confined placental mosaicism. Pregnancies with NIPT-indicated trisomy 2 are associated with elevated risks of fetal loss, small-for-gestational-age, and uniparental disomy. Fetal anomalies can include intrauterine growth restriction, oligohydramnios, ventriculomegaly, hydrocephalus, brain atrophy, and craniofacial dysmorphism. However, some cases of uniparental disomy of chromosome 2, particularly when associated with confined placental mosaicism, may lead to good postnatal catch-up growth or even normal phenotypes. If uniparental disomy in homozygosity for pathogenic variants, neurodevelopmental abnormalities may occur, which can sometimes be responsive to targeted treatment. [PMC12404953, PMC10965300, PMC10138005]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Myalgia-eosinophilia syndrome associated with tryptophan is a rare systemic disease characterized by severe myalgia and peripheral eosinophilia associated with tryptophan dietary supplementation. The symptoms do not subside after tryptophan discontinuation. Clinical presentation includes muscle tenderness and cramps, fatigue, weakness, paresthesia, peripheral edema, arthralgia, dyspnea, skin rash, dry mouth, and development of scleroderma-like skin abnormalities.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) emerged as an epidemic in 1989, directly linked to the consumption of L-tryptophan that originated from a single source. Following the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) ban on the sale of L-tryptophan, the incidence of EMS rapidly declined. Notably, no new cases have been described since the FDA ban was lifted in 2005, indicating that the epidemic was associated with a specific contaminated product rather than L-tryptophan itself. [PMC3848710, PMC1002528, PMC1679916, PMC1663365]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) is characterized by a subacute onset of myalgias and peripheral eosinophilia, often followed by chronic neuropathy and skin induration. Patients may experience fatigue, rash, fever, edema, alopecia, arthralgias, diminished joint motion, skin tightening, muscle cramping, and distal paresthesias. Respiratory symptoms like shortness of breath and pulmonary hypertension have been noted. Laboratory findings include leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and increased serum levels of aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase, and liver enzymes. Postmortem findings include abnormalities of the coronary arteries, neural structures, and cardiac conduction system. Skin and muscle biopsies show sclerosis or mixed inflammatory cell infiltration of the dermis, subcutis, and fascia, with eosinophils often present but vasculitis absent. [PMC3848710, PMC2376663, PMC1002528]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) is strongly associated with the ingestion of L-tryptophan. An epidemic in 1989 was linked to L-tryptophan originating from a single source. The incidence of EMS rapidly declined following the FDA ban on L-tryptophan sales, with no new cases reported since the ban was lifted in 2005. The pathogenesis may involve abnormalities in lymphokine secretion, with evidence of activated transforming growth factor β and interleukin-4 signaling observed in lesional skin. [PMC3848710, PMC1002528, PMC1679916, PMC1663365]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) is characterized by the subacute onset of myalgias and peripheral eosinophilia, often followed by chronic neuropathy and skin induration. A key diagnostic criterion is a history of L-tryptophan consumption. Laboratory abnormalities include leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, and elevated serum levels of aldolase, lactate dehydrogenase, and liver enzymes. Skin and muscle biopsies may reveal sclerosis or mixed inflammatory cell infiltration of the dermis, subcutis, and fascia, frequently with eosinophils. Abnormal chest radiographs have also been observed. [PMC3848710, PMC1002528]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for myalgia-eosinophilia syndrome include conditions that present with overlapping symptoms. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) should be considered, as it can manifest with myalgia, fever, and eosinophilia, potentially alongside cerebral infarction, painful paraplegia, or rhabdomyolysis. Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) syndrome and hypersensitivity syndrome to phenobarbital are also important, given their presentations of myalgia, eosinophilia, fever, rash, and systemic organ dysfunction. Eosinophilic fasciitis, especially when complicated by myopathy, and dermatomyositis in cases of prominent muscle weakness, warrant consideration. Additionally, the toxic oil syndrome shares comparative findings with eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome. [PMC12060753, PMC11922073, PMC7982268, PMC7759697, PMC4078519]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome is characterized by subacute onset of myalgias and peripheral eosinophilia, followed by chronic neuropathy and skin induration. Postmortem findings have revealed abnormalities of the coronary arteries, neural structures, and the heart's conduction system. Pulmonary hypertension was also observed in some patients, indicating potential for severe systemic involvement. [PMC3848710, PMC2376663, PMC1002528]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Autosomal dominant intermediate Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type E
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy disorder characterized by the typical CMT phenotype (slowly progressive distal muscle weakness and atrophy in upper and lower limbs, distal sensory loss in extremities, reduced or absent deep tendon reflexes and foot deformities) associated with focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (manifesting with proteinuria and progression to end-stage renal disease). Mild or moderate sensorineural hearing loss may also be associated. Nerve biopsy reveals both axonal and demyelinating changes and nerve conduction velocities vary from the demyelinating to axonal range (typically between 25-50m/sec).

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Renal disease is associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT), a common inherited neurological disorder. Three forms of CMT have been identified: CMT1 of the demyelinating type, CMT2 of the axonal defect type, and intermediate type (Int-CMT). INF2 is an important target for variants that cause the complex symptoms of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and CMT. the case of a 13-year-old female Chinese patient (born in 2011) with a rare co-occurrence of CMT1 and glomerulosclerosis (GS) (CMT1-GS). The patient presented with slowly progressive gait disorder with unsteadiness during walking, pes cavus, and kyphoscoliosis since the age of 1 year. Electrophysiological studies and brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed demyelinating features consistent with CMT1. At 12 years of age, she was hospitalised for hypertension and dizziness; her serum albumin was 27.9 g/L, serum... [PMC11603986]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Renal disease is associated with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease (CMT), a common inherited neurological disorder. Three forms of CMT have been identified: CMT1 of the demyelinating type, CMT2 of the axonal defect type, and intermediate type (Int-CMT). INF2 is an important target for variants that cause the complex symptoms of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) and CMT. the case of a 13-year-old female Chinese patient (born in 2011) with a rare co-occurrence of CMT1 and glomerulosclerosis (GS) (CMT1-GS). The patient presented with slowly progressive gait disorder with unsteadiness during walking, pes cavus, and kyphoscoliosis since the age of 1 year. Electrophysiological studies and brain magnetic resonance imaging revealed demyelinating features consistent with CMT1. At 12 years of age, she was hospitalised for hypertension and dizziness; her serum albumin was 27.9 g/L, serum... [PMC11603986]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves clinical evaluation for symptoms such as slowly progressive gait disorder, unsteadiness, pes cavus, and kyphoscoliosis, which may present early in life. Electrophysiological studies and brain magnetic resonance imaging can reveal demyelinating features consistent with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease. Given the association with renal disease, laboratory tests for serum albumin, creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate, and 24-hour urine protein are important, with renal biopsy potentially showing glomerulosclerosis. Definitive diagnosis is achieved through genetic testing, such as whole-exome sequencing, to identify pathogenic variants in genes like INF2. [PMC11603986]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The abstract describes a case of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1 and glomerulosclerosis (CMT1-GS) caused by a de novo heterozygous pathogenic variant in the INF2 gene. This finding is directly relevant to genetic counseling. A de novo variant indicates that the genetic change was not inherited from either parent, which typically implies a low recurrence risk for the parents' future offspring. However, as the variant is pathogenic and heterozygous, the affected individual would have a 50% chance of passing it on to their children, consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. [PMC11603986]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Autosomal dominant intermediate Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type E, particularly when associated with INF2 variants, can involve slowly progressive neurological symptoms such as gait disorder, unsteadiness, pes cavus, and kyphoscoliosis, which may manifest from an early age (e.g., 1 year). Renal complications, including glomerulosclerosis, can also occur and may lead to deteriorating renal function, potentially necessitating a kidney transplant, as observed in a patient at 13 years of age. [PMC11603986]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare cono-truncal anomaly in which both the aorta and pulmonary artery originate, either entirely or predominantly, from the morphologic right ventricle.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Double outlet right ventricle (DORV) accounts for about 2-3% of all congenital heart defects, with a birth prevalence rate of 1/ 10,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical picture varies widely, depending on the combination of the abnormalities present. Symptoms are generally observed during the first days or weeks of life. Cyanosis is the most frequent sign. Tachypnea or breathlessness, poor feeding and slow weight gain are also common. Tachycardia and/or heart murmur may also be observed. DORV is always associated with a ventricular septal defect (VSD) that allows blood to drain from the left ventricle. DORV is classified into sub-types, based on the relationship of the VSD (subaortic, doubly committed, subpulmonary or non-committed) with the great arteries. Other cardiac anomalies frequently associated with DORV include pulmonary stenosis, various degrees of left and right ventricular hypoplasia, atrioventricular (AV) septal defects, and straddling AV valves. Extracardiac anomalies, such as heterotaxy (polysplenia, asplenia, situs ambiguous) intestinal malrotation and ciliary dysfunction could be associated. It is important to figure out that DORV is not a congenital heart disease per se but a mode of ventriculo-arterial connection. Therefore there are several clinical types of DORV, depending on the presence of a pulmonary stenosis and of associated lesions. The functional classification has identified 5 types of DORV: DORV-VSD type, DORV-Fallot, DORV-Taussig Bing, DORV-non committed VSD, DORV-AVSD-heterotaxy. Each type has a specific clinical presentation and surgical treatment.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: DORV results from a failure in the fetal development of the cono-truncus, which is the primary outlet of the heart during embryonic development. The cono-truncal anomalies result in neural crest and second heart field dysfunction. Cardiac progenitor cells are controlled by various genes, such as GDF1 (19p13.11) and CFC1 (2q21.2), which when mutated can result in DORV. DORV is associated with chromosomal anomalies such as 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, trisomy 13, trisomy 18 and CHARGE syndrome and others.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on 3D echocardiography showing both great arteries arising from the right ventricle. In complex forms, cardiac catheterization-angiography, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and /or computed tomography (CT) scan are required. Recently, 3D printed models have been very useful to plane the surgery.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes transposition of the great arteries, tetralogy of Fallot, ventricular septal defect, and double outlet left ventricle.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: DORV can be diagnosed by fetal echocardiography with a good degree of accuracy when the two vessels arise entirely from the right ventricle.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: DORV is a sporadic disease. Consanguinity seems to be a risk factor. Genetic counseling is not possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: In the presence of two viable ventricles, biventricular repair is the optimal treatment for DORV and it is quite safely achieved in the simple forms (DORV-VSD type, DORV-Fallot type and DORV-TGA type). In the complex forms (DORV with non-committed VSD, DORV-atrioventricular septal defect-pulmonary stenosis-heterotaxy), univentricular repair (Fontan operation) is often preferred by a number of teams, while biventricular repair is performed in selected cases in advanced pediatric heart surgery centers.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Without treatment, prognosis is poor due to severe cyanosis, congestive heart failure or pulmonary hypertension. With biventricular repair, patients have, on average, a normal life expectancy, with possible risk or re-operation. All patients that have received surgery for a DORV require life-long surveillance by a cardiologist. Univentricular palliation requires a very close follow up.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Triple A syndrome is a very rare multisystem disease characterized by adrenal insufficiency with isolated glucocorticoid deficiency, achalasia, alacrima, autonomic dysfunction and neurodegeneration.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): 2A syndrome; 3A syndrome; 4A syndrome; AAA syndrome; Achalasia-addisonianism-alacrima syndrome; Adrenal insufficiency-achalasia-alacrima syndrome; Allgrove syndrome; Double A syndrome; Quaternary A syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown but less than 100 cases have been published since the first description in 1978.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The onset of Triple A syndrome varies between infancy and adulthood. When presenting in early childhood, alacrima and, possibly, achalasia are the indicative signs; in childhood and adolescence, onset is characterized by achalasia and adrenal insufficiency; while in adulthood, presentation is predominantly neurological with autonomous and polyneuropathic involvement. Alacrima, when present, is the first clinical sign, manifesting in the first months of life, but achalasia of the cardia, leading to dysphagia, is usually the first relevant symptom leading to diagnosis. Adrenal insufficiency may cause hypoglycemia and seizures. These three cardinal signs may not all be present, or be associated with autonomic dysfunction and other neurological features, leading to the ''double A'' or ''quaternary A'' denomination, respectively. Neurological manifestations are diverse: dysautonomia results in dyshidrosis and digestive, sexual, circulatory and urinary dysfunction; pyramidal syndrome and peripheral neuropathy lead to walking difficulties and sometimes to sensory deficit; and bulbar and facial deficiencies are responsible for velar insufficiency, tongue amyotrophy or paresis, orbicularis oris dysfunction and oropharyngeal dysphagia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by mutations in the AAAS gene (12q13), coding for the ALADIN nuclear pore scaffolding protein.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical examination and adrenal function testing. It can be confirmed by molecular testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Given that the presence of 2 among the 3 main clinical signs (achalasia, alacrima or adrenal insufficiency) is pathognomonic, differential diagnosis can be considered when only one clinical sign is observed, for example at the onset of the disease.
