All 22 affected subjects have soft tissue syndactyly of all fingers and all toes and 14 also have preaxial polydactyly of the hands and/or feet. In addition, 14 have a prominent upper sternum and/or a blind ending, inverted U shaped sinus in the anterior chest wall. Linkage studies and haplotype analysis carried out in 16 affected and nine unaffected members of this family showed that the underlying locus maps to a 6.4 cM interval on chromosome 7q36, between EN2 and D7S2423, a region to which a locus for preaxial polydactyly and triphalangeal thumb-polysyndactyly has previously... [PMC1734869]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis includes F syndrome (acropectorovertebral syndrome), which is described as a related but potentially distinct dominantly inherited skeletal dysplasia, possibly representing another manifestation of the same genetic entity. Furthermore, conditions characterized by preaxial polydactyly and triphalangeal thumb-polysyndactyly should be considered, as their loci have previously been mapped to the same 7q36 region. This shared genetic region and overlapping features like polydactyly suggest a common underlying mechanism, potentially involving misregulation of SHH. [PMC1734869]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Ring chromosome 3 syndrome is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome with a highly variable phenotype principally characterized by pre- and postnatal growth retardation, short stature, developmental delay, mild to severe intellectual disability, microcephaly and mild dysmorphic features (incl. triangular face, dysplastic ears, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, broad nasal bridge, full nasal tip, long philtrum, downturned corners of the mouth, and micro/retrognathia). Additional manifestations reported include hypotonia, mild articular limitation, hearing loss, digital anomalies (i.e. clinodacytyly, brachydactyly), café-au-lait patches and hypospadias.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Ring chromosome 3 syndrome presents with a spectrum of clinical features, including mental retardation and pre- and postnatal growth retardation, which can manifest as short stature. Patients often exhibit microcephaly, hypertonia, and digital anomalies. A characteristic facies is also noted, comprising ptosis, epicanthal folds, a broad nasal root, down-turned corners of the mouth, and dysplastic ears. While some cases present with a milder phenotype, the syndrome's features are primarily associated with deletion of 3p26 to pter. [PMC1016983, PMC1048968]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Ring chromosome 3 syndrome is characterized by the presence of a ring chromosome 3, which can arise de novo. Karyotypes such as 46,XX, r(3)(p26.2q29) and 46,XY,r3 (p26 leads to q29) have been identified. The clinical syndrome is primarily derived from the deletion of the 3p26 to pter region. This genetic anomaly can manifest with a range of phenotypes, from mild, including short stature, to more severe presentations involving mental retardation, pre- and postnatal growth retardation, microcephaly, and specific dysmorphic features. It has also been associated with Cornelia de Lange syndrome. [PMC1016983, PMC1017144, PMC1048968]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of ring chromosome 3 syndrome is established through karyotyping, which identifies the characteristic 46,XX or XY, r(3) chromosome. This genetic anomaly, often noted as r(3)(p26.2q29) or r3 (p26 leads to q29), can be detected in peripheral lymphocytes and cultured fibroblasts. Patients are typically investigated for clinical features such as short stature, mental retardation, and poor growth, leading to the discovery of the de novo ring chromosome 3. [PMC1016983, PMC1048968]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Ring chromosome 3 syndrome shares phenotypic features with deletion 3p, including mental retardation, pre- and postnatal growth retardation, microcephaly, hypertonia, digital anomalies, and a characteristic facies with ptosis, epicanthal folds, broad nasal root, down-turned corners of the mouth, and dysplastic ears. Additionally, Cornelia de Lange syndrome has been observed in conjunction with ring chromosome 3, suggesting a potential overlap or shared diagnostic considerations. [PMC1017144, PMC1048968]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Ring chromosome 3 syndrome can arise de novo, as observed in an 18-year-old female with a mild phenotype. However, the syndrome presents with a spectrum of severity, with other cases showing mental retardation, pre- and postnatal growth retardation, microcephaly, hypertonia, digital anomalies, and characteristic facial features. The specific karyotype 46,XX, r(3)(p26.2q29) or 46,XY,r3 (p26 leads to q29) is associated with these features, which are thought to derive mainly from deletion of 3p26 leads to pter. [PMC1016983, PMC1048968]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: an 18 year old female with a de novo ring chromosome 3 found after investigation for short stature. Her karyotype was interpreted as 46,XX, r(3)(p26.2q29). Her phenotype is milder than previously reported cases and illustrates the mild end of the spectrum of the ring chromosome 3 phenotype. [PMC1016983]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A primary bone dysplasia with micromelia characterized by micromelia, macrocephaly, narrow thorax, and distinctive facial features. It includes TD, type 1 (TD1) and TD, type 2 (TD2), that can be differentiated from each other by femur and skull shape.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Thanatophoric dysplasia (TD) estimated incidence is about 1/20,000 to 1/50,000 births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Characteristic morphological features are seen on prenatal ultrasounds. Late in the 1st trimester, shortening of the long bones is apparent on ultrasound along with increased nuchal translucency. In the 2nd trimester a marked growth deficiency (limb length below 5th percentile) is noted along with relative macrocephaly, a well mineralized skull, and narrow thorax with flattened vertebral bodies. Bowed ''telephone receiver'' femurs (in TD1), cloverleaf skull (in TD2 and a few cases of TD1) and polyhydramnios can also be seen. Neonates are macrocephalic with a large anterior fontanelle, frontal bossing, severe midface hypoplasia and proptosis. The thorax is narrow and bell-shaped. There is significant micromelia with redundant skin folds and brachydactyly with a trident hand configuration is common. Generalized hypotonia is present. CNS abnormalities can include temporal lobe dysplasia, hydrocephalus, and injury from critical foramen magnum stenosis. Rarely, cardiac and renal abnormalities have been reported as well as seizures.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: TD is caused by mutations in the fibroblast growth factor receptor 3 (FGFR3) gene (4p16.3) which cause overactivity of the FGFR3 protein, resulting in the disturbances in bone growth and other tissues that are characteristic of TD.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is usually made in the 2nd to 3rd trimester but is possible earlier with short limbs identified during standard 1st trimester dimensional ultrasound. Molecular genetic testing can be used to screen for FGFR3 mutations and definitely diagnose TD.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include homozygous achondroplasia, achondrogenesis (types 1A, 1B, and 2), SADDAN, short rib-polydactyly syndromes, osteogenesis imperfecta type 2, platyspondylic lethal skeletal dysplasias, dyssegmental dysplasia Silverman-Handmaker type, and campomelic dysplasia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is usually suspected by prenatal ultrasound and can be confirmed by molecular analysis of amniocytes, or by chorionic villus sampling (CVS), or recently by cell free fetal DNA.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: TD is inherited autosomal dominantly but the majority of cases are due to a de novo mutation in the proband. Genetic counseling allows families who have already had one child with TD to know that recurrence rate is about 2%, so the likelihood of having a healthy child is high.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Prenatally, treatment aims to avoid potential pregnancy and delivery complications. Postnatally, management should focus on the parents' wishes for provision of comfort-care for the newborn versus aggressive management. Respiratory support with a tracheostomy and ventilation is essential for survival in all infants. Hydrocephaly can be treated with the placement of a shunt. Suboccipital decompression can be done when needed to relieve craniocervical junction constriction. Antiepileptic drugs can be given to those with seizures. Hearing aids can be provided to those with hearing loss.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor with death occurring in utero or shortly after birth in almost all cases. Death is likely due to respiratory insufficiency and/or spinal cord/brain stem compression. A few rare cases have been reported where patients survived into childhood with significant medical intervention.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inborn error of metabolism characterized by abnormal accumulation of plasma cystathionine and subsequent increased urinary excretion due to cystathionine gamma-lyase deficiency. The condition is considered benign without pathological relevance. Mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Cystathionase deficiency; Gamma-cystathionase deficiency; Cystathionine gamma-lyase deficiency syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: studies of six individuals with marked elevations of cystathionine in plasma and/or urine. Studies of CTH, the gene that encodes cystathionine gamma-lyase, revealed the presence among these individuals of either homozygous or compound heterozygous forms of a novel large deletion, p.Gly57_Gln196del, two novel missense mutations, c.589C>T (p.Arg197Cys) and c.932C>T (p.Thr311Ile), and one previously reported alteration, c.200C>T (p.Thr67Ile). Another novel missense mutation, c.185G>T (p.Arg62His), was found in heterozygous form in three mildly hypercystathioninemic members of a Taiwanese family. In one severely hypercystathioninemic individual no CTH mutation was found. Brief clinical histories of the cystathioninemic/cystathioninuric patients are presented. Most of the novel mutations were expressed and the CTH activities of the mutant proteins determined. The crystal structure of the... [PMC2752209]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Studies of individuals with marked elevations of cystathionine in plasma and/or urine, including those with homozygous or compound heterozygous inactivating CTH mutations, have been conducted. Despite severe loss of cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH) activity, the experience with these patients provides no evidence of adverse clinical effects. Some individuals had mild plasma total homocysteine elevations, but no other clinical symptoms were reported. [PMC2752209]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Cystathioninuria is characterized by marked elevations of cystathionine in plasma and/or urine. The condition is primarily associated with mutations in the CTH gene, which encodes cystathionine gamma-lyase. Identified mutations include homozygous or compound heterozygous forms of a novel large deletion (p.Gly57_Gln196del), two novel missense mutations (c.589C>T (p.Arg197Cys) and c.932C>T (p.Thr311Ile)), and a previously reported alteration (c.200C>T (p.Thr67Ile)). Another novel missense mutation (c.185G>T (p.Arg62His)) has been found in heterozygous form. While most cases are linked to CTH mutations, one severely hypercystathioninemic individual showed no CTH mutation. Inactivating CTH mutations can also lead to mild plasma total homocysteine elevations. [PMC2752209]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of cystathioninuria involves detecting marked elevations of cystathionine in plasma and/or urine. Genetic studies identify homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the CTH gene, such as p.Gly57_Gln196del, c.589C>T, c.932C>T, c.200C>T, and c.185G>T. However, CTH mutations are not always found in severely hypercystathioninemic individuals. In some cases, a greater level of plasma cystathionine is observed only after methionine loading. [PMC2752209]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: In medical practice, conditions such as renal iminoglycinuria and alpha 1-antitrypsin deficiency may be relevant for differential diagnosis, particularly when observed within the same family as cystathioninuria. [PMC1704166]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Cystathioninuria is a familial condition linked to mutations in the CTH gene, which encodes cystathionine gamma-lyase. Affected individuals typically present with homozygous or compound heterozygous forms of inactivating CTH mutations, including specific deletions and missense mutations. Heterozygous carriers of certain mutations, such as c.185G>T, may exhibit mild hypercystathioninemia. A common polymorphism, c.1208G>T, when homozygous, can lead to elevated plasma cystathionine after methionine loading in otherwise healthy individuals. Despite severe loss of CTH activity due to these mutations, current experience provides no evidence of adverse clinical effects. [PMC2752209, PMC1704166]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: studies of six individuals with marked elevations of cystathionine in plasma and/or urine. Studies of CTH, the gene that encodes cystathionine gamma-lyase, revealed the presence among these individuals of either homozygous or compound heterozygous forms of a novel large deletion, p.Gly57_Gln196del, two novel missense mutations, c.589C>T (p.Arg197Cys) and c.932C>T (p.Thr311Ile), and one previously reported alteration, c.200C>T (p.Thr67Ile). Another novel missense mutation, c.185G>T (p.Arg62His), was found in heterozygous form in three mildly hypercystathioninemic members of a Taiwanese family. In one severely hypercystathioninemic individual no CTH mutation was found. Brief clinical histories of the cystathioninemic/cystathioninuric patients are presented. Most of the novel mutations were expressed and the CTH activities of the mutant proteins determined. The crystal structure of the... [PMC2752209]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Based on the experience with reported patients, there is no evidence that severe loss of cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH) activity, which characterizes cystathioninuria, is accompanied by adverse clinical effects. This suggests a generally benign prognosis for individuals with the condition. [PMC2752209]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, primary bone dysplasia characterized by rhizomelic limb shortening, punctate calcifications in cartilage with epiphyseal and metaphyseal abnormalities (chondrodysplasia punctata) and coronal cleft vertebrae associated with profound postnatal growth deficiency, early-onset cataracts, severe intellectual disability and seizures.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Rhizomelic chondrodysplasia punctata (RCDP) prevalence is estimated to be lower than 1/100,000. The disorder is pan ethnic.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Presentation is at birth with severe joint contractures; cataracts may be present or appear in the first few months of life. Respiratory distress and feeding difficulties are commonly observed after birth. Whilst birth parameters (weight, length, and head circumference) are in the lower range from normal, profound postnatal growth retardation ensues. Rhizomelic limb shortening is typically greater in the humerus than the femur. Other skeletal abnormalities include punctate calcifications in cartilage with epiphyseal and metaphyseal abnormalities (chondrodysplasia punctata) and coronal cleft vertebrae. Intellectual disability is severe, and the majority of children develop seizures.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by defective plasmalogen biosynthesis and impaired peroxisome function. The majority of patients have variants in the PEX7 gene (6q21-q22.2, RDCP type 1) encoding the peroxisomal targeting signal 2 receptor which plays an important role in peroxisomal protein import. Biallelic variants in the GNPAT gene (1q42) encoding dihydroxyacetone phosphate acyltransferase cause RDCP type 2, variants in the AGPS gene (2q31) encoding peroxisomal alkyldihydroxyacetonephosphate synthase cause RDCP type 3, and variants in the PEX5 gene (12p13.31) encoding the peroxisomal targeting signal 1 receptor cause RDCP type 5.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected on clinical and radiologic findings and confirmed by either biochemical or molecular testing. Sub-typing requires molecular testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The principle differential diagnosis is Zellweger syndrome. It also includes Warfarin embryopathy, fatty acyl-CoA reductase 1 deficiency, and Chondrodysplasia punctata, tibia-metacarpal type.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is feasible for at risk pregnancies where the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disease is transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner. Genetic counseling should be proposed to at risk couples (where both parents are unaffected carriers of the disease) informing them that the risk of having and affected child is 25% for each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is supportive. Cataract extraction may restore some vision. Physical therapy is recommended to improve contractures; orthopedic procedures may improve function in some individuals. Dietary restriction of phytanic acid to avoid the consequences of phytanic acid accumulation over time may benefit individuals with milder forms of RCDP. Gastrostomy tube may be considered for poor weight gain, feeding intolerance, aspiration, and gastroesophageal reflux. Anti-seizure medications may be considered for seizures particularly where seizures are progressive, continuous and apparently painful, or significantly interfering with a child's interaction with the environment.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: RCDP has a severe prognosis with death generally occurring during the first decade of life, mainly due to respiratory complications; a proportion may die in the neonatal period. Greater than 90% of individuals with RCDP survive the first year of life, and about 75% live to school age. Those with less severe plasmalogen deficiency, had improved survivability compared with those with very low classical plasmalogen levels.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare subtype of autosomal dominant limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, with a variable age of onset, characterized by progressive, proximal weakness and wasting of the shoulder and pelvic musculature (with the pelvic girdle, and especially the ileopsoas muscle, being more affected) and frequent association of calf hypertrophy, dysphagia, arachnodactyly with or without finger contractures and/or distal and axial muscle involvement. Additional features include an abnormal gait, exercise intolerance, myalgia, fatigue and respiratory insufficiency. Cardiac conduction defects are typically not observed.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): LGMD1F; Autosomal dominant limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 1F; LGMD type 1F; Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 1F

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiology of this limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is associated with mutations in the TNPO3 gene. This link is supported by molecular and histopathological studies conducted on sporadic patients identified with TNPO3 mutations and presenting with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy. [PMC6299540]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves identifying mutations in the PLEC gene, such as the c.1_9del mutation, often in individuals with slowly progressive limb-girdle weakness. Muscle biopsies typically show dystrophic changes. Neurological examination may reveal ptosis, facial weakness, fatigability, and muscle cramps. Electrophysiological studies, including repetitive nerve stimulation and single-fiber electromyography, can detect a borderline decrement and high jitter, respectively. Muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features also contribute to the diagnostic characterization. [PMC7397187]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: We identified the known c.1_9del mutation in the PLEC gene in four unrelated females from consanguineous families of Turkish origin. All individuals presented with slowly progressive limb-girdle weakness without any dermatological findings, and dystrophic changes observed in their muscle biopsies. Additionally, the neurological examination revealed ptosis, facial weakness, fatigability, and muscle cramps in all four cases. In two patients, repetitive nerve stimulation showed a borderline decrement and a high jitter was detected in all patients by single-fiber electromyography. Clinical improvement was observed after treatment with pyridostigmine and salbutamol was started. We further characterize the phenotype of patients with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R17 clinically, by muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features and by describing a common 3.8 Mb haplotype in three... [PMC7397187]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: We identified the known c.1_9del mutation in the PLEC gene in four unrelated females from consanguineous families of Turkish origin. All individuals presented with slowly progressive limb-girdle weakness without any dermatological findings, and dystrophic changes observed in their muscle biopsies. Additionally, the neurological examination revealed ptosis, facial weakness, fatigability, and muscle cramps in all four cases. In two patients, repetitive nerve stimulation showed a borderline decrement and a high jitter was detected in all patients by single-fiber electromyography. Clinical improvement was observed after treatment with pyridostigmine and salbutamol was started. We further characterize the phenotype of patients with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R17 clinically, by muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features and by describing a common 3.8 Mb haplotype in three... [PMC7397187]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Clinical improvement has been observed with treatment. Patients showed improvement after the initiation of pyridostigmine and salbutamol. These treatments were associated with positive outcomes in individuals presenting with slowly progressive limb-girdle weakness, ptosis, facial weakness, fatigability, and muscle cramps. [PMC7397187]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The condition is characterized by slowly progressive limb-girdle weakness. Clinical improvement has been observed in affected individuals following the initiation of treatment with pyridostigmine and salbutamol, indicating that symptoms can be managed. [PMC7397187]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, acquired, life-threatening, infectious disease due to the tick-borne bacteria Rickettsia rickettsii characterized by an acute onset of fever, malaise, and severe headache, variably accompanied by myalgia, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and photophobia, associating (2-5 days after fever onset) a typically erythematous, blanching or non-blanching, maculopapluar rash with petechiae, starting on the wrists and ankles and progressing centrifugally to the palms and soles and centripetally to the arms, legs and trunk. Additonal variable features may include conjunctivitis, mucosal ulcers, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, jaundice, pneumonia, hepatomegaly, renal failure, meningismus, amnesia, optic disc edema, and ocular arterial occlusion.

DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) is often initiated empirically based on clinical signs, symptoms, and epidemiological settings, supported by laboratory findings such as hyponatremia, leukocytosis, or thrombocytopenia. Confirmatory include serological testing for IgG antibodies, typically involving acute and convalescent samples to demonstrate a four-fold increase in titers. Molecular diagnostic tests, such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays, are also employed, utilizing samples like postmortem tissue, biopsy material, or crusts from inoculation eschars. However, species-specific confirmatory testing faces challenges due to cross-reactivity in some molecular assays, potentially leading to misidentification of Rickettsia species. Bacterial isolation is another diagnostic approach. [PMC12404551, PMC11210658, PMC10859820, PMC10710119, PMC9390100]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) is a tick-borne infection caused by Rickettsia rickettsii. a series of two cases of pregnant patients who showed up at the emergency room of a hospital in Nuevo León, Mexico. Both patients lived in environments where R. rickettsii is endemic and they presented with several days of symptoms, including fever. Both patients developed a rash and had stillbirths during their hospital stay. Treatment with doxycycline was delayed, with fatal in both patients. Diagnosis of RMSF was confirmed via polymerase chain reaction assay postmortem. The need to link epidemiological clues with clinical data is critical in the diagnosis and early treatment of RMSF to prevent maternal deaths. [PMC10859820]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Rocky Mountain spotted fever (RMSF) is a serious and potentially fatal tick-borne disease, with numerous reported deaths. Delays in diagnosis and prompt initiation of appropriate treatment, especially with doxycycline, are critical factors contributing to severe illness, morbidity, and mortality. The disease can progress rapidly, leading to life-threatening consequences such as respiratory failure and stillbirths in pregnant patients. Patients may also develop severe neurological manifestations, including seizures, aphasia, hemiparesis, and long-term central nervous system impairment. Early recognition and treatment are vital to avert severe outcomes. [PMC11602018, PMC11210667, PMC11210658, PMC10946421, PMC10859820]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare epilepsy syndrome characterized by adolescence/young adulthood onset of myoclonic with or without other generalized seizure types in an otherwise healthy individual. The electroencephalogram (EEG) shows 3-5.5 Hz generalized spike-waves and polyspike-waves. Photosensitivity is common.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (JME) ranges from 1/3,333 to 1/10,000 people (<30 years old), with slight female preponderance. JME accounts for approximately 9.3% of all epilepsies (among patients <30 years of age).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: JME mostly appears in the second decade of life. It is characterized by myoclonic seizures that typically occur shortly after awakening and when tired. Myoclonic seizures may be triggered by photic stimulation. Sleep deprivation is an important provoking factor. Generalized tonic-clonic seizures occur in 90% of patients, often preceded by a series of myoclonic jerks. Absence seizures occur in a third of patients. Cognition is typically normal, although mild neuropsychiatric symptoms may be associated including executive function and attention impairment, anxiety, depression and impulsiveness.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: JME has a strong genetic component following a complex pattern of inheritance which is likely polygenic; to date, 8 genes have been associated with the disease (CILK1, CACNB4, EFHC1, GABRA1, GABRD, KCNQ3, JRK and CLCN2).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the electroclinical picture. EEG background activity is normal. Interictal EEG (in untreated patients) shows discharges of generalized polyspikes and waves and spike-waves at the frequency of 3-5.5 Hz. A photo paroxysmal response may be elicited in up to 90% of untreated individuals, mainly if the EEG is recorded in the morning. Sleep deprivation usually elicits the generalized epileptic activity and may be required to confirm the diagnosis in patients with normal awake EEG. Neuroimaging is normal and it is not required for the diagnosis in individuals with a typical clinical picture. Genetic testing is not part of routine diagnostic evaluation.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes: juvenile absence epilepsy, epilepsy with generalized tonic-clonic seizure alone, epilepsy with eyelid myoclonia, progressive myoclonic epilepsies (PME), familial adult myoclonic epilepsy (FAME), epilepsy with myoclonic absences, psychogenic non-epileptic seizures.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: As other idiopathic generalized epilepsies (IGE), JME has a ''complex'' inheritance. Genetic counseling is difficult in an individual patient, since JME is probably polygenic. This polygenic basis of the IGE suggest that variation in many alleles confer a low to moderate risk to express the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Monotherapy with sodium valproate is the most effective treatment in controlling myoclonic, generalized tonic-clonic, and absence seizures. In women of childbearing potential, levetiracetam and lamotrigine are considered the first-choice treatment, given the high risk of fetal malformations and of cognitive and behavioral impairments in children born to women given valproate.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis of JME is usually favorable, with good therapy responsiveness. However, relapse of seizures after the withdrawal of antiseizure medication occurs in up to 90% of individuals.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare progressive peroxisomal disorder characterized by endocrine dysfunction (adrenal failure and sometimes testicular insufficiency), progressive myelopathy, peripheral neuropathy and, variably, progressive leukodystrophy.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy (X-ALD) is the most common peroxisomal disorder with an estimated birth prevalence of 1/17,000 (male and female). It has been reported throughout the world.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: X-ALD affects males and females, although symptoms and disease progression differ. The age of onset is highly variable and the rate of progression is unpredictable. Male patients usually present in childhood with signs and symptoms of adrenal failure (80% of male patients develop adrenal failure before the age of 18) or with a rapidly progressive leukodystrophy (40% of male patients before the age of 18, with a lifetime prevalence of 60%). Leukodystrophy is initially clinically silent, but eventually neuropsychiatric symptoms develop, followed by focal deficits like hemiparesis and auditory agnosia, and occasionally epileptic seizures. In early adulthood male patients develop a progressive myelopathy (and peripheral neuropathy) with a gait disorder and incontinence. Progression is slow (over years). Penetrance of this myelopathy is complete, although age of onset and progression are highly variable (some patients require a walking aid whilst others remain ambulatory). Female patients virtually never develop adrenal failure or leukodystrophy. About 90% develop a myelopathy and peripheral neuropathy, but at a later age (after 40 years of age) and with slower progression (over decades) than in males.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: X-ALD is caused by variants of ABCD1 (Xq28), with about 900 different mutations reported. There is no geno-phenotype correlation. The encoded protein peroxisomal transmembrane protein is involved in the transport of very long-chain fatty acid CoA-esters (VLCFA) from the cytosol into the peroxisome. Although the exact pathophysiology is poorly understood, perturbed VLCFA homeostasis in glial cells may contribute to the destabilization of the myelin sheath and impairment of axonal function.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: If there is clinical suspicion, the diagnosis is established by determining plasma VLCFA (C26:0 and C26:0/C22:0 ratio) which is increased in all male patients; up to 15% of female patients have normal VLCFA. Recently, C26:0-lysophosphatidylcholine in bloodspots or plasma has been validated as diagnostic marker, and is elevated in all male and virtually all female patients. The diagnosis can be confirmed by ABCD1 mutation analysis. If necessary, functional assays in cultured skin fibroblasts are available. In case of leukodystrophy, the MRI pattern is virtually pathognomonic. Adrenal failure can be established with an ACTH stimulation test. Newborn screening for X-ALD has been recently implemented in certain regions.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Testing for X-ALD is recommended in all males presenting with adrenal failure (especially in cases of isolated glucocorticoid deficiency). In adult men or women presenting with a chronic myelopathy, the differential diagnosis is large and includes both acquired and genetic disorders. There is no relevant differential diagnosis for presentation with leukodystrophy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: In case of a positive family history and a fetus at risk, genetic prenatal diagnosis is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is X-linked. Male patients transmit the disorder to all of their daughters, but never to a son. Female patients transmit the disorder to 50% of their sons and daughters. In case a patient is diagnosed, family screening and counseling is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Adrenal insufficiency in X-ALD is treated by hydrocortisone (and if needed fludrocortisone) by an endocrinologist. For the progressive myelopathy there is currently no disease modifying treatment available. The leukodystrophy is treatable with allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant (HCT), although the outcome is only acceptable when treated in the early stages (Loes score < 9). Autologous HCT after ex vivo lentiviral gene therapy is pending approval in the U.S.A and Europe.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Pre-symptomatic diagnosis permits monitoring for the occurrence of adrenal failure and the onset of cerebral ALD. If appropriate treatment is initiated, severe morbidity and mortality can be prevented. There is currently no treatment to prevent the occurrence or progression of the myelopathy. However, with appropriate supportive care life expectancy is near normal.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Bloom syndrome is a rare disorder associated with pre- and postnatal growth deficiency, a telangiectatic erythematous rash of the face and other sun-exposed areas, insulin resistance and predisposition to early onset and recurrent cancer of multiple organ systems.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Bloom syndrome (BSyn) overall prevalence is unknown, but in the Ashkenazi Jewish population it is estimated at approximately 1/ 48,000 births. A founder mutation, known as BLMash is present in approximately 1 in 100 persons of Ashkenazi Jewish background. There are also founder mutations in the Slavic and Hispanic populations.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Individuals with BSyn show proportionate growth deficiency of prenatal onset (average birth weight 1757 g) and continuing throughout life (average adult height of 149 cm for men and 138 cm for women). Dolichocephaly, narrow face, prominent nose and ears, and malar and mandibular hypoplasia can be observed. Subcutaneous adipose tissue is sparse. Telangiectatic erythema appears during the first 1-2 years of life on the face (in particular the cheek), dorsum of the hands and other sun-exposed areas. Café-au-lait macules and hypopigmented skin lesions are common. Children with BSyn characteristically feed slowly, have a decreased appetite and eat a limited variety of foods. Despite nutritional interventions, weight gain is modest and children are rarely in the normal range for growth. One major feature of Bsyn is a greatly increased predisposition to cancers in a distribution corresponding to the general population but occurring at a much younger age. Survivors of a first cancer may have multiple cancers in their lifetime. Most men with BSyn have azoospermia or severe oligospermia, while women are often fertile but may begin menopause prematurely.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Bloom syndrome is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. The BLM gene codes for a RecQ helicase that forms a complex with two other proteins, DNA topoisomerase IIIα and RMI.BLM heterozygotes are healthy and without any clinical features of the disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of BSyn is suspected clinically by identification of characteristic features and is confirmed by identification of biallelic pathogenic variants of the BLM gene on molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis of Bloom syndrome includes Fanconi anemia, Silver-Russell syndrome, Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, ataxia-telangiectasia, and Nijmegen breakage syndrome. Three other disorders also may be of interest in a differential diagnosis. RECQ-mediated genome instability 1, RECQ-mediated genome instability 2, Microcephaly, growth restriction, & increased sister-chromatid exchange 2.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis of at-risk pregnancies is possible by cytogenetic (SCE) or molecular genetic testing (BLM sequencing and deletion/duplication) of fetal cells obtained by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling. Molecular genetic testing is preferred.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is symptomatic. Increased calorie density formulas and foods may promote weight gain and increased growth. Although growth hormone treatment may improve linear growth, many clinicians caution against its use because of reports of early onset of cancer in some treated children. Standard antibiotic regimens are used to treat infections. If the serum levels of immunoglobulins are low and the patient is experiencing repeated infections, some have been treated with intravenous or subcutaneous immunoglobulins. Skin protection, including covering exposed skin and use of a broad-spectrum sunscreen with at least 30 SPF is crucial to reduce the sun-sensitive skin rash. Health supervision recommendations for persons with Bloom syndrome have been published, including recommendations for cancer surveillance. Due to hypersensitivity of patients to chemotherapy, reduced dosage and/or duration of therapy is recommended, usually beginning with 50% of the weight-based dosage. Caution should be exercised with use of ionizing radiation or alkylating agents, particularly busulfan, cyclophosphamide or melphalan.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The high occurrence of cancer reduces life expectancy. The median overall life expectancy is approximately 30 years, with cancer and related complications as the leading cause of death.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is a rare, slowly progressive liver disease characterized by inflammation and destruction of the intra- and/or extra-hepatic bile ducts that lead to cholestasis, liver fibrosis, liver cirrhosis and ultimately liver failure.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of PSC in Europe ranges from 1/446,000-1/6,170. A male preponderance is observed with a male to female ratio of approximately 2:1.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: PSC can occur at any age with a peak incidence around 40 years of age. Symptoms and clinical findings are variable, depending on the stage of the disease. In early stages, unspecific manifestations such as fever, fatigue, pruritus, malaise, abdominal pain, and weight loss are reported, however about 40-50% of patients may be asymptomatic at time of diagnosis. Hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, jaundice, portal hypertension and, in more advanced cases, spider angiomata, ascites and muscle atrophy are observed. The disease course is also highly variable, but in the majority of cases, PSC is slowly progressive, leading to liver cirrhosis, liver failure and the need for liver transplantation over a period of 13-21 years following diagnosis. Several immune-mediated comorbidities are observed in PSC. The most common co-existing condition is inflammatory bowel disease, reported in up to 60-80% of patients of Northern European decent. Other immune-mediated conditions, such as autoimmune hepatitis, thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes mellitus, and celiac disease, are also observed with slightly increased frequencies in PSC patients. A proportion of PSC patients develop malignancies; mainly cholangiocarcinoma, but also increased risk of carcinoma of the large intestine in patients with concomitant IBD. Small-duct PSC is a PSC-variant manifesting with chronic cholestasis, biochemical and histological findings similar to those found in PSC, and a normal cholangiography.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The precise etiology of PSC has not yet been established, but it is believed to be multifactorial. Genetic susceptibility factors are known to be involved, and a strong association to genetic variants within the HLA-region on chromosome 6 is observed. The disease is thought to be related to an abnormal immune response to a still unidentified environmental stimulus.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: PSC is suspected based on clinical manifestations and altered liver function tests and diagnosis is confirmed through magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) or endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) showing bile duct changes with strictures and dilatations characteristic of the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other hepatic diseases, such as autoimmune hepatitis and primary biliary cholangitis. Exclusion of multiple secondary causes leading to PSC-like bile duct changes, such as IgG4-associated sclerosing cholangitis, mast cell cholangiopathy, infections, biliary calculi or trauma, and other identifiable causes of insults to the biliary tree (leading to the ERCP or MRCP features seen in PSC) is mandatory to establish the diagnosis of PSC.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Immunosuppressants and chelators are used to treat the symptoms and manage the complications, however, to date there are no medical therapies that cure or alter the disease course of PSC. Replacement therapy of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K is frequently necessary since patients frequently present deficiency of these vitamins. Liver transplantation is currently the only definitive treatment for patients with advanced disease and the majority of patients require a liver transplantation 13-21 years after diagnosis; either due to disease progression or disease complications, such as treatment-resistant bacterial cholangitis. Endoscopic dilatation, with or without stenting, of biliary strictures may be performed to relieve symptoms of biliary obstruction.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis after liver transplantation is generally good, however, in a proportion of patients PSC may recur in the transplanted liver, with recurrence rates varying from 10-37%.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Rationale: Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) is characterized by idiopathic intra- and extrahepatic bile duct inflammation and biliary fibrotic changes. Recurrent bile duct stones due to PLKR and UGT1A1 mutation is an extremely rare complications of PSC. Patient concerns: A 26-year-old male patient complains a history of recurrent yellow skin and urine for over a year. Diagnoses: Following dynamic magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography imaging, colonoscopic manifestation, liver biopsy and whole exome sequencing, the patient was finally diagnosed with PSC - ulcerative colitis with PLKR and UGT1A1 mutation. Interventions: Following resolution of the obstruction, a long-term regimen of 1000 mg/d ursodeoxycholic acid in combination with 10 mg/d obeticholic acid to improve cholestasis, 8 g/d colestyramine to facilitate adsorption of excess bile acids and 1.2 g/d rifaximin to prevent... [PMC11709192]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome due to lysyl hydroxylase 1 deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare subtype of kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome characterized by congenital muscle hypotonia, congenital or early-onset kyphoscoliosis (progressive or non-progressive), and generalized joint hypermobility with dislocations/subluxations (in particular of the shoulders, hips, and knees). Additional common features are skin hyperextensibility, easy bruising of the skin, rupture/aneurysm of a medium-sized artery, osteopenia/osteoporosis, blue sclerae, umbilical or inguinal hernia, chest deformity, marfanoid habitus, talipes equinovarus, and refractive errors. Subtype-specific manifestations include skin fragility, atrophic scarring, scleral/ocular fragility/rupture, microcornea, and facial dysmorphology (like low‐set ears, epicanthal folds, down‐slanting palpebral fissures, high palate). Molecular testing is obligatory to confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): EDS VIA; Ocular-scoliotic EDS; kEDS-PLOD1; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type 6A; Cutis hyperelastica; Lysyl hydroxylase-deficient EDS; Kyphoscoliotic EDS due to lysyl hydroxylase 1 deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (kEDS) due to lysyl hydroxylase 1 deficiency is a rare, autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder. While cases have been reported globally, the first case of PLOD1-related kEDS of Chinese origin was identified in a 17-year-old male. Rare cases have also been described in Korean siblings, and affected brothers have been reported, highlighting its familial occurrence. [PMC11061726, PMC7599977, PMC7073314, PMC6040561, PMC1918329]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: PLOD1 -related kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a rare, autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder characterized by congenital hypotonia, early-onset, progressive kyphoscoliosis, and generalized joint hypermobility. PLOD1 -kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is also associated with heightened vascular fragility, resulting in an elevated susceptibility to recurrent vascular complications such as arterial aneurysms, dissection, and spontaneous arterial rupture. the cases of two affected brothers: a 13-year-old boy presenting with spontaneous rupture of a celiac artery aneurysm and a 10-year-old boy presenting with a rapidly enlarging celiac artery aneurysm requiring urgent repair. The corpus callosum plays a vital role in brain function. In particular, in the trunk of the corpus callosum, in the course of various diseases, there may be temporary, reversible changes... [PMC11061726, PMC9407725, PMC7599977, PMC7073314, PMC6040561]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome due to lysyl hydroxylase 1 deficiency should be differentiated from other connective tissue disorders presenting with similar features. These include B3GALT6-related disorders, characterized by severe early-onset spinal deformities and kyphoscoliosis. Other Ehlers-Danlos syndrome subtypes, such as arthrochalasia-type EDS and classical EDS (due to COL5A1 or COL5A2 mutations), also present with severe kyphoscoliosis or scoliosis, skin hyperextensibility, and joint hypermobility. Loeys-Dietz syndrome, an autosomal dominant connective tissue disease, can also manifest with scoliosis and vascular abnormalities. Additionally, pathogenic variants in lysyl hydroxylase 3 can cause a multisystem connective tissue disorder with features of collagen-related disorders. [PMC12214426, PMC12227340, PMC9761383, PMC8172199, PMC8135155]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (kEDS) due to lysyl hydroxylase 1 deficiency is an autosomal recessive connective tissue disorder caused by mutations in the PLOD1 gene, with both homozygous and compound heterozygous variants reported. Genetic counseling should highlight the recessive inheritance pattern, implying that parents are typically asymptomatic carriers. The condition is characterized by congenital hypotonia, early-onset progressive kyphoscoliosis, generalized joint hypermobility, and severe skin hyperextensibility and fragility. A significant feature is heightened vascular fragility, leading to an elevated susceptibility to recurrent arterial aneurysms, dissection, and spontaneous rupture, which can occur even in early childhood. Intrafamilial variability in clinical severity and age of kyphoscoliosis onset has been observed. [PMC11061726, PMC7599977, PMC7073314, PMC6040561, PMC1918329]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Diencephalic syndrome (DS) is a rare condition characterized by profound emaciation and failure to thrive (with normal caloric intake and normal linear growth), hyperalertness, hyperkinesia and euphoria, in the presence of hypothalamic tumors.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Diencephalic cachexia; Diencephalic syndrome of childhood; Diencephalic syndrome of emaciation; Russell diencephalic cachexia; Russell syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: DS usually presents in infants or young children (mean age 6 months), but can also occur rarely in older children and adults. DS usually occurs in the presence of low grade astrocytoma/glioma brain tumors of the hypothalamus, which may extend into the optic pathway. These tumors are usually more aggressive and appear at a younger age when associated with DS. Rarely, DS can be secondary to craniopharyngioma, as well as other suprasellar tumors. Manifestations of DS include weight loss, eventually leading to severe emaciation (despite normal caloric intake and linear growth) with an absence of subcutaneous fat, as well as hyperalertness, hyperkinesia, and cheerfulness extending to euphoria in some. Nystagmus, strabismus, decreased visual acuity (and very rarely blindness), optic pallor, hydrocephalus, headache, somnolence, and vomiting have also been reported in some cases. Hypothalamic obesity may occur due to hypothalamic damage. Normal or precocious intellectual development is noted. Rarely, tumors may also be associated with neurofibromatosis type 1.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: A variety of chiasmatic and hypothalamic low-grade gliomas have been reported to be associated with DS, most commonly pilocytic and pilomyxoid astrocytoma, but there are case reports of craniopharyngioma, suprasellar ependymoma, suprasellar germinoma, suprasellar epidermoid cyst, and hypothalamic spongioblastoma. These tumors may lead to hypothalamic dysfunction and/or degeneration of the optic nerve. The pathogenesis of DS is unknown. Recently, it was proposed that leptin may be dysregulated, but further studies are needed.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: When DS is suspected clinically (failure to thrive in children despite normal caloric intake), gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging of the cranium, as well as of the spine (due to frequent leptomeningeal seeding) is performed, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis may also be necessary. Ophthalmologic examination should be performed to check for any visual abnormalities. Growth hormone and ghrelin levels are increased and insulin and leptin levels are decreased, but those changes may be secondary to the patient's body mass index.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes gastrointestinal disorders that lead to severe weight loss such celiac disease.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment aims at removing or reducing the size of the tumor, by surgical or non-surgical methods. Since complete resection of the tumor is not possible due to its location, tumor resection is usually partial and is generally followed by chemotherapy. Radiotherapy is not commonly used, as the patients are young. Patients also require nutritional supplementation (orally or via nasogastric feeding tube or gastrostomy) for malnutrition while symptomatic. Follow-up after completion of treatment includes regular life-long oncologic, neurologic, ophthalmologic and clinical assessments as precocious puberty and pituitary hormone deficiencies may develop.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the histological type and grade of tumor but is poorer in patients with DS than in patients with similar tumors who do not present with DS. Frequently, these tumors continue to progress despite treatment. If untreated, patients have an average survival time of less than 12 months after diagnosis, but with proper treatment the long-term survival is greatly improved.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: This syndrome is characterized by severe immunodeficiency, osteopetrosis, lymphedema and anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It has been described in a few unrelated male patients born to mothers with mild incontinentia pigmenti.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The first two reported children died before three years of age from multiple infections with Gram-positive cocci, Gram-negative bacilli, mycobacteria, and fungi.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is classified as a X-linked osteopetrosis and is caused by mutations in the IKBKG (NEMO) gene (Xq28).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia-immunodeficiency-osteopetrosis-lymphedema syndrome, also known as OL-EDA-ID Syndrome, involves the identification of a novel hypomorphic NEMO mutation. This genetic finding is associated with the severe clinical presentation of the syndrome. [PMC5226985]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: OL-EDA-ID Syndrome: a Novel Hypomorphic NEMO Mutation Associated with a Severe Clinical Presentation and Transient HLH. [PMC5226985]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: OL-EDA-ID Syndrome: a Novel Hypomorphic NEMO Mutation Associated with a Severe Clinical Presentation and Transient HLH. [PMC5226985]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (MCAD) deficiency (MCADD) is an inborn error of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation characterized by a rapidly progressive metabolic crisis, often presenting as hypoketotic hypoglycemia, lethargy, vomiting, seizures and coma, which can be fatal in the absence of emergency medical intervention.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): ACADM deficiency; Carnitine deficiency secondary to medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency; MCAD deficiency; MCADD; Medium chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated birth prevalence of MCADD is thought to range from 1/4,900 to 1/27,000 in Caucasian populations and is highest in individuals of Northern European descent. The worldwide birth prevalence is 1/14,600.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: MCADD usually presents 3 to 24 months after birth in previously healthy infants. However, neonatal presentations are well described as are those in adults, given sufficient metabolic stress (such as significant alcohol ingestion). Nevertheless, many affected individuals remain asymptomatic throughout life. Typically hypoketotic hypoglycemia, lethargy and vomiting are triggered by an infection, fasting or surgery. Some patients, however, can present with a progressive metabolic crisis despite ketosis and normal blood glucose. Rarely patients may present in crisis with ''paradoxically'' gross ketosis. During a crisis, a patient may manifest with lethargy, emesis, respiratory arrest, seizures, hepatomegaly and rapid progression to cardiac arrest unless emergency treatment is implemented. Potential brain injury occurring during these episodes can lead to an increased risk of long term neurological damage. Sudden unexplained death can sometimes be the first manifestation of this disease. Historically, about 25% of undiagnosed patients die during their first presentation of a crisis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MCADD is caused by mutations in the ACADM gene (1p31) which encodes the mitochondrial MCAD protein. The most prevalent mutation, c.985A>G, (K329E), p.(Lys329Glu), accounted for about 80% of clinical disease prior to newborn screening programs but many more individuals are now being identified with other ACADM mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is through the identification of a characteristic abnormal pattern in dried blood spots or plasma of acylcarnitines species (increased C6, C8 and increased ratio of C8/C10 with abnormal urine organic acid findings of C6 to C10 dicarboxylic acids, hexanoylglycine and suberylglycine). Final confirmation is by mutation analysis. MCADD is now included in newborn screening programs in many European countries such as the UK, Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal and Spain.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other disorders of mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation including multiple acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (MADD).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: MCADD is inherited autosomal recessively. Genetic counseling is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Strict avoidance of fasting is the primary objective. Medium chain triglycerides should be avoided but no other special dietary restrictions are required. Guidelines are available for the safe interval time between feeds for infants and young children. The use of low dose carnitine supplementation in patients who develop a low blood carnitine status remains controversial. In symptomatic patients, simple carbohydrates are given by mouth (glucose tablets) or intravenously until blood glucose level is maintained at above 5 mmol/L. During intercurrent infections, an emergency regimen should be made available. Immediate medical attention is needed in case of decompensation. Artificial sweeteners should be avoided.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is excellent in diagnosed patients who avoid fasting and who are managed appropriately during an intercurrent illness/ metabolic crisis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare metabolic myopathy presenting during childhood, and characterized clinically by growth failure, severe muscle weakness, and moderate sensorineural deafness and biochemically by metabolic acidosis, elevated serum pyruvate concentration, hyperalaninemia and hyperalaninuria. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1973.

DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Myopathy, lactic acidosis, and sideroblastic anemia 2 (MLASA2) is an autosomal recessive mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic variants in YARS2. YARS2 variants confer heterogeneous phenotypes ranging from the full MLASA syndrome to a clinically unaffected state. Symptom onset is most common in the first decade of life but can occur in adulthood and has been reported following intercurrent illness. Early death can result from respiratory muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy. a case of MLASA2 with compound heterozygous YARS2 pathogenic variants; a known pathogenic nonsense variant [NM_001040436.3:c.98C>A (p.Ser33Ter)] and a likely pathogenic missense variant not previously associated with disease [NM_001040436.3:c.948G>T (p.Arg316Ser)]. The proband initially presented with a relatively mild phenotype of myopathy and lactic acidosis. During pregnancy, anemia emerged as an additional... [PMC9541592]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Mitochondrial myopathy-lactic acidosis-deafness syndrome encompasses genetically heterogeneous disorders with various inheritance patterns. Autosomal recessive inheritance is observed in conditions caused by mutations in nuclear genes such as YARS2, ISCU (which can also be de novo dominant), POLG, SLC25A42, and PUS1. Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations, including those in MT-ATP6 (which can be de novo and heteroplasmic) or the maternally inherited A3243G mutation, also cause these syndromes. Phenotypic heterogeneity is common, influenced by factors like mtDNA genetic background, nuclear modifiers, and environmental stressors. Early genetic diagnosis, often involving direct sequence analysis of relevant genes, is crucial for accurate counseling. Specific considerations, such as careful counseling regarding pregnancy due to risks of disease exacerbation, are important for affected individuals. [PMC9938677, PMC9541592, PMC5740555, PMC4703200, PMC4900140]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Historically, treatment for mitochondrial diseases has been challenging, though advancements are improving understanding and management. Early genetic diagnosis is essential for counseling and to facilitate appropriate supportive therapy. Specific supportive measures mentioned include gavage feeding and ventilatory support, particularly in cases of reversible mitochondrial myopathy requiring intensive treatment until spontaneous improvement. Coenzyme Q10 administration has been reported to decrease plasma lactate levels and slightly improve muscle weakness, though it did not affect CSF lactate. Additionally, careful counseling is needed for patients considering pregnancy due to the risk of disease exacerbation and complications. [PMC11724432, PMC9541592, PMC3884767, PMC1793596, PMC1032560]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic disorder of urea cycle metabolism characterized by either a neonatal-onset with manifestations of lethargy, poor feeding, vomiting and tachypnea or, more commonly, presentations in infancy, childhood or adulthood with chronic neurocognitive deficits, acute encephalopathy and/or coagulation defects or other chronic liver dysfunction.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): HHH syndrome; ORNT1 deficiency; Ornithine carrier deficiency; Triple H syndrome; Ornithine translocase deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: More than 100 cases have been reported in the literature to date. The prevalence in Northern Saskatchewan, Canada is especially high due to a founder effect and is estimated in this population at 1/1550 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Age of onset can range from the neonatal period to adulthood and a wide phenotypic spectrum is noted. The neonatal presentation usually begins a few days after birth with lethargy, somnolence, refusal to feed, vomiting, tachypnea with respiratory alkalosis, and/or seizures. Onset of symptoms (ranging from mild to severe) in the majority of patients occurs in infancy, childhood and adulthood with episodes of confusion, forgetfulness, hyperammonemic coma, intellectual disability, developmental delay, spastic paraplegia, cerebellar ataxia, learning difficulties, unexplained seizures, liver dysfunction (rarely failure) and coagulopathy with factor VII-, IX- and X-deficiencies. An aversion to protein-rich foods before diagnosis is often reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is due to mutations in the SLC25A15 gene (13q14) encoding the mitochondrial ornithine transporter 1 (ORNT1) which plays a role in ornithine transport across the mitochondrial membrane and consecutively in mitochondrial protein synthesis, metabolism of arginine and lysine, and synthesis of polyamines. Mutations in this protein disrupt the urea cycle, resulting in hyperornithinemia, hyperammonemia and homocitrullinuria. Patients with a complete ORNT1 deficiency present in the neonatal period with severe hyperammonemia whereas those with a partial deficiency present later, between infancy to adulthood.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical findings and specific metabolic abnormalities. Laboratory tests usually reveal increased urinary excretion of orotic acid, homocitrulline and uracil, and a rise in the levels of plasma polyamines, ornithine, glutamine, alanine, and liver transaminases. Plasma ammonia levels are elevated episodically or postprandially and plasma ornithine is chronically elevated and is a hallmark of the disease as is the presence of homocitrulline in urine. Molecular genetic testing confirms diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other urea cycle disorders as well as lysinuric protein intolerance. Hyperinsulinism-hyperammonemia syndrome, pyruvate carboxylase deficiency and secondary causes of hyperammonemia should also be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible in families with a known disease causing mutation on both alleles.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal recessive; where both parents are unaffected carriers, there is a 25% risk of inheriting the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment involves the adherence to a low protein diet along with citrulline or arginine supplementation. In resistant cases, sodium benzoate and/or sodium or glycerol phenylbutyrate may be necessary for control of plasma ammonia levels. Patients should be monitored during times of stress (e.g. pregnancy, surgery, intercurrent infections) and when taking certain medications (i.e. corticosteroids) as they can trigger an episode of hyperammonemia. Hyperammonemic coma is treated in a tertiary care center where plasma ammonia levels must be lowered (by hemodialysis or hemofiltration), ammonia scavenger therapy implemented, catabolism reversed (with glucose and lipid infusions) and special care taken to reduce the risk of neurological damage.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With early diagnosis and proper adherence to treatment protocol the prognosis is better than for most other urea cycle defects. However, patients remain at risk for metabolic decompensation throughout life and irreversible neurological complications can occur if treatment is delayed.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Tetrasomy 9p is a rare autosomal anomaly characterized by pre- and postnatal growth retardation, psychomotor delay, mild to moderate intellectual disability, hypotonia, microcephaly, dysmorphic features (ocular hypertelorism, low-set, malformed ears, bulbous/beaked nose, microretrognathia, enophthalmos/micropthalmia, epicanthus, strabismus), cleft lip/palate, skeletal abnormalities (hypoplastic nails/distal phalanges, short stature, short neck, contractures), congenital heart defects, renal and urogenital malformations (renal hypoplasia, genital hypoplasia, cryptorchidism).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Tetrasomy 9p is described as a rare chromosomal abnormality. Cases, such as a mosaic de novo tetrasomy 9p identified postnatally in an infant with multiple congenital malformations, have been reported. The condition has been observed, for example, for the first time in Central Brazil, highlighting its rarity and the importance of advanced diagnostic tools like Chromosomal Microarray Analysis for identification. [PMC6128999]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Tetrasomy 9p syndrome is a rare chromosomal abnormality characterized by a variety of physical and developmental abnormalities, often identified prenatally. Fetal manifestations can include intrauterine growth restriction, Dandy-Walker malformation, ventriculomegaly, agenesis of the cerebellar vermis (sometimes with rhombencephalosynapsis), cardiac anomalies (including congenital heart disease like valvular stenosis), renal anomalies, and facial abnormalities or dysmorphic facial features. Postnatally, patients may present with mental retardation, hydrocephalus, and skeletal anomalies. Mosaic forms of tetrasomy 9p have also been associated with inflammatory bowel disease, increased interferon activation, and immune dysregulation leading to persistent infections like adenovirus B3, which can result in bronchiolitis obliterans. [PMC10568385, PMC10760254, PMC9662610, PMC6821155, PMC6198380]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Tetrasomy 9p syndrome is a rare chromosomal abnormality characterized by the presence of a supernumerary isochromosome 9p, which typically consists of two copies of the 9p arm, leading to a karyotype such as 47,XY,+idic (9) (q13). The condition can manifest as mosaic or non-mosaic, with mosaic cases often arising de novo. The duplicated region on chromosome 9p varies in size and location, encompassing areas like 9p24.3 to p13.1 or 9p24.3q13. More complex structural variants at 9p24, involving interspersed duplications and inversions, have also been identified, sometimes forming chimeric transcripts. Diagnosis relies on various genetic analysis techniques, including karyotyping, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT). [PMC12261823, PMC10568385, PMC10760254, PMC9662610, PMC6128999]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Tetrasomy 9p syndrome often relies on a combination of genetic analysis techniques, particularly in prenatal settings. Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) can initially indicate 9p duplication mosaicism. Traditional karyotyping, while used on cultured amniocytes, may miss mosaic cases or show lower mosaic ratios compared to other . Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) are crucial for detecting mosaicism, determining break-points, and assessing mosaic levels, with CMA being a powerful tool for identifying the origin of supernumerary marker chromosomes. CNV-seq analysis on uncultured amniocytes is also recommended, often in conjunction with karyotype analysis on cultured amniocytes, as it can detect mosaic tetrasomy 9p missed by traditional karyotyping. Ultrasound examinations can reveal associated fetal anomalies. In one case, the GALT gene dosage effect confirmed tetrasomy 9p. [PMC12261823, PMC10568385, PMC9662610, PMC6128999, PMC2593768]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: In prenatal diagnosis, tetrasomy 9p syndrome, including mosaic forms, should be considered when non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPT) indicates 9p duplication mosaicism. It is important to differentiate from other forms of 9p duplication mosaicism or complex mosaicism involving trisomy 9 and trisomy 9p. Furthermore, in fetuses presenting with cerebellar malformations, such as rhombencephalosynapsis or agenesis of the cerebellar vermis (both cystic and non-cystic types), tetrasomy 9p should be taken into account, as these findings are associated with the syndrome, including the Dandy-Walker anomaly. [PMC10568385, PMC2593768]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of tetrasomy 9p syndrome often begins with non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPT), which can indicate 9p duplication mosaicism or gain. Ultrasound examinations may reveal associated features such as fetal growth restriction, cardiac anomalies, ventriculomegaly, renal anomalies, or cerebellar malformations like Dandy-Walker or rhombencephalosynapsis. Definitive diagnosis typically requires a combination of genetic analysis techniques. While traditional karyotyping can identify supernumerary chromosomes, it may miss mosaic tetrasomy 9p or underestimate mosaic levels compared to chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). CNV-seq on uncultured amniocytes is also recommended for detecting mosaicism. The combined use of these various is crucial for accurately determining breakpoints and mosaic levels, especially for complex structural variants. [PMC12261823, PMC10568385, PMC10760254, PMC9662610, PMC2593768]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for tetrasomy 9p, particularly mosaic forms, is challenging due to variable clinical outcomes, which can range from benign conditions to adverse outcomes with multiple malformations such as Dandy-Walker, cardiac anomalies, and facial abnormalities. Prenatal diagnosis often begins with non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT), but accurate determination of breakpoints and mosaic levels requires a combined approach using multiple techniques, including karyotype analysis, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), and CNV-seq. Although genotype-phenotype correlation can be elusive, familial cases with segregating rearrangements can utilize genetic biomarkers for reproductive options like embryo selection. Informed decision-making is crucial for pregnant women facing such circumstances. [PMC12261823, PMC10568385, PMC10760254, PMC9662610]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management strategies include specific treatments for complications and reproductive planning. For persistent adenovirus infections, cidofovir was used, and standard therapy with pulsed steroids was applied for associated bronchiolitis obliterans. It is suggested that earlier antiviral therapy might reduce the severity of such complications, given the association of mosaic tetrasomy 9p with immune dysregulation. Additionally, identifying specific 9p rearrangements can enable embryo selection, offering a reproductive management option for families with segregating congenital traits. [PMC10760254, PMC6198380]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Tetrasomy 9p syndrome is highly variable, ranging from a benign condition with a normal clinical phenotype to severe adverse outcomes, including early infant death in cases with multiple congenital malformations. Individuals may present with a distinctive malformation syndrome encompassing mental retardation, hydrocephalus, dysmorphic facial features, congenital heart disease, and skeletal and renal anomalies. The condition can also be associated with specific long-term complications such as inflammatory bowel disease driven by interferon activation, and persistent infections leading to severe respiratory issues like bronchiolitis obliterans, potentially due to immune dysregulation. The severity and outcome appear to be influenced by the specific mosaicism and the extent of the duplicated region. [PMC12261823, PMC10568385, PMC6821155, PMC6198380, PMC6128999]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A constitutional genomic disorder due to the presence of a supernumerary derivative 22 chromosome and characterized by severe intellectual disability, characteristic facial dysmorphism (micrognathia, hooded eyelids, upslanting downslanting parebral fissures, deep set eyes, low hanging columnella and long philtrum), congenital heart defects and kidney abnormalities.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: A small supernumerary marker chromosome (sSMC) is a structurally abnormal chromosome. It is an additional chromosome smaller than one chromosome most often lacking a distinct banding pattern and is rarely identifiable by conventional banding cytogenetic analysis. The origin and composition of an sSMC is recognizable by molecular cytogenetic analysis. These sSMCs are seen in different shapes, including the ring, centric minute, and inverted duplication shapes. The effects of sSMCs on the phenotype depend on factors such as size, genetic content, and the level of the mosaicism. The presence of an sSMC causes partial tris- or tetrasomy, and 70% of the sSMC carriers are clinically normal, while 30% are abnormal in some way. In 70% of the cases the sSMC is de novo, in 20% it is inherited from the mother, and in 10% it is inherited from the father. An sSMC can be causative for specific... [PMC4544121]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Emanuel syndrome is caused by a small supernumerary marker chromosome (sSMC), which is an additional, structurally abnormal chromosome. These sSMCs are typically smaller than one chromosome, often lack a distinct banding pattern, and are identifiable by molecular cytogenetic analysis. The presence of an sSMC in partial trisomy or tetrasomy. While 70% of sSMC carriers are clinically normal, 30% exhibit abnormalities. The sSMC is de novo in 70% of cases, inherited from the mother in 20%, and from the father in 10%. [PMC4544121]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Emanuel syndrome is caused by a small supernumerary marker chromosome (sSMC), which is a structurally abnormal, additional chromosome. These sSMCs often lack a distinct banding pattern and are rarely identifiable by conventional banding cytogenetic analysis. Therefore, the origin and composition of an sSMC, which is causative for Emanuel syndrome, are recognizable by molecular cytogenetic analysis. [PMC4544121]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Emanuel syndrome is caused by a small supernumerary marker chromosome (sSMC), which is an additional, structurally abnormal chromosome. Other specific syndromes that can also be caused by sSMCs include Pallister-Killian syndrome and cat eye syndrome. The phenotypic effects of sSMCs depend on factors such as size, genetic content, and the level of mosaicism, making molecular cytogenetic analysis crucial for identification and differentiation. [PMC4544121]

DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling is relevant for Emanuel syndrome, which can be caused by a small supernumerary marker chromosome (sSMC). These sSMCs are de novo in 70% of cases, inherited from the mother in 20%, and from the father in 10%. The phenotypic effects of sSMCs depend on factors such as size, genetic content, and the level of mosaicism. Furthermore, familial complex chromosome rearrangements, like a balanced translocation involving chromosomes 1, 8, and 11, can lead to reproductive failure. Genetic counseling can provide insight into possible meiotic segregations and the clinical phenotypes that could arise from unbalanced products of conception. [PMC5427656, PMC4544121]
