The most frequently associated features include bilateral sensorineural deafness, heart involvement (cardiomyopathy, cardiac conduction defect), central nervous system involvement (cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, bilateral facial weakness, intellectual deficit), skeletal muscle myopathy, intestinal disorders, endocrine disorders (delayed puberty, hypoparathyroidism, diabetes), and renal failure. The disease progresses slowly, over decades, with new symptoms appearing and previous symptoms slowly worsening. A very few cases of Pearson syndrome have progressed into KSS.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: KSS is caused by deletions of large portions of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), resulting in the loss of genes involved in the oxidative phosphorylation pathway. Deletions are heteroplasmic (i.e. a single cell can harbor both deleted and normal DNA molecules). Symptoms only appear if the proportion of abnormal DNA is high. The abnormal DNA threshold depends on the organ (e.g. about 60% for the skeletal striated muscle). Exceptional cases of KSS may be observed in the absence of a typical single large mtDNA deletion. They may be due either to point mutations located in the mtDNA encompassing tRNA genes or in nuclear genes involved in mtDNA maintenance (i.e. RRM2B).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Clinical diagnostic criteria of the disorder include the triad of progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, and onset before 20 years of age, plus at least one of the followings: heart block, cerebellar symptoms, or cerebrospinal fluid protein levels above 100 mg/dl. Apart from clinical features, muscle pathology and molecular genetic analysis can play a great role in the diagnostic workup. Muscle pathology showed ragged-red fibers (RRF), ragged-blue fibers (RBF), or cytochrome c-oxidase (COX)-negative fibers in almost all patients. Diagnosis can be confirmed by the detection of a large deletion of mtDNA (1.3-10 kb) in a clinically or morphologically affected tissue (usually skeletal muscle).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include any disease caused by large mtDNA deletions or with an overlapping clinical picture, such as Pearson syndrome or maternally-inherited progressive external ophthalmoplegia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is usually not performed.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Most cases of KSS are sporadic. Deletions of mtDNA are only exceptionally transmitted from one generation to the next. Men do not transmit their mtDNA to their offspring. The risk of a woman, carrying a large size mtDNA deletion, transmitting the deletion to her child has been estimated to be less than 4%. The exceptional cases of KSS due to causes other than a large size mtDNA deletion follow the transmission associated with the gene involved (maternal transmission in the case of mtDNA point mutations or autosomal recessive in the case of nuclear gene mutations).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment of KSS is supportive. Regular follow-up with a cardiologist is recommended. In those with high-grade heart block, a permanent pacemaker/implantable cardioverter-defibrillator device may be suggested and improves the prognosis. Hearing aids may be given to those with sensorineural deafness. Supplementation with coenzyme Q10 has been beneficial in some cases. Ophthalmologic manifestations may be treated by surgery but there is a high risk of recurrence and possible ocular complications.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis essentially depends on the number of organs involved and, in each of them, on the proportion of the abnormal mtDNA. In the majority of cases, life expectancy can be normal with appropriate support.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Acute myeloid leukaemia with myelodysplasia-related features
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare acute myeloid leukemia (AML) characterized by the presence of acute leukemia with at least 20% peripheral blood or bone marrow blasts with morphological features of myelodysplasia, or occurrence in patients with a prior history of a myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) or myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm, with MDS-related cytogenetic abnormalities, in the absence of specific genetic abnormalities characteristic of AML with recurrent genetic abnormalities. Prior cytotoxic or radiation therapy for an unrelated disease must be excluded. The condition occurs mainly in elderly patients and is rare in children. Patients often present with severe pancytopenia. Prognosis is generally poor.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): AML with multilineage dysplasia; Acute myeloid leukemia with multilineage dysplasia; AML with myelodysplasia-related features

DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for acute myeloid leukemia with myelodysplasia-related features encompass morphologic, cytochemical, and immunophenotypic criteria. Flow cytometric characterization, utilizing surface and cytoplasmic markers, is a key diagnostic approach for identifying immunophenotypes and subtypes of acute leukemia. Cytogenetic analysis, including bone marrow chromosome analysis, detects chromosomal abnormalities like translocations, though subtle rearrangements may require metaphase FISH analysis. FISH is crucial for detecting specific rearrangements such as MECOM-R, and a reflex FISH analysis is recommended in myeloid neoplasms showing -7/del(7q). RT-PCR and sequencing can identify fusion partners like MLL-SEPT9, and genetic diagnosis is used for mutations such as GATA2. Histologic evaluation is also important. [PMC11830883, PMC9856433, PMC6489290, PMC3307482, PMC2768487]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is a treatment option, considered a definitive cure for pediatric acute myeloid leukemia, though it carries risks of relapse and transplant-related mortality. While HSCT has been performed, it can be unsuccessful or lead to complications such as graft-versus-host-disease related infection, prompting careful risk assessment. Chemotherapy, including cytarabine and daunomycin with high-dose dexamethasone, has been used for remission induction. Decitabine therapy has shown response in de novo myelodysplastic syndrome. For specific genetic abnormalities like PDGFRB mutations, tyrosine kinase inhibitors are suggested as potentially safe and effective alternatives. Research is also exploring novel approaches, such as multivalent CAR T cells, to enhance HSCT efficacy and safety. [PMC11872492, PMC8501773, PMC6489290, PMC3307482, PMC2768487]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) with myelodysplasia-related features is often associated with an inferior prognosis. MECOM rearrangement (3q26.2 aberrations) leads to dismal outcomes, with a median overall survival of 14 months, and is frequently accompanied by cytopenia and morphological dysplasia. GATA2 mutations also confer a high risk of developing myelodysplastic syndrome or AML, with observed progression from myelodysplastic pancytopenia to refractory anemia with excess blasts type II. Relapsed AML generally carries a dismal prognosis, and even high-risk patients undergoing hematopoietic stem cell transplantation may experience relapse and high transplant-related mortality. [PMC11830883, PMC11872492, PMC9856433, PMC6489290, PMC3307482]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Sialidosis type 2 (ST-2) is a rare lysosomal storage disease, and the severe, early onset form of sialidosis characterized by a progressively severe mucopolysaccharidosis-like phenotype (coarse facies, dysostosis multiplex, hepatosplenomegaly), macular cherry-red spots as well as psychomotor and developmental delay. ST-2 displays a broad spectrum of clinical severity with antenatal/congenital, infantile and juvenile presentations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of ST-2 is unknown. The prevalence of sialidosis (types 1 and 2 combined) has been estimated at approximately 1/5,000,000-1/1,500,000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: ST-2 has a wide range of clinical manifestations and is usually divided into congenital/antenatal, infantile and juvenile forms. The congenital/antenatal form is characterized by non-immune hydrops fetalis, or ascites, presenting in utero or at birth and by the development of a mucopolysaccharidosis-like phenotype including coarse facial features, dysostosis multiplex, hepatosplenomegaly, and umbilical and inguinal hernias. Surviving children and patients with the infantile onset form (before 12 months of age) are characterized by a mucopolysaccharidosis-like phenotype that includes coarse facies, dysosotosis multiplex, kyphosis, short stature (with a slowing of growth towards 18 months of age), hepatosplenomegaly, hearing impairment, cherry-red spot on the retina (a constant feature after 3 years of age), corneal opacities (rarely) and speech and developmental delay, followed by psychomotor regression and myoclonus and ataxia in some cases. Renal disease (nephrosialidosis) has been reported in some patients. The juvenile form usually presents after the age of 2 with less pronounced coarse facies, angiokeratoma, myoclonic seizures, macular cherry red spots, and psychomotor regression.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: ST-2 is due to a mutation of the N-acetyl-alpha-neuraminidase-1 (NEU1) gene (6p21) encoding the lysosomal enzyme neuraminidase, that initiates the degradation of sialoglycoconjugates in lysosomes. Mutations lead to a deficiency in enzyme activity and consequently to an accumulation of sialyloligosaccharides in tissues. In general, a higher residual neuraminidase activity is associated with milder symptoms and a longer lifespan.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: An ophthalmological examination (fundoscopy) can visualize the bilateral macular cherry-red spots. Neuroimaging shows varying degrees of brain and cerebellar atrophy. The diagnosis is suspected by detection of urinary sialyloligosaccharide excretion and must be confirmed by demonstration of the neuraminidase enzyme deficiency (in the presence of normal beta-galactosidase activity) in leukocytes or, preferably, in cultured fibroblasts. Molecular genetic testing revealing causal mutation(s) can also confirm the diagnosis. The presence of echographic signs (such as hydrops, edema, ascites) may aid in diagnosing antenatal forms during pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses include galactosialidosis (characterized by deficiencies in both beta galactosidase and neuraminidase) and mucopolysaccharidosis type 1, 2 or 6. Many patients of the juvenile sub-group, in particular, may appear to have a form of galactosialidosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis can be performed by measurement of enzyme activity or by molecular genetic analysis if the underlying molecular defect in the family is well established
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: ST-2 is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Genetic counseling is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for ST-2 and management is multidisciplinary involving mainly palliative care. Anti-convulsants may be used to treat myoclonic seizures, but are only rarely effective. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation has not been successful in preventing psychomotor regression, bone changes or nephrosialidosis.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis depends on the form of ST-2. The congenital form leads to still-birth or death within the first two years of life. For the other forms, life expectancy does not generally exceed two decades.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare and highly aggressive myeloid malignancy characterized by predominant cutaneous involvement with concomitant or subsequent bone marrow, lymph node and visceral involvement, as well as central nervous system (CNS) disease. It derives from the precursors of plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: US incidence ranges from 500 to 1000 cases per year; global point prevalence is estimated at 12/100,000. Incidence is higher in patients aged ≥ 60 years and in males; ~10% of cases occur in children.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: BPDCN affects patients of all ages but is most common in the elderly. Median age at onset is 60-70 years. It is characterized by skin and bone marrow involvement, but may involve lymph nodes, peripheral blood, liver, spleen and the CNS. The most common clinical presentation is asymptomatic solitary or multiple skin lesions (either isolated purplish nodules, isolated bruise-like papules, or disseminated purplish nodules/macules/papules). Some patients may present with leukemia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: BPDCN derives from the precursors of pDC. There is no single cytogenetic or molecular change characteristic of BPDCN.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis requires biopsy of the affected area(s) with morphologic assessment and immunophenotyping. Skin biopsy shows a diffuse, monomorphous infiltrate of medium-sized blast cells resembling lymphoblasts or myeloblasts with massive dermis. Immunohistochemical diagnostic criteria are expression of CD123 (in all cases), CD4 and/or CD56, or one other pDC marker; or expression of any three pDC markers (CD123, TCF4, TCL1, CD303, CD304, CD4, CD56) and no expression of CD3, CD14, CD19, CD34, lysozyme, and myeloperoxidase.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes acute myeloid leukemia (AML), chronic myelomonocytic leukemia, nasal-type extranodal NK/T cell lymphoma, subcutaneous panniculitis-like T cell lymphoma, and cutaneous T cell lymphoma.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Tagraxofusp, a CD123-directed therapy, is the only drug approved for patients aged ≥2 years with newly diagnosed and relapsed/refractory BPDCN in the USA, or for adults with newly diagnosed BPDCN in Europe. Tagraxofusp, typical chemotherapy regimens for acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphocytic leukemia, or lymphoma induction chemotherapies, are recommended as first-line treatment by the NCCN AML guideline. However, the chemotherapy regimens are associated with more toxicities, as well as lower survival rates and are not FDA/EMA-approved. Intrathecal chemotherapy should be considered for patients with documented CNS disease at diagnosis. Management strategies should vary according to patients' age and fitness. Off protocol approaches and participation in clinical trials can be considered in young/fit patients. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) offers the best chance of long-term disease-free survival and should be considered in first remission for all eligible patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Historically, prognosis is poor. Median overall survival (OS) ranges from 8 to 12 months following chemotherapy and is 15.7 months following tagraxofusp. Median OS is longer in patients who were bridged to HSCT.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm (BPDCN) is a rare, aggressive hematodermic malignancy derived from plasmacytoid dendritic cell precursors. Despite advances in our understanding of tumor cell surface markers, the pathogenesis of BPDCN remains largely unknown. No standard or optimal treatments are available for BPDCN, and the prognosis is usually poor. herein a case of BPDCN that harbored multiple genetic mutations in epigenetic modifiers such as TET2 and ZRSR2 . Genetic studies in patients with BPDCN may provide insights into the underlying pathogenesis, prediction of clinical prognosis, and development of better targeted therapeutics for this rare clinical entity. [PMC7871073]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Familial reactive perforating collagenosis is a very rare genetic skin disease characterized by transepidermal elimination of collagen fibers presenting as recurrent spontaneously involuting keratotic papules or nodules.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Familial Reactive Perforating Collagenosis (FRPC) is an extremely rare benign dermatosis, with fewer than 50 cases reported in the literature globally. It frequently presents during infancy or early childhood, though cases with adolescence-onset have also been documented. [PMC11348990, PMC5265844]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Familial reactive perforating collagenosis (FRPC) is a very rare, benign dermatosis, typically presenting in early childhood, though adolescence-onset cases have been reported. It is characterized by transepidermal clearance of altered collagen and excessive excretion of keratin. Clinically, patients develop generalized multiple discrete papules and nodules covered with central keratotic plugs, often found on the face, neck, abdomen, and extensor regions of the extremities. Histopathological analysis reveals crateriform invaginations in the epidermis filled with inflammatory lymphocytes and basophilic debris, perforated by basophilic collagen bundles from the underlying dermis. Unlike some acquired forms, FRPC is not associated with systemic diseases. [PMC11348990, PMC9726282]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Familial Reactive Perforating Collagenosis (FRPC) is a rare, benign dermatosis, with its pathophysiology remaining elusive due to the limited number of reported cases. It is characterized by the transepidermal clearance of altered collagen, where basophilic collagen bundles from the underlying dermis perforate the epidermis. FRPC is frequently presented during early childhood, though adolescence-onset cases exist, and is not associated with systemic diseases, unlike acquired forms of reactive perforating collagenosis. The familial nature is evidenced by similar symptoms acknowledged in family members. [PMC11348990, PMC9726282, PMC5265844]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of familial reactive perforating collagenosis (FRPC) relies on both clinical and histopathological findings. Clinically, patients present with generalized multiple discrete papules covered with central keratotic plugs, often itchy, on various body regions, with similar symptoms frequently acknowledged in family members. Histopathological analysis of skin biopsies is crucial, revealing crateriform invagination in the epidermis filled with inflammatory lymphocytes and basophilic debris, and basophilic collagen bundles perforating the epidermis from the underlying dermis. Degenerated collagen fibers can be identified by elastic fiber stain. High clinical suspicion is required, and the timing of the skin biopsy may be crucial for diagnosis. [PMC11348990, PMC9726282, PMC5265844]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The variable skin rash of reactive perforating collagenosis can mimic conditions such as systemic lupus erythematosus and vasculitis. Furthermore, reactive perforating collagenosis is typically linked to systemic conditions including renal failure or hepatic disease, which should be considered in the differential diagnosis. [PMC9726282]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Familial reactive perforating collagenosis (FRPC) is a rare dermatosis with a familial presentation. Cases have been reported in siblings and other family members, indicating a genetic component. For instance, similar symptoms were acknowledged in the family members of a patient, and the condition has been observed in two siblings. While its pathophysiology remains elusive, the familial nature suggests that genetic counseling may be relevant for affected families. [PMC11348990, PMC3794328]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: There is no standard treatment agreed upon for Familial Reactive Perforating Collagenosis. However, topical corticosteroids, such as desoximetasone cream, have been reported to achieve near-complete resolution of skin papules in some patients, suggesting they are a potential treatment option. Other reported treatments for reactive perforating collagenosis include systemic antihistamines, oral isotretinoin, and phototherapy. For acquired forms, managing coexisting systemic diseases and the use of compound glycyrrhizin tablets have also been noted to lead to improvement. [PMC11348990, PMC9726282, PMC5265844]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Familial Reactive Perforating Collagenosis is described as a benign dermatosis and is not associated with systemic diseases. In one reported case, skin papules showed near-complete resolution after 4 weeks of topical corticosteroid treatment, suggesting a favorable prognosis for the dermatological manifestations with appropriate management. [PMC11348990]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare childhood-onset epilepsy characterized by sudden onset, short lasting absence associated with rhythmical myoclonia of head and shoulders.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Exact incidence of this rare epilepsy syndrome is unknown. Both sexes are affected, with a male predominance (70%).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Seizure onset is between 1 to 12 years of age (peak 7 years) and characterized by absences associated with rhythmical jerks of head/shoulders. Other seizure types (generalized tonic-clonic, atonic seizures and typical absences) occur in the majority of patients. At presentation, approximately half the children are developmentally and neurologically normal; a spectrum of learning disability is eventually seen in 70% of cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Currently, the etiology is unidentified in the majority of cases. In 30% of cases, a genetic cause can be found with possible polygenic etiologies. SLC2A1 variants (1p34.2), causing GLUT1 deficiency, are one of the most common monogenic etiologies of myoclonic absences. There is one case report of a translocation resulting in a truncation in the SYNGAP1 gene causing epilepsy with myoclonic absences. A family history (usually of generalized seizures) is present in 20% of cases. Rarely, there is a family history of febrile seizures.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Micro-array and dedicated epilepsy panels can show pathogenic mutations. On electroencephalogram (EEG), generalized spike-and-wave discharges and polyspike-and-wave discharges may occur. Background is otherwise normal. Ictal EEG: regular 3-Hz generalized spike-and-wave accompanies myoclonic absences. Electromyography recordings from the upper arm show a constant relationship between the bilateral myoclonic jerks and spike-and-waves. High resolution magnetic resonance imaging is required to exclude structural brain abnormality although neuroimaging is usually normal. However, mild non-specific diffuse atrophy is seen in some cases.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (atypical absences may occur with rhythmic myoclonic jerking but EEG background is typically abnormal), myoclonic seizures due to structural brain abnormality, childhood absence epilepsy with a common EEG pattern but the description of the seizure is different, progressive myoclonic epilepsies, and myoclonic atonic epilepsy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Not relevant.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In case of a monogenic etiology or a chromosomal anomaly, genetic counseling can be provided.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Seizures are often difficult to treat and may continue into adulthood. Anti-seizure drugs for absence seizures can be used: sodium valproate, ethosuximide, zonisamide, topiramate, or levetiracetam.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Seizures are usually difficult to control. Later on, in adolescence and adulthood, other (generalized) seizures may develop in almost half of patients. Sometimes an evolution towards juvenile myoclonic epilepsy is seen. Cognitive function seems to be preserved in children in whom myoclonic absences are controlled.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare developmental disorder characterized by facial, limbs and genital features, and a disproportionate acromelic short stature.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Aarskog syndrome; Faciodigitogenital syndrome; Faciogenital dysplasia
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: AAS prevalence is not known, but less than 100 cases have been reported in the literature since the first description in 1970. However, prevalence estimates are thought to be around 1/25,000. About 40 molecularly proven cases are published worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: AAS predominantly concerns males. Facial features include widow's peak and hypertelorism, both observed in female carriers, and downslanting palpebral fissures, broad nasal bridge, anteversed nostrils, low set and protuberant ears, maxillary hypoplasia and transverse crease below the lower lip. AAS patients have short and broad hands and feet, interdigital webbing, clinodactyly, and hyperextension of proximal interphalangeal joints and flexion at distal interphalangeal joints causing swan neck deformity of fingers. Size is generally normal at birth, but growth is slow in infancy and childhood, leading to short stature until puberty, which is often delayed. A growth spurt in late teens, generally, results in a moderate short stature. Genital anomalies may include cryptorchidism, macroorchidism, shawl scrotum and, more rarely, hypospadias. Fertility is normal. Female carriers may have only a subtle phenotype with hypertelorism and widow's peak. Patients may present a neurodevelopmental phenotype with learning and behavioural disabilities that are often confined to early childhood. When present, mental impairment is rarely severe.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Although clinically and genetically heterogeneous, the best characterized form of the disorder is caused by mutations in the FGD1 gene (faciogenital dysplasia 1 gene; Xp11.21). Other gene(s) might be involved since most familial cases still do not have identified genetic cause.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Clinical diagnosis is based on physical examination and the recognition of the most distinctive clinical hallmarks. Molecular genetics, based on analysis of the FGD1 gene, may confirm diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: When molecular diagnosis is not conclusive, all possible options for differential diagnosis should still be considered, including Noonan syndrome, SHORT syndrome, pseudohypoparathyroidism and Robinow syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis for pregnancies at increased risk is technically possible when the disease-causing mutation in the family is known (the majority of mutations are family specific). However, prenatal testing is unlikely to be requested frequently, because usually physical signs can be mild and the clinical heterogeneity makes difficult a prediction of the phenotype, even within the same family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: AAS is an X-linked disease, but autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive transmissions have also been reported. Genetic counseling thus requires in depth investigation of patient's family history.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative treatment for AAS. Preliminary results of growth hormone administration in childhood do not seem to show a significant effect. Learning problems and attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), in case, may require a neuropsychiatric intervention.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The majority of patients present a good prognosis. Typically, they have a good evolution into adulthood with an age-related improvement of mental status.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common subtype of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) in adults characterized by a median age of presentation in the sixth decade of life (but also rarely occurring in adolescents and children) with the initial presentation being single or multiple rapidly growing masses (that may or may not be painful) in nodal or extranodal sites (such as thyroid, skin, breast, gastrointestinal tract, testes, bone, or brain) and that can be accompanied by symptoms of fever, night sweats and weight loss. DLBCL has an aggressive disease course, with the elderly having a poorer prognosis than younger patients, and with relapses being common.

DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling may be relevant for individuals with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) in specific contexts. Gain-of-function mutations in the PIK3CD gene, such as c.3061G>A p.Glu1021Lys, are associated with Activated phosphoinositide 3-kinase δ syndrome (APDS1), an inborn error of immunity that can lead to EBV-positive DLBCL. Additionally, germline mutations have been identified in patients presenting with concurrent extrathymic DLBCL and thymoma, suggesting a genetic predisposition in these cases. These findings highlight the role of inherited genetic factors in the pathogenesis of certain DLBCL subtypes. [PMC12095188, PMC12283472]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare form of congenital disorders of N-linked glycosylation characterized by gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea, vomiting, feeding problems with failure to thrive, protein-losing enteropathy), edema and ascites (including hydrops fetalis), hepatomegaly, renal tubulopathy, coagulation anomalies due to thrombocytopenia, brain involvement (psychomotor delay, seizures, ataxia), facial dysmorphism (low-set ears and retrognathia), pes equinovarus, and muscular hypotonia. Cataracts may also be observed. Prognosis is usually poor. The disease is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the gene ALG8 (11q14.1), resulting in a block in the initial step of protein glycosylation.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CDG syndrome type Ih; CDG-Ih; CDG1H; Carbohydrate deficient glycoprotein syndrome type Ih; Congenital disorder of glycosylation type 1h; Congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ih; Glucosyltransferase 2 deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: In a systematic literature review of congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) presenting with nonimmune hydrops fetalis (NIHF), ALG8 was identified as one of the causative genes. Among 15 distinct families with CDG and NIHF, ALG8 was reported in 13% (2/15) of cases. This highlights ALG8-CDG as a rare but significant etiology within the spectrum of CDG causing NIHF, a condition associated with poor prognosis in affected infants. [PMC11894479]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: ALG8-CDG is associated with nonimmune hydrops fetalis (NIHF). In cases of congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) presenting with NIHF, common features include facial dysmorphism, central nervous system abnormalities such as cerebellar atrophy, and cardiovascular abnormalities, frequently hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Thrombocytopenia is also reported. The prognosis is poor, with a high mortality rate in infancy and significant developmental delays in survivors. Therefore, ALG8-CDG should be considered in the differential diagnosis of NIHF, especially when cerebellar atrophy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or thrombocytopenia are present. [PMC11894479]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: ALG8-CDG is a congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG) that can be an etiology for nonimmune hydrops fetalis (NIHF). In a systematic review of CDG cases presenting with NIHF, the ALG8 gene was identified in 13% (2/15) of distinct families where a specific gene was reported. This indicates that mutations in the ALG8 gene are a cause of this form of CDG, particularly when associated with NIHF. [PMC11894479]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG), including ALG8-CDG, is frequently established postnatally. Genetic testing is a key diagnostic method, with ALG8 being one of the genes identified in patients presenting with nonimmune hydrops fetalis (NIHF). Isoelectric focusing of serum transferrin, which can show a type 1 pattern, has also been utilized for diagnosis. CDG should be considered in the differential diagnosis for NIHF, especially in the presence of cerebellar atrophy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or thrombocytopenia. [PMC11894479]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: ALG8-CDG, particularly when presenting with nonimmune hydrops fetalis (NIHF), should be differentiated from numerous other etiologies of NIHF. Congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) should be included in the differential diagnosis of NIHF, especially in the presence of cerebellar atrophy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or thrombocytopenia. Within the CDG spectrum associated with NIHF, other genetic causes such as PMM2, ALG9, ALG1, MGAT2, and COG6 should also be considered. [PMC11894479]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: ALG8 is one of the congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) genes associated with nonimmune hydrops fetalis (NIHF). While recognition of CDG in NIHF is challenging and diagnosis is mostly postnatal, prenatal identification is important due to the poor prognosis. CDG should be considered in the differential diagnosis of NIHF, particularly in the presence of cerebellar atrophy, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or thrombocytopenia, to guide counseling regarding pregnancy management. [PMC11894479]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: ALG8 is one of the genes associated with congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) that can lead to nonimmune hydrops fetalis (NIHF), accounting for 13% of reported cases in distinct families. Infants with NIHF due to CDG, including ALG8-CDG, have a poor prognosis, with a high mortality rate in live births (71% died at a median age of 34 days). For survivors, significant developmental delays are common. Therefore, prenatal identification of these disorders is crucial to guide genetic counseling with families regarding pregnancy management, given the severe outcomes. [PMC11894479]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Numerous etiologies may lead to nonimmune hydrops fetalis (NIHF) including congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG). Recognition of CDG in NIHF is challenging. reviews prenatal and neonatal characteristics of CDG presenting with NIHF. A systematic literature search was performed. Thirteen articles met the inclusion criteria. Twenty-one cases with NIHF associated with a CDG were reported. There were 17 live births, three pregnancy terminations, and one fetal demise. Timing of CDG diagnosis was reported mostly postnatally (90%; 10/11). Postnatal genetic testing was reported in 18 patients; three patients were diagnosed by isoelectric focusing of serum transferrin that showed a type 1 pattern. The genes reported for CDG with NIHF for 15 distinct families include: PMM2 in 47% (7/15), ALG9 in 20% (3/15), ALG8 in 13% (2/15), ALG1 in 7% (1/15), MGAT2 in 7% (1/15), and COG6 7% (1/15). In our... [PMC11894479]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: ALG8-CDG, when presenting with nonimmune hydrops fetalis (NIHF), is associated with a poor prognosis. Among infants with congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG) and NIHF, 71% died at a median age of 34 days (range 1-185). For those who survived past the neonatal period, 80% experienced significant reported developmental delays. This highlights the severe outcomes for affected individuals. [PMC11894479]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Intellectual disability-developmental delay-contractures syndrome, formerly known as Wieacker-Wolff syndrome, is a severe X-linked recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by severe contractures (arthrogryposis) and intellectual disability.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence and incidence rates are not known. The syndrome has been reported in 5 families to date, with fewer than 30 affected individuals described. Affected patients are male, while carrier females are often asymptomatic. Cases have been reported from Germany, France, the Netherlands, Australia, and the United States.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The syndrome is characterized by an association of arthrogryposis multiplexa congenita and intellectual disability. Affected patients are born with severe contractures (arthrogryposis) and muscle weakness causing respiratory distress. Intellectual disability and delayed motor development are found in all patients. Facial weakness (ptosis) and bulbar weakness (feeding difficulty), characteristic dysmorphic facial features (possibly including long flat philtrum, low-set ears, high-arched palate, and carp-shaped mouth), and skeletal abnormalities (camptodactyly, hip dislocation, scoliosis, kyphosis, lordosis and pes equinovarus) have been reported. Other neurological signs may include spasticity and seizures. Heterozygous female carriers may also be affected, but to a lesser degree (intellectual disability, distal muscle weakness, camptodactyly, joint contractures, and pes equinovarus).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Intellectual disability-developmental delay-contractures syndrome is caused by mutations in the ZC4H2 gene (Xq11.1) that is presumed to play a role in neuronal function during fetal growth.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder follows an X-linked recessive pattern on inheritance. Simplex cases are also found. Genetic counseling should be provided to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Wieacker-Wolff syndrome primarily involves genetic testing. Whole exome sequencing (WES) is a key method used to identify mutations, particularly in the ZC4H2 gene, which is associated with the disease pathogenesis. WES can also reveal multilocus pathogenic variations, and quantitative Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) analysis may aid in dissecting complex blended phenotypes. In female heterozygous carriers, X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) pattern analysis can be performed. Brain MRI may show non-specific myelination abnormalities, while other extensive genetic and metabolic work may be negative. [PMC8837671, PMC8903185, PMC7005642]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Wieacker-Wolff syndrome (WWS), linked to variants in ZC4H2, can be part of a complex neurodevelopmental disorder with a blended phenotype resulting from multilocus pathogenic variation. In such cases, the clinical presentation is not solely explained by WWS but by the combined effects of multiple disease-contributing genes. Therefore, other conditions, such as limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (linked to CAPN3) and congenital myasthenia (linked to MUSK), should be considered in the differential diagnosis, particularly when WWS-like features are observed alongside other atypical or severe symptoms. Quantitative Human Phenotype Ontology analysis can aid in dissecting the phenotypic contributions of individual genes in these complex presentations. [PMC8837671]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Duane retraction syndrome and arthrogryposis multiplex congenita have an incidence of approximately 1:1500-1:3000 live births. However, the association of these two entities with a Marcus-Gunn might be a rare and, until now, under-recognized clinical presentation of the Wieacker-Wolff Syndrome. Patient and a 7-year-old female with dysmorphic features, global developmental delay, arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (AMC), Duane retraction syndrome (DRS), and unilateral Marcus Gunn jaw winking. Whole Exome Sequencing showed a de novo premature stop codon in ZC4H2. Extensive genetic and metabolic work was negative otherwise and Brain MRI showed delayed non-specific myelination abnormalities. She continues to have significant delays but does not have regression, seizures or other neurological complications. She has required a multidisciplinary approach for the management of her multiple... [PMC8903185]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Wieacker-Wolff syndrome involves significant global developmental delays and multiple contractures that necessitate a multidisciplinary management approach. In one reported case of a 7-year-old female, despite these challenges, there was no evidence of regression, seizures, or other neurological complications, suggesting a stable course in some individuals. [PMC8903185]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Microphthalmia-ankyloblepharon-intellectual disability syndrome is characterized by microphthalmia, ankyloblepharon and intellectual deficit. It has been described in seven male patients from two generations of a Northern Ireland family. The causative gene is localized to the Xq27-q28 region. The syndrome is transmitted as an X-linked recessive trait.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Lenz microphthalmia syndrome (LMS) is a genetically heterogeneous X-linked disorder. In one family, a mutation in the intron 7 splice donor site (c.471+2T→A) of the N-acetyltransferase NAA10 gene was identified as the disease-causing gene. This NAA10 mutation, which leads to aberrant transcripts and lack of full-length protein expression, is concluded to be the cause of LMS in this family. The etiology is likely mediated through the dysregulation of the retinoic acid signalling pathway, affecting genes such as BMP4 and STRA6, which are associated with genetic forms of anophthalmia. [PMC4278941]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Lenz microphthalmia syndrome, characterized by microphthalmia/anophthalmia, skeletal abnormalities, and intellectual disability, can involve genetic testing. Exome sequencing has been used to identify disease-causing mutations, such as a splice donor mutation in the NAA10 gene. Further diagnostic confirmation can include linkage studies to map the disease locus, cDNA analysis to detect aberrant transcripts, and assessment of NAA10 protein expression in patient fibroblasts. Molecular assays, such as expression arrays, can reveal dysregulation of associated genes, and retinol uptake assays may show decreased retinol uptake in patient cells, indicating dysregulation of the retinoic acid signaling pathway. [PMC4278941]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Lenz microphthalmia syndrome (LMS) is an X-linked disorder characterized by microphthalmia/anophthalmia, skeletal abnormalities, genitourinary malformations, and anomalies of the digits, ears, and teeth. Intellectual disability and seizure disorders are seen in about 60% of affected males. A splice donor mutation in the NAA10 gene has been identified as a cause of LMS. Ogden syndrome, which is also associated with NAA10 mutations, is clinically distinct from LMS. [PMC4278941]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Lenz microphthalmia syndrome (LMS) is an X-linked disorder. A splice donor mutation in the N-acetyltransferase NAA10 gene (c.471+2T→A) was identified as the cause in one family, with the mutation co-segregating with the phenotype in three affected brothers. This gene is located at Xq27-Xq28. It is important to note that NAA10 mutations have also been associated with Ogden syndrome, which is clinically distinct from LMS, suggesting genetic heterogeneity or variable phenotypic expression depending on the specific mutation. [PMC4278941]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inflammatory multisystem disorder characterized clinically by four cardinal signs: fever of unknown origin, arthralgia or arthritis, hyperleucocytosis, and typical skin rash.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence and incidence data are difficult to determine given the broad, non-specific clinical presentation of adult-onset Still disease (AOSD). The estimated prevalence of AOSD is more than 1/100,000 population. There is a slightly higher number of affected women than affected men.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: AOSD primarily affects young adults, although older patients have been reported. The presenting features are variable and may include high fever (>39°C) with daily spikes, sore throat or pharyngitis, arthralgia or arthritis (>65% of patients), transient maculopapular rash, and more rarely myalgia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and serositis. Arthritis may involve any joint and can migrate in early disease and then stabilize with time. Arthralgia is usually correlated with fever spikes. Rash mostly consists of transient, small, discrete, salmon-pink, non-pruritic macules or maculopapules that often occur concomitantly with fever and generally spare the face, palms and soles of the feet. Pleuritis or pericarditis are commonly found. Patients may lose weight and have a generally poor overall health status. Three different disease courses have been described: self-limited, systemic course with a single flare and complete remission within 2 to 4 weeks, intermittent course with recurrence of systemic or articular flares after remission of 2 weeks to 2years, and a primarily articular chronic course (with erosions in a 1/3 patients). Some affected individuals have a history of systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of AOSD and its underlying pathogenetic mechanisms are not known. No risk factors for the disease have been identified so far, but environmental factors are suspected. Several infectious conditions have been reported to be associated with onset of the disease (e.g. Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human immunodeficiency virus, Coxsackie virus, hepatitis A, B, and C viruses, and Mycoplasma pneumoniae).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The non-specific clinical features of AOSD make diagnosis difficult. No serological marker is currently available. AOSD is a diagnosis of exclusion. Two sets of classification criteria, Yamaguchi and Fautrel, exist. Major diagnostic criteria include arthralgia for more than 2 weeks, intermittent high fever for more than 1 week, characteristic rash, and white blood cell count above 10,000. Minor criteria include sore throat, lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly, abnormal liver function tests, and negative rheumatoid factor and ANA. Elevated ferritin is often found and may assist in diagnosis, especially if it is associated with a low level of glycosylated ferritin.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Many other inflammatory, neoplastic, and infectious conditions with a similar presentation must be ruled out in order to diagnose AOSD. Differential diagnoses include infections (endocarditis, occult infections, secondary syphilis, viral rash), malignancies (lymphoma) or autoimmune diseases (such as polyarteritis nodosa, vasculitis, or polymyositis).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: AOSD is a sporadic non-inheritable disease and genetic counseling is therefore not needed.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The aim is to achieve complete remission and prevent joint damage through treatment. Treatment-free remission is possible but the risk of relapse remains present throughout life Multidisciplinary rounds in contact with a reference center are highly recommended. The mainstay of first-line treatment is prednisone, and most guidelines tend to recommend an early association with biologic therapies (anti-IL1 agents (anakinra, canakinumab), and anti-IL-6 agents (tocilizumab)), in order to allow a rapid tapering of prednisone and hence prevent steroid-induced complications. Methotrexate and tumor necrosis factor blockers may be used in chronic articular forms, but have limited efficacy in systemic forms. Regular clinical and biological monitoring (initially tight) is necessary.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The overall prognosis is generally good, but acute life-threatening manifestations may occur in rare cases. The most classical complication is macrophage activation syndrome but blood coagulation disorders, fulminant hepatitis, cardiac and pulmonary complications may occur. Some patients with chronic disease and major joint involvement may have significantly altered quality of life, but this tends to disappear thanks to a better and earlier management with biologics.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 is an uniparental disomy of paternal origin that most likely do not have any phenotypic expression except from cases of homozygosity for a recessive disease mutation for which only father is a carrier (e.g., cystic fibrosis, congenital chloride diarrhea, sensorineural hearing loss).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Uniparental disomy for maternal chromosome 7 has been described in three patients with recessive disorders. Short stature in each of these patients has been explained by the effect of imprinting of growth-related genes on maternal chromosome 7. Alternatively, although less likely, all these patients may be homozygous for a rare recessive mutation. Here both paternal isodisomy for chromosome 7 and normal growth in a patient with a recessive disorder, congenital chloride diarrhea. She had inherited only paternal alleles at 10 loci and was homozygous for another 10 chromosome 7 loci studied. Her physical status and laboratory tests were normal except for a mild high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. As the patient has normal stature, it is likely that the paternal chromosome 7 lacks the suggested maternal imprinting effect on growth. Paternal isodisomy for human chromosome 7 may have... [PMC1918292]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Paternal uniparental disomy for chromosome 7 is compatible with normal growth and development, with patients typically exhibiting normal stature and overall physical status. One reported case showed normal laboratory tests, with the only noted clinical feature being a mild high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. This suggests that paternal isodisomy for human chromosome 7 may have no significant phenotypic effect on growth. [PMC1918292]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 (UPD7), specifically paternal isodisomy, involves inheriting only paternal alleles at multiple loci on chromosome 7, leading to homozygosity for these loci. This genetic mechanism can result in recessive disorders if the paternal chromosome carries a recessive mutation, as observed in a patient with congenital chloride diarrhea. Unlike maternal UPD7, paternal UPD7 is compatible with normal growth and development, as the paternal chromosome 7 lacks the imprinting effect on growth-related genes seen with maternal inheritance. The described patient also presented with mild high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. [PMC1918292]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Purpose: The prevalence of low birth weight (LBW) is increased in subjects born after assisted reproduction technology (ART), and defective imprinting has frequently been identified in patients with Beckwith-Wiedermann and Angelman syndromes conceived by ART. Thus, we examined methylation pattern in a girl born after ART who had Silver-Russell syndrome (SRS) which can be caused by maternal uniparental disomy for chromosome 7 and by hypomethylation of the differentially methylated region (DMR) of H19. We examined methylation status of 31 cytosines at the CpG dinucleotides in the DMR of PEG1/MEST on 7q32.2 and 23 cytosines at the CpG dinucleotides in the DMR of H19 on 11p15, using leukocyte genomic DNA. Eight of the 31 cytosines in the patient and four of the 31 cytosines in the father were hypermethylated in the PEG1/MEST-DMR. In the H19-DMR, no abnormal methylation pattern was... [PMC3455069, PMC1698557, PMC1051738, PMC1918292, PMC1683410]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 (pUPD7) primarily involves distinguishing it from maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 (mUPD7). Unlike mUPD7, which is associated with conditions such as Silver-Russell Syndrome (SRS) and developmental verbal dyspraxia (DVD) characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth failure, pUPD7 is generally compatible with normal growth and development. Individuals with pUPD7 do not exhibit DVD, as the paternal chromosome 7 lacks the maternal imprinting effect on growth. Therefore, conditions presenting with growth retardation or DVD would suggest mUPD7 rather than pUPD7. [PMC10624206, PMC3455069, PMC1698557, PMC1051738, PMC1918292]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: The association of maternal uniparental disomy for chromosome 7 and postnatal growth failure has been reported in four cases and suggests the presence of genomic imprinting of one or more growth related genes on chromosome 7. However, in the reported cases, the possibility of homozygosity for a recessive mutation could not be excluded as the cause of the growth failure as in all cases isodisomy rather than heterodisomy for chromosome 7 was present. a case of prenatal and postnatal growth retardation associated with a prenatal diagnosis of mosaicism for trisomy 7 confined to the placenta. DNA typing of polymorphic markers on chromosome 7 has established that the zygote originated as a trisomy 7 with two maternal and one paternal chromosomes 7 with subsequent loss of the paternal chromosome resulting in a disomic child with maternal heterodisomy for chromosome 7. The growth failure seen... [PMC1051738]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 (UPD7) is generally compatible with normal growth and development, as the paternal chromosome 7 appears to lack the imprinting effect on growth seen with maternal UPD7. Individuals with paternal UPD7 do not typically present with developmental verbal dyspraxia. However, paternal isodisomy for chromosome 7 can lead to recessive disorders if the individual inherits two copies of a paternal allele carrying a pathogenic variant, as observed in cases of congenital chloride diarrhea. Genetic counseling should therefore consider the potential for recessive conditions while noting the absence of certain phenotypes associated with maternal UPD7. [PMC1698557, PMC1918292]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Paternal isodisomy for chromosome 7 is generally compatible with normal growth and development. One patient with this condition exhibited normal physical status and laboratory tests, with the exception of a mild high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss. It is suggested that paternal chromosome 7 lacks the imprinting effect on growth seen with maternal chromosome 7, and therefore, paternal isodisomy may have no phenotypic effect on growth. [PMC1698557, PMC1918292]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A congenital cardiac malformation characterized by a communication between the atrial chambers of the heart.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): ASD; Atrial septal defect; Interauricular communication

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Overall, openings between the atrial chambers account for about 6 to 8% of all congenitally malformed hearts. As a group, the prevalence at birth is between 6 to 9/10000; however, this is likely an underestimated due to the asymptomatic nature of the disease. The female-to-male ratio is 2-4:1.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: There are four types of defects, named according to their position relative to the atrial septum. The ostium secundum defect is the most common type, accounting for three-quarters of all cases, located to the region of the oval fossa, most commonly due to a deficiency of the primary atrial septum (septum primum) but deficiency of the septum secundum (superior interatrial fold) may also contribute. The ostium primum defect, which accounts for one-sixth of defects, is in reality an atrioventricular septal defect, with shunting exclusively at atrial level. Only these two defects are true atrial septal defects. The sinus venosus defect (one-tenth of cases) is a hole outside the confines of the oval fossa, through which a caval vein and/or pulmonary vein(s) override the atrial septum or the septum secundum (superior interatrial fold) producing an interatrial or anomalous veno-atrial communication.The rarest defect, the coronary sinus defect, is a communication between the left atrium and the coronary sinus allowing interatrial communication through the orifice of the coronary sinus, and is due to absence or partial unroofing of the coronary sinus. Interatrial communications are most often asymptomatic in childhood but clinical manifestations can include: rapid breathing, shortness of breath, fatigue, sweating, palpitations, frequent respiratory infections, and poor growth. Symptoms often manifest by the age of 30 to 40 years. Adults with interatrial communications are at increased risk of developing pulmonary arterial hypertension, heart failure, arrhythmias, and stroke. About one third of affected children have an associated hereditary syndrome, such as Down's syndrome, Alagille syndrome, Holt-Oram syndrome, Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, or Noonan syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Several susceptibility genes have been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The defect is most often suspected during a physical examination. Cardiac auscultation reveals a systolic outflow murmur. Echocardiography, chest X-ray and electrocardiogram, and cardiac catheterization may help the diagnosis, although the latter technique is now rarely required for diagnostic purposes.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other congenital cardiac anomalies that result in left-to-right shunt at the atrial level, including partial atrioventricular septal defect and anomalous pulmonary venous return.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: A significant defect may be diagnosed during fetal life, although prenatal diagnosis is difficult as interatrial communication is an integral part of fetal circulation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Most defects occur sporadically as a result of spontaneous genetic mutations, but hereditary forms have been reported. Familial secundum defects can be associated with mutations in transcription factors NKX2.5 (5q34), GATA4 (8p23.1), TBX6 (16p11.2), along with conduction disorders such as atrioventricular block.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Closure of the defect is recommended if left-to-right shunt is important with right ventricular overload and dilatation. Transcatheter device closure is nowadays the treatment of choice for secundum defects beyond the infant period. For other types of interatrial communications, and in large secundum defects with deficient rims, open-heart surgery is indicated, and is complication-free in the majority of cases. Whatever the technique used, closure of the defect is rarely indicated before the age of 3 years. Large defects should be closed before the second decade of life.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Small-to-moderate defects may be asymptomatic and life expectancy is not reduced. In some children, small openings may close spontaneously (occurring in up to four-fifths of cases with small openings in the first 18 months of life). In some patients with large defects, Eisenmenger reaction can occur after the first decade of life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Chronic pneumonitis of infancy is a rare pediatric form of interstitial lung disease (ILD).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of this disease is not known.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical and radiologic features are similar to those observed in other forms of ILD (cough, tachypnea, and infiltrative opacities on chest imaging). Specific histological abnormalities include diffuse thickening of alveolar septa, hyperplasia of type 2 alveolar epithelial cells (AEC), and presence of primitive mesenchymal cells within the alveolar septa. In some cases, foci of pulmonary proteinosis-like material have been observed in air spaces.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is poor with a high mortality rate.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic malformation syndrome characterized by congenital anomalies (microcephaly, specific facial characteristics, and broad thumbs and halluces), short stature, intellectual disability and behavioral characteristics.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Broad thumb-hallux syndrome; Broad thumbs-halluces syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Birth prevalence is estimated at around 1/100,000 to 125,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Facial features, which become more prominent with age, include highly arched eyebrows, long eyelashes, downslanting palpebral fissures, convex nasal ridge, low hanging columella, highly arched palate and micrognathia. Talon cusps are very frequent on the permanent incisors. An unusual smile with almost complete closure of the eyes is present in most individuals. Other physical findings may include eye anomalies (nasolacrimal duct obstruction, congenital glaucoma, refractive errors), a variety of congenital heart defects (e.g. ventricular and atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus), joint hypermobility, and skin anomalies (in particular keloid formation). Feeding difficulties are frequently observed in the first year, and respiratory tract infections are very common in infancy and childhood. Constipation is generally a life-long problem, and patients may become overweight during late childhood or early puberty. The children have a marked ability to establish excellent social contacts. In adulthood, sudden mood changes and obsessive-compulsive behavior may gradually become more frequent. Other than previously thought, persons with Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome under the age of 40 have no increased risk of getting malignant tumors. It is unclear whether this risk is increased in the elderly with Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Causes of Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome include: a microdeletion of chromosome 16p13.3 or chromosome 22q13.2, a variant in CREB-binding protein (CREBBP, 16p13.3) or a variant in E1A-binding protein p300 (EP300, 22q13.2). CREBBP and EP300 show a very high degree of homology and both play important roles as transcriptional coactivators; however, the exact pathogenesis of the syndrome remains uncertain. There is no significant genotype-phenotype correlation, except in the case of individuals with a EP300 mutation who on average have a higher level of functioning, less marked distal limb malformations, and a more pronounced microcephaly.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is in essence based on clinical examination. A cytogenetic or molecular abnormality can be detected in about 65% of individuals.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The syndrome can sometimes be difficult to differentiate from Saethre-Chotzen syndrome, Floating Harbor syndrome and Cornelia de Lange syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: If a cytogenetic or molecular abnormality is found in the affected child, reliable prenatal diagnosis is possible in future pregnancies through chorionic villus biopsy. Prenatal ultrasound only rarely allows a reliable diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The syndrome is almost always sporadic, most cases resulting from de novo mutations. For a couple with an affected child, accumulating data suggest a recurrence risk of approximately 0.5%. If a person with Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome is able to reproduce, the recurrence risk is 50% as the transmission is autosomal dominant.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: All individuals should have a cardiac assessment at the time of diagnosis and should be checked for hearing loss or diminished vision (every 3 years in children and every 5 years in adults). Specialized educational programs are required, with early emphasis on psychomotor development and speech therapy. Children should be tested at regular intervals with a systematic developmental assessment starting at age 3-4 years, to ensure adequate educational support compatible with each child's potential. If surgery is required, individuals undergoing general anesthesia should be under the care of an anesthesiologist comfortable with complex airway problems and aware of the increased risk of aspiration and cardiac arrhythmia upon the use of cardioactive drugs.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy does not seem to be explicitly altered.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare syndromic retinitis pigmentosa characterized by pigmentary retinopathy, diabetes mellitus with hyperinsulinism, acanthosis nigricans, secondary cataracts, neurogenic deafness, short stature mild hypogonadism in males and polycystic ovaries with oligomenorrhea in females. Inheritance is thought to be autosomal recessive. It can be distinguished from Alstrom syndrome by the presence of intellectual disability and the absence of renal insufficiency. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1993.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Edwards-Sethi syndrome; Retinitis pigmentosa-intellectual disability-sensorineural hearing loss-hypogenitalism syndrome; Retinitis pigmentosa-intellectual disability- labyrinthine deafness-hypogenitalism syndrome

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked syndromic intellectual disability characterized by congenital and permanent vocal cord paralysis causing severe congenital laryngeal stridor, associated with intellectual disability in male patients. Other presenting symptoms may include weak cry, cough, cyanosis, neonatal asphyxia, feeding difficulty, aspiration, and bronchiectasis. Microcephaly, tone abnormalities, visual and hearing impairment may also be associated features.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Laryngeal abductor paralysis-intellectual disability syndrome is a congenital condition with a familial basis. One reported family included a brother and three sisters, born to remotely consanguineous parents, who presented with congenital laryngeal abductor paralysis and moderate mental retardation. Their mother also had unilateral laryngeal abductor paralysis. Inheritance is most likely autosomal dominant with variable expression, though autosomal recessive and X-linked inheritance are also considered possible. [PMC1017266]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Laryngeal abductor paralysis-intellectual disability syndrome is characterized by congenital laryngeal abductor paralysis and moderate mental retardation. Microcephaly may also be present at birth in some affected individuals. The condition exhibits variable expression, as some family members can present with laryngeal abductor paralysis alone, without intellectual disability. [PMC1017266]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiology of laryngeal abductor paralysis-intellectual disability syndrome is likely genetic, with familial cases reported. In one family, a brother and two sisters from remotely consanguineous parents were affected, and their mother also presented with unilateral laryngeal abductor paralysis. While mental deficiency in some siblings was considered potentially related to birth asphyxia, microcephaly at birth in one suggested an intrinsic cause. Inheritance is most likely autosomal dominant with variable expression, though autosomal recessive and X-linked inheritance are also considered possible modes of transmission. [PMC1017266]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Laryngeal abductor paralysis-intellectual disability syndrome is based on the presence of congenital laryngeal abductor paralysis and moderate mental retardation. Laryngoscopy can be used to confirm laryngeal abductor paralysis, which may present unilaterally. Microcephaly at birth has also been noted in affected individuals. Familial cases suggest genetic evaluation, with potential inheritance patterns including autosomal dominant with variable expression, autosomal recessive, or X-linked. [PMC1017266]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for Laryngeal abductor paralysis-intellectual disability syndrome should consider several possible inheritance patterns. Autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expression is suggested, as seen in a family where a healthy mother with unilateral laryngeal abductor paralysis had children with both paralysis and mental retardation. Autosomal recessive inheritance is also possible, especially given the remote consanguinity of the parents, where the mother could be an affected homozygote and both parents carriers. X-linked inheritance is another potential mode of transmission. The variable expression observed, where affected individuals can present with different severities, is an important consideration for counseling. [PMC1017266]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Rabies is a viral zoonosis leading to a fatal encephalopathy if not treated.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Epidemiology depends on the control level of the pathogen and its animal vectors, so the rabies is much more prevalent in the developing world than in developed countries. The WHO estimates that around 50,000 persons die each year from rabies.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Rabies evolution follows a three steps path. After a contact (bite) with an infected animal, incubation lasts 20 to 90 days while patients remain asymptomatic. This duration varies with the quantity and the location of the inoculum. It can extend to several years in rare cases. The second phase, the prodromal period, lasts 2 to 10 days and is characterized by paresthesia or pain at the inoculation site. Other nonspecific symptoms may occur, including malaise, anorexia, headaches, fever, chills, pharyngitis, nausea, emesis, diarrhea, anxiety, agitation, insomnia and depression. The third phase is the most distinctive one, named the acute neurologic period. It is associated to clear central nervous system (CNS) involvement, its duration is 2 to 7 days and it can be of two kinds: the furious rabies or the paralytic rabies. In the first case, patients show agitation, hyperactivity, restlessness, trashing, biting, confusion or hallucinations. Hydrophobia and aerophobia are pathognomonic for rabies and occur in 50% of patients. After hours or days these signs appear by bouts - during less than 5 minutes - alternating with calm phases of lucidity. Seizures may occur. The terminal evolution of this phase is cardiorespiratory arrest or paralysis. In the second case, also named apathetic rabies, paralysis develops from the outset with fever, headache and nuchal rigidity. In both cases, the terminal evolution, if untreated, is coma and death.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Rabies is caused by infection of a virus of the Lyssavirus genus. Infection occurs in a large majority through the bite of a rabid dog and more generally through contact of broken skin or mucous membrane with infected saliva, CNS tissue or aerosolized secretions from infected animals. Lyssavirus are neurotropic viruses that escape immune system invading peripheral nerve ending. Incubation duration depends on the time needed to invade the CNS.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical examination, early signs being paresthesia or pain at the inoculum site, and firmly relies on PCR detection of viral RNA in the saliva, the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or in a nuchal skin biopsy, on blood or CSF serological findings.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Tetanus is the main differential diagnosis which also includes other types of encephalomyelitis and neuropaludism.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Standardized vaccination procedures are established for pre- or post-exposure situations. In case of exposition, rapid washing, antisepsis and vaccine administration could be associated to a serotherapy protocol consisting of immunoglobulins injection at the inoculum site. Each infection has to be declared.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: If not treated, rabies is always fatal. Treatment has to be administrated during the incubation period to be efficient.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A group of inherited epidermolysis bullosa (EB) characterized by cutaneous and mucosal fragility resulting in blisters and superficial ulcerations that develop below the lamina densa of the cutaneous basement membrane and that heal with significant scarring and milia formation. Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa (DEB) comprises four major and several rare sub-types with the three most common being intermediate dominant DEB, severe recessive DEB and intermediate recessive DEB.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): DEB; Dermolytic epidermolysis bullosa; Epidermolysis bullosa dystrophica

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: DEB is the second most common form of EB, the first being EB simplex. Based on recent data, the prevalence in Europe ranges between 1/120,000-350,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical picture varies widely, ranging from mild localized to severe generalized involvement. Onset is usually at birth but a delayed onset in infancy, childhood or adolescence can also be observed in milder subtypes. Skin lesions, forming spontaneously or in response to friction, may show a generalized or a localized distribution, particularly on the hands, feet or pretibial areas. Healing of blisters is associated with atrophic or, more rarely, hypertrophic scarring, albopapuloid lesions, milia formation and dystrophic nails. Excessive scarring can lead to highly disabling hand/foot deformities. Mucosal involvement is common and most frequently manifests with oral cavity lesions and esophageal strictures. The eyes and the genitourinary tract can also be affected. Skin and mucosal involvement can lead to anemia, iron deficiency, osteopenia/osteoporosis, growth delay and, rarely, renal failure. DEB patients are also at a higher risk of occurrence of squamous cell carcinomas (SCC).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: DEB is caused by mutations in the COL7A1 (3p21.31) gene encoding type VII collagen. Mutations are either autosomal dominant (dominant DEB) or recessive (recessive DEB), and alter the function or reduce or disrupt the production of collagen VII. This impairs its assembly into anchoring fibrils that anchor the basement membrane to the underlying dermis, resulting in a cleavage plane below the lamina densa, within the upper papillary dermis. In the case of severe recessive DEB there is no collagen VII production.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected at clinical examination. It is confirmed by biopsy of skin samples by immunofluorescence antigen mapping and/or transmission electron microscopy (showing a blister cleavage plane beneath the lamina densa of the cutaneous basement membrane zone), and by COL7A1 mutation screening.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other forms of EB. During the neonatal period and infancy, it may also include aplasia cutis congenita, herpes simplex infection, epidermolytic ichthyosis, bullous impetigo, staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome, linear IgA bullous dermatosis, bullous pemphigoid, neonatal pemphigus and pemphigoid gestationis. For rare forms of DEB with a late onset, differential diagnosis includes acquired skin disorders such as lichen planus or autoimmune bullous diseases.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis should be offered to affect families with recessive severe DEB.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling should be offered to affect families and depends on the inheritance type and form of DEB.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is preventive and symptomatic and requires an inter- and multidisciplinary approach. Protective padding of the skin and careful wound care reduces blistering, scarring and prevents secondary infection. Treatment of pain and itching is highly warranted but partly limited in effectiveness. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy are necessary to delay gradual loss of mobility and autonomy. Hand deformities can be treated surgically, but have a high recurrence. Nutritional requirements should be evaluated by a dietitian and gastrostomy feeding may be necessary. Esophageal strictures are treated by balloon dilatation with fluoroscopic guidance. Transfusions, iron supplementation, and erythropoietin administration improve anemia and iron deficiency. A regular follow-up with complete skin checks and biopsies is necessary for the surveillance of SCC development. Psychological support should be offered.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the subtype. Patients with dominant DEB usually have a normal life expectancy. Patients with severe recessive DEB are at high risk of mortality primarily from metastatic SCC, less frequently from chronic renal failure, sepsis and dilated cardiomyopathy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hemoglobin E disease (HbE) is a hemoglobinopathy characterized by production of abnormal variant hemoglobin known as hemoglobin E, with a generally benign, asymptomatic presentation.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Hemoglobin E (HbE) affects at least 1 million people worldwide and is among the most common inherited diseases. It is a structural hemoglobin variant characteristic of the Southeast Asian population. The carrier frequency of HbE/beta-thalassemia is highest in Southeast Asia, with a notable frequency in the northeast region of India, where Hb E is also common among distinct tribal populations. While rare, Hb E has been detected in European populations, such as in Croatia, and its appearance in Europe is attributed to migration, making it a public health issue in multiethnic populations. Combined heterozygosity for Hb Paksé and Hb E is occasionally described in East Asia, and combined heterozygosity for Hb S and E is a rare condition with approximately 46 cases reported worldwide. [PMC12031744, PMC9906172, PMC8327456, PMC5082216]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hemoglobin E (Hb E) is a structural hemoglobin variant and a common inherited cause of anemia, with clinical manifestations varying by genetic combination. Combined heterozygosity for Hb E and other variants, such as Hb Paksé, can be asymptomatic, presenting with microcytic anemia without iron deficiency. Compound heterozygosity for Hb S and E (Hb SE disease) is generally a benign clinical condition. However, Hb E/beta-thalassemia can lead to pallor, weakness, moderate hepatosplenomegaly, and may involve adrenal extramedullary hematopoiesis. This form also presents challenges in managing anemia, particularly during pregnancy, and is rarely associated with Moyamoya syndrome, a progressive cerebrovascular disease that can manifest as choreoathetoid movements. Distinguishing homozygous Hb E disease from Hb E/beta-thalassemia can be challenging due to their clinical and hematological similarities. [PMC12031744, PMC9906172, PMC8327456, PMC7802720, PMC6198700]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hemoglobin E disease is an inherited disorder of globin chain synthesis, characterized as a structural hemoglobin variant. It is specifically a β-thalassemia variant, identified by genetic sequencing as HbE β2 CD 26 [G > A] (HBB: c.79 G > A). This condition can occur as a single variant or in combined heterozygosity with other hemoglobin variants, such as Hb Paksé or hemoglobin S. While characteristic of South East Asian populations, its appearance in other regions is noted as a result of migration. [PMC12031744, PMC8327456, PMC5082216]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Hemoglobin E can be initially suspected during routine hematological examinations, especially when microcytic anemia without iron deficiency is observed. Further diagnostic steps include hemoglobin typing and the detection of structural variants, such as through capillary zone electrophoresis. Genetic sequencing or genetic testing is crucial to confirm specific hemoglobin E mutations, like HBB: c.79 G > A. These facilitate clinical recognition and help avoid misdiagnosis of conditions like sideropenic anemia. Screening programs and family screening are also employed to identify affected individuals and carriers. [PMC12031744, PMC8327456, PMC5082216]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis for Hemoglobin E disease includes conditions with similar hematological profiles or those that might be confused with it. It is crucial to distinguish homozygous Hemoglobin E disease from HbE/β-thalassemia, as both are clinically and hematologically similar.
