These advanced confirm the chromosomal origin and precisely map genomic variations, which are essential for understanding the diverse phenotypic spectrum. [PMC6180451, PMC5687301, PMC3599180, PMC3410245, PMC1682952]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Ring chromosome 6 (r(6)) is a rare disorder that mainly occurs as a de novo event. Genetic counseling should address the wide phenotypic spectrum, which can range from an almost normal phenotype to severe malformations and intellectual disability. This variability depends on factors such as breakpoints, the size of involved regions, copy number alterations, and mosaicism of cells. The severity of the phenotype appears to be related to the size of the terminal deletions. [PMC6180451, PMC3599180]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for ring chromosome 6 syndrome addresses specific congenital anomalies. In one reported case, a male infant with a large patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and associated heart failure symptoms recovered after ligation of the PDA. Other clinical features, such as infantile failure to thrive and delayed milestones, were observed during follow-up, but specific management for these aspects is not detailed in the provided information. [PMC3410245]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Ring chromosome 6 syndrome is highly variable, with a phenotypic spectrum ranging from nearly normal to severe developmental delay, intellectual disability, and multiple congenital anomalies. Clinical severity is influenced by factors such as breakpoints, the size of the involved region, copy number alterations, and mosaicism. Common features include central nervous system anomalies, growth retardation, and facial dysmorphism. While one infant recovered from heart failure symptoms after intervention, he subsequently experienced infantile failure to thrive and delayed milestones, highlighting the long-term challenges. [PMC6180451, PMC5687301, PMC3599180, PMC3410245, PMC1682952]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Piebaldism is a rare congenital pigmentation skin disorder characterized by the presence of hypopigmented and depigmented skin areas (leukoderma) on various parts of the body, preferentially on the forehead, chest, abdomen, upper arms, and lower extremities, that are associated with a white forelock (poliosis), and in some cases with hypopigmented and depigmented eyebrows and eyelashes.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Piebaldism is characterized by congenital pigmentary defects, including a white hair forelock (poliosis) and congenital leukoderma, which presents as amelanotic white macules, often with hyperpigmented macules within them, typically on the ventral body and extremities. Other variable manifestations can include auburn hair color. Some patients may also exhibit multiple café-au-lait macules and intertriginous freckling. Rarely, a complex auditory-pigmentary multisystem phenotype may occur, featuring congenital sensorineural hearing loss, inborn pigmentary defects of the iris, hair, and skin, and severe neuropsychiatric impairment, especially in dual locus inherited syndromes. [PMC6681376, PMC3755434, PMC3967413, PMC3054053, PMC53036]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Piebaldism is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder of melanocyte development, classified as a neurocristopathy resulting from altered neural crest cell development. It is mostly caused by mutations in the KIT gene (c-kit protooncogene), which is critical for melanoblast development and maps to chromosome 4q12. Identified KIT mutations include splicing mutations and heterozygous deletions of the entire gene. While KIT mutations are the main cause, some complex cases may involve co-occurrence with other genetic alterations, such as a deletion at chromosome 15q13.3, leading to a dual locus inherited syndrome. KIT mutations may also be associated with auburn hair color and can influence other cutaneous manifestations like café-au-lait macules and freckling, potentially through a common pathway with SPRED1. [PMC6681376, PMC3755434, PMC3967413, PMC1051037, PMC53036]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Piebaldism is primarily diagnosed based on characteristic clinical findings, including a congenital white forelock, localized poliosis, and amelanotic white macules, which may contain hyperpigmented macules and involve ventral and extremity depigmentation. Genetic analysis is crucial for confirmation, often identifying pathogenic variants, splicing mutations, or heterozygous deletions in the KIT gene. Molecular investigations, such as mutation screening, Southern blot analysis, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), are employed to detect these KIT gene alterations. Cytogenetic investigation can also reveal deletions or translocations involving chromosome 4q12. While typical pigmentary defects are key, the presence of other features like café-au-lait macules or intertriginous freckling can complicate the diagnostic process. [PMC6681376, PMC3755434, PMC3967413, PMC1051037, PMC3054053]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Piebaldism, characterized by inborn pigmentary defects of hair and skin, including white forelock and leukoderma, and sometimes congenital sensorineural hearing loss, is an auditory-pigmentary disorder caused by KIT mutations. Other auditory-pigmentary disorders that may be considered include Waardenburg syndromes, oculocutaneous albinism, and Tietz syndrome. Oculocutaneous albinism specifically involves pigmentation of eyes, hair, and skin due to tyrosinase gene mutations. Griscelli syndrome, characterized by hypopigmentation, immunodeficiency, and neurological features, also presents with pigmentary dilution; Griscelli syndrome type 3 specifically involves pigmentary dilution of skin and hair without other systemic abnormalities. Chedíak-Higashi Syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder, presents with partial oculocutaneous albinism alongside immunodeficiency, bleeding tendencies, and neurological deficits. The presence of multiple café-au-lait macules and intertriginous freckling in patients with piebaldism may also lead to consideration of neurofibromatosis type 1 or Legius syndrome. [PMC11730025, PMC8109045, PMC7678511, PMC6681376, PMC5987098]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Piebaldism is an autosomal dominant disorder primarily caused by mutations in the KIT gene, located on chromosome 4, and can be inherited in a familial pattern. It is characterized by congenital white hair forelock and depigmentation, but genetic counseling should address the variable phenotype and potential for complex genetic scenarios. For example, a dual locus inherited syndrome involving a KIT mutation and a deletion at chromosome 15q13.3 can lead to sensorineural deafness and neuropsychiatric impairment. Additionally, features like café-au-lait macules and intertriginous freckling, while sometimes attributed to neurofibromatosis type 1, may also be seen in piebaldism due to KIT and SPRED1 interactions. KIT mutations can also influence hair color, such as auburn. [PMC6681376, PMC3755434, PMC3967413, PMC1051037, PMC3054053]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Congenital sensorineural hearing loss may occur in association with inborn pigmentary defects of the iris, hair, and skin. These conditions, named auditory-pigmentary disorders (APDs), represent extremely heterogeneous hereditary diseases, including Waardenburg syndromes, oculocutaneous albinism, Tietz syndrome, and piebaldism. APDs are part of the neurocristopathies, a group of congenital multisystem disorders caused by an altered development of the neural crest cells, multipotent progenitors of a wide variety of different lineages, including those differentiating into peripheral nervous system glial cells and melanocytes. on clinical and genetic findings of two monozygotic twins from a large Albanian family who showed a complex phenotype featured by sensorineural congenital deafness, severe neuropsychiatric impairment, and inborn pigmentary defects of hair and skin. The genetic... [PMC6681376, PMC53036]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Persistent placoid maculopathy is characterised by white plaque-like lesions involving the macula but sparing the peripapillary areas of both eyes. It has been described in five patients. In contrast to patients with macular serpiginous choroiditis presenting with similar lesions, the five patients reported so far with persistent placoid maculopathy had good visual acuity until the onset of choroidal neovascularization (CNV) or pigmentary mottling. The macular lesions fade after several months or years, but the vascular anomalies persist leading to a loss of central vision.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Persistent placoid maculopathy is described as a rare and previously unreported clinical entity, appearing to be a new disease. Case series have documented its occurrence in patients, with one study reviewing five patients aged 50 to 68 years seen across different centers from 1999 to 2006. Another case series presented four patients, with ages ranging from 49 to 65 years. The condition is characterized as an idiopathic bilateral chorioretinopathy. [PMC12057242, PMC1809922]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Persistent placoid maculopathy (PPM) is a rare, idiopathic bilateral chorioretinopathy characterized by choriocapillaris hypoperfusion. Patients typically present with sudden-onset or persistent bilateral central scotomas and varying visual acuity. Ophthalmological examination reveals well-delineated whitish or yellowish plaque-like macular lesions, which may fade over months to years. Multimodal imaging shows bilateral hyperautofluorescent lesions, early-phase hyper-fluorescent staining on fluorescein angiography that intensifies late, and persistent hypofluorescence on indocyanine green angiography. Optical coherence tomography may reveal focal deposits at the retinal pigment epithelium and disruption of outer photoreceptor bands, alongside significant macular choriocapillaris flow deficits. Complications such as choroidal neovascularization, submacular hemorrhage, and complete macular chorioretinal atrophy are common, often leading to central vision loss or disciform macular scars. [PMC12057242, PMC10111074, PMC1809922]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Persistent placoid maculopathy is defined as an idiopathic bilateral chorioretinopathy. However, case reports suggest potential associations. In one instance, the condition was diagnosed in a patient with a history of scalp tenderness and jaw claudication, with a temporal artery biopsy confirming giant cell arteritis. Another case involved a patient receiving immunosuppressive therapy, where corticosteroid treatment led to a decrease in chorioretinal lesions and vision recovery. [PMC12057242]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Persistent placoid maculopathy is diagnosed based on clinical presentation and multimodal imaging. Patients typically present with sudden-onset central scotomas, bilateral blurred vision, or sudden vision loss, and exhibit well-delineated whitish or yellowish plaque-like macular lesions. Multimodal imaging includes autofluorescence, which shows bilateral hyperautofluorescent lesions. Fluorescein angiography reveals early-phase hyper-fluorescent staining that intensifies in late phases, or well-defined early hypofluorescent areas that partially fill in. Indocyanine green angiography consistently displays persistent hypofluorescence. Swept source optical coherence tomography (SS-OCT) B-scans show bilateral focal deposits at the retinal pigment epithelium and disruption of outer photoreceptor bands. SS-OCT angiography (SS-OCTA) quantifies choriocapillaris flow deficits, indicating significant impairment of macular perfusion. [PMC12057242, PMC10111074, PMC1809922]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Persistent placoid maculopathy superficially resembles macular serpiginous choroiditis, sharing some lesion characteristics. However, it differs in its clinical course and effect on visual acuity. Unlike serpiginous choroiditis, visual acuity often remains good despite early foveal involvement until complications like choroidal neovascularization (CNV) develop. The white macular lesions of persistent placoid maculopathy fade over time, and chorioretinal scar formation is typically absent unless related to CNV, which contrasts with serpiginous choroiditis. Additionally, giant cell arteritis has been reported in a patient diagnosed with persistent placoid maculopathy, suggesting it may be considered in the differential or as a co-occurring condition. [PMC12057242, PMC1809922]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management approaches for persistent placoid maculopathy vary depending on presentation and complications. Corticosteroid treatment has been shown to improve visual acuity, facilitate recovery of outer photoreceptor bands, and enhance choriocapillaris perfusion, leading to decreased chorioretinal lesions and vision recovery in some cases. However, in one instance associated with giant cell arteritis, corticosteroids did not prevent complete macular chorioretinal atrophy. Complications like choroidal neovascularization can be managed with intravitreal injections of Aflibercept, sometimes preceded by sub-tenon triamcinolone injection, which may improve visual acuity. Surgery with pneumatic displacement combined with intravitreal Aflibercept was also performed for submacular hemorrhage, though without observed visual improvement in that specific case. [PMC12057242, PMC10111074]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for persistent placoid maculopathy is variable. While some cases show improvement in visual acuity and outer retinal anatomy, particularly with corticosteroid treatment leading to improved choriocapillaris perfusion, severe outcomes are also reported. A significant complication is choroidal neovascularization (CNV), which developed in the majority of eyes (9 out of 10 in one series), often converting to disciform macular scars and leading to central vision loss. Other complications include complete macular chorioretinal atrophy and submacular hemorrhage, which can result in no visual improvement. Although the characteristic white macular lesions may fade over months to years, angiographic findings often persist longer. [PMC12057242, PMC10111074, PMC1809922]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hereditary Transthyretin (TTR)-related systemic amyloidosis (ATTR) with predominant cardiac involvement resulting from myocardial infiltration of abnormal amyloid protein.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Global prevalence is unknown. The prevalence of the Val122Ile variant has been estimated to be 3.5% in American population of African descent, corresponding to potentially 1.6 million carriers in the USA. However, the actual penetrance in this population is unknown, with estimates as low as 10%.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients present during late adulthood with restrictive cardiomyopathy (with varying degrees of chronic heart failure and possible brady/tachyarrhythmias). Cardiomyopathy may be accompanied by sensorimotor/autonomic polyneuropathy but in many patients carrying this variant the phenotypic expression may remain exclusively cardiac.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Several specific TTR mutations are associated with predominant cardiac involvement. Among these, V122I is particularly common among African-Americans (3.5% of the population).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The gold standard for diagnosis of amyloidosis is histological analysis and Congo red staining of biopsy specimens. Detection of the specific TTR mutation allows confirmation of the diagnosis. A high level of diagnostic suspicion of cardiac amyloidosis can be generated by characteristic echocardiographic and ECG findings, and confirmed by bone tracer scintigraphy and/or magnetic resonance imaging with late enhancement. A family history of cardiac disease may suggest hereditary ATTR amyloidosis etiology.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include other infiltrative/storage myocardial diseases, including other types of cardiac amyloidosis, such as AL amyloidosis. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy should also be included in the differential diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Considering the late-onset phenotype and the increasing availability of disease-modifying therapies, antenatal diagnosis has a very limited role in this specific condition.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Hereditary ATTR amyloidosis is dominantly transmitted. Genetic counseling is generally highly recommended to at-risk patients' relatives, informing them there is a 50% risk of inheritance in siblings and offspring. For the Val122Ile variant in African-Americans, it is particularly important to discuss the low penetrance and possible gender-related variations, with a higher disease rate observed in males over the age of 70. Factors affecting penetrance are still unknown. In general, pre-symptomatic testing is increasingly offered in hereditary ATTR amyloidosis due to emerging disease-modifying therapies.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Close monitoring of cardiac function and symptoms by an expert cardiologist is recommended. Supportive therapy plays a major role. Disease modifying therapy is available for hereditary V122I amyloidosis. Patient with exclusive cardiomyopathy can be treated with the TTR stabilizer tafamidis at the dose of 61 mg/day. Patients presenting with a mixed phenotype (cardiomyopathy associated with polyneuropathy) are eligible to a gene-silencing treatment, including the RNAi agent patisiran (or vutrisiran, where already available) and the antisense oligonucleotide inotersen.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is driven by the severity of cardiomyopathy. A validated prognostic staging system for patients with hereditary ATTRV122I amyloidosis is the NAC staging system, in which survival correlates with NT-proBNP concentration and eGFR at diagnosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital malformation of the lower spinal segments characterized by a high truncated conus with either aplasia or hypoplasia of the sacrum and lumbar spine. Coexisting malformations of gastrointestinal, genitourinary, skeletal, nervous system are commonly described.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Caudal dysgenesis syndrome; Caudal dysplasia; Caudal regression sequence

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Whilst the exact prevalence at birth is unknown, the incidence of caudal regression syndrome (CRS) is estimated between 1/20,000-100,000 pregnancies. Maternal diabetes is a major risk factor for developing CRS, and the disorder is up to 200 fold more frequent in this group of patients than in the general population.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The spectrum of anomalies affecting the caudal end of the trunk vary from isolated partial agenesis of the sacrococcygeal spine to more severe deformities. The caudal malformation can result in deformities of the pelvis (typically fusion of the iliac wings), anomalies of the lower extremities (i.e. flexion of the knees, varus position of the feet) and motor and neurological deficits of varying degrees of severity (i.e. spontaneous motor activity and impaired deep tendon reflexes of lower limbs). Additional complications of the genitourinary, gastrointestinal and respiratory systems may occur. Genitourinary anomalies can involve unilateral or bilateral renal agenesis, renal ectopia and fused ureters, and generally lead to urinary obstruction, neurogenic bladder, enuresis, or vesicoureteral reflux. Gastrointestinal anomalies can involve inability to control bowel movements (incontinence, encopresis) and an imperforate anus. Congenital heart anomalies are frequently observed. Cases with Chiari I malformation, holoprosencephaly, chronic hypertension and cleft lip and palate have also been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The malformations are believed to result from impaired development of the mesoderm prior to 4 weeks gestation. However, vascular steal or hypoperfusion with fetal hypoxemia is also hypothesized due to a few descriptions of a single umbilical cord. Several etiologic factors have been suggested and include maternal diabetes, hypoperfusion, as well as a genetic predisposition (for example mutation in VANGL1 gene (1p13.1), CELSR1 (22q13.31) and, FUZ gene (19q13.33).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on antenatal ultrasound examination in the first trimester of pregnancy in the most severe cases. The severity of the disease is determined by examination of the newborn by means of postnatal ultrasonographic and nuclear magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnosis is sirenomelia. CRS has also been associated with the VACTERL syndrome, and Currarino syndrome is a form of caudal regression syndrome characterized by the classic triad of presacral mass, sacral bone defect and anorectal malformation. Due to the similarity between sirenomelia, VACTERL and CRS, the distinction between these defects is debated.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: In severe forms, diagnosis is easier in the first trimester and more difficult later in pregnancy due to oligohydramnios. Sacrococcygeal dysgenesis, abrupt termination of spinal cord, and other anomalies (cardiac, renal, gastrointestinal, lower limbs) can be diagnosed in the second or third trimester. Fetal MRI can be useful in difficult cases or to better define anomalies.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The most severe cases of CRS appear to be sporadic but the milder forms appear to be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with variable phenotypes.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment and management is supportive and requires a multidisciplinary approach by neurosurgeons, orthopedics, urologists, nephrologists, physical therapists, and psychologists. Neurogenic bladder is commonly described and clean intermittent catheterization and/or anticholinergic drug administration are generally required to treat urological disorders. Surgical interventions such as vesicoureteral reimplantation, cystostomy, Mitrofanoff are commonly performed in order to improve quality of life, urinary continence, and preserve renal function. Surgical reconstruction (Pena Procedure) can be required for imperforate anus, although colostomy may be required in some cases. Depending on the severity of the syndrome, orthopedic interventions may also be required.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor and is mainly related to urological and cardiac malformations. Early neonatal death in the severe forms occurs from cardiac, renal and respiratory complications. Surviving infants usually have normal cognitive function.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare renal disease characterized by the association of X-linked Alport syndrome (glomerular nephropathy, sensorineural deafness and ocular anomalies) and benign proliferation of visceral smooth muscle cells along the gastrointestinal, respiratory, and female genital tracts and clinically manifests with dysphagia, dyspnea, cough, stridor, postprandial vomiting, retrosternal or epigastric pain, recurrent pneumonia, and clitoral hypertrophy in females.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of X-linked Alport syndrome-diffuse leiomyomatosis (XLAS-DL) is unknown. It affects both males and females.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Symptoms of glomerular disease (hematuria, progressive proteinuria and renal impairment) typically appear late in childhood, and in males is more severe with faster progression. Patients also have sensorineural deafness and ocular anomalies (anterior lenticonus, congenital cataracts, corneal opacities, maculopathy, fleck retinopathy and temporal retinal thinning). Diffuse leiomyomatosis is severe in males and in females, and typically involves the esophagus, causing dysphagia, postprandial vomiting and retrosternal or epigastric pain. Tracheobronchial lesions lead to dyspnea, cough, stridor and recurrent pneumonia due to aspiration. Affected females show clitoral hypertrophy and variable involvement of labia majora and uterus. Perirectal or perineal leiomyomas are uncommon and associated with constipation.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: XLAS-DL is due to contiguous gene deletions encompassing the 5' ends of COL4A5 (Xq22.3) and COL4A6 (Xq22.3) genes, which respectively encode the alpha-5 and alpha-6 chain of type IV collagen. COL4A5 is an integral component of the type IV collagen 3,4,5 network, a key component of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM), and COL4A6 is a component of the type IV collagen 5,5,6 network present in Bowman's capsule but not in the healthy GBM.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: X-linked Alport syndrome is suspected on clinical presentation and family history of hematuria, deafness and/or renal impairment, and is confirmed by genetic analysis of COL4 genes. Histological evaluation of the kidney is valuable in case of equivocal or unavailable genetic testing. Immunohistochemical assays can also be performed on kidney and skin specimens, and electron microscopy provides ultrastructural analysis of basement membranes. An abnormal expression pattern of type IV collagen chains confirms the diagnosis; however, a normal expression does not eliminate diagnosis. The diagnosis of leiomyomatosis requires a biopsy of the affected tissue. Radiological imaging can identify lesions and the associated deformation of the affected tract.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis regarding the combination of glomerular disease with deafness includes Fechtner syndrome, MYH9-related disease, MELAS and May-Hegglin thrombocytopenia. The main differential diagnosis for glomerular hematuria is IgA nephropathy, familial benign hematuria and membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Leiomyomata can occur as sporadic benign smooth muscle tumors, without AS.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal testing for at risk pregnancies is possible where the COL4A5-COL4A6 deletion has been previously identified in a family member, and if a molecular diagnosis of the inherited deletion can be reliably performed.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: XLAS-DL is transmitted as X-linked dominant trait and, thus, heterozygous females will also express the disease. Genetic counseling for affected families is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Regular monitoring of blood pressure and urinalysis are important to identify hypertension or microalbuminuria/proteinuria and treat accordingly with angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors/angiotensin receptor blockers. This additionally permits timely clinical management of chronic kidney disease, including eventual renal replacement therapy with either preemptive transplantation or dialysis. Surgical intervention is required for symptomatic leiomyomas. Ocular manifestations rarely need intervention but an ophthalmologist is helpful for diagnosis since ocular involvement is often asymptomatic. Audiological evaluation should be performed regularly and hearing aids should be prescribed when appropriate.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis of AS is poor due to the progression to ESRD (often affecting young adults). Renal transplantation is successful in individuals with AS, since development of anti-glomerular basement membrane antibodies is a rare event.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, isolated, diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma disorder characterized by red-yellow, moderate to severe hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles, extending to the dorsal aspects of the hands, feet and/or wrists and involving the skin over the Achilles' tendon (transgrediens), gradually worsening with age (progrediens) to include patchy hyperkeratosis over the shins, knees, elbows and, sometimes, skin flexures. Hyperhidrosis is usually associated. Histologically, either epidermolytic or nonepidermolytic changes may be seen.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Greither disease; Keratosis extremitatum hereditaria progrediens; Keratosis palmoplantaris transgrediens et progrediens; Progressive diffuse PPK; Progressive diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma; Transgrediens et progrediens PPK

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Transgrediens et progrediens palmoplantar keratoderma, exemplified by Greither syndrome, is characterized by diffuse, thick, scaly yellow palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK). This PPK exhibits a transgrediens pattern with an erythematous border, extending up to the Achilles' tendon. Additionally, patients may present with patchy hyperkeratotic plaques over the knees, shins, thighs, elbows, knuckles, and axillary folds. This phenotype can be associated with KRT1 mutations. [PMC8886511]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Transgrediens et progrediens palmoplantar keratoderma, such as Greither syndrome, is an autosomal dominant disorder. It is caused by mutations in the KRT1 gene. Generally, palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK) develops as a compensatory hyperproliferation of the epidermis and excessive production of stratum corneum. This occurs in response to altered cornification of the palmoplantar skin due to mutations in genes encoding proteins involved in this process. Hereditary PPK exhibits wide genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity. [PMC8886511, PMC6615398]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of transgrediens et progrediens palmoplantar keratoderma, such as Greither syndrome, relies on recognizing characteristic clinical patterns. These include diffuse, thick, scaly yellow palmoplantar keratoderma with transgrediens and an erythematous border extending to the Achilles' tendon, often accompanied by patchy hyperkeratotic plaques on the knees, shins, thighs, elbows, knuckles, and axillary folds. While clinical features are crucial, molecular studies are imperative for accurate classification, especially given the genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity of hereditary palmoplantar keratoderma. KRT1 mutations are associated with Greither-like presentations. [PMC8886511, PMC6615398]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Greither syndrome, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by KRT1 mutation, presents with diffuse, thick, scaly yellow palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK) with transgrediens and an erythematous border extending up to the Achilles' tendon, along with patchy hyperkeratotic plaques over the knees, shins, thighs, elbows, knuckles, and axillary folds. Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis (AEI), particularly when caused by KRT1 mutations, can phenotypically mimic Greither disease, presenting with Greither-like PPK that extends to the dorsal aspects of the hands and feet up to the Achilles' tendon, and patchy hyperkeratotic plaques over areas like the elbows and axillary folds. [PMC8886511]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Hereditary palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK) with transgrediens, such as Greither syndrome, is an autosomal dominant disorder often linked to mutations in genes like KRT1. Given the wide genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity of hereditary PPK, an accurate diagnosis based solely on clinical features can be challenging. Therefore, molecular studies are imperative for precise classification and diagnosis. This molecular confirmation is crucial for providing appropriate genetic counseling, although recognizing clinical patterns can also assist in the diagnostic process. [PMC8886511, PMC6615398]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: The ridged skin of the palms and soles has several unique features: (i) presence of dermatoglyphics created by alternating ridges and grooves forming a unique pattern, (ii) presence of the highest density of eccrine sweat glands and absence of pilosebaceous units, and (iii) differential expression of keratins compared to the glabrous skin. These features explain the preferential localization of palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK) and several of its characteristic clinical features. PPK develops as a compensatory hyperproliferation of the epidermis and excessive production of stratum corneum in response to altered cornification of the palmoplantar skin due to mutations in the genes encoding several of the proteins involved in it. PPK can manifest as diffuse, focal, striate, or punctate forms per se or as a feature of several dermatological or systemic diseases. There is a wide genetic and... [PMC6615398]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: BACKGROUND Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis is a rare form of epidermolytic ichthyosis caused by specific pathogenic variants of KRT1 and KRT10. Classically, it manifests at birth with variable degrees of erythroderma and superficial erosions, which subsequently improve with time. Later, it is characterized by a cyclic history of annular hyperkeratotic erythematous plaques over the trunk and proximal extremities, with or without palmoplantar keratoderma. Greither syndrome, another autosomal dominant disorder of KRT1 mutation, is demonstrated by the diffuse, thick, scaly yellow PPK with transgrediens and erythematous border extending up to the Achilles' tendon, patchy hyperkeratotic plaques over the knees, shins, thighs, elbows, knuckles, and axillary folds. a patient with clinical findings consistent with annular epidermolytic ichthyosis mimicking Greither disease with a likely... [PMC8886511]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Singleton-Merten dysplasia is characterized by dental dysplasia, progressive calcification of the thoracic aorta with stenosis, osteoporosis and expansion of the marrow cavities in hand bones. Additional features included generalized muscle weakness and atrophy, and chronic psoriasiform skin eruptions. It has been reported in four unrelated patients (male and female) and in a family with multiple affected members (male).

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Singleton-Merten syndrome (SMS) is a type I interferonopathy caused by gain-of-function mutations in genes like IFIH1 or DDX58, leading to overactivation of type I interferon signaling. Clinically, it presents with a broad spectrum of features. Dental anomalies are common, including dysplasia, root formation issues, impacted teeth, internal resorption, alveolar bone loss, and early tooth loss, though atypical forms may have normal dentition. Skeletal abnormalities include osteoporosis, acro-osteolysis, widened phalangeal medullary cavities, tendon rupture, and arthropathy. Cardiovascular manifestations are significant, with aortic and cardiac valve calcifications, critical or progressive aortic stenosis, and rhythm disturbances, often being a major cause of mortality. Other features include muscular weakness, failure to thrive, glaucoma, psoriasis, chilblain lupus-like cutaneous lesions, and neurological involvement such as generalized epilepsy, spasticity, basal ganglia calcification, and developmental delay, with severity varying by genotype. [PMC11977043, PMC12095186, PMC11420756, PMC8995680, PMC6394545]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Singleton-Merten syndrome is a type I interferonopathy primarily caused by heterozygous gain-of-function mutations in the IFIH1 gene. IFIH1 encodes the pattern recognition receptor MDA5, and its mutations lead to overactivation of type I interferon (IFN) signaling, resulting in autoinflammation and an enhanced interferon response. Pathogenic variants in DDX58, which encodes RIG-I, also cause Singleton-Merten syndrome, including both atypical and classic forms. DDX58 alterations similarly confer constitutive activation, leading to increased IFN activity and IFN-stimulated gene expression. [PMC11977043, PMC8995680, PMC6394545, PMC5439407, PMC4745891]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Singleton-Merten syndrome (SMS) involves genetic testing, primarily whole exome sequencing or next-generation sequencing, to identify pathogenic gain-of-function mutations in the IFIH1 or DDX58 genes. Early genetic diagnosis is crucial. Functional studies assessing type I interferon (IFN) production or interferon-stimulated gene (ISG) expression in whole blood or patient cells can confirm constitutive upregulation or enhanced interferon signaling, which is characteristic of the disease. Clinical phenotyping, including assessment of dental anomalies, skeletal abnormalities, and other systemic features, guides the diagnostic process. Imaging techniques such as panoramic radiographs and cone beam computed tomography (CBCT) are utilized to evaluate dental and maxillofacial challenges, including root formation anomalies and impacted teeth. [PMC11977043, PMC11420756, PMC8995680, PMC6394545, PMC5439407]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Singleton-Merten syndrome (SMS) exhibits significant phenotypic overlap with Aicardi-Goutières syndrome (AGS), with both conditions considered part of the Type I interferonopathy spectrum. Specifically, IFIH1-related disorders can present with features from both SMS and AGS, as demonstrated by cases with the Arg822Gln mutation in IFIH1, which can cause a spectrum of disease including neurological involvement. The phenotypic spectrum associated with IFIH1 mutations also extends to dermatological involvement, sometimes resembling familial chilblain lupus, further highlighting the overlap between AGS and SMS. [PMC11977043, PMC5439407, PMC4745891]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: This case report describes the prosthetic rehabilitation of a 15-year-old female patient with a rare IFIH1-related interferonopathy, presenting features from both Aicardi-Goutières Syndrome (AGS) and Singleton-Merten Syndrome (SMS). The report highlights the unique dental and maxillofacial challenges, and the multidisciplinary treatment approach required in such patients. The patient underwent a comprehensive prosthetic rehabilitation, which included two stages of extractions, followed by the fabrication of a complete upper denture and a two-implant-retained mandibular overdenture. Pre- and post-treatment assessments, including panoramic radiographs and cone beam computed tomography (CBCT), were utilized to guide treatment. Initial assessments revealed root formation anomalies, multiple impacted teeth, internal resorption, and associated dental anomalies. Following extractions and ridge... [PMC11977043, PMC11420756, PMC8995680, PMC6394545, PMC5439407]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Precision treatment with the Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor ruxolitinib has shown efficacy in Singleton-Merten syndrome 1 (SGMRT1), resolving psoriatic skin lesions, normalizing the IFN signature, and improving muscular weakness, osteopenia, and growth. Cardiovascular complications, such as critical aortic stenosis and progressive supra-aortic stenosis, may require interventions like transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI) or urgent surgery. Dental anomalies and bone fragility necessitate comprehensive prosthetic rehabilitation, which can include extractions and implant-retained dentures. A multidisciplinary approach, early genetic diagnosis, and thorough treatment planning are critical for managing the diverse manifestations of the syndrome. [PMC11977043, PMC12095186, PMC8995680, PMC4158224]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Singleton-Merten syndrome is variable, with cardiovascular involvement, including progressive supra-aortic stenosis and rhythm disturbances, identified as a major cause of mortality. However, critical cardiac issues can be successfully managed with interventions such as transcatheter valve implantation. Neurological outcomes, particularly for generalized epilepsy, can be favorable, with some patients becoming seizure-free, depending on specific IFIH1 variants. Genotype-phenotype correlations exist, where different IFIH1 variants are associated with varying neurological severity, from normal neurodevelopment to refractory epilepsy and severe developmental delay. Targeted treatments, such as JAK inhibition, can lead to sustained improvement in symptoms like psoriasis, muscular weakness, osteopenia, and growth. Early genetic diagnosis and thorough treatment planning are critical for optimal patient outcomes. [PMC11977043, PMC12095186, PMC11420756, PMC8995680, PMC6394545]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Isolated glycerol kinase deficiency (GKD) is a very rare X-linked disorder of glycerol metabolism characterized biochemically by elevated plasma and urine glycerol levels, and clinically by variable neurometabolic manifestations, depending on the age of onset, and varying from a life-threatening childhood metabolic crisis to an asymptomatic adult form (infantile GKD, juvenile GKD, and adult GKD).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Isolated glycerol kinase deficiency (GKD) is an X-linked recessive disorder, primarily affecting males. The clinical and biochemical picture is highly variable, ranging from asymptomatic adult "pseudohypertriglyceridaemia" to childhood metabolic crises, which may include gastrointestinal symptoms with ketoacidosis or hypoglycaemia, or recurrent convulsions. Familial cases have been reported, and one family showed a high prevalence of diabetes mellitus. So far, no genotype-phenotype correlation can be established in these GKD families. [PMC1051390, PMC372524]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Isolated glycerol kinase deficiency (GKD) presents with a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations, ranging from asymptomatic adult "pseudohypertriglyceridaemia" to severe childhood metabolic crises. Asymptomatic individuals typically exhibit hyperglycerolaemia and glyceroluria, leading to falsely elevated triglyceride levels that are unresponsive to treatment and often result in misdiagnosis. Symptomatic presentations can include gastrointestinal symptoms with ketoacidosis or hypoglycaemia, recurrent convulsions, psychomotor retardation, growth delay, bone dysplasia, and mental retardation. Phenotypic variation is common, even among individuals with the same mutation, and no clear genotype-phenotype correlation has been established, suggesting other factors may influence disease severity. [PMC8928288, PMC4612542, PMC1734616, PMC1051390, PMC1915081]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Isolated glycerol kinase deficiency (GKD) is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the Xp21 glycerol kinase (GK) gene, leading to a deficiency or absence of ATP:glycerol phosphotransferase activity. Identified mutations include extensive deletions, such as exon 17 deletions, as well as nonsense mutations (e.g., R413X), missense mutations (e.g., W503R, D440V), splice-site mutations, insertions, and terminations causing premature truncation of the GK polypeptide chain. The GK gene structure has been characterized, with reports of 20 or 21 exons. Despite diverse mutations, studies consistently show no clear genotype-phenotype correlation, with significant phenotypic variability observed even among individuals with identical mutations, suggesting additional influencing factors. [PMC1734616, PMC1051390, PMC1915081, PMC372524]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of glycerol kinase deficiency relies on a combination of biochemical and genetic findings. Characteristic biochemical markers include hyperglycerolaemia and glyceroluria, often detected through routine lipid tests, urinary glycerol tests, or urine organic acid analysis. Pseudohypertriglyceridemia, where high triglyceride values are reported by glycerol-measuring analyzers despite clear serum, is a common indicator, clarified by a 'glycerol blank' test. Enzymatic confirmation can involve demonstrating defective 14C-glycerol incorporation in fibroblasts or negligible glycerokinase activity in leukocyte homogenates. Ultimately, definitive diagnosis is established through genetic testing, such as gene screening, mutation screening of the GK gene via PCR and direct sequencing, or identifying deletions involving the GK gene on the Xp21 chromosome. [PMC9434940, PMC8928288, PMC10228193, PMC8543963, PMC5198007]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Isolated glycerol kinase deficiency (IGKD) must be differentiated from complex glycerol kinase deficiency (CGKD), which is a rare genetic syndrome caused by microdeletions in Xp21. CGKD involves co-occurrence of glycerol kinase deficiency with conditions like adrenal hypoplasia/insufficiency and Duchenne muscular dystrophy. Additionally, IGKD can present as pseudo-hypertriglyceridaemia, where elevated glycerol levels lead to falsely high triglyceride readings, often misdiagnosed as true hypertriglyceridaemia. This can result in unnecessary hypolipidaemic treatments, especially when the apparent hypertriglyceridaemia is unresponsive to therapy despite a clear serum sample. [PMC9434940, PMC8928288, PMC10228193, PMC8543963, PMC5198007]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Isolated glycerol kinase deficiency is an X-linked recessive disorder. Genetic counseling should address the significant phenotypic variability, which ranges from asymptomatic individuals to those with severe symptoms, even within the same family carrying identical mutations. Studies consistently demonstrate no clear correlation between the specific genotype and the clinical phenotype or disease severity. This suggests that other factors, such as metabolic or environmental stress or interactions with functional polymorphisms in other genes, may influence the expression of the disease. [PMC1734616, PMC1051390, PMC1915081, PMC372524]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of isolated glycerol kinase deficiency primarily involves avoiding unnecessary interventions for pseudo-hypertriglyceridemia. Patients are often misdiagnosed with true hypertriglyceridemia due to falsely elevated triglyceride values caused by excess serum glycerol. Consequently, they may be subjected to aggressive hypolipidemic drugs and lifestyle changes, which are ineffective in lowering triglyceride levels. Recognition of this asymptomatic condition is crucial to prevent such unnecessary treatments and to avoid overestimating cardiovascular risk. Discontinuation or modification of primary triglyceride-lowering agents is indicated once the correct diagnosis is established. [PMC8928288, PMC4612542]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: A 52-year-old man with a longstanding history of hypertriglyceridaemia (approximately 7 mmol/L (600 mg/dL)), unresponsive to treatment, presented to a lipid-specialty clinic. Additional triglyceride-lowering therapies were added with no effect. It was then noted that despite the apparent hypertriglyceridaemia, his serum sample was clear. A 'glycerol blank' was then requested from an advanced lipid laboratory, which reported a triglyceride value of 0.7 mmol/L (62 mg/dL). These findings suggest isolated asymptomatic glycerol kinase deficiency (GKD) or 'pseudohypertriglyceridaemia'. The falsely elevated triglyceride values in such individuals are a result of excess serum glycerol and clinical laboratories measuring glycerol to report triglyceride concentrations. After discontinuation or modification of the patient's primary triglyceride-lowering agents, the lipid panels and triglyceride... [PMC4612542, PMC1734616, PMC1051390, PMC1915081]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital, distal arthogryposis syndrome characterized by microstomia, whistling-face appearance, Chin with V- or H- shaped creased, and prominent nasolabial folds; most patients present club foot and congenital joint contractures of the hands and feet. It is the most severe form of distal arthrogryposis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Craniocarpotarsal dysplasia; Craniocarpotarsal dystrophy; Distal arthrogryposis type 2A; Whistling face syndrome; Freeman-Burian syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Approximately 100 cases of Freeman-Sheldon syndrome (FSS) have been reported to date; no gender predominance is reported and the distribution is worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Facial features include prominent forehead and eyebrow ridges, hypertelorism, epicanthus, telecanthus, down-slanting palpebral fissures, deep-set eyes, full cheeks, low-set ears, midface hypoplasia, a short nose and long philtrum, deep nasolabial folds, high-arched palate, and chin with a V- or H-shaped crease. The hallmark feature is small mouth with a whistling appearance. Dental crowding and difficulty in maintaining oral hygiene are reported, as well as hearing loss. Multiple contractures in the hands and feet are found at birth and are non-progressive; they cause camptodactyly, ulnar deviation of wrist and fingers, clubfoot, and overlapping fingers. Kyphoscoliosis is a frequent feature; congenital dislocation of the hip is rare. Ocular features include hypertelorism, strabismus, ptosis and blepharophimosis. Delayed growth is almost universal, but cognitive performances are generally normal. Infancy may be characterized by failure-to-thrive, due to microstomia, micrognathia and high palate. Other problems occurring with higher frequency in FSS are sleep apnea, dysglycemia, hyperhidrosis, diarrhea, constipation and gastro-esophageal reflux disease. An increased risk of adverse event during anesthesia is reported, mainly due to difficult intubation (because of orofacial contractures and structural anomalies, limited neck mobility, spinal deformities), difficult vascular access, and susceptibility to malignant hyperthermia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FSS is caused by homozygous mutations in MYH3, encoding for embryonic myosin heavy chain 3, a primary component of fetal myotubules; this protein has a central role during fetal muscular development, while postnatally it is progressively replaced by other isoforms. The switch in myosin expression pattern could explain why contractures are congenital and non-progressive. Mutations in NALCN have been identified in a few cases.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on both physical findings and genetic testing on MYH3. Diagnostic criteria have been proposed and include two or more of the following signs: distal arthrogryposis, microstomia, whistling-face, nasolabial creases, and H-shaped chin dimple. In some cases of clinically diagnosed FSS, mutations in NALCN have been detected. Of note, at least 7% of clinical FSS cases are not explained by known pathological allelic variations.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis mainly includes other distal arthrogryposis such as digitotalar dymorphism (which lacks craniofacial features), Sheldon-Hall syndrome (clinically less severe), Gordon syndrome, trismus-pseudocamptodactyly syndrome, and autosomal dominant multiple pterygium syndrome. Schwartz-Jampel syndrome and CLIFAHDD (congenital contractures of the limbs and face, hypotonia, and developmental delay) are also to be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Pre-conception and pre-natal tests are possible, when a relative carries a known pathogenic variant. Prenatal ultrasound can also be useful.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Most cases are sporadic (de novo) autosomal dominant mutations; an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern has also been described and seems to be associated with a more severe clinical presentation. Genetic counselling may be offered for patients who have a child with FSS.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: No specific pharmacological therapy is available. Patients should have craniofacial and orthopedic consultation as early in life as possible, in order to undertake proper operative measures (e.g. oral commissuroplasties, dental treatment, blepharoplasty, myringotomies). Operative correction of lower deformities often results in poor outcome. Bracing and physiotherapy (including the Ponseti method) are the cornerstones of non-operative therapy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Aspiration and respiratory complications may lead to early mortality. Surviving infants usually have normal life expectancy. Quality of life is generally impaired by the multiple malformations and functional repercussions.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A mild subtype of autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy characterized by a variable onset (ranging from infancy to adolescence) of progressive proximal upper and lower limb muscle weakness and atrophy. Mild scapular winging, calf hypertrophy, and lack of respiratory and cardiac involvement are also observed.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): LGMD2G; Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy due to telethonin deficiency; Autosomal recessive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2G; Telethonin-related LGMD R7; LGMD type 2G; LGMD due to telethonin deficiency; Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy type 2G

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Telethonin-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R7 (LGMD2G) is a rare hereditary muscle disease. It was originally described in Brazilian patients, with four families reported. Subsequently, cases have been identified in other populations, including Chinese, Moldavian, and Portuguese patients, indicating a wider geographical distribution. While specific mutations have been identified in these populations, the actual frequency of this disease remains unknown. However, its identification outside the Brazilian population suggests that telethonin mutation-associated LGMD should be considered worldwide. [PMC2954583, PMC2592511]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Telethonin-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R7 typically presents with slowly progressive muscle weakness, often beginning in the early teens or twenties. Patients experience prominent weakness in the proximal lower extremities, distal anterior compartment of the legs, and sometimes the upper limbs and shoulder girdle. Associated features can include muscle atrophy in the thighs, legs, and arms, marked calf hypertrophy, painful calf cramps, mild scapular winging, and hyperlordosis. Muscle biopsies show mild dystrophic changes and complete telethonin deficiency. In some cases, mutant telethonin may be linked to autoimmune manifestations, such as systemic sclerosis with severe restrictive lung disease. [PMC9472154, PMC2954583, PMC2592511]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Telethonin-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R7 (LGMD2G) is an autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in the telethonin (TCAP) gene, located on chromosome 17q11-12. Specific mutations identified include homozygous c.157C > T (p.Gln53X) and homozygous Trp25X. The Trp25X mutation in early termination of transcription, leading to complete telethonin deficiency. Abnormal telethonin can compromise the integrity of the sarcomere structure, potentially causing rhabdomyolysis and exposing immunogenic sequences to the immune system. This abnormal protein may act as an immunogenic target, as suggested by its role in the development of systemic sclerosis in one patient. [PMC9472154, PMC2954583, PMC2592511]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Telethonin-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R7 involves molecular analysis to identify homozygous mutations in the TCAP gene, such as c.157C > T or Trp25X. Clinical examination reveals progressive proximal and distal limb weakness, muscle atrophy, and sometimes calf hypertrophy or painful cramps. Muscle MRI can show severe symmetrical atrophy in thigh and leg compartments. Further diagnostic support comes from muscle biopsy, which may exhibit mild dystrophic changes and lobulated fibers, and from immunofluorescence and Western blot assays demonstrating complete telethonin deficiency. [PMC2954583, PMC2592511]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Telethonin-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R7 (LGMD2G) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by homozygous mutations in the telethonin (TCAP) gene, located on chromosome 17q11-12. Specific mutations identified include c.157C > T (p.Gln53X) and Trp25X, both leading to telethonin deficiency. While initially described in Brazilian patients, cases have since been reported in Moldavian, Chinese, and Portuguese individuals, indicating a worldwide distribution. Genetic counseling should address the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, the TCAP gene involvement, and the implications for family planning, although the exact frequency of the disease remains unknown. [PMC2954583, PMC2592511]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Telethonin-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R7 is characterized by slowly progressive muscle weakness, typically manifesting in adolescence or early adulthood. Patients experience prominent weakness in proximal lower extremities and distal anterior leg compartments, with milder involvement of shoulder girdle muscles. Associated features can include calf hypertrophy, muscle atrophy, scapular winging, and hyperlordosis. A severe complication, restrictive lung disease due to fibrosing interstitial pneumonia secondary to systemic sclerosis, has been reported in a patient with a TCAP gene mutation, suggesting potential for serious systemic involvement. [PMC9472154, PMC2954583, PMC2592511]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare endocrine disease characterized by lentigines with a specific peri-orifical distribution, blue nevus, myxomas, various endocrine tumors including primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD), acromegaly, thyroid tumors, and a wide range of other tumors.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Carney syndrome; Myxoma-spotty pigmentation-endocrine overactivity syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Carney complex (CNC) is a rare disease with more than 750 cases reported in the scientific and medical literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Lentigines with a specific peri-orifical distribution, blue nevus (particularly epithelioid blue nevus), and cutaneous myxomas, with a classical distribution in the eyelids, nipples, external ear canal or genitalia, are frequent and very suggestive of the diagnosis. The most common endocrine gland manifestations are of Cushing syndrome (CS) due to primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease (PPNAD), large cell calcifying Sertoli cell tumors, thyroid tumors, and acromegaly. Myxomas can also be observed in the heart and breast. Cardiac myxomas are diagnosed at a median age of 50 but may occur in early childhood, can develop in any cardiac chamber, and may be multiple and/or recurrent.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In more than 70% of cases, CNC is related to mutations of the PRKAR1A gene coding for regulatory subunit R1alpha of protein kinase A. The mutation c.709-7del6 is mostly associated with isolated PPNAD, and the mutation c.491-492del is associated with more frequent cardiac myxomas, lentigines and thyroid tumors. Deleterious PDE11A variants have been described in patients with PRKAR1A mutations, with more frequent PPNAD and testicular tumors. A germline triplication mutation involving PRKACB, the gene encoding the catalytic subunit beta of the protein kinase A, has been described in a young woman with acromegaly, lentigines and myxomas who did not harbor a PRKAR1A mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made if two major features are present (e.g. peri-orifical lentigines, myxomas, PPNAD), or one major feature with a supplementary criterion such as a PRKAR1A mutation or an affected first-degree relative. Patients with CNC, or with a genetic predisposition to CNC, should have regular screening for manifestations of the disease. Clinical work-up for all the manifestations of CNC should be performed at least once a year in all patients and should start in infancy.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The heterogeneity of the manifestations of CNC implies that differential diagnosis should be discussed for each of its numerous manifestations: i.e. differential diagnosis of PPNAD can be the others causes of adrenal Cushing syndrome; PPNAD can be isolated without others manifestations of CNC and no genetic variant of PRKAR1A, or be part of a classic CNC associated with another main feature like lentiginosis and/or myxoma.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible where the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in one of the 2 parents.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: About 70% of the cases are familial with an autosomal dominant transmission. Genetic analysis should be proposed to all patients with CNC. In a second step, a genome-wide study may be discussed. Genetic counseling should be proposed in families with a known disease-causing mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Cardiac myxomas require surgical removal. Treatment of the other manifestations of CNC should be discussed and may include follow-up, surgery, or medical treatment depending on the location of the tumor, it's size, existence of hormonal excess or volume-related clinical signs, and the suspicion of malignancy. Bilateral adrenalectomy is the most common treatment for CS due to PPNAD.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Cardiac myxoma complications and other tumors development can greatly impact the lifespan of CNC patients.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive acromesomelic dysplasia characterized by severe dwarfism (adult height <120 cm), both axial and appendicular involvement (shortening of the middle and distal segments of limbs and vertebral shortening), and with normal facial appearance and intelligence. It is a less severe form than acromesomelic dysplasia, Grebe type and acromesomelic dysplasia, Hunter-Thomson type .

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Maroteaux type (AMDM) is a rare autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia with an estimated prevalence of 1:1,000,000. It is characterized by severe dwarfism with shortening of the middle and distal segments of the limbs. Genetic heterogeneity has been observed, with some families showing linkage to chromosome 9p13-q12, while others do not, which may account for the variable clinical and radiological severity of AMDM. [PMC12186393, PMC1734441]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Maroteaux type (AMDM), is a rare autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia characterized by severe dwarfism and disproportionate short stature. It typically involves extreme shortening of the forelimbs and shortening of the middle and distal segments of the limbs. The phenotypic spectrum can include abnormal changes of the appendicular and axial skeleton. Clinical and radiological severity is variable, with some patients showing no involvement of the distal lower limbs, a variability attributed to genetic heterogeneity. [PMC12186393, PMC7127880, PMC1734441]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Maroteaux type (AMDM) is an autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia. It is caused by variants in the NPR2 gene, with specific pathogenic variants such as C.2965 C > T (p.Arg989*) and C.2291T > C (p.Leu764Pro) being identified. The AMDM gene has been mapped to human chromosome 9p13-q12. Genetic heterogeneity is suggested, as linkage to this region is not observed in all affected families, which may account for the variable clinical and radiological severity of the disease. [PMC12186393, PMC1734441]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Acromesomelic dysplasia, Maroteaux type, involves assessing characteristic clinical features such as severe dwarfism, disproportionate short stature, and abnormal changes in the appendicular and axial skeleton, particularly shortening of the middle and distal limb segments. Molecular genetic detection is emphasized, with diagnostic exome sequencing used to identify variants in the NPR2 gene. Sanger sequencing can confirm the inheritance pattern of these variants. Genetic mapping techniques, including homozygosity mapping and linkage analysis to chromosome 9p13-q12, have also been employed to identify the disease gene and can aid in diagnosis, including the identification of milder forms. [PMC12186393, PMC1734441]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia Maroteaux type (AMDM) is an autosomal recessive disorder belonging to the group of acromesomelic dysplasias. AMDM is characterised by severe dwarfism with shortening of the middle and distal segments of the limbs. An AMDM gene has recently been mapped to human chromosome 9p13-q12 by homozygosity mapping in four consanguineous families. Here, we show linkage of the disease gene to chromosome 9p13-q12 in four of five consanguineous AMDM families and its exclusion in a fifth family with two children affected with a mild form of the disease. suggests that genetic heterogeneity accounts for the variable clinical and radiological severity of AMDM. [PMC1734441]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Maroteaux type (AMDM) is an autosomal recessive disorder. Affected individuals are typically compound heterozygous for variants in genes like NPR2, inheriting one mutated allele from each phenotypically normal, heterozygous carrier parent. While an AMDM gene has been mapped to human chromosome 9p13-q12, genetic heterogeneity is observed, suggesting that different genetic causes or loci can lead to the condition. This heterogeneity may also account for the variable clinical and radiological severity seen in AMDM, which is an important consideration for genetic counseling regarding diagnosis and recurrence risk. [PMC12186393, PMC1734441]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Currently, over 500 rare genetic bone disorders are identified. These diseases are often accompanied by dental abnormalities, which are sometimes the first clue for an early diagnosis. However, not many dentists are sufficiently familiar with phenotypic abnormalities and treatment approaches when they encounter patients with rare diseases. Such patients often need dental treatment but have difficulties in finding a dentist who can treat them appropriately. Herein we focus on major dental phenotypes and summarize their potential causes and mechanisms, if known. We discuss representative diseases, dental treatments, and their effect on the oral health of patients and on oral health-related quality of life. can serve as a starting point for dentists to contribute to early diagnosis and further investigate the best treatment options for patients with rare disorders, with the goal of... [PMC11068025]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, rapidly progressive, and histologically distinct, form of idiopathic interstitial pneumonia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP) is estimated at 1 in 25,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: AIP occurs over a wide age range, with a mean age of approximately 50 years. There is no sex predominance or association with smoking. The onset is acute/subacute (1±3 weeks), with dyspnoea and cough followed by rapid development of respiratory failure and the need for mechanical ventilation in the vast majority of the patients. Fever is present in almost half of the patients on presentation and a history of viral-like symptomatology exists in most cases but extensive investigations for bacterial and viral agents are negative.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: No etiology is known for AIP. There is no genetic predisposition identified.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The chest radiograph and high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) scan is abnormal; chest CT manifestations of AIP are bilateral, extensive, and sometimes patchy. They show alveolar densities associated with areas of ground glass attenuation. Consolidation is seen in the majority of cases, but is not as common as ground glass attenuation. Lung biopsies from patients with AIP show histologic features of the acute and/or organising phases of diffuse alveolar damage (DAD). The exudative phase shows oedema, hyaline membranes, and microvascular thrombi. The organising phase shows loose organising fibrosis, mostly within alveolar septa, and type II pneumocyte hyperplasia. The diagnosis of AIP is made in the appropriate clinical setting in a patient who has a clinical, radiological and histopathological presentations compatible with acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) but without a clear etiology.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis, histologically and clinically, includes acute exacerbation of pulmonary fibrosis, DAD in patients with collagen vascular diseases, DAD of known cause (ARDS), infection (especially Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia and legionellosis) and drug-induced pneumonitis, as well as hypersensitivity pneumonitis and acute eosinophilic pneumonia.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no proven treatment, however supportive care with mechanical ventilation, occasionally extracorporeal membrane oxygenation, high-dose corticosteroids, and often intravenous pulse cyclophosphamide, are usually provided.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is severe and early mortality is high, with a mortality rate over 50% within six months after onset.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A malformation syndrome reported in offspring (children and grandchildren) of women exposed to diethylstilbestrol (DES) during pregnancy and is characterized by reproductive tract malformations, decreased fertility and increased risk of developing clear cell carcinoma of the vagina and cervix in young women. Reproductive malformations reported in DES syndrome include small, T-shaped uteri and other uterotubal anomalies that increase the risk of miscarriages in women and epididymal cysts, microphallus, cryptorchidism, or testicular hypoplasia in men. DES, a synthetic nonsteroidal estrogen was widely prescribed from 1940-1970 to prevent miscarriage.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): DES embryofetopathy; DES syndrome; Diethylstilbestrol embryofetopathy; Distilbene embryofetopathy

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 4 syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 4 is an uniparental disomy of maternal origin that most likely does not have any phenotypic expression except from cases of homozygosity for a recessive disease mutation for which only mother is a carrier.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 4, specifically segmental UPD 4, is considered a rare genetic event. As of the reported case, this specific segmental UPD 4 has not been previously documented in the medical literature. This suggests that the condition is either extremely uncommon or has been largely unrecognized and unreported. [PMC6978399]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 4 can result in diverse clinical presentations, often manifesting as specific autosomal recessive disorders. One reported case involved Wolfram syndrome type 1, characterized by optic atrophy and diabetes mellitus, with the patient developing diabetes mellitus at 11 years and experiencing a rapid reduction in visual acuity at 17.8 years. Another patient presented with cblA type methylmalonic acidemia, an autosomal recessive disorder of organic acid metabolism, which led to an acute metabolic crisis after vaccination. [PMC8348440, PMC6978399]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Maternal uniparental disomy (UPD) of chromosome 4 is an underlying cause for specific genetic disorders, occurring when both copies of a chromosome or a chromosomal segment are inherited from the mother. This mechanism has been linked to Wolfram syndrome type 1 (WFS1) due to a novel homozygous pathogenic variant in the WFS1 gene, inherited maternally with uniparental mero-isodisomy of chromosome 4. Similarly, cblA type methylmalonic acidemia (MMA) resulted from a homozygous pathogenic variant in the MMAA gene, inherited solely from the mother due to maternal UPD on chromosome 4q26-q35.2. This leads to a homozygous pathogenic variant that does not conform to typical Mendelian inheritance. Segmental UPD 4 is considered rare. [PMC8348440, PMC6978399]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 4 can be diagnosed using chromosomal microarray analysis or high-resolution SNP-array analysis, which can identify segmental uniparental disomy on chromosome 4. Genetic testing for specific gene variants, such as in the WFS1 or MMAA genes, may reveal homozygous pathogenic variants. When these variants are inherited from only one parent, it can suggest uniparental disomy, prompting further chromosomal analysis. [PMC8348440, PMC8261101, PMC6978399]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 4 can lead to the homozygous expression of maternally inherited pathogenic variants, resulting in specific autosomal recessive disorders. For instance, Wolfram syndrome type 1, characterized by optic atrophy and diabetes mellitus, has been observed in a patient with partial uniparental mero-isodisomy of chromosome 4 and a homozygous WFS1 gene variant inherited from the mother. Similarly, cblA type methylmalonic acidemia, presenting with acute metabolic crisis, has been linked to maternal uniparental disomy on chromosome 4q26-q35.2, leading to a homozygous pathogenic variant in the MMAA gene. Therefore, these conditions should be considered in the differential diagnosis when maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 4 is identified. [PMC8348440, PMC6978399]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Small supernumerary marker chromosomes (sSMCs) are chromosomal fragments with abnormal structures found in patients with fertility problems and developmental delay. They may be detected in amniotic cell karyotypes. sSMCs are categorized as hereditary or de novo. Here, a case of prenatal de novo 4q11q12 sSMC and its molecular cytogenetic features which had no apparent phenotypic abnormality. Case: The fetus of a 36-yr-old pregnant woman was detected positive for Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) at the 16 th wk of gestation. Quantitative fluorescent polymerase chain reaction technique was applied for the rapid detection of numerical aneuploidy of chromosomes X, Y, 13, 18, and 21 microsatellites. Array comparative genomic hybridization (array CGH) technique was also conducted following the karyotype analysis of amniotic cells. The karyotype analysis was also done for the parents. Quantitative... [PMC8261101]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Maternal uniparental disomy (UPD) of chromosome 4 can lead to autosomal recessive disorders if the mother is a heterozygous carrier for a pathogenic variant on this chromosome. In such instances, the child inherits two copies of the affected chromosome segment solely from the mother, resulting in homozygosity for the variant and disease manifestation. For example, Wolfram syndrome type 1 has been reported due to a maternal inherited mutation with uniparental mero-isodisomy of chromosome 4, where the mother was heterozygous and the patient homozygous for the variant. Similarly, methylmalonic acidemia (cblA type) was observed in a patient with maternal UPD 4q26-q35.2, where the MMAA gene was inherited only from the mother with the same pathogenic variant on both alleles, explaining a non-Mendelian inheritance pattern. [PMC8348440, PMC6978399]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Wolfram syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by optic atrophy and diabetes mellitus. Wolfram syndrome type 1 (WFS1) is caused by bi-allelic pathogenic variations in the wolframin gene. We described the first case of WFS1 due to a maternal inherited mutation with uniparental mero-isodisomy of chromosome 4. Diabetes mellitus was diagnosed at 11 years of age, with negative anti-beta cells antibodies. Blood glucose control was optimal with low insulin requirement. No pathogenic variations in the most frequent gene causative of maturity-onset diabetes of the young subtypes were detected. At 17.8 years old, a rapid reduction in visual acuity occurred. Genetic testing revealed the novel homozygous variant c.1369A>G; p.Arg457Gly in the exon 8 of wolframin gene. It was detected in a heterozygous state only in the mother while the father showed a wild type sequence. In... [PMC8348440]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Wolfram syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by optic atrophy and diabetes mellitus. Wolfram syndrome type 1 (WFS1) is caused by bi-allelic pathogenic variations in the wolframin gene. We described the first case of WFS1 due to a maternal inherited mutation with uniparental mero-isodisomy of chromosome 4. Diabetes mellitus was diagnosed at 11 years of age, with negative anti-beta cells antibodies. Blood glucose control was optimal with low insulin requirement. No pathogenic variations in the most frequent gene causative of maturity-onset diabetes of the young subtypes were detected. At 17.8 years old, a rapid reduction in visual acuity occurred. Genetic testing revealed the novel homozygous variant c.1369A>G; p.Arg457Gly in the exon 8 of wolframin gene. It was detected in a heterozygous state only in the mother while the father showed a wild type sequence. In... [PMC8348440, PMC6978399]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by anomalous ossification and skeletal patterning of the axial and appendicular skeleton, facial dysmorphism and conductive and sensorineural hearing loss.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, over 100 cases have been described in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Frontometaphyseal dysplasia (FMD) is a congenital disorder and the cardinal manifestations in males are skeletal dysplasia (skull base sclerosis; distal phalangeal hypoplasia; progressive contractures of the hand over the first two decades resulting in marked limitation of movement at the interphalangeal, metacarpophalangeal joints, wrists, elbows, knees, and ankles); mild but progressive scoliosis; limb bowing; campomelia), facial dysmorphism (supraorbital hyperostosis, downslanting palpebral fissures, ocular hypertelorism, broad nasal bridge and nasal tip, hypodontia, oligodontia and occasionally craniosynostosis) and conductive and sensorineural hearing loss. Extraskeletal manifestations include congenital heart malformation (interauricular communication, ventricular septal defect, congenital pulmonary valve stenosis, aortic dilatation), congenital subglottic stenosis, an asthenic build, and underdevelopment of the musculature, most notably around the shoulder girdle and in the intrinsic muscles of the hands (common). Males with FMD can present with ureteric and/or urethral obstruction most frequently at the vesicoureteric junction (leading to hydronephrosis). Intelligence is normal. Females are less severely affected and present the characteristic craniofacial features, scoliosis but absent or attenuated digital, cardiorespiratory, and urologic anomalies.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The exact pathogenesis of FMD is still unknown, however around half of cases of FMD are caused by gain of function mutations in the gene FLNA (Xq28) that encodes filamin A. There is evidence for a second autosomal locus for FMD that to date remains uncharacterized. FMD is allelic with 4 other skeletal dysplasias (otopalatodigital syndrome type 1 and 2 (OPD1 and OPD2, respectively), terminal osseous dysplasia - pigmentary defects (TOD) and Melnick-Needles syndrome (MNS)).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Many pedigrees are consistent with X-linked dominant inheritance. Male-to-male transmission has not been reported. The risk of transmitting the mutation in each pregnancy is 50%; males inheriting the mutation will be affected while females who inherit the mutation are less severely affected.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Frontometaphyseal dysplasia (FMD) relies on clinical, radiological, and genetic findings.
