Clinically, patients exhibit distinctive features such as skeletal dysplasia, facial dysmorphism, extremities anomalies, and deafness, with specific presentations including congenital glaucoma, craniofacial dysmorphism, xerosis, poikiloderma, acro-osteolysis, keratitis, camptodactyly, and flexion contractures. Radiological assessment may reveal bowed long bones with cortical thickening, distal phalangeal osteolysis, widespread cranial sclerosis, and craniosynostosis, often involving multiple sutures. Genetically, FMD is associated with mutations in the FLNA gene, identifiable through like whole genome sequencing. FMD2 is linked to pathogenic variants, including missense variants, in the MAP3K7 gene. Filaminopathy should be considered in the differential diagnosis of craniosynostosis, especially with atypical cranial or skeletal features. [PMC7304360, PMC6076188, PMC4519681, PMC1181949, PMC1015795]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Frontometaphyseal dysplasia (FMD) shares phenotypic overlap with several conditions. Craniometaphyseal dysplasia presents with similar facial dimorphism, prominent supraorbital bridges, and metaphyseal involvement. Cardiospondylocarpofacial syndrome (CSCFS), an allelic disorder to FMD type 2 (MAP3K7 variants), exhibits overlapping features such as valvular heart disease, short stature, skeletal fusions, and facial dysmorphisms, including flexion contractures and widely spaced toes. FMD type 1 is caused by FLNA mutations, which also cause periventricular nodular heterotopia (PVNH) and otopalatodigital spectrum disorders (OPDS), with FMD being part of the OPDS spectrum. A filaminopathy should be considered in the differential for craniosynostosis with atypical features. Some FMD features, like xerosis and poikiloderma, may also be consistent with xeroderma pigmentosum variant. [PMC11649263, PMC7304360, PMC6076188, PMC5891500, PMC4519681]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Frontometaphyseal dysplasia addresses specific complications. For craniofacial dimorphism and retrognathia, fronto-orbital cranioplasty combined with orthognathic surgery has been performed. Cutaneous lesions like xerosis and poikiloderma, along with keratitis, may be managed with anti-inflammatory treatment, sunscreens, and moisturizers, though keratitis can still severely impact sight. Obstructive uropathy, such as posterior urethral valves and bladder neck stenosis, can be treated with transurethral resection of urethral valves and bladder neck, alongside open cystolithotomy for bladder stones, leading to normal voiding. [PMC11649263, PMC6076188, PMC3268711]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Frontometaphyseal dysplasia can lead to significant long-term complications, including deafness and degenerative osteoarthropathy in weight-bearing joints. Patients may also develop acro-osteolysis and keratitis, with the latter potentially seriously weakening sight. Cutaneous lesions can develop slowly over several years. In one reported case, metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma was a fatal complication five years after diagnosis. [PMC6076188, PMC1048490]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inborn error of metabolism characterized by congenital hypertryptophanemia and hyperserotonemia. Patients are typically asymptomatic, although developmental delay, intellectual disability, and behavioral abnormalities, among others, have been reported in association.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hypertryptophanemia, specifically when due to tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase deficiency, is characterized by a biochemical phenotype of hypertryptophanemia and hyperserotoninemia. The underlying etiology involves compound heterozygosity for specific variants in the TDO2 gene. However, this biochemical profile does not appear to have significant clinical consequences in affected individuals. [PMC5421356]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hypertryptophanemia has been confirmed in humans due to tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase deficiency. This deficiency is caused by mutations in the TDO2 gene. In the first reported human case, compound heterozygosity for two rare variants, c.324G>C (p.Met108Ile) and c.491dup (p.Ile165Aspfs*12), was identified. The c.491dup variant prevents the production of soluble protein, while the c.324G>C variant leads to a catalytically less efficient enzyme that is prone to proteolytic degradation. [PMC5421356]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of hypertryptophanemia due to tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase deficiency is established by sequencing the TDO2 gene to identify underlying genetic variants, such as compound heterozygosity. The pathogenicity of these identified variants is subsequently confirmed through molecular-level studies. The biochemical phenotype, characterized by hypertryptophanemia and hyperserotoninemia, also contributes to the diagnostic assessment. [PMC5421356]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Hypertryptophanemia is caused by tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase deficiency, with the underlying etiology established by sequencing the TDO2 gene. The first human case involved compound heterozygosity for two rare variants, c.324G>C and c.491dup, indicating an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Molecular studies confirmed the pathogenicity of these variants, showing one does not produce soluble protein and the other in a catalytically less efficient enzyme prone to degradation. Importantly, the biochemical phenotype of hypertryptophanemia and hyperserotoninemia does not appear to have significant clinical consequences. [PMC5421356]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The biochemical phenotype of hypertryptophanemia and hyperserotoninemia, as observed in the first human case due to tryptophan 2,3-dioxygenase deficiency, does not appear to have significant clinical consequences. This suggests a generally benign prognosis for individuals with this condition. [PMC5421356]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: X-linked intellectual disability, Stevenson type is characterised by intellectual deficit, hypotonia, absent deep tendon reflexes, tapered fingers and excessive fingerprint arches, genu valgum, a characteristic face and small teeth. It has been described in four males from two generations of one family. The causative gene appears to be located in the q13 region of the X chromosome.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Stevenson type, is an X-linked condition affecting males. It was initially described in four males across two generations within a single white family of European ancestry. Female carriers do not exhibit symptoms. Genetic linkage analysis identified tight linkage to DXS1166 and DXS995 in Xq13 and Xq21 respectively. [PMC1050968]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Stevenson type, is characterized by distinctive facial features including a square configuration, tented upper lip, and thickening of the helices, upper eyelids, and alae nasi. Affected males present with poor muscle tone (hypotonia), absent deep tendon reflexes (areflexia), tapered fingers, excessive fingerprint arches, and genu valgum. Cognitive impairment is mild to moderate, with reported IQ scores between 40-51. Growth parameters, including head circumference, height, and weight, are typically comparable to or greater than unaffected male siblings. The condition is X-linked, with carriers showing no manifestations. [PMC1050968]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Stevenson type, is an X-linked condition, indicating a genetic basis linked to the X chromosome. It has been identified in males across two generations within a white family of European ancestry. Genetic linkage analysis further pinpointed its locus, showing tight linkage to markers DXS1166 in Xq13 and DXS995 in Xq21. [PMC1050968]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis is based on a distinctive clinical presentation, including characteristic facies (square configuration, tented upper lip, thickened helices, upper eyelids, and alae nasi), hypotonia, areflexia, tapered fingers, excessive fingerprint arches, and genu valgum. Affected males exhibit mild-moderate intellectual disability, with documented IQ scores between 40-51. Growth parameters (head circumference, height, weight) are typically comparable to unaffected male siblings. Genetic linkage analysis has identified tight linkage to markers DXS1166 and DXS995 in Xq13 and Xq21, respectively. [PMC1050968]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Stevenson type, is characterized by distinctive facies, hypotonia, areflexia, tapered fingers, excessive fingerprint arches, genu valgum, and mild-moderate intellectual disability. While this X-linked condition appears to be different from other syndromes with mental retardation, it shares certain similarities with the alpha thalassaemia-mental retardation syndrome (ATR-X). [PMC1050968]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Stevenson type, follows an X-linked inheritance pattern, affecting males. The condition has been observed in multiple males across generations within families. Female carriers typically do not exhibit any heterozygote manifestations. Linkage analysis has identified tight linkage to markers DXS1166 and DXS995 in Xq13 and Xq21, which can be relevant for genetic counseling and family planning. [PMC1050968]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Affected males experience mild-to-moderate intellectual disability, with documented IQ scores ranging between 40 and 51. Physical growth, including head circumference, height, and weight, is comparable to or greater than unaffected male siblings at both birth and maturity. Carriers of the condition do not show any heterozygote manifestations. [PMC1050968]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare cytotoxic cutaneous alpha-beta T-cell lymphoma characterized by solitary or multiple erythematous subcutaneous nodules and plaques that can be localized to the lower extremities or generalized. It has been recognized as a distinct subset of peripheral T-cell lymphomas originating and presenting primarily in the subcutaneous fat tissue and often associated with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact incidence is unknown but estimated around 1/10,000,000 individuals per year in Europe. A slight female preponderance has been reported. Median age of diagnosis is around 40 years old, but cases are reported from 1 to 90 years old.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma (SPTCL) is characterized by solitary or multiple erythematous subcutaneous nodules and plaques (proliferation of T lymphocytes and macrophages in the subcutaneous fat lobule), which appear in crops and are localized to the lower extremities or may be more generalized. Systemic manifestations include fever, chills, malaise, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, mucosal ulcers, and serosal effusions. SPTCL may be accompanied by hemophagocytic syndrome (characterized by the proliferation of histiocytes and phagocytosis of blood elements, hepatosplenomegaly, and coagulopathy and reported in approximately 30-40% of cases), which may be fatal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is not completely understood. An infectious trigger events has been described in some pediatric cases. Recently, germline homozygous mutation of HAVCR2 has been associated with SPTCL in 32 to 85% of patients.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Repeated biopsies may be required to establish the diagnosis. Pathology is characterized by CD8+ T cells expressing alpha-beta T cell antigen receptors (TCRs) and infiltrating subcutaneous adipose tissue, rimming adipocytes in a lace-like pattern, and adipocyte necrosis. The immunophenotype of the lymphoma is CD8+, CD56-, CD30-, granzymeB+, TiA-1, betaF1+. Molecular clonality assay should exclude gamma-delta T cell lymphoma which has a more aggressive course and is considered as a distinct entity.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other lymphomas as well as atypical lobular panniculitis and cytophagic histiocytic panniculitis. Lupus panniculitis can be excluded by the frequent MxA staining on lymphocytes, macrophages and on clusters of CD123+CD303+ PDC, and by the presence of lymphoid follicles and B cells.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission of HAVCR2-associated risk is autosomal recessive with incomplete penetrance. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having a child with heterozygous HAVCR2 variant at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: SPTCL may be rapidly fatal or indolent. Most patients respond to immunosuppressive drugs (ciclosporin A, corticosteroids, hydroxychloroquine or methotrexate). Systemic chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone) is an available option in severe case or when associated with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation has been proposed in severe cases and is a curative treatment option, especially in HAVCR2-variant cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: SPTCL is a life-threatening disease with a good prognosis in most cases. 2-years overall survival is estimated around 90% and complete remission around 80% with immunosuppressive drugs.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare developmental defect during embryogenesis characterised by an absence of the lens. CPAK can be associated with variable secondary ocular defects.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Congenital primary aphakia (CPAK) prevalance is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: CPAK is a congenital eye defect presenting at birth with no lens formation, resulting from a failure of lens induction from the surface ectoderm and aborted lens development. CPAK is often associated with other ocular anomalies, including aplasia/dysplasia of the anterior segment of the eye, microphthalmia, glaucoma.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CPAK is caused by variants in the FOXE3 gene. Most cases are autosomal recessive. It is important to note that both dominant and recessive variants in FOXE3 are associated with a variable mixed phenotype of developmental eye disorders including anterior segment dysgenesis, microphthalmia, Peters anomaly, sclerocornea, early-onset cataract, glaucoma and ocular coloboma.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Molecular diagnosis can be made through genetic testing, for example whole exome/genome sequencing and can be validated by bi-directional Sanger sequencing. Clinical diagnosis can be made based on clinical examination and confirmed with ultrasound. Anterior segment ultrasound biomicroscopy may aid detection of co-existent anterior segment dysgenesis. Due to the association of CPAK and the rubella virus, a TORCH complex evalutation is also recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Transabdominal ultrasound at 23 weeks gestation has detected CPAK.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic testing for FOXE3 variants will provide a molecular diagnosis. This yields information regarding carrier status and provide choices that would not otherwise be available to facilitate decision making for the patient and their family. Genetic testing is essential for defining inheritance patterns, carrier status and enabling effective genetic counselling with consequent implications for prenatal or pre-implantation genetic diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: CPAK should be managed by specialists with expertise in the condition. Supportive measures for those with sight impairment include involvement of social services. Regular follow-up will be required to monitor progression of associated anterior segment dysgenesis and glaucoma with medical and surgical interventions where needed. Intraocular surgery is not advised unless steps are taken to avoid inflammatory membrane formation and subsequent retinal detachment. Regular refraction to reduce/prevent amblyopia. Genetic counselling should be offered to the family.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Early diagnosis will enable prompt supportive treatment.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare acute myeloid leukemia that occurs predominantly in childhood and particularly in children with Down syndrome (DS-AMKL). Nonspecific symptoms may be irritability, weakness, and dizziness while specific symptoms include pallor, fever, mucocutaneous bleeding, hepatosplenomegaly, neurological manifestations and rarely lymphadenopathy. Acute panmyelosis with myelofibrosis may also be associated with AMKL. In contrast to DS-AMKL (around 80 % survival), non-DS-AMKL is an AML subgroup associated with poor prognosis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): AMKL; AML M7; Acute megakaryocytic leukemia; Acute myeloid leukemia M7

DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Down syndrome myeloid hyperplasia includes transient abnormal myelopoiesis (TAM) and the myeloid leukemia associated with Down syndrome (ML-DS). The mutation of GATA1 gene is essential in the development of Down syndrome combined with TAM or ML-DS. Some patients with TAM are asymptomatic and may also present with severe manifestations such as hepatosplenomegaly and hydrops. two cases of prenatally diagnosed TAM. One case was a rare placental low percentage 21 trisomy mosiacism, resulting in the occurrence of a false negative NIPT. The final diagnosis was made at 36 weeks of gestation when ultrasound revealed significant enlargement of the foetal liver and spleen and an enlarged heart; the foetus eventually died in utero. We detected a placenta with a low percentage (5-8%) of trisomy 21 mosiacism by Copy Number Variation Sequencing (CNV-seq) and Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH).... [PMC10588144]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inborn error of metabolism characterized by elevated levels of imino acids (proline, hydroxyproline) and glycine in urine due to defective reabsorption in the kidney. The condition is considered benign and not associated with any specific clinical phenotype. Mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Cystathioninuria, renal iminoglycinuria and...alpha 1-antitrypsin...deficiency in the same family: relevance in medical practice. [PMC1704166]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Iminoglycinuria has been observed to co-occur with other conditions within the same family, such as cystathioninuria and alpha 1-antitrypsin deficiency. The presence of these conditions together may be relevant for medical practice when considering a differential diagnosis. [PMC1704166]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inherited inborn error of metabolism resulting in a severe zinc deficiency and characterized by acral dermatitis, alopecia, diarrhea and growth failure.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): AEZ; Inherited zinc deficiency; Acrodermatitis enteropathica, zinc deficiency type

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of Acrodermatitis enteropathica (AE) is unknown. It is more common in the North-West of Tunisia.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: AE usually presents in the first 4-10 weeks of life in infants that are not breast-fed and at around the time of weaning in breast-fed infants, as cow's milk contains more zinc-binding phytates that impede zinc absorption. AE is characterized by eczematous pink scaly plaques that can become pustular, vesiculobullous, psoriasisform or crusted. Lesions usually involve the acral, periorificial and typically the anogenital areas. Skin lesions may evolve into erosions without treatment and are susceptible to secondary staphylococcal and candidal infections. Diarrhea, generalized alopecia and Beau-Reil lines on the nails are frequent manifestations. Paronychia, conjunctivitis, blepharitis and erythematous oral mucous membranes are also sometimes observed. Other features associated with severe and chronic zinc deficiency include failure to thrive, mental slowness, photophobia, hypogeusia, anemia, poor wound healing, hypogonadism in males, and delayed puberty.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: AE is due to a mutation in the SLC39A4 gene (8q24.3) that encodes a zinc transporter protein (called the Zip4 transporter). Zip4 is needed for the transcellular absorption of zinc into the enterocytes of the duodenum and jejunum where the ZnT-zinc transporters (that are not affected) allow for the transport of zinc into the bloodstream. Mutations in the SLC39A4 lead to zinc malapsorption. This can only be corrected by a high dietary intake of zinc that allows for a small fraction of zinc to be absorbed paracellularly, without the aid of Zip4.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical findings (diarrhea and acral dermatitis) as well as laboratory testing. Patients have low plasma zinc concentrations and low levels of serum alkaline phosphatase. Molecular genetic testing can identify a mutation in the SLC39A4 gene, confirming diagnosis of AE.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include impetigo contagiosa, candidiasis, psoriasis, and other pathogen-related skin diseases. Sickle cell disease and related diseases, non-genetic or acquired causes of zinc deficiency such as glucagonoma, chronic liver and renal diseases, nutritional deficiency, chronic inflammatory bowel diseases, AIDS, burn injuries, and excessive perspiration in hot climates should also be excluded.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: AE is inherited autosomal recessively. Genetic counseling is recommended to identify other affected family members before the onset of symptoms.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for AE. In the majority of cases, zinc supplementation therapy results in the disappearance of AE symptoms, but this treatment is life-long and relapses can occur. Initial dosages of 5-10 mg/kg/day of elemental zinc, followed by maintenance doses of 1-2 mg/kg/day are recommended and are taken orally. Zinc sulphate is the best tolerated preparation, in most cases, but it can also be administered as acetate, gluconate and amino acid chelates. Zinc and copper levels should be monitored regularly. Dosages need to be increased during periods of growth, such as adolescence and during pregnancy, when relapses can occur.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With adherence to life-long zinc substitution therapy, the prognosis is good. Only when infants are left untreated can the disease be fatal.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, malignant, primary thymic neoplasm originating from neuroendocrine cells, presenting as a mass within the anterior mediastinum. Patients typically present with nonspecific symptoms, such as chest pain, cough, shortness of breath, or in some cases, superior vena cava syndrome, although patients could be asymptomatic during the early stages or present with multiple endocrine neoplasia type I. Ectopic production of ACTH and serotonin can lead to Cushing syndrome and carcinoid syndrome, respectively.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Atypical carcinoid of the thymus is an exceptionally rare neuroendocrine tumor originating from neuroendocrine cells within the thymus. These tumors often present with no symptoms or with nonspecific clinical signs, making early diagnosis particularly challenging. Despite their rarity, atypical carcinoids are clinically significant due to their aggressive nature and relatively poor prognosis. Early detection and appropriate management are therefore crucial to improving patient outcomes. In , the case of a 64-year-old patient in whom an atypical carcinoid of the thymus was incidentally discovered following a thoracic computed tomography scan performed for unrelated reasons. Imaging revealed a suspicious anterior mediastinal mass, which was subsequently surgically resected. Histopathological examination, supported by immunohistochemical analysis, confirmed the diagnosis of an atypical... [PMC12372005, PMC12191037, PMC11176988, PMC11390396, PMC10238025]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of thymic neuroendocrine tumors typically involves surgical resection as the cornerstone for localized disease, with complete resection being crucial. Minimally invasive approaches like thoracoscopic excision or single-incision port robot-assisted surgery are utilized, and complex surgery with vascular replacement may be necessary for advanced cases. For advanced or recurrent disease, systemic therapies include platinum-based chemotherapy, everolimus, somatostatin analogs, and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy. Immunotherapy and radioimmunotherapy are emerging options. In cases of severe hypercortisolism due to ectopic ACTH syndrome, steroid inhibitors such as ketoconazole, metyrapone, or osilodrostat are used, with etomidate serving as an intravenous option for rapid cortisol reduction. A multidisciplinary approach and prolonged, lifelong surveillance are essential due to the aggressive nature and high recurrence rate of these tumors. [PMC11760978, PMC11920866, PMC11894571, PMC12191037, PMC11558849]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Thymic neuroendocrine tumors (NETT), particularly atypical carcinoids, are malignant and exhibit aggressive behavior, often leading to a relatively poor prognosis. They are frequently diagnosed at an advanced stage due to nonspecific symptoms, and delayed diagnosis can result in disease progression. Prognosis largely depends on tumor stage, differentiation, resectability, and functional activity. A high recurrence rate necessitates prolonged and even lifelong surveillance. Managing advanced or recurrent disease is challenging, with limited effective options for patients who do not respond to initial therapies in the metastatic setting. Early diagnosis, complete surgical resection, and tailored adjuvant treatments are crucial for improving survival outcomes. [PMC11760978, PMC12372005, PMC11894571, PMC12191037, PMC11211248]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) is a rare malformation syndrome caused by excessive maternal consumption of alcohol during pregnancy. It is characterized by prenatal and/or postnatal growth deficiency (weight and/or height <10th percentile), a unique cluster of minor facial anomalies (short palpebral fissures, flat and smooth philtrum, and thin upper lip) and severe central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities including microcephaly, and cognitive and behavioral impairment (intellectual disability, deficit in general cognition, learning and language, executive function, visual-spatial processing, memory, and attention).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): ARBD; ARND; Alcohol-related birth defects; Alcohol-related neurodevelopmental disorder; FAS; FASD; Fetal alcohol spectrum disorders

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) is a prevalent condition, with recent estimates indicating that it afflicts up to 5% of American children. This suggests a significant public health impact within the United States population. [PMC7891191]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) encompasses a broad range of disabilities resulting from prenatal alcohol exposure. Clinical manifestations include characteristic facial features such as microcephaly, epicanthal folds, flat midface, low nasal bridge, indistinct philtrum, and a thin upper lip. Individuals often present with growth restriction, intellectual impairment, and neurodevelopmental delay. Severe behavioral problems, including aggression, tantrums, self-harm, anxiety, and defiant behavior, are common, with many meeting criteria for autism spectrum disorder. Neurological findings can include porencephaly, cerebral hemisphere asymmetry, and temporal lobe abnormalities, potentially leading to secondary psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia. Ocular anomalies, such as optic nerve hypoplasia and lens opacification, are reported. Cardiac defects, including ventricular and atrial septal defects, conotruncal defects, and rhythm alterations, along with mitral incompetence, can also occur. Myasthenia gravis has also been uniquely associated. [PMC11988866, PMC10527597, PMC7891191, PMC7402805, PMC7196488]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Fetal alcohol syndrome (FAS) and fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) are complex malformative diseases caused by the teratogenic effect of alcohol consumed during pregnancy, particularly maternal alcohol abuse throughout pregnancy, especially in the first trimester. Alcohol is described as a teratogenic agent producing dysmorphism and multisystem problems, with moderate to excessive prenatal alcohol exposure being the primary etiological factor. The severity and clinical presentation can be influenced by genetic risk or protective factors, such as FMR1 mutations or specific microdeletions (e.g., 18q12.3-q21.1), and environmental factors, which can have an additive effect. Alcohol is preferentially toxic to temporal lobe patterning during gestation. [PMC11988866, PMC10527597, PMC7402805, PMC7196488, PMC6923862]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) involves identifying characteristic facial features such as microcephaly, epicanthal folds, flat midface, low nasal bridge, indistinct philtrum, and a thin upper lip. Imaging studies, including echocardiograms for cardiac defects and brain magnetic resonance imaging for cerebral abnormalities like asymmetry, hypoplasia, ventricular dilatation, and porencephaly, also contribute to diagnosis. Crucially, ethylglucuronide (EtG) concentration in the neonate's hair, measured by liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, can detect prenatal alcohol exposure, significantly improving diagnosis, particularly when maternal alcohol consumption is not reported. [PMC7402805]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis of Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) can be challenging, particularly in neonates and infants. Fragile X Syndrome (FXS) is a key consideration, as both conditions are common causes of intellectual disability and can co-occur, leading to more severe phenotypes with shared features like autism spectrum disorder and severe behavioral problems. Other genetic diseases and chromosomal abnormalities, such as 18q deletion syndrome, should also be excluded, as they can present with similar clinical findings including growth restriction, developmental delay, intellectual deficiency, and abnormal facial features. Rare neurological diseases like porencephaly may also prompt consideration of FASD. [PMC11988866, PMC10527597, PMC7402805, PMC7196488]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: While Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) is caused by prenatal alcohol exposure, genetic factors can significantly influence its clinical presentation and severity. Genetic counseling should consider the importance of adequate chromosomal testing and other genetic analyses to exclude genetic diseases with similar clinical findings, such as microdeletions or Fragile X Syndrome, which can co-occur and exacerbate the phenotype. Such testing can help explain phenotypic discordancy among individuals with similar prenatal alcohol exposure and is crucial for differential diagnosis in complex alcohol-induced developmental disorders. [PMC11988866, PMC10527597, PMC7402805, PMC7196488]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Research on pharmacological modalities for Fetal Alcohol Spectrum Disorder (FASD) is limited, primarily focusing on stimulants for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder or second-generation atypical antipsychotics for aggression. A retrospective case series explored the effect of cannabis, mostly cannabidiol (CBD), on severe disruptive behavior in children and young adults with FASD. observed a marked and statistically significant decrease in disruptive behavior scores after cannabis use. These findings suggest that CBD may offer a beneficial approach for managing serious disruptive behavior in FASD, warranting further investigation through well-controlled studies. [PMC7891191]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder (FASD) encompasses a broad range of disabilities, often leading to intellectual impairment, neurodevelopmental delay, and autism spectrum disorder. Individuals frequently exhibit severe behavioral problems, including aggression, tantrums, self-harming, anxiety, and defiant behavior, though some disruptive behaviors may improve with interventions like cannabidiol. Neurological complications can include porencephaly and temporal lobe pathology, which may contribute to the development of secondary psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia in adolescence. Cardiac anomalies, including congenital structural heart defects and asymptomatic rhythm alterations, are also associated with FASD. The prognosis can be significantly worsened when FASD co-occurs with other conditions like Fragile X Syndrome, resulting in a much more severe clinical presentation and intellectual impairment, further complicated by environmental factors. [PMC11988866, PMC10527597, PMC7891191, PMC7402805, PMC6923862]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: LCAT (lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase) deficiency is a rare lipoprotein metabolism disorder characterized clinically by corneal opacities, and sometimes renal failure and hemolytic anemia, and biochemically by severely reduced HDL cholesterol.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of LCAT deficiency is unknown. About 125 cases have been reported to date worldwide. Most cases were reported in Europe, Japan and Canada.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Age of onset is variable but most patients are diagnosed during adulthood. Two familial forms of LCAT deficiency have been reported: familial LCAT deficiency (FLD) characterized by corneal opacities, anemia and renal insufficiency, and Fish-eye disease (FED) characterized by corneal opacities and sometimes atherosclerosis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: LCAT deficiency is caused by deficient or absent catalytic activity of the LCAT enzyme, which catalyzes the formation of cholesterol esters in lipoproteins and is encoded by the LCAT gene (16q22.1). Accumulation of unesterified cholesterol in the body, e.g. in the cornea, erythrocytes and kidneys, is thought to underlie the clinical manifestations. To date, more than 85 mutations in the LCAT gene have been identified. LCAT deficiency follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Nephrotic syndrome (NS) is characterized by proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia. Apart from the traditional causes of NS, such as minimal change disease, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, diabetes, infections, malignancies, autoimmune conditions, and nephrotoxic agents, there are also rare causes of NS, whose knowledge is of the utmost importance. The aim of this article was to highlight the less well-known causes that have a significant impact on diagnosis and treatment. Genetic syndromes such as Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia, familial lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase deficiency with two clinical variants (fish-eye Disease and the p.Leu364Pro mutation), lead to NS through mechanisms involving podocyte and lipid metabolism dysfunction. Congenital disorders of glycosylation and Nail-Patella Syndrome emphasize the role of deranged protein processing and... [PMC12383661, PMC11822860, PMC8953693, PMC3736715, PMC3373316]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for LCAT deficiency includes other genetic syndromes causing nephrotic syndrome, such as Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia, congenital disorders of glycosylation, and Nail-Patella Syndrome. An immune-mediated acquired LCAT deficiency, caused by inhibitory anti-LCAT antibodies, can present with glomerular lesions and foam cell accumulation similar to familial LCAT deficiency (FLD), but may also feature membranous nephropathy, which is not typical of FLD. Furthermore, a frameshift mutation in the apolipoprotein A-I gene can lead to HDL deficiency, corneal opacities, and partial LCAT deficiency, clinically resembling fish-eye disease, despite a wild-type LCAT sequence. Distinguishing these conditions often relies on genetic analysis, renal biopsy with histopathological and electron microscopy findings, and specific antibody testing. [PMC12383661, PMC3736715, PMC295069]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: LCAT deficiency, encompassing familial LCAT deficiency (FLD) and fish-eye disease (FED), is a rare autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in the LCAT gene. Genetic analysis is essential for prompt recognition and diagnosis. Affected individuals are typically homozygous or compound heterozygous for LCAT mutations. Heterozygous carriers of the LCAT gene defect can be identified, often presenting with half-normal enzyme levels or reduced HDL-cholesterol and apolipoprotein A-I levels. Family analysis and genetic testing are crucial for establishing the causal relationship between mutations and the biochemical phenotype, aiding in counseling for affected families. [PMC12383661, PMC11822860, PMC8953693, PMC3373316, PMC3361081]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Currently, no specific treatment is available for familial LCAT deficiency, though novel therapeutics are under development, with restoring LCAT activity to subnormal levels suggested as a potential strategy to prevent renal disease progression. Management focuses on addressing specific manifestations. For renal disease, conservative therapies, including careful control of blood pressure and lifestyle measures to optimize non-HDL lipoproteins, are important. Monitoring markers of anemia and controlling hypercholesterolemia and hypertriglyceridemia may also improve renal prognosis. For end-stage renal disease, kidney and liver transplantations have been performed. Ophthalmologic interventions, such as deep lamellar keratoplasty, phacoemulsification, and intraocular lens insertion, are used to treat corneal opacities and cataracts. [PMC12383661, PMC11822860, PMC8953693, PMC8473656, PMC3736715]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, autosomal recessive, acid sphingomyelinase deficiency characterized clinically by onset in infancy or early childhood with failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly, interstitial lung disease and rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disorders.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Infantile neurovisceral ASMD; Niemann-Pick disease type A; NPD-A

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The birth prevalence of acid sphingomyelinase deficiency (combined both Niemann-Pick disease (NPD) types A and B) is estimated between 1/167,000-250,000 in Europe. Niemann-Pick disease type A (NPD-A) is more prevalent in the Ashkenazi Jewish population, where the estimated birth rate is estimated at 1/33,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The first symptom in NPD-A is hepatosplenomegaly, usually noted in the first few months of life. Other non-neurological findings include feeding problems, failure to thrive, gastrointestinal complaints (e.g., constipation, diarrhea, and vomiting), recurrent respiratory infections, persistently elevated transaminases, and irritability. Early neurological manifestations include muscular hypotonia, weakness and feeding difficulties. Affected infants have decreased linear growth and body weight. By 6 months of age, global development delay becomes evident and regression of developmental milestones is noted. With advancing age, the loss of motor function and the deterioration of intellectual capabilities are progressively debilitating. A classic cherry-red spot of the macula of the retina is eventually present in all affected children after 6 months of age. Interstitial lung disease results in frequent respiratory infections and often respiratory failure. Osteoporosis is common, presumably due to infiltration and poor nutrition.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: NPDA is caused by mutations in the sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 1 (SMPD1) gene (locus 11p15.4), leading to decreased activity of acid sphingomyelinase (ASM), which results in lysosomal accumulation of sphingomyelin (SM) and secondary increases in the concentrations of cholesterol and other lipids.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of NPD-A is established by detection of biallelic pathogenic variants in SMPD1 and/or residual acid sphingomyelinase enzyme activity (in peripheral blood lymphocytes, cultured skin fibroblasts or dry blood spots (DBS)). The de-acylated form of sphingomyelin (lyso-SPM) is increased in NPD-A and could be measured in plasma and DBS. Bone marrow examination reveals the histochemical characteristic, ''Niemann-Pick'' foam cells.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other lysosomal storage diseases such as Gaucher disease, GM1-and GM2-gangliosidosis, Niemann-Pick disease type C, lysosomal acid lipase deficiency, hematologic malignancy, and primary hepatic disease (e.g., fatty liver, autoimmune, chronic hepatitis B-related, cryptogenic cirrhosis).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis for pregnancies at increased risk is possible by testing of ASM enzyme activity or by DNA analysis if both SMPD1 pathogenic variants in the family are known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: NPD-A is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Currently, only supportive care is available for patients with NPD-A. The disease is best managed by an interprofessional team that includes a gastroenterologist, endocrinologist, neurologist, and geneticist. Also, family care, nursing support, and social support are an integral part of the management.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The clinical course is characterized by a brief period of normal development followed by a severe neurodegenerative course and death in the first 5 years of life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare group of genetic connective tissue disorders characterized by ophthalmic, auditory, orofacial and articular manifestations. The two main clinical forms are clinically distinguished by the vitreous phenotype; stickler type 1 by a vestigial vitreous gel in the immediate retrolental space, bordered by a distinct folded membrane, and Stickler type 2 by sparse and irregularly thickened bundles of ﬁbers throughout the vitreous cavity.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence at birth has been estimated at around 1/7,500 to 1/9,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Ocular manifestations include a high risk of retinal detachment, congenital abnormalities of vitreous development, congenital myopia and congenital cataract. Retinal paravascular lattice degeneration may develop in adulthood. Orofacial features include Pierre Robin sequence (PRS), cleft palate and midfacial hypoplasia. In addition, congenital high-frequency sensorineural deficit is common and variable conductive hearing loss may also occur. Musculoskeletal problems include spinal abnormalities, hypermobility, epiphyseal dysplasia and premature osteoarthritis. Two other forms are characterized by the ocular-only (autosomal dominant rhegmatogenous retinal detachment) or systemic-only (Stickler syndrome type 3) manifestations.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Stickler syndrome is an inherited connective tissue disorder most commonly caused by mutations in the genes encoding collagen types II (COL2A1, 12q13.11), IX (COL9A1, 6q13; COL9A2, 1p34.2; COL9A3, 20q13.33), and XI (COL11A1, 1p21.1), but rarer non-collagen gene variants have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made on the basis of clinical and ophthalmic examination and confirmed by molecular genetic analysis. Vitreous phenotyping is helpful in segregating sub-types as many of the other shared clinical features are similar.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses includes spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita, spondyloperipheral dysplasia, Kniest dysplasia, Wagner syndrome, Knobloch syndrome, multiple epiphyseal dysplasia, metatropic dysplasia, Marfan syndrome and Marshall syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis may be possible. First trimester prenatal diagnosis based on the analysis of linked markers may be possible. In second trimester, ultrasound may be helpful in detecting features such as micrognathia or cleft palate, but their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance for Stickler syndrome type 1 and 2 is autosomal dominant; the risk of disease transmission to offspring is 50%. Autosomal recessive inheritance is rarely observed but should be considered if there is a history of consanguinity. However, there is wide variation in clinical expression of the disease. The disease is highly penetrant but with wide variability in its extraocular phenotype. Affected family members in the high risk sub-groups should be offered prophylactic treatment to reduce the risk of retinal detachment and be offered genetic counselling.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management should be multidisciplinary and as clinical expression is very variable, treatment needs to be adapted to each case. Patients with PRS or cleft palate will require referral to a specialist multidisciplinary cleft team for assessment and management. This may also include speech therapy for patients with sub-clinical or soft palate cleft. Any refractive error should be corrected and prophylactic retinopexy discussed for the high risk variants. For type 1 Stickler syndrome, retinopexy substantially reduces the risk of giant retinal tear detachment. Patients should be warned of the signs and symptoms of retinal detachment and have rapid access to specialist vitreoretinal expertise in the event of such a development. Cataract is common and the surgical management, particularly in the pediatric sub-group requires specialist care. All affected patients should be referred for specialist audiology assessment if this has not already been undertaken by the cleft team. Patients may be unaware of sub-clinical hearing loss, particularly if present from birth. Although intellect is normal, pre-verbal children may need additional educational support with respect to their auditory and visual impairment. Specialist rheumatology and orthopedic management may be required for the associated arthropathy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis of the disease is generally good. There is no direct reduction on life expectancy. The quality of life will differ depending on clinical expression, age of diagnosis and degree (if any) of associated visual loss, deafness, speech impairment and arthropathy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare generalized, genetic disorder of proximal tubular transport characterized by excessive urine output with loss of low molecular weight solutes (amino acids, glucose, low-molecular weight proteins, organic acids, carnitine, calcium, phosphate, potassium, bicarbonate) and water, and which can be life threatening.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Primary Fanconi renal syndrome; DeToni-Debré-Fanconi syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of the condition is not known.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset is typically between infancy and childhood with symptoms related to tubular loss of nutrients, water and electrolytes. Typical clinical features include failure to thrive and rickets, normoglycemic glycosuria and polyuria with bicarbonaturia leading to hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis. Nephrocalcinosis and kidney stones are less common.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The genetic etiology has been identified in a handful of families, and includes mutations in either GATM (15q21.1), involved in mitochondrial function, EHHADH (3q27.2), due to a specific mutation (c.7G>A) that introduces a mitochondrial targeting motif, or SLC34A1 (5q35.3) which encodes the proximal tubular sodium-phosphate transporter, NaPi-IIa. However, the disease may be due to unidentified mutations. Of note, the gene SLC34A1 is also associated with two other diseases: autosomal recessive infantile hypercalcemia and dominant hypophosphatemia with nephrolithiasis or osteoporosis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation as well as plasma electrolytes levels and evaluation of urinary solute excretion (aminoaciduria, proteinuria, phosphaturia, calciuria, uricosuria, glycosuria).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Before the diagnosis of primary Fanconi renotubular syndrome is made all causes of secondary Fanconi syndrome must be ruled out, including both inherited (cystinosis, tyrosinemia type I, fructosemia, Wilson's disease, galactosemia, glycogen storage disease, Dent disease, Oculocerebrorenal syndrome of Lowe, arthrogryposis-renal dysfunction-cholestasis (ARC) syndrome, mitochondrial cytopathies) and acquired disorders (drug or heavy metal poisoning, malignancies).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The majority of reported cases are sporadic and may be associated with de novo mutations. However, hereditary forms have been reported. The pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant for EHHADH and GATM, and autosomal recessive for SLC34A1. The risk of transmission to offspring is 50% for autosomal dominant disease and, where both parents are heterozygous for the pathogenic mutation, 25% in autosomal recessive disease.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic. Kidney transplantation is curative.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With adequate fluid, electrolyte and nutrient supplementation, adequate physical and neurocognitive development is usually possible. Mutations in GATM are associated with progressive chronic kidney disease, whereas this has not been observed with EHHADH-associated disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, highly variable, multisystemic disorder mainly characterized by short stature, distinctive facial features, congenital heart defects, cardiomyopathy and an increased risk to develop tumors in childhood.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The birth prevalence of Noonan syndrome (NS) is estimated between 1:1000 to 1:2500.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: NS typically presents in the neonatal period with feeding difficulties and failure to thrive. Characteristic facial features are often more obvious in infancy : high broad forehead, hypertelorism, palpebral ptosis and downward slanting palpebral fissures, low-set, thick, posteriorly rotated ears, deep philtrum, micrognathia, curly hair and a short neck with sometimes a pterygium colli. With age, the face becomes triangular, with marked skinfolds. The most common congenital heart defect is pulmonary valve stenosis (50-60%) with pulmonic valve dysplasia and various types of cardiac malformations (atrial septal defects, ventricular septal defects ect.). Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy of antenatal onset is common (20%) and may be stable or rapidly progressive. Dilation of coronary arteries and moya-moya disease may develop with aging. Growth delay affects 50%, uncommonly associated with growth hormone deficiency. Weight gain is difficult and many patients remain lean throughout life. Major orthopedic manifestations include sternal deformity, talipes equinovarus, and progressive scoliosis (onset at adolescence). Skin is often dry and sometimes hyperkeratotic on hands and feet. Hair is curly and may be thick or sparse. Peripheral lymphedema may be present and may be progressive and extensive in some. Ocular anomalies (strabismus, refractive errors), and dental crowding are common. Hearing loss is present in 10%. Delayed speech and learning difficulties affect 30-40%. Intellectual disability (often mild) is present in 10-20%. Dyspraxia (clumsiness), attention deficit disorder, agitation, mood disorders and emotional disturbances are not rare, as well as difficulties in identifying and expressing emotions, which can lead to more difficult social interactions. Motor development and puberty are delayed and short stature is present in 50%. Unilateral or bilateral cryptorchidism is present in two-thirds of boys, and hypofertility may affect males, but not females. Thyroid dysfunction may occur. Coagulation defects are frequent but rarely clinically significant. In childhood, there is an increased risk of tumors and leukemias (noteworthy juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia), with a cumulative cancer risk of about 4% by age 20. The risk of common adult cancer does not appear increased.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: NS is caused by mutations in PTPN11 (12q24.13) seen in 50% of cases, SOS1 (2p22.1) in 15%, RAF1 (3p25.2), RIT1 (1q22) and LZTR1(22q11.21), and less commonly in other genes associated with the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway. The clinical spectrum of NS may differ slightly between causative genes, and some forms have been described as ''Noonan like'' (NS-like disorder with juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia and NS-like disorder with loose anagen hair).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis relies on clinical manifestations but may be difficult because of the highly variable presentation. Molecular genetic testing of the causative genes helps diagnosis and genetic counseling. Mild cases may remain undiagnosed and only brought to clinical attention in adulthood after the birth of a more severely affected child.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Cardio-Facio-Cutaneous syndrome, Costello syndrome, Neurofibromatosis type 1, Noonan syndrome with multiple lentigines (all RASopathies), Baraitser-Winter, Aarskog and Escobar syndromes.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible on chorionic villi or amniotic fluid. Prenatal signs of NS are nonspecific: increased nuchal translucency, cystic hygroma and/or ascites (that may lead to fetal demise), polyhydramnios, cardiomyopathy and congenital heart defect.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance of NS is autosomal dominant, except LZTR1 which can be either dominant or recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment requires a multidisciplinary approach. Cardiovascular anomalies are treated with standard approaches. Treatment of growth retardation with growth hormone is still controversial. Developmental disabilities should be addressed early.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is variable since the presentation ranges from mild/unrecognized manifestations in adulthood to severe disorder with life-threatening heart disease or malignancy in infancy. Severe cardiomyopathy may lead to early demise.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Uncombable hair syndrome (UHS), or pili trianguli et canaliculi, is a rare scalp hair shaft dysplasia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset is usually between ages 3 months and 12 years. Hair becomes progressively silvery-blond or straw-colored, dry and disordered, standing out from the scalp and growing in different directions, and being unmanageable to comb it flat. The quantity of hair stays normal. Microscopic analysis reveals a longitudinal groove of the hair shaft with a triangular or kidney-shaped section. The anomaly is clinically detectable when approximately 50% of hairs are affected. Several conditions have been reported to occur with UHS such as ectodermal dysplasia, retinal dysplasia, retinal pigmentary dystrophy, juvenile cataract, digit abnormalities, tooth enamel anomalies, oligodontia, phalango-epiphyseal dysplasia, alopecia areata, atopic eczema, and ichthyosis vulgaris.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The stiffness and brightness of hair are supposed to result from a misshapen dermal papilla inducing an anomaly in the keratinization of the inner root sheath.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on clinical and microscopic observation, but electron microscopic analysis of hair shaft can eliminate other hair anomalies.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Rapp-Hodgkin ectodermal dysplasia, loose anagen hair syndrome, ectrodactyly, cleft/lip palate syndrome, familial tricho-odonto-onchyial ectodermal dysplasia with syndactyly and other ectodermal dysplasias.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: UHS is likely to be an autosomal dominant inherited disease with a variable penetrance but no causal gene has been identified yet.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: UHS spontaneously regresses in late childhood and only gentle care including conditioners, soft brushes and avoidance of harsh treatments cares of the hair are recommended. Biotin treatment as been used in several patients and might be useful to control nail fragility, leading to acclaimed increase in hair growth after 4 months of supplementation.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Uncombable hair syndrome typically manifests during early childhood. The condition generally lessens as children grow older, often resolving gradually by puberty. In some cases, a temporary change in hair shaft appearance can occur, with one reported instance of abrupt resolution after nine months. [PMC6489048, PMC1627762]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Bleeding diathesis due to a collagen receptor defect
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic coagulation disorder characterized by a mild to moderate bleeding tendency due to impaired platelet activation and aggregation in response to collagen, or impaired platelet-vessel wall interaction, resulting from a collagen receptor defect. Patients manifest with ecchymoses, epistaxis, menorrhagia, and/or post-traumatic and post-surgery bleeding complications. Laboratory analysis reveals prolonged bleeding time and, occasionally, mild thrombocytopenia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: CD36 deficiency, which involves a collagen receptor, is a rare condition. It exhibits a disproportionately higher prevalence in individuals of East Asian, African, and Arabian descent. The co-occurrence of CD36 deficiency with other platelet glycoprotein deficiencies, such as Glanzmann thrombasthenia, is exceedingly rare, estimated at approximately 1 in 100 million. Awareness of these coexisting platelet disorders and their ramifications is limited due to their stochastic rarity. [PMC12005580]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Patients with this condition, exemplified by the β3(R760C) mutation, present with macrothrombocytopenia, characterized by decreased platelet counts and reduced expression of αIIbβ3 and glycoprotein IV (GPVI). This leads to impaired platelet aggregation, spreading on fibrinogen, and agonist-induced P-selectin expression. Megakaryocytes show impaired filopodia and lamellipodia formation, as well as abnormal proplatelet formation. The mutation also impairs both inside-out and outside-in signaling of αIIbβ3, affecting actin rearrangement and RhoA activation, and in a shortened platelet life span. [PMC12320448]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The bleeding diathesis is caused by a specific nonactivating β3(R760C) mutation in the ITGB3 gene. This mutation leads to macrothrombocytopenia, characterized by reduced expression of αIIbβ3 and glycoprotein IV (GPVI). The underlying mechanism involves impaired inside-out and outside-in signaling of αIIbβ3, which subsequently in abnormal actin rearrangement and impaired RhoA activation. These cellular dysfunctions are identified as major contributors to the development of macrothrombocytopenia. [PMC12320448]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves identifying specific genetic mutations, such as the β3(R760C) mutation, which is associated with macrothrombocytopenia. Key diagnostic indicators include reduced platelet counts and decreased expression of αIIbβ3 and glycoprotein IV (GPVI). Platelet function tests reveal impaired aggregation, agonist-induced JON/A binding, P-selectin expression, and spreading on fibrinogen. Further assessment may show impaired filopodia and lamellipodia formation, abnormal proplatelet formation, and significantly impaired RhoA activation, reflecting defects in αIIbβ3 signaling and actin rearrangement. [PMC12320448]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for bleeding diathesis include other platelet glycoprotein deficiencies. Glanzmann thrombasthenia, a rare autosomal recessive bleeding disorder, from GP IIb/IIIa deficiency or dysfunction, impairing platelet aggregation. Platelet GP IV (CD36) deficiency, which has a limited role in primary hemostasis, can also contribute to bleeding and may coexist with other platelet disorders. Congenital macrothrombocytopenia, particularly with ITGB3 mutations, can also cause bleeding diathesis due to impaired αIIbβ3/RhoA pathway, reduced αIIbβ3 and glycoprotein VI (GPVI) expression, and impaired platelet aggregation and spreading. [PMC12005580, PMC12320448]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The macrothrombocytopenia associated with the β3(R760C) mutation in ITGB3 appears to be inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, as the phenotype was observed in heterozygous individuals within a family study. This mutation leads to reduced expression of αIIbβ3 and glycoprotein IV, impairing platelet function. While heterozygous individuals exhibit macrothrombocytopenia, studies in knockin mice suggest a more severe reduction in platelet counts in homozygous individuals. [PMC12320448]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management is complicated by the development of antibodies against missing platelet glycoproteins, leading to immune-mediated platelet transfusion refractoriness and unresponsiveness to platelet transfusions when most needed. In cases of dual glycoprotein deficiencies, finding crossmatch-compatible platelets is particularly challenging due to the rarity of specific deficient blood donors. Therefore, thorough evaluation of platelet glycoprotein deficiencies is important to prevent future antibody formation or reduce bleeding risk with pre-existing antibodies. [PMC12005580]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Almost all mutations of ITGA2B or ITGB3 identified in congenital macrothrombocytopenia induce constitutive activation of αIIbβ3. However, whether concomitant αIIbβ3 activation is essential for macrothrombocytopenia development remains unknown. Recently, we identified the β3(R760C) mutation that does not induce αIIbβ3 activation in a patient with macrothrombocytopenia. The family study showed that macrothrombocytopenia with reduced expression of αIIbβ3 and glycoprotein IV (GPVI) appeared to be associated with patients heterozygous for β3(R760C). We generated β3(R760C) knockin (KI) mice and investigated the effects of the mutation on platelet/megakaryote biology. Macrothrombocytopenia was decreased to 76% and 40% of platelet counts in heterozygous (Hetero) and homozygous (Homo) KI mice, respectively, when compared with the wild-type mice. Platelet αIIbβ3 and GPVI expression were decreased... [PMC12320448]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by lissencephaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum and other cerebral structural anomalies, early-onset intractable seizures, and ambiguous genitalia. Consequences of hypothalamic dysfunction, such as disturbed temperature regulation, may be observed. Additional anomalies including dysmorphic craniofacial features have been reported. The disease is fatal in infancy or childhood in males, while female carriers may be unaffected or show a milder phenotype with developmental delay, behavioral abnormalities, and seizures.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): X-linked lissencephaly with ambiguous genitalia; X-linked lissencephaly-corpus callosum agenesis-genital anomalies syndrome; XLAG (X-linked lissencephaly with abnormal genitalia) syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: X-linked lissencephaly with abnormal genitalia (XLAG) is a severe phenotype resulting from truncating variants or complete loss-of-function mutations in the ARX gene. This condition is characterized by malformations of the brain, specifically lissencephaly, and ambiguous or abnormal genitalia. The severe presentation of XLAG is distinct from other ARX-related phenotypes, such as infantile spasms, which may occur with different types of mutations or reinitiation of translation leading to a less severe outcome. [PMC4930085]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: X-linked lissencephaly with abnormal genitalia (XLAG) is caused by mutations in the Aristaless-related homeobox (ARX) gene, which are associated with a broad spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders. Truncating variants in ARX generally result in the severe XLAG phenotype, characterized by malformations of the brain and genitalia. However, other ARX variants, such as polyalanine expansions, missense variants, or premature termination mutations that allow for reinitiation of mRNA translation, can lead to milder phenotypes like infantile spasms or other neurodevelopmental delays, often due to reduced levels of N-terminally truncated protein. Female carriers of ARX variants can also exhibit a wide range of phenotypes, from normal cognitive development to intellectual disability, developmental delay, and other neurodevelopmental disorders, sometimes with milder symptoms than affected males. [PMC11476583, PMC9949785, PMC4930085]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: The ARX mutations encompass a nearly continuous spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), ranging from lissencephaly to Proud syndrome, as well as infantile spasms without brain malformations, and including both syndromic and non-syndromic intellectual disabilities (IDs). worsening neuropsychiatric symptoms in the offspring of a Korean family with ID/developmental delay (DD) caused by a novel ARX p.Lys385Ter variant. Sequential genetic testing was performed to investigate the ID, DD, agenesis of the corpus callosum (ACC), and developmental epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) observed in the proband. A comprehensive trio clinical exome sequencing approach using a Celemics G-Mendeliome Clinical Exome Sequencing Panel was employed. Given the clinical manifestations observed in the proband, gene panel sequencing identified a heterozygous ARX variant, c.1153A>T/p.Lys385Ter (Reference... [PMC11476583, PMC11353499, PMC9949785]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for X-linked lissencephaly with abnormal genitalia (XLAG) includes other ARX-related neurodevelopmental disorders, which encompass a spectrum from lissencephaly to Proud syndrome, infantile spasms, and intellectual disabilities. While severe truncating ARX variants typically cause XLAG, specific early premature termination mutations in ARX can lead to reinitiation of translation, resulting in milder phenotypes like infantile spasms without the severe brain and genitalia malformations. Female carriers of ARX variants can also exhibit a wide range of phenotypes, including intellectual disability, developmental delay, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and developmental epileptic encephalopathy. Additionally, tubulinopathies, such as those caused by novel TUBA1A variants, can present with lissencephaly, brain malformations, and hypoplastic genitalia, requiring differentiation from conditions like Walker-Warburg Syndrome. [PMC11476583, PMC11353499, PMC9949785, PMC4930085]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Tubulinopathies are associated with malformations of cortical development but not Walker-Warburg Syndrome. Intensive monitoring of a Croatian infant presenting as Walker-Warburg Syndrome in utero began at 21 weeks due to increased growth of cerebral ventricles and foetal biparietal diameter. Monitoring continued until Caesarean delivery at 34 weeks where the infant was eutrophic. Clinical assessment of a progressive neurological disorder of unknown aetiology found a macrocephalic head and markedly hypoplastic genitalia with a micropenis. Neurological examination showed generalized hypotonia with very rare spontaneous movements, hypotonia-induced respiratory insufficiency and ventilator dependence, and generalized myoclonus intensifying during manipulation. With clinical features of hypotonia, lissencephaly, and brain malformations, Walker-Warburg Syndrome was suspected; however, eye... [PMC11353499]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for ARX-related disorders requires careful consideration due to the X-linked inheritance pattern and significant phenotypic variability. While truncating variants generally lead to severe X-linked lissencephaly with ambiguous genitalia in males, female carriers can exhibit a wide spectrum of phenotypes, ranging from normal cognitive development to intellectual disability, developmental delay, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and developmental epileptic encephalopathy. ARX variants can also cause phenotypes in females, sometimes through de novo mutations. The specific mutation type can influence severity, as some early truncating variants may allow for reinitiation of translation, leading to a milder phenotype compared to complete loss-of-function mutations. [PMC11476583, PMC9949785, PMC4930085]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for individuals with ARX gene variants primarily involves symptomatic and supportive therapies for neurological manifestations. A case report highlights the use of dual antiepilepsy drug therapy, complemented by physiotherapy, speech therapy, occupational therapy, and oral motor exercises. Additionally, genetic counseling is an important aspect of management for ARX families, given the wide range of phenotypes that can be observed, particularly in female carriers. [PMC11476583, PMC9949785]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: X-linked lissencephaly with abnormal genitalia (XLAG), typically resulting from truncating ARX variants, is generally a severe neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by brain malformations and ambiguous genitalia. However, the prognosis can vary with the specific mutation; premature termination mutations that allow for reinitiation of mRNA translation, even at low levels of truncated protein, can lead to an improved phenotype compared to complete loss-of-function mutations. The spectrum of ARX-related disorders can include worsening neuropsychiatric symptoms. Female carriers exhibit a wide range of phenotypes, from normal cognitive development to intellectual disability, developmental delay, and epileptic encephalopathy, often with milder symptoms than affected males. [PMC11476583, PMC9949785, PMC4930085]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Bacterial toxic shock syndrome (TSS) is a potentially fatal, acute disease characterized by a sudden onset of high fever along with nausea, myalgia, vomiting and multisystem organ involvement, potentially leading to shock and death. TSS is mediated by superantigenic toxins, usually caused by an infection with Staphylococcus aureus in staphylococcal TSS or Streptococcus pyogenes in streptococcal TSS.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The worldwide prevalence is estimated at 1/30, 000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease affects mainly young adult women with no previous medical conditions. However, non-menstrual TSS, which can also be observed in men and children, represents up to 50% of Staphylococcal TSS cases. Onset is sudden and includes high fever (>38.9Â°C), nausea, diarrhea, vomiting, myalgia, abdominal pain and sore throat. Staphylococcal TSS almost always exhibits an erythematous rash and skin peeling as one of its manifestations, whereas it is very rarely seen in streptococcal TSS, which can show signs of soft tissue infection. Serious manifestations include confusion, shock, renal and myocardial dysfunction, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and coma.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Staphylococcal TSS is due to an infection with Staphylococcus aureus and streptococcal TSS is due to an infection with Streptococcus pyogenes, or rarely, group C or G Streptococcus. Superantigens produced by both bacteria are responsible for the massive and sudden immune reaction seen in TSS. Both forms have been associated with recent traumas (surgery or childbirth) and viral infections, while staphylococcal TSS has also been associated with high absorbency tampon use.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cranio-cerebello-cardiac (3C) syndrome is a rare multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by craniofacial (prominent occiput and forehead, hypertelorism, ocular coloboma, cleft palate), cerebellar (Dandy-Walker malformation, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia) and cardiac (tetralogy of Fallot, atrial and ventricular septal defects) anomalies.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date < 50 cases have been described. The syndrome appears to be panethnic.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: 3C syndrome is a congenital disorder characterized by distinctive craniofacial features including, in decreasing frequency, low-set ears, hypertelorism, down-slanting palpebral fissures, depressed nasal bridge, prominent occiput, prominent forehead, cleft palate, micrognathia, ocular coloboma. Additional craniofacial features encompass nevus flammeus (on forehead), low posterior hairline, sparse scalp hair, eyebrows and eyelashes, open mouth with protruding tongue, and short neck. In 80% of cases, cerebellar anomalies are present and include primarily Dandy-Walker malformation or Dandy-Walker variant, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia and enlargement of cisterna magma. Affected individuals have gross motor and speech delay and intellectual disability. The cardiovascular anomalies include atrial and ventricular septal defects, patent arterial duct, tetralogy of Fallot, double outlet right ventricle, hypoplastic left heart syndrome, aortic or pulmonary stenosis, and other valvular anomalies. Postnatal short stature is noted in most patients, and growth hormone deficiency has been reported in two patients. Additional anomalies, noted in >10% of patients, include feeding difficulties, single umbilical artery, small hands with single transverse crease, camptodactyly, equinovarus deformity, hydronephrosis, shallow scrotum, undescended testis, cryptorchidism, micropenis, hypospadias, nail hypoplasia, hearing loss, malrotation of the gut. Skeletal defects may be present with rib and vertebral anomalies (hemivertebrae). Rarely observed features include ocular (congenital glaucoma, optic nerve atrophy with eyelid ptosis, heteochromatic iris, posterior embryotoxon), renal (multicystic dysplastic kidney, horseshoe kidneys, unilateral renal agenesis) and anal (anal atresia, anteriorly placed anus malformations) anomalies. Single occurrences of renal hypoplasia, nipple hypoplasia, penile hypoplasia, unilateral adrenal aplasia, immunodeficiency have also been reported
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The exact etiology is still unknown but mutations in KIAA0196 (8q24.13; coding for strumpellin) have been identified in a First Nations cohort and these mutations may be involved in the pathophysiology of 3C syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnostic criteria for 3C syndrome include congenital heart malformation(s) other than isolated patent arterial duct; Dandy-Walker malformation, cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, or enlarged cisterna; and cleft palate, ocular coloboma or four of the following: prominent occiput, prominent forehead, hypertelorism, micrognathia, downslanting palpebral fissures, depressed nasal bridge, low-set ears.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Joubert syndrome, Ellis Van Creveld syndrome, Cornelia de Lange syndrome, distal monosomy 6p and Dandy Walker malformation.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis may be suspected after an ultrasound examination revealing characteristic major structural anomalies of 3C syndrome. Prenatal testing is available for families in which the disease-causing mutations have been previously identified.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Sporadic and familial cases have been reported. Transmission is autosomal recessive. Phenotypic variability exists between siblings.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is mainly symptomatic and multidisciplinary approaches including educational programs, physical, occupational, and speech therapy may help to improve hypotonia and reduce motor developmental delay. Cardiac malformation requires specific care, often surgery.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is determined by the cardiovascular malformation. Motor delay is common and associated with hypotonia secondary to cerebellar anomalies.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare medullar disease characterized by cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)-filled cavities (syrinx) inside the spinal cord as a result of an obstruction to CSF flow, either at the craniovertebral junction (Chiari malformation) or in the perimedullary subarachnoid spaces (arachnoiditis).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Estimated prevalence is 8.4/100,000. Cases of autosomal recessive familial syringomyelia have been reported with an estimated incidence of 2% of all syringomyelia cases.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Although syringomyelia can lead to disruption of neural connections in the spinal cord and to neurological damage, 50% of patients (when all types of syrinxes are considered) will experience no or only mild disability. In symptomatic patients, onset is usually marked by pain and sensory disturbances, varying from complete absence of sensation, pins and needles or temperature sensing alterations, to increased sensation to stimuli. Although there are no clear clinical clues at neurological examination, a 'cape-like' sensory dissociation (loss of the ability to distinguish between hot and cold with intact light-touch sensation in the upper limbs and torso), as well as reduced upper limb reflexes, are quite specific initial findings when present. Motor symptoms usually range from varying degrees of weakness to spasticity and loss of autonomy. Alterations in bladder and sexual function may also be present.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Syringomyelia is due to obstruction of CSF flow either at the craniovertebral junction (e.g. Chiari malformation) or in the perimedullary subarachnoid spaces (e.g. arachnoiditis). Chiari malformations can be associated with other craniovertebral junction malformations (e.g. basilar invagination) or neural tube defects (Chiari II malformation). Spinal arachnoiditis can be either idiopathic or secondary (postinfectious, posttraumatic, posthemorrhagic, postoperative).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Neurological examination and MRI are required for diagnosis. MRI is the gold standard and reveals a fluid filled cavity with variable degrees of vertical and horizontal extension within the spinal cord ranging from involvement of one level up to extension over the entire spinal cord. The signal characteristics on MRI are usually quite similar to those of CSF.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes persistent or dilated central canal (hydromyelia, slits), myelomalacia, tumoral cysts, myelitis, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and multiple sclerosis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management consists of long-term follow up and surgery in cases of progressive neurological deterioration. The goal of surgery is to restore CSF flow either at the craniovertebral junction in case of Chiari malformation (foramen magnum decompression) or in the perimedullary subarachnoid spaces in case of arachnoiditis (arachnoidolysis).
