If not possible, or in case of failure, a shunting procedure can be performed to drain the syrinx, either to the peritoneal space (syringoperitoneal shunt) or pleural space (syringopleural shunt).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Around 50% of Chiari malformation type I patients with syringomyelia remain neurologically stable. In cases with progressive deterioration, surgical intervention usually prevents clinical progression. In cases of posttraumatic syringomyelia due to spinal cord compression, reconstruction of the spinal canal appears to yield similar results. Prognosis is worse for cases in which the only surgical option is direct shunting of the syrinx, as this often leads to neurological deficit and recurrence. Persistent or dilated central canal, which is not a syringomyelia, has a benign natural history with usually no progression neither clinically nor radiologically.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, inherited bleeding disorder characterized by defective platelet adhesion and secondary coagulation defect that manifests as abnormal bleeding of variable severity occurring either spontaneously or in association with an invasive procedure. Three main subtypes are defined based on the type of von Willebrand factor defect: partial (type 1) or total (type 3) deficiency, and qualitative/functional anomalies (type 2).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Hereditary von Willebrand disease; Hereditary pseudohaemophilia

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of Von Willebrand disease (VWD) in the general population is estimated at between 0.6 and 1.3% (including all forms) depending on the study, but the prevalence of symptomatic VWD that requires specific treatment is approximately 1/10 000. Type 3 VWD is much more rare (1/1 000 000).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Age of onset varies, with earlier onset being associated with more severe VWF deficiency. The disease manifests as abnormal bleeding of variable severity occurring either spontaneously or in association with an invasive procedure. The bleeding anomalies are generally characterized by mucocutaneous hemorrhage (epistaxis, menorrhagia, bleeding from minor wounds, etc.) but hematomas and hemarthrosis may occur in more severe forms.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: VWD is caused by mutations in the VWF gene (12p13.3) encoding the multimeric VWF protein. The VWF protein has an intraplatelet, endothelial and plasmatic localization and plays essential roles both in the interaction of platelets with the injured vessel wall and in the transport and stabilization of factor VIII (FVIII).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on laboratory tests involving functional and immunological assays of VWF and FVIII levels. Determination of the type of VWD requires other specific tests such as studies of the distribution of VWF multimers.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Measurements of VWF levels (antigen and functions) generally allow VWD to be distinguished from hemophilia A. However, these tests do not allow differentiation of type 2N VWD, which requires more specific assays. Differentiation between acquired von Willebrand syndrome (AVWS), which occurs in association with another underlying pathology, and inherited VWD is more problematic. The fact that individuals in the general population belonging to blood group O may also have moderately lower levels of VWF should also be taken into consideration in the differential diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: In at risk pregnancies, the identification of underlying VWF mutations may be used for prenatal diagnosis of type 3 VWD.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: VWD is most often transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner, however, the mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive for type 3 VWD and for some of the type 2 subtypes. Genetic counseling should be proposed to inform patients about the severity of the disease and the associated risks, and to allow screening for detection of other affected family members. For couples at risk of having a child with type 3 disease, genetic counseling may be best discussed in a specialized multidisciplinary center.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management depends on the type of VWD. Desmopressin is generally an effective preventative or curative treatment for abnormal bleeding in type 1 VWD. In patients with type 2 disease, the response to desmopressin is variable and substitution therapy with purified human VWF is often required. Desmopressin does not constitute an effective treatment for patients with type 3 disease, and thus these individuals require substitution therapy with purified human VWF associated, at least for the first injection, with FVIII.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: For patients managed within specialized hemostasis hospital centers, the prognosis is favorable, even for those with the most severe forms of the disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Scleroderma is a rare autoimmune connective tissue disorder characterized by abnormal hardening of the skin and, sometimes, other organs. It is classified into two main forms: localized scleroderma and systemic sclerosis (SSc), the latter comprising three subsets; diffuse cutaneous SSc (dcSSc), limited cutaneous SSc (lcSSc) and limited SSc (lSSc).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is estimated at around 1-9/100,000 for localized scleroderma, and 1/6,500 adults for systemic sclerosis. Women are predominantly affected (F/M sex ratio around 4:1).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Localized scleroderma is the cutaneous form of scleroderma characterized by fibrosis of the skin causing cutaneous plaques (morphea) or strips (linear scleroderma). Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a generalized disorder characterized by fibrosis and vascular obliteration in the skin and organs, particularly, lungs, heart, and digestive tract.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The exact cause of scleroderma is unknown. The disease originates from an autoimmune reaction which leads to localized overproduction of collagen. In some cases, the condition is associated with exposure to chemicals. Other suggested causes include genetic and infectious mechanisms.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of scleroderma involves various approaches depending on organ involvement and disease severity. Immunosuppressive agents like cyclophosphamide, tocilizumab, glucocorticoids, hydroxychloroquine, mycophenolate mofetil, and rituximab are used for systemic manifestations, with combination therapies showing potential for refractory cases. For scleroderma renal crisis, ACE-inhibitors such as captopril are crucial, and rapid recognition is important. Pulmonary hypertension may be treated with intravenous epoprostenol, inhaled treprostinil, ambrisentan, and tadalafil, though caution is needed for pulmonary veno-occlusive disease, which may benefit from diuretics. Gastrointestinal complications can be managed with endoscopic interventions like argon plasma coagulation and pharmacological therapies. Co-occurring conditions like adrenocortical adenoma or lung infections may require surgical treatment, and a gluten-free diet is advised for celiac disease. Multidisciplinary management and early diagnosis are key for optimal patient outcomes. [PMC12267156, PMC12179478, PMC12060736, PMC12035258, PMC11991400]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare contiguous gene deletion syndrome of chromosome 17p13.3 characterized by classical lissencephaly, distinct facial dysmorphism, seizures and severe to profound intellectual disability. Additional congenital malformations can be part of the condition.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Lissencephaly due to 17p13.3 deletion; Monosomy 17p13.3; Telomeric deletion 17p

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Miller-Dieker Syndrome (MDS) is undoubtedly a rare condition. The exact prevalence remains unknown. The limited epidemiological data available do not distinguish MDS from other classic lissencephalies, which have an estimated birth incidence to ranging from 1 in 85,000 to 1 in 25,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: MDS is associated with several clinical manifestations, including: a) lissencephaly, characterized by a smooth brain with agyria or pachygyria due to abnormal neuronal migration; b) facial dysmorphism, including a prominent forehead, vertical forehead creases, short nose, thin vermillion border, micrognathia and low-set ears; c) developmental delay and intellectual disability, whereby most affected individuals show important developmental delay and severe to profound intellectual disability; d) seizures, with a significant proportion of patients presenting with drug-resistant seizures; e) growth retardation, with individuals often showing intrauterine growth retardation, failure to thrive and microcephaly; and f) other congenital anomalies, including congenital heart defects, renal and urogenital anomalies (e.g. renal cysts, pelvic kidneys, cryptorchidism) and gastrointestinal anomalies (e.g. duodenal atresia, omphalocele), which are occasionally present.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MDS is caused by a deletion of chromosome 17p13.3, including the PAFAH1B1 and YWHAE genes. The size of the deleted region varies amongst affected individuals.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: In patients with clinical manifestations suggestive of MDS, MRI typically reveals agyria/pachygyria with an hourglass configuration. The genetic diagnosis can be established through chromosomal microarray analysis or CNV analysis using exome or genome sequencing data.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Several diseases may have phenotypic overlap with MDS, including classic lissencephalies due to other genetic etiologies, isolated lissencephaly type 1 without known genetic defects, subcortical band heterotopia and cobblestone lissencephaly.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound may reveal some structural brain anomalies indicative of lissencephaly and/or other congenital anomalies other associated findings (e.g., mild ventriculomegaly, intrauterine growth retardation, cardiac anomalies or polyhydramnios) which are usually not detectable before the second or third trimester. Fetal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) serves as a supplemental diagnostic tool to further characterize structural brain anomalies. Amniocentesis with chromosomal microarray analysis or CNV analysis on exome or genome sequencing data may confirm the MDS diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The 17p13.3 deletion causing MDS often arises de novo, with a low recurrence risk for parents. However, in case of a telomeric deletion, a parent may carry a balanced chromosomal rearrangement with a higher recurrence risk. Genetic counseling is essential to provide appropriate information about recurrence risk, available testing, such as invasive prenatal diagnosis and preimplantation testing, and implications of a diagnosis for family planning.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management of children with MDS is symptomatic and supportive. Gastrostomy is often required to ensure adequate nutrition and prevent aspiration, given the known swallowing and feeding difficulties. Multiple anti-epileptic medications are typically used to control seizures (which are often refractory).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor. Developmental milestones are rarely achieved. Most of the affected children die prematurely due to aspiration pneumonia and refractory seizures. However, individual cases were reported to have survived into late adolescence/early adulthood.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multisystem disorder characterized by neonatal/childhood hypotonia, mild to moderate developmental delay or intellectual disability, epilepsy, dysmorphic facial features, hypermetropia, congenital heart anomalies, congenital renal/urologic anomalies, musculoskeletal problems, and a friendly/amiable disposition.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of this disorder is unknown; however, the prevalence of the 17q21.31 deletion is approximately 1/55,000 individuals. The prevalence of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in KANSL1 cannot be ascertained with precision owing to the limited number of cases identified thus far. Males and females are affected equally.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Hypotonia is most evident between the neonatal period and infancy with poor sucking and slow feeding, but may persist throughout life. Feeding difficulties may require hospitalization and/or nasogastric tube feeding in some neonates. Tracheo/Laryngomalacia is a common feature. Global psychomotor developmental delay is noted in all individuals from an early age, although the level of developmental delay varies significantly. The majority of individuals with Koolen-de Vries syndrome (KdVS) function in the mild to moderate range of intellectual disability. Oral hypotonia and apraxia in infancy and preschool, associated with severely delayed speech development is one of the hall marks of KdVS. A history of epilepsy is noted in ~30-50% of all cases and other neurological problems may also be present. The facial dysmorphism is characterized by upslanted palpebral fissures, blepharophimosis, epicanthal folds, ptosis, a pear-shaped nose with bulbous nasal tip, and large / protruding ears. Short stature, pectus excavatum, spine anomalies, dislocation of the hip(s), long slender fingers and slender lower limbs, and positional deformities of the hands/feet have been reported. Other features include heart defects (bicuspid aortic valve, atrial and ventricular septal defects), kidney and urologic anomalies, and cryptorchidism.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: KdVS is typically a sporadic disorder caused either by a 17q21.31 deletion encompassing the KAT8 regulatory NSL complex subunit 1 (KANSL1) gene or a mutation of the KANSL1 gene.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Molecular genetic testing approaches can include a combination of chromosomal microarray (CMA), a multigene panel, and comprehensive genomic testing (exome sequencing, exome array, genome sequencing). In individuals with normal CMA results, targeted Sanger sequencing of the KANSL1-gene testing can be considered based on the clinical findings.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Prader-Willi syndrome in the neonatal period and 22q11.2 deletion syndrome, fragile X syndrome, Angelman syndrome and blepharophimosis-intellectual disability syndrome, SBBYS type in older patients.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Almost all cases correspond to a single occurrence in a family, but prenatal testing can be offered for at risk pregnancies.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling should be proposed to parents of affected individuals. Whilst almost all affected individuals represent simplex cases (i.e., a single affected individuals in the family) with a very small risk of sibling recurrence, the pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant and thus the risk to offspring of affected individuals inheriting KdVS is 50%
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Affected individuals should have routine examinations by the primary care physician and pediatrician. Cardiac investigations, and kidney and urologic evaluations are warranted. Speech production requires intensive motor speech treatment in preschool years and language development requires focused intervention and augmentative (sign language) or alternative (communication device) support until oral speech and language develops. Regular check up by a dermatologist can be considered in case of multiple nevi. Referral to other specialists is indicated if neurological or other systemic problems are suspected.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Longitudinal data are insufficient to determine life expectancy, although survival into adulthood is typical, autonomy is likely to be limited and affected individuals will probably require life-long support from caregivers.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Triploidy is a rare chromosomal anomaly, polyploidy, characterized by early in utero growth restriction, and multiple birth defects, including neural tube defects, facial abnormalities, cleft lip/palate, congenital heart anomalies, genital malformations, and peripheral skeletal abnormalities. It is usually prenatally lethal.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Triploidy is a lethal chromosomal numeric abnormality, occurring in 2-3% of conceptuses and accounting for approximately 20% of chromosomally abnormal first-trimester miscarriages. Its estimated prevalence decreases significantly with gestational age, from 1 in 3,500 pregnancies at 12 weeks to 1 in 250,000 at 20 weeks. Most affected pregnancies result in early miscarriage, with very few surviving to term. While generally understood as a sporadic disorder with no recognized risk of recurrence, recurrent triploidy has been reported, and investigations suggest a possible genetic predisposition of maternal origin in some cases, including associations with NLRP7 mutations or failure to complete maternal meiosis II. [PMC11957313, PMC7929808, PMC5511524, PMC4381034, PMC3823570]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Triploidy syndrome is a lethal chromosomal disorder characterized by an extra set of haploid chromosomes (69, XXX; 69, XXY; or 69, XYY). Most affected pregnancies result in early miscarriage, with very few fetuses surviving to term. Ultrasound examinations often reveal multiple severe fetal anomalies early in gestation, including asymmetric intrauterine growth retardation, septated cystic hygroma, subcutaneous edema, ascites, pleural and pericardial effusions, and cardiac or renal abnormalities. Specific malformations reported include alobar holoprosencephaly (with cyclopia and severe facial anomalies), sacral meningocele, spina bifida (in 25% of late triploids), syndactyly of hands and feet, single palmar creases, hypoplasia of adrenals and ovaries, hypertrophy of thigh muscles, and other brain abnormalities. The placenta can be large and show hydatidiform degeneration, particularly with 69XXX triploidy. Maternal complications such as hypertension, acute dyspnoea, and pre-eclampsia may also occur. The prognosis is extremely poor, with affected infants rarely surviving beyond the neonatal period. [PMC11957313, PMC7929808, PMC8112748, PMC8343603, PMC5511524]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Triploidy is a lethal chromosomal numeric abnormality characterized by an extra set of haploid chromosomes, resulting in 69 chromosomes (e.g., 69,XXX; 69,XXY; 69,XYY). While often sporadic, recurrent triploidy has been reported, suggesting a genetic predisposition. Mechanisms include digyny, where an extra maternal haploid set is present, and fertilization with more than one sperm (polyspermy). Recurrent cases can arise from a failure to complete maternal meiosis II, with candidate genes like PLCD4 and OSBPL5 implicated in oocyte maturation or activation. NLRP7 mutations are also associated with recurrent triploid conceptions, potentially due to impaired prevention of polyspermic fertilization. [PMC11957313, PMC7929808, PMC8343603, PMC5511524, PMC4381034]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of triploidy syndrome is typically suspected by antepartum ultrasound, which can reveal various fetal anomalies such as cystic hygroma, holoprosencephaly, intrauterine growth retardation, subcutaneous edema, ascites, and cardiac or renal abnormalities early in pregnancy. Biochemical maternal serum screening during the second trimester may also indicate the condition, though non-invasive prenatal screens are considered unreliable for definitive detection. Confirmation requires invasive testing of fetal cells, such as amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, followed by karyotype analysis. Cytogenetic investigations, including banding and fluorescence techniques, and DNA analysis, are used to confirm the abnormal number of 69 chromosomes. Pathological examination of the embryo, fetal autopsy, and placental pathological study can reaffirm antenatal diagnostics. [PMC11957313, PMC7929808, PMC8112748, PMC8343603, PMC5511524]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Triploidy syndrome, a lethal chromosomal abnormality, presents with features that overlap with other genetic conditions. Prenatal ultrasound findings such as cystic hygroma, intrauterine growth retardation, subcutaneous edema, ascites, pleural/pericardial effusions, and cardiac or renal abnormalities necessitate genetic work-up, as these can also be seen with other chromosomal abnormalities, including Down syndrome, or even a 'normal' karyotype. Triploidy is also a cause of partial hydatidiform mole and spontaneous abortion, requiring differentiation from other causes of molar pregnancies and reproductive wastage, some of which are linked to NLRP7 mutations. Specific fetal anomalies like syndactyly and spina bifida are also observed in other conditions. [PMC8112748, PMC5511524, PMC3823570, PMC1013443]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: BACKGROUND Fetal triploidy is a rare, lethal disorder characterized by an extra set of haploid chromosomes resulting in 69 chromosomes (69, XXX; 69, XXY; or 69, XYY). Fetal anomalies and occasionally maternal complications such as hypertension result in a high fetal loss rate during gestation. It is estimated to be present in 1: 250 000 pregnancies at 20 weeks, and very few survive to term. Diagnosis is suspected by antepartum ultrasound and confirmed by invasive testing of fetal cells by karyotype. Management includes pregnancy termination or pregnancy continuation based on the patient's choice. Whether a cesarean delivery should be performed for a nonmaternal indication in a triploid pregnancy is controversial. CASE REPORT A 17-year-old primagravida presented at 33 weeks post-last menstrual period with several weeks of lower abdominal pain and nausea. She had received prenatal care at... [PMC11957313, PMC7929808, PMC8112748, PMC8343603, PMC5511524]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for triploidy syndrome involves informing parents about its lethal nature and very poor fetal prognosis. Diagnosis is typically suspected by antepartum ultrasound and confirmed by invasive testing, such as amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, as non-invasive prenatal screens are unreliable for definitive detection. Upon confirmation, parents are offered options including pregnancy termination or continuation, with the understanding that declining a cesarean delivery for non-maternal indications is also a choice. While triploidy is generally considered a sporadic disorder with no recognizable recurrence risk, several cases of recurrent triploidy have been reported, suggesting a potential underlying genetic predisposition, possibly of maternal origin or linked to specific gene mutations like NLRP7. Therefore, investigation into an underlying genetic mechanism is recommended in recurrent cases to provide more accurate counseling. [PMC11957313, PMC7929808, PMC8112748, PMC8343603, PMC5511524]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Given triploidy is a lethal disorder, management options include pregnancy termination or continuation, based on patient choice. Due to the very poor fetal outcome and major malformations, elective termination is a common decision. Genetic counseling is crucial, and patients must be thoroughly informed about the short and long-term fetal prognosis. Diagnostic steps, such as ultrasound and genetic work-up via amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling, are mandatory to inform these management decisions. The performance of a cesarean delivery for non-maternal indications in a triploid pregnancy is controversial, with declining it being an important option. [PMC11957313, PMC7929808, PMC8112748, PMC8343603, PMC5511524]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Triploidy syndrome is consistently described as a lethal chromosomal disorder with a very poor prognosis. Most pregnancies result in early miscarriage, and there is a high fetal loss rate during gestation, with very few surviving to term. Chances of thriving through the second trimester are very slim. When diagnosed, pregnancies are often terminated due to major fetal malformations. In rare instances where infants are born, survival is typically very short, as exemplified by an infant dying on day 20 of life. [PMC11957313, PMC7929808, PMC8112748, PMC8343603, PMC5511524]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A group of rare genetic hypopigmentation disorders characterized by a generalized reduction in pigmentation of hair, skin and eyes and variable ocular findings including nystagmus, reduced visual acuity and photophobia. Variants include OCA1A (the most severe form), OCA1B, OCA1-minimal pigment (OCA1-MP), OCA1-temperature sensitive (OCA1-TS), OCA2, OCA3, OCA4, OCA5, OCA6, OCA7 and OCA8.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a group of rare, genetically heterogeneous autosomal recessive disorders. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS), which includes oculocutaneous albinism, is also a rare autosomal recessive condition with a globally low incidence. OCA type II is noted as the most common subtype among African and African Americans. The prevalence of these conditions may be under-reported, particularly in regions with high rates of consanguinity and endogamy, such as the Middle East, suggesting a higher unrecognized prevalence. Molecular testing is crucial for accurate diagnosis, especially in populations with higher disease prevalence. [PMC11908729, PMC11240142, PMC10767448]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) is a group of rare autosomal recessive genetic disorders characterized by congenital melanin deficiency and defects in melanin biosynthesis, resulting in hypopigmentation of the skin, hair, and eyes. Specific types of OCA are linked to mutations in different genes. For instance, OCA type 2 (OCA2) is commonly associated with variants in the OCA2 gene, which encodes a protein critical for melanosomal pH regulation and melanin biosynthesis. OCA type 1B (OCA1B) is caused by variants in the Tyrosinase (TYR) gene, leading to deficient expression of melanogenic enzymes. A newer type, OCA8, from pathogenic variants in the DCT gene, which may regulate L-Dopa levels and retinal signaling. Additionally, oculocutaneous albinism can be a feature of Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS), a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in BLOC-1 subunits, which are involved in the biogenesis of melanosomes and other lysosome-related organelles. [PMC12247470, PMC11908729, PMC11824501, PMC12396517, PMC12303592]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Melanin deposition in the kidney is rare and appears limited to the conditions of oculocutaneous albinism and malignant melanoma with melanuria. Melanin is generally an insoluble polymer, and it is curious how people with albinism who have little or no skin pigmentation can secrete melanin into the bloodstream, have it pass through the glomerular filtration barrier, and be absorbed by renal tubules. The concentration and solubility of melanin were analyzed in kidney tissue and urine of a renal transplant donor who had a pre-nephrectomy biopsy performed on a black kidney. Genetic testing of a donor blood sample found a novel homozygous Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS) HPS1 mutation (c.70G > T; p.Glu24Ter). Melanin was extracted from a 24-hour urine collection, and tissue and urine melanin concentrations were determined by spectrophotometry. In the kidney, non-melanosomal melanin was... [PMC12247470, PMC11908729, PMC11824501, PMC12303592, PMC11654439]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Oculocutaneous albinism (OCA) must be differentiated from other conditions presenting with hypopigmentation. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome (HPS) is a primary differential, characterized by oculocutaneous albinism, bleeding diathesis, and potential multi-organ involvement such as pulmonary fibrosis, granulomatous colitis, and kidney melanosis. Mutations in BLOC-1 subunits cause HPS, which can be clinically confused with other forms of albinism, necessitating molecular testing to distinguish between HPS and specific OCA types, such as OCA1B due to Tyrosinase gene variants. Additionally, amelanotic melanoma can be a diagnostic pitfall in individuals with oculocutaneous albinism. Kidney melanosis, when present, is a rare finding associated with oculocutaneous albinism and malignant melanoma with melanuria. [PMC12247470, PMC11908729, PMC12090962, PMC12396517, PMC11240142]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis for oculocutaneous albinism is possible, as demonstrated by genetic testing in amniotic fluid. In one instance, a gross exon 10-19 deletion variant in the OCA2 gene, identified in a family with OCA, was not detected in the amniotic fluid of the proband's sister, indicating the feasibility of prenatal genetic screening for known pathogenic variants. [PMC10767448]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Hemolytic anemia due to red cell pyruvate kinase deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic metabolic disorder due to pyruvate kinase deficiency characterized by a variable degree of chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia resulting in a variable clinical manifestations ranging from fatal anemia at birth to a to a fully compensated hemolysis without apparent anemia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Pyruvate kinase (PK) deficiency is the most frequent cause of congenital nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia with a prevalence estimated at 1/20,000 in the general white population.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinically, PK-deficient patients suffer from a highly variable degree of chronic hemolysis, ranging from severe neonatal jaundice and fatal anemia at birth, severe transfusion-dependent chronic hemolysis, moderate hemolysis with exacerbation during infection, to a fully compensated hemolysis without apparent anemia. Symptoms are usually present at birth but, due to the variable severity, may not be recognized or acknowledged until later. Chronic icterus, gallstones, iron overload and splenomegaly are common findings.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Erythrocyte PK deficiency is caused by mutations in the PKLR gene (1q22). To date, more than 290 mutations in PKLR have been reported. PK is a key regulatory enzyme of glycolysis and two major metabolic abnormalities result from PK deficiency: ATP depletion and increased 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) content. The precise mechanisms that cause extravascular hemolysis are as yet unknown, but an important feature involves the selective sequestration of PK-deficient young red blood cells, in particular reticulocytes, by the spleen. The increased 2,3-DPG levels ameliorate the anemia by lowering the oxygen-affinity of hemoglobin.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis may be considered on the basis of the clinical features and laboratory findings: a variable degree of anemia, reticulocytosis, increased non-conjugated bilirubin, and decreased levels of haptoglobin. Red blood cell morphology is essentially normal. PK deficiency is diagnosed by measuring PK enzymatic activity. Importantly, due to the fact that the enzymatic activity is red cell age-dependent, a deficiency of PK may be masked by reticulocytosis. Simultaneous measurement of another red cell age-specific enzyme, e.g. hexokinase, may therefore be helpful. Confirmation of the diagnosis requires genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Secondary PK deficiency has also been reported, occurring in the context of hematological diseases (acute/chronic leukemia, myelodysplastic syndromes and sideroblastic anemia). In case of persistent normocytic hemolytic anemia in which hemoglobin abnormalities and antiglobulin reactions have been excluded, spherocytes are absent, and osmotic fragility is normal, the diagnosis of hereditary nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia should be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Erythrocyte PK deficiency is an autosomal recessive disease and genetic counseling should be offered to affected families. Where both parents are unaffected carriers, there is a 25% risk of disease transmission to offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The mainstay of treatment is blood transfusion and, in severe cases, splenectomy. The latter should be based on the patient's ability to tolerate the anemia. As a result of splenectomy, transfusion needs are reduced in many patients. Splenectomy is often accompanied by a considerable increase in reticulocyte counts. Bone marrow transplantation can cure PK deficiency but is rarely performed. Small molecule activator therapy is currently in clinical trials.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable depending on the severity of the anemia, but as in other chronic hemolytic disorders, gallstones and iron overload may develop, requiring appropriate treatment.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare lysosomal disease characterized by an accumulation of cystine inside the lysosomes, causing damage in different organs and tissues, particularly in the kidneys and eyes. Three clinical forms have been described: nephropathic infantile, nephropathic juvenile and ocular.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence at birth is estimated at around 1/100,000- 1/200,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In the infantile form (the most common), the first clinical signs appear between 3 and 6 months of age, with a polyuria-polydipsia syndrome and marked growth delay secondary to a generalized proximal tubular dysfunction with severe fluid-electrolyte balance alterations (renal Fanconi syndrome). Hypophosphatemic rickets causing bone deformities are also observed. Ocular involvement caused by cystine deposits in the cornea is responsible for photophobia which usually appears after 3 years of age. Cystine deposits in various organs progressively lead to hypothyroidism, insulin-dependent diabetes, hepatosplenomegaly with portal hypertension in some patients, and muscle and cerebral involvement. In the absence of specific treatment, the disease progresses to end stage renal failure before the age of 10. The first symptoms of juvenile cystinosis (< 5% of patients), typically appear around 6-8 years of age with a milder form of proximal tubulopathy and/or proteinuria in nephrotic syndrome. Progression to renal failure occurs later than in the infantile form. Finally, the ocular form is observed in adults who are generally asymptomatic and may suffer only from photophobia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Cystinosis is due to a defect in cystine transport out of lysosomes. The causative gene, CTNS (17p13), encodes cystinosin, a lysosomal membrane protein. Mutations in this gene have been detected for all 3 forms of the disease, with a 57-kb deletion detected in 60%-70% of alleles in patients from Northern Europe. Severe truncating mutations cause a more severe disease (infantile form) while mutations allowing the protein residual function cause milder phenotypes (juvenile or ocular).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on blood and urine analysis showing features of renal Fanconi syndrome (metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hyperaminoaciduria, glycosuria, low molecular weight proteinuria), detection of cystine crystals in the cornea and determination of elevated cystine levels in leucocytes. It is confirmed by CTNS gene analysis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other diseases causing renal Fanconi syndrome (Lowe syndrome, Dent disease, galactosemia, fructose intolerance, thyrosinemia, mitochondrial nephropathies, Wilson disease, Fanconi-Bickel syndrome, lysinuric protein intolerance, idiopathic Fanconi syndromes, secondary Fanconi syndrome due to drug toxicity or substance abuse, recovery of acute tubulus necrosis), diseases causing phosphaturia and rickets, and proteinuria of unknown etiology.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: A prenatal, genetic diagnosis is possible in families with a previously affected child.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling is recommended for affected families. The risk of disease transmission is 25% where both parents are unaffected carriers; disease severity depends on the mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment consists of administering electrolytes, alkali, phosphate and vitamin D supplements; indomethacin, which improves the general status and growth; and cysteamine. Cysteamine lowers the cystine content in the lysosomes, thereby slowing or even stopping the progression to renal failure and the development of extra-renal manifestations. The side effects of cysteamine include gastrointestinal symptoms, bad breath, sweat odor and allergic reactions. A delayed-released formulation has been developed and approved in the USA and Europe, which allows patients to receive cysteamine twice a day, thus improving compliance and quality of life. Topical cysteamine eye drops (0.5%) are also needed as systemic cysteamine has no effect on cystine corneal deposits.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy has significantly improved with therapy. Cysteamine delays the need for renal replacement therapy. The disease does not recur in the graft after renal transplantation but continues to progress in other organs and may cause complications (swallowing dysfunction, neurologic complications, lung disease) that may worsen the prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic lipodystrophy characterized by a loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue from the trunk, buttocks and limbs; fat accumulation in the neck, face, axillary and pelvic regions; muscular hypertrophy; and usually associated with metabolic complications such as insulin resistance, diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia and liver steatosis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Dunnigan syndrome; FPLD2; Familial partial lipodystrophy type 2

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Familial partial lipodystrophy, Dunnigan type (FPLD2) is the most frequent form of familial partial lipodystrophy (FPLD) for which the prevalence is estimated at less than 1/100,000 in Europe; although, this is likely an underestimate.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset of lipodystrophy usually occurs at or around puberty, with regional loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue from the limbs, buttocks and trunk, followed by a progressive fat accumulation on the face, neck and axillary regions giving patients a cushingoid appearance. Females often have a more severe phenotype than males. An increased skeletal muscle volume and mass is also noted. Prominent veins (due to lipoatrophy) are noted in the limbs. Metabolic complications appear progressively in adolescence or in adulthood and include insulin resistance, diabetes, hepatic steatosis, acanthosis nigricans, high blood pressure, and premature atherosclerosis with an increased risk of coronary heart disease. Some patients may display the features of polycystic ovary syndrome such as hirsutism, oligomenorrhea, polycystic ovaries and infertility. All patients are typically predisposed to early cardiovascular diseases. Other manifestations may include complications of diabetes, recurrent acute pancreatitis and liver steatohepatitis or cirrhosis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FPLD2 is caused by mutations in the LMNA gene (1q22) encoding the nuclear intermediate filaments A-type lamins. Typical forms of FPLD2 are mainly due to heterozygous substitutions at the 482nd codon of the gene (p.R482W/Q or L mutation). Other monoallelic or biallelic LMNA pathogenic variants are rarely found, and are more frequently associated with atypical forms of lipodystrophies, associated or not with other laminopathic phenotypes (muscular and/or cardiac dystrophies, accelerated aging).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made by clinical examination, analysis of fat distribution by imaging (MRI, CT-scan and whole-body dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry) and evaluation of metabolic status (hypertriglyceridemia, low levels of high density lipoprotein (HDL)-cholesterol in the blood, hyperinsulinemia, altered glucose tolerance, low circulating levels of leptin and adiponectin). Body mass index is usually normal. Liver enzyme levels should be measured and ultrasonography of liver should be performed, and with transient elastography if a fatty liver disease is suspected. Cardiovascular investigations are needed to search for rhythm and conduction disturbances, and early atherosclerosis. Molecular genetic testing confirms diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other forms of FPLD as well as Cushing syndrome, type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome and acquired lipodystrophy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis could be discussed in families with a known disease causing mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: FPLD2 is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner; where there is an affected parent, the risk of disease transmission is 50%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment consists of correcting metabolic abnormalities and managing complications. Monitoring diet (reduced intake of dietary fats and carbohydrates) and maintaining daily physical activity can improve the metabolic complications of lipodystrophy. Insulin sensitizers (mainly metformin) and lipid-lowering drugs (statins, or fibrates in case of major hypertriglyceridemia) can also be helpful. Diabetes may require other non-specific treatments, along with insulin. The orphan drug metreleptin is authorized under exceptional circumstances in Europe for the treatment of metabolic complications of partial forms of lipodystrophies, in adults and children above the age of 12 years, where standard treatments have failed. Further studies are required to investigate the benefits and risks of treatment. Regular cardiac monitoring is recommended. Ethinylestradiol should be avoided in women with FPLD2. Plastic surgery can help some patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is linked to the severity of associated comorbidities (diabetes, pancreatitis, cardiovascular diseases).

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare primary immunodeficiency due to a defect in innate immunity characterized by a marked decrease or absence of myeloperoxidase activity in neutrophils and monocytes. Clinically, most patients are asymptomatic. Occasionally, severe infectious complications may occur, particularly recurrent candida infections, being especially severe in the setting of comorbid diabetes mellitus.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) deficiency is described as a common inherited disorder. It is linked to an increased susceptibility to infection and malignancy. [PMC508882]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) deficiency is characterized by less efficient microbial killing by neutrophils compared to normal cells. Despite this, individuals with MPO deficiency frequently do not experience life-threatening infectious complications, leading some to consider the MPO oxidant system as ancillary. However, the essential contribution of MPO to innate host defense may become manifest when exposure to pathogens overwhelms the capacity of other host defense mechanisms. [PMC3545676]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) deficiency is an inherited disorder caused by mutations in the MPO gene. One identified mutation, R499C (arginine to cysteine), in exon 9, leads to the absence of MPO peptides, potentially due to impaired heme binding. Another novel missense mutation, Y173C (tyrosine to cysteine), in a precursor protein that is glycosylated and acquires heme but fails to be proteolytically processed or secreted. This mutant protein remains associated with chaperones in the endoplasmic reticulum and is subsequently degraded by the proteasome, highlighting a role for proteasome-mediated quality control in this form of hereditary MPO deficiency. [PMC6032473, PMC508882]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of myeloperoxidase deficiency involves detecting the absence of MPO activity, often following an initial screening assay that may show an abnormal hematograph. Western blot analysis can confirm the absence of MPO peptides. Genetic analysis, utilizing standard PCR techniques for amplification and sequencing, is employed to identify specific mutations in the MPO gene, such as the R499C or Y173C missense mutations, which are associated with the deficiency. [PMC6032473, PMC508882]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD) should be considered in the differential diagnosis. CGD is an inborn error of immunity caused by an impaired respiratory burst reaction in phagocytes, leading to an increased risk for invasive bacterial and fungal infections, particularly with S. aureus and Aspergillus spp. Patients with CGD also experience autoinflammation. Diagnosis involves measuring reactive oxygen intermediates generated by the NADPH oxidase in peripheral blood phagocytes upon in vitro activation. [PMC11239527]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) deficiency is an inherited disorder linked to specific mutations in the MPO gene. Genetic analysis has identified a nonsynonymous arginine to cysteine substitution (R499C) in exon 9 in a Japanese patient with complete MPO deficiency, a mutation not found in controls. Another novel missense mutation, Y173C, has been identified, which leads to impaired MPO processing and degradation via the proteasome. These mutations highlight the genetic basis of MPO deficiency, affecting MPO synthesis, processing, or heme binding. [PMC6032473, PMC508882]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Myeloperoxidase deficiency is linked to increased susceptibility to infection and malignancy. While life-threatening infectious complications are frequently absent, microbial killing by MPO-deficient cells is less efficient than by normal neutrophils. The essential contribution of MPO to innate host defense becomes apparent when exposure to pathogens overwhelms the capacity of other host defense mechanisms. Therefore, individuals with MPO deficiency may face a higher risk of infection and malignancy, despite often not experiencing severe infectious outcomes. [PMC3545676, PMC508882]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare primary bone dysplasia with decreased bone density disorder characterized by multiple doughnut-shaped hyperostotic or osteosclerotic calvarial lesions (manifesting with cranial lumps) associated with numerous pathologic fractures, elevated serum alkaline phosphatase levels and osteopenia.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Calvarial doughnut lesions-bone fragility syndrome, also known as osteoporosis with calvarial doughnut lesions (OP-CDL), presents with moderate to severe skeletal fragility. This condition is characterized by childhood-onset symptoms, including multiple long-bone fractures, scoliosis, and bone deformities. A distinctive feature is the presence of variable cranial hyperostotic lesions, specifically multiple calvarial doughnut lesions (CDLs) or calvarial bumps, which exhibit central radiolucency and peripheral radiopacity. [PMC8531111]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Calvarial doughnut lesions-bone fragility syndrome, also known as osteoporosis with calvarial doughnut lesions (OP-CDL), is a heritable disease characterized by skeletal fragility. Mutations in SGMS2, encoding sphingomyelin synthetase 2, result in aberrant sphingomyelin metabolism and lead to this condition. Additionally, a novel IFITM5 missense mutation (c.143A>G, p.N48S) has been identified in individuals with the OP-CDL phenotype, expanding its genetic spectrum. IFITM5 encodes the osteoblast-restricted protein BRIL, which is implicated in cranial skeletogenesis, and pathogenic variants in this gene can lead to diverse phenotypic consequences. [PMC8531111]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves recognizing the characteristic skeletal phenotype, which includes childhood-onset skeletal fragility with multiple long-bone fractures, scoliosis, and bone deformities. Key radiological features are multiple calvarial doughnut lesions or bumps exhibiting central radiolucency and peripheral radiopacity. Genetic testing is crucial; while SGMS2 sequencing may be considered, whole-exome sequencing can identify novel genetic variants, such as IFITM5 mutations, expanding the known genetic causes of the condition. [PMC8531111]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for calvarial doughnut lesions-bone fragility syndrome includes other heritable diseases with skeletal fragility, such as osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) and other decreased bone density disorders. Specifically, osteoporosis with calvarial doughnut lesions (OP-CDL) caused by SGMS2 mutations should be considered, as it presents with a similar skeletal phenotype and cranial hyperostotic lesions. While IFITM5 mutations are associated with OI type V, which involves hyperplastic callus formation, the phenotype of calvarial doughnut lesions is distinct from OI type V. [PMC8531111]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Calvarial doughnut lesions-bone fragility syndrome is a heritable disease with skeletal fragility. Genetic counseling should address the known genetic heterogeneity, as mutations in SGMS2 are associated with osteoporosis with calvarial doughnut lesions (OP-CDL). Additionally, novel IFITM5 variants, such as a missense mutation c.143A>G (p.N48S), have been identified in patients with OP-CDL, expanding the genetic spectrum. It is important to note that IFITM5 variants can lead to diverse phenotypic consequences, including OI type V, and some identified variants may be classified as Variants of Uncertain Significance. [PMC8531111]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An extremely rare and highly aggressive neoplasm, usually manifesting in the third to fourth decade of life, affecting males and females equally, and characterized by the onset of high fever, weight loss, jaundice, skin infiltration, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe anemia. It has a fulminant and rapidly fatal disease course with the progressive appearance of multiorgan failure and disseminated intravascular coagulation.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): ANKCL; Aggressive NK-cell lymphoma; NK-cell LGL leukemia; NK-cell large granular lymphocyte leukemia

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Aggressive NK-cell leukemia (ANKL) is a rare and highly malignant lymphoproliferative disorder, especially uncommon in children. It predominantly affects populations in Asia, East Asia, and Latin America, and is particularly common among the Asian population. The disease is closely linked to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection and is associated with prior systemic chronic active EBV disease. In one study of Chinese patients, the median age was 42 years, ranging from 22 to 50 years. [PMC12283809, PMC10557268, PMC9168658, PMC4097262]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Aggressive NK-cell leukemia (ANKL) is a rare and highly malignant lymphoproliferative disorder associated with poor prognosis and high mortality rates. The disease is closely linked to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and predominantly affects populations in Asia and Latin America. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) has emerged as a promising treatment strategy, yet its efficacy and prognosis in ANKL patients remain to be systematically evaluated. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis by searching PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library for studies published up to April 2025. The objective was to evaluate the outcomes of allo-HSCT in patients with ANKL. Six studies met the inclusion criteria. The primary outcomes included overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS), reported as hazard ratios (HRs), as well as standardized... [PMC12283809, PMC12219632, PMC10557268, PMC9838178, PMC9168658]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Aggressive NK-cell leukemia (ANKL) is strongly linked to Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection and is often considered to be caused by it. The disease is frequently associated with prior systemic chronic active EBV disease, where EBV may infect progenitor cells, leading to neoplastic transformation. While most cases are EBV-positive, some have been reported as EBV-negative. Genetically, ANKL is characterized by a higher mutation frequency of FAT family genes and specific copy number alterations, including 11q loss and 4q loss. It is broadly classified as a clonal disorder. [PMC12283809, PMC12219632, PMC10557268, PMC9168658, PMC5548667]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Aggressive NK-cell leukemia (ANKL) involves a multimodal approach. Bone marrow examination, including aspirate and trephine biopsy, is crucial, often revealing characteristic large granular lymphocytes with azurophilic granules. Immunophenotyping by flow cytometry and immunohistochemistry identifies typical markers such as CD3ε+, CD56+, CD16+, Granzyme B+, and TIA-1+. Molecular include PCR for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), EBER-ISH, and genetic analyses like targeted sequencing for FAT family gene mutations (e.g., FAT1) and copy number alterations (e.g., 11q loss, 4q loss). T-cell receptor γ gene rearrangement analysis typically shows germline configuration. Clinical features, such as hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis or specific organ involvement, also guide diagnosis, which can be challenging due to overlap with extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma and systemic EBV-positive T-cell lymphoma. [PMC12219632, PMC10953786, PMC10557268, PMC10516508, PMC9838178]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Aggressive NK-cell leukemia (ANKL) presents diagnostic challenges due to overlapping features with several other conditions. It is often confused with extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma (ENKTL), especially with bone marrow involvement, though genetic differences like FAT family gene mutations and 11q/4q loss, alongside a more acute clinical course, can aid distinction. ANKL can also be indistinguishable from systemic chronic active Epstein-Barr virus (CAEBV) infection and other EBV-positive T-cell and NK-cell proliferations, including systemic EBV-positive T-cell lymphoma of childhood (SEBVTCL). Clinical manifestations of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) are common in ANKL, leading to potential misdiagnosis as HLH. Other clonal large granular lymphocyte disorders, such as T-cell LGL leukemia and chronic lymphoproliferative disorders of NK cells, are also in the differential. Flow cytometric immunophenotyping, molecular biological techniques, and bone marrow analyses are crucial for accurate diagnosis. [PMC12219632, PMC10953786, PMC10557268, PMC10516508, PMC9168658]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Aggressive NK-cell leukemia (ANKL) shares common clinicopathological features with extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma with bone marrow (BM) involvement (ENKTL-BM), making their distinction challenging in BM examination. Despite numerous studies, genetic differences between the two diseases remained largely unclear. To investigate the genetic and clinical differences between ANKL and ENKTL-BM, we performed targeted sequencing of 282 genes and survival analyses on 15 ANKL and 5 ENKTL-BM patients. Mutation frequency of FAT family genes was higher in ANKL than in ENKTL-BM (80.0% vs. 0.0%, P = 0.004), and FAT1 gene mutations were associated with significantly lower survival rates in ANKL patients (P = 0.002). Copy number alterations including 11q loss and 4q loss were detected exclusively in ANKL. The interval from symptom onset to death was significantly shorter (113.0 vs. 440.5 days, P = 0.027)... [PMC12219632]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Aggressive NK-cell leukemia (ANKL) is associated with a poor prognosis. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) has emerged as a promising treatment strategy, demonstrating a statistically significant survival benefit. While some patients experienced temporary relief with chemotherapy, and one case survived over 30 months with splenectomy and chemotherapy, L-asparaginase containing chemotherapy has shown very poor responses. New therapeutic regimens, including allo-HSCT, require optimization to improve outcomes. [PMC12283809, PMC9168658, PMC5548667, PMC5474018, PMC4097262]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Aggressive NK-cell leukemia (ANKL) is a highly malignant disorder associated with a very aggressive clinical course, poor prognosis, and high mortality rates. The interval from symptom onset to death is significantly shorter in ANKL compared to extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma with bone marrow involvement, with patients often experiencing rapid decline and death within weeks to months. FAT1 gene mutations are associated with significantly lower survival rates in ANKL patients and are considered novel prognostic factors. While response to L-asparaginase containing chemotherapy can be very bad, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) has demonstrated a statistically significant survival benefit and improved progression-free survival, with some patients surviving over 18-30 months following this or other optimized regimens. [PMC12283809, PMC12219632, PMC9168658, PMC5474018, PMC4097262]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic form of low-renin hypertension characterized by hypertension associated with decreased plasma levels of potassium and aldosterone.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Liddle syndrome prevalence is unknown. The condition is considered rare with less than 80 families reported worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease can be clinically heterogeneous, ranging from mild to severe. Most patients are diagnosed in young adulthood, although the diagnosis may be made as early as in infancy, especially when family screening of an affected patient is performed. The typical clinical features are resistance to treatment with conventional anti-hypertensives, salt-sensitive arterial hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis often associated with a family history of early-onset hypertension and sudden death. Associated manifestations of hypokalemia may include muscular weakness, polyuria/polydipsia. Sudden death due to stroke or myocardial infarction or associated with malignant arrhythmias elicited by severe hypokalemia has been reported. Mild forms with essential normal plasma electrolytes have also been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Liddle syndrome is due to gain-of-function mutations in the genes SCNN1A (16p13), SCNN1B (16p12.2-p12.1) and SCNN1G (16p12.2), encoding, respectively, the alpha, beta and gamma subunits of the epithelial sodium channel (ENaC), a key protein involved in sodium reabsorption in the distal renal tubules. Physiologically, ENaC channel abundance is regulated by aldosterone. The gain-of-function mutations causing Liddle syndrome impair the retrieval from the apical membrane and subsequent degradation of ENaC by the ubiquitin proteasome pathway. The prolonged tenancy of mutated ENaC in the membrane results in increased sodium reabsorption independent of aldosterone with consequent hypertension.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected by the detection of hypertension, associated with hypokalemic alkalosis and suppressed renin and aldosterone, especially in the presence of a relevant family history. It can be confirmed by genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Liddle syndrome needs to be distinguished from other forms of hypertension with hypokalemic alkalosis. The suppressed renin and aldosterone levels separate it from primary and secondary forms of hyperaldosteronism, such as Conn syndrome or renovascular hypertension. A family history consistent with dominant inheritance, a urine steroid profile and genetic testing can separate it from apparent mineralocorticoid excess and glucocorticoid remediable hypertension.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant, the risk to offspring of inheriting the mutation from an affected parent is 50%. Given the variable phenotype reported in some families, genetic screening should be performed in first-degree relatives of a mutation carrier.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is based on administration of potassium-sparing diuretics, such as amiloride or triamterene, which act by blocking ENaC activity. This results in reduction of blood pressure and correction of hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis. Conventional antihypertensive therapies are not effective. Patients must also follow a low sodium diet.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With adequate treatment, prognosis is good. Without treatment, cardiovascular and renal complications usually occur.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic, syndromic glomerular disorder characterized by the association of progressive glomerular nephropathy and 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis with a high risk of developing gonadoblastoma.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, less than 150 cases have been described.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Nephropathy is the hallmark of the disease. It develops during childhood presenting as persistent proteinuria and subsequently steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome (SRNS) and progresses to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) in the second or third decade of life. On renal biopsy, focal segmental glomeruloscrelosis (FSGS) is the most common histopathological finding. Individuals have a 46, XY karyotype and present with female external genitalia, complete gonadal dysgenesis and have a higher risk of gonadoblastoma. These individuals are later evaluated for delayed puberty or primary amenorrhea. Since (modest) breast development occurs also without estrogen stimulus, failure to recognize a delayed puberty is not rare. In addition, the clinical picture may be confused by attributing pubertal delay to previous immunosuppressive therapy, renal insufficiency itself or renal transplantation. Complete gonadal dysgenesis results in infertility, female external genitalia and presence of Mullerian structures. Wilms tumor is not common in individuals with Frasier syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Frasier syndrome has been associated to specific pathogenic variants affecting nucleotides 4-5 of the intron 9 (previously referred to as IVS9+4; IVS9+5) in the WT1 gene (11p13). WT1 encodes for a protein that serves as regulatory transcription factor important both for renal and gonadal development.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is suspected on childhood onset of progressive glomerulopathy with findings of FSGS on histological analysis. Phenotypic females with delayed puberty or primary amenorrhea, should be carefully evaluated for signs of nephropathy. When the clinical findings suggest the diagnosis of WT1 associated disorders, single gene testing of the hotspot 8-9 exons with adjacent introns can be performed. Karyotype testing is recommended for all individuals with WT1 intron 9 pathogenic variants.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnosis is idiopathic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, and other WT1 associated diseases including Denys-Drash syndrome, genetic steroid resistant nephrotic syndrome and disorders of testicular development.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Most affected individuals have a de novo pathogenic variant and hence negative family history; however, autosomal dominant inheritance has been reported. Where karyotyping is indicated, pre-testing genetic counselling on the possibility of detecting sex reversal should be offered.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is multidisciplinary and should involve a nephrologist for management of chronic renal failure (initially with nephroprotective medical therapy and afterwards with renal replacement therapies or transplantation when ESRD occurs), an endocrinologists for treatment of associated disorder of testicular development, and oncologists and surgeons to evaluate the need for an early gonadectomy in order to prevent tumorigenesis. Preemptive bilateral gonadectomy at the time of renal transplant or placement of a peritoneal dialysis catheter might be an option.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: There is limited information on life expectancy. After kidney transplantation, nephrotic syndrome does not recur. 46,XY individuals with complete gonadal dysgenesis are infertile.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS) characterized by neonatal onset of systemic inflammation, urticarial skin rash and arthritis/arthralgia resulting in severe arthropathy and central nervous system involvement (including chronic aseptic meningitis, brain atrophy and sensorineural hearing loss).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): IOMID syndrome; Infantile-onset multisystem inflammatory disease; NOMID syndrome; Neonatal-onset multisystem inflammatory disease; Prieur-Griscelli syndrome; Chronic infantile neurological cutaneous and articular syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Whilst the exact prevalence of chronic infantile neurological, cutaneous, and articular (CINCA) syndrome is unknown, it is estimated that the whole spectrum of CAPS has a prevalence of 1/360,000 in France, CINCA being the less common form. In the Eurofever registry, collecting information on over 250 patients with NLRP3 mutation, about 25% of the patients present the most severe CINCA phenotype.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset typically occurs within the first hours/days of life with an urticarial rash, persistent elevation of acute phase reactants, and intermittent fever (which may be low-grade or absent). Typical facial features include frontal bossing and saddle back nose. The rash is typically non-pruritic and changes distribution during the day, without vasculitic alterations. Central nervous system manifestations include chronic aseptic meningitis, which, if left untreated, leads to brain atrophy, severe intellectual disability and sensorineural hearing loss. Typical neurological symptoms include chronic irritability, headache, early morning nausea, vomiting and, rarely, seizures. Ocular manifestations may include conjunctivitis, papilledema, optic nerve atrophy and progressive vision loss. Early degenerative arthropathy frequently involves large joints and causes deformities and contractures.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Mutations (usually de novo ) in the NLRP3 gene (chromosome 1q44) are identified in the majority of patients; however 30-35% of affected individuals lack a detectable mutation. Most of these patients display a somatic mosaicism for NLRP3. The NLRP3 gene plays a key role in innate immunity, encoding a component of the NLRP3-inflammasome, with gain of function mutations leading to overproduction of interleukin 1beta (IL-1beta).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The general consensus is that the clinical picture of CINCA is sufficient for diagnosis. Laboratory analyses document a nonspecific inflammatory syndrome with anemia, granulocyte hyperleukocytosis, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and elevated concentrations of C reactive protein. No autoantibodies or immune deficiencies are detected. Skin biopsy shows a neutrophilc dermatosis with massive perivascular neutrophil infiltration without signs of vasculitis. Brain MRI shows evident signs of meningitis with a possible inflammatory involvement of the inner ear. Ophthalmological examination may reveal papilledema. Genetic testing usually detects de-novo NLRP3 mutations but is not obligatory for diagnosis. In the absence of a positive standard genetic test, NLRP3 somatic mosaicism should be investigated
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: An infectious disease is often suspected at disease onset. CINCA should be differentiated from similar monogenic or multifactorial autoinflammatory diseases, including, systemic onset juvenile idiopathic arthritis, tumor necrosis factor receptor 1 associated periodic syndrome, and the severe form of mevalonate kinase deficiency, CANDLE syndrome as well as the milder phenotype associated to mutations of NLRP3 (familial cold urticarial and Muckle-Wells syndrome).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant. Affected patients carrying a germinal mutation have a 50% risk of transmitting the disease to each child. In case of somatic mosaicism, risk depends on the possible presence of somatic mutations in reproductive organs of the parents.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Therapeutic approaches using numerous anti-inflammatory drugs and immunosuppressants have provided disappointing results. Corticosteroids can partially improve the symptoms but at the cost of high toxicity. Anakinra (a receptor antagonist of interleukin-1) and canakinumab (a monoclonal antibody against IL-1beta) have proved to be efficient against inflammatory signs, as well as against intracranial hypertension and hearing loss.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Without adequate and timely treatment, quality of life is often poor. Syndrome severity is wide-ranging and the functional prognosis depends on the degree of neurological manifestations (such as intellectual disability and hearing loss) and the occurrence of tendinous retractions.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS) is a life-long, autoinflammatory disease associated with a gain-of-function mutation in the nucleotide-binding domain, leucine-rich repeat family, pyrin domain containing 3 (NLRP3) gene, which result in uncontrolled production of IL-1β and chronic inflammation. Chronic infantile neurologic cutaneous and articular (CINCA) syndrome/neonatal-Onset multisystem inflammatory disease (NOMID) is the most severe form of CAPS. Although the first symptoms may be presented at birth, there are few reports on the involvement of the placenta and umbilical cord in the disease. Therefore, herein a preterm case of CINCA/NOMID syndrome and confirms intrauterine-onset inflammation with conclusive evidence by using fetal and placental histopathological examination. The female patient was born at 33weeks of gestation by emergency caesarean section and weighted at... [PMC8165790]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare chromosomal anomaly characterized by highly variable manifestations, ranging from a severe phenotype which presents with lissencephaly and severe intellectual disability to a milder phenotype that includes short stature, microcephaly, intellectual disability, seizures (that may be pharmacoresistant), café-au-lait spots, retinal flecks and minor facial dysmorphism, depending on the presence or absence of the Miller-Dieker critical region.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Ring chromosome 17 syndrome is phenotypically heterogeneous, ranging from severe Miller-Dieker syndrome to milder forms. Common features include mental and motor retardation, seizures, short stature, muscular hypotonia, and microcephaly. Distinctive findings often include café au lait spots and retinal flecking or freckling. Other reported features encompass intrauterine growth retardation, clinodactyly, and minor facial dysmorphic features. In severe cases, lissencephaly, dysphagia, failure to thrive, and intractable convulsions leading to early mortality have been observed. Dermatoglyphic abnormalities and unspecified genital abnormalities have also been noted in some patients. [PMC12131107, PMC1793146, PMC504131, PMC1048713]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Ring chromosome 17 syndrome is caused by the presence of a ring chromosome 17, which can occur in a mosaic form. This chromosomal abnormality is associated with a wide range of clinical features, and phenotypic heterogeneity can be influenced by the specific breakpoints on chromosome 17. Associated deletions, such as the 17p13.3 deletion, may also be present and involve genes like PAFAH1B1, YWHAE, and CRK, contributing to the varied clinical presentation. Abnormalities of chromosome 17 are implicated in conditions such as retinal pigment epithelial or photoreceptor dysfunction. [PMC12131107, PMC504131, PMC1048713]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Ring chromosome 17 syndrome can be challenging, as arrays and sequencing may have limitations in identifying structural variants. While CGH arrays can detect associated deletions, such as 17p13.3 deletions involving YWHAE and CRK, they may miss the ring chromosome itself. Cytogenetic analysis of G-banded chromosomes is crucial for revealing mosaic ring chromosome 17. Optical genome mapping (OGM) has been shown to simultaneously identify both 17p13.3 deletions and mosaic ring chromosome 17, and is suggested as a potential first-tier test, possibly in conjunction with exome sequencing. [PMC12131107]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Ring chromosome 17 syndrome shares significant phenotypic overlap with 17p13.3 deletion syndrome, both presenting with features ranging from Miller-Dieker syndrome (characterized by lissencephaly, hypotonia, and severe intellectual disability due to PAFAH1B1 deletion) to milder phenotypes including microcephaly, seizures, and developmental delay, often involving YWHAE and CRK gene deletions. Distinguishing features for ring chromosome 17 syndrome include café au lait spots and retinal or axillary freckling, which are not typically seen in 17p13.3 deletion syndrome. Diagnostic like CGH arrays may initially suggest 17p13.3 deletion, necessitating further cytogenetic analysis or optical genome mapping to identify mosaic ring chromosome 17. [PMC12131107]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for ring chromosome 17 syndrome involves explaining its significant phenotypic heterogeneity, which ranges from severe Miller-Dieker syndrome (associated with PAFAH1B1 gene deletion, lissencephaly, and profound intellectual disability) to milder presentations (linked to YWHAE and CRK gene deletions, microcephaly, seizures, and developmental delay). This clinical variability is often attributed to differences in breakpoints on chromosome 17. Diagnostic are crucial, as arrays may have limitations in identifying structural variants like mosaic ring chromosomes, necessitating further investigation with cytogenetic analysis or optical genome mapping, particularly when atypical phenotypic features are present. [PMC12131107, PMC1048713]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Ring chromosome 17 syndrome is heterogeneous, with clinical features ranging from severe to milder phenotypes. The most severe form, resembling Miller-Dieker syndrome, is characterized by lissencephaly, severe intellectual disability, and intractable convulsions, which can lead to early mortality, as observed in an infant who died at 9 months. Milder presentations include microcephaly, seizures, delayed development, short stature, and intellectual disability, with individuals surviving into childhood. Common findings across cases include mental and motor retardation, seizures, short stature, muscular hypotonia, and microcephaly. The variability in clinical outcomes is likely due to differences in the breakpoints on chromosome 17. [PMC12131107, PMC1793146, PMC1048713]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A spondylodysplasic dysplasia clinically characterized by postnatal progressive vertebral fusions frequently manifesting as block vertebrae, contributing to an shortened trunk and hence disproportionate short stature, scoliosis, lordosis, carpal and tarsal synostosis and infrequently, club feet.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Spondylocarpotarsal synostosis (SCT) is very rare. To date, less than 40 cases have been reported in the medical literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: While the clinical onset is postnatal, the diagnosis becomes clinically evident in early in childhood. Primary clinical characteristics of SCT syndrome include progressive vertebral fusions manifesting as block vertebrae leading to a shortened trunk resulting in disproportionate short stature that becomes apparent with physical growth. Scoliosis, lordosis, carpal and tarsal synostosis are frequent with club feet being observed in a minority of cases. A mild facial dysmorphism with a round face with frontal bossing and anteverted nostrils can be evident. Midline cleft palate, conductive hearing loss, joint laxity and dental enamel hypoplasia are uncommonly reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: SCT syndrome is due to biallelic mutations in FLNB (localized to 3p14.3) that encodes cytoskeletal protein filamin B. A very similar condition is caused by either monoallelic or biallelic mutations in MYH3.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is confirmed by skeletal x-rays and genetic testing. Radiographs demonstrate progressive vertebral fusions and lumbar spine, carpal and tarsal synostosis without rib anomalies. Occasionally, delayed ossification of epiphyses and bilateral epiphyseal femur dysplasia are reported.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis may include isolated Klippel-Feil syndrome and other vertebral dysplasias, such as autosomal dominant spondylocostal dysplasia and multiple synostoses syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: SCT syndrome follows an autosomal recessive inheritance (FLNB, MYH3) or occasionally autosomal dominant inheritance (MYH3). Genetic counseling should be proposed to at risk couples informing them that there is 25% (autosomal recessive) or 50% (autosomal dominant) risk of tranmitting the disease to offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management involves ophthalmologic, audiologic and spine assessments. Scoliosis is treated medically; no effective surgical intervention has been described. The cervical spine should be evaluated for features of instability prior to general anesthesia. Pain management is indispensable as patients suffer from much continuing physical pain due to the spinal deformities and fused block vertebrae.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: It has not been formally evaluated if SCT syndrome affects life expectancy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of Spondylocarpotarsal synostosis (specifically CPSFS1A) is achievable through genetic analysis. In one reported case, genomic DNA was extracted from a fetus, and whole-exome sequencing of the proband, followed by Sanger sequencing, identified a novel pathogenic variant in the MYH3 gene. This variant was confirmed to cosegregate with the condition within the family. Based on this genetic finding, the pregnancy was selectively terminated due to the fetus being genetically affected, providing evidence for genetic counseling and pregnancy management. [PMC7549579]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare distal myopathy characterized by weakness in the distal upper extremities, usually finger and wrist extensors which later progresses to all hand muscles and distal lower extremity, primarily in toe and ankle extensors.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Distal myopathy, Welander type (WDM) prevalence is unknown. The condition is mainly restricted to a geographical area around the Baltic Sea especially in Finland and Sweden (mid-eastern region), where the estimated prevalence is 1/10,000. However, some patients have been reported in the United Kingdom.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: WDM is a late adult-onset disorder (onset between 40 and 60 years) characterized by initial weakness of index finger extensors followed by extension weakness in the other fingers. Weakness slowly progresses to all hand and lower leg muscles. In the lower limb, the anterior tibial muscle and toe extensors are typically affected leading to walking difficulties and steppage gait.
