DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: PPARG-related familial partial lipodystrophy (FPLD3) is a very rare autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by mutations in the PPARG gene. Familial partial lipodystrophies are generally described as very rare inherited conditions, with FPLD3 specifically noted as rare. While numerous genes are implicated in FPLD, PPARG mutations are a known cause of FPLD3. Case reports describe affected individuals and kindreds from various populations, and one review identified a total of 58 FPLD3 patients from previous studies. [PMC11593357, PMC11196099, PMC11580599, PMC9001891, PMC8217860]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: PPARG-related familial partial lipodystrophy (FPLD3) is an inherited disorder characterized by partial loss of adipose tissue, typically affecting the upper and lower extremities, face, hips, and limbs. This lipoatrophy is frequently accompanied by severe metabolic complications, including profound insulin resistance, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus, severe hypertriglyceridemia, and hypertension. Patients may also experience recurrent pancreatitis, fatty liver, liver dysfunction, albuminuria, diabetic peripheral neuropathy, and depressed high-density lipoprotein cholesterol. Subnormal leptin secretion is a noted feature. Clinical presentation can range from elevated triglycerides in prepubescent individuals to severe, difficult-to-manage diabetes and cardiovascular disease in adults. [PMC11593357, PMC11580599, PMC9001891, PMC8217860, PMC1368963]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: PPARG-related familial partial lipodystrophy type 3 (FPLD3) is a rare, autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by heterozygous, loss-of-function mutations in the PPARG gene, which encodes peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (PPARγ). These mutations lead to PPAR-gamma deficiency through mechanisms such as haploinsufficiency or dominant-negative interference with the wild-type receptor. Specific novel mutations identified include c.1024C>T p.(Gln342Ter), Y151C, c.929T>C (p.F310S), Glu157Gly, L451P, and Y355X. These variants can cause intra- and/or intermolecular defects, including impaired cofactor binding, reduced RXRα heterodimerization, and transcriptional inactivity or instability of the mutant protein. [PMC11593357, PMC11196099, PMC11580599, PMC9001891, PMC8217860]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of PPARG-related familial partial lipodystrophy primarily relies on genetic testing, including whole exome sequencing (WES) and Sanger analysis to detect and confirm PPARG gene mutations. Targeted gene panels, which may include nuclear and mitochondrial genes, are also employed. Computational prediction tools (e.g., MT, DANN, CADD, BayesDel, fitCons) are utilized to assess the pathogenicity of identified variants. Further analysis can involve protein modeling (e.g., AlphaFold) and molecular docking. Careful phenotypic and genotypic reanalysis is crucial, with physical examination emphasized for young patients presenting with severe metabolic syndromes. Early clinical recognition of FPLD syndromes is important to prevent complications. [PMC11593357, PMC11196099, PMC11580599, PMC9001891, PMC8217860]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: PPARG-related familial partial lipodystrophy (FPLD) is frequently misdiagnosed as common metabolic conditions, including type 1 or type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hypertriglyceridemia, due to shared features like severe insulin resistance. Patients presenting with difficult-to-classify or challenging-to-manage diabetes should prompt consideration of FPLD syndromes. The differential diagnosis also includes other genetic forms of partial lipodystrophy, such as FPLD1 linked to Mysterin variants, and mitochondrial diseases, as exemplified by a case with an m.A8344G mitochondrial variant presenting with an FPLD phenotype and additional systemic features. Careful phenotypic and genotypic reanalysis is crucial for accurate molecular diagnosis. [PMC11196099, PMC11580599, PMC8217860, PMC7662064]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: PPARG-related familial partial lipodystrophy type 3 (FPLD3) is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder caused by heterozygous mutations in the PPARG gene. Genetic testing, including whole exome sequencing and Sanger analysis, is crucial for diagnosis and confirmation of pathogenic variants. Early recognition of FPLD syndromes through genetic testing is important, especially in young patients with severe metabolic syndromes or difficult-to-classify diabetes. Family members can be assessed, as unaffected individuals may not carry the mutation, while pre-pubescent relatives might show metabolic abnormalities even without overt lipodystrophy, indicating variable expressivity and the need for family screening. [PMC11593357, PMC11196099, PMC11580599, PMC9001891, PMC8217860]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of PPARG-related familial partial lipodystrophy aims to prevent and improve complications. PPARG agonists, particularly Pioglitazone, are considered preferred agents. Pioglitazone has demonstrated dramatic responses, improving patient responsiveness to hypoglycemic and antihypertensive therapy, normalizing fasting blood glucose and glycosylated hemoglobin, and enhancing PPARγ activation for better clinical outcomes. Additionally, Metreleptin, a synthetic analogue of human leptin, has shown efficacy in a patient with a novel PPARG mutation, significantly reducing HbA1c and fasting plasma triglycerides, suggesting it may be an effective treatment for FPLD3. [PMC11593357, PMC11580599, PMC8217860]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: PPARG-related familial partial lipodystrophy is associated with severe metabolic complications including uncontrolled diabetes, profound insulin resistance, severe hypertriglyceridemia, hypertension, and recurrent pancreatitis. Without early recognition, patients may develop multiple manifestations of cardiovascular disease. However, treatment with PPARγ agonists like Pioglitazone can lead to dramatic improvements in clinical outcomes, with fasting blood glucose and glycosylated hemoglobin approaching normal levels. Metreleptin treatment has also shown efficacy in reducing HbA1c and fasting plasma triglycerides. Therefore, while the condition presents with significant metabolic challenges, effective management can substantially improve the prognosis and prevent severe complications. [PMC11593357, PMC11580599, PMC8217860, PMC1368963]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked syndromic intellectual disability characterized by global developmental delay and severe intellectual disability, seizures, and recurrent lower respiratory tract infections, resulting in premature death in affected males. Additional reported manifestations include mild dysmorphic facial features (such as epicanthic folds, high nasal bridge, or small mouth), gait disturbances, brisk tendon reflexes, delayed bone age, and tapering fingers. No evident heterozygous manifestation has been reported in females.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Pai type, is an X-linked recessive syndrome characterized by mental retardation, minor dysmorphism, and premature death in affected males. The minor anomalies observed are not distinctive enough to suggest a unique syndrome, and the condition does not present with features of Waisman-Laxova or PPM-X syndromes. The possibility of allelism with other non-specific XLMR syndromes mapped to Xq28 could not be excluded. [PMC1050990]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Pai type, is an X-linked recessive disorder. A linkage study in a four-generation family mapped the gene locus to a 7 Mb region on Xq28, specifically between markers DXS1113 and DXS1108. This condition is characterized by X-linked recessive mental retardation, minor dysmorphism, and premature death in affected males. While the specific gene responsible was not identified, the locus was strongly implicated. Allelism with other non-specific X-linked mental retardation syndromes also mapped to Xq28 could not be excluded. [PMC1050990]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves genetic linkage studies, initially using microsatellite-based polymorphic loci across the X chromosome to identify linkage to Xq28. Further analysis can pinpoint a specific haplotype of Xq28 markers, such as those bounded by DXS1113 and DXS1108, which cosegregates with the X-linked recessive mental retardation. Strong evidence for the gene locus within the 7 Mb region of Xq28 is provided by two-point lod scores greater than 3.0. This genetic information allows at-risk female relatives to know their genotype and enables prenatal diagnosis for heterozygotes. [PMC1050990]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Patients did not present with features characteristic of Waisman-Laxova syndrome or PPM-X syndrome. However, the possibility of allelism with other non-specific X-linked mental retardation syndromes, including MRX3, MRX16, MRX25, MRX28, and MRX41, all mapped to Xq28, could not be excluded. The minor anomalies observed were not distinctive enough to suggest a unique syndrome, complicating differentiation from other Xq28-linked XLMR conditions. [PMC1050990]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: For families with known genetic risk, female relatives can benefit from genetic testing to determine their carrier status. Heterozygous carriers have the opportunity to undergo prenatal diagnosis to assess the fetal genotype for X-linked intellectual disability, Pai type. [PMC1050990]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Pai type, is an X-linked recessive disorder characterized by mental retardation, minor dysmorphism, and premature death in affected males. Genetic counseling is crucial for families, as multiple female relatives at risk can benefit from knowing their genotype. Heterozygous females, identified through genetic testing, have the opportunity to undergo prenatal diagnosis for future pregnancies. [PMC1050990]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Efforts to understand the genetic basis of mental retardation are greatly assisted by the identification of families with multiple relatives with mental retardation that clinical geneticists encounter in the routine practice of their profession. Here a linkage study of a four generation family in which X linked recessive mental retardation (XLMR) is associated with minor dysmorphism and premature death of the affected males. Microsatellite based polymorphic loci evenly spaced over the entire X chromosome were used initially to detect linkage to Xq28. Further analysis identified a haplotype of Xq28 markers bounded proximally by locus DXS1113 and distally by DXS1108 that cosegregated with XLMR in this family. Two point lod scores > 3.0 provided strong evidence that the gene locus responsible for XLMR in this family is within this 7 Mb region of Xq28. The minor anomalies noted in some... [PMC1050990]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Affected males with X-linked intellectual disability, Pai type, experience premature death. This X-linked recessive syndrome is also characterized by mental retardation and mild dysmorphism, as identified in a four-generation family study. The available information primarily focuses on the genetic mapping of the disorder to Xq28, with limited details provided regarding the specific long-term clinical progression or other prognostic indicators beyond the early mortality. [PMC1050990]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare variety of migraine with aura characterized by the presence of a motor weakness during the aura. There are two main forms depending on the familial history: patients with at least one first- or second-degree relative who has aura including motor weakness have familial hemiplegic migraine (FHM); patients without such familial history have sporadic hemiplegic migraine (SHM).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of hemiplegic migraine (HM) is one in 10,000, with FHM and SHM being equally frequent.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Typical HM attacks are characterised by motor weakness that is always associated with other aura symptoms, the most frequent being sensory, visual and speech disorders. In addition, basilar-type symptoms occur in up to 70% of patients. Severe attacks may occur in both FHM and SHM with prolonged hemiplegia, confusion, coma, fever and seizures. The clinical spectrum also includes permanent cerebellar signs (nystagmus, ataxia, dysarthria) and less frequently various types of seizures and intellectual deficit.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The three causative genes identified so far encode ion-transporters (CACNA1A, ATP1A2 and SCNA1). Molecular diagnosis is now possible through screening of these three genes.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: FHM is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment involves the same approaches used for other varieties of migraine with aura, with the exception that triptans are contraindicated in FHM/SHM. Based on new pathophysiological insights, preventive treatments using various antiepileptic agents seem promising.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is usually good.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inflammatory and autoimmune disease with epilepsy characterized by unilateral hemispheric atrophy, associated with drug-resistant focal epilepsy, progressive hemiplegia, and cognitive decline. The disease mainly affects children and begins with a prodromal period with mild hemiparesis or infrequent seizures lasting up to several years. The acute stage is marked by frequent seizures arising from one cerebral hemisphere, followed by a residual stage with persistent severe neurological deficits and relapsing epilepsy.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Rasmussen's encephalitis (RE) is a rare, progressive, chronic neurological disorder primarily affecting one cerebral hemisphere, typically in pediatric individuals, though 10% of cases occur in adolescents and adults. It is characterized by progressive focal epilepsy, often drug-resistant and manifesting as epilepsia partialis continua, and unilateral cerebral atrophy. Patients also develop motor and cognitive impairment. Atypical presentations include delayed-onset seizures or initial limb motor disorders without immediate seizures. Neuroimaging reveals progressive unilateral hemispheric atrophy with multifocal abnormal signals on MRI and decreased metabolism in the affected hemisphere on PET, which can also show unihemispheric hypometabolism and crossed cerebellar diaschisis early. EEG exhibits asymmetric background rhythms with slow waves and epileptiform discharges in the affected hemisphere. Histopathological examination shows T-cell-dominated encephalitis, activated microglial cells, reactive astrogliosis, cortical inflammation, neuronal degeneration, and gliosis. [PMC12205137, PMC12014926, PMC11515774, PMC11313535, PMC11001175]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Rasmussen encephalitis (RE) can be challenging to diagnose, especially in atypical presentations. Conditions considered in the differential diagnosis include autoimmune encephalitis, such as Anti-Hu encephalitis, particularly in cases presenting with epilepsia partialis continua (EPC) and brain lesions resembling RE. Unilateral primary angiitis of the CNS (PACNS) and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disease are also important considerations, especially in patients with unihemispheric disease, an indolent course, and seizures. The presence of predominantly unilateral symptoms, lateralized EEG findings, and progressive unilateral hemispheric atrophy on imaging are key features that guide the differential workup. [PMC12014926, PMC10834122, PMC11305367, PMC10585676]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Rasmussen's encephalitis (RE) is a rare, chronic, neurological disorder characterized by progressive focal epilepsy and hemispheric atrophy. Late-onset RE poses diagnostic challenges due to atypical clinical features and nonspecific early MRI findings. This case series underscores the value of [18F]FDG PET in detecting unihemispheric hypometabolism and crossed cerebellar diaschisis at diagnosis, before MRI changes appear. During follow-up, PET identified active disease through hypermetabolic foci or pseudo-normalized metabolism, indicative of subclinical seizures, while stable hypometabolism signaled quiescence. Combining PET with MRI enhances diagnostic accuracy and guides treatment decisions in managing RE. We retrospectively analyzed the clinical characteristics of three ARE cases with delayed-onset seizures treated at Peking University First Hospital and Sanbo Brain Hospital from... [PMC12205137, PMC12014926, PMC11515774, PMC11313535, PMC11596482]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: 46,XY difference of sex development due to 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 3 deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare difference of sex development characterized by 17-beta hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 3 deficiency that affects individuals with a 46,XY karyotype leading to underandrogenization of the genitalia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 3 deficiency; 17-ketoreductase deficiency; 17-ketosteroidreductase deficiency; 46,XY disorder of sex development due to 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase 3 deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Estimated prevalence at birth has been reported to be 1/147,000 in the Netherlands; the prevalence may be higher elsewhere, especially in populations with high consanguinity.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical presentation is variable. Atypical external genitalia with variable phallic size and posterior labioscrotal fusion are often noticed at birth. Patients with typical female-appearing external genitalia may present with inguinal hernia in childhood. Although some patients, with less severe enzyme defiency, are assigned males at birth, affected individuals are often assigned females at birth. However, at puberty, a portion of these patients develop signs of unusual androgenization (phallic enlargement, male secondary sexual characteristics) as the result of increased testosterone (due to conversion of androstenedione by 17-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase isoenzymes). Testes can be abdominal, inguinal, or in the labioscrotal folds. The internal urogenital tract is developed to a variable extent, and Müllerian structures are absent. All affected individuals are infertile.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The condition is caused by mutations in the HSD17B3 gene (9q22) encoding an enzyme expressed predominantly in the testes that converts androstenedione to testosterone. The variable clinical phenotype may be related to partial activity of the enzyme or activity of isoenzymes.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Hormonal evaluation demonstrates increased androstenedione and low testosterone levels, with an elevated androstenedione/testosterone ratio. The Sertoli cell markers, serum AMH and inhibin B, are usually in the typical age-related reference range for males. Before puberty, an hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin) stimulation test is often necessary for diagnosis, since basal levels may be uninformative. Therefore, recent consensus statements recommend the molecular genetic analysis of the HSD17B3 gene as a primary diagnostic approach.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes disorders of androgen synthesis such as 5-alpha-reductase 2 deficiency, complete and partial androgen insensitivity syndromes and partial gonadal dysgenesis (caused by NR5A1 mutations for example).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is available for the kindred of affected patients if causal pathogenic variants have been identified. Atypical fetal genitalia may be seen on prenatal ultrasound.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The condition follows an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Parents of an affected individual should be informed that there is a 25% of chance of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: If diagnosed at birth, gender assignment should be discussed openly with the family and an evaluation should be done at a DSD center. Any genital surgery demands a thorough assessment and is restricted in several countries in childhood. Early gonadectomy is unnecessary. Depending on gender identity development, some adolescents may demand a gender change whereas others may request treatment to prevent pubertal androgenization and to induce female puberty.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy and overall morbidity (other than related to untreated hormone deficiency) are not altered. The impact on genital development, puberty and adult sexual functioning is usually severe and may require endocrine and/or surgical treatment, as well as psychological counseling.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A fetopathy that is likely to occur when a cytomegalovirus (CMV) infected pregnant woman transmits the virus in utero. Children born with congenital CMV infection may present with hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, jaundice, pneumonitis, fetal growth retardation, petechiae, purpura, and thrombocytopenia. Congenital CMV infection can equally result in major neurological sequelae, including microcephaly, intracranial calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss, chorioretinitis, intellectual and motor disabilities, and seizure disorders. CMV disease sequelae caused by a primary infection are usually more severe than those caused by the reactivation of a latent infection.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Mother-to-child transmission of cytomegalovirus syndrome; Antenatal cytomegalovirus infection; Antenatal CMV infection

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection is the most common congenital infection worldwide and the leading infectious cause of birth defects, including damage to the brain. It is also one of the leading causes of congenital hearing loss in newborns. The incidence of congenital cytomegalovirus infection is around 1%, depending on the region. In a rural German study, 54.8% of pregnant women were CMV seronegative, with a seroconversion rate of 0.37-1.42%. Low uptake of CMV serological testing indicates low risk awareness among pregnant women and healthcare professionals. Even a partially effective vaccine against human cytomegalovirus would have a major effect on global health consequences. [PMC11684802, PMC12110699, PMC10148470]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Fetal cytomegalovirus syndrome can lead to abortion or perinatal death. Common prenatal abnormalities include small for gestational age, ventriculomegaly, and hyperechogenic bowels. Prenatal MRI frequently reveals subependymal cysts, which correlate with neurological complications such as speech delay. Other fetal brain alterations, including microcephaly and cortical dysplasia, have been reported. Postnatally, hearing loss, ranging from mild to severe, is a significant complication, with a correlation noted between hearing loss and ventriculomegaly. Placentitis may also be present. [PMC12110699, PMC9865737, PMC2431643]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Fetal cytomegalovirus syndrome (cCMV) is caused by human cytomegalovirus (HCMV), which is the most common congenital infection worldwide and a leading infectious cause of birth defects. The incidence of congenital CMV infection is around 1%. Intrauterine CMV transmission poses significant risks to fetal development, particularly affecting the nervous system, and is a primary cause of congenital hearing loss. Pathological findings include placentitis, fetal brain alterations such as microcephaly and cortical dysplasia, and other prenatal abnormalities like small for gestational age, ventriculomegaly, and hyperechogenic bowels. A correlation has been observed between CMV DNA loads in fetal organs and the extent of infection, with a potent pro-inflammatory condition at the placental level potentially contributing to cCMV. CMV is recognized as part of the TORCH complex of infections that can cause congenital abnormalities during pregnancy. [PMC11684802, PMC12110699, PMC11209383, PMC10148470, PMC9865737]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for fetal cytomegalovirus syndrome encompass maternal, fetal, and neonatal screening. Maternal serological tests, including CMV IgG and IgM antibodies, are used to determine seroprevalence and identify seroconversion during pregnancy, with low IgG avidity correlating with fetal transmission. Fetal diagnosis can involve detecting CMV DNA in amniotic fluid or ascites via abdominocentesis using PCR. Predictive ultrasound findings such as small for gestational age, ventriculomegaly, and hyperechogenic bowels may prompt further investigation, including prenatal MRI to identify abnormalities like subependymal cysts. Post-termination, real-time PCR for CMV DNA loads in fetal organs and histopathological examination with CMV-specific immunostaining are utilized. Overall, the performance of TORCH diagnostic assays is variable, highlighting the importance of confirmatory testing. [PMC12110699, PMC11209383, PMC10148470, PMC9865737, PMC6927310]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Fetal cytomegalovirus syndrome is part of the TORCH complex, which includes other infections causing congenital abnormalities. The differential diagnosis should consider other TORCH pathogens such as Toxoplasma gondii, parvovirus B19, and rubella virus. Zika virus is also recognized as an emerging TORCH infection with similar presentations, further complicating diagnosis due to overlapping clinical features and variable diagnostic assay performance for these congenital infections. [PMC6927310]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of fetal cytomegalovirus infection involves several approaches. Maternal serological testing, though often underutilized, can identify seronegative women and seroconversion, with low maternal IgG avidity potentially correlating with fetal transmission. Fetal diagnosis can be achieved by detecting CMV DNA via PCR in amniotic fluid or ascites obtained through abdominocentesis. Ultrasound is crucial for identifying predictive abnormalities such as small for gestational age, ventriculomegaly, and hyperechogenic bowels, and can help estimate outcomes. In cases of suspicious ultrasound findings, prenatal MRI is recommended to detect abnormalities like subependymal cysts and assess neurological complications. Overall, diagnostic assays for congenital infections show variable performance, highlighting the need for confirmatory testing. [PMC12110699, PMC11209383, PMC10148470, PMC9865737, PMC6927310]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Background/CMV (cytomegalovirus) is associated with several developmental disorders. The incidence of congenital cytomegalovirus infection is around 1%, depending on the region. Previous prospective studies have shown that certain ultrasound findings are predictive factors for prenatal CMV infection. During this systematic review, we searched PubMed and Embas. Out of 569 , 19 met our search criteria (we included cases where prenatally positive amniocentesis PCR for CMV was performed or autopsy confirmed the CMV diagnosis). A total of 237 cases were reported from 19 studies. In 64 cases, abortion or perinatal death occurred. The most common prenatal abnormalities were small for gestational age (n = 47), ventriculomegaly (n = 51), and hyperechogenic bowels (n = 39). A subependymal cyst was the most common prenatal MRI abnormality (n = 20). Hearing loss was observed in 61 cases (42 mild,... [PMC12110699, PMC10148470, PMC9865737, PMC6927310]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: The pursuit of a vaccine against the human cytomegalovirus (HCMV) has been ongoing for more than 50 years. HCMV is the leading infectious cause of birth defects, including damage to the brain, and is a common cause of complications in organ transplantation. The complex biology of HCMV has made vaccine development difficult, but a recent meeting sponsored by the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases in September of 2023 brought together experts from academia, industry, and federal agencies to discuss progress in the field. The meeting reviewed the status of candidate HCMV vaccines under study and the challenges in clinical trial design in demonstrating efficacy against congenital CMV infection or the reduction of HCMV disease following solid organ transplantation or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Discussion in the meeting revealed that, with the numerous... [PMC11684802, PMC10148470]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Fetal cytomegalovirus syndrome is associated with severe outcomes, including abortion or perinatal death, which occurred in 64 out of 237 cases in one systematic review. Common prenatal abnormalities include small for gestational age, ventriculomegaly, and hyperechogenic bowels. Neurological complications are frequent, with speech delay being the most common, and subependymal cysts, often detected by MRI, are associated with these complications. Hearing loss, ranging from mild to severe, is also observed in many cases and correlates with ventriculomegaly. Fetal brain alterations such as microcephaly and cortical dysplasia have also been reported. Ultrasound signals may be useful for estimating the outcome. [PMC12110699, PMC9865737]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare chronic encephalitis developing up to several years after congenital rubella virus infection or rubella infection in childhood, characterized by slowly progressive, wide-spread neurological symptoms, like cognitive decline, cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, and seizures, amongst others. Progredient deterioration of the neurological disease eventually leads to the death of the patient.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Rubella panencephalitis, or acute encephalitis following rubella virus infection, is considered a very rare neurological complication. One report described a single case of postrubella polyradiculoneuritis combined with encephalitis. Another report detailed a family cluster in India, where two out of three atypical rubella cases presented with acute encephalitis and were fatal. A separate case involved a 17-year-old male in Korea who developed meningoencephalitis during a rubella epidemic. [PMC6154155, PMC3054242]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Rubella infection can lead to severe neurological complications, including acute encephalitis, which has been fatal in some cases. Atypical presentations are observed, where some individuals may experience only mild febrile illness, while others develop acute encephalitis. Neurological manifestations can include suspected meningoencephalitis, symmetrical hyporeflexic weakness of all four extremities, and urinary disturbance. Rare cases have shown involvement of both central and peripheral nerves, presenting as polyradiculoneuropathy with multifocal conduction block. [PMC6154155, PMC3054242]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Rubella panencephalitis is a rare neurological complication directly linked to rubella virus infection. The rubella virus can be isolated from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in individuals with postnatal rubella encephalitis. Confirmation of rubella virus infection can also be achieved through the detection of rubella IgM antibody titers in both serum and CSF. Cases of acute encephalitis associated with rubella have been reported, sometimes resulting in fatal outcomes. [PMC6154155, PMC3054242, PMC1632541]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of rubella panencephalitis can involve several . Rubella IgM antibody titers are measured in both serum and cerebrospinal fluid, often using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Next-generation sequencing has also been employed to confirm rubella. Furthermore, rubella virus can be isolated from cerebrospinal fluid. Electrophysiologic studies may reveal peripheral polyradiculoneuropathy, and electroencephalogram (EEG) can show unusual patterns associated with rubella encephalitis. [PMC6154155, PMC3054242, PMC1028780, PMC1632541]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: In cases of acute encephalitis associated with rubella, the prognosis can be severe. For instance, in a family cluster of atypical rubella, two patients who developed acute encephalitis ultimately died from the disease. This suggests that rubella-associated encephalitis can lead to fatal outcomes. [PMC6154155]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic, congenital malformation syndrome characterized by microcephaly, short stature and numerous digital anomalies (brachymesophanlangy, fifth finger clinodactyly, syndactyly of toes and hypoplastic thumbs), mild learning deficit and short palpebral fissures. The two subtypes are clinically distinguished by the presence (type 1) or absence (type 2) gastrointestinal atresia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Brunner-Winter syndrome; Digital anomalies with short palpebral fissures and atresia of esophagus or duodenum; FGLDS; FS; MMT; MODED syndrome; Microcephaly-digital anomalies-normal intelligence syndrome; Microcephaly-intellectual disability-tracheoesophageal fistula syndrome; Microcephaly-oculo-digito-esophageal-duodenal syndrome syndrome; ODED syndrome; Oculo-digito-esophageal-duodenal syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: a case of fetal microcephaly found during the second trimester ultrasound and confirmed by further ultrasound scans and fetal MRI. The array comparative genomic hybridisation analysis of the fetus and the male parent showed a 1.5 Mb deletion overlapping the Feingold syndrome region, an autosomal dominant syndrome that can cause microcephaly, facial/hand abnormalities, mild neurodevelopmental delay and others. This case illustrates the need for a detailed investigation by a multidisciplinary team to provide prenatal counselling regarding a postnatal outcome to the parents and orient their decision towards the continuation or termination of pregnancy. Feingold syndrome (FGLDS1) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the MYCN oncogene on the short arm of chromosome 2 (2p24.1). It is characterised by microcephaly, digital abnormalities, oesophageal and duodenal atresias,... [PMC10008251, PMC4244445]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Feingold syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by microcephaly, various digital abnormalities, and neurodevelopmental or cognitive impairments, including mild delay, learning disability, mental retardation, memory, sleep, and psychiatric issues. Feingold syndrome type 1 (FGLDS1) is associated with oesophageal and duodenal atresias, and facial/hand abnormalities. Feingold syndrome type 2 (FGLDS2) shares skeletal abnormalities but typically lacks gastrointestinal atresia, instead presenting with short stature, growth hormone deficiency, aortic dilation, cardiac anomalies, and phalangeal joint contractures. Prenatal diagnosis of fetal microcephaly is possible. [PMC10008251, PMC8751417, PMC7038632, PMC4244445]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Feingold syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder with distinct genetic etiologies for its two types. Feingold syndrome type 1 (FGLDS1) is caused by mutations or deletions in the MYCN oncogene on the short arm of chromosome 2 (2p24.1), including de novo copy-number losses. Feingold syndrome type 2 (FGLDS2) is associated with hemizygous microdeletions of the MIR17HG gene on chromosome 13q31.3. These genetic alterations lead to the characteristic features of the syndrome, with FGLDS2 typically lacking the gastrointestinal atresia seen in FGLDS1. [PMC10008251, PMC8751417, PMC7038632, PMC4244445]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Feingold syndrome involves both clinical assessment and genetic testing. Prenatally, fetal microcephaly identified via second-trimester ultrasound and confirmed by fetal MRI can lead to further investigation. Genetic confirmation often utilizes array comparative genomic hybridisation (aCGH) to detect deletions, such as a 1.5 Mb deletion overlapping the Feingold syndrome region. Postnatally, genome sequencing (GS) is a valuable tool for identifying various variant types, including copy-number losses in the MYCN gene for Feingold syndrome type 1, and mosaic variants. Comparative genomic hybridisation array testing can also confirm microdeletions, such as those in the MIR17HG gene associated with Feingold syndrome type 2. Comprehensive genetic analysis combined with detailed clinical phenotyping is essential for accurate diagnosis. [PMC10008251, PMC8751417, PMC4244445]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Feingold syndrome can present with a complex phenotype, and its features may overlap with other genetic conditions. In one reported case, an individual with suspected leukodystrophy and features such as hearing loss, clinodactyly, rotated thumbs, tapered fingers, and simplified palmar crease was found to have Feingold syndrome alongside Pol III-related leukodystrophy and COL2A1-related disorders. This illustrates that multiple diagnoses can contribute to an individual's overall presentation, emphasizing the need for comprehensive genetic analysis in complex cases. [PMC8751417]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of Feingold syndrome type 1 can be initiated by detecting fetal microcephaly during a second-trimester ultrasound, with further confirmation possible through additional ultrasound scans and fetal MRI. Definitive diagnosis involves array comparative genomic hybridization analysis, which can identify a deletion overlapping the Feingold syndrome region in the fetus. A multidisciplinary team is crucial for providing comprehensive prenatal counseling to parents, informing them about potential postnatal outcomes and assisting in decisions regarding the continuation or termination of the pregnancy. [PMC10008251]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for Feingold syndrome is essential, given its autosomal dominant inheritance and the potential for de novo variants. Prenatal diagnosis, often prompted by findings such as fetal microcephaly, necessitates detailed investigation by a multidisciplinary team to provide comprehensive information regarding postnatal outcomes. This enables parents to make informed decisions about the continuation or termination of pregnancy. The diagnostic process can be complex, especially when multiple genetic diagnoses are present, highlighting the importance of comprehensive genetic analysis, such as genome sequencing, and detailed clinical phenotyping to ensure accurate counseling and optimal clinical care for individuals and their families. [PMC10008251, PMC8751417]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management involves comprehensive genetic analysis and detailed clinical phenotyping to guide clinical care and genetic counseling. For patients with Feingold syndrome type 2, specific recommendations include echocardiography at diagnosis and evaluation for growth hormone deficiency in those with short stature. Growth hormone therapy has been successfully used to treat growth hormone deficiency. Prenatal counseling by a multidisciplinary team is also important for parents regarding postnatal outcomes. [PMC10008251, PMC8751417, PMC7038632, PMC4244445]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Feingold syndrome can lead to a range of postnatal outcomes, including microcephaly, facial and hand abnormalities, and mild neurodevelopmental delay. These potential manifestations are significant enough to be a focus of prenatal counseling, guiding parental decisions regarding the continuation or termination of pregnancy. The syndrome's impact on development and physical features is a key consideration for the long-term outlook. [PMC10008251]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hunter-McAlpine craniosynostosis is characterised by craniosynostosis, intellectual deficit, short stature, facial dysmorphism (oval face with almond-shaped palpebral fissures, droopy eyelids and a small nose) and minor distal anomalies. It has been described in 10 patients. Transmission is autosomal dominant and the syndrome is associated with partial duplication of the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q35-5qter).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: A partial duplication of the distal long arm of chromosome 5 (5q35-->qter) is known to be associated with a distinct phenotype referred to as Hunter-McAlpine syndrome. Clinical spectrum of this disorder mainly consists of mental retardation, microcephaly, short stature, skeletal anomalies, and craniofacial dysmorphism featuring flat facies, micrognathia, large, low-set dysplastic ears, hypertelorism, almond-shaped, down-slanted palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, small nose, long philtrum, small mouth, and thin upper lip. Less frequent remarkable findings include craniosynostosis, heart defect, hypoplastic phalanges, preaxial polydactyly, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, and inguinal hernia. In most patients with a partial duplication of 5q the aberration occurred due to an inherited unbalanced translocation, therefore the phenotype was not reflective of pure trisomy 5q. on a 9.5-year-old... [PMC3576294, PMC1013640]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hunter-McAlpine syndrome is characterized by mental retardation, microcephaly, and short stature. A distinct craniofacial dysmorphism includes a small oval or flat face, micrognathia, large low-set dysplastic ears, hypertelorism, almond-shaped or down-slanted palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, a small nose, long philtrum, small mouth, and thin upper lip. Skeletal anomalies are common, such as hypoplastic phalanges, brachyphalangy, and occasionally radial agenesis or preaxial polydactyly. Less frequent findings include craniosynostosis, heart defects, hypospadias, cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia, choroidal and retinal coloboma, and abnormal biliary vesicle. The clinical expression can be variable. [PMC3576294, PMC1013640]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hunter-McAlpine syndrome is associated with a partial duplication of the distal long arm of chromosome 5 (5q35-->qter), with a pure distal microduplication of 5q35.2-5q35.3 being considered causative for the phenotype. This chromosomal aberration can result from inherited unbalanced translocations or de novo chromosomal rearrangements. The syndrome has been observed to occur in families across multiple generations, with variable expression among affected individuals. Parents in the direct line of transmission may show few overt signs, though specific skeletal profiles can indicate carrier status. [PMC3576294, PMC1013640]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Hunter-McAlpine syndrome is primarily based on a distinct clinical phenotype, which includes mental retardation, microcephaly, short stature, skeletal anomalies, and characteristic craniofacial dysmorphism. Genetic testing, specifically array comparative genomic hybridization, can detect a partial duplication on 5q35.2-5q35.3, which is known to be associated with the syndrome. While other genetic analyses like karyotype, sequencing, and MLPA for TBX5 and SALL4 genes may be performed, they were unremarkable in one reported case. A metacarpal/phalangeal profile has also been suggested as a sensitive indicator, particularly for carrier status. [PMC3576294, PMC1013640]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Hunter-McAlpine syndrome, associated with a partial duplication of 5q35-->qter, is characterized by mental retardation, microcephaly, short stature, skeletal anomalies, and craniofacial dysmorphism, with less frequent findings including heart defects and hypoplastic phalanges. However, other conditions should be considered in the differential, particularly if features such as bilateral radial agenesis with absent thumbs, ulnar hypoplasia with bowing, choroidal and retinal coloboma, or abnormal biliary vesicles are present, as these have not been noted in pure 5q trisomy patients, even when some Hunter-McAlpine features are observed. [PMC3576294]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Hunter-McAlpine syndrome is associated with a partial duplication of the distal long arm of chromosome 5 (5q35-->qter), which can occur due to a de novo chromosomal rearrangement or be inherited. Familial cases demonstrate vertical transmission across generations. Expression of the syndrome is variable, and parents in the direct line of transmission may show few overt signs of the disease. However, a specific metacarpal/phalangeal profile has been suggested as a sensitive indicator of carrier status. Genetic testing, such as array comparative genomic hybridization, can detect the causative duplication, even when standard karyotype or gene-specific tests are unremarkable. [PMC3576294, PMC1013640]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic cerebral small vessel disease characterized by amyloid deposition in the cerebral blood vessels leading to predominantly hemorrhagic strokes, focal neurological deficits, and progressive cognitive decline eventually leading to dementia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): HCHWA; Hereditary cerebral hemorrhage with amyloidosis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown. HCHWA has been described in several families from all over the world. The estimated number of affected patients is between 300 and 400.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Unlike sporadic forms of cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA), HCHWA usually presents in younger patients (<55 years of age) and has more severe manifestations. Clinical features depend on the HCHWA disease type, with 7 discovered to date: Icelandic, Dutch, Arctic, Piedmont, Iowa, Flemish and Italian. In general, patients present with either a stroke (with headache, nausea, vomiting, focal neurological deficits, and alterations in consciousness) or progressive dementia of the Alzheimer type. Transient neurological symptoms lasting a few minutes to a few hours, and seizures can also occur. Microbleeds and hemorrhages can occur throughout the brain, and are caused by involvement of the vessels in the cerebral cortex and the meninges. Hemorrhages tend to recur. Cognitive decline is progressive and can lead to dementia, either in a stepwise fashion or slowly progressive as in Alzheimer's disease.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Most forms of HCHWA (Dutch, Arctic, Piedmont, Iowa, Flemish and Italian) are due to a point-mutation in the APP gene on chromosome 21q21.2, which encodes the beta-amyloid precursor protein. This mutation causes increased accumulation of amyloid-beta protein in the walls of cerebral arteries and capillaries. This can lead to rupture or narrowing of the blood vessels, leading to hemorrhagic or non-hemorrhagic stroke. Sometimes the affected blood vessels show signs of inflammation (CAA-angiitis). Only one form of HCHWA, Icelandic type, is due to a mutation in the CST3 gene on chromosome 20p11.2, encoding the precursor protein cystatin C.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: For a probable diagnosis of HCHWA a detailed family history, and (preferably) a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan should be performed. Typically, the MRI shows multiple lobar (cortical, subcortical) hemorrhages and leukoencephalopathy. In the presence of otherwise unexplained lobar hemorrhages and a typical family history, the finding of a causative mutation is sufficient for a definite diagnosis of HCHWA in vivo. At postmortem examination severe CAA, and cortical, lobar or subcortical hemorrhages are found.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include all other conditions that could cause lobar intracerebral hemorrhage such as coagulopathies, vasculitis, intravascular large B-cell lymphoma, CNS neoplasms, cavernous malformations, cerebral vascular malformation and antecedent trauma
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible but is rarely performed.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The presently known types of HCHWA are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Screening of family members of patients with HCHWA is recommended, because of the possibility of genetic counseling. Presymptomatic genetic testing is offered.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no known acute or preventive treatment for cerebral hemorrhages in HCHWA. Antihypertensive therapy is recommended, even in cases of mild to moderate hypertension, but its efficacy is not evidence-based. Corticosteroids can ameliorate symptoms caused by CAA-related inflammation. Patients experiencing seizures should be given antiepileptic drugs. Surgical hematoma evacuation is rarely performed for HCHWA because of the poor outcome associated with severe neurological deficits.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is often poor.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, clinically heterogeneous, multisystemic inflammatory disease characterized by inflammation of the cartilage and proteoglycan rich structures leading to cartilage damage along with joint, ocular and cardiovascular involvement.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence and annual incidence of Relapsing polychondritis (RP) are not known. The estimated incidence is 1/285,000. The sex ratio appears to be equal and all ethnic groups seem to be affected (with more cases reported among Caucasians).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset is generally sudden and most commonly occurs in the 5th decade of life (age 40 to 55). Cases with early and late onset do occur. RP follows a flaring and remitting course. Clinical manifestations vary from intermittent auricular and nasal chondritis, to occasional organ or life-threatening complications. Unilateral or bilateral external ear inflammation with pain, tenderness, swelling, erythema, and discoloration, limited to the cartilaginous portion of the pinna with characteristic sparing of the lobule, is one of the hallmark features of RP (90-95% of patients). Auricular collapse or inflammation of vestibular structures can lead to conductive or sensorineural hearing loss. Other associated complications include nausea, vomiting, tinnitus, vertigo and ataxia. Nasal chondritis with sudden pain and tenderness is found at some stage of the disease in more than 50% of patients. Nasal cartilage may be severely damaged resulting in saddle nose deformity. Some patients develop potentially serious laryngotracheal involvement with hoarseness, aphonia, stridor and wheezing, dyspnea, or even airway collapse. Joint pain lasting weeks or months is found in most patients (>70%) and is often the presenting feature (30%). Cardiovascular manifestations (25-50%) include large vessel vasculitis, aneurysmal involvement, and aortic or mitral valve disease. Ocular manifestations reported are proptosis, conjunctivitis, ulcerative keratitis, episcleritis/scleritis, uveitis, and periorbital edema. Cutaneous manifestations that may precede chondritis include aphthosis, nodules, purpura, and papules. Neurological manifestations are due to vasculitis of central or peripheral nervous system. Renal involvement is rare. MAGIC syndrome represents a subset of patients with RP who also have mouth and genital ulcers, which are features of Behçet disease.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The exact etiopathogenesis of RP is not known but it is thought to be an immune-mediated disease. A complex cytokine network is thought to be involved in the recruitment of infiltrating cells in RP lesions.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: There is no single blood or imaging test that can be used to diagnose this condition. The diagnosis is generally based upon the detection of a combination of clinical presentations. According to the most accepted and widely used diagnostic criteria, three of the following six features are required to make a diagnosis of RP: bilateral auricular chondritis, nonerosive seronegative inflammatory polyarthritis, nasal chondritis, ocular inflammation, respiratory tract chondritis, and audiovestibular damage.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include granulomatosis with polyangiitis, eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, Behçet disease, and leprosy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is primarily symptomatic and no standard therapeutic protocol has been established due to the rarity of the disease. In less severe cases, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, dapsone, and colchicine may be used. In severe cases with organic involvement, systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone or rarely intravenous methylprednisolone) are required. Methotrexate, azathioprine, cyclosporine and chlorambucil may constitute an alternative. Use of biological agents like anti TNFs, tocilizumab, anakinra, rituximab and abatacept has been reported with various efficacy in case reports and small case series. A relapsing polychondritis disease activity index (RPDAI) and damage index (RPDAM) has been validated for assessing disease activity and damage respectively.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is generally good in the majority of cases, but the disease may occasionally follow a severe, life-threatening course, with respiratory complications (tracheal collapse and infections) as the primary cause of mortality. Cardiovascular involvement may also lead to a fatal outcome.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Mosaic trisomy 5 is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome with a variable phenotype ranging from clinically normal to patients presenting intrauterine growth retardation, congenital heart anomalies (mainly ventricular septal defect), multiple dysmorphic features (e.g. hypertelorism, prominent nasal bridge) and other congenital anomalies (incl. eventration of diaphragm, agenesis of corpus callosum, cloverleaf skull, clinodactyly, anteriorly placed anus). Psychomotor development may be normal in spite of low growth parameters being associated.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Clinical features of mosaic trisomy 5 syndrome can include bilateral congenital diaphragmatic hernia, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, atrial septal defect, and hypothyroidism. Affected individuals may also present with a specific facial configuration, macroglossia, and talipes equinovarus. Prenatal findings can include polyhydramnios and levocardia. [PMC7945345]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Bilateral congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is very rare. A few studies have reported the pathogenic role of 5p in CDH. A 23-year-old primigravida Japanese woman was referred for the following abnormal findings at 33 weeks of gestation: polyhydramnios, macroglossia, talipes equinovarus, and levocardia. A marker chromosome was detected by amniocentesis. Fluorescence in situ hybridization with whole chromosome paint 5 and nucleolus organizer region probes confirmed its origin from chromosome 5 and an acrocentric chromosome. [PMC7945345]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis can involve prenatal detection of a marker chromosome via amniocentesis. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with whole chromosome paint 5 and nucleolus organizer region probes can confirm the origin of the marker chromosome from chromosome 5 and an acrocentric chromosome. Postnatally, karyotyping of peripheral blood can be performed to confirm the findings. [PMC7945345]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A form of hereditary episodic ataxia (EA) characterized by paroxysmal episodes of ataxia lasting hours, with interictal nystagmus and mildly progressive ataxia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Familial paroxysmal ataxia, also referred to as familial periodic cerebellar ataxia or episodic ataxia type 2 (EA2), is a rare, autosomal dominant condition. It typically presents with paroxysmal attacks of ataxia, often with onset in childhood or early adolescence. The disease is associated with mutations in the CACNA1A gene. The phenotypic spectrum is broad, encompassing not only ataxia but also conditions like familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 (FHM1), and can include atypical presentations such as childhood epilepsy or late-onset non-episodic progressive gait ataxia. The genetic overlap with other neurological disorders can complicate diagnosis. [PMC8702007, PMC7312673, PMC1042501]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Familial paroxysmal ataxia, also known as episodic ataxia type 2 (EA2) or familial periodic cerebellar ataxia (FPCA), is characterized by paroxysmal attacks of ataxia, typically with onset in childhood or early adolescence. The clinical spectrum can include atypical manifestations such as childhood absence epilepsy and, later in life, non-episodic, slowly progressive gait ataxia. Persistent diplopia due to superior oblique palsies has also been observed, even between ataxic attacks. These diverse presentations expand the known phenotypic spectrum of CACNA1A-related diseases. [PMC7312673, PMC1042501]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Familial paroxysmal ataxia, particularly Episodic Ataxia type 2 (EA2), is primarily caused by mutations in the CACNA1A gene, which encodes the α1A subunit of P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (Cav2.1). Identified mutations include missense and splice site variants, which can lead to a complete loss of P/Q calcium channel function. CACNA1A is also implicated in Familial Hemiplegic Migraine type 1 (FHM1) and Spinocerebellar Ataxia type 6, indicating these are allelic disorders with genetic and phenotypic overlap. The spectrum of CACNA1A-related diseases is broad, encompassing paroxysmal ataxia, episodic hemiplegia, childhood epilepsy, and late-onset non-episodic progressive gait ataxia. [PMC8702007, PMC7312673, PMC1274487]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of familial paroxysmal ataxia and related conditions, such as familial hemiplegic migraine type 1, relies on both clinical assessment and genetic testing. Whole-exome sequencing or gene panel sequencing for hereditary ataxias can identify pathogenic mutations in the CACNA1A gene, which encodes the Cav2.1 subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels. Genetic testing is considered an indispensable method, particularly for identifying atypical presentations. Further characterization of identified genetic defects can involve RT-PCR analysis of patient skin fibroblasts to confirm splice site alterations, and functional studies like two-electrode voltage-clamp recordings to assess channel function. [PMC8702007, PMC7312673]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Familial paroxysmal ataxia, particularly episodic ataxia type 2 (EA2), shares genetic and phenotypic overlap with several neurological disorders, making differential diagnosis challenging. Conditions to consider include familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 (FHM1) and spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 (SCA6), all of which are allelic disorders of the CACNA1A gene. Atypical presentations of CACNA1A-related diseases, such as episodic hemiplegia without migraine or childhood epilepsy followed by late-onset non-episodic gait ataxia, further complicate diagnosis due to blurred genotype-phenotype correlations. Genetic testing is crucial for identifying these conditions. [PMC8702007, PMC7312673, PMC1274487]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Familial paroxysmal ataxia and related conditions, such as familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 and episodic ataxia type 2, are often inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Mutations in the CACNA1A gene, encoding the alpha1A subunit of P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels, are frequently implicated in these allelic disorders. However, the genotype-phenotype correlation is complex, with significant genetic overlap and atypical symptoms blurring the distinction between conditions like EA2, spinocerebellar ataxia type 6, and FHM type 1. Various mutation types, including missense, protein truncating, and expansion mutations, can lead to similar phenotypes, often by causing a complete loss of P/Q channel function. Genetic testing is indispensable for identifying atypical presentations and confirming diagnosis, given the expanding phenotypic spectrum of CACNA1A-related diseases. [PMC8702007, PMC7312673, PMC1274487, PMC1042501]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management strategies for familial paroxysmal ataxia include pharmacological interventions. Oral acetazolamide (250 mg twice daily) has been effective in preventing periodic symptoms and relieving persistent diplopia in familial periodic cerebellar ataxia. However, prophylactic therapy with flunarizine (5 mg daily) for familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 was found to be ineffective, as attack intensity remained unchanged, leading to its termination after a few weeks. [PMC8702007, PMC1042501]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: For an atypical presentation of CACNA1A-associated disease, a patient exhibited childhood epilepsy followed by late-onset, slowly progressive non-episodic gait ataxia. This expands the phenotypic spectrum. While typical episodic ataxia type 2 (EA2) involves paroxysmal attacks of ataxia with onset in childhood or early adolescence, the long-term progression of these typical forms is not detailed. The presence of atypical symptoms and genetic overlap can complicate diagnosis, potentially delaying therapeutic intervention. [PMC7312673]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Craniosynostosis - anal anomalies - porokeratosis, or CDAGS, is a very rare condition characterized by craniosynostosis and clavicular hypoplasia, (C), delayed closure of the fontanel (D), anal anomalies (A), genitourinary malformations (G) and skin eruption (S).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It has been described in seven patients from four unrelated families.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Cranial abnormalities include a coronal synostosis with wide-open anterior and posterior fontanels and large parietal foramina. In some patients the skin eruption has been classified as porokeratosis (a disorder of keratinization). Sensorineural hearing loss and mild to severe developmental delay are common.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The condition is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Craniosynostosis-anal anomalies-porokeratosis syndrome is distinct from other craniosynostosis syndromes, such as Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Apert, and Beare-Stevenson syndromes, which are typically associated with autosomal dominant mutations in FGFR1, FGFR2, and FGFR3 genes. In contrast, individuals with craniosynostosis-anal anomalies-porokeratosis syndrome do not carry any of the common FGFR mutations. The observed pedigree patterns suggest an autosomal or X-linked recessive inheritance for this condition. [PMC1051430]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Craniosynostosis-anal anomalies-porokeratosis syndrome is based on the clinical recognition of the triad of coronal craniosynostosis, anal anomalies, and porokeratosis. This combination of features distinguishes it from other craniosynostosis syndromes like Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Apert, and Beare-Stevenson syndromes, which are typically associated with common fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR) gene mutations and autosomal dominant inheritance. In contrast, affected individuals with this syndrome do not carry common FGFR mutations, and the pedigree suggests an autosomal or X-linked recessive inheritance pattern. [PMC1051430]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for Craniosynostosis-anal anomalies-porokeratosis syndrome include Crouzon, Pfeiffer, Apert, and Beare-Stevenson syndromes. These conditions also present with craniosynostosis and may involve cutaneous or anal anomalies. However, these syndromes are typically associated with mutations in FGFR1, FGFR2, and FGFR3 genes and exhibit an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. In contrast, Craniosynostosis-anal anomalies-porokeratosis syndrome cases do not carry common FGFR mutations, and the pedigree suggests an autosomal or X-linked recessive inheritance. [PMC1051430]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A demyelinating disorder of the central nervous system.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): ADEM; Acute disseminated encephalitis; Acute demyelinating encephalomyelitis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence rate has been estimated at 1 in 125,000-250,000 per year.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Children younger than 10 years are predominantly affected. A seasonal winter and spring peaks have been registered. The disease usually develops after acute viral or bacterial infection or vaccination, with a sudden onset of irritability and lethargy after a prodromal period of 1-4 weeks. Major symptoms include fever, headache, drowsiness, changes in mental status, seizures and coma. Weakness, vomiting, weight loss, stiff neck, ataxia, bilateral optic neuritis and delirium are common. Peripheral nervous system involvement (paralysis of a single limb or hemiplegia) occurs in 5-45% of cases, according to literature data. Although initially the symptoms of ADEM may be mild, they worsen rapidly within several hours to four days. Pathologically, ADEM is characterized by bilateral large and confluent lesions in cerebral and cerebellar white matter; basal ganglia and gray matter may also be involved. ADEM lesions in the spinal cord are continuous and extending to multiple levels. Some authors consider the disease as a variant or borderline form of multiple sclerosis (MS).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: ADEM is considered as an immune-mediated disorder of the central nervous system. It can arise spontaneously but in most cases the disease is triggered by infectious disease or vaccinations. Links between the Pasteur rabies vaccine and ADEM have been documented. Immunizations less frequently associated with ADEM include pertussis, measles, Japanese B virus, tetanus, influenza.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the clinical history and magnetic resonance imaging, which is the diagnostic modality of choice.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: MS is the main differential diagnosis. The differentiation between ADEM and a first episode of MS can be very difficult but has important prognostic and treatment implications. Differential diagnosis also includes infectious encephalitis, Guillain-Barré syndrome, glioblastoma multiforme, Schilder's disease, psychotic disorders with acute onset, toxic/metabolic encephalopathy, vasculitis, nonvasculitic autoimmune encephalopathy, meningitis, metastatic tumor.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Currently, immunosuppression with corticosteroids for the acute events is the mainstay of treatment. In patients refractory to steroid therapy, plasmapheresis or intravenous immunoglobulin therapy can be used. Symptomatic and supportive treatments are recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: ADEM is typically a monophasic (single episode) disease with generally favorable outcome. Average time to recover is one to six months. Relapses may occur in 5-25% of cases, generally 6-18 months after the onset. Fulminant presentation with cerebral edema requiring critical intensive care is rare.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by variable expression of the holoprosencephaly (HPE) spectrum in association with ectrodactyly, cleft lip/palate and/or other ectodermal anomalies. Developmental delay of variable severity and endocrine abnormalities are often associated.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Approximately 35 patients have been described in the literature to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Presentation is heterogeneous; cerebral malformations may present as lobar, semi-lobar and alobar HPE, or milder midline anomalies, such as arhinencephaly, or corpus callosum agenesis. Microcephaly, hypotelorism or hypertelorism, and malformed ears may be observed. Ectrodactyly affects hands and/or feet with variable severity and may involve one to four limbs. Over half of reported individuals have cleft lip and/or palate, which may be uni- or bilateral. Midline brain malformation involving the hypothalamo-pituitary axis may lead a range of endocrine disorders including growth hormone deficiency and subsequent short stature, central diabetes insipidus with a risk of hypernatremic dehydratation, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, cryptorchidism, micropenis or hypospadias, as well as temperature dysregulation and erratic sleep patterns. Developmental delay is often observed and intellectual disability ranges from mild to severe. In severe cases, individuals are nonverbal, spastic and non-ambulatory. The severity of the neurological impairment in part correlates to the severity of the brain malformation. Seizures are possible. There has been anecdotal reports of skull defects, vertebral anomalies, radial aplasia, eye anomalies, and cardiac malformation.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Hartsfield syndrome is most often caused by the presence of heterozygous pathogenic variants in the FGFR1 gene (8p11.23), although bi-allelic pathogenic variants have been described in a minority of patients.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Confirmation of clinical diagnosis is based on FGFR1 sequencing by targeted sanger sequencing, or via NGS (next generation sequencing) multigene panel including FGFR1.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The association of HPE and ectrodactyly is quite unique to Hartsfield syndrome. Phenotypic overlap can be observed in Kallman syndrome, isolated congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, EEC (ectrodactyly ectodermal dysplasia and cleft lip/palate syndrome), HPE, and septo-optic dysplasia spectrum.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: For parents of an index individual, prenatal diagnosis in subsequent pregnancies should be discussed. Diagnosis involves genetic testing for FGFR1 in the presence of the ultrasound findings of HPE and/or ectrodactyly.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Depending on the variants identified, transmission of Hartsfield syndrome can follow an autosomal dominant or recessive mode of inheritance. In most cases, heterozygous FGFR1 variants occur de novo. Several occurrences of parental germline mosaicisms, with recurrences in the sibship, have been reported. Although not known, the recurrence risk in siblings is thus much higher than the usual theoretical 1% estimated risk in the presence of an apparent de novo variant. Recurrence risk is 25% in each pregnancy if bi-allelic variants are identified in the index sib.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management and treatment are based on the phenotype. Severity of the HPE must be evaluated by neuroimaging. Spasticity and the possibility of seizures must be assessed. Antiepileptic drugs, physical and occupational therapy may be needed. Nutritional and feeding status should be evaluated. Surgery may be required to treat cleft lip/palate and ectrodactyly. The possibility of endocrine deficiency must be evaluated (growth hormone deficiency, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and central diabetes insipidus). Central diabetes insipidus may require treatment with desmopressin.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of the phenotype.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Platyspondylic lethal skeletal dysplasia (PLSD), Torrance type (PLSD-T) is a skeletal dysplasia characterised by severe limb shortening (short and broad long bones), platyspondyly with wafer-like vertebral bodies, short ribs with anterior cupping, severe hypoplasia of the lower ilia and radial bowing. Histological findings include slightly enlarged chondrocytes and hypercellularity. The prevalence is unknown. The disorder is transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait and is caused by mutations in the C-propeptide domain of the COL2A1 gene. Although PLSD-T is generally lethal, survival to adulthood has been reported in two families.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): PLSD-T; Platyspondylic dysplasia, Torrance-Luton type; Platyspondylic lethal skeletal dysplasia, Torrance type

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Odontochondrodysplasia (ODCD, OMIM #184260) is a rare, non-lethal skeletal dysplasia characterized by involvement of the spine and metaphyseal regions of the long bones, pulmonary hypoplasia, short stature, joint hypermobility, and dentinogenesis imperfecta. ODCD is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion with an unknown frequency caused by mutations of the thyroid hormone receptor interactor 11 gene ( TRIP11 ; OMIM *604505). The TRIP11 gene encodes the Golgi microtubule-associated protein 210 (GMAP-210), which is an indispensable protein for the function of the Golgi apparatus. DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Systemic capillary leak syndrome (SCLS) is a severe systemic disease due to increased capillary permeability, characterized by episodes of hypotension, edema and hypovolemia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Capillary hyperpermeability syndrome; Capillary leak syndrome; Clarkson disease; Idiopathic capillary leak syndrome; SCLS

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: SCLS has been reported in less than 150 cases since its first description in 1960.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Mean age of onset is 45 and pediatric or geriatric cases are rare. The disease is characterized by alternance of crises and quiescent phases. Delay between crises is a few weeks to several years. They have been reported following infection, mostly of the upper airways, during perimenstrual or post-partum periods and, more rarely, after intense physical effort. They last days or weeks, can be of variable severity, from grade 1 (hypotension responding to oral hydration) to grade 4 (fatal attacks), and have a 3-step evolution. Crises may start with prodromes such as generalized weakness, fatigue, myalgias, orthostatic hypotension, possible digestive (diarrea, abdominal pain) and ENT (rhinorrhea, cough) manifestations, occasional fever and weight gain. The leak phase follows with oliguria, arterial hypotension and rapid development of edema of the face or the upper limbs but sparing the lungs. Hypotension may lead to hypovolemic shock with preserved consciousness. In the post-leak phase, massive edema resorption leads to polyuria and weight loss. Biological features are a characteristic association of hemoconcentration with hypoalbuminemia without albuminuria, hyperleukocytosis and a proteinemia drop in the 350-750 kDa range. Chronic cases have been reported with a continuous generalized edema, visceral effusions, hypotension and hemoconcentration being more subtle. Complications may occur in acute and post-leak phases: in the former, they include compartment syndrome with rhabdomyolysis, cardiac arrythmias, thrombosis, pancreatitis, pericarditis, seizures, cerebral edema or thickening of the myocardium. Rhabdomyolysis and fatal pericarditis may also occur in the post-leak phase, but cardiovascular overload is more frequent. Fatal acute lung edema has also been reported at this stage. Renal failure may result from hypoperfusion-induced acute tubular necrosis and rhabdomyolysis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: SCLS is caused by capillary hyperpermeability of unknown etiology. Several physiopathological hypotheses have been considered such as an inflammation-mediated mechanism or a damage of the capillary endothelium by the monoclonal gammopathy.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on physical and biological examination, recurrence of crises, association of hemoconcentration with hypoalbuminemia being strong indicators. The presence of an anomalous monoclonal immunoglobulin termed paraprotein is suggestive but not diagnostic.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes sepsis, anaphylaxis, any other cause of capillary leakage and inferior vena cavainterruption. Chronic cases might be misdiagnosed as Gleich syndrome, venous stasis, protein-losing enteropathy and nephrotic syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative treatment, thus management is symptomatic and prophylactic. Intravenous fluids administration is not recommended as it fails to increase arterial pressure and worsens edema, furthermore it increases the risk of vascular overload in the post-leak phase. Oral electrolyte-containing fluids can reduce the attack severity if taken early, thus patient education to detect early signs of prodrome is crucial. Beta-adrenergic agonists (terbutaline) and phosphodiesterase inhibitors (theophylline) have shown good results in few cases but have serious side effects; intra-venous immunoglobulines are a promising prophylactic strategy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Despite progress in diagnosis and management that has prolonged the survival of patients, prognosis remains poor as mortality reaches 30-40% after 10 years.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Systemic capillary leak syndrome (SCLS) has been genetically linked to pathogenic variants in the TLN1 gene. A rare heterozygous splice-site variant in TLN1 was identified in a familial SCLS case, suggesting an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with incomplete penetrance. This genetic finding provides insight into the molecular mechanism of the disease. [PMC11665552]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hereditary, metabolic disease characterized by serum levels of alpha-1-antitrypsin (AAT) that are well below the normal range. In the most severe form, the disease can clinically manifest with chronic liver disorders (cirrhosis, fibrosis), respiratory disorders (emphysema, bronchiectasis), and rarely panniculitis or vasculitis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of the genetic condition at birth is estimated between 1/1,600-5,000 in Western Europe and in the USA.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The severe form, caused by homozygous Z variant in the gene SERPINA1, is the most clinically relevant and referred to here as Z-AATD. Z-AATD has an extraordinary heterogeneous disease course. Some individuals remain healthy, while others develop a severe lung or liver disease, rarely both. The age of onset is variable in Z-AATD, liver disease presents typically in newborn/early childhood age or later on in adult life (typically at ≥ 40 years of age). Z-AATD can lead to neonatal cholestasis in about 10 % of the affected infants and about 30-50% of these will develop chronic progressive liver disease. About 10% of adults develop liver cirrhosis. Onset of lung disease is generally between 20 and 50 years of age. The main pulmonary manifestations include early onset panacinar emphysema, bronchiectasis, bronchial asthma or vasculitis presenting with persistent, dyspnea, cough, wheezing, and production of sputum. Smoking is a major factor affecting the course of the pulmonary manifestations, and is associated with earlier onset. Other features include weight loss, recurrent respiratory infections, and fatigue. Panniculitis of variable severity and developing at any age is a rare disease manifestation. A strongly increased risk of developing liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma has been reported. The course may be severe in the absence of appropriate treatment and continued tobacco smoking.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is due to variants in SERPINA1 (14q32.13). Major gene sequencing efforts carried out in disease populations disclosed more than 100 rare SERPINA1 variants which may cause the absence of circulating AAT (null alleles), poor AAT secretion from hepatocytes (deficiency alleles) or even form a modified enzyme inhibitory activity (dysfunctional alleles). The low levels of the serine protease inhibitor alpha-1-antitrypsin, involved in regulation of neutrophil elastase and proteinase 3, leads to alveolar damage. The pathophysiology of lung alveolar damage is based on the protease-antiprotease balance hypothesis.
