DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Manifestations are non-specific and therefore may lead to delayed diagnosis. Liver and lung diseases are investigated with imaging and biopsies. The diagnosis is based on detection of low serum concentrations of AAT and molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses include asthma in younger patients and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in older individuals. Chronic viral hepatitis, hemochromatosis, Wilson disease, non-alcoholic/alcoholic fatty liver and primary biliary cirrhosis should be considered as alternative causes of liver disease.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: When mutations have been identified in an affected family, prenatal diagnosis is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance is autosomal recessive and genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them of the 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is currently no curative treatment. Treatment is similar to that used for COPD and emphysema and aims at reducing symptoms and slowing progression. Long-acting bronchodilators, antibiotics, corticosteroid inhalations, and long-acting beta-agonists are the mainstay of treatment. Another treatment option in severe cases involves augmentation therapy with administration of purified human AAT to reach normal physiological levels. Smoking and exposure to tobacco smoke should be avoided. Vaccines for common respiratory disorders may be beneficial. Lung transplantation may be required for end-stage lung disease. Likewise, liver transplantation can be considered for advanced liver disease. Panniculitis usually responds to treatment with intravenous augmentation of AAT. Several treatments for lung and liver disease are currently in clinical trials.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is generally very good in non-smokers. Smoking is known to exacerbate the disease and leads to poorer outcomes. Obesity, diabetes, alcohol misuse, metabolic syndrome and male sex are risk factors for liver disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An acute arboviral infection caused by an alphavirus of the Togaviridae family transmitted by an infected mosquito, that is characterized by the onset of flulike symptoms including fever, chills, weakness, headache, vomiting, abdominal pain with diarrhea, myalgia, leucocytosis, and hematuria, rapidly progressing to diffuse central nervous system (CNS) involvement with confusion, somnolence, or even coma. Seizures, which may progress to status epilepticus and neurologic sequelae, cranial nerve palsies, and photophobia may occur. EEE is associated with a high rate of morbidity and mortality.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) is a rare, potentially fatal neuroinvasive disease with a high mortality rate exceeding 30%. In the United States, an average of 8 cases are reported annually, though 38 cases were confirmed in 2019 across 10 states. EEE also occurs in Latin America, with outbreaks reported in Panama affecting both humans and horses. Transmission is primarily mosquito-borne, with enzootic lineages identified in affected regions. Human cases can arise from increased contact with these enzootic transmission cycles, genetic changes in viral strains, or an altered host range. Additionally, EEEV transmission through solid organ transplant from an infected donor has been demonstrated. [PMC8784058, PMC6488434, PMC3839813]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) typically presents with fever, flu-like symptoms, headache, confusion, and altered mental status, often progressing rapidly to severe neurological manifestations. Patients commonly experience seizures, including generalized tonic-clonic, focal, or nonconvulsive status epilepticus, along with focal neurological deficits and brain lesions. Diagnostic findings include EEE-specific IgM antibodies in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which also shows elevated protein, red blood cells, and white blood cells with lymphocytic or neutrophil predominance. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) frequently reveals T2 hyperintensities in the basal ganglia, thalamus, cortical regions, and hippocampi, sometimes with encapsulation. Electroencephalogram (EEG) findings vary from normal to focal irritability or spikes. EEE carries a high mortality rate, often exceeding 30%. Survivors may require mechanical ventilation and can experience neurological sequelae such as impaired memory, though full recovery is possible. [PMC11688096, PMC8784058, PMC4885365, PMC3839813]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) is caused by the Eastern equine encephalitis virus (EEEV), an alphavirus within the Togaviridae family. Madariaga virus (MADV), formerly known as South American variants of EEEV, is also associated with neurological conditions. EEEV is primarily transmitted by mosquitoes, but transmission through solid organ transplant from an infected donor has also been documented. Phylogenetic analyses indicate enzootic lineages of EEEV, and antigenic subtypes of the virus have been identified. Factors such as ecological changes increasing human contact with enzootic transmission cycles, genetic changes in viral strains leading to increased human virulence, or an altered host range may contribute to human cases. [PMC6488434, PMC4458814, PMC3839813, PMC269613]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) is confirmed by detecting EEE-specific IgM antibodies in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) or by demonstrating a rise in IgG and IgM antibody titres in convalescent serum samples. EEEV RNA can also be detected in serum, and the virus can be isolated from CSF or tissue. CSF analysis typically reveals elevated protein, red blood cells, and elevated white blood cells, with normal or high glucose. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) often shows T2 hyperintensities or abnormal T2 and FLAIR signals in regions such as the basal ganglia, thalamus, cortical areas, ventricular nuclei, hippocampi, and frontal/parietal regions, sometimes with evidence of encapsulation. Electroencephalogram (EEG) findings can range from normal to focal irritability, spikes, or nonconvulsive status epilepticus. [PMC11688096, PMC8784058, PMC6488434, PMC4885365, PMC4458814]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for Eastern equine encephalitis (EEE) includes other encephalitic viruses. Venezuelan equine encephalitis (VEE) virus causes similar neurologic disease and encephalitis, with co-infections reported. Madariaga virus (MADV), formerly known as South American variants of EEE virus, is associated with acute disseminated encephalomyelitis (ADEM) and should be included in the etiologic differential diagnosis in endemic countries. Additionally, Powassan virus (POWV), a tick-borne encephalitic virus endemic to Canada, the United States, and Russia, also causes human cases of encephalitis, particularly in the northeastern and midwestern United States. [PMC12225551, PMC4458814, PMC3839813]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for Eastern equine encephalitis is primarily supportive. This includes anticonvulsant therapy, often using levetiracetam, to manage seizures, and mechanical ventilation for respiratory support when required. Empiric antibiotics and antivirals may be initiated until the diagnosis is confirmed. Some patients have also received immunomodulatory treatments such as high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone or intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG). [PMC11688096, PMC8784058, PMC4885365, PMC4458814]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Eastern equine encephalitis is a severe neuroinvasive disease with a high mortality rate, often reported as exceeding 30% in some series, and 25% in others. Neuroinvasive infection can directly contribute to death. Among survivors, neurological sequelae are common, including brain lesions, seizures that may evolve to status epilepticus, and impaired memory, often requiring discharge to rehabilitation facilities and extensive physical therapy. While some patients may recover fully, others experience persistent cognitive deficits. [PMC11688096, PMC8784058, PMC6488434, PMC4885365, PMC3839813]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Sanjad-Sakati syndrome (SSS), also known as hypoparathyroidism - intellectual disability-dysmorphism, is a rare multiple congenital anomaly syndrome, mainly occurring in the Middle East and the Arabian Gulf countries, characterized by intrauterine growth restriction at birth, microcephaly, congenital hypoparathyroidism (that can cause hypocalcemic tetany or seizures in infancy), severe growth retardation, typical facial features (long narrow face, deep-set eyes, beaked nose, floppy and large ears, long philtrum, thin lips and micrognathia), and mild to moderate intellectual deficiency. Ocular findings (i.e. nanophthalmos, retinal vascular tortuosity and corneal opacification/clouding) and superior mesenteric artery syndrome have also been reported. Although SSS shares the same locus with the autosomal recessive form of Kenny-Caffey syndrome, the latter differs from SSS by its normal intelligence and skeletal features.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): HRD syndrome; Hypoparathyroidism-intellectual disability-dysmorphism syndrome; Hypoparathyroidism-short stature-intellectual disability-seizures syndrome; Richardson-Kirk syndrome; SSS

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Sanjad-Sakati syndrome (SSS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder, though its prevalence is unknown. Historically, reported patients were almost exclusively from the Arabian Peninsula, linked to the ancestral "Bedouin mutation" (c.155-166del of the TBCE gene). This mutation has also been identified in a Moroccan patient, reflecting Arabian origins in that population. More recently, a novel variant (c.100 + 1G > A) of the TBCE gene has been found in patients of Central-Eastern European descent, suggesting a potential founder mutation in this group and indicating a broader clinical phenotype associated with pathogenic TBCE variants. [PMC12000180, PMC6074128]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Sanjad-Sakati syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by growth and psychomotor retardation, intellectual disability, and epilepsy, which can include status epilepticus. Common dysmorphic features include microcephaly, thin lips, beaked nose, low set ears, retrognathic mandible, and other facial, eye, and dental anomalies. Oral manifestations may involve oligodontia/hypodontia, small dental arches, a high arched palate, deep overbite, and increased overjet. Endocrine abnormalities include congenital hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism, and hypocalcemia, sometimes with bilateral calcification of basal ganglia. Abnormalities of the extremities and cryptorchidism in males are also reported. A novel TBCE variant (c.100 + 1G > A) can present with a milder course, lacking calcium-phosphate metabolism deviations or CNS pathology on MRI, but may include rigid spine, eosinophilia, neutropenia, and nocturnal hypoxemia. [PMC12000180, PMC6062658, PMC6074128, PMC3603786]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Sanjad-Sakati syndrome (SSS) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the TBCE gene. The ancestral mutation, c.155-166del, known as "the Bedouin mutation," is commonly found in homozygous patients, particularly those from the Arabian Peninsula and individuals of Arabian origin. A novel pathogenic variant, c.100 + 1G > A, has been identified in patients of Central-Eastern European descent, suggesting a potential founder mutation in this population. Homozygous carriers of the c.100 + 1G > A variant exhibit a markedly milder clinical course. [PMC12000180, PMC6074128]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: three patients with the novel variant c.100 + 1G > A of the TBCE gene and describe the presented clinical phenotype in detail. We also systematically reviewed the literature for clinical similarities and dissimilarities among all known patients with pathogenic TBCE variants. The clinical phenotype observed in patients with pathogenic TBCE variants is broader than previously described. Homozygous carriers of the c.100 + 1G > A variant exhibit a markedly milder clinical course, with no deviations in the calcium-phosphate metabolism and central nervous system pathology in MRI studies. Additionally, two patients manifest highly specific symptoms such as a rigid spine, eosinophilia, neutropenia, and nocturnal hypoxemia. Furthermore, cryptorchidism was observed in male patients. The identification of the pathogenic c.100 + 1G > A variant has thus far been limited to patients of... [PMC12000180, PMC6062658, PMC6074128, PMC3603786]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Sanjad-Sakati syndrome (SSS) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by the c.155-166del ("Bedouin mutation") in the TBCE gene, characterized by congenital hypothyroidism, growth and psychomotor retardation, epilepsy, and dysmorphic features. A distinct phenotype associated with the c.100 + 1G > A variant of the TBCE gene should be considered in the differential diagnosis. This variant presents with a markedly milder clinical course, notably lacking deviations in calcium-phosphate metabolism and central nervous system pathology on MRI, which are features of SSS. Additionally, patients with the c.100 + 1G > A variant may exhibit specific symptoms such as a rigid spine, eosinophilia, neutropenia, nocturnal hypoxemia, and cryptorchidism, and are typically of Central-Eastern European descent, contrasting with the Arabian Peninsula origin of most SSS patients. [PMC12000180, PMC6074128]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: three patients with the novel variant c.100 + 1G > A of the TBCE gene and describe the presented clinical phenotype in detail. We also systematically reviewed the literature for clinical similarities and dissimilarities among all known patients with pathogenic TBCE variants. The clinical phenotype observed in patients with pathogenic TBCE variants is broader than previously described. Homozygous carriers of the c.100 + 1G > A variant exhibit a markedly milder clinical course, with no deviations in the calcium-phosphate metabolism and central nervous system pathology in MRI studies. Additionally, two patients manifest highly specific symptoms such as a rigid spine, eosinophilia, neutropenia, and nocturnal hypoxemia. Furthermore, cryptorchidism was observed in male patients. The identification of the pathogenic c.100 + 1G > A variant has thus far been limited to patients of... [PMC12000180, PMC6074128]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for Sanjad-Sakati syndrome addresses specific manifestations. Hypocalcemia and hypoparathyroidism are treated with intravenous calcium gluconate, followed by oral calcium and calcitriol. Orofacial features, including oligodontia and small dental arches, may necessitate dental rehabilitation with prosthetic crowns, stainless steel crowns, and removable partial prostheses, though such care can be complicated by intellectual, neurological, and endocrine abnormalities. Genetic counseling is also an important component of patient management. [PMC6062658, PMC6074128, PMC3603786]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: For homozygous carriers of the c.100 + 1G > A variant of the TBCE gene, a markedly milder clinical course is observed. These individuals show no deviations in calcium-phosphate metabolism and no central nervous system pathology in MRI studies. This suggests that the prognosis can vary significantly depending on the specific genetic variant, with some variants leading to a less severe presentation. [PMC12000180]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 2
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy characterized by profound and universal sensory loss involving large and small fiber nerves.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Autosomal recessive sensory radicular neuropathy; HSAN2; Neurogenic acroosteolysis; Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type II

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, less than 100 cases have been reported. There is no sex preference or particular ethnic preponderance.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset is typically in infancy and is non-progressive. Initial symptoms (from birth to 3 years) include lack of crying with trauma, self-mutilation (tongue, lips), swallowing and feeding problems. Gastroesophageal reflux is common. Sensory dysfunction is manifested by reduced or absent pain and temperature perception, and depressed or absent deep tendon reflexes. Corneal reflexes are reduced or absent. Muscle strength is preserved and there is no atrophy. Sensation to fine touch, position, vibration, taste, and gag reflexes may be diminished. Unrecognized injuries (e.g., burns, skin and corneal ulcers) and fractures of hands, feet, and limbs, sometimes resulting in osteomyelitis, as well as Charcot joints are frequent. Some patients have hearing loss. Autonomic involvement is limited to reduced lacrimation. Patients do not typically have orthostatic hypotension or sweating abnormalities.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Causal mutations in several genes have been identified and include SCN9A (2q24.3), WNK1 (12p13.33), RETREG1 (5p15.1), and KIF1A (2q37.3), all of which appear to be involved in the development of sensory nerves.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based upon clinical features (congenital onset of severe reduction in sensory modalities and deep tendon reflexes resulting in injuries and self-mutilation). Neurophysiological evaluation (showing slow sensory conduction velocities and amplitudes), electromyogram and electroencephalographic studies support the diagnosis. Targeted genetic testing identifying described mutations in causatives genes is confirmatory. For cases in which no genetic mutation can be identified with targeted genetic testing, whole exome sequencing may identify novel variants/genes.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes the other hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies, the most similar of which include hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 4 (characterized by complete lack of pain and complete lack of sweating), familial dysautonomia (accompanied by baroreflex abnormalities with paroxysmal episodes of nausea, retching, vomiting and hypertension) and hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1 (typically adult-onset).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal recessive. Where both parents are unaffected carriers, the risk of disease transmission to offspring is 25%. Offspring of affected individuals are obligate carriers. Penetrance is always complete, but the severity of the disease is variable.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is symptomatic and preventative. If feeding problems compromise nutrition and if gastroesophageal reflux is also present, fundoplication with gastrostomy might be considered. Parents' and patients' education is required to learn how to avoid injury and be alert for signs of unrecognized trauma. Reduced lacrimation requires artificial tears and corneal protective lenses to prevent corneal ulcers.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: No natural history studies have been performed. Most patients reach adulthood.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, small-vessel vasculitis characterized by skin purpura, arthritis, abdominal and/or renal involvement, IgA tissue deposits (arterioles, capillaries, and venules) and circulating IgA immune complexes.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Anaphylactoid purpura; Henoch-Schönlein purpura; IgA vasculitis; Purpura rheumatica; Rheumatoid purpura

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The disease usually affects children and is rare in adults. Annual incidence in children is estimated at between 1/4,880 and 1/6,660, whereas it is estimated at around 1/1,000,000 in adults. The male-to-female ratio is 1.5:1.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients present with vascular purpura that is usually symmetrical and primarily localized to the buttocks and legs. In adults it is more frequently complicated by necrotic or hemorrhagic bullous lesions. The lesions progressively regress, disappear after a few days and, in 80% of cases, never reappear. Patients also present with arthralgia, predominantly involving the knees and ankles. Abdominal pain is common and may be associated with life-threatening gastrointestinal bleeding. Renal involvement is more severe and frequent in adults. It usually consists of microscopic hematuria with varying degrees of proteinuria. Nephrotic syndrome, renal failure, and hypertension may also occur. Other manifestations are rare but may include headaches, seizures, paresis, orchiepididymitis, uretritis, pancreatitis, myositis, episcleritis, pulmonary bleeding and myocarditis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is associated with deposition of IgA-dominant immune complexes in arterioles, capillaries, and venules, but the exact etiology remains unknown. Several different viral or bacterial organisms, drugs, foods, and insect bites have been implicated as the initiating factors of the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on clinical and histopathological findings. Examination of skin and kidney biopsies reveals tissue deposition of IgA with circulating IgA immune complexes.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other causes of purpura such as thrombopenia, hemopathy or infectious diseases. In adults, ANCA associated vasculitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and mixed cryoglobulinemia should also be considered in the differential diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The treatment is symptomatic. The use of steroids and/or immunosuppressors is controversial but may be considered in case of severe gastrointestinal or renal manifestations. Renin-angiotensin-system blockers should be started as soon as the proteinuria/creatinine ratio is greater than 50 mg/mmol.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Gastrointestinal or pulmonary bleeding can be life-threatening. The long term prognosis depends on the extent of the renal involvement. Long term follow-up studies of adult series show that end-stage renal failure may occur in up to one-third of patients.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Congenitally uncorrected transposition of the great arteries
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Congenitally uncorrected transposition of the great arteries (congenitally uncorrected TGA), also referred to as complete transposition, is a congenital cardiac malformation characterized by atrioventricular concordance and ventriculoarterial (VA) discordance.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Congenitally uncorrected transposition of the great vessels; Isolated ventriculoarterial discordance; Ventriculoarterial discordance with atrioventricular concordance; D-transposition of the great arteries; Dextro-transposition of the great arteries

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence is estimated at 1 in 3,500-5,000 live births, with a male-to-female ratio of 1.5 to 3.2:1.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In 50% of cases, the VA discordance is an isolated finding. In 10% of cases, TGA is associated with noncardiac malformations. The association with other cardiac malformations such as ventricular septal defect (VSD) and left ventricular outflow tract obstruction is frequent and dictates the timing and clinical presentation, which consists of cyanosis with or without congestive heart failure. The onset and severity depend on anatomical and functional variants that influence the degree of mixing between the two circulatory systems. If no obstructive lesions are present and there is a large VSD, cyanosis may go undetected and only be perceived during episodes of crying or agitation. In these cases, signs of congestive heart failure prevail.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The exact etiology remains unknown. Some associated risk factors (gestational diabetes mellitus, maternal exposure to rodenticides and herbicides, and maternal use of antiepileptic drugs) have been proposed. Mutations in the growth differentiation factor-1 gene (GDF1), the mediator complex subunit 13-like gene (MED13L) and the gene encoding the cryptic protein (CFC1) have been shown to be implicated in discordant VA connections, but they account for only a small minority of congenitally uncorrected TGA cases.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is confirmed by echocardiography, which also provides information about the morphological details required for future surgical management.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include other causes of central neonatal cyanosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis by fetal echocardiography is feasible and useful as it may improve early neonatal management and reduce morbidity and mortality.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Palliative treatment with prostaglandin E1 and balloon atrial septostomy are usually required soon after birth. Surgical correction is performed at a later stage. Usually, the Jatene arterial switch operation is the procedure of choice. Whenever this operation is not feasible, an adequate alternative surgical approach should be implemented.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With the advent of newer and improved surgical techniques and improved post-operative intensive care, the long-term survival is approximately 90% at 15 years of age. However, exercise performance, cognitive function and quality of life may be impaired.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inflammatory rheumatic disease characterized by juvenile onset arthritis that affects fewer than 5 joints during the first 6 months after disease onset.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence of juvenile idiopathic arthritis in Caucasians is 8.3/100,000. Oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis is the most common form in North America and Europe, comprising 30% to 60% of children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis. It affects girls more than boys and is rare in individuals of African, Native American or Sourthern Asian descent.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease is typically asymmetrical, affecting between one to four joints, predominantly those of the lower limbs (knee or foot) although the wrist and elbows could be rarely affected. Onset occurs between the ages of 2 and 4. The disease is divided into persistent oligoarthritis, in which there is no more than 4 joints involved after the first six months of illness, and extended oligoarthritis, in which there is involvement of more than 4 joints involved after the first six months. Pain is not a constant feature in young children and the most common reasons for seeking medical advice are an increase in the volume of the joint and/or limping. The association of this form of arthritis with nonsymptomatic iridocyclitis (no pain or visible redness) is a specific feature that is present in a third of cases. Systemic manifestations other than uveitis are characteristically absent. Therefore, fever, rash, or other constitutional symptoms suggest a different diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is not currently known. All juvenile idiopathic arthritis subtypes are most likely complex genetic traits as they lack single-gene, Mendelian patterns of inheritance. Inherited risk factors for both disease susceptibility and disease severity have been reported; the highly polymorphic HLA genes confer the strongest genetic effects.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the clinical manifestations, and exclusion of other potential causes. The presence of iridocyclitis and/or antinuclear antibodies without fever or psoriasis are strong diagnostic indicators. Exclusion criteria includes presence of systemic arthritis, psoriasis, ankylosing spondylarthritis, enthesitis and arthritis, sacroiliitis with an inflammatory enteropathy or acute anterior uveitis in the patient or a first-degree relative. In addition, HLA B27-positivity in males with onset of arthritis after 6 years of age and presence of rheumatoid factor IgM must be excluded.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis principally includes the other subtypes of juvenile idiopathic arthritis as well as Lyme disease, inflammatory bowel disease, pigmented villonodular synovitis, malignancy, plant thorn synovitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, or tuberculosis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: First step of treatment is non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent (NSAID) , but their efficacy is quite rare. Intra-articular glucocorticoids injections are often necessary and effective. Methotrexate and, if ineffective, biologics are recommended for children with disease that extends to involve five or more joints or require repeat injections.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Several long-term complications may occur, the most frequent and significant ones being temporomandibular joint arthritis with retrognatism, uveitis complications (glaucoma or synechia), leg-length discrepancy in case of delayed diagnosis. Arthritis may extend to involve five or more joints within several years of diagnosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder involving multiple structure of the eye characterized by reduced visual acuity in males due to juvenile macular degeneration. Clinical features such as vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment, and neovascular glaucoma can be observed in advanced stages.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: X-linked retinoschisis prevalence is estimated to range between 1/5,000-1/25,000 males worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: XLRS is a symmetrical bilateral macular disorder with onset in the first decade of life. It manifests with poor vision and reading difficulties. In severe cases, nystagmus may also be observed. Severe cases involve full-thickness retinal detachment that leads to impaired vision or blindness. In more advanced stages of the disease, vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment, and neovascular glaucoma, which may induce severe loss of vision, can be seen. Correlation exists between visual acuity, patient age, and OCT features. There is clinical variability. Female carriers rarely have any vision impairment.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by mutations on the RS1 gene (Xp22.2-p22.1), including missense, nonsense, frameshift, and splice site mutations, deletions, and insertions. RS1 codes for retinoschisin, an adhesive protein, localized in photoreceptors and bipolar cells, and secreted in the extracellular matrix. In the adult retina, retinoschisin is essential for maintaining the structural and functional integrity of the retina and participates in molecular pathways at the photoreceptor bipolar synapse.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of XLRS can be made clinically, based on fundus appearance. Fundus examination shows microcystic changes of the macular region of the retina and areas of splitting within the nerve fiber layer, or schisis (spoked-wheel pattern), and vitreous veils. Electroretinogram (ERG) usually shows generalized cone system dysfunction with a reduction in the amplitude of the beta-wave and a relative preservation of the negative alpha-wave in scotopic ERG (electronegative rods and mixed ERG) and a normal photopic ERG. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) shows schisis areas in the macular region. There is also a family history consistent with X-linked inheritance. Molecular genetic analysis by direct sequencing of the RS1 gene detects mutations in approximately 90% of patients. NGS panels for Inherited Retinal dystrophies, including the RS1 gene represent also an appropriate approach.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes retinitis pigmentosa and Goldmann-Favre syndrome. The presence of an autosomal recessive inheritance, severe nyctalopia, pigmentary retinopathy, and reduced alpha- and beta-waves on the electroretinogram (ERG) help to differentiate Goldmann-Favre syndrome from XLRS.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: There are more than 290 mutations described in RS1, most missense (~51%). Nonsense, splicing, small indels and CNVs variants have also been reported. XLRS is inherited in an X-linked manner, with a carrier female having a 50% risk of transmitting the mutation to her offspring. Carrier testing for at-risk female relatives and prenatal diagnosis for pregnancies at increased risk are possible if a RS1 mutation is identified in an affected family member.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management includes periodic ophthalmologic examination to monitor progression of XLRS. Additionally, patients are informed about possible ophthalmic complications that can be surgically treated (i.e., retinal detachment, vitreous haemorrhage, cataracts or strabismus). Therefore, patient education and close follow-up are the only clinical alternatives to early identification and treatment of vision-threatening complications.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: In XLRS, vision slowly decreases until adolescence, and then in most patients remains relatively stable during young adulthood. The disease does not progress again until the fourth or fifth decade of life, when a significant decline in visual acuity typically occurs.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Wells syndrome is characterised by the presence of recurrent cellulitis-like eruptions with eosinophilia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Approximately 80 cases have been described in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The lesions are usually filled with fluid, tender and progress to form hardened plaques of edema and erythema. They usually resolve without scarring.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Histological studies reveal flame figures and heavy infiltration of eosinophils and histiocytes.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The syndrome is usually sporadic but familial cases have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Wells syndrome often involves addressing underlying triggers, as seen with oral terbinafine resolving cases linked to fungal infections. While initial treatments like steroids, antibiotics, and methotrexate may be ineffective in some instances, established anti-neutrophilic drugs such as dapsone, colchicine, and tetracyclines are also utilized, often off-label, for eosinophilic dermatoses. For refractory or relapsing disease, emerging therapies include biologics like dupilumab and mepolizumab, topical ruxolitinib, and abrocitinib, which have shown complete or near-complete resolution, though recurrences are common. JAK1/JAK2 inhibitors, such as baricitinib, also demonstrate potential, achieving complete clinical remission in refractory cases by targeting the activated type 2 inflammatory pathways. [PMC12149015, PMC11969056, PMC11673839, PMC10285679]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Neonatal diabetes-congenital hypothyroidism-congenital glaucoma-hepatic fibrosis-polycystic kidneys syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic disease characterized by intrauterine growth retardation, permanent neonatal diabetes mellitus, and congenital hypothyroidism. Additional manifestations include congenital glaucoma, hepatic disease (hepatitis, fibrosis, and cirrhosis), polycystic kidneys, exocrine pancreatic dysfunction, sensorineural hearing impairment, developmental delay, and mild facial dysmorphism (such as flat nasal bridge, epicanthal folds, long philtrum, and low-set ears), among others.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: This syndrome, caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the GLIS3 gene, is a rare condition. As of 2023, at least 22 cases have been described, contributing to the characterization of its genotypic and phenotypic spectra. Earlier reports from 2017 noted 12 reported patients, with additional cases subsequently identified. [PMC10683540, PMC5335837]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: The syndrome, caused by GLIS3 gene mutations, is characterized by neonatal diabetes and congenital hypothyroidism. Common accompanying features include congenital glaucoma, cholestatic hepatic fibrosis, polycystic kidney disease, developmental delay, and dysmorphic facial features. Other reported manifestations encompass pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, sensorineural deafness, osteopenia, and skeletal anomalies. Additional features like small for gestational age, choanal atresia, and craniosynostosis have also been described. While external genitalia abnormalities were noted in one case, their association might be coincidental. The phenotypic expression can vary, with some individuals not developing all described features during follow-up. [PMC10683540, PMC5335837]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The syndrome is a rare condition caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the GLIS3 gene, which encodes the transcription factor GLIS3. Mutations in this gene are a known cause of neonatal diabetes and congenital hypothyroidism. Additional features associated with GLIS3 mutations include congenital glaucoma, hepatic fibrosis, and polycystic kidneys. Reported cases have confirmed homozygous GLIS3 gene mutations in affected individuals. [PMC10683540, PMC5335837]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of this syndrome is primarily based on identifying homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the GLIS3 gene. Genetic testing, such as detecting an exon 10-11 deletion in GLIS3, confirms the condition. It is suggested that infants presenting with neonatal diabetes associated with dysmorphism should be screened for GLIS3 gene mutations to establish a diagnosis. [PMC10683540, PMC5335837]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The constellation of neonatal diabetes and congenital hypothyroidism, especially when accompanied by congenital glaucoma, hepatic fibrosis, polycystic kidneys, and facial dysmorphism, is highly suggestive of GLIS3 gene mutations. Additional features such as developmental delay, osteopenia, sensorineural deafness, choanal atresia, craniosynostosis, and pancreatic exocrine insufficiency further characterize the syndrome. Infants presenting with neonatal diabetes associated with dysmorphism should be screened for GLIS3 gene mutations. [PMC5335837]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The syndrome is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the GLIS3 gene, indicating an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. This is supported by cases reported in consanguineous parents. Genetic counseling should inform families about the recurrence risk associated with this mode of inheritance. Screening for GLIS3 gene mutations is suggested for infants presenting with neonatal diabetes associated with dysmorphism. [PMC10683540, PMC5335837]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for this rare syndrome, caused by GLIS3 mutations, can involve a wide range of phenotypic features. While many cases are described, long-term survival is possible. One patient with neonatal diabetes, congenital hypothyroidism, congenital glaucoma, developmental delay, and facial dysmorphism survived for 17 years. Notably, during this extended follow-up, no signs of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, liver and kidney diseases, deafness, osteopenia, or bone fracture were observed, despite these being described features of the syndrome. This case represents one of the oldest surviving individuals with a GLIS3 mutation, contributing to the characterization of the syndrome's long-term phenotypic spectrum. [PMC10683540]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Thomas syndrome is characterised by renal anomalies, cardiac malformations and cleft lip or palate. It has been described in six patients. Transmission was suggested to be autosomal recessive.

A rare parasitic disorder that occurs after ingestion of eggs of Echinococcus multilocularis and characterized by an initial asymptomatic incubation period of many years followed by a chronic course where the clinical manifestations include epigastric pain and jaundice.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: E.multilocularis is endemic in the northern hemisphere and central Europe and the incidence in Europe is estimated to range between 1/10,000,000-1/330,000. Hot spots are in Western parts of China and Central Asia. People at high risk include dog-owners, including farmers, or others who have contact with wild foxes, or their stool.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The peak age group in Europe is 50-60 years. After an asymptomatic period of >10 years, the parasite invades mainly the liver forming slow-growing, minute vesicles comparable to a sponge. As the lesion gets larger, the central part may become necrotic, and appears as a pseudocyst. Calcifications can frequently be seen. The clinical manifestations include epigastric pain and jaundice which may be followed by fever, anemia and weight loss. Invasion of the bile ducts leads to cholangitis, portal hypertension, and biliary cirrhosis. The disease can progress to the cirrhotic stage after a long latent, asymptomatic period. Extrahepatic manifestation as primary disease is very rare (1%). 13% of cases present as multiorgan disease where the metacestode infiltrates the neighborhood of the liver, and/or sets metastasis involving the lungs, spleen, bones and/or brain. Lung or brain involvement is characterized by exertional dyspnea, dysarthria, hemiparesis and cranial nerve palsies.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Alveolar echinococcosis (AE) occurs after ingestion of eggs of the parasite E.multilocularis. Wild carnivores, mainly foxes, are the most important definitive hosts but domestic dogs and cats may also serve as definite hosts by ingestion of infected wild rodents. Human are accidental intermediate hosts and are affected by the intermediate metacestode stage of the parasite.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of AE is based on: typical organ lesions detected by imaging techniques such as ultrasound (large hepatic mass with juxtaposed areas of internal hyper- and hypoechogenicity, irregular margins, and scattered calcification, and/or a pseudocyst with a large area of central necrosis surrounded by an irregular ring-like region of hyperechogenicity representing fibrous tissue), CT (indistinct solid tumors with central necrotic areas, plaque like calcifications), and MRI; detection of specific serum antibodies by ELISA or by immunochromatographic test; specific staining of metacestode in histo-or immunohistopathology; and detection of E. multilocularis nucleic acid in a clinical specimen.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes benign or malignant neoplasms, focal hepatic lesions, and abscesses.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The mainstay for AE treatment remains an interdisciplinary management guided by gastroenterologists, surgeons, radiologists and parasitologists. Radical surgery is indicated if lesion can be excised with safety margins. Long-term antiparasitic treatment with albendazole is mandatory. Preventive measures include avoidance of contact with fox feces, use of praziquantel-impregnated baits, regular treatment of dogs or cats with praziquantel, as well as hand washing and improved hygiene.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: AE is one of the most dangerous zoonotic diseases in the world and if untreated prognosis is poor. Early diagnosis and treatment of AE, especially during the asymptomatic period, are important for reducing morbidity and mortality. Patients succumb to hepatic failure, invasion of contiguous structures, or, less frequently, involvement of the brain. Mortality rates have traditionally been high, ranging between 50% and 75%. However, in recent years major achievement has been reached by careful management of AE cases, and life-expectancy of patients is approaching that of the general population.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Hydatid disease, caused by the larval form of Echinococcus granulosus, is a rare but potentially life-threatening condition during pregnancy, with an estimated incidence of 1 in 20,000 to 30,000 gestations. Physiological immunosuppression and increased placental steroid levels during pregnancy may promote cyst growth, elevating the risk of rupture, which can result in anaphylactic shock, sepsis, or widespread peritoneal dissemination. Diagnostic imaging, particularly ultrasonography, plays a central role in detection, while treatment decisions are complicated by the lack of standardized guidelines and the need to balance maternal-fetal safety. This case report describes a 29-year-old pregnant woman at 22 weeks' gestation who was incidentally diagnosed with two large hepatic hydatid cysts during a routine ultrasound. Given the high rupture risk, she underwent successful laparoscopic... [PMC12295198]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare metabolic disorder for which two forms have been described. Lack of activity of the erythrocyte isoform of adenosine monophosphate (AMP) deaminase has been described in subjects with low plasma uric acid levels without obvious clinical relevance and will not be described further. Myoadenylate deaminase deficiency is an inherited disorder of muscular energy metabolism with a lack of AMP deaminase activity in skeletal muscle. It is characterised by exercise-induced muscle pain, cramps and/or early fatigue.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): AMP deaminase deficiency; Myoadenylate deaminase deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: About 1-2% of the Caucasian population carries the genetic defect causing myoadenylate deaminase deficiency, but only a minority of carriers develop symptoms. The prevalence is unknown but several hundred patients with the disorder have been reported in case reports and patient series. Men and women are equally affected.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The vast majority of patients suffer from post-exercise symptoms: rapid fatigue, cramps or myalgias. Approximately equal proportions of the patients first develop symptoms during childhood, adolescence, or as young or older adults. After progression of the symptoms over the first few years, the clinical course usually stabilises. There is no evidence of muscular dystrophy or muscular wasting. The disorder exclusively affects skeletal muscle. Smooth muscle or other organs are not affected as the disorder is associated with a specific lack of skeletal muscle adenylate deaminase activity.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The vast majority of patients with this disease are homozygous for the nonsense C34-T mutation in the AMPD1 (adenosine monophosphate deaminase 1) gene. This mutation creates an early stop codon thus preventing the synthesis of an enzymatically active protein. The deficiency disrupts the purine nucleotide cycle, and thus muscle energy production. Surprisingly, however, asymptomatic AMP deaminase-deficient subjects have been reported, indicating that additional factors are likely to be involved in the development of myopathic symptoms.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on histochemical staining or biochemical analysis of a muscle biopsy showing a lack of muscle adenylate deaminase activity, or on molecular identification of the disease-causing mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Unfortunately, there is no medical cure for this disorder. Symptoms improve with administration of D-ribose. However, the effects of this sugar are only short-tem and it has no beneficial effect during subsequent days.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: When evaluating severe rhabdomyolysis, particularly in the context of Plasmodium vivax malaria, adenosine monophosphate deaminase deficiency should be considered. However, rhabdomyolysis can occur due to P. vivax infection alone, even without myophosphorylase or deaminase deficiency, as observed in a 16-year-old boy. This contrasts with other reported cases where P. vivax infection and rhabdomyolysis were associated with myoadenylate deaminase deficiency, highlighting the need to differentiate between these potential causes. [PMC2911169]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: MyoAdenylate Deaminase Deficiency (MADD) is a relatively common metabolic disorder of the skeletal muscle. Patients with MADD usually show an impaired bioenergetic production and a clinical spectrum with either exercise-induced muscle pain, fatigue and/or rhabdomyolysis. Left ventricular hypertrophy as well as other types of cardiac involvement have been reported in patients with primary MADD. herein a case of a 61-year-old woman with biochemical and genetic evidence of Myo-Adenylate Deaminase deficiency, in whom we found a right ventricular hypertrophic cardiomyopathy leading to severe outflow tract dynamic obstruction. A patient with symptoms of easy fatigability, postexercise myalgias, and delayed recovery of muscle strength after activity is described. Skeletal muscle from this patient had <1.0% normal myoadenylate deaminase activity and NH(3) was not released from muscle after... [PMC3185826, PMC371628]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A extremely rare, genetic malformation syndrome characterized by hypoplastic amelogenesis imperfecta (hypoplastic dental enamel) and nephrocalcinosis (precipitation of calcium salts in renal tissue). Oral manifestations include yellow and misshaped teeth, delayed tooth eruption, and intrapulpal calcifications. Nephrocalcinosis is often asymptomatic but can progress during late childhood or early adulthood to impaired renal function, recurrent urinary infections, renal tubular acidosis, and rarely to end-stage renal failure.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Enamel-renal syndrome (ERS) is characterized by disturbed amelogenesis, manifesting as severe enamel hypoplasia, agenesis, or thin, discolored, and misshapen teeth, often leading to delayed or failed tooth eruption, intrapulpal calcifications, and localized gingival hyperplasia. Renal features include nephrocalcinosis, presenting as medullary calcium deposits, bilateral multiple calculi, and small papillary tip calcifications. Patients may also exhibit hypophosphatemia, hypocitraturia, and hypocalciuria, though renal function can remain normal. The syndrome is associated with bi-allelic pathogenic variants in FAM20A. [PMC11457907, PMC11284857, PMC9017830, PMC6848751, PMC3865794]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Enamel-renal syndrome (ERS) is caused by bi-allelic, likely pathogenic or pathogenic variants in the FAM20A gene. These include biallelic loss-of-function mutations, frameshift mutations, splice junction alterations, missense mutations, and single nucleotide deletions. FAM20A is likely a secretory pathway kinase, and its loss-of-function mutations lead to pathology where its phosphorylations are necessary for normal development or homeostasis. FAM20A is localized in secretory-stage ameloblasts, odontoblasts, the eruption pathway, and renal tubules. Mutations in FAM20A disrupt dental follicle cells, impeding proper tooth eruption, and also affect the homeostasis of gingival epithelium and connective tissues. [PMC11457907, PMC11284857, PMC6848751, PMC3865794]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Enamel-renal syndrome (ERS) is primarily based on its characteristic features of disturbed amelogenesis and nephrocalcinosis. Clinical examination often reveals severe enamel hypoplasia, delayed tooth eruption, misshapen teeth, and localized gingival hyperplasia. Genetic confirmation is achieved by identifying bi-allelic pathogenic variants in FAM20A, frequently through whole-exome sequencing. Nephrological investigations are crucial, involving imaging to detect nephrocalcinosis, medullary calcium deposits, or calculi. Additionally, urine analysis may show hypocitraturia and hypocalciuria, and blood tests can indicate hypophosphatemia and increased alkaline phosphatase. [PMC11457907, PMC6848751, PMC3865794, PMC3669991]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for Enamel-renal syndrome, which involves both dental and renal manifestations, includes other conditions affecting tooth development and systemic health. Amelogenesis imperfecta, an inherited disorder of dental enamel, is particularly relevant as it can present with associated renal disease. Other genetic disorders that cause abnormal tooth eruption due to dental follicle cell disruption include Cleidocranial dysplasia, osteosclerosis, mucopolysaccharidosis type VI, and dentin dysplasia. Additionally, regional odontodysplasia and multiple calcific hyperplastic dental follicles are involved in tooth eruption failure, although these are not linked to gene mutations. [PMC11284857, PMC9017830]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Enamel-renal syndrome is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by bi-allelic likely pathogenic or pathogenic variants in the FAM20A gene. Genetic analyses have identified various FAM20A mutations, including splice junction alterations, missense mutations, and single nucleotide deletions, which are associated with the disease phenotype. For instance, homozygosity for a specific FAM20A variant has been genetically confirmed in affected individuals. Loss-of-function mutations in FAM20A are believed to cause the pathology. Genetic confirmation is crucial, as diagnostic delay can occur, highlighting the importance of early identification for appropriate management. [PMC11457907, PMC3865794]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Enamel-renal syndrome involves extensive dental treatment, often requiring rehabilitation for functional and aesthetic requirements, which may need revision. The dental prognosis is influenced by anatomical variations and patient cooperation. Renal management addresses nephrocalcinosis and stone formation; one reported case used potassium citrate to decrease the risk of progressive renal stone formation due to hypocitraturia and hypocalciuria. Lifelong surveillance of renal function is recommended, although the prognosis for renal function appears good. Multidisciplinary dental and medical management is crucial for this syndromic disorder. [PMC11457907, PMC3669991]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Knowledge regarding the long-term prognosis of Enamel-renal syndrome is generally lacking, and the complex nature of the condition can endanger both dental and general health. The dental prognosis following rehabilitation is influenced by anatomical variations and patient cooperation. While the prognosis for renal function appears to be good, lifelong surveillance of renal function is recommended to monitor for potential complications. [PMC11457907]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Reducing body myopathy (RBM) is a rare muscle disorder marked by progressive muscle weakness and the presence of characteristic inclusion bodies in affected muscle fibres.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown: although some sporadic cases have been described, only four families with RBM have been reported in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The age of onset, speed of progression and severity of the disease vary significantly between patients, even between affected members of the same family. Although early development is generally normal (up to 2 years of age), onset during infancy or early childhood appears to be associated with severe myopathy, hypotonia and rapidly progressive muscle weakness leading to death due to respiratory insufficiency within the first five years of life. Onset during childhood or adulthood is characterised by mainly proximal muscle weakness, a rigid spine syndrome and a slowly progressive disease course.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Both sporadic and familial cases of RBM are caused by mutations in the gene encoding the four-and-a-half LIM domain 1 protein (FHL1; Xq27.2).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: As the clinical picture is highly variable (EMG reveals mixed myogenic patterns), diagnosis relies on recognition of the typical histopathological findings at muscle biopsy: the non-membrane-bound inclusions reduce nitro-blue tetrazolium (hence the name `reducing body myopathy') and are located in the cytoplasm, usually close to the degenerating nucleus. Electron microscopy reveals that the inclusions consist of a fine granular material and immunohistochemical analysis reveals the presence of aggresome-like proteins.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include other disorders with reducing bodies (e.g. acid maltase deficiency) and other congenital myopathies in familial cases. Sarcotubular myopathy may also be considered in patients with less severe forms of the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The mode of transmission remains unclear. There are no reports of male-to-male transmission in familial cases and cases of severely affected females have been reported. X-linked dominant, semi-dominant and recessive inheritance have been suggested and skewed X-inactivation has not been excluded.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is supportive and should be multidisciplinary (involving a neurologist, orthopaedic surgeon and physical therapist).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is generally severe: disease progression results in loss of ambulation, and death due to respiratory failure occurs even in patients with later-onset slowly progressive forms of the disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, congenital, vascular anomaly syndrome characterized by venous or, on occasion, arterial malformations which lead to soft tissue hypertrophy and bone hypoplasia. Affected limb is generally shortened, highly deformed, painful and edematous and associates bone and muscle hypotrophy. Single parts, or multiple small parts, of limbs are typically affected but more extensive involvement, including complete extremity, shoulder girdle and axilla, has been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: The association between congenital vascular malformations and altered bone growth, the so-called vascular bone syndrome, is well documented. Various eponymous syndromes each with their individual traits, such as Klippel-Trenaunay, Parkes-Weber and Servelle-Martorell syndrome have been described, along with variations. on a previously undescribed case of congenital vascular malformation associated with multiple skeletal abnormalities affecting the skull, vertebrae and right upper limb, and discuss the literature. [PMC5696949]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The association between congenital vascular malformations and altered bone growth, termed vascular bone syndrome, encompasses various eponymous syndromes. These include Klippel-Trenaunay, Parkes-Weber, and Servelle-Martorell syndromes, each with distinct traits and variations. [PMC5696949]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A distinct form of duodenal atresia in which the head of the pancreas forms a ring around the second portion of the duodenum.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The annual incidence is estimated at around 1/50,000 births, representing 10% of all cases of duodenal stenosis.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: During the neonatal period, the clinical picture is dominated by epigastric distension with vomiting, which is nonbilious as the obstruction is usually supra-vaterian (above the junction of the biliary ducts). As in other forms of duodenal atresia, malformations of the cranial intestine are also frequently present in patients with annular pancreas. Cardiac anomalies may also be present and are more frequent in the context of notochord induction anomalies or deficiency. Chromosomal abnormalities are present in one-third of cases of annular pancreas, with trisomy 21 (followed by trisomy 18 and 13) being the most frequently detected anomaly.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Annular pancreas is an embryopathy resulting from an anomaly occurring early (towards the fourth week) in development. It is a distinct form of duodenal atresia, rather than a pancreatic anomaly, and should not be confused with other congenital malformations of the pancreas or pancreaticobiliary ducts (such as anomalies of the pancreaticobiliary junction) for which the diagnosis cannot be made until childhood or adulthood.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of annular pancreas is often made before birth through ultrasound findings showing duodenal dilation and through difficulties in observing peri-duodenal pancreatic development. In cases where the diagnosis is not made prenatally, it is made in the neonatal period on the basis of the clinical picture and imagining studies (abdominal radiography and ultrasound).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include other forms of duodenal stenosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis allows management to be planned in a specialized center immediately after birth.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Investigations using a gastric tube allow drainage of the digestive tract prior to the site of obstruction. Treatment is surgical and is performed in the neonatal period.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis for annular pancreas is very favorable, but the overall prognosis depends on the presence of associated malformations.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Annular pancreas (AP) is a congenital defect with a suggested genetic contribution, supported by a few reported familial cases. Exome sequencing studies have identified rare heterozygous missense variants in genes such as IQGAP1 and NRCAM in a subset of affected individuals, with these genes being crucial for cell polarization and migration. Other rare heterozygous missense variants have also been found in PDX1 and FOXF1, genes previously associated with AP. These findings raise the possibility that AP may be related to abnormal cell migration due to specific genetic variants. [PMC10568395]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Lichen amyloidosis is a rare chronic form of cutaneous amyloidosis, a skin disease characterized by the accumulation of amyloid deposits in the dermis, clinically characterized by the development of pruritic, often pigmented, hyperkeratotic papules on trunk and extremities, especially on the shins, and histologically by the deposition of amyloid or amyloid-like proteins in the papillary dermis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Lichen amyloidosis (LA), a type of primary localized cutaneous amyloidosis (PLCA), is more frequently observed in Asian populations, with an estimated prevalence of 0.98/10,000, compared to European/Caucasian populations where it is considered very rare and epidemiologic data are limited. A Central European study of PLCA patients found a higher proportion of females (16 males/25 females) and a mean age at LA onset of 46.7 years (range 14-73 years). In this population, LA commonly affects the extensor surface of the lower extremities. Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis (CLA) can also be detected at an early age (childhood to young adulthood) and is associated with Medullary Thyroid Cancer (MTC) and Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Type 2 (MEN2), particularly with RET pathogenic variants, such as at codon 634. Females appear more prone to MEN2-CLA, which often presents in the scapular region of the upper back. [PMC11431960, PMC10743860, PMC8541328]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Lichen amyloidosis (LA) is associated with several factors. Genetic predisposition includes RET pathogenic variants, particularly at codon 634, which are strongly linked to cutaneous lichen amyloidosis (CLA) in Medullary Thyroid Cancer (MTC)/Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN2). Other non-C634 germline RET variants (V804M, S891A, C611Y) have also been implicated. LA can also be associated with endocrine diseases, such as type 2 diabetes mellitus and thyroid disorders like post-thyroidectomy hypothyroidism due to papillary thyroid carcinoma. Furthermore, LA has been reported in association with autoimmune conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis. One hypothesis suggests CLA may be secondary to long-term pruritus or notalgia paresthetica. [PMC11431960, PMC9789704, PMC9969724]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of lichen amyloidosis primarily relies on histopathological examination, which reveals amyloid deposition in the papillary dermis. This is particularly recommended for hyperkeratotic lesions in patients with endocrine diseases. Dermoscopy serves as a useful non-invasive tool, characterized by central white hubs with grayish-brown dots and globules, and sometimes vascular structures like red globules or branching lines. Furthermore, cutaneous lichen amyloidosis can be a diagnostic clue for Medullary Thyroid Cancer/Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2, especially in the presence of specific RET pathogenic variants, and RET screening protocols may aid in early detection. [PMC11431960, PMC9789704, PMC8541328]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Lichen amyloidosis (LA) can co-exist with Acquired Reactive Perforating Collagenosis (ARPC), particularly in patients with endocrine conditions such as type 2 diabetes mellitus and thyroid disorders, including papillary thyroid carcinoma and hypothyroidism. Histopathological examination is essential to confirm LA and distinguish it from ARPC in such cases. Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis (CLA) also has a strong association with Medullary Thyroid Cancer (MTC) in Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), often linked to specific RET pathogenic variants, where CLA may be detected before MTC. Notalgia paresthetica has also been hypothesized as a secondary cause for CLA. [PMC11431960, PMC9789704]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Lichen amyloidosis (CLA) is associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2A (MEN2A), particularly in the context of Medullary Thyroid Cancer (MTC). This association is linked to germline pathogenic variants in the RET gene, with the majority of MEN2A-CLA patients having variants at codon 634, though other RET variants are also implicated. MEN syndromes, including MEN2, exhibit significant genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity, meaning the same RET mutation within a family may not lead to identical CLA presentations. CLA can manifest early, often preceding MTC identification, suggesting its utility in early RET screening protocols. Genetic counseling should address the variable expressivity and penetrance of RET mutations, the potential for early detection of associated conditions, and implications for family members given the autosomal dominant nature of some associated syndromes like MEN1. [PMC11431960, PMC11432259, PMC7451451]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: There is currently no standard treatment for lichen amyloidosis, and a wide range of therapeutic options are applied. Topical corticosteroids, such as clobetasol propionate ointment, are among the most prescribed and have shown effectiveness, sometimes with occlusion. Systemic acitretin has demonstrated excellent responses in severe and extensive cases, and is recommended for recalcitrant disease. Abrocitinib, an oral Janus kinase 1 inhibitor, significantly improved pruritus and lesions in a case of lichen amyloidosis co-existing with severe atopic dermatitis. Other treatments mentioned include nemolizumab, dexamethasone oral mini pulse therapy, and retinoic acid gel. Further randomized controlled trials and guidelines are needed to establish optimal management strategies. [PMC12328671, PMC11602498, PMC10743860, PMC10373807, PMC9789704]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked syndromic intellectual disability characterized by intellectual impairment of variable severity, progressive lower limb spasticity, and diffuse palmoplantar hyperkeratosis. Additional manifestations include pes cavus, extensor plantar responses, hand tremor, and mild dysmorphic facial features.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Sjögren-Larsson syndrome (SLS) is a rare neurometabolic syndrome caused by deficient fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase. Patients exhibit intellectual disability, spastic paraplegia, and ichthyosis. The accumulation of fatty alcohols and fatty aldehydes has been demonstrated in plasma and skin but never in brain. Brain magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy studies, however, have shown an abundant lipid peak in the white matter of patients with SLS, suggesting lipid accumulation in the brain as well. Using histopathology, mass spectrometry imaging, and lipidomics, we studied the morphology and the lipidome of a postmortem brain of a 65-year-old female patient with genetically confirmed SLS and compared the with a matched control brain. Histopathological analyses revealed structural white matter abnormalities with the presence of small lipid droplets, deficient myelin, and astrogliosis.... [PMC7689726]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Paraplegia-intellectual disability-hyperkeratosis syndrome, also known as Sjögren-Larsson syndrome (SLS), is a rare neurometabolic disorder caused by deficient fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase. Patients exhibit intellectual disability, spastic paraplegia, and ichthyosis. The condition involves the accumulation of fatty alcohols and fatty aldehydes in plasma and skin. Brain magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy show lipid accumulation in white matter, with histopathological analyses revealing structural white matter abnormalities, lipid droplets, deficient myelin, and astrogliosis. Severely disturbed lipid profiles, including the accumulation of fatty alcohols and ether lipids, are found in both white and gray matter, indicating it is not solely a leukoencephalopathy. [PMC7689726]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Sjögren-Larsson syndrome (SLS) is a neurometabolic disorder caused by deficient fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase. This enzyme deficiency leads to the accumulation of fatty alcohols and fatty aldehydes in various tissues, including the brain. In the central nervous system, this accumulation in a profound disruption of the brain lipidome, characterized by an imbalance between ether lipid and glycero(phospho)lipid metabolism. Histopathological findings include structural white matter abnormalities, lipid droplet accumulation, deficient myelin, and astrogliosis, affecting both white and gray matter. Astrocytes and microglia may also contribute to the impairment of myelin maintenance. [PMC7689726]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Sjögren-Larsson syndrome (SLS) is confirmed genetically. Biochemical analysis can demonstrate the accumulation of fatty alcohols and fatty aldehydes in plasma and skin. Brain magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy studies are also utilized, typically revealing an abundant lipid peak in the white matter. Postmortem examination further characterizes the disease, showing structural white matter abnormalities, lipid droplets, deficient myelin, and astrogliosis, alongside disturbed brain lipid profiles with accumulated fatty alcohols and ether lipids. [PMC7689726]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Sjögren-Larsson syndrome (SLS) is a rare neurometabolic syndrome caused by deficient fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase. Patients exhibit intellectual disability, spastic paraplegia, and ichthyosis. The accumulation of fatty alcohols and fatty aldehydes has been demonstrated in plasma and skin but never in brain. Brain magnetic resonance imaging and spectroscopy studies, however, have shown an abundant lipid peak in the white matter of patients with SLS, suggesting lipid accumulation in the brain as well. Using histopathology, mass spectrometry imaging, and lipidomics, we studied the morphology and the lipidome of a postmortem brain of a 65-year-old female patient with genetically confirmed SLS and compared the with a matched control brain. Histopathological analyses revealed structural white matter abnormalities with the presence of small lipid droplets, deficient myelin, and astrogliosis.... [PMC7689726]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare difference of sex development (DSD) characterized by the presence of female external genitalia, ambiguous genitalia or variable defects in virilization in a 46,XY individual with absent or partial responsiveness to age-appropriate levels of androgens. It comprises two clinical subgroups: complete AIS (CAIS) and partial AIS (PAIS).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): AIS; Androgen resistance syndrome; Goldberg-Maxwell syndrome; Morris syndrome; Testicular feminization syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) is consistently described as a rare disorder. It is a rare Mendelian disorder caused by mutations in the androgen receptor gene, and complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS) is also noted as a rare 46,XY disorder of sex development. The condition is considered rare, even in twins, and individual cases are often highlighted as uncommon. [PMC12188037, PMC11907799, PMC10889606, PMC10956715]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) is a rare 46,XY disorder of sex development characterized by varying degrees of undervirilization despite a normal male karyotype and normal to high testosterone levels, typically due to mutations in the androgen receptor gene or epigenetic repression. Complete AIS (CAIS) presents with a female phenotype, including female external genitalia, breast development, and primary amenorrhea. Internally, individuals lack a uterus and ovaries but possess cryptorchid gonads (testicles). These gonads are prone to developing various tumors, such as germ cell tumors, Sertoli cell hamartomas, adenomas, and Sertoli-Leydig cell tumors. Müllerian duct remnants, including rudimentary uteri and fallopian tubes, can also coexist, expanding the clinical spectrum. Patients may also experience infertility and psychological difficulties. [PMC12188037, PMC11907799, PMC12148651, PMC11603565, PMC11251026]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Complete androgen insensitivity syndrome is a rare 46,XY disorder of sex development caused by mutations in the androgen receptor gene, resulting in androgen resistance despite a normal male karyotype. Individuals with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome typically present with female external genitalia, primary amenorrhea, and a heightened risk of gonadal germ cell tumors. Herein, the case of a 30-year-old woman who was diagnosed with complete androgen insensitivity syndrome at 18 years of age during evaluation for primary amenorrhea. Chromosomal analysis revealed a 46,XY karyotype, and imaging confirmed the absence of a uterus and ovaries. Despite medical advice for prophylactic gonadectomy, the patient delayed surgery and later presented with a palpable abdominal mass. Genetic analysis identified a novel hemizygous germline missense mutation, c.1768G>T (p.G590W), in exon 2 of the... [PMC12188037, PMC11907799, PMC12148651, PMC11603565, PMC11251026]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS), particularly complete AIS (CAIS), presents diagnostic challenges and can be initially misdiagnosed as Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome. It is also differentiated from other 46, XY Disorders of Sex Development (DSD), such as pure 46, XY gonadal dysgenesis. A key distinction is that CAIS patients never menstruate, while individuals with pure gonadal dysgenesis may achieve regular menstrual cycles with estrogen replacement therapy. Both CAIS and pure 46, XY gonadal dysgenesis are forms of 46, XY DSD and carry an elevated risk of gonadal malignancy. [PMC11603565, PMC11191977, PMC11291305]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of complete androgen insensitivity syndrome (CAIS) can be initiated through such as amniocentesis. In one reported case, a discrepancy between the karyotype identified via amniocentesis and the phenotype observed at birth prompted the diagnosis shortly after birth. This early detection allowed for longitudinal evaluation of the gonads from birth through puberty. [PMC12148651]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of complete androgen insensitivity syndrome primarily involves prophylactic gonadectomy due to the elevated risk of gonadal malignancy, although the optimal timing remains controversial. While some cases emphasize early gonadectomy, others suggest it may be safely deferred until post-puberty with careful monitoring. Following gonadectomy, hormone replacement therapy, typically estrogen, is critical for promoting secondary sexual characteristics, preventing estrogen deficiency, and addressing osteoporosis. Multidisciplinary care, including psychological support and patient counseling, is essential for optimizing outcomes and ensuring patient-centered management. In cases where malignancy develops, tumor resection and chemotherapy may be required. [PMC12188037, PMC11907799, PMC12148651, PMC11603565, PMC11191977]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Refractory cytopenias with multilineage dysplasia (RCMD) is a frequent subtype of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) characterized by 1 or more cytopenias in the peripheral blood and dysplasia in 2 or more myeloid lineages.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Exact prevalence is unknown but RCMD accounts for about 30% of patients with MDS which has a prevalence estimated to be 1/25,000 to 1/33,000. The disease tends to occur in older adults with a male predominance.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most patients are asymptomatic at presentation, and the disorder is detected incidentally. Some patients may have fatigue (anemia), a tendency to bleed or bruise (thrombocytopenia), or susceptibility to infections (neutropenia). Laboratory findings show one or more cytopenias.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is not known but is thought to involve inherited susceptibility or hematopoietic stem cell damage.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The hematological parameters used to define RCMD are as follows: less than 1% blasts in peripheral blood or less than 5% in bone marrow, multilineage dysplasia sometimes with ring sideroblasts, and no Auer rods (abnormal, needle-shaped or round inclusions in the cytoplasm of myeloblasts and promyelocytes).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Median survival of 17 to 33 months has been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: In recent years, advances in genetics and the integration of clinical-grade next-generation sequencing (NGS) assays into patient care have facilitated broader recognition of hereditary hematopoietic malignancy (HHM) among clinicians, in addition to the identification and characterization of novel HHM syndromes. Studies on genetic risk distribution within affected families and unique considerations of HHM biology represent exciting areas of translational research. More recently, data are now emerging pertaining to unique aspects of clinical management of malignancies arising in the context of pathogenic germline mutations, with particular emphasis on chemotherapy responsiveness. In this article, we explore considerations surrounding allogeneic transplantation in the context of HHMs. We review pre- and post-transplant patient implications, including genetic testing donor selection and... [PMC10213438, PMC8104173, PMC185849]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pentalogy of Cantrell (POC) is a lethal multiple congenital anomalies syndrome, characterized by the presence of 5 major malformations: midline supraumbilical abdominal wall defect, lower sternal defect, diaphragmatic pericardial defect, anterior diaphragmatic defect and various intracardiac malformations.
