Ectopia cordis (EC) is often found in fetuses with POC.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Cantrell deformity; Cantrell syndrome; Thoraco-abdominal syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of POC is estimated to be 1/65,000-1/200,000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: POC is a congenital disorder characterized by the presence of 5 major malformations: midline supraumbilical abdominal wall defect (diastasis recti, epigastric and umbilical hernia), lower sternal defect (sternal cleft, absent xiphoid process, short sternum and defective formation of lower two third), diaphragmatic pericardial defect, anterior diaphragmatic defect and heart malformations (ventricular septal defect (72%), interauricular communication (35%), cardiac diverticulum (32%), congenital pulmonary valve stenosis (PS; 31%) (isolated PS or in combination with double outlet right ventricle in fetuses with EC and univentricular heart in fetuses without EC), tetralogy of Fallot (17%), dextrocardia (15%), and transposition of the great arteries (TGA; 6%)). Thoraco-abdominal wall defects may lead to omphalocele and EC, with the heart located outside the thoracic wall and sometimes covered by pigmented loose skin. The heart can be partially or completely repositioned into the thoracic cavity when the patient is in a supine position. Neonates usually present with severe respiratory distress and cyanosis. Additional features that may be observed include craniofacial and central nervous system (CNS) anomalies (cleft lip and/or palate, encephalocele, craniorachischisis and hydrocephalus), limb defects (club foot, absence of tibia/radius, hand and foot oligodactyly, phocomelia, and abdominal organ defects (gallbladder agenesis and polysplenia, as part of heterotaxia). POC may occur in association with Trisomy 13, 18, Down syndrome and Turner syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of POC is still unknown. It has been postulated that at around 14 to 18 days post conception, a failure of the lateral mesodermal folds to migrate to the midline may cause the sternal and abdominal wall defects and abnormal development of the septum transversum result in defects in the anterior diaphragm and pericardium.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of complete POC relies on the following classification: class 1, a definite diagnosis, when all 5 defects are present; class 2, a probable diagnosis with 4 defects being present, including intracardiac and ventral wall abnormalities; and class 3, an incomplete expression with various combinations of defects being present, including a sternal abnormality.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes limb body wall complex, omphalocele, thoracic EC and amniotic bands.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis can be made in first-trimester ultrasonography by detection of multiple thoraco-abdominal defects, including EC and CNS anomalies.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: POC usually occurs sporadically but rare cases of chromosomal anomalies, autosomal or X-linked transmission have also been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is surgical, consisting of palliative repair of the ventral hernia and diaphragmatic defect and palliative or corrective repair of the cardiovascular anomalies. Surgical repair to relocate the heart into the chest cavity is usually performed in the neonatal period or in infancy. For patients unable to tolerate a single-staged approach, an intraoperative ''heart restoring'' trial may be proposed. If heart position can be successfully restored without obvious hemodynamic changes, one-staged operation is advised; if hemodynamic changes are minor, a combined operation may be possible.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis of POC is poor and only few patients survive through early childhood. The main causes of death are tachyarrhythmias, bradycardia, low blood pressure, rupture of the diverticulum, and heart failure.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Recombinant 8 (rec(8)) syndrome, also known as San Luis Valley syndrome, is a complex chromosomal disorder that is due to a parental pericentric inversion of chromosome 8 and is characterized by major congenital heart anomalies, urogenital malformations, moderate to severe intellectual deficiency and mild craniofacial dysmorphism.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Duplication 8q/deletion 8p; Rec(8) syndrome; Rec8 syndrome; Recombinant chromosome 8 syndrome; San Luis Valley syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown but the syndrome is rare. Rec(8) syndrome occurs typically in people with Hispanic ancestry from the Southwestern United States and is thought to be due to a single founder who emigrated from Spain to Colorado or New Mexico in the 17th or 18th century.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Rec(8) syndrome is characterized by major congenital heart anomalies, comprising complex conotruncal abnormalities often accompanied by patent ductus arteriosus or persistent left superior vena cava (PLSVC) or nonconotruncal anomalies including pulmonic stenosis, ventricular septal defect (VSD), patent ductus arteriosus and PLSVC; urogenital malformations such as cryptorchidism and hypoplastic scrotum in males; moderate intellectual disability; and mild craniofacial dysmorphism including abnormal hair whorl, low posterior hairline, wide face, hypertelorism, infraorbital creases, anteverted nares, thin upper lip, downturned mouth, gingival hyperplasia, abnormal tooth development, micrognathia, mal-shaped and low-set ears. Other findings include developmental delay, spasticity, leading to orthopedic complications such as scoliosis, seizures and recurring otitis media or hearing loss. Individuals with rec(8) syndrome generally present solid social and nonverbal communication skills and an overall good nature despite their intellectual disability.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Rec(8) syndrome is a complex chromosomal disorder, rec(8)dup(8q)inv(8)(p23.1q22.1) due to a parental pericentric inversion of chromosome 8 [inv(8)(p23.1q22.1)] with presumed constant breaking points in this Hispanic population and variants in other populations.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical manifestations leading to chromosomal analysis by classical or molecular karyotyping.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other chromosomal anomalies involving chromosome 8, Bardet-Biedl syndrome, Williams syndrome and Noonan syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling and cytogenetic analysis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling is recommended and needs karyotyping of the parents in order to evaluate the risk of recurrence. Segregation analysis has ascertained a 6.2% risk for a carrier parent to have a child with rec(8) syndrome with the transmission rate being higher in carrier mothers (59%) than fathers (42%).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management involves cardiac surgery in case of cardiac malformations and a multidisciplinary approach including hearing screening, evaluation of reflux and constipation and full developmental assessment with periodic follow-up. Regular neurodevelopmental screening and participation in individually adapted therapy programs are recommended. Orthopedic surgery has been shown to give suboptimal results due to the intellectual deficit impeding rehabilitation.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable, depending on the severity of congenital heart disease. Historically, life expectancy past early childhood was very low, however with the increased quality and early treatment intervention the majority may live into adulthood. Exact life expectancy is unknown.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hair disorder characterized by the appearance of lustreless, curly, frizzy, and coarse hair generally during adolescence predominantly in the frontal, temporal, and vertex regions of the scalp. Eyelashes, as well as growth and pigmentation of the hair, may also be affected.

A rare neuroendocrine neoplasm (NEN) characterized by severe peptic disease (ulcers/esophageal disease) caused by hypergastrinemia secondary to a gastrin-secreting NEN (gastrinoma) resulting in increased gastric acid secretion.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence is estimated at 1-3 cases per million. The condition is slightly more common in females than males (sex ratio of 1.3:1).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Sporadic non-inherited ZES (75%) onset is usually in the fifth decade of life, but is 10 years earlier if part of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) (25%). Abdominal pain, typically in the upper abdomen due to peptic ulcer disease (PUD), and diarrhea are the most frequent manifestations. Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) is present in 44% of cases. Other signs include nausea, vomiting, malabsorption, and weight loss. Some patients present with ulcer complications (gastrointestinal bleeding, perforation and penetration).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: ZES is caused by a gastrin-secreting tumor (gastrinoma), usually located in the duodenum (50-85%), pancreas, abdominal lymph nodes or, in rare cases, ectopic locations (heart, ovary, liver, mesentery, etc.). MEN1 is caused by mutations in MEN1 (11q13) encoding menin, a protein which binds and regulates the activity of numerous transcription factors.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is first suspected on the basis of the clinical manifestations of severe, recurrent, or resistant PUD/GERD. Elevated fasting serum gastrin (FSG) levels are almost invariably present. FSG levels >10-fold higher than normal and gastric pH <2 confirm the diagnosis (40% of cases). If FSG levels are elevated <10-fold and gastric pH is <2, secretin stimulation (abnormal: increase >120 pg/ML) and basal acid (abnormal: >15 mEq/hr-basal) tests performed in a specialty center are recommended (60% of cases). Imaging (somatostatin receptor scintigraphy, CT/MRI scan, abdominal or endoscopic ultrasound) is required to localize/stage the gastrinoma. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy may be indicated to detect duodenal ulcerations and assess presence of prominent gastric folds (>90% of cases).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other causes of hypergastrinemia with increased acid output, and elevated FSG levels. The latter includes H. pylori infections, retained gastric antrum, gastric outlet obstruction, renal failure, antral G cell syndromes, idiopathic gastroesophageal reflux or peptic ulcer disease, and the former includes all physiological causes of hypergastrinemia (atrophic gastritis, pernicious anemia, H. pylori infections) or use of potent antisecretory drugs such as proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs)/vonoprazan.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal genetic testing may allow diagnosis of MEN1 but not gastrinomas.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Patients with MEN1 must be counseled about its autosomal dominant inheritance.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Gastric acid hypersecretion must be controlled short- and long-term. Oral H(+)-K(+)-ATPase inhibitors (PPIs) are the drugs of choice because of their long duration of action and potency (administered in 1-2 doses/day). Intravenous PPIs are effective when oral drugs cannot be taken. Histamine H2-receptor antagonists can also be effective but frequent high doses are needed by many patients. Potassium-competitive acid blockers such as vonorazan are potent, long-acting acid blockers can also be effective. Management also includes treatment of the tumor itself (60-90% are malignant). For localized disease in non-MEN1 patients, surgery is recommended if not medically contraindicated. For advanced metastatic disease, numerous antitumor therapies are used including chemotherapy, biotherapy (somatostatin/interferon analogues), embolization of hepatic metastases and aggressive surgery. A number of newer treatments including somatostatin receptor-mediated radiotherapy, novel chemotherapeutic agents and growth factor/tyrosine kinase/mTor inhibitors (sunitinib/everolimus), are also increasingly used. The treatment of gastrinomas in MEN1/ZES patients without distal metastases is controversial with most recommending a watch/wait approach if NET <1.5-2 cm on imaging is present.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: In the absence of liver metastases, the prognosis is favorable (10-year survival rate of 90-100%). Patients with liver metastases (65-75%) have a 10-year survival rate of 20-40%. Patients with MEN1 are rarely cured surgically due to the presence of multiple tumors and lymph node metastases, however, only 15% pursue an aggressive course and 10-year survival is 80-98%.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Sézary syndrome (SS) is an aggressive form of cutaneous T-cell lymphoma characterized by a triad of erythroderma, lymphadenopathy and circulating atypical lymphocytes (Sézary cells).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: SS has an annual incidence rate of 1/10,000,000 and represents 3% of all cutaneous lymphomas.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: SS develops most frequently in men, in most cases during their fifth decade of life and progresses rapidly. SS correspond to stages IVA2 and IVB of T-cell cutaneous lymphoma. Patients present with a scaling erythroderma and infiltration often manifesting with leonine facies and severe pruritus. Alopecia, ectropium, mild palmoplantar keratoderma and nail onychodystrophy may be present. Lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are observed. Patients often shiver and complain of chills and general fatigue.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: SS has been linked to a wide range of chromosomal anomalies, in particular rearrangements in the 6q23-27 region leading to alterations in the MYB proto-oncogene and the interleukin-22 receptor subunit alpha-2 gene (IL22RA2), but its etiology remains unclear.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Criteria that define SS are currently the following: an absolute Sézary cell count of 1,000 cells/mm3 or greater (B2 stage); an increase in CD3 or CD4 positive cells resulting in a CD4/CD8 ratio of 10 or greater; aberrant expression of pan T cell markers (i.e. deficient CD7 expression on T cells); increased relative or absolute lymphocyte counts with evidence of an identical T cell clone in the blood and skin by Southern blot or PCR technique. Skin biopsy may be not conclusive.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes adverse drug reactions, classical mycosis fungoides and other forms of primary cutaneous T cell lymphoma as well as other causes of erythroderma such as psoriasis, atopic dermatitis and pityriasis rubra pilaris.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Assessment includes chest X-ray, computed tomography scan, magnetic resonance imaging and PET scan and an initial lymph node biopsy. Bimonthly extracorporeal photopheresis treatment may be combined with low doses of methotrexate, bexarotene or interferon-alpha. In advanced or non-responsive cases, chemotherapy with liposomal doxorubicine, gemcitabine or alemtuzumab may be considered. In cases of relapse, treatment may include total skin electron beam therapy and allogeneic stem cell transplantion.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor, with median survival of patients being approximately 5 years, and is dependent upon initial presentation and evolution.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis (IJO) is a primary condition of bone demineralization that presents with pain in the back and extremities, walking difficulties, multiple fractures, and radiological evidence of osteoporosis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact prevalence is unknown but several hundreds of cases have been reported in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset usually occurs in the prepubertal period, between 8 and 12 years of age. The first sign of IJO is usually pain in the lower back, hips and feet. Knee and ankle pain, kyphosis, loss of height and a sunken chest may also be present. Low bone mineral density, vertebral collapse and metaphyseal compression fractures of the long bones are common.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of idiopathic juvenile osteoporosis remains unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation, skeletal X-rays and bone density tests (dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry, dual photon absorptiometry and quantitative computed tomography).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Osteogenesis imperfecta is the main differential diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is aimed at protecting the spine and other bones from fracture. Physical therapy and exercise (avoiding weight-bearing activities), and other supportive measures are mandatory. There is no established treatment strategy. Treatments with calcium and/or vitamin D, fluoride, calcitonin, and bisphosphonates (in severe, long-lasting cases) have been reported with unequivocal efficacy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The disease is self-limiting with spontaneous resolution after the onset of puberty. Rarely, in more severe cases, permanent disability (kyphoscoliosis and rib deformity) can develop.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Familial cold urticaria (FCAS) is the mildest form of cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS) and is characterized by recurrent episodes of urticaria-like skin rash triggered by exposure to cold associated with low-grade fever, general malaise, eye redness and arthralgia/myalgia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): FCAS; FCU; Familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact prevalence of FCAS is unknown. Most cases have been published in the USA, and this CAPS phenotype could be less frequent in Europe in comparison with MWS and CINCA.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: FCAS generally starts in childhood (<10 years, often at birth), but may occasionally start later, and is characterized by recurrent episodes of non-pruritic urticaria-like rash triggered by exposure to cold (5 minutes to 3 hours and not necessarily by touch). Lesions last about 12 hours (range 30 minutes to 72 hours) and are typically associated with a burning sensation. Low-grade, daylong episodes of fever, malaise, conjunctivitis, and abdominal discomfort are also observed. Polyarthralgias involving hands, knees, and ankles are very common and incapacitating. Other joints involved are feet, wrists, and elbows. Profuse sweating, drowsiness, headache, extreme thirst, and nausea are also noticed after cold exposure. Amyloidosis, arthritis are uncommon while deafness, lymphadenopathy, and serositis are absent
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FCAS is caused by gain-of-function point mutations in the NLRP3 gene (1q44), which encodes cryopyrin. Mutations in NLRP3 gene ultimately lead to the increased secretion of the proinflammatory cytokine interleukin (IL)-1 beta and dysregulated inflammation. Mutations in this gene may also cause two additional forms of CAPS which are Muckle-Wells syndrome (MWS) and CINCA syndrome, demonstrating that all three disorders are allelic. Some patients with a classical phenotype of FCAS, MWS or CINCA syndrome may not have mutations in NLRP3, suggesting involvement of additional genes. In addition, somatic NLRP3 mosaicism could explain 30-60% of patients with negative conventional genetic testing. Patients carrying identical amino acid substitution may present with distinctly different clinical subtypes, suggesting that additional genetic and/or environmental modifying factors are required to define the clinical phenotype.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant. Genetic counseling may be proposed and the recurrence risk is 50%.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of familial cold urticaria and related autoinflammatory syndromes primarily involves genetic testing. Whole exome sequencing or targeted gene sequencing can identify gain-of-function mutations or variants in genes such as NLRP3 (also known as CIAS1), NLRC4, NLRP12, and MEFV. Specific mutations like p.R262W in NLRP3, p.A441V in NLRP3, p.A439V in NLRP3, and various mutations in NLRC4 (e.g., c.A91C, c.1202T>C, c.390delG) have been reported. Additionally, laboratory findings often show elevated inflammatory markers, including leukocyte count, neutrophil count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive protein (CRP), serum amyloid A (SAA), and interleukin-1β (IL-1β). Histological examination of skin lesions may reveal neutrophilic dermatitis. The interpretation of genetic variants, particularly in NLRP12, should be cautiously combined with clinical and paraclinical data. [PMC11487858, PMC9918341, PMC8562517, PMC6911267, PMC6477140]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome (FCAS), a phenotype of cryopyrin-associated periodic syndromes (CAPS), often involves targeted therapy. Interleukin-1 (IL-1) inhibitors, such as anakinra, have demonstrated dramatic responses, inducing disease remission and improving symptoms like hearing loss in related conditions. Other IL-1 inhibitors like canakinumab and rilonacept are also used. Colchicine has been reported to reduce the frequency and severity of skin rash and leg edema in suspected FCAS. Supportive measures include preventing cold exposure, such as using forced-air warming systems during surgery. While effective, IL-1 inhibitors carry risks, including infections, injection site reactions, and other adverse events, especially in pediatric populations, necessitating careful consideration of benefits versus risks. In oligosymptomatic children, IL-1 blockade may be postponed. [PMC12288570, PMC11487858, PMC9552617, PMC6911267, PMC6477140]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal trisomy 22q is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from the partial duplication of the long arm of chromosome 22, with variable phenotype principally characterized by varying degrees of intellectual disabilty and developmental delay, pre- and postnatal growth deficiency, hypotonia, and craniofacial dysmorphism (incl. microcephaly, hypertelorism, narrow and upslanted palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, low-set dysplastic ears, broad and depressed nasal bridge, cleft lip an/or palate, long philtrum, retro/micrognathia). Congenital heart defects, as well as cerebral, skeletal, renal and genital anomalies, have also been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal trisomy 6p and 20q owing to the concurrent transposition of distal 6p and 20q to the 22q telomere: a genomic polymorphism? [PMC1735572]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS), caused by deletions at 22q13.3 and pathogenic variants in the SHANK3 gene, is a rare developmental disorder characterized by hypotonia, developmental delay (DD), intellectual disability (ID), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), dysmorphic features, absence of or delayed language, and other features. Conventional karyotyping, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), and whole exome sequencing (WES) have been used to detect genetic defects causing PMS. We summarized the genetic and clinical findings from prenatal to postnatal stages of detected cases of PMS and mapped potential candidate haploinsufficient genes for deletions of 22q13. summarize the laboratory findings, genetic defects, and genotype-phenotype correlations for Chinese patients with PMS. Seven prenatal cases and fourteen postnatal cases were diagnosed with PMS in our center. Thirteen cases had a... [PMC9470928]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive form of lipodystrophy characterized by the association of generalized lipoatrophy with acromegaloid features, muscle hypertrophy, insulin resistance, hypertriglyceridemia, and liver steatosis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): BSCL; Berardinelli-Seip syndrome; Berardinelli-Seip congenital lipodystrophy; CGL

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Presentation is typically in the first months of life with failure to thrive, hepatomegaly, generalized lipoatrophy, prominent musculature, umbilical prominence, acromegaloid features of extremities. Hypertriglyceridemia, insulin resistance, hyperglycemia and liver steatosis can be present in infancy, or diagnosed in late childhood, adolescence or adulthood. Accelerated growth in infancy, virilization of female patients and precocious puberty have been reported in some cases. High blood pressure, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and bone cysts are frequent complications. Mild intellectual disability can be present, mainly in CGL related to BSCL2. Muscular dystrophy and cardiac arrhythmia are reported in CGL related to CAVIN1.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Two main causative genes have been identified: AGPAT2 (9q34), encoding a key enzyme in triglyceride biosynthesis (1-acyl-glycerol-3-phosphate-O-acyltransferase-2), BSCL2 (11q13), encoding the reticulum endoplasmic seipin protein. A few cases of CGL are due to biallelic pathogenic variants in CAV1 (7q31.2) and CAVIN1 (17q21.2), encoding respectively caveolin-1 and cavin-1, which are major components of specialized plasma membrane microdomains called caveolae. Generalized lipodystrophy is described in rare patients with biallelic pathogenic variants in the genes PPARG (3p25.2) or LMNA (1q22), for which heterozygous mutations are associated with familial partial lipodystrophy.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of CGL is based on recognition of the clinical picture and associated metabolic disturbances including low serum leptin levels. The differential diagnosis of each monogenic form of the disease requires genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: CGL may occur as a feature in other diseases. Differential diagnoses include acquired generalized lipodystrophy (which occurs mainly in the context of auto-immune diseases), monogenic syndromes of insulin resistance, autoinflammatory diseases, partial forms of lipodystrophy and premature ageing syndromes.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis can be discussed in families with a known disease causing mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Couples in which each member carries at least one pathogenic variant should be informed that the risk of disease transmission to their offspring is 25%. A positive genetic test in an adult patient may lead to test the carriership of his/her partner.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Diet should be carefully managed, avoiding overfeeding in patients with CGL who are typically hyperphagic due to leptin deficiency. A low glycemic-index and low fat diet, supplemented with medium chain triglycerides in infants/children, is usually needed to manage insulin resistance, diabetes and hypertriglyceridemia. Exercise should be encouraged in the absence of cardiac complications. Insulin sensitizers (mainly metformin) and lipid-lowering drugs (statins, or fibrates in case of major hypertriglyceridemia) are helpful. Diabetes may require other non-specific treatments, along with insulin. The orphan drug metreleptin is authorized in Europe, as a therapeutic option in addition to diet, for the treatment of metabolic complications of generalized lipodystrophy associated with leptin deficiency, in adults and children above the age of 2 years. Regular metabolic, hepatic and cardiac monitoring is recommended. Ethinylestradiol should be avoided in women with CGL.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the presence of associated complications. Complications of diabetes, liver disease, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are significant causes of morbidity and early mortality.
DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Congenital generalized lipodystrophy (CGL) is a rare, autosomal recessive, hereditary disease. It is characterized by abnormal adipose tissue deposition and is frequently associated with metabolic changes. CGL is considered one of the severe insulin resistance syndromes, which are a heterogeneous group of rare disorders. Its reported prevalence is less than 1 in 10 million. [PMC12192740, PMC11021684, PMC10369054, PMC10126596, PMC8961907]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A sclerosing disorder of the skeleton characterized by increased bone density that classically displays the radiographic sign of ''sandwich vertebrae'' (dense bands of sclerosis parallel to the vertebral endplates).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is estimated to be 1/20,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset of the disease is typically in late childhood or adolescence. The main manifestations are confined to the skeleton, including fractures, scoliosis, hip osteoarthritis and osteomyelitis, particularly affecting the mandible in association with dental abscess or caries. Cranial nerve compression is a rare but important complication, with hearing and visual loss affecting around 5% of individuals. Moderate bone marrow failure is described occasionally.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by heterozygous mutations in the chloride channel 7 (ClCN7) gene (16p13).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical findings and largely depends on the radiographic appearance of the skeleton. Genetic testing is available and can be used to confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other subtypes of osteopetrosis, fluorosis, beryllium, lead and bismuth poisoning, myelofibrosis, Paget's disease (sclerosing form) and malignancies (lymphoma, osteoblastic cancer metastases).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible if the mutation causing the condition in the family is known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Albers-Schönberg osteopetrosis is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner. Genetic counseling should be offered to families. Each child of an affected individual has 50% risk of being affected. The parents of the proband should be carefully evaluated for signs of osteopetrosis, including radiographic studies of the skeleton.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: At present, there is no effective medical treatment for osteopetrosis. Management is supportive and aims at providing multidisciplinary surveillance and symptomatic treatment.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Clinical manifestations may worsen over time but life expectancy is usually normal.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A tropical disease mainly found in latin America and transmitted by triatomine insects (mostly Triatoma infestans and Rhodnius prolixus and Panstrongylus megistus) harboring the hemoflagellate protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi. The disease is characterized by an acute phase which is either asymptomatic or manifest with fever, inflammation at the inoculation site (inoculation chancre or chagoma), unilateral palpebral edema called the Romaña sign (when the triatomine bite occurs near the eye), enlarged lymph nodes, and splenomegaly. The chronic phase is lifelong and development of chagasic cardiomyopathy (30%; complex arrhythmias, heart failure, and thromboembolic events), digestive (10%; megaoesophagus and megacolon), neurological (10%; stroke, peripheral neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction), or mixed alterations (10%) may be observed. These can all lead to high morbidity and mortality rates.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: American trypanosomiasis, or Chagas disease, is characterized by acute and chronic phases, with reactivations possible, particularly in immunosuppressed individuals such as HIV patients or heart transplant recipients. The acute phase can present with symptoms including fever, headache, asthenia, adynamia, dysuria, and lymphadenopathy, with an average incubation period of about 14 days in orally transmitted cases. Neurological manifestations, such as focal neurological deficits and single lesions predominantly involving white matter in the central nervous system, are a severe complication of reactivation, especially post-transplant. In blood donors, bimodal distributions of anti-Trypanosoma cruzi antibody levels have been observed, with lower levels potentially associated with spontaneous parasite clearance. [PMC12017318, PMC12124490, PMC11609539, PMC11300699, PMC11441692]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Patients with American trypanosomiasis may present with non-specific symptoms such as fever, headache, asthenia, adynamia, and dysuria. In such cases, other conditions like symptomatic urinary tract infection and malaria should be considered in the differential diagnosis, as these can present similarly. For patients with neurological manifestations, especially those with concomitant immunosuppression such as HIV, a comprehensive diagnostic approach is necessary to confirm Trypanosoma cruzi. [PMC11609539, PMC11300699]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Chagas disease, caused by Trypanosoma cruzi , is a parasitic zoonosis with significant health impacts, particularly in Latin America. While traditionally associated with vector-borne transmission, increased migration has expanded its reach into urban and non-endemic regions. Congenital transmission has become a critical route of infection, involving intricate maternal-fetal immune interactions that challenge diagnosis and treatment. synthesizes findings from three RNA-seq studies that explore the molecular underpinnings of congenital Chagas disease, emphasizing differentially expressed genes (DEGs) implicated in host-pathogen interactions. The DAVID tool analysis highlighted the overexpression of genes associated with the innate immune response, including pro-inflammatory cytokines that drive chemotaxis and neutrophil activation. Additionally, calcium-dependent pathways critical for... [PMC11858232]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Current management of American trypanosomiasis primarily involves antiparasitic agents such as benznidazole and nifurtimox. Benznidazole is used for acute cases and for preemptive therapy to prevent T. cruzi reactivation in immunocompromised patients, with parasitemia monitoring by qPCR recommended for early intervention. Nifurtimox has also been used, including in HIV co-infected patients. However, current therapies are limited by reduced efficacy, high toxicity, emerging resistance, and a lack of diverse options. Immunocompromised individuals are at high risk for lethal T. cruzi reactivation, necessitating tailored management and close monitoring. Rapid surveillance and early treatment are crucial, especially in acute outbreaks. There is an urgent need for new therapeutic strategies due to these challenges. [PMC12129137, PMC12029465, PMC11800084, PMC11609539, PMC11300699]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare syndromic intestinal malformation characterized by the association of marfanoid features (including marfanoid habitus, severe myopia, retinal detachment, and mitral valve prolapse) with visceral diverticula (inguinal and/or femoral hernia and diverticula of the large and small bowel or urinary bladder). Some patients also had diaphragmatic eventration. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1996.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Marfanoid syndrome, De Silva type, appears to be an extremely rare condition. Visceral diverticula, a key feature, have been described in only a few adults with marfanoid features and recessive inheritance. A report details two siblings from a consanguineous marriage presenting with marfanoid features, visceral diverticula, and diaphragmatic eventration, suggesting a pattern of recessive inheritance. The limited number of reported cases indicates its rarity. [PMC1511712]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Individuals with Marfanoid syndrome, De Silva type, exhibit marfanoid features, which can overlap with other connective tissue disorders. Distinctive clinical manifestations include visceral diverticula and diaphragmatic eventration. These features have been reported in siblings from consanguineous marriages, suggesting a recessive inheritance pattern. [PMC1511712]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The marfanoid phenotype, particularly when presenting with visceral diverticula, has been associated with recessive inheritance. This is supported by observations of affected siblings from consanguineous marriages who exhibit marfanoid features, visceral diverticula, and diaphragmatic eventration. The condition is considered a connective tissue disorder with diverse manifestations. [PMC1511712]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Marfan's syndrome has diverse manifestations that overlap with those seen in other connective tissue disorders. Visceral diverticula have been described only once in four adults with marfanoid features of recessive inheritance. Two siblings of a consanguineous marriage with marfanoid features, visceral diverticula, and diaphragmatic eventration are reported. [PMC1511712]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Marfan's syndrome has diverse manifestations that overlap with those seen in other connective tissue disorders. Individuals with marfanoid features, especially those with recessive inheritance, visceral diverticula, and diaphragmatic eventration, may present similarly to other connective tissue disorders. Therefore, the differential diagnosis should include other conditions that share these marfanoid characteristics. [PMC1511712]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The marfanoid phenotype, which includes visceral diverticula and diaphragmatic eventration, has been described with a recessive inheritance pattern. This pattern was observed in siblings from a consanguineous marriage, indicating a potential for recurrence in families with affected individuals, especially in the context of consanguinity. [PMC1511712]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare subtype of autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia type I characterized by involuntary movements, ataxia, epilepsy, mental disorders, cognitive decline and prominent anticipation.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Worldwide prevalence is unknown. However, the disease is found most commonly in Japan where the prevalence is estimated to be 1/208,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Age of onset ranges from 1 to 60 years (mean age = 28.8 years). Patients with earlier onset (below 20 years of age) tend to show myoclonus epilepsy and intellectual deficit. Patients with late onset (over 40 years of age) tend to present with cerebellar ataxia, choreoathetosis and dementia. Clinical features and the age of onset are significantly correlated with the size of CAG repeats. Head magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows atrophy of cerebellum, brainstem, cerebrum and high signal has been shown in periventricular white matter.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Unstable expansion of CAG repeats in the ATN1 gene (12p13.31) has been demonstrated.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor. DRPLA progresses rather rapidly. The mean disease duration is about 13 years. Recurrent seizures and dysphagia with frequent fluid and food aspiration lead to bronchopneumonia and subsequent death. However, some patients can reach 60 years of age or more.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A group of myeloid hemopathies characterized by blood cytopenias, marrow dysplasia and a high risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The annual incidence is 1/17,000-25,000 people, with a median age at diagnosis of 70 years. Only 5-10% of patients are diagnosed below the age of 50.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical symptoms are consequences of blood cytopenias, mainly anemia (e.g. fatigue, dyspnea, possible angina, etc.), and less often of thrombocytopenia (spontaneous bleeding) or neutropenia (bacterial or less often fungal infections).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is unknown in 80% of the cases. In the remaining 20% it has either acquired causes (previous treatment with chemo or radiotherapy, occupational exposure to benzene derivatives or ionizing radiation) or inherited causes, such as inherited gene point mutations mainly in DDX41, GATA2, RUNX, and telomerase genes, or DNA instability (Fanconi anemia patients are prone to develop MDS).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Blood count reveals aregenerative anemia, which is often macrocytic, with or without neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. Cytological/ Histological analysis of bone marrow aspirate or biopsy generally reveals hypercellularity, with dysplasia in one to three myeloid lineages, without (<5%) or with (5-20%) excess of blasts. Cytogenetics of bone marrow show acquired clonal abnormality in 50 % of the cases, especially chromosome loss (-7, del 5q, del 20q) or gain (+8). Marrow cell mutations analysis by NGS method reveals at least one acquired mutation in myeloid genes panel in 90% of the cases especially in spliceosome genes (SF3B1,SRSF2), epigenetic genes (TET2, DNMT3a, ASXL1), RUNX1, or TP53.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other bone marrow failures such as aplastic anemia, AML, or peripheral and clonal hematopoiesis in the elderly.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management and treatment depends on the prognostic score of patients in the revised International Prognostic Scoring System for Myelodysplastic Syndromes (IPSS-R), recently improved by the addition of acquired mutations (IPSS-M). Higher risk MDS are treated with allogeneic bone marrow transplantation when possible, otherwise with hypomethylating agents (azacytidine, decitabine), and less often chemotherapy. Lower risk MDS patients receive treatment for anemia with erythropoietin or derivatives, or other drugs in specific cases (lenalidomide in case of 5q deletion; Luspatercept in MDS with ringed sideroblasts).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: MDS may progress into AML in ~30% of patients. The prognosis differs depending on a set of criteria scored by the IPSS-R and IPSS-M, including the number and importance of cytopenias, marrow blast percentage, and marrow cytogenetic abnormalities. This score separates schematically patients into lower risk (mainly characterized by anemia and less often thrombocytopenia) and higher risk (with generally severe cytopenias, including also neutropenia) of progression to AML, into five (IPSS-R) or six (IPSS-M) categories going from very low risk (2.8% risk of transformation into AML by 4 years) to very high risk (42.8% risk of transformation into AML by 4 years).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: H3K4 methylation, primarily mediated by MLL family proteins, plays a pivotal role in the epigenetic regulation of gene transcription. Among the MLL family, KMT2A is known for its critical role in hematopoiesis. MLL family proteins feature C-terminal SET catalytic domains, requiring the formation of MLL complexes with proteins like DPY30 to maximize their enzymatic activity. Deletion of DPY30 in a significant reduction in H3K4me1, H3K4me2, and H3K4me3 levels in bone marrow (BM) cells, underscoring the essential role of DPY30 in facilitating optimal catalytic activity within MLL family complexes. Here, a unique case of myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS) associated with a novel t(2;19)(p23;q13.3) translocation. A 22-year-old pregnant woman initially sought consultation due to thrombocytopenia, which temporarily improved following a miscarriage. However, she later presented with progressive... [PMC12079049]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Congenital Tufting Enteropathy is a rare congenital enteropathy presenting with early-onset severe and intractable diarrhea that leads to irreversible intestinal failure.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Intestinal epithelial dysplasia; IED; Non-syndromic congenital tufting enteropathy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: No epidemiological data is available, however, the prevalence can be estimated at around 1/200,000 births in Europe. The prevalence is higher in areas with high degrees of consanguinity, but cases have been reported worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most affected patients develop digestive intolerance with vomiting and watery diarrhea within the first few months of life. Diarrhea is severe, chronic and persistent despite bowel rest, resulting in electrolyte imbalance and dehydration. Moreover, an intestinal insufficiency leads to malabsorption, malnutrition, and growth impairment. Although most children present with isolated diarrhea, a small number of congenital tufting enteropathy (CTE) patients present with a syndromic form where diarrhea is associated with non-specific punctuated keratitis, and various malformations such as choanal atresia, esophageal atresia, imperforate anus, dysmorphic features, skeletal dysplasia, and (in one case) Dubowitz syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CTE is related to abnormal enterocyte development and differentiation. Mutations in the EPCAM gene (2p21) are seen in 73% of CTE patients and are associated with the isolated intestinal disease. Mutations in the SPINT2 gene (19q13.2) are seen in 21% of CTE cases which are clinically characterized by the syndromic form of the disease. Rarely, CTE patients may present with isolated diarrhea but have no mutations in either EPCAM or SPINT2.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the combination of clinical and histological criteria. A congenital chronic diarrhea in the absence of an infectious or an inflammatory process, in association with various degrees of small and large bowel villous atrophy and specific histological abnormalities involving the focal crowding of surface enterocytes resembling ''tufts'', and branching crypts, allow for the diagnosis of CTE. When not all criteria are obvious one can be helped by the association of the non-syndromic form of the disease with negative EpCAM immunostaining on patient's duodenal biopsies; or conversely in case of the syndromic form of the disease with a normal EpCAM immunostaining. To date, SPINT2 immunostaining on duodenal biopsies seems useless for the diagnosis. Molecular genetic testing, identifying a mutation in the EPCAM gene or SPINT2 can confirm diagnosis, however, some CTE patients do not have any identified genetic mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis primarily includes other protracted congenital diarrhea disorders such as microvillus inclusion disease, congenital chloride diarrhea, congenital sodium diarrhea, and syndromic diarrhea, as well as glucose-galactose malabsorption.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is available but can only be offered to families where a first case has already been described. The rarity of CTE and the absence of prenatal signs do not make it an appropriate candidate for either antenatal or postnatal mass screening.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: CTE is transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner with high prevalence of consanguinity and affected siblings in families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: To date there is no known curative treatment for CTE. Oral or enteral feedings worsen the diarrhea, however they should be maintained at the minimum tolerated level. CTE patients require daily, long-term parenteral support in order to maintain an adequate nutritional status. Life threatening complications related to intestinal failure and long-term parenteral nutrition may become an indication for intestinal transplantation, thus timing of referral to an expert center is crucial before the onset of severe complications.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Currently, children with CTE reach adulthood if long-term parenteral nutrition is conducted appropriately in an experienced center, otherwise the long-term prognosis may be reserved due to the complications of this delicate palliative treatment.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal dominant syndromic lymphedema characterized by lower-limb lymphedema and varying degrees of abnormal growth of eyelashes from the orifices of the Meibomian glands (distichiasis), with occasional associated manifestations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Lymphedema-distichiasis syndrome is characterized by primary lower limb lymphedema (with or without genital edema in males) usually starting in childhood or puberty (but in some cases later or, occasionally, at birth) and associated with distichiasis (extra eyelashes growing from the Meibomian gland orifices in the inner eyelid). Ptosis of the eyelid(s) is frequent. Other associated manifestations can include: heart abnormalities, cleft palate (with or without Pierre Robin sequence), renal malformations, varicose veins and extradural cysts. Distichiasis may lead to infection (styes), congenital ectropion, photophobia corneal abrasion or ulceration.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The causative gene is FOXC2 (previously referred to as MFH1, located at 16q24.3), coding for transcription factor FOXC2.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected on clinical presentation with the presence of 'extra' eyelashes arising from the inner eyelid, ptosis and lower limb lymphedema; although the latter may not present until later in childhood or adolescence. The condition can usually be confirmed by genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other conditions presenting with late onset (i.e. not congenital) lymphedema of the lower limbs. This includes Meige disease, Noonan syndrome, Emberger syndrome (part of the GATA2 deficiency spectrum) and CELSR-related lymphedema.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible where the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in a family member. The nuchal translucency, visible by sonograph, is often slightly increased (3mm to 4.5mm). The fetus may develop fetal hydrops in the second trimester. There may be congenital heart disease and or congenital renal malformations.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is autosomal dominant. Although the condition is usually inherited from an affected parent, some cases occur sporadically. Genetic counseling should be offered to affected individuals informing them that there is a 50% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The standard treatment for the lower limb (and genital) lymphedema are made-to-measure compression garments with the option of intensive bandaging for moderate to severe swelling. Skin care is necessary to prevent infections. Every newly diagnosed patient should have a renal ultrasound and echocardiogram to exclude congenital malformations. They should also be examined for a cleft of the hard or soft palate. The distichiasis is often problematic, and they may require to be plucked or even electrolysis. If severe, they may require lamellar eyelid division and cryotherapy to the posterior lamella.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The severity may vary even within families. A normal life span is expected but there is a high mortality with the rare complication of fetal hydrops. Approximately 7% will have congenital heart disease but it is not usually severe. There is a high morbidity associated with recurrent cellulitis of the edematous limbs.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, endocrine disease characterized by autoimmune Addison disease associated with autoimmune thyroid disease or type I diabetes mellitus, or both, and without chronic candidiasis. Additional endocrine (hypogonadism, hypoparathyroidism) and non-endocrine diseases (vitiligo, autoimmune hepatitis, autoimmune gastritis, pernicious anemia, and myasthenia gravies) may be present.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): APS type 2; APS2; Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2; Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2; Autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes-Addison disease syndrome; Schmidt syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy type 2 (APS-2) is a rare autoimmune disorder, though it is considered the most common among the autoimmune polyendocrine syndromes. It typically manifests in early adulthood, but pediatric cases are extremely rare, with the youngest reported patient being 3 years old. Presentations involving the full triad of primary adrenal insufficiency, autoimmune thyroid disease, and type 1 diabetes mellitus are rare, and even rarer when complicated by adrenal crisis. The comorbidity of APS-2 with stiff person syndrome is exceptionally rare and often underdiagnosed. The condition's rarity, especially in childhood, and the frequency of unrevealed or incomplete forms suggest potential underrecognition. [PMC12098416, PMC12046904, PMC11746041, PMC12274025, PMC11067522]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Whole genome sequencing in one patient with autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type II (APS II) found no genetic variants associated with component diseases, though human leukocyte antigen typing revealed DR3/DR4 and DQ8/DQ2 heterozygosity associated with APS II. Another case also showed susceptible HLA alleles. A patient with comorbid MELAS syndrome and APS II had a heteroplasmic point mutation in the MT-ND4 gene, but the association of this specific MELAS variant with APS II had not been previously described. The provided abstracts do not offer further information regarding genetic counseling for APS II. [PMC9130185, PMC7140544, PMC6437310]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy type 2 primarily involves hormone replacement therapy for affected endocrine glands. This includes glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids for primary adrenal insufficiency, levothyroxine for hypothyroidism, and insulin for type 1 diabetes. Emergency treatment for adrenal crisis involves high-dose intravenous glucocorticoids and sodium supplementation. Other treatments mentioned include carbimazole and propranolol for Graves' thyrotoxicosis, hydroxocobalamin for pernicious anemia, and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) for anti-GAD65 antibody-associated stiff person syndrome. Immunosuppressants and thymectomy may be used for thymoma-associated myasthenia gravis. Regular monitoring, dosage titration, and careful adrenal function screening before initiating thyroid therapy are crucial to prevent complications like adrenal crisis and ensure a good prognosis. Early diagnosis and prompt treatment are emphasized to reduce morbidity and mortality. [PMC12098416, PMC11746041, PMC12274025, PMC11067522, PMC10387197]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Radiation myelitis is a rare neurological disease characterized by the development of paresthesias, as well as, in severe cases, progressive paresis and paralysis following irradiation of tumors in which the spinal cord is included within the radiation field. Symptoms may develop months or years after radiation therapy was administered.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Reported cases of radiation myelitis include a 68-year-old man and a 71-year-old Caucasian female. These instances indicate that the condition can manifest in older adults, though the provided abstracts do not offer a broader age range or typical age of onset for the general population. [PMC6868866, PMC4313465]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Radiation myelitis is a rare but devastating complication following therapeutic irradiation when the spinal cord is included within the radiation field. The calculated probability of this complication after radiotherapy alone is statistically measurable at 0.02%. Symptoms are usually delayed, most often appearing about 6 to 24 months following irradiation. Concomitant use of certain drugs, such as gefitinib, may also play a role in its development. [PMC4634631, PMC4313465]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Radiation myelitis is a rare but devastating neurological complication that typically follows therapeutic irradiation when the spinal cord is included within the radiation field. Symptoms are usually delayed, appearing 6 to 24 months post-irradiation, and can include motor deficits (e.g., plegia, paralysis), sphincter dysfunction (urinary and anal incontinence), and diminished bilateral deep and superficial sensitivity. These neurological symptoms can be progressive. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) often reveals spinal abnormalities or signal alterations suggestive of myelitis, usually matching the irradiated area, though MRI findings may not always correlate with clinical progression. Concomitant treatments like immunotherapy or targeted therapy may contribute to its development, potentially through an enhanced inflammatory reaction or radiation recall phenomenon. [PMC6868866, PMC4634631, PMC4313465]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Radiation myelitis is a rare but devastating complication following therapeutic irradiation to neoplasms when the spinal cord is included within the radiation field. Symptoms are typically delayed, often appearing 6 to 24 months after irradiation, with the confinement within the radiation field and latency of appearance being characteristic. While primarily caused by radiotherapy, other treatments can contribute to its development. Immunotherapy, such as pembrolizumab, may contribute by enhancing an inflammatory reaction on a focal post-radiation chronic inflammatory state, even with relatively low radiation doses. Targeted therapies like gefitinib can also play a role, and radiation recall myelitis has been described with chemotherapy and targeted therapy. The probability of this complication after radiotherapy alone is statistically measurable at a low level of 0.02%. [PMC6868866, PMC4634631, PMC4313465]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of radiation myelitis is primarily based on clinical presentation, patient history, and imaging findings. Symptoms such as motor deficits, sphincter dysfunction, or paralysis typically emerge after a latent period, commonly 6 to 24 months following irradiation, with abnormalities confined to the radiation field. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a key diagnostic tool, revealing characteristic changes, spinal abnormalities, or signal alterations in the spinal cord. MRI also helps exclude other causes like bony or intraspinal tumor progression. Differential diagnoses, such as paraneoplastic myelopathy, can be refuted by tests like negative autologous antibody assays. [PMC6868866, PMC4634631, PMC4313465]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: When diagnosing radiation myelitis, it is crucial to exclude other causes of myelopathy. Tumor progression or intraspinal tumor recurrence should be considered, though MRI may show spinal cord signal alteration without bony or intraspinal tumor growth. Paraneoplastic myelopathy can be ruled out by negative autoantibody tests. Myelitis can also be an adverse effect of immunotherapy, chemotherapy, or targeted therapy, sometimes presenting as a radiation recall phenomenon. The combined effects of radiotherapy with immunotherapy or targeted therapy may also contribute to an enhanced inflammatory reaction, making the distinction challenging. [PMC6868866, PMC4313465]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: No treatment has proved universally satisfactory for radiation myelitis. Steroid treatment has shown varied efficacy, leading to rapid and complete recovery in one case, particularly when combined with discontinuation of concomitant immunotherapy. However, another case reported no response to steroids. While mesenchymal stem cell transplantation is a promising strategy for central nervous system disorders, it has not been established as a therapeutic option for radiation myelitis. [PMC6868866, PMC4634631, PMC4313465]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Radiation myelitis is a devastating complication for which no treatment has proved satisfactory. Neurological symptoms can be progressive, leading to severe deficits such as complete plegia, sensory loss, and incontinence, with some cases showing no response to steroids. While MRI findings may sometimes ameliorate, clinical symptoms can remain stable or worsen. However, in a specific case of myelitis associated with both radiotherapy and immunotherapy, rapid and complete recovery was observed after immunotherapy discontinuation and steroid treatment, although other similar cases did not achieve complete recovery. [PMC6868866, PMC4634631, PMC4313465]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:97349

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Postencephalitic parkinsonism can manifest as a rapidly progressive atypical parkinsonism or Parkinson-like syndrome following various viral encephalitic illnesses, including those caused by SARS-CoV-2, dengue, or Epstein-Barr virus. Patients typically present with new-onset parkinsonism without prior history of symptoms. Evidence of encephalitis may be found through cerebrospinal fluid analysis and electroencephalogram. Neuroimaging, such as FDG-PET/CT, can reveal distinctive metabolic alterations, including cortical hypo-metabolism and hyper-metabolism in the brainstem, mesial temporal lobes, and basal ganglia. While some patients show marked improvement with levodopa, they may develop early onset "on-off" phenomena. An immune-mediated etiology has been suggested in some cases, though immunotherapy may not always be effective. The diagnosis, though rarely considered today, has been observed in recent patients. [PMC8059684, PMC5708097, PMC1763051, PMC491565, PMC491086]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Postencephalitic parkinsonism can arise following various encephalitic illnesses. Recent observations suggest that SARS-CoV-2 infection may trigger an encephalitis with prominent parkinsonism, with a possible immune-mediated etiology. Dengue viral infection has also been linked to post encephalitic parkinsonism, evidenced by positive IgM antibodies against dengue virus in cerebrospinal fluid. Epstein-Barr virus encephalitis can also present with a Parkinson-like syndrome. Historically, the diagnosis of encephalitis lethargica is also associated with this condition. [PMC8059684, PMC5708097, PMC1763051, PMC491565, PMC491086]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of post-encephalitic parkinsonism relies on clinical suspicion, particularly in cases of atypical parkinsonism following an encephalitic event. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis is crucial, often revealing evidence of encephalitis, specific viral antibodies (e.g., dengue IgM), and oligoclonal protein bands. These oligoclonal bands may be useful for diagnostic purposes, particularly in differentiating from idiopathic Parkinson's disease. Electroencephalogram (EEG) can also show evidence of encephalitis. Neuroimaging, such as FDG-PET/CT, may reveal distinctive brain metabolic alterations, including cortical hypo-metabolism and hyper-metabolism in the brainstem, mesial temporal lobes, and basal ganglia, which are reminiscent of the condition. MRI can further evaluate structural correlates. [PMC8059684, PMC5708097, PMC491086, PMC1082966]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for postencephalitic parkinsonism includes idiopathic Parkinson's disease, which typically lacks oligoclonal protein bands in the cerebrospinal fluid. There is also a possible clinical overlap with progressive supranuclear palsy. More recently, SARS-CoV-2-related encephalitis with prominent parkinsonism has been described, presenting with rapidly progressive atypical parkinsonism and distinctive brain metabolic alterations reminiscent of those observed in post-encephalitic parkinsonism. [PMC8059684, PMC486383, PMC1082966]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management approaches for postencephalitic parkinsonism include pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions. Levodopa (carbidopa/levodopa) has demonstrated marked or striking improvement in patients, including children, although some may experience early onset of "on-off" fluctuations in response. A novel, minimally invasive approach using bright light treatment has also shown promise in restoring sleep and improving depression, anxiety, and cognitive changes in patients with post-encephalitic symptoms. Conversely, immunotherapy did not yield favorable responses in cases of SARS-CoV-2-related encephalitis with prominent parkinsonism. [PMC11520186, PMC8059684, PMC5708097, PMC491565]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Patients with post-encephalitic parkinsonism can experience initial marked improvement with levodopa therapy. However, some individuals, including children, may rapidly develop predictable and unpredictable 'on-off' fluctuations in their response to levodopa within weeks of treatment initiation. In certain contexts, such as SARS-CoV-2-related parkinsonism, patients might not respond favorably to immunotherapy. For related post-encephalitic symptoms like insomnia, depression, anxiety, and cognitive changes, bright light treatment has demonstrated recovery maintained for weeks to months. [PMC11520186, PMC8059684, PMC5708097, PMC8094307, PMC491565]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Peters plus syndrome is an autosomal recessively inherited syndromic developmental defect of the eye characterized by a variable phenotype including Peters anomaly and other anterior chamber eye anomalies, short limbs, limb abnormalities (i.e. rhizomelia and brachydactyly), characteristic facial features (upper lip with cupid bow, short palpebral fissures), cleft lip/palate, and mild to severe developmental delay/intellectual disability. Other associated abnormalities reported in some patients include congenital heart defects (i.e. hypoplastic left heart, absence of right pulmonary vein, bicuspid pulmonary valve), genitourinary anomalies (hydronephrosis, renal hypoplasia, renal and ureteral duplication, multicystic dysplastic kidneys, glomerulocystic kidneys) and congenital hypothyroidism.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Krause-Kivlin syndrome; Krause-van Schooneveld-Kivlin syndrome; Peters anomaly with short limb dwarfism

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Peters plus syndrome is described as a rare to very rare congenital disorder. It is most commonly inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, often associated with homozygous B3GLCT mutations. Consanguinity has been noted, which is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. A common mutation, c.660 + 1G > A, has been reported to account for 75% of mutant alleles in some affected populations. [PMC7092513, PMC6928627, PMC6334245, PMC2755183, PMC1016833]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Peters plus syndrome (PPS) is a rare congenital disorder characterized by a combination of ocular Peters anomaly and systemic abnormalities. Ocular findings predominantly include anterior segment defects such as corneal opacity and iridocorneal adhesions, but can also involve microphthalmia, hyperechogenic lenses, and atypical bilateral chorioretinal atrophy. Systemic features often include short stature, hand anomalies like brachydactyly, distinctive craniofacial defects (e.g., hypotelorism, retrognathia), and skeletal defects. Other reported anomalies include hydrocephalus, mild ventriculomegaly, and absence of the cavum septum pellucidum. PPS is most commonly inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, with mutations in the B3GLCT gene (also referred to as B3GALTL) being a primary cause, leading to a glycosylation disorder. Peters plus-like phenotypes without B3GLCT mutations have been observed, and other genetic variants can be associated with Peters anomaly spectrum disorders. [PMC12250460, PMC7092513, PMC6928627, PMC6334245, PMC2755183]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Peters anomaly (PA) is a rare congenital disorder within the anterior segment dysgenesis (ASD) spectrum, characterized by corneal opacity, iridocorneal adhesions, and potential systemic involvement. The genetic basis of PA and related syndromes are complex and incompletely understood. investigates novel genetic variants and their clinical impact in two unrelated individuals diagnosed with PA spectrum disorder. Whole-exome sequencing (WES), long-range PCR, and breakpoint analysis were applied to identify pathogenic variants. In the first patient, a heterozygous ~1.6 Mb deletion was detected, spanning the genes PEX2 and ZFHX4 (GRCh37 chr8:g.76760782_78342600del). The second patient carried a heterozygous FOXC1 variant (NM_001453.3:c.310A>G), classified as likely pathogenic. Both variants were confirmed by Sanger sequencing and considered de novo, as they were not present in the biological... [PMC12250460, PMC10798386, PMC7092513, PMC6928627, PMC6334245]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for Peters plus syndrome primarily involve genetic analysis. Next-generation sequencing, including whole-exome and trio sequencing, is utilized to identify pathogenic variants in genes such as B3GLCT (also referred to as B3GALTL), PEX2, ZFHX4, and FOXC1. Comprehensive genomic analysis, including long-range PCR, breakpoint analysis, and microarray, can detect specific deletions like a 781-kb deletion of 13q12.3 or a ~1.6 Mb deletion spanning PEX2 and ZFHX4. Automated text mining tools combined with variant filtering can accelerate the identification of genetic variants. Prenatal diagnosis may involve ultrasound examination for ocular, craniofacial, and skeletal anomalies, followed by amniocentesis and microarray analysis. Clinical evaluation and fetal autopsy findings are also suggestive, particularly for Peters plus-like syndrome when B3GALTL mutations are absent. [PMC12250460, PMC6928627, PMC6334245, PMC2736557, PMC2755183]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for Peters plus syndrome includes Peters anomaly, which presents with isolated ocular manifestations without the systemic features characteristic of Peters plus syndrome. Peters plus-like syndromes, often lacking B3GALTL gene mutations despite phenotypic overlap, should also be considered, as these can be associated with other genetic variants such as deletions spanning PEX2 and ZFHX4. Other syndromic cases involving Peters anomaly but lacking the full spectrum of classic Peters plus features and B3GALTL mutations also fall within the differential. Additionally, fucosidosis, an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease, has been noted in a patient subsequently diagnosed with Kivlin (Peters plus) syndrome, suggesting potential overlap or initial diagnostic confusion. [PMC12250460, PMC6334245, PMC2755183, PMC1050861]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of Peters plus syndrome or Peters plus-like syndrome can be achieved through prenatal evaluation. Ultrasound examination may reveal findings such as hyperechogenic lenses, microphthalmia, hypotelorism, retrognathia, mild ventriculomegaly, absence of the cavum septum pellucidum, and short stature. Amniocentesis and microarray analysis can also be performed, though normal chromosomal copy numbers, including the B3GALTL gene, might lead to a diagnosis of Peters plus-like syndrome. Obstetricians should consider this condition when ocular, craniofacial, and skeletal anomalies are detected prenatally, particularly in the absence of a B3GALTL gene mutation. [PMC6334245]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Peters plus syndrome is most commonly inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern, typically associated with homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the B3GLCT (also referred to as B3GALTL) gene. Specific pathogenic variants in B3GLCT, such as c.660+1G>A, c.459+1G>A, c.230insT, and c.755delC, have been identified. While B3GLCT mutations are strongly implicated in typical Peters plus syndrome, some Peters plus-like phenotypes or syndromic cases with Peters anomaly may not involve this gene, suggesting genetic heterogeneity. De novo heterozygous variants, including deletions spanning PEX2 and ZFHX4 or FOXC1 variants, have also been reported in Peters anomaly spectrum disorders with Peters plus-like features. Comprehensive genomic analysis, including next-generation sequencing, is important for diagnosis and to expand the understanding of the genetic landscape. [PMC12250460, PMC10798386, PMC7092513, PMC6928627, PMC6334245]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Peters' anomaly (PA) is a manifestation of complex disorders in the development of the anterior segment of the eye. The most recognizable feature of the disease is a doughnut-shaped central corneal opacity and adhesions between the opacity and underlying iris. Glaucoma is observed in 30-70% of patients, with up to 50% of the patients showing concomitant vision-threatening disorders. Up to 60% of patients have systemic abnormalities or developmental delays. Being a rare malformation, PA is one of the most common congenital indications for corneal transplantation in infants. Penetrating keratoplasty is used as the primary method of treatment in cases with corneal opacification of a degree that forbids visual development in both eyes. The heterogeneity of co-occurring ophthalmic and systemic malformations in the spectrum of PA determines the wide range of success, defined by various... [PMC10816361, PMC10798386]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Peters plus syndrome can be severe, with one reported case of in utero mort fetalis at the 23rd gestational week. The syndrome includes ocular anterior segment defects of classic Peters' anomaly, for which pediatric corneal grafting is associated with a higher graft failure rate and worse visual prognosis compared to adult procedures. Furthermore, up to 60% of patients with Peters' anomaly, a key feature of the syndrome, experience concomitant vision-threatening disorders, systemic abnormalities, or developmental delays. [PMC10816361, PMC10798386, PMC6334245]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, congenital, fetal lower urinary tract obstruction (LUTO) anomaly characterized by an abnormal congenital obstructing membrane or leaflets that are located within the posterior urethra associated with significant obstruction of the male bladder restricting normal bladder emptying.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal recessive, Not applicable, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It is the most common anomaly of LUTO with a prevalence estimated at 1/4,750-6,250 male births. Posterior urethral valves (PUV) occur exclusively in males.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: PUV represents a spectrum of severity ranging from a disease fatal in infancy to a disease that is minimal and may not manifest until later in life. In the most severe cases, characterized by antenatal oligohydramnios or anhydramnios, the newborn may presents with severe pulmonary distress and features of Potter sequence including wide-set eyes, flattened nose, receding chin and large, low-set ears deficient in cartilage. In toddlers and older children PUV may present with urinary incontinence, poor growth, urinary tract infections, hypertension, lethargy and ultimately renal failure.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The embryology of the urethra is not completely understood, particularly as it pertains to pathologic anomalies. Several different theories have been proposed in the development of PUV. It represents a spectrum of severity based on the timing and severity of obstruction. Congenital obstruction of the urinary tract at a critical time in organogenesis has a profound and lifelong effect on kidney, ureteral and bladder function. The inability of urine to pass out of the body of the fetus results in oligohydramnios which in turn may lead to pulmonary hypoplasia and the features of Potter sequence.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Postnatal diagnosis is suggested on renal ultrasound with findings of dilated, thick-walled bladder and a dilated posterior urethra. Postnatal diagnosis is confirmed with voiding cystotourethrography and cystoscopy.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include anterior urethral valves, congenital urethral stricture, urethral atresia and Prune Belly syndrome. The diagnosis is then confirmed by postnatal physical examination and postnatal renal ultrasonography along with voiding cystourethrography.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is based on ultrasound, possibly aided by magnetic resonance imaging studies. PUV is characterized by variably enlarged thick-walled, non-emptying urinary bladder and a dilated posterior urethra. Counseling is dependent upon the ultrasound findings that also suggest possible associated renal dysplasia at the time of prenatal diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The majority of cases occur sporadically; however, some rare cases observed in siblings indicate autosomal recessive or x-linked recessive inheritance.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Antenatal treatment involves urinary decompression with a vesico-amniotic shunt. Postnatally, PUV is treated using primary valve ablation or creation of a vesicostomy. Further surgical intervention is dependent on the status of the bladder function as well as renal function. Immediately after birth, infants are placed on antibiotic prophylaxis and a means of draining their bladder is accomplished using suprapubic or transurethral catheter diversion. Pulmonary function is assessed and fluid and electrolyte management performed.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis of PUV is variable depending on the degree of severity of the LUTO. Patients may be susceptible to urinary incontinence, urinary tract infections and progressive renal damage. Approximately one third of patients born with PUV progress to end stage renal disease and all patients need periodic long-term urologic follow-up care. Without intervention, patients are at risk of renal failure and bladder dysfunction. Fertility may be compromised in patients who are uremic.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A form of amyloidosis affecting patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), on long term dialysis characterized by the accumulation of amyloid fibrils consisting of beta 2 microglobulin (β2M) deposits in the musculoskeletal system leading to carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS), chronic arthropathy, cystic bone lesions, destructive osteoarthropathy, and pathologic fractures.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): ABeta2Mwt amyloidosis; Dialysis-related amyloidosis; Dialysis-related arthropathy; Wild type ABeta2-microglobulinic amyloidosis

DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: No effective treatment is currently available for dialysis-related amyloidosis (DRA). Interventions focus on improving beta-2 microglobulin (B2M) clearance, such as switching to hemodialysis membranes that effectively absorb B2M, which can ameliorate symptoms. Doxycycline has shown an antalgic effect, reducing osteoarticular pain, though this effect appears independent of inflammation. Haptoglobin is identified as a potential extracellular chaperone that prevents B2M fibril formation, reduces cytotoxicity, and promotes degradation, suggesting promising therapeutic implications. Despite these options, there is a need to translate improved B2M clearance into improved quality of life for patients undergoing long-term dialysis. [PMC8815520, PMC5943088, PMC5586015, PMC3820869]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Wild type ABeta2M amyloidosis, or dialysis-related amyloidosis, can lead to severe and invalidating outcomes in long-term dialysis patients. Complications such as Charcot neuroarthropathy carry a poor prognosis and high risk of lower limb amputation. The disease can cause destructive arthritis and systemic inflammatory signs, significantly impacting quality of life. Visceral organ involvement, including intramural coronary amyloidosis leading to myocardial ischemia and infarction, or widespread visceral deposits causing acute pulmonary edema and hemorrhage, can be fatal.
