While modern hemodialysis has reduced its incidence, the condition remains a serious concern, with a need to translate improved beta-2 microglobulin clearance into better patient outcomes. [PMC10009628, PMC7021141, PMC8815520, PMC5943088, PMC5586015]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A disorder of most severe form of alopecia areata, an inflammatory disease of the hair follicle, which is characterized by a complete loss of hair of the scalp and all the hair-bearing areas of the body.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Alopecia universalis is a rare form of alopecia areata. It has been associated with solid malignancies, with an adjusted odds ratio of 2.10. Cases of alopecia universalis have also been reported following the administration of a heterologous COVID-19 vaccine scheme, with onset between 3 and 17 days after vaccination. Additionally, the condition has been observed after treatment with simvastatin and ezetimibe. [PMC11473577, PMC9968192, PMC9563873]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Atrichia congenita with papular lesions (APL), a rare autosomal recessive form of alopecia, can mimic alopecia universalis. Other conditions that may present similarly include Vitamin D dependent rickets and ectodermal dysplasia. Proper diagnosis of APL, which may present with distinct dermoscopic features like the "Cluster of Stars" appearance, is important to avoid unnecessary treatments. [PMC12252010]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for alopecia universalis involves considering conditions with known genetic bases that may present similarly. For instance, atrichia congenita with papular lesions (APL), an autosomal recessive form of alopecia, can mimic alopecia universalis, necessitating counseling regarding its inheritance pattern if diagnosed. Furthermore, specific variants in the HR gene, such as c.3215T > A p.(Val1072Glu), have been identified as potential risk factors for Alopecia Areata, a broader condition that includes alopecia universalis. These variants are noted for their potentially deleterious effect on protein function, indicating a genetic component that may be discussed during counseling. [PMC12252010, PMC10136600]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Alopecia Universalis (AU) increasingly focuses on Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors, which have demonstrated significant therapeutic effects. Tofacitinib has successfully treated AU in multiple cases, including refractory forms, and upadacitinib has shown success in children. Baricitinib and deuruxolitinib are also promising for severe alopecia areata, which can progress to AU. While traditional treatments like systemic or local glucocorticoids, minoxidil, and immunomodulators (e.g., azathioprine, methotrexate) have been used, they often have limited efficacy or high recurrence. Diphenylcyclopropenone is effective for severe alopecia areata, though platelet-rich plasma is not an effective adjunct. For pediatric alopecia areata, topical corticosteroids are preferred first-line, followed by contact immunotherapy, with JAK inhibitors emerging as novel options. Patients on JAK inhibitors require regular lab monitoring due to potential side effects, and systemic exposure is necessary for efficacy. [PMC12021876, PMC12251980, PMC12010142, PMC12189223, PMC11649032]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Mosaic variegated aneuploidy (MVA) syndrome is a chromosomal anomaly characterized by multiple mosaic aneuploidies that leads to a variety of phenotypic abnormalities and cancer predisposition.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, 41 cases of MVA have been described in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The most common clinical features are growth retardation of prenatal onset, microcephaly, developmental delay, structural central nervous system and ophthalmological anomalies (e.g. cataract, corneal opacities, microphthalmia and glaucoma), and mild dysmorphic features, including triangular facies, micrognathia, and epicanthic folds. Additional features include oligohydramnios, ventricular dilatation, Dandy-Walker malformation, fetal ascites, and increased nuchal translucency. Cancer occurs in approximately 1/3 of individuals. Wilms tumor, rhabdomyosarcoma, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and granulosa cell malignant tumor of the ovary all occur before the age of 5 years. In one individual, carcinoma of the ampulla of Vater and of the colon occurred in adulthood.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MVA is due to defective cell division, leading to aberrant disjunction of chromosomes during mitosis. This results in a high proportion (>10%) of aneuploid cells. Mutations of the BUB1B and CEP57 genes have been identified in individuals with MVA. BUB1B encodes BUBR1, a key protein in the mitotic spindle checkpoint. CEP57 is a centrosomal protein involved in nucleating and stabilizing microtubules. Individuals with BUB1B mutations have a high incidence of cancer (approximately 75%). No individual with a CEP57 mutation has thus far been diagnosed with cancer.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of MVA is based on cytogenetic analysis showing variable aneuploidy.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Aneuploidy can be a feature of chromosomal instability syndromes including Roberts syndrome, ataxia telangiectasia, xeroderma pigmentosum, Bloom syndrome, Werner syndrome and Nijmegen breakage syndrome. Microcephaly with chromosome instability can occur in Fanconi anemia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal karyotype can be undertaken by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. This allows prenatal diagnosis of familial recurrence or investigation of abnormal sonographic findings consistent with MVA.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: MVA is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. The parents of an affected child are obligate carriers. Recurrence risk to siblings is 25%. Carrier testing for at-risk family members of individuals with biallelic BUB1B or CEP57 mutations is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Clinical management depends on the affected individual's specific needs (e.g.: growth hormone therapy for the treatment of growth failure). Cases with a cytogenetic confirmation of MVA syndrome and/or demonstrated BUB1B mutations should be offered Wilms tumor surveillance with renal ultrasonography every three to four months until five years.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is related to the nature of the malformations and the risk of malignancy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Simple (monoclonal) cryoglobulinemia or type I cryoglobulinemia refers to the presence in the serum of one isotype or subclass of immunoglobulin (Ig) that precipitates reversibly below 37°C.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: This serological disorder is almost invariably associated with well-known hematological disorders, usually B-cell dyscrasias (multiple myeloma, WaldenstrÃ¶m macroglobulinemia, or chronic lymphocytic leukemia). Type I cryoglobulinemia is frequently asymptomatic per se but patients may develop acrocyanosis, retinal hemorrhage, Raynaud's phenomenon, and arterial thrombosis. These symptoms may be the expression of hyperviscosity syndrome due to high levels of monoclonal cryoglobulins. The cryoprecipitate in type I cryoglobulinemia is usually composed of IgG or IgM, but infrequent cases with IgA and very rarely monoclonal light-chain protein cryoprecipitation have been reported. Type I cryoglobulins lack rheumatoid factor activity (RF) and do not easily activate complement.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The pathogenetic processes in simple cryoglobulinemia generally appear to be related to those of the underlying lymphoproliferative diseases. The mechanisms of cryoprecipitation are poorly understood but may be partially related to the structure of the component immunoglobulin heavy and light chains.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on detection of cryoglobulins through blood sampling, clotting, and serum separation (carried out at 37°C), and cryoglobulin isolation and cryocrit determination (carried out at 4°C). Ig composition is commonly evaluated by simple diffusion on agarose gels or by immunoelectrophoresis (performed at 37°C to avoid precipitation and loss of cryoglobulins during the procedures).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The principle differential diagnosis is mixed cryoglobulinemia (MC type II-III). Type I cryoglobulinemia and MC type II-III are two distinct clinico-serological entities. In contrast to type I cryoglobulinemia, the cryoprecipitate in MC type II-III is composed ofimmune complexes containing polyclonal IgGs and mono- (type II) or polyclonal (type III) IgMs. Patients with simple cryoglobulinemia lack the typical vasculitic manifestations and serological findings (RF positivity and low complement C4) that characterize MC patients. Clinical course, treatment, and prognosis of type I cryoglobulinemia largely depend on the underlying disorder. Patients with a benign monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance are generally asymptomatic or present with a mild disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Plasma exchange treatment, with/without steroids and/or immunosuppressors, is beneficial for simple cryoglobulinemia patients presenting with clinically overt hyperviscosity syndrome. In patients with malignant B-cell neoplasias, the chemotherapy may lead to resolution of this serological manifestation.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Successful management of neonatal cryoglobulinaemia after a gemellar pregnancy in a woman with symptomatic type I cryoglobulinaemia. [PMC1754881]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis of type I cryoglobulinemia is variable, largely dependent on the underlying hematological malignancy and treatment response. While some reports suggest an unsatisfactory prognosis, successful treatment of associated conditions like smoldering multiple myeloma, plasma cell neoplasm, or monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance can lead to marked responses, symptom improvement, and sustained remission for several years. However, severe and refractory cases can result in significant organ damage, including necrosis necessitating amputations, especially with delayed diagnosis or treatment. In contrast, COVID-19-triggered type I cryoglobulinemia may follow a mild, self-limiting course, and neonatal cases have been successfully managed. [PMC12351230, PMC11861407, PMC11512869, PMC10937136, PMC10347500]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hyperpigmentation of the skin disease characterized by the congenital to infantile-onset of bilateral, diffuse (occasionally localized), reticulate (swirls and streaks), macular hyperpigmentation following the lines of Blaschko, typically involving the trunk, limbs, head and neck (but sparing palms, soles and mucosa), without preceding inflammation, blistering or atrophy. Occasionally, extracutaneous abnormalities, including autism, seizures, cardiac defects, skeletal abnormalities and developmental delay, may be associated. Histologically, basal and/or suprabasal melanosis, without pigment incontinence, is observed.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis is a rare skin pigmentation disorder, characterized by linear streaks and whorls of hyperpigmented macules along Blaschko's lines. Lesions are commonly restricted to the trunk, neck, and extremities, sparing the face, palms, soles, and mucosae. Associated with this, certain cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, neurological, and developmental anomalies have been reported in the literature. Herein, a rare case of linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis involving the face, with musculoskeletal, genital, aural, and ocular abnormalities. [PMC10810383]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis is a rare skin pigmentation disorder characterized by linear streaks and whorls of hyperpigmented macules along Blaschko's lines. Lesions are commonly restricted to the trunk, neck, and extremities, typically sparing the face, palms, soles, and mucosae. However, facial involvement has been reported in rare cases. The condition can be associated with various systemic anomalies, including cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, neurological, and developmental issues. Specific abnormalities like genital, aural, and ocular problems have also been noted. [PMC10810383]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis is a rare skin pigmentation disorder characterized by hyperpigmented macules in linear streaks and whorls along Blaschko's lines. It is considered a case of pigmentary mosaicism. The condition is associated with genetic mosaicism, sometimes presenting with twin spotting. [PMC10810383, PMC8202472]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Incontinentia pigmenti (IP) is a rare X-linked geno-dermatosis characterized by numerous findings. Skin biopsy and histopathological analysis are considered as minor criteria for the diagnosis of IP. We assume that dermoscopy can assist the earlier diagnosis of IP. To gain experience in earlier diagnosis of IP by observing dermoscopic findings of cutaneous changes. We revised confirmed cases of IP and examined them using dermoscopy, comparing histopathological and dermoscopic . Stage I presented solitary and grouped vesicles in linear arrangement on erythematous skin. Early stage II presented star-shaped verrucous lesions on erythematous or pigmented skin. In well-developed lesions, dotted vessels surround keratotic part, some with thrombosed capillaries, resembling a viral wart. Stage III presented linear brown dots on the pigmented areas. Dermoscopic image was uniform in all the... [PMC9464546]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis is a rare skin pigmentation disorder, characterized by linear streaks and whorls of hyperpigmented macules along Blaschko's lines. Lesions are commonly restricted to the trunk, neck, and extremities, sparing the face, palms, soles, and mucosae. Associated with this, certain cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, neurological, and developmental anomalies have been reported in the literature. Herein, a rare case of linear and whorled nevoid hypermelanosis involving the face, with musculoskeletal, genital, aural, and ocular abnormalities. [PMC10810383]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Autosomal dominant hyper-IgE syndrome due to STAT3 deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A very rare primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the clinical triad of high serum IgE (>2000 IU/ml), recurring staphylococcal skin abscesses, and recurrent pneumonia with formation of pneumatoceles.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): AD-HIES due to STAT3 deficiency; Autosomal dominant HIES due to STAT3 deficiency; Job syndrome; Buckley syndrome; Autosomal dominant hyperimmunoglobulin E syndrome due to signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 protein deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence is estimated at around 1/1,000,000. The syndrome affects males and females equally.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: AD-HIES typically first manifests with neonatal rash but it affects the immune system, connective tissue, skeleton, and dental development, with variations in severity. Eczema, recurrent skin abscesses, pneumonia with pneumatocele formation, mucocutaneous candidiasis, elevated serum IgE levels, and eosinophilia are the most common features of immune deficiency/dysregulation. Severe recurrent respiratory infections that may lead to chronic respiratory insufficiency are frequent. A distinctive facial appearance is described (rough skin, facial asymmetry, a prominent forehead, deep-set eyes, broad nasal bridge and a fleshy nasal tip, prognathism), along with midline anomalies. Recurrent pathological fractures occur in about 50% of patients (long bones and ribs). Scoliosis of varying degrees of severity is seen in more than 60%. Anomalies of dentinogenesis are a consistent feature. Reduced resorption of primary tooth roots may lead to prolonged retention of primary teeth, which in turn prevents the appropriate eruption of permanent teeth. Vascular features (coronary and aortic aneurysms, thrombosis of the cerebellar artery and congenital patent ductus venosus) have also been reported. Ocular complications may include xanthelasmas, giant chalasias, eyelid nodules, strabismus, and retinal detachment with complicated cataracts. There is also an increased risk of autoimmune and lymphoproliferative diseases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In 70% of patients, the phenotype is associated with heterozygous mutations of the signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 gene (STAT3; 17q21.31). STAT3 plays a key role in the signal transduction of a broad range of cytokines (control of infections caused by fungi and extracellular bacteria). The etiology in the remaining 30% is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnostic hallmark is increased serum immunoglobulin E (IgE) levels exceeding 2000 U/ml, often higher than 5000 U/ml. A clinical scoring sheet has been defined to assess the probability of diagnosis. Total IgE concentration > 1000 IU/ml and weighted score of clinical features > 30 indicates AD-HIES due to STAT3 deficiency, and a dominant-negative heterozygous mutation in STAT3 provides a definitive diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include cystic fibrosis and chronic granulomatous disease, as well as severe atopic dermatitis and HIV-infection. A clinically distinct autosomal recessive hyper-IgE syndrome has also been described (AR-HIES).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis for pregnancies at increased risk is possible if the disease-causing mutation in the family is known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The majority of AD-HIES cases are caused by de novo mutations and are therefore sporadic but autosomal dominant transmission is characteristic for STAT3 mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The therapeutic approach involves prevention and management of infections with long-term administration of systemic antibiotics and antifungals. Lung abscesses may require surgery but possible complications require close attention. The role of hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has to be evaluated further.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Although HIES is associated with significant morbidity and mortality, adequate care, close monitoring, and patient compliance improve the prognosis and can lead to survival of 50 years of age or over.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cytophagic histiocytic panniculitis (CHP) is a very rare form of panniculitis manifesting as recurrent multiple subcutaneous nodules (which may progressively become ecchymotic and ulcerated), and histologically characterized by lobular panniculitis with lymphocytic and histiocytic infiltration in the subcutaneous adipose tissue.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact prevalence is unknown, but less than 100 cases have been reported (mostly middle-aged and elderly patients).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The histiocytic infiltration often involves lymph nodes, bone marrow and other tissues of the reticuloendothelial system. Severe fever, malaise, pancytopenia, hepatosplenomegaly, and mucosal ulcers are common systemic symptoms.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology remains unclear. In more than 50% of cases, the disease occurs in immunocompromised patients (those with immunodeficiency, autoimmune disease or hematological disease) and is triggered by an infection (mainly with a virus from the herpes-virus family).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on the histological features of fat infiltration.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes malignant histiocytosis and virus-associated hemophagocytic syndrome, as well as systemic Weber-Christian panniculitis. A search for subcutaneous T-cell lymphoma is mandatory.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management involves symptomatic treatment and systemic chemotherapy. Combinations of cytotoxic and immunosuppressive drugs have been reported to be efficient. Chemotherapy followed by stem cell rescue should be considered in severe cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Although remissions have been reported, the disease tends to follow a chronic course often complicated by terminal hemorrhagic diathesis and organ system failure.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Cytophagic histiocytic panniculitis is a rare disease, associated with either nonmalignant conditions or subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma, and often also associated with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). the case of a 11-year-old boy with a history of secondary HLH who, after a local trauma, developed a painful, indurated plaque over the right thigh associated with relapsing HLH. Histopathologic findings from skin biopsy specimens revealed significant lobular panniculitis with benign histiocytes showing hemophagocytosis. High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone and cyclosporine A treatment was highly effective. A genetic study after a new, relapsing episode of HLH revealed an heterozygous missense mutation on STX 11 gene inherited from the mother. Cytophagic histiocytic panniculitis with fatal haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis in a paediatric patient with... [PMC3974103, PMC2014859]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare skeletal dysplasia characterized by peculiar facial anomalies, Pierre Robin sequence, cleft palate, shortening and bowing of long bones. Sexual ambiguity or female external genitalia is possible in individuals with a male karyotype.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Although epidemiological data is limited, prevalence at birth has been suggested at approximately 1/40,000-80,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical features include a relatively large head, Pierre Robin sequence with cleft palate, flat face, laryngotracheomalacia, respiratory distress, 11 pairs of ribs, ambiguous genitalia or normal female external genitalia in an individual with a 46,XY karyotype. It also includes dislocated hips, short bowed femura and tibiae (lower limbs more frequently than upper limbs), pretibial skin dimples (bowing of the lower leg is often associated with a skin dimple over the apex of curve) and clubfeet. A few cases of a variant syndrome, referred to as ``acampomelic campomelic dysplasia'' have been described. This variant can be distinguished by the lack of long bone curvature. Many infants die in the neonatal period; additional problems identified in long-term survivors include short stature, cervical spine instability with cord compression, progressive kyphoscoliosis, and hearing impairment. In some cases developmental delay is described.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disorder is autosomal dominant; however, most cases are due to heterozygous de novo mutations in the SOX9 gene (localized to 17q24). In rare individuals the disorder is caused by chromosomal recombination (deletion or translocation) involving the region 17q24.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis in based on peculiar facial anomalies (flat face, long philtrum, micrognathia), short stature and specific radiological findings (bowed femura and tibiae, dislocated hip, hypoplastic scapulae, hypoplastic and nonmineralized thoracic vertebral pedicles).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: In the prenatal period, differential diagnoses include osteogenesis imperfecta type 2 and 3, hypophosphatasia and thanatophoric dysplasia and Stuve-Wiedemann syndrome; after birth, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita (SEDC), diastrophic dysplasia and Larsen syndrome may be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Diagnosis is generally suspected prenatally during the second trimester ultrasound examination, based on the observation of delayed growth associated with bowed femura and tibiae. Prenatal genetic testing can be performed through chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis when there is a suspicion of the diagnosis or in familial cases where an abnormality of the chromosomal region has already been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Most cases arise sporadically and in these cases the recurrence risk in siblings of a proband is at estimated 2% (due to germline mosaicism). Approximately 5% of cases are a result of chromosomal recombination involving the region 17q24 and, in rare cases, there may be familial transmission. For this reason, genetic counseling is recommended for couples potentially at risk.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic and follows standard protocols for cleft palate, clubfeet, hip subluxations, cervical instability and kyphoscoliosis. In individuals with a 46,XY karyotype and undermasculinization of the genitalia, the gonads should be removed due to the increased risk for gonadoblastoma. Hearing aids for those with hearing impairment.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Newborns suffering from campomelic dysplasia often die soon after birth as a result of respiratory insufficiency, but about 10 % of individuals survive. Complications (such as kyphoscoliosis, recurrent respiratory infections, hearing loss, light to moderate learning difficulties, small size and hip dislocation) can arise as the patients age.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 4
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Congenital bile acid synthesis defect type 4 (BAS defect type 4) is an anomaly of bile acid synthesis characterized by mild cholestatic liver disease, fat malabsorption and/or neurological disease.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): 2-methylacyl-CoA racemase deficiency; AMACR deficiency; Alpha-methyl-acyl-CoA racemase deficiency; Liver disease-retinitis pigmentosa-polyneuropathy-epilepsy syndrome; BASD4

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Five cases have been reported to date: two siblings presenting with neonatal cholestasis and three adults with neurological disease.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical presentation of this defect varies. Infants present with severe fat and fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies, hematochezia and mild cholestasis, whereas adults present with various neurological disorders. It is possible that the adults had undocumented mild liver disease and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency in earlier life that led to neurological disease.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: BAS defect type 4 is caused by a mutation in the AMACR gene (5p13.2-q11.1).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on liquid secondary ionization mass spectrometry (LSIMS), gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and electrospray ionization-tandem mass spectrometry analysis of urine, serum and bile.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is based on primary bile acid therapy with cholic acid. Dietary restriction of phytanic and pristanic acids is likely to be necessary in the long term to prevent neurotoxicity.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for bile acid synthesis defects can be influenced by treatment. Bile acid replacement therapy may delay or stabilize disease progression by improving biochemical profiles. For specific defects like α-methylacyl-CoA racemase (AMACR) deficiency, early diagnosis is important as patients may benefit from restricted dietary intake. Cholic acid treatment in children with certain defects, including AMACR deficiency, is generally well tolerated, leading to normalized transaminase levels and no clinically relevant changes in liver elasticity, neurological assessment, or growth. However, adults may experience more side effects, and the balance of benefits versus side effects can be negative, with one adult developing hepatocellular carcinoma during treatment. Without intervention, conditions like adult-onset AMACR deficiency can manifest as a complex phenotype including severe neurological features such as peripheral neuropathy, epilepsy, and relapsing encephalopathy, alongside other systemic complications. [PMC12247693, PMC3567975]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive acromesomelic dysplasia characterized by severe dwarfism at birth, abnormalities confined to limbs, severe shortening and deformity of long bones, fusion or absence of carpal and tarsal bones, ball shaped fingers and, occasionally, polydactyly and absent joints. As seen in acromesomelic dysplasia, Hunter-Thomson type and acromesomelic dysplasia, Maroteaux Type, facial features and intelligence are normal.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Grebe dysplasia, Hunter-Thompson dysplasia, and du Pan dysplasia constitute a spectrum of skeletal dysplasias inherited as an autosomal recessive trait characterized by short stature, severe acromesomelic shortening of the limbs, and normal axial skeleton. The majority of patients with these disorders have biallelic loss-of-function mutations of GDF5. In single instances, Grebe dysplasia and a Grebe dysplasia-like phenotype with genital anomalies have been shown to be caused by mutations in BMPR1B, encoding a GDF5 receptor. We clinically and radiologically characterised an acromesomelic chondrodysplasia in an adult woman born to consanguineous parents. We sequenced GDF5 and BMPR1B on DNA of the proposita. We performed 3D structural analysis and luciferase reporter assays to functionally investigate the identified BMPR1B mutation. We extend the genotype-phenotype correlation in the... [PMC4482310, PMC4023204, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Grebe type, is an autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia characterized by short stature, a normal axial skeleton, and severe acromesomelic shortening of the limbs. This disproportionate shortening predominantly affects the middle (forearms and forelegs) and distal segments (hands and feet) of the appendicular skeleton. Clinical findings consistent with ACD-type Grebe include severe brachydactyly, ulnar deviation of the hands, aplasia of the fibula, and fusion of carpal/tarsal bones. Some patients, particularly those with specific BMPR1B mutations, may also present with genital anomalies such as hypoplasia of the uterus and ovarian dysfunction, which can distinguish their phenotype from GDF5-associated chondrodysplasias. Grebe dysplasia is considered a more severe form within the acromesomelic chondrodysplasia spectrum. [PMC4482310, PMC4023204, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Grebe type, is an autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia. The majority of patients have biallelic loss-of-function mutations in GDF5. However, mutations in BMPR1B, which encodes a GDF5 receptor, also cause Grebe dysplasia or Grebe-like phenotypes, sometimes with additional genital anomalies. Identified BMPR1B mutations include homozygous missense, nonsense, and deletion mutations, all leading to a loss of function by hindering receptor activation by GDF5 or causing reduced protein translation. The phenotypic severity may correlate with the extent of functional impairment of the GDF5-BMPR1B ligand-receptor pair. Heterozygous carriers typically show mild or non-penetrant phenotypes, distinct from dominant-negative BMPR1B mutations. [PMC4482310, PMC4023204, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Acromesomelic dysplasia, Grebe type, relies on clinical and radiological characterization, which typically reveals short stature, severe acromesomelic limb shortening, and a normal axial skeleton. Specific findings include aplasia of the fibula, severe brachydactyly, ulnar deviation of hands, and fusion of carpal/tarsal bones; genital anomalies may also be present. Genetic analysis is essential, identifying biallelic loss-of-function mutations in GDF5 or homozygous mutations in BMPR1B. Functional assays, such as 3D structural analysis and luciferase reporter assays, can further confirm the pathogenic impact of identified BMPR1B mutations by demonstrating loss of function or hindered receptor activation. [PMC4482310, PMC4023204, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Grebe type, is part of a spectrum of autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasias that includes Hunter-Thompson and du Pan dysplasias. These conditions are characterized by short stature, severe acromesomelic shortening of the limbs, and a normal axial skeleton. While the majority of patients with these disorders have biallelic loss-of-function mutations of GDF5, Grebe dysplasia and Grebe-like phenotypes with genital anomalies can also be caused by mutations in BMPR1B. Du Pan dysplasia, a milder form, can result from hypomorphic BMPR1B mutations. A distinct subtype of acromesomelic chondrodysplasia, caused by a homozygous BMPR1B mutation, presents with additional genital anomalies and a distinct limb phenotype, differentiating it from GDF5-associated chondrodysplasias. This condition is also distinct from brachydactyly type A2, which involves heterozygous BMPR1B mutations. [PMC4482310, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Grebe type, is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. The majority of patients have biallelic loss-of-function mutations in GDF5, while mutations in BMPR1B have also been identified as causative. Affected individuals are typically homozygous for these mutations, often observed in consanguineous families. Heterozygous carriers of BMPR1B mutations associated with the recessive Grebe type may exhibit mild brachydactyly or be non-penetrant, distinguishing it from autosomal-dominant brachydactyly-type A2 caused by dominant-negative BMPR1B mutations. Genetic counseling should address the recessive inheritance pattern and the specific genes involved. [PMC4482310, PMC4023204, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Grebe dysplasia, Hunter-Thompson dysplasia, and du Pan dysplasia constitute a spectrum of skeletal dysplasias inherited as an autosomal recessive trait characterized by short stature, severe acromesomelic shortening of the limbs, and normal axial skeleton. The majority of patients with these disorders have biallelic loss-of-function mutations of GDF5. In single instances, Grebe dysplasia and a Grebe dysplasia-like phenotype with genital anomalies have been shown to be caused by mutations in BMPR1B, encoding a GDF5 receptor. We clinically and radiologically characterised an acromesomelic chondrodysplasia in an adult woman born to consanguineous parents. We sequenced GDF5 and BMPR1B on DNA of the proposita. We performed 3D structural analysis and luciferase reporter assays to functionally investigate the identified BMPR1B mutation. We extend the genotype-phenotype correlation in the... [PMC4482310]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurodegenerative disorder of the astrocytes comprised of two clinical forms: Alexander disease (AxD) type I and type II manifesting with various degrees of macrocephaly, spasticity, ataxia and seizures and leading to psychomotor regression and death.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown. One population based study in Japan estimated an annual incidence of 1/ 2.7 million.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical presentation depends on the subtype. Previously, AxD was classified either as infantile, juvenile or adult, based simply on age of onset. The currently used classification system is based on a constellation of clinical and radiologic features and includes AxD type I and AxD type II. AxD type I is more likely to be of early onset (mean 1.74 years) and shorter survival (median 14 years) whereas type II exhibits onset throughout the lifespan (mean 21.64 years, but can occur in early childhood) and has longer survival (median 25 years). The two types also differ in their clinical symptoms. AxD type I manifests with symptoms of encephalopathy, epilepsy and failure to thrive and has an infantile presentation, while patients with AxD type II manifest with bulbar, autonomic and motor signs such as dysarthria, dysphonia, dysphagia, ataxia, spastic paraparesis and palatal myoclonus. AxD type II also has a slower progression and cognitive impairment can be completely absent.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In the vast majority (95%) of patients, AxD is caused by gain-of-function de novo mutations in the glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) gene. Several familial cases have also been reported with autosomal dominant transmission. This gene encodes GFAP, the major intermediate filament protein found in astrocytes. The over-expression and accumulation of this mutant protein leads to the formation of astrocytic inclusion bodies (Rosenthal fibers) throughout the central nervous system (CNS). It is currently unknown how Rosenthal fibers are involved in disease pathogenesis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Alexander disease is an autosomal dominant leukodystrophy caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the glial fibrillar acidic protein (GFAP) gene. Although increasingly recognised, there is evidence that Alexander disease, particularly later-onset disease, is significantly underdiagnosed and its true prevalence is unknown (the only population-based prevalence was estimated at one in 2.7 million). Using the extensive UK Biobank dataset, we analysed the frequency of pathogenic and likely pathogenic variants, GFAP variants, within the UK population and identified clinical and radiological phenotypes linked to these variants. Pathogenic, likely pathogenic and GFAP variants of uncertain significance were identified in the UK Biobank whole-exome sequencing data (n=4 70 000). Demographic information, previous medical history-including symptoms associated with Alexander disease-collected... [PMC12322464, PMC10970303, PMC11288593, PMC10061190, PMC6967083]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Alexander disease is an autosomal dominant leukodystrophy caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the GFAP gene. Genetic analysis, including Sanger sequencing and whole-exome sequencing, is crucial for diagnosis, identifying both inherited and de novo mutations. Familial cases demonstrate an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, with evidence suggesting genetic anticipation where offspring may have an earlier age of onset. The prevalence of pathogenic GFAP variants in the general population is higher than previously estimated, indicating potential under-reporting, misdiagnosis, or reduced penetrance, which are important considerations for genetic counseling. [PMC12322464, PMC10864087, PMC9464415, PMC9277918, PMC9178008]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Alexander disease primarily involves symptomatic care. While no curative treatment exists, interventions include ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement for hydrocephalus and various anti-seizure medications, although seizures can be refractory. Amoxicillin has been reported to improve irritability by modulating glutamate levels, and perampanel, an AMPA receptor antagonist, has shown efficacy for seizures. In late-onset cases, prednisolone may alleviate vomiting and weight loss. Respiratory difficulties and sleep apnea can be managed with variable positive pressure ventilation. Anesthetic sensitivity due to astrocyte dysfunction necessitates careful, EEG-guided anesthesia during procedures. [PMC11761024, PMC11633705, PMC10970303, PMC9277918, PMC5534752]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Type I Alexander disease in humans is associated with a poor prognosis, presenting with paroxysmal neurodegeneration, refractory epilepsy, and encephalopathy in the first years of life. In canine cases, the disease is progressive, leading to euthanasia due to suspected poor prognosis or death from respiratory failure after slow neurological deterioration. While symptomatic treatments like amoxicillin and perampanel may improve specific symptoms such as irritability and seizures, the overall long-term prognosis remains poor. [PMC11633705, PMC10061190, PMC7719875]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare restrictive cardiomyopathy characterized by hypereosinophilia and fibrous thickening of the endocardium, with usually large thrombi against the ventricle walls, that can lead to cardiovascular complications such as heart failure and thromboembolism. It manifests with symptoms like edema, fatigue and shortness of breath. It is usually secondary to eosinophil-associated tissue damage and is associated with idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome, chronic eosinophilic leukemia, carcinoma, or lymphoma.

DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Loeffler endocarditis (LE) is the cardiac manifestation of hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES), which must be distinguished from other causes of persistent eosinophilia, including helminth infections, drug reactions, malignancies, and immunologic, inflammatory, and allergic diseases. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) can cause endocardial fibrosis or LE-like cardiac manifestations. As a form of primary restrictive cardiomyopathy, LE is differentiated from other causes such as sarcoidosis, storage diseases, desminopathy, and hemochromatosis. Non-specified T-cell lymphoma can also cause endocarditis parietalis fibroplastica Löfflein. Other conditions to rule out include chronic eosinophilic leukaemia, FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, PDGFRB mutation, abnormal myeloid maturation, and lymphoproliferative disorders. [PMC11631239, PMC9025762, PMC6536155, PMC5346256, PMC5020759]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Loeffler's endocarditis (LE) is the cardiac manifestation of hypereosinophilic syndrome. a case of LE in a 45-year-old female, resulting in diffuse endothelial fibrosis and severe right-sided heart failure. The patient was admitted with dyspnoea and oedema, with haematology revealing an absolute eosinophil count of 20.9 × 10 9 . Imaging showed near-complete obliteration of the right ventricular apical and formation of thromboses. Endomyocardial biopsy indicated diffuse fibrous hyperplasia of the endocardium with fibrinous thrombi rich in eosinophils. Molecular and cytogenetic analyses of bone marrow cells showed no signs of FIP1L1-PDGFRA fusion, PDGFRB mutation, abnormal myeloid maturation, or a lymphoproliferative disorder. Flow cytometry indicated no clonality, ruling out chronic eosinophilic leukaemia. Gene mutation screening discovered a p.L583_A586delinesS mutation in the JAK2... [PMC11631239, PMC5882404]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Loeffler endocarditis primarily involves corticosteroids, such as prednisone or prednisolone, which rapidly decrease eosinophil levels, relieve myocardial thickening, and improve cardiac function. Anticoagulant therapy, including warfarin, is crucial for managing intracardiac thrombi and preventing thromboembolic complications, with early initiation of both steroids and anticoagulation being beneficial for prognosis. For specific genetic mutations like JAK2, targeted therapies such as ruxolitinib may normalize eosinophil levels, though cardiac damage can be irreversible. In cases of severe, irreversible cardiac damage and refractory heart failure, heart transplantation may be considered. Multimodality imaging, including echocardiography and cardiac MRI, is important for early detection and monitoring treatment response. [PMC12393971, PMC12107866, PMC11631239, PMC11473627, PMC8713406]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Loeffler endocarditis is associated with high morbidity and mortality, often carrying a pessimistic prognosis, particularly with cardiac involvement and intracardiac thrombus, with one review reporting a 27.3% mortality rate. Heart failure and lack of anticoagulation are linked to poor outcomes. However, early detection and treatment are crucial, as early disease often responds well to corticosteroids. Treatment with steroids and anticoagulation can lead to rapid recovery, relief of myocardial thickening, and improved cardiac function. While cardiac damage can be irreversible, sometimes necessitating heart transplantation and subsequent complications, patients can gradually recover. Recurrence is possible if immunosuppression is stopped. Multiparametric cardiac MRI can assist in individual prognosis assessment and therapy monitoring. [PMC12393971, PMC12107866, PMC11631239, PMC9742649, PMC8713406]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Glycogen storage disease due to muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A form of glycogen storage disease (GSD) characterized by exercise intolerance and rhabdomyolysis episodes, due to a deficiency of the muscle isoform of glycogen phosphorylase.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): GSD due to muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency; GSD type 5; Glycogen storage disease type 5; Glycogenosis due to muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency; Glycogenosis type 5; McArdle disease; Myophosphorylase deficiency; GSD type V; Glycogen storage disease type V; Glycogenosis type V

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence has been estimated to be 1 in 100,000 to 170,000 people.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset typically occurs in childhood or adolescence. Patients present with a syndrome of muscular exercise intolerance with myalgia, cramps, fatigue, and moderate muscle weakness may appear after the age of 40 years in less than 30% of patients. Massive elevation of creatine-kinase and rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria (dark urine) after exercise is noted in around 50% of patients, potentially leading to acute kidney failure. A ''second wind'' phenomenon with relief of myalgia and fatigue after a few minutes of rest is observed in most patients. Some patients may have very moderate forms.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The condition is caused by mutations in the PYGM gene (11q13), leading to muscle phosphorylase deficiency, an enzyme involved in the first step of glycogenolysis. About 180 pathogenic or likely-pathogenic variants have been identified in patients. The variant p.(Arg50*) accounts for most of the alleles present in the Caucasian populations.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Forearm non-ischaemic exercise test always reveal a blunted lactate increase, and increased ammonia levels. CK levels are generally increased at rest. Diagnosis is confirmed by PYGM gene analysis. When performed, muscle biopsy shows subsarcolemmal vacuoles, increased glycogen content on PAS staining, and absence of myophosphorylase activity.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include other GSD manifesting with exercise intolerance and with rhabdomyolysis episodes (in particular GSD type 7) and other metabolic myopathies such as lipid storage myopathies and mitochondrial disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis and preimplantation genetic testing are usually not offered to at-risk couples.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy, and to at-risk relatives.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is based on controlled regular physical activity in order to avoid muscle deconditioning and develop mitochondrial oxidation capacities in muscles. Sucrose intake before exercise can markedly improve exercise tolerance. Clinical trials are currently assessing the potential benefit of ketogenic diet.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is favorable, without limitation of life-expectancy. Rhabdomyolysis episodes may be avoided in limiting strenuous exercises, but can be exceptionally life-threatening in case of unaccustomed exercise. However, myoglobinuria may lead to potentially life-threatening renal failure.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Crouzon disease is characterized by craniosynostosis and facial hypoplasia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated prevalence in the general population of Europe is 0.9/100,000 .
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Craniosynostosis is variable but many sutures are usually involved. The facial dysmorphology is characterized by ocular hypertelorism, small beaked nose, proptosis, exophthalmos, hypoplastic maxilla and mandibular prognathism. The synostosis is evolutive and is usually either not visible or only slightly visible at birth. It usually manifests by the age of 2 years and becomes progressively more severe. However, precocious and congenital forms have been reported in which hypoplasia of the upper maxilla is pronounced and leads to respiratory difficulties, and the exophthalmia is severe resulting in palpebral malocclusion. Hydrocephaly, descent of the cerebellar tonsils and anomalies in jugular venous drainage are also frequently observed in Crouzon disease and may pose therapeutic problems. Two thirds of patients with Crouzon disease have intracranial hypertension, which may lead to blindness.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Crouzon disease is caused by mutations of the fibroblast growth factor receptor FGFR2 (10q25.3-q26) with 80% being located to the immunoglobulin (Ig)-like domain III (IgIII domain) of the extracellular region and an additional 20% of mutations being located in the IgI-IgII domains, transmembrane and tyrosine kinase regions. A distinct form of Crouzon disease associated with acanthosis nigricans has been reported and is caused by a specific mutation (p.Ala391Glu) in the transmembrane domain of another protein from the same family, FGFR3 (Crouzon syndrome - acanthosisnigricans). Moreover, mutations in ERF (19q13.2) gene encoding the ETS2 repressor, resulting in anosteogenic stimulation, have been associated to a Crouzon-like syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disease is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner with variable penetrance.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Surgical interventions are aimed at preventing cerebral, ophthalmological or respiratory complications and correcting the cranio-facial dysmorphy. The craniofacial surgical approach adopted needs to take into account both the cranial and facial synostosis and should be tailored to each patient.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Crouzon syndrome can be suspected in the antenatal period via ultrasonographic assessment. Once suspected, advanced imaging such as three-dimensional computed tomography may be requested to show early signs of cranial sutures fusion. Genetic testing, including the identification of FGFR2 mutations, is valuable for prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling. Whole exome sequencing combined with dynamic ultrasound assessments can also contribute to prenatal diagnosis, as demonstrated by a family with a history of Crouzon syndrome successfully having a healthy baby through this approach. [PMC9622563, PMC8857571, PMC5865782]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Opsismodysplasia is a skeletal dysplasia characterized by congenital dwarfism and facial dysmorphism.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Twenty five cases (16 males and 9 females) have been reported in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disorder is evident at birth. The facial dysmorphism includes macrocephaly, prominent brow, large fontanels, depressed nasal bridge, a small nose, anteverted nares and a long philtrum, hypertelorism, and exophthalmos. Additional features include a short neck, narrow thorax, predominantly rhizomelic micromelia with very short long bones, short feet and hands, muscular hypotonia, severe platyspondyly, marked delay of bone maturation, and increased susceptibility to respiratory infections.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Etiology remains unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Autosomal recessive transmission has been suggested.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of opsismodysplasia involves evaluating clinical features such as short limbs with flared metaphyses, bowed radii, femora and tibiae, irregular ossification of hands and feet, and marked platyspondyly. Radiological and chondro-osseous findings are also relevant. Genetic testing, specifically whole-exome sequencing, can identify unique compound heterozygous variants in the INPPL1 gene. The absence of the SHIP2 protein, encoded by INPPL1, can be confirmed by immunoblot analysis on amniocytes. [PMC4995133, PMC1735387]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: identify the genetic basis of a severe skeletal lethal dysplasia. The main clinical features of two affected fetuses included short limbs with flared metaphyses, bowed radii, femora and tibiae, irregular ossification of hands and feet, and marked platyspondyly. Affected and nonaffected family members were subjected to whole-exome sequencing, followed by immunoblot analysis on amniocytes isolated from one of the affected individuals. Unique compound heterozygous variants in the inositol polyphosphate phosphatase-like 1 (INPPL1) gene encoding the SHIP2 protein were identified in both affected individuals. One variant was inherited from each unaffected parent. Both allelic variants, c.(2327-1G>C);(1150_1151delGA), are predicted to result in premature stop codons leading to nonsense-mediated mRNA decay of the mutant alleles and no production of SHIP2. The absence of SHIP2 was confirmed by... [PMC4995133]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of opsismodysplasia can be achieved by identifying characteristic skeletal features in affected fetuses, including short limbs with flared metaphyses, bowed radii, femora, and tibiae, irregular ossification of hands and feet, and marked platyspondyly. Genetic testing, such as whole-exome sequencing, can identify unique compound heterozygous variants in the INPPL1 gene. Additionally, immunoblot analysis on amniocytes isolated from affected individuals can confirm the absence of the SHIP2 protein, which is the genetic basis of this severe skeletal dysplasia. [PMC4995133]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Severe opsismodysplasia, characterized by features such as short limbs, bowed bones, irregular ossification, and platyspondyly, is identified as a skeletal lethal dysplasia. This severe form, linked to the complete absence of the SHIP2 protein due to INPPL1 mutations, indicates a very poor prognosis, likely leading to lethality. Opsismodysplasia generally involves significant delayed bone formation. [PMC4995133]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder of lysine and tryptophan metabolism characterized by 2-aminoadipic and 2-oxoadipic aciduria. Patients may also present with increased urinary excretion of alpha-hydroxyadipic acid. Variable clinical presentations have been found in patients including hypotonia, developmental delay, mild to severe intellectual disability, ataxia, epilepsy, and behavioral disorders (most commonly attention deficit hyperactivity disorder). However, many individuals with the biochemical phenotype are completely asymptomatic and thus the clinical significance of the condition is questionable.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: 2-aminoadipic and 2-oxoadipic aciduria is a metabolic condition characterized by abnormalities in metabolite profiles, specifically increased levels of 2-aminoadipate and 2-oxoadipate. Clinically, this disorder has been associated with varying neurological symptoms. The underlying molecular cause involves mutations in the DHTKD1 gene, which codes for an enzyme mediating a step in the L-lysine-degradation pathway, leading to impaired turnover of decarboxylation 2-oxoadipate to glutaryl-CoA. [PMC3516599]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: 2-aminoadipic 2-oxoadipic aciduria is caused by mutations in the DHTKD1 gene. This gene codes for dehydrogenase E1 and transketolase domain-containing protein 1, which is part of a 2-oxoglutarate-dehydrogenase-complex-like protein. DHTKD1 mediates the final step in the L-lysine-degradation pathway, specifically the decarboxylation of 2-oxoadipate to glutaryl-CoA. Mutations, such as compound heterozygosity for c.1A>G and c.2185G>A (p.Gly729Arg) or c.2185G>A with c.1228C>T (p.Arg410*), impair this turnover, leading to the characteristic aciduria. [PMC3516599]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of 2-aminoadipic and 2-oxoadipic aciduria relies on identifying abnormalities in metabolite profiles, particularly increased levels of 2-oxoadipate, which can be observed in individual-derived fibroblasts. Molecular diagnosis is established through genetic testing, such as exome sequencing or sequence analysis, to identify causative mutations in the DHTKD1 gene. Specific mutations, including c.1A>G, c.2185G>A (p.Gly729Arg), and c.1228C>T (p.Arg410*), have been linked to the condition. [PMC3516599]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: 2-aminoadipic 2-oxoadipic aciduria is caused by mutations in the DHTKD1 gene. Affected individuals have been found to carry compound heterozygous mutations in DHTKD1, such as an initiating methionine mutation (c.1A>G) and a missense mutation (c.2185G>A [p.Gly729Arg]), or a missense mutation (c.2185G>A [p.Gly729Arg]) with a nonsense mutation (c.1228C>T [p.Arg410(*)]). This genetic basis indicates an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. [PMC3516599]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare chromosomal anomaly of chromosome 13 characterized by a widely variable phenotype (ranging from mild to severe) principally characterized by intrauterine growth retardation, developmental delay, short stature, moderate to severe intellectual deficit, microcephaly, facial dysmorphism (i.e. upslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, abnormal ears, broad nasal bridge, high arched palate, micrognathia, small mouth, and thin lips), hands and feet anomalies, and genital abnormalities. Additional features reported include behavioral problems, hearing and speech disorders, congenital heart defects, cerebral malformations, and anal atresia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Ring chromosome 13 syndrome is a rare condition, with a general frequency for ring chromosomes estimated at 1 in 50,000, and specifically for chromosome 13 at 1 in 58,000. It typically presents as a syndromic situation characterized by developmental delay, mental retardation, and CNS, skeletal, or organ anomalies. However, cases with isolated manifestations, such as male infertility, have also been reported. Despite these estimated occurrences, patients with ring chromosomes reported in the literature account for less than 1% of their actual occurrence, indicating significant under-representation and diagnostic challenges. [PMC10189157, PMC9519620]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Ring chromosome 13 syndrome typically presents as a syndromic situation characterized by developmental delay, intellectual disability, and severe growth retardation. Common features include dysmorphies such as microcephalus, hypertelorism, low-set ears, wide nasal bridge, short philtrum, digital anomalies, and microphtalmia. Central nervous system, skeletal, and other organ anomalies, including corpus callosum agenesis, anencephaly, and ambiguous genitalia, are also reported. The clinical phenotype is highly heterogeneous, ranging from multiple malformations to isolated features like male infertility or early-onset diabetes mellitus. This variability is influenced by the amount and site of genetic material loss, specific gene deletions (e.g., MIR17HG, ZIC2, EFNB2, IRS2), and the dynamic mosaicism of the ring chromosome. [PMC10189157, PMC9519620, PMC6949681, PMC7389945, PMC6169464]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for ring chromosome 13 syndrome involve a combination of cytogenetic and molecular techniques. Prenatal detection often begins with ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging to identify associated anomalies. Karyotyping, including high-resolution banding (e.g., GTW-banding, RBG banding), is a primary method for identifying the ring chromosome and mosaicism. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is also employed to detect the ring and characterize terminal deletions. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) or array-based comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) is crucial for identifying copy number variants, deletions, and duplications, and for revealing qualitative genetic differences. Whole exome sequencing (WES) or whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is recommended, particularly when initial karyotype and CMA are negative, to further characterize genomic alterations. DNA polymorphism analysis can determine the parental origin of the ring chromosome. Despite these advancements, standardized laboratory practices for analyzing the cellular behavior and genomic imbalances of ring chromosomes are currently lacking. [PMC12217963, PMC10189157, PMC9541672, PMC9519620, PMC6949681]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Ring chromosome 13 syndrome presents with a heterogeneous phenotype, often overlapping with other chromosome 13 aberrations. Differential diagnoses include trisomy 13, as patients with ring 13 may exhibit features of trisomy 13, and duplication 13q, which can also resemble trisomy 13. Conditions like microdeletion 13q and mosaic monosomy 13 should also be considered, given their similar abnormalities of external genitalia and facial dysmorphia. The clinical spectrum of ring 13 can also resemble other deletion syndromes, depending on the specific genetic material lost. When ambiguous genitalia is present, sex chromosome disorders and other autosomal chromosome anomalies should be considered. Furthermore, for cases presenting with corpus callosum abnormalities, various other genetic causes identified through karyotyping, chromosomal microarray, or exome sequencing should be evaluated. [PMC12217963, PMC9541672, PMC6949681, PMC4141575, PMC1684954]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of ring chromosome 13 is possible, with one case of a fetus with mosaic ring chromosome 13 being characterized, highlighting its rarity. Rare chromosome 13 aberrations, which include ring chromosome 13, are identified in prenatal tests and may present with various sonographic features. These can include abnormalities of the external genitalia and facial dysmorphia, or features resembling trisomy 13. Genetic testing, such as karyotyping, chromosomal microarray analysis, and exome sequencing, is employed for prenatal detection of genetic causes, especially when fetal anomalies like corpus callosum abnormalities are identified via ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging. [PMC12217963, PMC9541672, PMC5742933]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for ring chromosome 13 syndrome is challenging due to its rarity and highly variable clinical presentation, which can include developmental delay, intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, organ anomalies, and even isolated infertility. Diagnosis typically involves karyotyping, FISH, CMA, and whole-exome sequencing, especially for prenatal cases with corpus callosum abnormalities or other anomalies. The phenotypic spectrum is determined by the amount and site of genetic material loss, specific gene deletions, and dynamic mosaicism. However, under-representation of clinical cases and a lack of comprehensive diagnostic analysis hinder evidence-based interpretation of clinico-cytogenomic correlations and management recommendations, though standardized approaches are a future prospect. [PMC12217963, PMC10189157, PMC9541672, PMC9519620, PMC6949681]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Ring chromosomes are the result of breakage and re-union of distal ends of chromosomal arms. They have a general frequency of 1 in 50,000 and 1 in 58,000 for chromosome 13. Ring chromosome 13 is usually presented as a syndromic situation stigmatized by particular features, including developmental delay, mental retardation and CNS, skeletal or organ anomalies. As an experimental study, here a 31 years old male with no major phenotypic manifestation who was evaluated for azoospermia, while his karyotype revealed presence of a mosaic ring chromosome 13. He had a history of bilateral varicocelectomy and no other major finding in his routine infertility work up was determined. Genetic counseling did not provide any clue for mental disability or dysmorphic features. Pathology examination of the testicular tissue revealed very scarce number of spermatid/spermatozoa within the tubules in... [PMC10189157]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Human ring chromosomes (RCs) are rare diseases with an estimated newborn incidence of 1/50,000 and an annual occurrence of 2,800 patients globally. Over the past 60 years, banding cytogenetics, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), chromosome microarray analysis (CMA), and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) has been used to detect an RC and further characterize its genomic alterations. Ring syndrome featuring sever growth retardation and variable intellectual disability has been considered as general clinical presentations for all RCs due to the cellular losses from the dynamic mosaicism of RC instability through mitosis. Cytogenomic heterogeneity ranging from simple complete RCs to complex rearranged RCs and variable RC intolerance with different relative frequencies have been observed. Clinical heterogeneity, including chromosome-specific deletion and duplication syndromes,... [PMC9519620, PMC6949681, PMC7389945, PMC6169464, PMC4141575]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Reynolds syndrome (RS) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by the association of primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC) with limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis (lcSSc).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Primary biliary cirrhosis and systemic scleroderma

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of systemic sclerosis (SSc) in PBC patients is 5-15%. Conversely, the prevalence of PBC in SSc patients is about 2%. Females are more affected.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset occurs between 30-65 years. RS associates the features of PBC (fatigue, pruritus due to cholestasis, hepatomegaly) with most features of lcSSC (cutaneous calcifications, digital ulcers, facial telangiectasias, calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, esophageal involvement and sclerodactyly). In 50% of cases, symptoms of scleroderma occur prior to those of PBC. About 25-50 % of newly diagnosed RS patients have hyperpigmentation of skin, and jaundice at a later stage. Inflammatory arthropathies are observed in approximately 40% of patients with PBC. In some, RS is associated with other autoimmune diseases such as Sjögren's syndrome, autoimmune hemolytic anemia and (in one case) with thymoma. An overlap syndrome between nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver, PBC, and lcSSc may exist.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The pathological mechanism of RS has not yet been established, but it is assumed to be an auto-immune disorder. A heterozygous missense mutation in LBR exon 9 was identified in a Caucasian woman with RS. The mutation was predicted to induce a change in Lamin B receptor tertiary structure. Mutations in LBR may either have a direct pathogenic effect or constitute a predisposing factor in conjunction with other genetic and environmental factors.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of RS relies on the clinical findings for lcSSc and, for PBC, on the biochemical evidence of cholestasis which is based on marked elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase enzymes and IgM concentrations, a positive test for serum mitochondrial antibody, histologic evidence of non suppurative destructive cholangitis and destruction of interlobular bile ducts. An elevated serum bilirubin is a poor prognostic sign. Specific autoantibodies associated with both facets of the disease (antimitochondrial antibodies for PBC and anticentromere/antitopoisomerase for SSc), and suggestive microscopical abnormalities in the skin and liver have been found in patients affected with RS. Furthermore, a higher prevalence of clonal populations of CD8+ TCRBV3+ T cells has been found in RS.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The association with primary sclerosing cholangitis and SSc is extremely rare. Cholestasis in SSc patients may also reflect liver congestion due to right-sided heart failure in cases with severe pulmonary hypertension. Medications (antibiotics, anabolic steroids, birth control pills, chlorpromazine, cimetidine, estradiol) may cause cholestasis similar to that of PBC.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: RS occurs sporadically, but rare familial cases with an unknown inheritance pattern have been observed.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for RS and management is mainly supportive. It includes physiotherapeutic assistance and treatment of PBC with ursodeoxycholic acid so as to normalize the cholestatic parameters. Potential hepatotoxic drugs such as bosentan monohydrate or methotrexate can be used to treat some SSc manifestations, if transaminases are < 3 fold the upper limit of normal and remains < 3 fold the upper limit of normal over time.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver is a rare complication in those with SSc. Patients usually have a good prognosis, particularly when UDCA treatment is started in the early stages. RS prognosis depends on PBC's severity, but also depends on SSc evolution, as lcSSc has a higher risk of pulmonary arterial hypertension. The regular evaluation of liver function tests is useful for monitoring disease progression. Advanced age, hyperbilirubinemia, low serum albumin and cirrhotic liver biopsy indicate a worse prognosis. Survival of patients with RS seems to be better than that of patients with PBC alone.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Ménétrier disease (MD) is a rare premalignant hyperproliferative gastropathy characterized by massive overgrowth of foveolar cells in the gastric lining, resulting in large gastric folds, and manifesting with epigastric pain, nausea, vomiting, peripheral edema and, less commonly, anorexia and weight loss.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Hypoproteinemic hypertrophic gastropathy; Giant hypertrophic gastritis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Exact prevalence and incidence data are not available. MD appears to affect males slightly more than females.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The usual age of onset is between 30 and 60 years (average 55 years), although cases in childhood have been reported. The childhood variant often involves sudden onset and spontaneous regression. In adults, onset is often insidious with a wide spectrum of clinical manifestations. Affected patients typically present with abdominal pain, vomiting and nausea. Edema of peripheral tissues is often found. Other symptoms include asthenia, anorexia, and weight loss. Some individuals with MD are only mildly affected or are asymptomatic. Loss of protein from the gastrointestinal tract leads to hypoalbuminemia and peripheral edema. Mucosal ulceration is also described and can result in gastrointestinal bleeding. Disease course tends to be progressive, leading to gastric adenocarcinoma in 2-15% of cases. Complications include severe or recurrent infections and vascular thromboembolism.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is currently unknown but is thought to be acquired and to involve enhanced epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling in the gastric mucosa with local overproduction of transforming growth factor-alpha (TGF-alpha). In children, some MD cases have been linked to cytomegalovirus (CMV) and in adults some have been linked to Helicobacter pylori; however, the possible role of these infections remains to be elucidated. Rare familial cases point to a possible genetic component. The mechanism(s) underlying carcinogenesis in MD remain unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: MD is suspected on the basis of the constellation of clinical signs and symptoms but there are no formal diagnostic criteria. Diagnosis requires gastroscopic examination (showing enlarged gastric folds primarily involving the gastric corpus) with biopsy, preferably of full thickness gastric mucosa, which reveals characteristic histological features (extensive foveolar hyperplasia with corkscrew morphology in the absence of distortion of overall linear architecture, decreased or absent parietal cells, variable amounts of chronic inflammation with scattered clusters of eosinophils, and scattered strands of smooth muscle between mucous glands). Gastric acid secretion is generally markedly decreased or absent, while gastric mucous secretion is elevated. Serum gastrin levels remain relatively normal.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, hypertrophic hypersecretory gastropathy, hypertrophic lymphocytic gastritis, infiltrating neoplasm, polyps, and polyposis syndromes (e.g. juvenile polyposis syndrome, Peutz-Jeghers syndrome, and gastric adenocarcinoma and proximal polyposis of the stomach).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: MD is an acquired gastropathy but a genetic predisposition with autosomal dominant inheritance has been suggested in a few families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no recommended standard treatment. In some patients, treatment may be limited to supportive care with a high-protein diet. Inconsistent results have been achieved with anticholinergic drugs, acid suppression therapy, treatment against CMV infection in children, and H. pylori eradication in adults. Treatment with cetuximab, an EGFR neutralizing monoclonal antibody, has been successfully carried out. If there is concern about malignant transformation or in severe cases, partial or total gastrectomy may be required. Although there is no official recommendation, endoscopic surveillance may be offered every 1-3 years.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: MD tends to be a progressive disorder. Most of the patients ultimately require gastrectomy, either due to worsening symptoms or the risk of developing gastric cancer. The risk of malignant transformation is not well characterized.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, adrenogenital syndrome characterized by generalized, partial tissue insensitivity to glucocorticoids leading to variable phenotype, including asymptomatic individuals with only biochemical alterations or patients with ambiguous genitalia at birth in females, hypertension, acne, hirsutism, precocious puberty, male-pattern hair loss, anxiety and depression in both sexes, menstrual irregularities in women, and oligospermia in men.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Generalized glucocorticoid resistance syndrome is a rare genetic disorder, considerably rarer than 11β-hydroxylase deficiency, which is itself a relatively uncommon cause of male precocity. It can present as a sporadic or familial condition, caused by mutations in the gene encoding the glucocorticoid receptor. Specific mutations associated with the syndrome are rarely observed in patient cohorts or public databases. The condition may be underdiagnosed, particularly in low-income countries, due to challenges in differentiating it from other conditions like 11β-hydroxylase deficiency using less specific immunoassays. [PMC7050302, PMC5840839, PMC4010692]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of generalized glucocorticoid resistance syndrome relies on biochemical, dynamic, and genetic evaluations. Key biochemical markers include elevated serum, salivary, and 24-hour urinary cortisol, often with normal or slightly elevated ACTH, and increased dehydroepiandrosterone-sulfate and androstenedione. A characteristic finding is resistance to dexamethasone suppression. Genetic testing, typically Sanger sequencing of the NR3C1 gene, identifies mutations in the glucocorticoid receptor, such as p.E198X, p.R714Q, V575G, or I729V. In some instances, chromosomal microdeletion analysis, like for 16p11.2, may reveal ZNF764 haploinsufficiency. Functional assays demonstrating decreased receptor affinity for dexamethasone or thermolability can also support the diagnosis. Differentiation from 11β-hydroxylase deficiency is crucial, as older cortisol immunoassays may show falsely elevated due to cross-reactivity with 11-deoxycortisol, necessitating highly specific assays. [PMC7050302, PMC10913058, PMC5840839, PMC4010692, PMC3410270]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Generalized glucocorticoid resistance syndrome (PGRS) must be differentiated from 11β-hydroxylase deficiency (11-BHD), as both can present with gonadotropin-releasing hormone-independent isosexual male precocity. While PGRS is considerably rarer, other clinical, biochemical, or radiological parameters are often indistinguishable. The primary distinction lies in serum and urinary cortisol levels, which are elevated in PGRS but low or low-normal in 11-BHD. However, older immunoassays may show falsely elevated serum cortisol in 11-BHD due to cross-reactivity with accumulated 11-deoxycortisol, potentially leading to misdiagnosis of 11-BHD as PGRS. Therefore, highly specific cortisol assays are crucial for accurate differentiation. [PMC7050302]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The primary cause of branchio-oto-renal syndrome (BORS) is mutations in the EYA1 gene. The aim of was to investigate the clinical characteristics associated with induced podocyte reappearance in children with BORS and EYA1 mutations. We collected clinical and genetic data from a 4-year-old girl diagnosed with BORS and her family. Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) were derived from peripheral blood mononuclear cells of both the patient and healthy individuals, which were differentiated into podocytes in vitro. RNA-seq was used to analyze differentially expressed genes in both groups. Here, the proband, along with his brother and mother, exhibited symptoms of BORS. WES analysis identified a heterozygous splicing variant at the EYA1 locus: c.1050 + 5G > A, inherited from his mother. The proband was initially glucocorticoid-resistant. After tacrolimus treatment, his urine... [PMC12276159, PMC10913058, PMC5840839, PMC4010692, PMC3410270]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis of generalized glucocorticoid resistance syndrome is highly variable. It can present with severe, life-threatening complications such as hypertensive encephalopathy and punctate microinfarcts, which may require high doses of dexamethasone for control. However, the condition can also manifest with a mild phenotype, with fatigue as the only symptom, or even be clinically asymptomatic despite genetic mutations. The same genetic mutation can lead to distinct clinical presentations, suggesting the influence of other modifying factors on the disease course. [PMC12276159, PMC10913058, PMC5840839, PMC4010692, PMC423813]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by auditory canal atresia (resulting in moderate conductive hearing loss) associated with intellectual disability, ventricular septal defect, umbilical hernia, anteriorly displaced anus, various skeletal anomalies (such as mild clubfoot, long fifth fingers, proximally placed thumbs), and craniofacial dysmorphism which includes brachycephaly, prominent forehead, flattened occiput, midface hypoplasia, anteverted nares, and low set, posteriorly rotated ears with overlapping superior helix. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1987.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Aural atresia-multiple congenital anomalies-intellectual disability syndrome
