DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare infantile epilepsy syndrome characterized by an infantile-onset of sudden, frequent and generalized myoclonic seizures that occur in neurologically and developmentally normal patients, and later resolve during childhood with a generally favorable outcome.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Benign myoclonus epilepsy of infancy; Benign myoclonic epilepsy of infancy; MEI

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: MEI represents less than 2% of all epilepsies with onset in infancy, and occurs nearly twice as much in boys than girls.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: MEI typically occurs during infancy and is not associated to any developmental or neurological disorder. Seizures manifest as very sudden, brief and unexpected myoclonic jerks and can present as isolated events or in clusters of a few seconds duration, during wakefulness and/or in the first stages of sleep, and may be increased by drowsiness. They mostly affect the upper limbs (bilaterally) and the head, and may be accompanied by characteristic vocalizations and a quick upward deviation of the eyes. Myoclonic jerks are initially subtle at onset, then become more frequent and remarkable after a few weeks. They occur in variable intensity in the same child and when comparing children and/or episodes, and in rare severe cases may cause sudden falls. Seizures usually present spontaneously, although a variant phenotype described as reflex MEI has also been reported, with triggering by various sensory stimuli (acoustic, tactile, thermal, photic or proprioceptive). At diagnosis, myoclonic seizure is the only seizure type. However, a history of febrile seizure is not uncommon. The disease might resolve spontaneously, but most patients will be controlled with a monotherapy of antiseizure medication. Most of the patients have a favorable outcome. However, neurodevelopmental abnormalities were reported in some patients, including mild intellectual disability, behavioral disorders (e.g. ADHD, personality changes), learning disabilities, language impairment and poor coordination.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The genetic and molecular factors underlying MEI remain unknown. A history of febrile seizures was reported in some patients, as well as the presence of other types of genetic generalized epilepsy in some families.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is confirmed by electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring that may be supported by video recordings of the myoclonic episodes. Ictal EEG typically shows generalized discharges of polyspikes, polyspikes-and-waves, or spikes-and-waves associated with isolated or rhythmic myoclonic jerks. Background EEG is usually normal, although interictal abnormalities have been reported in rare cases, including focal paroxysmal discharges (often during sleep) and nonspecific myoclonic jerks.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other myoclonic epilepsies of genetic (chromosomal/gene), metabolic (lysosomal disease) or structural origin. In some cases, infantile spasms are considered. Other types of myoclonic epilepsies occur in young children, such as familial infantile myoclonic epilepsy, epilepsy with myoclonic-atonic seizure epilepsy, and epilepsy with myoclonic absences.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment with valproate or levetiracetam has shown very good response in MEI patients. Neuropsychological assessment should be carried out for the management of cases with a less favorable outcome.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The disease is associated with a good prognosis, as the myoclonic jerks generally subside in childhood with or without treatment. However, a less favorable and variable neurodevelopmental outcome was noted in some patients. A later-onset of other types of epilepsies was reported in rare cases, such as juvenile myoclonic epilepsy or myoclonic-astatic epilepsy.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The genetic generalized epilepsies (GGEs) have been proved to generate from genetic impact by twin studies and family studies. The genetic mechanisms of generalized epilepsies are always updating over time. Although the genetics of GGE is complex, there are always new susceptibility genes coming up as well as copy number variations which can lead to important breakthroughs in exploring the problem. At the same time, the development of ClinGen fades out some of the candidate genes. This means we have to figure out what accounts for a reliable gene for GGE, in another word, which gene has sufficient evidence for GGE. This will improve our understanding of the genetic mechanisms of GGE. In , important up-to-date genetic mechanisms of GGE were discussed. [PMC11960252]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Craniometadiaphyseal dysplasia, wormian bone type is an extremely rare craniotubular bone dysplasia syndrome described in fewer than 10 patients to date. Clinical manifestations include macrocephaly, frontal bossing, malar hypoplasia, prominent mandible and dental hypoplasia. Other skeletal anomalies include abnormal bone modeling in tubular bones, multiple wormian bones and deformities of chest, pelvis and elbows. An increased risk of fractures is noted.

A rare punctate palmoplantar keratoderma characterized by multiple small, round to oval or rhomboid, yellowish, hyperkeratotic papules and plaques most commonly localized to the palms of the hands and soles of the feet, potentially extending to the dorsum of the hands and feet in severe cases. Histopathological analysis shows hyperkeratosis, epidermal hypertrophy, and fragmentation and rarefaction of elastic fibers. The condition can be sporadic or familial.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): AKE; PPKP3; Punctate palmoplantar hyperkeratosis type 3; Punctate palmoplantar keratoderma type 3

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Acrokeratoelastoidosis is a rare condition, with only around 40 cases reported worldwide. It is primarily an autosomal dominant disorder, and most reported cases are familial. The condition has been observed globally, including a sporadic case reported from Saudi Arabia, which was the first from that region. Given its rarity, little is known about the disease, and further studies and case reports are needed to understand its characteristics and etiology. [PMC11959294, PMC4031972]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Acrokeratoelastoidosis is characterized by multiple hyperkeratotic papules. These lesions typically present bilaterally on the palms, soles, and dorsum of the hands and feet. However, sporadic cases with unilateral keratosis on the hand and foot have also been reported. [PMC4031972]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Acrokeratoelastoidosis (AKE) is an autosomal dominant disorder, though the specific gene mutation responsible remains unknown. It is characterized by the degeneration and/or fragmentation of elastic fibers. While most reported cases are familial, sporadic occurrences have also been noted. The co-occurrence of AKE with ARCL1A cutis laxa, a disorder linked to fibulin five gene mutations, suggests that fibulin gene alterations might contribute to AKE's pathogenesis. Overall, little is known about the disease's etiology, and further studies are required to understand its underlying mechanisms. [PMC11959294, PMC4031972]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Acrokeratoelastoidosis of Costa requires histopathological examination. This method is essential for differentiating it from focal acral hyperkeratosis. The key distinguishing feature is the absence of elastorrhexis in the histopathological findings, which is necessary for a correct diagnosis. [PMC4155971]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Acrokeratoelastoidosis of Costa (AKE) shares clinical features with focal acral hyperkeratosis, a rare autosomal dominant genodermatosis characterized by keratotic papules on the hands and feet. The primary distinction lies in histopathological examination, as AKE presents with elastorrhexis, which is absent in focal acral hyperkeratosis. Another condition to consider is cutis laxa type ARCL1A. Both AKE and ARCL1A are disorders of elastic fibers characterized by elastin degeneration and/or fragmentation. While AKE is an autosomal dominant disorder with an unknown gene mutation, ARCL1A is associated with a fibulin five gene mutation. The co-occurrence of these conditions in families suggests a possible shared pathogenesis, potentially involving fibulin gene alterations in AKE. [PMC11959294, PMC4155971]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Acrokeratoelastoidosis (AKE) is considered an autosomal dominant disorder, although the specific gene mutation responsible remains unknown. Most reported cases are familial, consistent with an inherited pattern, but sporadic cases have also been observed. While AKE involves elastic fiber degeneration, its pathogenesis is thought to be distinct from other conditions like cutis laxa type ARCL1A, which is associated with a fibulin five gene mutation. Further research is needed to fully understand the pathogenesis of AKE. [PMC11959294, PMC4155971, PMC4031972]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Acrokeratoelastoidosis is a rare condition characterized by bilateral multiple hyperkeratotic papules on the palms, soles, and dorsum of the hands and feet. To the best of our knowledge, only around 40 cases of acrokeratoelastoidosis have been reported worldwide, which are mostly familial. the first case from Saudi Arabia in a 5-year-old Saudi girl of Arabian origin, who presented symptoms of acrokeratoelastoidosis with unilateral sporadic keratosis on her left hand and left foot. We also review the clinical and histopathologic features, etiology, differential diagnosis and its treatment. Given the rarity of acrokeratoelastoidosis, little is known about the disease. Further studies are required to understand the pathogenesis of the disease for better treatment options. Additional case reports of acrokeratoelastoidosis will help in recognizing risk factors, patient characteristics,... [PMC4031972]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurologic disease characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness associated with uncontrollable sleep urges and cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone while awake, often triggered by pleasant emotions).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Gélineau disease; Narcolepsy-cataplexy; Hypocretin/orexin deficiency syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Narcolepsy type 1 prevalence is estimated between 1/2,000 and 1/5,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The age of onset varies between 10 and 30 years old and symptoms are lifelong. The average time between the age of appearance of the symptoms and the diagnosis is still very long, 10 years. Other, non specific, clinical signs include hypnagogic hallucinations, sleep paralysis, disturbed nocturnal sleep, and weight gain, especially in children.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is due to loss or impairment of the orexin/hypocretin neurons of the lateral hypothalamus that results in decreased hypocretin-1 levels in the cerebrospinal fluid. An autoimmune origin for the disease is highly suspected, particularly environmental factors interacting with susceptibility genes (more than 98% of the patients carry the HLA-DQB1*0602 allele); however, this is unproven.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Definitive diagnosis requires the presence of clinical symptoms, characteristic polysomnography findings and/or low hypocretin-1 levels in cerebral spinal fluid. Nocturnal and daytime polysomnography demonstrate an average sleep latency of under eight minutes with at least two sleep onset rapid eye movement periods (SOREMP) on multiple sleep latency tests. The presence of low hypocretin-1 levels (<110 pg/ml) in the cerebrospinal fluid can confirm the diagnosis with an excellent sensibility and specificity.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Cataplexy must be typical to be confident with the diagnosis. In absence of typical cataplexy, other causes of sleepiness must be considered, such as chronic insufficient sleep, idiopathic hypersomnia or narcolepsy without cataplexy, now called narcolepsy type 2.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Rare familial cases have been reported (<2%); however the mode of inheritance is unclear.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is nowadays only symptomatic, as the loss of orexin neurons is irreversible. It comprises stimulants (modafinil, methylphenidate, amphetamine, pitolisant, solriamfetol), anticataplectic drugs (antidepressants) or sodium oxybate. First-line treatment of diurnal sleepiness is often with modafinil but it can be also with pitolisant or sodium oxybate. Second-line treatments are methylphenidate, solriamfetol or amphetamines. Sodium oxybate is efficient for sleepiness, cataplexy and disturbed nocturnal sleep. A good sleep hygiene is always recommended, with scheduled short naps, and regular sleep habits.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Narcolepsy can severely disable scholarly and professional performances. The evolution of the disease is often stable with a frequent improvement of sleepiness and cataplexy, but with age there is an aggravation of the poor quality of night sleep.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Glycogen storage disease due to glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Glycogen debranching enzyme (GDE) deficiency, or glycogen storage disease type 3 (GSD 3), is a form of glycogen storage disease characterized by severe muscle weakness and hepatopathy.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): GSDIII; Glycogen storage disease type 3; Glycogenosis due to glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency; Glycogenosis type 3; Limit dextrinosis; Amylo-1,6-glucosidase deficiency; Cori disease; Cori-Forbes disease; Forbes disease; GDE deficiency; GSD due to glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency; GSD type 3; Glycogen storage disease type III; Glycogenosis type III

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Estimated prevalence is approximately 1/100,000 births (it may be higher among North Africans).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: GSD 3 commonly occurs in early childhood. Children present with hepatomegaly, growth retardation and occasional seizures related to hypoglycemia. Hepatomegaly may disappear with adulthood. Muscle weakness is slowly progressive. Other frequently associated signs include muscular hypotonia and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Symptoms often improve at puberty, except in the few cases where cirrhosis or myopathy appears. Biological findings include hypoglycemia without acidosis, hypertriglyceridemia, and hypertransaminasemia during childhood.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by mutations in the AGL gene (1p21), leading to a deficiency in the GDE that works with the glycogen phosphorylase to catabolize glycogen. The deficiency may occur in the liver and muscle (GSD 3a) or only in the liver (GSD 3b).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on the evidence of enzymatic deficiency in fresh leukocytes, fibroblasts, or on a liver or a muscle biopsy. Unlike GSD type 1, there is a response to glucagon after meals.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include the other forms of glycogen storage diseases.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible by enzyme assay and/or DNA analysis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is based on a specific diet, with enteral nasogastric drip feeding at night in case of hypoglycemia, frequent meals, and uncooked starch supplements. For patients with myopathy, a high protein diet is also recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Rarely, patients may develop complications such as hepatic failure or hepatocellular carcinoma.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Rieger's anomaly is a congenital ocular defect caused by anterior segment dysgenesis and is characterized by severe anterior chamber deformity with prominent strands and marked atrophy of the iris stroma, with hole or pseudo-hole formation and corectopia. The term covers the association of these iris and pupil anomalies with the features of Axenfelds anomaly.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Rieger anomaly, also known as Axenfeld-Rieger Syndrome, is a rare autosomal dominant genetic disease. It is characterized by considerable expressive variability, manifesting with both ocular and non-ocular features. Current data report an incidence of 1:200,000 in the population. [PMC9264492]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Rieger anomaly, often part of Axenfeld-Rieger Syndrome (ARS), is primarily characterized by ocular abnormalities including posterior embryotoxon, iridocorneal adhesions, corectopia, iris hypoplasia, and developmental glaucoma, which is a main cause of visual morbidity. Other ocular findings can include foveal hypoplasia or anomaly (particularly with PITX2 mutations), optic disc coloboma, microspherophakia, and aniridia, with phenotype variability even between eyes. Non-ocular manifestations of ARS may include mild craniofacial and dental malformations such as hypodontia or delayed teething, and sometimes cardiovascular issues or redundant periumbilical skin. Rieger anomaly is also a defining feature of SHORT syndrome, which presents with short stature, hyperextensibility, ocular depression, teething delay, insulin resistance, and characteristic facies. It can also be associated with Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome. [PMC12315255, PMC11005067, PMC9264492, PMC9426135, PMC8704954]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: A 33-year-old man presented with short stature, thin build, hearing impairment, Rieger anomaly, and a history of inguinal hernia. He also exhibited characteristic facies, including a triangular face with a small chin, deeply set eyes, and low-set ears. He was born with intrauterine growth restriction and developed diabetes during adolescence, requiring high-dose insulin therapy. For 19 years, an accurate diagnosis was not made. We performed direct sequencing of the insulin receptor gene and exons 11-16 of the PIK3R1 gene, identifying a c.1957A>T mutation (p.Lys653*) in the PIK3R1 gene, which confirmed a diagnosis of SHORT syndrome. Suspecting SHORT syndrome in individuals who exhibit some of its typical symptoms may facilitate an accurate diagnosis and enable effective management of this condition. Purpose: Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome (ARS) is characterized by ocular anomalies including... [PMC12315255, PMC11005067, PMC11141933, PMC8008669, PMC8504897]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Rieger anomaly can be a feature of several genetic syndromes. SHORT syndrome, characterized by short stature, hyperextensibility, ocular depression, and teething delay, frequently includes Rieger anomaly. Axenfeld-Rieger syndrome (ARS) also presents with Axenfeld-Rieger anomaly, sometimes asymmetrically with aniridia, and non-ocular findings like flat midface and hypodontia. Peters' anomaly, distinct from Rieger anomaly but also involving anterior segment dysgenesis and central corneal opacification, has been associated with mutations in the RIEG1 gene, which is also linked to Rieger syndrome. Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome, caused by a deletion on chromosome 4p16.3, can manifest with Axenfeld's anomaly among other ocular and systemic features. [PMC12315255, PMC8504897, PMC6123033, PMC5823738, PMC4022398]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Rieger anomaly is often associated with Axenfeld-Rieger Syndrome (ARS) or SHORT syndrome, both of which are rare autosomal dominant genetic conditions. ARS is linked to mutations in genes such as PITX2, as observed in a three-generation family, and can present with considerable expressive variability, including asymmetric phenotypes and unusual ophthalmic features. SHORT syndrome, which includes Rieger anomaly, is caused by PIK3R1 mutations, which can occur de novo and be transmitted from parent to child. Given the wide spectrum of mutations and variable clinical presentation, genetic testing is advantageous for accurate diagnosis and understanding familial transmission. [PMC9264492, PMC8008669, PMC6123033, PMC5823738, PMC4022398]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis of Rieger anomaly is significantly influenced by ocular complications, with glaucoma identified as the main cause of visual morbidity and decreased visual acuity. Anterior segment defects, including iris abnormalities and iridocorneal adhesions, also contribute to visual impairment. Additionally, newly identified posterior segment anomalies, such as foveal hypoplasia (particularly in PITX2-ARS) and other retinal irregularities, can further contribute to visual acuity deficits. Patients may experience peripheral visual field loss. Regular and complete ophthalmological examinations are crucial for identifying and managing these progressive ocular defects, including ocular hypertension, to mitigate visual deterioration. [PMC11005067, PMC8008669, PMC7739019]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A clinically heterogeneous group of mitochondrial disorders characterized by a reduction of the mitochondrial DNA copy number in affected tissues without mutations or rearrangements in the mitochondrial DNA. It is phenotypically heterogeneous, and can affect a specific organ or a combination of organs, with the main presentations described being either hepatocerebral (i.e. hepatic dysfunction, psychomotor delay), myopathic (i.e. hypotonia, muscle weakness, bulbar weakness), encephalomyopathic (i.e. hypotonia, muscle weakness, psychomotor delay) or neurogastrointestinal (i.e gastrointestinal dysmotility, peripheral neuropathy). Additional phenotypes include fatal infantile lactic acidosis with methylmalonic aciduria, spastic ataxia (early-onset spastic ataxia-neuropathy syndrome), and Alpers syndrome.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndromes are rare genetic disorders. Encephalomyopathic mtDNA depletion syndrome 13 (MTDPS13), an autosomal recessive condition linked to FBXL4 gene variants, has an estimated prevalence of 1/100,000-400,000. FBXL4 defects, which contribute to MTDPS13, are found in approximately 0.7% of suspected mitochondrial disease cases. The condition exhibits variability in disease manifestation, with diagnoses sometimes occurring later than typical onset, underscoring the importance of early recognition. [PMC12064180]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: The mitochondrial m.3243 A > G variant is a prevalent mitochondrial disease mutation that causes multisystem maternal inheritance disorders. While clinical severity typically correlates with mutation load, symptom manifestation may be influenced by other variants and environmental factors. Notably, the m.3290T > C variant has been hypothesized as a potential protective variant for m.3243 A > G pathogenicity, though clinical evidence remains limited. Here we reported a six-generation Chinese pedigree carrying both m.3243 A > G and homoplasmic m.3290T > C variants. Clinical and genetic analyses revealed that carriers with extremely high m.3243 A > G heteroplasmy (> 95%) exhibited severe symptoms, whereas those with moderate or high levels showed limited or no clinical symptoms. Our findings provide novel evidence for the protective role of m.3290T > C in mitigating m.3243 A > G... [PMC12166622, PMC11912596, PMC11855138, PMC11669185, PMC12064180]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome primarily involves symptomatic care, such as dichloroacetic acid for lactic acidosis in FBXL4-related cases. Deoxynucleoside supplementation, specifically purine deoxynucleosides, has shown promise in a zebrafish model of RRM2B-related MDDS by increasing mtDNA copy numbers and improving movement, suggesting a potential therapeutic approach. For specific forms of MDDS presenting with liver failure, such as those caused by TFAM or MPV17 variants, liver transplantation has demonstrated favorable outcomes, normalizing liver function and improving survival, particularly in patients with isolated liver disease or without neurological symptoms. While targeted treatments are generally rare for mitochondrial diseases, supportive therapies like coenzyme Q10, acetylcarnitine, and multivitamins are also utilized. [PMC12085779, PMC12064180, PMC12301291, PMC11668023, PMC10919458]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pseudoachondroplasia is characterized by severe growth deficiency and deformations such as bow legs and hyperlordosis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is estimated at around 1/60,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disorder is usually discovered during the second year of life with the onset of slow growth and walking difficulties. The short stature becomes more prominent with age and the hands and feet appear short and wide. Joint laxity is a general feature, but predominantly affects the hands. Defective epiphyseal growth causes early arthrosis. The limb deformation is caused by metaphyseal lesions.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disorder is caused by small mutations or deletions in the COMP gene (19p13.1) coding for the cartilage oligomeric matrix protein.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made on the basis of epiphyseal and metaphyseal anomalies detected on radiographs during the second year of life.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The principle differential diagnosis is achondroplasia, but the craniofacial anomalies present in this disorder are absent in patients with pseudoachondroplasia and radiographic findings differ significantly. Forms of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia may also be included in the differential diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is feasible if the mutation has been detected in an affected parent.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant, but most isolated cases are due to de novo mutations. Genetic counseling may be proposed and the recurrence risk is 50%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is based on physiotherapy, management of the spinal deformation and corrective orthopedic surgery. Intensive physical activity should be avoided. The limb deformation should be corrected surgically at the end of the growth period.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The final height prognosis is variable but the short stature may be moderately severe.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A pneumoconiosis, characterized by granulomatous inflammation, that occurs in individuals who develop beryllium sensitization (BeS), a cell-mediated immune response to environmental and occupational beryllium exposure. BeS precedes the lung disease that may present with chronic dry cough, fatigue, weight loss, chest pain, and increasing dyspnea.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Chronic beryllium lung disease; Berylliosis; Chronic berylliosis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The number of workers exposed to beryllium has been estimated at 1 million in the US, although no accurate figure exists for the US or globally. The prevalence of BeS in those exposed ranges from 1 - 20%. Chronic beryllium disease (CBD) among those with BeS ranges from 15-100%.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients with CBD can range from those who are asymptomatic to those with severe lung dysfunction. Manifestations occur a few months to many years after exposure to beryllium and include chronic dry cough, dyspnea on exertion, chest pain, fatigue, fever, night sweats and weight loss. Additional extrapulmonary manifestations of dermatitis and skin granulomas have been reported. Progressive pulmonary fibrosis can eventually lead to cor pulmonale and respiratory failure. An increased risk of lung cancer among workers exposed to high levels of beryllium has also been observed.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CBD is caused by occupational or environmental exposure to beryllium and beryllium-containing alloys (usually by inhalation of dust or fumes but also via contact with skin). Over time, in a subset of individuals, a cell-mediated immune response to beryllium may occur, causing the development of sensitized T cells that accumulate within the lungs and eventually form granulomas which can lead to fibrosis. A genetic variant in the HLA-DPB1 gene (6p21.3) with the presence of a glutamic acid at amino acid position 69 has been associated with the development of BeS and CBD.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on a history of exposure to beryllium, characteristic clinical findings and laboratory testing. BeS can be detected with the beryllium lymphocyte proliferation test (BeLPT). Chest x-ray, CT scan of the lungs, exercise tolerance testing and pulmonary function tests can also aid in the diagnosis. Sampling of the lung with for example bronchoscopy with biopsy and bronchoalveolar lavage is usually required to demonstrate granulomatous inflammation in the lungs and or sensitization to beryllium
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses are sarcoidosis (most common), hypersensitivity pneumonitis and tuberculosis as well as other occupational lung diseases (such as silicosis).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for CBD. Treatment involves recommendations for cessation of beryllium exposure as medically prudent, and the use of immunosuppressive therapies, such as corticosteroids (prednisone). Early symptomatic disease may be treated with inhaled corticosteroids along with a short acting bronchodilator. Methotrexate and other immunosuppressive therapies can reduce steroid side effects. The efficacy of corticosteroids may be limited and relapses can occur after cessation of therapy or when dose is lowered. Those with advanced disease and major breathing difficulties may require oxygen supplementation. In severe cases, a lung transplant may be suggested. Patients should refrain from smoking. CBD may be prevented by providing exposed workers with respiratory protective devices and protective clothing and by minimizing exposure through use of workplace administration and engineering controls. The BeLPT is used to identify patients early on and to define workplace areas for modification in order to ultimately reduce additional BeS and CBD cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis varies, with some patients remaining clinically stable for many years and some experiencing a gradual worsening of symptoms over time. A debilitating course resulting in respiratory failure is also possible but regular monitoring and treatment can slow down the disease process.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Chronic beryllium disease (CBD) is a granulomatous disorder that develops in individuals exposed to beryllium who carry the HLA-DP2 protein, specifically the HLA-DP2*0201 allele, of the major histocompatibility complex class II. The disease is proposed to be caused by the exposure to beryllium in genetically susceptible individuals. The binding of beryllium to the HLA-DP2 protein alters its conformational and ionization properties, which can trigger an inappropriate signaling cascade upon peptide binding. [PMC4219729]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Glycogen storage disease due to glycogen branching enzyme deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Glycogen branching enzyme (GBE) deficiency (Andersen's disease or amylopectinosis), or glycogen storage disease type 4 (GSD4), is a rare and severe form of glycogen storage disease which accounts for approximately 3% of all the glycogen storage diseases.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): GSD due to glycogen branching enzyme deficiency; GSD type 4; Glycogen storage disease type 4; Glycogenosis due to glycogen branching enzyme deficiency; Glycogenosis type 4; Amylopectinosis; Andersen disease; GSD type IV; Glycogen storage disease type IV; Glycogenosis type IV

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical presentation is extremely heterogeneous and involves the liver or the neuromuscular system. In the classical form, children are normal at birth, but develop hepatomegaly, hypotonia, and developmental delay during their first months. The disease then rapidly progresses to cirrhosis with portal hypertension and ascites, ultimately causing death in early childhood. A non-progressing hepatic form has been reported in a few cases. In the neuromuscular presentation, the age of onset ranges from fetal to adult age. The most severe form starts before birth with decrease or absence of fetal movements, arthrogryposis, hypoplastic lungs, and perinatal death. Patients with congenital forms have severe hypotonia, cardiomyopathy, depressed respiration and neuronal involvement. Milder forms have been reported with later-onset, marked by muscular weakness or cardiomyopathy and heart failure. Neurological adult forms with central and peripheral nervous system dysfunction have also been described, such as Adult Polyglucosan Body Disease (APBD), which is characterized by widespread upper and lower motor neuron lesions.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by mutations in the GBE1 gene (3p12) encoding GBE. GBE deficiency results in storage of abnormal glycogen that resembles an amylopectin-like structure (polyglucosan).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on biochemical findings from a liver biopsy, revealing an abnormal glycogen content, and on the evidence of enzymatic deficiency in the liver, muscle, erythrocytes, or fibroblasts, and in the trophoblast or cultured amniotic cells.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include galactosemia, hydrops fetalis, and tyrosinemia.APBD can also present with or without GBE deficiency indicating that different biochemical defects could result in an identical phenotype.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible by enzyme assay and/or DNA analysis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no specific treatment. A liver transplant can be proposed in severe forms without associated heart disease.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is unfavorable for patients with perinatal onset and classic forms who do not undergo liver transplantation. Long-term prognosis for others depends on the extent, severity, and progression of the condition.
DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Glycogen storage disease due to glycogen branching enzyme deficiency, specifically Adult Polyglucosan Body Disease (APBD), is a rare, autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder. It is primarily caused by mutations in the GBE1 gene. While typically associated with Ashkenazi Jewish populations, it can also occur in other ethnic groups, as evidenced by cases in non-Ashkenazi Jewish patients, expanding its known phenotypic and genetic spectrum. [PMC11961938]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Galactosialidosis is a lysosomal storage disease characterized by coarse facial features, macular ''cherry red spot'', and dysostosis multiplex. Clinical presentation can be heterogenous ranging from a severe, early-onset, rapidly progressive infantile form to late onset, slowly progressive juvenile/adult form.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Goldberg syndrome; Neuraminidase deficiency with beta-galactosidase deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Galactosialidosis is consistently described as a rare lysosomal storage disease or a rare genetic disorder. Its rarity contributes to diagnostic challenges, as the full spectrum of phenotypic variation is not well characterized due to the limited number of reported patients and its low frequency. Specific cases, such as those identified in a Thai-Lahu family, represent novel findings and further expand the known clinical and genotypic spectrum of this rare condition. [PMC11982657, PMC4065856]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Galactosialidosis is a lysosomal storage disease with variable onset. Early infantile forms can present with common findings alongside multiple congenital abnormalities, including complex cyanotic congenital heart disease with dextrocardia and situs inversus. The late-infantile onset is characterized by developmental delay, visceromegaly, coarse facies, and cherry-red macula. Recurrent infections due to T-cell defects have also been reported in affected individuals. [PMC11982657, PMC1015996]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Galactosialidosis is a rare lysosomal storage disease caused by a defect in protective protein/cathepsin A (PPCA), which is encoded by the CTSA gene. Mutations in the CTSA gene, including novel homozygous missense variants and compound heterozygous mutations, are responsible for the disorder. These genetic alterations can impair the dimerization process of PPCA, disrupting its proper protein maturation or function and leading to significantly reduced PPCA activity. [PMC11982657, PMC4065856]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Galactosialidosis is initiated by characteristic clinical features, such as developmental delay, visceromegaly, coarse facies, and cherry-red macula. Lysosomal enzyme assays are a key diagnostic step, revealing undetectable or significantly reduced activity of protective protein/cathepsin A (PPCA). Molecular diagnosis is established through genetic testing, including whole-exome sequencing, to identify pathogenic variants in the CTSA gene. Biochemical studies can further confirm the molecular diagnosis, and in vitro functional analysis may support the impact of identified variants on PPCA activity. [PMC11982657, PMC4065856]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Galactosialidosis, a lysosomal storage disease, presents with features such as developmental delay, visceromegaly, coarse facies, and cherry-red macula. These clinical signs, particularly the cherry-red macula, necessitate differentiation from other lysosomal storage diseases. Additionally, recurrent infections due to T-cell defects, as observed in some cases, may lead to consideration of primary immunodeficiencies. However, genetic testing for Galactosialidosis typically reveals variants in the CTSA gene, and exome sequencing may rule out other primary immunodeficiency genes. [PMC11982657]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Galactosialidosis is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by mutations in the CTSA gene, which encodes protective protein/cathepsin A. Genetic studies have identified both homozygous and compound heterozygous CTSA variants in affected individuals. Given the broad and expanding clinical and genotypic spectrum of the disease, genomic sequencing approaches, such as whole-exome sequencing, are valuable tools for molecular diagnosis, often confirmed by biochemical studies. This genetic information is essential for counseling affected families regarding inheritance patterns and recurrence risks. [PMC11982657, PMC4065856]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Benign familial neonatal epilepsy (BFNE) is a rare genetic epilepsy syndrome characterized by the occurrence of afebrile seizures in otherwise healthy newborns with onset in the first few days of life.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): BFNS; Benign familial neonatal convulsions; Benign familial neonatal seizures; Benign familial neonatal epilepsy; SeLNE

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is currently unknown since this disorder is possibly overlooked. About 100 families have been reported to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Seizure onset is usually between the second and the eighth day of life, in otherwise healthy newborns. Seizures are mostly focal involving alternatively both sides of the body and apnea is frequently associated. Seizures can be isolated or in clusters, are generally brief and last 1-2 minutes. However, they can be very frequent, occurring up to 20 times a day, and may evolve into status epilepticus. Seizures can occur during wakefulness and/or sleep, and are of a mixed type, starting with tonic posture and apnea, and often progressing to clonic movements and motor automatisms. During the interictal period, neonates are neurologically normal, although some degree of sedation can be seen in response to anti-epileptic medications. Although most patients do receive antiepileptic treatment in the neonatal period, seizures have been shown to remit spontaneously after the first months of life, and are usually not seen after the first year of life. However, about 10 to 15% of patients have febrile or afebrile seizures later in childhood. Subsequent psychomotor development is normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: BFNE is a genetically heterogeneous disorder due to mutations in the KCNQ2 (20q13.33) and KCNQ3 (8q24) genes that both code for voltage-gated potassium channel subunits. Mutations in KCNQ2 are also responsible for KCNQ2-related epileptic encephalopathy, a severe form of neonatal epilepsy.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Electroclinical events are suggestive of the disorder. Asymmetric tonic posturing associated with apnea and followed by focal or bilateral clonic jerking is the typical seizure type. In BFNE, neonates are neurologically normal and neurocognitive development is normal. Ictal electroencephalogram (EEG) may show focal interictal abnormalities, mainly over the central regions, but otherwise the EEG background is normal. The diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes benign familial neonatal-infantile seizures and benign familial infantile epilepsy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible if the disease-causing mutation has already been identified in the family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant with incomplete penetrance. Genetic counseling should be offered to affected families informing them of the 50% risk the offspring has of inheriting the disease-causing mutation and therefore being affected with the disorder. Rare cases are due to de novo mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The use of anticonvulsant therapy (e.g. phenobarbital, phenytoin, valproate, carbamazepine) is needed in most cases to stop seizures in the neonatal period, particularly in cases with very frequent seizures or status epilepticus. Usually, patients require treatment for the first 6-12 months of life. However, it is important for clinicians and family to be aware that some patients require treatment beyond 12 months of age.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is good. Seizures normally disappear during the first year of life and patients do not display any neurological sequelae. Later seizures have been reported, including occasional febrile seizures and idiopathic epilepsy syndromes in childhood, in particular Rolandic epilepsy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic hypoaldosteronism that typically presents in infancy (earl-onset familial hypoaldosternism) as a life-threatening electrolyte imbalance (failure to thrive, recurrent vomiting, and severe dehydration). A history of fever, diarrhoea, lethargy, poor weight gain, poor feeding since birth may also be present. Older subjects (late-onset familial hypoaldosteronism) are less severely affected or asymptomatic.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Familial hypoaldosteronism is a rare group of disorders, with most reported cases being sporadic. Its inheritance patterns vary, including autosomal recessive forms like aldosterone synthase deficiency and corticosterone methyloxidase deficiency type 2, X-linked forms such as adrenal hypoplasia congenita, and autosomal dominant forms linked to renin gene mutations. The condition typically presents in the early neonatal period or early childhood, often with a salt-wasting syndrome. [PMC10938521, PMC8272273, PMC8186340, PMC6549270, PMC10118833]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Isolated aldosterone synthase deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in CYP11B2 , resulting in impaired aldosterone synthesis. on a neonate with isolated aldosterone synthase deficiency caused by a novel homozygous CYP11B2 variant Chr8:NM_000498.3:c.400G>A p.(Gly134Arg). The patient presented shortly after birth with severe signs of aldosterone deficiency. Interestingly, segregation analysis revealed that the patient’s asymptomatic father was also homozygous for the CYP11B2 variant. Biochemical evaluation of the father indicated subclinical enzyme impairment, characterized by elevated aldosterone precursors. Apparently, this homozygous variant led to different clinical phenotypes in two affected relatives. DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Familial hypoaldosteronism is primarily a genetic disorder resulting from impaired aldosterone synthesis or function. A common cause is aldosterone synthase deficiency (also known as corticosterone methyloxidase deficiency types 1 and 2), an autosomal recessive condition caused by pathogenic or inactivating mutations in the CYP11B2 gene. These mutations lead to a block in aldosterone synthesis, with specific homozygous and compound heterozygous variants identified. Other etiologies include pseudo-hypoaldosteronism type 1, linked to mutations in the NR3C2 gene, and X-linked Adrenal Hypoplasia Congenita, caused by mutations in the NR0B1/DAX-1 gene, which can present with isolated hypoaldosteronism. Deficiency of 18-dehydrogenase has also been identified as a cause of blocked aldosterone synthesis. [PMC10938521, PMC8272273, PMC8186340, PMC6549270, PMC10118833]

DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of familial hypoaldosteronism typically involves mineralocorticoid replacement therapy, with oral fludrocortisone being a preferred treatment. This therapy has been shown to correct electrolyte imbalances, improve blood pressure, and enhance renal function in conditions such as aldosterone synthase deficiency, 18-dehydrogenase deficiency, and those caused by dominant renin gene mutations or X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita. In cases like X-linked adrenal hypoplasia congenita, hydrocortisone may also be required if full adrenal insufficiency develops. For Liddle's-like syndrome, characterized by hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism, potassium-sparing diuretics such as triamterene or amiloride can drastically improve the condition. Regular follow-up visits are recommended to monitor patient response. [PMC6549270, PMC10118833, PMC5966895, PMC4264543, PMC1546099]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic, syndromic eye disorder characterized by progressive joint stiffness, glaucoma, short stature and lens dislocation. This syndrome shows similarities to Moore-Federman syndrome.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: The syndrome, consistent with Weill-Marchesani syndrome, is a rare genetic disorder characterized by short stature, joint stiffness, and ocular abnormalities including microspherophakia and glaucoma. ADAMTS18-related ocular pathology, which can present with changes in lens dimensions and anterior segment dysgenesis, is also described as rare with few reported cases. While specific prevalence figures are not provided, both conditions are consistently noted for their rarity. [PMC11788680, PMC8175056]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Glaucoma-ectopia lentis-microspherophakia-stiff joints-short stature syndrome, also known as Weill-Marchesani syndrome, is characterized by short stature, brachydactyly, and joint stiffness. Ocular abnormalities are prominent, including microspherophakia, glaucoma (often narrow-angle with elevated intraocular pressure), lens subluxation, and severe myopia. Patients may also present with phenotypic dysmorphic features, and cardiac defects can occur occasionally. Glaucoma treatment is considered a significant challenge in this syndrome. [PMC8175056]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Glaucoma-ectopia lentis-microspherophakia-stiff joints-short stature syndrome, also known as Weill-Marchesani syndrome (WMS), is caused by homozygous mutations in the FBN1, ADAMTS10, ADAMTS17, or LTBP2 genes. Despite genetic heterogeneity, the syndrome is clinically homogeneous. The precise disease-causing mechanism is not fully understood but is thought to involve abnormal actin distribution and organization in fibroblasts, resulting from impaired connections between extracellular matrix components and the cytoskeleton. [PMC8175056]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis relies on a constellation of clinical features, including short stature, brachydactyly, joint stiffness, and ocular abnormalities such as microspherophakia and glaucoma. Other phenotypic findings may encompass distinctive facies, refractive error, anterior segment dysgenesis, retinal dystrophy, and changes in lens dimensions and shape. Radiological findings also contribute to the diagnostic process. Molecular examination, often via next-generation sequencing gene panels, can identify pathogenic variants in genes like ADAMTS18, FBN1, ADAMTS10, ADAMTS17, or LTBP2. Additionally, growth hormone provocation tests may be utilized. [PMC11788680, PMC8175056]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Weill-Marchesani syndrome (WMS) is a key differential diagnosis, characterized by short stature, brachydactyly, and joint stiffness. Ocular abnormalities are prominent, including microspherophakia, glaucoma, and lens subluxation. WMS is a rare genetic disorder caused by homozygous mutations in the FBN1, ADAMTS10, ADAMTS17, or LTBP2 genes, and despite genetic heterogeneity, it presents with a clinically homogeneous phenotype. [PMC8175056]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for this rare condition is informed by its genetic heterogeneity and variable manifestations. Pathogenic variants have been identified in genes such as ADAMTS18, FBN1, ADAMTS10, ADAMTS17, and LTBP2. Inheritance patterns include homozygous and compound heterozygous mutations. Molecular examination, including carrier gene testing or next-generation sequencing, can confirm familial or de novo variants. This knowledge aids in counseling patients regarding the genotypic and phenotypic spectrum of the disease. [PMC11788680, PMC8175056]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management primarily focuses on ocular complications, with glaucoma treatment being the greatest challenge. This involves surgical interventions such as lensectomy and scleral-fixated intraocular lens implantation, in addition to drug therapy to control intraocular pressure. [PMC8175056]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Purpose: ADAMTS18 -related ocular pathology is rare with few described cases. Features include distinctive facies, refractive error, anterior segment dysgenesis, and retinal dystrophy. Previous patients were found to have homozygous variants in ADAMTS18 . Here, a patient with compound heterozygous ADAMTS18 -related pathology and its associated findings. Observations: A 37-year-old male with a history of bilateral congenital nasolacrimal duct obstruction, dry eye syndrome, mild myopia, and accommodative esotropia presented to the Retina Service. He was found to have multiple features of anterior segment dysgenesis and retinal dystrophy, some of which have not been previously reported in association with ADAMTS18 variants. An inherited retinal disease (IRD) next-generation sequencing gene panel revealed heterozygous ADAMTS18 variants, both classified by the performing laboratory as likely... [PMC11788680]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, inherited disorder characterized by non-malignant lymphoproliferation, multilineage cytopenias, and a lifelong increased risk of Hodgkin's and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of ALPS is unknown. It has been characterized in more than 500 patients to date and has been reported worldwide in various ethnic groups.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: ALPS is clinically heterogeneous with the following primary clinical signs: lymphoproliferation, manifesting as lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly with or without hypersplenism, often improving with age, autoimmune disease, mostly involving blood cells, and an increased risk of lymphoma lifelong. Many patients develop non-malignant lymphoproliferation during the first years of life. Clinical manifestations of autoimmunity in the form of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, or autoimmune hepatitis are of variable severity but these signs are often absent at the time of diagnosis. Autoimmunity has been reported to potentially affect almost any organ, leading to uveitis, pulmonary fibrosis, gastritis, colitis, nephritis, urticaria, arthritis, or rarely autoimmune neurological complications. The disease course is also variable. Several genetic subtypes based on the causative genes and types of mutations have been proposed and result in often similar clinical presentations and outcomes. These include ALPS-FAS, ALPS-FASLG (FASgene), ALPS-CASP10 (CASP10), and ALPS-U (undetermined genetic defect).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: ALPS is caused by defective lymphocyte homeostasis. Germline mutations in the FAS (10q24.1), FASLG (1q23), or CASP10 (2q33-q34) genes are known to be associated with ALPS. 75% of cases are associated with heterozygous mutations in FAS. The second largest group (10%) has somatic mutations in FAS, while CASP10 (2-3%) and FASLG (<1%) mutations are extremely rarely reported. Some patients do not have mutations in any of these genes (ALPS-U). More recently one case of an ALPS-like disorder due to mutation in the PRKCD gene (3p21.31) was reported. This patient however did not have elevated DNT cells and hence does not fit the diagnostic criteria.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical, laboratory and genetic findings. A definitive diagnosis is established in the presence of both of the required diagnostic criteria, i.e. chronic non-malignant, non-infectious lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegalyand elevated TCR alpha/beta-double-negative T cells (DNTs) with normal or elevated lymphocyte counts, along with one primary accessory criterion, including defective lymphocyte apoptosis, and germline or somatic mutations in FAS, FASLG or CASP10.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Depending on the specific genetic mutation, inheritance may be autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Some patients may require chronic immunosuppressive therapies with sirolimus and mycophenolate mofetil.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis for ALPS patients remains guarded. ALPS-FAS patients have a significantly increased risk of non-Hodgkin's and Hodgkin's lymphoma which can occur at any age and responds to conventional chemotherapy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hereditary disorder due to autosomal dominant transmission with hamartosis characterized by multiple early-onset basal cell carcinoma (BCC), multiple jaw keratocysts and skeletal abnormalities.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Basal cell nevus syndrome; Gorlin-Goltz syndrome; NBCCS; Nevoid basal cell carcinoma syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of Gorlin syndrome (GS) is estimated to be 1/31,000-1/164,000 in Europe. Birth prevalence in the UK is reported to be 1/19,000. Males and females are equally affected.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: GS is characterized by the early onset of mandibular odontogenic keratocysts (2nd decade of life) and/or multiple BCCs (most commonly seen on the face, back and chest - 3rd decade of life). Approximately 60% of individuals have a recognizable appearance with macrocephaly, frontal bossing, coarse facial features, and facial milia. Ectopic calcification, particularly in the falx, is present in more than 90% of affected individuals by age 20 years. Palmar or plantar pits (asymmetrical, 2-3 mm in diameter, 1-3 mm in depth and developing in the 2nd decade) and skeletal anomalies (fusion of vertebrae, wedge-shaped vertebrae, bifid or fused ribs, hemivertebra, kyphoscoliosis, pectus deformity, sprengel deformity, syndactyly, polydactylia) are also reported. Additional features include facial dysmorphism (cleft lip/palate, macrocephaly), eye anomalies (cataract, coloboma, microphthalmos) and lymphomesenteric cysts. A predisposition to malignant or benign tumors such as medulloblastoma, meningioma, papillary fibroelastoma of the heart, ovarian fibroma (commonly bilateral and calcified), fibrosarcoma, nephroblastoma is observed.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: GS is caused by loss of functions due to mutations in the tumor suppressor gene PTCH1 (9q22.1-q31), which encodes the receptor of the sonic hedgehog ligand. Environmental exposure and other modifier genes (SUFU; PTCH2) may contribute to the variable expressivity observed in the clinical presentation. Mutations in PTCH1 also account for the majority of features in monosomy 9q22.3.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based upon presence of two major criteria and one minor criterion or one major and three minor criteria. Physical examination, radiography, ophthalmologic evaluation, dentist or orthodontist examination, skin examination, ultrasound test and echocardiography are essential to identify the criteria leading the diagnosis. Identification of a heterozygous germline PTCH1 or SUFU pathogenic variant on molecular genetic testing establishes the diagnosis if clinical features are inconclusive.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes: Sotos syndrome, Brooke-Spiegler syndrome, Bazex syndrome, Rombo syndrome, Muir-Torre syndrome, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, isolated hydrocephaly or megalencephaly, an autosomal dominant or X-linked syndrome of hypotrichosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible with ultrasound scans and DNA analysis extracted from fetal cells after amniocentesis or chronic villus sampling. Preimplantation genetic diagnosis may be proposed to families in which the pathogenic variant has been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant, with high penetrance and variable expressivity. Genetic counselling, including testing family members to distinguish familial mutations from de novo pathogenic variants, and assessment of genetic cancer risk should be offered. The optimal time for determination of genetic risk and discussion of the availability of prenatal testing is before pregnancy. It is appropriate to offer genetic counseling (including discussion of potential risks to offspring and reproductive options) to young adults who are affected or at risk.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The treatment of choice for multiple BCC consists of a combined approach including surgery supplemented by cryotherapy, laser, photodynamic therapy or topical treatments. Use of oral retinoids is also suggested. Oral vismodegib may reduce development of BCC but adverse events are common. Sonic hedgehog inhibitors may be particularly helpful with lesions around the eyes. Radiation therapy must be avoided as it can cause invasion of BCC years later. Photodynamic therapy is particularly suitable for thin lesions of <2 mm on ultrasound. Surgical treatment using Mohs' microsurgery appears particularly effective. Jaw keratocysts are often recurrent and demand repeated surgical excisions. Ovarian fibroma is usually managed with conservative surgery to preserve normal ovarian tissue.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy in GS is not affected. Early diagnosis is important due to susceptibility to multiple neoplasms in early age. Ovarian tumors are usually benign with risk of recurrence. In young patients, mandibular odontogenic keratocysts can cause displacement of developing teeth and may be associated with unerupted teeth and cause root resorption.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma, characterized by the infiltration of monoclonal lymphoplasmacytic cells in the bone marrow and the production of serum immunoglobulin M (IgM) monoclonal protein.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Waldenström macroglobulinemia (WM) has an overall incidence ranging between 1 in 123,000 and 1 in 263,000 persons/year in Europe and the USA, respectively and represents approximately 1-2% of all hematological malignancies. The median age at diagnosis is 72 years, and it is twice as frequent in men.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: WM is preceded by an early precursor stage, termed IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (IgM-MGUS), and a subsequent stage, termed smoldering WM. Both stages are asymptomatic, although smoldering WM is associated with an increased risk of progression to symptomatic WM. Symptoms in WM are either related to the proliferation of tumoral cells or directly to the secreted IgM paraprotein. Fatigue related to normochromic normocytic anemia is the most common presenting symptom (80%). Less frequently, patients present lymphadenopathy and/or hepato/splenomegaly (20-25%), hyperviscosity syndrome (15-25%), with blurred vision, headache, epistaxis, and more rarely retinal hemorrhage or serious neurologic complications (mental confusion, stroke), which occurred mainly when IgM levels were >5 g/dL. Bleeding symptoms can occur due to acquired von Willebrand disease and/or thrombocytopenia. IgM-related neuropathy is seen in approximately 20-30% of cases; the most frequent being anti-myelin-associated glycoprotein (MAG) neuropathy which typically presents as gradually worsening distal sensory loss and ataxic gait. Visceral infiltration is rare but may target the kidney, lungs/pleura and central nervous system (Bing-Neel syndrome). Major complications include bone marrow failure, autoimmune cytopenia, large B-cell lymphoma, and infections.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Exact etiology is unknown. Familial predisposition has been described in around 20-30% of WM cases, and first-degree relatives of WM patients have an increased risk of developing the disease. The most important acquired risk factor is preexisting IgM-MGUS.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is confirmed by the identification by electrophoresis and immunofixation of an IgM monoclonal protein in the serum and a bone marrow biopsy showing infiltration of clonal lymphoplasmacytic cells. WM's pathologic designation is lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma (IgM-type) according to the WHO Classification of Tumors. Cells test typically negative for CD3, CD10, CD5, CD23 and CD103 markers but express pan B cell markers CD19 and CD20. The MYD88 L265P mutation is present in around 95% of WM patients and is a reliable molecular diagnostic tool to distinguish WM from other closely-related B-cell chronic lymphoproliferative disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other forms of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, notably marginal zone lymphoma; IgM-multiple myeloma; B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia; and IgM-MGUS monoclonal gammapathies of undetermined significance. Infections like hepatitis, AIDS, and various rheumatological disorders also raise IgM levels.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for WM. Asymptomatic/smoldering WM patients are simply monitored and have a life expectancy similar to the one of age-matched general population. Treatments given to symptomatic patients depend on many factors (e.g. age, comorbidities, need for rapid response, genetics) and rely on two main therapeutic options: chemoimmunotherapy (CIT) and BTK inhibitors (BTKi). CIT, consisting in the combination of an anti-CD20 antibody and an alkylating agent is the standard first-line treatment in most countries. The most widely used CIT regimen is the combination of dexamethasone-rituximab-cyclophosphamide (DRC) which can be offered to patients of all ages, especially those who are frail, and do not require rapid disease control. Bendamustine-rituximab (BR) is mostly used in fit patients, particularly when rapid disease control is needed. Bortezomib-based therapies as BR provide rapid disease control. BTKi (ibrutinib, zanubrutinib) have been approved for symptomatic WM patients as a first-line treatment, particularly for those who are not candidates for chemo-immunotherapy, and in relapsing patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: For symptomatic WM, the median survival time after starting treatment is around 10 years and is continuously improving.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital disorder of copper metabolism with severe multisystemic manifestations that are primarily characterized by progressive neurodegeneration and marked connective tissue anomalies. A pathognomonic feature is the typical sparse, abnormal steely hair.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Menkes kinky hair disease; MD; Menkes syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence at birth is estimated at 1/300,000 and 1/360,000 in Europe and Japan, respectivley. In Australia, the birth prevalence is much higher (1/50,000-100,000), likely due to a founder effect. The disorder is X-linked and thus primarily affects males.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Menkes disease (MD) manifests in the neonatal period. Most patients are born at term with appropriate birth measurements. Cephalohematomas and spontaneous fractures are occasionally observed at birth. In the early neonatal period, patients may present with prolonged jaundice, hypothermia, hypoglycemia and feeding difficulties. Pectus excavatum and umbilical and inguinal hernias have also been reported. Unusual sparse and dull scalp hair is often the initial observation at the age of 1-2 months. Characteristically, the hair appears hypopigmented/depigmented, resembles steel wool and is friable, especially in the areas of the scalp subjected to friction. Additional symptoms are failure to thrive, poor eating, vomiting, and diarrhea. The appearance of pale skin, frontal or occipital bossing, micrognathia and pudgy cheeks may be observed. Patients develop gradual motor dysfunction and seizures. Muscular hypotonia in early life is replaced later-on by spasticity and weakness of the extremities. The clinical course is usually severe. Variable forms exist with occipital horn syndrome (OHS) being the mildest recognized form, which further presents with prominent bony exostoses and bladder diverticula.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MD is caused by pathogenic variants in ATP7A (Xq21.1) encoding a membrane bound copper-transport protein (Cu2+-transporting ATPase-alpha polypeptide). To date, about 300 different variants in this gene have been reported. There is no obvious correlation between the variants and the clinical course.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Initial diagnosis is based on clinical features (typical hair changes associated with hypotonia and delayed neuromotor development) and supported by demonstration of reduced levels of serum copper and ceruloplasmin. However, in the neonatal period these markers should be interpreted with caution, as their levels are also low in healthy newborns. In this period, plasma catecholamine analysis (ratio of DOPA to dihydroxyphenylglycol), indicative of dopamine beta-hydroxylase deficiency, may be used as a diagnostic test when the clinical diagnosis suggests MD. Although not specific, other laboratory investigations are useful to complete the clinical work up, these include light microscopy (for hair), radiological imaging (for generalized osteoporosis, metaphyseal flaring and spurs in the long bones, diaphyseal periosteal reaction and thickening, and Wormian bones in the cranial sutures), and arteriography (arterial tortuosity, especially of the intracranial arteries). Definitive diagnosis is based on molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Marfan syndrome, cutis laxa syndromes, mitochondrial disorders, osteogenesis imperfecta and child abuse.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible where the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in a family member and the preferred situation is to determine the carrier status of the mother prior to pregnancy and prenatal diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is X-linked recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to couples where the mother is a carrier of a pathogenic variant, informing them that the risk for a male fetus to be affected is 50% at each pregnancy. In rare cases, a female fetus may be affected (manifesting heterozygote) and this possibility should also be considered during genetic counselling. Similarly, germ-line mosaicism has been described and, although probably infrequent, it should also be discussed when counselling non-carrier mothers of singleton cases.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is mainly symptomatic. Early parenteral copper-histidine supplementation may modify disease progression and some symptoms by providing extra copper to tissue and to copper-dependent enzymes. Oral administration of copper is ineffective as it is trapped in the intestines.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor and patients usually die in early childhood. However, careful medical care, and possibly copper administration, may extend life span.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A congenital malformation syndrome characterized by mandibulofacial dystosis (malar hypoplasia, micrognathia, external ear malformations) and variable preaxial limb defects.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Mandibulofacial dysostosis with preaxial limb anomalies; NAFD; Nager acrofacial dysostosis; Preaxial acrodysostosis
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown; more than 100 cases of NAFD have been published.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: NAFD is characterized by mandibulofacial anomalies that include downward slant of palpebral fissures, ptosis of upper lids, coloboma of lower lids, deficiency of eyelashes of the medial one-third to two-thirds of the lower eyelids, hypoplasia of the malar eminences, hypoplasia of the maxilla, cleft palate, absence or hypopoplasia of the palatal velum, choanal atresia, extension of a ''tongue'' of temporal hair down the sides of the cheeks. Cleft lip is rare. Limb defects are predominantly preaxial with hypoplasia or absence of thumbs being the most characteristic feature, frequently associated with radio-ulnar synostosis and/or aplasia/hypoplasia of the radius. Triphalangeal thumbs and other abnormalities of the digits have also been reported and a small percentage of patients also have lower limb malformations. Otologic and oral anomalies frequently lead to bilateral conductive hearing loss, speech difficulties and upper respiratory airways obstruction. Most Nager syndrome individuals have normal vision and intelligence.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In approximately 50% of patients, NAFD has been associated with heterozygous mutations in the SF3B4 gene (1q21.2), coding for a component of the splicing machinery.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on physical and radiological examination or the identification of a mutation in SF3B4.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis may include mandibulofacial dysostosis syndromes such as Treacher-Collins syndrome, and other acrofacial dysostoses (AFD) such as the AFD Catania type, the AFD Palagonia type, the AFD Genee-Wiedemann type, the AFD Rodriquez type as well as mandibulofacial dysostosis with microcephaly. Patients with the oculoauriculovertebral (OAV) spectrum may also have overlapping features.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis can be performed by ultrasonography or molecular testing of SF3B4.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Nager syndrome is likely genetically heterogenous with confirmed autosomal dominant inheritance, but autosomal recessive inheritance is suspected based on sibling recurrence in consanguineous families. Genetic counseling requires careful evaluation of parents and sibs of an affected child, in order to determine if the disease has a familial origin or if it occurred sporadically. If one parent is mildly affected, recurrence risk is 50% and a 25% risk cannot be excluded when parents are apparently normal.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management must focus on neonatal respiratory distress (tracheostomy) and feeding difficulties (gastrostomy). Surgery can be considered for repair of clefts, management of severe micrognathia as well as temporomandibular joint dysfunction. Hearing aids can be proposed. Language and phonological impairment must be managed by a specific speech therapy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: After infancy, most patients are healthy and are presumed to have a normal lifespan. Ongoing medical issues are usually only related to airway obstruction or temporomandibular joint dysfunction in patients with more severe manbibular malformations.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Esophageal carcinoma (EC) is a tumor arising in the epithelial cells lining the esophagus and can be divided into two subtypes: esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated annual incidence of EC in Europe is approximately 1/13,300.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease usually presents between the ages of 50-70 years. It is often asymptomatic until it has reached an advanced disease stage with the first symptoms usually being difficulty in swallowing (dysphagia), especially present when swallowing dry foods. Unintentional weight loss is also common. Manifestations of back or chest pain, hoarseness of voice, unexplained coughing, protracted hiccups, and severe reflux may be presenting or associated symptoms. More rarely, neck swelling from adenopathies may be the initial manifestation.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is unknown but many risk factors for esophageal cancer have been identified. Alcohol abuse, smoking, lye ingestion, radiation therapy and achalasia are associated with ESCC. EAC is associated with Barrett's esophagus, which is intestinal metaplasia (replacement of normal esophageal epithelia by intestinal epithelia), associated with chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease. EAC has also been associated with obesity, in particular visceral obesity and metabolic syndromes which are more common in men than in women.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: A de novo whitish subepithelial lesion (SEL) with irregular vascular hyperplasia was detected in the lower thoracic esophagus during endoscopic surveillance. Special types of esophageal cancer were suspected; however, endoscopic biopsy specimens were inadequate for a diagnosis. Ten days later, endoscopic ultrasound showed a 7-mm homogeneously hypoechoic round mass in the submucosa, and a biopsy confirmed a histological diagnosis of esophageal neuroendocrine carcinoma (eNEC). Based on the clinical diagnosis of cT2N0M0, subtotal esophagectomy followed by adjuvant chemotherapy was performed immediately after endoscopic reexamination revealing a 20-mm reddish SEL. We herein report the marked changes in endoscopic findings of eNEC within 1.5 months. An 80-year-old woman with a history of endoscopic balloon dilation for esophageal stricture caused by accidental ingestion of caustic soda... [PMC12222931, PMC11785629, PMC12309025, PMC11129664, PMC11347470]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling may be relevant for individuals with a family history of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (EC). A case report describes a patient with early-onset EC who had a family history of the disease, alongside other risk factors such as consuming high-temperature and pickled foods. This suggests that a family history, particularly in patients with achalasia of the cardia, may contribute to the early development of EC. Clinicians should consider family history as a high-risk factor when assessing patients and planning follow-up, especially after procedures like per-oral endoscopic myotomy. [PMC10843513]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Esophageal carcinoma, particularly advanced squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC), synchronous multiple primary esophageal cancer (SMPEC), primary small cell carcinoma (PSCCE), and SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated esophageal carcinoma (UEC), generally carries a poor prognosis. These aggressive malignancies are often diagnosed at advanced stages, with PSCCE and SMARCA4-deficient UEC showing particularly short survival times (e.g., median 2.6 months). Aggressive metastasis and a high risk of recurrence after resection further contribute to poor outcomes. However, some advanced ESCC cases have demonstrated improved progression-free survival (e.g., 12 to over 36 months) and even complete remission with multi-modality treatments, including chemotherapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, oncolytic adenovirus, and localized radiotherapy. [PMC12256217, PMC12023257, PMC11920187, PMC11867956, PMC11129664]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism characterized by hypogonadism due to selective deficiency of follicle stimulating hormone (FSH). Clinical manifestations are primary amenorrhea, absent or incomplete breast development, and infertility in women, and small testes, azoospermia, and infertility in men. Luteinizing hormone is elevated in the gonadotropin-releasing hormone stimulation test, while the FSH response is impaired.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Isolated follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) deficiency presents with primary subfertility or infertility in both sexes. In females, clinical features include primary amenorrhea and impaired pubertal development, with undetectable basal and GnRH-stimulated serum FSH. A genetic cause, such as a homozygous nonsense mutation in the FSHβ gene, can lead to disturbed production of bioactive FSH. Males present with primary subfertility, non-obstructive azoospermia, and low seminal fluid volume, despite normal external genitalia, potency, and libido. They exhibit an isolated FSH deficiency with elevated testosterone and normal luteinizing hormone and prolactin levels, typically without structural abnormalities on imaging. [PMC7311626, PMC5769506]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Isolated follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) deficiency can stem from genetic mutations affecting pituitary development or the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis. A homozygous nonsense mutation in the FSHβ gene, such as Arg97X, can disturb the structural stability of the FSH protein, leading to its deficiency despite normal mRNA and protein expression. Furthermore, the synthesis of FSH by pituitary gonadotrope cells is critically regulated by specific signaling molecules and transcription factors. SMAD3 is required for FSH synthesis in vivo, and its absence, particularly with SMAD4, in nearly undetectable FSHβ mRNA levels. Similarly, forkhead protein L2 (FOXL2) is an essential gonadotrope-restricted transcription factor for selective FSH synthesis, with its ablation leading to diminished pituitary FSHβ mRNA production and FSH deficiency. [PMC8708611, PMC7311626, PMC5313102, PMC3589670]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of isolated follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) deficiency involves evaluating reproductive endocrine parameters. This typically reveals undetectable basal and GnRH-stimulated serum FSH in females, or an isolated FSH deficiency with normal luteinizing hormone and prolactin but elevated testosterone in males. Genetic testing, specifically DNA sequencing of the FSHβ gene, is used to identify causative mutations, such as the homozygous nonsense mutation Arg97X. Imaging studies, including CT scans and pituitary MRI, are often performed to exclude other pathologies and are typically normal. Panel testing for congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which can involve a curated set of genes, is also a relevant genetic diagnostic approach. [PMC10133250, PMC7311626, PMC5769506]
