DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Bone is the most frequently affected organ (80% of cases), followed by the skin (35% of cases) and then the pituitary gland (25% of cases). However, involvement of these organs does not affect the vital prognosis. Involvement of the hematopoietic system (cytopenia), lungs and liver is much less common (15-20% of cases) but results in more severe disease. The aggressive nature of the hematological forms in young children, the long-term sequelae associated with lung and liver (sclerosing cholangitis) involvement, and the neurodegenerative manifestations (2-5% of cases) make LCH a severe disease. The disease may occur as one or several crises. It may result in aesthetic or functional sequelae with variable expression depending on the sites involved (deafness, respiratory or hepatic failure, diabetes insipidus, growth hormone deficiency, and cerebellar syndrome). In adults, the clinical picture is characterized by isolated lung disease, with a strong association with smoking.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The origin of the LCH lesions, originally thought to be neoplastic proliferation of Langerhans cells, was found to instead be similar to proliferation of immature myeloid precursors, with activation of one gene of the MAPK/ERK pathway (most frequently BRAF) involving the macrophagic cells.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of LCH usually relies on histological and immunohistochemical analysis of the affected tissues. A thoracic CT scan showing typical radiological findings may allow diagnosis in adults with isolated lung involvement.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: A large range of alternative diagnoses may be considered, depending on the associated clinical picture and radiological findings.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The choice of therapeutic approach depends on the extent of disease, determined by routine examinations (clinical examination, hemogram, liver function tests, and bone and chest radiographs). Local treatment is usually effective for forms limited to one organ. In children, treatment of the systemic forms relies on the combination of corticosteroids and vinblastine. Smoking cessation is necessary for adults with lung involvement. Second-line treatments are available in specialized centers for patients with progressive disease. Given the polymorphic and chronic nature of the disease, management of LCH should be multidisciplinary. Treatment protocols for adult forms of the disease are less well established than those for patients with childhood onset. Long-term follow-up is needed for detection and management of later-onset sequelae.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The vital prognosis is not usually affected in childhood forms, except in cases with hematological involvement resistant to first-line therapies.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cardiomyopathy-hypotonia-lactic acidosis syndrome is characterised by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, muscular hypotonia and the presence of lactic acidosis at birth. It has been described in two sisters (both of whom died within the first year of life) from a nonconsanguineous Turkish family. The syndrome is caused by a homozygous point mutation in the exon 3A of the SLC25A3 gene encoding a mitochondrial membrane transporter.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Cardiomyopathy-hypotonia-lactic acidosis syndrome is a fatal infantile disorder, often presenting congenitally with severe lactic acidosis, muscular hypotonia, and cardiomyopathy, including hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and cardiomegaly. Affected infants typically die within the first year of life, with familial cases reported. Pathological findings can include increased numbers of skeletal muscle mitochondria, fatty infiltration of the viscera, and spongy encephalopathy. High lactate-to-pyruvate ratios and hypermetabolism may also be observed. [PMC1821108, PMC442203]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Cardiomyopathy-hypotonia-lactic acidosis syndrome is caused by various mitochondrial defects affecting oxidative phosphorylation. One identified etiology is a homozygous mutation in the SLC25A3 gene, leading to mitochondrial phosphate-carrier deficiency and impaired ATP synthesis in muscle. Another cause is a familial deficiency of the reduced nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide dehydrogenase component of complex I of mitochondrial electron transport, which impairs the oxidation of NADH-linked substrates. Both defects result in a disorder of oxidative phosphorylation. [PMC1821108, PMC442203]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of cardiomyopathy-hypotonia-lactic acidosis syndrome involves evaluating clinical features like lactic acidosis, hypotonia, and cardiomyopathy, often accompanied by elevated lactate and lactate-to-pyruvate ratios. Genetic testing can identify specific mutations, such as a homozygous c.215G->A in SLC25A3. Further investigation includes functional studies of mitochondria from muscle or liver biopsies, demonstrating deficiencies in ATP synthesis or NADH-linked substrate oxidation. Enzyme activity assays, particularly for mitochondrial NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I), can confirm defects in mitochondria and fibroblasts. Histopathological examination of muscle may also reveal increased mitochondrial numbers. [PMC1821108, PMC442203]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: A key differential diagnosis includes familial deficiency of a component of mitochondrial NADH dehydrogenase (complex I), which presents with fatal congenital lactic acidosis, hypotonia, and cardiomyopathy. This condition is characterized by a high lactate-to-pyruvate ratio, hypermetabolism, and pathological findings such as increased skeletal muscle mitochondria, cardiomegaly, fatty visceral infiltration, and spongy encephalopathy. Deficient NADH dehydrogenase activity (complex I) is observed in affected individuals. [PMC442203]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The syndrome is caused by genetic mutations, with cases reported in siblings. One study identified a homozygous mutation in the SLC25A3 gene in two affected siblings, indicating an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Another report described a familial deficiency of mitochondrial NADH dehydrogenase (complex I) in an infant whose sister had died with a similar disorder, also consistent with recessive inheritance. Genetic counseling should address the familial nature and the likely autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. [PMC1821108, PMC442203]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Cardiomyopathy-hypotonia-lactic acidosis syndrome is severe, with reported cases indicating a fatal outcome in infancy. Two siblings with mitochondrial phosphate-carrier deficiency died within their first year of life. Similarly, an infant with a deficiency of the NADH dehydrogenase component of complex I, along with his sister, experienced a fatal congenital lactic acidosis. [PMC1821108, PMC442203]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A drug-related embryofetopathy that can occur when an embryo/fetus is exposed to the anticonvulsant drug phenytoin, characterized by distinct craniofacial anomalies (hypertelorism and epicanthal folds, short nose and deep nasal bridge, malformed and low set ears, short neck) as well as hypoplastic distal phalanges and underdevelopment of nails of fingers and toes, prenatal and postnatal growth retardation, and neurological impairment (at a 2-3 times higher risk than that of the general population) including cognitive deficits and motor developmental delay. Less commonly, microcephaly, ocular defects, oral clefts, umbilical and inguinal hernias, hypospadias and cardiac anomalies have also been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: two children with mild mental retardation and appreciable articulation difficulties whose mothers took phenobarbitone and phenytoin throughout their pregnancies. The speech difficulties in both children were due to malfunction of an anatomically normal palate. Two cases are reported of prolonged hypocalcaemia with tetany in infants born at term, whose mothers had been treated with phenytoin and phenobarbitone in high doses. Both infants presented with jitteriness and tetany in the first and second weeks of life, and in both the hypocalcaemia was resistant to therapy over a longer period. An effect on the fetal vitamin D metabolism by phenytoin and phenobarbitone, resulting in defective bone mineralization and neonatal hypocalcaemia is suggested. [PMC1628867, PMC1546284]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Fetal hydantoin syndrome can manifest with a range of clinical features. Affected children may present with mild mental retardation and appreciable articulation difficulties, often due to functional palatal incompetence where an anatomically normal palate malfunctions. Neonatal presentations can include prolonged hypocalcaemia with tetany and jitteriness, typically appearing in the first and second weeks of life. This hypocalcaemia is often resistant to therapy and is suggested to result from defective bone mineralization due to an effect on fetal vitamin D metabolism. [PMC1628867, PMC1546284]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Fetal hydantoin syndrome is associated with maternal exposure to anticonvulsant drugs, specifically phenytoin and phenobarbitone, during pregnancy. This exposure has been linked to several developmental issues in affected children. These include functional palatal incompetence, leading to articulation difficulties and mild mental retardation. Additionally, high-dose maternal treatment with these drugs can result in prolonged neonatal hypocalcaemia with tetany, which is suggested to be due to an effect on fetal vitamin D metabolism, causing defective bone mineralization. [PMC1628867, PMC1546284]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for fetal hydantoin syndrome would address the risks associated with maternal exposure to anticonvulsant drugs, specifically phenytoin and phenobarbitone, during pregnancy. Such exposure has been linked to developmental challenges in offspring, including mild mental retardation and articulation difficulties due to functional palatal incompetence. Additionally, infants exposed *in utero* may present with prolonged neonatal hypocalcaemia and tetany, which can be resistant to therapy and are suggested to result from an effect on fetal vitamin D metabolism leading to defective bone mineralization. Counseling should focus on managing anticonvulsant therapy during pregnancy to mitigate these potential adverse outcomes. [PMC1628867, PMC1546284]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Two cases are reported of prolonged hypocalcaemia with tetany in infants born at term, whose mothers had been treated with phenytoin and phenobarbitone in high doses. Both infants presented with jitteriness and tetany in the first and second weeks of life, and in both the hypocalcaemia was resistant to therapy over a longer period. An effect on the fetal vitamin D metabolism by phenytoin and phenobarbitone, resulting in defective bone mineralization and neonatal hypocalcaemia is suggested. [PMC1546284]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for affected individuals can include long-term developmental challenges. Children may experience mild mental retardation and appreciable articulation difficulties, often due to functional palatal incompetence despite an anatomically normal palate. Neonatally, prolonged hypocalcaemia with tetany has been reported, which can be resistant to therapy over an extended period and is associated with defective bone mineralization. [PMC1628867, PMC1546284]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare late-onset neurodegenerative disease characterized by ocular motor dysfunction, postural instability, akinesia-rigidity, and cognitive dysfunction.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Estimates of prevalence of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) range between 1/13,000-34,000. It mainly affects adults older than 50 years of age.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: PSP usually manifests during the sixth or seventh decade of life. Five clinical variants have been described with clinicopathological correlations. Classical PSP (Richardson's syndrome) is the most common clinical variant and manifests with slowing of vertical saccadic eye movements, falls due to postural instability, axial akinetic-rigid syndrome, and cognitive impairment. Progressively patients develop other problems such as problems in speech and eventually a supranuclear gaze palsy and difficulties in swallowing. PSP with predominant Parkinsonism (PSP-P) is characterized by prominent early parkinsonism (tremor, limb bradykinesia, axial and limb rigidity) rather than falls and cognitive change. Over the years, patients ultimately develop clinical features characteristic of classical PSP. PSP with progressive gait freezing (PSP-PGF) is characterized by progressive freezing of gait, speech and writing early in the disease course. Later, axial rigidity, and facial immobility can occur, and supranuclear downgaze paresis may emerge after a decade. PSP with predominant corticobasal syndrome (PSP-CBS) is characterized by progressive apraxia/cortical sensory loss and limb rigidity/bradykinesia dystonia/myoclonus. PSP with predominant speech/language disorder (PSP-SL) is characterized by speech anomalies (apraxia of speech, agrammatism, nonfluent/agrammatic variant of primary progressive aphasia). Motor symptoms appear later in the course of the disease. PSP with predominant frontal presentation (PSP-F) presents with frontal cognitive/behavioral symptoms. Other variant manifestations of PSP include PSP with predominant ocular motor dysfunction (PSP-OM), PSP with predominant postural instability (PSP-PI), and PSP with predominant frontal presentation (PSP-F).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: PSP is a 4R tauopathy composed of a preponderance of four-repeat (exon 10 positive) tau isoforms and a characteristic biochemical profile (doublet tau 64 and tau 69). The MAPT H1-clade specific sub-haplotype, H1c, is a risk factor for this disease. PSP is also characterized by deficits in several neurotransmitter systems (e.g., dopaminergic, cholinergic, GABAergic). The factors that initiate tau-neurodegeneration are unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the clinical picture and neuropsychological evaluation. On autopsy, PSP is characterized neuropathologically by neuronal loss and gliosis with tau-immunoreactive astrocytic plaques and neurofibrillary tangles in the brainstem and basal ganglia more than in cerebral cortex and cerebellum. Differences in the anatomical distribution of accumulation of phosphorylated tau protein correlate with the clinical variants.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Parkinson disease and other atypical parkinsonian disorders (APD) such as multiple system atrophy and corticobasal degeneration. Similar eye movement abnormalities can occur in Niemann-Pick disease type C and Whipple disease.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: PSP is a sporadic, non-hereditary disease.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no treatment curing the disease. Some drugs, depending on the clinical variant, reduce morbidity and improve quality of life (e.g., levodopa responsiveness of patients with PSP-Parkinsonism). Amantadine may improve gait freezing, coenzyme Q10 may positively affect motor and cognitive dysfunction, and other anticholinergic medications occasionally improve voice and speech disturbance.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Progressively, patients become wheel-chair dependent due to the frequent falls. Difficulties in breathing and swallowing, and infections are the main causes of death, generally 6-12 years after onset of the disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare pituitary tumor originating from normally hormone-producing cells of the adenohypophysis, characterized by a sellar or extrasellar mass manifesting with clinical signs secondary to mass effect, but without evidence for hormonal hypersecretion. Typical manifestations are visual disturbances, headaches, cranial nerve dysfunction, and hypopituitarism but the mass may also be discovered incidentally.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of pituitary adenoma in the general population ranges between 1/1000 - 1,300; non-functioning pituitary adenoma (NFPA) accounts for 15-30% of these. Annual incidence is estimated at 1/100,000 worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: NFPA is most often diagnosed in middle-aged adults (average age 50-60 years). The vast majority of NFPAs are revealed by mass effects on anatomic structures in the vicinity of the pituitary (headache, optic chiasm compression) and/or on pituitary hormonal function, leading to hypopituitarism. Pituitary stalk compression can also produce hyperprolactinemia causing amenorrhea and galactorrhea. Pituitary apoplexy may be the presenting feature of NFPA, with severe headaches of sudden onset, meningismus, a variably depressed sensorium, and visual disturbances. However, an increasing proportion of pituitary tumors are detected incidentally on computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain performed for unrelated reasons. Very rarely, gonadotropin hypersecretion can stimulate the gonads: macro-orchidism has been reported in males and an ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome in premenopausal women with FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone)-secreting tumors.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: NFPAs are sporadic in the vast majority. The gene aryl hydrocarbon receptor interacting protein, AIP (11q13.3), has been identified as a susceptibility factor, particularly in cases of familial isolated pituitary adenomas (FIPA) or when NFPA begins in childhood or adolescence. NFPA may also be part of multiple endocrine neoplasia syndrome such as MEN1 (gene MEN1, 11q13).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Assessment of tumor volume and extension is based on imaging studies (MRI). Potential visual problems related to compression of optic pathways are diagnosed by evaluation of visual acuity, visual fields and occasionally optic coherence tomography (OCT). Hypopituitarism is diagnosed by measurement of the various pituitary hormones and hormones from the target glands (cortisol, thyroid hormones, etc.). Dynamic tests may be necessary, particularly for assessment of corticotropic axis. Hyperprolactinemia may be found related to pituitary stalk compression and disinhibition of the dopaminergic tone that normally acts at the level of pituitary lactotrophs. Gonadotropins serum levels, particularly FSH may be increased arguing for the gonadotroph nature of the NFPA.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: In case of hyperprolactinemia, prolactin (PRL) serum levels are always below 150-200 ng/ml in patients with NFPAs. This distinguishes them from macroprolactinomas, which are associated with much higher PRL levels proportional to tumor size. Other differential diagnoses include other tumors of the sellar region (meningiomas, craniopharyngiomas, metastasis, etc.) and inflammatory process (hypophysitis, sarcoidosis, histiocytosis).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is aimed at correcting (or preventing) tumor compression by excising the disease-causing lesion. Transsphenoidal surgery is often the first-line treatment. If a tumor remnant persists (a frequent situation in patients with large and often invasive adenomas), watchful waiting is preferred to routine radiotherapy, as long as the tumor residue does not grow. NFPA can sometimes recur even after complete resection. Postoperative irradiation is only considered in case of residual tumor growth or relapse. NFPA discovered incidentally may require a different approach, especially when they are small and/or remote from the optic pathways. If hypopituitarism persists, adequate hormone replacement is indicated.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: A small excess mortality rate in women and in patients with a young age at diagnosis has been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Visual field compression by a non-secreting pituitary tumour during pregnancy. [PMC539368]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN-1) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by pituitary tumors, among others. Approximately 40% of MEN-1 patients harbor a pituitary adenoma. Therefore, genetic counseling may be relevant for individuals with pituitary adenomas, particularly if other features of MEN-1 are present, given its autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. [PMC6592835]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare primordial growth disorder characterized by low birth weight, reduced birth length, severe postnatal growth restriction, large head size, a spectrum of minor anomalies (including facial dysmorphism) and normal intelligence.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Approximately 200 cases have been reported to date and the condition is rare. However, the phenotype is likely under-recognized.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Infants present with severe prenatal and postnatal growth retardation, birth weight usually at or below the 2nd centile. Growth impairment is greater in those with CUL7 variants. The head circumference is relatively large. Characteristic facial features include: triangular-shaped face, pointed chin, frontal bossing, hypoplastic midface, fleshy, upturned nose , prominent mouth and lips. These features often become less noticeable with age. Short broad neck and thorax, prominent trapezii, winged scapulae, square shoulders, hyperlordosis and clinodactyly of the fifth finger are seen in some children. Prominent fleshy heels in infancy are a common and distinctive feature. Joint hypermobility and an increased risk of congenital hip dislocation may be present. Hyperlordosis can cause back pain. Intelligence is unaffected and development is usually normal. Some cases of impaired fertility and hypospadias have been noted in males , though this is not universal, while females have normal ovarian function. Patients reach a final adult height of about 120-130 cm (5-6 standard deviations below the mean).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Pathogenic variants in three different genes are known to cause 3M syndrome. Variants in in the CUL7 at 6p21.1 are found in around 75% patients. Other genes known to be involved are OBSL1 (2q35), in 20% of cases and CCDC8 (19q13.33) in 5% of cases. The precise mechanisms leading to growth failure in 3M syndrome remain unclear although the poor response to growth hormone in many patients indicates a degree of resistance to the GH/IGF1 pathway.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based primarily on clinical features (e.g. low birth weight, severe growth retardation, prominent fleshy heels). In some, specific radiological findings will be found including slender/ 'gracile' long bones, relatively tall vertebral bodies, foreshortening of vertebral bodies with increasing age, small pelvic bones and a broad thorax with slender and horizontal ribs. The occurrence of these radiological findings, however, is highly variable. Children with 3M syndrome usually have normal GH levels. Molecular genetic testing can identify pathogenic variants in one of the causal genes, confirming diagnosis in the majority of cases. Some children with 3M syndrome demonstrate normal-high baseline insulin-like growth factor (IGF-I) concentrations.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Silver-Russell syndrome, Dubowitz syndrome, Mulibrey nanism, fetal alcohol syndrome, and microdeletion of chromosome 20p13p12.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal and preimplantation diagnosis is possible in families with a known disease causing variant.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: 3M syndrome is inherited autosomal recessively and genetic counseling is recommended for affected families. In a family with an index patient, the sibling recurrence risk is 25%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Once diagnosed the child should be seen by a pediatric endocrinologist for monitoring of growth and pubertal progress and for consideration of recombinant human growth hormone (GH) therapy. Monitoring of growth every 6-12 months is recommended until achievement of final height. Adaptive aids for people with short stature and physiotherapy are possible treatment options. Newborns should have a hip ultrasound scan to screen for developmental dysplasia of the hip. Children can be treated with recombinant human growth hormone. In general, the response to treatment is relatively poor, however a trial of treatment over 1 year may show a reasonable response. Overall treatment with growth hormone is more successful if started early and continued long term. The issue of fertility should be discussed with male patients at the end of puberty and semen analysis offered.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: 3M syndrome is not a life-threatening condition and the prognosis is good.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A clinically variable form of isolated agammaglobulinemia, an inherited immunodeficiency disorder, characterized in affected males by recurrent bacterial infections during infancy.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Estimated prevalence is 1/350,000 to 1/700,000. Annual incidence is not known. The disorder has been reported in various ethnic groups worldwide. Only males are affected and females are asymptomatic carriers.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Affected individuals are usually healthy in the first few months of life due to residual maternal immunoglobulins. The majority of patients develop recurrent or persistent bacterial infections, most commonly caused by S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae, within the first two years of life,: otitis media, conjunctivitis, sinusitis, respiratory infections, diarrhea and skin infections (impetigo, cellulitis, abscesses, and furuncles). Other severe infections may include empyema, meningitis, sepsis, or septic arthritis. Pyoderma or cellulitis (associated with neutropenia) and pseudomonas or staphylococcal sepsis are frequent presenting findings, particularly in patients less than 12 months of age. Lymph nodes, tonsils, and other lymphoid tissues are unusually small or absent. Rare patients are reported to have vitiligo, erythematous rash, or alopecia totalis. Infections tend to persist throughout adulthood. Affected patients are reported to have a higher susceptibility to severe and chronic enteroviral infections. Growth and development are usually normal. Some patients have a less severe clinical presentation and are not recognized as immunodeficient until 10 years of age or later. Complications of X-linked agammaglobulinemia (XLA) include progressive lung disease, chronic sinusitis, inflammatory bowel disease, arthritis , as well as neurological changes.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: XLA is caused by mutations in the BTK gene (Xq21.33-q22) involved in B lymphocyte differentiation and maturation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: A diagnosis of XLA should be considered in patients with recurrent or persistent otitis media, pneumonia, sinusitis, and conjunctivitis starting before age five years or severe bacterial infections such as sepsis, meningitis, cellulitis, or empyema. A family history consistent with X-linked transmission also points to this diagnosis. Suspicion can be confirmed with blood tests showing low serum Ig and markedly reduced B lymphocyte counts. Molecular genetic testing can also be used to establish or confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include autosomal recessive or dominant agammaglobulinemia, common variable immunodeficiency (CVID), hyper IgM syndrome and severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible following identification of the disease-causing mutation in the family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: XLA, as the name indicates, follows an X-linked pattern of inheritance. Nearly 50% of cases are familial, while the remainder are thought to be related to de novo mutations. Genetic counseling should be provided to members of affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative treatment for XLA but good disease control can be achieved through consistent gammaglobulin therapy. This can be given intravenously (400-600 mg/kg every 3 to 4 weeks) or subcutaneously (100 mg/kg every week). Therapy should be started as early as possible. Some immunologists advocate chronic prophylactic antibiotics and treatment of acute infections should be prolonged and at maximal doses of antibiotics.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Most patients with XLA lead a normal life. Life expectancy may be reduced in some patients as a result of complications such as severe infections and chronic pulmonary damage. Early therapeutic measures and treatment compliance are major prognostic factors.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A clinically heterogeneous progressive condition characterized by a combination of proximal neurogenic muscle weakness, sensory-motor neuropathy, ataxia, and pigmentary retinopathy.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Neurogenic muscle weakness-ataxia-retinitis pigmentosa syndrome; Neuropathy-ataxia-retinitis pigmentosa syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Wordwide prevalence is unknown but may be estimated at 0.8-1/100,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: NARP (Neuropathy, Ataxia, and Retinitis Pigmentosa) syndrome is characterized by a great phenotypic variability and habitually clearly manifests in young adulthood. Early childhood manifestations often describe learning difficulties, developmental delay and ataxia, whereas ocular signs, proximal neurogenic muscle weakness with sensory neuropathy usually develop in the second decade of life. Ocular manifestations are variable and range from early salt and pepper retinopathy to retinitis pigmentosa, sluggish pupils, nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, night blindness and loss of visual field. Other features may include short stature, seizures, corticospinal tract atrophy, depression, dementia, sleep apnea, hearing loss or cardiac arrhythmias.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: NARP syndrome is caused in the large majority of patients by a m.8993T>C/G in the subunit 6 of mitochondrial H(+)-ATPase gene (MTATP6). Most NARP patients have 70-90% mutated mitochondrial DNA. The m.8993T>G mutation is also present in 8-10% of patients with Leigh syndrome when mutated mitochondrial DNA is > 90%. Less common ATP6 heteroplasmic mutations include m.8839G>C, m.8989G>C, m.8618-8619insT, m.9032T>C, and m.9127-9128 delAT microdeletion, all identified in single families.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical manifestations, electroretinogram, and genetic testing. Peripheral neuropathy may be demonstrated by electromyography, whereas an MRI may pick up cerebral and cerebellar atrophy in later stages. Serum lactate may be normal or elevated. At muscle biopsy, histochemical or biochemical signs of oxidative phosphorylation may be absent.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes maternally inherited Leigh syndrome (MILS, like NARP syndrome part of the same group of disorders of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation), Refsum disease, Cockayne syndrome, abetalipoproteinemia, Usher syndrome, neurological complication of lipidosis or rare cases of spinocerebellar disorder/ataxia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling and cytogenetic analysis if the mutation has been identified in an affected family member. Preimplantation genetic diagnosis is available for affected couples in few centers.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: NARP syndrome is a maternally inherited syndrome and women can transmit to all their offspring. Clinical severity usually depends on the mutation load. There must be extreme caution in predictive counseling because of the genetic shift between mother and offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management and treatment is only supportive and may include sodium bicarbonate or sodium citrate for acute aggravation of acidosis; antioxidant treatment, treatment of epileptic seizures by appropriate anticonvulsants; treatment of dystonia (e.g., benzhexol, baclofen, tetrabenazine, and gabapentin); and anticongestive therapy in case of cardiomyopathy. Patients require psychological support and should be followed up periodically by neurologists, ophthalmologists and cardiologists to monitor disease progression. Agents to avoid include Sodium Valproate, barbiturates and anesthesia (in general) as well as dichloroacetate.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: As NARP syndrome is progressive, patients may become increasingly dependent of others. The quality of life is severely reduced. Patients may go blind and deaf and may experience depression and dementia. Due to the progressive neurogenic muscle weakness patients may become wheelchair bound.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare ciliopathy characterized by the association of nephronophthisis and liver fibrosis. Renal manifestations include chronic renal failure, polyuria, polydipsia, anemia, as well as increased echogenicity on renal ultrasound and interstitial fibrosis and tubular dilation on biopsy. Hepatic involvement manifests as hepatosplenomegaly with extensive fibrosis, destruction of the bile ducts, and cholestasis. Mild psychomotor retardation and ocular symptoms, such as strabismus, nystagmus, retinal degeneration, and anisocoria, have been reported in some patients.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Senior-Boichis syndrome, specifically nephronophthisis 13 caused by WDR19 variants, presents with a combination of renal and extrarenal manifestations. Clinical features include mild proteinuria without hematuria, kidney dysfunction, and hepatosplenomegaly. Blood tests may reveal pancytopenia and mild elevation of liver enzymes. Biopsies can suggest nephronophthisis and congenital hepatic fibrosis. The condition can lead to the need for liver and kidney transplantation, highlighting the importance of early diagnosis, especially when extrarenal symptoms coexist with kidney dysfunction and mild proteinuria. [PMC11608199]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: a case of nephronophthisis 13 that resulted from WDR19 variants. The patient, a nine-year-old Japanese boy, had detection of mild proteinuria during a school urine screening. Urinalysis revealed mild proteinuria without hematuria. Blood tests indicated pancytopenia, mild elevation of liver enzymes, and kidney dysfunction. Ultrasound examination disclosed hepatosplenomegaly. Abdominal computed tomography and bone marrow assessments ruled out malignant tumors. Subsequent kidney and liver biopsies suggested nephronophthisis and congenital hepatic fibrosis. Furthermore, comprehensive genetic analysis through next-generation sequencing revealed compound heterozygous variants in WDR19 (NM_025132.4), including the previously reported c.3533G > A, p.(Arg1178Gln), and c.3703G > A, p.(Glu1235Lys) variants, confirming the diagnosis of nephronophthisis 13. There is potential need for liver and... [PMC11608199]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Senior-Boichis syndrome, a form of nephronophthisis, often begins with opportunistic findings such as mild proteinuria during urine screening. Subsequent investigations may include urinalysis, blood tests revealing pancytopenia, elevated liver enzymes, and kidney dysfunction. Imaging like ultrasound can show hepatosplenomegaly. Kidney and liver biopsies may suggest nephronophthisis and congenital hepatic fibrosis. Comprehensive genetic analysis, particularly next-generation sequencing, is invaluable for confirming the diagnosis by identifying causative gene variants, such as those in WDR19. Early diagnosis is crucial for managing complications and preparing for potential transplantation. [PMC11608199]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Nephronophthisis, a group of disorders including Senior-Boichis syndrome, should be considered in the differential diagnosis when patients present with coexisting extrarenal symptoms and kidney dysfunction. Specifically, the presence of mild proteinuria, pancytopenia, mild elevation of liver enzymes, hepatosplenomegaly, and congenital hepatic fibrosis alongside kidney dysfunction warrants consideration. Genetic testing, such as next-generation sequencing, is important for accurate diagnosis given the diverse symptoms and numerous causative genes. [PMC11608199]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Senior-Boichis syndrome, specifically nephronophthisis 13, is caused by WDR19 variants, often presenting as compound heterozygous variants, which implies an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Genetic testing is crucial for an accurate diagnosis, especially given the diverse symptoms and numerous causative genes associated with nephronophthisis. Next-generation sequencing is invaluable for genetic diagnosis. Early genetic diagnosis is important for managing complications and preparing for potential organ transplantation. [PMC11608199]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: There is potential need for liver and kidney transplantation in patients with Senior-Boichis syndrome, particularly when hepatic fibrosis and kidney insufficiency are present. Early diagnosis is crucial to mitigate delays in treating complications associated with kidney and hepatic insufficiency and to facilitate preparation for transplantation. [PMC11608199]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Senior-Boichis syndrome, characterized by nephronophthisis and congenital hepatic fibrosis, often involves progressive kidney and hepatic insufficiency. Patients may develop pancytopenia, mild elevation of liver enzymes, and hepatosplenomegaly. There is a potential need for liver and kidney transplantation due to these complications. Early diagnosis is crucial to mitigate delays in treating complications associated with kidney and hepatic insufficiency and to facilitate preparation for transplantation. [PMC11608199]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, non-syndromic respiratory or mediastinal malformation characterized by unilateral complete absence of lung tissue, bronchi, and pulmonary vessels. It may be isolated or associated with congenital malformations, most commonly with heart anomalies. Presentation is highly variable including airway narrowing, stridor, respiratory distress, recurrent respiratory tract infections, and pulmonary hypertension.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Pulmonary agenesis is a rare to exceedingly rare congenital anomaly, with bilateral forms being extremely rare. It is often detected in early childhood, though some individuals remain asymptomatic and undiagnosed until adulthood. While the main etiology is unknown, genetic factors, iatrogenic causes, viral factors, and vitamin A deficiency during early pregnancy are suggested contributors. The condition can occur in isolation or in association with other congenital malformations, including cardiac, gastrointestinal, and skeletal anomalies, as seen in syndromes like VACTERL-H, MCOPS9, and LADD syndrome. Right-sided pulmonary agenesis is considered rarer than left-sided. [PMC12129118, PMC11376699, PMC11046135, PMC10712378, PMC10456747]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Prenatal diagnosis of pulmonary agenesis is possible, primarily through ultrasonography, though it can be challenging, particularly for bilateral forms or when associated with complex syndromes like VACTERL-H. Ultrasonography can suspect unilateral pulmonary agenesis as early as 22 weeks gestation, sometimes prompted by findings such as hydramnios or fetal heart malposition. Fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be used to confirm suspected cases, especially for bilateral pulmonary agenesis. When multiple anomalies are present, including ventriculomegaly, an abnormally positioned heart, or upper-limb abnormalities, systematic ultrasonographic examinations are recommended. Genetic testing, such as whole-exome sequencing, can confirm syndromic forms of pulmonary agenesis. Accurate prenatal diagnosis is crucial, especially for bilateral agenesis which is incompatible with extrauterine life, and requires differentiation from other thoracic abnormalities. [PMC10456747, PMC7507429, PMC7727913, PMC4955509, PMC2799641]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare sex chromosome aneuploidy where males receive an additional Y chromosome, that is characterized clinically by tall stature evident from childhood, macrocephaly, facial features (mild hypertelorism, low set ears, a mildly flat malar region), speech delay and an increased risk for social and emotional difficulties, attention deficit hyperactive disorder and autistic spectrum disorder.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Jacobs syndrome; Double Y syndrome; XYY syndrome; Y disomy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: 47,XYY syndrome, or Jacobs syndrome, is a common chromosomal disorder affecting approximately one in 1000 live-born male infants. Despite this incidence, the condition is often asymptomatic or mildly expressed, and its diagnosis is frequently missed due to variable clinical symptoms. It can be identified incidentally during genetic analysis for other conditions. Early studies erroneously linked the syndrome to aggressive behavior, but recent evidence contradicts this. The syndrome is associated with an increased risk of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders, underscoring the importance of early diagnosis for appropriate management. [PMC11906151, PMC8809031, PMC6235860, PMC5354807, PMC3902449]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: 47,XYY syndrome is a chromosomal disorder often asymptomatic or mildly expressed, though clinical symptoms are variable and diagnosis can be missed. Affected individuals typically present with a male phenotype, tending to be tall and thin, with normal physical structure and secondary sexual characteristics. However, rare cases with a female phenotype, short stature, and undeveloped sex characteristics have been reported. Common features include an increased risk of learning difficulties, delayed language skills, speech delay, and hyperactivity. There are also increased rates of attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, autism spectrum disorder, major depressive disorder, and anxiety disorders. Physical manifestations can include childhood acne, tooth-size increase, over-retained deciduous teeth, and cardiac anomalies like a prolonged P-R interval. Infertility is common, often due to impaired gonadal function, with findings such as oligozoospermia, azoospermia, Sertoli cell-only syndrome, lower testosterone, and elevated LH and FSH. Congenital bilateral absence of the vas deferens and pituitary hyperplasia have also been noted. [PMC11906151, PMC8809031, PMC7232388, PMC7092595, PMC6235860]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: 47,XYY syndrome is diagnosed through cytogenetic or genetic analysis. Karyotype analysis is a primary method, revealing the 47,XYY karyotype or mosaic forms like 46,XY/47,XYY. Chromosomal microarray examination can also identify the condition. Early detection may occur incidentally during genetic analysis for other conditions, such as cardiac anomalies, or be prompted by clinical signs like childhood acne. For couples with 47,XYY males, preimplantation genetic testing (PGT), including next-generation sequencing-based PGT, can be performed, though its necessity is debated unless other indications are present. [PMC12012309, PMC8809031, PMC7232388, PMC7092595, PMC3902449]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) for 47,XYY syndrome males might not be necessary unless other indications are present. A pilot study revealed a low chance (1.55%) of sex chromosome abnormalities in embryos from 47,XYY syndrome patients undergoing PGT. Importantly, no differences were observed in biochemical pregnancy, implantation, clinical pregnancy, ongoing pregnancy, pregnancy loss, live birth, or preterm delivery rates between PGT-embryo transfer and conventional IVF/ICSI-embryo transfer cycles. Neonatal outcomes, including gestational age, birthweight, and congenital anomalies, were also comparable. Therefore, PGT may not be a necessity for 47,XYY syndrome males. [PMC12012309]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Purpose: This pilot study explore the necessity for 47,XYY syndrome males (couples) to perform PGT rather than conventional In Vitro Fertilization (IVF)/Intracytoplasmic Sperm Injection (ICSI) cycles. A retrospective cohort study was conducted with 36 nonmosaic and mosaic 47,XYY syndrome patients (couples) undergoing 43 oocyte retrieval cycles (37 planned for PGT and 6 for IVF/ICSI) between December 2017 and December 2023. The couples were given either next-generation sequencing-based PGT or conventional IVF/ICSI followed by 45 embryo transfer (ET) cycles (38 from PGT and 7 from IVF/ICSI). The detailed cytogenetic of the 129 embryos from PGT were analyzed, and the pregnancy and neonatal outcomes between PGT-ET and conventional IVF/ICSI-ET cycles were compared. The PGT showed that the chance of sex chromosome abnormalities was low (1.55%), with chromosomal errors being observed more... [PMC12012309, PMC11906151, PMC8809031, PMC7232388, PMC7092595]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of 47,XYY syndrome involves a multidisciplinary approach to address endocrine, reproductive, and oral health issues. Counseling is recommended for infertility, hormonal imbalances, and to improve quality of life. Regular monitoring for hypogonadism and consideration of hormone therapy are important. For fertility challenges, assisted reproductive technologies (ART) are recommended, including intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) for fertility assessment, and in vitro fertilization (IVF) with donor sperm as an option. Preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) may not be necessary for 47,XYY males unless other indications are present. Awareness of the increased risk for neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders can inform appropriate management. [PMC12012309, PMC11906151, PMC8809031, PMC7232388, PMC7092595]

A retrospective cohort study was conducted with 36 nonmosaic and mosaic 47,XYY syndrome patients (couples) undergoing 43 oocyte retrieval cycles (37 planned for PGT and 6 for IVF/ICSI) between December 2017 and December 2023. The couples were given either next-generation sequencing-based PGT or conventional IVF/ICSI followed by 45 embryo transfer (ET) cycles (38 from PGT and 7 from IVF/ICSI). The detailed cytogenetic of the 129 embryos from PGT were analyzed, and the pregnancy and neonatal outcomes between PGT-ET and conventional IVF/ICSI-ET cycles were compared.
