Understanding these patterns can improve embryo selection, reduce miscarriage risks, and enhance genetic counseling. At the same time, due to the limited data on potential comorbidities in affected children, our findings support both clinicians and patients in making informed decisions. The retrospective clinical study included 461 PGT-A biopsies from our clinic database (September 2023-December 2024) to determine whether specific chromosome regions or individual chromosomes (C) are more likely to be mosaic or aneuploid. Among the 461 embryos analyzed in our clinic, the incidence rate of mosaicism was 16.70% whereas the aneuploidy rate was 32.10%. Our showed that mosaicism tends... [PMC12155553, PMC5690727, PMC7512120]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Whole-genome oligonucleotide single-nucleotide polymorphism (oligo-SNP) arrays enable simultaneous interrogation of copy number variations (CNVs), copy neutral regions of homozygosity (ROH) and uniparental disomy (UPD). Structural variation in the human genome contributes significantly to genetic variation, and often has deleterious effects leading to disease causation. Co-occurrence of CNV and regions of allelic homozygosity in tandem involving the same chromosomal arm are extremely rare. Replication-based mechanisms such as microhomology-mediated break-induced replication (MMBIR) are recent models predicted to induce structural rearrangements and gene dosage aberrations; however, supportive evidence in humans for one-ended DNA break repair coupled with MMBIR giving rise to interstitial copy number gains and distal loss of heterozygosity has not been documented. on the identification... [PMC4266739, PMC2682770]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare glomerular disease characterized by a pattern of glomerular injury on kidney biopsy with characteristic light microscopic changes: mesangial hypercellularity, endocapillary proliferation, and thickening of the glomerular basement membrane (GBM). On the basis of immunofluorescence (IF) the disorder is divided into C3 glomerulopathy (C3G) or immunoglobulin-mediated membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis. Through electron microscopy C3G is further divided into Dense deposit disease, with highly electrondense deposits in the glomerular basement membrane, and C3 glomerulonephritis, with mesangial, intramembranous, subendothelial and subepithelial deposits. Secondary causes (autoimmune, infectious, malignancies) are excluded.
A rare, chronic, relapsing, multisystemic vasculitis characterized by mucocutaneous lesions, as well as articular, vascular, ocular and central nervous system manifestations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Behçet disease (BD) is most often reported in populations along the Silk Road, with highest prevalence reported in Turkey at >1/1,000, versus 1/10,000 in Japan. European cases are more often described in Mediterranean countries.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset most commonly occurs in adults (mean 30 years of age), but pediatric cases have been reported. Relapsing episodes of round oral aphthae with sharp erythematous and elevated borders (1-3 cm diameter) may be accompanied by genital aphthae (>50% of cases); cutaneous features may include pseudo-folliculitis and erythema nodosum. Ocular disorders (posterior uveitis, retinal vasculitis) occur in over 50% of BD patients. Arthralgia and/or non-erosive, asymmetric, arthritis affecting mainly large articulation (knees, ankles ect.) are frequent (45%) and can occur as an initial symptom. Vasculitis in BD is more frequent in the venous system where thromboses in femoro-iliac, superior and inferior vena cava and cerebral territories may occur. Rarer arterial thromboses and aneurysms primarily affect the pulmonary and aorta vessels. Neurological manifestations (neuro-BD) are frequent (>20%), and may include headache, fever, pyramidal signs with hemiparesis, cranial nerve damage, meningitis, behavioral changes and sphincter dysfunction. Aphthoid and/or ulcerative lesions may affect the whole digestive tract but mainly the ileo-caecum and ascending colon, potentially leading to hemorrhages and perforations.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Of unknown origin, genetic predisposition in BD may allow certain infectious (in particular Streptococcus sanguis) and/or environmental insults to trigger symptoms involving sporadic inflammatory attacks reminiscent of auto-inflammatory disorders due to cross reactions with oral mucosa antigens. HLAB5101 antigen is associated to BD in 50-60% of patients. NF-kB activation and aberrant cytokine levels (eg- IL-6, TNF-a, IL-8, IL-12, IL-17 and IL-21) have been implicated in the pathogenesis of BD. A familial, autosomal dominant form of BD, A20 haploinsufficiency, is linked to mutations in TNFAIP3(6q23.3).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of BD is essentially clinical and is based on the international classification criteria, which are sensitive and specific. The presence of recurrent oral ulceration (at least 3 times over 12 months; 2 points), genital ulceration (2 points), uveitis (2 points), skin lesions (1 point), cardiovascular (1 point), neurologic (1 point) and/or pathergy reaction (1 point). Behçet disease is retained with 4 or more points. Other elements may contribute to the diagnosis. Isolated severe visceral involvement (e.g. vena cava, cerebral and/or subhepatic vein thrombosis, pulmonary aneurysms, neurological involvement and/or retinal vasculitis) can be inaugural and should evoke BD; therefore, systematic request of an expert opinion is recommended. A family history of BD also increases the probability of diagnosis. Searching for the HLA-B51 haplotype is not a strong diagnostic element, but can be useful in situations of diagnostic uncertainty.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis depends on upon the manifestations, herpes ulcerations, spondylo-arthropathies, infectious uveitis, relapsing polychondritis, sarcoidosis, antiphospholipid syndrome, Takayasu arteritis, Crohn's disease, infectious meningo-encephalitis or multiple sclerosis may be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Anti-inflammatory steroids are the basis of treatment; however, corticodependance and relapses may occur upon discontinuation. Concurrent administration of immunosuppresive drugs (e.g. azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate or mycophenolate mofetil), are also prescribed but their action is delayed. Anti-TNF and alpha-interferon (2a or 2b) are efficient, particularly in severe uveitis, and antiplatelet or anticoagulation treatments are discussed in case of vascular thrombosis. Colchicine relieves mucocutaneous symptoms. Apremilast has been recently approved in refractory oral ulceration of BD. Efficacy is dependent upon rapid initiation and patient compliance.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: In the absence of treatment, the prognosis is severe due to ocular involvement leading potentially to blindness, the risk of lethal arterial rupture, large vessel thrombosis and neurological symptoms potentially causing encephalopathy or cerebral hypertension that may lead to a loss of autonomy. Intensive care coupled with close multidisciplinary follow-up, and adapted immunosuppressive treatment has been shown to reduce morbidity and mortality.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Behçet's disease (BD) during pregnancy is a relatively rare condition, and there are currently no established guidelines for its management. The effects of BD on both mothers and children remain unclear. In , the diagnostic and treatment processes for a patient with BD during pregnancy. A 20-year-old woman, gravida 2, para 1, presented to our inpatient department with recurrent oral and genital ulcers at 28 weeks and 3 days of gestation. Given the complexity of the patient's condition, we initiated the first multidisciplinary consultation to establish appropriate treatment regimens. However, the initial treatment was ineffective, and the patient experienced a fever for four days. Consequently, we conducted a second multidisciplinary consultation. The final treatment regimen included azithromycin, hydroxychloroquine, prednisone, and low-molecular-weight heparin calcium. The clinical... [PMC11761207]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Behçet disease (BD) is associated with genetic predisposition, and its clinical presentation can overlap with other genetically driven autoinflammatory conditions. Chromosomal abnormalities, such as Trisomy 8, and specific genetic variants (e.g., in NRAS, JAK2, MEFV, PTPN11, SALL1) have been identified in patients with BD-like symptoms, including de novo mutations. Notably, Deficiency of Adenosine Deaminase 2 (DADA2), a monogenic disorder caused by biallelic ADA2 mutations, can mimic BD, often presenting with HLA-B*51 positivity and a familial pattern. Therefore, genetic and chromosomal analysis is recommended for patients with BD-like symptoms, especially those not fully meeting diagnostic criteria or with a family history, to ensure accurate diagnosis and appropriate management. [PMC12364497, PMC12149140, PMC11913947, PMC11781933, PMC12228353]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Primary hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis without severe ocular involvement
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Familial primary hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis without severe ocular involvement (FHHN) is a form of familial primary hypomagnesemia (FPH), characterized by recurrent urinary tract infections, nephrolithiasis, bilateral nephrocalcinosis, renal magnesium (Mg) wasting, hypercalciuria and kidney failure.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): FHHNC without severe ocular involvement; HOMG3; Renal hypomagnesemia type 3

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, more than 110 individuals have been reported in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: FHHN has an onset in childhood and the clinical manifestations are recurrent urinary tract infections, polyuria, polydipsia, enuresis, hematuria, nephrolithiasis and bilateral nephrocalcinosis. Some patients fail to thrive during early childhood and experience seizures, vomiting, abdominal pain, tetany and rarely rickets. Ocular involvement is rare and when observed it is relatively mild (myopia, hypermetropia, astigmatism and strabism). Approximately one third of patients progress to renal failure or end-stage renal disease (ESRD) during adolescence.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FHHN is characterized by impaired tubular reabsorption of Mg and calcium (Ca) in the thick ascending limb of Henle's loop due to mutations in CLDN16 (3q27), which encodes claudin-16 (previously known as paracellin 1). A significant residual function is observed in several missense mutations, whereas a complete loss of claudin-16 function appears to be more severe (disease presenting earlier and often progressing to kidney failure at a significantly younger age).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them of the 25% risk of having an affected child.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Hypocalcemia is an electrolyte disorder that can be effectively corrected. However, in its severe form, it poses significant risks, including potentially fatal symptoms such as electrocardiographic changes that may lead to sudden cardiac arrest if not treated promptly. the case of a young female patient who presented with multiple episodes of tonic posturing and altered level of consciousness. Diagnostic evaluation revealed severe hypocalcemia with hypomagnesemia, QT prolongation, and episodes of non-sustained ventricular tachycardia. The condition was managed with calcium and magnesium supplementation. Further investigations revealed a novel missense mutation in transient receptor potential melastatin 3 (TRPM3). Discussion: Hypocalcemic seizures are rare in adults and are typically associated with severe hypocalcemia and cardiovascular instability, including ventricular dysrhythmias.... [PMC12124228, PMC11593538, PMC7667358, PMC6045852, PMC4487846]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for conditions involving hypomagnesemia and hypocalcemia include primary hypoparathyroidism, Bartter syndrome type 5 (CaSR mutation), Gitelman syndrome, and claudin mutations. A novel TRPM3 missense mutation has also been identified, causing severe hypocalcemia with hypomagnesemia and impacting kidney resorption of calcium and divalent ions. Additionally, drug-induced causes such as omeprazole-induced hypomagnesaemia should be considered, which can lead to hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and renal tubular acidosis. Epilepsy may also be a differential diagnosis in patients presenting with seizures due to severe hypocalcemia. [PMC12124228, PMC7348324]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management strategies include calcium and magnesium supplementation, which have shown marked improvement in symptoms such as seizures and cardiac function in some patients. However, in cases associated with CLDN16 mutations, treatments involving calcitriol, calcium, thiazide diuretics, and magnesium supplements have often failed to halt disease progression. These patients frequently advance to end-stage renal disease, necessitating interventions like renal transplantation. [PMC12124228, PMC6045852, PMC4487846, PMC2562370]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The disease is frequently complicated by progressive chronic renal failure, often leading to end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Progression to ESRD can occur early in infancy or later in adulthood, with reported cases reaching ESRD by ages 25 or 36, or within five years of symptom onset. Therapy, including magnesium supplements, calcitriol, calcium, and thiazide diuretics, may fail to halt disease progression, necessitating renal transplantation. One patient's sibling died from renal failure at age 25. [PMC6045852, PMC4487846, PMC2562370]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cutis laxa (CL) is an inherited or acquired connective tissue disorder characterized by wrinkled, redundant and sagging inelastic skin associated with skeletal and developmental anomalies and, in some cases, with severe systemic involvement. Several different forms of inherited CL have been described, differentiated on the basis of the mode of inheritance and differences in the extent of internal organ involvement, associated anomalies and disease severity.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable, X-linked recessive
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Cutis laxa can manifest congenitally, with cases diagnosed at birth or presenting in early childhood, such as a 5-year-old girl with congenital skin wrinkles or a 26-month-old girl with developmental delay. Some forms, like autosomal-recessive cutis laxa type 2, are characterized by intrauterine growth retardation, suggesting prenatal onset. Additionally, an acquired form of cutis laxa has been observed in adult patients. [PMC12171241, PMC11865015, PMC11446081, PMC11341742, PMC10230959]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Most cases of CL are inherited, with prevalence at birth being estimated at around 1/1,000,000 and only around 200 families being reported in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Autosomal recessive types of CL (ARCL) appear to be the most common forms with two subtypes being described: ARCL1 and ARCL2. ARCL1 is the most severe form of CL with generalized involvement leading to life-threatening complications (lung atelectesias and emphysema, vascular anomalies, and gastrointestinal and genitourinary tract diverticuli). ARCL2 appears to cover a spectrum of disorders ranging in severity from the wrinkly skin syndrome to more severe disease associated with growth and developmental delay, and skeletal anomalies (classic ARCL2, Debré type). De Barsy syndrome and geroderma osteodysplastica also show significant clinical overlap with ARCL2. Occipital horn syndrome (X-linked cutis laxa (XRCL)) is very similar to ARCL2; however, several patients present a more severe phenotype and systemic involvement. Autosomal dominant CL (ADCL) is generally a mild cutaneous disorder but systemic manifestations (hernias, cardiac valve anomalies, cardiovascular manifestations, gastrointestinal diverticuli and emphysema) have been noted in some cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Although the underlying etiology remains unknown in many patients with the inherited forms of CL, several genes have been implicated: FBLN5 , EFEMP2 and LTBP4 in ARCL1 (14q32.1, 11q13 and 19q13.1-q13.2) , ATP6V0A2 and PYCR1 in ARCL2 (12q24.3 and 17q25.3), and ELN and FBLN5 in ADCL (7q11.2 and 14q32.1). Homozygous ELNmutations have also been indentified in four patients with a mild form of ARCL.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is often problematic due to the considerable clinical overlap between the hereditary forms. The diagnostic approach should include a detailed physical examination, family history, skeletal survey, developmental assessment, imaging studies, histological analysis, liver function tests and biochemical analysis, kidney ultrasound, and ophthalmological and cardiac evaluation.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnosis is the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes but similar skin manifestations may also occur in patients with Williams syndrome, pseudoxanthoma elasticum, Hutchinson Gilford syndrome, Barber Say syndrome, Costello syndrome, Cardio-Facio-Cutaneous syndrome and Kabuki syndrome. Inherited forms of CL should also be distinguished from acquired CL which is commonly preceded by urticaria, angioedema, local or generalized inflammatory skin disease or drug hypersensitivity reactions.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is feasible by molecular testing for families in which the genetic anomaly has been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Correct diagnosis of the hereditary forms is essential for providing adapted genetic counseling to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no efficient treatment for CL and management is symptomatic. Plastic surgery is not generally indicated for the cutaneous manifestations in inherited forms.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable, ranging from a usually fatal outcome in childhood in ARCL1 to a normal life expectancy in less severe forms.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by severe global developmental delay, osteogenesis imperfecta, presence of wormian bones, seizures, ocular abnormalities (blue sclerae, optic atrophy, retinal detachment), and dysmorphic facial features (including frontal bossing, low anterior hairline, medial flare of the eyebrows, long eyelashes, hypertelorism, depressed nasal bridge, and low-set, large ears). There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1994.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: As a result of a whole-exome sequencing study, three mutant alleles in SEC24D, a gene encoding a component of the COPII complex involved in protein export from the ER: the truncating mutation c.613C>T (p.Gln205(∗)) and the missense mutations c.3044C>T (p.Ser1015Phe, located in a cargo-binding pocket) and c.2933A>C (p.Gln978Pro, located in the gelsolin-like domain). Three individuals from two families affected by a similar skeletal phenotype were each compound heterozygous for two of these mutant alleles, with c.3044C>T being embedded in a 14 Mb founder haplotype shared by all three. The affected individuals were a 7-year-old boy with a phenotype most closely resembling Cole-Carpenter syndrome and two fetuses initially suspected to have a severe type of osteogenesis imperfecta. All three displayed a severely disturbed ossification of the skull and multiple fractures with prenatal onset.... [PMC4375534, PMC4375435]

DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic approaches involve genetic testing, specifically whole-exome sequencing, which has identified mutations in genes such as SEC24D and P4HB in individuals presenting with phenotypes resembling Cole-Carpenter syndrome or severe osteogenesis imperfecta. Further cellular analysis of skin fibroblasts can reveal characteristic findings. These include inefficient ER export of procollagen and dilated ER tubules, observed through electron and immunofluorescence microscopy, or signs of increased endoplasmic reticulum stress. [PMC4375534, PMC4375435]

Another condition to consider is cranio-lentico-sutural dysplasia (CLSD), caused by SEC23A mutations. CLSD displays an overlapping craniofacial phenotype but is not characterized by generalized bone fragility and presents with cataracts. [PMC4375534, PMC4375435]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis is possible, as evidenced by two fetuses initially suspected of having a severe form of osteogenesis imperfecta. These affected fetuses displayed severely disturbed ossification of the skull and multiple fractures, with the onset of these skeletal abnormalities occurring prenatally. This suggests that characteristic features of the syndrome, particularly severe skeletal manifestations, can be identified before birth. [PMC4375534]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Humero-radial synostosis is a rare, genetic, congenital joint formation defect disorder characterized by uni- or bilateral fusion of the humerus and radius bones at the elbow level, with or without associated ulnar and carpal/metacarpal deficiency, leading to loss of elbow motion and, in many cases, functional arm incapacity. Bowing of radius may be additionally present.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Isolated humero-radial synostosis is considered a rare deformity. To date, a little more than 150 patients have been described with this condition. It is more commonly observed in individuals with deficient ulnar formation or those affected by syndromes such as Antley-Bixler and Hermann. [PMC10310413]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Isolated humero-radial synostosis is characterized by the union of the humerus and radius at the elbow, forming a single, longer bone and resulting in the lack of a functional elbow joint. This fusion leads to stiffness and causes significant disability, the severity of which varies based on hand function, elbow positioning, mobility of adjacent joints, and the function of the contralateral limb. Fractures in the fused bone are considered not uncommon, despite the rarity of the condition, and have been described in clinical cases. [PMC10310413]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Humeroradial synostosis, defined as the union of two originally separated bones, is more commonly observed in individuals with deficient ulnar formation, such as Bayne type-IV ulnar formation failure, or as a feature of conditions like Antley-Bixler syndrome. Antley-Bixler syndrome is linked to specific mutations in the NADPH-cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase (POR) gene, which can be inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. These POR mutations affect P450 metabolism and may impact FGF signaling pathways, both of which are crucial for proper bone development, leading to skeletal defects including radiohumeral synostosis. [PMC10310413, PMC4687943, PMC3783497, PMC6057845]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Prenatal diagnosis of severe bone diseases is challenging and requires complete and precise analysis of fetal anomalies to guide genetic investigation and parental counselling. a rare case of Antley-Bixler syndrome prenatally diagnosed at 26 weeks' gestation by ultrasound and computed tomography in a 28-year-old woman with a history of early termination of pregnancy for "malposition of the inferior limbs". The prenatal ultrasound scan showed severe femoral bowing and frontal bossing. Taking into account the high probability of a recurrent severe skeletal disorder, a computed tomography (CT) scan was proposed. CT findings revealed bilateral femora deformation, craniosynostosis, severe midface hypoplasia, and radiohumeral synostosis. These anomalies strongly suggested Antley-Bixler syndrome. Sequencing of the POR gene in the fetus and the parents revealed compound heterozygous mutations... [PMC4687943]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Humeroradial synostosis can be a feature of more complex conditions rather than an isolated deformity. It is more commonly observed in individuals with deficient ulnar formation or those affected by syndromes such as Antley-Bixler and Hermann syndromes. Antley-Bixler syndrome, for example, presents with radiohumeral synostosis alongside cardinal features like craniosynostosis, severe mid-face hypoplasia, frontal bossing, and femoral bowing. Asymmetrical tetraphocomelia is another condition associated with radiohumeral synostosis, necessitating careful evaluation to distinguish isolated cases from syndromic presentations. [PMC10310413, PMC4687943, PMC6074508, PMC6057845]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Prenatal diagnosis of severe bone diseases, including those featuring radiohumeral synostosis, can be challenging. In one instance, radiohumeral synostosis was identified as part of Antley-Bixler syndrome at 26 weeks' gestation. Initial prenatal ultrasound scans revealed severe femoral bowing and frontal bossing. A computed tomography (CT) scan was subsequently utilized, confirming radiohumeral synostosis alongside other skeletal and facial anomalies. Precise analysis of ultrasonographic images is the primary diagnostic step, and CT may serve as a valuable adjunct for diagnosis and prognosis assessment in suspected severe fetal inherited disorders during the late mid-trimester. [PMC4687943]

Taking into account the high probability of a recurrent severe skeletal disorder, a computed tomography (CT) scan was proposed. CT findings revealed bilateral femora deformation, craniosynostosis, severe midface hypoplasia, and radiohumeral synostosis. These anomalies strongly suggested Antley-Bixler syndrome. Sequencing of the POR gene in the fetus and the parents revealed compound heterozygous mutations... [PMC4687943, PMC6057845]

At the elbow, humeroradial or longitudinal synostosis causes significant disability, which varies depending on hand function, elbow positioning, adjacent joints mobility and contralateral limb function. It is estimated that, to date, a little more than 150 patients have been described with this deformity, which is more common in subjects with deficient ulnar formation or affected by conditions such as Antley-Bixler and Hermann syndromes. The lack of the elbow joint, with the formation of a longer bone due to humerus-radius fusion, in stiffness. As such, it is assumed that fractures in this topography are not uncommon. However, since synostosis is rare, this lesion was only described twice in the literature. two patients with a fracture of the single bone formed by a humeroradial synostosis and Bayne... [PMC10310413, PMC4687943]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Isolated humero-radial synostosis causes significant disability due to the lack of an elbow joint and resulting stiffness. The extent of disability varies depending on hand function, elbow positioning, mobility of adjacent joints, and contralateral limb function. Fractures in the fused bone can occur, and successful surgical treatment has been described. Adequate treatment is crucial to avoid compromising the daily activities of patients who have adapted to their deformity, thereby preventing further worsening of the affected limb's function. [PMC10310413]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic proximal spinal muscular atrophy characterized by degeneration of alpha motor neurons in the anterior horns of the spinal cord and lower brain stem manifesting with onset of progressive proximal muscle weakness (legs greater than arms) between 18 months and adulthood. Motor development is heterogeneous but walking is typically acquired.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Juvenile spinal muscular atrophy; Kugelberg-Welander disease; SMA type 3; SMA type III; SMA-III; SMA3

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The average prevalence at birth of proximal spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is estimated at 1/12,000, of which more than 10% account for type 3. Prevalence worldwide ranges between 1/70,00-285,000, although studies are limited.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease manifests between 18 months of age and adulthood, typically presenting with frequent falls, difficulty climbing steps and proximal weakness. Patients are subdivided based on age of onset: early onset is between 18 months and 3 years of age (type 3a) and is associated with a plateau in motor development, reduced or absent reflexes, finger polymyoclonus tremor and, frequently, loss of ambulation before or around puberty. Later onset (type 3b), between 3 and 21 years of age, is associated with comparatively milder decline in gross motor function. The muscle weakness predominantly affects the legs and hip muscles and then progresses to the shoulders and arms. Abnormal gait characteristics are common in order to compensate for weakness. Typically, patients are spared scoliosis and respiratory muscle weakness but these may be a feature after loss of ambulation. Cognition is normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is a result of degeneration and loss of the lower motor neurons in the spinal cord and the brain stem nuclei. Causal homozygous mutations/deletions in the SMN1 gene (5q12.2-q13.3) are responsible. SMN1 encodes the survival motor neuron protein (SMN) which is known to participate in critical pathways related to RNA processing and transport. Modifier genes include SMN2 (5q13.2), a homologous centromeric copy of SMN1, and NAIP (5q13.1), encoding neuronal apoptosis inhibitory protein. Type 3 is associated with 3-4 copy numbers of SMN2.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The disease is suspected based on clinical history and examination. The gold standard in diagnosis is genetic testing of SMN1 deletion/mutation. Muscle biopsy and electromyography should not be performed in a typical presentation.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other disorders of the peripheral nervous system including myopathies or muscular dystrophies (dystrophinopathies, limb girdle muscular dystrophy, metabolic myopathies, or inflammatory myopathies), inflammatory neuropathies (Guillain-Barré syndrome), neuromuscular junction disorders (myasthenia gravis or congenital myasthenic syndromes), and other motor neuron disorders (non-5q form of SMA or late onset hexosaminidase A deficiency).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible through molecular analysis of amniocytes or chorionic villus samples.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive but around 2% of cases are caused by de novo mutations. Genetic counseling should be offered to patients and their families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Symptomatic management is multidisciplinary and aims to improve quality of life. Physiotherapy and occupational therapies are recommended and include exercise programs. Clinical evaluations should include timed function tests including the six-minute walk test. Nusinersen, an antisense oligonucleotide, is approved for treatment of SMA in Europe and the USA. Real world data following commercial availability of the drug suggest efficacy in type 3 children and adult patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: A wheelchair may be required during childhood for some patients (more commonly those with type 3a), whilst others retain the ability to walk into adulthood. Progression is slow and life expectancy is typically normal. Data on long-term outcomes with nusinersen treatment are not currently available.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A toxin-mediated infection due to the anaerobic bacteria Clostridium tetani and characterized by spasms and contractions of the skeletal muscles, the disease is often lethal.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Tetanus has almost disappeared from countries where a vaccination policy is ensured and implemented. Annual incidence in developed countries is less than 1 / 1,000,000 inhabitants, and mainly affects patients over 70 years of age. The annual incidence is 100 to 200 times higher in the poorest countries. There are no international statistics on the number of adult cases. In 2015, the number of newborn deaths recorded was 34,000. In 2018 neonatal and maternal tetanus was eliminated in 14 of the 57 countries deemed to be at high risk.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Tetanus can occur at all ages. The first symptoms appear 4 to 20 days after a wound contamination and begin by a trismus. In a few hours or a few days (depending on the severity), these painful contractures will spread to the whole body; they can be accompanied by dysautonomics disorders. Death can occur from respiratory blockade.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Tetanus caused by Clostridium Tetani, a bacterium found in almost all soils and animal droppings and present as spores. It enters the body through a contaminated wound, and produces a neurotropic toxin which gains, following the nervous axes, the neuromuscular junctions where it attaches, causing spasms and contractures of the striated muscles.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is exclusively based on clinical signs.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes local causes of trismus, muscular dystonia induced by certain drugs, and much more rarely, meningitis or certain forms of hysteria.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic and aims to control contractures with large doses of muscle relaxant drugs or even prolonged curarization, until the toxin is removed, which often requires respiratory resuscitation. The only effective treatment is vaccination. It is 100% effective and there are almost no contraindications. In practice, a vaccine recipient (three injections and a booster after one year, followed by the scheduled booster) will never get tetanus. For injured individuals whose vaccination status is uncertain, the risk of tetanus is constant, and the systematic administration of specific gamma globulin necessary.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is variable. The disease lasts from 2 to 4 weeks, the mortality varying between 20 and 80% depending on the severity of the disease, the age of the patient and the local possibilities of resuscitation.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Genetic epilepsy with febrile seizure plus
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare familial epilepsy syndrome characterized by febrile, focal and generalized seizures, with a spectrum of phenotypes largely variable among different family members.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): GEFS+; Generalized epilepsy with febrile seizures plus

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Genetic epilepsy with febrile seizures plus (GEFS+) is common with hundreds of cases described. However, its exact prevalence and incidence are unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: GEFS+ spectrum can range from febrile seizures (FS) and FS plus (FS+) to more severe phenotypes with myoclonic atonic seizures or Dravet syndrome (DS), also including genetic, generalized and focal epilepsies. FS+ is the most common phenotype, described as FS with infancy onset (below 1 year of age) persisting beyond the age of 6 years, with possible evolution to afebrile generalized tonic-clonic, myoclonic, atonic or absence seizures, usually remitting by late childhood or early adolescence. Occasional seizures in adulthood and focal seizures can also be observed. Despite FS being the hallmark of GEFS+ not all affected family members present with fever sensitivity. Typically, neurological examination and cognition are normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: GEFS+ is genetically heterogeneous. More than 300 SCN1A (2q24.3) pathogenic variants have been associated with the GEFS+ spectrum. Other genes involved are SCN1B (19q13.12), SCN2A (2q24.3), SCN9A (2q24.3), FGF13 (Xq26.3-q27.1), GABRG2 (5q34) and GABRD (1p36.3). STX1B (16p11.2) or PRRT2 (16p11.2) have been found in some families. HCN1 (5p12) and ADGRV1 (5q14.3) are possible susceptibility genes.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: GEFS+ is diagnosed clinically through the seizure type, EEG pattern, and family history. Molecular genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include self-limited familial infantile seizures due to PRRT2 pathogenic variants, classic glucose transporter type 1 deficiency syndrome, and other symptomatic epilepsies.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Given the broad phenotypic GEFS+ spectrum, prenatal diagnosis is not recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In most families, GEFS+ is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with incomplete penetrance. In a few cases, the inheritance is more complex, likely due to genetic and/or environmental modifiers. Recently, sporadic cases with FS+ have been also described. Genetic counseling is possible in families with a known disease-causing gene variant. However, precise phenotypes cannot be predicted due to the large intra-familial phenotypic variability.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: In most individuals with GEFS+ treatment may not be necessary; regular electro-clinical and neuropsychological follow-up are recommended. Seizures in FS+ are usually responsive to anti-seizure medications (ASMs) whenever needed. Seizure outcome for other epilepsies within the GEFS+ spectrum depends on the epilepsy syndrome. Most effective ASMs are valproic acid, benzodiazepines, ethosuximide, levetiracetam, topiramate and perampanel; lamotrigine and phenytoin should not be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The overall prognosis depends on the exact GEFS+ phenotype. In individuals with FS/FS+, seizures are often self-limited by puberty. Individuals with more severe phenotypes may require life-long treatment and have neurocognitive sequelae.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is a rare disease due to a severely impaired central autonomic control of breathing and dysfunction of the autonomous nervous system.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CCHS; Ondine syndrome; Congenital central alveolar hypoventilation syndrome; Ondine curse

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence is estimated to be at 1 of 200 000 livebirths.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Association with a Hirschsprung's disease is observed in 16% of the cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: A heterozygous mutation of PHOX-2B gene is found in 90% of the patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Despite a high mortality rate and a lifelong dependence to mechanical ventilation, the long-term outcome of CCHS should be ultimately improved by multidisciplinary and coordinated follow-up of the patients.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is primarily confirmed by molecular testing for paired-like homeobox 2B (PHOX2B) gene mutations, which can involve next-generation sequencing, Sanger sequencing, fluorescent probe PCR, capillary electrophoresis, or detection of whole gene deletions. Polysomnography is a crucial diagnostic tool, demonstrating central and obstructive sleep apnea, hypoxemia, and hypoventilation, often worsening in non-rapid eye movement sleep. The absence of hypercapnic ventilatory response is a key clinical clue, and incorporating capnography in polysomnography is important for accurate detection of hypoventilation. Other indicators like respiratory acidosis and elevated serum bicarbonate may be observed, and an exhaustive etiological study is performed to exclude primary pulmonary, cardiac, metabolic, or neurological diseases. Atypical presentations, sometimes lacking overt hypoventilation, underscore the need for expanded genetic testing to identify PHOX2B variants. [PMC12225278, PMC11019219, PMC10724499, PMC10235709, PMC8867765]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) includes other causes of neonatal apnea and hypoventilation, such as primary pulmonary, cardiac, metabolic, and neurological diseases. Acquired central hypoventilation syndrome, or Ondine's curse, resulting from brainstem injury (e.g., lateral medullary infarction) must also be considered. CCHS can present atypically, with obstructive or central sleep apnea as the primary feature, even in the absence of overt alveolar hypoventilation, making it crucial to differentiate from other sleep-disordered breathing conditions. Given that CCHS is a neurocristopathy, associated conditions like Hirschsprung disease, neuroblastoma, schwannomas, and pheochromocytomas should prompt genetic investigation for CCHS. Furthermore, unexplained alveolar hypoventilation, even in adults or with late-onset, warrants consideration of CCHS. [PMC12225278, PMC11019219, PMC11050951, PMC10476029, PMC10235709]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by pathogenic variants in paired-like homeobox 2B ( PHOX2B ) gene. Characteristics of neonatal-onset CCHS cases have not been well assessed. The aim of is to expand current knowledge of clinical and genetic features of neonates with CCHS and provide data on the genotype-phenotype correlation. We made a retrospective analysis of 14 neonates carrying PHOX2B pathogenic variants from 2014 to 2019 and we reviewed previously published neonatal-onset cases. Clinical and genetic data were analyzed. Moreover, genotype-phenotype correlation analysis was performed. We identified a total of 60 neonatal-onset CCHS cases (35 males and 25 females) including 14 novel cases from our local cohort. Nearly 20% (18.2%) of the patients were born prematurely. Nearly half (46.2%) of the patients had abnormal family... [PMC8107878]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Paired-like homeobox 2B gene variants cause congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (CCHS) characterized by abnormal ventilatory control necessitating lifelong assisted ventilation (AV). a 3-year-old female who presented with apnea, hypoxemia, hypoventilation requiring AV, and Hirschsprung's disease during infancy followed by resolution of hypoventilation. At 3 weeks, polysomnography showed obstructive and central sleep apnea, oxygen desaturations, and hypoventilation. A novel, heterozygous, paternal-inherited 2.77-Mb deletion in chromosome 4p14-p13 resulted in deletion of the entire paired-like homeobox 2B gene, confirming the diagnosis of CCHS. Paired-like homeobox 2B whole-gene deletions are categorized as nonpolyalanine repeat mutations. AV via tracheostomy was utilized during sleep. At 2.8 years, diagnostic polysomnography was performed due to suboptimal adherence to AV that... [PMC12225278, PMC11019219, PMC10550651, PMC8867765, PMC8883077]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare focal childhood epilepsy characterized by seizures involving unilateral facial sensory-motor symptoms, with electroencephalogram (EEG) showing sharp biphasic waves over the rolandic region. It is an age-related epilepsy, with excellent outcome. Self-Limited Epilepsy with CentroTemporal Spikes (SeLECTS) was formerly known as benign Rolandic epilepsy or benign epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): BRE; Benign epilepsy of childhood with centrotemporal spikes; Benign familial epilepsy of childhood with rolandic spikes; Benign rolandic epilepsy; Centrotemporal epilepsy; BECRS; BECTS; Rolandic epilepsy; SeLECTS

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: SeLECTS is the most common childhood epilepsy and accounts for 6-7% of all childhood epilepsies. Its annual incidence has been estimated to be approximately 1/10,000-20,000 in children within 15 years. This epilepsy primarily affects boys (60%) and children aged 6 to 11 years.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset is between 3 and 14 years, in otherwise normal children. Seizures usually occur during sleep or drowsy states and are characterized by short episodes of unilateral somatosensory symptoms such as numbness, tingling, and drooling. These symptoms primarily affect pharynx, tongue, face, lips and sometimes hand. Speech may temporarily cease during these episodes, although comprehension remains intact. In some cases, these seizures have the potential to progress into bilateral tonic-clonic seizures. However, it is important to note that the occurrence of status epilepticus as a result of these seizures is quite rare. During the course of illness, seizures may alternate between one side and the other. Longer attacks can be followed by post-ictal hemiplegia. Additionally, some children may have selective neuropsychological impairment affecting language, attention, visuomotor skills and behavior. They usually do not outlast the period of active seizures. Seizure remission occurs within 2-4 years from the onset. The majority of patients have <10 seizures and 10-20% have a single seizure.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Etiology of SeLECTS is still unknown. Complex inheritance is suspected, as an increased rate of SeLECTS, febrile seizures, and epilepsy-aphasia spectrum disorders were found among relatives. However, usually no single causative gene can be identified in these families. Pathogenesis seems to be related with the critical and vulnerable phase of brain maturation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of SeLECTS relies on the clinical features and on EEG findings. EEG shows a normal background activity with slow, biphasic, high amplitude, centrotemporal spikes, activated by drowsiness sleep. In typical clinical presentations, brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is not necessary for diagnosis. However, if it is performed, the results are typically normal.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other self-limited focal epilepsies of childhood (Self-limited Epilepsy with Autonomic Features, Photosensitive Occipital Lobe Epilepsy and Childhood Occipital Visual Epilepsy). Structural etiologies causing similar symptoms are excluded with brain MRI.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Currently, the majority of children with SeLECTS do not exhibit any identified pathogenic gene variants. However, individuals with SeLECTS who have heterozygous pathogenic variants in GRIN2A may experience progression to epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The majority of patients, who have a single or few seizures, do not require treatment. Only patients with frequent seizures (10-20%) may need treatment for a short time. For such cases, sulthiame, oxcarbamazepine, carbamazepine, and clobazam are initially considered.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis of SeLECTS is favorable since nearly 90% of patients remit before puberty. Anti-seizure medications (ASMs) are usually effective in treating seizures. The likelihood of seizure remission is excellent, even for individuals who initially struggle to control their seizures. In rare cases (<1%), SeLECTS may evolve to epileptic encephalopathy with spike-wave activation in sleep with cognitive and language regression.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A spectrum of congenital malformative disorders characterized by the co-occurrence of distal limb anomalies (usually bilateral cleft feet and/or hands) and renal defects (e.g. unilateral or bilateral agenesis), that can be associated with a variety of other anomalies such as those of genitourinary tract (genital anomalies, ureteral hypoplasias, vesicoureteral reflux), abdominal well defects, intestinal atresias, and lung malformations. Familial cases have been reported in which an autosomal recessive inheritance was suspected.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: A primiparous woman in her late 30s at 28+1 weeks' gestation presented with a 3-day history of abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea and vomiting and was diagnosed with starvation ketoacidosis. A routine admission swab returned positive for COVID-19. She had been diagnosed with acrorenal syndrome from birth. Three days post admission, she deteriorated rapidly into respiratory failure requiring intubation and ventilation. She was treated with dexamethasone, prophylactic enoxaparin, a course of piperacillin/tazobactam followed by meropenem and fluconazole and 8 cycles of proning. An emergency caesarean section was performed on day 12 of hospital admission at 29+5 weeks' gestation to improve maternal oxygenation and ventilation. The baby had deformities consistent with acrorenal syndrome but no evidence of COVID-19. She spent 23 days in the intensive care unit. Our case describes an... [PMC8565554]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hereditary folate malabsorption (HFM) is an inherited disorder of folate transport characterized by a systemic and central nervous system (CNS) folate deficiency manifesting as megaloblastic anemia, failure to thrive, diarrhea and/or oral mucositis, immunologic dysfunction and neurological disorders.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown. Approximately 30 cases have been reported to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset usually occurs a few months after birth. Manifestations include failure to thrive, diarrhea and/or mouth ulcers, various neurological manifestations (motor impairment, seizures, developmental delay, cognitive and behavioral disorders), megaloblastic anemia and hypoimmunoglobulinemia. Megaloblastic anemia is the primary manifestation of HFM and can be very severe if untreated. Hypoimmunoglobulinemia results in unusual infections with Pneumocystis jiroveccii, C. difficile and cytomegalovirus (CMV) which can be recurrent and life-threatening in undiagnosed infants. Neurological manifestations may be the presenting symptoms in some but are absent in others. Seizures, if present, begin in infancy or later in childhood. Intracranial calcifications have been observed in some.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: HFM is caused by mutations in the SLC46A1 gene found on chromosome 17q11.2 which encodes the proton-coupled folate transporter (PCFT). PCFT is essential for intestinal folate absorption and transport of folates across the blood-cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) barrier. A defect in this protein leads to a systemic folate and CNS folate deficiency. Infants cannot absorb adequate folate from breast milk/formula and become deficient once their stores accumulated during gestation are exhausted.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical and laboratory findings. It is confirmed by findings of an impaired absorption of an oral folate load (even after correction of serum folate concentration) and a low CSF folate concentration (0-1.5nM). Bone marrow biopsy confirms the presence of megaloblastic anemia. Sequence analysis of the SLC46A1 coding region can identify any mutations present in the gene, also confirming diagnosis of HFM.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The immunodeficiency seen in HFM may resemble severe combined immune deficiency (SCID). Other differential diagnoses include methionine synthase deficiency with megaloblastic anemia and developmental delay, formiminoglutamic aciduria, tyrosinemia type 1, methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase deficiency and erythroleukemia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible via prenatal testing. Screening of newborns with a family history of HFM allows for early diagnosis and treatment with folate immediately after birth, before symptoms occur.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: HFM is inherited autosomal recessively. Genetic counseling is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: High dose oral or parenteral 5-formyltetrahydrofolate (5-formylTHF) and oral L-5-methyltetrahydrofolate (L-5-methylTHF) are the two types of reduced folates used to treat HFM. Dosage is monitored and adjusted (individualized for each patient) so that the CSF folate levels remain within the normal range (around 100nM in infants-2 year olds). Folic acid should not be used as it binds to folate receptors and blocks folate transport. If anemia is severe, a transfusion may be necessary. Early treatment with reduced folates before the appearance of symptoms can prevent the metabolic consequences of HFM. Patients should have regular blood tests to monitor complete blood count, serum and CSF folate and homocysteine concentrations and serum immunoglobulin concentrations.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With proper treatment the prognosis is good and reversal of most of the systemic consequences of the disease is usually achieved. Only when untreated is the prognosis poor.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, hyperpigmentation of the skin disease characterized by adulthood-onset of reticular, reddish-brown to dark-brown, macular and/or comedone-like, hyperkeratotic papules with hypopigmented macules, predominantly affecting flexural areas and, on occasion, progressing to involve trunk and acral regions. Histologically, epidermal acanthosis, thin, branch-like, rete ridges, and a tendency for acantholysis and pigmentary incontinence is observed.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Dowling-Degos disease (DDD) is a rare genodermatosis, typically inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, sometimes with variable penetrance. It commonly manifests in late childhood, adolescence, or after puberty. While it appears in both genders, it is more frequently observed in females. Familial cases have been reported, and specific presentations, such as vulvar involvement, are considered rare findings. [PMC12232819, PMC12259490, PMC10885078, PMC10010119, PMC8202491]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Dowling-Degos disease (DDD) is a rare, autosomal dominant genodermatosis that typically presents in late childhood, adolescence, or after puberty, and is more common in females. It is characterized by acquired reticular hyperpigmentation, manifesting as brown to black macules and papules in a clustered or reticulated pattern, primarily at flexural sites such as the axilla, groin, elbow, face, neck, trunk, vulvar, perianal, and forehead. Associated features can include comedone-like follicular papules, pitted perioral scars, eczematous plaques, and follicular-centric lesions. DDD has also been associated with hidradenitis suppurativa and seborrhoeic keratosis. Diagnosis relies on clinical and histopathological correlation, and the condition can cause significant psychological distress and impact quality of life. [PMC12232819, PMC12259490, PMC10010119, PMC7914397, PMC3173736]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Dowling-Degos disease is established through the correlation of clinical and histopathological findings. Clinically, it is characterized by acquired reticular hyperpigmentation, often at flexural sites, with comedone-like follicular papules and pitted perioral scars. Histopathological examination, typically performed on punch biopsies with haematoxylin-eosin staining, reveals features consistent with the disease. Genetic analysis, such as whole exome sequencing, can identify underlying mutations in genes like POFUT1 or KRT5, which may be necessary to confirm the diagnosis, particularly in cases with overlapping clinical features or atypical presentations. [PMC12232819, PMC12259490, PMC7914397, PMC4150463, PMC3173736]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Dowling-Degos disease (DDD) is a rare genodermatosis with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, though variable penetrance has been noted. It is caused by germline heterozygous mutations, including those in the KRT5 and POFUT1 genes. Postzygotic mutations in POFUT1 can also occur, leading to distinct clinical presentations. Due to its hereditary nature, genetic counseling is provided to affected individuals and their families, which includes discussing the prognosis, treatment options, and long-term management strategies. Family history often reveals similar lesions in relatives, underscoring the genetic basis of the disease. [PMC12232819, PMC12259490, PMC10885078, PMC7914397, PMC4150463]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Dowling-Degos disease can be challenging, with no established guidelines and limited effectiveness for various treatments. Initial attempts with Triderma cream may not yield improvement. However, a case demonstrated significant fading of lesions after 8 months with a regimen of sunblock, depigmenting agents, and moisturizers. Genetic counseling is important due to the hereditary nature, and long-term management strategies should be emphasized. A multidisciplinary approach is essential for improving patient outcomes and managing the elevated risk of skin cancers. [PMC12232819, PMC12259490, PMC10885078]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Dowling-Degos disease can cause significant psychological distress and a decline in quality of life. Patients with the condition also have an elevated risk of skin cancers. Furthermore, Dowling-Degos disease should be considered a comorbid factor for hidradenitis suppurativa, potentially being responsible for its development in susceptible individuals. Long-term management strategies are emphasized. [PMC12232819, PMC12259490, PMC10010119]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurocutaneous disorder caused by an inborn error of lipid metabolism and characterized by congenital ichthyosis, intellectual deficit, and spasticity.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is estimated at 1/250,000 worldwide, but the syndrome is more common in Sweden due to a founder effect.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical features develop perinatally and during infancy. Patients tend to be born preterm. Hyperkeratosis is usually present at birth and progresses to a generalized ichthyosis, particularly prominent on flexural areas, the nape of the neck, the trunk and the extremities. Pruritus is a prominent feature. Erythematous dermatitis is often present at birth, and then tends to fade with increasing age. Neurological signs appear during the first two years of life and consist of delay in reaching motor milestones due to spastic diplegia or, much less commonly, spastic tetraplegia. Approximately one-half of patients are non-ambulatory. Seizures occur in about 40% of cases. Intellectual deficit varies from mild to severe, although rare patients with normal intellect have been reported. Delayed speech and dysarthria are common. Ophthalmologic involvement is often present and is characterized by retinal crystalline inclusions (so-called glistening white dots) surrounding the fovea. Photophobia and myopia are common.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: SLS is caused by mutations in the ALDH3A2 gene (17p11.2) encoding fatty aldehyde dehydrogenase (FALDH), an enzyme that catalyzes the oxidation of fatty aldehydes to fatty acids. More than 90 mutations in ALDH3A2 have been identified, including amino acid substitutions, deletions, insertions, splicing errors and contiguous gene deletions.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: SLS is diagnosed based on the clinical features, and by measuring FALDH or fatty alcohol oxidoreductase (FAO) activity in cultured fibroblasts from skin biopsies. DNA-based diagnosis is possible by directly sequencing the ALDH3A2 gene and identifying pathogenic mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: In early infancy, before the onset of spasticity, the differential diagnosis includes other forms of congenital ichthyosis including lamellar ichthyosis and congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma. Once neurologic symptoms appear, the differential diagnosis includes other neuro-ichthyotic syndromes such as neutral lipid storage disease (Chanarin-Dorfman syndrome), ELOVL4 deficiency, multiple sulfatase deficiency and Refsum disease.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible through biochemical or molecular analysis of amniocytes or chorionic villus cells.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management should be multidisciplinary including neurologists, dermatologists, ophthalmologists, orthopedic surgeons, and physiotherapists. The treatment of ichthyosis consists of topical application of moisturizing creams and keratolytic agents, or use of systemic retinoids. Seizures usually respond to anti-convulsant medications and spasticity is alleviated by botulinum toxin injections or surgical procedures. Special diets with medium-chain fatty acid supplements may help the ichthyosis, but effects are limited.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Patients usually survive until adulthood but require life-long care. Minimal progression of the neurologic findings or intellectual deficit occurs after puberty. Patients with early symptoms tend to be more severely affected.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Mosaic trisomy 14 is a rare chromosomal anomaly disorder, with a highly variable phenotype, principally characterized by growth and developmental delay, intellectual disability, body asymmetry/hypotonia, congenital heart defects, genitourinary abnormalities (cryptorchidism, micropenis, large clitoris, labial swelling), and abnormal skin hyperpigmentation. Patients usually present with craniofacial dysmorphism such as microcephaly, abnormal palpebral fissure, hypertelorism, ear abnormalities, broad nose, low-set ears, micro/retro-gnathia, and cleft or highly arched palate.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Mosaic trisomy 14 syndrome presents with a distinctive clinical picture, primarily characterized by developmental retardation, ranging from mild psychomotor to severe. Common craniofacial dysmorphism includes a wide flat nose with a bulbous or wide tip, a large mouth with turned down corners (sometimes with protruding lips), low-set dysplastic ears, and retrognathia. Patients may also exhibit palatal anomalies, such as a high arched or cleft palate, and digital anomalies, including curved fifth fingers or contractions and deviations. Other reported features encompass skeletal abnormalities like pectus carinatum, retarded bone age, and skeletal asymmetry, along with congenital malformations such as atrial septal defect, failure to thrive, a short neck with redundant skin folds, and cryptorchidism. Abnormalities of neutrophil nuclei, similar to those in trisomy 13 syndrome, have also been noted. [PMC1049549, PMC1049351, PMC1048663, PMC1013561]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Mosaic trisomy 14 syndrome is caused by the presence of an extra chromosome 14, or a segment of it (14q), in a mosaic proportion of cells. The extra chromosome 14 can arise from either a second paternal meiotic error or an early mitotic error. In some instances, the chromosomal imbalance is attributed to the dissociation of a balanced 14q15q translocation, leading to the subsequent formation of a 14q isochromosome. One reported case also identified mosaic trisomy 14 in conjunction with maternal uniparental disomy for chromosome 14, which was associated with the loss of a chromosome 14 from somatic cells with t(13;14) trisomy 14. [PMC1682257, PMC1049549, PMC1048663]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Postnatal diagnosis of mosaic trisomy 14 syndrome involves cytogenetic analysis, which has identified trisomic cells in blood lymphocytes and skin fibroblasts. DNA analysis, including polymorphic markers, can also reveal the condition and help determine the parental origin of chromosomes or the extra chromosome's origin through non-disjunction studies. For prenatal diagnosis, a silicon-based microfluidic platform can capture circulating fetal nucleated red blood cells from maternal blood. These captured cells are then suitable for fluorescent in situ hybridization or molecular genetic analyses to facilitate genetic diagnosis. [PMC6413103, PMC1682257, PMC1049549]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Mosaic trisomy 14 syndrome shares features with other chromosomal abnormalities. Neutrophil nuclear abnormalities, such as multiple pedunculated or sessile projections, are similar to those characteristically associated with trisomy 13 syndrome. Additionally, patients with mosaic trisomy 14 exhibit common features with cases of atypical D trisomy (Snodgrass category II), including developmental retardation, characteristic facial features like a wide flat nose and large mouth, short neck, low-set ears, retrognathia, and digital and palatal anomalies. [PMC1049351, PMC1013561]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Circulating fetal cells (CFCs) in maternal blood are rare but have a strong potential to be the target for noninvasive prenatal diagnosis (NIPD). "Cell Reveal TM system" is a silicon-based microfluidic platform capable to capture rare cell populations in human circulation. The platform is recently optimized to enhance the capture efficiency and system automation. In , spiking tests of SK-BR-3 breast cancer cells were used for the evaluation of capture efficiency. Then, peripheral bloods from 14 pregnant women whose fetuses have evidenced non-maternal genomic markers (e.g., de novo pathogenic copy number changes) were tested for the capture of circulating fetal nucleated red blood cells (fnRBCs). Captured cells were subjected to fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) on chip or recovered by an automated cell picker for molecular genetic analyses. The capture rate for the spiking tests... [PMC6413103]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The genetic origins of mosaic trisomy 14 are varied. Non-disjunction events, either a second paternal meiotic error or an early mitotic error, have been identified as causes. In some cases, the chromosomal imbalance may result from the dissociation of a balanced translocation, such as a 14q15q translocation, followed by isochromosome formation. Uniparental disomy for chromosome 14 can also occur concurrently, particularly in individuals with de novo Robertsonian translocations and mosaic trisomy 14, which can complicate the assessment of the mosaicism's phenotypic contribution. [PMC1682257, PMC1049549, PMC1048663]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Mosaic trisomy 14 syndrome is observed in liveborn infants, with reported cases surviving into childhood, including a 2-year-old and a 9-year-old. The condition is consistently associated with developmental retardation, which can range from mild psychomotor retardation to severe developmental delay. Other features include failure to thrive and various congenital malformations. In one instance, hydrocephalus resolved spontaneously during the first year of life. The clinical picture suggests a distinctive syndrome. [PMC1682257, PMC1049549, PMC1049351, PMC1048663, PMC1013561]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Growth delay due to insulin-like growth factor type 1 deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Growth delay due to insulin-like growth factor I deficiency is characterised by the association of intrauterine and postnatal growth retardation with sensorineural deafness and intellectual deficit.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Growth delay-hearing loss-intellectual disability syndrome; IGF-1 deficiency; Primary insulin-like growth factor deficiency; Growth delay-deafness-intellectual disability syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The syndrome is extremely rare and only four cases have been reported in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Addition clinical features include microcephaly, adiposity, and insulin resistance. Partial gonadal dysfunction and osteoporosis may also be present. A case of partial IGF-I deficiency has also been described and was associated with pre- and postnatal growth retardation and microcephaly but the developmental delay was mild and hearing tests were normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: IGF-I deficiency is caused by homozygous mutations in the insulin-like growth factor 1 gene (IGFI; 12q22-q24.1). IGF-I is essential for foetal and postnatal growth, brain development and metabolism.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on direct sequencing of the five IGF1 exons and of the intron-exon junctions. Measurement of IGF-I levels can be used for diagnosis but the circulating levels of IGF-I vary between patients (ranging from undetectable, low to very high) depending on the molecular defect present and on the immunoassay used.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include growth hormone deficiency and growth hormone resistance (caused by GH receptor or STAT5b anomalies), growth delay due to insulin-like growth factor I resistance and primary acid-labile subunit (ALS) deficiency syndrome, as well as secondary IGF-I deficiency due to nutritional problems.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is feasible for families with an identified IGF1 mutation proven to be responsible for the disease phenotype of intrauterine and postnatal growth delay associated with intellectual deficit.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: IGF-I deficiency is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait. Affected families should be offered genetic counselling and informed of a 25% risk of recurrence.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management involves nutritional and developmental support, together with screening for deafness. Growth velocity in patients with partial IGF-I deficiency can be increased by recombinant growth hormone (GH) therapy. Recombinant IGF-I therapy can be used in patients with complete IGF-I deficiency or those showing an insufficient response to recombinant GH treatment.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for growth delay due to insulin-like growth factor type 1 deficiency can be favorable depending on the underlying cause and treatment. In cases where IGF-1 deficiency is caused by a treatable condition, such as a hepatocellular adenoma, surgical resection can normalize IGF-1 levels, blood pressure, lipid profile, ovarian function, and lead to gains in height and reduction in waist circumference. For deficiencies impacting IGF-1 bioavailability, such as PAPP-A2 deficiency, treatment with recombinant human IGF-1 has been shown to improve growth velocity and height. [PMC11391839, PMC5393598]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Camurati-Engelmann disease (CED) is a rare, clinically variable bone dysplasia syndrome characterized by hyperostosis of the long bones, skull, spine and pelvis, associated with severe pain in the extremities, a wide-based waddling gait, joint contractures, muscle weakness and easy fatigability.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown but more than 300 cases have been reported to date. CED has been described in various ethnic groups, and males and females are affected equally.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most of the clinical signs are related to hyperostosis and sclerosis. The age of onset and severity are highly variable, even within the same family. The average age of onset is about 13 years and almost always before 30 years. Patients generally present with pain in the extremities, waddling gait, easy fatigability, and muscle weakness. Pain may be severe, constant and aching and is exacerbated by cold weather and physical activity. Other signs include decreased muscle mass, joint contractures, and sometimes marfanoid body habitus. Later in life, severely affected individuals may present facial abnormalities such as frontal bossing and enlarged mandible, as well as facial paralysis. Other signs of musculoskeletal involvement include lumbar lordosis, kyphosis, scoliosis, coxa valga, genu valgum, and flat feet. Involvement of the orbit may lead to proptosis, papilledema, epiphora, glaucoma, and subluxation of the globe. Conductive and/or sensorineural hearing loss is found in less than 20% of patients. Occasional associated systemic features include anemia, leukocytopenia, and hepatosplenomegaly. Rare signs include sensory loss, slurred speech, dysphagia, cerebellar ataxia, anorexia, decreased subcutaneous tissue, hyperhidrosis of the extremities, delayed dentition, extensive dental caries, delayed puberty, hypogonadism and bladder incontinence.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In more than 90% of patients, mutations in the transforming growth factor TGFB1 gene (19q13.1) are detected.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of CED is based on the clinical and radiographic signs and can be confirmed by molecular genetic testing. CED should be suspected in patients with proximal muscle weakness and hyperostosis of one or more of the long bones on radiographic imaging. The radiographic hallmark of the disorder is bilateral, sometimes symmetrical, periosteal and endosteal bony sclerosis of the diaphyses of long bones resulting in cortical thickening. Skull, spine and pelvic involvement may be found on radiographic examination.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Camurati-Engelmann disease has characteristic clinical and radiological findings, reducing the need for extensive differential diagnosis. Disorders to consider include craniodiaphyseal dysplasia, autosomal dominant Kenny-Caffey syndrome, juvenile Paget disease, Ghosal hematodiaphyseal dysplasia, Worth type autosomal dominant osteosclerosis, sclerosteosis and hyperostosis corticalis generalisata.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis for at-risk pregnancies is possible when the disease-causing mutation has been identified in a family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: CED is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait with reduced penetrance. The number of cases caused by de novo mutations is not known. Reduced penetrance complicates genetic counseling.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: No disease-modifying treatment is available. Corticosteroids are reported to relieve the symptoms of CED. Analgesics and non-pharmacological methods can be used to treat pain. NSAIDs and bisphosphonates have been found to be ineffective.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: CED is a progressive disorder and prognosis is poor. Depending on the severity, quality of life is impaired by pain and reduced mobility.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare group of genetic, cardiac rhythm diseases characterized by a prolongation of the QT interval at basal electrocardiography (ECG) and by a high risk of life-threatening arrhythmias.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The most prevalent form, Romano-Ward syndrome (RWS), has a prevalence close to 1/2,500 live births. The other forms of familial LQTS are extremely rare.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The two cardinal manifestations of LQTS are syncopal episodes, which may lead to cardiac arrest and sudden cardiac death, and electrocardiographic abnormalities: prolongation of the QT interval and T wave abnormalities. Where there are no extracardiac features, the disease is referred to as RWS. RWS related to SCN5A is sometimes associated with 2:1 atrioventricular block and very early occurrence of cardiac arrhythmias, especially in de novo cases. The Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome also has congenital deafness. Timothy syndrome can be associated with syndactyly, facial dysmorphism and neurodevelopmental features. The Andersen-Tawil syndrome is no longer considered part of LQTS.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: All the LQTS genes identified so far encode cardiac ion channel subunits or proteins involved in modulating ionic currents. Mutations in the genes that encode the cardiac potassium and sodium channels (KCNQ1, 11p15.5-p15.4 ; KCNH2, 7q36.1 ; SCN5A, 3p22.2) mainly cause the disease by prolonging the duration of repolarization and, thus, of the action potential. KCNQ1 is the most common LQTS variant.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Given the characteristic features of LQTS, the typical cases present no diagnostic difficulties for physicians aware of the disease. However, borderline cases are more complex and require the evaluation of various electrocardiographic, clinical, and familial findings, as proposed in the specific diagnostic criteria (the Schwartz score). The molecular screening is now part of the diagnostic process.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis must be made with epilepsy, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT), and drug-induced LQTS.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis should be considered when one of the parents has LQTS.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance may be autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive and depends on the genes involved and the form of familial LQTS. Genetic counseling should be offered to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment should always begin with beta-blockers, unless there are valid contraindications. If the patient has a further syncopal episode despite a full dose beta-blockade, left cardiac sympathetic denervation (LCSD) should be performed without hesitation. Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) therapy should be considered when the degree of protection afforded by beta-blockers and LCSD does not appear sufficient, with the final decision being based on individual patient characteristics (age, sex, clinical history, genetic subgroup including mutation-specific features in some cases, and the presence of ECG signs from 24-hour Holter recordings, indicating high electrical instability).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is usually good in patients that are correctly diagnosed and treated. The exceptions are patients with Timothy syndrome, Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome patients carrying KCNQ1 mutations and patients with LQTS related to either Calmodulin, TRDN or SCN5A variants.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic peripheral neuropathy characterized by complete congenital insensitivity to painful stimuli, commonly associated with neuropathic arthropathy. In addition, patients are typically anosmic.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Congenital insensitivity to pain (CIP) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Congenital indifference to pain is also described as a rare and debilitating congenital disease. The condition presents with a spectrum of clinical features. [PMC6767138, PMC4242143]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Congenital insensitivity to pain (CIP) is a rare, debilitating, autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a spectrum of clinical features. Patients exhibit congenital indifference to pain, including a lack of mechanical nociception and diminished ability to detect heat and cool stimulation. Associated sensory deficits often include anosmia or hyposmia, and sometimes hypogeusia. While patients may show no autonomic reflex to surgical stimuli, they can still develop autonomic responses like tachycardia, hypertension, and pyrexia, which may indicate underlying conditions such as infection. Some forms of the disorder involve devastating and fatal autonomic dysfunction. Histologically, there is a lack of Meissner's corpuscles and loss of epidermal nociceptors, though autonomic organ innervation can be normal. Radiographic presentations, such as a mass of the distal femur, have also been observed. [PMC12049192, PMC6767138, PMC4242143]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Congenital insensitivity to pain (CIP) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in different genes, indicating genetic heterogeneity. Mutations in SCN9A are implicated in CIP.
