DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Antibiotic treatment (tetracycline, doxycycline, erythromycin, ceftriaxone, chloramphenicol or penicillin G) is effective. Of important note, within a few hours after the start of antibiotic treatment, a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction (JHR) may occur, starting with restlessness, a chill phase with intense rigors, a sharp rise in body temperature, pulse and respiratory rates, and sometimes delirium, and followed by a flush phase with systemic vasodilatation, a massive drop in blood pressure, profuse sweating, and slowly declining body temperature. Though rarely fatal, JHR increases the risk for (lethal) complications. Prevention revolves around eradication of the hosts and vector control, i.e. hygiene measures, repellents, acaricides and rodenticides.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The case fatality rate is 4-10%. There are no relevant studies on long term prognosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Ticks are vectors of public health concern because the pathogens they transmit can cause detrimental diseases in humans. Lyme disease, tick-borne relapsing fever, human granulocytic anaplasmosis, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, tick-borne encephalitis, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, and babesiosis are some of the most common diseases caused by the pathogens transmitted by ticks. The overlap between human activities and tick habitats is growing, contributing to an increase in tick-borne disease cases. Unfortunately, pregnancy as a risk factor for tick-borne diseases is largely ignored. In this narrative review we use case reports, epidemiological studies, and animal studies to evaluate the maternal, pregnancy, and fetal outcomes caused by Lyme disease, tick-borne relapsing fever, human granulocytic anaplasmosis, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, tick-borne encephalitis, Crimean-Congo... [PMC11598240]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis is a rare disorder characterized by osteopetrosis, renal tubular acidosis (RTA), and neurological disorders related to cerebral calcifications.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Carbonic anhydrase 2 deficiency; Guibaud-Vainsel syndrome; Marble brain disease; Mixed RTA; Mixed renal tubular acidosis; Renal tubular acidosis type 3

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of this disorder is not known. Fewer than 100 cases have been reported to date. Many reports involved families of North African and Middle Eastern descent, but cases have been documented worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients present a triad of mild osteopetrosis, mixed proximal and distal RTA, and intracerebral calcifications. Other clinical manifestations include fractures, growth failure and short stature, developmental delay, intellectual deficit, dental malocclusions/malalignment, cranial nerve compression and hearing impairment.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis is caused by mutations in the CA2 gene (8q22) encoding carbonic anhydrase II.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on radiological findings in the presence of acidosis and intracerebral calcifications, and can be confirmed by molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible if the mutation(s) causing the condition in the family are known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic. Referral to a renal physician to manage the acidosis is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Severity is variable but the disorder has a milder course than in patients with classic osteopetrosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for osteopetrosis with renal tubular acidosis primarily includes carbonic anhydrase II (CAII) deficiency, which is the most common cause and from mutations in the CA2 gene. However, a phenocopy of CAII deficiency can occur due to the coinheritance of two distinct recessive disorders: osteopetrosis caused by a TCIRG1 deletion and distal renal tubular acidosis from an ATP6V1B1 mutation. Additionally, an unusual presentation of autosomal dominant osteopetrosis, typically associated with CLCN7 mutations (Albers-Schonberg disease), has been reported with coexistent renal tubular acidosis, renal stones, epilepsy, and blindness, expanding the genetic considerations. [PMC6499615, PMC5132132, PMC1735376]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:2207

DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Typically, primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) develops as a result of multiglandular hyperplasia, parathyroid cancer, or parathyroid adenoma. Patients usually present with skeletal manifestations such as low-trauma fractures. Osteitis fibrosa cystica (OFC) is a classic yet rare skeletal manifestation of advanced PHPT currently reported in less than 2% of patients. a case of a 29-year-old Indian female who presented with a femur fracture and mandibular OFC 20 days after delivery. The painless mandibular swelling gradually progressed from the third month of pregnancy. The biochemical and radiological investigations were indicative of PHPT-associated OFC. After the excision of the three-and-a-half parathyroid gland, histology revealed benign cystic adenomas and hyperplasia. Based on the associated clinical manifestations, OFC was suspected. Clinical exome sequencing revealed CDC73 (+)... [PMC11604356, PMC10214968, PMC8981180]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal dominant disorder characterized by aplasia, atresia or hypoplasia of the lacrimal and salivary glands leading to varying features since infancy such as recurrent eye infections, irritable eyes, epiphora, xerostomia, dental caries, dental erosion and oral inflammation.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): ALSG; Congenital absence of lacrimal puncta and salivary glands
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Lacrimo-auriculo-dento-digital (LADD) syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in one of the three genes: fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2), FGFR3, or FGF10. Affected patients have hypoplasia/aplasia of lacrimal ducts/glands, hypoplasia/aplasia of salivary glands, dental anomalies, ear anomalies, hearing loss, and digital anomalies. Proband was an 11-year-old male with xerostomia, xerophthalmia, and a referring diagnosis of Sjogren syndrome. He presented with microdontia, hypodontia, low-set/cupped ear auricles, and hearing loss in the left ear. Whole exome sequencing (WES) was performed on proband. Variations and segregation within the family were verified using Sanger sequencing. Molecular studies revealed a novel heterozygous missense mutation in exon 11 of FGFR2: c.1547C>T (p.Ala516Val), compatible with LADD syndrome. To the best of our knowledge,... [PMC7549548]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands (ALSG syndrome) is a rarely diagnosed condition. The clinically overlapping lacrimo-auriculo-dento-digital (LADD) syndrome, which includes hypoplasia/aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands, is described as a rare autosomal dominant disorder. A literature review of LADD syndrome summarized 23 case reports/series, and the first family report in Korea suggests its infrequent occurrence. The combination of xerostomia and xerophthalmia in affected patients may lead to misdiagnosis, such as Sjogren syndrome. [PMC7549548, PMC2626586]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands (ALSG) syndrome is a rare autosomal-dominant disorder characterized by combined aplasia, hypoplasia, or atresia of lacrimal points and salivary glands. Patients typically suffer from xerostomia, epiphora, and severe dental caries. Aberrations of the Fibroblast Growth Factor 10 (FGF10) gene are causative for this disorder. A clinically overlapping condition, lacrimo-auriculo-dento-digital (LADD) syndrome, also presents with hypoplasia/aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands, xerostomia, and xerophthalmia. LADD syndrome, caused by mutations in FGFR2, FGFR3, or FGF10, additionally involves dental, ear, and digital anomalies. The combination of xerostomia and xerophthalmia may lead to a misdiagnosis of Sjogren syndrome. [PMC7549548, PMC2626586]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands (ALSG) syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder primarily caused by aberrations of the Fibroblast Growth Factor 10 (FGF10) gene. A novel heterozygous intronic variation in FGF10 (c.430-1, G > A) has been identified, which derogates the regular splice acceptor site. This condition can also be a feature of Lacrimo-auriculo-dento-digital (LADD) syndrome, another rare autosomal dominant disorder. LADD syndrome is caused by mutations in one of three genes: fibroblast growth factor receptor 2 (FGFR2), FGFR3, or FGF10. A novel heterozygous missense mutation in exon 11 of FGFR2 (c.1547C>T (p.Ala516Val)) has been found in patients with LADD syndrome. [PMC7549548, PMC2626586]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands (ALSG) involves recognizing clinical features such as xerostomia, xerophthalmia, epiphora, and severe dental caries, which may sometimes be misdiagnosed as Sjogren syndrome. Molecular genetic testing is crucial for confirmation. Whole exome sequencing (WES) is a useful clinical tool for identifying causative gene mutations. Specifically, sequence analysis of the FGF10 gene is performed for ALSG syndrome, while LADD syndrome, which shares overlapping features, involves mutations in FGFR2, FGFR3, or FGF10. Sanger sequencing can be used to verify identified variations and their segregation within families. Transcript analysis of FGF10 from primary fibroblasts has also been employed. [PMC7549548, PMC2626586]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands includes Lacrimo-auriculo-dento-digital (LADD) syndrome, which presents with similar hypoplasia or aplasia of these glands but also involves dental, ear, hearing, and digital anomalies. The clinical presentation of xerostomia and xerophthalmia, common in both conditions, may lead to a misdiagnosis of Sjogren syndrome. [PMC7549548, PMC2626586]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Aplasia of lacrimal and salivary glands (ALSG) syndrome and the clinically overlapping lacrimo-auriculo-dento-digital (LADD) syndrome are rare autosomal dominant disorders. ALSG is caused by aberrations in the Fibroblast Growth Factor 10 (FGF10) gene, while LADD syndrome can result from mutations in FGFR2, FGFR3, or FGF10. Molecular studies, including whole exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing, are utilized to identify causative heterozygous mutations, such as novel intronic alterations in FGF10 or missense mutations in FGFR2. Genetic counseling should address the autosomal dominant inheritance pattern and the potential for misdiagnosis, as LADD syndrome may be confused with Sjogren syndrome. [PMC7549548, PMC2626586]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pityriasis rubra pilaris is a rare chronic papulosquamous disorder of unknown etiology characterized by small follicular papules, scaly red-orange patches, and palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, which may progress to plaques or erythroderma. Although most of the cases are sporadic and acquired, a familial form of the disease exists.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is a rare inflammatory skin disease that occurs in adults of all ages and in children. While its etiology is largely unknown, genetic factors, specifically CARD14 mutations, have been implicated, sometimes presenting with early onset and an autosomal dominant family history. PRP has also been reported in association with certain medications, including ponatinib and topical imiquimod, and as a paraneoplastic phenomenon. Furthermore, cases have been observed following COVID-19 infection and various COVID-19 vaccinations, such as Pfizer-BioNTech, Oxford-AstraZeneca, Moderna, CoronaVac, and ChAdOx1. In one systematic review, PRP accounted for 16% of pityriasis eruptions reported after COVID-19 inoculations. [PMC11596965, PMC11221136, PMC10859040, PMC11355122, PMC10589495]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is a rare, chronic, inflammatory, papulosquamous, scaly, keratotic skin disease with varied clinical manifestations and phenotypic variability across all ages. It is primarily characterized by scaly plaques and keratinized hair follicles. Patients may present with generalized papular erythema, diffuse erythematosquamous plaques, and prominent palmoplantar hyperkeratosis or keratoderma. Scalp involvement can manifest as white-silvery scales forming triangular hair casts. Lesions often appear as erythematous papules and plaques, sometimes with demarcated areas of spared skin, affecting the trunk, extremities, neck, and face. Gain-of-function mutations in CARD14 are associated with a distinct form, CARD14-associated papulosquamous eruption (CAPE), which may feature early onset, prominent facial involvement, and an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. [PMC11907769, PMC11596965, PMC11355122, PMC9541132, PMC9775151]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiology of Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is largely unknown, but several factors have been implicated. Genetic gain-of-function mutations in CARD14 are involved in PRP pathogenesis, activating the NF-kB signaling pathway. These mutations are associated with CARD14-associated papulosquamous eruption (CAPE), which presents with PRP features, particularly in early-onset cases with an autosomal dominant trait. PRP has also been reported following certain medications, including ponatinib and topical imiquimod 5, and as a paraneoplastic phenomenon. Furthermore, PRP or PRP-like eruptions have been observed after SARS-CoV-2 infection and various COVID-19 vaccinations, such as Pfizer-BioNTech, Oxford-AstraZeneca, Moderna, CoronaVac, and ChAdOx1. [PMC11221136, PMC10859040, PMC10589495, PMC10480444, PMC11017724]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) presents a diagnostic challenge due to its varied clinical manifestations. Diagnosis involves evaluating clinical, trichoscopic, and histopathological features. For scalp involvement, trichoscopy may reveal white-silvery scales forming triangular hair casts. Clinical findings can include generalized papular erythema, diffuse erythematosquamous plaques, and palmoplantar keratoderma. Differential diagnoses are important, as conditions like atypical Grover's disease can present with PRP-like lesions. In pediatric patients with early-onset PRP-like features, prominent facial involvement, family history, and resistance to conventional therapy, testing for CARD14 mutations should be considered to distinguish CARD14-associated papulosquamous eruption (CAPE) from classical PRP. [PMC11596965, PMC8578307, PMC8054706, PMC8007481]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) presents diagnostic challenges due to its varied clinical manifestations, including scalp involvement. Differential diagnoses include psoriasis, particularly in pediatric patients where initial treatment for psoriasis may occur before a PRP diagnosis. CARD14-associated papulosquamous eruption (CAPE) also encompasses features ranging from psoriasis to PRP, with specific characteristics distinguishing it. Atypical Grover's disease can present with PRP-like lesions. Additionally, various pityriasis eruptions, such as pityriasis rosea, pityriasis lichenoides et varioliformis acuta, and pityriasis lichenoides chronica, have been reported, sometimes as PRP-like eruptions, especially following COVID-19 vaccinations. [PMC11596965, PMC11017724, PMC9541132, PMC9544444, PMC8444918]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) can be associated with gain-of-function mutations in the CARD14 gene, which activate the NF-kB signaling pathway. These CARD14 mutations are linked to an autosomal dominant trait, particularly in cases termed CARD14-associated papulosquamous eruption (CAPE). Genetic testing for CARD14 mutations should be considered in pediatric patients presenting with early-onset features of PRP or psoriasis, especially if the condition is resistant to conventional therapies. This information is crucial for understanding inheritance patterns and guiding diagnostic approaches. [PMC9775151, PMC8578307]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) presents a therapeutic challenge, often proving resistant to common topical and conventional systemic therapies, with no universally satisfactory clinical options available. Small molecule drugs, including apremilast, upadacitinib, abrocitinib, and tofacitinib, have demonstrated good efficacy and safety, particularly in refractory cases or those unresponsive to biologics, though data is limited by small sample sizes. Biologic agents, such as IL-17 and IL-23 inhibitors, and ustekinumab (an IL-12/23p40 inhibitor), are emerging as promising treatments, with ustekinumab showing successful or excellent responses in some patients, including children. Bimekizumab is also noted for refractory erythrodermic PRP. While these biologics are often used off-label, treatment decisions are largely guided by clinical experience and case reports due to the rarity of the condition. Oral isotretinoin, rehydrating cream, cetirizine, and prednisolone have also shown successful outcomes in specific cases. [PMC11907769, PMC12339111, PMC11596965, PMC11221136, PMC11355122]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Pityriasis rubra pilaris (PRP) is a chronic skin disease that significantly impacts the patient's quality of life and is considered one of the intractable conditions in dermatology. The disease often proves resistant to common topical and conventional systemic therapies. Despite these challenges, PRP is known for its possible spontaneous remission. For instance, one pediatric case of PRP post-COVID-19 infection showed clinical resolution of lesions within three months. [PMC11907769, PMC11355122, PMC8578307, PMC8054706]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A primary adrenal insufficiency caused by a sudden defective production of adrenal steroids (cortisol and aldosterone). It represents an emergency, thus the rapid recognition and prompt therapy are critical for survival even before the diagnosis is made.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Adrenal crisis; Adrenocortical crisis; Acute adrenal failure; Acute adrenocortical insufficiency; Addisonian crisis
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal recessive, Not applicable, X-linked dominant

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Acute adrenal insufficiency (AAI) exact prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease may occur at any age. The onset is often sudden. The initial presentation may be non specific and may be limited to abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, tachycardia, and fever. Asymptomatic hypoglycemia, Hypoglycemic seizures or symptoms of dehydration are common manifestations seen in children. If untreated, shock and bilateral adrenal hemorrhage can rapidly lead to death.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Steroid withdrawal is the most common cause of AAI in patients with chronic adrenal insufficiency. A precipitating illness (severe infection, acute myocardial infarction, stroke), surgery without adrenal support, pregnancy, any acute or chronic disease, or acute trauma are other potential causes of an acute adrenal crisis. AAI may result from an acute exacerbation of chronic primary adrenal insufficiency (CPAI). Adrenal destruction may be associated with autoimmune adrenalitis (Addison disease), isolated or in the context of autoimmune polyendocrinopathy type 1, 2 or 4. It can also be caused by medications that reduce steroid metabolism for patients with tuberculosis, opportunistic mycoses and viral infections in immunocompromised patients and adrenal metastases. Adrenal destruction may occur in the absence of CPAI history and may be due to bilateral massive adrenal hemorrhage (BMAH) as seen in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. AAI may also result from corticotroph insufficiency, either isolated or more often resulting from complete anterior pituitary insufficiency. Chronic glucocorticoid therapy (exogenous steroid such oral prednisolone or inhaled steroid) is also a cause of adrenal insufficiency (secondary adrenal insufficiency). Abrupt withdrawal of treatment may result in acute adrenal insufficiency.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The clinical signs are nonspecific but the diagnosis of AAI is suspected if a patient presents with hypotonia or shock that responds poorly to catecholamines. Laboratory exams show signs of adrenal insufficiency (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia and elevated natriuresis, hyperkaliemia, hemoconcentration, metabolic acidosis and functional renal failure) confirmed by hypocortisolemia, increased ACTH (Adreno CorticoTropic Hormone), and an insufficient response to rapid ACTH stimulation testing that leads to the diagnosis of absolute and peripheral AAI. The mineralocorticoid insufficiency, when present, can be confirmed by low aldosterone levels and high plasma renin activity (PRA). The etiological diagnosis is based on various imaging exams (CT-scan, ultrasound, or MRI). In case of anterior pituitary insufficiency, ACTH is low.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Secondary adrenal insufficiency needs to be eliminated. Peritonitis is often a differential diagnosis as well as other causes of adrenal destruction such as bilateral adrenalectomy, Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome, autoimmune adrenalitis, infectious adrenalitis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Immediate treatment in an intensive care unit is necessary. Administration of 100 mg hydrocortisone i.v. (followed by 100-200 mg over 24 hours) combined with fluid resuscitation (1L saline solution during first hour, 500ml during second hour) is the standard treatment for an adrenal crisis. In children the dosage is based on 2 mg/kg/every 6 hours and hydroelectrolytic re-equilibration based on 3l/m2/d. During this time cardiac monitoring is essential. Antibiotics, vasopressors, heparin, packed red blood cells, platelets, cryoprecipitates and fresh frozen plasma are also administered if needed. Preventive strategies include dosage increase of oral steroid hormones during times of stress in those with CPIA or intramuscular, intraveinous or sub cutaneous injection. Patients and their families should also be educated on what to do during an adrenal crisis.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis varies depending on the etiologies, but is generally correlated with the rapidity of diagnosis and medical assistance. Death is rare when the patients receive appropriate medical assistance.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Acute adrenal insufficiency can be a manifestation of underlying genetic disorders. Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH), a group of autosomal recessive diseases caused by enzyme deficiencies in steroidogenesis (e.g., 21-hydroxylase deficiency confirmed by CYP21A2 gene mutation), is a notable example. Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, another rare autosomal recessive disorder of cholesterol biosynthesis, can also present with acute adrenal crisis. Genetic testing plays a role in diagnosing these hereditary conditions. [PMC12125153, PMC10089040, PMC6441270, PMC6085650]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal monosomy 7p is a partial autosomal monosomy characterized by developmental delay and intellectual disability, digital anomalies, congenital heart and urogenital anomalies, and specific craniofacial features, commonly including craniosynostosis.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Subchromosomal deletions and duplications could currently be detected by noninvasive preliminary screening (NIPS). However, NIPS is a screening test that requires further diagnosis. Here a fetus with an autosomal abnormality revealed by NIPS and conventional karyotype combined with copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq) confirmed the fetus with an unbalanced translocation. Patient concern: This was the fourth pregnancy of a 30-year-old woman who underwent 2 spontaneous abortions and gave birth to a child with a normal phenotype. The woman and her husband were healthy and nonconsanguineous. NIPS indicated a repeat of about 19-Mb fragment at the region of 16q22.1-q22.4 at 17-week gestation. Diagnoses: The combination of traditional karyotype and CNV-seq could better locate the abnormal chromosomal region and further identify the source of fetal chromosomal abnormalities.... [PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal deletion 7p syndrome is caused by a subchromosomal deletion in the distal region of chromosome 7p, specifically 7p22.3-p22.2, involving approximately 3.86-Mb. This deletion can arise from an unbalanced translocation, such as 46,XX,der(7)t(7;16)(p22;q23), which may be inherited from a parent carrying a balanced translocation, like 46,XY, t (7;16) (p22;q23). [PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Noninvasive preliminary screening (NIPS) can detect subchromosomal deletions, but it is a screening test requiring further diagnosis. Conventional karyotype combined with copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq) is a useful tool to confirm and precisely locate abnormal chromosomal regions, and to identify the source of fetal chromosomal abnormalities. Fetal morphology can also be evaluated by ultrasound examination, which may reveal features like micrognathia. [PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis can be initiated by noninvasive preliminary screening (NIPS), which may indicate subchromosomal abnormalities, though it requires further diagnostic confirmation. Traditional karyotyping combined with Copy Number Variations sequencing (CNV-seq) can then precisely locate the deletion, such as a 3.86-Mb deletion in 7p22.3-p22.2. Prenatal ultrasound examination may reveal associated fetal morphological anomalies, including micrognathia. Parental karyotyping can also identify the source of the abnormality, such as an inherited unbalanced translocation. [PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for distal deletion 7p syndrome should consider the possibility of parental chromosomal rearrangements. In one reported case, a fetus with a 3.86-Mb deletion in 7p22.3-p22.2 inherited an abnormal chromosome 7 from its father, who carried a balanced translocation t(7;16)(p22;q23). Noninvasive preliminary screening (NIPS) can indicate such abnormalities, but definitive diagnosis requires conventional karyotype and copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq) to precisely locate the abnormal region and identify the source of the chromosomal abnormality. This highlights the importance of parental karyotyping to assess recurrence risk. [PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Subchromosomal deletions and duplications could currently be detected by noninvasive preliminary screening (NIPS). However, NIPS is a screening test that requires further diagnosis. Here a fetus with an autosomal abnormality revealed by NIPS and conventional karyotype combined with copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq) confirmed the fetus with an unbalanced translocation. Patient concern: This was the fourth pregnancy of a 30-year-old woman who underwent 2 spontaneous abortions and gave birth to a child with a normal phenotype. The woman and her husband were healthy and nonconsanguineous. NIPS indicated a repeat of about 19-Mb fragment at the region of 16q22.1-q22.4 at 17-week gestation. Diagnoses: The combination of traditional karyotype and CNV-seq could better locate the abnormal chromosomal region and further identify the source of fetal chromosomal abnormalities.... [PMC7899829]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Optic pathway glioma (OPG) is a benign tumor that develop along the optic nerve (chiasm, tracts, and radiations) characterized by impairment or loss of vision and may be accompanied by diencephalic symptoms such as reduced growth and alteration in sleeping patterns. OPG are often linked to neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Optic pathway glioma (OPG) is strongly associated with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), a common autosomal dominant genetic disorder affecting approximately 1 in 5000 people. While OPG typically presents in childhood in individuals with NF1, it is rarely found in adults. Reported cases include children as young as 2.5 and 3 years old, as well as adults aged 52 and 75 years. Unusual co-occurrences of OPG have also been noted in patients with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease type 2 and in hybrid phakomatosis involving tuberous sclerosis. [PMC9410573, PMC7434601, PMC4678666, PMC4302466, PMC2621301]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Optic pathway gliomas (OPGs) are commonly associated with vision loss, particularly in children, and can present with symptoms such as visual disturbance, progressive visual acuity loss, visual field defects (e.g., quadrantopsia, total scotoma), proptosis, strabismus, exotropia, limitation in adduction, optic disc edema, enlarged blind spot, and optic disc pallor. In rare cases, visual field defects may fluctuate, correlating with the menstrual cycle. OPGs can involve the optic nerve, chiasm, optic tracts, and optic radiations, sometimes extending to the brainstem or showing extensive intraocular involvement with subretinal fluid and hemorrhage. Pathologically, they are often pilocytic astrocytomas (WHO grade I), but malignant forms like glioblastoma can occur, which are rare and rapidly lethal. OPGs are frequently associated with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), where they can be asymptomatic or lead to severe visual compromise, motor deficits, or central precocious puberty, especially with chiasmatic involvement. In NF1, T2 hyperintensities may also be observed, which can rarely evolve into cystic masses with neurological signs like hemiparesis. [PMC9410573, PMC11587496, PMC7167457, PMC5857244, PMC5346192]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Optic pathway glioma (OPG) is frequently associated with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), a common autosomal dominant genetic disorder. In children, OPG is the most frequently identified tumor in NF1. The etiology in NF1 involves the loss of tumor suppressor function of the neurofibromin gene, often due to mutations such as R681X or 4-bp deletions, leading to truncated neurofibromin. A positive family history of NF1 is also noted. In rare cases of hybrid phakomatosis involving both NF1 and tuberous sclerosis, defective tumor-suppressor genes may lead to an increased propensity for tumor formation and rapid growth of optic glioma. [PMC7434601, PMC5081233, PMC4678666, PMC4302466, PMC3908353]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Rationale: Benign optic nerve gliomas were rarely found in adults, and total resection of these lesions seems impossible. to share a rare clinical case with an unusual and instructive treatment process. Patient concerns: A 52-year-old woman complained of a 4-month history of visual disturbance. Automated perimetry revealed visual field defect in her both eyes. Diagnosis: This patient was diagnosed with optic nerve glioma. We found its pathological features consistent with the pilocytic astrocytomas (WHO grade I). Interventions: A total resection of the tumor was smoothly performed. Outcomes: Repeat MRI 3 months after the surgery demonstrated no recurrence of the lesion. Two years of postoperative telephone follow-up showed a stable status of improved vision. Lessons: We reported this interesting case to show a rare kind of condition regarding optic nerve gliomas in adults, which might... [PMC9410573, PMC11587496, PMC6959466, PMC5346192, PMC4818450]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Optic pathway glioma is frequently associated with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), an autosomal dominant genetic disorder with an extremely variable phenotype. NF1 is caused by mutations in the NF1 tumor suppressor gene, which can be identified through genetic analysis, including mutational analysis and next-generation sequencing. The mutational spectrum is wide and complex, and NF1 can arise from novel mutations or be inherited, as evidenced by positive family histories. Early and regular ophthalmological assessment is paramount for individuals suspected or confirmed to have NF1 to detect optic pathway gliomas. Co-occurrence with other autosomal dominant conditions like ADPKD has been noted, but without an additive effect on tumor severity. [PMC7434601, PMC5081233, PMC4678666, PMC4302466, PMC2621301]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare syndromic lymphedema characterized by the association of primary lymphedema, intestinal lymphangiectasia, intellectual deficit and unusual facial characteristics.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact prevalence is unknown but around 100 cases have been reported in the literature. The entity occurs in all ethnic groups.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The lymphedema has invariably been present at birth, and is mainly present in the lower limbs and genitalia, although it can also be present elsewhere, including ascites. Lymphangiectasia is common in the intestines but can also be present in lungs, pericardium, thyroid and kidneys. The degree of intellectual deficit is highly variable, even within a single family. Facial characteristics are a flat face, a broad and depressed nasal bridge, hypertelorism, epicanthi, a small mouth, and low-set ears with a narrow meatus. Other features include mild growth retardation, delayed puberty, tooth anomalies, gingival hypertrophy, seizures, and blood vessel anomalies.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome can be caused by bi-allelic variants in CCBE1 (18q21.32), FAT4 (4q28.1) or ADAMTS3 (4q13.3).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on the clinical phenotype. Intestinal lymphangiectasia may be suspected because of hypogammaglobulinemia, hypoalbuminemia, and lymphopenia, but a definitive diagnosis can only be made by biopsies (often several are needed). Molecular studies may confirm the clinical diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other entities associated with congenital lymphedema such as Noonan syndrome, Milroy syndrome and cholestasis-lymphedema syndrome, and Van Maldergem syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal genetic testing is possible in families with known mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The syndrome is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait and genetic counseling is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative therapy, only supportive management including decongestive therapy for edema control, typically needing lymphologists. Rarely surgery is performed. Medium-chain triglyceride-rich diet is usually helpful because of the intestinal lymphangiectasias but recurrent albumin infusions are not uncommon. Vitamin and electrolyte supplements should be considered. Pulmonary lymphangiectasia may need temporary artificial ventilation (positive end-expiratory pressure). Penicillin prophylaxis may be needed to prevent erysipelas.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The signs and symptoms vary widely among affected individuals and even those within the same family. The course of the lymphedema may vary considerably within a person, for instance by hormonal influences, but often for unknown reasons. Life expectancy depends on the severity of manifestations, and may lead to early death.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) characterized by extreme skin fragility and laxity, a prominent facial gestalt, excessive bruising and, sometimes, major complications due to visceral and vascular fragility.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Dermatosparaxis EDS; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type 7C; dEDS; Human dermatosparaxis EDS VIIC

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Dermatosparaxis Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (dEDS) is a rare monogenic disease resulting from biallelic defects in the ADAMTS2 gene, which causes a loss of enzyme activity and retention of N-propeptides in type I procollagen. The condition is hallmarked by extreme fragility of the skin and other soft connective tissues. Defining characteristics include tissue fragility, skin hyperextensibility, and joint hypermobility. Severe manifestations, observed in animal models, include multifocal wounds, atrophic scars, narrowed palpebral fissures, and joint-associated swellings, often leading to severe skin fragility. Dermal tissues exhibit characteristic hieroglyphic-like figures of collagen fibrils. [PMC12362006, PMC9690363]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked genetic condition due to deficiency of the lysosomal-associated membrane protein 2 (LAMP2) characterized by severe cardiomyopathy and variable degrees of muscle weakness, frequently associated with intellectual deficits (in males).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): GSD due to LAMP-2 deficiency; Glycogenosis due to LAMP-2 deficiency; Lysosomal glycogen storage disease with normal acid maltase activity; GSD, type 2B; GSD, type IIb; Glycogen storage disease, type IIb; Glycogen storage disease, type 2B; Glycogen storage disease due to LAMP-2 deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: More than 100 families have been described in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease classically manifests in males at a median age of 13-14 years. The clinical picture may be severe in both sexes, but onset generally occurs later in females and disease progression tends to be slower in females.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by mutations in the LAMP2 gene, localised to Xq24. The LAMP2 protein is an essential component of the lysosomal membrane and appears to play a role in autophagosome-lysosome fusion and the cellular process of autophagy. Originally the condition was classified as a 'glycogen storage disease' reflecting elevated glycogen visible on histological analysis; however, as the condition is not due to a specific defect in glycogen storage, the name Danon disease is currently preferred.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The main diagnostic method is molecular genetic testing for identification of loss-of-function variants in LAMP2. Histological and/or electron microscopy findings of cytoplasmic vacuoles and increased cellular glycogen levels can be suggestive of the diagnosis. Exclusion of Pompe disease should be done if LAMP2 molecular testing is non-conclusive. Staining of LAMP-2 protein revealing reduced or absence in males heart, muscle, lymphocytes, may also be performed for diagnosis, but is not widely available clinically. Identification of a LAMP2 pathogenic variant in a proband allows cascade testing of other at-risk relatives.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include X-linked myopathy with excessive autophagia (XMEA) and glycogen storage disease type 2.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis of at-risk pregnancies can be done if a known LAMP2 pathogenic variant has been detected in a parent (typically detected in the mother as males with this disease have reduce reproductive fitness).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling is recommended for the X-linked inheritance pattern seen in the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no specific treatment for this disease. Symptomatic treatment is required for the cardiac manifestations and patients may require a heart transplant.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Patients are at risk of sudden death due to arrhythmia and/or heart failure during early adulthood. Death or transplant occurs at median ages in males and females of 19-21 years and 34-38 years, respectively.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Familial idiopathic dilatation of the right atrium
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital heart malformation of unknown etiology that is characterized by an extremely dilated right atrium, and that is usually asymptomatic and fortuitously discovered by echocardiography or chest radiography, and can be sometimes associated with other anomalies such as atrial arrhythmias (e.g. atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, supraventricular tachycardia), severe tricuspid regurgitation, or atrial thrombus that could lead to potentially life-threatening thromboembolic complications.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Idiopathic dilatation of the right atrium is a rare malformation. It is characterized by disproportionate growth of the right atrium in the absence of an identifiable cause. The condition is infrequently encountered, as highlighted by its description as a rare entity in medical literature. [PMC10406491]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Idiopathic dilatation of the right atrium is a rare malformation characterized by disproportionate growth of the right atrium in the absence of a justifying cause, and can be diagnosed in fetal life. It is frequently recognized accidentally due to an enlarged cardiac silhouette on routine chest radiography. While some patients are asymptomatic, enlargement of the right atrium can cause symptoms such as progressive dyspnoea, palpitations, and atrial fibrillation. Complications include secondary tricuspid regurgitation due to annular dilatation, arrhythmias, and thrombus formation, which may lead to pulmonary embolism, stroke, or rarely, sudden death due to left ventricular compression. The enlarged atrium can also compress adjacent structures like the left atrium, left ventricle, and pulmonary vessels. Resected atrial tissue may show wall thinning and focal fibrosis. [PMC10406491, PMC6029170, PMC4281571]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Familial idiopathic dilatation of the right atrium can be associated with Holt-Oram syndrome, an autosomal dominant genetic condition. This syndrome is characterized by congenital heart malformations, including significant enlargement of the right atrium, and abnormalities in the bones of the upper limb. The underlying mutation can be inherited, but many cases arise from new mutations in individuals without a family history of the disorder. [PMC11800680]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of idiopathic dilatation of the right atrium can occur prenatally, with detection possible during fetal life. Postnatally, it is frequently identified incidentally through routine chest radiography, which may reveal an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Further evaluation often includes echocardiography, which shows massive right atrial enlargement and may detect associated features like tricuspid regurgitation or dysplastic tricuspid valve. Cardiac computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging can provide detailed visualization of the enlarged right atrium and its compression of surrounding structures. Surgical examination of resected atrial tissue can confirm wall thinning and focal fibrosis, establishing the idiopathic nature of the dilation. [PMC10406491, PMC11800680, PMC6029170, PMC4281571]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for conditions involving right atrial enlargement or abnormalities include Holt-Oram syndrome and congenital right atrial aneurysm. Holt-Oram syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic condition characterized by upper limb abnormalities and congenital heart malformation, which can include significant enlargement of the right atrium without tricuspid regurgitation. Congenital right atrial aneurysm is another consideration, sometimes associated with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome and presenting with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. [PMC11800680, PMC9632392]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Idiopathic dilatation of the right atrium can be diagnosed during fetal life. Prenatal detection of significant enlargement of the right atrium, without tricuspid regurgitation, has been observed during routine anatomy scans in the second trimester. [PMC10406491, PMC11800680]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: To detect common congenital disorders in Holt-Oram syndrome. a case of a 32 years old primigravida pregnant woman affected by Holt-Oram syndrome referred to our institution for second trimester routine anatomy scan. The ultrasound reported a bilateral aplasia radii, slightly curved ulna and bilateral twisted hand with four digital rays. A significant enlargement of the right atrium without tricuspid regurgitation was also detected. The patient refused the amniocentesis and the postnatal evaluation confirmed the diagnosis of Holt-Oram syndrome. Holt-Oram syndrome is an autosomal dominant genetic condition. It is characterized by abnormalities in the bones of the upper limb and congenital heart malformation. The mutation can be inherited, but most cases result from a new mutation in patients without family history of the disorder. [PMC11800680]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management primarily involves surgical intervention for symptomatic patients. Procedures include resection of the right atrial aneurysm or plication of the enlarged right atrium, often combined with tricuspid valve repair, such as annuloplasty. Surgery is indicated for symptoms like dyspnoea, palpitations, and chest discomfort, as well as for associated arrhythmias (e.g., supraventricular tachycardia, atrial fibrillation), secondary tricuspid regurgitation, thrombus formation, or compression of other cardiac structures. In one case, radiofrequency ablation was ineffective prior to surgical resection. Successful outcomes include improved symptoms, reduced atrial volume, and restoration of normal sinus rhythm. [PMC9632392, PMC6029170, PMC4281571]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Familial idiopathic dilatation of the right atrium can lead to significant complications including arrhythmias such as paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia and atrial fibrillation, secondary tricuspid regurgitation, and thrombus formation, which may result in pulmonary embolism or stroke. Compression of adjacent cardiac structures like the left atrium, left ventricle, and pulmonary vessels can also occur, causing symptoms such as dyspnoea, palpitations, and chest discomfort. Rarely, sudden death has been reported. However, surgical interventions such as aneurysm resection, right atrial plication, and tricuspid valve repair have shown successful outcomes, leading to symptom relief, reduced cardiac enlargement, and improved patient well-being at follow-up. [PMC9632392, PMC6029170, PMC4281571]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare dendritic cell neoplasm characterized by a proliferation of spindled to ovoid cells with morphological and immunophenotypic features of follicular dendritic cells. Conventional follicular dendritic cell sarcomas are negative for EBV. The tumor arises as a painless, slow-growing mass in lymph nodes (most often cervical), extranodal sites (such as tonsils, gastrointestinal tract, soft tissue, mediastinum, or lung, among others), or both. Paraneoplastic pemphigus may occur in rare cases. Predictive factors are tumor size, presence of coagulative necrosis, mitotic count, and presence of significant cytological atypia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Rationale: Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma (FDCS) is an exceptionally rare mesenchymal tumor, with gastric involvement being scarcely reported (only 7 prior cases). This case highlights the diagnostic challenges and underscores the importance of multimodal imaging in identifying this malignancy, particularly in extra-nodal sites like the stomach. Patient concerns: A 25-year-old male presented with acute abdominal pain and a palpable mid-abdominal mass. He denied weight loss, fever, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Laboratory tests revealed elevated squamous cell carcinoma-related antigen (3.6 ng/mL). Diagnoses: Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed a 68 × 47 × 91 mm soft tissue mass in the gastric antrum, vascularized by the left gastric artery. Positron emission tomography/CT demonstrated intense FDG uptake (SUVmax 25.48). Magnetic resonance images showed a... [PMC12237314, PMC12101044, PMC11829389, PMC12267037, PMC12191123]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Rationale: Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma (FDCS) is an exceptionally rare mesenchymal tumor, with gastric involvement being scarcely reported (only 7 prior cases). This case highlights the diagnostic challenges and underscores the importance of multimodal imaging in identifying this malignancy, particularly in extra-nodal sites like the stomach. Patient concerns: A 25-year-old male presented with acute abdominal pain and a palpable mid-abdominal mass. He denied weight loss, fever, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Laboratory tests revealed elevated squamous cell carcinoma-related antigen (3.6 ng/mL). Diagnoses: Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed a 68 × 47 × 91 mm soft tissue mass in the gastric antrum, vascularized by the left gastric artery. Positron emission tomography/CT demonstrated intense FDG uptake (SUVmax 25.48). Magnetic resonance images showed a... [PMC12237314, PMC12101044, PMC11829389, PMC12267037, PMC12191123]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma (FDCS) poses diagnostic challenges, especially in extranodal sites, due to nonspecific presentations and overlapping features with other conditions. Gastric FDCS can be misdiagnosed as gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) or Castleman disease. Renal FDCS may initially be identified as sarcomatoid renal cell carcinoma. The Epstein-Barr virus-positive inflammatory variant with significant granuloma can be confused with other granulomatous diseases. Accurate diagnosis requires distinguishing FDCS from other hematologic malignancies, including histiocytic and classical dendritic/Langerhans cell neoplasms, and other solid non-hematopoietic cancers, primarily through pathological morphology and immunohistochemical analysis. [PMC12237314, PMC11829389, PMC12191123, PMC11191520, PMC10870656]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Complete surgical excision or resection is the standard and preferred primary treatment for localized follicular dendritic cell sarcoma. In several reported cases, patients remained recurrence-free or alive after surgery, sometimes without additional adjuvant therapy. However, chemotherapy has been administered post-resection in some instances, and it is suggested for recurrences. For metastatic disease, there is no standard treatment protocol, but a PD-1 inhibitor combined with chemotherapy (e.g., epirubicin plus ifosfamide) has shown promising as a first-line option, achieving partial response and extended progression-free survival. Long-term follow-up is necessary to monitor for recurrence or metastasis. [PMC12237314, PMC12101044, PMC11829389, PMC12351499, PMC11634961]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma (FDCS) is considered a low-grade malignancy, but it carries a propensity for recurrence and metastasis, requiring long-term follow-up. Complete surgical excision is the primary treatment, with several reported cases showing patients remaining recurrence-free for extended periods, even without adjuvant therapy. For metastatic FDCS, a PD-1 inhibitor combined with chemotherapy demonstrated a partial response and a relatively long progression-free survival in one instance. The EBV-positive inflammatory subtype is also a low-grade malignancy, with patients alive at follow-up, although overall prognosis can vary. [PMC12237314, PMC12101044, PMC11829389, PMC12351499, PMC10994431]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal trisomy of the long arm of chromosome 10 (10q) is characterized by pre- and postnatal growth retardation, a pattern of specific facial features, hypotonia, and developmental and psychomotor delay.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, approximately 40 cases of trisomy 10q have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most cases are diagnosed in infancy or in childhood. The range and severity of symptoms and physical findings may vary from case to case, depending upon the exact length and location of the duplicated portion of chromosome 10q. Characteristic craniofacial findings include a flat round face with full cheeks and a large prominent forehead, highly arched eyebrows, short and narrow palpebral fissures (blepharophimosis), widely spaced eyes with telecanthus, a short nose, a bow-shaped mouth with a prominent upper lip, and a small mandible. A few major malformations have also been reported, including renal and cardiac anomalies. Minor defects of the hands and/or feet, bone anomalies and cryptorchidism are frequent signs.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The duplicated region almost always includes 10qter, with the most frequent proximal breakpoint at 10q24 (with variation from q22 to q25). Interstitial duplications of 10q have also been reported. Most cases of distal trisomy 10q result from of a parental balanced translocation or pericentric inversion, and may be accompanied by another chromosomal imbalance. Intrachromosomal duplications or de novo translocations are also observed.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected on the basis of the clinical features and is confirmed by karyotyping and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with specific 10q probes.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible using cytogenetic tools.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The risk of recurrence for siblings depends on the parental karyotypes.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is multidisciplinary and symptomatic only. Early educational (speech, occupational and physical therapy) and rehabilitation programs should be offered to all patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable. A number of reported patients died in infancy from respiratory problems.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Unbalanced translocations between the q arm of chromosomes 5 and 13 are exceedingly rare and there is only one reported case with distal trisomy 5q/monosomy 13q. In , a second patient with a similar rearrangement arising from a paternal balanced translocation. Karyotype analysis was performed on the proband and their parents. Microarray was also conducted on the proband. Our patient was found to have global developmental delay, distinct facial features, short stature, growth hormone deficiency, delayed puberty, and brain anomalies including a small pituitary. Karyotype and microarray analysis revealed a terminal duplication of chromosome regions 5q33.3 to 5qter and a terminal deletion of chromosome regions 13q34 to 13qter that resulted from a balanced translocation in her father. The endocrine abnormalities and neuroimaging findings have not been previously described in patients with... [PMC8606198]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic keratinization disorder which is classically characterized by keratotic papules, acral pits, and acral wart-like lesions that can be associated with a trigger, and may occur anywhere on the body (including mucosal surfaces). Extracutaneous manifestations may include, nail anomalies, blepharitis, dry eye, neuropsychiatric illness and, recurrent parotid gland obstruction and xerostomia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of Darier disease (DD) is estimated at around 1/30,000 in Europe.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Darier disease is a debilitating and chronic condition, with both cutaneous and extra-cutaneous manifestations, which can have a severe impact on patients' general health and quality of life. The cutaneous and extra-cutaneous manifestations have variable expression within and between families. Exacerbations may be triggered by summer, sweating, exposure to sunlight, mental distress, contact with wool and febrile illness. Classical lesions are characterized by keratotic papules (typically occurring on the trunk), acral pits (occurring on palms and soles) and acral wart-like lesions (typically occurring on the hands, particularly after soaking in water). Non-classical lesions may include acral keratoderma, leukodermic macules, giant comedones, vegetations and acral hemorrhagic blisters, and may co-exist with classical lesions. However, non-classical lesions are rare. Lesions can occur anywhere on the body with no specific location. Nail abnormalities include V-shaped notches at the free edge of nail, longitudinal red and white lines, ridging and splitting. Genital involvement, especially on female genitalia, is more frequent in patients with severe disease. Oral mucosal lesions may be found. Extra-cutaneous manifestations vary within and between families and may include, blepharitis, dry eye, neuropsychiatric illness, epilepsy (often only before age 20), learning disabilities, recurrent parotid gland obstruction and xerostomia. Staph aureus colonization in skin & nares is frequent and corresponds with extent of skin area affected and disease severity.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: DD is caused by mutations in the ATP2A2 gene (12q23-q24.1) encoding the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+ ATPase isoform 2 (SERCA2), which has a central role in intracellular calcium signaling.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on histological examination of skin lesion biopsies revealing hyperkeratosis, focal dyskeratosis and suprabasal acantholysis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Hailey-Hailey disease, Grover disease (transient acantholytic dermatosis), seborrheic dermatitis, pemphigus, and warty dyskeratoma.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: The prenatal diagnostic tests and procedures are available for affected couples where the genetic variant has been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is autosomal-dominant with complete and delayed penetrance, and variable expression. Genetic counselling is advised for affected patients to discuss identification of the mutation, the pattern of inheritance as well as the prenatal diagnostic tests and procedures available.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management and treatment are based on case reports and case series reported in the literature as well as clinical experience. The full extent of the disease should be assessed by a dermatologist and includes assessment of the skin involvement (including staph aureus colonization), the extracutaneous involvement (neuropsychiatric illness etc.), family history and triggering factors. Current treatment is symptomatic and includes topical and systemic therapy as well as minimizing exposure to triggers. For patients prone to secondary skin infections, a diluted bleach bath may be considered. Other therapies reported include injection of botulinum toxin to decrease sweating, surgical excision, electrosurgical excision, dermabrasion, laser ablation, photodynamic therapy and electron beam radiation. Extracutaneous manifestations should be treated according to standard protocols.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The disease is characterized by a chronic cycle with acute exacerbations and does not improve with age. In assessing the prognosis, it is very important to consider the extracutaneous manifestations of the disease. Secondary bacterial and viral infections were reported as causes of morbidity and mortality in a few cases.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic syndromic intellectual disability characterized by global developmental delay, intellectual disability, infantile or childhood onset of progressive ataxia, and bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment. Variable features include signs of upper and lower motor neuron disease, peripheral neuropathy, myopathic facies, lower limb muscle wasting, and heel contractures. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1993.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Reardon-Baraitser syndrome; Ataxia-hearing loss-intellectual disability syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Ataxia-deafness-intellectual disability syndrome is a familial disorder characterized by developmental delay or mental retardation, ataxia, and deafness. Specific clinical features include progressive spinocerebellar ataxia, sensorineural deafness, and signs of peripheral neuropathy, which can manifest as polyneuropathy. Congenital cataract has also been observed. Progressive hearing loss, ataxia, and polyneuropathy may become evident in the third decade. [PMC1016502, PMC1017170]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for ataxia-deafness-intellectual disability syndrome includes other conditions causing familial ataxia, deafness, and developmental delay. Specifically, for syndromes presenting with mental retardation, congenital cataract, progressive spinocerebellar ataxia, sensorineural deafness, and peripheral neuropathy, the syndromes described by Berman et al and Koletzko et al are considered. [PMC1016502, PMC1017170]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The syndrome is described as a familial disorder, with cases reported in brothers and sisters, indicating an inherited basis. The clinical features, including ataxia, deafness, and intellectual disability, are consistent across affected family members. Differential diagnosis with other syndromes presenting similar features is important for accurate diagnosis and counseling. [PMC1016502, PMC1017170]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The disorder is characterized by progressive spinocerebellar ataxia, progressive hearing loss, and signs of peripheral neuropathy. These progressive symptoms, including hearing loss, ataxia, and polyneuropathy, typically become evident in the third decade of life. [PMC1017170]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare vascular condition characterized by the sudden blockage of an artery supplying blood to the limbs by a blood clot, causing acute limb ischemia. The clinical presentation is variable and depends on the time course of vessel occlusion, the presence of an underlying vascular disease, and the recruitment of collateral circulation. Symptoms can develop over a period of hours to days and typically include limb pain, pallor, absent pulse, poikilothermia, paresthesia, and limb paralysis. The condition can quickly progress to infarction and loss of the limb.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Peripheral arterial disease affects over 230 million people worldwide, with acute peripheral arterial occlusion being a potential manifestation. COVID-19 infection is a predisposing factor for arterial thrombotic events, including peripheral arterial thrombosis and acute limb ischemia. A high incidence of these events has been confirmed, particularly in critically ill COVID-19 patients, but also in those with asymptomatic or mild forms. Delayed vascular arterial complications, such as arterial thrombotic sequelae and acute limb ischemia, can also occur after COVID-19 infection. Rare complications like stent migration can occur following endovascular revascularization for iliac artery occlusions. [PMC12371380, PMC10251170, PMC8087612]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Peripheral arterial disease affects over 230 million people worldwide, presenting as intermittent claudication or critical limb ischemia. Endovascular revascularization, with self-expanding stents, has proven effective in treating iliac artery occlusions. However, rare complications like stent migration can occur. a rare case of common iliac artery stent migration across the aortic bifurcation. Case summary: A 64-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension was evaluated for ischemic rest pain. He underwent iliac artery stenting and later developed worsening leg pain. Angiography revealed stent migration across the aortic bifurcation eventually managed percutaneously. Discussion: Stent migration while rare has been reported in the venous system, but reports of retrograde arterial stent migration are very rare. This case offers valuable insights into endovascular management of complex... [PMC12371380, PMC10615444, PMC10251170, PMC9636630, PMC9158042]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Rationale: Cystic medial degeneration Erdheim-Gsell is a vascular pathology mainly of the large vessels, which is mostly associated with Marfan syndrome or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. The clinical findings of this entity are aneurysms of the aorta or large peripheral arteries which usually present in an acute setting due to rupture of an aneurysm. Patient concerns: a case of a 43-year-old Caucasian male with histologically proven cystic medial degeneration of the lower limb vessels mimicking peripheral artery occlusive disease. Despite antiplatelet and anticoagulant treatment, the patient suffered multiple vascular stenosis and occlusions. Diagnoses: Multiple arterial stenoses and thromboses leading to peripheral artery occlusive disease caused by cystic medial degeneration Erdheim-Gsell. Interventions: Multiple surgical and endovascular interventions including bypass graft and... [PMC5708978]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Campomelia, Cumming type, is characterized by the association of limb defects and multivisceral anomalies.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The syndrome has been reported in eight infants from four different families.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Skeletal features include tetramelic campomelia and short long bones. Extraskeletal manifestations may include cervical lymphocele, generalized hydrops, polycystic kidneys, pancreas and liver, fibrotic liver or pancreas, polysplenia, heterotaxia, lung hypoplastia, short bowel. All newborns reported so far were either stillborn or died shortly after birth.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In one of the affected families, three sibs with identical features born to first-cousin parents have been reported, suggestive of autosomal recessive mode of inheritance.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: A late adolescent primigravida was found to have a fetus with a cystic hygroma and significant shortening of the limbs on first-trimester ultrasound. She underwent chorionic villus sampling with normal microarray result. In the early second trimester, the fetus was found to have the absence of all four limbs and a thorough skeletal dysplasia workup was pursued, identifying a variant in the FLNB gene (c.62C>G). The patient underwent termination of pregnancy. The care of this patient was expedited by first-trimester sonographic evidence of limb abnormalities enabling timely clinical management. [PMC10921501]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis can be initiated by first-trimester ultrasound, which may reveal limb abnormalities such as significant shortening or absence of limbs, and cystic hygroma. Further investigation can include chorionic villus sampling, which, despite a normal microarray result, can lead to the identification of specific genetic variants, such as a c.62C>G variant in the FLNB gene, confirming the diagnosis of severe skeletal dysplasia. [PMC10921501]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of Campomelia, Cumming type, can be achieved through ultrasound, with findings such as cystic hygroma and significant limb shortening or absence observed as early as the first trimester. These sonographic abnormalities can expedite clinical management. A thorough skeletal dysplasia workup, including genetic testing, can identify variants in the FLNB gene, confirming the diagnosis in the early second trimester. [PMC10921501]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: A late adolescent primigravida was found to have a fetus with a cystic hygroma and significant shortening of the limbs on first-trimester ultrasound. She underwent chorionic villus sampling with normal microarray result. In the early second trimester, the fetus was found to have the absence of all four limbs and a thorough skeletal dysplasia workup was pursued, identifying a variant in the FLNB gene (c.62C>G). The patient underwent termination of pregnancy. The care of this patient was expedited by first-trimester sonographic evidence of limb abnormalities enabling timely clinical management. [PMC10921501]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: A late adolescent primigravida was found to have a fetus with a cystic hygroma and significant shortening of the limbs on first-trimester ultrasound. She underwent chorionic villus sampling with normal microarray result. In the early second trimester, the fetus was found to have the absence of all four limbs and a thorough skeletal dysplasia workup was pursued, identifying a variant in the FLNB gene (c.62C>G). The patient underwent termination of pregnancy. The care of this patient was expedited by first-trimester sonographic evidence of limb abnormalities enabling timely clinical management. [PMC10921501]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Rare cutaneous lupus erythematosus (CLE) is an autoimmune disease that denotes a heterogeneous spectrum of clinical manifestations affecting the skin and can be divided into 4 categories: acute CLE (ACLE); subacute CLE (SCLE); chronic CLE (CCLE; the most diverse form); and intermittent CLE (ICLE). CLE can either occur alone or associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Incidence is estimated to be 1/25,000 in USA, and it affects predominantly women. CLE occurs more in patients with a family history of lupus or other autoimmune diseases.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: CLE usually appears between 20-70 years but it has also been described in children (0-18 years). There are 4 main types of CLE: ACLE which presents as prominent non scarring-rash on cheeks and nose (''butterfly rash'', localized form) or more rarely, by a widespread eruption of red, symmetric, maculopapular lesions with accentuation of the UV-exposed areas (''maculopapular lupus rash'', generalized form); SCLE which presents with red, raised, scaly rash on sun-exposed areas of the body (annular/polycyclic form or papulosquamous form); CCLE which presents either as red to purple, well demarcated, scaly rash on the scalp, face, ears, and other sun-exposed areas (discoid LE; DLE), as frostbites (Chilblain LE; ChLE), or as painful subcutaneous nodules (LE profundus; LEP); and ICLE or LE tumidus (LET) presenting as red, swollen, urticaria-like plaques. Cutaneous manifestations appear in 72-85% of SLE patients.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Etiology is still elusive but it is thought to be multifactorial, involving a genetic predisposition. The disease is then triggered by UV radiation, infections (cytomegalovirus, hepatitis C, Epstein-Barr virus), hormones (estrogens, prolactin), and exposure to drugs and chemicals, which initiate an inflammatory process. Cytokines and chemokines are involved in propagating inflammatory responses, suppressing tolerogenic components of the immune system. Autoreactive B cells are intrinsic to lupus pathogenesis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on family history, clinical and laboratory findings (detection of antibodies anti-nuclear antigens (ANA)), histological examinations of skin biopsy which show superficial and deep perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrate, interface-dermatitis and thickening of the basement membrane as a late consequence. The epidermis is atrophic with necrotic keratinocytes. Diagnosis is confirmed by direct immunofluorescence (detects deposits of immunoglobulins and complement component C3 and IgG at the dermo epidermal junction) and photoprovocation.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis depends on subtypes and includes: ACLE: dermatomyositis, erythema multiforme, drug-induced photosensitivity, dermatitis (atopic, contact), exanthema (viral, drug-induced), rosacea, seborrheic dermatitis. SCLE: classic mycosis fungoides, pityriasis rubra pilaris, vitiligo, tinea corporis, erythema anulare centrifugum, granuloma annulare, erythema gyratum repens, psoriasis. DLE: sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, leprosy, classic mycosis fungoides, cutaneous pseudolymphoma, granuloma faciale, nummular eczema, psoriasis, squamous and basal cell carcinoma, rosacea, lichen planus. ChLE: frostbites. LEP: subcutaneous panniculitis-like T-cell lymphoma, erythema nodosum. LET: Jessner lymphocytic infiltration of the skin, polymorphous light eruption, reticular erythematosus mucinosis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment goals are to improve skin appearance, limit scarring, and prevent new skin lesions. This includes use of UV light protection; topical therapy (corticosteroids and/or calcineurin inhibitors); and antimalarial therapy that may improve CLE and delay progression to SLE. For patients refractory to antimalarials, immunosupressive and immunomodulatory therapy (systemic corticosteroids, methotrexate, oral retinoids) may be proposed.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: CLE is a chronic skin disease, with significant impact on the patients' quotidian. Risk of SCLE and CCLE patients developing SLE is <10%. ACLE is associated with SLE.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Primary progressive freezing gait is a rare, heterogeneous, progressively incapacitating neurodegenerative disease characterized by freezing of gait (usually during the first 3 years), later associating postural instability, eventually resulting in a wheelchair-bound state. Other features may include mild bradykinesia, rigidity, postural tremor, hyperreflexia, speech disorder and dementia. The disease is unresponsive to dopaminergic treatments.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Primary progressive freezing gait (PPFG) is characterized by a solitary symptom of sudden transient breaks on walking, which slowly progresses over several years. Standard imaging, such as magnetic resonance imaging and PET scans, typically appears unremarkable, and the gait difficulty is not affected by dopamine agonist medication. Diagnosis is based on these clinical symptoms and imaging findings. Diffusion tensor tractography may reveal degeneration of the corticofugal tract from the supplementary motor area, characterized by partial tearing, thinning, and reduced fractional anisotropy and tract volume, which is attributed to the occurrence of PPFG. [PMC5428604]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Primary progressive freezing gait (PPFG) may be attributed to the degeneration of corticofugal fibers. In a case report, a patient with PPFG exhibited degeneration of the corticofugal tract (CFT) originating from the supplementary motor area (SMA), as evidenced by diffusion tensor tractography (DTT). The CFT from the left SMA was observed to be partially torn and thinned, with significantly lower fractional anisotropy and tract volume compared to normal controls. This lesion in the CFT from the left SMA is suggested as a pathological mechanism contributing to the gait difficulties seen in PPFG. [PMC5428604]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of primary progressive freezing gait (PPFG) is based on clinical symptoms, specifically a solitary and slowly progressive freezing gait. Standard imaging, such as magnetic resonance imaging and F-florinated-N-3-fluoropropyl-2-β-carboxymethoxy-3-β-(4-lodophenyl) nortropane positron emission tomography scanning, may be unremarkable, and symptoms are not affected by dopamine agonist medication. Diffusion tensor tractography (DTT) can reveal degeneration, such as partial tearing and thinning of the corticofugal tract from the supplementary motor area, with reduced fractional anisotropy values and tract volume compared to controls, which may be attributed to the condition. [PMC5428604]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Rationale: To report a patient with primary progressive freezing gait (PPFG) whose degeneration of corticofugal tract (CFT) from the supplementary motor area (SMA) was demonstrated using diffusion tensor tractography (DTT). Patient concerns: A 66-year-old woman presented with a solitary symptom of a sudden transient break on walking (i.e., freezing gait), which slowly progressed for 4 years. Diagnoses: Imaging evidence using magnetic resonance imaging and F-florinated-N-3-fluoropropyl-2-β-carboxymethoxy-3-β-(4-lodophenyl) nortropane positron emission tomography scanning was unremarkable, and our patient's symptom was not affected by dopamine agonist medication. Based on the clinical symptoms and imaging findings, we diagnosed our patient as having PPFG. Interventions: From the patient and 20 age- and sex- matched normal controls, diffusion tensor imaging data were acquired using a 1.5 T... [PMC5428604]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Primary progressive freezing gait is characterized by a slow progression of symptoms. In one reported case, a 66-year-old woman experienced a solitary symptom of freezing gait which slowly progressed over four years. This suggests a chronic and gradually worsening course of the condition. [PMC5428604]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Glycogen storage disease due to muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare form of glycogen storage disease (GSD) characterized classically by exertional fatigue and muscular exercise intolerance. It occurs typically in childhood and adolescence.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): GSD due to muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency; GSD type 7; Glycogen storage disease type 7; Glycogenosis due to muscle phosphofructokinase deficiency; Glycogenosis type 7; Tarui disease; GSD type VII; Glycogen storage disease type VII; Glycogenosis type VII

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: More than 100 cases have been reported worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical signs are muscular exercise intolerance (often with rhabdomyolysis) with muscle cramps and pain during exercise. The patients do not show a second wind phenomenon, and symptoms may worsen after glucose intake. Compensated hemolysis (increased bilirubin and reticulocytes) and hyperuricemia are frequently associated.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The condition is caused by mutations in the PFKM gene (12q13) encoding the muscular isoenzyme of PFK, a key enzyme in the regulation of anaerobic glycolysis which has 3 isoenzymes (for the muscle, liver, and platelets).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Non-invasive diagnostic confirmation is made by molecular analysis of PFKM gene. When performed, muscle biopsy typically shows vacuolar myopathy, increased glycogen content and PFK enzyme deficiency. Polyglucosan bodies may be observed in some cases.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include the other forms of muscular glycogen storage disease (GSD type 5 and other glycolysis enzyme deficiencies).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are usually not offered to at-risk couples.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy and to at-risk relatives for carrier testing.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Rhabdomyolysis episodes may be prevented by avoiding strenuous exercise. It should be noted that carbohydrates induce lower muscular performance (due to the decreased amounts of free fatty acids and ketone bodies).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Myoglobinuria may lead to renal failure.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare lethal combination of manifestations including short stature, congenital cataracts, encephalopathy with epileptic fits, and postmortem confirmation of nephropathy (renal tubular necrosis). There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1963.
