DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare orodental disease characterized by localized developmental anomaly of the dental tissues, with enamel and dentin hypomineralization affecting one (odontodysplasia) or several (regional odontodysplasia; ROD) teeth (deciduous and permanent, with teeth of the maxilla more frequently involved).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown but around 180 cases have been reported in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The defects involve both primary and permanent dentitions in the majority of the cases. The teeth of individuals with ROD are usually hypoplastic, small and atypically shaped with surface pits and grooves and a yellowish or brownish discoloration. Early loss of primary teeth is described. The condition usually affects the maxilla more than the mandible and is generally unilateral. Other common features include eruption failure or delay, and facial swellings (cellulitis), abscesses or fistulae in the absence of caries. Radiographic examination reveals a lack of contrast between enamel and dentin, with very thin (ghost-like) layers. Both dentin and enamel are hypomineralized. The pulp looks large and pulp stones or denticles can be seen. Histological features include mixed areas of cellular, amorphous and interglobular dentin. The enamel is hypoplastic, and hypocalcified areas and invaginations from the enamel surface into the dentin layer have been observed and may result in bacterial contamination of the pulp, leading to pulpitis or necrosis. The bone itself is not affected.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The underlying cause of ROD is still a matter of debate but various etiological factors have been suggested such as local circulatory disorders, viral infections, local trauma, pharmacotherapy during pregnancy, facial asymmetry or a combination of these factors. Some familial cases may also point towards a genetic etiology.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis should be suspected on the basis of the clinical aspect of the teeth, or upon presentation with failure of eruption, or pulpitis or necrosis in absence of caries. The diagnosis may be confirmed by radiography revealing the typical ''ghost-like'' appearance of the teeth and the presence of enamel and dentin with similar radiodensities.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes dentinogenesis imperfecta, dentin dysplasia and amelogenesis imperfecta.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is mainly conservative and includes treatment of the pulpitis and necrosis when necessary, with the aim of trying to maintain the affected teeth as long as possible to permit normal jaw development. If extraction is required, the extracted teeth should be replaced with removable appliances to maintain aesthetic appearance and function, and to avoid overeruption of opposing teeth and preserve the normal vertical dimension. Some patients benefit from autotransplants. Prosthesis and implants can be considered when craniofacial development is complete.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis for patients is good, especially when the condition is diagnosed and managed during the early stages. Life-long treatment is expected.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An inborn error of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) metabolism characterized by recurrent ketoacidotic comas or transient vomiting, dehydration, hypotonia and intellectual deficit, which responds to vitamin B12. There are three types: cblA, cblB and cblD-variant 2 (cblDv2).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Adenosylcobalamin deficiency; Vitamin B12-responsive methylmalonic aciduria

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, over 120 patients with cblA, 66 patients with cblB and 6 patients with cblDv2 have been reported. Prevalence of 1/48,000-1/61,000 have been reported for methylmalonic acidemia (MA) of all causes in North America, and 1/26,000 in China, but only a subset of this is vitamin B12-responsive MA.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients usually present in infancy or early childhood with features including lethargy, failure to thrive, recurrent vomiting, dehydration, respiratory distress, muscle hypotonia, hepatomegaly and coma. They may also show signs of anemia (not megaloblastic), have potentially life-threatening ketoacidosis and/or hyperammonemia, and developmental delay and intellectual deficit, with metabolic stroke affecting the brain stem. MA frequently leads to end-stage renal failure by adolescence or adulthood. Patients with cblB are usually more severely affected than patients with cblA.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Vitamin B12-responsive MA is caused by defects in the synthesis of adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl). There are three distinct complementation classes, cblA, B and Dv2. cblA is caused by mutations in the MMAA gene (4q31.1-2); cblB by the MMAB gene (12q24.1); and cblDv2 by the MMADHC gene (2q23.2). The previously reported cblH disorder has been shown to be cblDv2.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on increased methylmalonic acid in blood and urine. Neonatal screening for propionylcarnitine and/or increased propionylcarnitine-to-acetylcarnitine ratio in dried blood spots by tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) has become common, but specific identification of methylmalonic acid remains crucial.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include MA with homocystinuria, caused by defects in cblC, D and F, which can be differentiated by the presence of megaloblastic anemia, or vitamin B12-unresponsive MA without homocystinuria, which also can present early in life (<1 to 4 weeks) with similar symptoms. Complementation analysis can be used to identify the group involved, or sequencing of the causative genes to identify the affected gene.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible by measurement of methylmalonate in amniotic fluid and maternal urine at mid-trimester and by studies of functional mutase activity and cobalamin metabolism in cultured amniotic fluid cells. Molecular diagnosis is possible if the gene affected and the mutation(s) in the family are known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive (1 in 4 recurrence risk/pregnancy).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment involves a protein-restricted diet, which should be instituted as soon as life-threatening manifestations such as ketoacidosis or hyperammonemia have been resolved, and intramuscular injections of vitamin B12, with or without carnitine (mainly effective in cblA). A good response to cobalamin supplementation has been reported in most cblA patients and in nearly half cblB patients. Oral antibiotics may also be useful to reduce propionic acid from gut flora.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis varies with the complement involved, with cblA patients having the most favorable prognosis (most patients well at ages up to 30 years) and cblB patients less favorable. cblDv2 appears similar to cblA, although the number of patients is small. One complication in long-term surviving patients is chronic renal failure.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Deletion 5q35 refers to the different congenital malformation syndromes resulting from deletions of variable extent of the terminal part of the long arm of chromosome 5 (5q), spanning the region from 5q35.1 to 5q35.3 . The most significant anomaly is a recurring deletion in 5q35.2 comprising the NSD1 gene that causes Sotos syndrome that is characterized by cardinal features including excessive growth during childhood, macrocephaly, distinctive facial gestalt and various degrees of learning difficulty. Subtelomeric deletions of the terminal 3.5 Mb region on 5q35.3 are very rare, characterized by prenatal lymphedema with increased nuchal translucency, pronounced muscular hypotonia in infancy, borderline intelligence, postnatal short stature due to growth hormone deficiency, and a variety of minor anomalies such as mildly bell-shaped chest, minor congenital heart defects and a distinct facial gestalt. Larger deletions including bands 5q35.1, 5q35.2 and 5q35.3 cause a more severe phenotype that associates severe developmental delay with microcephaly, and significant cardiac defects (e.g. atrial septal defect with/without atrioventricular conduction defects, Ebstein anomaly, tetralogy of Fallot) linked to haploinsufficiency of NKX2.5 (5q35.1). Various combinations of signs may result from deletions of variable extent depending on the genes comprised in the deleted segment.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Del (5)(q35); Del (5)(qter); Distal 5q deletion; Monosomy 5q35; Telomeric deletion 5q

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: The 5q deletion syndrome is a relatively rare condition caused by the monoallelic interstitial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5. Patients described in literature usually present variable dysmorphic features, behavioral disturbance, and intellectual disability (ID); moreover, the involvement of the APC gene (5q22.2) in the deletion predisposes them to tumoral syndromes (Familial Adenomatous Polyposis and Gardner syndrome). Although the development of gastrointestinal tract malignancies has been extensively described, the genetic causes underlying neurologic manifestations have never been investigated. In , we described a new patient with a 19.85 Mb interstitial deletion identified by array-CGH and compared the deletions and the phenotypes reported in other patients already described in the literature and the Decipher database. Patients described in literature usually present variable dysmorphic features, behavioral disturbance, and intellectual disability (ID); moreover, the involvement of the APC gene (5q22.2) in the deletion predisposes them to tumoral syndromes (Familial Adenomatous Polyposis and Gardner syndrome). Although the development of gastrointestinal tract malignancies has been extensively described, the genetic causes underlying neurologic manifestations have never been investigated. DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The 5q deletion syndrome is a relatively rare condition caused by the monoallelic interstitial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5. Patients described in literature usually present variable dysmorphic features, behavioral disturbance, and intellectual disability (ID); moreover, the involvement of the APC gene (5q22.2) in the deletion predisposes them to tumoral syndromes (Familial Adenomatous Polyposis and Gardner syndrome). Although the development of gastrointestinal tract malignancies has been extensively described, the genetic causes underlying neurologic manifestations have never been investigated. In , we described a new patient with a 19.85 Mb interstitial deletion identified by array-CGH and compared the deletions and the phenotypes reported in other patients already described in the literature and the Decipher database. Overlapping deletions allowed us to highlight a... [PMC10379344, PMC3790513, PMC3384815]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of 5q deletion syndrome involves various cytogenetic and molecular . Karyotype analysis and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) are employed, though smaller or cryptic deletions may not always be identified by these techniques. Array-CGH and microarray are also utilized to detect interstitial deletions. Single-nucleotide polymorphism arrays (SNP-A) are particularly useful for identifying diminutive somatic deletions, defining breakpoints, and characterizing complex rearrangements like ring chromosomes, which may be cryptic to conventional cytogenetics or FISH. FISH can also be applied to monitor treatment response by evaluating peripheral blood cells. [PMC10379344, PMC9635032, PMC8606198, PMC3790513, PMC3384815]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Classical 5q- syndrome, an acquired macrocytic anemia of the elderly, and Diamond Blackfan anemia (DBA), an inherited red cell aplasia, are characterized by a paucity of erythroid precursors and involve deletions in the 5q region, including RPS14. Diminutive mosaic deletions in 5q, leading to RPS14 haploinsufficiency, have also been identified in patients with nonclassical DBA and myelodysplastic syndrome, presenting with hypoproliferative anemias. These conditions represent important differential diagnoses for disorders involving 5q deletions. [PMC10717177, PMC9235249, PMC8606198, PMC3790513]

It has shown therapeutic efficacy in patients with associated mastocytosis or chronic myeloproliferative neoplasia. However, some patients may become refractory to lenalidomide, acquire secondary cytogenetic abnormalities, and evolve into acute leukemia, particularly if pre-existing TP53 mutated subclones are present. Azacitidine has also been used successfully for acute myeloid leukemia with concomitant del(5q). [PMC9635032, PMC6506002, PMC6122386, PMC5486789, PMC5111523]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare lysosomal lipid storage disease characterized by variable clinical signs, depending on the age of onset, such as prolonged unexplained neonatal jaundice or cholestasis, isolated unexplained splenomegaly, and progressive, often severe neurological symptoms such as cognitive decline, cerebellar ataxia, vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (VSPG), dysarthria, dysphagia, dystonia, seizures, gelastic cataplexy, and psychiatric disorders.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence at birth of Niemann-Pick disease type C (NPDC) ranges between 1/45,000-286,000 worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical onset and presentation is heterogeneous. NPDC is classically a neurovisceral condition with hepatosplenomegaly usually preceding the neurological symptoms, occurring in infancy or childhood but possibly occurring much later. Some patients exhibit lung disease early on and a small subset of patients can develop rapidly deteriorating hepatic or respiratory failure in early infancy. Neurological onset varies between early infancy to adulthood. Typically, neurologic involvement is progressive and consists mainly of dystonia, cerebellar ataxia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and progressive dementia. VSGP and cataplexy (with or without narcolepsy) are characteristic. Psychiatric disturbances are frequent in late-onset patients.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Most patients (95%) have mutations in the NPC1 gene (localized to 18q11.2), which encodes a membrane glycoprotein. The remainder have mutations in the NPC2 gene (localized to 14q24.3 ), which encodes a soluble lysosomal protein that binds cholesterol. The loss of function of those proteins blocks cholesterol egress from lysosomes leading to accumulation of lipid membrane components (unesterified cholesterol, glucosylceramide, and gangliosides) in the late endosomal/lysosomal compartment of the cell.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of NPDC must be confirmed by mutation analysis and, if necessary, filipin test (based on the reaction of unesterified cholesterol with fluorescent antibiotic filipin). Several biomarkers are used alone or in combination as a first-line test to screen for NPDC: oxysterols (cholestane-3β, 5α, 6β-triol); lyso-SM-509 and lyso-sphingomyelin. Foam cells and sea-blue histiocytes are usually present in the bone marrow.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: In the first 2 years of life, NPDC must be differentiated from Niemann-Pick types A and B, Wolman disease, Gaucher disease type II/III, idiopathic neonatal hepatitis, and other causes of cholestatic jaundice. In older children and adults, neurodegenerative disorders such as mitochondrial diseases, Wilson disease, late-onset lysosomal storage diseases, Friedreich Ataxia, progressive supranuclear palsy, Huntington disease, Alzheimer disease, Pick disease, frontotemporal dementias, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, primary psychiatric illnesses must be ruled out. Acquired conditions such as pineal region or midbrain tumors, attention-deficit disorder, learning disabilities, absence seizures, other dementia illnesses, HIV encephalopathy, sleep disorders, and syncope also should also be included in the differential diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis of NPDC should be offered to couples at risk. Molecular genetic analysis is the preferred strategy.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: NPDC is an autosomal recessive disease. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management of NPDC remains largely symptomatic. Treatment with an iminosugar inhibitor of glucosylceramide synthase (miglustat) was approved for the management of neurologic manifestations of NPDC in several countries. There are presently some therapies under investigation, including 2-hydroxypropyl-beta-cyclodextrin and arimoclomol.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Lifespan varies from a few days (in case of fetal hydrops) to a few decades. Death in early infancy can be due to either liver failure or severe pulmonary insufficiency (usually before 3-6 months). Early infantile, severe, neurological onset is often fatal between 3-5 years of age, late-infantile neurologic onset typically between 7-12, and juvenile neurologic onset between adolescence and 30 years of age.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Trichinellosis is a zoonotic parasitic disease caused by the consumption of raw or undercooked meat (pork and wild game) infected by nematodes of the genus Trichinella and that is characterized by an enteral (intestinal) phase, that can be asymptomatic or that can manifests with diarrhea, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain, and a parenteral (muscular) phase, manifesting with fever, periorbital edema, muscle swelling and pain, weakness, and in some cases, skin rash and peripheral edema. Rarely, potentially fatal cardiac (i.e. myocarditis), pulmonary (i.e. pneumonitis, respiratory failure), and nervous system (i.e. meningoencephalitis) complications may occur.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Trichinellosis is a cosmopolitan foodborne zoonosis, recognized as a global food safety and public health problem, with cases reported across Europe, Africa, North America, South America, and Asia. Infection occurs through the consumption of raw or undercooked meat from infected animals. Wild boar is a primary source of human infection, implicated in outbreaks in Iran, Turkey, Romania, Italy, the United States, and Korea. Domestic pigs are also significant reservoirs, particularly in areas with traditional free-ranging farming practices or where slaughter waste is used as feed, as seen in Romania and Senegal. Other animal sources include bear meat, wild carnivores like jackals and wolves, badgers, and even soft-shelled turtles. Outbreaks frequently involve families or groups, often linked to cultural traditions of consuming raw or homemade meat products. While rates have declined in some regions due to improved practices, trichinellosis remains a concern, with ongoing surveillance and public education recommended. [PMC11466378, PMC11452060, PMC9932804, PMC10051731, PMC9631380]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Trichinellosis presents with a wide range of intermittent symptoms, often with a gradual onset, sometimes mimicking systemic inflammatory diseases. Common manifestations include prolonged fever, myalgias, arthralgias, headache, dry cough, rash, and gastrointestinal symptoms like diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Hallmarks can include ophthalmic and musculoskeletal signs such as periorbital edema, conjunctival hemorrhage, subungual splinter hemorrhage, and myositis. Laboratory findings frequently show eosinophilia, though it can be normal in rare presentations like pleural effusion. Elevated creatinine phosphokinase may also be observed. Complications, affecting neurological, cardiovascular, or respiratory systems, occur in a minority of patients. Diagnosis is guided by clinical history, especially raw meat consumption, and confirmed by positive Trichinella serology or muscle biopsy. [PMC9903410, PMC10051731, PMC8561047, PMC8082078, PMC8536450]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurovascular malformation characterized by massive dilation of one or more dural sinuses typically associated with arteriovenous shunts. Anatomic types are the lateral type involving the jugular bulb, which presents with minimal symptoms, and the usually symptomatic midline type involving the confluens sinuum (torcular Herophili) and adjacent posterior sinuses. Complications include sinus thrombosis, venous infarction, and cerebral hemorrhage, as well as cardiac failure, macrocrania, and hydrocephalus. Spontaneous regression of the malformation may occur.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Cranial dural arteriovenous fistula; Cranial dural arteriovenous malformations

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Dural arteriovenous fistulas, such as lower cervical arteriovenous fistulas, are considered rare vascular malformations. Spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas are the most common type of spinal arteriovenous malformation. Demographically, lower cervical AVFs show an equal distribution between sexes, with a mean age of 48.68 years (range 4-76 years). However, medullary bridging vein-draining dural arteriovenous fistulas in the foramen magnum region exhibit a male predominance. [PMC12264256, PMC12370346, PMC11802681]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula usually has an insidious clinical course and is easily misdiagnosed. In some cases, acute exacerbation occurs following certain triggers, such as corticosteroid use and lumbar puncture. Here, we introduce a rare case of spinal dural arteriovenous fistula with acute onset, rapid progression, and no cause. A 76-year-old Chinese male patient presented with numbness and weakness of the lower limbs that rapidly progressed to complete paralysis within 4 days. Patient was diagnosed with spinal dural arteriovenous fistula after magnetic resonance imaging and spinal vascular angiography, undergoing bilateral internal iliac artery embolization 2 weeks later, and started rehabilitation 40 days later but only received minimal improvement 1 year thereafter. This case highlights that spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas cannot be excluded in acute-onset or rapidly... [PMC12330131, PMC12303420, PMC12187352, PMC11723842, PMC11949654]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiology of dural arteriovenous fistulas can be varied. Some cases, particularly spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas, may present with acute onset without an identifiable cause. In other instances, acute exacerbations of spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas have been linked to specific triggers such as corticosteroid use and lumbar puncture. Furthermore, a genetic predisposition has been observed, with dural arteriovenous fistulas reported in patients with Cowden syndrome, an autosomal dominant condition associated with PTEN gene mutations. [PMC12330131, PMC11949654]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of dural arteriovenous fistulas (DAVFs) relies on various imaging modalities. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) scans can identify lesions or associated complications like subarachnoid hemorrhage. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA), including spinal vascular angiography and selective spinal angiography, is a key method for revealing DAVFs and their angioarchitecture. Advances in DSA and 3D reconstruction imaging provide a more precise understanding of the shunt and vascular access route. Additionally, intraoperative angiography is helpful for identifying spinal DAVFs prior to electrocoagulation. [PMC12330131, PMC12303420, PMC12187352, PMC11723842, PMC11735054]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Determining the differential diagnosis of small scalp cysts identified on a fetus is difficult. In particular, many physicians have difficulty differentiating small meningoceles from small scalp cysts during the prenatal period. Volume contrast imaging increases contrast between tissues, thereby allowing an enhanced view of target structures. A 15 × 5 mm scalp cyst was identified on a fetus during a prenatal ultrasonography examination performed at 20 weeks of gestation. The cyst was not connected to the blood flow, and did not include the tissue of the brain parenchyma. Ventriculomegaly and other structural abnormalities were not observed. Based on these findings, we suspected a sinus pericranii or fetal epidermal cyst. The size of the fetal scalp cyst was stable, and the growth of the fetus remained normal until birth. The diagnosis of a small meningocele was confirmed postnatally,... [PMC11735054]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Dural arteriovenous fistulas (AVFs) can be observed in patients with Cowden syndrome (CS), an autosomal dominant condition. Most individuals with CS harbor mutations in the phosphatase and tensin homolog (PTEN) gene. Vascular malformations are common in CS, suggesting a genetic predisposition for dural AVFs in this context. Therefore, genetic evaluation for CS and PTEN mutations may be relevant for patients presenting with dural AVFs. [PMC11949654]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistula usually has an insidious clinical course and is easily misdiagnosed. In some cases, acute exacerbation occurs following certain triggers, such as corticosteroid use and lumbar puncture. Here, we introduce a rare case of spinal dural arteriovenous fistula with acute onset, rapid progression, and no cause. A 76-year-old Chinese male patient presented with numbness and weakness of the lower limbs that rapidly progressed to complete paralysis within 4 days. Patient was diagnosed with spinal dural arteriovenous fistula after magnetic resonance imaging and spinal vascular angiography, undergoing bilateral internal iliac artery embolization 2 weeks later, and started rehabilitation 40 days later but only received minimal improvement 1 year thereafter. This case highlights that spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas cannot be excluded in acute-onset or rapidly... [PMC12330131, PMC12303420, PMC12187352, PMC11766481, PMC11723842]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for dural sinus malformations is variable, depending on factors such as location, presentation, and treatment. Many patients experience good recovery, with resolution of symptoms and no recurrence following successful endovascular or surgical intervention. For instance, patients with foramen magnum or jugular foramen DAVFs often recover well with no further neurological deficits. However, acute onset with rapid neurological progression, especially to complete paraplegia, can lead to a poor prognosis even after prompt treatment. Complex venous drainage patterns, such as perimedullary and retrograde drainage, are associated with worse outcomes. While hydrocephalus often resolves spontaneously post-treatment, acute worsening can occur. Some cases may experience recurrence or require prolonged observation after embolization. Overall, early diagnosis and tailored management are crucial for optimizing patient outcomes. [PMC12330131, PMC12303420, PMC12187352, PMC11723842, PMC11949654]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, severe, interstitial lung disease characterized by insidious onset with subacute or chronic non-specific respiratory manifestations (dyspnea, cough, wheezing) often associated with systemic manifestations (fatigue, malaise, weight loss) and a history of asthma (up to half of patients). Eosinophilia is present in most cases, usually in excess of 1000 cells/mm3.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Idiopathic chronic eosinophilic pneumonia (ICEP) is a rare disease. It is consistently described as a rare interstitial lung disease of unknown cause or etiology. The disorder has been observed in both pediatric and adult populations. [PMC10851541, PMC10483178, PMC7868209]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Craniosynostosis is defined as the premature fusion of one or more cranial sutures leading to secondary distortion of skull shape resulting in skull deformities with a variable presentation. Craniosynostosis may occur in an isolated setting or as part of a syndrome.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable, Unknown, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of craniosynostosis relies on a combination of . Clinical examination and phenotypic characterization, including distinctive facial features, skull abnormalities, and limb anomalies, serve as important diagnostic clues. Genetic testing, encompassing genomic screening, exome analysis, and molecular testing, is crucial for identifying pathogenic gene variants and confirming specific syndromes, often guided by consensus-based algorithms and pedigree analysis. Imaging techniques are also vital, with prenatal diagnosis possible through ultrasound and MRI. Postnatally, cranial computed tomography with three-dimensional reconstruction is utilized. Early and accurate diagnosis is essential for appropriate medical management and genetic counseling. [PMC11985952, PMC12405648, PMC12367812, PMC11049481, PMC11191325]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Prenatal diagnosis of craniosynostosis, including specific syndromes like Apert and Pfeiffer, is possible through advanced imaging techniques and molecular testing. Ultrasound examinations can identify characteristic features such as skull-shaped abnormalities, facial anomalies like hypertelorism or midface hypoplasia, and limb deformities like syndactyly. These detected anomalies are often confirmed postnatally. Early diagnosis is crucial for assessing the severity of the condition and providing appropriate parental counseling. [PMC11651975, PMC11276282, PMC10656109]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic ocular disease characterized by congenital nystagmus (horizontal, vertical and/or torsional), foveal hypoplasia, presenile cataracts (with typical onset in the second to third decade of life), and normal irides. Corneal pannus and/or optic nerve hypoplasia may also be present.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Myelodysplastic syndrome associated with isolated del(5q) chromosome abnormality
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare myelodysplastic syndrome characterized by macrocytic anemia (with or without other cytopenias and/or thrombocytosis), and with del(5q) occurring either in isolation, or with one other cytogenetic abnormality, other than monosomy 7 or del(7q). The bone marrow is typically hypercellular with erythroid hypoplasia and increased numbers of megakaryocytes, which show non-lobated and hypolobated nuclei. Myeloblasts constitute less than 5% of the nucleated bone marrow cells and less than 1% of the peripheral blood leukocytes. Auer rods are absent. Ring sideroblasts may be observed. Patients present with anemia and often thrombocytosis, while thrombocytopenia or pancytopenia are uncommon. Transformation to acute myeloid leukemia may occur in a small number of patients.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Myelodysplastic syndrome with isolated del(5q) is an acquired macrocytic anemia, typically affecting the elderly, and is characterized by a paucity of erythroid precursors in the bone marrow. Patients often present with progressive anemia and thrombocytopenia, frequently leading to red blood cell transfusion dependency, though white blood cell counts may be normal. RPS14 deletions are implicated in the pathogenesis, with anemia potentially stemming from excessive intracellular heme. While generally having an indolent course and favorable prognosis, rare progression to high-risk MDS, acute myeloid leukemia, or acute lymphoblastic leukemia can occur. Rare associations, such as with cKIT D816V positive mastocytosis, have also been reported. [PMC9185154, PMC6506002, PMC6344201, PMC6122386, PMC5256528]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Lenalidomide is a primary treatment for myelodysplastic syndrome with isolated del(5q), approved for lower-risk, transfusion-dependent patients. It effectively reduces transfusion dependency and can achieve erythroid and cytogenetic responses, with durable remissions reported. However, treatment can lead to hematological toxicities and the emergence of new mutations, such as TP53, or progression to acute leukemias like AML or B-ALL, sometimes with acquired additional genetic abnormalities. For these progressions or lenalidomide resistance, salvage therapies including decitabine or multi-agent chemotherapy regimens have been utilized. [PMC10988196, PMC10058431, PMC6506002, PMC6344201, PMC6122386]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Emergence of TP53 mutation during lenalidomide therapy of myelodysplastic syndrome with del(5q) and its subsequent disappearance following salvage therapy with decitabine. Myelodysplastic neoplasm (MDS) represents a heterogeneous group of myeloid disorders that originate from the hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells that lead to the development of clonal hematopoiesis. MDS was characterized by an increased risk of transformation into acute myeloid leukemia (AML). In recent years, with the aid of next-generation sequencing (NGS), an increasing number of molecular aberrations were discovered, such as recurrent mutations in FLT3 , NPM1 , DNMT3A , TP53 , NRAS , and RUNX1 genes. During MDS progression to leukemia, the order of gene mutation acquisition is not random and is important when considering the prognostic impact. Moreover, the co-occurrence of certain gene mutations is not... [PMC10988196, PMC10058431, PMC6344201, PMC6122386, PMC5256528]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital laryngeal anomaly characterized by an abnormal dilation of the laryngeal saccule that is filled with air, maintains communication with the laryngeal lumen, and is either confined to the false vocal fold or extends upward, protruding through the thyrohyoid membrane to the neck. Symptoms may include cough, hoarseness, stridor, sore throat and uni- or bilateral swelling of the neck. Blockage of the laryngocele neck can result isn laryngomucocele, and forms laryngopyocele when infected.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Laryngocele is a rare or uncommon condition, representing a benign dilatation of the laryngeal saccule. It can be congenital, affecting newborns and infants, or acquired, presenting across a wide age range, including elderly patients up to 91 years. Both congenital and acquired factors are implicated in its development. While many laryngoceles are asymptomatic and found frequently in pathology studies, symptomatic cases can lead to significant clinical complaints. Rarely, laryngocele may be associated with supraglottic squamous cell carcinoma or occur as a rare complication in patients with a history of tracheostomy. [PMC8915273, PMC7268503, PMC5892799, PMC6129081, PMC5018709]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Laryngocele is defined as a rare, benign, cystic or abnormal dilatation of the laryngeal saccule, forming an air sac that can extend internally into the airway or externally through the thyrohyoid membrane. While many laryngoceles are asymptomatic, they can present as a swelling on one or both sides of the neck, sometimes pulsatile. Clinical manifestations, when present, often include dyspnoea, difficulty breathing, stridor, change in voice, hoarseness, cough, sore throat, dysphagia, or regurgitation. Congenital laryngocele is an uncommon cause of neonatal stridor. It can be an airway emergency, causing severe respiratory distress and obstruction. Complications include infection, leading to laryngopyocele, and aspiration. Laryngoceles can also mimic other entities, such as a thyroid nodule. [PMC11273564, PMC8915273, PMC9402881, PMC7268503, PMC6721084]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiology of laryngocele is not fully understood, but both congenital and acquired factors are implicated in its development. Congenital laryngocele is recognized as an uncommon cause of neonatal stridor. Acquired forms may arise from local mechanical conditions, and it has been reported as a rare complication following surgical tracheostomy. Additionally, laryngocele may be associated with supraglottic squamous cell carcinoma. [PMC7268503, PMC2640037, PMC1676021]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of laryngocele typically involves a combination of imaging and endoscopic examinations. Computed tomography (CT) scans, including contrast-enhanced CT of the neck, are considered the most effective imaging method for diagnosis, confirming the presence of a laryngocele and differentiating it from other entities like thyroid nodules or parapharyngeal abscesses. Plain radiography can also reveal laryngeal masses or air-filled sacs. Endoscopic such as flexible nasopharyngolaryngoscopy, fiberoptic bronchoscopy, and videolaryngoscopy are crucial for visualizing the laryngeal area. Doppler ultrasonography and fine-needle aspiration biopsy may be utilized, with cytopathological analysis and histopathological findings contributing to the definitive diagnosis. Clinical findings also play a role, and timely aspiration can be both diagnostic and therapeutic. [PMC11273564, PMC8915273, PMC9402881, PMC6721084, PMC5892799]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Laryngocele can present with varied clinical manifestations, often mimicking other conditions. It has been reported to mimic a thyroid nodule, leading to initial misdiagnosis during evaluation for suspected thyroid pathology. In acute presentations, such as severe respiratory distress with neck swelling, laryngocele was initially misdiagnosed as a parapharyngeal abscess. A high index of suspicion for laryngocele is recommended when patients present with stridor and pulsatile neck swelling, considering its potential to be mistaken for other entities. [PMC8915273, PMC9402881, PMC6129081, PMC2640037]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of laryngoceles primarily involves surgical intervention, which is considered the treatment of choice. For internal laryngoceles, microlaryngoscopy, often utilizing a CO2 laser, has become the main therapeutic procedure. Combined or external laryngoceles are typically managed with an external surgical approach. In cases of acute airway obstruction, emergency interventions such as tracheostomy may be necessary to secure the airway, though timely aspiration might help avoid this. Successful surgical excision, marsupialization, or drainage generally leads to symptom resolution and prevents recurrence. [PMC11273564, PMC8915273, PMC7268503, PMC6721084, PMC5892799]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Laryngoceles are generally benign, but can cause significant complications including acute airway obstruction, infection (pyocele formation), and aspiration, sometimes necessitating emergency tracheostomy. However, with correct diagnosis and proper treatment, such as surgical excision, aspiration, or marsupialization, the prognosis is often good. Clinical signs typically resolve immediately after removal of the mass, and recurrence may not be observed during follow-up. Even in severe cases requiring urgent intervention, patients can recover well and achieve a patent airway. Asymptomatic laryngoceles may remain stable under continued follow-up. [PMC11273564, PMC8915273, PMC9402881, PMC7268503, PMC6721084]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome is characterised by fusion of the carpals, tarsals, and phalanges.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Less than 10 affected families have been described so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: At birth, patients present with stiffness of the proximal interphalangeal joint of the fifth digit, with or without bony synostosis. Proximo-distal progression leads to involvement of the fourth, third and then the second digits. Other anomalies include brachydactyly, humeroradial synostoses and, in some cases, short stature.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Causative mutations in the NOG gene have recently been identified, showing that this syndrome is an allelic variant of symphalangism.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome can be distinguished from multiple synostoses syndrome and proximal symphalangism by the absence of hearing loss.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis can be suspected antenatally via scanning. At birth, reduced range of motion in digits, elbows, and ankles may indicate the condition. In affected individuals, the diagnosis is confirmed by identifying synostosis of the wrist, ankle, and digits, as well as extensive coalition of tarsal and carpal bones, which can progress to fixed flexion deformities. [PMC6557331]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal scanning can raise suspicion for tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome, as observed in a case where a baby's condition was suspected prenatally. This early suspicion was later confirmed at birth, with the newborn presenting reduced range of motion in the digits, elbows, and ankles. [PMC6557331]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for Tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome, a progressive condition, may involve surgical interventions. For individuals experiencing progression of the disease, such as fixed flexion deformities and extensive bone coalition, regular osteotomies have been required. These procedures improve limb functioning and enhance the quality of life for affected individuals. [PMC6557331]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Tarsal-carpal coalition syndrome is a progressive condition involving synostosis of the wrist, ankle, and digits. Affected individuals may be born with reduced range of motion in their digits, elbows, and ankles. The condition can progress to involve fixed flexion deformities and extensive coalition of tarsal and carpal bones. Regular osteotomies may be required to improve limb functioning and quality of life. [PMC6557331]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Juvenile Paget disease is a very rare form of Paget disease of the bone characterized by a general increase in bone turnover with increased bone resorption and deposition, resulting in cortical and trabecular thickening, and clinically presenting as progressive skeletal deformities, growth impairment, fractures, vertebral collapse, skull enlargement and sensorineural hearing loss.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Familial osteoectasia; Hereditary hyperphosphatasia; JPG; Hyperostosis corticalis deformans juvenilis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Juvenile Paget disease (JPD) is a very rare autosomal recessive bone disease. It is primarily caused by biallelic inactivating mutations, often homozygous, in the TNFRSF11B gene, which encodes osteoprotegerin. Compound heterozygous variants in TNFRSF11B have been reported, though less frequently. A distinct form, JPD2, can be associated with heterozygous activating mutations in the TNFRSF11A gene. The disease is considered ultra-rare, with individual cases being the first reported in certain regions, highlighting its infrequent occurrence. [PMC12333066, PMC11994531, PMC10406616, PMC5111855, PMC4410173]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Juvenile Paget disease (JPD) is a rare, often autosomal recessive, bone disorder characterized by markedly escalated or generalized rapid bone turnover. Clinical manifestations typically include early-onset bone pain, recurrent fractures, and progressive skeletal deformities such as macrocephaly, arched chest, lower extremity valgosity, and bowing of the thighs and shins. Extraskeletal features are common and can involve deafness (mixed, conductive, or sensorineural hearing loss, sometimes with missing ossicles or eroded cochleas), angioid stripes of the choroidea, temporary immunodeficiency, and auricular ossification. Other reported complications include craniosynostosis, progressive external tooth root resorption, and bilateral cavernous internal carotid aneurysms. In some adults, retinopathy from vascular microcalcification can lead to blindness. Biochemical markers show markedly increased serum alkaline phosphatase activity. [PMC12333066, PMC10406616, PMC5111855, PMC4410173, PMC4189967]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Juvenile Paget disease (JPD) is a rare autosomal recessive bone disease primarily caused by biallelic inactivating mutations in the TNFRSF11B gene, which encodes osteoprotegerin (OPG). Most published JPD cases involve homozygous TNFRSF11B variants, but compound heterozygous variants have also been reported. OPG is an important regulator of osteoresorption, and its deficiency leads to escalated bone metabolism and rapid bone turnover. JPD can also be associated with activating mutations within TNFRSF11A, which encodes RANK, such as heterozygous insertional duplications. Other causes of JPD remain unknown. [PMC12333066, PMC11994531, PMC10406616, PMC5111855, PMC4410173]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Juvenile Paget disease (JPD) relies on a combination of clinical, biochemical, radiological, and genetic findings. Clinically, patients present with skeletal deformities, bone pain, fractures, macrocephaly, and hearing impairment, with auricular ossification also noted in some cases. Biochemical studies typically show markedly increased serum alkaline phosphatase activity, elevated bone turnover markers, and sometimes low serum osteoprotegerin (OPG) with elevated RANKL. Radiological assessments may reveal acquired tubular bone widening, cortical thickening, coarse trabeculation, and low bone mineral density. Genetic testing is crucial, identifying loss-of-function mutations or compound heterozygous variants in TNFRSF11B (JPD1), or activating duplications in TNFRSF11A (JPD2), using such as Sanger sequencing or next-generation sequencing. Histopathology can also show accelerated remodeling with abundant osteoclasts. [PMC12333066, PMC10406616, PMC5111855, PMC4410173, PMC4189967]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Juvenile Paget disease (JPD) is a rare Mendelian disorder characterized by rapid bone turnover, skeletal pain, and deformity. While JPD is typically an autosomal recessive condition caused by loss-of-function mutations in TNFRSF11B (JPD1), it can also arise from heterozygous constitutive activation of TNFRSF11A (JPD2). Other Mendelian osteolytic disorders caused by activating duplications in TNFRSF11A, such as familial expansile osteolysis (FEO), expansile skeletal hyperphosphatasia (ESH), early-onset familial Paget's disease of bone (PDB2), and panostotic expansile bone disease (PEBD), present with accelerated bone remodeling and can have overlapping phenotypes, making them important differential considerations. These conditions are part of a spectrum of disorders involving aberrant osteoclastogenesis. [PMC10406616, PMC5111855, PMC4189967]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Treatment for Juvenile Paget disease is largely empirical, focusing on antiresorption therapy to prevent fractures, deformities, and improve quality of life. Bisphosphonates, including zoledronic acid, alendronate, and pamidronate, are used to suppress accelerated bone turnover, reduce bone pain, and improve symptoms, though relapse can occur if discontinued. Zoledronic acid has shown effectiveness but its long-term clinical outcomes are unclear and it can cause hypocalcemia. Denosumab is a long-term option that normalizes alkaline phosphatase, improves mobility, and prevents further hearing deterioration and new fractures, proving safe and effective for skeletal disease. However, denosumab may not prevent retinopathy, and bisphosphonates might exacerbate auricular ossification. Vitamin D repletion is also an effective part of therapy, particularly when combined with pamidronate. [PMC12333066, PMC11994531, PMC10406616, PMC5111855, PMC4410173]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Juvenile Paget disease is characterized by skeletal deformities, fractures, bone pain, and extraskeletal manifestations like hearing impairment and retinopathy. Early diagnosis and antiresorption treatment can prevent further fractures and deformity progression, improving quality of life. Long-term denosumab therapy in adults has shown effectiveness in normalizing bone turnover markers, reducing bone pain, improving mobility, and preventing new fractures and further hearing deterioration. However, it may not prevent retinopathy, with some patients developing sudden vision loss in adulthood. Auricular ossification is a recognized feature, potentially exacerbated by bisphosphonate treatment, and may lead to difficult tracheal intubation. While bisphosphonates suppress bone turnover and improve symptoms, their long-term effects on clinical outcomes are not fully clear, and relapse occurs upon discontinuation. Severe complications like bilateral cavernous internal carotid aneurysms have also been reported. [PMC12333066, PMC11994531, PMC10406616, PMC5111855, PMC4410173]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A clonal B-cell disorder characterized by the aggregation and deposition of insoluble amyloid fibrils derived from misfolding of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains. It usually presents as systemic AL amyloidosis with involvement of one or more parenchymal organ(s) and, less frequently, as localized amyloidosis with usually nodular deposits restricted to a single organ and/or system.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It represents the most common type of systemic amyloidosis in western countries; in Europe and the USA the incidence ranges from 1/80,000-330,000 and prevalence between 1/17,000-50,000. AL amyloidosis affects men slightly more often than women.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The average age of diagnosed patients is 63 years. The clinical manifestations depend on organ involvement and general symptoms, such as fatigue and weight loss, can also occur. The heart (approximately 80%) and the kidneys (65%) are the most commonly involved organs, followed by soft tissues, liver, peripheral and autonomic nervous system, and gastrointestinal tract. This can result in fluid retention, dyspnea, arrhythmias, liver enlargement, macroglossia, swelling if the submandibular glands, carpal tunnel syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, hypotension, diarrhea or constipation. Localized AL amyloidosis can affect the skin, the respiratory, gastrointestinal and urinary tract, and the eye.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: AL amyloidosis results from conformational changes of monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains produced by a usually small B-cell (most commonly plasma cell) clone. These light chains misfold, aggregate, and deposit in tissue in the form of fibrils. Organ dysfunction and damage is dependent on a direct toxic effect of monoclonal light chains, particularly in the heart, and on the mechanical effect of deposits.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of systemic AL amyloidosis is established by demonstrating amyloid deposits (red-green birefringence with Congo red staining under cross-polarized light) in the affected organ by biopsy or other less invasive alternatives (e.g. subcutaneous fat aspirate) and by demonstrating that amyloid fibrils are formed by immunoglobulin light chains (amyloid typing). Amyloid typing can be achieved by immunohistochemical staining, immunofluorescence on renal biopsies in patients with kidney involvement, and mass spectrometry. A B-cell clone producing a light chain of the same isotype as that documented in the deposits should be searched for and demonstrated. The presence and severity of organ involvement should be assessed (by echocardiography, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, measurement of proteinuria and renal and liver function parameters) and graded. Cardiac and renal staging systems based on natriuretic peptide type-B or its N-terminal pro-hormone, troponin, free light chain proteinuria, and glomerular filtration rate accurately predict the risk of death and progression to dialysis. Localized AL amyloidosis is diagnosed by biopsy of the deposits.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Systemic AL amyloidosis should be distinguished from other forms of systemic amyloidosis and from non-amyloid light chain deposition disease.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment of systemic AL amyloidosis is based on therapies targeting the underlying plasma clone aiming at reducing the supply of the amyloid-forming light chain. Successful treatment can improve organ involvement and extend survival. The only licensed therapy is the combination of daratumumab, cyclophosphamide, bortezomib, and dexamethasone (Dara-CyBorD). Other effective regimens are bortezomib, melphalan, dexamethasone (BMDex) and CyBorD. Autologous stem cell transplant is effective and induces long term survival in responders, but only a minority of patients (approximately 20%) are fit enough to safely undergo this procedure. Relapsed and refractory patients are usually rescued with immunomodulatory drugs, such as lenalidomide and pomalidomide. Patients in whom the disease is not caused by a plasma cell clone are treated with regimens used in the corresponding B cell malignancy. Localized AL amyloidosis is treated by surgical removal of the amyloid deposits when this is necessary and possible.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis of systemic AL amyloidosis depends on the presence and severity of heart involvement and on response to therapy. Patients who are diagnosed when advanced heart involvement is already established are at high risk of early death (within a few months), whereas patients who attain rapid and deep response to therapy can enjoy a prolonged survival. Localized AL amyloidosis has a largely better outcome and only exceptionally is it life threatening.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inherited cancer-predisposing syndrome characterized by the presence of juvenile hamartomatous polyps in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): JIP; JPS; Juvenile gastrointestinal polyposis; Juvenile intestinal polyposis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence ranges from 1/100,000 to 1/160,000; 1/1,000,000 for juvenile polyposis of infancy (JPI).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Juvenile polyposis syndrome (JPS) is diagnosed if any of the following criteria are met: a) ≥5 juvenile polyps in the large bowel; b) multiple juvenile polyps throughout the GI tract; c) any number of juvenile polyps (JP) and a family history of JPS. JPS is genetically and clinically heterogeneous, with a strong genotype-phenotype correlation. It is distinct from solitary juvenile polyp, which is a common sporadic entity. Polyps may develop at any age. Most affected individuals present polyps by adolescence/early adulthood. JPs are benign but malignant transformation can occur. The large bowel is the most common site of cancer. Gastric cancer and significant gastric polyposis are seen almost uniquely in SMAD4 pathogenic variant (PV) carriers. JPI is a severe form caused by de novo microdeletions involving BMPR1A and PTEN. New JPI cases most commonly present with rectal bleeding and anemia, and may also present with failure to thrive or protein losing enteropathy. SMAD4 PVs may cause a hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) overlap syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: JPS is caused by constitutional PVs in SMAD4 (18q21.1), and BMPR1A (10q22.3), the latter either in isolation or as part of a microdeletion also involving PTEN in JPI. No genetic alterations are found in 50% of JPS patients.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is clinical or genetic. Clinical diagnosis is based on clinical findings, family history, endoscopic findings, and polyp histology. Small JPs are often confused with inflammatory polyps at initial histological assessment as they may not have developed all the classical features of a juvenile-type hamartoma. Molecular genetic testing confirms the diagnosis in carriers of constitutional PVs.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other hamartomatous polyposis syndromes such as PTEN-hamartoma-tumor and Peutz-Jeghers syndromes. SMAD4 PV carriers may have similar gastric appearance to Menetriers disease and Cronkhite-Canada syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is an option for family planning.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The mode of inheritance is autosomal dominant; each child has a 50% risk of inhering the PV.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Colonoscopy surveillance is recommended every 1-3 years (depending on polyp burden), starting between 12 and 15 years of age for both BMPR1A and SMAD4 PV carriers. Most patients can be managed endoscopically but surgery may be required for patients with severe large bowel disease to manage polyp related complications and/or cancer prevention. Upper GI endoscopy, 1-3 yearly should start sometime between adolescence and age 18 for SMAD4, and between adolescence and age 25 for BMPR1A PV carriers. Patients with a SMAD4 PV should be screened and monitored for HHT manifestations. CT scan of the chest to look for pulmonary arteriovenous malformation, transthoracic echocardiogram to assess for aortopathy and valvular heart disease, and video capsule endoscopy (VCE) to assess for small bowel angioectasia, are the most commonly recommended screening modalities. They may be repeated in case of findings in the initial screening or concerns during the patient's follow-up. Early therapy with mTOR inhibitors has shown promise as effective pharmacological treatment in JPI.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: JPS prognosis mostly depends on the risk of developing GI cancer. The cumulative cancer risk is 20% by 35 years old and 68% by 60 years old. However, the data for cancer risk is subject to significant ascertainment bias and may not reflect real life risks when on appropriate surveillance. JPI was associated with very poor prognosis and children rarely survived. Early data on the use of mTOR inhibitors are encouraging, and longer-term survival seems a very real possibility. For patients with JPS/HHT overlap, HHT may be the major determinant of prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A parasitic disease caused by different species of the genus Leishmania, transmitted through the bite of hematophagous female phlebotomine sand flies. The clinical spectrum ranges from asymptomatic to clinically overt disease which can remain localized to the skin or disseminate to the upper oral and respiratory mucous membranes or throughout the reticulo-endothelial system. Three main clinical syndromes have been described: visceral (or Kala-Azar; with fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly), cutaneous, and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (cutaneous or mucocutaneous ulceration).

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: presents the case of a 54-year-old woman, otherwise healthy, who presented with a 4-month history of red plaques with central ulceration, which had initially developed from painless papules. The lesions appeared on her right arm and trunk, two months after her travel to Morocco. Physical examination revealed a 7 cm × 5 cm red plaque with central ulceration and crusting on her right arm, along with papules and plaques on her trunk. Based on microbiological, histopathological, and PCR , the patient was diagnosed with Old World cutaneous leishmaniasis. After receiving two sessions of intralesional pentavalent antimonial treatment, the patient was left with only a minor scar and experienced negligible side effects, except for moderate aching during therapy. Leishmaniasis is a potentially life-threatening protozoan infection that presents with many clinical manifestations, including... [PMC12222432, PMC12176833, PMC12172367, PMC12142294, PMC12114399]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Leishmaniasis relies on identifying the parasite or its genetic material. Histopathological examination of biopsies from affected tissues, including skin, liver, tonsils, or larynx, frequently reveals Leishmania amastigotes within macrophages or suspicious inclusions. Molecular techniques, such as PCR, real-time PCR, and PCR-RFLP, are essential for confirming Leishmania DNA and for species identification from samples like skin scrapings, cotton swabs, or bone marrow. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) offers a rapid and accurate diagnostic approach, applicable to peripheral blood and bone marrow, especially in non-endemic areas or when traditional are insufficient. Cytological examinations and bone marrow smears also aid in diagnosis, particularly for visceral forms. [PMC12222432, PMC12176833, PMC12172367, PMC12142294, PMC12114399]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Familial melanoma (FM) is a rare inherited form of melanoma characterized by development of histologically confirmed melanoma in two first degree relatives or more relatives in an affected family.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: FM is thought to account for about 10% of all cases of cutaneous melanoma. Melanoma primarily affects populations of European origin. Incidence is higher in geographical regions with greater sun exposure (southern USA, Australia, New Zealand). Incidence was estimated at 1/90,000 in Europe in 2012.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Familial melanoma tends to occur earlier than non-familial melanoma. The average age of onset is often between 30 and 40 years, while non-familial melanoma typically occurs in the general population between 50 and 60. Earlier and later onset is nonetheless reported in some families. A higher frequency of multiple primary melanomas is also found. Melanoma generally presents as a pigmented lesion on the skin. It is often asymmetrical with irregular borders and color variegation. The diameter is often greater than 6 mm. The most common sites are the trunk, lower legs and back. All four main clinicopathologic subtypes of primary cutaneous melanoma described (spreading melanoma, nodular melanoma, lentigo maligna melanoma, and acral lentiginous melanoma) are observed. A variety of growth patterns are found with progression to a potential for metastasis to other organs. Atypical moles are often found in families with FM.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The risk of familial melanoma is closely related to a wide range of genetic alterations in susceptibility genes but also appears to be influenced by phenotypic risk factors, such as pigmentation, freckling and nevi and sun reactions but also exposure to UV radiation. Complex interactions between genetic and environmental factors are therefore thought to underlie FM. The most common high-penetrance susceptibility gene implicated in FM is CDKN2A, accounting for predisposition in approximately 20% of FM. CDK4, another high risk gene, is rarely involved. Mutations of BAP1,POT1, TERF2IP, ACD,and TERT have recently been reported and penetrance remains to be determined. Medium penetrance genes include MITF and MC1R. Some twenty common genetic variants modulate risk for melanoma in low clustering families.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: FM is suspected in individuals when two or more close relatives have developed melanoma. A new or changing skin mole should be assessed to identify melanoma. Changes include color, border, size, and symmetry.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses are seborrheic keratosis, atypical mole, familial atypical multiple mole melanoma and skin carcinoma.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In some affected families, susceptibility is consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance but in most cases, a polygenic mode of inheritance appears likely. Patients should be informed that a family history of melanoma in one close relative is associated with an average 2-fold increased risk. History in more than one relative and relevant personal phenotypic characteristics such as multiple pigmented atypical melanocytic lesions result in a significantly higher risk.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Long-term screening of individuals at high risk and monitoring in FM families is recommended. This involves a total-body skin examination by a qualified dermatologist every six months. Self-examination of skin should be encouraged. Treatment is similar to sporadic melanoma and is largely based on surgery at initial stages.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable and depends on time of diagnosis, thickness, presence of ulceration, mitotic index, and possible lymph node involvement, and distant metastatic disease. Early diagnosis (with thin Breslow thickness) is associated with a high percentage of cure. Monitoring of melanoma families aims to detect melanoma offering skin surveillance resulting in a favorable prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pellagra is a nutritional disorder caused by a deficiency in niacin (vitamin B3) or its precursor (tryptophan) that is mainly observed in Asia and Africa where it is generally due to poor nutrition. It is characterized by dermatitis (symmetrical photodistributed erythema that may be accompanied by vesicles and bullae, and that develops into hyperkeratotic and hyperpigmented skin), gastrointestinal symptoms (diarrhea), and neuropsychiatric disorders (dementia). It can be life-threatening without a correct management.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Pellagra can manifest across a broad age spectrum, from childhood to advanced age. While it seldom occurs in children, a case of a 12-year-old female has been reported. Adult cases span from a 27-year-old woman to individuals in their 40s, 50s, and 60s. Furthermore, diagnoses in elderly patients, including a 70-year-old man and a man in his 80s, indicate that onset can occur later in life. [PMC11282565, PMC9639017, PMC8363969, PMC7357129, PMC6814328]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An ectodermal dysplasia syndrome with defining features of ankyloblepharon filiforme adnatum (AFA), ectodermal abnormalities and a cleft lip and/or palate.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Ankyloblepharon-ectodermal defects-cleft lip/palate syndrome (AEC syndrome) prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: A history of skin erosions, especially of the scalp neonatally is typical. Congenital erythroderma occurs in 78%. Skin erosions often persist intermittently for many years, evolving into alopecia and cutaneous scarring of the skin. Wound healing appears to be delayed. Other prevalent skin manifestations include hyperpigmentation and/or hypopigmentation, often reticulated, and palmar and plantar changes with effaced dermatoglyphics. Nail changes are universal and variable and include hyperconvexity, pseudoptyergium and frayed distal margin with nail plate resorption. Hypotrichosis is common and hair is thin, brittle, wiry and uncombable. Mild hypohidrosis is always present. Nearly all cases have clefting abnormalities, ranging from submusous cleft palate, to soft and/or hard cleft palate, cleft lip or a combination. Other oroauditory findings include recurrent otitis media, canal stenosis and over 90% have a conductive hearing loss associated with a delay of speech development. AFA affects most neonates (70%) but is not always evident as these may autolyse or be lysed by a healthcare provider applying ophthalmic antibiotic ointment at birth. Eyes often are deficient of lacrimal puncta. In childhood, other facial features become more apparent and include broad nasal root, hypoplastic alae nasi, short philtrum, thin vermillion border, maxillary hypoplasia and small mandible. Over time, cone-shaped teeth and hypodontia become evident. Other anomalies are limb changes with syndactyly of fingers and toes most common, hypospadias (males 78%) and trismus (less frequently described). Failure to thrive, growth delay and gastrointestinal issues are also common.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: AEC is an autosomal dominant condition caused by pathogenic (usually missense) changes in the Tumor suppressor gene TP63. Over 4/5th of the reported pathogenic variants occur in the sterile alpha motif (SAM) domain, and about 1/5th occur in the transactivation inhibitory (TI) domain of TP63.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Clinical features can be diagnostic. Light or scanning microscopy of the hair in combination with genetic testing may ascertain diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis may include epidermolysis bullosa simplex, disorders of cornification, CHAND syndrome and hypohidrotic ectodermal dysplasia. Allelic disorders include Acro-dermal-ungual-lacrimal-tooth (ADULT) syndrome, ectrodactyly-ectodermal dysplasia clefting (EEC) syndrome, limb-mammary syndrome and split hand/foot malformation type 4. AEC is generally distinguished from these other disorders by clinical features (particularly scalp erosions) as well as the location of the TP63 change. The Rapp-Hodgkin syndrome is not a separate disease entity, but is now considered part of the disease spectrum of AEC syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: In case of family history, prenatal diagnosis is possible by genetic testing of amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: AEC syndrome follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. About 70% of cases are caused by a de novo change in TP63. In case of family history, genetic counseling is recommended. Genetic counseling should be proposed to individuals having the pathogenic variants, informing them that there is 50% risk of passing the mutation to offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: AFA and cleft palate may require surgical intervention, as well as dental abnormalities requiring prosthetics. Efforts to prevent secondary infections in skin erosions comprise gentle wound care and dilute bleach soaks. Secondary infections should be cultured and treated appropriately. Extra care should be taken to avoid complications in infants with severe skin erosions. Extensive grafting procedures are not recommended. Hearing loss, growth and gastrointestinal problems should be monitored regularly. Gastrostomy is common. Psychological consequences of ectodermal defects should be addressed.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Overall prognosis is good with most having normal life expectancy. Unfortunately infants with extensive skin erosions are at risk of premature death due to complications including sepsis and fluid/electrolyte abnormalities. Quality of life and psychosocial functioning is often mildly but variably impacted.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare skin tumor characterized by predominantly intraepithelial growth of an adenocarcinoma which may either arise primarily in the skin (primary extramammary Paget disease) or result from intraepithelial spread of a visceral carcinoma (secondary extramammary Paget disease). The lesion is typically located in the anogenital region, presenting as a scaly, oozing, pruritic or painful erythematous plaque often resembling eczema. It may exhibit an invasive component with a significant risk of lymph node metastasis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Perianal Paget's disease (PPD) is a rare condition which is often associated with underlying malignancy. To definitively rule out malignancy, excision biopsy is required. Surgery is the mainstay of treatment for this condition. A male patient in his 70s was referred to the colorectal outpatient clinic by a dermatologist with a punch biopsy result demonstrating PPD. His only presenting complaint was pruritus ani. Repeat biopsies confirmed the diagnosis of PPD and flexible sigmoidoscopy excluded luminal pathology. With complete preoperative work-up, a wide local excision was performed with a concurrent defunctioning colostomy to reduce local contamination and facilitate healing of delayed closure with both VY and mucosal advancement flaps. Delayed closure allows time to confirm histology prior to definitive closure. We conclude that PPD is a rare condition which requires extensive and... [PMC12214454, PMC12298491, PMC12341820, PMC11233530, PMC11230674]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Extramammary Paget disease (EMPD) is a rare intraepithelial adenocarcinoma originating from apocrine glands, primarily affecting the anogenital and axillary regions, including the vulva, perianal area, scrotum, and penis. It can also occur in ectopic, non-apocrine sites such as the scalp, oral mucosa, anterior chest, and buttocks, sometimes at multiple sites. Clinically, EMPD often presents as persistent erythematous lesions, patchy erythema, or pigmented plaques, which may be large and can ulcerate. Symptoms like pruritus ani are reported. Due to its varied manifestations and resemblance to inflammatory dermatoses or other pigmented lesions, EMPD is frequently misdiagnosed. It is often associated with underlying malignancy, necessitating comprehensive systemic evaluation. [PMC12214454, PMC12135345, PMC12298491, PMC12341820, PMC12275371]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Extramammary Paget disease (EMPD) is a rare intraepithelial adenocarcinoma that primarily originates from apocrine glands, predominantly affecting areas rich in these glands such as the anogenital, axillary, vulvar, perianal, scrotal, and penile regions. It can be classified as either primary or secondary in origin. Secondary EMPD may arise from pagetoid spread of an underlying malignancy, such as vulvar or esophageal adenocarcinoma. Primary EMPD is also often associated with underlying malignancy. Ectopic EMPD can occur in non-apocrine sites like the scalp, sometimes associated with other neoplasms such as an atypical meningioma. Genomic analysis of metastatic EMPD has revealed copy number variations and enrichment in signaling pathways like TGFβ and FGFR1. [PMC12214454, PMC12135345, PMC12298491, PMC12341820, PMC11329320]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Extramammary Paget disease (EMPD) primarily relies on histopathological biopsy, which is considered the most important and definitive method. This includes excision, punch, and rapid intraoperative frozen biopsies, with specialized techniques like modified clock mapping biopsy used to assess disease extent preoperatively. Immunohistochemical examination is crucial for confirming the diagnosis, differentiating EMPD from other conditions, and identifying specific markers such as CK20, CK7, HER2, estrogen receptor, and Ki-67. A comprehensive systemic evaluation, including imaging like CT scans and flexible sigmoidoscopy, is warranted to rule out underlying malignancies or identify associated lesions. Whole genome sequencing may be performed in metastatic cases to understand the genomic landscape. [PMC12214454, PMC12135345, PMC12298491, PMC12341820, PMC12275371]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Extramammary Paget's disease (EMPD) is often misdiagnosed due to its varied manifestations. Clinically, ectopic EMPD can resemble inflammatory dermatoses, and pigmented EMPD can be mistaken for superficial spreading melanoma, Bowen's disease, pigmented superficial basal cell carcinoma, or seborrheic keratosis. Histologically, pagetoid spread from other adenocarcinomas, such as vulvar adenocarcinoma, can present a similar appearance, termed secondary extramammary Paget's disease. Accurate differential diagnosis, particularly for atypical lesions and pigmented variants, relies on histopathological and immunohistochemical analyses. [PMC12135345, PMC12298491, PMC12341820, PMC11416748]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Extramammary Paget disease is predominantly surgical, with wide local excision being the mainstay. Preoperative assessment, such as clock mapping biopsy, and intraoperative rapid frozen pathological examination are crucial to ensure negative surgical margins and reduce recurrence. For large surgical wounds, skin flap transplantation may be used. However, complete surgical excision can be challenging, and local recurrence is common. Alternative or adjunctive therapies include radiotherapy, Mohs micrographic surgery, and photodynamic therapy. For advanced, Her-2-positive cases, anti-Her-2 therapy, such as disitamab vedotin combined with immunotherapy, has demonstrated efficacy. A comprehensive systemic evaluation is warranted due to the potential association with underlying malignancies. [PMC12257348, PMC12214454, PMC12298491, PMC12341820, PMC11233530]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Traditional boluses for pelvic lesions present challenges, including compromised skin dose coverage from large air gaps in treatment plans and increased uncertainties in treatment delivery due to variations in bolus fitting. evaluates the clinical benefits of a patient-specific, 3D-printed bolus (pBolus) in external beam radiation therapy (EBRT) for extramammary Paget's disease in the inguinal fold. A three-dimensional (3D) conformal plan utilizing the pBolus was compared to a conventional Superflab bolus (sBolus) under identical beam arrangements. The pBolus improved dose conformity by reducing air gaps in the treatment plan, and therefore, it was selected for clinical treatment. Weekly setup imaging revealed air gaps predominantly along the inguinal fold, demonstrating overall consistency in bolus fitting with minor air gap variations. Additionally, in vivo dosimetry confirmed dose... [PMC12257348, PMC12214454, PMC12135345, PMC12197883, PMC12298491]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, acquired motor neuron disease characterized by a slowly progressive, unilateral, ascending or descending hemiplegia, associated to unilateral or asymmetrical pyramidal signs and no sensory loss. It is a diagnosis of exclusion and controversy exists regarding whether the presence of bulbar symptoms, sphincter disturbances, fasciculations or cognitive manifestations characterize the disease.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Mills' syndrome is a purely clinical description characterized by progressive spastic hemiparesis, which can manifest as ascending or descending progressive hemiplegia. It is considered a hemiplegic form of primary lateral sclerosis. The syndrome is reserved for patients where no other explanation for the progressive spastic hemiparesis can be found. Active pathology, such as microglial activation in the superior frontal region or a high cervical cord inflammatory lesion, may be detectable many years after symptom onset, even in cases with clinically similar presentations. [PMC1739672, PMC485513]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Mills' syndrome is primarily a clinical description for patients presenting with progressive spastic hemiparesis, an isolated upper motor neuron syndrome, for which no other explanation can be found. While its precise etiology is varied, active pathology, indicated by microglial activation, has been detected in the motor cortex or superior frontal region in some patients. In other cases, a high cervical cord inflammatory lesion suggests an extra-cerebral inflammatory disease. The syndrome has also been considered a hemiplegic form of primary lateral sclerosis. Pathology can be detectable many years after symptom onset and occur in disparate sites with clinically similar presentations. [PMC1739672, PMC485513]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Mills syndrome is a purely clinical description, diagnosed in patients presenting with progressive spastic hemiparesis when no other explanation can be found. Positron emission tomography (PET) using (11)C-(R)-PK11195 has been utilized to explore active pathology in vivo in clinically similar isolated upper motor neuron syndromes, revealing microglial activation in the motor cortex or superior frontal region. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can identify other conditions, such as high cervical cord inflammatory lesions, which would exclude a diagnosis of Mills syndrome. [PMC1739672]
