DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Mills' syndrome is a purely clinical description reserved for patients presenting with progressive spastic hemiparesis for which no other explanation can be found. It is closely considered in relation to Primary Lateral Sclerosis (PLS), with some suggesting it may represent a hemiplegic form of PLS. Other differential considerations include isolated upper motor neuron syndromes and conditions such as high cervical cord inflammatory lesions or other extra-cerebral inflammatory disease. Positron emission tomography (PET) can aid in differentiation, demonstrating active pathology in disparate sites with clinically similar presentations, such as microglial activation in the motor cortex or superior frontal region, or no focal cerebral pathology in cases of cervical cord lesions. [PMC1739672, PMC485513]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Mills' syndrome is characterized by progressive spastic hemiparesis or ascending/descending progressive hemiplegia. Active pathology, such as microglial activation, may be detectable many years after the onset of symptoms, indicating a chronic and worsening course. The condition is considered a purely clinical description for progressive spastic hemiparesis without other explanation, and it has been questioned whether it represents a hemiplegic form of primary lateral sclerosis. [PMC1739672, PMC485513]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Congenital hypothyroidism (CH) is defined as a thyroid hormone deficiency present from birth.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It occurs in approximately 1/2,000 to 1/4,000 newborns and is more common in Asian, Native American, and Hispanic infants.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical manifestations are often subtle or not present at birth, probably as a result of trans-placental passage of some maternal thyroid hormone and the fact that many infants have some thyroid production of their own. More specific symptoms often do not develop until several months of age. Common clinical features include decreased activity and increased sleep, feeding difficulty and constipation, prolonged jaundice, myxedematous facies, large fontanels (especially posterior), macroglossia, a distended abdomen with umbilical hernia, and hypotonia. Slow linear growth and developmental delay are usually apparent by 4-6 months of age. Without treatment CH results in severe intellectual deficit and short stature.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CH can be divided into permanent (with primary, secondary, or peripheral causes) or transient forms. Causes of primary CH include thyroid dysgenesis (85% of cases) and inborn errors of thyroid hormone biosynthesis (dyshormonogenesis, 10-15% of cases). The cause of thyroid dysgenesis remains unknown in the vast majority of cases. Secondary or central CH results from thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) deficiency and is usually associated with congenital hypopituitarism. Peripheral CH results from defects in thyroid hormone transport, metabolism, or action as in Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome or as a result of peripheral resistance to thyroid hormones. CH may also occur as part of a syndrome, for example in the Pendred and Bamforth-Lazarus syndromes. Transient CH most commonly occurs in preterm infants born in areas of endemic iodine deficiency. In Western countries, transient hypothyroidism is more likely to be associated with exposure to excess iodine, or with maternal thyroid blocking antibodies.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: In countries with newborn screening programs (with either a primary thyroxine (T4)-follow-up TSH or primary TSH test), infants are diagnosed after detection by screening tests finding an elevated serum TSH level and low T4 or free T4 level. Other diagnostic tests (thyroid radionuclide uptake and scan, thyroid sonography, or serum thyroglobulin determination) may help pinpoint the underlying etiology and separate transient from permanent cases.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: If a familial form of CH is discovered, this will guide genetic counseling. Thyroid dysgenesis is usually a sporadic disorder; thyroid dyshormonogenesis is autosomal recessive, with a recurrence risk of 25%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Etiological diagnosis is not necessary when initiating thyroid hormone treatment. Levothyroxine is the treatment of choice; the recommended starting dose is 10-15 mcg/kg/day. The immediate goals of treatment are to raise the serum T4 above 130 nmol/L (10 ug/dL) as rapidly as possible; with these starting doses, serum TSH usually normalizes in 2-4 weeks. Frequent laboratory monitoring in infancy is essential to ensure optimal neurocognitive outcome. Serum TSH and T4 or free T4 should be measured every 1-2 months in the first 6 months of life, every 3 months between 6 months and 3 years of age, and 4 weeks after any dose change.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis of infants started on treatment early is excellent, with IQs similar to sibling or classmate controls. Lower neurocognitive outcomes may occur in those infants started after more than 30 days of age, on lower l-thyroxine doses than currently recommended, and in those infants with more severe hypothyroidism.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Worldwide newborn screening (NBS) programmes detect one in 2000-4000 newborns with forms of congenital hypothyroidism (CH). However, some newborns such as premature born babies, are at increased risk for a false-negative test result caused by delayed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) elevation through an immature hypothalamic-pituitary axis. a case of a premature newborn in which CH remained undetected. At the age of 3 months cardiorespiratory incidents increased, bradycardia, hypothermia and seizures developed. Investigation revealed severe hypotonic hyponatraemia (85 mmol/L), severe CH (TSH 300 mIU/L, free T4 2 pmol/L), renal insufficiency and metabolic acidosis. High urine osmolality, low urine sodium concentration and an extremely activated renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system suggested a low effective circulating volume. This case report describes hypothyroid-induced hyponatraemia... [PMC11795244, PMC12371337, PMC11972869, PMC11163313, PMC11515955]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Chédiak-Higashi syndrome (CHS) is a rare severe genetic disorder generally characterized by partial oculocutaneous albinism (OCA), severe immunodeficiency, mild bleeding, neurological dysfunction and lymphoproliferative disorder. A classic, early-onset form and an attenuated, later-onset form (Atypical CHS) have been described.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Exact prevalence is difficult to determine; fewer than 500 cases have been reported. Many patients likely remain undiagnosed because of variability in clinical signs. No gender or ethnic predilection has been found.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients with CHS mostly have partial OCA involving the hair, skin, and eyes. Reduced iris pigmentation may be associated with nystagmus, and visual acuity may be impaired. Infections that are predominantly bacterial, but also of viral or fungal origin, begin to occur in infancy and may be severe, affecting primarily the skin and upper respiratory tract. Periodontitis has often been reported. Manifestations of increased bleeding tendency are generally mild and include epistaxis, gum bleeding and easy bruising. Cognitive deficits are often noted in childhood. Most patients develop neurological features by early adulthood as the disease progresses including ataxia, tremor, absent deep-tendon reflexes, and peripheral neuropathy. Some patients have Parkinsonian features with bradykinesia and rigidity. About 85% of CHS patients develop the accelerated phase, a lymphoproliferative disorder which involves fever, anemia, neutropenia, and occasionally thrombocytopenia, as well as lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Loss-of-function mutations in the LYST lysosomal trafficking regulator gene (1q42.1-q42.2) are associated with the severe, childhood-onset form of CHS. Missense mutations appear to underlie the atypical form.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected in individuals with partial OCA, a history of severe or frequent infections, and minor bleeding tendency. The main criterion is peroxidase-positive giant inclusions in white blood cells identified on the peripheral blood smear. Deficiency of platelet-dense bodies found via whole-mount electron microscopy is also characteristic. Molecular genetic testing supports diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include oculocutaneous albinism, Hermansky Pudlak syndrome (specifically HPS-2 caused by mutations in AP3B1), Cross syndrome and Griscelli disease.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis of CHS is available clinically by amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling and requires prior identification of the genetic mutation in the family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: CHS follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. Genetic counseling should be provided to asymptomatic carriers and to affected adults.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The hematological and immunological manifestations can be treated by allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) upon diagnosis. HSCT is more successful when performed before the accelerated phase, but does not alter progression of neurological dysfunction. Management of the acceleration phase involves combination therapy with etoposide, dexamethasone, and cyclosporine (the same as for familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)). Infections should be treated promptly with antibiotics or antivirals and exposure to infectious agents avoided. Desmopressin can be used for bleeding prophylaxis. Standard therapeutic measures should be adopted to improve visual acuity and to manage neurological manifestations. Patients should use sunscreen and wear protective UV sunglasses.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Without treatment, prognosis is very poor. Primary causes of mortality in the first 10 years of life are development of the accelerated phase and overwhelming infection. Neurologic manifestations occur in individuals despite bone marrow transplantation.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A teratologic disorder associated with intrauterine exposure of phenobarbital during the first trimester of pregnancy. Infants are usually asymptomatic but an increased risk of intellectual disability, tetralogy of Fallot, unilateral cleft lip, hypoplasia of the mitral valve and some other mild abnormalities such as hypertelorism, epicanthus, hypoplasia and low insertion of the nose, low insertion of the ears, prognathism, ﬁnger hypoplasia, brachydactyly and hypospadias have been reported in rare cases.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Phenobarbital embryopathy can manifest with a range of clinical features. Affected children may present with mild mental retardation and appreciable articulation difficulties, which can be attributed to functional palatal incompetence despite an anatomically normal palate. Neonatal complications include prolonged hypocalcaemia with tetany, typically appearing in the first and second weeks of life as jitteriness and tetany. This hypocalcaemia can be resistant to therapy over a longer period and is associated with defective bone mineralization. These conditions are observed in infants whose mothers were exposed to phenobarbitone during pregnancy. [PMC1628867, PMC1546284]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Fetal exposure to antiseizure medications (ASMs), including phenobarbitone, is linked to an elevated risk of congenital malformations. Mechanistically, ASMs can induce global DNA hypomethylation, dysregulate epigenetic regulators, and cause site-specific hypermethylation at key developmental genes. This leads to the downregulation of developmentally critical proteins, with integrative analyses revealing coordinated regulation of target genes linked to congenital abnormalities. Phenobarbitone exposure during pregnancy has been associated with functional palatal incompetence, mild mental retardation, and neonatal hypocalcaemia. The hypocalcaemia is suggested to result from an effect on fetal vitamin D metabolism, leading to defective bone mineralization. Folic acid co-treatment has been shown to partially restore DNA methylation and reverse some proteomic disruptions. [PMC12387082, PMC1628867, PMC1546284]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Fetal exposure to antiseizure medications, including phenobarbitone, elevates the risk of congenital malformations by inducing global DNA hypomethylation and dysregulating epigenetic regulators, which impacts key developmental genes and proteins. Offspring may present with mild mental retardation, articulation difficulties due to functional palatal incompetence, or prolonged neonatal hypocalcaemia with tetany, potentially linked to defective bone mineralization. Integrated analyses suggest that folic acid co-treatment can partially restore DNA methylation and reverse some epigenetic and proteomic disruptions, offering a potential strategy to mitigate these teratogenic effects. Counseling should address the risks associated with maternal phenobarbitone use and the potential protective role of folic acid supplementation. [PMC12387082, PMC1628867, PMC1546284]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Folic acid supplementation shows potential to mitigate the teratogenic impact of antiseizure medications, including phenobarbital, on developmental pathways. Studies indicate that folic acid co-treatment can partially restore DNA methylation and reverse the downregulation of developmentally critical proteins, thereby countering epigenetic and proteomic disruptions linked to congenital abnormalities. These findings offer mechanistic insight and support folic acid's role in mitigating the effects of phenobarbital embryopathy. [PMC12387082, PMC10658473]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Children exposed to phenobarbital prenatally may experience long-term developmental challenges, including mild mental retardation and appreciable articulation difficulties due to functional palatal incompetence. Neonates can present with prolonged hypocalcemia and tetany, which may be resistant to therapy over a longer period and are suggested to be linked to defective bone mineralization. These findings indicate a prognosis that can involve persistent neurological, speech, and metabolic complications. [PMC1628867, PMC1546284]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, severe disorder of urea cycle metabolism typically characterized by either a neonatal-onset of severe hyperammonemia that occurs few days after birth and manifests with lethargy, vomiting, hypothermia, seizures, coma and death or a presentation outside the newborn period at any age with (sometimes) milder symptoms of hyperammonemia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CPS1 deficiency; CPS1D; Carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase I deficiency; Carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The worldwide prevalence ranges between 1/526,000-1,300,000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In the neonatal-onset form of carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency (CPS1D), patients are usually healthy at birth but after few days they begin to manifest with lethargy and unwillingness to feed. Severe hyperammonemia continues and manifests with vomiting, hypothermia, hypotonia, seizures, coma, and can lead to death. Outside the newborn period, patients can present at any time in life. Risk factors for manifestation include catabolic stressors such as fasting and intercurrent illness. Manifestations include hyperammonemia with irritability, lethargy, headache, seizures, confusion, avoidance of high-protein meals, axial hypotonia and cognitive disability.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CPS1D is due to mutations in the CPS1 gene (2p) that encodes carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase I (CPS1), an enzyme located in the mitochondrial matrix of hepatocytes and epithelial cells of intestinal mucosa that controls the first step of the urea cycle where ammonia is converted into carbamoyl-phosphate. Mutations in this gene lead to an interruption in the urea cycle and excess nitrogen is not converted to urea for excretion by the kidneys, leading to hyperammonemia.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based mainly on clinical findings and laboratory test results. Biochemical findings include severe hyperammonemia with very low plasma levels of citrulline and arginine, high plasma levels of glutamine, increased transaminases and low or normal levels of orotic acid in the urine. Molecular genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses mainly include other urea cycle disorders and organic acidurias. Amino acid profiles will distinguish CPS1D from argininosuccinic aciduria, citrullinemia type I and arginase deficiency while orotic acid in urine should help to distinguish from ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency. Another more recent differential diagnosis is hyperammonemic encephalopathy due to carbonic anhydrase VA deficiency.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible in families with a known disease causing mutation on both alleles.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: CPS1D is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner; there is a 25% risk of inheriting the disease where both parents are unaffected carriers.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Patients presenting with a hyperammonemic coma must be treated immediately in a tertiary care center where plasma ammonia levels must be lowered (by hemodialysis or hemofiltration methods), ammonia scavenger therapy implemented, catabolism reversed (through glucose and lipid infusions) and special care taken to reduce the risk of neurological damage (EEG surveillance and treatment of seizures, if necessary). A life-long diet low in natural protein, supplements of essential amino acids, citrulline and arginine as needed, nitrogen scavenger therapy (sodium benzoate and/or sodium or glycerol phenylbutyrate) and appropriate nutritional support to avoid catabolic stress are recommended. Early liver transplantation for those with neonatal-onset CPS1D can correct metabolic abnormalities but does not reverse any neurological complications. Valproic acid should be avoided.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on disease severity but is considered bleak in patients with early neonatal disease. With early diagnosis and optimal treatment started without any delay, the prognosis improves. Episodes of hyperammonemic coma of long duration are associated with a poor neurological outlook.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare developmental defect during embryogenesis with digit duplication, polydactyly, syndactyly, and/or hyperphalangy characterized by multiple congenital anomaly syndrome.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The precise estimates of birth prevalence are difficult to determine, as ascertainment is erratic (estimated range 1-9/1,000,000).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The primary findings include widely spaced eyes, macrocephaly with frontal bossing, and pre- or post-axial polydactyly and cutaneous syndactyly. The polydactyly is most commonly preaxial in the feet and postaxial in the hands, with variable cutaneous syndactyly, but the limb findings vary significantly. Other low frequency findings include central nervous system (CNS) anomalies, hernias, and cognitive impairment.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: GCPS is caused by loss of function on chromosome 7p14.1 in the transcription factor gene GLI3.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Clinical diagnosis is challenging because the findings of GCPS are relatively non-specific, and no specific and sensitive clinical criteria have been delineated. A presumptive diagnosis of GCPS can be made if the patient has the classic triad of preaxial polydactyly with cutaneous syndactyly of at least one limb, hypertelorism, and macrocephaly. Individuals with a phenotype consistent with GCPS (but which may not manifest all three attributes listed above) and a GLI3 pathogenic variant may be diagnosed definitively with GCPS. In addition, individuals with a GCPS-consistent phenotype who are related to a definitively diagnosed family member in a pattern consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance may also be diagnosed definitively.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include preaxial polydactyly type 4, the GCPS contiguous gene syndrome, acrocallosal syndrome, Gorlin syndrome, Carpenter syndrome, and Teebi syndrome. The disorder is allelic to Pallister-Hall syndrome and one form of the acrocallosal syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal molecular diagnosis is technically feasible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Genetic counseling should be proposed to individuals having the disease-causing mutation informing them that there is 50% risk of passing the pathogenic variant to offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment of the disorder is symptomatic, with plastic or orthopedic surgery indicated for significant limb malformations.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis for is generally excellent. There may be a slight increase in the incidence of developmental delay or cognitive impairment. Patients with large deletions that include GLI3 may have a poorer prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Jeune syndrome, also called asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy, is a short-rib dysplasia characterized by a narrow thorax, short limbs and radiological skeletal abnormalities including 'trident' aspect of the acetabula and metaphyseal changes.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy of the newborn; JATD; Jeune asphyxiating thoracic dystrophy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence at birth is unknown but is estimated to be 1-5/500,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The syndrome is recognizable during the antenatal period or at birth. In rare cases, postaxial polydactyly may also be present. The narrow thorax may cause neonatal respiratory failure, and may be associated with persistent respiratory manifestations. Some cases are severe while others have a benign course. The growth rate is variable but may be almost normal. Hepatic and renal failure has been reported in rare cases (liver fibrosis or nephronophthisis) occurring at any age. Retinal pigmentary degeneration could also be observed. Intellectual development is normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The molecular basis of the syndrome has been partially elucidated indicating involvement of the IFT80 (3q25.33), DYNC2H1 (11q22.3), WDR19 (4p14) and TTC21B (2q24.3) genes, each encoding an intraflagellar transport protein, which confirms that Jeune syndrome belongs to the ciliopathies group. Mutations in other genes may also be implicated in the disease and remain to be identified.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on radiologic findings: ribs are short and the pelvis has an abnormal morphology, with a horizontal acetabular roof and a trident aspect formed by a median protrusion and two lateral spurs. Hands are normal or short with possible cone-shaped epiphyses in the phalanges.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis should include thoracolaryngopelvic dysplasia, Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, Sensenbrenner syndrome and paternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 14.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Molecular diagnosis must be confirmed in the proband before proposing prenatal molecular testing. In other cases, only a careful antenatal ultrasound examination can detect the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The syndrome is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait. The recurrence risk is 25% for every pregnancy after the birth of an affected child.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment consists of management of respiratory infections, which may lead to severe complications. Renal and hepatic function should be monitored regularly, and retinal examination performed.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable depending of the visceral associated diseases, and the risk of severe respiratory complications decreases after 2 years of age.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Oral-facial-digital syndrome, type 8 is characterized by tongue lobulation, hypoplasia of the epiglottis, median cleft upper lip, broad or bifid nasal tip, hypertelorism or telecanthus, bilateral preaxial and postaxial polydactyly, abnormal tibiae and/or radii, duplication of the halluces, short stature, and mild intellectual deficit.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): OFD8; Oral-facial-digital syndrome type 8; Oral-facial-digital syndrome, Edwards type; Orofaciodigital syndrome, Edwards type

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The syndrome has been described in one family with four affected males in three generations.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Increased susceptibility to respiratory infections has been noted.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: X-linked recessive transmission has been suggested, but the causative gene has not yet been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: a male infant with hypertelorism, median pseudo-cleft of the upper lip and cleft palate, lobulated tongue, hypoplastic larynx and epiglottis, mesomelic shortening of limbs with particularly short and broad tibiae, polydactyly of the upper limbs, severely hypoplastic external genitalia with anorchidism, anal atresia, severe congenital heart defect, and renal agenesis. These features show considerable overlap with severe Majewski type short rib-polydactyly syndrome and so expand the known spectrum of anomalies in orofaciodigital syndrome type IV. [PMC1017006]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: a male infant with hypertelorism, median pseudo-cleft of the upper lip and cleft palate, lobulated tongue, hypoplastic larynx and epiglottis, mesomelic shortening of limbs with particularly short and broad tibiae, polydactyly of the upper limbs, severely hypoplastic external genitalia with anorchidism, anal atresia, severe congenital heart defect, and renal agenesis. These features show considerable overlap with severe Majewski type short rib-polydactyly syndrome and so expand the known spectrum of anomalies in orofaciodigital syndrome type IV. [PMC1017006]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: a male infant with hypertelorism, median pseudo-cleft of the upper lip and cleft palate, lobulated tongue, hypoplastic larynx and epiglottis, mesomelic shortening of limbs with particularly short and broad tibiae, polydactyly of the upper limbs, severely hypoplastic external genitalia with anorchidism, anal atresia, severe congenital heart defect, and renal agenesis. These features show considerable overlap with severe Majewski type short rib-polydactyly syndrome and so expand the known spectrum of anomalies in orofaciodigital syndrome type IV. [PMC1017006]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Early-onset progressive leukoencephalopathy-central nervous system calcification-deafness-visual impairment syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic neurological disorder characterized by early-onset progressive leukoencephalopathy, severe developmental delay, early-onset or congenital deafness (only few cases reported without hearing loss), and visual impairment. All patients manifest calcifications in brain and spinal cord. Cognitive impairment, seizures, hypotonia, spastic tetraplegia or quadriplegia are observed in the majority of the patients. Variable features may include microcephaly and anemia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Early onset progressive leukoencephalopathy- central nervous system calcification- hearing loss-visual impairment syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: The clinical picture is varied, often including intracerebral calcifications, specifically bilateral striato-pallidal calcifications. Patients may present with a pyramidal syndrome, characterized by upper limb tremors and dysgraphia. Ophthalmological findings include distance vision disorder, poor visual acuity, and macular degeneration. Associated features can include failure to thrive, short stature, and microcrania. The combination of cerebral calcification of the basal ganglia, failure to thrive, and macular degeneration represents a particular phenotype. [PMC11215278]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: The clinical picture of intracerebral calcification is so varied that it constitutes an essential element of a wide range of clinical syndromes of variable expression that continue to be described. In this article, we discuss the diagnostic possibilities of basal ganglia calcification considering the association of failure to thrive and macular degeneration in our patient. Case: A 17-year-old male patient of Congolese origin consulted us for a pyramidal syndrome consisting of upper limb tremors during mobilization and dysgraphia. The patient also presented with a distance vision disorder for which the ophthalmological examination revealed poor visual acuity in both eyes (2/10) and macular degeneration in the left eye. On physical examination, we noted a short stature with a small head circumference in relation to age. The brain scan revealed the presence of bilateral striato-pallidal... [PMC11215278]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The presence of intracerebral calcifications, particularly in the basal ganglia, is a key feature that necessitates a broad differential diagnosis. Conditions like Fahr's disease should be considered when striato-pallidal calcifications are observed. Furthermore, the association of failure to thrive, macular degeneration, and basal ganglia calcifications suggests a range of syndromic hypotheses, with Rajab-type cerebral calcification being a likely consideration. The varied clinical presentation of intracerebral calcification means it is an essential element of many syndromes. [PMC11215278]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A malignant hepatic tumor, typically affecting the pediatric population, arising mostly in an otherwise healthy liver. The most common signs are abdominal distension and abdominal mass. Sometimes patients present with anorexia, weight loss, fatigue. Most HBLs are sporadic, but some cases are associated with genetic factors, especially overgrowth syndromes, such as Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) or hemihypertrophy, and familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Hepatoblastoma (HB) accounts for about 0,5-2% of all pediatric tumors and for 2/3 of primary hepatic tumors in children. Its incidence is estimated to be 1/1,000,000 in Europe and 1-1,5/1,000,000 in USA. A slight male predilection (1.5:1 to 2:1) has been observed. The incidence of HBL in children has been increasing by about 5% annually.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The age of disease onset lies in infancy or early childhood (median age of occurrence is 18 months and 90% of HBs present before 5 years). The most common signs are: (1) abdominal distension and abdominal mass, (2) anorexia, weight loss, fatigue, (3) abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, (4) jaundice is less frequently observed, (5) anemia and thrombocytosis detected by laboratory tests. Rare cases present with precocious puberty/virilization due to beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) secretion by the tumor. FAP and BWS are associated with an increased risk of HB. Trisomy 13 and 18, Goldenhar syndrome, Noonan syndrome, Fragile X syndrome, Sotos syndrome, Prader-Willi syndrome, Prune belly syndrome, Aicardi syndrome and neurofibromatosis type 1 may also predispose to HB. Genetic syndromes are associated with 20% of HB cases. High-risk patients are those with distant metastases, very low initial alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level (under 100 ng/ml), older age (over 8 years), tumor rupture at diagnosis and/or tumor involvement of all 4 hepatic sections.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of HB is still unknown. However, it is hypothesized to derive from primary hepatoblasts, and likely from less differentiated hepatic stem cells or human fetal liver multi-potent progenitor cells (hFLMPCs). Mutations of the genes APC (5q21-q22), AXIN1 (16p13.3) and AXIN2 (17q24.1), that prevent degradation of beta-catenin, have been found in syndromic forms of HB but have rarely been described in sporadic HB. However, a high rate of oncogenic mutations of the beta-catenin gene (CTNNB1; 3p21) (60%-70%) has been reported in HB and it is thought to be associated with constitutive activation of the Wnt/beta-catenin signaling pathway. Overall, Wnt pathway abnormalities account for up to 90% of genetic defects in hepatoblastoma tumor.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes: (1) hemangioma and infantile hemangioendothelioma (IHE), (2) hepatic mesenchymal hamartoma, (3) focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH), (4) pediatric hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), (5) undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma of the liver (UESL), (6) embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (eRMS), (7) rhabdoid tumor of the liver, (8) hepatic adenoma.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: A diagnostic tumor biopsy should be mandatory for all patients with primary liver tumor. HB is definitely a surgical tumor. Surgery remains the cornerstone of management and complete resection is crucial for cure. In most cases complete resection of the tumor can be achieved with a partial hepatectomy (hemihepatectomy). The PRETEXT (PRETreatment EXtent of Disease) system (based on liver anatomy and imaging) is used for assessment of chemotherapy response and planning the extent of liver resection. Resection at diagnosis is currently recommended for very low risk tumors (PRETEXT I/II, M-, surgically resectable at diagnosis (VPEFR-), and additionally in PRETEXT II: age under 8 years, AFP over100 ng/ml) and only when a segmentectomy or hemihepatectomy with at least 1 cm margin on middle hepatic vein and/or bifurcation of portal vein is possible. For unresectable tumors, preoperative chemotherapy (mostly systemic or, in highly selected cases, transcatheter arterial chemoembolization [TACE], sometimes combined with systemic chemotherapy) is used. Total hepatectomy with liver transplantation is a treatment option for HB in conditions where the tumors remain unresectable after chemotherapy or for multifocal HB invading all 4 sections of the liver. 10-20% of all HB cases require liver transplantation. In most cases postoperative chemotherapy is used routinely.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Current prognosis for patients with resectable tumors and no high risk features is fairly favorable (90%), whereas the outcome for those with metastases is around 50-70%, while the prognosis of patients with non-resectable or recurrent disease is relatively poor (around 20-30%). Relapse in HB occurs in less than 12% of the children who have achieved complete remission.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: reports a case of hepatoblastoma with onset at 30-weeks' gestation and rapid growth rate. DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA) is a retinal dystrophy defined by blindness and responses to electrophysiological stimulation (Ganzfeld electroretinogram (ERG)) below threshold, associated with severe visual impairment within the first year of life.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of LCA is 1/50,000 - 1/33,000 live births and accounts for 5% of all retinal dystrophies and 20% of blindness in school age children.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: LCA is characterized by severely reduced visual acuity (less or equal 20/400) or blindness within in the first year of life. Sluggish pupillary responses, roving eye movement, photophobia, high hyperopia, nystagmus, convergent strabismus, or keratoconus may occur depending on the genetic cause. The Franceschetti's oculo-digital sign, comprising eye poking, pressing, and rubbing is pathognomonic. LCA may be associated with mutations in genes linked to syndromes presenting with neurodevelopmental delay, intellectual disability, oculomotor apraxia-type behavior (difficulty moving the eye) and renal dysfunction.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: To date, mutations in genes encoding retina specific proteins have been reported to cause LCA. This includes GUCY2D (17p13.1), CEP290 (12q21.33), RPGRIP1 (14q11.2), RDH12 (14q24.1), SPATA7 (14q31.3), AIPL1 (17p13.1), RD3 (1q32.3), CRB1 (1q31-q32.1), CRX (19q13.3), IMPDH1 (7q31.3-q32), IQCB1 (3q21.1), KCNJ13 (2q37), LCA5 (6q14), NMNAT1 (1p36.22), and TULP1 (6p21.3). These mutations cause severe functional impairment or are mostly related to retinal dystrophies. Mutations in CRX or IMPDH1 genes may cause an early and severe onset disease. Patients with GUCY2D mutations present with very slow progressive morphological degeneration and a mostly functional defect.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on clinical observation which shows a pupillary response that may be sluggish or near-absent in early life; on funduscopy findings revealing attenuation of retinal vessels along with variable signs of retinal degeneration (from almost unremarkable to an overall granulated appearance). Diagnosis is confirmed by sedated ERG close to or below threshold. Molecular diagnosis is indispensable and may be performed using an arrayed primer extension (APEX) chip (tests a subset of known mutations in known LCA genes; diagnosis achieved in 50-70% of cases) and next generation sequencing (NGS) (covering the whole sequence of the known reported genes; this is the preferable method covering up to 90% of patients). Confirmation of identified mutations and segregation analysis in the parents by Sanger sequencing is the final step.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes retinitis pigmentosa, Alström syndrome, Joubert syndrome, Stargardt disease, Senior-Loken syndrome, Conorenal syndrome and infantile neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis. Cortical blindness is a frequent misdiagnosis when there is limited access to functional testing or high resolution morphological examination.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis may be offered by specialized laboratories for at-risk couples with identified disease-causing mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: LCA is typically an autosomal recessive inherited disease. Rarely, mutations within CRX or IMPDH1 genes are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner that may overlap with the diagnosis of LCA.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Currently LCA is an incurable disease. Treatment is mainly supportive and includes correction of refractive error and use of low-vision aids. Repeated poking and pressing on the eyes should be discouraged. Periodic ophthalmic evaluation and assessment of the presence of amblyopia, glaucoma, or cataract should be achieved. Therapies are presently being investigated, including gene therapy (particularly for RPGRIP and CEP290) and optogenetics (genetic targeting of light-sensing molecules to residual cells in a degenerate retina).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Vision commonly declines with age until complete blindness is observed most often latest by the third or fourth decade of life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare immune disease characterized by progressive immunodeficiency leading to recurrent and opportunistic infections, autoimmunity and malignancy as well as neurologic manifestations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, more than 70 patients have been reported with Purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) deficiency in the world literature. PNP deficiency accounts for less than 4% of patients with severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: PNP deficiency typically manifests in the 1st years of life, with recurrent, opportunistic infections caused by bacterial, viral (such as varicella zoster virus), and fungal (such as Pneumocystis carinii) pathogens. The susceptibility to infections is variable ranging from classical SCID in infancy to infrequent infections during childhood and even the 2nd decade of life. Failure to thrive has also been reported. Up to 2/3 of patients have neurologic involvement including motor system dysfunction, hyper/hypotonia, spastic paresis, ataxia, hyperactivity, and behavioral problems. Cerebrovascular accidents and sensorineural deafness are less commonly observed. The neurologic involvement often precedes immune abnormalities. Autoimmune manifestations are reported in 1/3 of cases and include autoimmune hemolytic anemia, immune thrombocytopenic purpura and systemic lupus erythematosus.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: PNP deficiency is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the PNP gene (14q11.2) which encodes a key enzyme (PNP) in the purine salvage pathway. PNP is vital for removal of metabolites of DNA breakdown and promotes recycling of purine bases. Lack of PNP allows intracellular accumulation of such metabolites which are particularly toxic to immature lymphoid cells, leading to lymphopenia and impaired cell-mediated immunity. Intracellular accumulation of purine bases has also been suggested to cause neuronal cell apoptosis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the clinical examination and on laboratory findings showing leukopenia, severe lymphopenia with low CD3, CD4, and CD8 counts and variable B cell function and immunoglobulin levels. Neutropenia has also been reported. Hallmark diagnostic markers of PNP deficiency include hypouricemia, complete or near complete absence of PNP activity in red blood cell lysate and increased urine or blood levels of inosine, guanosine and their deoxy forms. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic screening of PNP.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes aplastic anemias, SCID, severe combined immunodeficiency due to adenosine deaminase deficiency, ataxia-telangiectasia, and viral meningoencephalitis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Measurement of T cell receptor excision circles during newborn screening for SCID can detect some patients suffering from PNP deficiency, although removal of metabolites by maternal PNP may delay the deleterious effects on PNP-deficient lymphocytes. Few newborn screening programs also measure purine metabolites in dried blood spots.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be proposed to affected families informing them of a 25% risk of transmitting the disease where both parents are unaffected carriers.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Specific enzyme replacement is not available for PNP deficiency, although frequent red blood cells transfusions rich in PNP have been shown to provide temporary benefit. Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is the only treatment option for the severe immune deficiency. Transplanted cells deliver the missing enzyme, thereby improving purine homeostasis. Supportive treatment, including intravenous immunoglobulin therapy, prophylaxis for Pneumocystis carinii, and physical, occupational, and speech therapy, reduces the risk of infection and may encourage optimal neurologic development for patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: If left untreated, prognosis is poor and patients usually die in the first decade of life, often succumbing to infections. Few patients have reached the 2nd and even 3rd decade of life. After HSCT from family or unrelated donors, patients may achieve successful immune reconstitution and are free from infections. Nevertheless, even with HSCT, improvement of neurological deficits is not definite.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A genetically and clinically heterogeneous group of slowly progressive neurological disorders which in the pure form is characterized by pyramidal signs (weakness, spasticity, brisk tendon reflexes, and extensor plantar responses) predominantly affecting the lower limbs and with possible association of sphincter disturbances and deep sensory loss; and in the complex form by the addition of variable neurological or non-neurological features.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Familial spastic paraplegia; HSP; Hereditary spastic paraparesis; SPG; Strümpell-Lorrain disease
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of hereditary spastic paraplegia (HSP) is highly variable, ranging from 1/11,000-77,000 in Europe.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinically, HSPs can be divided into the pure and complex form. Pure HSPs are characterized by slowly progressive lower extremity spasticity and weakness, often associated with urinary disturbances, and deep sensory abnormalities (reduction of lower extremity vibration sense). Complex forms of HSP forms are characterized by the presence of additional neurological or non-neurological features. Neurological features may include cerebellar dysfunction (ataxia, nystagmus, tremor), axonal or demyelinating peripheral neuropathy (sensory and/or motor disturbances), cognitive impairment (dysexecutive syndrome, dementia), sensory impairment (optic, auditive neuropathy), epilepsy, myopathic features (ptosis, opthalmoparesis), extrapyramidal features (Parkinsonism, chorea, dystonia), psychiatric disturbances, and brain and spine imaging abnormalities (brain white matter alterations, thin corpus callosum, brain iron accumulation, cerebellar atrophy) which may be suggestive of a genetic subtype. Non-neurological manifestations may include ophthalmological abnormalities (cataracts, retinitis pigmentosa, macular degeneration), and orthopedic abnormalities (scoliosis, joint dislocation, and different foot deformities).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is due to the dysfunction of the upper motor neurons of the corticospinal tract. To date, more than 80 genes have been linked. The encoded proteins are involved in many processes, including axonal transport, myelination, endo-membrane trafficking, mitochondria functions, complex lipid and nucleotide metabolism. The most common causative genes include SPAST (2p22.3), ATL1 (14q22.1), REEP1 (2p11.2) and KIF5A (12q.13.3) for autosomal dominant HSPs, and SPG7 (16q24.3), SPG11 (15q21.1), and CYP7B1 (8q12.3) for autosomal recessive HSP. However, a significant number of patients are without a genetic diagnosis after systematic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the clinical symptoms, neurological examination, progressive course of the disease, biomarker dosages, brain and spine MRI, family history, molecular genetic testing, and exclusion of the differential diagnoses.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes multiple sclerosis, spinal vascular abnormality, vitamin B12 deficiency, HTLVI infection, primary lateral sclerosis, diplegic cerebral palsy, metabolic genetic diseases (dopa-responsive dystonia, leukodystrophies, brain metal accumulation disorders).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Genetic testing is possible where a mutation has previously been identified in a family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Patterns of inheritance include mostly autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive, and rarely X-linked and mitochondrial. In addition, multiple recessive and dominant forms exist for the genes KIF1C (17p13.2), REEP2 (5q31.2), ALDH18A1 (10q24.1), ERLIN2 (8p11.23). SPAST (2p22.3), ATL1 (14q22.1), REEP1 (2p11.2) are usually associated with the pure form, autosomal recessive forms often lead to more complicated phenotypes, while some genes are associated with both phenotypes. High intrafamilial variability and incomplete penetrance are frequent.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is symptomatic with physiotherapy, anti-spasticity drugs (baclofen, tizanidine, diazepam, botulinum toxin), and orthoses.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the phenotype (pure/complex form), genotype, and is highly variable due to incomplete penetrance and variable gene expression.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hyaline fibromatosis syndrome characterized by papulo-nodular skin lesions (especially around the head and neck), soft tissue masses, gingival hypertrophy, joint contractures, and osteolytic bone lesions in variable degrees. Joint contractures may cripple patients and delay normal motor development if occuring in infancy. Severe gingival hyperplasia can interfere with eating and delay dentition. Histopathology analysis of involved tissues reveals cords of spindle-shaped cells embedded in an amorphous, hyaline material.

DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis (JHF) is primarily based on characteristic clinical manifestations, including skin lesions such as nodules, papules, plaques, and swellings, along with gingival hypertrophy, joint contractures, and bone anomalies. Histopathological examination of affected tissues, often from skin biopsies, reveals dermal and subcutaneous deposits of amorphous eosinophilic hyaline material, sometimes showing collagen VI accumulation. Definitive diagnosis is achieved through genetic analysis, typically involving whole-exome sequencing or Sanger sequencing, to identify pathogenic mutations in the ANTXR2 gene. Molecular diagnosis is essential for accurate confirmation, genetic counseling, and presymptomatic or prenatal diagnosis. [PMC9245060, PMC9356561, PMC8927703, PMC8501544, PMC10421683]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis is possible through molecular genetic testing, particularly after identifying pathogenic variants in the ANTXR2 (CMG2) gene in a proband. Genetic information from proband mutations has been utilized for prenatal diagnosis in affected families. This molecular diagnosis is important for genetic counseling and early recognition of the condition. [PMC10421683, PMC4158768]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Juvenile hyaline fibromatosis (JHF) is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the ANTXR2 (CMG2) gene, with over 40 mutations identified. The condition is often observed in individuals from consanguineous backgrounds, particularly in regions with higher rates of interfamilial marriages. Genetic molecular testing is essential for accurate diagnosis and to identify specific pathogenic variants, which can inform genotype-phenotype correlations. Genetic counseling is a critical component of holistic management for affected families, enabling presymptomatic diagnosis in at-risk relatives and facilitating prenatal diagnosis based on proband mutation information. Early recognition and molecular diagnosis are important for effective genetic counseling and early treatment planning. [PMC9245060, PMC8927703, PMC10421683, PMC7645300, PMC5970508]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for Juvenile Hyaline Fibromatosis is primarily symptomatic, as no standard treatment exists. Surgical excision is a common approach for cutaneous lesions, tumor masses, gingival hypertrophy, and joint contractures, with early surgical treatment providing instantaneous and more sustainable relief, though recurrences are noted. Intraregional steroid injections may prevent relapse after surgery, and corticosteroid therapy can offer temporary outcomes. Anesthetic management may present difficulties with patient positioning and airway. Non-operative , such as early hip spica for fractures, are also employed, alongside preventative measures for bone health. In severe cases, intravenous gamma globulin has improved recurrent infections and diarrhea. Physical education interventions have shown gains in mobility, range of motion, and quality of life. A multidisciplinary team approach, including genetic counseling and molecular diagnosis, is crucial for comprehensive management. [PMC10082625, PMC9245060, PMC9356561, PMC8984057, PMC8927703]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Facial onset sensory and motor neuronopathy
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Facial onset sensory and motor neuronopathy is characterised initially by paraesthesia and numbness in the region of the trigeminal nerve distribution, which later progresses to involve the scalp, neck, upper trunk and upper limbs. Onset of motor manifestations occurs later with cramps, fasciculations, dysphagia, dysarthria, muscle weakness and atrophy. This syndrome has been described in four males and appears to be a slowly progressive neurodegenerative disease.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Facial-onset sensory and motor neuronopathy (FOSMN) is described as a greatly rare disease. There have been few reports regarding its occurrence, particularly in association with other conditions like myasthenia gravis, further emphasizing its infrequent presentation. [PMC10659734]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Facial onset sensory and motor neuronopathy (FOSMN) is a rare neurodegenerative disease. Clinical presentation can include right-side facial numbness and right-eyelid incomplete closure, followed by slurred speech and dysphagia, with symptoms gradually progressing. In some cases, taste loss may be the sole presenting symptom. One reported case also showed co-occurrence with myasthenia gravis, characterized by positive anti-AchR and anti-Titin antibodies. [PMC10659734, PMC8611768]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Autopsy evidence suggests that Facial-onset sensory and motor neuronopathy (FOSMN) is associated with neurodegeneration. While the etiology is not fully elucidated, immune dysfunction has been hypothesized as a potential pathogenesis, particularly in cases where FOSMN co-occurs with other autoimmune disorders like myasthenia gravis. However, definite evidence to support this hypothesis is lacking, and further studies are needed. [PMC10659734]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital malformation characterized by absent or severely underdeveloped eyelids (ablepharon), a lateral enlargement of the mouth (macrostomia), malformed external ears, and redundant skin folds.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Less than 30 cases have been reported in the literature worldwide to date, with no evident ethnic or sex-related predominance. The true prevalence is unknown, but it is likely to be far below 1 in 1,000,000. Current definitions qualify it as an ultra-rare disease.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: All reported patients exhibited ablepharon and macrostomia. Other frequently observed features (>70%) include malformed, low-set ears, absent or sparse eyebrows, redundant skin folds, sparse scalp hair, hypoplastic or absent nipples, and genital anomalies affecting both sexes (e.g., micropenis or hypoplastic labia majora). Less frequently reported anomalies (20-50%) include abdominal wall defects (e.g., omphalocele), anteriorly placed anus, syndactyly, camptodactyly, ichthyotic skin, and dental anomalies. Symptoms are typically apparent at birth. Visual impairment can result from inadequate eyelid coverage. Mild developmental delay has been described in a subset of patients; however, in genetically confirmed cases with a TWIST2 variant, cognitive development is often normal. Significant intellectual disability is not a common feature.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: AMS is caused by a specific heterozygous pathogenic variant in the TWIST2 gene (chr2q37.3), which encodes a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that regulates mesenchymal differentiation and is involved in craniofacial and ectodermal development. To date, all genetically confirmed cases carry the same pathogenic missense variant: c.223G>A (p.Glu75Lys).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on recognition of the characteristic craniofacial phenotype, particularly the combination of ablepharon and macrostomia. In case of clinical suspicion, targeted sequencing of TWIST2 can confirm the diagnosis. The absence of a pathogenic variant makes the diagnosis improbable, since genetic heterogeneity has not been observed to date. With the increasing use of whole exome or genome sequencing as first-tier diagnostics in patients with congenital anomalies, AMS may also be diagnosed genetically even without initial clinical suspicion.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses include Barber-Say syndrome, Sweeney-Cox syndrome, FRAS1-FREM1-complex-related conditions (Fraser syndrome, MOTA syndrome), BILU syndrome, and Neu-Laxova syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Absent eyelid structures or a characteristically wide oral opening may be detected prenatally by ultrasound. Given the syndrome's rarity and its lack of striking prenatal morphologic characteristics, a specific prenatal suspicion is unlikely in the absence of family history. However, broad genomic approaches such as exome or genome sequencing in the context of fetal anomalies may reveal a causative TWIST2 variant. If a familial variant is known, targeted prenatal testing via chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis is feasible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance is autosomal dominant. Most affected individuals have a de novo TWIST2 variant, but transmission from an affected parent has been observed. Cases of parental mosaicism with only mild features (e.g., subtle eyelid anomalies) have been reported. A careful clinical evaluation of both parents for subtle signs suggestive of mosaicism is recommended in all apparently sporadic cases to inform recurrence risk.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is symptomatic and multidisciplinary. Immediate ocular lubrication and corneal protection are essential to prevent damage due to absent eyelids. Surgical interventions address eyelid, lip, ear, and genital anomalies, often in staged procedures. Developmental and supportive therapies are tailored to individual needs.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With appropriate medical and surgical care, individuals may achieve good functional and cognitive outcomes. Visual impairment and facial appearance may impact quality of life. Life expectancy is not typically reduced, but long-term data remain limited due to the rarity of the condition.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Mitochondrial myopathy and sideroblastic anemia belongs to the heterogeneous family of metabolic myopathies. It is characterised by progressive exercise intolerance manifesting in childhood, onset of sideroblastic anaemia around adolescence, lactic acidaemia, and mitochondrial myopathy.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): MLASA; Myopathy, lactic acidosis and sideroblastic anemia

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Less than 10 cases have been described so far.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: A 656C-->T mutation in the nuclear pseudouridine synthase 1 gene (PUS1), localised to 12q24.33, has recently been identified in some patients. Deficient pseudouridylation of mitochondrial tRNAs may be responsible for the oxidative phosphorylation disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Muscle biopsy demonstrates low activity of complexes 1 and 4 of the respiratory chain and paracrystalline inclusions can be revealed in most mitochondria by electron microscopy.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Mitochondrial myopathy, lactic acidosis, and sideroblastic anemia (MLASA) is a rare condition characterized by early-onset myopathy, lactic acidosis, and sideroblastic anemia, though onset can also occur in adulthood or following intercurrent illness. Patients may initially present with anemia, with ringed sideroblasts and transfusion dependency developing later. Other common features include poor weight gain, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and severe myopathy leading to respiratory failure. Specific genetic mutations can lead to additional symptoms, such as developmental delay, sensorineural hearing loss, epilepsy, agenesis of the corpus callosum, failure to thrive, and stroke-like episodes. The disease can be exacerbated by events like pregnancy, leading to severe cardiorespiratory decompensation, and early death can result from respiratory muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy. [PMC9541592, PMC4253070, PMC3884767, PMC2598032]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for mitochondrial myopathy, lactic acidosis, and sideroblastic anemia (MLASA) includes other nuclear-encoded disorders of mitochondrial translation, which are clinically and genetically heterogeneous. These broader disorders can involve defects in mitochondrial aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases or other factors for protein synthesis. Initially, anemia in MLASA patients may be misattributed to iron deficiency. For a definitive diagnosis of MLASA, direct sequence analysis of YARS2 and PUS1 genes is recommended, distinguishing it from other potential causes of similar symptoms. [PMC3884767]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Myopathy, lactic acidosis, and sideroblastic anemia 2 (MLASA2) is an autosomal recessive mitochondrial disorder caused by pathogenic variants in YARS2. YARS2 variants confer heterogeneous phenotypes ranging from the full MLASA syndrome to a clinically unaffected state. Symptom onset is most common in the first decade of life but can occur in adulthood and has been reported following intercurrent illness. Early death can result from respiratory muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy. a case of MLASA2 with compound heterozygous YARS2 pathogenic variants; a known pathogenic nonsense variant [NM_001040436.3:c.98C>A (p.Ser33Ter)] and a likely pathogenic missense variant not previously associated with disease [NM_001040436.3:c.948G>T (p.Arg316Ser)]. The proband initially presented with a relatively mild phenotype of myopathy and lactic acidosis. During pregnancy, anemia emerged as an additional... [PMC9541592, PMC3884767]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management primarily involves appropriate supportive therapy. This may include ventilatory support for severe myopathy leading to respiratory failure, and transfusions for anemia. Early genetic diagnosis is essential for counseling. Furthermore, careful counseling and caution are advised for patients considering pregnancy due to the risk of disease exacerbation and complications. [PMC9541592, PMC3884767]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for mitochondrial myopathy and sideroblastic anemia (MLASA) is heterogeneous, with phenotypes ranging from mild to severe. Symptom onset can occur in the first decade of life, adulthood, or following intercurrent illness. Early death can result from respiratory muscle weakness and cardiomyopathy. The disease may involve progressive features such as anemia, lactic acidosis, poor weight gain, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and severe myopathy leading to respiratory failure requiring ventilatory support. Pregnancy can exacerbate the condition, leading to severe cardiorespiratory decompensation. Early genetic diagnosis is essential for counseling and to facilitate appropriate supportive therapy. [PMC9541592, PMC3884767]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare retinal dystrophy characterized by photophobia, progressive loss of visual acuity, nystagmus, visual field abnormalities, abnormal color vision, and psychophysical and electrophysiological evidence of abnormal cone function. Progressive cone dystrophy usually presents in childhood or early adult life, and patients tend to develop rod photoreceptor dysfunction in later life.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Progressive cone dystrophy is an inherited retinal disorder characterized by significant genetic and phenotypic heterogeneity. It can be inherited in an autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive manner. Numerous familial cases have been reported across diverse populations, including Chinese, Indian, and Japanese families. While specific syndromic forms, such as TUBB4B-associated sensorineural disease, are noted as very rare with a limited number of reported families, a general prevalence for progressive cone dystrophy is not provided in the available literature. [PMC11775458, PMC8116265, PMC6133598, PMC5627817, PMC5158031]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Progressive cone dystrophy is a genetically heterogeneous disorder. Autosomal dominant forms have been linked to mutations in genes such as GUCA1A, where a novel Asn104His variant alters cGMP signaling by hyperactivating retinal guanylate cyclase. Other identified causes include a novel frameshift mutation (c.538dupG:p.Val180fs) in CRX, and mutations in GUCY2D, such as a novel p.T849A missense mutation and the R787C mutation associated with CORD6. Mutations in TUBB4B, including a novel Lys350Thr variant, are also associated with progressive cone-rod dystrophy, often presenting with early onset sensorineural hearing loss. Additionally, trinucleotide repeat expansions in ATXN7 cause cone-rod dystrophy in patients with spinocerebellar ataxia type 7. Autosomal recessive forms include those caused by frameshift mutations in CNGB3 and homozygous nonsense mutations in GNAT1, which can lead to rod-cone dystrophy. [PMC11775458, PMC8509414, PMC8116265, PMC6133598, PMC6687076]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) is a frequent manifestation of syndromic inherited retinal diseases (IRDs), exemplified by the very rare form of autosomal-dominant Leber congenital amaurosis with early onset deafness (LCAEOD; OMIM #617879). LCAEOD was first described in 2017 in four families segregating heterozygous missense mutations in TUBB4B, a gene encoding a β-tubulin isotype. To date, only eight more families with similar TUBB4B-associated sensorineural disease (SND) have been reported. Most cases harbored missense variants affecting the same amino acid (Arg391) and only three families segregated variants involving different residues (Tyr310, Arg390). We performed whole-exome sequencing and a full ophthalmological and audiological examination of the affected members in an Italian family segregating syndromic IRD with early onset deafness. We identified a novel, ultra-rare,... [PMC11775458, PMC8116265, PMC6133598, PMC5627817, PMC5158031]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Progressive cone dystrophy, while primarily affecting cone function, can involve mild rod system impairment, distinguishing it from a full cone-rod dystrophy. However, conditions presenting with a cone-rod dystrophy phenotype, such as Spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 (SCA7), should be considered in the differential diagnosis. SCA7 is characterized by progressive bilateral visual loss and specific retinal imaging findings. Additionally, rod-cone dystrophy, which can be caused by mutations in genes like GNAT1, represents another related progressive inherited retinal disorder to differentiate. [PMC8116265, PMC5158031, PMC1298768]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Progressive cone dystrophy and cone-rod dystrophy demonstrate significant genetic heterogeneity, with both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance patterns identified. Autosomal dominant forms are associated with mutations in genes such as TUBB4B, GUCA1A, ATXN7 (in SCA7), CRX, and GUCY2D (also known as retGC-1 or ROS-GC1), where specific variants like missense or frameshift mutations segregate with the disease in affected families. For ATXN7, trinucleotide repeat expansions show a positive correlation between repeat length and disease severity. Autosomal recessive forms have been linked to mutations in genes like CNGB3 and GNAT1, with GNAT1 mutations exhibiting variable phenotypes and modes of inheritance. Molecular genetic analysis, including whole-exome sequencing, is crucial for identifying pathogenic variants and confirming inheritance patterns within families. [PMC11775458, PMC8509414, PMC8116265, PMC6133598, PMC6687076]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: with recombinant reconstituted system mimicking the cellular conditions of the native cones documents that photoreceptor ROS-GC1 is modulated by gaseous CO 2 . Mechanistically, CO 2 is sensed by carbonic anhydrase (CAII), generates bicarbonate that, in turn, directly targets the core catalytic domain of ROS-GC1, and activates it to increased synthesis of cyclic GMP. This, then, functions as a second messenger for the cone phototransduction. The study demonstrates that, in contrast to the Ca 2+ -modulated phototransduction, the CO 2 pathway is Ca 2+ -independent, yet is linked with it and synergizes it. It, through R 787 C mutation in the third heptad of the signal helix domain of ROS-GC1, affects cone-rod dystrophy, CORD6. CORD6 is caused firstly by lowered basal and GCAP1-dependent ROS-GC1 activity and secondly, by a shift in Ca 2+ sensitivity of the ROS-GC1/GCAP1 complex that remains... [PMC6687076]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Progressive cone dystrophy is characterized by progressive bilateral visual loss, with the disease's nature evident from changes in visual performance over several years. Onset of visual deterioration typically occurs in the third or fourth decade. In early stages, a severe defect in blue sensitivity may be present even when visual acuity is near normal. The degree of cone-rod dystrophy and progression can be positively related to age and genetic factors, such as the number of CAG repeats in SCA7. Peripheral cones may be affected earlier and more severely than central ones, leading to widespread loss of cone function and, in advanced stages, potential mild impairment of the rod system. [PMC8116265, PMC1042376, PMC1298768]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic disorder characterized by craniosynostosis, craniofacial and skeletal abnormalities, marfanoid habitus, cardiac anomalies, neurological abnormalities, and intellectual disability.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (SGS) is an extremely rare collagenopathy and a rare congenital disorder. Since its discovery in 1982, approximately 50-60 cases of SGS have been recorded in the literature worldwide. [PMC7816931, PMC6770791, PMC6698069]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (SGS) is an extremely rare collagenopathy, often caused by autosomal-dominant mutations in the SKI proto-oncogene. This disorder affects bone and vascular development, resulting in craniosynostosis, scoliosis, chest deformities, and aortic root dilation. Patients may also experience central nervous system problems, including Chiari 1 malformation, hydrocephalus, and dilation of the lateral ventricles, alongside intellectual disability and affected mentation. Ocular manifestations such as oculo-motility disorder, hypoplastic bilateral medial recti, and large A-pattern exotropia have been observed. Connective tissue symptoms can involve dural and vascular problems, with cervical spinal instability and Scheuermann's disease also reported. The symptoms of SGS closely parallel those of related collagenopathies involving the TGF-ß signaling pathway. [PMC8206384, PMC7816931, PMC6770791, PMC6698069, PMC5371443]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (SGS) is most often caused by autosomal-dominant mutations in the SKI proto-oncogene, which is a component of the transforming growth factor beta (TGF-ß) signaling pathway. This condition is considered an extremely rare collagenopathy. Additionally, mutations in B3GAT3, encoding a glucuronyltransferase, have been described in patients with variable phenotypes resembling SGS, placing it within a group of linkeropathies. Symptoms of SGS can parallel those of related collagenopathies involving mutations in the TGF-ß signaling pathway, making accurate diagnosis challenging without genetic testing. [PMC6770791, PMC6698069]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Accurate diagnosis of Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (SGS) is often difficult due to its significant phenotypic overlap with other collagenopathies and connective tissue disorders, such as Marfan, Larsen, Antley-Bixler, and Ehlers-Danlos syndromes. Genetic testing is essential for confirmation, primarily targeting mutations in the SKI proto-oncogene, which is the most common cause, or B3GAT3 variants, which can present with SGS-like features. Early clinical recognition is crucial, involving awareness of syndromic associations like craniosynostosis, skeletal abnormalities, intellectual disability, and specific ocular findings such as hypoplastic medial recti, which may be identified on imaging. [PMC7816931, PMC6770791, PMC6698069, PMC5371443]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (SGS) shares phenotypic features with several other conditions, making differential diagnosis challenging. There is considerable clinical overlap with Marfan syndrome and Loeys-Dietz syndrome, particularly in features like thoracic aortic aneurysm, connective tissue findings, and craniofacial dysmorphism. A human importin-β-related disorder caused by IPO8 variants also presents with similar features including early-onset TAA, motor developmental delay, and craniofacial dysmorphism. Linkeropathies, such as those with B3GAT3 mutations, can resemble SGS, as well as Larsen, Antley-Bixler, and Geroderma osteodysplastica syndromes, forming a continuum with Ehlers-Danlos and skeletal disorders. Additionally, syndromic craniosynostosis, sometimes with oculo-motility disorders, can resemble SGS. The symptoms of SGS, a collagenopathy involving the TGF-ß signaling pathway, closely parallel those of related collagenopathies, often necessitating genetic testing for accurate diagnosis. [PMC8206384, PMC7816931, PMC6770791, PMC6698069, PMC5371443]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome (SGS) is most often caused by autosomal-dominant mutations in the SKI proto-oncogene, which is part of the TGF-ß signaling pathway. Accurate diagnosis is challenging without genetic testing, as SGS symptoms closely resemble those of other collagenopathies involving the TGF-ß pathway. Conditions with clinical overlap or phenotypes resembling SGS can also be caused by other genetic mutations, such as bi-allelic loss-of-function variants in IPO8 or mutations in B3GAT3. Early diagnosis is crucial for better outcomes and to reduce the psychological and financial burden on the patient and family, with counseling helping to address concerns. [PMC8206384, PMC6770791, PMC6698069, PMC5371443]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management primarily involves surgical interventions for various manifestations. Craniofacial surgery, including midface distraction, is used to address craniosynostosis and related facial deformities, with early diagnosis and intervention correlating with better outcomes and potentially averting intellectual disability and neurological deficits. Surgical occipital-C4 fusion can resolve severe cervical spinal instability. Ophthalmologists should be aware of the challenges in managing oculo-motility disorders and large squints. A critical consideration for midface distraction surgery is the anticipated risk of extreme blood loss due to insufficient dura and prominent vasculature. Family counseling is also noted to help lessen concerns. [PMC7816931, PMC6698069, PMC5371443]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Shprintzen-Goldberg syndrome has an enormous negative impact, particularly when diagnosis is late, limiting effective interventions. However, early diagnosis is crucial, as timely craniofacial surgery can lead to significantly better outcomes. Such early interventions are essential to avoid intellectual disability and other neurological deficits. While surgery can be remarkably helpful, procedures like midface distraction carry risks, including extreme blood loss due to associated dural and vascular problems. The disorder affects bone, vascular, and central nervous system development, necessitating careful management. [PMC6698069, PMC5371443]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Mosaic trisomy 22 is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, with a highly variable phenotype, principally characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth delay, mild to severe intellectual disability, hemiatrophy, webbed neck, ocular and cutaneous pigmentary anomalies, craniofacial dysmorphic features (e.g. microcephaly, upslanted palpebral fissures, ptosis, ear malformations, flat nasal bridge, micrognathia) and cardiac abnormalities (including ventricular and atrial septal defect, pulmonary or aortic stenosis). Hearing loss and limb malformations (e.g. cubitus valgus, syn/brachydactyly), as well as renal and genital anomalies, have also been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Mosaic trisomy 22 syndrome is an extremely rare autosomal anomaly compatible with life, with only about 25 postnatal and 18 prenatal cases described in the literature so far. Diagnosis is frequently delayed due to the negative selection of trisomic cells in blood, and the percentage of mosaicism can vary among different tissues. While mosaicism, including trisomy 22, is observed in IVF embryos, the syndrome itself remains exceptionally uncommon. [PMC12155553, PMC10970670, PMC7938395]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Mosaic trisomy 22 syndrome is a rare autosomal anomaly with a variable phenotype, where severity depends on the count of trisomic cells. Key features include facial and body asymmetry, often presenting as hemiatrophy or unilateral radial aplasia, and facial dysmorphisms such as abnormal ears, cleft palate, or a flattened nasal bridge. Patients frequently exhibit congenital heart defects, growth failure or general hypotrophy, and variable degrees of neurodevelopmental delay or mental retardation. Other reported manifestations include webbed neck, microcephaly, genital anomalies, dysplastic toenails, hypotonic muscle, hearing loss, and skin pigmentary anomalies. Diagnosis can be challenging due to the varying mosaicism percentage across tissues. [PMC10970670, PMC7938395, PMC10228565, PMC1050079, PMC1048799]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of mosaic trisomy 22 syndrome can be challenging due to variable mosaicism percentages across tissues and negative selection of trisomic cells in blood, often necessitating further testing. Prenatally, NIPT plus combined with ultrasound is an optimal screening strategy for rare autosomal trisomies, significantly improving detection rates compared to standard NIPT, despite NIPT plus alone having a higher false positive rate. Echocardiography is also suggested for early detection of congenital heart defects. Postnatally, cytogenetic analyses, such as G-banding, are crucial. Repeated cytogenetic investigations on large numbers of cells from various tissues, including blood, bone marrow, and skin biopsies, are often required, especially when clinical features like asymmetry are present or initial blood tests show low-level mosaicism. [PMC11997100, PMC10970670, PMC7938395, PMC1734329, PMC1050079]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis for mosaic trisomy 22 syndrome includes other chromosomal anomalies, particularly those involving chromosome 22. Phelan-McDermid syndrome, caused by 22q13.3 deletions or SHANK3 variants, presents with hypotonia, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and dysmorphic features. Ring chromosome 22, especially when mosaic or associated with duplications leading to features consistent with cat eye syndrome, can also manifest with overlapping phenotypes. More broadly, other forms of chromosome mosaicism may cause subtle and asymmetrical clinical features, mental retardation, dysmorphism, and skin pigmentary anomalies, necessitating active cytogenetic investigation. [PMC9470928, PMC1734329, PMC1050079]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Mosaic trisomy 22 mosaicism is an extremely rare condition, with only about 18 prenatal cases described, which restricts genetic counseling due to scattered information and a dearth of data.
