We evaluated silent SNHL in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) receiving tacrolimus and the different factors affecting it compared to healthy controls. In this case control study, hearing functions were studied in 42 KTRs receiving tacrolimus as maintenance immunosuppressive therapy for more than 3 months in comparison to 27 age- and gender-matched healthy subjects using tympanometry, pure-tone audiometry (PTA), extended high frequency audiometry (EHFA), and transient evoked oto-acoustic emissions (TEOAEs). Also, different factors were studied in relation to SNHL. PTA showed that 23.8%, 21.4%, and 4.8% had mild, moderate, and severe SNHL, respectively. One-fifth of KTRs had severe SNHL, according to EHFA. According to... [PMC11762832, PMC12015281, PMC5843986, PMC4918683]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: It has been claimed that tacrolimus may have harmful effects on the auditory system, where it has been linked to ototoxicity and sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). We evaluated silent SNHL in kidney transplant recipients (KTRs) receiving tacrolimus and the different factors affecting it compared to healthy controls. In this case control study, hearing functions were studied in 42 KTRs receiving tacrolimus as maintenance immunosuppressive therapy for more than 3 months in comparison to 27 age- and gender-matched healthy subjects using tympanometry, pure-tone audiometry (PTA), extended high frequency audiometry (EHFA), and transient evoked oto-acoustic emissions (TEOAEs). Also, different factors were studied in relation to SNHL. PTA showed that 23.8%, 21.4%, and 4.8% had mild, moderate, and severe SNHL, respectively. One-fifth of KTRs had severe SNHL, according to EHFA. According to... [PMC11762832, PMC6354463, PMC4680576]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) can be associated with various factors. Immunosuppressive therapy with tacrolimus, particularly higher trough levels, has been linked to SNHL in kidney transplant recipients. Environmental exposures such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) are positively correlated with decreased hearing, and occupational noise exposure, including in call centers, is a known cause of hearing loss, with a synergistic effect observed with pesticides. Traumatic injury to the vestibulocochlear nerve, even without a temporal bone fracture, can result in sudden total hearing loss. Furthermore, specific microRNAs like miR-431, secreted by vestibular schwannomas, can increase the inner ear's vulnerability to noise trauma. In rare cases, sudden onset SNHL has been reported following rabies vaccination, with associated findings of Epstein-Barr virus and anticochlear antibodies. [PMC11762832, PMC12408137, PMC12015281, PMC10598552, PMC6354463]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) include pure-tone audiometry, extended high frequency audiometry, tympanometry, and otoacoustic emissions (e.g., transient evoked or distortion product). Auditory brainstem response testing can also be employed. For sudden onset SNHL, further investigations may involve MRI of the internal acoustic meatus, viral serology (e.g., for Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus), syphilis screening, and anticochlear antibody testing. Otoscopy is a standard examination, and computerized tomography scans can identify middle ear fluid or traumatic injuries. [PMC11762832, PMC10598552, PMC6354463, PMC5843986, PMC4680576]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL) can be associated with various factors. Tacrolimus, an immunosuppressive therapy, has been linked to ototoxicity and SNHL in kidney transplant recipients, with higher trough levels correlating with hearing loss. Exposure to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), including 1-Hydroxynaphthalene and 1-Hydroxypyrene, is positively correlated with decreased hearing. Vestibular schwannoma typically presents with SNHL, and its secreted miR-431 can increase inner ear vulnerability to noise trauma. Traumatic vestibulocochlear nerve injury in the internal acoustic canal can cause sudden-onset total hearing loss, even without a temporal bone fracture. Occupational hearing loss may result from noise exposure, such as in call centers, and a synergy between noise and pesticide exposure has been observed. Additionally, sudden onset SNHL has been reported following rabies vaccination. [PMC11762832, PMC12015281, PMC10598552, PMC6354463, PMC5843986]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Initial treatment for sudden sensorineural hearing loss may involve a course of high-dose oral prednisolone and acyclovir, which in one reported case led to a small improvement in hearing thresholds. Salvage intratympanic steroid injections were also attempted in this case, but they did not result in further hearing improvement. [PMC4680576]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Vestibular schwannoma (VS) is an intracranial tumor that arises on the vestibular branch of cranial nerve VIII and typically presents with sensorineural hearing loss (SNHL). The mechanisms of this SNHL are postulated to involve alterations in the inner ear's microenvironment mediated by the genetic cargo of VS-secreted extracellular vesicles (EVs). to identify the EV cargo associated with poor hearing and determine whether its delivery caused hearing loss and cochlear damage in a mouse model in vivo. VS tissue was collected from routinely resected tumors of patients with good (VS-GH) or poor (VS-PH) pre-surgical hearing measured via pure-tone average and word recognition scores. Next-generation sequencing was performed on RNA isolated from cultured primary human VS cells and EVs from VS-conditioned media, stratified by patients' hearing ability. microRNA expression levels were compared... DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare skin disease of unknown origin characterized by macrocheilia and secretions of thick saliva from swollen labial minor salivary glands.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Cheilitis glandularis (CG) prevalence is unknown. Less than a 100 cases have been reported to date, predominantly in adult males, and more rarely in adult females.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical picture of CG consists of variable degrees of macrocheilia accompanied by the presence of red, dilated ostia of minor salivary glands on the vermilion area. A thick, mucoid material can be obtained from these ostia by manual expression. This viscous saliva often sticks to the vermilion causing discomfort to the patient. Hardening of superficial and deep tissues, including minor salivary glands, may occur. Rarely they may suppurate and drain a purulent discharge (cheilitis apostematosa profunda). Changes occur more frequently on the lower lip, but the upper lip is occasionally affected. Because of the macrocheilia, the vermilion is more exposed to ultra-violet radiation, which may lead to chronic actinic cheilitis and squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip in rare cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Cheilitis glandularis occurs more frequently in fair skinned adults and albino patients seem particularly prone, suggesting an influence of sunlight exposure. Nonetheless, the actual cause of CG remains unknown. Some consider CG as an inflammatory glandular disease while others think it merely represents a clinical reaction pattern to external trauma (mechanic, actinic) with no relation to salivary involvement as salivary glands have been found to be normal in some patients. Recently, changes in the immunohistochemical expression of water flow channels have been demonstrated in cases of CG.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is mostly clinical. Histopathologic findings in the vermilion vary from spongiotic changes to chronic actinic epithelial damage, including superficial squamous cell carcinoma. Changes in minor salivary glands include chronic sialadenitis with dilated acinar lobules and ducts. Excretory ducts are ectatic and ductal metaplasia can be observed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis may include cheilitis granulomatosa, cutaneous lupus erythematosus, angioedema, atopic cheilitis, actinic cheilitis, cheilitis artefacta, exfoliative cheilitis, ointment pseudo-cheilitis and benign and malignant minor salivary gland tumours (e.g. cystadenoma, cystadenocarcinoma and mucoepidermoid carcinoma).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Mild cases do not require specific treatment. A lower lip vermilionectomy followed by careful dissection of the minor labial salivary glands is recommended for symptomatic and/or albino patients and is the only curative treatment for CG. Intralesional corticosteroids and oral antibiotics are ineffective. Long-term follow up is recommended, especially in very fair-skinned or albino patients, as the risk of labial squamous cell carcinoma is higher in these patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With proper treatment and surveillance, the prognosis is good.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD) is a heterogeneous group of muscular dystrophies characterized by proximal weakness affecting the pelvic and shoulder girdles. Cardiac and respiratory impairment may be observed in certain forms of LGMD.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated prevalence for all forms of LGMD ranges from 1/44,000 to 1/123,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: LGMD ranges from severe forms with onset in the first decade and rapid progression (resembling Duchenne muscular dystrophy) to milder forms with late onset and slower progression (similar to Becker muscular dystrophy). LGMD is characterized by weakness and wasting predominantly of the limb musculature (proximal greater than distal). The initial presentations are usually weakness of the hip and proximal leg muscles. Affected individuals usually have normal early motor and intellectual milestones and show a positive Gowers' sign. Cardiac involvement in the form of dilated or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and dysrhythmias are present in LGMD 2C-F, 2I, 2W, 2X, 1B, and 1E. At some stage, when upper arm muscles are involved, all subtypes may also have respiratory muscle weakness with nocturnal hypoventilation, in particular type 2I where it is noted from an earlier stage. Additional clinical features include a waddling gait, muscle pain during exercise, hypertrophy of the deltoids and quadriceps, and muscle wasting, affecting either the pelvis and/or shoulder girdle. The facial muscles are usually spared or involved only minimally.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: LGMD is caused by mutations in more than 25 genes which encode numerous components of the myofiber, contractile apparatus, nuclear lamina, sarcolemma or the cytoplasm.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of LGMD involves physical examination and muscle biopsy, which reveals fiber size variation including (non specific) fiber hypertrophy, scattered degenerating and regenerating muscle fibers, and a mild increase in perimysial tissue. Serum creatine-kinase can be normal or mildly to grossly elevated. Diagnosis of a specific LGMD subtype can be achieved by biochemical protein testing performed on muscle biopsies, followed by confirmation with genetic testing. Genetic testing, using panels, is becoming more readily available and can confirm diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis of LGMD includes facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy, Emery-Dreifuss muscular dystrophy, congenital muscular dystrophy, polymyositis, myotonic, myofibrillar, distal and metabolic myopathy, collagen 6-related disorders and dermatomyosistis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is available when a causative gene in a family is known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: There are at least 30 different genetic forms of LGMD, among which the type 1 LGMDs (LGMD1) are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and the type 2 LGMDs (LGMD2) are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Genetic counseling should be offered to families according to the mode of inheritance.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment of LGMD remains palliative and supportive and includes weight control to avoid obesity, physical therapy and stretching exercises to promote mobility and prevent contractures, use of mechanical aids to help ambulation and mobility, surgical intervention for orthopedic complications, use of respiratory aids when indicated, monitoring for cardiomyopathy in LGMD types with cardiac involvement, and social as well as emotional support and stimulation.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The clinical course of LGMD is typically progressive, although it is highly variable and is dependent on the severity of the individual genetic mutation. In most childhood onset forms of LGMD (in particular the rapidly progressive forms), ambulation is achieved but is invariably lost in later years. In other forms of LGMD, ambulation can be maintained and wheelchair assistance needed only later in life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by severe intellectual deficit, Dandy-Walker malformation, macrocephaly, severe myopia, brachytelephalangy with short and broad fingernails, and dysmorphic facial features (such as thick eyebrows, synophrys, epicanthal folds, low-set ears, short philtrum, and high-arched palate). Additional reported manifestations include seizures and skeletal and genital anomalies, among others. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1989.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The syndrome is associated with a de novo complex chromosome rearrangement and an interstitial microdeletion on chromosome 15. This 1.6 Mb deletion is located at chromosome band 15q14 and is considered the smallest genomic region of overlap in patients with 15q14 deletion. This specific microdeletion plays a relevant role in the phenotype expression and delineates a novel recurrent syndrome. [PMC3096895]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Complex chromosome rearrangements are constitutional structural rearrangements involving three or more chromosomes or having more than two breakpoints. These are rarely seen in the general population but their frequency should be much higher due to balanced states with no phenotypic presentation. These abnormalities preferentially occur de novo during spermatogenesis and are transmitted in families through oogenesis.Here, a de novo complex chromosome rearrangement that interests eight chromosomes in eighteen-year-old boy with an abnormal phenotype consisting in moderate developmental delay, cleft palate, and facial dysmorphisms.Standard G-banding revealed four apparently balanced translocations [corrected] involving the chromosomes 1;13, 3;19, 9;15 and 14;18 that appeared to be reciprocal. Array-based comparative genomic hybridization analysis showed no imbalances at all the breakpoints... [PMC3096895]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The syndrome is associated with a de novo complex chromosome rearrangement, which includes an interstitial microdeletion on chromosome 15q14. While complex chromosome rearrangements preferentially occur de novo during spermatogenesis, they can also be transmitted in families through oogenesis. Therefore, genetic counseling should consider both sporadic de novo occurrences and potential familial transmission. [PMC3096895]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare skeletal developmental defect characterized by congenital upward translocation of the upper cervical spine and clivus into the foramen magnum. It can be asymptomatic or associated with severe neurological dysfunction.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Primary basilar invagination is the commonest malformation of the craniocervical junction. Its prevalence in the general population is estimated to be 1%. It is a well-recognized cause of neck pain and can be easily overlooked, often mistaken for a musculoskeletal disorder. [PMC4707768]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Primary basilar invagination (BI) is a craniocervical junction malformation where the odontoid peg projects above the foramen magnum, often co-occurring with atlantoaxial dislocation and occipitalized C1 arch. It is a recognized cause of neck pain, which can be intermittent and mechanical, along with occipital headache. Patients may experience neurological symptoms such as drop attacks, facial numbness, and poorly defined upper extremity muscle weakness, indicating potential spinal cord pressure. Clinical severity can be assessed using grading systems like Nurick's. Imaging findings, including MRI, reveal basilar impression and improvements in traditional indices, while occipito-C2 pseudo-joints and asymmetrical pseudo-joints causing coronal/neck tilt are also noted. [PMC6603831, PMC4707768]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Primary basilar invagination is an abnormality and the commonest malformation of the craniocervical junction. It is considered a craniovertebral congenital anomaly, characterized by the odontoid peg projecting above the foramen magnum. [PMC4707768]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of basilar invagination is based on patient symptoms, such as drop attacks, facial numbness, and upper extremity muscle weakness, in conjunction with physical examination findings like the modified Sharp-Purser test. Diagnostic imaging plays a crucial role, primarily involving magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) scans. These imaging modalities are used to evaluate atlanto-dental interval, basilar invagination, hyper-lordosis, neck tilt, sagittal and coronal inclination, cranio-cervical tilt, pseudo-joints, and anomalous vertebral artery. Traditional indices, including Chamberlein line, McRae line, atlanto-dental interval, and Ranawat line, are also utilized for diagnosis. [PMC6603831, PMC4707768]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Primary basilar invagination can be easily overlooked and mistaken for common musculoskeletal disorders, particularly those presenting with neck pain and occipital headache. Neck pain is a frequent musculoskeletal complaint, but it can mask more serious underlying pathology such as craniovertebral congenital anomalies. Therefore, musculoskeletal disorders causing neck pain and headache should be considered in the differential diagnosis. [PMC4707768]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Surgical correction is the recommended treatment for basilar invagination, especially when life-threatening symptoms or pressure on the spinal cord are present. The Distraction, Compression, Extension, and Reduction (DCER) technique, utilizing a posterior-only approach, is effective for reducing, realigning, and relieving cranio-spinal compression. This technique may incorporate joint remodeling or extra-articular distraction, and customized instruments and implants, such as PSC spacers and the universal craniovertebral junction reducer, enhance its safety and effectiveness. Surgical intervention has demonstrated significant improvements in neurological grading and various anatomical indices. [PMC6603831, PMC4707768]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Surgical intervention, such as the DCER technique, can significantly improve the prognosis for patients with basilar invagination. Studies show a marked improvement in neurological status, with Nurick's grading improving from an average of 3.14 to 1.22 following surgery. Additionally, traditional indices like the Chamberlein line, McRae line, atlanto-dental interval, and Ranawat line all show significant improvement, indicating successful reduction and realignment of cranio-spinal compression. Cervical hyperlordosis also improves significantly, suggesting a favorable outcome with appropriate surgical management. [PMC6603831]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Transcobalamin deficiency (TC) is a disorder of cobalamin transport that usually presents during the first few months of life and is characterized by megaloblastic anemia, failure to thrive, vomiting, weakness and pancytopenia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Inherited deficiency of transcobalamin; Transcobalamin II deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, more than 40 cases of TC have been described in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: TC typically manifests in the first few months of life. Patients present with one or more of the following signs: weight loss, failure to thrive, diarrhea, vomiting, lethargy, irritability, pallor, ulcers of oral mucous membranes and impaired development. Myoclonus, decreased reflexes in the lower extremities and toe-walking may be observed. Severe infections (i.e. Pneumocystis carinii, pneumococcal meningitis, Escherichia coli, urinary tract infection, Salmonella sepsis, aseptic meningitis and gastro-enteritis) in the first year of life are also reported. In rare cases, the disease may be asymptomatic. Metabolic stroke and peripheral neuropathy have been observed in one case.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: TC is caused by mutations in the TCN2 gene (22q12.2) which encodes transcobalamin, a transporter of cobalamin (vitamin B12). Cobalamin has an important role in the metabolism of both homocysteine and methylmalonic acid as a cofactor for methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, respectively. Methionine synthase helps to maintain levels of methionine and its derivative, S-adenosylmethionine, which is required for neurotransmitter synthesis and methylation of DNA, RNA, lipids and proteins. It also prevents accumulation of homocysteine.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on laboratory findings showing pancytopenia (or isolated megaloblastic anemia or combined anemia and leucopenia) and accumulation of homocysteine and methylmalonic acid. Methionine concentration may be reduced. Serum cobalamin levels are typically not low (most circulating cobalamin bound to haptocorrin). Reduction of unsaturated B12 binding capacity (test must be carried out before starting treatment with vitamin B12) and Holo- TC levels are observed. Diagnosis is confirmed by quantification of total transcobalamin in serum or plasma or by genetic screening of TCN2. Postnatal diagnosis may be achieved by screening newborn serum by tandem mass spectroscopy to detect the presence of C3-carnitines derived from methylmalonic acid.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes inherited disorders of intestinal cobalamin absorption (Gräsbeck-Imerslund disease and congenital intrinsic factor deficiency); inborn errors of cellular cobalamin metabolism, in particular the forms resulting in combined homocystinuria and methylmalonic aciduria (cblC, cblD, cblF, cblJ and cblX); and pernicious anemia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is based on genetic screening of TCN2 or incubation of amniocytes in medium lacking any exogenous source of transcobalamin supplemented with radiolabeled cobalamin followed by measurement of transcobalamin-bound cobalamin.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment of TC involves maintenance of a very high serum cobalamin concentration (1,000-10,000 pg/ml) by intramuscular (IM) administration of hydroxocobalamin. Oral treatment or treatment with cyanocobalamin instead of hydroxocobalamin may result in poorer outcomes. Treatment with IM hydroxocobalamin at least once a week is recommended, with monitoring of biochemical and hematological parameters to ensure that treatment is effective. Follow-up into adulthood for asymptomatic children who continue to have abnormal metabolite excretion is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: TC is a severe, life-threatening and rapidly progressing disease. Treatment, started early, is highly effective and reverses the clinical and hematological manifestations of the disease. If left untreated, immunologic deficiency (marked hypogammaglobulinemia with absence of specific antibody production after antigenic stimulation) and neurological problems (severe intellectual disabilities, ataxia, and pyramidal deficit) can develop.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Wrinkly skin syndrome (WSS) is characterized by wrinkling of the skin of the dorsum of the hands and feet, an increased number of palmar and plantar creases, wrinkled abdominal skin, multiple skeletal abnormalities (joint laxity and congenital hip dislocation), late closing of the anterior fontanel, microcephaly, pre- and postnatal growth retardation, developmental delay and facial dysmorphism (a broad nasal bridge, downslanting palpebral fissures and hypertelorism).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown but only around 30 cases have been reported in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Although the clinical picture is milder, WSS also shows significant overlap with classic features of ARCL2 (also known as DebrÃ©-type cutis laxa), leading to the suggestion that WSS and ARCL2 are variable manifestations of the same disorder. The clinical spectrum in WSS also closely resembles that of geroderma osteodysplastica (GO) and to some extent that of De Barsy syndrome (DBS).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Although the etiology in some patients remains unknown, mutations in the ATP6V0A2 gene (12q24.31) have been identified both in patients with WSS and in those with autosomal recessive cutis laxa (ARCL) type 2. Mutations in the PYCR1 gene (17q25.3) have recently been identified in patients with phenotypes (wrinkly skin, osteopenia and progeroid features) overlapping with ARCL2, GO and DBS.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Histological findings are not pathognomonic for WSS (elastic fiber abnormalities may be mild or nonspecific) but may allow WSS to be distinguished from ARCL2 and ARCL1.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: WSS is transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Patients with WSS syndrome have a variable outcome. The prognosis depends on the underlying mutation and appears to be most benign in children with a mutation in the ATP6V0A2 gene.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Wrinkly skin syndrome is clinically diagnosed alongside De Barsy syndrome (DBS). Progeroid disorders overlapping with DBS are collectively denoted as autosomal-recessive cutis laxa type 3 (ARCL3), which are caused by biallelic mutations in PYCR1 or ALDH18A1. Furthermore, an autosomal-dominant form of cutis laxa with progeroid features, caused by recurrent de novo heterozygous mutations affecting the Arg138 residue of pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS) encoded by ALDH18A1, should be considered, as these mutations were identified in individuals initially diagnosed with either DBS or wrinkly skin syndrome. [PMC4564990]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:96321
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Polyploidy syndrome, particularly triploidy, is frequently identified prenatally, with most pregnancies ending as early miscarriage or spontaneous abortion. Triploid gestations can be detected as early as 8.5 weeks or through amniocentesis in the second trimester, though chances of thriving through this period are very slim. While most cases do not progress beyond early fetal development, tetraploidy has been observed in liveborn infants, with one case reported at 3 months of age. [PMC7929808, PMC3823570, PMC2745218, PMC1017283]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Polyploidy syndrome, particularly triploidy, is generally understood as a sporadic genetic disorder, with most affected pregnancies ending in early miscarriage and very slim chances of thriving past the second trimester. However, recurrent triploid pregnancies have been observed, suggesting a possible maternal genetic predisposition. Mutations in NLRP7 are associated with recurrent triploid and dispermic conceptions, indicating that some oocytes may fail to prevent polyspermic fertilization. Tetraploidy is exceedingly rare in liveborn infants; only seven cases of 92,XXYY karyotype have been reported. [PMC7929808, PMC3823570, PMC1017283]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Polyploidy, particularly triploidy, is frequently associated with early miscarriage, though some pregnancies can progress to the second trimester. Fetal manifestations observed in triploidy include holoprosencephaly. Liveborn infants with tetraploidy have presented with severely delayed growth, neurodevelopmental delay, and cleft lip. Maternal complications of triploid pregnancies can include early-onset preeclampsia, HELLP syndrome, and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome, which may manifest as delayed-onset bilateral cystic ovarian enlargement. Pathological findings in triploid conceptions can range from partial hydatidiform mole to spontaneous abortion, though placental histology may also be normal. Recurrent triploidy may suggest a genetic predisposition, with NLRP7 mutations linked to triploid spontaneous abortions and various types of hydatidiform moles. [PMC7929808, PMC7783603, PMC3823570, PMC2745218, PMC1017283]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Triploidy is generally understood as a sporadic genetic disorder without a recognized risk of recurrence or identifiable risk factors. However, cases of recurrent triploid pregnancies, even from different fathers, suggest a potential maternal genetic predisposition, indicating a need for further investigation into underlying genetic mechanisms. Mutations in the NLRP7 gene have been associated with recurrent triploid conceptions and hydatidiform moles. These mutations can lead to oocytes that are unable to prevent polyspermic fertilization, resulting in triploidy and contributing to spontaneous abortions. [PMC7929808, PMC3823570]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for polyploidy include karyotyping, which can be performed on samples such as amniocentesis, peripheral blood, and skin fibroblast cultures to reveal triploid or tetraploid karyotypes. Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH) studies are also employed, for instance, to detect gene rearrangements and polyploidy of specific genes. Flow cytometry can identify non-diploid cells. Additionally, histopathological examination is used for characterizing molar tissues and spontaneous abortions, while prenatal laboratorial markers and sonographic features contribute to the analysis of fetal development. [PMC7929808, PMC7413957, PMC3823570, PMC1017283]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: A 32-year-old woman underwent a medical termination in the second trimester of a spontaneously conceived triploid pregnancy after developing early-onset preeclampsia with subsequent haemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count (HELLP) syndrome. Placental histology was normal (non-molar) and unusually, she developed ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) 4 weeks later. She was managed conservatively following multidisciplinary team input to exclude malignant pathology. The rarity of late-onset spontaneous OHSS could have resulted in inappropriate surgical management. In the absence of supportive treatment there is also a risk of the condition progressing to a critical stage. Follow-up ultrasonography after termination of pregnancy should be considered for women with evidence of ovarian hyperstimulation, particularly if other risk factors for OHSS are present.... [PMC7783603, PMC4209769, PMC3823570]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of triploidy can be achieved through amniocentesis, which reveals a triploid karyotype, often leading to elective termination. Sonographic features, such as holoprosencephaly, can be observed in early gestation, as early as 8.5 weeks. While triploidy is typically considered a sporadic disorder, recurrent cases reaching the second trimester suggest a potential genetic predisposition of maternal origin, necessitating further investigation to enable better genetic and obstetric counseling. Prenatal laboratorial markers and clinical course are also analyzed in these cases. [PMC7929808, PMC2745218]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: While triploidy is generally considered a sporadic genetic disorder with no recognized recurrence risk, evidence suggests that recurrent triploid pregnancies can occur, pointing to a potential genetic predisposition. Mutations in the NLRP7 gene have been associated with recurrent triploid and dispermic conceptions, as well as various types of hydatidiform moles and triploid spontaneous abortions, indicating an inability of some oocytes to prevent polyspermic fertilization. Therefore, in cases of recurrent triploidy, particularly those of maternal origin, investigation for an underlying genetic mechanism, such as NLRP7 mutations, is crucial for improved genetic and obstetric counseling. [PMC7929808, PMC3823570]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of polyploidy syndrome, specifically triploidy, may involve medical termination of pregnancy, particularly if maternal complications such as early-onset preeclampsia or HELLP syndrome develop. Subsequent maternal complications, like ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), are managed conservatively with multidisciplinary team input to rule out malignancy. Supportive treatment is crucial for OHSS to prevent progression to a critical stage. Follow-up ultrasonography is recommended for women with signs of ovarian hyperstimulation after termination of a triploid pregnancy. [PMC7783603]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Triploidy typically in early miscarriage, with very slim chances of fetal survival past the second trimester. In cases where triploidy reaches the second trimester, elective termination is often decided. Recurrent triploid conceptions, sometimes associated with genetic factors like NLRP7 mutations, can manifest as spontaneous abortions or partial hydatidiform moles. Tetraploidy is exceedingly rare in liveborn infants, with only a few reported cases. These liveborn infants exhibit severe developmental and growth delays, along with congenital anomalies such as cleft lip. [PMC7929808, PMC3823570, PMC1017283]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare spotted fever rickettsiosis caused by infection with the tick-borne bacterium Rickettsia conorii, characterized by the onset of fever after an incubation period of about a week, followed by a centripetally spreading maculopapular rash, which may evolve into a petechial form. Accompanying symptoms are headaches, myalgia and/or arthralgia, among others. The typical ''tache noire'' may be observed at the site of the tick bite for several days. The disease is endemic in Africa, Southern Europe, and India.

A rare form of hereditary nonpolyposis colon cancer (HNPCC) characterized by predisposition to a wide variety of cancers, including neoplasms of the digestive tract, urinary tract, endometrium, ovary, brain, and prostate, as well as sebaceous skin tumors. LS-associated tumors are typically characterized by the presence of microsatellite instability (MSI) and loss of expression of MMR proteins in tumor tissue.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The population prevalence of germline pathogenic variants in the MMR genes has been estimated at 1:279. Cancer type incidences vary with the affected gene, sex, and population. LS accounts for approximately 3% of colorectal (CRC) and endometrial cancers (EC).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: LS-associated cancer usually occurs in adulthood, at earlier ages compared to the general population. CRC is the predominant LS-associated cancer; it has an increased risk of being synchronous or metachronous and is typically located in the proximal colon; symptoms include abdominal pain, iron deficiency or signs of colonic obstruction. EC is the most prevalent LS-associated cancer in women and manifests with pelvic pain and menorrhea. Other LS-associated cancers include ovarian, stomach, hepatobiliary tract, pancreas, small intestine, urinary tract, prostate, brain (mainly glioblastoma) and skin cancers (sebaceous adenomas/carcinomas/epitheliomas and keratoacanthomas). Muir-Torre and Turcot syndromes were terms used to describe patients with skin neoplasia, or with tumors of the colon and central nervous system, respectively. Several other cancer types have been reported to occur in individuals with Lynch syndrome (e.g., sarcomas, adrenocortical carcinoma, breast cancer).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: LS is caused by heterozygous pathogenic germline variants affecting DNA mismatch repair (MMR) genes (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2). Other variants involve C-terminal deletions of EPCAM leading to methylation of the adjacent MSH2 promoter in epithelial tissue. Rarely, LS is due to constitutional inactivation of MLH1 by epimutation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Amsterdam/revised Bethesda criteria fail to identify up to 50% of LS patients. MSI analysis and/or immunohistochemical analysis of MMR protein expression in CRC and EC is recommended for all patients. Universal or age-dependent somatic and/or germline genetic testing of these patients is undergoing evaluation. Cascade testing should follow the identification of an individual with a MMR pathogenic mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes several forms of attenuated polyposis, particularly recessive tumor syndromes associated with germline biallelic pathogenic variants in MUTYH, NTHL1, MBD4, or MSH3, polymerase proofreading-related adenomatous polyposis, constitutional MMR deficiency, and other cancer predisposition syndromes such as PTEN hamartoma tumor or Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Unexplained cases might be classified as Lynch-like syndrome or familial CRC type X, depending on the status of the MMR system in the tumors.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Due to the high risk of synchronous or metachronous tumors, patients should be included in surveillance programs consisting of colonoscopy with removal of precancerous polyps, and transvaginal ultrasound examination and endometrial biopsy (with yearly education on EC and ovarian cancer) for women, every 1-2 years starting at the age of 20-25 years. Full colectomy should be considered in LS-CRC patients. Screening may start at an earlier age depending on family history. Aspirin decreases the risk of CRC. Prophylactic hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy can be proposed to women after childbearing age. Treatments supporting anti-tumoral immune response show great success against MSI-high tumors.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Early diagnosis and surveillance significantly reduce morbidity and mortality. LS-associated tumors tend to have a better prognosis at similar stage compared with microsatellite stable tumors.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare partial autosomal monosomy characterized by global developmental delay, intellectual disability, multiple cartilaginous exostoses, and craniofacial anomalies (such as brachycephaly, biparietal foramina, large fontanels, craniosynostosis, ptosis, epicanthic folds, prominent nasal bridge with broad, depressed nasal tip, hypoplastic nares, short philtrum, downturned upper lip, and micrognathia). Additional reported features include behavioral abnormalities, myopia, strabismus, and sensorineural hearing loss, among others.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Potocki-Shaffer syndrome is a rare contiguous gene deletion syndrome, characterized by deletions in the 11p11.2p12 region. Both Potocki-Shaffer syndrome and WAGR syndrome are described as very rare. While specific prevalence figures are not provided, its rarity is highlighted by reports of individual cases, such as the first Korean patient identified with the condition. [PMC7245943, PMC4310950]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Potocki-Shaffer syndrome (PSS) is a contiguous gene deletion disorder with cardinal features including multiple exostoses, biparietal or parietal foramina, intellectual disability, and craniofacial anomalies. Multiple exostoses are attributed to EXT2 involvement, and biparietal foramina to ALX4. Haploinsufficiency of PHF21A contributes to intellectual disability and craniofacial anomalies, and is also associated with epilepsy, hypotonia, autism spectrum disorder, and neurobehavioral problems. Other characteristic features can include developmental delay, dysmorphic face, enlarged anterior fontanels, and genitourinary abnormalities. Overgrowth has been occasionally reported. [PMC9783151, PMC7245943, PMC6805429, PMC6460561, PMC4310950]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Potocki-Shaffer syndrome (PSS) is a rare contiguous gene deletion disorder caused by haploinsufficiency of genes located on chromosome 11p11.2. The cardinal features are linked to specific gene involvement: haploinsufficiency of PHF21A is associated with intellectual disability, craniofacial anomalies, epilepsy, hypotonia, and neurobehavioral problems, as PHF21A encodes BHC80, a component of the LSD1-CoREST complex that modulates neuronal genes. ALX4 involvement causes biparietal foramina, and EXT2 haploinsufficiency leads to multiple exostoses. Deletions in this region can vary in size, and de novo truncating variants or other mutations in PHF21A alone can also cause a related syndromic intellectual disability with similar features. [PMC9783151, PMC7245943, PMC6805429, PMC6460561, PMC4310950]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Potocki-Shaffer syndrome is primarily achieved through genetic testing. employed include SNP array, high-resolution microarray, whole exome sequencing (including trio WES), Sanger sequencing, targeted gene panel sequencing, and MiSeq sequencing to identify deletions or variants in associated genes. Clinical suspicion is raised by characteristic features such as multiple exostoses, biparietal foramina, developmental delay, intellectual disability, and craniofacial anomalies, which can be further investigated with skull radiographs and other radiological examinations. Genetic testing enables early diagnosis, and advanced prenatal diagnosis may be considered in cases with prenatal indicators like oligohydramnios. Protein-DNA modeling can also be used to substantiate the pathogenicity of identified mutations. [PMC9783151, PMC7245943, PMC6805429, PMC4310950]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Potocki-Shaffer syndrome (PSS), a contiguous gene deletion disorder, requires differentiation from conditions with overlapping features or shared chromosomal regions. A PHF21A-related disorder, caused by variants solely in the PHF21A gene, is a key differential; while not fitting a PSS diagnosis, it shares intellectual disability, epilepsy, hypotonia, and dysmorphic features. Furthermore, WAGR syndrome, an 11p13 deletion syndrome characterized by Wilms tumor, aniridia, genitourinary abnormalities, and mental retardation, can co-occur with PSS in patients with larger 11p deletions, necessitating careful diagnostic consideration. [PMC9783151, PMC7245943, PMC3746256]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Oligohydramnios has been identified as a prenatal symptom associated with Potocki-Shaffer syndrome. The presence of oligohydramnios might indicate the need for advanced prenatal diagnosis, suggesting the possibility of antenatal detection for this condition. [PMC7245943]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Potocki-Shaffer syndrome (PSS) is a contiguous gene deletion disorder caused by haploinsufficiency of genes, including PHF21A, ALX4, and EXT2, located on chromosome 11p11.2. While many cases arise from de novo deletions or mutations, paternally inherited mosaicism has been reported. Genetic testing, utilizing such as SNP array, high-resolution microarray, whole exome sequencing, and Sanger sequencing, can confirm the diagnosis, sometimes at a young age. The possibility of prenatal diagnosis exists, with oligohydramnios potentially serving as an indicator. Genetic counseling should address the variable clinical presentation, which depends on the specific genes affected, such as EXT2 for multiple exostoses, ALX4 for biparietal foramina, and PHF21A for intellectual disability and craniofacial anomalies. [PMC9783151, PMC7245943, PMC6805429, PMC6460561, PMC4310950]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Potocki-Shaffer syndrome (PSS, OMIM #601224) is a rare contiguous gene deletion syndrome caused by haploinsufficiency of genes located on the 11p11.2p12. Affected individuals have a number of characteristic features including multiple exostoses, biparietal foramina, abnormalities of genitourinary system, hypotonia, developmental delay, and intellectual disability. here on the first Korean case of an 8-yr-old boy with PSS diagnosed by high resolution microarray. Initial evaluation was done at age 6 months because of a history of developmental delay, hypotonia, and dysmorphic face. Coronal craniosynostosis and enlarged parietal foramina were found on skull radiographs. At age 6 yr, he had severe global developmental delay. Multiple exostoses of long bones were detected during a radiological check-up. Based on the clinical and radiological features, PSS was highly suspected. Subsequently,... [PMC4310950]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Individuals with Potocki-Shaffer syndrome experience developmental delay, which can be severe and profound, necessitating ongoing rehabilitation therapy. Multiple exostoses are also a characteristic feature, and their progression requires continuous monitoring. Other features include hypotonia, intellectual disability, and abnormalities of the genitourinary system. [PMC4310950]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia (TCPT) is a contiguous gene syndrome characterized by mild bleeding tendency, variable thrombocytopenia (THC), dysmorphic facies, abnormal giant alpha-granules in platelets and dysmegakaryopoiesis.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia, a feature of 11q23 deletion syndrome (Jacobsen syndrome), is characterized by growth retardation, psychomotor retardation, facial dysmorphism, and multiple congenital abnormalities. Patients present with thrombocytopenia, and bleeding severity can be unexpectedly severe, sometimes disproportionate to platelet counts. Specific manifestations may include skull deformities, facial asymmetry, low-set ears, inguinal hernia, flat feet, and crowded toes. Coagulation abnormalities, such as prolonged prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time, can also be present. Peripheral blood smears reveal two distinct platelet sizes, both containing large α-granules, and severe bleeding often necessitates transfusions. [PMC5757304]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia is associated with 11q23 deletion syndrome, also known as Jacobsen syndrome, which is characterized by thrombocytopenia. The etiology involves a deletion of the 13.0 Mb region on chromosome 11q, specifically from 11q24.1 to the q terminus, which includes the FLI1 gene. This genetic deletion in a low platelet count and abnormal platelet morphology, featuring two different sizes of platelets containing large α-granules. [PMC5757304]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of 11q23 deletion syndrome, which includes Paris-Trousseau thrombocytopenia, can be made prenatally via amniocentesis. Postnatally, array comparative genomic hybridization analysis identifies a deletion of the 13.0 Mb region from 11q24.1 to the q terminus, encoding FLI1. Peripheral blood analysis typically reveals a low platelet count and features two different sizes of platelets containing large α-granules. Coagulation abnormalities, such as prolonged prothrombin time-international normalized ratio and activated partial thromboplastin time, may also be observed. [PMC5757304]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Jacobsen syndrome, also known as 11q23 deletion syndrome, should be considered in the differential diagnosis of thrombocytopenia. This syndrome is characterized by growth retardation, psychomotor retardation, facial dysmorphism, multiple congenital abnormalities, and thrombocytopenia, often with severe bleeding. Patients may present with a low platelet count and peripheral blood featuring two different sizes of platelets containing large α-granules. The diagnosis is associated with a deletion of regions on 11q, which can include FLI1. [PMC5757304]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Prenatal diagnosis of 11q23 deletion syndrome, which includes thrombocytopenia and a deletion encoding FLI1, has been achieved through amniocentesis and array comparative genomic hybridization analysis. Such early diagnosis allows for careful management and vigilant perinatal care, including consideration of a cesarean section, which can help avoid massive bleeding and serious sequelae in affected newborns. [PMC5757304]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Prenatal diagnosis of 11q23 deletion syndrome, which involves a deletion encoding FLI1, can be made by amniocentesis. Such prenatal diagnosis is warranted to facilitate careful management and vigilant perinatal care, including consideration of a cesarean section. This proactive approach can help avoid massive bleeding and serious sequelae in affected newborns. [PMC5757304]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management involves careful perinatal care, particularly following prenatal diagnosis. A cesarean section may be warranted for delivery. In cases of severe bleeding, treatment has included multiple platelet transfusions and fresh frozen plasma transfusions. Vigilant management can help avoid massive bleeding and serious sequelae. [PMC5757304]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Patients with 11q23 deletion syndrome, which includes thrombocytopenia, can experience severe bleeding, sometimes more severe than predicted by platelet counts. However, careful management, including prenatal diagnosis and vigilant perinatal care, can mitigate severe outcomes. In one reported case, despite severe bleeding requiring multiple transfusions, massive bleeding and serious sequelae were avoided, with only petechial hemorrhage observed, highlighting the importance of early intervention. [PMC5757304]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare acute encephalopathy with inflammation-mediated status epilepticus characterized by infancy-onset of refractory unilateral, mainly clonic status epilepticus during or shortly after a febrile episode without evidence of central nervous system infection, followed by permanent or transient hemiplegia with a minimum duration of one week. The majority of children develop pharmaco-resistant epilepsy a few months later. Brain imaging shows edematous swelling of the affected hemisphere at the time of the initial status, followed by hemiatrophy that does not correlate with any vascular territory.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy (HHE) syndrome typically presents during infancy or early childhood, often with an infantile presentation of febrile focal motor status epilepticus. Reported cases include children ranging from 6 months to 4 years of age. Specific examples include an 11-month-old girl, a 20-month-old girl, and a 4-year-old girl, all diagnosed with HHE syndrome. [PMC8183818, PMC7847093, PMC7163536, PMC3962940]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy (HHE) syndrome is an uncommon pediatric epilepsy syndrome, typically presenting in infancy or early childhood. It is described as an uncommon outcome of prolonged focal status epilepticus in childhood. While the syndrome is poorly understood, only a very small minority of cases are associated with an underlying genetic or metabolic abnormality. Cobalamin C deficiency has been identified as a potential contributing factor in some cases. [PMC7847093, PMC7163536, PMC3962940]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy (HHE) syndrome is an uncommon pediatric condition typically presenting in infancy or early childhood with prolonged, often febrile, focal motor status epilepticus or unilateral convulsive seizures. This initial phase is followed by transient or permanent hemiplegia on the affected side. Months to years later, chronic epilepsy with recurrent focal seizures often develops, which can be refractory to treatment. Patients frequently experience neurodevelopmental or severe developmental delay. Neuroimaging may reveal brain atrophy, particularly on the hemisphere contralateral to the hemiplegia. HHE syndrome has been associated with underlying genetic or metabolic abnormalities, such as cobalamin C deficiency or medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD), and infections like human herpesvirus 6. [PMC9712474, PMC8183818, PMC7847093, PMC7163536, PMC3962940]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy syndrome is poorly understood, with only a small minority of cases associated with an underlying genetic or metabolic abnormality. Specific metabolic conditions identified as possible etiologies include medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD) and genetic cobalamin C deficiency. Acute encephalopathy with biphasic seizures and late reduced diffusion (AESD), potentially associated with human herpesvirus 6, has also been linked to HHE syndrome. These findings highlight the importance of considering metabolic diseases and infections as possible etiologies, especially in cases of unknown origin. [PMC9712474, PMC8183818, PMC7163536]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy (HHE) syndrome is primarily based on the characteristic clinical course, which includes initial sudden and prolonged unilateral convulsive seizures, followed by hemiplegia and subsequent epilepsy. Neuroimaging, particularly MRI, is crucial, typically revealing brain atrophy more pronounced on the hemisphere contralateral to the hemiplegia, along with ventricular dilation. In cases of unknown etiology, investigations may include DNA tests of blood and cerebrospinal fluid for viral agents like human herpesvirus 6, and screening for inborn errors of metabolism such as medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency, especially in adults not screened at birth. Confirmation of the syndrome can also involve observing the response to seizure control and the recovery of hemiplegia over time. [PMC9712474, PMC8183818, PMC3962940]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy syndrome (HHE syndrome) include metabolic disorders such as medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD) and genetic cobalamin C deficiency, both of which have been associated with HHE syndrome presentations. Acute encephalopathy with biphasic seizures and late reduced diffusion (AESD) can also overlap with HHE syndrome, as observed in some cases. Considering these conditions is important, particularly for treatable metabolic etiologies, to provide timely and targeted treatment. [PMC9712474, PMC8183818, PMC7163536]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy syndrome is rarely associated with underlying genetic or metabolic abnormalities. However, specific genetic conditions such as medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency (MCADD) and genetic cobalamin C deficiency have been identified as potential etiologies. For cases of unknown origin, particularly in adults not screened at birth, investigation for treatable inborn errors of metabolism like MCADD is advised to enable timely and targeted treatment. The association with genetic cobalamin C deficiency further underscores the importance of considering metabolic disorders in patients presenting with acute deterioration, suggesting derangements in cobalamin metabolism as a possible contributing factor. [PMC9712474, PMC7163536]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy syndrome primarily involves seizure control, which can be prolonged and difficult, sometimes requiring various anticonvulsants like midazolam infusion, carbamazepine, or valproate, and potentially surgery. Good seizure control is highlighted as essential for improving outcomes. Investigation for underlying treatable metabolic conditions, such as medium-chain acyl-coenzyme A dehydrogenase deficiency or cobalamin C deficiency, is advised, as timely and targeted treatment of these etiologies may prevent developmental delay and progression. Pharmacotherapy and rehabilitation therapy are also utilized, which can lead to recovery of physical function, though mild developmental delays may still be observed. [PMC9712474, PMC8183818, PMC7847093, PMC7163536, PMC3962940]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy (HHE) syndrome often involves chronic, drug-resistant epilepsy and significant neurodevelopmental delay, which can be severe. Hemiplegia may be permanent, though it can resolve in approximately 20% of cases, with rehabilitation potentially aiding physical function recovery. Neurological sequelae are common, impacting daily living and schooling. Severe presentations can lead to complications like progressive cerebral edema, herniation, and even death, particularly in cases progressing to super refractory status epilepticus. Early diagnosis and effective seizure control are considered crucial for potentially improving long-term outcomes. [PMC9712474, PMC8183818, PMC7847093, PMC7163536, PMC3962940]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hereditary patellar dysostosis characterized by nail hypoplasia or aplasia, aplastic or hypoplastic patellae, elbow dysplasia, and the presence of iliac horns as well as renal and ocular anomalies.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The reported prevalence is 1/50,000; however, epidemiological studies are lacking.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Nail-patella syndrome (NPS) is a multisystemic disorder characterized by significant inter- and intrafamilial variability in clinical manifestations and severity of the disease. Cases can range from mild with no functional impact to severe leading to disability. The classical tetrad involves nails dysplasia, absent or hypoplastic patellae, presence of iliac horns, and elbow deformities. Adults can have a slight lower bone mineral density of the hip and spine (8 -20%) leading to a higher risk of fractures and scoliosis. Glaucoma and ocular hypertension have been described in NPS patients and may require early ophthalmological screening. Renal complications are reported in 30-60% of the cases. Other extraskeletal abnormalities described are loss of the normal skin creases over the distal interphalangeal joints and, neurological symptoms such as numbness, tingling and neuropathic pain.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: NPS is an autosomal-dominant disorder and the majority of the cases are caused by LMX1B mutations (9q33.3) leading to loss of function of the LMX1B protein. About 10% are caused by a de novo pathogenic variant.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on clinical findings. Molecular test can identified the LMX1B gene mutations in around 95% of the cases, thus helping to confirm the clinical diagnosis or cases where clinical signs and symptoms are not clear.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: As patients with NPS may present a broad phenotypic spectrum, differential diagnosis may be necessary, as the association of systemic and musculoskeletal findings may also occur in other genetic syndromes including Coffin-Siris, Meier-Gorlin, Genitopatellar, RAPADILINO, DOORS, and coxopodopatellar syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possibile when there is a positive familiar history for the disorder. Some skeletal signs (ie, talipes equinovarus or large iliac horns) may be identified on fetal ultrasound examination in the third trimester of pregnancy. When the disease-causative variant is found in the affected individual of the family, prenatal testing for a pregnancy at increased risk and preimplantation genetic diagnosis are possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: NPS is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Each child of an NPS affected individual has a 50% chance of inheriting the LMX1B pathogenic variant of the disease. The penetrance of the disease is complete, but the clinical expression is variable even in individuals of the same family. About 90% of NPS patients have an affected parent. In NPS, somatic and germline mosaicism has been reported in unaffected parents.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The management and treatment is focused on the clinical manifestations, which may require a multidisciplinary team. Joint limitations or anatomical abnormalities may need surgical treatment. Early ocular and renal screening may be helpful and a medical follow up can be required if any alteration is identified. Pain management is important and physical and pharmacological options are available.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Patients with NPS live a normal lifespan. The renal pathology is a major determinant of the prognosis, as proteinuria, hypertension, and hematuria occur in 30 - 60% of the patients; 5 % progress to chronic renal failure.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Loose anagen syndrome is a rare benign hair disorder affecting predominantly blond females in childhood and characterized by the presence of hair that can be easily and painlessly pulled out. Most of the hair is in the anagen phase and lacks an external epithelial sheath. Hair grows back quickly and the condition improves spontaneously with aging. Loose anagen hair can be associated with other anomalies, such as coloboma.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Loose anagen syndrome, often referred to as Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair (NS-LAH), is a rasopathy caused by mutations in genes such as SHOC2 or PPP1CB. It is characterized by distinctive hair anomalies, including sparse, slow-growing, or unruly hair, alongside developmental delay and short stature. Common features include characteristic facial dysmorphism, cardiac anomalies such as septal defects, and hypotonia. Patients may also present with skin hyperpigmentation, ligamentous laxity, feeding difficulties, and structural brain abnormalities like relative megalencephaly or cerebellar tonsillar ectopia. Hematological issues such as thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, or myelofibrosis, and monogenic lupus with nephritis, have also been reported. [PMC10797908, PMC10697549, PMC5134331, PMC3787995, PMC4231415]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Loose anagen syndrome, particularly in its Noonan-like presentation (NS-LAH), is primarily caused by germline mutations in genes encoding proteins of the RAS/MAPK pathway, classifying it as a RASopathy. Specifically, mutations in the SHOC2 gene, such as the recurrent c.4A>G (p.Ser2Gly) variant, are responsible for NS-LAH. These SHOC2 variants affect the Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor (EGFR)-mediated Extracellular signal-Regulated Kinase (ERK1/2) pathway, influencing ERK1/2 and AKT downstream signaling. Mutant SHOC2 can impair interaction with protein phosphatase 1c (PP1c), leading to insufficient RAF-1 kinase activation. Additionally, recurrent de novo missense mutations in the PPP1CB gene have been identified, causing a novel rasopathy that closely resembles NS-LAH by affecting RAF dephosphorylation within the RAS/MAPK pathway. [PMC10797908, PMC11373329, PMC10697549, PMC5134331, PMC4407356]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: BACKGROUND RASopathies involve mutations in genes that encode proteins participating in the RAS-mitogen-activated protein kinase pathway and are a collection of multisystem disorders that clinically overlap. Variants in the SHOC2 gene have been reported in Noonan-like syndrome, which include distinct facial features, short stature, congenital cardiac defects, developmental delays, bleeding disorders, and loose anagen hair. is of a 7-year-old girl with the c.4A>G (p.Ser2Gly) variant of the SHOC2 gene, consistent with Noonan-like syndrome, with loose anagen hair, presenting with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura and autoimmune hemolytic anemia. CASE REPORT The child had a medical history of 7 hospitalizations at our institution. At the age of 2 months, she underwent surgical correction for ventricular and atrial septal defects. At the age of 2 years, tonsil and adenoid removal surgery... [PMC10697549, PMC5134331, PMC3787995, PMC4231415]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Loose anagen syndrome, particularly in its Noonan-like presentation, overlaps with a spectrum of RASopathies. These include Noonan syndrome, LEOPARD syndrome, Costello syndrome, cardio-facio-cutaneous syndrome, Neurofibromatosis-1, and Legius syndrome, all caused by mutations in the RAS-MAPK pathway. A novel rasopathy caused by recurrent de novo missense mutations in PPP1CB closely resembles Noonan syndrome with loose anagen hair. Additionally, monogenic lupus has been reported in a child with Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair, suggesting it can be part of the presentation. [PMC10797908, PMC10697549, PMC5134331, PMC4407356, PMC4213265]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for individuals with loose anagen hair, particularly in the context of Noonan-like syndrome (a RASopathy), can involve a range of significant complications. Patients may experience severe short stature, often linked to growth hormone deficiency or insensitivity, and cognitive deficits or developmental delay. Neurological complications are common, including structural brain anomalies such as megalencephaly, enlarged subarachnoid spaces, cerebellar tonsillar ectopia (potentially progressing to Chiari 1 malformation), Dandy-Walker malformation, optic nerve hypoplasia, and ventriculomegaly. Feeding difficulties, sometimes requiring feeding tubes, are also reported. Cardiac anomalies are frequent. Furthermore, severe systemic complications can arise, such as the development of monogenic systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus nephritis, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and myelofibrosis. [PMC10797908, PMC10697549, PMC5134331, PMC3787995, PMC4231415]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked congenital myopathy characterized by numerous centrally placed nuclei on muscle biopsy and that presents at birth with marked weakness, hypotonia and respiratory failure.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The birth prevalence of X-linked centronuclear myopathy (XLMTM) is estimated at 1/50,000 males.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease is characterized by a severe phenotype in males presenting at birth with marked weakness, hypotonia and respiratory failure. Signs of antenatal onset are frequent and comprise reduced fetal movements and polyhydramnios. Thinning of the ribs is observed on chest radiographs of the newborn. Birth asphyxia may be the presenting feature. A family history of either male neonatal deaths or miscarriages is common. Affected infants are often macrosomic, with a body length above the 90th centile and large head circumference. External ophthalmoplegia is commonly associated. Testes are frequently undescended. Pyloric stenosis and cavernous hemangiomas of the liver have been reported in some long-term survivors.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: XLMTM is caused by mutations in the myotubularin (MTM1); Xq27.3-q28) gene.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on typical histopathological findings on muscle biopsy in combination with suggestive clinical features. Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses include congenital myotonic dystrophy and other conditions characterized by severe neonatal hypotonia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible where the mutation has been previously identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is x-linked recessive. Where the female is a carrier, the risk to male offspring inheriting the disease is 50%; female offspring have a 50% risk of being carriers. The degree of disease penetrance depends on skewed X-inactivation; the majority of female disease carriers are asymptomatic but may show signs of only mild muscle weakness or urinary incontinence, indicating smooth muscle involvement. Genetic counseling should be offered to all patients and families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is currently no curative treatment available. Management is supportive and based on a multidisciplinary approach.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: In the majority of cases, the course is fatal within the first months of life. A proportion of affected males may survive into their teens or beyond. In these cases, the survival depends on a substantial degree of medical intervention and often constant ventilation.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hypothalamic hamartomas with gelastic seizures is a rare cerebral malformation with epilepsy syndrome characterized by early-onset gelastic (i.e. ictal laughter) or dacrystic (i.e., ictal crying) seizures due to non-neoplastic developmental malformation - hypothalamic hamartomas. In many patients, seizures progress to other seizure types including focal and generalized seizures, with concomitant cognitive decline and behavioral disorders. Some patients also present a precocious puberty.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): GS-HH; Hypothalamic hamartoma with gelastic seizures

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hypothalamic hamartomas (HHs) are associated with pharmacoresistant epilepsy. Stereotactic radiofrequency thermocoagulation (SRT) shows promise as a disconnecting intervention. Although magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is typically used to determine the attachment and intervention side, it presents challenges in cases of bilaterally attached HH, where the epileptogenic side is unclear. The lateralizing potential of electroclinical parameters in such cases remains uncertain. This retrospective study evaluates the lateralization value of specific parameters, particularly in patients with unilateral HH, to improve future diagnostics and treatment approaches for bilateral HH. Four lateralizing parameters-semiology, ictal electroencephalography (EEG), and interictal epileptiform discharges during awake (IEDs w ) and sleep states (IEDs s )-were assessed for correlation with HH attachment side... [PMC11908668, PMC11852620, PMC12371641, PMC10040029, PMC11960393]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Autosomal recessive primary microcephaly (MCPH) is a rare genetically heterogeneous disorder of neurogenic brain development characterized by reduced head circumference at birth with no gross anomalies of brain architecture and variable degrees of intellectual impairment.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): MCPH; Microcephalia vera; Microcephaly vera; True microcephaly

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Exact prevalence of non-syndromic microcephaly is not known. MCPH is more common in Asian and Middle Eastern populations than in Caucasians, in whom an annual incidence of 1/1,000,000 is reported. It is more common in specific populations, e.g. northern Pakistanis. Consanguinity appears to play a role in incidence.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients have a reduction in head circumference (HC) at birth of at least 2 standard deviations (SD) below ethnically matched, age- and sex-related mean values. Microcephaly can be observed by week 32 of pregnancy. Subsequent head growth is very slow, and HC worsens during infancy: below -3SD before 6 months, and usually between -4SD and -12SD in adults. Mild to moderate non-progressive intellectual impairment is found, in the absence of any significant neurological deficit. Seizures may be present (10%). Delay in early motor milestones and speech delay are common. Most patients have hyperactive behavior.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Ten subtypes based on the 11 genes have been differentiated. However, patients are basically phenotypically indistinguishable. MCPH is caused by mutations in MCPH1, WDR62, CDK5RAP2, CEP152, ASPM, CENPJ, STIL, CEP63, CEP135 , CASC5 and PHC1. These mutations appear to lead to reduced generation of cerebral cortical neurons during embryonic neurogenesis. Some patients do not harbor these mutations. Some carry mutations in one of the genes of Meier-Gorlin syndrome, i.e. CDC6, CDT1, ORC1, ORC4, ORC6.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is generally based on clinical signs. Reduced occipitofrontal circumference along with mild to moderate cognitive impairment, in the absence of other malformations or dysmorphism, and with normal height to mildly shortened height, are the most common diagnostic criteria. MRI shows grossly normal, proportionately small-sized brain with some degree of gyral simplification, and small normal brainstem and cerebellum. Patients with mutations in WDR62 may show more severe cortical anomalies and may not fulfill the common criteria of MCPH. Molecular genetic testing is available for several genes. The condition can be diagnosed on prenatal ultrasound but absence of microcephaly does not exclude the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: MCPH and Seckel syndrome belong to a clinical continuum, as mutations of some genes (CENPJ, CEP152) result in either phenotype. The distinction between MCPH and Seckel relies on a historical distinction between microcephalic patients with normal stature and patients with reduced stature. Normal fundus examination is important to distinguish MCPH from the microcephaly-chorioretinopathy syndromes. MRI is crucial to distinguish MCPH from other disorders with congenital microcephaly, such as lissencephaly, Norman-Roberts type or infectious embryofetopathies. Assessment of maternal serum phenylalaninemia is mandatory to exclude maternal phenylketonuria.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal testing and carrier testing are available for families with known gene mutations. When no mutation is identified, fetal MRI could be advised, but normal findings do not exclude the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Exact genotype-phenotype correlations have not been established.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no specific etiologic treatment. Physical and speech therapy may be beneficial. Seizures are usually stabilized with common anticonvulsants. Ritalin may reduce hyperactivity.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Vital prognosis depends on severity and related manifestations but is generally good.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:285
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): EDS-HT; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome hypermobility type; EDS III; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type 3; hEDS; Hypermobile EDS

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Background/To provide a large-scale analysis on the demographics and ocular comorbidities in Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome (EDS) patients in the US. Subjects/This is an exploratory cross-sectional study comparing medical records of EDS patients to the general population on demographic variables and ICD-10 ocular diagnoses. A research platform with de-identified EHR data of over 99 million patients across 60 healthcare organizations was utilized. Groups were stratified by 30-year age groups. Patients aged 0-61+ with an ICD-10 diagnosis of EDS (76,526), the general platform population aged 0-61+ (99,836,639), and patients with a concurrent ICD-10 ocular diagnosis were queried to determine the prevalence of EDS across demographic variables, ocular disease, and odds of ocular disease. Statistical analysis was conducted using Microsoft Excel and R studio, using p < 0.01 and 95% confidence intervals... [PMC12209458]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (formerly Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type 3) is characterized by joint hypermobility and clinical manifestations in the absence of other systemic diseases, necessitating their exclusion. A specific rare form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, resulting from the total absence of the alpha2(I) chain of collagen type I, can present with a phenotype reminiscent of mild hypermobility EDS during childhood. This condition requires biochemical analysis of collagens for detection. Connective tissue disorders, a heterogeneous group including heritable disorders affecting collagen-containing structures, also require differentiation from overlapping diseases. [PMC10418020, PMC8149255, PMC2564565]

Two inherited pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants were identified; a previously reported deletion resulting in a TNXA/TNXB chimeric gene and a novel frameshift variant.
