DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Triatrial heart is a rare congenital heart defect characterized by a fibro-muscular membrane dividing the left or right atrium into two chambers. Cor triatriatum sinister (CTS), the subdivision of the left atrium, is the more common form, accounting for up to 0.4% of congenital heart disease. The right atrial equivalent, cor triatriatum dexter (CTD), is rarer, representing up to 0.025% of the burden of congenital heart disease. [PMC11448167]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of triatrial heart primarily relies on multimodality imaging for accurate anatomical assessment, differentiation from other anomalies, and surgical planning. Echocardiography, including transthoracic, transesophageal, 3D transesophageal, and intracardiac echocardiography, is a key diagnostic tool, revealing fibromuscular membranes and associated anomalies. Computed tomography, including cardiac CT and CT angiography, further clarifies intricate anatomy. Magnetic resonance imaging is also utilized. Cardiac catheterization can confirm shunts and assess pressure gradients. For complex cases, 3D heart printing can facilitate virtual surgical planning. [PMC12273821, PMC12160066, PMC12313162, PMC12348748, PMC11193257]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of conditions involving an echogenic membrane in the right atrium, such as persistent right venous valve causing supravalvular tricuspid valve obstruction and secondary right ventricle hypoplasia, is possible. Prenatal sonography can detect these abnormalities, with one case reported at 31 weeks of gestation. Precise identification of variant forms and related flow patterns is crucial for informing patient management decisions. [PMC10753248]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Oculo-auriculo-vertebral spectrum is a heterogeneous group of genetic disorder, also known as Goldenhar Syndrome, which has several phenotypic features including craniofacial anomalies, cardiac, vertebral and central nervous system defects. Cardiovascular anomalies include ventricular septal defects, atrial septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, Tetralogy of Fallot, double outlet right ventricle, aberrant right subclavian artery, coarctation of aorta, transposition of the great arteries, double inlet left ventricle, cor triatriatum, pulmonary artery stenosis, aortic stenosis, persistent left superior vena cava, partially or totally abnormal pulmonary venous return and bicuspid aortic valve. Persistent fifth aortic arch, also named as double lumen aortic arch, is a very rare cardivascular anomaly and usually associate other cardiac defects. a 7 month old patient with... [PMC8862463]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Botulism is a rare acquired neuromuscular junction disease, characterized by descending flaccid paralysis caused by botulinum neurotoxins (BoNTs), including four clinical forms with different modes of acquisition.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Estimated global prevalence is less than 1/1,000,000. Annual incidence in Western countries is estimated at 1/2,000,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The incubation period usually lasts 12 to 36 h, sometimes up to 5-8 days depending on the disease form. The typical clinical picture includes symmetrical cranial nerve palsies followed by symmetrical descending flaccid motor paralysis, with cholinergic dysautonomia. Initial symptoms include blurry vision (accommodation defects, diplopia) with bilateral ptosis, followed by dysautonomic symptoms (dry mouth and eyes, mydriasis, dysphagia, dysarthria, urinary retention and constipation). In the severe forms, paralysis concerns the neck, shoulder, and proximal muscles, followed by involvement of the muscles of the distal upper extremities, the diaphragm and respiratory muscles, which may result in respiratory compromise or arrest. The sensory system and intellectual functions remain unaffected.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Clinical manifestations are common to all forms, whatever the mode of acquisition. Foodborne botulism caused by consumption of foods contaminated with BoNTs (homemade or traditional canned-foods, ham, pork products, etc) is the most frequent form of botulism in adults. Intestinal colonization by Clostridium botulinum and in situ toxin production is observed in young infants (infant botulism) and certain adults with risk factors (adult intestinal botulism). Wound (or inoculation) botulism, through infection of wounds, is rare and mainly occurs in injection drug users; inhalational botulism and iatrogenic botulism have also been reported. Botulism is due to BoNTs produced by C. botulinum and, very rarely, by certain related Clostridia, rod-shaped, strictly anaerobic and sporulating bacteria, i.e neurotoxigenic strains of C. baratii and C. butyricum. There are seven types of BoNTs (A to G) with different antigenic properties. Types A, B, E and, more rarely F, are associated with human botulism. At the site of absorption or adsorption, BoNT diffuses via the blood to the presynaptic membrane of skeletal and autonomic cholinergic nerves. BoNT binds to and enters peripheral cholinergic terminals and causes a block of acetylcholine release, with ensuing flaccid paralysis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is essentially clinical in the first stage; the electromyography (EMG) pattern is characterized by brief, small, abundant potentials (BSAPs). Confirmation is based on BoNT detection in serum, stools, and/or food samples. The detection of BoNT-producing Clostridium in cultures from stools and food or wound samples also supports the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis, depending on the disease form, in adults or infants, includes myasthenia, Guillain-Barré syndrome (and Miller Fisher syndrome), Lambert-Eaton syndrome, bacterial and chemical food poisoning or chemical intoxication.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic. Management is based on supportive care and respiratory assistance with recovery in severe cases, in an intensive care unit (ICU). Anti-toxin therapy is effective when it is administrated at the onset of symptoms. In Europe, the formulation currently available for adults is trivalent (anti-A, B, E). A heptavalent (anti-A to G) product is also available. In the USA, bivalent (anti A, B) and monovalent (anti-E) antitoxins are distributed; for infant botulism, a human derived botulinum immune globulin (BIG-IV, anti-A-B) is available.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis varies depending on the different forms of botulism, but is generally correlated with the rapidity of diagnosis and medical assistance. Death resulting from respiratory failure is rare when the patients receive appropriate medical assistance.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: GNE myopathy is a rare autosomal recessive distal myopathy characterized by early adult-onset, slowly to moderately progressive distal muscle weakness that preferentially affects the tibialis anterior muscle and that usually spares the quadriceps femoris. Muscle biopsy reveals presence of rimmed vacuoles.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): DMRV; Distal myopathy with rimmed vacuoles; HIBM2; Hereditary inclusion body myopathy type 2; IBM2; Inclusion body myopathy type 2; Nonaka myopathy; Quadriceps-sparing myopathy; Distal myopathy, Nonaka type

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Worldwide prevalence is estimated at 1/1,000,000, however it is more frequent in populations of Persian Jewish and Japanese ethnicity.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease usually starts during the third decade of life (but the onset may range from the early teens to the 5th decade). Typically, distal weakness in the legs with foot drop is the first sign, followed by (usually) slow progression to the proximal muscles (thigh) and the upper limbs (hand muscles). Shoulder girdle muscles are subsequently involved, with relative sparing of the triceps. Neck flexor muscles are also commonly affected. A unique clinical pattern of this myopathy is sparing of quadriceps in spite of major involvement of other thigh muscles. Unusual patterns of onset in proximal lower limb musculature and even in the upper limbs have been observed. Ocular, pharyngeal, and cardiac muscles are usually spared. Respiratory muscles are generally not affected until the very late stages in wheelchair-bound patients. Occasionally, affected individuals may present facial weakness.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: GNE myopathy is caused by biallelic mutations in the GNE gene (9p13.3) which encodes a bi-functional enzyme involved in the sialic acid biosynthetic pathway. Mutations in this gene result in a 30-60% decrease in enzyme activity leading to a decreased sialylation of glycoproteins and glycolipids. Hyposialylation appears to be involved in disease pathogenesis, but the process by which a defect in GNE leads to muscle disease is still elusive. With increasing number of patients, genotype-phenotype correlations are currently emerging.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected in individuals with early-onset foot drop, negative dominant family history, sustained quadriceps sparing despite marked weakness of all other thigh muscles, modest elevation of serum creatine kinase (2-5x), muscle biopsy showing fiber size variation (with atrophy) and presence of rimmed vacuoles and congophilic protein aggregates. MRI reveals a characteristic pattern of muscle involvement with (from the early stages of the disease) severe fatty-fibrous replacement of the biceps femoris short head muscles, accompanied by less severe involvement of the gluteus minimus, tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis and digitorum longus, soleus and gastrocnemius medialis muscles. Genetic screening revealing pathogenic variants in GNE confirms the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other adult-onset distal myopathies with rimmed vacuolar pathology (i.e. distal myopathy, Welander type; tibial muscular dystrophy; adult-onset distal myopathy due to VCP mutation; and vocal cord and pharyngeal distal myopathy), myofibrillar myopathies, and Laing early-onset distal myopathy.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them of the 25% risk of having an affected child.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: In the absence of a proven effective therapy, management remains mainly supportive. Metabolic supplementation with sialic acid or a precursor of sialic acid, as well as gene therapy, are under investigation.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Most patients become wheelchair-bound after 15-20 years of disease onset. About 5% of patients have atypical early involvement of the quadriceps muscle resulting in earlier non-ambulation.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare deletion of all or part of the short arm of chromosome 18 characterized by a highly variable phenotype, most commonly including global developmental delay, short stature, and dysmorphic facial features.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Monosomy 18p syndrome incidence is estimated to be about 1:50,000 live birth. A female-to-male ratio of 3:2 has been observed.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Monosomy 18p syndrome has unspecific clinical features that vary considerably within patients depending on the deletion size and specific breakpoints. Most common features include global developmental delay, moderate-to-severe intellectual disability, and short stature. Movement disorders such as dystonia and hypotonia have been frequently reported. Patients often present with dysmorphic facial features such as a round face, epicanthic folds, strabismus, ptosis, hypertelorism, short and protruding philtrum, downturned corners of mouth, and protruding ears with hypoplastic antihelix. Microcephaly, micrognathia, dental anomalies, and a short neck are also frequently present. White matter abnormalities have been reported in >50%, pituitary abnormalities and holoprosencephaly in 10-15% of affected individuals. Congenital heart defects, skeletal malformations, immunodeficiency, and genitourinary malformations have been described.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In two-thirds of the cases, 18p- syndrome is due to a mere terminal deletion occurring de novo. In the remaining cases, the following are possible: a de novo translocation with loss of 18p, missegregation of a parental translocation or inversion, or a ring chromosome 18. Parental transmission of monosomy 18p syndrome has been reported. In approximately half of the cases, the breakpoint occurs in the centromeric region, while in the other cases, breakpoints are distributed throughout the entire 18p region. There appear to be genotype-phenotype correlations and dosage-sensitive genes, but these remain to be fully established.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on cytogenetic analysis such as karyotyping including FISH and SNP array or on NGS-based CNV analysis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis may include a wide number of syndromes with short stature and intellectual deficiency.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis. Preimplantation genetic diagnosis is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Recurrence risk for siblings is low for de novo deletions and translocations, but is significant if a parental rearrangement is present. Affected individuals have a 50% risk of having an affected child.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is symptom-based and requires a multidisciplinary approach that may include occupational, physical, and speech therapy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy does not seem significantly reduced, but can be reduced in patients with severe brain malformations.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Trisomy 9p is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from a partial or complete trisomy of the short arm of chromosome 9, with a wide phenotypic variablility, typically characterized by intellectual disability, craniofacial dysmorphism (e.g. microcephaly, large anterior fontanel, hypertelorism, strabismus, downslanting palpebral fissures, malformed, low-set, protruding ears, bulbous nose, macrostomia, down-turned corners of mouth, micrognathia), digital anomalies (brachydactyly and clinodactyly), and short stature. Less frequently patients present with cardiopathy and renal, skeletal, and central nervous system malformations.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Duplication 9p; Duplication of the short arm of chromosome 9; Trisomy of the short arm of chromosome 9

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Trisomy 9p is described as the fourth most frequent chromosome anomaly and a common autosomal trisomy. To date, over 150 patients with 9p duplication have been reported. The duplicated segment is most often derived from a parent who is a reciprocal translocation carrier. However, approximately 15 cases of de novo 9p duplication have also been described. Familial occurrences, including the first reported instance in two successive generations, indicate its hereditary potential. [PMC8489072, PMC4868013, PMC4438924, PMC3711006, PMC1050821]

[PMC12097821, PMC11607743, PMC10099690, PMC8489072, PMC4868013]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Trisomy 9p syndrome involves various cytogenetic and molecular to identify the characteristic chromosomal abnormalities. Conventional karyotype analysis, often utilizing G-banding or GTG-banding techniques, is a primary diagnostic tool. More detailed characterization of rearrangements and confirmation of findings can be achieved through spectral karyotyping, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), M-FISH, and molecular cytogenetics with multicolor banding probes. Advanced molecular approaches such as copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq), chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), and OaCGH (Oligonucleotide array Comparative Genomic Hybridization) are employed to detect submicroscopic aberrations and define breakpoint regions. High-resolution whole-genome sequencing and sequence analyses of microdissected chromosomes further contribute to precise breakpoint definition, aiding in genetic counseling and understanding the origin of these complex chromosomal changes. His medical history included strabismus, cryptorchidism, and severe intellectual disabilities. He also had epilepsy. His mother seemed to have slight intellectual disability. A physical examination revealed malformations. The lateral and fourth ventricles were dilated using computed tomography. CGG repeats in the 5' untranslated region of FMR1 gene were normal. G-banding and spectral karyotyping revealed a novel unbalanced X-autosomal translocation, with a karyotype of 46,Y,der(X)t(X;9)(p22.33;p12); distal trisomy of 9p and distal Xp nullisomy. here, a case of a neonate with an unbalanced chromosomal translocation due to a maternal chromosomal translocation carriage that resulted in the presence of trisomy 9p combined with a... [PMC12097821, PMC11607743, PMC10099690, PMC10476427, PMC9137177]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for Trisomy 9p syndrome addresses specific complications, such as congenital hydrocephalus, which may require complex and individualized therapeutic approaches. In one reported case, hydrocephalus caused by excessive cerebrospinal fluid production necessitated multiple interventions, including ventriculoperitoneal and ventriculoatrial shunts. Endoscopic choroid plexus coagulation was performed to reduce fluid production, complemented by pharmaceutical treatment with acetazolamide and furosemide. Coexisting conditions like congenital heart disease can further complicate the therapeutic strategy. [PMC9137177]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Acquired monoclonal Ig light chain-associated Fanconi syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare monoclonal gammopathy characterized by renal proximal tubule dysfunction secondary to monoclonal kappa light chain deposits in proximal tubular cells. Clinical presentation is with variable chronic kidney disease, low molecular weight proteinuria, aminoaciduria, hyperphosphaturia, uricosuria, bicarbonaturia, and non-diabetic glycosuria. Renal phosphate and urate wasting may cause hypophosphatemia and hypouricaemia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Acquired monoclonal immunoglobulin light chain-associated Fanconi syndrome; Acquired Fanconi syndrome secondary to monoclonal gammopathy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, less than 100 cases have been reported in the medical literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Presentation is often in patients over 50 years of age with a degree of chronic kidney disease (CKD). There will be low molecular weight proteinuria, generalised aminoaciduria, uricosuria, phosphaturia, bicarbonaturia (which may cause a mild metabolic acidosis) and normoglycemic glycosuria. Low molecular weight proteinuria is the most sensitive test, and non-diabetic glycosuria is the most specific. There may be hypophosphatemia and hypouricemia and/or a mild metabolic acidosis. Urinary phosphate wasting may be severe enough to cause bone demineralization and rickets in children or osteomalacia in adults. Bone pain or pathological fractures are a possible presentation of this condition. The disease often occurs in the setting of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance and less commonly in multiple myeloma or Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Typically, the monoclonal light chains are of the variable kappa-1 (VK1) subgroup which resist proteolysis in the proximal tubular cells, and results in self-aggregation and crystal formation in the endolysosomal compartment.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made by demonstrating the renal Fanconi syndrome with the presence of low molecular weight proteinuria (and phosphaturia or glycosuria, if present) along with a monoclonal gammopathy. The diagnosis may be confirmed by a kidney biopsy (which may be indicated when establishing the diagnosis of myeloma). Findings on light microscopy include atrophy, dedifferentiation and intracytoplasmic inclusions in the proximal tubule epithelium. Proximal tubule cells are typically positive for kappa LCs (and less frequently lambda LCs) on immunofluorescence. Ultrastructural studies reveal crystals (rhomboid), located in proximal tubular cells lysosomes or free in the cytoplasm. Additional investigations required include bone marrow aspiration or biopsy to identify the clone, and evaluation of serum and urine immunoglobulin free light chains.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis should include other types of monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (AL amyloidosis, monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease, and myeloma cast nephropathy), in addition to other causes of FS (including autoimmune disorders, drugs, or heavy metal poisoning).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: If there is severe urinary phosphate wasting, or osteomalacia (low bone mineral density) then phosphate supplements should be given. Bone demineralization starts before the serum phosphate falls. All patients with an associated overt lymphoid disorder should receive appropriate chemotherapy. Otherwise, treatment should be adapted to the degree of renal failure. CKD 1-3 stages: chemotherapy should be considered to slow progression to ESRD. Cyclophosphamide, bortezomib or thalidomide-based treatment are the best options. High dose melphalan (HDM) supported by autologous peripheral blood cell transplantation (ASCT) may be performed in selected nonresponding patients, although the benefit of this strategy remains to be proven. CKD 4-5 stages: patients who are eligible for renal allograft, chemotherapy (including HDM/ASCT) should be considered prior to transplantation. In patients not eligible for renal transplantation, introduction of chemotherapy has no benefit.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Progression of CKD is slow.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare mycosis caused by ubiquitous, opportunistic fungi of the order Mucorales, characterized by tissue infarction and necrosis due to invasion of the vasculature by hyphae. The spectrum of clinical manifestations depends on the route of infection and includes rhinocerebral, pulmonary, cutaneous, gastrointestinal, renal, and disseminated forms. The disease is usually rapidly progressive and associated with high mortality.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: The global incidence of invasive mucormycosis (mucor) infection is on the rise due in part to an increased utilization of immunosuppressive therapies to treat malignancies and autoimmune diseases. While cirrhosis has previously been considered a risk factor for fungal infections, very little is known about the inciting factors precipitating development of isolated cutaneous mucormycosis infection. This form of mucor poses a significant mortality risk despite antifungal and surgical treatments and has been documented in only 5 patients with cirrhosis prior to our case report. This case report presents the sixth documented case of cutaneous mucormycosis in a patient with cirrhosis and explore nosocomial etiologies for its progression to clinically significant infection. Mucormycosis is a rare opportunistic fungal infection usually seen in patients with diabetic ketoacidosis or severe... [PMC12276409, PMC12220414, PMC12049641, PMC12332211, PMC11980106]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Zygomycosis, an aggressive and life-threatening opportunistic fungal infection, primarily affects immunocompromised individuals, including those with diabetes, hematologic malignancies, solid organ transplants, or cirrhosis. It manifests in various forms: rhino-orbital disease, which can masquerade as acute dacryocystitis and lead to orbital involvement or maxillary osteonecrosis; pulmonary mucormycosis, presenting with fever, cough, and rapidly progressive lung cavities; and hepatic or gastrointestinal forms, characterized by fever, abdominal pain, and potential organ failure or perforation. Cutaneous mucormycosis can be acute and fatal or chronic with an indolent course. The infection is known for its rapid progression, angioinvasive nature, and high morbidity and mortality, often leading to sepsis and multiorgan failure. [PMC12276409, PMC12220414, PMC12148331, PMC12049641, PMC12332211]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Zygomycosis, often referred to as mucormycosis, is a rare, aggressive, and life-threatening opportunistic fungal infection caused by various Mucorales fungi, including Rhizopus arrhizus, Mucor variabilis, Lichtheimia ramosa, Rhizopus microsporus, Rhizomucor pusillus, Cunninghamella bertholletiae, and Mucor indicus. It predominantly affects immunocompromised individuals. Common predisposing conditions include diabetes (especially poorly controlled type 2 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis), hematologic malignancies, solid organ transplantation, severe aplastic anemia, and those undergoing chemotherapy or immunosuppressive therapies. Other risk factors include cirrhosis, trauma history, ICU admission, corticosteroid treatment, concurrent COVID-19 infection, and contact with contaminated water. [PMC12276409, PMC12220414, PMC12148331, PMC12049641, PMC12332211]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Severe aplastic anemia (SAA) is an uncommon life-threatening disorder characterized by hypocellular bone marrow and pancytopenia. It is typically associated with immune-mediated mechanisms, requiring immunosuppressive therapy (IST) or hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT). Infections, especially invasive fungal infections such as mucormycosis and aspergillosis, constitute principal causes of morbidity and mortality in patients with SAA. Genetic predispositions, including perforin (PRF1) polymorphisms, may further complicate disease outcomes by impairing immune function. a case of a 36-year-old female patient diagnosed with SAA, for whom IST was considered, due to the unavailability of a matched sibling donor for HSCT. The patient presented with a feverish condition and deep neck space abscesses were revealed by imaging, caused by invasive aspergillosis. To prioritize infection... [PMC12101316]

While cirrhosis has previously been considered a risk factor for fungal infections, very little is known about the inciting factors precipitating development of isolated cutaneous mucormycosis infection. DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic hepatic disease characterized by very high serum bilirubin levels in a newborn, clinically presenting as jaundice during the first few days of life. The condition is usually self-resolving, although in some cases it can lead to kernicterus with corresponding symptoms (including lethargy, high-pitched crying, hypotonia, missing reflexes, vomiting, or seizures, among others), which may result in chronic disability and even death.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Transient familial neonatal hyperbilirubinemia presents as unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia or jaundice in newborns, often associated with breast milk jaundice and UGT1A1 polymorphisms. It can manifest as intense yellowing of the skin and eyes, with bilirubin levels sometimes requiring interventions like exchange transfusion. While typically benign with good clinical condition and growth, some cases may show elevated liver and biliary enzymes. Importantly, other causes of jaundice, such as hemolytic diseases, infections, or metabolic disorders, are usually ruled out. Liver function tests normalize by 6-7 months of life, highlighting its transient nature. [PMC4039948, PMC3639837]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Neonatal hyperbilirubinemia, including prolonged jaundice, can stem from deficient activity of the UGT1A1 gene, which is essential for bilirubin conjugation. Gilbert's syndrome, characterized by reduced UGT1A1 activity, is linked to prevalent UGT1A1 polymorphisms, such as G71R and A(TA)7TAA. The G71R polymorphism has been associated with breastfeeding jaundice and neonatal hyperbilirubinemia in both term and preterm infants. Breast milk jaundice, a form of neonatal jaundice related to breastfeeding, may also present with transient elevations in liver and biliary enzymes. Genetic testing for Gilbert's syndrome should be considered for infants with prolonged jaundice and a positive family history. [PMC11015704, PMC4039948, PMC3639837]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Phytobacter diazotrophicus (P. diazotrophicus) is an opportunistic pathogen that causes nosocomial outbreaks and sepsis. However, there are no reports of P. diazotrophicus isolated from human blood in China. A 27-day-old female infant was admitted to our hospital with fever and high bilirubin levels. The clinical features included jaundice, abnormal coagulation, cholestasis, fever, convulsions, weak muscle tension, sucking weakness, ascites, abnormal tyrosine metabolism, cerebral oedema, abnormal liver function, clavicle fracture, and haemolytic anaemia. The strain isolated from the patient's blood was identified as P. diazotrophicus by whole-genome sequencing (WGS). Galactosemia type 1 (GALAC1) was diagnosed using whole-exome sequencing (WES). Based on drug sensitivity , 10 days of anti-infective treatment with meropenem combined with lactose-free milk powder improved symptoms. P.... [PMC11186240, PMC11015704, PMC8130366, PMC4039948, PMC3639837]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for neonatal hyperbilirubinemia and jaundice encompasses various conditions. These include breast milk jaundice, which can be associated with elevated liver and biliary enzymes, and genetic disorders affecting bilirubin conjugation, such as Gilbert's Syndrome or UGT1A1 polymorphisms (e.g., G71R). Neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis caused by citrin deficiency (NICCD) is another common form of neonatal jaundice. More severe etiologies include metabolic diseases like Galactosemia type 1, which can present with high bilirubin levels, cholestasis, and other systemic features, often complicated by sepsis. When hyperbilirubinemia is exaggerated, it is important to exclude haemolytic diseases, infections, or hypothyroidism. [PMC11186240, PMC11015704, PMC8130366, PMC4039948, PMC3639837]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic testing should be considered for infants with prolonged jaundice, especially when there is a positive family history of conditions like Gilbert's Syndrome. Genetic analysis can identify specific polymorphisms in genes such as UGT1A1 (e.g., G71R) or mutations in SLC25A13, which are associated with reduced bilirubin conjugation or neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis, respectively. Such testing requires informed parental consent and helps in diagnosing the underlying cause of hyperbilirubinemia. [PMC11015704, PMC8130366, PMC3639837]
