DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Shigellosis is a bacterial infection leading to dysentery and is caused by Shigella, which are small, ubiquitous Gram-negative bacteria belonging to the enterobacteria family. There are four species: S. dysenteriae, S. flexneri, S. boydii and S. sonnei, all of which cause bacillary dysentery and are strictly limited to human hosts.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinically, after an incubation period of 2-3 days, dysenteric syndrome appears, with 10-30 glairy, bloody watery stools per day, a high temperature (40°C) and abdominal pain. Examination of the intestinal mucosa with endoscopy shows multiple ulcerations.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In western Europe, cases of shigellosis are either imported or limited to small familial epidemics and usually food-borne. They are mostly due to S. sonnei. The virulence of shigellas is a result of their ability to invade the intestinal epithelium by passing between contiguous epithelial cells, leading to the destruction of the intestinal mucosa.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on evidence of the bacilli in stools.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment revolves around administration of antibiotics, quinolones and cotrimoxazole, and rehydration to alleviate symptoms. Strict isolation of affected individuals is essential to limit epidemics. The disease is notifiable
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Shigellosis can present with symptoms that mimic other severe conditions, making differential diagnosis crucial. Systemic inflammatory syndromes, including sepsis and multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C), may be suspected, particularly in cases with shock, cardiac dysfunction, and hyperinflammation. Neurological manifestations, such as altered mental status, can lead to an initial suspicion of bacterial meningitis or viral encephalitis, requiring differentiation from Shigella-associated encephalopathy. Furthermore, laboratory identification can be challenging, as Shigella species may be misidentified as Escherichia coli by conventional and even some newer technologies like MALDI-TOF, especially in blood cultures. [PMC12166990, PMC6904198, PMC5775773, PMC4422933]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A disorder defining by the association of Perineal hemangioma, External genitalia malformations, Lipomyelomeningocele, Vesicorenal abnormalities, Imperforate anus, and Skin tag. Eleven cases have been reported.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): PELVIS syndrome; Perineal hemangioma-external genitalia malformations-lipomyelomeningocele-vesicorenal abnormalities-imperforate anus-skin tag syndrome; SACRAL syndrome; Lower body hemangioma-urogenital anomalies-myelopathy-bony deformities-anorectal and arterial malformations-renal anomalies syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Perineal groove is a well-defined clinical entity that belongs to a broader group of anorectal malformations. It is characterized by a non-epithelialized mucous membrane that appears as an erythematous sulcus in the perineal midline, extending from the posterior vaginal fourchette to the anterior anal orifice. The defect is gradually cicatrized, unless there are complications like infection, defecation disorders, trauma, and bleeding. The differential diagnosis includes several other conditions like trauma, infection, irritant dermatitis, lichen sclerosis, and ulcerated hemangioma. Since it is a rare malformation, it is often misdiagnosed and its presence often elicits unnecessary diagnostic workup and intervention. In this respect, neonatologists, dermatologists, or pediatric surgeons may under- or overestimate it. four cases of perineal groove out of 2250 live births at a Greek... [PMC6724277]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Perineal groove is a well-defined clinical entity that belongs to a broader group of anorectal malformations. It is characterized by a non-epithelialized mucous membrane that appears as an erythematous sulcus in the perineal midline, extending from the posterior vaginal fourchette to the anterior anal orifice. In this respect, neonatologists, dermatologists, or pediatric surgeons may under- or overestimate it. four cases of perineal groove out of 2250 live births at a Greek... [PMC6724277]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Cavernous hemangioma is a congenital, benign vascular tumor that occurs in the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Scrotal hemangiomas are rare entities and are usually diagnosed in childhood. Adult scrotal hemangiomas are also extremely rare. They are infrequently encountered in adults because they are usually removed in childhood. Urologists often face difficulties in deciding surgery to treat a genital cavernous hemangioma. Here, a case of scrotal cavernous hemangioma that involved the entire penis and scrotum, and extended to the perineum in a 44-year-old man, and we review the literature. [PMC11917761]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: This syndrome is characterized by osteopetrosis, agenesis of the corpus callosum, cerebral atrophy and a small hippocampus.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It has been described in a brother and a sister born to nonconsanguineous Caucasian parents.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The children died at the ages of 1 and 9 months, respectively. Several additional cases combining axonal dystrophy and osteopetrosis have been described.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology remains unclear.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Autosomal recessive inheritance has been suggested.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital nephrotic syndrome characterized by massive protein loss and marked edema manifesting in utero or during the first 3 months of life.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: This type of nephrotic syndrome is more frequent in Finland with a prevalence of 1/8,200 births. The disease is observed in various ethnic groups worldwide but the prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Affected children show massive proteinuria and edema starting in utero (fetal hydrops). Children usually have low birth weight and are born prematurely; the weight of the placenta constitutes more than 25% of the birth weight. Severe nephrotic syndrome develops soon after birth; typical features include hypoalbuminemia, hyperlipidemia, hypothyreosis, abdominal distension and edema with associated failure to thrive, increased susceptibility to thromboembolic events and severe infections. Histologically, microcystic dilatations of the tubules are seen whereas glomeruli are only slightly modified initially, with variable mesangial cell hypercellularity and/or endocapillary hypercellularity. Electron microscopy shows glomerular effacement of the podocytes.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by recessive mutations in the NPHS1 gene (19q13). NPHS1 encodes for Nephrin, a zipper-like protein, which is essential for the porous structure of the glomerular slit diaphragm. To date more than 200 NPHS1 mutations have been detected but two of them have a particular high frequency in affected Finnish children, one is a two base pair deletion in exon 2 resulting in a truncated protein (Fin-major) and the other is a nonsense mutation in exon 26 (Fin minor). These two mutations are observed in 94% of Finnish patients but are quite rare outside Finland.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is suspected on clinical grounds and confirmed by genetic analysis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other forms of early onset nephrotic syndrome, including Denys Drash syndrome, Pierson syndrome, Galloway Mowat syndrome, Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia and congenital membranous nephropathy due to maternal anti-neutral endopeptidase alloimmunization.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal proteinuria results in an up to 10-fold increase in alpha-fetoprotein concentrations as early as in the 15th week of gestation, with a parallel but smaller rise in the maternal serum level. However, heterozygous mutations in the NPHS1 gene can also lead to increased levels of alpha-fetoprotein, leading to misdiagnosis. Reliable antenatal diagnosis is achieved by gene analysis on a trophoblastic sample.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of disease transmission is autosomal recessive. The risk of recurrence in siblings of an affected individual is 25%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The nephrotic syndrome does not respond to any immunosuppressive therapy and treatment is largely symptomatic, comprising frequent albumin infusions, protein-rich diet, anti-proteinuric pharmacotherapy with RAS (renin-angiotensin system) inhibitors and indomethacin, anticoagulation, thyroid hormone supplementation and aggressive treatment of infections. In case of failure to thrive despite these measures, uni- or bilateral nephrectomy may be necessary to stop the massive protein loss.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With adequate supportive care, most children survive long-term but develop end-stage kidney disease requiring renal replacement therapy within the first 2-3 years of life. Five-year patient and graft survival after transplantation is around 90%, similar as in infants with other causes of end-stage kidney disease. Post-transplant disease recurrence is limited to patients who are homozygous for the Fin major mutation, who have a 30% risk to develop de novo glomerulonephritis due to circulating anti-nephrin antibodies.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by the association of camptodactyly, multiple eye defects (fibrosis of the medial rectus muscle, severe myopia, ptosis and exophthalmos), scoliosis, flexion contractures and facial anomalies (arched eyebrows, facial asymmetry with an abnormal skull shape, a prominent nose, small mouth, low-set and dysplastic ears, and a low nuchal hairline).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Distal arthrogryposis type 5D (DA5D) is an autosomal recessive disease. The clinical symptoms include contractures of the joints of limbs, especially camptodactyly of the hands and/or feet, unilateral ptosis, a round-shaped face, arched eyebrows, and micrognathia, without ophthalmoplegia. ECEL1 is a DA5D causative gene that encodes a membrane-bound metalloprotease. ECEL1 plays important roles in the final axonal arborization of motor nerves in limb skeletal muscles and neuromuscular junction formation during prenatal development. A DA5D family with webbing of the elbows and fingers was recruited. We performed whole-exome sequencing (WES) and filtered mutations by disease-causing genes of arthrogryposis multiplex congenita (AMC). Mutational analysis and cosegregation confirmation were then performed. We identified novel compound heterozygous mutations of ECEL1 (NM_004826: c.69C>A, p.C23∗... [PMC7273484, PMC5789735, PMC5588382, PMC1050402]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: The syndrome is characterized by multiple congenital joint contractures, including camptodactyly of the hands and/or feet, and flexion contractures of the elbows, shoulders, and knees. Facial dysmorphic features often include ptosis, blepharophimosis, micrognathia or microretrognathia, a round-shaped face, arched eyebrows, and antimongoloid eye slant. Other skeletal anomalies reported are arachnodactyly, slender ribs, hooked lateral clavicular ends, bilateral radial head dislocations, short distal ulnae, and vertebral anomalies. Skin webs or pterygium may be present, affecting the neck, elbows, and fingers. Additional features can include joint laxity, flat feet, recurrent patellar dislocations, short stature, developmental delay, and conductive deafness. Respiratory impairment and orchidopexy have also been noted. [PMC7273484, PMC5789735, PMC5588382, PMC1050402]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The camptodactyly-joint contractures-facial skeletal defects syndrome can manifest as several distinct autosomal recessive conditions. Distal arthrogryposis type 5D (DA5D), an autosomal recessive disease, is caused by mutations in the ECEL1 gene, which plays roles in motor nerve axonal arborization and neuromuscular junction formation. Specific novel compound heterozygous mutations (c.69C>A, p.C23∗ and c.1810G>A, p.G604R) and a homozygous splice site mutation (c.1184+1G>T) in ECEL1 have been identified in affected individuals. Another autosomal recessive condition, Van Den Ende-Gupta Syndrome (VDEGS), is associated with a homozygous mutation in the SCARF2 gene (c.773G > A (p. Cys258Tyr)). Multiple pterygium syndrome, also inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, presents with similar features. [PMC7273484, PMC5789735, PMC5588382, PMC1050402]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, including features like camptodactyly, joint contractures, and facial dysmorphism. Genetic testing is a key diagnostic method. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) or full gene sequencing is used to identify causative mutations. For instance, mutations in the ECEL1 gene are identified in distal arthrogryposis type 5D, while Van Den Ende-Gupta Syndrome is diagnosed by mutations in the SCARF2 gene. Mutational analysis and cosegregation confirmation are performed to detect and confirm these pathogenic variants. [PMC7273484, PMC5789735, PMC5588382]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses include distal arthrogryposis type 5D (DA5D), an autosomal recessive condition characterized by limb joint contractures, camptodactyly, ptosis, and micrognathia. Van Den Ende-Gupta Syndrome (VDEGS), also autosomal recessive, presents with camptodactyly, elbow flexion contractures, blepharophimosis, and various skeletal anomalies such as slender ribs and radial head dislocations. Multiple pterygium syndrome is another consideration, featuring multiple congenital joint contractures, camptodactyly, skin webs, ptosis, and antimongoloid eye slant. [PMC7273484, PMC5789735, PMC5588382, PMC1050402]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Several syndromes characterized by camptodactyly, joint contractures, and facial skeletal defects, such as distal arthrogryposis type 5D (DA5D), Van Den Ende-Gupta Syndrome (VDEGS), and multiple pterygium syndrome, are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Affected individuals with DA5D may have novel compound heterozygous or homozygous mutations in the ECEL1 gene. Similarly, VDEGS is associated with homozygous mutations in SCARF2. In autosomal recessive inheritance, unaffected parents of affected children are typically heterozygous carriers of the causative mutation, as observed in families with VDEGS and DA5D, including those with consanguineous parents. [PMC7273484, PMC5789735, PMC5588382, PMC1050402]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: The aim of this work was to report a case of an Emirati child who presented with developmental delay and multiple congenital abnormalities that are consistent with distal arthrogryposis type 5D. Clinical presentation and intervention: The clinical presentation comprised contractures of the shoulders, elbows, and knees in addition to camptodactyly and neck pterygium. The facial dysmorphic features noted include ptosis and microretrognathia. Importantly, left orchidopexy was also observed and corrected surgically. Whole exome sequencing revealed that the patient is homozygous for the novel c.1184+1G>T variant in endothelin-converting enzyme-like 1 (ECEL1). This is a case of a novel homozygous splice site mutation in the ECEL1 gene in a child with a phenotype consistent with distal arthrogryposis type 5D. The child was born to consanguineous Emirati parents heterozygous for the novel ECEL1... [PMC5588382]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for individuals with this syndrome is characterized by potential morbidity, particularly secondary to respiratory impairment. Conductive deafness may also be a feature of the syndrome, contributing to the overall clinical course. These factors highlight key areas of concern in the long-term management and outlook for affected individuals. [PMC1050402]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital malformation syndrome characterized by bilateral absence/hypoplasia of the radii with presence of both thumbs, and thrombocytopenia. Additional manifestations can include cow's milk allergy, anomalies of the lower limbs, heart and genitourinary system.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of thrombocytopenia-absent radius (TAR) syndrome is estimated at around 1/100,000-200,000 people.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Individuals with TAR syndrome almost always have bilateral absence or hypoplasia of the radii. The thumbs are always present, which is highly specific for TAR syndrome. Upper limbs may be more severely affected (hypoplasia or absence of the ulnae and/or humeri, fingers syndactyly, fifth-finger clinodactyly). Lower limbs are affected in almost 50% of cases with variable severity (hip dislocation, coxa valga, femoral and/or tibial torsion, genu varum, absence of the patella). The most severe limb involvement is tetraphocomelia. Thrombocytopenia is congenital or develop within the first few weeks to months of life. Usually, platelet counts remain low during the first two years of life; then, they increase but do not normalize. Additional recurrent manifestations include: cardiac anomalies (atrial and/or ventricular septal defect, patent foramen ovale), gastro-intestinal involvement (cow's milk allergy, increased susceptibility to gastro-enteritis), genitourinary anomalies (kidney agenesis or malrotation, horseshoe kidney, hydronephrosis, pyelectasis). Other rare manifestations include Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome, rib and vertebral anomalies, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, transient leukemoid reaction, acute myeloid or lymphoblastic leukemia. Cognitive development is usually normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: TAR syndrome is caused by compound heterozygosity for a null (most often a 1q21.1 deletion including RBM8A) and a hypomorphic RBM8A allele.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made on the clinical signs and confirmed by molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses are other disorders associated with radial aplasia, with a genetic etiology (Holt-Oram syndrome, ESCO2-spectrum disorder, Fanconi anemia, RAPADILINO syndrome, SALL4-related disorders), or not (VACTERL association, thalidomide embryopathy, fetal valproate spectrum disorder).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis may be suspected by fetal ultrasound examination identifying radial anomalies, and confirmed by molecular genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: TAR syndrome is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Penetrance is complete, with variable expressivity. Several characteristics are unusual in autosomal recessive disorders: null alleles are rare and can occur de novo in the proband, the percentage of affected sibs is consequently lower than expected; hypomorphic alleles are common, therefore an apparent parent-to-child transmission can be observed resulting in pseudo-dominant inheritance. Biallelic carriers of hypomorphic variants are asymptomatic.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative treatment for TAR syndrome. Symptomatic treatment of manifestations and prevention of complications include: early detection of thrombocytopenia, prevention of bleeding and hemorrhage, platelet transfusions in case of severe thrombocytopenia, surgical interventions if required to manage cardiac, urinary or skeletal malformations, avoidance of cow's milk.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable and mainly conditioned by the severity of thrombocytopenia and its complications (intracranial, digestive hemorrhage). Cardiac defects, renal malformations, acute complications of cow's milk intolerance, acute leukemia can also affect the prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: X-linked sideroblastic anemia and spinocerebellar ataxia
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare syndromic, inherited form of sideroblastic anemia characterized by mild to moderate anemia (with hypochromia and microcytosis) and early-onset, non- or slowly progressive spinocerebellar ataxia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Pagon-Bird-Detter syndrome; X-linked sideroblastic anemia with ataxia; XLSA-A

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: X-linked sideroblastic anemia and ataxia (XLSA-A) prevalence is unknown. Less than 20 genetically confirmed patients have been reported to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: .XLSA-A usually presents before the age of 3 years. Anemia is usually asymptomatic. In males, spinocerebellar symptoms are apparent in childhood and can include delayed walking, predominantly truncal ataxia, dysmetria and dysdiadochokinesis. Dysarthria and intention tremor are sometimes present. Ataxia may improve over time, but in the fifth to sixth decade of life a slow deterioration of walking is noted. Upper motor neuron signs in the legs such as equivocal or extensor plantar responses, brisk deep tendon reflexes and unsustained ankle clonus are sometimes present. Strabismus, as well as mild learning disability and depression, have also been reported in some, but intellectual abilities are generally within the normal range. Hepatic and systemic iron overload does not occur. Females are clinically asymptomatic.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: XLSA-A is caused by mutations in the ABCB7 gene (Xq13.3), encoding a mitochondrial ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter protein, which plays a role in heme production and iron homeostasis. A pathogenic variant in this gene alters the availability of reduced iron and therefore disrupts heme biosynthesis. The ABCB7 gene is highly expressed in both the bone marrow and the cerebellum, which may explain ataxia.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the presence of characteristic neurological and blood test findings. Mild to moderate hypochromic, microcytic anemia is noted in all males and both whole blood total erythrocyte protoporphyrin (TEP) and zinc erythrocyte protoporphyrin (ZnEP) are elevated. Bone marrow examination demonstrates the presence of increased iron stores with ring sideroblasts and peripheral blood smear reveals Pappenheimer bodies. In the majority of cases magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows cerebellar atrophy/hypoplasia. Female carriers display hematological abnormalities. Molecular genetic testing identifies a ABCB7 gene variation, confirming the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnosis includes other forms/causes of ataxia that typically present before the age of 3 years such as ataxia-telangiectasia, infantile-onset spinocerebellar ataxia, congenital disorder of glycosylation, and cerebellar malformations (e.g. Dandy-Walker malformation). Ataxia with vitamin E deficiency, Friedreich ataxia, ataxia - oculomotor apraxia type 1 and 2, and X linked sideroblastic anemia , the most common form of congenital sideroblastic anemia (without ataxia), should also be excluded.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal testing is possible in families with a known ABCB7 mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is X-linked recessive and gentic counselling should be offerend to affected families. Where the female is a carrier, the risk to male offspring inheriting the disease is 50%, female offspring have a 50% risk of being carriers. Where a male is affected, female offspring are obligate carriers, and male offspring do not inherit the pathogenic mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for XLSA-A and treatment is symptomatic. Anemia does not require treatment. Early physical therapy may aid in the acquisition of gross motor skills. Ankle fixation orthoses and walkers may be required to aid with mobility. Weighted eating utensils promote independent skills in children. Speech therapy is recommended for those with dysarthria. Crutches or a wheelchair may be needed by some patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: While prognosis information is limited due to very few existing reports, XLSA-A does not appear to have a significant impact on life expectancy. Quality of life, however, can be significantly affected.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare mature T-cell neoplasm characterized by proliferation of small to medium-sized prolymphocytes with a mature post-thymic T-cell phenotype, involving the peripheral blood, bone marrow, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, and sometimes the skin. T-cell receptor genes are clonally rearranged. Patients typically present with hepatosplenomegaly, generalized lymphadenopathy, high leukocyte count with normal serum immunoglobulins, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. HTLV-1 serology is negative. The disease course is aggressive with generally poor prognosis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) is a rare, aggressive neoplasm of mature T-cells, most frequently affecting patients in their seventh decade of life. It is considered the most common mature T-cell leukemia in Central Europe. The disease typically presents at an advanced stage, often manifested by rapidly increasing lymphocytosis, marked bone marrow infiltration, splenomegaly, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and B symptoms. In 10-15% of cases, diagnosis is made incidentally in otherwise asymptomatic patients. [PMC12027594, PMC11371457, PMC10669936, PMC10419310]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: We encountered a patient with composite mantle cell lymphoma (MCL) and T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (T-PLL) who presented with inactive disease to active T-PLL over 8 years. A 71-year-old man was diagnosed with MCL with an atypical T-cell population showing CD2+, CD3-, CD4+, CD7+, CD8-, and CD25+; however, the cause of the T-cell population could not be determined at the first MCL diagnosis. When MCL relapsed approximately 8 years after the initial treatment, T-PLL was definitively diagnosed using the T-PLL International Study Group criteria. MCL and T-PLL were determined to coexist in the lymph nodes and bone marrow by histological or flowcytometry analysis. Retrospective flow cytometry and T-cell receptor-polymerase chain reaction analysis of the stored samples suggested that the T-cell population noted at the time of initial MCL diagnosis eight years earlier was the same clone of... [PMC12351245, PMC11915055, PMC12151792, PMC12027594, PMC11371457]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Alemtuzumab remains the frontline therapy for T-cell prolymphocytic leukemia, achieving high response rates, but these responses are rarely durable. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (alloHSCT) is considered the only curative option and significantly improves outcomes for selected patients, often following alemtuzumab, though many patients are ineligible. Relapse after alloHSCT can be managed with donor-lymphocyte infusions. Emerging therapeutic approaches include JAK/STAT inhibitors, targeting recurrent mutations and constitutive activation. Dual STAT3/STAT5 inhibition, particularly in combination with hypomethylating agents like azacytidine or BCL2-targeting agents like venetoclax, shows promising anti-leukemic potential, as venetoclax monotherapy has limited efficacy and combined BCL2 and MCL1 inhibition is synergistic. [PMC11915055, PMC12133589, PMC12027594, PMC11534987, PMC11371457]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare imprinting disorder, characterized by fetal growth restriction with no catch-up associated with feeding anomalies and dysmorphic features

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence of SRS is estimated around 1/16,000 cases.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The diagnosis is clinical, using the Netchine-Harbison clinical scoring system, and SRS is suspected if at least 4 of the following items are present: a) being born small for gestational age (birth weight and/or birth length ≤−2 SDS for gestational age); b) relative macrocephaly at birth (head circumference at birth≥1.5 SDS above birth weight and/or length SDS); c) postnatal growth failure (height at 24 ± 1 months ≤−2 SDS and/or height ≤−2 SDS below mid-parental target height); d) protruding forehead (projecting beyond the facial plane on a side view as a toddler (1-3 years); e) body asymmetry (leg length discrepancy (LLD) of ≥0.5 cm or arm asymmetry or LLD <0.5 cm with at least two other asymmetrical body part (one non-face)); and f) feeding difficulties and/or low BMI (BMI ≤−2 SDS at 24 months or current use of a feeding tube or cyproheptadine for appetite stimulation). Fifth finger clinodactyly is also frequently reported. Gastroesophageal reflux and constipation are common. Speech and/or motor delay and hypotonia have been reported. Patients also present with hypoglycaemia, premature aggressive adrenarche, early central puberty and insulin resistance during childhood.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The most common underlying mechanism is a loss of methylation on chromosome 11p15 at IGF2/H19:IG-DMR identified in around 60% of the patients. A maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 7 (upd(7)mat) is identified in ∼10% of the patients. Because of the clinical overlapping with Temple syndrome, anomalies at chromosome 14q32 are also frequently identified. Some rare genetic anomalies have also been reported in IGF2, HMGA2, CDKN1C or PLAG1 genes, however, the molecular etiology remains unknown in around 40% of patients with a positive clinical score.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The first line molecular diagnosis relies on methylation analysis at IGF2/H19:IG-DMR and search for upd(7)mat with genomic arrays. Chromosome 14 anomalies or rare genetic anomalies should be driven as molecular alternative diagnosis. As methylation anomalies occur in a mosaic manner, a skin biopsy to evaluate a second tissue can be proposed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis can be classified according to head circumference. In case of relative macrocephaly: 3M, SHORT, Floating-Harbor or, IMAGe syndrome can be evoked. Whereas, in case of microcephaly: IGF1R gene defects, Bloom, Nijmegen breakage or Meier-Gorlin syndrome can be differential diagnoses.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Fetal growth retardation can be observed by ultrasound during pregnancy. Antenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are available for some rare genetic causes of SRS, but methylation analysis is not reliable and not recommended for clinical outcome prediction.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In most cases, the overall risk of recurrence in siblings is low (11p15 anomalies). However, some familial cases with genetic anomalies can have an elevated recurrence risk.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management require a multidisciplinary approach in an expert center. Expert guidelines are available. Hypoglycemia, nutritional and pubertal aspects should be closely monitored. Recombinant growth hormone therapy can improve final height and body composition in these patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Few long-term studies are available. SRS is associated with increased risk of metabolic syndrome, obesity and cardiovascular disease in adulthood.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, non-syndromic developmental defect of the eye disorder, with high clinical and genetic heterogeneity, most frequently characterized by bilateral, symmetrical, non-progressive cataracts which present at birth or in early-childhood. Additional ocular manifestations (e.g. anterior segment dysgenesis, colobomas, nystagmus, microcornea, microphthalmia, myopia) may be associated, however other organs/systems are usually not affected.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of congenital cataracts is possible through fetal ultrasonography, with cases reported as early as 21 to 25 weeks of gestation. This method is particularly valuable for proactive fetal monitoring in genetically predisposed cases or those with a family history of congenital cataracts. Following ultrasound detection, genetic analysis, such as Whole Exome Sequencing, can confirm a genetic diagnosis by identifying specific gene variants, like a homozygous CRYBB1 variant, consistent with isolated autosomal recessive cataract. Early detection allows for timely postnatal management and treatment planning. [PMC10901674, PMC7469896]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare soft tissue tumor characterized by a slowly growing mass typically involving tendons and aponeuroses of the extremities, composed of polygonal or spindle-shaped cells with melanocytic differentiation. The tumor typically affects young adults, who often present with pain or tenderness at the tumor site. Prognosis is poor with high recurrence rates and frequent metastasis, especially to lymph nodes, lung, and bones.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Clear cell sarcoma of the tendons and aponeuroses

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) of soft tissue, a rare and aggressive melanocytic tumor, is an extremely rare form of sarcoma, representing less than 1% of all soft-tissue sarcomas. Its population-adjusted incidence ranges from 0.012 to 0.027 per 100,000, with incidence remaining stable in recent years. This tumor predominantly affects young to middle-aged adults, equally impacting both sexes, and is typically found in the tendinous sheaths and aponeuroses of the limbs, particularly the lower extremities. Gastrointestinal localization is exceptional, though related malignant gastrointestinal neuroectodermal tumors (MGNET) can occur in extragastrointestinal sites. CCS is highly aggressive, with over 30% of patients presenting with distant or lymphatic metastasis at diagnosis, and it has a high recurrence rate exceeding 80% in the first year. Prognosis is poor, and Black patients have been associated with shorter survival durations. [PMC12111261, PMC12239694, PMC11205295, PMC11100201, PMC11263060]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) of soft tissue is a rare and aggressive neoplasm originating from the neural crest, often misidentified due to its phenotypic resemblance to malignant melanoma. It is considered a melanocytic-differentiated tumor with morphological, structural, and immunohistochemical similarities to malignant melanoma. The pathognomonic genetic alteration for CCS is the gene fusion of Ewing sarcoma breakpoint region 1 (EWSR1) with activating transcription factor 1 (ATF1). Related entities, such as malignant gastrointestinal neuroectodermal tumor (MGNET), are also characterized by recurrent EWSR1 chromosomal rearrangements, specifically EWSR1::CREB1 fusions, and typically exhibit low tumor mutational burden and microsatellite stability. [PMC12111261, PMC11205295, PMC11100201, PMC8870546]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, non-syndromic, hereditary palmoplantar keratoderma characterized by diffuse, yellowish, thick hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles with a sharp demarcation at the volar border and an erythematous margin, and the epidermolytic pattern of changes on the skin biopsy, including perinuclear vacuolization, granular degeneration of keratinocytes in the spinous and granular layer, and tonofilament aggregates. Painful fissures and hyperhidrosis are frequently associated.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Diffuse erythrodermic palmoplantar keratoderma, Voerner type; Diffuse erythrodermic palmoplantar keratoderma, Vörner type; EPPK; Epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma of Voerner; Epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma of Vörner

DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (EPPK) includes other forms of palmoplantar keratoderma (PPK) and ichthyoses. Annular epidermolytic ichthyosis (AEI), a subtype of epidermolytic ichthyosis, can mimic Greither disease or erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva (EKVP), all presenting with PPK. AEI is characterized by migratory scaly plaques and PPK, with histopathology showing epidermolytic hyperkeratosis. Greither disease presents with diffuse, thick, scaly yellow PPK. EKVP-like phenotypes can also result from partial loss of function ABCA12 mutations, leading to patchy ichthyosis and erythrodermia with PPK. Palmoplantar keratoderma with deafness (PPKDFN), caused by GJB2 variants, involves severe palmoplantar hyperkeratosis. Ichthyosis Hystrix of Curth-Macklin, another epidermolytic ichthyosis, features generalized spiky hyperkeratosis and typical PPK. Additionally, diffuse non-epidermolytic PPK of Bothnian type, caused by AQP5 mutations, presents with PPK and hyperhidrosis. Autosomal recessive forms of epidermolytic PPK also exist, distinct from the autosomal dominant entity. [PMC10530436, PMC8886511, PMC9354265, PMC7335885, PMC7903949]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (EPPK, OMIM 144200) is an autosomal dominant inherited disease, clinically characterized by diffuse yellowish thickening of the skin on the palms and soles, usually with erythematous borders developing during the first weeks or months after birth. Pathogenesis of EPPK is determined by mutations in the keratin gene (KRT9). Thirty three mutations in the KRT9 gene from 100 EPPK families have been identified. Among these, 23 mutations are located in the 1A region (a mutation hot spot region), 7 are located in the 2B region, and the remaining 3 are synonymous mutations. In , three heterozygous mutations (p.N161S, p.R163W, and p.R163Q), located in regions of the gene encoding the conserved central a-helix rod domain, were detected in the KRT9 gene of the three large Chinese families. confirms that codon 163 (48 of 100 cases) is a hot spot mutation site... [PMC6330350]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Vunakizumab, an anti-IL-17A monoclonal antibody, has shown potential in treating epidermolytic ichthyosis, a condition that can involve palmoplantar hyperkeratosis. In a case of a 4-year-old boy with epidermolytic ichthyosis due to a KRT1 gene mutation, a three-month treatment with Vunakizumab significantly alleviated symptoms, including palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, and normalized inflammatory factor levels. This suggests a promising new therapeutic option for skin cornification disorders. [PMC12122345]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare group of primary bone dysplasia disorders characterized by the association of epiphyseal anomalies of long bones causing joint pain early in life, recurrent osteochondritis and early arthrosis. This group contains an heterogeneous group of diseases with variable expression. Common reported clinical signs include waddling gait and pain at onset, and moderate short stature. Some forms are mainly limited to the femoral epiphyses, while several other syndromes are characterized by the association of multiple epiphyseal dysplasia with other clinical manifestations such as myopia, deafness and facial dysmorphism. Diagnosis relies on identification of the radiological features.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous group of skeletal diseases, with mutations in at least six genes identified as causative. Autosomal dominant forms are linked to mutations in genes encoding cartilage oligomeric matrix protein (COMP), matrilin-3 (MATN3), and type IX collagen (COL9A1, COL9A2, COL9A3), with COMP mutations being the most common. Recessive MED (rMED or MED-4) is caused by mutations in the SLC26A2 (also known as DTDST) gene. Additionally, complex genomic rearrangements, such as a 6p25 rearrangement, have been implicated in some cases. Novel pathogenic variants and compound heterozygous mutations in these genes continue to expand the known genetic spectrum of MED. [PMC11593528, PMC8123746, PMC7140548, PMC5934830, PMC4236474]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous condition diagnosed through a combination of clinical, radiological, and molecular findings. Initial clinical manifestations often appear in childhood, including joint pain, stiffness, mild short stature, abnormal gait, and joint deformities such as bent lower limbs, scoliosis, or osteochondritis dissecans. Radiological examination reveals characteristic epiphyseal abnormalities, such as abnormally small and/or irregular epiphyses, hip dysplasia, brachydactyly, abnormal cartilage development, and joint space widening, with specific findings like a multilayered patella also reported. Molecular diagnosis is critical, utilizing next-generation sequencing and Sanger sequencing to identify pathogenic variants in genes such as COMP, MATN3, COL9A1, COL9A2, COL9A3, and SLC26A2 (DTDST), confirming the diagnosis and informing genetic counseling. [PMC11593528, PMC10853925, PMC8123746, PMC7140548, PMC5934830]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (MED) is a genetically heterogeneous condition with both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance patterns. Autosomal dominant forms are caused by mutations in genes such as COMP, MATN3, COL9A1, COL9A2, and COL9A3, with de novo mutations also reported (e.g., MATN3). Recessive forms, such as MED-4, are linked to mutations in SLC26A2 (also known as DTDST), where affected individuals may be homozygous or compound heterozygous, inheriting mutations from carrier parents. Molecular diagnosis is crucial for accurate genetic counseling and prognosis, especially given the clinical variability and the potential for multilocus genomic variations. Carrier status can be confirmed through segregation analysis. [PMC11593528, PMC8123746, PMC7140548, PMC5934830, PMC4236474]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Surgical treatment has been successfully applied for specific complications in multiple epiphyseal dysplasia. For instance, habitual patella dislocation, even when involving a multilayered patella, has been managed with medialization of the tibial tuberosity, leading to excellent clinical outcomes. [PMC2902411]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome (SLOS) is characterized by multiple congenital anomalies, intellectual deficit, and behavioral problems.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: SLOS is most common in central and northern Europe with an estimated incidence of around 1/ 20,000 to 1/ 40,000 births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease is present at birth, but may be detected in later childhood or adulthood in mild forms. Patients present with growth retardation and intellectual deficit. Behavioral problems include multiple autistic traits, hyperactivity, self-injurious behavior and sleep disturbances. The structural brain anomalies may include hypoplasia or absence of the corpus callosum, and holoprosencephaly. Microcephaly (80% of cases), bitemporal narrowing, ptosis, a broad nasal bridge, short nasal root, anteverted nares (90% of cases), a small chin, and micrognathia are common craniofacial features. Occasionally, cataract, strabismus, and nystagmus are observed. Other clinical features include cleft palate or bifid uvula (1/3 of patients), photosensitivity, rhizomelia and postaxial polydactyly of the hands or feet, syndactyly of the 2nd and 3rd toes (95% of cases), and short and proximally placed thumbs. Genital anomalies (small penis, hypospadias, ambiguous genitalia) are frequent in males (70% of cases). Cardiovascular anomalies (atrial and ventricular septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, atrioventricular canal) can be present. Gastrointestinal anomalies including poor feeding, gastroesophageal reflux, pyloric stenosis, malrotation, and colonic aganglionosis are frequent.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: SLOS is due to an inborn error of cholesterol synthesis and is caused by mutations in the DHCR7 gene (11q13.4) leading to deficiency of the enzyme 3 beta-hydroxysterol-delta 7-reductase that converts 7-dehydrocholesterol (7DHC) to cholesterol.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the detection of elevated 7DHC levels in plasma or tissues. Mutation analysis confirms the diagnosis. Imaging studies (CT, MRI, echocardiogram) may be performed to detect malformations.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: he differential diagnosis includes lathosterolosis, desmosterolosis, Dubowitz syndrome, Cornelia De Lange syndrome, oculo-digito-esophago-duodenal syndrome, Noonan syndrome, Pallister-Hall syndrome, trisomy 13 and trisomy 18, and pseudotrisomy 13.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis may be suspected at fetal ultrasonography and should be confirmed by analysis of amniotic fluid or chorionic villous samples, measurements of 7DHC content and mutation analysis if DHCR7 mutations have already been identified in the family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is symptomatic and most patients are treated with dietary cholesterol supplementation. Treatment trials are underway investigating combined treatment with cholesterol supplementation and a HMG CoA reductase inhibitor (simvastatin). Surgery is proposed in case of secondary problems due to malformations.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of the disease and on the associated malformations. Heart disease and brain malformations may be lethal. Some individuals live into adulthood. Mildly affected individuals may be able to live and work in a group home setting.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare cranial malformation characterized by hyperostosis frontalis interna, variably associated with metabolic and endocrine disorders (such as obesity, diabetes mellitus, and hirsutism, among others). Compression by calvarial thickening may lead to cerebral atrophy and present with cognitive impairment, neuropsychiatric symptoms, headaches, and epilepsy. The condition predominantly affects women.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Morgagni-Stewart-Morel syndrome is characterized by internal frontal hyperostosis, a proliferation of the frontal bone. This condition can manifest in isolation or in association with neuropsychiatric, metabolic, and endocrine symptoms. Neuropsychiatric manifestations can reveal the syndrome, including cognitive decline, impaired executive functions, psychiatric disorders, and possibly memory loss. These symptoms may arise from frontal lobe compression due to extensive hyperostosis frontalis interna. [PMC12150029, PMC4543109]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Morgagni-Stewart-Morel syndrome is characterized by internal frontal hyperostosis, which is a proliferation of the frontal bone. This hyperostosis can occur in isolation or in association with a range of symptoms, including neuropsychiatric, metabolic, and endocrine manifestations. These associated symptoms, along with the frontal hyperostosis, collectively form the syndrome. The pathophysiology of the syndrome is a subject of literature review. [PMC12150029]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Morgagni-Stewart-Morel syndrome is diagnosed by identifying internal frontal hyperostosis in association with neuropsychiatric, metabolic, and endocrine symptoms. Neuropsychiatric manifestations, such as cognitive decline, can be a revealing presentation. Hyperostosis frontalis interna, a key component, is often discovered on MRI examination during assessment for cognitive decline. Neuropsychological evaluations are used to assess associated cognitive impairment. Diagnosis relies on a combination of clinical presentation and imaging findings. [PMC12150029, PMC8693403, PMC7332183, PMC6957065, PMC6699430]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Leontiasis ossea, also known as craniofacial fibrous dysplasia, is a rare form of osseous hypertrophy of the facial bones associated with chronic kidney disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism. As the condition progresses, changes in bone structure can lead to severe facial disfigurement, respiratory difficulties, dysarthria, and dysphagia. the case of an approximately 30-year-old male with a long-standing history of end-stage renal disease who experienced rapidly progressing facial swelling and underlying bone changes following a period of poor access to dialysis. Despite brief symptomatic improvement following parathyroidectomy, the patient's hyperparathyroidism ultimately persisted. Subsequent immunomodulator therapy again offered subjective improvements but was discontinued in the setting of adverse effects. We provide a brief overview of the pathophysiology of leontiasis ossea,... [PMC11700241, PMC8693403, PMC6957065, PMC6699430, PMC2807558]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Leontiasis ossea, also known as craniofacial fibrous dysplasia, is a rare form of osseous hypertrophy of the facial bones associated with chronic kidney disease and secondary hyperparathyroidism. As the condition progresses, changes in bone structure can lead to severe facial disfigurement, respiratory difficulties, dysarthria, and dysphagia. the case of an approximately 30-year-old male with a long-standing history of end-stage renal disease who experienced rapidly progressing facial swelling and underlying bone changes following a period of poor access to dialysis. Despite brief symptomatic improvement following parathyroidectomy, the patient's hyperparathyroidism ultimately persisted. Subsequent immunomodulator therapy again offered subjective improvements but was discontinued in the setting of adverse effects. We provide a brief overview of the pathophysiology of leontiasis ossea,... [PMC11700241, PMC8693403, PMC6699430]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Morgagni-Stewart-Morel syndrome, particularly its hyperostosis frontalis interna component, can lead to significant cognitive and psychiatric impairments. Patients may experience cognitive decline, including deficits in executive functions, working memory, and potentially memory loss. Psychiatric disorders have also been observed. These issues are attributed to the compression of the frontal lobe, specifically the dorsolateral frontal cortex, by the extensive hyperostosis, resulting in selective cognitive impairment. [PMC4543109, PMC2169696]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A non-progressive autosomal dominant macular disorder of congenital or infantile onset characterized by loss of central vision, the accumulation of drusen in the macula and atrophy of photoreceptor cells with a variable phenotype at macular examination.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CAPE dystrophy; CAPED; Central areolar pigment epithelial dystrophy; Central retinal pigment epithelial dystrophy; MCDR1; NCMD; North Carolina macular dystrophy, retinal 1; Progressive foveal dystrophy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: North Carolina macular dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition. It has been identified in a Danish family, representing the first pedigree from Scandinavia, and a case in Australia was reported, believed to be the first confirmed case in that country. The condition is prone to misdiagnosis, often mistaken for congenital ocular toxoplasmosis, which raises questions about how many other cases are misdiagnosed and suggests that its true prevalence may be underestimated. [PMC6857771, PMC3002954]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: North Carolina macular dystrophy (NCMD) is an autosomal dominant, non-progressive developmental maculopathy, considered a focal macular dystrophy with highly variable expressivity and no correlation between age and severity. Patients present with well-demarcated macular lesions; mild forms show small drusen-like yellowish lesions that are hyperautofluorescent, while more severe forms exhibit hyperpigmented foveal lesions surrounded by confluent hyperautofluorescence. These lesions differ from drusen as they lack accumulation of material between the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch's membrane. Histopathologically, they are characterized by focal absence of photoreceptor cells and retinal pigment epithelium, attenuated Bruch's membrane, and marked choriocapillaris atrophy. NCMD's variable phenotype can overlap with age-related macular degeneration and be misdiagnosed as congenital ocular toxoplasmosis. [PMC7245606, PMC6857771, PMC3002954, PMC1359015]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: North Carolina macular dystrophy (NCMD) is an autosomal dominant maculopathy. It is associated with genetic variants on chromosome 6, including a unique heterozygous transversion (chr6:100040974A>C) within the PRDM13 upstream region and a single base substitution (chromosome 6: 99,593,111 (G>C)). A heterozygous deletion in the CFH gene (c.2247_2252del) on chromosome 6 has also been identified in some affected individuals, potentially acting as a modifier gene. However, NCMD in other families has been linked to a region on chromosome 5p (5p13-p15), overlapping the previously mapped macular dystrophy (MCDR3) locus, indicating genetic heterogeneity. [PMC7245606, PMC6857771, PMC3002954]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of North Carolina macular dystrophy (NCMD) relies on a combination of clinical, imaging, electrophysiological, and genetic . Clinical examination typically includes visual acuity testing, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, indirect ophthalmoscopy, fundus photography, Goldmann perimetry, dark adaptation, and color vision testing. Imaging techniques like optical coherence tomography and fundus autofluorescence reveal characteristic macular lesions, such as hyperautofluorescent areas and hyperpigmented foveal lesions. Electroretinography (full-field and focal) may also be employed. Genetic analysis, utilizing Sanger sequencing, whole exome sequencing, comparative genomic hybridization, and genome-wide SNP scans, is crucial for confirming the diagnosis by identifying specific variants, for example, in PRDM13 or on chromosome 6. Histopathologic examination, when performed, shows focal absence of photoreceptor cells and retinal pigment epithelium. The wide phenotypic variability and overlap with conditions like age-related macular degeneration and congenital ocular toxoplasmosis can make accurate diagnosis challenging. [PMC7245606, PMC6857771, PMC3002954, PMC1359015]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: North Carolina macular dystrophy (NCMD) presents with a wide spectrum of clinical phenotypes that can overlap with other conditions, making diagnosis challenging. It has been misdiagnosed as congenital ocular toxoplasmosis due to clinical similarities. The phenotype can also overlap with age-related macular degeneration (AMD), particularly dry AMD, and NCMD lesions may appear drusen-like, although they differ in their underlying pathology. [PMC7245606, PMC6857771, PMC3002954]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: North Carolina macular dystrophy is an autosomal dominant maculopathy with variable expressivity. Genetic counseling should address its autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis, which is important given the wide spectrum of clinical phenotypes that can overlap with other conditions like age-related macular degeneration or ocular toxoplasmosis, making clinical diagnosis challenging. NCMD has been associated with variants in the PRDM13 gene on chromosome 6, while other families show linkage to a locus on chromosome 5p. A CFH gene variant may also act as a modifier, contributing to phenotypic variability. [PMC7245606, PMC6857771, PMC3002954]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: North Carolina macular dystrophy (NCMD) is considered a non-progressive developmental disorder. It presents with variable expressivity and a wide spectrum of clinical phenotypes. There is no correlation between age and the severity of the maculopathy. [PMC7245606]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare 46,XY difference of sex development due to impaired androgen production characterized by impaired normal male sexual development. The severity of the disorder varies and can manifest in its severe form with complete 46,XY male pseudohermaphroditism, including low testosterone and high luteinizing hormone levels, absent development of secondary male sex characteristics and lack of breast development. Patients with the milder form can have a wider range of phenotypes, ranging from micropenis to severe hypospadias.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): 46,XY DSD due to LH resistance or LHB deficiency; 46,XY DSD due to luteinizing hormone resistance or luteinizing hormone beta subunit deficiency; 46,XY disorder of sex development due to LH resistance or LHB deficiency; 46,XY disorder of sex development due to luteinizing hormone resistance or luteinizing hormone beta subunit deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Leydig cell hypoplasia (LCH) is a rare condition, with available data primarily limited to case series. A systematic review, including patients from a single center, identified 88 patients from 59 families with LHCGR-inactivating variants. Of these, 70 were 46,XY patients and 18 were 46,XX patients, presenting with various clinical features. [PMC11466245]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Leydig cell hypoplasia (LCH), caused by inactivating variants in the LHCGR gene, is a rare disorder of sexual differentiation in males. 46,XY individuals typically present with atypical genitalia, which can include hypospadias, micropenis, undescended testes, or female external genitalia with bilateral testes; many are raised as females. Pubertal delay is common, characterized by low basal and hCG-stimulated testosterone, high luteinizing hormone (LH), and sometimes elevated follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). While pubertal LH inaction is uniform, the severity of antenatal human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) inaction is variable. In 46,XX individuals, LCH manifests as oligo/amenorrhea and/or anovulatory infertility, often with polycystic ovaries and elevated LH. [PMC11219444, PMC11466245, PMC6571543, PMC4695626]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for conditions involving Leydig cell dysfunction or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism often includes human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) or other exogenous gonadotropins with luteinizing hormone (LH) activity. Treatment with hCG has been shown to increase serum testosterone concentrations, promote the appearance of male secondary sex characteristics, and increase the size of external genitalia. In patients with selective LH deficiency, hCG treatment can restore spermatogenesis and normalize seminal parameters, thereby improving male fertility. While the critical role of LH in spermatogenesis is recognized, further research is needed to establish the most effective dosages and treatment durations for LH-containing drugs. [PMC11726975, PMC5984881, PMC4265034, PMC1704396]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Primary lymphedema is a lymphatic system malformation characterized by swelling of an extremity that can be associated with other lymphatic effusions, due to an underlying developmental anomaly of the lymphatic system (abnormal lymphangiogenesis). It can be hereditary or not and be congenital or late onset.

DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of primary lymphedema often begins with a clinical assessment, relying on thorough patient history and physical examination. Genetic diagnosis involves identifying variants in genes such as FOXC2, FLT4, SOX18, and HGF. Advanced imaging techniques include indocyanine green lymphography for visualizing dermal backflow, particularly in eyelid lymphedema. For primary intestinal lymphangiectasia, diagnosis integrates clinical, endoscopic, histological, and radiological evaluations, with 99mTc-labeled albumin macroaggregate scintigraphy confirming protein loss. A multidisciplinary approach is crucial for accurate diagnosis. [PMC11962590, PMC11612690, PMC11122351, PMC11022294, PMC11896721]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Primary lymphedema is frequently linked to hereditary factors and is associated with variants in several genes, including FOXC2, FLT4, and SOX18. A novel mutation in the hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) gene has also been identified in familial cases, consistent with an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. Genetic diagnosis is part of understanding complex presentations, such as primary lymphedema combined with tuberous sclerosis complex. [PMC11612690, PMC11122351]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An interstitial lung disease with a poor prognosis, that is characterized by the progressive formation of scar tissue within the lungs in the absence of any known cause.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) incidence appears to be increasing. Reported incidences range from 0.2 per 100.000 per year to 94 per 100.000 per year. The prevalence is estimated to be higher in men than in women.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The mean age at presentation is 66 years. IPF initially usually manifests with symptoms of breathlessness on exertion and dry coughing. Auscultation of the lungs reveals early inspiratory crackles, predominantly located in the lower posterior lung zones. Clubbing is found in approximately 50% of IPF patients typically exertional dyspnea progresses over a period of months to years. In practice patients are often misdiagnosed.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is not yet completely understood. The current conceptual model is that environmental factors may cause microscopic damage in the lungs and that in susceptible people this may lead to a disturbed healing reaction that will result in an ongoing process of scar formation in the lung. This will ultimately lead to loss of lung function.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: IPF is recognized on high-resolution computed tomography by peripheral, subpleural lower lobe reticular opacities in association with subpleural honeycomb changes. IPF is associated with a pathological lesion known as usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP). The UIP pattern consists of normal lung alternating with patches of dense fibrosis, taking the form of collagen sheets. The diagnosis of IPF requires correlation of the clinical setting with radiographic images. If these are non-conclusive a lung biopsy can be considered, though potential implications and associated risks should always be weighed and discussed. The diagnosis of IPF can be made by defined criteria that have been published in guidelines endorsed by several professional societies.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other idiopathic interstitial pneumonias, connective tissue diseases (systemic sclerosis, polymyositis, rheumatoid arthritis), forme fruste of autoimmune disorders, chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis + and other environmental (sometimes occupational) exposures. In a subgroup of patients with pulmonary fibrosis, despite thorough investigations, no definite diagnosis can be made and this group is than labeled as unclassifiable- pulmonary fibrosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In patients that present one or more family members with pulmonary fibrosis, genetic counseling should be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Pharmacological management: Two medications, pirfenidone and nintedanib, are recommended in the current international guidelines for the treatment of IPF. These medication slow down disease progression, as measured by decline in forced vital capacity by approximately 50% and are safe. Besides these, multiple new molecular therapeutic targets have been identified and several clinical trials are investigating the efficacy of novel medications. These non pharmacological management approaches aim to improve or maintain quality of life and sometimes also life longer. Preventative measures as smoking cessation, influenza and pneumococcal vaccination are recommended. Supplemental oxygen is recommended for patients with an oxyhemoglobin saturation of less than 88% and reduces exertional dyspnea and improves exercise capacity for patients. Pulmonary rehabilitation and measures aimed at symptom relieve improve health related quality of life for patients. In a subgroup of patient lung transplantation may be an option.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The median survival without treatment is 2 to 5 years from the time of diagnosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare syndrome variably characterized by chronic cholestasis due to paucity of intrahepatic bile ducts, peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis, vertebrae segmentation anomalies, characteristic facies, posterior embryotoxon/anterior segment abnormalities, pigmentary retinopathy, and dysplastic kidneys.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Alagille-Watson syndrome; Arteriohepatic dysplasia; Syndromic bile duct paucity

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is approximately 1/70,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease may manifest in newborns by prolonged jaundice due to conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and/or cardiac signs and symptoms. Cardiac abnormalities include pulmonary atresia or stenosis, atrial and/or ventricular septal defects, tetralogy of Fallot, and patent ductus arteriosus. Cholestasis manifests by conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, hepatosplenomegaly, hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and coagulopathy. Pruritus and xanthomas may occur. Minor skeletal abnormalities include butterfly hemivertebrae (around 50% of cases), and shortening of the radius, ulna, and phalanges. Characteristic facial features, if present, are usually apparent from childhood and include prominent forehead, deep-set eyes, upslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, flat nasal root, and pointed chin. Ophthalmic anomalies include posterior embryotoxon (75% of cases), Axenfeld anomaly, pigmentary retinopathy, papillary and optic disc anomalies. Growth delay, fat malabsorption (rickets may occur), and sometimes developmental delay occur. Small and dysplastic kidneys (common in AGS type 2), and hypothyroidism may be present.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: AGS is most commonly due to JAG1 (20p12) gene mutations (AGS type 1), encoding a Notch signaling pathway ligand. AGS type 2 is due to NOTCH2 gene mutations (1p12).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on the clinical picture and liver biopsy revealing chronic cholestasis and paucity of interlobular bile ducts. Imaging (abdominal ultrasonography, cholangiography) helps to identify biliary anatomy. Screening for ophthalmic, skeletal, vascular and endocrine (thyroid) abnormalities should be performed. DNA sequencing may confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include biliary atresia, congenital hepatic fibrosis, cystic fibrosis, neonatal jaundice, polycystic kidney disease, progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, and tyrosinemia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: If a pathogenic mutation has been identified, prenatal genetic diagnosis is possible on DNA from chorionic villous tissue or cultured amniocytes. Otherwise, detailed fetal ultrasonography may identify cardiac and/or renal anomalies if present.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant, but reduced penetrance (up to 50% of cases) and somatic mosaicism (~8%) are common.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is non-specific and includes high-carbohydrates and high-medium chain triglyceride diets and vitamin supplementation. Pruritus may be reduced by cholestyramine or rifampin. Liver transplantation may be necessary for patients with refractory disease. Cardiac or vascular procedures may be required for significant symptomatic lesions.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is usually favorable, but complications such as cirrhosis, variceal hemorrhage, refractory ascites, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis may occur. The disease usually stabilizes between ages 4 and 10 years. When hepatic failure and/or cardiac lesions are present, mortality risk is increased.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Congenital stationary night blindness (CSNB) refers to a non-progressive group of retinal disorders characterized by night or dim light vision disturbance or delayed dark adaptation, poor visual acuity (ranging from 20/30 to 20/200), myopia (ranging from low (-0.25 diopters [D] to -4.75 D) to high (≥-10.00 D)), nystagmus, strabismus, normal color vision and fundus abnormalities.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Congenital stationary night blindness (CSNB) is characterized by night blindness, often from an early age, and can include photophobia, nystagmus, myopia, strabismus, and reduced or preserved visual acuity. Color vision may be mildly changed or normal. Fundus appearance is often normal, though some forms like fundus albipunctatus show small white dots, and Åland island eye disease presents with ocular hypopigmentation. Electroretinography (ERG) is diagnostic, showing characteristic abnormalities. Complete CSNB (cCSNB) typically presents with a lack of rod response, severely reduced dark-adapted b-wave amplitude, and undetectable S-cone ERG b-wave, indicating anomalous postreceptor retinal circuitry. Incomplete CSNB (iCSNB) also shows reduced rod-driven postreceptor responses. Autosomal dominant forms can exhibit a Riggs-type ERG with loss of the rod a-wave and small b-waves. [PMC10672672, PMC7911795, PMC5937575, PMC8325388, PMC3542465]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Congenital stationary night blindness (CSNB) is a clinically and genetically heterogeneous retinal disorder. Various genetic mutations are implicated in its etiology. Biallelic missense mutations in the LRAT gene, such as c.197G>A and c.557A>C, are associated with fundus albipunctatus, a rare form of CSNB. X-linked incomplete CSNB and Åland island eye disease are caused by variants in the CACNA1F gene, including a novel splice-site variant c.4294-11C>G. Autosomal dominant Riggs type CSNB can result from a novel heterozygous missense mutation in GNAT1 (c.155T>A p.Ile52Asn). Autosomal-recessive complete CSNB is linked to mutations in TRPM1, GRM6 (including novel deletions), NYX, GPR179, and LRIT3. LRIT3 mutations include missense (e.g., c.983G>A), nonsense (e.g., c.1318C>T), and deletion variants. [PMC10672672, PMC7911795, PMC7105792, PMC5937575, PMC8325388]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Congenital stationary night blindness (CSNB) is a genetically heterogeneous disorder with diverse inheritance patterns. X-linked forms are associated with genes like CACNA1F, where variants are found in a hemizygous state in affected individuals and heterozygous in asymptomatic mothers. Autosomal recessive inheritance is linked to mutations in genes such as LRAT, LRIT3, GRM6, TRPM1, and GPR179, with biallelic mutations identified in some cases. Autosomal dominant CSNB has also been reported, including those caused by mutations in GNAT1, which cosegregate with the phenotype. Genetic testing is essential for diagnosis, identifying specific gene mutations, and expanding the known mutational spectrum. In complex presentations, co-existing retinal dystrophies should be considered. [PMC10672672, PMC7911795, PMC7105792, PMC5937575, PMC8325388]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: There are currently no available treatments for fundus albipunctatus (FAP), a rare form of congenital stationary night blindness. Management focuses on understanding the genetic landscape of the condition. [PMC10672672]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Congenital stationary night blindness (CSNB) is generally characterized by a non-progressive course. For instance, in fundus albipunctatus (FAP) associated with LRAT gene mutations, ophthalmic imaging and best-corrected visual acuity have been observed to remain stable over a 23-year period. Similarly, Åland Island Eye Disease and incomplete CSNB, linked to CACNA1F variants, are explicitly described as non-progressive disorders, with affected individuals experiencing night blindness from an early age and generally normal visual acuities. While one older patient with dominantly inherited CSNB showed areas of peripheral chorioretinal atrophy, the condition is largely considered stationary. [PMC10672672, PMC7911795, PMC1772254]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Congenital analbuminemia (CAA) is characterized by the absence or dramatic reduction of circulating human serum albumin (HSA).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence has been estimated at approximately 1 case per million population, with less than 50 cases being reported in the literature so far. The disorder occurs with no geographic, sex or ethnic predilection.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In the majority of cases, CAA is diagnosed in adulthood. Although albumin is the most abundant plasma protein and has many functions, patients with CAA present with only a few mild clinical signs and biochemical abnormalities: fatigue, low blood pressure, edema, increased concentration of several plasma proteins and a prolonged albumin half-life. HSA is either absent or present at very low levels (<1 g/L) but liver function is normal and there is an absence of conditions leading to significant protein loss. The mildness of the clinical manifestations is attributed to the compensatory increase in hepatic biosynthesis of other plasma proteins, notably a compensatory increase in serum globulin concentrations. However, CAA patients may develop lipodystrophy and hypercholesterolemia, possibly leading to premature atherosclerosis and cardiovascular events. Rarely, CAA may be complicated by hypercoagulability, osteoporosis and respiratory tract infections. The disorder appears to be more severe in the fetus or during early infancy, as intrauterine growth retardation and intrauterine death have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disorder is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the gene coding for HSA (ALB; 4q13.3). More than ten different causative mutations have been identified to date. The Kayseri mutation (a homozygous AT deletion at nucleotides c.228-229, the 91st and 92nd bases of exon 3) appears to be the most common cause of analbuminemia in humans.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on laboratory analysis of blood specimens (albumin immunoassays and serum protein electrophoresis). DNA analysis is required for identification of the mutation involved.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include a wide number of pathological conditions that present with reduction of HSA (glomerulonephritis, nephrosis, ascites, systemic lupus erythematosus, intestinal lymphangiectasia, and protein-losing enteropathies).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: CAA is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait and consanguinity has been shown in all reported cases with available genealogic data.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: CAA is a relatively benign and tolerable condition. Management aims at prophylaxis and treatment of the possible cardiovascular complications related to hypercholesterolemia and atherosclerosis. Drugs that bind to the albumin plasma protein fraction should be used with caution in patients with CAA.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Congenital analbuminemia is often characterized by a lack of clinical symptoms, with the virtual absence of albumin being tolerable despite its multiple functions. When symptoms do occur, they are rare and may include fatigue, ankle edema, and hypotension. Even in challenging situations like pregnancy, patients can have a normal delivery with proper management, as demonstrated by a case where polyhydramnios was successfully managed with albumin transfusions, leading to no intrapartum or postpartum complications. [PMC6597461, PMC5293980, PMC44823]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic disorder caused by deletions in the long arm of chromosome 11 (11q) and mainly characterized by craniofacial dysmorphism, congenital heart disease, intellectual disability, Paris Trousseau bleeding disorder, structural kidney defects and immunodeficiency.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Chromosome 11q deletion syndrome; Del(11)(q23.3); Del(11)(qter); Distal deletion 11q; Distal monosomy 11q; Monosomy 11qter; Telomeric deletion 11q; 11q terminal deletion syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Whilst prevalence of Jacobsen syndrome is unknown, the birth prevalence has been suggested at 1/50,000-100,000 in the United States, with a female/male ratio of 2:1.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Jacobsen syndrome is contiguous gene disorder, characterized by craniofacial dysmorphism (skull deformities, hypertelorism, ptosis, coloboma, downslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, a broad nasal bridge, short nose, V-shaped mouth, and small, low-set and posteriorly rotated ears), craniosynostosis, eye abnormalities, congenital heart disease, intellectual disability, behavioral problems including ADHD and autism, seizures, Paris-Trousseau bleeding disorder, structural kidney defects and other urogenital anomalies including undescended testes in males, chronic constipation, pyloric stenosis, and immunodeficiency.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is caused by deletion of one copy of the long arm of chromosome 11 (11q). Most of the deletions are terminal, i.e. extending to the end of the chromosome. The deletion size ranges from ~7 to ~16Mb, with the proximal breakpoint within or telomeric to subband 11q23.3 and the deletion usually extending to the telomere. Interstitial deletions in this region and terminal deletions less than 7Mb can cause a ''partial Jacobsen syndrome'' phenotype. In a minority of cases the breakpoint is at the FRA11B fragile site. There are a few reported cases of mosaicism for the deletion, which may lessen the severity of the clinical phenotype.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical findings and confirmed by array comparative genomic hybridization, and/or FISH.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses may include the Turner and Noonan syndromes, as well as acquired thrombocytopenia due to sepsis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis of 11q deletion is possible through array comparative genomic hybridization analysis of genomic DNA from amniocytes or chorionic villus samples. Deletions can also potentially be detected by non-invasive prenatal testing from a maternal blood sample, although the reliability of this test for Jacobsen syndrome is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: About 90% of cases are de novo. The remainder are inherited from an affected parent, either from one carrying a balanced translocation (giving rise to an unbalanced translocation in the offspring) or from a parent carrying a terminal 11q deletion. Genetic counseling is not possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is multi-disciplinary and requires evaluation by a pediatrician, pediatric cardiologist, neurologist, hematologist, allergy/immunologist, endocrinologist and ophthalmologist. Additional subspecialty evaluations might include neurosurgery, urology, and nephrology. Follow-up with subspecialists varies between individuals, depending on need. Most individuals with JS have intellectual disability (ranging from mild learning disabilities to severe intellectual disability) and behavioral problems, requiring care by a pediatrician specializing in behavioral/developmental disabilities. Psychological and psychiatric care may also be warranted. Cardiac malformations can be severe and require heart surgery in the neonatal period. Newborns with Jacobsen syndrome may also have feeding difficulties requiring tube feeding. Special attention should be devoted to hematological problems.
