DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Historically, the most common causes of death in people with JS have been from congenital heart disease, bleeding and immunodeficiency. Early diagnosis of the syndrome can lead to lifesaving interventions including the need for prophylactic platelet transfusions at times of risk to prevent bleeding, prophylactic antibiotic or IVIG infusions to prevent life-threatening infections, early medical or surgical intervention for complex congenital heart defects, and brain imaging to identify potential life-threatening brain aneurysms. Intellectual disability can range from mild to severe. For patients who survive the neonatal period and infancy, the life expectancy remains unknown.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome is a rare, fatal, autosomal dominant and premature aging disease, beginning in childhood and characterized by growth reduction, failure to thrive, a typical facial appearance (prominent forehead, protuberant eyes, thin nose with a beaked tip, thin lips, micrognathia and protruding ears) and distinct dermatologic features (generalized alopecia, aged-looking skin, sclerotic and dimpled skin over the abdomen and extremities, prominent cutaneous vasculature, dyspigmentation, nail hypoplasia and loss of subcutaneous fat).

DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Laminopathiesrepresent a rare group of genetic disorders affecting various organs and tissues, including the skin, muscles, adipose tissue, bone, and cardiovascular system. The LMNA gene, the most common pathogenic gene responsible for laminopathies, harbors variants that can lead to diverse clinical phenotypes, such as progeroid syndromes, lipodystrophies, muscular dystrophies, and cardiomyopathies. presents a case of a young female patient who presented with prediabetes, secondary amenorrhea, and secondary osteoporosis. A 28-year-old female presented to our clinic with complaints of amenorrhea and decreased bone mineral density. She exhibited pronounced facial abnormalities and underdeveloped secondary sexual characteristics. Laboratory investigations revealed hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, prediabetes and hyperlipidemia. Significant mitral annular calcification was revealed via... [PMC12288645, PMC10965776, PMC10887809, PMC10815864, PMC11503585]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) includes both disease-modifying and comprehensive supportive approaches. Farnesyltransferase inhibitors and genetic interventions like CRISPR-Cas9 show potential in mitigating progerin-associated symptoms, with emerging therapies such as rapamycin, sulforaphane, and MG132 also holding promise. Cord blood cell therapy has demonstrated therapeutic effects, improving growth rate, joint flexibility, and cardiovascular parameters like pulse wave velocity and dyslipidemia. Comprehensive management includes growth hormone therapy, retinoids, and dental care. Cardiovascular complications are significant, with conservative medical management, including anticoagulation and antiplatelet therapy, used for conditions like carotid dissection, and medication with aggressive risk factor control for events like NSTEMI. Anesthetic management requires careful assessment due to potential airway challenges and comorbidities, with spinal anesthesia reported as an option. [PMC11466922, PMC11650505, PMC11480815, PMC8922814, PMC9279580]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by cutaneous mastocytosis, microcephaly, microtia and/or hearing loss, hypotonia and skeletal anomalies (e.g. clinodactyly, camptodactyly, scoliosis). Additional common features are short stature, intellectual disability and difficulties. Facial dysmorphism may include upslanted palpebral fissures, highly arched palate and micrognathia. Rarely, seizures and asymmetrically small feet have been reported.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Mastocytosis-short stature-hearing loss syndrome; Cutaneous mastocytosis-hearing loss-microtia syndrome; Mastocytosis-short stature-deafness syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Cutaneous mastocytosis-deafness-microtia syndrome is characterized by an aggressive form of systemic congenital mastocytosis, often presenting with significant global developmental delay, deafness, and multiple anomalies. Previously reported pediatric patients also exhibit cutaneous mastocytosis, microcephaly, microtia, and/or hearing loss. A germinoma presenting as an invasive spinal mass has been observed. The syndrome is associated with a KIT alteration, specifically NM_000222.3(KIT):c2447A > 7 pAsp816Val, and overexpression of C-kit in tumor cells. [PMC10605361]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiology of cutaneous mastocytosis-deafness-microtia syndrome (MIM 248910) has not yet been definitively determined. However, a case presenting with an aggressive form of systemic congenital mastocytosis, global developmental delay, deafness, and multiple anomalies revealed a KIT alteration (NM_000222.3(KIT):c2447A > 7 pAsp816Val) and a likely pathogenic variant in peripheral blood and skin lesions. C-kit was also overexpressed in spinal tumor cells. This finding extends the spectrum of KIT-related disorders and provides clues regarding the potential etiology of a syndromic form of congenital mastocytosis. [PMC10605361]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of cutaneous mastocytosis-deafness-microtia syndrome involves a combination of clinical evaluation and genetic testing. Clinical features include cutaneous mastocytosis, deafness, and microtia, often alongside developmental delay and other anomalies. Molecular genetic studies, such as whole-exome sequencing, are crucial for identifying specific KIT alterations, like NM_000222.3(KIT):c2447A > 7 pAsp816Val, in DNA from peripheral blood and skin lesions. Additionally, C-kit overexpression may be detected in tumor cells. Extensive cytogenetic and metabolic studies can also contribute to the diagnostic process. [PMC10605361]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for Cutaneous mastocytosis-deafness-microtia syndrome includes other syndromic forms of mastocytosis, particularly those presenting with similar features such as microcephaly, microtia, and/or hearing loss. Previously, a condition described as mastocytosis, conductive hearing loss, and microtia (OMIM 248910) had an undetermined etiology. The identification of KIT alterations in patients with these features suggests that KIT-related disorders should be considered, as they may extend the recognized spectrum of such syndromic forms of congenital mastocytosis. [PMC10605361]

One reported case described an aggressive form of systemic congenital mastocytosis, leading to significant global developmental delay, deafness, and multiple anomalies. This patient also developed an invasive spinal germinoma at 4 years of age. The presence of KIT alterations suggests potential targets for therapy, but the long-term benefits of targeted treatments are still under evaluation. [PMC10605361]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Double-outlet left ventricle (DOLV) is an extremely rare congenital cardiac malformation in which both the aorta and the pulmonary artery arise, either exclusively or predominantly, from the morphologic left ventricle.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown. The birth prevalence is estimated at less than 1/ 200,000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: DOLV usually manifests during the neonatal period with cyanosis, tachypnea, exertional dyspnea, failure to thrive, sweating (especially during feeding), unresponsiveness and/or fatigue. DOLV occurs most commonly in the form of atrial situs solitus with atrioventricular (AV) concordance but is often associated with cardiac anomalies such as a ventricular septal defect (VSD), an atrial septal defect, pulmonary stenosis, right ventricular hypoplasia, patent ductus arteriosus, and tricuspid atresia. The clinical manifestations depend largely on the type of the associated cardiac defects, e.g. pulmonary or aortic outflow tract obstruction resulting from pulmonary or aortic valve stenosis respectively. DOLV is classified into two sub-types depending on the location of the VSD and the position of the great arteries: DOLV with normal great arteries (DOLV NGA type) with subpulmonary or doubly committed subarterial VSD and levo-position of the anterior pulmonary artery; and DOLV with transposition of the great arteries (DOLV TGA type) with subaortic or doubly committed subarterial VSD and levoposition of the anterior aorta. The two sub-types are almost clinically indistinguishable, apart from cyanosis being more prominent in TGA type.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiopathology is not clearly understood. Embryologically, DOLV could result from excessive leftward shift of the embryonic conotruncus, anomalous differential absorption of sub-pulmonic and sub-aortic conus, or anomalous differential conal growth.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on 2-D echocardiography combined with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showing both great arteries arising from the morphologic left ventricle. Chest X-ray and/or cardiac catheterization can also be performed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes transposition of the great arteries and double outlet right ventricle.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal echocardiographic diagnosis is possible but very difficult.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: DOLV is a sporadic disease.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Biventricular repair is the usual treatment for DOLV and is usually accomplished by an intraventricular baffle procedure, by the Rastelli procedure or by a variant of the Lecompte operation. Pulmonary root translocation from the left to the right ventricle can also be performed and provides excellent anatomic and hemodynamic repair. When other cardiac malformations are present, other techniques can be used such as Fontan-type cavopulmonary derivation in the presence of right ventricular hypoplasia.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: DOLV is associated with high mortality, generally due to heart failure, myocardial infarction or aortic thrombosis. With surgery, the five-year survival rate is estimated at 70-75%. Most patients will continue to present with residual cardiac anomalies, such as aortic or mitral valve regurgitation, arrhythmias or hypertension.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital anomaly of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) in which one or both kidneys (unilateral or bilateral MCDK respectively) are large, distended by multiple cysts, and non-functional. Unilateral MCDK is typically asymptomatic if the other kidney is fully functional but may occasionally present with abdominal obstructive signs when the cysts become too large. Bilateral MCDK is considered a lethal entity and neonates present with features of the Potter sequence, severe pulmonary hypoplasia and severe renal failure, and generally die shortly after birth.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Multicystic dysplastic kidney may present as an abdominal lump, as observed in a 3-year-old male child with a left-sided mass. Radiological examination typically reveals a cystic mass in the affected kidney. Diagnosis can be challenging, with initial clinical and radiological findings potentially suggesting other conditions like multicystic nephroma, and cytology often proving inconclusive. A definitive diagnosis is established through histological examination. [PMC3094784]

She was born dead to a 28 year old mother, showing a hydropic change, narrow thorax, and shortened limbs with postaxial heptasyndactyly of both hands and feet. Radiologic examination revealed short horizontal ribs, curved short tubular limb bones, small ilia and scapula, and a mild vertebral abnormality. Postmortem examination disclosed pulmonary hypoplasia, pancreatic cysts, hepatic fibrosis, and left persistent superior vena cava. In addition this case had bilateral huge polycystic renal dysplasia that was seldom described in any type of SRPS. Histologic... [PMC3054471]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Clinical and radiological examinations can suggest a tentative diagnosis, revealing a cystic mass. However, cytology may be inconclusive. A definitive diagnosis often requires histological examination, typically performed after nephrectomy. [PMC3094784]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Multicystic dysplastic kidney can present a diagnostic dilemma, particularly when distinguishing it from other cystic renal masses. Clinical and radiological examinations may lead to a tentative diagnosis of multicystic nephroma. However, a definitive diagnosis often requires histological examination to differentiate it from other conditions. [PMC3094784]

She was born dead to a 28 year old mother, showing a hydropic change, narrow thorax, and shortened limbs with postaxial heptasyndactyly of both hands and feet. Radiologic examination revealed short horizontal ribs, curved short tubular limb bones, small ilia and scapula, and a mild vertebral abnormality. Postmortem examination disclosed pulmonary hypoplasia, pancreatic cysts, hepatic fibrosis, and left persistent superior vena cava. In addition this case had bilateral huge polycystic renal dysplasia that was seldom described in any type of SRPS. Histologic... [PMC3054471]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: A 3-year-old male child had left-sided abdominal lump for 4 months. Radiological examination revealed a cystic mass in the left kidney. A tentative diagnosis of multicystic nephroma was made on clinical and radiological examination. Cytology was inconclusive. Nephrectomy was done. A final diagnosis of multicystic dysplasia was made on histological examination. [PMC3094784]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Tibial aplasia-ectrodactyly syndrome is a rare condition characterized by congenital ectrodactylous limb malformations associated with tibial aplasia or hypoplasia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Aplasia of tibia with split-hand/split-foot deformity; SHFLD syndrome; SHFM associated with aplasia of long bones; Split hand/foot malformation with long bone deficiency; Split-hand/foot malformation associated with aplasia of long bones; TH-SHFM; Tibial hemimelia with split hand/foot malformation; Tibial hemimelia-ectrodactyly syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence is estimated to be approximately 1 in 1,000,000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The expression of the phenotype is highly variable and ranges from bilateral aplasia of tibiae and split-hand/split-foot deformity (tetramonodactyly or transverse hemimelia) to the mildest visible manifestation, hypoplastic big toes. Additional malformations may include distal hypoplasia or bifurcation of femora, hypo- or aplasia of ulnae, and minor anomalies such as aplasia of patellae, postaxial and intermediate polydactyly in association with split-hand deformity, and cup-shaped ears.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Two susceptibility loci at 1q42.2-q43 and 6q14.1 have been identified, leading to the hypothesis that this syndrome fits the model of digenic inheritance.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Overlap with the Gollop-Wolfgang syndrome has been described.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The syndrome is generally inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with reduced penetrance. Autosomal recessive inheritance has also been proposed in some families.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis typically involves clinical examination to identify characteristic limb deformities, including tibial hemimelia, ectrodactyly, and bifid femur. Imaging studies are crucial for confirming skeletal abnormalities and classifying the extent of tibial deficiency. Genetic testing plays a significant role, with such as array comparative genomic hybridization (array CGH) and quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) used to detect duplications or triplications in regions like 17p13.3, particularly involving the BHLHA9 gene. Genetic evaluation may also explore variants in genes such as COL11A2 and EVC2, with segregation studies and breakpoint analysis further characterizing genetic rearrangements. [PMC12030042, PMC9419377, PMC6570964, PMC5015155]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of tibial aplasia-ectrodactyly syndrome emphasizes early diagnosis and a multidisciplinary approach. Surgical interventions may include resection of a bifid femur. Knee disarticulation is frequently necessary, particularly in the absence of a viable tibial anlage, especially with femoral bifurcation, or when the knee extensor mechanism is lacking. Conversely, tibiofibular synostosis is a suitable option if a proximal tibial anlage and good quadriceps function are present. Limb salvage techniques remain challenging. Patients can achieve ambulation with the aid of prostheses or ankle-foot orthoses. [PMC12030042, PMC6191263]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Tibial aplasia-ectrodactyly syndrome often involves significant limb length discrepancy and skeletal abnormalities. In cases with absent proximal tibial anlage or femoral bifurcation, knee disarticulation is frequently necessary, as limb salvage techniques remain challenging. However, with appropriate surgical interventions, such as tibiofibular synostosis when a proximal tibial anlage and good quadriceps function are present, patients can achieve ambulation, potentially with prostheses or ankle-foot orthoses. Early diagnosis and a multidisciplinary approach are important for managing the condition. [PMC12030042, PMC6191263]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic form of pontocerebellar hypoplasia (PCH) characterized by neocortical and pontocerebellar hypoplasia with pons and cerebellum equally affected and that clinically manifests with neonatal hypotonia and impaired swallowing followed by seizures, optic atrophy and short stature from infancy onward. Movement disorders, as seen in other forms of PCH, are absent.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Cerebellar atrophy with progressive microcephaly; PCH3

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Pontocerebellar hypoplasia type 3 (PCH3) is reported in only 3 families.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Neonatally, PCH3 is characterized by hypotonia and impaired swallowing. From infancy onwards, the main features of PCH3 include progressive microcephaly with brachycephaly, optic atrophy, seizures during the first year of life, severe developmental delay, truncal hypotonia, with increased limb deep tendon reflexes and signs of spasticity of the limbs. Other characteristics such as facial dysmorphism (low set ears and prominent eyes), short stature and low weight are also reported. None of the clinical findings are specific. Characteristic movement disorders, as seen in PCH type 2, appear to be absent.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Mutations in the PCLO gene (7q21.11) has been identified in a family from the Sultanate of Oman. It is however unclear if PCLO mutations are causative in the other reported PCH3 families reported in literature. PCH3 is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: MRI demonstrates neocortical and pontocerebellar hypoplasia with pons and cerebellum equally affected, a small brainstem, prominent sulci and lateral ventricles and decreased cerebral white matter volume. Genetic testing is recommended to confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Due to phenotypic overlap, other subtypes of PCH should be considered, as well as mutations in the CASK gene. Congenital disorder of glycosylation type 1A (CDG1A) caused by mutations in the PMM2 gene can resemble PCH.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal detection of PCH by ultrasound is unreliable, since cerebellar abnormalities are often not detected at time of the routine screening for structural abnormalities at 20 weeks of gestation. In families in which the causal mutation is detected, prenatal testing or pre-implantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) should be offered.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: PCH3 is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Genetic counseling is recommended for families of individuals with PCH3. For parents of an affected individual, there is a 25% recurrence risk of having another affected child.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic in PCH.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: There is no information on life expectancy, but reported PCH3 patients do not appear to regress.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare non-syndromic cerebral malformation due to abnormal neuronal migration characterized by clusters of disorganized neurons in abnormal locations such as periventricular and subcortical. The extent of the lesions ranges from isolated single to bilateral confluent nodules. Pediatric patients typically show variable degrees of developmental delay, intellectual disability, and intractable epilepsy, and concomitant cerebral and/or systemic malformations are frequent. Milder forms may present with onset of seizures in adulthood.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked dominant

DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of nodular neuronal heterotopia can be initiated by routine fetal imaging, with follow-up MRI confirming neurological malformations such as periventricular nodular heterotopia (PVNH) and absence of the corpus callosum. These imaging findings often prompt genetic evaluation, which can identify causal variants in genes like FLNA, LAMC3, or NEDD4L. Familial genetic analysis may reveal the same variants in asymptomatic relatives. Additionally, severe prenatal neurodevelopmental manifestations, including hypokinesia and flexion contractures, have been associated with familial NEDD4L variants. [PMC7916305, PMC8740014, PMC6305664]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Stereotactic electroencephalography (SEEG) is an important invasive assessment method in epilepsy surgery. After electrode implantation, SEEG-guided radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RF-TC) is performed on the discharge initiation and rapid propagation areas by monitoring intracranial electroencephalography. We also sought to determine whether these changes, along with clinical characteristics, could serve as predictive factors for postoperative seizure outcomes. Three-minute segments of SEEG signals were analyzed in 44 patients before and after RF-TC. We used Anywave software to quantify the rate of spikes, rate of... DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder of multiple glycosylation pathways characterized by global developmental delay, motor skills delay, hypotonia, seizures, microcephaly and eye abnormalities (including retinopathy, nystagmus, strabismus) with varying onset and severity. Additional clinical features may include peripheral neuropathy, dysmorphic features (facial and limb abnormalities), ataxia and severe gastrointestinal involvement.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CDG syndrome type Ie; CDG-Ie; CDG1E; Carbohydrate deficient glycoprotein syndrome type Ie; Congenital disorder of glycosylation type 1e; Congenital disorder of glycosylation type Ie; Dol-P-mannosyltransferase deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: DPM1-CDG, also known as CDG-Ie, is a congenital disorder of glycosylation typically presenting with severe mental and psychomotor retardation. It is characterized by altered isoelectric focusing patterns of serum transferrin. Affected individuals produce a truncated dolichol-linked precursor oligosaccharide with 5 mannose residues, instead of the normal 9, and show approximately 95% deficiency in dolichol-phosphate-mannose synthase activity in fibroblasts. [PMC377427]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: DPM1-CDG, also known as CDG-Ie, is a congenital disorder of glycosylation resulting from metabolic deficiencies in glycoprotein biosynthesis. The condition is caused by defects in the DPM1 gene, which encodes the catalytic subunit of dolichol-phosphate-mannose (Dol-P-Man) synthase. Patients exhibit approximately 95% deficiency in Dol-P-Man synthase activity, leading to the production of a truncated dolichol-linked precursor oligosaccharide with 5 mannose residues instead of the normal 9. Specific DPM1 gene alterations identified include a C(274)G point mutation causing an R(92)G change, and a 13-bp deletion. [PMC377427]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of DPM1-CDG, a congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG-Ie), can be initiated by recognizing altered isoelectric focusing (IEF) patterns of serum transferrin. Further analysis involves metabolic labeling of fibroblasts with 2-(3)Hmannose, revealing a truncated dolichol-linked precursor oligosaccharide with 5 mannose residues. Additionally, fibroblast microsomes show approximately 95% deficiency in dolichol-phosphate-mannose synthase activity and an increased K(m) for GDP-Man. Definitive diagnosis is achieved through genetic analysis of the DPM1 gene, identifying specific mutations such as a C(274)G point mutation or a 13-bp deletion. [PMC377427]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: SLC37A4 encodes an endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-localized multitransmembrane protein required for transporting glucose-6-phosphate (Glc-6P) into the ER. Once transported into the ER, Glc-6P is subsequently hydrolyzed by tissue-specific phosphatases to glucose and inorganic phosphate during times of glucose depletion. DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Desmosterolosis is a very rare sterol biosynthesis disorder characterized by multiple congenital anomalies, failure to thrive, and intellectual disability, with elevated levels of desmosterol.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Only 9 cases have been reported in the literature to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Desmosterolosis presents at birth with growth restriction, spasticity with variable degrees of hand contractures, either microcephaly or relative macrocephaly, and microretrognathia. Transient neonatal seizures, nystagmus, strabismus and failure to thrive are also seen in most cases. Intellectual disability occurs in all patients and is first noted by delayed milestones for speech and adaptive, fine and gross motor development. Less common manifestations reported include hirsutism, facial dysmorphism (downslanting palpebral fissures, bilateral epicanthal folds, submucous cleft palate, and thick alveolar ridges), sensorineural hearing loss, patent arterial duct, ambiguous genitalia, bilateral clubfeet, muscle wasting, and cutis aplasia. Optic atrophy, corpus callosum agenesis and loss of white matter are also noted.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Desmosterolosis is due to mutations in the DHCR24 gene (1p32.3) encoding 3-beta-hydroxysterol delta-24-reductase. This enzyme catalyzes the conversion of desmosterol (the cholesterol precursor) to cholesterol, which is highly involved in embryonic development and morphogenesis. Reduced enzyme activity leads to the accumulation of desmosterol and a lack of cholesterol, disrupting antenatal and postnatal development.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Desmosterolosis is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and genetic counseling is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Desmosterolosis is primarily established by detecting significantly elevated plasma desmosterol levels through sterol quantitation. This initial evaluation is typically followed by genetic testing to confirm the diagnosis, identifying mutations in the DHCR24 gene. In some cases, reduced enzyme activity of DHCR24, assessed through like expression of patient cDNA, can also contribute to establishing the diagnosis. [PMC5963269, PMC4995031]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Desmosterolosis should be considered in the differential diagnosis for patients presenting with a constellation of symptoms including agenesis or dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, cerebral white matter atrophy, and ventriculomegaly. Other features prompting consideration include psychomotor developmental delay, failure to thrive, spasticity, retromicrognathia (with or without cleft palate), and hand contractures. Given the nonspecific nature of its clinical presentation, early screening for cholesterol synthesis defects should be entertained, especially in children from consanguineous matings who may be at higher risk for rare recessive disorders. [PMC5963269, PMC4076431]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic brachydactyly syndrome characterized by the association of brachydactyly type E with hypertension (due to vascular or neurovascular anomalies) as well as the additional features of short stature and low birth weight (compared to non-affected family members), stocky build and a round face. The onset of hypertension is often in childhood.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Bilginturan brachydactyly; Bilginturan syndrome; Brachydactyly type E, with short stature and hypertension

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Brachydactyly-arterial hypertension syndrome, caused by pathogenic variants in the PDE3A gene, was first reported in 2015. To date, there are only a few documented reports of this syndrome, indicating its rarity. The exact prevalence or incidence is not specified in the available literature. [PMC7336660]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Brachydactyly-arterial hypertension syndrome is characterized by hypertension and brachydactyly type E, with short stature also observed. The hypertension can be severe, leading to complications such as renal insufficiency, hypertensive encephalopathy, hypertensive heart disease, and fundus hemorrhage. Cardiac and renal damage associated with the condition may be reversible with strict blood pressure control. The syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by pathogenic variants in the PDE3A gene. [PMC10918729, PMC7336660]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Brachydactyly-arterial hypertension syndrome, also known as autosomal dominant hypertension with brachydactyly type E syndrome, is caused by pathogenic variants in the PDE3A gene. These variants are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. A specific de novo heterozygous missense PDE3A variant (c.1346G > A, p.Gly449Asp) has been identified, which is predicted to affect protein function. This variant was absent in healthy controls and parents, supporting its de novo origin and link to the syndrome. [PMC7336660]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Genetic diagnosis for this syndrome often involves whole-exome sequencing to identify pathogenic variants in the PDE3A gene, such as heterozygous missense variants. This process typically includes bioinformatics analysis and filtering against healthy control databases. Quantitative real-time PCR can be utilized to identify pathogenic copy number variations. Identified variants are then confirmed using Sanger sequencing, which also helps to determine their de novo status or presence in family members and control populations. [PMC7336660]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Brachydactyly-arterial hypertension syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition caused by pathogenic variants in the PDE3A gene. Genetic testing, such as whole-exome sequencing, can identify these variants. A de novo heterozygous missense PDE3A variant (c.1346G > A, p.Gly449Asp) was identified in one proband, indicating that the variant was absent in the healthy parents. This highlights the possibility of de novo mutations, which is an important consideration for genetic counseling regarding recurrence risk. [PMC7336660]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management centers on strict blood pressure control. A case report described a teenager with severe hypertension, brachydactyly type E, and short stature who developed cardiac damage and renal insufficiency. These complications were successfully reversed and returned to normal following strict antihypertensive treatment. This suggests that the cardiac and renal damage are consequences of uncontrolled hypertension, rather than direct effects of the syndrome, and can be mitigated through effective blood pressure management. [PMC10918729]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Cardiac and renal damage associated with severe hypertension in Brachydactyly-arterial hypertension syndrome can be reversed with strict blood pressure control. A case report demonstrated that a patient with severe hypertension, brachydactyly type E, and short stature experienced a return to normal cardiac and renal function after treatment. This suggests that the hypertension and brachydactyly syndrome alone do not directly cause cardiac and renal damage, but rather the uncontrolled hypertension leads to these complications, which are amenable to treatment. [PMC10918729]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Ring chromosome 1 syndrome is an autosomal anomaly characterized by variable clinical features, most commonly including significant intrauterine and postnatal growth failure, developmental delay, intellectual disability, microcephaly, and dysmorphic facial features. Some less frequent clinical features are dysgenesis of corpus callosum, atrial septal defect, rocker bottom feet and clinodactyly.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Ring chromosomes are estimated to occur in 3/10000 newborns and the simultaneous occurrence of two autosomal rings must be a very rare event. Recently, the characterisation of these markers using fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) has greatly enhanced cytogenetic-phenotypic correlations in patients with these marker chromosomes. This kind of analysis enabled us to clarify a unique karyotype containing a r(1) and a r(16) in identical twins born after a 26 week gestation with minimal somatic abnormalities. The origin of the rings was identified using a satellite and whole chromosome painting probes. FISH analysis showed the same abnormal female karyotype in both twins, 48,XX,+r(1)(p13q21),+r(16)(p11q11).ish r(1) (D1Z5+,wcpl+), r(16)(D16Z2+,wcp16+) in about two thirds of the cells. Each also had minor clones with a normal female karyotype or with one or the other supernumerary ring.... [PMC1762981]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Ring chromosome 1 syndrome can manifest with varied clinical features. Reported cases include developmental delay and oligospermia. The phenotype appears to correlate with the specific structure of the ring chromosome 1, ranging from normal or mild to abnormal. One patient was noted to have a radial ray defect. In some instances, individuals with ring chromosome 1, particularly when co-occurring with another ring chromosome, may present with minimal somatic abnormalities and prematurity. The diverse origins of these ring chromosomes complicate attempts to define clear phenotype-genotype relationships. [PMC1734780, PMC1734276, PMC1734252, PMC1762981, PMC1049333]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Ring chromosome 1 syndrome involves the formation of ring chromosomes derived from chromosome 1. These can manifest as supernumerary marker chromosomes, potentially of paternal origin, and may be associated with maternal uniparental disomy 1. The mitotic stabilization of acentric ring chromosomes can occur through neocentromere formation, as observed in a stable ring 1p32-p36.1 chromosome. The origins of these ring chromosomes are diverse, including those consisting of 1q12 heterochromatin and short arm pericentric euchromatin, or non-contiguous chromosome 1 euchromatin. The specific composition of the ring chromosome influences the associated phenotype. [PMC1734780, PMC1734276, PMC1734252]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for ring chromosome 1 syndrome primarily involve cytogenetic analysis. Conventional cytogenetics, GTL banding analysis, and CBG banding are utilized. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is a crucial technique, employing various probes such as telomeric, reverse painting, satellite, and whole chromosome painting probes, as well as specific BAC clones (e.g., BAC923C6). FISH and molecular cytogenetic analyses enhance the characterization of ring chromosomes and aid in genotype-phenotype correlations. The presence of key centromere binding proteins (CENP-E, CENP-F, INCENP) can also indicate neocentromere activity, which contributes to the mitotic stability of acentric ring chromosomes. [PMC3702848, PMC1734276, PMC1734252, PMC1762981]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis may include other chromosomal abnormalities involving chromosome 1, such as a supernumerary marker chromosome (1) or maternal uniparental disomy 1, particularly in cases presenting with developmental delay. The simultaneous occurrence of multiple autosomal ring chromosomes, such as r(1) and r(16), has also been reported, which may represent a distinct chromosome disorder. These cases can present with minimal somatic abnormalities, highlighting the need for detailed cytogenetic analysis, including FISH, to clarify unique karyotypes. [PMC1734780, PMC1762981]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Ring chromosomes are estimated to occur in 3/10000 newborns and the simultaneous occurrence of two autosomal rings must be a very rare event. Recently, the characterisation of these markers using fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH) has greatly enhanced cytogenetic-phenotypic correlations in patients with these marker chromosomes. This kind of analysis enabled us to clarify a unique karyotype containing a r(1) and a r(16) in identical twins born after a 26 week gestation with minimal somatic abnormalities. The origin of the rings was identified using a satellite and whole chromosome painting probes. FISH analysis showed the same abnormal female karyotype in both twins, 48,XX,+r(1)(p13q21),+r(16)(p11q11).ish r(1) (D1Z5+,wcpl+), r(16)(D16Z2+,wcp16+) in about two thirds of the cells. Each also had minor clones with a normal female karyotype or with one or the other supernumerary ring.... [PMC1762981]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for ring chromosome 1 syndrome is complicated by the diversity of origins of r(1)s, which hampers attempts to define clear phenotype-genotype relationships. Different structural compositions of accessory small ring chromosomes derived from chromosome 1, such as those involving 1q12 heterochromatin and pericentric euchromatin, or contiguous versus non-contiguous euchromatin, are associated with a range of phenotypes from normal or mild to abnormal. Supernumerary ring chromosome 1 can be of paternal origin, and cases may involve maternal uniparental disomy 1. Mosaicism, where individuals have clones with normal karyotypes or different ring chromosomes, has also been observed. The formation of neocentromeres can contribute to the mitotic stabilization of these acentric ring chromosomes. [PMC1734780, PMC1734276, PMC1734252, PMC1762981, PMC1049333]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for individuals with ring chromosome 1 syndrome is variable, depending on the specific characteristics of the ring chromosome. Patients with r(1) chromosomes consisting of 1q12 heterochromatin and short arm pericentric euchromatin extending to at least BAC923C6 are associated with a normal or mild phenotype. Conversely, patients presenting with abnormal phenotypes possess different types of rings, such as those with contiguous pericentric short arm euchromatin extending beyond BAC923C6 or non-contiguous chromosome 1 euchromatin. The diverse origins of these r(1)s make it challenging to define precise phenotype-genotype relationships, which can complicate prognostic assessments. [PMC1734252]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD), a non-Langerhans form of histiocytosis, is a multisystemic disease characterized by various manifestations such as skeletal involvement with bone pain, exophthalmos, diabetes insipidus, renal impairment and central nervous system (CNS) and/or cardiovascular involvement.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown. More than 500 cases (<15 pediatric) have been reported since 1930.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: ECD usually presents in adults aged 40-60 with a 3:1 male to female ratio. Clinical course varies from asymptomatic to multisystemic, life-threatening forms. The pathognomonic feature of ECD is osteosclerosis of the long bones manifesting as bone pain, mainly affecting the distal lowerlimbs (50% of cases). Pituitary gland infiltration leads to diabetes insipidus and rarely hyperprolactinemia and gonadotropin insufficiency. Constitutional symptoms include fever, weakness and weight loss. Infiltrations in other organs can lead to intracranial hypertension, exophthalmos, papilledema, adrenal insufficiency, xanthelasmas and papulonodular skin lesions. CNS involvement can cause cerebellar and pyramidal syndromes, headaches, seizures, cognitive impairment, cranial nerve palsies and sensory disturbances. A frequent cardiovascular involvement is the ''coated aorta''. Renal arteries can also be involved, leading to reno-vascular hypertension. Pericardial involvement may be complicated by a tamponade. Pseudo-tumoral infiltration of the right atrium is also seen. Dyspnea, due to lung infiltration, has been reported. Pseudo retroperitoneal fibrosis is sometimes complicated by bilateral hydronephrosis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Etiology is unknown but it is thought to be either a reactive or neoplastic disorder. Elevated levels of interferon-alpha (IFN-alpha), interleukin (IL)-7, IL-12, monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 and decreased levels of IL-4 found in ECD patients support an associated systemic immune Th-1 oriented perturbation. Recent findings of mutations in the BRAF proto-oncogene in > 50% of ECD cases clearly add further complexity to the pathophysiology of ECD.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The hallmark histological finding is the xanthogranulomatous or xanthomatous infiltration of tissues with spumous histiocytes. Immunohistochemical staining of a biopsy sample is CD68-positive and CD1a-negative. Bone x-rays usually display bilateral and symmetric cortical osteosclerosis of the long bones, while technetium 99m bone scintigraphy shows almost constantly evidence of symmetric and abnormally strong labeling of the distal ends of the long bones of the lower limbs (and sometimes the upper limbs). Abdominal CT scan may show a ''hairy kidney'' appearance (in 50%) which can be biopsied.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Langerhans' cell histiocytosis, Rosai-Dorfman disease, Takayasu arteritis, Wegener's granulomatosis, primary hypophysitis, chronic recurrent multifocal osteomyelitis, malignancies, neurosarcoidosis, mycobacterial infections and metabolic disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: First line treatment is the administration of standard or pegylated IFN-alpha for all forms of ECD with higher doses (9 million units, 3 times per week) required on a long-term basis for those with CNS and cardiac localizations (if well tolerated). Bisphosphonates may be given to alleviate bone pain. Cladribine can be given to those with orbital involvement that have been resistant to other forms of treatment. Anakinra can improve symptoms of mild forms of ECD in patients where IFN-alpha was ineffective. Recently, infliximab and vemurafenib have been used with some success, this latter drug seeming very promising for patients with a BRAFV600 mutation. PET scans are recommended for the assessment of disease activity.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: ECD has a variable prognosis but is overall poorer in those with CNS involvement. Before IFN-alpha, the mean survival after diagnosis was 19.2 months. Nowadays, with IFN-alpha treatments, the mortality rate is only 26%, and 5-year survival is 68%.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Erdheim-Chester disease (ECD) is an exceedingly rare non-Langerhans histiocytosis. While often affecting the skeleton, cardiovascular system, and kidneys, pancreatic involvement remains uncommon and can mimic more prevalent conditions such as autoimmune or chronic pancreatitis. A 58-year-old female presented with a two-year history of bilateral lower limb edema and a year-long course of recurrent abdominal pain. Imaging suggested necrotizing pancreatitis and retroperitoneal infiltration, yet serum IgG4 levels were normal. A CT-guided biopsy of the pancreas and retroperitoneum revealed diffuse proliferation of foamy histiocytes (CD68 + , CD163 + , CD1α - ) carrying the BRAF V600E mutation, confirming ECD. Supportive therapy and corticosteroids temporarily relieved symptoms, but targeted treatment was delayed due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Subsequent follow-up revealed significant clinical... [PMC12301201, PMC12241793, PMC12105831, PMC11936638, PMC11670472]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare infectious disease caused by inhalation of the opportunistic fungus aspergillus that can lead to the following manifestations: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA), aspergilloma, chronic necrotizing pulmonary aspergillosis (CNPA), and invasive aspergillosis (IA). Aspergilloma occurs in patients with cavitary lung disease and results in a fungal mass with variable clinical presentations from asymptomatic to life-threatening (massive hemoptysis). CNPA manifests as subacute pneumonia in patients with underlying disease. IA is disseminated aspergillosis that eventually invades other organs. Cutaneous aspergillosis is usually the dermatological manifestation of IA that manifests as erythematous-to-violaceous plaques or papules, often characterized by a central necrotic ulcer or eschar.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Aspergillosis manifests in diverse ways, often influenced by the patient's immune status and affected organs. Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA) can present with cough, blood-tinged sputum, and sore throat, sometimes mimicking lung cancer, and is associated with high mortality. Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis (CCPA) is characterized by multiple pulmonary cavities, chronic cough, fever, and rarely, pneumothorax. Systemic forms may involve fever, pneumonic infiltration, and lymphadenopathy. Isolated renal and urinary tract aspergillosis, though uncommon, typically causes flank pain, fever, and lower urinary tract symptoms. Rare presentations include retroperitoneal aspergilloma, which can appear as a mass, and lung abscesses. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA) is observed in patients with cystic fibrosis and asthma. Key risk factors include immunodeficiencies (e.g., interferon-gamma receptor 1, CARD9, chronic granulomatous disease), diabetes mellitus, HIV, haematological malignancies, liver cirrhosis, tuberculosis, and immunosuppressive therapies. [PMC12151011, PMC10240762, PMC9909941, PMC10734358, PMC8330574]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of aspergillosis relies on a combination of . Imaging, including CT scans and abdominal ultrasound, can reveal characteristic features such as pulmonary opacities or cavitating nodules. Pathological biopsy and histopathology are crucial for confirming the presence of aspergillus hyphae. Laboratory diagnostics encompass PCR of whole blood, fungal culture from various samples like bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or urine, and KOH staining. Serum markers such as galactomannan and IgG for Aspergillus fumigatus are also utilized, alongside advanced techniques like metagenome next-generation sequencing (mNGS) from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid and molecular identification for species typing. Antifungal susceptibility testing further guides treatment, and diagnosis may be supported by established criteria. [PMC12151011, PMC10240762, PMC9909941, PMC10734358, PMC8330574]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Aspergillosis can be challenging to diagnose due to its nonspecific clinical and imaging manifestations, often leading to misdiagnosis. Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis is frequently misdiagnosed as lung cancer, while retroperitoneal aspergilloma can present as a malignant tumor, such as liposarcoma. Furthermore, aspergillosis can occur as a coinfection with other pathogens, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis and other fungal infections like mucormycosis or Exophiala spinifera, particularly in immunocompromised individuals. [PMC12151011, PMC9909941, PMC8254622, PMC8315308, PMC6069780]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Aspergillosis can be associated with various inherited immunodeficiencies. Germline mutations in STAT3, such as the N-terminal domain p.Trp37* variant, define a novel allelic form of STAT3 deficiency linked to chronic pulmonary aspergillosis and minor Hyper-IgE syndrome signs. Interferon-gamma receptor 1 deficiency, involving mutations in IFNGR1, IFNGR2, or STAT1 genes, and SH2B3 mutations are associated with an increased risk for systemic aspergillosis. Inherited Caspase-associated recruitment domain-9 (CARD9) deficiency, an inborn error of immunity, predisposes individuals to invasive fungal infections, including chronic invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, often due to homozygous loss-of-function mutations. Additionally, underlying chronic granulomatous disease, including X-linked carrier states with gp91(phox) deficiency, can lead to Aspergillus colonization and related conditions. Genetic counseling should consider these inherited predispositions in affected individuals and their families. [PMC11811237, PMC10240762, PMC8315308, PMC1746555]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Aspergillosis, particularly invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA), is associated with a high mortality rate, especially with emerging drug-resistant species like Aspergillus lentulus or in lethal coinfections such as with mucormycosis. For isolated renal and urinary tract aspergillosis, all-cause mortality was 24.4%. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical, with antifungal therapy (AFT) leading to symptom improvement and reduced inflammation in some cases. While high survival frequency was observed in COVID-19 patients receiving combination or prolonged AFT, meta-analysis showed no significant difference in all-cause mortality, possibly due to confounding factors like delayed diagnosis. Surgical resection, alongside AFT, can improve outcomes in localized infections or coinfections. However, sustained clinical remission may not always be achieved, particularly in patients with inherited immune deficiencies or in those with species exhibiting reduced antifungal susceptibility. [PMC12151011, PMC9909941, PMC10734358, PMC9333218, PMC8254622]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cataract-glaucoma syndrome is characterised by the association of total bilateral congenital cataract with the secondary occurrence of glaucoma appearing at ages varying between 10 and 40 years.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Congenital cataract-anterior segment mesenchymal dysgenesis syndrome; Congenital cataract-ASD syndrome; Congenital cataract-ASMD syndrome; Congenital cataract-ASGD syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: This very rare syndrome has only been described in three families, one of which contained a few dozen affected individuals spanning eight generations.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is caused by dysfunction of the PITX3 gene (localised to 10q25). This gene codes for a transcription factor involved in the development of the lens and anterior segment of the eye.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The cataract can be managed by classical surgery. Yearly monitoring of ocular tonus is advised; hypertonia is treated classically when it appears.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is good if the disease is correctly treated, but can lead to blindness if diagnosis is delayed.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Congenital or childhood cataracts are a primary clinical feature, presenting as various types including posterior-polar, total, and zonular cataracts. Blue dot opacity has also been observed. When one allele of PITX3 is mutated, dominant cataract and anterior segment mesenchymal dysgenesis occur. Homozygous PITX3 mutations are associated with microphtalmia and brain malformations. Autosomal recessive congenital cataract can also be associated with mental retardation. [PMC2956670, PMC2848917]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic primarily involve molecular analysis to identify genetic etiologies. This includes polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and direct sequencing of candidate genes such as CRYBB2, GJA3, and PITX3. The goal is to detect specific mutations or polymorphisms that co-segregate with the congenital cataract and anterior segment dysgenesis phenotype, distinguishing them from common variations or those not linked to the disease. [PMC2956670, PMC2848917]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Conditions caused by PITX3 mutations should be considered in the differential diagnosis. Heterozygous PITX3 mutations are associated with dominant cataract and anterior segment mesenchymal dysgenesis. Homozygous PITX3 mutations can lead to microphthalmia with brain malformations. However, some cases of autosomal recessive congenital cataract associated with mental retardation may not involve PITX3 mutations, indicating other genetic etiologies. [PMC2848917]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An extremely rare type of arthrogryposis multiplex congenita characterized by the combination of multiple joint contractures with movement limitation, microstomia with a whistling appearance of the mouth that may cause feeding, swallowing, and speech difficulties, a distinctive expressionless facies, severe developmental delay, central and autonomous nervous system dysfunction (excessive salivation, temperature instability, myoclonic epileptic fits, bradycardia), occasionally Pierre-Robin sequence, and lethality generally occurring during the first months of life. Arthrogryposis multiplex congenita-whistling face syndrome has been suggested to be a fetal akinesia deformation sequence.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Clinical manifestations observed in a child with this syndrome include distal arthrogryposis, whistling face, and progressive neurological deterioration. [PMC1734551]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis involves progressive neurological deterioration, as observed in a child with distal arthrogryposis and whistling face. [PMC1734551]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Erythema elevatum diutinum (EED) is a distinctive form of chronic cutaneous vasculitis, belonging to the group of the neutrophilic dermatoses.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It is very rare, although the exact prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease manifests as chronic, red to purple papules, located mainly on the dorsal aspect of the main joints (knees, elbows, hands and feet). Acute lesions may appear bullous, necrotic or hemorrhagic. Older lesions are yellowish or brown.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: EED is not an inherited disease and the exact aetiology remains unknown. EED is a reactive process, which may occur in isolation or in the context of an inflammatory or systemic disease, or in association with blood abnormalities (gammopathies) or infections (including HIV infection).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made on the basis of the clinical presentation and after histological analysis of skin biopsies by a dermatopathologist.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: EED should be distinguished from other types of papular or nodular dermatoses, as well as fibrous tumors and xanthomas.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management includes a complete clinical examination by a dermatologist, together with screening for infections, digestive disorders, and gammopathies (serum electrophoresis). Dapsone is the first line of treatment for EED. Treatment must be monitored clinically and by blood examination. In cases were dapsone is inefficient or poorly tolerated, other drugs may provide an effective treatment.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Although EED is a chronic condition, it is usually sensitive to treatment and the prognosis is good.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Joubert syndrome with hepatic defect is a very rare subtype of Joubert syndrome and related disorders (JSRD) characterized by the neurological features of JS associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis (CHF).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): COACH syndrome; Cerebellar vermis hypoplasia-oligophrenia-congenital ataxia-coloboma-hepatic fibrosis; Gentile syndrome; JS-H; Joubert syndrome with congenital hepatic fibrosis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The age of onset and severity of hepatic manifestations are variable. Some patients may also present chorioretinal or optic nerve colobomas and nephronophthisis (NPH), but these are not mandatory features.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Over 70% of cases are due to mutations in the TMEM67 gene (8q22.1).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Joubert syndrome with hepatic defect (COACH syndrome) is based on clinical findings including intellectual impairment, hypotonia, and ataxia, supported by brain imaging showing the molar tooth sign or cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, combined with clinically apparent liver disease. Genetic testing is crucial, with MKS3 mutations being responsible for the majority of cases. MKS3 should be the first gene tested in patients with Joubert syndrome-related disorder and liver disease or coloboma, followed by CC2D2A and RPGRIP1L. Liver biopsies can reveal changes consistent with congenital hepatic fibrosis or ductal plate malformation. [PMC3501959]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Joubert syndrome with hepatic defect, also known as COACH syndrome, is characterized by Joubert syndrome related disorder (JSRD) and clinically apparent liver disease. Genetic testing is crucial for diagnosis, with mutations in MKS3 accounting for the majority of cases. Minor contributions come from CC2D2A and RPGRIP1L mutations. Therefore, MKS3 should be the initial gene tested in patients presenting with JSRD alongside liver disease or coloboma, followed by CC2D2A and RPGRIP1L. Liver biopsies from affected individuals reveal changes consistent with congenital hepatic fibrosis/ductal plate malformation. [PMC3501959]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: To identify genetic causes of COACH syndrome COACH syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterised by Cerebellar vermis hypoplasia, Oligophrenia (developmental delay/mental retardation), Ataxia, Coloboma, and Hepatic fibrosis. The vermis hypoplasia falls in a spectrum of mid-hindbrain malformation called the molar tooth sign (MTS), making COACH a Joubert syndrome related disorder (JSRD). In a cohort of 251 families with JSRD, 26 subjects in 23 families met criteria for COACH syndrome, defined as JSRD plus clinically apparent liver disease. Diagnostic criteria for JSRD were clinical findings (intellectual impairment, hypotonia, ataxia) plus supportive brain imaging findings (MTS or cerebellar vermis hypoplasia). MKS3/TMEM67 was sequenced in all subjects for whom DNA was available. In COACH subjects without MKS3 mutations, CC2D2A, RPGRIP1L and CEP290 were also sequenced.... [PMC3501959]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A disorder that is characterised by the association of a non-progressive congenital ataxia, severe intellectual deficit, optic atrophy and structural anomalies of the skin vessels. It has been described in five children from a large consanguineous Lebanese family. Short stature and microcephaly were also reported. Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Cerebellar ataxia-intellectual disability-optic atrophy-skin abnormalities syndrome; SCAR5

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pilomatrixoma is a rare and benign hair cell-derived tumor occurring mostly in young adults (usually under the age of 20) and characterized as a 3-30 mm solitary, painless, firm, mobile, deep dermal or subcutaneous tumor, most commonly found in the head, neck or upper extremities. When superficial, the tumors tint the skin blue-red. Multiple pilomatrixomas are seen in myotonic dystrophy, Gardner syndrome, Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome, and Turner syndrome.

DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Pilomatrixoma often presents with atypical morphology, making diagnosis challenging and leading to misdiagnosis, particularly in unusual locations or in elderly patients. Common differential diagnoses include epidermoid cyst, sebaceous cyst, and fibroma. In older patients or those with a history of malignancy, it may be mistaken for malignant tumors, metastasis, or cancer recurrence. Atypical forms can mimic cystic or hemorrhagic malignant conditions, or present as a cutaneous horn in pediatric patients. It should also be considered in the differential diagnosis of ear lobule neoplasms and subcutaneous nodules, even those with a malignant character on radiological imaging. [PMC12108143, PMC12316045, PMC12268492, PMC11407096, PMC11135972]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Multiple pilomatricomas can be associated with genetic mutations and syndromic disorders, most commonly including Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome, Gardner syndrome, myotonic dystrophy, Turner syndrome, and Sotos syndrome. Genetic tests can confirm these syndromic diagnoses in patients presenting with multiple pilomatricomas. At a molecular level, pilomatricomas are characterized by activating mutations in the beta-catenin (CTNNB1) gene. [PMC12033402, PMC11170102, PMC10591970]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: The primary treatment for pilomatrixoma is complete surgical excision, which is associated with low recurrence rates. While clinical diagnosis can be challenging, often leading to misdiagnosis, histopathological examination is crucial for confirmation. Diagnostic aids like ultrasound imaging, fine-needle aspiration, or Tru-cut biopsy can help characterize the tumor and guide treatment planning. For the rare malignant variant, pilomatrix carcinoma, wide excision, lymphadenectomy, and adjuvant radiotherapy are recommended. Chemotherapy is generally ineffective, but PDL1 antibodies and CDK4/6 inhibitors may be considered as alternative treatment options. [PMC12108143, PMC12316045, PMC12268492, PMC12033402, PMC11170102]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Pilomatrixoma is a benign tumor with an excellent prognosis following complete surgical excision. It typically has a low recurrence rate, with one study reporting 1.0% and others observing no recurrence at follow-up. While malignant transformation of pilomatricomas has been described as a possible tumor evolution, no such cases were observed in a large series of 105 patients. Pilomatrix carcinoma, an aggressive malignant variant with metastatic potential, represents a distinct entity. [PMC12316045, PMC12268492, PMC12033402, PMC11170102, PMC11313151]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic, multisystemic lysosomal disease characterized by specific cutaneous (angiokeratoma), neurological (pain), renal (proteinuria, chronic kidney failure), cardiovascular (cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia), cochleo-vestibular and cerebrovascular manifestations (transient ischemic attacks, strokes). The phenotypic expression depends on age of onset and, in females, the level of X-inactivation.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency; Anderson-Fabry disease; FD

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Worldwide, the average prevalence at birth is approximately 1/15,000, but Fabry disease is an underdiagnosed condition and the frequency may be higher.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical picture covers a wide spectrum ranging from mild cases in some heterozygous females, to severe cases in classically affected hemizygous males with no residual alpha-galactosidase A activity. The classical form typically has onset in childhood and may have all the characteristic neurological, cutaneous, renal, cardiovascular, cochleo-vestibular and cerebrovascular signs of the disease. Female patients may have very mild to severe symptoms. Pain is a common early symptom (chronic pain characterized by burning and tingling paresthesia and occasional episodic crises) but may wane in adulthood. Anhidrosis or hypohidrosis may occur causing heat and exercise intolerance. Other signs include angiokeratoma, corneal deposits, tinnitus, hearing loss, fatigue, cardiac and cerebrovascular abnormalities (left ventricular hypertrophy, arrhythmia), dyspnea, and chronic kidney disease. The later-onset form starts in adulthood and in such cases cardiac involvement is the prevailing feature.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Fabry disease is a disorder of glycosphingolipid metabolism caused by the functional deficiency of the lysosomal alpha-galactosidase due to pathogenic variants in the GLA gene (Xq21.3-q22). Deficient activity results in accumulation of globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) and its deacylated form, lyso-Gb3, within lysosomes which is then believed to trigger a cascade of cellular events.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The definitive laboratory diagnosis involves demonstration of marked enzyme deficiency in hemizygous males and identification of a pathogenic variant in GLA. Enzyme analysis may occasionally help to detect heterozygotes but is often inconclusive due to X-chromosomal inactivation, making molecular testing (GLA genotyping) of females mandatory.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: In childhood, other possible causes of pain such as rheumatoid arthritis and "growing pains" must be ruled out. In adulthood, multiple sclerosis and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) are occasionally considered.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis, available by determination of DNA testing in chorionic villi or cultured amniotic cells is, for ethical reasons, only considered in male fetuses (after non-invasive prenatal testing for fetal sex determination). Pre-implantation genetic diagnosis is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is X-linked. The existence of atypical, later-onset, variants and the availability of specific therapies for Fabry disease should be considered when delivering genetic counseling.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: A disease-specific therapeutic option (enzyme replacement therapy using in vitro engineered alpha-galactosidase A) has been available since 2001 and meta-analyses of its long-term efficacy suggest promising outcomes. Enzyme enhancement with a pharmacological chaperone is approved in patients with amenable GLA variants following recent clinical trials. Plant-derived enzyme replacement therapy, substrate reduction therapy (SRT) and gene therapy using adeno-associated viral vectors are currently under investigation in clinical trials. Conventional management consists of pain relief with analgesic drugs, nephroprotection (angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors or angiotensin receptors blockers), antiarrhythmic agents, pace-maker or implantable cardioverter defibrillator, dialysis, and kidney transplant.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With age, progressive damage to tissues develops, leading to organ failure. End-stage renal disease and life-threatening cardiovascular or cerebrovascular complications limit the life-expectancy of untreated males and females versus the general population.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Folinic acid-responsive seizures is a very rare neonatal epileptic encephalopathy disorder characterized clinically by myoclonic and clonic, or clonic seizures associated with apnea occurring several hours to 5 days after birth and responding to folinic acid.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Folinic acid-responsive seizures (FARS) are a rare treatable cause of neonatal epilepsy. While typically presenting in the neonatal period, there are also case reports of patients who develop seizures at a later age. [PMC4727671]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Folinic acid-responsive seizures (FARS) are a rare treatable cause of neonatal epilepsy, though seizures can also present at a later age and be intractable. The condition is characterized by impaired folate transport into the central nervous system, leading to cerebral folate deficiency. Neurological manifestations include progressive psychomotor retardation, behavioral disorders, and global developmental delay. Some patients, particularly those with hereditary folate malabsorption, may also exhibit systemic features such as macrocytic anemia, recurrent infections, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, diarrhea, and mouth ulcers. Genetic mutations in genes like ALDH7A1, SLC46A1, or FOLR1 are associated with these presentations. [PMC5815676, PMC4727671]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Folinic acid-responsive seizures (FARS) are a rare treatable cause of neonatal epilepsy with several identified etiologies. Hereditary folate malabsorption (HFM), caused by mutations in the SLC46A1 gene, leads to impaired intestinal folate absorption and central nervous system folate transport, resulting in systemic and neurological folate deficiency. FARS are also associated with mutations in the ALDH7A1 gene. Additionally, mutations in the FOLR1 gene can cause cerebral folate deficiency by affecting CSF folate transport, even without systemic folate deficiency. These conditions manifest with neurological deficits and early-onset seizures, and respond to folinic acid supplementation. [PMC5815676, PMC4727671]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of folinic acid-responsive seizures relies on specialized tests. Genetic testing can identify mutations in genes such as SLC46A1, associated with hereditary folate malabsorption, or ALDH7A1 and FOLR1, linked to cerebral folate deficiency. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis is also key, revealing characteristic peaks on monoamine metabolite analysis in some cases, or very low 5-methyltetrahydrofolate (5-MTHF) levels, particularly in cerebral folate deficiency. Early diagnosis with these specialized tests is crucial for favorable outcomes. [PMC5815676, PMC4727671]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Folinic acid-responsive seizures (FARS) and related conditions like hereditary folate malabsorption (HFM) have a genetic basis. FARS can be associated with mutations in the ALDH7A1 gene, which is also characteristic of pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy. Novel mutations in the FOLR1 gene have been identified, affecting CSF folate transport and leading to cerebral folate deficiency, as observed in affected siblings. HFM has also been linked to novel mutations in the SLC46A1 gene. The identification of these specific gene mutations and their occurrence in families underscore the hereditary nature of these conditions, making genetic testing and counseling relevant for diagnosis and family planning. [PMC5815676, PMC4727671]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Folinic acid supplementation is the primary and effective treatment for folinic acid-responsive seizures, including those associated with hereditary folate malabsorption and cerebral folate deficiency. For hereditary folate malabsorption, folinic acid improves macrocytic anemia, recurrent infections, and neurological deficits such as psychomotor retardation and seizures. In cerebral folate deficiency, folinic acid therapy can lead to dramatic improvements, including complete seizure control, enhanced social interaction, and improved mobility. Early diagnosis and initiation of folinic acid treatment are crucial for achieving favorable, potentially life-changing outcomes. [PMC5815676, PMC4727671]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Folinic acid supplementation is effective and may offer life-changing therapy for patients. Without treatment, patients may experience progressive psychomotor retardation, behavioral disorders, and early-onset or intractable seizures. With folinic acid, the response can be dramatic, leading to complete seizure control, improved social interaction, and enhanced mobility. Early diagnosis is crucial for achieving a favorable outcome. [PMC5815676, PMC4727671]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Butyrylcholinesterase (BChE) deficiency is a metabolic disorder characterised by prolonged apnoea after the use of certain anaesthetic drugs, including the muscle relaxants succinylcholine or mivacurium and other ester local anaesthetics. The duration of the prolonged apnoea varies significantly depending on the extent of the enzyme deficiency.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of BChE deficiency is highest in the Caucasian population with between 3.4 and 4% of the population displaying a partial enzyme deficiency leading to slightly prolonged apnoea (between 5 minutes and 1 hour) and 1 in 2500 individuals showing a prolongation of more than 1 hour. Individuals with undetectable levels of BChE activity display a severe prolongation lasting more than 8 hours. The prevalence of this severe form is estimated at 1 in 100 000 individuals.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: BChE deficiency is a multifactorial disorder. It is caused by mutations in the BChE gene. The BChE gene is located at the E1 locus on chromosome 3 (3q26.1-q26.2) and multiple atypical variants have been identified. However, BChE deficiency and sensitivity to anaesthetic drugs may also occur during pregnancy, in neonates or in association with other pathologies (chronic infections, malnutrition, liver disease, certain cancers etc.).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis can be made by analysis of enzyme activity in plasma samples, combined with dibucaine and fluoride inhibition tests. DNA analysis, although not carried out routinely, can be used to identify heterozygous carriers of atypical alleles.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The hereditary condition is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Affected individuals are asymptomatic unless exposed to neuromuscular blocking agents, however, prolonged respiratory paralysis following anaesthesia makes mechanical ventilation essential until the excess aesthetic agent is metabolised permitting normal neuromuscular function.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hereditary butyrylcholinesterase deficiency typically presents unexpectedly as prolonged muscle paralysis, apnea, or delayed emergence from general anesthesia after the administration of neuromuscular blocking agents such as succinylcholine or mivacurium. Patients often appear healthy and well-developed, with the deficiency usually discovered during anesthetic complications. Other reported clinical features include an increased risk of atraumatic glenohumeral joint dislocation in the immediate postoperative period. In one pediatric case, intellectual disability was identified as a potential associated phenotype. [PMC12337535, PMC12002386, PMC11951739, PMC11460908, PMC7813341]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Hereditary butyrylcholinesterase deficiency should be included in the differential diagnosis of delayed emergence, prolonged apnea, or paralysis following the administration of neuromuscular blocking agents such as mivacurium or succinylcholine during general anesthesia. This condition often presents unexpectedly. When low serum cholinesterase levels are observed, it is crucial to exclude common acquired causes, including liver disease, drug toxicity, and chronic illness, before confirming a congenital deficiency. [PMC12337535, PMC11951739, PMC11460908, PMC6314751]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Hereditary butyrylcholinesterase deficiency is often asymptomatic, with patients generally appearing healthy and well-developed, and clinical manifestations typically not significant. However, a major prognostic concern is the risk of severe, acute complications following exposure to certain neuromuscular blocking agents like succinylcholine or mivacurium during general anesthesia. These can lead to prolonged postoperative paralysis, apnea, and asphyxia, which are uncommon but very serious, potentially requiring intensive care and ventilatory support. While such acute events usually resolve without long-term sequelae, there is a reported risk of death. Additionally, an increased risk of atraumatic glenohumeral dislocation in the immediate postoperative period has been noted, and one case report suggested intellectual disability as a probable associated phenotype. [PMC12337535, PMC12002386, PMC11951739, PMC11460908, PMC6314751]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A chronic infectious disease affecting primarily the skin and peripheral nervous system.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Worldwide annual incidence is estimated at 250,000 cases, with a large majority in India and Brazil.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: A wide clinical spectrum has been described from a polar tuberculoid (localized) form (TT) to a polar lepromatous (disseminated) one (LL). Borderline forms exist: borderline tuberculoid, borderline borderline and borderline lepromatous (BT, BB, BL). Tuberculoid leprosy (TLep) or paucibacillary form includes TT and BT and lepromatous leprosy (LLep) or multibacillary form includes LL, BL and BB. The incubation time ranges from several months to more than 20 years and does not exceed 5 years in TLep. After contact with Mycobacterium leprae, only 5% of patients develop the disease, almost all with cutaneous lesions and variably severe peripheral neuropathy. In TLep, initially a few large lesions are found (1 to 10). They appear as well demarcated hypopigmented, macules or erythematous plaques. A characteristic loss of sensation at the skin lesion is always present. In LLep, the cutaneous lesions are numerous (10 to 100 or more), normoesthesic, poorly demarcated hypopigmented macules or erythematous papules or nodules and sometimes plaques and may induce diffuse infiltration causing a leonine facies. Mucosas are affected leading in severe cases to nasal destruction, and corneal or laryngeal impairment. Visceral involvement (adenopathies, hepato-splenomegaly or orchiepididymitis) may be present. Neural involvement affects especially the ulnar, median, radial, external popliteal and tibial posterior nerves, with a greater risk in TLep than LLep of distal (hands and feet) anesthesia, palsy (foot drop or clawed hands) and amyotrophy. About 40% of patients may develop 2 types of reactional states: 1) reversal reaction (RR; inflammation of the skin lesions and severe acute neuritis) or down-grading reaction (increased number of lesions) and 2) erythema nodosum leprosum (ENL; vasculitis with painful and eruptive erythematous nodules, fever, neuritis and joint swelling) or Lucio's phenomenon (granulomatous vasculitis with painful necrotic macules).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by M. leprae, a mycobacterium for which the main reservoir is humans and some species of armadillos. Recently M. lepromatosis was identified as causing some LLep cases. Possible predisposing genetic factors have been found.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical, histopathological and bacteriological findings. Skin biopsy is used to determine the form. Examination of slit skin smears enables quantitative evaluation of the bacterial load, usually low or nil in TLep and always high in LLep. PCR assays in tissue may accurately detect M. leprae's 16s rRNA in LLep cases and gene mutations inducing antibiotic resistance. It is generally negative in TLep and only gives a qualitative score.
