DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes hypochromic eczematides, annular granuloma, annular erythema, dermatophyties and annular sarcoidosis in TLep, and pityriasis versicolor, post-inflammatory hypomelanosis, hypochromic or papulo-nodular sarcoidosis, Kaposi sarcoma, syphilis, lymphoma, cutaneous leukemia in LLep.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There are 2 treatment groups: paucibacillary (PB; up to 5 skin lesions) and multibacillary (MB; more than 5). The recommended therapy combines 2 antibiotics (for PB) or 3 (for MB): rifampicin, dapsone and clofazimine. In some cases, other drugs can be used (ofloxacin, minocycline, clarithromycin). Treatment duration is 6 months for PB and at least 1 year for MB. Reactional states can be treated with systemic corticosteroids and sometimes surgical neurolysis for RR, and thalidomide, corticosteroids or pentoxifylline for ENL.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is favorable when antibacillary and anti-reactional treatments are rapidly instituted. If not, the disease may lead to definitive neurological disabilities.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Renpenning syndrome is an X-linked intellectual disability syndrome (XLMR) characterized by intellectual deficiency, microcephaly, leanness and mild short stature.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): X-linked intellectual disability due to PQBP1 mutations; X-linked intellectual disability, Renpenning type

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The main clinical manifestations of Renpenning syndrome are usually moderate intellectual deficiency, leanness, microcephaly and short stature (relative to familial target measurements) and sometimes small testes (testicular volumes below 15 ml), that are noticed at puberty. Manifestations are expressed only in males, and female carriers show normal facial features, growth development and intelligence. Small head and brain sizes are noted at birth. Characteristic craniofacial features include long triangular faces with upslanting palpebral fissures, half-depilated eyebrows, large ridged or bulbous nose with overhanging columella, short philtrum, and cupped and laterally protruding ears. Patients are thin and show failure to thrive. Delayed motor and language development is noticed in children from an early age. Moderate to severe intellectual deficiency is seen in two thirds of cases. Muscular atrophy is also observed affecting mostly the spine and back muscles resulting in fall of head, upper back curve loss and an appearance of scapula alata. Metacarpophalangeal ankylosis of the thumb and muscular atrophy of the intrinsic muscles of the hand can occur in some cases. Although uncommon, cardiac malformations (atrial septal defect), cleft palate, ocular colobomas and imperforate anus have been noted in a few patients. Phenotypic variants grouped under Renpenning syndrome include Golabi-Ito-Hall syndrome, Hamel cerebro-palato-cardiac syndrome, Porteous syndrome, Sutherland-Haan syndrome, MRX55 and three other XLMR families. Hamel cerebro-palato-cardiac syndrome usually has the most severe manifestations.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Renpenning syndrome is an X-linked condition caused by mutations in the polyglutamine tract-binding protein 1 (PQBP1) gene, encoding a nuclear protein that regulates pre-mRNA splicing and transcription. Six of the seven mutations discovered in the PQBP1 gene result in a truncated protein whereas a missense mutation that does not affect the length of the mutated protein is seen in Golabi-Ito-Hall syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on inheritance of clinical manifestations of Renpenning syndrome. It is often difficult if there is only one male with intellectual deficiency in a family, but it must be suggested even in sporadic cases. Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows no obvious gyral reduction, which contrasts with frank microcephaly. PQBP1 gene screening for a mutation can confirm diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Fragile X syndrome is a differential diagnosis but microcephaly is not a feature. Other causes of microcephaly such as fetal CMV infection, fetal alcohol syndrome, maternal phenylketonuria, autosomal recessive microcephalies and Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome should be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: If a mutation is identified, prenatal diagnosis may be proposed to parents for further pregnancies. In sporadic cases, germinal mosaicism should be ruled out on prenatal setting.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Renpenning syndrome follows an X-linked recessive pattern of inheritance. Genetic testing is possible to identify carrier females and to inform them of the risk of passing on the gene to their offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management for Renpenning syndrome involves early education and intervention by trained therapists and treatment of any associated symptoms (cardiac defect, hypospadias, conductive deafness, strabismus). Children need to attend special education courses at school due to learning disabilities.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: There is no cure for Renpenning syndrome but in most cases there is no decrease in life expectancy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal monosomy 9p is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from a partial deletion of the short arm of chromosome 9, with a highly variable phenotype typically characterized by intellectual disability, craniofacial dysmorphism (trigonocephaly, upslanting palpebral fissures, hypoplastic supraorbital ridges), abnormal digits (long middle phalanges with short distal phalanges), as well as frequent association with genitourinary abnormalities (cryptorchidism, hypospadias, ambiguous genitalia, 46,XY testicular dysgenesis). Congenital hypothyroidism and cardiovascular defects have been reported in some cases. Patients present an increased risk for gonadoblastoma.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Distal deletion 9p syndrome is a rare chromosomal abnormality. While previous studies were limited by small sample sizes, a recent worldwide cohort analyzed genetic data from 719 individuals, making it the largest study on 9p-related syndromes to date. This condition exhibits a significant gender bias, with a notable enrichment for females. Additionally, simultaneous deletions and duplications involving 9p are rarely reported. [PMC9445862, PMC8756500]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Distal deletion 9p syndrome presents with a wide spectrum of manifestations, commonly including developmental delay/intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, and hypotonia. Craniofacial anomalies such as trigonocephaly are frequently observed, with an association to the FREM1 gene. Genital defects and gonadal dysfunction are common in XY individuals, often presenting as ambiguous genitalia, undescended testes, or sex reversal. Other reported features include congenital heart disease, psychiatric diagnoses, autism spectrum disorder, speech and language impairment, chronic constipation, atopic disease, vision problems, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and neonatal hypoglycemia. Brain anomalies and fair hair have also been noted in some patients. [PMC11369271, PMC9445862, PMC8606205, PMC8756500, PMC8136447]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Using a new analytic method ("unique non-overlapping region" (UNOR) analysis), we characterized the genotypes and phenotypes of a large cohort of individuals diagnosed with chromosome 9p deletion syndrome (9PMS) and defined critical genomic regions. We extracted phenotypic information from 48 individuals with 9PMS from medical records and used a guided interview with caregivers to clarify ambiguities. Using high-resolution whole-genome sequencing for breakpoint definition, we aligned deletions and drew virtual breakpoints to obtain UNORs associated with phenotypic characteristics. We next extracted genotype and phenotype data for 57 individuals identified from a systematic review of the 9PMS literature and analyzed these as above. Common phenotypic features included developmental delay/intellectual disability, dysmorphic features, hypotonia, genital defects in XY individuals,... [PMC11369271, PMC10099690, PMC9445862, PMC8606205, PMC8756500]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive acromesomelic dysplasia characterized by severe dwarfism (adult height approximately 120 cm) with abnormalities limited to the limbs (affecting the lower limbs more than upper limbs, with middle and distal segments being the most affected), severe shortening, absence or fusion of tubular bones of hands and feet and large joint dislocations. As seen in acromesomelic dysplasia, Grebe type and acromesomelic dysplasia, Maroteaux type, facial features and intelligence are normal.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Hunter-Thompson type, is part of a spectrum of skeletal dysplasias inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. The majority of patients with these disorders have biallelic loss-of-function mutations in GDF5. In some instances, mutations in BMPR1B, encoding a GDF5 receptor, have been identified as the cause, sometimes presenting with additional features like genital anomalies. Affected individuals have been reported from consanguineous families, consistent with its autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. [PMC4482310, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Grebe dysplasia, Hunter-Thompson dysplasia, and du Pan dysplasia constitute a spectrum of skeletal dysplasias inherited as an autosomal recessive trait characterized by short stature, severe acromesomelic shortening of the limbs, and normal axial skeleton. The majority of patients with these disorders have biallelic loss-of-function mutations of GDF5. In single instances, Grebe dysplasia and a Grebe dysplasia-like phenotype with genital anomalies have been shown to be caused by mutations in BMPR1B, encoding a GDF5 receptor. We clinically and radiologically characterised an acromesomelic chondrodysplasia in an adult woman born to consanguineous parents. We sequenced GDF5 and BMPR1B on DNA of the proposita. We performed 3D structural analysis and luciferase reporter assays to functionally investigate the identified BMPR1B mutation. We extend the genotype-phenotype correlation in the... [PMC4482310, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Hunter-Thompson type, is an autosomal recessive skeletal dysplasia that is part of a spectrum including Grebe and du Pan dysplasias. The majority of patients with these disorders, including Hunter-Thompson type, have biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the GDF5 gene. In some instances, mutations in BMPR1B, which encodes a GDF5 receptor, have been linked to Grebe dysplasia, du Pan dysplasia, and a distinct acromesomelic chondrodysplasia with genital anomalies. The phenotypic severity across this spectrum of related disorders may be influenced by the extent of functional impairment in the GDF5-BMPR1B ligand-receptor pair. [PMC4482310, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of acromesomelic dysplasia, including the Hunter-Thompson type, relies on clinical and radiological characterization. These conditions are typically identified by features such as short stature, severe acromesomelic shortening of the limbs, and a normal axial skeleton, often presenting with specific limb malformations like brachydactyly, aplasia of the fibula, ulnar deviation, and fusion of carpal/tarsal bones. Genetic analysis is crucial, primarily involving sequencing of GDF5 and BMPR1B, as biallelic loss-of-function mutations in GDF5 or mutations in BMPR1B are causative. Functional investigations, such as 3D structural analysis and luciferase reporter assays, can further characterize identified mutations. [PMC4482310, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Hunter-Thompson type, is part of a spectrum of skeletal dysplasias that includes Grebe dysplasia and du Pan dysplasia. These conditions are characterized by short stature, severe acromesomelic shortening of the limbs, and a normal axial skeleton. While the majority of patients with these disorders have biallelic loss-of-function mutations in GDF5, mutations in BMPR1B, which encodes a GDF5 receptor, can also cause Grebe dysplasia and du Pan dysplasia. A distinct subtype of acromesomelic chondrodysplasia caused by a homozygous BMPR1B mutation presents with genital anomalies and a unique limb phenotype, differentiating it from GDF5-associated chondrodysplasias like Hunter-Thompson type, despite some skeletal overlap. The phenotypic severity across this spectrum is linked to the extent of functional impairment of the GDF5-BMPR1B ligand-receptor pair. [PMC4482310, PMC1736042]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Acromesomelic dysplasia, Hunter-Thompson type, along with Grebe and du Pan dysplasias, are inherited as autosomal recessive traits. The majority of patients with these disorders have biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the GDF5 gene. However, mutations in BMPR1B, which encodes a GDF5 receptor, can also cause these conditions, including du Pan dysplasia and a subtype with genital anomalies. These BMPR1B mutations are typically homozygous and lead to a loss of function, distinguishing them from dominant negative effects seen with heterozygous BMPR1B mutations in other conditions. The occurrence in individuals from consanguineous families further supports the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. [PMC4482310, PMC1736042]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A small vessel vasculitis characterized by neutrophilic inflammation predominantly limited to the superficial cutaneous postcapillary venules and without systemic vasculitis or glomerulonephritis. Typical presentation is of unifocal or multifocal palpable purpura on the lower extremities.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The annual incidence of leukocytoclastic vasculitis in the United States is estimated at 1/220,000, of which 45% consist of cutaneous small vessel vasculitis.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease onset can occur at any age, and typically presents with non-blanching, palpable purpura and/or petechiae of the lower extremities with unifocal or multifocal distribution. The lesions may coalesce, ulcerate or be surrounded by hemorrhagic bullae. Urticarial lesion can also be observed. Lesions are usually not painful, although they may cause burning and itching. Histological characteristics are non-specific for the disease and include neutrophilic infiltration of the dermal small blood vessel walls, as well as, fibrinoid necrosis and disruption of the vessel wall, leukocytoclasia, endothelial swelling, and erythrocytes extravasation. As the lesion gets older, neutrophils diminish, and lymphocytes become prominent.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease may be idiopathic (in up to 50% of cases) or secondary to infections, medications, connective tissue diseases, or malignancy. The disease occurs due to the deposition of immune complexes (IC) on the wall of post-capillary venules, which then activates both complement pathways, leading to degranulation of mast cells and neutrophil chemotaxis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is one of exclusion. In general, skin biopsy samples from lesions between 24-48 hours old, should be examined with light microscopy and direct immunofluorescence. A complete history, review of systems, physical examination, and selected laboratory studies also should be performed to assess for inciting causes or extracutaneous involvement.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnosis is of systemic small vessel vasculitides with cutaneous presentation and includes antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis, immunoglobulin A vasculitis. Other conditions with similar histopathology include infective endocarditis, macular purpura owing to trauma, skin fragility, pigmented purpuric dermatosis, septic emboli, and livedoid vasculopathy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment varies and depends on the chronicity of the disease, the severity of cutaneous involvement, and the presence or absence of both an underlying cause. An isolated episode associated with a known inciting factor may be managed by removal or treatment of the trigger, along with symptomatic measures. First-line systemic treatments for chronic, idiopathic disease include colchicine or dapsone, used singly or in combination. Recurrent, chronic, or severely symptomatic disease that does not respond to the aforementioned therapies may require initiation of an immunosuppressive agent such as azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, methotrexate, or rituximab.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The clinical outcome is typically good with 90% resolving in weeks to months of onset, but may be complicated by the occurrence of ulcers (treatment prolongation, infections and scarring). The reported relapse rate is between 8-25%.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Ring chromosome 12 syndrome is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome with a highly variable phenotype principally characterized by postnatal growth retardation, variable degrees of developmental delay and intellectual disability, microcephaly and facial dysmorphism (incl. epicanthal folds, low-set, cupped ears, prominent nose with flat nasal bridge, high arched palate, micrognathia). Skeletal abnormalities (e.g. pectus excavatum, clinodactyly), congenital heart malformations, cryptorchidism, café-au-lait spots and epilepsy have also been reported.
A rare kidney malformation characterized by a reduction of 80% in nephron number and a marked hypertrophy of the glomeruli and tubules.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown. The male to female ratio is of 3:1.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Oligomeganephronia is usually detected on routine ultrasound screening with small but normal shaped kidneys. Birth weight is often below the average value. Patients may present at birth with polyuria/polydipsia or signs of kidney dysfunction. During the first year of life, the usual symptom is persistent anorexia with vomiting, fever, and growth delay. Chronic kidney disease typically occurs during childhood or adolescence. Adult-onset oligomeganephronia has been reported in some rare cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of oligomeganephronia is not fully understood, but is hypothesized to be caused by premature termination of nephrogenesis. This may be linked to the same factors as renal hypoplasia, but with a more severe reduction in nephron numbers. Such factors include intrauterine growth restriction, maternal diseases (diabetes, hypertension), maternal drug intake (inhibitors of the renin-angiotensin system or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs)) or intoxication (smoking and alcohol). Premature birth (before the 36th week) is also a risk factor due to incomplete nephrogenesis. Oligomeganephronia can occur as part of a multi-organ syndrome such as renal coloboma syndrome, which is caused by mutations in the PAX2 gene (10q24.31), or can be caused by chromosomal disorders including 22q11 deletion syndrome or Wolf-Hirschhorn syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis can be suspected by bilateral, small and echogenic kidneys on ultrasound. CT-scan may, in addition to small, normal-shaped kidneys, show a thickened cortex and medulla with striated nephrograms. The diagnosis is confirmed histologically by a reduced number of nephrons, hypertrophic glomeruli with diameters being two to three times the normal size, hypertrophic tubules and thickening of Bowman's capsule. Both kidneys are symmetrically affected.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes renal dysplasia, nephronophthisis, autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease, kidney infarction or ischemic kidney disease, and diffuse kidney parenchymal disease.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal ultrasonographic screening allows detection of oligomeganephronia from midway through gestation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Most cases are sporadic, but familial occurrence has been described.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Angiotensin-converting-enzyme inhibitors may slow the progression of the disease. Once having reached the stage of kidney failure, management includes a dialysis-transplantation program.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With the increasing metabolic demands on the kidney during growth, a decline in kidney function is seen resulting in chronic kidney disease at a mean age of 10 years (range 6 months to 20 years).

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A congenital, extracardiac channel which connects the ascending aorta above the sinotubular junction to the cavity of the left, or (less commonly) right ventricle.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact incidence is unknown, estimates ranging from 0.5% of fetal cardiac malformations to less than 0.1% of congenitally malformed hearts in clinico-pathological series. Approximately 130 cases have been reported in the literature, about twice as many cases in males as in females.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Associated defects, usually involving the proximal coronary arteries, or the aortic or pulmonary valves, are present in nearly half the cases. Occasional patients present with an asymptomatic heart murmur and cardiac enlargement, but most suffer heart failure in the first year of life.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of aorto-ventricular tunnel is uncertain. It appears to result from a combination of maldevelopment of the cushions which give rise to the pulmonary and aortic roots, and abnormal separation of these structures.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Echocardiography is the diagnostic investigation of choice. Antenatal diagnosis by fetal echocardiography is reliable after 18 weeks gestation.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Aorto-ventricular tunnel must be distinguished from other lesions which cause rapid run-off of blood from the aorta and produce cardiac failure.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Optimal management of symptomatic aorto-ventricular tunnel consists of diagnosis by echocardiography, complimented with cardiac catheterization as needed to elucidate coronary arterial origins or associated defects, and prompt surgical repair. Observation of the exceedingly rare, asymptomatic patient with a small tunnel may be justified by occasional spontaneous closure. All patients require life-long follow-up for recurrence of the tunnel, aortic valve incompetence, left ventricular function, and aneurysmal enlargement of the ascending aorta.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Aorto-left ventricular tunnel (ALVT) is a rare congenital heart defect, and its prenatal diagnosis is even rarer. It can be diagnosed by antenatal ultrasound or fetal echocardiography, with characteristics including an increased cardiac-thorax ratio, increased left ventricular end-diastolic diameter, and a dysplastic aortic valve. Extracardiac malformations are uncommon. While some fetuses with hydrops may die early, ALVT carries a good prognosis in the absence of fetal hydrops, particularly if the fetus survives to 24 weeks without this complication. Prompt neonatal management following antenatal diagnosis can help prevent perinatal morbidity and mortality. [PMC10617269, PMC9303731]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for aorto-ventricular tunnel is largely favorable, with a reported death rate of 5.7% among 177 patients who underwent surgery or transcatheter closure. However, the condition is also associated with a high mortality rate, though no specific risk factors for death were found. Fetal prognosis is good in the absence of hydrops, with fetuses surviving to 24 weeks without hydrops likely to have a good outcome; hydrops prior to 24 weeks was associated with fetal death. Postoperative complications, such as mild residual aortic regurgitation (present in 22.7% of cases), may hamper long-term prognosis. Prompt neonatal management and surgical repair can lead to survival and good functional status. [PMC11868909, PMC10617269, PMC10067305, PMC9303731, PMC5826325]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A form of leukodystrophy that is characterized by infantile-onset macrocephaly, often with mild neurologic signs at presentation (such as mild motor delay), which worsen with time, leading to poor ambulation, falls, ataxia, spasticity, increasing seizures and cognitive decline. Brain magnetic resonance imaging reveals diffusely abnormal and mildly swollen white matter as well as subcortical cysts in the anterior temporal and frontoparietal regions.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): MLC; Megalencephalic leukodystrophy; Megalencephaly-cystic leukodystrophy syndrome; Vacuolating megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts; Van der Knaap syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. It is observed more commonly in certain ethnicities with high rates of consanguinity, notably within the Agrawal community in India. To date, genetic variants have been identified in 508 patients with MLC confirmed by MRI diagnosis, compiled from both a database and published literature. [PMC10938252, PMC4513453]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC) is characterized by infantile-onset macrocephaly, often presenting at birth or during infancy, and chronic edema of the brain white matter. Patients typically experience progressive motor dysfunction, including ataxia and spasticity, along with epilepsy and slow cognitive decline or mild mental retardation. MRI findings are hallmark, showing diffuse subcortical leukoencephalopathy with cystic white matter degeneration. Atypical presentations can include internal capsule, brainstem, and cerebellum involvement, subependymal nodular heterotopia, subependymal cysts, cortical laminar necrosis, and, rarely, bipolar disorder. [PMC11669955, PMC10938252, PMC10114270, PMC7333431, PMC4757224]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC) is an autosomal recessive disorder. Classic MLC is caused by bi-allelic recessive pathogenic variants in the MLC1 gene, which encodes a novel protein, or in GLIALCAM (also called HEPACAM). Heterozygous dominant pathogenic variants in GLIALCAM can lead to remitting MLC. Rare patients with heterozygous dominant variants in GPRC5B have also been described with classic MLC, and bi-allelic recessive variants in AQP4 have been identified in remitting MLC. The disease occurs more commonly in some ethnicities where consanguinity is common, consistent with its recessive inheritance. [PMC10938252, PMC4757224, PMC4577658, PMC4513453]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Here, we discuss a rare and to our knowledge, the first case of an atypical Van der Knaap's disease in a 6-year-old boy who presented with motor difficulties, developmental delay, cognitive impairment, seizures. The objective of is to highlight its unusual findings on MRI including internal capsule, brainstem, cerebellum involvement; subependymal nodular heterotopia, subependymal cysts, cortical laminar necrosis along with typical findings of megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy and subcortical cysts. The study also underscores the clinical implications of this complex pathology, with emphasis on comprehensive neuroradiological evaluation for atypical presentations to guide better diagnostic and management outcomes. Here, we discuss a rare and to our knowledge, the first case of an atypical Van der Knaap's disease in a 6-year-old boy who presented with motor difficulties, developmental... [PMC11669955, PMC10938252, PMC8993180, PMC6660666, PMC4757224]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC) includes other hereditary neurometabolic diseases, which often present with variable and superimposable clinical and radiological features. Conditions such as RNASET2-deficient leukoencephalopathy, congenital cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, and Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome (AGS) share overlapping clinical and radiologic features. RNASET2-deficient leukoencephalopathy, for instance, can present with white matter involvement without megalencephaly, distinguishing it from typical MLC. Comprehensive neuroradiological evaluation, including MRI, is crucial for identifying distinctive findings and differentiating MLC from these conditions, particularly in atypical presentations. [PMC11669955, PMC8993180, PMC6660666, PMC4757224]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC) is primarily an autosomal recessive disorder, with increased prevalence in populations where consanguinity is common. Classic MLC is caused by bi-allelic recessive pathogenic variants in MLC1 or GLIALCAM. Remitting MLC can result from heterozygous dominant pathogenic variants in GLIALCAM or bi-allelic recessive variants in AQP4. Rare cases of classic MLC have also been linked to heterozygous dominant variants in GPRC5B. Genetic analysis can identify variants in these genes, including MLC1, GLIALCAM, GPRC5B, and AQP4. [PMC10938252, PMC4757224, PMC4577658, PMC4513453]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: There is no specific or curative treatment available for Megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts. Management is primarily supportive, focusing on symptomatic relief and rehabilitation. Medical interventions address symptoms such as seizures and psychiatric manifestations like catatonia or bipolar disorder, using medications like olanzapine, sertraline, and carbamazepine. Rehabilitation, including occupational therapy, speech therapy, physiotherapy procedures, and psychomotor stimulation, is crucial for improving motor functions and overall quality of life, with early referral being important. [PMC10938252, PMC10114270, PMC7333431, PMC4577658]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The leukodystrophy megalencephalic leukoencephalopathy with subcortical cysts (MLC) is characterized by infantile-onset macrocephaly and chronic edema of the brain white matter. With delayed onset, patients typically experience motor problems, epilepsy and slow cognitive decline. No treatment is available. Classic MLC is caused by bi-allelic recessive pathogenic variants in MLC1 or GLIALCAM (also called HEPACAM ). Heterozygous dominant pathogenic variants in GLIALCAM lead to remitting MLC, where patients show a similar phenotype in early life, followed by normalization of white matter edema and no clinical regression. Rare patients with heterozygous dominant variants in GPRC5B and classic MLC were recently described. In addition, two siblings with bi-allelic recessive variants in AQP4 and remitting MLC have been identified. The last systematic overview of variants linked to MLC dates... [PMC10938252, PMC10114270, PMC7333431, PMC4577658]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome characterized by childhood or adolescence onset of severe, intractable periodontitis, lack of attached gingiva, and presence of pretibial plaques. Additional manifestations are easy bruising, hypermobility mainly of the distal joints, skin hyperextensibility and fragility, abnormal scarring, recurrent infections, hernias, marfanoid facial features, acrogeria, and prominent vasculature.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Periodontal EDS; EDS VIII; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome type 8; Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, periodontitis type; pEDS

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder. Only a limited number of patients and pedigrees with this condition have been reported, indicating its rarity. One cohort identified 21 adults from 12 families, with a male to female ratio of 5:16. In this group, the age at molecular diagnosis ranged from 21 to 73 years, with a mean of 45 years. [PMC10264792, PMC3548259]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS) is characterized by severe early-onset periodontitis, often presenting in early childhood with severe tooth mobility, gingival bleeding, and precocious loss of deciduous teeth, along with generalized lack of attached gingiva, alveolar bone loss, and gingival recession. Beyond oral manifestations, patients frequently exhibit pretibial plaques, skin hyperextensibility, skin fragility, and easy bruising. Other features can include joint hypermobility, vocal changes, and early-onset osteoarthritis. In adults, leukodystrophy has also been identified. While a spectrum of joint and skin manifestations is common, their presence can be variable, and microscopic evidence of collagen disorganization may be detectable even when these signs are subtle. [PMC9979821, PMC10264792, PMC7912441, PMC3548259, PMC3314117]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS) is a rare autosomal dominant disorder. It is characterized by deleterious pathogenic heterozygous variants in the C1R and C1S genes, which encode components of the complement system. C1R variants have been identified in all families in some cohorts, and a novel missense mutation in C1R (c.658T>G; p.Cys220Gly) has been reported in affected individuals. [PMC10264792, PMC7912441, PMC3548259]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS) is established through clinical and molecular assessment. Clinically, it is characterized by severe early-onset periodontitis and generalized lack of attached gingiva, which is considered pathognomonic. Other features, as per the 2017 International EDS Classification, include pretibial plaques, joint hypermobility, and skin hyperextensibility. Molecular diagnosis involves identifying pathogenic heterozygous variants in C1R and C1S, typically through genetic analysis such as exome and Sanger sequencing. Physical and dental evaluations are integral to the assessment. Microscopic evidence of collagen disorganization may be detectable, and transmission electron microscopy and fibroblast studies can be performed in some cases. The diagnosis should be considered in familial forms of periodontitis, even when associated skin and joint manifestations are not prominent. [PMC10264792, PMC7912441, PMC3548259]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS), previously known as EDS type VIII, is characterized by early severe periodontitis, often with generalized lack of attached gingiva and precocious dental loss. This specific periodontal phenotype helps distinguish it from other forms of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, such as classical EDS, which may also present with joint hypermobility and skin manifestations. Marfan Syndrome, a systemic connective tissue disorder, can also involve severe periodontitis and generalized oral inflammation, suggesting it as a differential. Furthermore, pEDS should be considered in familial forms of periodontitis, even when associated skin and joint manifestations are not overtly present, due to the clinical variability of the disorder. [PMC7912441, PMC6485202, PMC3548259]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (pEDS) is an autosomal dominant disorder, with pathogenic heterozygous variants identified in the C1R and C1S genes. Molecular diagnosis is available through genetic services, confirming C1R variants in affected families. Familial forms of periodontitis, even without overt connective tissue signs, should prompt consideration of pEDS. Due to its autosomal dominant inheritance, familial monitoring is strongly recommended to identify affected individuals and provide appropriate management. The disorder can exhibit clinical variability within families. [PMC9979821, PMC10264792, PMC7912441, PMC3548259]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome primarily involves strict supragingival biofilm control, utilizing both mechanical and chemical strategies. Dental extractions may be necessary for severely affected teeth. Scaling and root planing are performed on remaining teeth, and patients should be included in a periodontal maintenance program to prevent disease recurrence. Familial monitoring is also recommended. [PMC9979821]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Periodontal Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is characterized by severe, early-onset periodontitis, often beginning in deciduous teeth, leading to precocious dental loss. Patients may experience severe tooth mobility, gingival bleeding, generalized alveolar bone loss, and gingival recession. Despite strict supragingival biofilm control and periodontal maintenance programs, multiple dental extractions may be required. Beyond dental manifestations, the disorder is clinically variable and can include a spectrum of joint and skin manifestations, with early-onset osteoarthritis being a reported complication. Microscopic evidence of collagen disorganization is detectable. [PMC9979821, PMC7912441, PMC3548259, PMC3314117]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:90058

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: The incidence of traumatic cauda equina syndrome (CES) in Victoria, Australia, ranged from 0.56 to 2.51 per million per year. Most affected individuals were men (67%), with a median age at injury of 41 years. Road trauma was the most common cause, accounting for 35% of cases. While the incidence rate of traumatic CES was low, most people experienced long-term sequelae, including problems with health-related quality of life, disability, and return to work, as well as bowel and bladder issues. [PMC11907211]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: There are some cases of Klippel-Feil syndrome with spinal cord injury in clinical work. However, there is no literature report on Brown-Sequard syndrome after trauma. a case of Brown-Sequard syndrome following minor trauma in a patient with KFS type III. Her Brown-Sequard syndrome is caused by Klippel-Feil syndrome. We found a 38-year-old female patient with KFS in our clinical work. She was unconscious on the spot following a minor traumatic episode. After treatment, her whole body was numb and limb activity was limited. Half an hour later, she felt numb and weak in the right limb and weak in the left limb. She had no previous hypertension, diabetes, or coronary heart disease. After one-month treatment of medication, hyperbaric oxygen, rehabilitation, and acupuncture in our hospital, her muscle strength partially recovered, but the treatment effect was still not satisfactory. Then, she... [PMC10494414]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Osteosarcoma is a primary malignant tumour of the skeleton characterised by the direct formation of immature bone or osteoid tissue by the tumour cells.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Classic osteosarcoma is a rare (0.2% of all malignant tumours) highly malignant tumour, with an estimated incidence of 3 cases/million population/year.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Osteosarcoma arises predominantly in the long bones and rarely in the soft tissues. The age at presentation ranges from 10 to 25 years of age.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Plain radiographs, computed tomography, magnetic resonance imaging, angiography and dynamic bone scintigraphy are used for diagnosis, evaluation the extent of tumour involvement and for making decisions about the type of operation and, if necessary, the type of reconstruction required.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: In the past, all patients with osteosarcoma were treated by amputation but the cure rate was under 10% and almost all patients died within a year from diagnosis. At present, the percentage of patients cured varies between 60% and 70% for localised osteosarcoma at onset (80% of cases) treated in specialised bone tumour centres with pre- and postoperative chemotherapy associated with surgery. Surgery is conservative (limb salvage) in more than 90% of patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is more severe (cure rate about 30%) for tumours located in the axial skeleton and in patients with metastasis at onset.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Osteosarcoma, particularly its variants, presents diagnostic challenges. Giant cell-rich osteosarcoma (GCRO) can be misdiagnosed as a giant-cell bone tumor or an aneurysmal bone cyst, especially when presenting as pure osteolytic bone lesions in young adults. Small cell osteosarcoma (SCOS) requires careful differentiation from other small cell tumors. Furthermore, radiation-induced osteosarcoma (RIOS) in its early stages can be confused with bone changes following radiotherapy or appearance deformities after surgery. [PMC12147397, PMC11706910, PMC12373421]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare mature B-cell neoplasm characterized by clonal proliferation of B-cell prolymphocytes, with prolymphocytes constituting more than 55% of lymphoid cells in peripheral blood. IG genes are clonally rearranged. Neoplastic cells are present in the bone marrow, peripheral blood, and spleen. Patients usually present with B symptoms, massive splenomegaly but absent or minimal lymphadenopathy, rapidly increasing lymphocyte count, anemia, and thrombocytopenia. Therapy response is poor.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (B-PLL) is an extremely rare disease, accounting for approximately 1% of lymphocytic leukemias. It generally occurs in older people, most frequently affecting patients in their seventh decade of life. B-PLL comprises conditions with unfavorable outcomes. [PMC12027594, PMC7868445, PMC8101659, PMC4867829]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (B-PLL) is an extremely rare and aggressive leukemia, typically affecting older individuals, often in their seventh decade. It is characterized by rapidly increasing leukocytosis, very high white blood cell counts, and the presence of over 55% prolymphocytes in the peripheral blood. Patients commonly present with massive splenomegaly, weakness, and varying degrees of lymphadenopathy, which can be minimal or generalized. Morphologically, Auer Rod-Like Inclusions may be observed, and flow cytometry can show B cells dimmer on CD45 and brighter on CD20 compared to typical B-CLL. The disease can transform from chronic lymphocytic leukemia and may lead to complications like systemic capillary leak syndrome. B-PLL generally carries a poor prognosis, with a median survival of approximately 3 years, though some patients may experience prolonged survival. [PMC12027594, PMC9052906, PMC7868445, PMC7757465, PMC8101659]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The pathogenesis of B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (B-PLL) is not completely understood. Mutations in MYC are presumed to play a role in its development. B-PLL can also arise as a transformation from chronic lymphocytic leukemia, where new complex cytogenetics may develop. TP53 mutations have been observed in cases of B-PLL. [PMC9052906, PMC7868445]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (B-PLL) relies on integrating clinical, morphological, immunophenotypic, and cytogenetic findings. Key characteristics include massive splenomegaly, minimal or no lymphadenopathy, and very high white blood cell counts. Morphological examination of peripheral blood typically reveals more than 55% prolymphocytes. Immunophenotypic analysis, such as flow cytometry, may show B cells with dimmer CD45 and brighter CD20 expression. Cytogenetic studies, including fluorescent in situ hybridization, can identify complex cytogenetics. These combined approaches are crucial for distinguishing B-PLL from other lymphoproliferative disorders. [PMC7868445, PMC8101659, PMC6863028]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (B-PLL) requires careful differentiation from other chronic lymphoproliferative disorders, including chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and de novo CLL/prolymphocytic leukemia. Key distinguishing features include the presence of over 55% prolymphocytes in the peripheral blood, massive splenomegaly, minimal or absent lymphadenopathy, and very high white blood cell counts. Immunophenotypic analysis, such as B cells appearing dimmer on CD45 and brighter on CD20 compared to typical B-CLL, also aids in diagnosis. Integrating clinical profile, morphological findings, immunophenotyping, and cytogenetic studies is crucial for accurate differentiation due to varied treatment and prognosis. [PMC7868445, PMC8101659]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (B-PLL) often draws from chronic lymphocytic leukemia strategies, with CD20 antibodies considered first-line therapy. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (alloHSCT) offers a prospect of cure for selected patients, with favorable outcomes reported, though pre-transplant performance status and comorbidity index are important considerations. While B-PLL can be resistant to many chemotherapies and targeted agents like alemtuzumab and thalidomide, specific regimens have shown promise. These include zanubrutinib, rituximab, and lenalidomide, or obinutuzumab and venetoclax, as well as chemoimmunotherapy which can resolve complications like systemic capillary leak syndrome. Salvage R-CHOP, potentially sensitized by phenylethyl isothiocyanate (PEITC), has also led to disease stabilization enabling subsequent alloHSCT. [PMC12027594, PMC9052906, PMC7868445, PMC7757465, PMC4867829]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia (B-PLL) is an aggressive disease generally associated with a poor prognosis, with a reported median survival of only 3 years. It is often resistant to most chemotherapy and newer targeted therapies, though a subset of patients may experience prolonged survival. Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (alloHSCT) significantly improves outcomes for selected patients, offering a prospect of cure, particularly in those with favorable pre-transplant performance status and comorbidity index. Specific treatment regimens, such as zanubrutinib, rituximab, and lenalidomide, have also shown to induce deep and durable remission, even in TP53-mutated cases. Furthermore, some treatments can lead to disease stabilization, enabling subsequent transplantation and favorable outcomes. [PMC12027594, PMC9052906, PMC8101659, PMC4867829]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: X-linked sideroblastic anemia is a constitutional microcytic, hypochromic anemia of varying severity that is clinically characterized by manifestations of anemia and iron overload and that may respond to treatment with pyridoxine and folic acid.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown. Around 200 cases and fewer than 100 unrelated probands are described in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The anemia can present at any age from birth to the 9th decade. Some patients are asymptomatic and are detected incidentally by hematological screening or through a family study. Clinical features are those of anemia and/or iron overload such as pallor, fatigue, weakness. Breathlessness, mild splenomegaly, cardiac problems, abnormal liver function, hyperglycemia, glucose intolerance and skin hyperpigmentation are seen more rarely.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: SA is due to inherited or de novo mutations in the ALAS2 gene (Xp11.21) encoding the erythroid form of delta amino levulinic acid synthase (ALAS2), which altered function leads to impaired heme synthesis. The increased ineffective and expanded erythropoiesis leads to increased absorption of dietary iron and a risk of iron overload. Female carriers are usually unaffected, however, one quarter of probands are female who have X-chromosome inactivation skewed against the unaffected allele and almost half of the female probands have macrocytic rather than microcytic red blood cells due to the heterozygous inheritance of a severe/null allele.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis requires a full blood and reticulocyte count, measurement of iron stores, exclusion of thalassemia as a cause, bone marrow aspirate showing ringed sideroblasts, and mutation analysis of the ALAS2 gene.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include other types of inherited sideroblastic anemia and in case of macrocytic red cells in females also acquired myelodysplasia (refractory anemia with ringed sideroblasts or RARS. Most female carriers show some evidence of microcytic, hypochromic red blood cells but hematological parameters cannot be relied upon for genetic counseling purposes and DNA analysis is required.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is rarely indicated or requested, but should be offered in case of family history.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling for the family of affected individuals is recommended, as early diagnosis in a child may be of great benefit for treatment of anemia and prevention of iron overload, the main cause of early death in the past.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is supportive and involves hematological monitoring, the surveillance of iron levels, lifetime pyridoxine supplementation in those who respond and folic acid supplementation. Pyridoxine response varies in degree and is rarely complete. Prophylactic occasional phlebotomy can be performed to prevent iron overload, if anemia is very mild or corrected by pyridoxine. If iron overload has already developed, phlebotomy, iron chelation or a combination of both can be used to normalize iron levels. In some cases iron depletion may simultaneously increase the hemoglobin level. Blood transfusions may be needed on occasion but are only required on a regular basis for those most severely affected.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable but for patients with pyridoxine-responsive anemia whose iron stores are kept low, normal life expectancy should be achievable.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, syndromic intellectual disability characterized by short stature, sparse hair, characteristic coarse face, brachydactyly with prominent interphalangeal joints, seizures and intellectual disability. Facial characteristics include triangular shaped face, dense and prominent eyelashes, rounded premaxilla, broad nasal base, thick alae nasi, upturned nasal tip, broad philtrum, thin upper vermilion, thick and everted lower vermilion and wide mouth.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Although the prevalence of the disorder is unknown, it is thought to be less than 1/1,000,000. To date, there are fewer than 100 molecularly confirmed, affected individuals reported in the literature. No significant difference in male-to-female ratio or geographical distribution has been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: At birth, patients may be small for gestational age (one-third of cases), have facial hypertrichosis, a low anterior-lateral hairline, and microcephaly (one-quarter). Postnatally, microcephaly and proportional short stature is present in over half of the patients. Sparse scalp hair is present in almost all patients and may be evident in the first months of life. Prominent inter-phalangeal joints due to decreased subcutaneous fat, are the most characteristic sign, and may be accompanied by fetal pads (half of patients). Radiological findings of the hands include short metacarpals, short phalanges, cone-shaped epiphyses, and ivory epiphyses in a few cases. Patients can show mild shortening of the toes, sandal gap and some thickening of the distal phalanx of the hallux. Most of these characteristics, particularly limbs and facial features, tend to be more evident with time. Hypotonia is reported in one third of patients, but major motor milestones such as sitting and walking independently are usually not very delayed. Intellectual disability (ID) is severe in nearly half, moderate in a third, and mild in the remainder of cases. Nearly a third never develop speech or language skills. Epilepsy occurs in two-thirds of patients, with onset between 18 to 24 months, and may correlate with regression. Seizure type is variable, even within the same individual and can be difficult to manage. Disposition is generally happy and very friendly, but temper outbursts and bouts of aggression are possible. Other congenital anomalies are variably observed.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disorder is due to missense variants (80% of case) or intragenic deletions in SMARCA2 (9p24.3). This gene encodes a protein belonging to the ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling enzymes, implicated in the regulation of gene expression and cell cycle control. In almost 17% of patients, no variant has been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected on peculiar combination of facial features with sparse hair, intellectual disability, brachydactyly with prominent interphalangeal joints and seizures. Molecular diagnosis is based on identification of variants in SMARCA2.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Coffin-Siris syndrome, Williams syndrome and Cornelia de Lange syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: If the pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, prenatal testing for pregnancies at theoretic increased risk is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant. To date, all affected individuals have had a de novo SMARCA2 pathogenic variant, suggesting a low risk to siblings. However, because of the theoretic possibility of parental germline mosaicism, the empiric recurrence risk to siblings is approximately 1%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Clinical management requires periodical evaluation by a child neurologist/neuropsychiatrist in order to monitor the evolution of the intellectual development or onset of seizures. Enabling and supporting therapies (including non-verbal communication) and special school program are required. Anti-epileptic drugs appear necessary for controlling seizures, sometimes unsuccessfully and with consequent need for hospitalization. Regular follow up of ophthalmologic and/or audiologic abnormalities is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable and is predominantly influenced by the age of onset of seizures and the difficulty in managing it. Independent living depends on the degree of intellectual disability, and is likely never totally achieved.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cat eye syndrome (CES) is a rare chromosomal disorder with a highly variable clinical presentation. Most patients have multiple malformations affecting the eyes (iris coloboma), ears (preauricular pits and/or tags), anal region (anal atresia), heart and kidneys. Intellectual disability is usually mild or borderline normal.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: CES has an estimated prevalence of 1/50,000 to 1/150,000 live births. Males and females appear to be affected equally.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: CES covers a very wide clinical spectrum in terms of features and severity, ranging from a normal phenotype to severe multisystemic disease. The 3 main visible characteristics are preauricular anomalies, anal atresia, and iris coloboma but none are found consistently. Preauricular skin tags and/or pits are the most consistent feature. The typical eye anomaly is absent in up to 50% of patients. Eye coloboma may involve the iris, the choroid and/or the retina. Less frequently, unilateral microphtalmia, aniridia, cornea clouding, cataract and/or Duane anomaly are observed. In addition to preauricular tags and/or pits, the external ears may be low-set and severely reduced with possible atresia of the external ear canal. Characteristic facial features are down-slanting palpebral fissures, inner epicanthic folds, hypertelorism, flat nasal bridge, and small mandible. Cleft lip/palate is sometimes observed. In some individuals, the anal canal is narrow or absent with a fistula from the rectum into an abnormal location (the bladder, vagina or perineum). The most frequently reported congenital heart defect is congenital total pulmonary venous return anomaly and, less frequently, tetralogy of Fallot. Congenital kidney abnormalities include absence of one or both kidneys, hydronephrosis, supernumerary kidneys, and/or renal hypoplasia. Skeletal abnormalities include spinal defects and limb malformations. Possible gastrointestinal malformations are biliary atresia, intestinal malrotation and/or Hirschsprung disease. Other variable features include hernias, cryptorchidism and hypospadias in males. Rarer malformations may affect almost every organ. Most patients have mild intellectual disability (although some moderate to severe) but a few have normal cognitive development. Short stature with growth hormone deficiency is possible in some cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Most patients harbor a small supernumerary bisatellited marker chromosome (sSMC) that results in partial tetrasomy of 22pter-22q11. In one third of cases, this extra chromosome is present in a mosaic state. Other cytogenetic anomalies have been rarely reported, including partial trisomy of chromosome 22 and intrachromosomal triplication of the 22q11 region.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis, suspected on the basis of clinical manifestations, is based on cytogenetic testing showing the presence of extra material derived from chromosome 22q11. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with specific probes is needed to detect a low level mosaicism.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other chromosomal disorders with overlapping phenotypes such as CHARGE syndrome and VACTERL/VATER association.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible through karyotyping and FISH analysis of prenatal samples.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The extra chromosome usually arises de novo.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Multidisciplinary management is necessary and depends on the specific symptoms that are apparent in each patient. Surgical correction is necessary for anal atresia and severe cardiac malformations. Bacterial infections should be anticipated and treated vigorously. Patients should be screened for visual and hearing impairment. Early intervention with educational support can be beneficial.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Some patients die from severe malformations in early infancy. Otherwise, life expectancy is generally not significantly reduced.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Tetrasomy 18p is a very rare structural chromosomal anomaly affecting multiple body systems and characterized clinically by craniofacial abnormalities, delayed development, cognitive impairment, changes in muscle tone, distinctive facial features, and rarely renal malformations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Tetrasomy 18p syndrome is a very rare chromosomal disorder, with most cases occurring de novo, although familial cases have also been reported. Low-level mosaicism for tetrasomy 18p is well tolerated and can be missed by certain diagnostic . This suggests that low-level mosaicism for the syndrome might be more common in the general population than currently recognized, primarily due to detection limitations. [PMC7963419, PMC5811181]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Tetrasomy 18p syndrome is a rare chromosomal disorder caused by the presence of isochromosome 18p. It is characterized mainly by developmental delays, cognitive impairment, and hypotonia. Typical dysmorphic features are common, and other reported anomalies include microcephaly, growth delay, and malformations affecting the cerebellum (such as partial agenesis of cerebellar vermis), kidneys, heart, and skeleton. The clinical presentation can vary, with some individuals exhibiting dysmorphic features and delayed neuro-motor development, while low-level mosaicism for i(18p) may be well tolerated and associated with a phenotypically normal state. [PMC7963419, PMC5811181]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Tetrasomy 18p syndrome is caused by the presence of isochromosome 18p [i(18p)], a supernumerary marker composed of two copies of the p arm of chromosome 18. Most cases are de novo, but familial cases have been reported, including those linked to inherited unbalanced reciprocal translocations. Mosaicism for tetrasomy 18p, often involving i(18p), is another recognized etiology, resulting from post-zygotic genetic variation or mutational events during meiotic or post-meiotic segregation. Low-level mosaicism for i(18p) might be more common than currently recognized. [PMC11593787, PMC7963419, PMC5811181, PMC5358428]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for Tetrasomy 18p syndrome include non-invasive prenatal screening tests (NIPT) for initial detection. Confirmation and characterization of aneuploidy involve a synergy of techniques such as cytogenetic analysis (karyotyping), FISH, SNP array, and array CGH. Karyotyping is particularly useful for identifying isochromosome 18p and detecting low-level mosaicism, which may be missed by other . When mosaicism is suspected, it is important to analyze multiple tissues, including blood, skin, hair follicles, and buccal mucosa, with non-invasive sampling complementing blood analysis. Whole-exome sequencing has also been employed. [PMC11593787, PMC7963419]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of Tetrasomy 18p syndrome can be suggested by non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPT) indicating a high risk for chromosome 18 aneuploidy. Subsequent confirmation typically involves invasive prenatal testing, employing a synergy of cytogenetic analysis, SNP array, and FISH techniques. For example, a partial tetrasomy 18p was characterized at 13+5 weeks gestation using these after a high-risk NIPT. Quantitative fluorescent PCR (QF-PCR) is also a rapid and accurate assay useful for diagnosing chromosome 18 aneuploidies. Sonographic fetal malformations may also prompt invasive prenatal investigations. [PMC11593787, PMC11272248, PMC3794322, PMC3653531]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Tetrasomy 18p syndrome is most often a de novo chromosomal disorder caused by an isochromosome 18p, though familial cases have been reported. It can arise from an inherited unbalanced reciprocal translocation from a balanced carrier parent, which carries a 50-80% risk for unbalanced chromosomal anomalies in offspring. Prenatal diagnosis may be indicated by a high-risk non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPT) for chromosome 18 aneuploidy, requiring confirmation and characterization using cytogenetic, FISH, and SNP-array techniques. Mosaicism for tetrasomy 18p can occur with variable phenotypic expression, and low-level mosaicism may be underrecognized. When mosaicism is suspected, studying multiple tissues like blood, skin, hair follicles, and buccal mucosa is recommended for comprehensive analysis. [PMC11593787, PMC7963419, PMC5811181]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Tetrasomy 18p syndrome is characterized by developmental delays, cognitive impairment, hypotonia, and dysmorphic features. The prognosis can be variable, as demonstrated by phenotypically discordant monozygotic twins where one presented with dysmorphic features and delayed neuro-motor development, while the other was phenotypically normal. Notably, low-level mosaic tetrasomy 18p has been observed to be well tolerated. [PMC7963419, PMC5811181]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare iron storage disorder present at birth characterized by the association of severe hepatocellular failure with hyperbilirubinemia, signs of hemorrhage, edema, ascites, hypoglycemia, and lactic acidosis with little to no elevation of transaminases. It is a distinct entity that differs from other forms of hemochromatosis with respect to its pathogenesis and molecular origin.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Neonatal hemochromatosis has been observed in multiple family members, including siblings and half-siblings, indicating a recurrent pattern. Cases have been reported in successive girls from different fathers, and in a brother, sister, and half-brother. The inheritance pattern is debated, with possibilities including incomplete penetrance or gonadal mosaicism for a dominant disorder, a maternal environmental factor, or a mitochondrial defect, rather than simple autosomal recessive inheritance. An association with the HLA haplotype (A3, B7) was noted in one affected family. [PMC1050628, PMC3049705, PMC1899670]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Neonatal hemochromatosis typically presents immediately after birth or in the first week of life with symptoms such as hypoglycemia, jaundice, coagulopathy, hypotonia, and respiratory difficulty, often leading to acute liver failure. Clinical features can include abnormal facial features, small liver and lungs, and a large spleen. Ocular manifestations like bilateral severe retinal edema with subretinal fluid and macular cherry-red spots have been observed, which may resolve after liver transplantation. Pathologically, the condition is characterized by siderotic cirrhosis, widespread parenchymal siderosis, and massive liver necrosis, with hemosiderin deposits found in various organs including the liver, pancreas, thyroid, myocardium, and renal tubules. The phenotypic expression can be variable, and while often fatal, liver transplantation offers a chance of survival. [PMC11290577, PMC3059895, PMC2528468, PMC3049705, PMC1899670]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Neonatal hemochromatosis involves abnormalities in cellular iron handling, leading to significant hepatic iron overload which is directly implicated in pathogenesis, often commencing as massive necrosis in midfetal life. The disease presents with widespread parenchymal siderosis and absent reticuloendothelial siderosis, a pattern shared with primary hemochromatosis. While the precise etiology remains undefined, recurrence in half-sibs suggests complex inheritance patterns beyond autosomal recessive, with possibilities including incomplete penetrance, gonadal mosaicism for a dominant disorder, a mitochondrial defect, or a maternal "environmental factor." Investigations into cellular iron response did not find primary abnormalities in transferrin-receptor or ferritin synthesis regulation by iron. [PMC1050628, PMC1879596, PMC1899670]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of neonatal hemochromatosis involves clinical presentation, pathological examination, and iron studies. Affected infants may present with hypotonia, jaundice, and respiratory difficulty. Postmortem or histological examination reveals siderotic cirrhosis, widespread parenchymal siderosis, and a coarsely nodular, fibrotic liver with multinucleated giant cells. A large amount of hemosiderin is typically observed in the liver, pancreatic acini, and thyroid follicular cells, with scanty amounts in myocardial fibers and renal tubular cells, notably without reticuloendothelial siderosis. Chemical assays demonstrate significantly increased hepatic iron concentration and an elevated hepatic iron to copper ratio. Antemortem iron metabolism studies in mothers may show hyperferremia, and other causes like congenital infection or immune-related hemolysis are absent. [PMC3049705, PMC1899670]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Neonatal hemochromatosis can present with features that mimic other conditions. Retinal findings, such as a macular cherry-red spot, can resemble those seen in many metabolic storage diseases. Clinically, it is important to rule out congenital infection, immune-related hemolysis, and exogenous iron uptake. The pattern of siderosis in neonatal hemochromatosis, characterized by widespread parenchymal iron deposition and absent reticuloendothelial siderosis, is similar to that observed in hereditary, secondary, and primary hemochromatosis, as well as adult idiopathic hemochromatosis. [PMC3059895, PMC3049705, PMC1879596, PMC1899670]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Three sibling and two isolated-case perinates (4 newborn, 1 stillborn) died with siderotic cirrhosis and widespread parenchymal siderosis, the latter similar to that seen in both hereditary and secondary hemochromatosis. Reticuloendothelial siderosis was absent, as occurs in primary hemochromatosis. Studies of iron metabolism were performed antemortem in two of the siblings and ante-, post- and internatally in their mother, who showed hyperferremia antenatally. The only finding in the affected family suggestive of hereditary hemochromatosis was the commonly associated HLA haplotype (A3, B7) in the mother and an infant. Liver morphology, including immunocytochemistry and ultrastructure, was similar in the 5 infants and suggested that liver disease commenced as massive necrosis in midfetal life. Histologic grading and chemical assays for iron and copper on liver and spleen of the 5 index... [PMC1899670]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The inheritance of neonatal hemochromatosis is complex, with observations of recurrence in half-sibs suggesting that autosomal recessive inheritance may not be the most suitable explanation. Alternative possibilities include incomplete penetrance or gonadal mosaicism for a dominant disorder, a maternal 'environmental factor,' or a mitochondrial defect. Due to these complexities, alternative modes of fertilization, such as donor insemination or in vitro fertilization with donor eggs, should be considered with caution. [PMC1050628]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Liver transplantation is considered the best treatment for neonatal hemochromatosis, especially in cases presenting with acute liver failure. Successful transplantation has been shown to resolve severe manifestations, such as bilateral retinal edema and subretinal fluid. Despite challenging perioperative management, liver transplantation has led to survival and improved outcomes in affected infants. [PMC3059895, PMC1050628, PMC2528468]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Neonatal hemochromatosis is a rare and often fatal metabolic disorder, frequently leading to death in the neonatal period, sometimes within hours of birth, or resulting in stillbirth. It presents with acute liver failure and rapid deterioration, with few survivors reported. However, liver transplantation is considered the best treatment option and can lead to improved outcomes, with one child reported well 18 months post-transplant. Successful transplantation has also been shown to resolve complications such as severe retinal edema. The disease can affect multiple siblings, highlighting its severe nature. [PMC3059895, PMC2528468, PMC3049705, PMC1899670]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, inherited, severe form of progressive myoclonus epilepsy characterized by drug-resistant epilepsy, myoclonus, and psychomotor deterioration affecting previously healthy children or adolescents.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): EPM2; PME type 2; Progressive myoclonic epilepsy type 2; Progressive myoclonus epilepsy type 2

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Lafora disease is ultrarare, with an estimated frequency of < 1 case per million individuals in the world. Prevalence rates are the highest in Mediterranean countries as well as North Africa, the Middle East, and some regions of Southern India.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset typically occurs during late childhood or adolescence, with generalized tonic-clonic seizures, myoclonus, and often focal occipital seizures with visual symptoms. Seizures gradually become difficult-to-treat and worsen, leading to episodes of status epilepticus. Myoclonus is a key feature and may present as myoclonic seizures but also as resting, action, and stimulus-induced myoclonus, becoming almost continuous in the advanced stages of the disease. Ataxia contributes to motor disability. Cognitive decline is invariably present; it manifests initially with school difficulties and progresses to dementia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Lafora disease is caused by biallelic mutations in the EPM2A or NHLRC1 (also known as EPM2B) genes, encoding the proteins laforin and malin, respectively, which are implicated in glycogen metabolism. Loss of function of either protein results in the build-up of insoluble polyglucosan aggregates known as Lafora bodies in different organs. Neurodegeneration and clinical manifestations are primarily due to the accumulation of Lafora bodies in the brain.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: At onset, the electroencephalogram (EEG) has a normal background, with generalized and, often, focal occipital epileptiform discharges that may be activated by photic stimulation. With time, the EEG background slows, and epileptiform abnormalities increase in prevalence becoming abundant or subcontinuous. Brain MRI is often unremarkable or shows variable degrees of cerebral and cerebellar atrophy. Brain FDG-PET can reveal extensive areas of decreased glucose metabolism that may correlate with disease progression. Targeted genetic testing of EPM2A and NHLRC1 is currently the reference standard to confirm the diagnosis in suspected cases. Biopsy of skin or other tissues might reveal Lafora bodies, but is fraught with false positive and false negative results.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: At onset, Lafora disease may mimic juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, which does not have a progressive course. In later disease stages, the clinical picture becomes quite characteristic, facilitating diagnosis. Atypical cases with slow progression may be confused with Unverricht-Lundborg disease.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal testing is possible for families in which the diagnosis has been confirmed by molecular testing.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling is recommended to inform parents of the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern; if both parents are carriers there is a 25% chance with each pregnancy that their child will develop the condition, a 50% chance that their child will be a carrier, and a 25% chance that their child will not be a carrier or have the condition.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is currently no cure for Lafora disease; antiseizure medications are used to manage both seizures and myoclonus. Psychological and social support is also essential for patients and their families. Metformin appears to slow disease progression. Various etiological therapies that may alter the course of Lafora disease are being developed, including gene or antisense oligonucleotide therapies and antibody-enzyme conjugates that can break down Lafora bodies.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Loss of autonomy usually occurs in late adolescence and death in young adulthood; half of the patients lose autonomy within 6 years and die within 11 years of disease onset. Death commonly results from status epilepticus or aspiration pneumonia and other complications of chronic neurodegeneration. Certain genetic variants can impact the prognosis and lead to either a more rapidly or slowly progressive form of the disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: 16p13.3 microduplication syndrome is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome resulting from a partial duplication of the short arm of chromosome 16 and manifesting with a variable phenotype which is mostly characterized by: mild to moderate intellectual deficit and developmental delay (particularly speech), normal growth, short, proximally implanted thumbs and other hand and feet malformations (such as camptodactyly, syndactyly, club feet), mild arthrogryposis and characteristic facies (upslanting, narrow palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, mid face hypoplasia, bulbous nasal tip and low set ears). Other reported manifestations include cryptorchidism, inguinal hernia and behavioral problems.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Distal duplication 16p; Distal trisomy 16p; Dup(16)(p13.3); Telomeric duplication 16p; Trisomy 16pter

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: 16p13.3 microduplication syndrome is a clinically recognizable disorder characterized by neurological impairment, developmental delay, and seizure disorder. Distinct facial anomalies include a high forehead, sparse eyebrows, blepharophimosis, short nose, everted upper lip, high-arched palate, wide-spaced teeth, and cupped anteverted ears. Patients may also present with microcephaly, hypopigmented macules, short 5th fingers, and sleep apnea due to enlarged tonsils. Midline abnormalities such as agenesis of the corpus callosum, imperforate anus, and bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia have been reported. A notable feature is susceptibility to vascular anomalies, including pulmonary hypertension, portal cavernoma, vascular ring, terminal hypoplasia of hands, and aplasia cutis. [PMC2986590, PMC1379634]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: 16p13.3 microduplication syndrome is caused by a duplication of the subtelomeric region of chromosome 16p. These duplications can arise de novo or result from the malsegregation of a balanced maternal translocation involving chromosome 16p. The duplicated regions have been measured to be approximately 8.5 Mb to 12 Mb, spanning 16p13.3p13.13 or 16p13.3p13.2. Unbalanced chromosomal translocations involving the segment distal to 16p13 have also been reported, leading to trisomy of 16p. [PMC2986590, PMC1379634]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of 16p13.3 microduplication syndrome relies on cytogenetic and molecular genetic techniques. Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) telomere analysis and subtelomeric analysis by FISH are employed to identify duplications of the subtelomeric region of chromosome 16p. The extent of these duplicated regions can be further characterized by array-comparative genome hybridization (array-CGH), which has revealed duplications ranging from approximately 8.5 Mb to 12 Mb on 16p13.3p13.13 or 16p13.3p13.2. Cytogenetic analysis, often in conjunction with FISH, can also detect unbalanced translocations involving the 16p13.3 segment. [PMC2986590, PMC1379634]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Phelan-McDermid syndrome (PMS), caused by deletions at 22q13.3 and pathogenic variants in the SHANK3 gene, is a rare developmental disorder characterized by hypotonia, developmental delay (DD), intellectual disability (ID), autism spectrum disorder (ASD), dysmorphic features, absence of or delayed language, and other features. Conventional karyotyping, chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA), and whole exome sequencing (WES) have been used to detect genetic defects causing PMS. We summarized the genetic and clinical findings from prenatal to postnatal stages of detected cases of PMS and mapped potential candidate haploinsufficient genes for deletions of 22q13. summarize the laboratory findings, genetic defects, and genotype-phenotype correlations for Chinese patients with PMS. Seven prenatal cases and fourteen postnatal cases were diagnosed with PMS in our center. Thirteen cases had a... [PMC9470928]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for 16p13.3 microduplication syndrome involves understanding its diverse genetic origins and clinical manifestations. The duplication can arise de novo, as observed in some cases involving the subtelomeric region of 16p. Alternatively, it may result from the malsegregation of a balanced parental chromosomal translocation, such as a t(16pter;21qter) or t(13;16)(q33;p13.3), leading to an unbalanced chromosomal complement. Clinical features associated with these duplications include distinct facial anomalies, neurological impairment, and susceptibility to vascular anomalies like pulmonary hypertension.
