DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Cross-sectional echocardiography can be used for diagnosis, as demonstrated in a case involving absence of aortic valve cusps with mitral atresia, a normal left ventricle, and an intact ventricular septum. However, echocardiography may suggest an alternate diagnosis if the hypoplastic aortic trunk is missed due to its small caliber. The final diagnosis can be clinched using dual source computed tomography, which clearly depicts the thin aortic trunk and coronary artery origins from the hypoplastic aortic root. Multi-detector computed tomography has also been utilized for diagnosis, particularly in cases with a well-developed left ventricle. [PMC5201087, PMC1024403]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Aortic atresia with an associated ventricular septal defect and adequate sized left ventricle is extremely rare. two cases in which an alternate diagnosis was suggested on echocardiography because the hypoplastic aortic trunk was missed due to its small caliber. The final diagnosis was, however, clinched on dual source computed tomography, which not only showed the thin aortic trunk but also clearly depicted the coronary artery origins from the hypoplastic aortic root. To the best of our knowledge, use of multi-detector computed tomography in aortic atresia with well developed left ventricle has not been reported in literature till date. [PMC5201087]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of congenital aortic valve atresia often involves surgical intervention. Palliative procedures, including atrial septectomy, pulmonary artery-aorta anastomosis, and pulmonary artery banding, are performed, particularly in the neonatal period. Ductal stenting can serve as a bridge procedure in small infants. Ventriculoaortic reconstitution is a potential treatment option, especially when the left heart chambers are adequate. While surgical correction is considered, its long-term prognosis can be guarded, particularly with severe left heart hypoplasia. Rarely, survival to adulthood without any surgical procedure has been reported. [PMC9564418, PMC1216816, PMC483094]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Congenital aortic valve atresia typically leads to death in the neonatal period, with survival being very rare, especially for extremely low birth weight infants. The long-term prognosis remains guarded even for survivors of palliative procedures, particularly when associated with severe hypoplasia of the left ventricle. However, in rare cases, patients have been reported to survive to adulthood without surgical intervention. [PMC9564418, PMC1216816, PMC483094]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Malignant sex cord stromal tumor of ovary
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Malignant sex cord stromal tumor (SCST) of ovary is a rare ovarian cancer arising from granulosa, theca, sertoli and leydig cells or stromal fibroblasts, occurring at any age and presenting with abdominal or pelvic mass, and characterized (with the exception of fibroma) by the production of sex steroids resulting in manifestations of hormone excess, with a relatively favorable prognosis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Malignant ovarian SCST; Malignant ovarian sex cord-stromal tumor

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Age related incidence rate was found to be 1 per 500,000 women. Sex cord stromal tumors constitute about 5% of ovarian malignancies.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Malignant SCST of ovary may occur at any age but usually occurs in child bearing or post menopausal age groups, presenting with manifestations of mass effect (abdominal pain or distention, gastrointestinal symptoms, or abdominal mass) and/or signs of sex hormone production (isosexual precocity including breast swelling and vaginal bleeding, primary or secondary amenorrhea, and/or virilization). Malignant SCST of ovary comprises the following 4 histological forms: gynandroblastoma; malignant granulosa cell tumor of ovary; malignant Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor of ovary; and malignant steroid cell tumor of ovary, not otherwise specified.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Mutations in the DICER1 (14q32.13) gene have been found to be a susceptibility factor for SCST, particularly in malignant Sertoli-Leydig cell tumor of ovary.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical features, particularly hormonal manifestations, and is supported by imaging (ultrasonogram, computed tomography) and tumor markers. Malignant granulosa cell tumor of ovary produces inhibin A and B which is helpful in diagnosis and follow-up. A FOXL2 mutation (3q23) has been found in most malignant granulosa cell tumors of the ovary, in adults. Chromosomal abnormalities have been recently detected among granulosa cell tumors and they include trisomy 12, monosomy 22 and chromosome 6 deletion. Diagnosis is confirmed by histological examination.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include the more common malignant ovarian germ cell tumor of ovary, small cell carcinoma of the ovary and ovarian metastasis of non-gonadal tumors. Malignant SCST of ovary is also found in association with enchondromatosis, Peutz Jeghers syndrome and Maffuci syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Surgery is performed for staging, histological confirmation and debulking. Total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salphingo-oopherectomy is often the initial management. Fertility sparing surgery is offered to patients with localized disease. In the absence of significant infiltration, preservation of the uterus along with the contralateral tube and ovary is attempted in children. Adjuvant chemotherapy is given to patients with advanced tumors.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Hormonal symptoms lead to earlier diagnosis and hence a better prognosis in many malignant SCST tumors of ovary. Initial stage at diagnosis is the main prognostic factor. Histological type, presence of atypia and mitotic rate are other important prognostic factors. Stage, tumor size and presence of residual tumor after surgery influence the risk of recurrence

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal anomaly characterized by variable clinical features, most commonly including hypotonia, neonatal feeding and respiratory difficulties, microcephaly, global developmental delay and intellectual disability, growth hormone deficiency, hypothyroidism, hearing loss, aural atresia, dysmorphic facial features and behavioral characteristics.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Ring chromosome 18 syndrome is consistently described as a rare or extremely rare chromosomal disorder or aberration. However, specific prevalence rates or the total number of reported cases for the syndrome itself are not provided in the abstracts. Case reports highlight its rarity in association with other conditions, such as the first reported case of its association with Prader-Willi syndrome, and the fourth reported case of a child with the syndrome undergoing surgical correction for an orofacial cleft. [PMC12051101, PMC11662835, PMC8500322, PMC3462387]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Ring chromosome 18 syndrome is a rare chromosomal disorder with a wide range of variable clinical presentations affecting multiple organ systems. Characteristic features often include craniofacial malformations or dysmorphic facial features such as hypertelorism, flat nasal bridge, micrognathia, "carp-shaped" mouth, and orofacial clefts. Patients commonly experience delayed development, intellectual disability, and hypotonia. Other reported findings include short stature, skeletal defects like scoliosis, craniosynostosis, hemivertebrae, and congenital heart defects. Autoimmune conditions such as thyroiditis, hypothyroidism, and insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, along with IgA deficiency, are also associated. Abnormal skin pigmentation, severe obstructive sleep apnea, and liver dysfunction have also been noted. Mosaicism is frequently observed and contributes to the phenotypic variability, often sharing features of 18q- and 18p- syndromes. [PMC12051101, PMC11662835, PMC8500322, PMC7517678, PMC3462387]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of ring chromosome 18 syndrome is possible, as evidenced by reported prenatal cases initially identified through GTG banding. These cases often present with complexity, requiring high-resolution molecular cytogenetics techniques such as fluorescence in situ hybridization, centromeric probes, multicolor banding, and locus-specific probes for chromosome 18. These advanced are crucial for characterizing dynamic mosaicism and establishing the relationship between the loss or gain of chromosomal material and the resulting phenotype. [PMC3957532]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Ring chromosome 18 syndrome requires a multidisciplinary approach focused on enhancing quality of life and preventing complications. Growth hormone therapy may be considered for short stature and can improve associated clinical features, including those seen in co-occurring Prader-Willi syndrome. Surgical correction, such as cleft palate repair, can significantly improve feeding, with techniques like acellular dermal matrix use potentially aiding healing. Hypothyroidism and associated liver dysfunction are managed effectively with levothyroxine therapy. For patients undergoing procedures requiring general anesthesia, preoperative evaluation for congenital heart defects and preparation for a potentially difficult airway are crucial. [PMC12051101, PMC11662835, PMC8500322, PMC3462387, PMC1779112]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic pulmonary disorder characterized by sweat, thick mucus secretions causing multisystem disease, chronic infections of the lungs, bulky diarrhea and short stature.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is the most common genetic disorder among Caucasians. In Europe, the average prevalence at birth is 1/5,000; the average prevalence in the general population is 1/9,000. There is wide variation in both rates depending on geographic location.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: CF is chronic and usually progressive. Symptoms often start at birth and involve the lungs and gastrointestinal tract. A common presentation might include thick secretions and chronic infections in the lung, bulky diarrhea and short stature. Abnormal airway secretions, inflammation and infections lead to bronchiectasis and early death. CF-related diabetes (CFRD) occurs at high frequency, rising to nearly 50% of patients surviving to age 50. Male sterility is common. Individuals with mild phenotypes may have mild or absent respiratory symptoms in childhood, but some may have infertility or may develop bronchiectasis or pancreatitis later in life. These individuals are typically diagnosed by newborn screening, but may be diagnosed later in life.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Abnormal chloride channel function causes high salt content sweat and highly viscous mucus secretions. CF is a monogenic autosomal recessive disease caused by CFTR mutations. Among thousands of mutations, less than 300 cause disease when present in a homozygous or compound heterozygous state. About 70% of patients are homozygous for the delta F508 allele; 30 other mutations account for 20% of cases. Genotype and phenotype correlate poorly, but mutations associated with pancreatic insufficiency lead to more severe phenotypes. Mutations permitting residual CFTR function (e.g. R117H) are associated with the milder phenotype. Many factors influence phenotype.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis requires a typical clinical syndrome and either laboratory confirmed CFTR protein dysfunction or presence of two disease-causing mutations of CFTR on heteroalleles. Sweat testing confirms protein dysfunction. Newborn screening may presumptively diagnose CF before symptoms.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Any cause of bronchiectasis may mimic CF including primary ciliary dyskinesia, immunodeficiency, autoimmune disease, untreated pneumonia, esophageal reflux, or anatomic limitation to airway clearance such as in scoliosis. Some unusual or rare conditions falsely elevate sweat chloride suggesting CF. Genetic testing helps in these cases.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: In at risk pregnancies, mutation analysis of chorionic villus samples after gestation week eight is possible for diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at risk couples carrying CF mutations (identified by birth of a child with CF, neonatal screening detection of carrier status or family history), informing them that the risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy is 25%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is transitioning from addressing symptoms to correcting biochemical defects. The oldest therapies include bronchial drainage and broad spectrum antibiotics for increasingly resistant pathogens. Pancreatic enzyme replacement with vitamin and calorie supplements improve digestion and nutrition. Insulin replacement for CFRD addresses lack of insulin release not seen in other types of diabetes. New CFTR modulators partly restore chloride channel function in about 90% of patients. However, they do not treat absent, truncated or severely malformed proteins.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Lung disease is the main driver of morbidity and mortality. However, non-specific treatments improved the expectation of life at birth to more than 35 years, and with the advent of CFTR modulator therapy life expectancy has increased to nearly 50 years. Prognosis for newborns with CF may soon approach that of general populations. However, aging CF patients may be more vulnerable to disease associated with aging than the general population.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: 17p11.2 microduplication syndrome is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from the partial duplication of the short arm of chromosome 17, typically characterized by hypotonia, poor feeding, failure to thrive, developmental delay (particularly cognitive and language deficits), mild-moderate intellectual deficit, and neuropsychiatric disorders (behavioral problems, anxiety, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, autistic spectrum disorder, bipolar disorder). Structural cardiovascular anomalies (dilated aortic root, bicommissural aortic valve, atrial/ventricular and septal defects) and sleep disturbance (obstructive and central sleep apnea) are also frequently associated.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: 17p11.2 microduplication syndrome, also known as Potocki-Lupski syndrome, presents with a range of clinical features. These include facial dysmorphism, which can be subtle, and varying degrees of cognitive impairment, from moderate to mild intellectual disability to severe mental retardation. Language developmental delay and expressive language impairment are commonly observed. Behavioral abnormalities, such as autism spectrum disorders, have been reported, though their manifestation can vary among individuals. Additional features may include scoliosis and/or kyphosis, and epilepsy. The syndrome has also been identified in patients diagnosed with atypical cerebral palsy. [PMC11988916, PMC4588678, PMC3524443, PMC1049020]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: 17p11.2 microduplication syndrome, also known as Potocki-Lupski syndrome, is caused by a duplication of the 17p11.2 region. This microduplication is reciprocal to the deletion that causes Smith-Magenis syndrome. The duplicated region can range from approximately 2.1 Mb to 3.7 Mb and may include genes such as RAI1 and SREBF. It is identified as a copy number variation, which can occur de novo. [PMC11988916, PMC4588678, PMC3524443, PMC1049020]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of 17p11.2 microduplication syndrome, also known as Potocki-Lupski syndrome, relies on genetic testing. used to identify the 17p11.2 duplication include multiplex ligation probe amplification (MLPA), array comparative genomic hybridization (array CGH), and chromosomal microarray (CMA). In some instances, whole exome sequencing (ES) and/or genome sequencing (GS) may be performed, often following routine karyotyping and CMA, to identify causative variants. Incorporating genetic testing into the diagnostic process is significant for understanding the molecular basis of associated conditions, such as atypical cerebral palsy. [PMC11988916, PMC4588678, PMC3524443]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Smith-Magenis syndrome, caused by the reciprocal deletion of the 17p11.2 region, is a primary differential diagnosis for 17p11.2 microduplication syndrome (Potocki-Lupski syndrome). Both syndromes involve alterations within the same -3.7-Mb region of 17p11.2. Additionally, 17p11.2 duplication has been identified as a genetic cause in cases of atypical cerebral palsy, a condition characterized by features such as scoliosis, epilepsy, and intellectual disability. [PMC11988916, PMC3524443]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: 17p11.2 microduplication syndrome, also known as Potocki-Lupski syndrome, is caused by a duplication in the 17p11.2 region and is the reciprocal disorder to Smith-Magenis syndrome. Diagnosis can be achieved through genetic testing such as chromosomal microarray (CMA), multiplex ligation probe amplification, and array comparative genomic hybridization (array CGH). Incorporating genetic testing into the diagnostic process is significant for understanding the molecular basis of atypical cerebral palsy and informing personalized treatment strategies. It is also possible to identify co-occurring duplications, such as in the Xq region. [PMC11988916, PMC4588678, PMC3524443]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Otospondylomegaepiphyseal dysplasia (OSMED) is an inborn error of cartilage collagen formation characterized by sensorineural hearing loss, enlarged epiphyses, skeletal dysplasia with disproportionately short limbs, vertebral body anomalies and a characteristic facies.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown but less than 30 cases have been described in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Typical facial features include midface hypoplasia, a short nose with anteverted nares and a flat nasal bridge, a long philtrum, cleft palate/bifid uvula, micrognathia, and hypertelorism. Joint pain and restricted mobility of the metacarpophalangeal joints appear during the second decade of life. The sensorineural hearing loss is generally described as moderate and nonprogressive. Early onset of osteoarthritis has also been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: OSMED is classed among the type XI collagenopathies as the majority of reported cases have been associated with homozygous mutations in the COL11A2 gene (6p21.3), encoding the alpha2 chain of type XI collagen.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made on the basis of the clinical phenotype and typical radiographic findings: shortening of the long bones (humerus, radius, ulna, tibia, and fibula) with large epiphyses and metaphyseal flaring, coronal clefting and mild to moderate platyspondyly.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: OSMED shows significant clinical overlap with Weissenbacher-Zweymuller syndrome (WZS) and Stickler syndrome. Whilst OSMED and Stickler syndrome can be distinguished early in life due to the absence of ocular anomalies in OSMED, differentiation of OSMED and WZS (also associated with heterozygous mutations in the COL11A2 gene) may be more problematic.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: OSMED is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic only, involving closure of the cleft palate, audiometry and adapted management of the hearing loss, and treatment of the joint pain.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis depends on the severity of the osteoarthritis (which may require early joint replacement), hearing loss and joint pain.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Bartter syndrome is a group of rare renal tubular disease characterized by impaired salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of Henle's loop and clinically by the association of hypokalemic alkalosis, hypercalciuria/nephrocalcinosis, increased levels of plasma renin and aldosterone, low blood pressure and vascular resistance to angiotensin II.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Renal tubular normotensive hypokalemic alkalosis with hypercalciuria; Salt-losing tubular disorder, Henle's loop type; Salt-wasting tubulopathy, Henle's loop type
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset: Adolescent, Adult, Antenatal, Childhood, Infancy, Neonatal

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence is estimated at 1/1000,000 in Europe.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Five distinct genotypes have been described, with four distinct clinical variants: an antenatal/infantile Bartter syndrome (most patients with genotypes I and II), characterized by polyhydramnios, premature delivery, polyuria, dehydration, hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis; an infantile Bartter syndrome with deafness (genotype IV), with congenital sensorineural deafness; classic Bartter syndrome (mostly patients with genotype III, but also some patients with genotype I and II), manifesting as polyuria-polydipsia in infancy-childhood through adulthood, dehydration and a variable delay in the height-weight growth curve; and autosomal dominant hypocalcemia with Bartter syndrome (patients with genotype V), associating chronic hypocalcemia and tubular salt wasting, hypokalemia and alkalosis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Bartter syndrome results from a defect in sodium, potassium and chloride reabsorption at the level of Henle's loop. They are caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in four genes encoding proteins involved in tubular fluid reabsorption in the thick ascending part of Henle's loop: SLC12A1 gene (15q15-21), encoding the sodium-potassium-chloride cotransporter NKCC2 in type I Bartter syndrome; KCNJ1 gene (11q24) encoding the potassium channel ROMK in type II; CLCNKB gene (1p36), encoding a basolateral chloride channel, in type III; and BSND gene (1p32.3), encoding barttin, the beta-subunit for the basolateral chloride channels, CLCNKA and CLCNKB in type IV. A final variant (type V) is associated with heterozygous activating mutations of the CASR gene (3q21.1), encoding the calcium sensing receptor.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the clinical picture, as well as in plasma and urine electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride, bicarbonate, magnesium, calcium), renin and aldosterone levels. Calcium levels in the urine may be normal to markedly increased. Hypocalcemia is observed in Bartter syndrome type V. Genetic testing provides the definite diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes pseudo-Bartter syndrome (diuretic abuse, surreptitious vomiting), Gitelman syndrome, cystic fibrosis and celiac disease.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Diagnostic testing of amniocytes might be indicated for mothers of affected children, or potential heterozygous carriers (close relatives of affected individuals).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Four of the genetic variants (types I,II,III,IV) of Bartter syndrome are transmitted following an autosomal recessive pattern whereas variant (type V) is transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment includes oral potassium supplements, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (e.g. indomethacin) and possibly potassium-sparing diuretics. In stressful situations (intecurrent diseases, surgical procedures, trauma) blood electrolyte levels may change rapidly, requiring prompt and vigorous intravenous treatment.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy may be reduced in severe cases but renal failure is rare. Quality of life may be poor, growth rate reduced, and hospitalization rate high.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, autosomal recessive systemic dysfunction of the hemostatic pathway, that is due to a defect in the coagulation factor XII (FXII or Hageman factor), and is either asymptomatic or characterized by a prolonged activated partial thromboplastin time and an increased risk for thromboembolism. FXII deficiency is strongly associated with primary recurrent abortions.

DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Congenital hemophilia A is a recessive inherited hemorrhagic disorder. According to the activity of functional coagulation factors, the severity of hemophilia A is divided into three levels: mild, moderate and severe. The first bleeding episode in severe and moderate congenital hemophilia A occurs mostly in early childhood and mainly involves soft tissue and joint bleeds. At present, there are limited reports on severe congenital hemophilia A with low factor XII (FXII) activity during the neonatal period. A 13-day-old neonate was admitted to the hospital with hematoma near the joints of both upper arms. Coagulation tests showed he had low activity of factor VIII (FVIII) and FXII. He was diagnosed with congenital hemophilia A and treated with human coagulation factor VIII (recombinant FVIII). Although the hematoma became smaller, FVIII activity was only increased to a certain extent and... [PMC8503991]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, benign, epidermal disease characterized by a solitary, asymptomatic, verrucous, skin-coloured to red-brown papule or nodule, which contains a central pore and keratotic plug, occuring most frequently on the scalp, face and neck (rarely, in the mouth, under the nail plate or on the mons pubis). Occasionally, lesions may be multiple and/or pruritic. Histologically, a well-circumscribed, cup-shaped, keratin-filled invagination, with prominent acantholytic dyskeratosis, suprabasilar clefts and villi projecting into the clefts, is observed.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Warty dyskeratoma is a rare condition or tumor, typically presenting as single or multiple papular or nodular lesions. It primarily affects adults, often middle-aged or elderly individuals, on the scalp, face, or neck, and sometimes the oral mucosa. While usually a single lesion, multiple warty dyskeratomas are very rare, mostly seen on the scalp. The etiopathogenesis may be multifactorial. Notably, warty dyskeratomas can also develop as a side effect of selective BRAF inhibitor therapy, presenting as single lesions or widespread eruptions. [PMC7772768, PMC4411912, PMC4838029]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Warty dyskeratoma is a rare, benign neoplasm presenting as single or multiple papular or nodular lesions, primarily on the skin of the scalp, face, or neck, and sometimes on the oral mucosa. Lesions often appear as a single papule or nodule with a central keratotic plug in middle-aged or elderly adults. Multiple lesions are very rare and mostly seen on the scalp. Histologically, it is characterized by a cup-shaped epidermal invagination with a plug of hyperparakeratosis, suprabasal acantholysis, and dyskeratosis. Dermoscopy may show a whitish collarette, light brown pigmentation, a central white structureless area, and rust-coloured blood crusts, though these features are not specific. The etiopathogenesis can be multifactorial, and warty dyskeratomas can also develop as a side effect of BRAF inhibitor therapy, sometimes presenting as widespread eruptions. [PMC7772768, PMC6857555, PMC4411912, PMC4838029]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiopathogenesis of warty dyskeratoma is considered multifactorial. Cases have been observed in a post-inflammatory context. Additionally, selective BRAF inhibitor therapy, including vemurafenib and dabrafenib, is associated with the development of warty dyskeratomas as a cutaneous side effect. These can manifest as single lesions or widespread eruptions with histopathologic findings of acantholytic dyskeratosis. [PMC7772768, PMC4838029]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Warty Dyskeratoma typically relies on histology, which reveals a cup-shaped epidermal invagination centered by a plug of epidermal hyperparakeratosis with suprabasal acantholysis and dyskeratosis. Dermoscopy can also be employed, showing features such as an eight-shape whitish collarette, light brown pigmentation, a central white structureless area, an adjacent rosette, and small rust-colored blood crusts. While dermoscopy is not specific, it may aid in ruling out other skin tumors. For new growths, especially in patients receiving BRAF inhibitor therapy, a low threshold for biopsy is recommended due to the potential for malignant lesions. [PMC7772768, PMC4838029]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Warty dyskeratoma (WD) can be confused with other skin tumors, and dermoscopy may assist in their exclusion. Histologically, WD shares features of acantholytic dyskeratosis with Darier-like or Grover-like rashes. Conditions such as squamous cell carcinomas, keratoacanthomas, and benign verrucous keratoses can also present, particularly as side effects of BRAF inhibitor therapy, and should be considered in the differential. Awareness of potential malignant lesions is necessary, especially in patients on such treatments, warranting a low threshold for biopsy of new growths. [PMC7772768, PMC4838029]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Warty dyskeratoma is consistently described as a benign neoplasm or growth. It presents as single or multiple papular or nodular lesions. The available information indicates its benign nature, with no details provided regarding its long-term course, potential for malignant transformation, or impact on overall health. [PMC7772768, PMC4838029]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hyperprolinemia type 2 is an autosomal recessive proline metabolism disorder due to pyroline-5-carboxylate dehydrogenase deficiency. The condition is often benign but clinical signs may include seizures, intellectual deficit and mild developmental delay.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Hyperprolinemia type 2 (HPII) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of proline metabolism. The manifestation typically occurs in neonatal age, early infancy, or early childhood. However, atypical late-onset cases have been reported, emphasizing the importance of diagnostic vigilance. At the time of , only four different pathogenic mutations were known to cause the disease. [PMC6935479]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hyperprolinemia type 2 (HPII) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of proline metabolism, typically manifesting in neonatal age, early infancy, or early childhood. Clinical features can include severe and potentially life-threatening symptoms. One reported case of late-onset HPII in a 64-year-old patient presented with a long history of abdominal pain, acute neuritis, multiple generalized epileptic seizures, vertical gaze palsy, and extensive lactic acidosis. This patient also exhibited secondary pyridoxine deficiency. Diagnosis involves detecting significantly increased proline levels in urine, CSF, and blood, and genetic analysis of the ALDH4A1 gene. [PMC6935479]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hyperprolinemia type 2 (HPII) is an autosomal recessive disorder of proline metabolism, caused by pathogenic mutations in the ALDH4A1 gene. While only a few pathogenic mutations were previously known, novel compound heterozygous variants have been identified, such as c.62 + 1G > A and c.349G > C, p.(Asp117His) in the ALDH4A1 gene. This genetic defect can lead to secondary pyridoxine deficiency. [PMC6935479]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Hyperprolinemia type 2 involves a thorough laboratory work-up. This includes measuring proline levels, which can be significantly increased (e.g., up to 400-times) in urine, cerebrospinal fluid, and blood. Additionally, a low vitamin B6 serum value may be found, consistent with secondary pyridoxine deficiency. Definitive diagnosis is confirmed by ALDH4A1 gene sequencing to identify pathogenic variants. [PMC6935479]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Hyperprolinemia type 2 is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the ALDH4A1 gene. Genetic counseling should inform families about this inheritance pattern, where affected individuals inherit two pathogenic variants, one from each carrier parent. Genetic testing, including gene sequencing, is crucial for diagnosis, identifying known or novel compound heterozygous variants. This genetic analysis is important for diagnostic vigilance and thorough work-up, even in cases with atypical or late manifestation. [PMC6935479]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for Hyperprolinemia type 2, particularly when associated with secondary pyridoxine deficiency and seizures, includes high-dose vitamin B6 therapy. In one reported case, this intervention successfully prevented further seizures. The condition is considered treatable, underscoring the importance of diagnostic vigilance and comprehensive laboratory work-up, including gene analysis, even in patients with atypical or late-onset manifestations. [PMC6935479]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Hyperprolinemia type 2 can have a severe and potentially life-threatening course, even with atypical late manifestation. Acute episodes may involve multiple generalized epileptic seizures, extensive lactic acidosis, and necessitate long-term sedation and ventilation due to secondary complications. Despite its potential severity, it is described as a treatable disease. For example, high-dose vitamin B6 therapy has been shown to prevent further seizures. The disease typically manifests in neonatal age, early infancy, or early childhood. [PMC6935479]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital patellar anomaly syndrome characterized by patellar aplasia or hypoplasia associated with microcephaly, characteristic coarse facial features (microcephaly, bitemporal narrowing, large, broad nose with high nasal bridge, prominent cheeks and micro/retrognathia or prognathism), arthrogryposis of the hips and knees, urogenital abnormalities and intellectual deficiency.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Absent patellae-scrotal hypoplasia-renal anomalies-facial dysmorphism-intellectual disability syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Genitopatellar syndrome (GPS) is a rare disorder. Early descriptions include seven children from five unrelated families, with recurrence in two families suggesting an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. The first genetically confirmed case in South Korea further underscores its rarity. [PMC6433568, PMC1734629]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Genitopatellar syndrome (GPS) is a rare disorder characterized by a constellation of features including patellar hypoplasia or absent patellae, flexion contractures of the lower limbs (knees, hips, club feet), psychomotor or mental retardation, and genital and renal anomalies. Dysmorphic features often include a coarse face, large nose with a high nasal bridge, and microcephaly. Other reported findings include agenesis of the corpus callosum, swallowing difficulties, micrognathia, pulmonary hypoplasia, bilateral hypoplasia of the ischia, and brachydactyly. The syndrome can be severe, with some cases resulting in prenatal termination or early childhood death, and survivors experiencing severe developmental delay. While de novo KAT6B gene mutations have been identified, recurrence in some families suggests an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. [PMC6433568, PMC1757222, PMC1734629]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Genitopatellar syndrome (GPS) is caused by mutations in the KAT6B gene, which encodes lysine acetyltransferase 6B. These mutations can be de novo, with examples including a 2-bp insertion leading to a frameshift and premature stop codon. The resulting truncated protein lacks a C-terminal transcription activation domain, which is thought to lead to dominant-negative or gain-of-function effects. Earlier observations, based on recurrence in families, suggested an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance for the condition. [PMC6433568, PMC4414115, PMC1734629]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Genitopatellar syndrome (GPS) is diagnosed by identifying mutations in the KAT6B gene, typically through whole exome sequencing, which has confirmed de novo KAT6B mutations in affected individuals. While high-resolution cytogenetic studies have been performed, they were consistently normal in reported cases, indicating they are not diagnostic. Prenatal ultrasound may detect associated features such as microcephaly and renal anomalies. [PMC6433568, PMC4414115, PMC1734629]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Genitopatellar syndrome (GTPTS) is characterized by absent patellae, genital and renal anomalies, facial dysmorphism, and mental retardation, distinguishing it from other previously reported hypoplastic patella syndromes. Mutations in KAT6B are associated with GTPTS, as well as Say-Barber-Biesecker-Young-Simpson (SBBYSS) syndrome. Furthermore, individuals presenting with blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES) features, but lacking FOXL2 mutations, may also have KAT6B mutations, expanding the phenotypic spectrum linked to this gene and suggesting a need for KAT6B testing in such cases. [PMC4414115, PMC1734629]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Prenatal ultrasound can detect features associated with Genitopatellar syndrome. In two reported cases, microcephaly and renal anomalies were identified antenatally, leading to termination of pregnancy at 27 weeks. [PMC1734629]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genitopatellar syndrome is associated with mutations in the KAT6B gene, which can be identified using whole exome sequencing. These mutations are frequently de novo and may exert a dominant-negative or gain-of-function effect. However, recurrence in some families has also suggested an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. The severe prognosis, including early mortality and profound developmental delay, along with the potential for prenatal detection of anomalies, underscores the importance of genetic evaluation and counseling for affected families. [PMC6433568, PMC4414115, PMC1734629]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Genitopatellar syndrome is severe. In some cases, prenatal detection of anomalies like microcephaly and renal issues led to termination of pregnancy. Among live births, three out of seven children died during the first years of life. The remaining two survivors exhibited severe developmental delay, indicating significant long-term neurological impairment. [PMC1734629]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Borjeson-Forssman-Lehmann syndrome (BFLS) is a rare X-linked obesity syndrome characterized by intellectual deficit, truncal obesity, characteristic facial features, hypogonadism, tapered fingers and short toes.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown. Approximately 50 patients have been reported, from 24 families and sporadic cases.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: BFLS is found mainly in boys, but several mild to moderately symptomatic females have been reported within known families, and as isolated cases. There is a wide variability in manifestations. At birth, large ears and small genitalia are occasionally evident. The head circumference is variable and hypotonia, leading to poor feeding, is seen in all infants. Developmental delay is often noted before the age of one. In late childhood, truncal obesity is apparent. Fingers are malleable and tapered and feet are usually broad with flexed, short toes. Most have short stature but some are of normal height. In adolescence, gynecomastia develops and genitalia usually remain small. Characteristic coarse facial features also appear in adolescence and include deep-set eyes, narrow forehead, supraorbital ridges, ptosis and large, fleshy earlobes, all of which become more pronounced in adulthood. Intellectual disability can range from mild to severe and is not progressive. Patients are usually sociable and friendly but some experience anxiety, depression and challenging or hypersexual behavior. Less common findings reported include acute precursor T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD), cleft lip/palate, hypopituitarism, hearing impairment, epilepsy and mild to generalized polyneuropathy. Females are mainly asymptomatic but in rare cases can exhibit learning problems along with some of the physical features seen in males.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: BFLS is caused by mutations in the PHF6 gene, located on Xq26, encoding PHF6, a protein involved in cell growth and proliferation. In general, mutations that result in loss or reduction of PHF6 expression result in more severe clinical symptoms. Loss-of-function mutations and skewed X-inactivation are thought to explain the rare occurrence of symptomatic females. Although most cases are inherited within families, several isolated cases have been reported, where the etiology is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: BFLS is suspected on clinical examination when the characteristic symptoms are present. A family history showing X-linked recessive inheritance as well as skewed X-chromosome inactivation in obligate female carriers is a strong additional indicator of BFLS. PHF6 mutation screening can confirm a diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Coffin-Lowry, Klinefelter, Prader-Willi, Bardet-Biedl, or Wilson-Turner syndromes.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: When a PHF6 mutation is known to exist in a parent, antenatal diagnosis is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance is X-linked and genetic counseling is possible to explain X-linkage to families and identify carrier females. Very few patients with BFLS reproduce, but asymptomatic female carriers can pass on the mutation to their children.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for BFLS. Treatment and management is symptomatic. Special education is started early and followed throughout adolescence and adulthood. A healthy diet is recommended. Adults require variable degrees of supervision which may include institutionalization in severe cases. Testosterone replacement therapy and/or a bilateral mastectomy may be considered for the treatment of gynecomastia. If seizures are present, antiepileptic drugs are prescribed. Symptomatic treatment for LCPD and hearing impairment is available. A social network is important as BFLS patients benefit from strong social relationships.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: BFLS is not life threatening but due to the intellectual disability encountered, quality of life is limited and life-long supervision is often necessary.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare chromosomal anomaly characterized by an intellectual deficiency, progressive microcephaly, seizures, growth delay, distinct facial dysmorphic features and various midline defects including cardiac, corpus callosum, gastro-oesophageal and urogenital anomalies.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Interstitial deletions of chromosome 1q are considered rare, with approximately 30 cases reported in the literature to date. This condition is recognized as the "interstitial 1q deletion syndrome." A more extensive comparative analysis of a larger number of patients with similar genetic profiles is needed for a more precise clinical and genomic characterization of this rare syndrome. [PMC11942503]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Interstitial deletions of chromosome 1q are rare, with about 30 cases reported in the literature. The phenotypical features of the affected subjects described so far include microcephaly, pre- and post-natal growth retardation, psychomotor delays, ear anomalies, brachydactyly, in addition to small hands and feet, and rarely a congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). Here, on a neonate with CDH, dysmorphic features, and multiple midline anomalies including a cleft palate, in whom an array-comparative genomic hybridization (a-CGH) analysis allowed the identification of an interstitial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 1. Our patient underwent a surgical correction of CDH on the fourth day of life, while that of cleft palate has been planned to be performed at 12 months. The few subjects suffering such rearrangement reported to date, along with the clinical and genetic profile of the... [PMC11942503, PMC6977633, PMC1685492]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal deletion 1q syndrome is caused by rare deletions of the long arm of chromosome 1 (1q). These genetic aberrations can manifest as interstitial deletions, as seen in cases of interstitial 1q deletion syndrome, or as terminal deletions, such as those involving regions 1q31 and q42.1. In reported cases, these deletions have been observed to appear de novo, with normal parental karyotypes and no family history of the condition. [PMC11942503, PMC6977633, PMC1685492]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of distal deletion 1q syndrome relies on genetic analysis. Array-comparative genomic hybridization (a-CGH) analysis can identify interstitial deletions of the long arm of chromosome 1. Karyotyping, specifically high-resolution G-banding, is used to detect chromosome 1 microdeletions. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and chromosome microdissection further confirm and define these chromosomal aberrations. [PMC11942503, PMC6977633, PMC1050918]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: a dysmorphic boy with a de novo partial trisomy 1q. The boy has microcephaly, bilateral cleft lip and palate, low set and dysmorphic ears, brain anomalies, pulmonary stenosis, duodenal obstruction, dysplastic kidneys, and bifid thumbs. The trisomic segment 1q32-qter is duplicated with an inverted insertion at 1p36.3. The aberration was initially detected at amniocentesis and confirmed and defined by GTG banding, chromosome microdissection, and FISH on postnatal blood samples. The parents had normal karyotypes. De novo partial duplications of chromosome 1q have rarely been reported. Comparison of our patient with other published pure trisomy 1q cases showed similarities which allowed the further delineation of the trisomy 1q syndrome. [PMC1050918]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: a dysmorphic boy with a de novo partial trisomy 1q. The boy has microcephaly, bilateral cleft lip and palate, low set and dysmorphic ears, brain anomalies, pulmonary stenosis, duodenal obstruction, dysplastic kidneys, and bifid thumbs. The trisomic segment 1q32-qter is duplicated with an inverted insertion at 1p36.3. The aberration was initially detected at amniocentesis and confirmed and defined by GTG banding, chromosome microdissection, and FISH on postnatal blood samples. The parents had normal karyotypes. De novo partial duplications of chromosome 1q have rarely been reported. Comparison of our patient with other published pure trisomy 1q cases showed similarities which allowed the further delineation of the trisomy 1q syndrome. [PMC1050918]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for distal deletion 1q syndrome typically addresses the de novo nature of the chromosomal aberration. In reported cases, the karyotypes of both parents were normal, and the deletion or duplication of 1q appeared to arise de novo. This indicates a sporadic occurrence rather than an inherited condition from carrier parents. Prenatal detection of such aberrations has been reported, for example, through amniocentesis, allowing for early diagnosis. [PMC6977633, PMC1050918, PMC1685492]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management involves surgical correction of specific congenital anomalies. For a patient with interstitial 1q deletion syndrome, a congenital diaphragmatic hernia was surgically corrected on the fourth day of life. Additionally, a cleft palate was planned for surgical repair at 12 months of age. These interventions address some of the phenotypic features associated with the syndrome. [PMC11942503]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare purine metabolism disorder due to inherited deficiency of the xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase enzyme and is characterized by very low (or undetectable) concentrations of uric acid in blood and urine and very high concentration of xanthine in urine, leading to urolithiasis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Classic xanthinuria; Xanthic urolithiasis; Xanthine stone disease

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of hereditary xanthinuria is not known, but about 150 patients have been described so far. Annual incidence has been estimated to be between 1:6,000 and 1:69,000. These rough estimates are due to the high rate of asymptomatic cases leading to underdiagnosis and the lack of newborn screening.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Symptom onset may be at any age. Approximately 50 % of the patients with classical hereditary xanthinuria present with symptoms of urinary tract infection, hematuria, renal colic, acute renal failure, crystalluria or urolithiasis. In some rare patients, renal disease may evolve to renal failure, or may even induce arthropathy, myopathy or duodenal ulcer.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Hereditary xanthinuria is due to mutations in the xanthine dehydrogenase (XDH, 2p23.1) or molybdenum cofactor sulfurase (MOCOS, 18q12.2) genes, resulting in failure to degrade hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid and leading to the accumulation of xanthine and, to a lesser extent, of hypoxanthine. Classical hereditary xanthinuria encompasses xanthinuria type I and II: type I is a simple xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase deficiency, due to mutations in XDH, whereas type II results from a combined deficiency of xanthine dehydrogenase and aldehyde oxidase, due to mutations in MOCOS. Both enzymatic deficiencies lead to an identical clinical phenotype.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on estimation of uric acid in blood and urine. If hypouricemia is confirmed, detailed purine metabolic investigation follows, and includes measurement of xanthine and hypoxanthine in urine and plasma. High urinary levels of xanthine are then typical for classical hereditary xanthinuria. In about half of patients, ultrasonography reveals the presence of xanthine urolithiasis. Additional methods for diagnostic confirmation and/or identification of the type of xanthinuria include allopurinol loading test, xanthine oxidase assay and molecular analysis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Hereditary xanthinuria is a clinical feature of molybdenum cofactor deficiency. The clinical picture of this disease is however much more severe, given the associated neurological damage and frequent infant death. Hypouricemia is also a biochemical marker for primary hereditary renal hypouricemia. Unlike hereditary xanthinuria, the excretion fraction of uric acid is elevated in renal hypouricemia.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Hereditary xanthinuria is an autosomal recessive disease, with a subsequent 25% recurrence risk.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative treatment. Low purine diet and high fluid intake is recommended. Since the solubility of xanthine is not affected by urinary pH, alkalization is of no value. When calculi are present, a pyelolithotomy might be necessary.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The overall prognosis is favorable, even though, in some cases, the disease progresses to end-stage renal insufficiency.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by cognitive impairment of variable severity, behavioral abnormalities, and sleep disturbance. Patients present with distinctive physical features and a wide range of malformations (e.g. cardiac, renal).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Smith-Magenis syndrome (SMS) has an estimated prevalence of 1/15,000-25,000 and has been identified worldwide in all ethnic groups, but is probably underdiagnosed. Males and females are affected equally.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients have a recognizable clinical picture. Craniofacial features include brachycephaly, a broad square-shaped face, synophrys, mildy upslanted palpebral fissures, midface retrusion with relative prognathism with age, and an everted upper lip with a ''tented'' appearance. Short stature is common in young patients, with height typically in the normal range as adults. Excess weight and/or obesity in teens and adults are common. Other skeletal anomalies include brachydactyly, clinodactyly of the 5th finger, 2-3 toe syndactyly and scoliosis. Otolaryngological problems such as velopharyngeal insufficiency, laryngeal anomalies, a hoarse deep voice and otitis media occur frequently. Hearing loss is frequent and may be mild to moderate. Ophthalmologic features (>80%) include strabismus, myopia, iris anomalies and retinal detachment (often resulting from violent behaviors). The majority of individuals function in the mild to moderate range of intellectual disability. Significant speech delay and maladaptive behaviors (outbursts/temper tantrums, nail yanking, insertion of foreign objects into body orifices, self-injurious behaviors, attention seeking, and anxiety) are common. Sleep disturbance is due to an inversion of the circadian rhythm of melatonin. Organ malformations include cardiac, renal and central nervous system abnormalities.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: SMS is typically a sporadic disorder caused either by a 17p11.2 deletion encompassing the retinoic acid-induced 1 (RAI1) gene (90%) or a mutation of the gene (10%). Patients with a mutation can have a less severe phenotype, and manifestations may have a later onset in the least severe cases.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on initial clinical suspicion followed by molecular confirmation of the genetic defect. Careful history-taking for birth defects, sleep disturbance, delayed milestones, chronic ear infections, self-injurious behaviors, and family history are important to recognize the characteristic features.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Down syndrome, Williams syndrome, brachydactyly-intellectual deficit syndrome (del 2q37), and Kleefstra syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Almost all cases correspond to a single occurrence in a family, but prenatal testing can be offered for at-risk pregnancies where the genetic alteration has been previously identified in an affected family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is autosomal dominant with most cases arising sporadically. Genetic counseling is recommended to affected families due the possibility of vertical transmission, parental germline mosaicism, and complex familial chromosome rearrangements. When a chromosomal deletion is identified, parental chromosomal testing is recommended to rule-out any translocation or other rearrangements that might affect the recurrence risk.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Appropriate assessment of the degree of cognitive, developmental, and behavioral deficits and of systemic/organ abnormality is essential for appropriate and specific management. Treatment is symptomatic and may include psychotropics intended to increase attention, decrease hyperactivity and stabilize behavior and treatment for sleep disorders. However, no single regimen has shown consistent efficacy. Family psychosocial support is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on age of diagnosis, disease severity, and precocity of therapeutic interventions.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare vascular anomaly characterized by the segmental narrowing of the abdominal and/or distal descending thoracic aorta, with varying involvement of the visceral and renal arteries, that commonly presents in children and young adults with early onset and refractory hypertension, abdominal angina, and lower-limb claudication, that can lead to life-threatening complications associated with severe hypertension (i.e. myocardial infarction, heart failure, aortic rupture, renal insufficiency and intracranial hemorrhage). It may be due to various congenital or acquired causes, but it is most often secondary to an acquired inflammatory disease (i.e. Takayasu arteritis or giant cell arteritis).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): MAC; Coarctation of the abdominal aorta; Mid-aortic dysplastic syndrome; Mid-aortic syndrome; Midaortic syndrome; Middle aortic coarctation; Abdominal coarctation

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Middle aortic syndrome (MAS), also known as middle aortic coarctation, is described as an exceedingly rare condition or vascular anomaly. It is characterized by narrowing of the distal thoracic and proximal abdominal aorta. Atypical aortic coarctation, which includes MAS, is often associated with various types of vasculitis syndromes, such as Takayasu arteritis or aortitis syndrome, and underlying genetic disorders like Down syndrome. Specific cases have been reported in individuals ranging from children to a 68-year-old woman, but the overall prevalence and typical demographic distribution are not detailed beyond its rarity. [PMC11336849, PMC10358302, PMC8815173, PMC7524094, PMC6849921]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Atypical aortic coarctation is an exceedingly rare condition, and there are very few reported cases of anesthetic management for bypass surgery in patients with severe impaired cardiac function. the anesthetic management of a 68-year-old woman with atypical aortic coarctation due to Takayasu arteritis and severely impaired cardiac function, who underwent ascending-to-abdominal aorta bypass surgery under extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO). The patient's severe cardiac dysfunction was due to sustained afterload from the coarctation, leading to recurrent episodes of heart failure. Surgical intervention was deemed necessary, and a decision was made to perform a bypass operation. The patient experienced a transient state of shock following induction of anesthesia, but subsequent perioperative care was safely managed with the implementation of ECMO. For bypass surgery performed on... [PMC11336849, PMC10358302, PMC8815173, PMC9152849, PMC8335882]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Middle aortic syndrome, often referred to as atypical aortic coarctation, is a rare vascular anomaly with diverse etiologies. It is frequently associated with various vasculitis syndromes, including Takayasu arteritis and other forms of aortitis. Underlying genetic disorders and congenital anomalies also contribute to its development, such as Down syndrome, atypical Shone's complex, bicuspid aortic valve, diffusely hypoplastic right aortic arch, and anomalous origins of subclavian arteries. Additionally, an atherosclerotic process has been identified as a cause in some atypical cases. [PMC11336849, PMC10358302, PMC9152849, PMC8335882, PMC7524094]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Middle aortic syndrome is commonly diagnosed by computed tomography angiography (CTA), which verifies long-segment narrowing, calcified plaques, renal artery involvement, and collateral vessels. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) can also be a first diagnostic tool, revealing segmental narrowing and calcified plaques, particularly in patients with hypertension and a marked pressure gradient between arms and legs. Abdominal vascular ultrasound may show narrowing extending to the abdominal aorta. Physical examination findings, such as a significant pressure gradient between arms and legs and weak peripheral pulses, are crucial for initial suspicion. Catheterization can further reveal pressure gradients between the ascending and descending aorta. [PMC8815173, PMC325552]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Coarctation of the aorta is a well-known congenital cardiovascular disorder that typically occurs within proximity to the ductus arteriosus. The ascending aorta, distal descending aorta, and abdominal aorta are segments which are prone to development of an atypical coarctation. The etiologies of atypical cases are usually associated with various types of vasculitis syndromes or underlying genetic disorders. In , a 24-year-old female patient with an ascending aortic coarctation which developed secondary to an atherosclerotic process. Midaortic syndrome is a rare vascular anomaly characterized by coarctation of the descending thoracic and abdominal aorta. Down syndrome is associated with multiple congenital cardiac malformations but is rarely associated with developmental vascular anomalies. Midaortic syndrome may result in severe renovascular hypertension that requires early intervention... [PMC10358302, PMC6849921]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Middle Aortic Syndrome primarily involves surgical and endovascular interventions. Surgical options include various bypass procedures such as ascending-to-abdominal aorta bypass, descending thoracic aorta-abdominal aorta bypass, axillofemoral bypass, axillo-iliac bypass, and reno-iliac arterial bypass, often performed to improve blood pressure control, alleviate heart failure, or restore blood flow to ischemic limbs and kidneys. Endovascular therapy, including stent or stent graft implantation, is also utilized, sometimes as an urgent measure for unstable patients or as a bridging procedure for subsequent open surgery. Hybrid techniques combining both approaches are also employed. Anesthetic management for surgery, especially in patients with severe cardiac dysfunction, requires meticulous planning and readiness for circulatory support like ECMO. Long-term follow-up is crucial to assess outcomes and prevent complications. [PMC11336849, PMC8815173, PMC9152849, PMC9610690, PMC8335882]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic nephropathy secondary to a disorder of purine metabolism characterized by the formation and hyperexcretion of 2,8-dihydroxyadenine (2,8-DHA) in urine, causing urolithiasis and crystalline nephropathy.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is estimated at 1/50,000 to 1/100,000 in Caucasian, 1/27,000 in Japanese and > 1/15,000 in Icelandic populations. Adenine phosphoribosyltransferase deficiency (APRT) deficiency appears to equally affect children and adults, male or female. In Caucasian populations, heterozygous prevalence is estimated between 0.4% and 1.2%.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical manifestations include symptoms usually associated with urolithiasis. Stones are typically radiolucent. Onset can be between infancy and the 4th decade of life, or sometimes even later. A small portion of patients remain asymptomatic. The disease can present not only as urolithiasis but also as crystalline nephropathy secondary to the precipitation of 2,8-DHA into renal parenchyma (DHA nephropathy). DHA nephropathy occurs most often in patients with repeated misdiagnosed episodes of urolithiasis and progressive worsening of renal function, but it may also present as acute renal failure. Rarely, DHA nephropathy may occur in patients who experienced only a few stone episodes. DHA nephropathy can evolve to end stage renal disease requiring dialysis and transplantation and can recur after transplantation causing rapid loss of graft function if left untreated.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: APRT deficiency is an autosomal recessive (AR) disorder caused by mutations in the APRT gene (16q24) encoding the APRT enzyme catalyzing AMP synthesis from adenine and 5'-phosphoribosyl-1-pyrophosphate. Two types of APRT deficiencies have been described, according to APRT activity in vitro; type I characterized by a total lack of APRT activity, found primarily in Caucasians, and type II, found only in Japan, characterized by a 10-25% APRT activity. This in vitro distinction has no known clinical significance.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Lack of awareness of APRT deficiency often causes a significant delay between the onset of symptoms and a proper diagnosis. Diagnosis is primarily based on identifying 2,8-DHA by examination of crystals or stones. Crystalluria examination can be used for diagnosis. In DHA nephropathy patients, crystals may also be identified in renal biopsy, although this invasive test is theoretically unnecessary. Crystals and stones should be analyzed by morphologic examination combined with infrared spectrometry and/or x-ray crystallography. Diagnosis can be confirmed by enzyme activity analysis in erythrocyte lysates. Genetic testing may be used for diagnosis but may be useful for familial screening.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Confusion frequently occurs between 2,8-DHA and uric acid stones, which are typically both radiolucent. Contrary to uric acid, 2,8-DHA stones do not respond to alkali therapy. Differential diagnosis also includes other radiolucent stones, such as cystine, xanthine and drugs.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling is possible but rarely indicated. However, given the AR transmission, siblings of the affected individual, even if they are asymptomatic, should be screened through DNA analysis or APRT activity.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: To prevent further 2,8-DHA formation, treatment consists of allopurinol daily (usually 10mg/kg per day in children and 300 mg per day in adults) together with a high fluid intake and low purine diet. In cases of acute or chronic renal failure, allopurinol doses should be reduced. Asymptomatic individuals should be treated by allopurinol to prevent renal complications. Febuxostat, another xanthine oxydase inhibitor, may be even more efficacious than allopurinol in reducing DHA excretion. It remains unknown how this translates into improved patient outcomes. Febuxostat should be recommended in allopurinol-intolerant patients and also in rare patients who do not respond well to allopurinol.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Early diagnosis is the key and prognosis depends on progression of this treatable disorder. Allopurinol therapy effectively prevents stone recurrence and can lead to an improvement or stabilization of renal function in most patients. Stone recurrence and renal complications are rare in patients who remain compliant with allopurinol therapy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Rheumatoid factor-positive polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare form of juvenile idiopathic arthritis characterized by distal and symmetrical polyarthritis (more than 5 joints) with presence of rheumatoid factor and possible evolution towards the appearance of erosions and joint destruction.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Rheumatoid factor-positive polyarticular JIA; Juvenile idiopathic rheumatoid factor-positive polyarthritis; Juvenile polyarthritis with rheumatoid factor

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The disorder occurs worldwide with regional variation in occurrence; prevalence in juvenile populations ranges from 1/10,000-350,000, and incidence ranges between 1/140,000-1,000,000. The disorder is less frequent in Asian populations. Females are predominantly affect with a female-to-male ratio of 8-9:1.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease is considered as the childhood onset of seropositive adult rheumatoid arthritis; it represents about 10% of all cases of JIA. Patients are frequently diagnosed in late childhood/adolescence, typically between the 10-12 years of age. As with adult rheumatoid arthritis (RA), patients have a chronic symmetric, erosive polyarticular arthritis. To have polyarticular RF-positive disease, the ILAR classification requires the involvement of 5 or more joints. Also, by definition, patients must have two positive tests for IgM rheumatoid factor (RF). Although anti-cyclic-citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibody status is not part of the ILAR criteria, children with childhood-onset RA also commonly have anti-CCP antibodies.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Rheumatoid factor-positive polyarthritis is an autoimmune inflammatory disease associated with enhanced lymphocyte activity and production of proinflammatory cytokines (IL1, IL6 and TNF alpha).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The international diagnostic criteria rely on the clinical, biological and radiological (joint erosion) features of the disease. Rheumatoid factor-positive polyarthritis is defined as the presence of arthritis affecting five or more joints at disease onset and by detection of rheumatoid factor in two tests carried out in the first six months of the disease course. Exclusion criteria are the presence of systemic arthritis or psoriasis in the patient, or a family history of psoriasis in one of the parents or first-degree relative, and HLA B27-positivity in males with onset of arthritis after 6 years of age. Other exclusion criteria include: the presence of ankylosing spondylarthritis, enthesitis and arthritis, sacroiliitis with an inflammatory enteropathy or acute anterior uveitis in the patient, or a family history of one of these conditions in a parent or first-degree relative.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include other polyarticular diseases: connective tissue disorders (lupus, dermatomyositis) and hematological diseases (notably, acute leukemia).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Patients should be managed by a multidisciplinary team, incorporating expertise in pediatric rheumatology, physiotherapy, psychology and infantile orthopedic care. Treatment is based on the association of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDS), disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) and rehabilitation. Methotrexate is used as first-line treatment and then in case of inefficacy or intolerance , biologics (anti-tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha, tocilizumab (anti-IL6 receptor) or abatacept (targeting T lymphocyte activation) could be prescribed. Corticotherapy, at low doses, can be used while waiting for the effectiveness of DMARDs. Rehabilitation will be associated if necessary to avoid joint limitation or amyotrophy. Intra-articular injection of delayed-action corticoids (triamcinolone hexacetonide) may be recommended in case of persistent localized arthritis.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Remission is rare during adulthood (10% of cases). In the vast majority of cases, the disease remains progressive and requires follow-up treatment. The risk of cartilage and bone damage has been significantly reduced with the use of rapid and more aggressive therapeutic strategies.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: A Mendelian monogenic autosomal dominant syndrome, coatomer-associated protein subunit alpha syndrome, has been identified in a patient presenting with rheumatoid factor-positive polyarthritis. This syndrome is linked to a heterozygous mutation (c.725T>G, p.Val242Gly) and is characterized by abnormal trafficking between the Golgi complex and the endoplasmic reticulum. It associates inflammatory arthritis with interstitial lung disease and several high-titer autoantibodies. Although no familial disease was reported in the specific case, the syndrome itself follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. [PMC7607568]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare systemic disease characterized by chronic inflammation of unknown etiology and occurring predominantly in males in the second to third decades of life, mainly in Southeast Asian countries. Patients present with painless soft tissue swelling most commonly involving the head and neck region, usually with salivary gland involvement (parotid and submandibular glands) and regional lymphadenopathy. Frequent laboratory findings are peripheral eosinophilia and raised serum IgE. The diagnosis is confirmed histopathologically by the presence of well-formed lymphoid follicles with eosinophilic infiltration and vascular proliferation in the biopsy.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Kimura disease is a rare, chronic inflammatory condition that primarily affects young to middle-aged Asian males or young men of East Asian descent. While predominantly observed in Asian populations, cases have been documented in other demographics, including African American individuals and in countries such as Ethiopia and Syria, though these occurrences are noted as rare or unusual presentations. The disease is characterized by a high recurrence rate. [PMC12075989, PMC12351233, PMC12256335, PMC12370539, PMC12103863]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Kimura disease is primarily confirmed by histopathological examination, which typically reveals proliferation of blood vessels, germinal centers in lymphoid follicles, variable fibrosis, and extensive eosinophil and lymphocyte infiltration. Clinical presentation often includes subcutaneous nodules, particularly in the head and neck, sometimes accompanied by regional lymphadenopathy. Characteristic laboratory findings include peripheral eosinophilia and elevated serum IgE levels. Fine-needle aspiration cytology can provide a presumptive diagnosis, especially in challenging anatomical locations, by identifying Warthin-Finkeldey-type multinucleated cells, eosinophilic infiltration, and vascular proliferation. Advanced imaging techniques, such as [18F]AlF-NOTA-FAPI-04 PET/CT, offer superior diagnostic accuracy by visualizing fibroblast activation compared to 18F-FDG PET/CT. [PMC12075989, PMC12351233, PMC12370539, PMC12103863, PMC10845772]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Kimura disease (KD) should be considered in the differential diagnosis of head and neck masses, subcutaneous nodules, and lymphadenopathy, especially when accompanied by peripheral eosinophilia and elevated IgE. Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) presents with overlapping clinical and imaging features, posing a diagnostic challenge. Angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia (ALHE) is also a related condition, with KD sometimes identified as a variant. Furthermore, given the prominent eosinophilia in KD, the differential diagnosis extends to other eosinophilic disorders. These include primary eosinophilia, such as clonal expansions with mutations like FIP1L1-PDGFRA, and secondary reactive eosinophilia associated with infections, allergic conditions, connective tissue disorders, vasculitis, malignancy, or endocrinopathies. [PMC12351233, PMC12145034, PMC10845772, PMC11130981, PMC11374520]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Kimura's disease (KD) is a rare, chronic inflammatory disorder that predominantly affects young men of East Asian descent. It is characterized by painless solid masses primarily localized to the deep subcutaneous tissues of the head and neck, eosinophilia, and elevated serum immunoglobulin E (IgE). While the exact cause remains unclear, the pathogenesis is thought to involve dysregulated immune responses, particularly those mediated by T-helper cells 2 (Th2), eosinophils, and IgE production. Advances in molecular biology have suggested that genetic factors play a significant role in the development and progression of this chronic inflammatory condition. Recent studies have implicated several genes and immune pathways in its development, and understanding these genetic components may provide insights into better diagnostic tools and therapeutic strategies for KD. In this regard,... [PMC11855017]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Kimura disease often involves surgical excision for localized lesions, which can be effective, though recurrence rates are high. For generalized or recurrent disease, corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone) are a common initial treatment, effectively controlling progression and managing relapses, sometimes in combination with radiotherapy. Long-term follow-up is crucial due to the chronic nature and high recurrence. In refractory cases, biological therapies like dupilumab, often combined with corticosteroids, have shown significant efficacy by reducing lesion size and inflammatory markers. Chemotherapy, such as CVP, may also be considered for uncontrolled disease. Specific complications like peripheral arterial occlusive disease can be managed with angioplasty and anticoagulants. [PMC12075989, PMC12351233, PMC12078088, PMC12370539, PMC12103863]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Kimura disease is a chronic inflammatory condition generally considered benign, but it is characterized by a high recurrence rate, often involving multiple sites over extended durations. While localized lesions treated with surgical excision can have favorable outcomes, relapses are common. However, these relapses can often be effectively managed with reinitiation of steroids or other treatments. Long-term follow-up is crucial due to the disease's chronic and recurrent nature. Although rare, complications such as peripheral arterial occlusive disease can occur, but successful management has been reported. Even refractory cases can achieve periods without recurrence with appropriate therapy. [PMC12075989, PMC12351233, PMC12078088, PMC12370539, PMC10845772]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA)-associated vasculitis characterized by necrotizing inflammation of small and medium vessels (capillaries, venules and arterioles), resulting in tissue ischemia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is estimated between 1/6,400 - 42,000 worldwide with annual incidence between 1/84,000-475,000. There is geographic and/or ethnic variation, with a higher incidence in colder regions and among Caucasians. Childhood-onset disease is characterized by female predominance, and adult-onset by a slight male predominance.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The average age of onset is 45 years but the disease may manifest at any age including childhood. The disease may present with various organ manifestations. Ear, nose and throat symptoms are present in 50-95% (persistent nasal obstruction, destructive sinusitis, crusting and/or hemorrhagic rhinitis, nasal septum deformity, saddle nose deformity, and otitis media), bronchopulmonary symptoms in 60-80% (nodules, alveolar hemorrage, bronchial and/or subglottic stenosis), and renal disease (typically extra-capillary necrotizing glomerulonephritis) in 60-80% of affected individuals. General signs (fever, arthralgia, myalgia, weight loss) are common. Skin lesions (purpura and cutaneous nodules) are observed in 10-50%, peripheral neuropathy (multineuritis) in 25%, central nervous system manifestations (headaches, sensorimotor deficit, hemiplegia and epilepsy) in 10%, and ocular anomalies (scleritis and orbital tumors) in 7-8% of patients.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The pathogenesis of GPA is still under study. Genetic susceptibility factors, environmental agents, infectious episodes and anomalies in innate and adaptive immunity seem to play a role in the development of all ANCA-associated vasculitides. Genetic variants appear to correlate with antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA) antigen specificity rather than with clinical phenotype. Thus, cytoplasmic-ANCAs directed to proteinase 3 (PR3-ANCA), found in 60-80% of GPA cases, are associated with genetic variants in HLA-DP1A and HLA-DP1B (6p21.32) which encode a class II major histocompatibility complex, SERPINA1 (14q32.13) encoding alpha-1 antitrypsin, and PRTN3 (19p13.3) encoding the autoantigen proteinase 3.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on clinical findings, imaging studies and biochemical testing, and detection of ANCAs in the serum, principally PR3-ANCAs. Histological analysis of biopsy specimens from affected organs confirms the diagnosis, showing necrotizing vasculitis and granulomatous inflammation.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other ANCA-associated vasculitides such as microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
