DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Induction therapy comprises steroid pulses combined with either intravenous Rituximab or Cyclophosphamide. Disease remission is achieved in more than 80% of patients with these protocols. In cases of lacking or insufficient response, plasma exchange can be considered. Azathioprine and Methotrexate are efficacious agents for maintenance immunosuppression whereas Mycophenolate-Mofetil is less effective. Leflunomide is an alternative option for individuals intolerant to Azathioprine or Methotrexate. Anti-TNF antibodies (e.g. Infliximab and Adalimumab) have shown promising results in clinical trials as steroid-sparing agents.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: While remission is achieved with treatment in 70-100% of cases, the disease relapses in more than 80% of patients within 10 years. Significant morbidity may emerge both from the disease and its treatment. Ten-year patient survival is around 75%.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Neovascular glaucoma is the most common type of secondary glaucoma, usually caused by diabetic retinopathy, central retinal vein occlusion and carotid artery obstruction but sometimes by trauma, uvietis or ocular tumors, and characterized by severe eye pain, synechial angle glaucoma, high intraocular pressure and leading to loss of vision.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Neovascular glaucoma can arise as a complication of other ocular conditions. In a study of 111 patients with retinal vein occlusions, 12 developed neovascular glaucoma. It is also observed in patients with cytomegalovirus (CMV) necrotizing retinopathy following haploidentical hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. In this specific population, the incidence of neovascular glaucoma was reported as 5.1% per case and 3.4% per eye, warranting long-term follow-up. [PMC10117181, PMC8210782]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Neovascular glaucoma can be associated with underlying genetic disorders. Pierson syndrome, an autosomal recessive condition caused by LAMB2 gene mutations, has been linked to neovascular glaucoma, with specific missense variants identified. Additionally, neovascular glaucoma in pediatric patients has been reported in association with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), which can be confirmed by genetic testing. Therefore, in young patients presenting with neovascular glaucoma, careful attention to family history and the overall patient condition is warranted. Molecular testing for conditions like NF1 may be necessary to ensure accurate diagnosis. [PMC9951501, PMC7451455, PMC7189718]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:86

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 is an uniparental disomy of maternal origin characterized by intrauterine growth retardation. Homozygosity for a recessive disease mutation for which only a mother is a carrier may lead to other phenotypes.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 (UPD(6)mat) is an extremely rare genetic condition, with few molecularly confirmed cases reported. Its clinical relevance is currently unclear, and it is considered an ultra-rare genetic disorder. A review of the literature identified 24 confirmed UPD(6)mat cases, underscoring its rarity. [PMC12026494, PMC5702562]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 (UPD(6)mat) is an extremely rare genetic condition with a variable clinical presentation. Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and preterm delivery are frequently observed, with many individuals born small for gestational age and experiencing failure to thrive. Neurodevelopmental issues, including developmental delay and autism spectrum disorder, are also common. Other reported features include dysmorphic features and sacrococcygeal teratoma. While a common UPD(6)mat phenotype is not always obvious, some features may arise from placental dysfunction due to trisomy 6 mosaicism or the unmasking of homozygous recessive mutations, such as early onset retinal dystrophy caused by a TULP1 variant. UPD(6)mat itself may act as a biomarker, indirectly identifying the cause of the phenotype. [PMC12026494, PMC6066270, PMC5702562]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 (UPD(6)mat) is an extremely rare genetic condition characterized by the inheritance of both copies of chromosome 6 from the mother. The exact molecular basis for its clinical relevance remains largely unknown, and UPD(6)mat itself may not be directly associated with a common phenotype, potentially acting as a biomarker. Proposed mechanisms include imprinting disturbances, similar to paternal UPD(6), and cryptic trisomy 6 mosaicism, particularly in heterodisomy. Placental dysfunction due to trisomy 6 mosaicism likely contributes to features such as intrauterine growth restriction and preterm delivery. Other observed clinical features can result from homozygosity of recessive mutations unmasked by the UPD, or from an undetected trisomy 6 cell line. No specific gene or consistent epigenetic abnormality has been identified as the primary cause of the overall UPD(6)mat phenotype. [PMC12026494, PMC6066270, PMC5702562]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 (UPD(6)mat) is confirmed through molecular diagnostic . These include single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays, which can detect the presence of uniparental disomy, and trio whole-exome sequencing. Molecular characterization is also used to identify isodisomic uniparental regions on chromosome 6. While cytogenetic data, such as karyotyping, may be available, and trisomy 6 mosaicism can be detected prenatally, molecular approaches are essential for confirming UPD(6)mat itself. [PMC12026494, PMC6066270, PMC5702562]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 (upd(6)mat) itself is not associated with a common clinical picture and can be regarded as a biomarker. However, it can unmask recessive mutations, leading to specific phenotypes. For example, a patient with upd(6)mat presented with early onset retinal dystrophy, including features overlapping Leber congenital amaurosis and retinitis pigmentosa, due to a homozygous TULP1 variant. Other clinical features observed in upd(6)mat patients, such as intrauterine growth restriction and preterm delivery, might be caused by placental dysfunction due to trisomy 6 mosaicism or by other undetected recessive mutations. Therefore, the differential diagnosis should consider conditions resulting from unmasked recessive variants on chromosome 6 and those associated with placental trisomy 6 mosaicism. [PMC6066270, PMC5702562]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 (UPD(6)mat) is frequently associated with prenatal findings such as intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and preterm delivery. While a common UPD(6)mat phenotype is not always obvious, placental dysfunction due to trisomy 6 mosaicism, which can be detected prenatally, likely contributes to these outcomes. The detection of UPD(6)mat itself, often considered a biomarker, prompts further clinical assessments and tests to identify the underlying cause of observed phenotypes. [PMC12026494, PMC5702562]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 (UPD(6)mat) is a rare genetic finding, often acting as a biomarker rather than the direct cause of a phenotype. Its detection is crucial for identifying underlying causes, which may include homozygosity for recessive mutations, such as a novel TULP1 variant, or mechanisms like imprinting disturbances and cryptic trisomy 6 mosaicism. Molecular diagnosis, including trio whole-exome sequencing and SNP arrays, is essential to confirm UPD(6)mat and unmask pathogenic variants, informing the mode of transmission and clinical management. Genetic counseling should incorporate a detailed list of clinical assessments and tests to guide diagnostic and management approaches for this ultra-rare disorder. [PMC12026494, PMC6066270, PMC5702562]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Uniparental disomy (UPD) is the inheritance of both copies of a chromosome from a single parent, leading to distinct genetic conditions. Maternal UPD of chromosome 6 (UPD(6)mat) is extremely rare, with few molecularly confirmed cases reported. a prematurely born female with isodisomic UPD(6)mat, presenting with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), developmental delay, autism spectrum disorder, dysmorphic features, and a sacrococcygeal teratoma. In addition, we reviewed 24 confirmed UPD(6)mat cases to assess clinical patterns in prenatal findings, birth outcomes, and postnatal features. Trio whole-exome sequencing revealed complete isodisomy of chromosome 6 and a de novo heterozygous DIAPH2 variant of uncertain significance. In the literature review, IUGR was present in 87% of cases, with most individuals born small for gestational age and preterm. Failure to thrive and... [PMC12026494, PMC6066270]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 6 (UPD(6)mat) is an ultra-rare condition with variable clinical relevance, and a common phenotype is not always obvious. However, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR), preterm delivery, and being small for gestational age are frequent, occurring in most reported cases. Neurodevelopmental issues, including developmental delay, autism spectrum disorder, and failure to thrive, are also commonly observed. Other features can include dysmorphic traits, sacrococcygeal teratoma, or early-onset retinal dystrophy, depending on unmasked recessive mutations. The UPD itself may act as a biomarker, with the phenotype potentially stemming from placental dysfunction or homozygosity of recessive mutations. [PMC12026494, PMC6066270, PMC5702562]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Drug-induced autoimmune hemolytic anemia is a type of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) that occurs as a reaction to therapeutic drugs, and can be due to various mechanisms.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Drug-induced AIHA is rare; annual incidence is estimated at about 1/1,000,000. It is more common in adults and is very rare in children, although some fatal cases in children have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease presents with anemia linked to hemolysis, and physical examination may show an enlarged spleen.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: To date about 100 drugs have been implicated in drug-induced AIHA, including: cephalosporins (primarily cefotetan and ceftriaxone), levodopa, methyldopa, penicillin and its derivatives, quinidine and some nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: It is important to consider drug-induced AIHA when a patient serologically presents as either warm- or cold-type AIHA to avoid erroneous diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Stopping the drug that is causing the problem may relieve or control the symptoms. Patients may also be given IV immunoglobulin and prednisone to reduce the immune response. Blood transfusion may be needed in severe cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is good if the causative drug is identified and the patient stops taking it. Death is a rare outcome, but has been reported particularly in children with AIHA caused by cefotetan and ceftriaxone.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A primary glomerular disease characterized by proteinuria, type IV renal tubular acidosis, microscopic hematuria and hypertension that may lead to end-stage renal failure in the second to sixth decade of life.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Fibronectin glomerulopathy exact prevalence is unknown. Only 20 families and 25 sporadic cases have been described in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Fibronectin glomerulopathy may present at different ages, although mostly in adolescence or early adulthood, with typical features of a nephrotic syndrome including hypertension, which can be severe, and edema, which initially develops around the eyes and legs but with time may become generalized. Patients may also present with varying degrees of renal failure that progressively worsen over several years, reaching end stage renal disease in the second to sixth decade of life.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Clustering of the disease within families indicates a genetic origin. In 40% of families, the disease is caused by heterozygous mutations in the FN1 gene (2q34) encoding fibronectin. Whole-genome linkage analysis in a large pedigree showed another disease locus on 1q32, however no specific candidate genes has been identified so far.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis rests on renal biopsy. Typical findings at light microscopy are enlarged glomeruli with deposits in the mesangium and subendothelial space, usually with scant immunoreactivity for immunoglobulins or complement factors. Electron microscopy reveals deposits mainly located in the subendothelial space but also in the subepithelial and intramembranous spaces. Homogeneous granular deposits dominate in most cases; in some an admixture of fibrils is observed. The most striking finding is the immunoreactivity of the glomerular deposits to fibronectin. Family history is supportive of the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other chronic non-amyloid glomerulopathies with organized deposits including mixed cryoglobulinemia, fibrillary glomerulonephritis, immunotactoid glomerulopathy, collagen type III glomerulopathy, systemic lupus erythematosus, diabetes glomerulopathy and other non-specific collagen deposition diseases. It is difficult to discriminate fibronectin glomerulopathy from membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis at light microscopy examination.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Segregation with disease appearance in successive generations is consistent with an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance with age-related penetrance. Genetic counseling should be proposed to individuals having the disease-causing mutation informing them that there is 50% risk of passing the mutation to offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no specific treatment for fibronectin glomerulopathy. Treatment of symptoms can include corticosteroids, diuretics and treatment for hypertension. Antiproteinuric and renoprotective treatment with ACE inhibitors or anti-AT1R antagonists could be of help to slow renal disease progression. More advanced cases of renal failure require renal dialysis or transplantation.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is uncertain, in some cases the disease follows an indolent course and in others it leads to end stage renal disease and chronic renal failure in the second to sixth decade of life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurologic disease characterized by impairment of higher visual processing skills and other posterior cortical functions without any evidence of ocular abnormalities, relatively intact memory and language in the early stages, and atrophy of posterior brain regions.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Benson syndrome; Biparietal Alzheimer disease; PCA

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Posterior Cortical Atrophy (PCA) prevalence is unknown, largely due to the lack of awareness of the syndrome, delayed diagnosis and the variable terminology referring to it (now partially addressed through international consensus criteria).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Early PCA symptoms include visuoperceptual and visuospatial dysfunction, apraxia and alexia. Features of Bálint syndrome (simultanagnosia, optic ataxia and oculomotor apraxia) and Gerstmann syndrome (acalculia, agraphia, finger agnosia and left-right disorientation) are commonly described. The disorder typical onset is between 50-65 years of age. Earliest reported symptoms include difficulties with complex visual behaviors (e.g. driving, reading, and telling the time from an analogue watch). Reading problems include getting lost on the page (visual disorientation), overlapping or miscombined letters (visual crowding) or better reading of small than large print. Odd visual manifestations like abnormally prolonged color after-images and perception of movement of static stimuli are also reported. People with PCA tend to have relatively well preserved memory, insight, and judgment early in the disease course, athough language problems (word finding problems, phonological errors) often emerge early. It should also be noted that PCA is a relatively heterogenous syndrome with some experiencing a very focal visual syndrome, whilst others show a more mixed cognitive picture with prominent visual but also evident episodic memory deficits from early in the disease course. Individuals with PCA often experience anxiety and depression from early on. Extrapyramidal signs, myoclonus, and grasp reflex have also been reported in PCA patients. An international consensus classification framework distinguishes two syndromic description levels. Classification 1 (PCA) defines the core clinical, cognitive, and neuroimaging features and exclusion criteria of the clinico-radiological syndrome. Classification level 2 (PCA-pure, PCA-plus) establishes whether, in addition to the core PCA syndrome, the core features of any other neurodegenerative syndromes are present.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: A third level of the international classification framework provides disease-level descriptions of the underlying causes of the PCA syndrome, based on available pathophysiological biomarker evidence. This distinguishes between Alzheimer's disease as the most common underlying pathology (PCA-AD), and other causes including Lewy Body disease (PCA-LBD), corticobasal degeneration (PCA-CBD) and prion disease (PCA-prion).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: PCA is an under-recognized disorder resulting often in a significant delay in diagnosis. Diagnosis of this clinico-radiological syndrome is based on neurological assessment, specific visual and cognitive testing, and (optional supportive) brain imaging and routine blood tests. MRI characteristically shows bilateral atrophy in the occipital, parietal and posterior temporal lobes, often asymmetric being more pronounced in the right hemisphere. Single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT) or PET show hypometabolism of the posterior cerebral areas as well as in the frontal eye fields in more advanced stages. Conclusive diagnosis of the underlying disease is confirmed on brain autopsy, though CSF and amyloid imaging may help to refine the clinical diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes the most commonly associated neuropathology Alzheimer disease, but may also include Lewy body disease, cortico-basal degeneration, and prion diseases such as Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is currently no cure for any of the neurodegenerative conditions that most commonly underly the PCA syndrome. Medications like acetylcholinesterase inhibitors, used in the treatment of Alzheimer's disease, are available and might bring relief for some symptoms. Management of PCA is based on visual aids, rehabilitation programs that include psychoeducation, compensatory strategies, and cognitive exercises to cope with visual disabilities. Antidepressant treatments may benefit individuals with PCA who have relatively preserve insight into their decline and often deal with depression, irritability, frustration and a loss of self-confidence. People with PCA and their caregivers are likely to have different needs to people with more typical presentations of Alzheimer's disease, and may benefit from specialized support groups.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor as PCA is progressive disorder. Life expectancy after PCA diagnosis is thought to be similar (8-12 years) to individuals affected with Alzheimer's disease.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for Posterior Cortical Atrophy (PCA) should consider the potential role of genetic variants, such as the GBA N370S variant, which has been identified in a PCA patient with a positive family history of Dementia with Lewy Bodies. While GBA variants are established risk factors for alpha-synucleinopathies like Parkinson's disease and Dementia with Lewy Bodies, this represents the first reported instance in PCA. Carriers of such variants may exhibit phenotypic overlaps across different neurodegenerative conditions. Next-generation sequencing can detect these variants, and reduced glucocerebrosidase activity can further support their pathogenicity. [PMC7802182]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare acute myeloid leukemia characterized by primary differentiation to basophils. Microscopically, peripheral blood and bone marrow blasts contain coarse cytoplasmic basophilic granules which are positive with metachromatic staining (toluidine blue). Electron microscopy confirms that granules show features characteristic of basophil precursors. Mature basophils are usually sparse. Patients may present with manifestations related to bone marrow failure, as well as hepatosplenomegaly, cutaneous involvement, lytic lesions, and hyperhistaminemia. The disease is associated with a poor prognosis.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Acute basophilic leukemia (ABL) is an uncommon subtype of acute leukemia, often presenting with clinical signs and symptoms related to hyper-histaminemia and bone marrow failure due to blast infiltration. Patients may or may not have circulating blasts. ABL can arise from chronic myeloid leukemia or transform from myelodysplastic syndrome, sometimes with abundant mast cells. Immunophenotypically, leukemic blasts typically express myeloid markers such as CD13 and CD33, and are positive for CD123, CD203c, CD11b, and CD294. KIT (CD117) can be positive or negative, while monocytic markers are usually negative. Genetic abnormalities include the t(X;6)(p11;q23) translocation resulting in the MYB-GATA1 fusion gene, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17(q10), der(22)t(9;22), monosomy 7, t(2;14), and MLL gene rearrangement. [PMC10493107, PMC9289198, PMC5385891, PMC3197559]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Acute basophilic leukemia (ABL) can arise from pre-existing hematologic conditions such as chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) or myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS). Genetic abnormalities are key to its etiology, including the t(X;6) (p11; q23) translocation, which in the MYB-GATA1 fusion gene and promotes basophilic differentiation by triggering NTRK1 and IL1RL1 transcription. Other identified fusions include PRKG2-PDGFRB. ABL transforming from CML may present with complex karyotypes like +8, i(17q)(q10), and der(22)t(9;22), while transformation from MDS can involve monosomy 7. Additionally, a three-way translocation t(12;15;17) (p13;q24;q21) leading to PML::RARA has been observed in acute promyelocytic leukemia with basophilic differentiation. Cases have also been reported to emerge from donor cells after allogeneic stem cell transplantation, associated with t(2;14) and MLL gene rearrangement, potentially linked to donor DNA repair gene polymorphisms. [PMC11203485, PMC10493107, PMC9289198, PMC7909134, PMC5385891]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for acute basophilic leukemia includes other myeloid neoplasms with basophilic differentiation. These encompass acute promyelocytic leukemia with basophilic differentiation, acute myeloid leukemia with basophilic differentiation (including cases transformed from myelodysplastic syndrome), and tryptase-positive acute myeloid leukemia. Myeloid neoplasms with PDGFRB rearrangement, particularly those presenting with basophilia and/or systemic mastocytosis, should also be considered. Additionally, myelomastocytic leukemia and mast cell leukemia, especially those without typical immunophenotype, require careful exclusion due to overlapping features. [PMC11203485, PMC9289198, PMC7909134, PMC5819157, PMC5385891]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: A 54-year-old woman was diagnosed with infiltrative ductal breast carcinoma. Two years after treatment, the patient developed an acute myeloid leukemia (AML) which harbored del(11q23) in 8% of the blast cells. The patient was submitted for allogeneic stem cell transplantation (aSCT) from her HLA-compatible sister. Ten months after transplantation, she relapsed with an AML with basophilic maturation characterized by CD45(low) CD33(high), CD117⁺, CD13(-/+), HLA Dr(high), CD123(high), and CD203c⁺ blast cells lacking expression of CD7, CD10, CD34, CD15, CD14, CD56, CD36, CD64, and cytoplasmic tryptase. Karyotype analysis showed the emergence of a new clone with t(2;14) and FISH analysis indicated the presence of MLL gene rearrangement consistent with del(11q23). Interestingly, AML blast cell DNA tested with microsatellite markers showed the same pattern as the donor's, suggesting that this... [PMC3197559]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Treatment strategies for leukemias with basophilic features include standard therapy with all-trans-retinoic acid (ATRA) and arsenic trioxide (ATO), which has led to complete remission in acute promyelocytic leukemia with basophilic differentiation. For myeloid tumors with basophilia and PDGFRB rearrangement, imatinib, azacitidine, and DHAG have been used, resulting in hematological, bone marrow morphological, and cytogenetic remission. Patients with PDGFRB abnormality are noted to have a good response to imatinib. [PMC11203485, PMC7909134, PMC3197559]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Acute basophilic leukemia (ABL) prognosis varies depending on the underlying context and genetic features. While basophilic differentiation has been associated with a poor prognosis in some reported cases, specific genetic abnormalities like PDGFRB rearrangement can lead to a good response to imatinib and complete remission. In contrast, ABL transformed from myelodysplastic syndrome may carry a poor prognosis, with one patient dying nine months after transformation when chemotherapy was refused. Relapse with basophilic maturation following allogeneic stem cell transplantation also indicates a poor outcome. However, some cases of acute promyelocytic leukemia with basophilic differentiation have shown prompt response to standard treatment. The role of abundant mast cells in ABL arising from chronic myeloid leukemia in prognosis warrants further study. [PMC11203485, PMC10493107, PMC7909134, PMC5385891, PMC3197559]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: X-linked intellectual disability-Dandy-Walker malformation-basal ganglia disease-seizures syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare central nervous system malformation characterized by severe intellectual deficit, early hypotonia with progression to spasticity and contractures, choreoathetosis, seizures, dysmorphic face (long face with prominent forehead), and brain imaging abnormalities such as Dandy-Walker malformation, and iron deposition.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: X-linked intellectual disability-Dandy-Walker malformation-basal ganglia disease-seizures syndrome, also known as Pettigrew syndrome, is a rare X-linked mental retardation caused by AP1S2 mutation. It was initially described in a four-generation family with nine affected individuals and has since been identified in other families, such as a Chinese pedigree with seven affected individuals. A review of the literature summarized the clinical manifestations of 59 patients with AP1S2 mutations. The syndrome's recognition has been complicated by highly variable expressivity, with affected families initially described under different OMIM numbers, but are now understood to represent the same condition. [PMC6422709, PMC3925263]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Pettigrew syndrome, an X-linked intellectual disability syndrome caused by AP1S2 mutations, presents with highly variable expressivity. Key features include intellectual disability, Dandy-Walker malformation, and basal ganglia disease, which may involve choreoathetosis or iron deposition. Patients commonly exhibit dysmorphic features, delayed walking, abnormal speech, hypotonia, and abnormal gait. Neurodevelopmental issues also encompass abnormal brain findings and behaviors such as aggression, ASD, and self-abuse. Seizures are frequently observed, particularly with splice site mutations, while nonsense mutations are more often associated with microcephaly. [PMC6422709, PMC3925263]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: X-linked intellectual disability-Dandy-Walker malformation-basal ganglia disease-seizures syndrome, also known as Pettigrew syndrome, is caused by mutations in the X-linked AP1S2 gene. Pathogenic point mutations affecting AP1S2 are associated with a broad spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders and dysmorphic features. Specific mutations identified include a novel splice site mutation (c.1-1 G>C) and a c.426+1 G>T mutation, which leads to a loss of 46 amino acids in the clathrin adaptor complex small chain domain. Patients with splice site mutations are more prone to seizures, while nonsense mutations are linked to microcephaly. The syndrome exhibits highly variable expressivity, complicating its recognition despite being associated with the same AP1S2 gene. [PMC6422709, PMC3925263]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of X-linked intellectual disability-Dandy-Walker malformation-basal ganglia disease-seizures syndrome, also known as Pettigrew syndrome, relies on identifying pathogenic mutations in the AP1S2 gene, often through X-chromosome exome sequencing. Clinical features such as facial dysmorphism, intellectual disability, Dandy-Walker malformation, and choreoathetosis are key, though expressivity is highly variable. Imaging studies may reveal iron deposition in the basal ganglia. Additionally, elevated neuron-specific enolase has been observed in some patients. Specific AP1S2 mutation types, like splice site or nonsense mutations, can correlate with particular clinical manifestations such as seizures or microcephaly. [PMC6422709, PMC3925263]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis is complicated by the highly variable expressivity of this X-linked intellectual disability syndrome, both within and between families. Most families affected by an AP1S2 mutation were initially described as having different disorders, assigned to at least three different OMIM numbers (MIM 300629, 300630, and 304340). However, analysis of the phenotype shows that these are all manifestations of the same syndrome, with the variability not explained by differences in mutation severity. [PMC3925263]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Pettigrew syndrome is an X-linked intellectual disability syndrome caused by mutations in the AP1S2 gene. The condition exhibits highly variable expressivity, both within and between families, which is not fully explained by differences in mutation severity. Specific mutation types may influence phenotypic presentation; for example, splice site mutations are more frequently associated with seizures, while nonsense mutations may predispose to microcephaly. Identification of AP1S2 mutations, as seen in multi-generational families, is crucial for diagnosis and genetic counseling regarding the X-linked inheritance pattern and the broad spectrum of neurodevelopmental disorders associated with these mutations. [PMC6422709, PMC3925263]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Pettigrew syndrome (PGS) is a rare X-linked mental retardation that caused by AP1S2 mutation. The pathogenesis of AP1S2 deficiency has remained elusive. The purpose of is to give a comprehensive overview of the phenotypic and genetic spectrum of AP1S2 mutations. systematically analyzed clinical features and genetic information of a Chinese family with AP1S2 variation, and reviewed previously reported literatures with the same gene variation. We identified a new c.1-1 G>C mutation in AP1S2 gene from a four generation family with seven affected individuals and found the elevated neuron-specific enolase (NSE) in a patient. We summarized the clinical manifestation of 59 patients with AP1S2 mutation. We found that pathogenic point mutations affecting AP1S2 are associated with dysmorphic features and neurodevelopmental problems, which included highly variable mental retardation (MR), delayed... [PMC6422709]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Developmental malformations-deafness-dystonia syndrome is characterised by the association of midline malformations, sensory hearing loss, and a delayed-onset generalised dystonia syndrome.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It has been described in two monozygotic twins.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is caused by a missense point mutation in the gene coding for beta-actin, a nonmuscle actin isoform. Mutations in nonmuscle actin isoforms may be associated with developmental anomalies and neurological disorders such as dystonia.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pili torti is a hair shaft abnormality characterized by flat hair that is twisted at irregular intervals. Hair is normal at birth but progressively stops growing long and becomes fragile. Pili torti can be isolated or occur in association with syndromes such as Menkes disease or Bazex syndrome.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Pili torti is a rare condition characterized by twisted hair shafts. It presents as either a congenital or acquired clinical presentation. Inherited forms may be isolated or associated with numerous genetic diseases and syndromes, while acquired forms have been described in various alopecias, neoplastic and systemic diseases, and can be drug-induced. The condition may also improve spontaneously after puberty. [PMC8432236, PMC4540501]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Pili torti is a rare condition characterized by hair shafts that are flattened at irregular intervals and twisted 180° along their long axis, resulting in increased fragility. Clinically, affected hairs are fragile, brittle, coarse, and lusterless, often presenting as difficult to comb. It can be congenital or acquired. Inherited forms may be isolated or associated with numerous genetic diseases, syndromes, or ectodermal dysplasias, including Menkes disease, Björnstad syndrome, Netherton syndrome, Rapp-Hodgkin syndrome, and Ankyloblepharon-ectodermal defects-cleft lip/palate syndrome. It may also be linked to neurological abnormalities, developmental delay, growth delay, or arginosuccinic aciduria. Acquired pili torti can be a feature of various alopecias, neoplastic and systemic diseases, or induced by certain drugs. Diagnosis is based on trichoscopic or microscopic examination, and a search for underlying conditions is recommended. The condition may spontaneously improve after puberty. [PMC8432236, PMC4540501, PMC1016033, PMC1438288]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Pili torti is a hair shaft disorder characterized by hairs flattened at irregular intervals and twisted 180° along their long axis. It is classified into inherited and acquired forms. Inherited forms may be isolated or associated with numerous genetic diseases and syndromes, including Menkes disease, Björnstad syndrome, Netherton syndrome, Bazex-Dupré-Christol syndrome, arginosuccinic aciduria, and various ectodermal dysplasias. It can also be a feature of unknown syndromes presenting with growth delay, developmental delay, and neurological abnormalities. Acquired pili torti has been described in various alopecias, neoplastic and systemic diseases, and may be induced by several drugs, such as epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors or oral retinoids. [PMC8432236, PMC4540501, PMC1016033, PMC1438288]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Pili torti is based on trichoscopic or microscopic examination, which reveals the hair shaft flattened at irregular intervals and twisted 180° along its long axis. Electron microscopic findings of the hair shaft can also be part of the diagnostic process. As Pili torti is a feature of numerous congenital and acquired conditions, a comprehensive search for signs of underlying disorders is recommended in every case. [PMC8432236, PMC1016033]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Pili torti is a feature of numerous congenital and acquired conditions, necessitating a broad differential diagnosis. Inherited forms can be isolated or associated with various genetic diseases and syndromes, including Menkes disease, Björnstad syndrome, Netherton syndrome, Bazex-Dupré-Christol syndrome, and arginosuccinic aciduria. It may also manifest as part of ectodermal dysplasias such as Rapp-Hodgkin syndrome and Ankyloblepharon-ectodermal defects-cleft lip/palate syndrome. Acquired pili torti has been observed in various alopecias (e.g., lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus erythematosus), neoplastic and systemic diseases (e.g., cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, anorexia nervosa), and can be drug-induced (e.g., by epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitors). Some presentations involve pili torti alongside growth delay, developmental delay, and neurological abnormalities, suggesting potentially unknown syndromes. Therefore, a comprehensive search for signs of underlying conditions is recommended in every case. [PMC8432236, PMC4540501, PMC1016033, PMC1438288]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Pili torti can be an inherited condition, occurring either in isolation or as a feature of numerous genetic diseases and syndromes, including Menkes disease, Björnstad syndrome, Netherton syndrome, Bazex-Dupré-Christol syndrome, Rapp-Hodgkin syndrome, Ankyloblepharon-ectodermal defects-cleft lip/palate syndrome, and arginosuccinic aciduria. It may also present as part of previously undescribed syndromes, such as that observed in consanguineous siblings with growth delay, developmental delay, and neurological abnormalities. Due to its diverse genetic associations, a comprehensive search for underlying conditions is recommended in every case to inform genetic counseling regarding inheritance patterns and potential recurrence risks. [PMC8432236, PMC1016033, PMC1438288]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Currently, there is no specific treatment available for pili torti. Despite the lack of targeted therapies, the condition, which is characterized by fragile, brittle, coarse, and lusterless hairs, may spontaneously improve after puberty. This suggests a potential natural resolution of the hair shaft abnormalities over time, although specific interventions are not described. [PMC4540501]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Pili torti is a rare hair shaft disorder characterized by fragile, brittle, coarse, and lusterless hairs. While there is no specific treatment available for this condition, the prognosis suggests a potential for spontaneous improvement. Specifically, the hair abnormalities associated with pili torti may resolve naturally after puberty. [PMC4540501]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare form of Legionellosis characterized by a severe, potentially fatal, pneumonia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The annual notification rate in 2009 from 25 EU Member States amounted to approximately 1/90,000. In France the annual incidence is around 1/50,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: LD has an incubation period of 2-10 days with fatigue and weakness often being the first signs of the disease. It manifests as pneumonia characterized by fever, cough, sputum production and shortness of breath. Other symptoms can include diarrhea, myalgia, headaches, confusion/delirium and nausea. LD is most severe in elderly and immunocompromised people (due to immunosuppressive therapy, especially with corticosteroids, transplants, hematologic malignancy or cancer), who are an ever-increasing risk group for infection. Other risk factors for LD include cigarette smoking, age over 50, male gender, diabetes, and chronic heart, lung or kidney disease.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: LD is caused by Legionella pneumophila (most commonly serogroup 1), a bacteria found in water and wet soil. Humans are infected by inhaling aerosols containing the bacteria, most commonly from showers, hot tubs, saunas or other bathing facilities. The same bacteria are responsible for Pontiac fever (PF) a mild form of LD. LD occurs sporadically and in outbreaks, with the sporadic form accounting for 65 to 80% of cases. Outbreaks are predominantly linked to contaminated aerosols from wet cooling systems or occur in hospitals, nursing homes or hotels.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: EU case definitions have been agreed upon associating clinical and laboratory criteria for case confirmation. Any person with pneumonia and one of the following criteria: isolation of Legionella spp. from respiratory secretions or any normally sterile site, detection of L. pneumophila antigen in urine or L. pneumophila serogroup 1-specific antibody response, are given a diagnosis of LD. Detection of Legionella spp. nucleic acid in a clinical specimen has been added as criteria for probable cases.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The disease has no particular clinical features that clearly distinguish it from other types of pneumonia. Other bacterial (Streptococcus pneumonia, Staphylococcus aureus and Haemophilus influenza) or viral infections that cause pneumonia need to be ruled out.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment involves antibiotics (usually macrolides and quinolones). Hospitalization is often required. Ventilatory support may be necessary in those with serious breathing difficulties. Legionella surveillance programs are based on notification of cases at a national and European level and on legislation for controlling the development of the bacteria in the aquatic environment.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: In most cases, LD is treated and cured with antibiotics but in those with compromised immune systems or underlying health conditions the prognosis can be poor. The overall case fatality rate is around 10-15%.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare embryonic tumor of the neuroepithelial tissue characterized clinically by increased intracranial pressure and cerebellar dysfunction, with the most common presenting symptoms being headache, vomiting, and ataxia. The disease can be classified according to histological (classic, anaplastic, large-cell, or desmoplatic medulloblastoma, or medulloblastoma with extensive nodularity) and molecular criteria (WNT-activated, sonic-hedgehog-activated, group 3, group 4).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Medulloblastoma (MB) is the most common malignant brain tumor in childhood. Annual incidence varies according to age a group, and is estimated in the USA at 0.47/100,000 in children (0-14 years of age), 0.11/100,000 in adolescents and young adults, 0.02/100,000 in adults (over 40 years of age). Males are more affected than females.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Age of disease onset is variable and can occur in patients ranging in age from the newborn period to adulthood (peak age at presentation is children 3-6 years, with only 25% of patients being between 15 and 44 years). The most common presenting symptoms are headache, vomiting, and ataxia. Additional features that may be observed include lethargy, motor or cranial nerve impairment, gaze palsy, visual impairment due to hydrocephalia, vertigo/hearing loss, behavioral changes/irritability, and extracranial pain (e.g. back pain in those with spinal metastases). Around 30% of pediatric cases present with metastases at diagnosis. Most metastases occur within the central nervous system by seeding via the cerebrospinal fluid (cranial or spinal), while spread to extracranial organs (e.g. bone marrow, liver, lungs) is very rare at diagnosis. In a minority of patients, MB is associated with Gorlin syndrome, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP; the association of FAP and MB is referred to as the Turcot syndrome with polyposis) or with Li-Fraumeni Syndrome. Increased susceptibility to certain tumors (neuroblastoma), hematological malignancies (acute lymphoblastic leukemia, acute myeloid leukemia) or disorders caused by mutations in genes encoding components of the RAS signaling pathway (Noonan syndrome or neurofibromatosis-Noonan syndrome) have been reported in MB.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: To date, the exact etiology of MB is still unknown but genomic data has identified multiple candidate genes that contribute to the pathogenesis of different subgroups of MB. This includes inhibitors of the sonic hedgehog pathway SUFU (10q24.32), Ptch1 (9q22.32), the RNA helicase DDX3X (Xp11.3-p11.23), chromatin regulators KDM6A (Xp11.2) and N-CoR complex genes BCOR (Xp11.4), and the Parkinson's disease genes KMT2D (12q13.12), SMARCA4 (19p13.3), MYC (8q24.21), MYCN (2p24.3), and TP53 (17p13.1).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: MB occurs in the vermis and 20% occurs in the hemispheres of the cerebellum. WNT-activated MB may arise from the dorsal brainstem. Histologically, MB is characterized by small, round cells that stain blue with haematoxylin spectrum and appearance ranges from tumors with extensive nodularity to those with large cell/anaplastic features. Apart from classical MB, four histological variants of MB are recognized: anaplastic MB, large cell MB, MB with extensive nodularity, and desmoplastic/nodular MB. Four different molecular subgroups (WNT-activated, sonic-hedgehog-activated, group 3, group 4) have been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other brain tumors (ependymoma, glial tumor, atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumor) and other causes of cerebellar alterations (infectious or cystic lesions, hemorrhages).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling is indicated in specific constellations, e.g. in sonic hedgehog-activated MB (Gorlin-syndrome, Li-Fraumeni-Syndrome, BRCA2), CTNNB1-negative WNT-activated MB (Turcot-syndrome).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Initially, patients need to be checked for increased intracranial pressure, which if present, needs to be controlled either by medication (e.g. steroids) or by neurosurgical drainage (e.g. external drainage). The postoperative treatment depends on age, histological and molecular subgroup, and result of staging assessments (cranial and spinal MRI, assessment of lumbar cerebrospinal fluid if lumbar puncture is not contraindicated). In children older than 3-5 years, combinations of chemotherapy and craniospinal irradiation are applied. In younger children, brain sparing therapies avoiding irradiation can be administered in very specific constellations.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The overall survival rates are now 80% in standard risk patients, and 30-60 % in high-risk patients. Relapse occurs in nearly 75% of pediatric cases within 2 years.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive cerebellar ataxia due to a DNA repair defect characterized by progressive neurological impairment with cerebellar syndrome, oculocutaneous telangiectasia, defects in B and T cell-mediated immunity, and increased susceptibility to malignancies (mainly lymphoid neoplasms). High sensitivity to ionizing radiation limits patient treatments.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is estimated to be 1/100,000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The first manifestations usually occur at 1-2 years of age with progressive walking difficulties, balance disorders followed by slurred speech, drooling and oculomotor apraxia. Choreoathetosis may appear around 9-10 years of age and worsen progressively. Intelligence is normal although slurred speech and drooling may be interpreted as intellectual deficiency. Cutaneo-mucosal telangiectasias (especially of the conjunctivae) usually appear around 3-6 years of age, or later. Immunodeficiency causes recurrent airway infections (otitis, sinusitis, bronchitis, pneumonia) which can lead to bronchiectasis and autoimmune/inflammatory features such as granulomas (mostly of the skin but also other organs); its severity varies widely between patients, from severe lymphopenia (including severe combined immune deficiency and/or severe hypogammaglobulinemia) to no overt biological abnormality. There is a high risk of malignancy, particularly of lymphoma and leukemia (in childhood and adolescence mostly), and carcinomas (in adulthood). Patients are highly sensitive to ionizing radiation, that are forbidden. X-rays imaging must be avoided. Other features include growth delay, infertility, glucose intolerance, non-alcoholic steatohepatitis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Ataxia-telangiectasia (A-T) is caused by loss of function biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) pathogenic variants (PVs) of the ATM gene (11q22.3) which encodes a protein kinase involved in double-strand-break DNA repair, notably in the Purkinje cells of the cerebellum and cutaneous and conjunctival endothelial cells. PVs induce stop codons or directly inactivate the kinase domain; some are hypomorphic and lead to an attenuated disease with late onset symptoms and dystonia.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Early diagnosis is difficult. Quasi-constant very high serum level of alpha-fetoprotein is a useful clinical sign. Cytogenetic analysis may help confirm the diagnosis (7;14 translocations) but few laboratories still perform it. Molecular analysis of the ATM gene confirms the diagnosis. Multigene panels for ataxias or immune deficiencies have now greatly facilitated A-T diagnosis and other differential diagnoses.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes ataxia-telangiectasia-like disorder and ataxia-oculomotor apraxia types 1 and 2.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal and preimplantation genetic diagnosis are possible when pathogenic variants have been identified in a family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling should be discussed due to the severity and incurability of the disease. Siblings of an affected individual have a 25% chance of being affected. The risk for couples with one PV carrier to have an affected child is estimated at 1/600-800. PV carriers are estimated to represent 1/150-200 of the general population. Genetic testing of the spouse may be discussed.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative therapy. Management is symptomatic and involves physiotherapy, speech therapy and treatment of the infection and pulmonary complications (chronic antibiotic prophylaxis and/or human polyvalent normal Immunoglobulin long-term replacement therapy). The cells of A-T patients show increased susceptibility to ionizing radiation; X-rays, radiotherapy, and some forms of chemotherapy should be used with caution or avoided. Affected children with classical A-T are often wheelchair bound by 10-11 years old. Beta-blockers may reduce trembling and improve fine movements performance. Nicotinamide riboside brings minor improvements of some neurological symptoms. Dexamethasone administration through autologous erythrocytes has shown promising results on neurologic features in clinical trials. Gene therapy using antisense oligonucleotides is currently under trial.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is severe due to the occurrence of respiratory infections, neurodegeneration, accelerated cutaneo-mucosal ageing and an increased risk of cancer (35% of patients develop cancer by the age of 20).

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inborn error of vitamin B12 (cobalamin) metabolism characterized by megaloblastic anemia, lethargy, failure to thrive, developmental delay, intellectual deficit and seizures. There are four complementation classes of cobalamin defects (cblC, cblD, cblF and cblJ) that are responsible for methylmalonic acidemia - homocystinuria (methylmalonic acidemia - homocystinuria cblC, cblD cblF and cblJ).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Combined defect in adenosylcobalamin and methylcobalamin synthesis; Methylmalonic aciduria with homocystinuria

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence in the USA, based on the California newborn screening program, has been estimated at 1/67,000 (for the cblC form). cblC is the most frequent type (over 550 cases). To date, rare cases of cblD (6 cases), cblF (15 cases) and cblJ (3 cases) have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset of the disorder can be between early infancy to adulthood. Patients with methylmalonic acidemia with homocystinuria of all types can present with developmental delay, signs of megaloblastic anemia (pallor, fatigue, and anorexia), lethargy and seizures. In addition, patients with cblC present with acute neurological deterioration, retinal deterioration, microcephaly and severe brain abnormalities including hydrocephalus, white matter abnormalities and unusual basal ganglia lesions. Patients with cblD present with severe learning difficulties, behavioral problems and movement and gait abnormalities and patients with cblF and cblJ present with feeding difficulties, hypotonia, stomatitis, mild facial dysmorphism, cardiac malformations, and skin rashes. Patients who become symptomatic beyond infancy may present with ataxia, dementia or psychosis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Methylmalonic acidemia - homocystinuria is caused by anomalies in the synthesis of both adenosylcobalamin (AdoCbl) and of methylcobalamin (MeCbl) resulting from genetic defects in the cbl complementation classes C, D, F and J. CblC is caused by mutations in the MMACHC gene (1p36.3), cblD by mutations in the MMADHC gene (2q23.2), cblF by mutations in the LMBRD1 gene (6q13) and cblJ by mutations in the ABCD4 gene.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Measurement of organic acids and amino acids, in particular evidence of increased total plasma homocysteine (tHcy), is suggestive of the disease. Diagnosis is confirmed by complementation analysis of cultured patient fibroblasts or by identification of mutations in the MMACHC, MMADHC, LMBRD1 or ABCD4 genes.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include acquired vitamin B12 deficiency, vitamin B12-responsive methylmalonic aciduria, and homocystinuria without methylmalonic aciduria. The combination of methylmalonic aciduria, homocystinuria and normal serum cobalamin concentrations is required to distinguish patients.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible by measurement of methylmalonate and homocysteine in amniotic fluid and maternal urine at mid-trimester and by studies of cobalamin metabolism in cultured amniotic fluid cells. Molecular diagnosis is possible when the affected gene and the mutation(s) segregating in the family are known. Prenatal therapy (treating the mother with hydroxycobalamin during pregnancy) has been reported in two cases with apparent success.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: All four forms of the disorder are transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner. Genetic counseling should be provided to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Patients are treated with intramuscular injections of hydroxycobalamin, oral betaine, and folic acid. Good metabolic control and correction of hematologic problems can sometimes be achieved with this treatment but most patients continue to have signs of motor and language delay, intellectual deficit and abnormal ophthalmologic findings. Early diagnosis and treatment are important.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is better in patients with later-onset disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Non-distal trisomy 13q is a rare chromosomal anomaly disorder, resulting from the partial duplication of the proximal long arm of chromosome 13, with a highly variable phenotype principally characterized by increased polymorphonuclear leucocyte projections and persistence of fetal hemoglobin, as well as growth and developmental delay and craniofacial dysmorphism (incl. microcephaly, depressed nasal bridge, stubby nose, low-set, malformed ears, cleft lip/palate, micrognathia). Strabismus, clinodactyly and undescended testes in males may also be associated.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Non-distal duplication 13q syndrome, characterized by partial trisomy 13q, has been observed to result from a paternal reciprocal Yq;13q translocation. This specific chromosomal rearrangement leads to the duplication of a segment on the long arm of chromosome 13. [PMC1016915]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: The concomitant occurrence of 8q duplication and 13q deletion is the first to be detected by noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) to date. Through case analysis, we could provide a clinical approach to pregnant women with chromosomal abnormalities revealed by NIPT. The combination of traditional karyotype and copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq) could better locate the abnormal chromosomal region and further identify the source of fetal chromosomal abnormalities. Simultaneously, we evaluated the fetal morphology by ultrasound examination. The karyotype of the fetus was 46,XY,der(13)t(8;13)(q22;q32)mat and CNV-seq showed that there was an approximately 45.26-Mb duplication in 8q22.2-q24.3 (101040001-146 300 000) and an approximately 9.54-Mb deletion in 13q33.2-q34 (105560001-115 100 000). Prenatal ultrasound revealed the fetal structural abnormalities presented with hypoplasia of... [PMC7496467]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: The concomitant occurrence of 8q duplication and 13q deletion is the first to be detected by noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) to date. Through case analysis, we could provide a clinical approach to pregnant women with chromosomal abnormalities revealed by NIPT. The combination of traditional karyotype and copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq) could better locate the abnormal chromosomal region and further identify the source of fetal chromosomal abnormalities. Simultaneously, we evaluated the fetal morphology by ultrasound examination. The karyotype of the fetus was 46,XY,der(13)t(8;13)(q22;q32)mat and CNV-seq showed that there was an approximately 45.26-Mb duplication in 8q22.2-q24.3 (101040001-146 300 000) and an approximately 9.54-Mb deletion in 13q33.2-q34 (105560001-115 100 000). Prenatal ultrasound revealed the fetal structural abnormalities presented with hypoplasia of... [PMC7496467]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for non-distal duplication 13q syndrome involves identifying the parental origin of the chromosomal abnormality. For example, partial trisomy 13q can result from a paternal reciprocal Yq;13q translocation. In cases of chromosomal abnormalities, such as those revealed by noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT), a combination of traditional karyotyping, copy number variation sequencing (CNV-seq), and ultrasonography can be used to locate the abnormal chromosomal region and identify the source of fetal chromosomal abnormalities, including those derived from a maternal balanced translocation. This comprehensive approach is valuable for pregnant women with abnormal NIPT . [PMC7496467, PMC1016915]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare acquired myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by an elevated absolute red blood cell mass (RBCM) caused by uncontrolled red blood cell production, frequently associated with uncontrolled white blood cell and platelet production.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Acquired primary erythrocytosis; Osler-Vaquez disease; PV; Polycythemia rubra vera; Vaquez disease

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence rate is estimated to range from 1 per 38,314 to 10,000,000 people. Polycythemia vera (PV) occurs at all ages but more common > 50 years old. Prevalence is difficult to estimate, widely ranging from 1 per 2,128 to 204,081 people in different studies (1 per 4,545 people in the USA).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Symptoms are often insidious at onset and may include headache, dizziness, vertigo, tinnitus, visual disturbances, and pruritus after bathing, a ruddy complexion that manifests in the face, palms, nailbeds, mucosa and conjunctiva. Erythromelalgia is infrequent but clinically impacting and manifests with sudden and transient erythema, warmth, and pain the extremities that is highly sensitive to aspirin. Complications may include arterial (cerebrovascular, myocardial or peripheral) thrombosis, angina pectoris or intermittent claudications, or venous thromboses including deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, splanchnic thrombosis (portal vein thrombosis and Budd-Chiari syndrome), bleeding (gum and/or gastrointestinal bleeding and ecchymoses) and splenomegaly. PV may transform with time into post-polycythemia vera myelofibrosis (~10-15% of cases 10-15 years after diagnosis). It may also evolve to an acute leukemia (~3-5% of cases) called blast phase, or occasionally to a myelodysplastic syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: PV is associated in > 95% of cases with a somatic mutation (JAK2 V617F) in exon 14 of the JAK2 gene (9p24) and, less frequently, a somatic mutation in exon 12 of JAK2, resulting in the uncontrolled activation of the JAK/STAT signaling pathway (proliferation and maturation of hematopoietic cells). This leads to blood hyperviscosity due to increased RBCM impairing microcirculation, increased spleen volume, and systemic inflammation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The 2022 WHO diagnostic criteria are: hemoglobin (Hb) > 165 g/L or hematocrit (Hct) > 49% in males; Hb > 160 g/L or Hct > 48% in females; V617F or exon 12 mutation of JAK2; evidence of a myeloproliferative disorder with involvement of the 3 myeloid lineages (panmyelosis) on bone marrow biopsy. In exceptional cases without mutation of JAK2, low circulating erythropoietin (EPO) levels must be demonstrated. The ICC criteria add that in situations where plasma volume is significantly expanded, findings of a RBCM increase > 125% of expected value may surrogate the artificial decrease of Hct level caused by hemodilution.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: In the case of a JAK2 somatic mutation, differential diagnosis includes other myeloproliferative neoplasms such as essential thrombocythemia and primary myelofibrosis, particularly prefibrotic forms of myelofibrosis. Otherwise, causes of secondary erythrocytosis should be considered. Familial forms of erythrocytosis should be excluded by genetic testing of EPO-R, VHL, EGLN1, HIF2A, EPAS1, hemoglobin genes (high oxygen affinity variants), PIEZO1, or HFE. After PV and all other reactive and genetic causes of polycythemia were excluded, the diagnosis of idiopathic erythrocytosis is reached.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: JAK2 mutations are somatic; no genetic counseling is necessary. Familial forms of PV have been described but remain exceedingly rare.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Patients should be individually assessed. In patients with low-risk (=patient < 60 years old and no history of thrombosis) and/or high-risk disease (= patient > 60 years old and/or history of thrombosis), a decrease of RBCM to 45% Hct by phlebotomy reduces the rate of cardiovascular events by 4-fold. In patients with high-risk disease, cytoreduction should be considered. Any effort to reduce generic cardiovascular risk factors should be pursued. Hydroxyurea is the reference drug in the elderly; in case of intolerance or refractoriness, ruxolitinib is the second line treatment. Ropeginterferon alfa-2b is approved for PV without splenomegaly, and may be also proposed to high-risk pregnant patients. In all patients, low-dose aspirin is recommended to reduce the risk of thrombosis, unless severe contraindications exist. In cases of previous venous events, oral anticoagulants are recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: PV is a chronic disease which impacts life expectancy. Main causes of death are cardiovascular events, disease progression to post-PV myelofibrosis, transformation to blast phase, second neoplasms, and infections.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Polycythemia vera has been diagnosed during pregnancy, sometimes concurrently with noncirrhotic portal hypertension. This indicates that antenatal diagnosis of the condition is possible. [PMC11104577]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Isolated complex I deficiency is a rare inborn error of metabolism due to mutations in nuclear or mitochondrial genes encoding subunits or assembly factors of the human mitochondrial complex I (NADH: ubiquinone oxidoreductase) and is characterized by a wide range of manifestations including marked and often fatal lactic acidosis, cardiomyopathy, leukoencephalopathy, pure myopathy and hepatopathy with tubulopathy. Among the numerous clinical phenotypes observed are Leigh syndrome, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy and MELAS syndrome.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Isolated NADH-coenzyme Q reductase deficiency; Isolated NADH-ubiquinone reductase deficiency; Isolated mitochondrial respiratory chain complex I deficiency; Isolated NADH-CoQ reductase deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal recessive, Mitochondrial inheritance, X-linked dominant

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Isolated complex I deficiency is described as the most common defect of the mitochondrial respiratory chain and the most common biochemical phenotype observed in individuals with mitochondrial disease, also being a common cause of mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation disease. It is an autosomal recessive disorder. While the overall condition is common among mitochondrial diseases, specific mutations, such as those in NDUFAF5, are rare, with only a few families reported. Genetic diversity includes founder variants in South Asian populations (NDUFV1), Ashkenazi founder mutations, and specific variants observed in individuals of Taiwanese descent and Caucasian populations, indicating population-specific genetic patterns. [PMC12288937, PMC7707637, PMC6189076, PMC5005451, PMC1236688]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of complex I deficiency is feasible. A biochemical diagnosis can be established on cultured amniocytes from a pregnancy. This can be further confirmed by identifying disease-causing mutations, such as in the NDUFS3 gene, within these amniotic cells. This method has been successfully utilized to confirm the diagnosis in subsequent pregnancies. [PMC1757256]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for isolated complex I deficiency, particularly in severe neonatal presentations, primarily involves intensive supportive care. This includes interventions such as tracheal intubation, mechanical ventilation, respiratory support, and antishock therapy to address critical conditions like respiratory and circulatory failure, and pulmonary hypertension. Some patients also received broad-spectrum antibiotics, oral coenzyme Q10, multivitamins, and idebenone. Despite these comprehensive interventions, the reported cases describe progressive deterioration and rapid fatality, indicating the severe and often lethal nature of the disease in these contexts. [PMC9410648, PMC9259100]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Diaphyseal medullary stenosis with malignant fibrous histiocytoma is a very rare autosomal dominant bone dysplasia/cancer syndrome characterized clinically by bone infarctions, cortical growth abnormalities, pathological fractures, and development of bone sarcoma (malignant fibrous histiocytoma).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Bone dysplasia-medullary fibrosarcoma syndrome; Diaphyseal medullary stenosis-malignant fibrous histiocytoma syndrome; Hardcastle syndrome

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare otorhinolaryngologic disease characterized by adult-onset progressive enophthalmos due to collapse of some or all of the maxillary sinus walls and remodeling of the orbital floor.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Imploding antrum syndrome; CMA grade 3; Chronic maxillary atelectasis grade III

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Its prevalence is unknown but around 550 cases have been reported in the literature so far. Patients typically present at 30-60 years old, with no sex predilection.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The progressive enophthalmos may occasionally be associated with hypoglobus, diplopia, headache, and facial pressure/pain. Patients sometimes report a history of remote episodes of sinusitis. The syndrome may be idiopathic or occur following a bony orbital decompression resulting from Graves' ophthalmopathy or orbital floor fracture.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The underlying mechanism involves obstruction of the ostiomeatal complex followed by development of hypoventilation and negative maxillary sinus pressure. This negative pressure subsequently collapses the sinus and causes inward bowing of the ipsilateral orbital floor.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made by facial computerized tomography (CT) scanning with coronal reconstructions, showing a collapse of the maxillary sinus wall(s) and opacification of the sinus cavity. The ostium of the maxillary sinus is occluded due to lateral retraction of the uncinate process and apposition against the inferomedial orbital wall. The middle meatus is enlarged.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis should include orbital floor 'blow-out' fractures, soft tissue atrophy, primary or secondary malignancy, orbital venous malformations, bone growth arrest following radiation therapy, congenital etiologies (minor forms of hemifacial microsomia, plagiocephaly, microphthalmos etc.) and pseudoenophthalmos (unilateral blepharoptosis, Horner syndrome, contralateral exophthalmos, contralateral high myopia and contralateral eyelid retraction).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Surgery is the only treatment. Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) is performed to open the ostiomeatal complex, with complete uncinectomy, and prevent development of negative maxillary pressure. Residual ophthalmic symptoms (e.g., enophthalmos) may be addressed by reconstructing the orbital floor in conjunction or in discontinuity with FESS.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Improvement in clinical symptoms, including enophthalmos and hypoglobus, is seen in a majority of patients.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: While Silent Sinus Syndrome is often considered an acquired condition, as illustrated by cases where maxillary sinuses were previously normal, recent observations suggest a more complex etiology. Familial clustering of chronic maxillary atelectasis and Silent Sinus Syndrome has been reported in three male family members, indicating a possible genetic or hereditary component to its development. This familial aspect is not commonly explored in the existing literature, suggesting that while some cases may be acquired, a predisposition or inherited factor might play a role in others. [PMC11796483, PMC7976156]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: VIPoma is an extremely rare type of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that secretes vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) leading to the manifestations of watery diarrhea, hypokalemia and achlorhydia or hypochhlorhydia (known as WDHA syndrome).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Diarrheogenic islet cell tumor; Pancreatic cholera; VIP-secreting tumor; Verner-Morrison syndrome; WDHA syndrome; Watery diarrhea-hypokalemia-achlorhydria syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence of VIPoma in the general population is of less than 1/10,000,000 individuals per year. There is a slight female predominance.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The median age of diagnosis is the fifth decade of life but VIPoma can occur at any age. The most common presentation includes chronic watery diarrhea (described as >3L/day, odorless, blood and mucus free and unaffected by fasting), hypokalemia (manifesting with muscle weakness, abdominal muscle cramps, or respiratory depression), and various dietary deficiencies (iron and B12 deficiency) caused by achlorhydia/hypochlorhydia. Other less common manifestations include nausea, vomiting, weight loss, bloating, indigestion, skin rash and facial flushing, backache and lethargy. In 60-80% of cases, metastasis has occurred at the time of diagnosis as symptoms usually only occur once a tumor has reached a certain size. The most common site of metastasis is liver but lung, lymph node and kidney involvement have also been reported. If untreated, prolonged dehydration can lead to renal failure and cardiac arrest. In rare cases, VIPomas are non-functional.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Most cases are sporadic but VIPomas can also occur in association with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1). VIPomas are, in 90% of cases, located in the pancreas (mainly in the body and tail) and are usually solitary with a diameter ranging from 1-7cm. The remainder (10%) originate from non-pancreatic tissue such as the colon, liver and neural crest-derived tissues (mainly pediatric cases). These tumors secrete VIP, which stimulates cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) production in the intestine, causing increased water and electrolyte secretion into the lumen. VIP also has an inhibitory effect on gastric mucosa parietal cells leading to decreased gastric acid production.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical, laboratory and imaging findings. Typical blood laboratory findings include elevated VIP levels (>200pg/mL is diagnostic), hypokalemia, hypochlorhydia or achlorhydia, hyperglycemia, hypercalcemia and non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Computed tomography (CT) and octreotide scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and endoscopic ultrasound can be used to localize neoplasms, confirming diagnosis. Immunohistochemically, VIPomas stain positively for VIP, synaptophysin, chromagranin A, somatostatin, neuron specific enolase and cytokeratin.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include all other causes of chronic diarrhea such as malabsorption syndrome, Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis, microscopic colitis, and gastrointestinal infections.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Initial treatment focuses on replacing the massive loss of fluids, restoring electrolyte levels and reversing acidosis. Some patients may require intravenous fluid and potassium replacement in a hospital setting. Octreotide (a somatostatin analogue) is successful in controlling diarrhea and reducing VIP hormone levels. Loperamide may also be used. Surgical resection is the standard treatment in those with primary or metastatic VIPoma. Unresectable metastatic disease has been treated with chemotherapy (docorubicin/streptozocin regimen) in some cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable and is dependent on many factors. In those with benign, surgically resectable tumors, the reported 5-year survival rate is almost 95%.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: VIPomas can be associated with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) syndrome. MEN1 is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by MEN1 gene mutations. Genetic testing can identify these mutations. For patients diagnosed with MEN1, genetic testing for family members is recommended to identify mutation carriers, as this can improve the prognosis for affected individuals. [PMC11406473, PMC4654027]

DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: A hybrid nerve sheath tumor is a biphasic, benign neoplasm of peripheral nerve sheaths, consisting of combinations of neurofibroma, schwannoma, or perineurioma. These tumors were recognized only recently, in 2013; they commonly occur sporadically but rarely with syndromic associations, such as neurofibromatosis syndrome, Carney complex, and schwannomatosis. With an occurrence of 1 in every 33,000 individuals, neurofibromatosis type 2 is a rare autosomal dominant condition characterized by bilateral vestibular schwannomas. Herein a serendipitous occurrence of a hybrid nerve sheath tumor with neurofibromatosis type 2 syndrome, with an emphasis on its diagnostic mimics.
