Neurological examination revealed increased motor... [PMC11866880, PMC11999759, PMC12247263, PMC11091025, PMC8482618]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Surgical excision is the primary treatment for perineuriomas. For benign forms, including extraneural, intraneural, soft tissue, pseudolipoblastic, and renal perineuriomas, simple or complete surgical resection is often curative, with recurrence being rare and prognosis generally good with early intervention. Intraneural perineuriomas may be managed with interfascicular neurolysis and targeted fascicular biopsy under electrophysiological monitoring, with decompression and neurolysis potentially improving neurological deficits, supported by rehabilitation. In malignant cases, resection is the primary option, though recurrence is common, necessitating further effective treatments for advanced disease; radiotherapy has been administered for dissemination, and NF2 mutations are identified as a potential therapeutic target. Accurate diagnosis is crucial to avoid overtreatment, as overall therapy remains variable. Multidisciplinary consultation is also noted in specific clinical scenarios. [PMC11866880, PMC11999759, PMC11933660, PMC10905452, PMC11091025]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Perineuriomas are generally benign tumors, with simple excision often curative and recurrence being rare or not observed in many reported cases, including soft tissue, pseudolipoblastic, and some hybrid types. Neurological deficits in intraneural perineuriomas may improve with surgical intervention. However, malignant perineurioma is a rare, aggressive counterpart that often recurs after resection, with one case reporting death from disease progression within six months. While most hybrid peripheral nerve sheath tumors are benign, rare local recurrence and malignant transformation have been reported. Limited follow-up data restricts a full understanding of recurrence rates for gastrointestinal tract perineuriomas. [PMC11999759, PMC11991822, PMC11091025, PMC11736673, PMC11573059]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Hereditary inclusion body myopathy-joint contractures-ophthalmoplegia syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic neuromuscular disease characterized by early onset of proximal or generalized muscle weakness, external ophthalmoplegia with or without ptosis, and joint contractures. Hypotonia, neonatal respiratory distress necessitating ventilation, and severe dysphagia have also been reported. The disease is of variable severity and non- or slowly progressive. Patients typically remain ambulatory. Muscle biopsy may show predominance of type 1 fibers, marked variability in fiber size, increased internal nuclei, and proliferation of perimysial and endomysial connective tissue.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): HIBM3; Hereditary inclusion body myopathy type 3; IBM3; Inclusion body myopathy type 3

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Hereditary inclusion body myopathy-joint contractures-ophthalmoplegia syndrome, caused by MYH2 mutations, is a rare neuromuscular disease. It exhibits both autosomal dominant and recessive inheritance patterns. While a single dominant missense mutation has been reported in one family, additional recessive mutations have been identified in a limited number of patients, such as five patients with four recessive mutations or seven patients across five families. The disease can affect multiple generations within a family, and de novo mutations have also been observed. Overall, it is considered a very rare disease, emphasizing the need for increased awareness. [PMC10023425, PMC8082902, PMC7507101, PMC6466613, PMC4023224]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hereditary inclusion body myopathy-joint contractures-ophthalmoplegia syndrome, caused by MYH2 mutations, presents with variable clinical features and inheritance patterns, including autosomal dominant and recessive forms. Dominant forms are typically characterized by progressive proximal limb weakness, ophthalmoplegia, and congenital joint contractures, with muscle biopsies often showing rimmed vacuoles and inclusions. Recessive forms can manifest as early-onset, non-progressive, mild-to-moderate diffuse weakness and ophthalmoplegia, with muscle biopsies revealing small or absent type 2A muscle fibers. However, some recessive cases may mimic dominant phenotypes with progressive proximal weakness and rimmed vacuoles. Other reported features include ptosis, dysphagia, respiratory distress, and late-pediatric onset. Pathological findings can also include myofilamentous tangles, nemaline rods, ring fibers, and disorganized myofibrils. [PMC10023425, PMC8082902, PMC7507101, PMC6466613, PMC4023224]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hereditary inclusion body myopathy-joint contractures-ophthalmoplegia syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the MYH2 gene, which encodes the skeletal muscle myosin heavy chain IIA (MyHC-IIA) isoform, expressed in fast type 2A muscle fibers. Both autosomal dominant and recessive inheritance patterns have been described, with mutations including splice-site, missense, truncating, and frame-shift variants. These mutations can lead to diverse pathological consequences, such as altered splicing, protein truncation, or changes in the catalytic motor head relay loop, potentially influencing myofibril disorganization. A hallmark pathological feature is the loss, atrophy, or reduction in the number and size of type 2A muscle fibers, sometimes with reduced or absent MyHC IIa transcript and protein expression. [PMC10023425, PMC8082902, PMC7507101, PMC6466613, PMC4023224]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of MYH2-associated myopathy, also known as hereditary inclusion body myopathy-joint contractures-ophthalmoplegia syndrome, integrates clinical findings, muscle biopsy, and genetic analysis. Clinically, patients present with ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, and progressive proximal muscle weakness, which can be accompanied by congenital joint contractures or severe early-onset symptoms like dysphagia. Muscle biopsy is a key diagnostic tool, consistently showing loss, atrophy, or absence of type 2A muscle fibers. Additional histopathological features may include rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, myofilamentous tangles, nemaline rods, and disorganized myofibrils, sometimes visualized by electron microscopy. Reduced or absent expression of MyHC IIa transcript and protein can also be observed. Genetic testing, utilizing such as next-generation sequencing, whole exome sequencing, and Sanger sequencing, identifies pathogenic MYH2 variants, often confirmed by segregation analysis, providing a definitive diagnosis. Muscle imaging may also contribute to the diagnostic process. [PMC10023425, PMC8082902, PMC7507101, PMC6466613, PMC4023224]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Hereditary inclusion body myopathy-joint contractures-ophthalmoplegia syndrome, initially described as hereditary inclusion body myopathy 3, is associated with dominant MYH2 mutations. These typically present with ophthalmoplegia, progressive proximal limb weakness, and often congenital joint contractures, with muscle biopsies revealing rimmed vacuoles, inclusions, and reduced type 2A fibers. Differential diagnosis includes recessive MYH2 myopathies, which usually manifest as early-onset, non-progressive weakness and ophthalmoplegia, characterized by a near or complete absence of type 2A fibers without vacuoles. However, some recessive MYH2 mutations can mimic the dominant phenotype, presenting with progressive proximal weakness and rimmed vacuoles. The clinical and pathological spectrum of MYH2 myopathies is expanding, with some dominant forms lacking classic features and novel pathological findings like nemaline rods being reported. [PMC10023425, PMC8082902, PMC7507101, PMC6466613, PMC4023224]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Hereditary inclusion body myopathy-joint contractures-ophthalmoplegia syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in the MYH2 gene and can be inherited in both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive patterns. Dominant forms typically present with progressive proximal weakness, ophthalmoplegia, and sometimes congenital contractures, often with rimmed vacuoles and type 2A fiber abnormalities on biopsy. Recessive forms are frequently characterized by early-onset, non-progressive, diffuse weakness and ophthalmoplegia, with a near or complete absence of type 2A fibers. However, the clinical and pathological spectrum is broad, with significant overlap; recessive genotypes can manifest phenotypes consistent with dominant forms, and dominant cases may lack classic features. De novo mutations have also been reported, expanding the known genetic and clinical findings. [PMC10023425, PMC8082902, PMC7507101, PMC6466613, PMC4023224]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for hereditary inclusion body myopathy-joint contractures-ophthalmoplegia syndrome varies depending on the inheritance pattern. Dominantly inherited forms typically manifest as a slowly progressive myopathy, often with progressive proximal limb weakness and ophthalmoplegia. In contrast, recessively inherited forms are generally characterized by early-onset, mild-to-moderate, and non-progressive diffuse weakness and ophthalmoplegia. However, some recessive MYH2 mutations can lead to a progressive phenotype that mimics dominant forms, with childhood-onset ophthalmoplegia and progressive proximal muscle weakness. Additionally, severe early-onset presentations, including dysphagia and respiratory distress, have been reported with de novo mutations. [PMC10023425, PMC7507101, PMC6466613, PMC4023224, PMC3639366]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hypotrichosis with juvenile macular degeneration (HJMD) is a very rare syndrome characterized by sparse and short hair from birth followed by progressive macular degeneration leading to blindness.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): HJMD; Hypotrichosis with juvenile macular dystrophy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown but approximately 50 patients have been described since the first characterization of the syndrome in 1935.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: HJMD patients present with short and sparse scalp hair since birth or first months of life, with no subsequent growth during life. A decade later, during the first to third decades of life, visual acuity decreases because of progressive macular degeneration, leading in many cases to blindness between the second and fourth decades of life. HJMD is sometimes associated with limb anomalies, in which case it is termed Ectodermal dysplasia, Ectrodactyly, and Macular dystrophy (EEM). Many patients display fair hair complexion as compared with their healthy siblings. The hair phenotype does not improve significantly with age, even though diffuse alopecia in infancy can evolve towards short and sparse hair in puberty.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: HJMD is caused by mutations in the CDH3 gene (16q22.1), encoding P-cadherin. P-cadherin is part of adherens junctions in various epithelia including the hair follicular epithelium. Moreover, P-cadherin is expressed in the retinal pigment epithelium.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the combined occurrence of hypotrichosis with characteristic degenerative changes and pigmentary abnormalities of the macula on fundoscopy. Where available, electrophysiologic studies can confirm abnormal function of the posterior pole. Additional tests of lesser diagnostic value include (1) histopathologic examination of scalp biopsies, revealing mostly vellus and catagen hair follicles with significantly reduced number of terminal hair follicles; (2) light microscopy and scanning electron microscopy of hair which can demonstrate various structural abnormalities including pseudomonilethrix, pili torti, longitudinal ridging, scaling and folding of the hair shaft.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes EEM syndrome, also caused by CDH3 mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: DNA-based prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling are available provided the underlying mutation is known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: As HJMD is an autosomal recessive disease, risk of recurrence is 25%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: No curative or palliative options exist for HJMD. However, educational measures can be implemented and psychological support should be provided once HJMD is diagnosed.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The most severe complication of HJMD is progressive macular degeneration leading to blindness between the second and fourth decades of life. Life expectancy is normal but quality of life can be reduced because of blindness and psychological impact due to the hair phenotype.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hemoglobin C disease (HbC) is a hemoglobinopathy characterized by production of abnormal variant hemoglobin known as hemoglobin C, with no or mild clinical manifestations (hemolytic anemia).

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: A 17-year-old male presented with acute hemolysis with stomatocytosis, elevated mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC), and osmotic gradient ektacytometry consistent with marked erythrocyte dehydration. Erythrocytes from both parents also demonstrated evidence of dehydration with elevated MCHC and abnormal ektacytometry, but neither to the degree of the patient. Genetic studies revealed the patient had hereditary xerocytosis (HX) due to a novel PIEZO1 mutation inherited from his mother and hemoglobin C (HbC) trait inherited from his father. HbC trait accentuated the erythrocyte dehydration of HX. Coinheritance of interrelated disorders and/or modifier alleles should be considered whenever severe erythrocyte dehydration is observed. Sickle cell nephropathy is a common complication in patients with sickle cell hemoglobinopathies. In these disorders, polymerization of mutated... [PMC5858911, PMC4849830, PMC1017523, PMC1042661]

In a patient presenting with acute hemolysis and co-inheritance of hereditary xerocytosis, HbC trait was associated with stomatocytosis, elevated mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration (MCHC), and osmotic gradient ektacytometry findings indicative of marked erythrocyte dehydration. These observations suggest that HbC trait can accentuate erythrocyte dehydration, which may be considered when severe erythrocyte dehydration is observed. [PMC5858911]

Monitoring of certain parameters such as venous and arterial oxygen content, hematocrit, acid base homeostasis, and body temperature are required for a superior outcome. Furthermore, perioperative exchange transfusion has a positive effect on the outcome of surgery and on the survival of patients undergoing heart surgery. DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by diffuse cartilage calcification, brachytelephalangism, peripheral pulmonary artery stenoses and facial dysmorphism. Vascular calcification has been reported in some cases.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: More than 40 cases have been reported in the literature so far, with the majority of patients being diagnosed during childhood or earlier.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The abnormal calcification principally involves the cartilage of the ears, nose, larynx and the tracheobronchial tree. Epiphyseal stippling of the long bones and calcification of the spinal column vertebrae have also been reported. The facial dysmorphism is characterized by maxillary and midface hypoplasia (broad and depressed nasal bridge with small alae nasi). Other associated features may include hearing loss and recurrent otitis and/or sinusitis, mild intellectual deficit, seizures/epilepsy, frequent respiratory infections, nasal speech and short stature. Patients may show vascular calcification, cerebral calcification, moyamoya and arterial stenosis. Additional findings of white matter anomalies, encephalomalacia, optic nerve atrophy, and lax and doughy skin with prominent skin folds were reported in one affected family.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the matrix Gla protein (MGP, located at 12p13.1-p12.3).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is usually suspected on the basis of the clinical presentation and radiographic examination, with abnormal cartilage calcification and brachytelephalangism being the cardinal signs of the syndrome. The diagnosis can be confirmed by gene mutation analysis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The principle differential diagnosis is X-linked recessive chondrodysplasia punctata, but abnormal calcification has also been observed in children with warfarin embryopathy and in those with combined vitamin K-dependent coagulation factor deficiency.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible where the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic and may involve angiographic dilatation for peripheral pulmonary artery stenosis and bronchodilating agents to relieve dyspnea and wheezing.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis for most patients is good, but life expectancy depends on the extent of the pulmonary involvement.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cholestasis-lymphedema syndrome is a rare genetic disorder characterized by neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis, often lessening and becoming intermittent with age, and severe chronic lymphedema which mainly affects the lower limbs. Patients often present with fat malabsorption leading to failure to thrive, fat soluble vitamin deficiency with bleeding, rickets, and neuropathy. In 25% of cases, cirrhosis occurs during childhood or later in life.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Cholestasis-lymphedema syndrome, also known as Aagenaes syndrome, has been observed with parent-child transmission, as evidenced by a mother and daughter presenting with features of the condition. While many previous cases have been associated with Norwegian ancestry and recessive inheritance, this specific pedigree suggests a dominant inheritance pattern and occurred in individuals without Norwegian ancestry. This indicates variability in its genetic transmission and ethnic distribution. [PMC1051095]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: a mother and daughter with features of Aagenaes syndrome. Unlike most previous cases, there is no Norwegian ancestry and the pedigree favours dominant rather than recessive inheritance. [PMC1051095]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiology of cholestasis-lymphedema syndrome involves a genetic component, with parent-child transmission observed. A specific case described a mother and daughter presenting with features of the syndrome. In this instance, the pedigree analysis suggested a dominant inheritance pattern, which differed from most previous cases. Furthermore, this particular family did not have Norwegian ancestry. [PMC1051095]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Parent-child transmission of cholestasis-lymphedema syndrome has been observed, with a mother and daughter presenting with features of the condition. The pedigree in such cases favors dominant rather than recessive inheritance. This suggests that the syndrome can be passed directly from an affected parent to their child. [PMC1051095]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A group of inherited epidermolysis bullosa characterized by involvement of the skin and mucous membranes, and is defined by the formation of blistering lesions between the epidermis and the dermis at the lamina lucida level of the cutaneous basement membrane zone and by healing of lesions with atrophy and/or exuberant granulation tissue formation.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Junctional epidermolysis bullosa (JEB) is the less common, but frequently early lethal form of EB. Point prevalence is generally below 1/1,000,000 worldwide except in the Netherlands where it is estimated at 1/475,000. Prevalence at birth ranges from 1/110,000-455,000 worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset is usually at birth with the exception of late-onset JEB. Several JEB subtypes have been described based on clinical features. All subtypes are characterized by the presence of enamel hypoplasia manifesting as localized or more extensive thimble-like pitting of some or all of the tooth surfaces. Blistering is usually associated with atrophic scarring or with exuberant granulation tissue formation and nail dystrophy. Additional skin findings may include congenital aplasia cutis and progressive hair loss. Mucosal involvement is constant, although of variable severity, and can affect the gastrointestinal, respiratory and genitourinary tracts and the eyes. Pyloric atresia is the hallmark of the JEB with pyloric atresia subtype. JEB is divided in the following subtypes: severe JEB, intermediate JEB, localized JEB, JEB with pyloric atresia (JEB-PA), JEB inversa, late-onset JEB, laryngo-onycho-cutaneous syndrome (LOC) syndrome and JEB with interstitial lung disease and nephrotic syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: JEB is caused by mutations in various genes, including COL17A1 (10q25.1), ITGA6 (2q31.1), ITGB4 (17q25.1), LAMA3 (18q11.2), LAMB3 (1q32.2), LAMC2 (1q25.3) and ITGA3 (17q21.33).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on determination of the level within which blisters develop on skin biopsy samples following minor traction to the skin. The recommended techniques are immunofluorescence antigen mapping and transmission electron microscopy. In JEB, the blister cleavage plane is localized within the lamina lucida of the cutaneous basement membrane zone. Subtypes are then defined on the basis of immunofluorescence and electron microscopic findings, and clinical presentation. Genetic testing should be always performed, as it is necessary for antenatal diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Diagnosis is usually straightforward with little need for extensive differential diagnosis. However, in the neonatal period, in utero Herpes simplex infection may need to be considered, especially if there is no family history of blistering disease or if the clinical findings are very atypical for EB. The differential diagnosis in neonates may include inherited or acquired skin disorders with a similar presentation.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis should always be offered to families at risk of having a child with severe JEB.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Parents of a child with JEB are obligate carriers of the pathogenic variants. For each pregnancy of the parents, the risk of having an affected child is 25%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Patients affected by most JEB forms require hospitalization in neonatal intensive care because of the severity skin lesions and extracutaneous manifestations, and should be monitored and treated for water-electrolyte balance, failure to thrive, anemia, infectious and respiratory complications, etc. Pain management is also extremely important in these patients and often requires opioids. Subsequently, patient management should involve a multidisciplinary team, to ensure coordinated care. Skin management is based on the avoidance of blistering by meticulous protective padding of the skin, avoidance of trauma in daily life, lancing and draining of new blisters, and prevention of secondary infection by careful wound care.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Patients with JEB, particularly those with severe subtypes (severe JEB, JEB-PA and JEB with interstitial lung disease and nephrotic syndrome) are at major risk of death during the first few years of life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease-deafness-intellectual disability syndrome is a rare demyelinating hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy characterized by early-onset, slowly progressive, distal muscular weakness and atrophy with no sensory impairment, congenital sensorineural deafness and mild intellectual disability (with absence of normal speech development). The absence of large myelinated fibers on sural nerve biopsy is equally characteristic of the disease.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with deafness, intellectual disability and absent sensory large myelinated fibers; Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease-hearing loss-intellectual disability syndrome; Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with hearing loss, intellectual disability and absent sensory large myelinated fibers; CMT-deafness-intellectual disability syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Cowchock syndrome (CMTX4) is a slowly progressive X-linked recessive disorder with axonal neuropathy, deafness, and cognitive impairment. The disease locus was previously mapped to an 11 cM region at chromosome X: q24-q26. Exome sequencing of an affected individual from the originally described family identified a missense change c.1478A>T (p.Glu493Val) in AIFM1, the gene encoding apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF) mitochondrion-associated 1. The change is at a highly conserved residue and cosegregated with the phenotype in the family. AIF is an FAD-dependent NADH oxidase that is imported into mitochondria. With apoptotic insults, a N-terminal transmembrane linker is cleaved off, producing a soluble fragment that is released into the cytosol and then transported into the nucleus, where it triggers caspase-independent apoptosis. Another AIFM1 mutation that predicts p.Arg201del has recently... [PMC3516602]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: A 9-yr 8-mo-old right-handed female presented with a history of gait difficulties, which first became apparent at age 9 mo of age, along with slurred speech and hand tremors while holding a tray. Her past medical history was significant for global developmental delay, and she was attending fourth grade special education classes. On examination, she had an ataxic gait, dysarthria, absent deep tendon reflexes, and flexor plantar responses. There were no signs of optic atrophy or hearing loss. Nerve conduction studies were consistent with an axonal neuropathy. A fascicular sural nerve biopsy showed a marked decrease of myelinated fibers larger than 6 µm in diameter as compared with an age-matched control. By electron microscopy, clusters of degenerating axonal mitochondria in both myelinated and unmyelinated fibers were frequently found. Whole-exome sequencing revealed a heterozygous... [PMC7304361, PMC3516602]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease-deafness-intellectual disability syndrome, also known as Cowchock syndrome (CMTX4), is an X-linked recessive disorder. It is caused by mutations in the AIFM1 gene, which encodes apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF) mitochondrion-associated 1. A specific missense change, c.1478A>T (p.Glu493Val), has been identified in affected individuals. This mutation alters the redox properties of the AIF protein, leading to increased cell death via apoptosis, without affecting the activity of the respiratory chain complexes. Other AIFM1 mutations have been linked to mitochondrial encephalomyopathy by impairing oxidative phosphorylation, expanding the spectrum of AIF-related diseases. [PMC3516602]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves a combination of clinical evaluation, neurophysiological studies, and genetic testing. Clinical examination may reveal an ataxic gait, dysarthria, absent deep tendon reflexes, and flexor plantar responses, alongside global developmental delay, cognitive impairment, and deafness. Nerve conduction studies are consistent with an axonal neuropathy. A fascicular sural nerve biopsy can show a decrease in myelinated fibers and degenerating axonal mitochondria. Definitive diagnosis often relies on genetic testing, such as whole-exome sequencing, to identify pathogenic variants in genes like MFN2 (e.g., c.314C > T (p.Thr105Met)) or AIFM1 (e.g., c.1478A>T (p.Glu493Val)), which cosegregate with the phenotype. [PMC7304361, PMC3516602]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Cowchock syndrome (CMTX4) is an important differential diagnosis, as it presents as a slowly progressive X-linked recessive disorder characterized by axonal neuropathy, deafness, and cognitive impairment. This syndrome is associated with mutations in AIFM1, the gene encoding apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF) mitochondrion-associated 1. While other AIFM1 mutations can cause severe mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, the specific mutation linked to Cowchock syndrome alters the redox properties of the AIF protein and increases cell death via apoptosis. [PMC3516602]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease-deafness-intellectual disability syndrome can be associated with mutations in different genes, influencing inheritance patterns. Cowchock syndrome (CMTX4), characterized by axonal neuropathy, deafness, and cognitive impairment, is an X-linked recessive disorder linked to mutations in AIFM1, with specific variants like c.1478A>T (p.Glu493Val) cosegregating with the phenotype in affected families. Separately, MFN2 variants, typically associated with autosomal dominant Charcot-Marie-Tooth Type 2A2A, can also present with intellectual disability and auditory impairment, alongside other variable phenotypes such as optic atrophy or spinal atrophy. Genetic testing for these genes can help determine the specific genetic cause and inform family risk assessment. [PMC7304361, PMC3516602]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease-deafness-intellectual disability syndrome, also known as Cowchock syndrome (CMTX4), is characterized as a slowly progressive X-linked recessive disorder. The condition involves axonal neuropathy, deafness, and cognitive impairment, which are the features that progress over time. [PMC3516602]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal trisomy 1p36 is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from the partial duplication of the short arm of chromosome 1, characterized by borderline to mild intellectual disability, mild developmental delay, metopic craniosynostosis and mild craniofacial dysmorphism (incl. slopping forehead, bitemporal narrowing, blepharophimosis). Other associated abnormalities may include growth retardation, microcephaly, large hands, syndactyly, supernumerary ribs, rectal stenosis and/or anterior displacement of anus. Congenital heart malformations (e.g. atrial septal defect, patent ductus arteriosus) have also been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Distal duplication 1p36 syndrome, characterized by 1p36 microduplications, is considered a rare event. In contrast, chromosome 1p36 deletion syndrome is one of the most common terminal subtelomeric microdeletion syndromes. The smallest reported case of 1p36 duplication to date involved a patient presenting with intellectual disability, microcephaly, epilepsy, and perisylvian polymicrogyria. [PMC7784979]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Distal 1p36 microduplications are rare chromosomal events. In one reported case, a patient with the smallest 1p36 duplication presented with intellectual disability, microcephaly, epilepsy, and perisylvian polymicrogyria. Polymicrogyria is a brain malformation phenotype that is also frequently present in patients with 1p36 monosomy. [PMC7784979]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal duplication 1p36 syndrome is a rare condition caused by 1p36 microduplications. The smallest reported case involved an intrachromosomal segment duplicated in mirror, which contained and disrupted the enolase 1 (ENO1) and RERE genes. Gene expression analysis in patient cells revealed reduced expression, mimicking haploinsufficiency. Experimental inactivation of Eno1 in rats resulted in brain development defects. Consequently, ENO1 is considered the most likely candidate gene contributing to the brain malformation phenotype observed in affected individuals. [PMC7784979]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Distal duplication 1p36 syndrome can be identified through various genetic diagnostic . High-resolution array comparative genomic hybridization (arrayCGH) has been utilized to detect 1p36 microduplications. Copy number analysis and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) are also employed, for instance, to reveal an extra copy of a gene inserted into chromosome 1p36. Chromosomal microarray analysis (CMA) is highly recommended for the evaluation of genetic disorders, including clinically significant copy number variants, and conventional karyotyping can identify structural chromosomal abnormalities. [PMC8577530, PMC7784979, PMC4557901]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Distal duplication 1p36 syndrome should be differentiated from chromosome 1p36 deletion syndrome, which is a more common subtelomeric microdeletion syndrome. While 1p36 deletion is associated with polymicrogyria and fetal akinesia, 1p36 duplication can also present with polymicrogyria, intellectual disability, microcephaly, and epilepsy. Additionally, other partial trisomies of chromosome 1, such as trisomy 1q syndrome, may present with multiple malformations, including brain anomalies, and could involve complex rearrangements affecting the 1p36 region. [PMC7784979, PMC6791227, PMC1050918]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of chromosomal aberrations involving 1p36 has been reported. In one case, a de novo partial trisomy 1q, with the trisomic segment 1q32-qter duplicated and an inverted insertion at 1p36.3, was initially detected at amniocentesis. This aberration was subsequently confirmed and further defined using GTG banding, chromosome microdissection, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) on postnatal blood samples. The parents in this case had normal karyotypes. [PMC1050918]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease (PMD) is an X-linked dysmyelinating disorder characterized by nystagmus, hypotonia, ataxia, progressive spasticity, and cognitive decline. PMD classically from a duplication of a genomic segment encompassing the entire PLP1 gene. Since the PLP1 gene is located in Xq22, PMD affects mostly boys. and Here the case of a girl with typical PMD. Copy number analysis of the PLP1 locus revealed a duplication of the entire gene and FISH analysis showed that the extra copy of the PLP1 gene was actually inserted in chromosome 1p36. This insertion of an additional copy of PLP1 in an autosome led to a functional duplication irrespective of the X-inactivation pattern. Subsequent overexpression of PLP1 was the cause of the PMD phenotype observed in this girl. Further sequencing of the breakpoint junction revealed a microhomology and thus suggested a replication based... [PMC4557901, PMC1050918]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma is a rare, indolent B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma characterized by abnormal clonal proliferation of mature B-lymphocytes with involvement in the spleen, bone marrow and, frequently, the blood. It usually presents with splenomegaly, lymphocytosis, anemia and/or thrombocytopenia. Hepatitis C virus and autoimmune manifestations, such as autoimmune hemolytic anemia and autoimmune thrombocytopenia, could be associated.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Splenic marginal zone lymphoma (SMZL) is a rare non-Hodgkin lymphoma, accounting for only 1-2.7% of all lymphomas, with SMZL presenting with monoclonal IgG being even rarer. Chronic antigenic stimulation is frequently implicated in its pathogenesis. While chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is often observed in SMZL patients in some geographical regions, a study in Turkey found a higher association with hepatitis B virus (HBV) positivity, suggesting it as a possible risk factor in that population. Germline disruptive variants in Protection of Telomeres 1 (POT1) have also been identified as a potential predisposing factor. The median age of patients in one cohort was 60 years, with a range of 35-87 years. [PMC10861014, PMC9028718, PMC8579832, PMC7532117, PMC7236417]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Translocations involving immunoglobin (IG) are common in B-cell neoplasms. These IG translocations lead to the disposition of the enhancer or promoter of an IG locus, typically IGH, to a proto-oncogene, resulting in the elevated expression of the cancer gene. IG fusions play an important role in the diagnosis, prognostication, and therapy selection of B-cell lymphomas. A t(14;22)(q32;q11) translocation involving IGH and IGL is rare in lymphomas. herein clinicopathological characteristics, response to treatment, and outcomes of a first splenic marginal zone lymphoma case with a t(14;22)(q32;q11) translocation involving IGH and IGL treated with rituximab, ibrutinib, and obinutuzumab. Studies of additional cases are needed to elucidate the potential role of the t(14;22) translocation in lymphomagenesis and prognostication. In indolent lymphomas, histological transformation (HT) often in a... [PMC12031878, PMC11971140, PMC10861014, PMC10983820, PMC9028718]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic skin disease belonging to the Mendelian Disorders of Cornification (MeDOC) and characterized by generalized hyperkeratosis and scaling of the skin. The condition is rather mild.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): RXLI; Steroid sulfatase deficiency; X-linked ichthyosis; XLI

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: RXLI affects almost exclusively males. It is the second most common type of ichthyosis with an estimated prevalence of 1/2,000 to 1/6,000 males.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset may occur within the first days of life with the development of generalized non-erythematous, polygonal, loosely adherent scales. These scales later evolve into grayish or blackish adherent scales that are pronounced on the trunk, the extensor and flexor sites of the extremities, and the neck (giving the ''dirty-neck'' appearance). Skin's folds, palms and soles, are normally spared. Scaling improves with age and during summer. Delayed birth (insufficient cervical dilatation) may be observed. Extracutaneous manifestations like testicular maldescent, attention deficit and hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) and/or corneal opacities are possible. Large deletions involving adjacent genes may result in more complex phenotypes (contiguous gene deletion syndromes like Kallman´s syndrome, the recessive form of X-linked chondrodysplasia punctata, short stature, intellectual disability, or central nervous systems anomalies).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: X-linked ichthyosis is an epidermal lipid metabolism anomaly due to inactivating mutations or deletions in the steroid sulfatase STS gene (Xp22.3). STS codes for a lipid hydrolase of the stratum corneum that participates in the regulation of permeability, barrier homeostasis and desquamation by catalyzing the hydrolysis of steroid sulfates (e.g. cholesterol sulfate CSO4, sulfated steroid hormones). STS deficiency leads to increased amounts of CSO4 that inhibit epidermal serine proteases, which in turn results in decreased desquamation of corneocytes with retention hyperkeratosis. There are some much rarer syndromic RXLI cases that are due to contiguous gene deletion affecting neighboring genes of the STS gene.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical findings and family history (scaling in male relatives, history of delayed birth). It is confirmed by biochemical (serum protein electrophoresis, STS activity test of fibroblasts or leukocytes) and molecular/cytogenetic analyses (polymerase chain reaction (PCR), multiple ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA), comparative genomic hybridization/comparative microarray analysis (CMA), fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH)). Histology or ultrastructure of the skin is helpful for the differentiation of ichthyosis vulgaris.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes ichthyosis vulgaris, autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI), namely lamellar ichthyosis, syndromic RLXI, or multiple sulfatase deficiency.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Maternal urine and serum steroid measurements may show decreased estrogen levels. Therefore, RXLI may be detected in utero, when maternal estriol levels are measured for prenatal screening for Down syndrome and other disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: XLRI is transmitted as an X-linked recessive trait: it affects males and is inherited through female carriers. Female patients have rarely been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment consists in hydrating and softening the skin with the use of lubricating bath oils and emollients containing humectants and keratolytics (e. g. urea, lactic acid, and glycolic acid). For adult patients, systemic retinoids are an option, e. g. during winter, when the ichthyosis is often more severe.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: RXLI represents a benign form of ichthyosis. The ichthyosis is life-long but hyperkeratosis and scaling may improve with age. Life expectancy is normal.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare chromosomal anomaly characterized by prenatal and postnatal growth retardation, developmental delay, intellectual impairment, dysmorphic signs and variable combination of congenital anomalies, including cardiovascular, genitourinary and skeletal anomalies and spectrum of caudal malformations.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: The clinical presentation of 3q duplication syndrome is highly variable, often influenced by the size of the duplicated segment. Characteristic features include hirsutism and facial dysmorphism, such as a square-shaped face, prominent nasal bridge, everted nostrils, hypertelorism, and palate abnormalities. Other reported findings encompass mental retardation, microcephaly, a high narrow forehead, and short stubby fingers. Skeletal anomalies, including short limbs, vertebral, thoracic, and digit abnormalities, and spina bifida, have been observed. Cardiovascular, urinogenital, and central nervous system abnormalities can also occur. Prenatal diagnoses have identified generalized hydrops foetalis, intrauterine growth retardation, and omphalocele. [PMC6567560, PMC1051066, PMC1050675, PMC1545362]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: 3q26 microduplication syndrome from a duplication of a fragment of the long arm of chromosome 3, commonly involving regions such as 3q21-qter, 3q26-qter, or 3q29. This genetic imbalance often arises from unbalanced chromosomal rearrangements, including familial or de novo translocations involving chromosome 3 and other chromosomes (e.g., 7, 6, 15, 11), or balanced insertions carried by a parent. Molecular karyotyping techniques like aCGH and FISH are valuable for precisely determining the size and origin of these imbalanced fragments. [PMC6567560, PMC1051364, PMC1051066, PMC1050675, PMC1545362]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for 3q duplication syndrome involve a combination of cytogenetic and molecular techniques. Karyotype analysis using GTG banding is a primary step, though it may not always resolve complex rearrangements. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) is crucial for identifying chromosomal regions, determining the origin of additional genetic material, and detecting both balanced and unbalanced translocations involving 3q. Molecular karyotyping techniques, such as array Comparative Genomic Hybridization (aCGH), are particularly valuable for precisely determining the size of imbalanced fragments and diagnosing submicroscopic deletions or duplications not detected by routine cytogenetic tests. aCGH can also characterize genetic material of unknown origin, but it does not identify balanced aberrations in carriers. These facilitate both prenatal and postnatal diagnosis. [PMC6567560, PMC1051364, PMC1051066]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis may include other conditions involving duplications of 3q, such as dup(3q) syndrome, which can present with features like omphalocele, short limbs, and intrauterine growth retardation. Blepharophimosis-ptosis-epicanthus inversus syndrome (BPES) should also be considered, especially given that some cases with cytogenetic abnormalities involve 3q22-q23. While a patient with trisomy for distal 3q (3q26-qter) presented with unilateral blepharophimosis, ptosis, and mental retardation, it differed from typical BPES by the unilateral ptosis and absence of epicanthus inversus. Additionally, distal del(11q) syndrome may share clinical features with partial 3q duplications. [PMC1051066, PMC1050675]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of 3q duplication syndrome is possible, though it is often diagnosed only after birth. Prenatal sonographic examination may reveal features such as generalized hydrops foetalis, short limbs, intrauterine growth retardation, and omphalocele. Karyotype analysis using GTG technique and FISH can identify chromosomal rearrangements and the origin of additional genetic material in a fetus. While conventional cytogenetic studies with high-resolution GTG banding or whole chromosome paint FISH may not always resolve complex rearrangements, molecular karyotyping techniques like array Comparative Genomic Hybridization (aCGH) are valuable. aCGH allows for precise determination of imbalanced fragment sizes and identification of submicroscopic deletions and duplications, particularly when routine cytogenetic tests are inconclusive. [PMC6567560, PMC1051364, PMC1050675]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for 3q duplication syndrome is informed by its variable presentation, which can arise de novo or from parental balanced chromosomal rearrangements, such as insertions or reciprocal translocations involving 3q. Balanced carriers may have offspring with different unbalanced karyotypes, leading to partial trisomy 3q. Phenotypic consequences are an important source of information for counseling, especially prenatally, though precise definition can be challenging due to varying sizes of duplications and involvement of other chromosomes. Prenatal diagnosis is possible using techniques like GTG karyotyping, FISH, and aCGH, with aCGH being valuable for precisely characterizing imbalanced fragments, although it does not identify balanced aberrations in carriers. [PMC6567560, PMC1051364, PMC1051066, PMC1050675, PMC1545362]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for 3q26 microduplication syndrome is variable, with the final clinical presentation difficult to define precisely due to differing duplication sizes and potential co-occurring chromosomal changes. Severe outcomes, including stillbirth and significant malformations, have been reported. Affected individuals frequently exhibit mental retardation, alongside a spectrum of dysmorphic features and abnormalities affecting various organ systems, such as cardiovascular, urinogenital, and central nervous system. The degree of trisomy may influence the syndrome's overall spectrum. [PMC6567560, PMC1051364, PMC1051066, PMC1050675, PMC1545362]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare cardiac disease characterized by acute occurrence of heart failure after an emotional or physical trigger; recovery of the wall motion abnormalities are observed within months. Symptoms are similar to acute coronary syndrome (ACS).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Ampulla cardiomyopathy; Apical ballooning syndrome; Ballooning cardiomyopathy; Stress cardiomyopathy; Takotsubo cardiomyopathy; Takotsubo syndrome; Transient left ventricular apical ballooning syndrome; Tako-Tsubo syndrome; Broken heart syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Takotsubo syndrome (TTS) is found in about 1-3% of all patients with symptoms of ACS; however, the prevalence is likely underestimated. Around 90% of TTS patients are women, typically postmenopausal but male and younger patients are diagnosed increasingly due to raised awareness of the syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In the acute phase, clinical presentation, electrocardiography (ECG) and cardiac biomarkers are similar to those of ACS. Typical symptoms are acute chest pain or dyspnea. Further symptoms can arise from complications of TTS, e.g. heart failure, cardiogenic shock, or cardiac arrest. New ECG changes or elevated cardiac biomarkers may or may not be present.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The underlying mechanisms of this syndrome remain incompletely understood. Recent findings show that specific alterations in neurological response and sympathetic activation after emotional stimuli are present in TTS. These findings confirm the importance of brain-heart interaction in the development of this process. Microcirculatory constriction is also proposed as an underlying mechanism.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is often challenging due to the similarity with ACS. Coronary angiography with left ventriculography is considered the gold standard diagnostic tool. The InterTAK (international takotsubo) Diagnostic Criteria have been developed to improve diagnosis and include the following: 1) transient left ventricular dysfunction presenting as either apical, midventricular, basal or focal wall motion abnormalities with possible right ventricular involvement, 2) a preceding emotional, physical, or combined trigger (although not obligatory), 3) neurological disorders can be possible triggers, 4) presence of new ECG abnormalities (ST-segment elevation or depression, T-wave inversion, or QTc prolongation), 5) elevated cardiac markers (especially brain natriuretic peptide), 6) significant coronary artery disease can coexist, 7) absence of myocarditis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include AMI, myocarditis, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, or peripartum cardiomyopathy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Due to difficulty in distinguishing TTS from ACS, patients should be transferred to a chest pain unit upon presentation and receive guideline based treatment of ACS. There are no randomized clinical trials to support specific acute or long term treatment recommendations in TTS. However, the consensus statement from an international TTS expert panel provides recommendations for optimal treatment of TTS patients. Electrocardiogram monitoring is essential as a prolonged QT-interval may trigger malignant ventricular arrhythmias (torsades de pointes) or atrioventricular-block. Cardiogenic shock or post cardiac arrest requires intensive care with treatment according to the presence or absence of pulmonary edema, low left ventricular ejection fraction, hypotension and bradycardia. In all cases, inotropic substances should be avoided. For long term treatment, angiotensin converting-enzyme inhibitors (ACEi) or angiotensin II receptor blockers (ARB) are recommended as they are associated with improved survival and lower recurrence rates. Echocardiography should be performed during the acute phase to exclude right ventricular involvement, left ventricular outflow tract obstruction or intraventricular thrombus. A follow-up echocardiography should be performed after discharge to confirm recovery.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The spectrum of TTS is wide and ranges from low to very high risk. In-hospital mortality and long-term outcome in TTS are similar compared to ACS. Recovery of the left ventricular regional systolic dysfunction is usually observed after 4-8 weeks. The risk of recurrence is around 5%.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Dermochondrocorneal dystrophy is characterised by osteochondrodystrophy of the hands and feet, corneal dystrophy and the presence of skin nodules clustered around the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, around the nose and ears and on the posterior surface of the elbow. Gingival lesions may also be present. It has been described in less than 20 patients. Transmission is autosomal recessive.

A rare intoxication with paraquat (a non-selective bipyridilium herbicide that has been banned in Europe), usually occurring through ingestion of the poison, and that presents with caustic injury of the oral cavity and pharynx, as well as nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain, lethargy, loss of consciousness and fever. Patients may develop potentially life-threatening complications such as hepatic dysfunction, acute tubular necrosis and renal insufficiency, and respiratory failure (due to pulmonary fibrosis) due to its inherent toxicity and lack of effective treatment. Intoxication via inhalation, injection and dermal or mucus contact have also been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Paraquat poisoning, commonly via oral ingestion but also through inhalation, skin absorption, or injection, is a life-threatening condition with a high mortality rate. Initial symptoms can include vomiting, dizziness, generalized body aches, chest pain, dysphagia, lip sores, swallowing difficulty, hypersalivation, or erosion of the tongue and pharyngeal wall. The toxicity rapidly progresses, causing oxidative stress and multiorgan damage, with a specific predilection for the lungs, leading to pulmonary fibrosis and respiratory distress. Other affected organs include the kidneys (acute kidney injury), liver (dysfunction), heart, and central nervous system. Gastrointestinal ulceration and necrosis are also common. Complications like mediastinal emphysema and multiorgan failure are frequent, often leading to death, though survival is possible with aggressive early management. [PMC11981316, PMC11515206, PMC11261553, PMC10579749, PMC9750538]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: reports on a 22-year-old male presenting with persistent chest pain accompanied by mediastinal emphysema. We firstly considered mediastinal emphysema induced by community acquired pneumonia. Pathogen detection was performed but no positive were found. Based on the of a subsequent lung CT scan, paraquat poisoning was suspected. Although there was no trace of paraquat in the blood, the nebulizer masks used by patient at home was found to be positive for paraquat. The diagnosis was ultimately established as paraquat poisoning via inhalation with mediastinal emphysema. This case report explores the clinical manifestations, diagnostic challenges, and treatment complexities of inhaled paraquat poisoning, emphasizing the importance of recognizing this rare poisoning route and its atypical symptoms. Paraquat (PQ) -induced pulmonary fibrosis poses a significant medical challenge due to limited... [PMC11515206, PMC11189367, PMC9750538, PMC9511329, PMC7722312]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: When patients present with persistent chest pain, retrosternal chest pain, or mediastinal emphysema/pneumomediastinum, other conditions are often initially considered. For example, mediastinal emphysema induced by community-acquired pneumonia was an initial differential diagnosis in one case. Paraquat poisoning, particularly from occult or inhaled exposure, should be suspected as a differential diagnosis when pneumomediastinum occurs without a recognizable cause, especially after other likely etiologies have been eliminated. [PMC11515206, PMC6320115]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Paraquat can cross the placental barrier and enter the fetus, as evidenced by its presence in fetal blood and amniotic fluid after maternal ingestion. In reported cases, paraquat concentrations in amniotic fluid were measured at 0.47 μg/mL and 0.673 μg/ml following maternal poisoning during gestational weeks 36 and 38, respectively. This indicates that paraquat can be detected in amniotic fluid, providing a potential avenue for antenatal assessment of fetal exposure. [PMC9511329, PMC6946536]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Paraquat poisoning is a life-threatening condition without a specific antidote, requiring mainly supportive care to reduce oxidative damage and organ dysfunction. Early decontamination with gastric lavage and activated charcoal is initiated. Treatment often includes corticosteroids, antioxidants (e.g., N-acetylcysteine, glutathione), and immunosuppressants such as cyclophosphamide. Hemoperfusion or hemodialysis is frequently employed, with early intervention potentially mitigating renal and hepatic damage. Despite aggressive management, the condition can rapidly progress to multiorgan failure, leading to a high mortality rate. Lung transplantation is considered for severe pulmonary fibrosis, and experimental therapies like enoxaparin and rapamycin show potential in improving outcomes. [PMC11981316, PMC10579749, PMC9750538, PMC8613450, PMC7722312]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Mitochondrial DNA-related cardiomyopathy and hearing loss
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare mitochondrial disease that has a heterogeneous clinical presentation characterized by the association of progressive sensorineural hearing loss with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and, in the majority of cases, encephalomyopathy symptoms such as ataxia, slurred speech, progressive external ophthalmoparesis (PEO), muscle weakness, myalgia, and exercise intolerance.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): mtDNA-related cardiomyopathy and deafness; Maternally-inherited cardiomyopathy and deafness; tRNA-LYS-related cardiomyopathy-hearing loss syndrome; mtDNA-related cardiomyopathy and hearing loss

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Mitochondrial DNA-related cardiomyopathy and hearing loss presents as a syndrome encompassing encephalomyopathy, sensorineural hearing loss, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Muscle biopsies from affected individuals demonstrate mitochondrial proliferation and partial defects in complexes I, III, and IV of the electron-transport chain. This condition is associated with specific mutations in the mitochondrial tRNA(Lys) gene, such as the G8363A mutation. Mutant genomes are found at high levels in muscle samples, particularly in cytochrome (c) oxidase-negative fibers, and at lower levels in blood. [PMC1914622]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The condition is caused by a novel G8363A mutation in the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) tRNA(Lys) gene. This mutation is associated with encephalomyopathy, sensorineural hearing loss, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Affected individuals exhibit mitochondrial proliferation and partial defects in electron-transport chain complexes I, III, and IV. The G8363A mutation is highly abundant in muscle samples from probands and present in maternal relatives, fulfilling accepted criteria for pathogenicity as it is absent in controls. [PMC1914622]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves genetic testing for specific mitochondrial DNA mutations, such as the G8363A mutation in the tRNA(Lys) gene, which can be detected in muscle and blood samples. Muscle biopsies from affected individuals show mitochondrial proliferation and partial defects of electron-transport chain complexes I, III, and IV. Single-muscle-fiber analysis can reveal significantly higher levels of mutant genomes in cytochrome c oxidase-negative fibers. The absence of these specific mutations in healthy controls and patients with other mitochondrial encephalomyopathies supports their diagnostic significance. [PMC1914622]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: A novel G8363A mutation in the mtDNA tRNA(Lys) gene was associated, in two unrelated families, with a syndrome consisting of encephalomyopathy, sensorineural hearing loss, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Muscle biopsies from the probands showed mitochondrial proliferation and partial defects of complexes I, III, and IV of the electron-transport chain. The G8363A mutation was very abundant (>95%) in muscle samples from the probands and was less copious in blood from 18 maternal relatives (mean 81.3% +/- 8.5%). Single-muscle-fiber analysis showed significantly higher levels of mutant genomes in cytochrome (c) oxidase-negative fibers than in cytochrome (c) oxidase-positive fibers. The mutation was not found in >200 individuals, including normal controls and patients with other mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, thus fulfilling accepted criteria for pathogenicity. [PMC1914622]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The condition is maternally inherited, associated with a novel G8363A mutation in the mitochondrial tRNA(Lys) gene. This mutation is highly abundant in muscle samples from affected individuals (>95%) and also present in blood from maternal relatives, though at lower, variable levels (mean 81.3% +/- 8.5%). The presence of the mutation in maternal relatives indicates a risk of transmission and potential for variable expression due to heteroplasmy. Its absence in over 200 controls, including patients with other mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, fulfills criteria for pathogenicity, which is essential for genetic counseling. [PMC1914622]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A primary immunodeficiency disease characterized by microthrombocytopenia, eczema, infections and an increased risk for autoimmune manifestations and malignancies.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence of WAS has been estimated at less than 1 in 100,000 live births. The disease almost exclusively affects males.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: WAS usually manifests in infancy but onset may also occur during the neonatal period. In most cases the first clinical features are hemorrhagic manifestations with petechiae, bruising, purpura, epistaxis, oral bleeding, bloody diarrhea and intracranial bleeding. Acute or chronic eczema is the second characteristic finding of WAS. Due to combined immunodeficiency, most patients also have airway, gut or skin infections caused by regular or opportunistic germs. Autoimmune manifestations are seen in approximately 40% of cases and include autoimmune hemolytic anemia, neutropenia, vasculitis, inflammatory bowel disease, renal disease, and arthritis. WAS patients have a higher risk of developing tumors (mainly B-cell lymphomas) at any age.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: WAS is due to hemizygous mutations in the WAS gene (Xp11.4-p11.21), coding for the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein, exclusively expressed in hematopoietic cells and having a major role in the reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, signal transduction and apoptosis. Usually, hypomorphic mutations in the WAS gene can lead to an attenuated form of WAS called X-linked thrombocytopenia with normal platelets (XLTT), that is characterized by mild to moderate thrombocytopenia and eczema and a lower risk of autoimmunity and malignancy, but usually showing no immunodeficiency. Recently, a mutation in the WIPF1 gene (WAS/WASL interacting protein family, member 1; 2q31.2), coding for a protein that stabilizes and prevents the degradation of WASp, was also found in a patient who displayed some features of WAS.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on family history, physical examination and laboratory investigations that reveal severe thrombocytopenia with reduced platelet size with a usually normal number of megakaryocytes, as well as altered antibody production (mainly antipolysaccharidic antibodies). Absent or decreased WAS protein levels and genetic testing confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Main differential diagnosis is acute or chronic idiopathic thrombocytopenia (ITP) or platelet alloimmunization in neonates.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is feasible in male fetuses when the causal mutation in the family is known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: WAS is an X-linked recessive disease. Carrier women have a 50% risk of transmitting the disease to their male progeny. Some de novo mutations might also occur.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The only curative treatment to date is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), performed as soon as possible with the best matched HLA donor. In young patients lacking a HLA matched donor, HSCT with a haploidentical donor can lead to a favorable outcome. Gene therapy, still experimental to date, may be a promising approach for patients lacking a suitable donor. Immunoglobulin replacement therapy and oral antibiotics prevent infections. Severe eczema requires treatment with topical or short-term systemic steroids. Treatments that could weaken the immune system (steroids, splenectomy, immunosuppressive agents) should be used with the highest caution by trained medical staff. Agonists of the thrombopoietin receptors (such as romiplostim and eltrombopag) can be used to increase the platelet count in severe refractory thrombocytopenia cases that are awaiting HSCT or gene therapy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: HSCT leads to an 80% survival rate, but when no donor is available, the overall prognosis is poor and life expectancy is reduced, especially when malignancy occurs.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Hydrocephalus with stenosis of the aqueduct of Sylvius
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A congenital, X-linked, clinical subtype of L1 syndrome characterized by severe hydrocephalus often of prenatal onset, adducted thumbs, spasticity (mostly evidenced by brisk tendon reflexes and extensor plantar responses) and moderate to severe intellectual disability. This subtype represents the severe end of the L1 syndrome spectrum and is associated with poor prognosis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Bickers-Adams syndrome; HSAS; X-linked HSAS; X-linked acqueductal stenosis; X-linked hydrocephalus; X-linked hydrocephalus with stenosis of aqueduct of Sylvius

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare osteochrondrosis characterized by chronic traction injury of the immature osteotendinous junction where the patellar tendon inserts into the inferior pole of the patella. It is typically seen in active adolescents. Patients present with point tenderness at the inferior pole of the patella associated with focal swelling and restriction of knee joint range of movement. Radiographic features include thickening of the proximal patellar tendon (potentially followed by dystrophic calcification and/or ossification) and fragmentation of the inferior pole of the patella.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Aseptic necrosis of patella; Osteochondrosis of patella

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease primarily affects physically active adolescents, typically between 9 and 17 years of age. It is commonly observed in males and is considered a sport-related condition. The disease presents as localized knee pain in this demographic. [PMC11438430, PMC6131294]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease (SLJD) commonly presents as localized knee pain in physically active adolescents, particularly males, aged 9-17 years. It can also manifest acutely with sudden pain, tenderness, and swelling over the patella, often following a noncontact injury. Diagnosis can be challenging due to other sport-related conditions affecting the distal patella in adolescents. Imaging, including ultrasound, MRI, and sometimes radiographs showing a minimally displaced distal patellar ossicle, are effective diagnostic tools to confirm SLJD and exclude other injuries. [PMC11438430, PMC6131294]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease (SLJD) is considered an osteochondrosis, characterized by osteonecrosis with reparative changes. It primarily affects physically active adolescents, particularly males, aged 9-17 years. The condition can present acutely following knee injuries, such as noncontact sports incidents. [PMC11438430, PMC6131294, PMC1888378]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease can be challenging, often presenting as localized knee pain in physically active adolescents, particularly males, sometimes acutely after injury, with tenderness and swelling over the patella. Radiographs may reveal features such as a minimally displaced distal patellar ossicle. Ultrasound and MRI are considered the most effective diagnostic tools, with MRI capable of excluding other injuries and documenting the disease. [PMC11438430, PMC6131294]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Rationale: Plentiful vascularity and lack of the physis are thought to render the patella less vulnerable to osteomyelitis. Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA) is an opportunistic pathogen predominantly affecting immunocompromised hosts. Despite the ubiquitous nature of PA, osteomyelitis of the patella caused by PA has been rarely reported in children. Patient concerns: A 5-year-old boy who had presented with a prolonged history of the left anterior knee pain following minor trauma was diagnosed with prepatellar bacterial cellulitis and bursitis. Afterward, a focal osteolytic lesion emerged at the ventral surface of the patella despite oral and intravenous antibiotic therapy lasting for weeks. We described clinical presentation as well as medical and surgical management of pediatric patellar osteomyelitis secondary to prepatellar septic bursitis. Diagnoses: Pseudomonas aeruginosa-associated... [PMC9936032, PMC9896215, PMC9771171, PMC9255640, PMC9137324]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Conservative treatment is the primary approach for Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease, often yielding positive outcomes within two to eight months. This management typically involves activity limitation, rest, cryotherapy, passive mobilization, muscle restraint, isometric exercise, and NSAIDs. In some acute presentations, brief knee immobilization has led to complete healing. Further cohort studies are recommended to refine the existing treatment database and management strategies. [PMC11438430, PMC6131294]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Sinding-Larsen-Johansson disease generally has a favorable prognosis with conservative management. Positive outcomes are typically observed within two to eight months with treatments focusing on activity limitation. One case report noted complete healing of the injury in four weeks following brief knee immobilization. The condition commonly presents in physically active adolescents and resolves with appropriate conservative care. [PMC11438430, PMC6131294]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Dubin-Johnson syndrome (DJS) is a benign, inherited liver disorder characterized clinically by chronic, predominantly conjugated, hyperbilirubinemia and histopathologically by black-brown pigment deposition in parenchymal liver cells.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Dubin-Sprinz disease; Hyperbilirubinemia type 2; Sprinz-Nelson syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence in the general population is unknown. DJS affects individuals of all ethnic origins but is most common among Iranian or Moroccan Jews, in which, due to founder mutations, it has been reported to occur in up to 1/1,300 individuals.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients usually present during adolescence or young adulthood with mild to moderate, recurrent jaundice without pruritus, often triggered by intercurrent illness, pregnancy, oral contraceptives or drugs. Abdominal pain and fatigue are sometimes observed during outbreaks and hepatosplenomegaly may be present in rare cases. Total serum bilirubin (mainly in the conjugated form: the proportion of conjugated to total serum bilirubin is 50-80%) is elevated, usually between 2 and 5 mg/dl (very rarely up to 20 mg/dl). Liver enzyme activities (i.e. aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase), total bile acid concentration, albumin level and prothrombin time are normal. An association with clotting factor VII deficiency can be observed, especially in Iranian and Moroccan Jews. Histological studies reveal a typical black-brown granular pigment deposition in the cytosol of hepatocytes, mostly in the centrilobular area, without other histological abnormalities.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: DJS is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is caused by homozygous mutations in the ABCC2 gene. ABCC2 encodes an ATP-dependent apical membrane transporter that mediates the efflux of bilirubin-glucuronides and other conjugated organic anions from the hepatocyte into bile.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis should be suspected in patients exhibiting isolated conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (i.e. without changes in liver enzyme activities) in the absence of any septic condition, ultrasound anomaly of the liver or potentially interfering drug. In this context, the characteristic urinary coproporphyrin excretion pattern (i.e. an elevated proportion of coproporphyrin I (over 80%) with a normal total coproporphyrin level) is usually diagnostic for DJS. 99mTc-HIDA cholescintigraphy, showing delayed or non-visualization of the gallbladder and bile ducts and prolonged visualization of the liver may also be useful. Definitive diagnosis can be obtained through molecular analysis of the ABCC2 gene. Although histological studies also allow a definitive diagnosis, liver biopsy is not systematically performed considering the invasive nature of the procedure together with the benign prognosis of the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnosis is another form of mainly conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, Rotor syndrome (RT).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative treatment for DJS, even though short-term administration of phenobarbital has been reported to reduce serum bilirubin level in some cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: DJS is a benign disorder and the prognosis for patients is good, highlighting the need for correct diagnosis to avoid unnecessary diagnostic procedures, treatment and follow-up. Progression to liver failure, cirrhosis or hepatic fibrosis is not observed.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A form of nonsyndromic craniosynostosis characterized by the premature fusion of the metopic suture.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Isolated metopic craniosynostosis; Non-syndromic metopic suture synostosis; Isolated trigonocephaly

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Incidence is estimated at 1/15,000 births. Males are more frequently affected than females (sex ratio of 2:1) and the frequency of trigonocephalic twins is high.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The premature closure of the metopic suture results in deformation of the anterior portion of the calvarium and a triangular-shaped forehead. In mild forms, only prominent ridging of the metopic suture is visible combined with a reduced width of the forehead; while in more severe forms marked narrowing of the frontal and temporal regions affects the supraorbital rims leading to hypotelorism. The psychomotor development of patients is usually normal but with a relatively high prevalence in the low average IQ range (< 85). The majority of cases are mild. Ridging of the metopic suture alone is considered a physiologic early closure of the suture and not an anomaly. The risk of developing elevated intracranial pressure is very low.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of isolated trigonocephaly remains to be delineated. Less than 10% of cases are associated with a genetic cause. However, the concordance rate of isolated trigonocephaly in monozygotic twins is 43%, suggesting that both genetic and environmental factors are involved in the etiology of this disorder. There is an overlap of pathogenic genetic causes between trigonocephaly and developmental delay.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical and ultrasound examination, radiological evaluation by X-rays, and 3D CT scans and/or black bone MRI of the skull. Premature fusion of the metopic suture may occur both in syndromic and in nonsyndromic forms of synostosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Metopic craniosynostosis can be found in syndromic forms; the differential diagnosis should include trisomy 13 and other chromosomal disorders (distal monosomy 9p and 11q), as well as C syndrome, and is based on the presence of multiple anomalies (including facial dysmorphism, organ anomalies and intellectual deficit). Fetal exposure to valproic acid during pregnancy can lead to trigonocephaly, which in this case is often associated with intellectual deficit and dysmorphic features, and therefore fetal valproate spectrum disorder should also be included in the differential diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is occasionaly made through ultrasound in which the characteristic head shape and closure of the metopic suture is identified.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic testing should be considered given the overlap between trigonocephaly and disorders with delayed development.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Surgery can be considered for correction of the skull deformation, especially in the severe presentation. The treatment of mild and moderate trigonocephaly is conservative; surgery is not systematically required. Establishing the added value of surgery within the spectrum of this disorders is part of ongoing research. Children with trigonocephaly are particularly at risk for ophthalmological problems, such as hyperopia, and have a higher prevalence of behavioral issues, including autism spectrum disorder and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder. These items should be taken into account in the treatment plan, regardless of surgery or not.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prevalence of an IQ below 80-85 is twice as high compared to the age-matched children.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hematological disease characterized by maternal alloimmunisation against fetal platelet antigens that are inherited from the father and different from those present in the mother, and usually presents as a severe isolated thrombocytopenia in otherwise healthy newborns.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence of fetal/neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopaenia (FNAIT) has been estimated between 1/800 to 1/2 000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: FNAIT has been considered to be the platelet counterpart of Rh Hemolytic Disease of the Newborn (RHD). Unlike RHD, FNAIT can occur during a first pregnancy. The spectrum of the disease may range from sub-clinical moderate thrombocytopenia to life-threatening bleeding in the neonatal period. Mildly affected infants may be asymptomatic. In those with severe thrombocytopenia, the most common presentations are petechiae, purpura or cephalohematoma at birth, associated with a major risk of intracranial hemorrhage (up to 20% of reported cases), which leads to death or neurological sequelae.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FNAIT results from the transplacental passage of maternal alloantibodies (which are IgG) against fetal platelet antigens which are inherited from the father. In Caucasians, the most frequent platelet antigen (HPA) involved in FNAIT is HPA-1a (anti-HPA-1a alloantibodies), which is located on glycoprotein IIIa (GPIIIa), accounting for 75-80% of cases. The other main antigens involved are HPA-2, HPA-3, HPA-5, and HPA-15. The mechanisms of maternal immunization are only partly understood. Fetal syncytiotrophoblasts express GPIIIa on their cell surface and the spread of their extracellular vesicles in the maternal circulating blood system may possibly be at the origin of immunization, beginning with the first pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Alloimmune thrombocytopenia is more often unexpected and is usually diagnosed after birth. Once suspected, the diagnosis is confirmed by demonstration of maternal antiplatelet alloantibodies directed against a paternal antigen inherited by the fetus/neonate.
