There is a well-established link between chronic Helicobacter pylori infection and gastric MALT lymphoma. In 40% of cases of gastric lymphoma associated with H. pylori infection and in 53% of cases of MALT lymphoma not associated with H. pylori infection, MALT lymphoma is associated with a translocation t(11;18)(q21;q21) leading to the fusion of two genes, BIRC3 and MALT1, implicated in apoptosis regulation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on histology of the lesion, as in all lymphomas, a complete blood count and biochemical analysis. Endoscopic examination is required for gastrointestinal or pulmonary lymphoma. MRI and CT scanning are required to determine the stage of the disease. Bone marrow biopsy is also performed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include B cell lymphomas, diffuse large B cell lymphomas, all other non-Hodgkin lymphomas, and infection with H. pylori.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: In cases with localized gastric involvement that are due to H. pylori, antibiotic therapy often results in regression of the lymphoma. In other cases, chemotherapy (chlorambucil, cyclophosphamide, or fludarabine) is required. Radiotherapy may be considered in cases of conjunctival lymphomas and in recurrent cases of localized forms, particularly gastric forms. Conjunctival MALT lymphoma is treated with interferon alpha-2a.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: These lymphomas evolve slowly. When the lymphoma is isolated, the 10yr-survival rate after treatment is around 75%.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, secondary glomerular disease characterized by proteinuria, dysproteinemias, nephrotic syndrome, and nodular glomerulopathy leading to renal failure, with or without extra-renal manifestations. The renal biopsy shows typical deposits of monoclonal immunoglobulins that do not show a fibrillar organization and are negative for Congo red staining. Associated signs and symptoms depend on the involvement of other organs, liver, heart, nerve fibers, gastrointestinal tract, or skin.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Non-amyloid monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition disease encompasses conditions like Light Chain Deposition Disease (LCDD) and Proliferative Glomerulonephritis with Monoclonal Immunoglobulin Deposits (PGNMID), characterized by the deposition of non-amyloid monoclonal immunoglobulins. LCDD primarily causes renal impairment, presenting with renal insufficiency, proteinuria, hematuria, and anemia, and can affect multiple organs, including the lungs, or co-occur with Sjögren's syndrome. PGNMID, a form of monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (MGRS), predominantly affects the kidneys, often presenting with hypertension, renal insufficiency, hematuria, and nephrotic syndrome, with poor renal outcomes including progression to end-stage kidney disease. It typically involves light chain restriction, often kappa, and can co-occur with thrombotic microangiopathy. IgM-MGRS can also manifest with renal impairment and anemia, potentially progressing to Waldenström macroglobulinemia. [PMC12275081, PMC12040654, PMC11973544, PMC12052853, PMC11936450]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Treatment strategies for non-amyloid monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition diseases, such as proliferative glomerulonephritis with monoclonal immunoglobulin deposition (PGNMID) and light chain deposition disease (LCDD), often involve clone-directed therapy. For PGNMID, this may include corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide, or bortezomib and plasma exchange, which have shown reduced proteinuria, stable renal function, and clinical stabilization. In IgM monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (MGRS) progressing to Waldenström macroglobulinemia, a Bruton's tyrosine kinase inhibitor like tirabrutinib rapidly resolved proteinuria and anemia. For LCDD, there is no universally accepted standard of care, but treatments used for multiple myeloma are recommended, including hematopoietic stem cell transplantation and chemotherapy with bortezomib, thalidomide, or dexamethasone. Bortezomib-based therapy appears favorable, and monoclonal antibodies like daratumumab have shown encouraging effects, leading to hematologic complete response and improved renal function. Frequent monitoring of free light chain levels is important, with a target of < 20 mg/L potentially improving kidney function. Renal allograft is not recommended for LCDD due to high relapse incidence. [PMC12275081, PMC12040654, PMC11973544, PMC12052853, PMC11936450]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic cerebral small vessel disease characterized by isolated marked tortuosity of second-order and third-order retinal arteries with normal first-order arteries and venous system, typically located in the macular and peripapillary area and developing during childhood or early adulthood. The disease may be asymptomatic, although most patients present variable degrees of transient vision loss due to retinal hemorrhage following physical exertion or minor trauma.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Retinal arteriolar tortuosity; Retinal hemorrhage with vascular tortuosity; Tortuosity of retinal arteries; Familial retinal arteriolar tortuosity

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Bilateral and multiple Valsalva-related sub-internal limiting membrane (ILM) hemorrhages in a familial retinal arteriolar tortuosity (FRAT) patient is rare, and we treated this patient by both observation and Neodymium yttrium aluminum garnet (Nd: YAG) laser membranotomy . A 13-year-old female student presented with sudden visual loss and central scotoma in both eyes after running 800 m at the school gym. The examination revealed six sub-ILM hemorrhages with the biggest hemorrhage measuring approximately 1.5-disc diameters (DD) in the right eye and two sub-ILM hemorrhages with the biggest one measuring 5.5 DD in the left eye. The patient was diagnosed as having Valsalva retinopathy associated with FRAT. Nd: YAG laser membranotomy was performed at the biggest hemorrhages and the rest hemorrhages were treated with observation in both eyes. The visual acuity recovered to 20/16 in the right... [PMC7161018, PMC2655750]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Familial isolated retinal arteriolar tortuosity (FRAT) is characterized by retinal arteriolar tortuosity. Clinical manifestations can include sudden visual loss, central scotoma, and recurrent vitreous hemorrhages. Patients may present with bilateral and multiple sub-internal limiting membrane hemorrhages, potentially triggered by Valsalva-like mechanisms, and epiretinal membrane formation has been observed. An association with internal carotid artery aneurysms has also been reported, suggesting possible involvement of the cerebral circulation. [PMC7161018, PMC2655750]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: A female infant born with a gestational age of 35 weeks and birth weight of 2500 g was referred for ophthalmic examination on the second postnatal day. Bilateral venous dilatation and arterial tortuosity, severe extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation, and peripheral ischemia were detected. Fluorescein angiography showed profoundly delayed arteriovenous transit and peripheral avascularity. Both eyes were treated with diode laser photocoagulation and bevacizumab injection. Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed hydrocephalus, ventricular dilatation, and cerebral atrophy. Her family history revealed that the patient’s brother presented to the ophthalmology outpatient clinic at postnatal 3 months with inoperable total retinal detachment and similar cranial MRI findings. No systemic or ocular findings were detected in the parents. A recent study showed that in 13 cases,... [PMC10750092, PMC10293751, PMC8183691, PMC7038593, PMC6896573]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of retinal arteriolar tortuosity typically involves a detailed ophthalmic examination. Fluorescein angiography can reveal prominent retinal arteriolar tortuosity and associated features like delayed arteriovenous transit. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) and adaptive optics retinal imaging are also employed, with semiautomated computer software capable of analyzing OCT-generated retinal vessel maps for tortuosity and dilation. For familial cases, whole exome sequencing can identify underlying genetic mutations, such as in the ACTA2 or ESAM genes, which are associated with syndromes presenting with retinal arteriolar tortuosity. [PMC10750092, PMC10842607, PMC8183691, PMC7038593]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Retinal arteriolar tortuosity can be a feature of several systemic conditions. Multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome (MSMDS), caused by ACTA2 gene mutations, presents with early-onset or prominent retinal arteriolar tortuosity, often alongside congenital mydriasis and other systemic issues like cerebrovascular disease. Neurofibromatosis type-1 can also manifest with retinal microvascular corkscrew tortuosity. In neonates, bi-allelic variants in the ESAM gene are associated with a neurodevelopmental disease featuring bilateral venous dilatation, arterial tortuosity, and extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation. Furthermore, bilateral arteriolar tortuosity has been observed in Waldenström macroglobulinemia, a hyperviscosity syndrome, where it may be an early sign. [PMC10750092, PMC10293751, PMC8183691, PMC7038593, PMC6896573]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for familial retinal arteriolar tortuosity involves considering different genetic etiologies and inheritance patterns. Bi-allelic variants in the ESAM gene are associated with a neurodevelopmental disease presenting with severe retinal findings in infants, where parents can be unaffected carriers. For these families, newborn siblings require detailed ophthalmic examination. Alternatively, heterozygous ACTA2 variants, potentially arising from somatic mosaicism in a parent, are linked to multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome, which includes retinal arteriolar tortuosity and cerebrovascular lesions. Genetic testing and family history assessment are crucial for identifying at-risk individuals and informing family planning. [PMC10750092, PMC7038593]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for complications of familial retinal arteriolar tortuosity (FRAT) may involve both observation and interventional procedures. In a case of bilateral and multiple sub-internal limiting membrane hemorrhages, treatment included Nd: YAG laser membranotomy for larger hemorrhages, while smaller ones were managed with observation. This approach led to visual acuity recovery. Nd: YAG laser can be considered for treating premacular hemorrhage in FRAT patients, particularly when rapid vision recovery is desired. [PMC7161018]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Patients with familial isolated retinal arteriolar tortuosity may experience acute events such as bilateral sub-internal limiting membrane hemorrhages, sometimes triggered by physical exertion, leading to sudden visual loss. While visual acuity can recover, potentially with laser intervention, complications like epiretinal membrane formation have been observed. Recurrent vitreous hemorrhages can also occur. Furthermore, there is a reported association with internal carotid artery aneurysms, suggesting potential systemic vascular involvement beyond the retina. [PMC7161018, PMC2655750]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: X-linked epilepsy-learning disabilities-behavior disorders syndrome is characterized by epilepsy, learning difficulties, macrocephaly, and aggressive behaviour. It has been described in males from a four-generation kindred. It is transmitted as an X-linked recessive trait and is likely to be caused by mutations in the gene encoding synapsin I (Xp11.3-q12).

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: The X-linked epilepsy-learning disabilities-behavior disorders syndrome presents with a variable phenotype in affected males. Some individuals exhibit epilepsy with normal intelligence, while others display a combination of epilepsy, learning difficulties, macrocephaly, and aggressive behavior. This spectrum of clinical features is observed within affected families. [PMC1735688]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The X-linked epilepsy-learning disabilities-behavior disorders syndrome is linked to a nonsense mutation in the SYN1 gene, which encodes synapsin I. This mutation was identified through linkage analysis in a four-generation family, where it segregated with the disease phenotype and was present in all affected males and female carriers, but absent in controls. Synapsin I is a synaptic vesicle-associated protein involved in the regulation of synaptogenesis and neurotransmitter release. The identified SYN1 nonsense mutation is considered the likely cause of the phenotype in affected individuals. [PMC1735688]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves genetic analysis. Linkage studies using X chromosome microsatellite polymorphisms, specifically between MAOB (Xp11.3) and DXS1275 (Xq12), can identify the disease-segregating region. Two-point linkage analysis demonstrated linkage with markers such as DXS1039 and DXS991. The causative gene, SYN1, can be screened for mutations by direct DNA sequencing of amplified products, as a nonsense mutation in SYN1 was identified in affected family members and female carriers. [PMC1735688]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: A four generation family is described in which some men of normal intelligence have epilepsy and others have various combinations of epilepsy, learning difficulties, macrocephaly, and aggressive behaviour. As the phenotype in this family is distinct from other X linked recessive disorders linkage studies were carried out. Linkage analysis was done using X chromosome microsatellite polymorphisms to define the interval containing the causative gene. Genes from within the region were considered possible candidates and one of these, SYN1, was screened for mutations by direct DNA sequencing of amplified products. Microsatellite analysis showed that the region between MAOB (Xp11.3) and DXS1275 (Xq12) segregated with the disease. Two point linkage analysis demonstrated linkage with DXS1039, lod score 4.06 at theta = 0, and DXS991, 3.63 at theta = 0. Candidate gene analysis led to... [PMC1735688]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The syndrome is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner, with a nonsense mutation in the SYN1 gene identified as the likely cause. This mutation is present in all affected males and female carriers. Affected males can present with a variable phenotype, ranging from epilepsy alone to a combination of epilepsy, learning difficulties, macrocephaly, and aggressive behavior. Genetic counseling should address the X-linked inheritance pattern, the identification of female carriers, and the potential for phenotypic variability in affected males. [PMC1735688]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, non-syndromic, posterior fossa malformation characterized by a cisterna magna that measures above 15 mm in length, 5 mm in height and 20 mm in width (or greater than 10 mm in fetuses) associated with a normal cerebellar vermis and absence of hydrocephalus. The majority of patients are asymptomatic; however, variable neurodevelopmental outcomes, including delayed speech and language development, motor development delay, visiospatial perception difficulties, and attention problems, has been observed in some patients.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Mega-cisterna magna can be identified across a wide age range. Prenatal diagnosis has been reported as early as 20 weeks and 3 days gestation. It has also been observed in early childhood, with cases diagnosed in a 2-year-7-month-old girl and a 3-year-old girl. In some syndromic contexts, such as TARP syndrome, structural brain abnormalities including mega-cisterna magna are present from birth or early infancy. Furthermore, a similar pattern of associated conditions, including mega-cisterna magna, has been confirmed in adults. [PMC11138330, PMC11402618, PMC8414764, PMC3183328]

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Mega cisterna magna (MCM) is a structural brain abnormality, often identified via imaging, and can be challenging to differentiate from a Blake's Pouch Cyst. It is frequently associated with a range of neurodevelopmental and syndromic conditions. These include diffuse periventricular nodular heterotopia, which presents with epilepsy, cardiovascular, and pulmonary pathologies. MCM is also observed in 16p11.2 microduplication syndrome, KIRREL3-related disorders (manifesting as intellectual disability, cerebellar hypoplasia, dysmorphic features, autism spectrum disorder, and apraxia of speech), and Raynaud-Claes type X-linked syndromic mental retardation (characterized by intellectual disability, language impairment, dysmorphic features, autistic traits, thin corpus callosum, and ventriculomegaly). Furthermore, MCM is a feature of TARP syndrome, which encompasses a broad spectrum of abnormalities including talipes equinovarus, atrial septal defect, Robin sequence, persistent superior vena cava, cerebellar hypoplasia, partial agenesis of the corpus callosum, and severe intellectual disability. MCM can influence cognitive function, behavior, and criminal responsibility. [PMC11938700, PMC11402618, PMC10454344, PMC10441694, PMC8414764]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Mega-cisterna magna has been observed in association with several genetic conditions. These include variants in the FLNA gene, often linked to periventricular nodular heterotopia, and variants in the KIRREL3 gene, which can also present with cerebellar hypoplasia. Other genetic associations include novel variants in the CLCN4 gene, leading to syndromic X-linked intellectual disability, and RBM10 gene mutations, characteristic of TARP syndrome. A case report also noted mega-cisterna magna in a child with 16p11.2 microduplication syndrome, though its direct causal link or phenotypic extension is still being explored. [PMC11402618, PMC10454344, PMC10441694, PMC8414764, PMC3183328]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for mega cisterna magna include prenatal ultrasound and neurosonography, which can identify the condition and lead to a hypothesis of associated anomalies like periventricular nodular heterotopia. This can be further supported by fetal and maternal brain MRI. Additionally, quantitative diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) parameters, such as apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) and exponential apparent diffusion coefficient (eADC), are effective in differentiating mega cisterna magna from cisterna magna arachnoid cysts. Genetic studies, such as whole exome sequencing, can supplement imaging findings to confirm underlying genetic etiologies. [PMC12257351, PMC11402618]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Mega-cisterna magna (MCM) must be differentiated from other posterior fossa fluid collections. Cisterna magna arachnoid cysts (CMAC) are a key differential, with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)-derived apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) and exponential apparent diffusion coefficient (eADC) parameters proving useful for distinction, as MCM exhibits significantly different values. Blake's Pouch Cyst (BPC) also presents with increased fluid in the cisterna magna, and it may be impossible to differentiate from MCM through image examination alone. While Joubert syndrome and Dandy-Walker malformation involve posterior fossa abnormalities, their direct differentiation from MCM is not detailed. [PMC12257351, PMC12268020, PMC10454344]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Mega cisterna magna can be identified prenatally. In one reported case, it was detected in a female fetus at 20 weeks and 3 days gestation during an ultrasound examination, alongside bilateral periventricular irregularities. Neurosonography was subsequently performed, leading to a hypothesis of diffuse periventricular nodular heterotopia, which was further supported by fetal MRI. [PMC11402618]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Mega-cisterna magna can be associated with various genetic conditions, necessitating genetic counseling. X-linked disorders, such as those involving FLNA, CLCN4, and RBM10 variants, have been identified, often inherited from mothers who may be healthy or mildly affected. Autosomal genetic causes include 16p11.2 microduplications and KIRREL3 variants, which can present with a range of neurodevelopmental and structural anomalies. Genetic testing, including chromosomal microarray and whole exome sequencing, is crucial for diagnosis. The variable expressivity and expanding phenotypic spectrum of these conditions underscore the importance of accurate diagnosis and comprehensive counseling for affected families, including prenatal considerations. [PMC11402618, PMC10454344, PMC10441694, PMC8414764, PMC3183328]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for mega cisterna magna appears to include a normal life expectancy, with no obvious increase in mortality, particularly when observed alongside conditions such as pituitary stalk duplication. However, mega cisterna magna can be associated with neurocognitive impairments that may influence behavior and complicate assessments, especially in forensic contexts. This suggests potential long-term cognitive or behavioral challenges, highlighting the need for comprehensive neurocognitive assessments to understand and manage these influences. [PMC11938700, PMC11138330]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Corneal dystrophy-perceptive deafness (CDPD) or Harboyan syndrome is a degenerative corneal disorder characterized by the association of congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy (CHED) with progressive, postlingual sensorineural hearing loss.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CDPD; Corneal dystrophy with progressive deafness; Harboyan syndrome; Corneal dystrophy with progressive hearing loss; Corneal dystrophy-perceptive hearing loss syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, 24 cases from 11 families of various origins (Asian Indian, South American Indian, Sephardi Jewish, Brazilian Portuguese, Dutch, Gypsy, Moroccan and Dominican) have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The ocular manifestations in CDPD include diffuse bilateral corneal edema occurring with severe corneal clouding, blurred vision, visual loss and nystagmus. They are apparent at birth or within the neonatal period and are indistinguishable from the ocular findings characterizing autosomal recessive CHED (CHED2). Hearing deficit in CDPD is slowly progressive and is typically identified in patients between 10 and 25 years of age. There are no reported cases with prelingual deafness, however, significant hearing loss in children as young as 4 years old has been detected by audiometry, suggesting that hearing may be affected early in the disease course, even at birth.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CDPD is caused by mutations in the SLC4A11 gene located at the CHED2 locus on chromosome 20p13-p12, indicating that CHED2 and CDPD are allelic disorders. A total of 62 different SLC4A11 mutations have been reported in 98 families (92 with CHED2 and six with CDPD).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical criteria, detailed ophthalmological assessment and audiometry. Molecular confirmation of the clinical diagnosis is feasible.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: A variety of genetic, metabolic, developmental and acquired diseases presenting with clouding of the cornea should be considered in the differential diagnosis (Peters anomaly, sclerocornea, limbal dermoids and congenital glaucoma). Audiometry must be performed to differentiate CDPD from CHED2. Autosomal recessive types of CHED (CHED2) and CDPD should be carefully distinguished from the less severe autosomal dominant type, CHED1.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: More than 50% of the reported CDPD cases have been associated with parental consanguinity and all reported cases have been consistent with autosomal recessive transmission.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The ocular abnormalities in patients with CDPD may be treated with topical hyperosmolar solutions. However, corneal transplantation (penetrating keratoplasty) represents the definitive treatment. Corneal transplantation results in substantial visual gains and has a relatively good surgical prognosis. Audiometric monitoring should be offered to all patients. Hearing aids may be necessary in adolescence.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The aim of was to describe the ocular phenotype in a case with Kearns-Sayre syndrome (KSS) spectrum and to determine if corneal endothelial cell dysfunction could be attributed to other known distinct genetic causes. Herein, genomic DNA was extracted from blood and exome sequencing was performed. Non-coding gene regions implicated in corneal endothelial dystrophies were screened by Sanger sequencing. In addition, a repeat expansion situated within an intron of TCF4 (termed CTG18.1) was genotyped using the short tandem repeat assay. The diagnosis of KSS spectrum was based on the presence of ptosis, chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia, pigmentary retinopathy, hearing loss, and muscle weakness, which were further supported by the detection of ~6.5 kb mtDNA deletion. At the age of 33 years, the proband's best corrected visual acuity was reduced to 0.04 in the right eye and 0.2 in... [PMC8702069]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare cardiac rhythm disease characterized by a transient or permanent absence of electrical and mechanical atrial activity. Electrocardiographic findings include bradycardia, ectopic supraventricular rhythms, lack of atrial excitability and absent P waves.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Isolated atrial cardiomyopathy with heart block

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Atrial standstill is characterized as a rare disorder of cardiac rhythm. However, the provided abstract primarily details a specific case of persistent atrial standstill that developed following a Cox-maze III procedure, rather than providing comprehensive epidemiological data for isolated atrial standstill. Consequently, specific prevalence or incidence rates, demographic distributions, or common risk factors for the isolated form of the condition are not elucidated. The overall epidemiology of isolated atrial standstill, beyond its general rarity, remains largely undescribed in the available information. [PMC6931504]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Atrial standstill is a rare cardiac rhythm disorder characterized by the total absence of electrical activity in one or both atria. Clinically, it can manifest with symptomatic pauses, low QRS voltage, QS complexes, and left ventricular dysfunction. It has been observed in pediatric patients with associated caveolin-3 mutations and in adults, including a 46-year-old female with giant cell myoendocarditis linked to SARS-CoV-2 and Parvovirus B19. It can also occur following procedures like the Cox-maze III, leading to pacemaker dependency. Complications include sudden cardiac death due to ventricular arrhythmias. Atrioventricular sequential pacing has been shown to restore mechanical atrial function. [PMC8426732, PMC6931504, PMC5778098]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Atrial standstill has been associated with several etiologies. One case described giant cell myocarditis, where SARS-CoV-2 and Parvovirus B19 were detected in the myocardium, suggesting a potential role in autoimmune myocarditis. Another instance reported persistent atrial standstill developing after a Cox-maze III procedure. Additionally, atrial standstill has been linked to a caveolin-3 mutation in a pediatric patient. [PMC8426732, PMC6931504, PMC5778098]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Atrial standstill is characterized by the total absence of electrical activity in one or both atria. Diagnosis involves identifying this absence, which may manifest as sinus arrest, potentially following atrial fibrillation or supraventricular tachycardia, and can be a feature of sick sinus syndrome. Other diagnostic findings may include low QRS voltage, QS complexes in V1-V5 leads, and left ventricular systolic and restrictive dysfunction. Magnetic resonance imaging can reveal subepicardial late gadolinium enhancement, while Doppler echocardiography may confirm the mechanical function of the atria. Endomyocardial biopsy is also mentioned in the diagnostic context. [PMC10507857, PMC8426732, PMC6931504]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for atrial standstill or related rhythm disturbances encompass various etiologies. These include post-procedural complications, such as sinus arrest following radiofrequency ablation, which may involve sinoatrial node injury, myocardial edema, propafenone poisoning, or autonomic dysfunction. Persistent atrial standstill has also been observed after the Cox-maze III procedure. Sick sinus syndrome, characterized by impaired sinoatrial node function, is another consideration, sometimes diagnosed after sinus arrest, potentially triggered by a trigeminal vagal reflex. Furthermore, atrial standstill can be associated with progressive chronic giant cell myoendocarditis, with detected SARS-CoV-2 and Parvovirus B19 in the myocardium. A genetic association with caveolin-3 mutation has also been reported in pediatric patients. [PMC11309667, PMC10507857, PMC8426732, PMC6931504, PMC5778098]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Isolated atrial standstill has been associated with specific genetic mutations, including caveolin-3. Mutations in the lamin A/C (LMNA) gene are also linked to cardiac conduction abnormalities, such as progressive atrioventricular block, and can present with a family history of cardiac disease and sudden cardiac death. Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy is an inherited disease, and genetic testing is important for patients with a family history of conduction abnormalities. Familial screening is recommended for inherited cardiac conditions to identify at-risk relatives. [PMC10314414, PMC8807425, PMC5778098, PMC2701154]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Rationale: Previous studies have found that the main treatment of sinus arrest is pacemaker treatment. It is rare to have 12 s of sinus arrest after radiofrequency ablation, and whether a permanent pacemaker is implanted immediately in this case is not described in the guidelines. Patient concerns: A 76-year-old male patient with persistent atrial fibrillation (AF) developed sinus arrest lasting 12 s in the early morning of the fourth day after using radiofrequency ablation for pulmonary vein isolation. Diagnosis: The patient was diagnosed with AF and sinus arrest. Interventions: The patient received cardiopulmonary resuscitation, intravenous injection of atropine 1 mg, and intravenous infusion of isoproterenol 1mg and immediately recovered consciousness thereafter. Approximately, 1.5 h later, the patient underwent surgery to install a temporary pacemaker in the right femoral vein.... [PMC11309667, PMC10507857, PMC8807425, PMC8495660, PMC8426732]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare heritable, glucocorticoid remediable form of primary aldosteronism (PA) characterized by early-onset hypertension, hyperaldosteronism, variable hypokalemia, low plasma renin activity (PRA), and abnormal production of 18-oxocortisol and 18-hydroxycortisol.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Dexamethasone-sensitive hypertension; FH-I; FH1; Familial hyperaldosteronism type 1; GRA; Glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism; Glucocorticoid-sensitive hypertension

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: PA is the most common form of secondary hypertension and is found in up to 10% of hypertensive patients. However, familial forms are rare and represent 6-7% of PA cases. Familial hyperaldosteronism type I (FH-I) is estimated at approximately 1% of all PA cases, but may reach 3% in the hypertensive pediatric population.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Hypertension of varying severity, even among members of the same family, manifests often before the age of 20. It can be accompanied with symptoms of severe hypertension such as headaches and nausea. Exogenous glucocorticoids are effective in reducing hyperaldosteronism and normalizing blood pressure. Cardiovascular complications due to aldosterone excess, such as fibrosis, left ventricular (LV) dysfunction, arrhythmias, and myocardial infarction, can be associated with the disease; abnormal cardiac function may manifest even in young normotensive patients. In adults, FH-I is associated with high risk of hemorrhagic stroke and ruptured intracranial aneurysms occurring at a young age.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FH-I is due to an unequal crossing over on the long arm of chromosome 8 between the CYP11B2 gene (coding for cytochrome P450 11B2 or aldosterone synthase), normally expressed in the zona glomerulosa (ZG), and the CYP11B1 gene (coding for the cytochrome P450 11B1 or steroid 11-beta-hydroxylase), normally expressed in the zona fasciculata (ZF), resulting in a chimeric gene composed of the adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-sensitive promoter of the CYP11B1 gene and the coding region of the CYP11B2gene. This leads to an excessive aldosterone synthase production in the zona fasciculata of the adrenal cortex, regulated by ACTH rather than by the renin-angiotensin system. Excessive aldosterone synthesis leads to increased sodium reabsorption, loss of potassium and subsequent increased water reabsorption.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is suggested by the clinical picture and a family history of early-onset hypertension and/or stroke. Blood and urinary tests show biological signs of primary aldosteronism, i.e. increased aldosterone levels and low plasma renin activity (tested after correction of potassium levels) with an abnormal aldosterone/renin ratio, associated or not with low serum potassium levels, and elevated urinary levels of the hybrid steroids 18-oxocortisol and 18-hydroxycortisol. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing providing evidence of the hybrid gene by Southern blot and/or long-range PCR. Many patients are diagnosed during familial genetic screening in case of family history.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The clinical presentation resembles that of the other familial forms of hyperaldosteronism (FH-II, FH-III). Specific features of FH-I are the presence of hybrid steroids 18-hydroxycortisol and 18-oxocortisol in the urine and the suppression of aldosterone by dexamethasone.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant and genetic counselling should be offered to affected individuals informing them that there is a 50% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Once the diagnosis is ascertained, small doses of glucocorticoids (dexamethasone at 0.125-0.250 mg/day or prednisone at 2.5 -5 mg/day) are sufficient to correct hypertension and reduce the production of aldosterone. Small doses are essential in order to avoid side effects of glucocorticoid treatment; complete suppression of ACTH-regulated hybrid gene activity is not necessary for controlling hypertension. In severe cases, dexamethasone can be combined with a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist and other non-specific antihypertensive drugs. Because of the side effects of glucocorticoids, in children eplerenone can be given instead.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With treatment, hypertension can be controlled for many years, and echocardiographic parameters maintained at normal values.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal monosomy 10q is a chromosomal anomaly involving terminal deletion of the long arm of chromosome 10 and is characterized by facial dysmorphism, pre- and postnatal growth retardation, cardiac and genital anomalies, and developmental delay.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Distal monosomy 10q; Monosomy 10qter; Telomeric deletion 10q; Deletion 10qter

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown but around 40 cases have been described in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: There is no specific clinical feature associated with this chromosome anomaly. Craniofacial features include hypertelorism, strabismus, a prominent or broad nasal bridge, and posteriorly rotated low-set ears. Hypotonia is frequent, and limited joint extensions and early scoliosis have been reported in a few cases. Cardiac defects are not a constant finding and vary to include patent ductus arteriosus, ventricular septal defect, tetralogy of Fallot and truncus arteriosus. Genital abnormalities have been mostly reported in males and include undescended testis, micropenis and a posterior urethral valve. Bladder distension due to cervical dysfunction may occur in females and may be evident during the antenatal period. Severe genital abnormalities (ambiguous external genitalia) have been reported in a few cases. Psychomotor retardation (generally described as mild) was present in all reported cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Distal monosomy 10q results from a subterminal 10q deletion with breakpoints in the 10q25 or 10q26 band leading to partial monosomy for the genes located in this area. Most of the reported cases involved de novo terminal deletions resulting from abnormal non-allelic homolog recombination during meiosis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made by molecular analysis. Comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) microarray or subterminal chromosome multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) may be necessary since conventional cytogenetic analysis may not be sensitive enough to detect very short subterminal deletions.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal molecular testing for the presence of a subterminal 10q deletion may be proposed in case of suspicion of a posterior urethral valve in males (associated or not with genital abnormalities) or in case of bladder distension in female fetuses. The risk of recurrence is low but prenatal screening for chromosomal abnormalities must be proposed, with the use of FISH markers for the 10q subterminal region.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is symptomatic only. Bladder dysfunction may require transient cystostomy. Special education programs to improve cognitive development are needed in most cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is unclear as there are no available data concerning long-term follow up, especially up until adult age.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Distal deletion 10q syndrome is a clinically heterogeneous disorder, and identified genotype-phenotype correlations are generally lacking, though specific genes like DOCK1 and INSYN2A are implicated in cognitive phenotypes. While the specific genes for some features remain elusive, monoallelic deletions of WDR11 and FGFR2 within 10q26.12q26.2 are associated with craniofacial dysmorphisms, growth retardation, intellectual disability, and cardiac diseases. Deletions can be inherited, as seen with a maternally inherited 10q26.13q26.2 deletion classified as likely pathogenic. Genetic testing, such as whole-exome sequencing, is useful for diagnosis and can reveal complex inheritance patterns, including deletions unmasking recessive mutations. Early genetic detection, alongside cardiac, audiologic, and cranial examinations, is recommended for diagnosis and management. [PMC11840842, PMC8278754]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal anomaly characterized by variable clinical features, most commonly including developmental delay, some degree of intellectual disability, facial dysmorphism, microcephaly, congenital heart anomalies, and variable genital, limb and skeletal anomalies.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Azoospermia and ring chromosome 9--a case report. [PMC4354179]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Ring chromosome 9 syndrome is characterized by the presence of a ring chromosome originating from chromosome 9. Molecular characterization, including fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with repetitive centromeric probes and chromosome painting, has been used to identify and confirm the origin of these small supernumerary ring chromosomes. These techniques determine that the ring chromosome specifically involves chromosome 9, excluding the involvement of additional chromosomes in the rearrangement. [PMC1682354]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Routine chromosome banding analysis may be insufficient for the identification of ring chromosomes. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) utilizing repetitive centromeric probes can determine the origin of supernumerary ring chromosomes, including those originating from chromosome 9. Chromosome painting with chromosome-specific libraries can further confirm the chromosomal origin and exclude the involvement of additional chromosomes in the rearrangements. Cytogenetic analyses are used to reveal such structural aberrations. [PMC3777464, PMC1682354]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Azoospermia and ring chromosome 9--a case report. [PMC4354179]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Azoospermia and ring chromosome 9--a case report. [PMC4354179]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic bone disease characterized by the association of osteogenesis imperfecta and congenital joint contractures.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown but > 60 cases have been reported in the literature so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The main features are osteoporosis, bone fragility (leading to recurrent fractures) and progressive multiple joint contractures of variable severity. They are often associated with pterygia, wormian bones, severe limbs malformation, talipes equinovarus, scoliosis due to vertebral deformities and short stature. Motor development is often affected with delayed sitting and walking. Orodental findings such as dental malocclusion, enamel hypoplasia or high-arched palate are sometimes described. Other facial abnormalities are sporadically described. Congenital heart disease was described in very rare cases. Cognitive development is generally not affected.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is caused by insertions, deletions or point mutations in the FKBP10 (17q21.2) gene (Bruck syndrome type 1) or point mutations in the PLOD2 (3q24) gene (Bruck syndrome type 2).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on examination of the clinical features, x-rays and can be confirmed by genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnoses are arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, osteogenesis imperfecta, different chondrodysplasias and chromosomal anomalies with short stature.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Ultrasound examination raises suspicion of bone shortening, bilateral fixed flexion of the elbow, wrist and knee joints, and talipes equinovarus. Prenatal molecular testing can confirm the clinical diagnosis; in some patients with spontaneous point mutations this might be challenging. Prenatal molecular testing is easier when a pathogenic variant has been identified in the family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% probability of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is similar to that of osteogenesis imperfecta and involves a multidisciplinary team. Cyclic intravenous therapy with bisphosphonates and vitamin D supplementation are the standard treatment options. Surgical corrections of bone and spinal malformations, and the prevention of dislocations of fractures by insertion of intramedullary rods and spinal rods, are also important. Bracing and surgery of the soft tissues can help slowing the progression of joint contractures. Physiotherapy can help improve motor function and prevent contractures. Occupational therapy, psychological and social support, should be offered.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is more severe than that of osteogenesis imperfecta depending on the severity of the joint contractures. Independent ambulation, if achieved, may be lost during childhood.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia of the liver
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A form of portosinusoidal vascular disease characterized histologically by the absence of cirrhosis and diffuse benign transformation of the hepatic parenchyma into multiple small nodules (typically 1-3 mm).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) is a rare disease that presents pathologically as diffuse hepatic nodules without fibrous septa. It is believed to be caused by vasculopathy against a background of various systemic diseases, such as hematologic, autoimmune, and drug-induced diseases, with various symptoms. In spite of the recent imaging advances, various atypical cases of nodular lesions are observed in daily clinical practice. Cases that do not completely meet these criteria are referred to as -like or -similar lesions in clinical situations, making it difficult to understand their pathogenesis. a case in which two hepatic nodular lesions were noted and difficult to differentiate from malignancy preoperatively. The lesions were laparoscopically resected and a pathological diagnosis with non-neoplastic liver regenerative nodules resembling NRH was made. A 49-year-old man with no... [PMC10834926, PMC9022230, PMC9650941, PMC9191568, PMC8436301]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Nodular regenerative hyperplasia (NRH) can occur in a familial pattern, with reports of sibling pairs affected in multiple families, sometimes without other underlying systemic diseases. Specific genetic factors have been identified in some cases, such as a mutation in the gene encoding for methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase, leading to hyperhomocysteinaemia. In such instances, treatment targeting the underlying metabolic defect, like folic acid and vitamin B supplementation, can normalize homocysteine levels. Familial cases may be associated with a poor clinical course and progressive renal failure. [PMC1774592, PMC1727622]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Glycogen storage disease due to glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inherited metabolic disease (comprising two major subtypes: type Ia and Ib) characterized by poor tolerance to fasting, growth delay and hepatomegaly resulting from accumulation of glycogen and fat in the liver.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): G6P deficiency; GSD due to G6P deficiency; GSD type 1; Glycogen storage disease due to G6P deficiency; Glycogen storage disease type 1; Glycogenosis type 1; Hepatorenal glycogenosis; Von Gierke disease; GSD type I; Glycogen storage disease type I; Glycogenosis type I

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown. Annual incidence at birth is around 1/100,000. Type Ia affects 80% of patients, and type Ib 20%.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease may manifest at birth by hepatomegaly or, more commonly, between the ages of three to four months by symptoms of fast-induced hypoglycemia. Patients have enlarged liver, growth delay, osteopenia, sometimes osteoporosis, full-cheeked round face, nephromegaly and frequent epistaxis due to platelet dysfunction. In addition, in type b, infections and inflammatory bowel disease are due to neutropenia and neutrophil dysfunction. Late complications are hepatic (hepatocellular adenomas and more rarely hepatocellular carcinoma) and renal (proteinuria and sometimes renal insufficiency).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is due to a dysfunction in the G6P system, a key step in glycemia regulation. Mutations in the G6PC gene (17q21) cause a deficit of the catalytic subunit G6P-alpha restricted to expression in the liver, kidney and intestine (type a), and mutations in the SLC37A4 gene (11q23) cause a deficit of the ubiquitously expressed G6P transporter (G6PT) or G6P translocase (type b).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation, and glycemia and lactacidemia levels, after a meal (hyperglycemia and hypolactacidemia), and after three to four hours fasting (hypoglycemia and hyperlactacidemia). Uric acid, triglycerides, and cholesterol serum levels are increased. There is no glycemic response to glucagon. Molecular genetic testing enables confirmation of diagnosis. Liver biopsy to measure G6P activity is no longer performed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include the other glycogenoses, in particular glycogen storage disease due to glycogen debranching enzyme deficiency (GDE deficiency) or GSD type III but in this case, glycemia and lactacidemia are high after a meal and low in a fasting period. Primary liver tumors and Pepper syndrome (hepatic metastases of neuroblastoma) may be evoked but easily ruled out through clinical and ultrasound data.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible where the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management aims at avoiding hypoglycemia (frequent meals, nocturnal enteral feeding through a nasogastric tube or a gastrostomy (only in type Ia patients), and later oral addition of uncooked starch), acidosis (restricted fructose and galactose intake, oral supplementation in bicarbonate), hypertriglyceridemia (diet, cholestyramine, statines), hyperuricemia (allopurinol) and hepatic complications. Renal protection using converting enzyme inhibitors must be started should microalbuminuria be detected. Liver transplantation, performed on the basis of poor metabolic control or hepatocarcinoma, corrects hypoglycemia, but renal involvement may continue to progress and neutropenia is not always corrected in type b. Kidney transplantation can be performed in case of severe renal failure. Combined liver-kidney grafts have been performed in a few cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With adapted management, prognosis is better: patients have almost normal life span.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare abdominal wall malformation characterized by the bowel protruding from the fetal abdomen on the right lateral base of the umbilical cord, and without a covering sac.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: In Europe, the average recorded prevalence of gastroschisis is 1/6,000 births with an increasing trend.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disorder occurs around the tenth week of gestation, and results in bowel protruding, without a covering sac. If the defect is large enough, other viscera (stomach, bladder and gonads) might be exteriorized in some cases by the end of gestation. The liver always remains intra-abdominal. Intestinal damage, bowel atresia and even bowel perforation may occur as a result from the primary defect. When the hernia ring is tight or decreasing in size, necrosis or progressive ischemia of the protruding intestines may be observed, resulting in some cases with poorer prognosis. Intestinal lesions are linked to the quality of the mesenteric vascularization more than to the contact between intestinal loops and amniotic fluid. Other malformations are only exceptionally associated.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Gastroschisis is believed to be a defect of the umbilical cord and ring, but the exact etiology remains unknown. Maternal age ( less than 20 years old) and maternal exposure to cigarette smoke could be risk factors. Genetic mutations and maternal genitourinary tract infections have been associated with an increased risk, but the exact pathological mechanisms remain elusive. Few familial cases have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is usually made before birth during prenatal ultrasound (US) in the first trimester, allowing the birth to be arranged in a specialized unit where surgery can be performed immediately and intensive neonatal support is available.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The only differential diagnosis is omphalocele which is more frequent, occurs earlier in embryonic development, and is associated in half of the cases with other malformations.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is nowadays made in the first trimester, and relies on the picture of intestinal loops floating freely outside the abdominal cavity, to the right of the cord. Fetal karyotype is not mandatory. Later in gestation, the US scan focuses on fetal growth, amniotic fluid amount, thickness and diameter of both intra and extra abdominal loops.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Gastroschisis is a surgical emergency. Primary abdominal closure is not always possible and different techniques of delayed management may be resorted to. Neonatal nutritional support is paramount. Early delivery is often proposed when intestinal complication is suspected.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is linked to the functional quality of the intestinal loops, but is excellent in more than 90% of cases.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for gastroschisis should consider the potential for co-occurring chromosomal abnormalities. In one reported case, a baby prenatally diagnosed with gastroschisis was confirmed to have Trisomy 21 through genetic examination. This suggests that attention should be paid to chromosomal abnormalities when abdominal wall closure defects are observed. [PMC4724109]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic odontal or periodontal disorder that represents a group of developmental conditions affecting the structure and clinical appearance of the enamel of all or nearly all the teeth in a more or less equal manner, and which may be associated with morphologic or biochemical changes elsewhere in the body.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked dominant

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence varies from 1:700 to 1:14,000, according to the populations studied.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The enamel may be hypoplastic, hypomineralised or both, and affected teeth may be discoloured, sensitive or prone to disintegration. Amelogenesis imperfecta (AI) exists in isolation or associated with other abnormalities as part of a syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In families with an X-linked form, it has been shown that the disorder may result from mutations in the amelogenin gene, AMELX. The enamelin gene, ENAM, is implicated in the pathogenesis of the dominant forms of AI. Autosomal recessive AI has been reported in families with known consanguinity.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the family history, pedigree plotting and meticulous clinical observation. At present, genetic diagnosis is only available as a research tool.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: It may be sporadic or show autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive or sex-linked inheritance.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The condition presents social and functional problems and leads to discomfort, but it may be managed by early vigorous intervention, both preventively and restoratively, with treatment continued throughout childhood and into adult life. In infancy, the primary dentition may be protected by the use of preformed metal crowns on posterior teeth. Longer-term care involves either crowns or, more frequently these days, adhesive, plastic restorations.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Amelogenesis imperfecta (AI) can be a key feature in several rare genetic syndromes. Kohlschutter-Tonz syndrome is characterized by AI alongside developmental delays and epilepsy. Heimler syndrome presents with AI, sensorineural hearing loss, retinitis pigmentosa, nail defects, and sometimes tooth agenesis or root maldevelopment. Jalili syndrome is an oculo-dental disorder encompassing cone-rod dystrophy and AI. Other conditions include a syndrome of short stature, skeletal dysplasia with scoliosis, and enamel renal syndrome, which involves AI and renal disease. Brachyolmia with AI is another distinct entity, presenting with skeletal dysplasia and severe enamel anomalies. [PMC12261647, PMC12172258, PMC12137488, PMC12050240, PMC10947733]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: a 2.2 year-old-boy, born of consanguineous marriage, referred for short stature, with history of neonatal death and skeletal deformities in his older sibling. Rhizo-mesomelic dwarfism was detected antenatally. Within 24 hours of birth, he developed multiple seizures. Examination revealed severe short stature, dolichocephaly, broad forehead, deep set eyes, low set ears, bulbous nose, small, irregular teeth, pointed chin, and triangular facies. He had rhizomelic shortening, stubby fingers, pes planus, and scanty hair. Neurological evaluation revealed ataxia, hypotonia, and global developmental delay. Skeletal survey radiograph revealed shallow acetabuli, short femurs and humerus, short, broad metacarpals and short cone-shaped phalanges with cupping of phalangeal bases. Clinical exome analysis revealed homozygous mutations involving the POC1A gene and the SLC13A5 gene responsible for SOFT... [PMC10947733]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Amelogenesis imperfecta (AI) is significantly improved with comprehensive, multidisciplinary, and long-term management. Early diagnosis and intervention are crucial, particularly in children, to enhance aesthetics, masticatory function, and overall quality of life, including psychological well-being. Without appropriate treatment, patients may experience reduced self-confidence, functional impairments, and aesthetic concerns. Multidisciplinary approaches, encompassing periodontal, orthodontic, orthognathic surgery, and prosthodontic rehabilitation, have demonstrated satisfactory functional and aesthetic outcomes, with some interventions showing stability over several years. In syndromic presentations, such as those associated with renal disease or skeletal dysplasia, timely diagnosis and intervention are vital to prevent severe complications and achieve good systemic outcomes. While complex, ongoing follow-ups are essential for effective long-term care. [PMC12261647, PMC12381680, PMC11665750, PMC11437823, PMC11322039]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, congenital, non-syndromic heart malformation characterized by partial or complete absence of tricuspid valve tissue and its apparatus, with an existing orifice. It can be isolated or associated with other heart anomalies. Clinical presentation is variable and may include syncope, arrhythmias, cyanosis, right heart dilatation and failure.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: A case of tricuspid valve agenesis involved the complete absence of the posterior tricuspid valve leaflet and its subvalvular apparatus, with only the valve annulus present in the corresponding position. The anterior and septal leaflets were observed to be normal. This condition presented in a 46-year-old male patient suffering from severe tricuspid valve regurgitation of unknown etiology, alongside an atrial septal aneurysm. [PMC3352735]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: a rare case of the absence of a posterior tricuspid valve leaflet. A male patient, aged 46, suffering from severe tricuspid valve regurgitation (TR) of unknown aetiology and atrial septal aneurysm was referred to our hospital for surgery. On surgical inspection, the posterior tricuspid valve leaflet and its subvalvular apparatus were completely absent and only the valve annulus was seen in the corresponding position. The anterior and septal leaflets were normal. We successfully reconstructed the tricuspid valve as follows: the head of an anterior papillary muscle was approximated to the ventricular septum (Sebening stitch). After the approximation of the centre of the tricuspid annulus of the anterior leaflet to the tricuspid annulus on the opposite side, a sizer of 29 mm in diameter was easily passed through the anterior orifice. The posterior orifice was closed with running sutures... [PMC3352735]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Surgical reconstruction is a described management approach for severe tricuspid valve defects, such as the absence of a posterior tricuspid valve leaflet, presenting with severe regurgitation. A technique involves approximating the head of an anterior papillary muscle to the ventricular septum and closing the posterior orifice with running sutures. If initial annulorrhaphy alone is insufficient, additional procedures like a Sebening stitch may be necessary to improve valve competence. This surgical intervention has been shown to reduce tricuspid regurgitation post-operatively. [PMC3352735]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: a rare case of the absence of a posterior tricuspid valve leaflet. A male patient, aged 46, suffering from severe tricuspid valve regurgitation (TR) of unknown aetiology and atrial septal aneurysm was referred to our hospital for surgery. On surgical inspection, the posterior tricuspid valve leaflet and its subvalvular apparatus were completely absent and only the valve annulus was seen in the corresponding position. The anterior and septal leaflets were normal. We successfully reconstructed the tricuspid valve as follows: the head of an anterior papillary muscle was approximated to the ventricular septum (Sebening stitch). After the approximation of the centre of the tricuspid annulus of the anterior leaflet to the tricuspid annulus on the opposite side, a sizer of 29 mm in diameter was easily passed through the anterior orifice. The posterior orifice was closed with running sutures... [PMC3352735]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, autosomal recessive congenital cerebellar ataxia characterized by congenital malformation of the brainstem and agenesis or hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis leading to an abnormal respiratory pattern, nystagmus, hypotonia, ataxia, and delay in achieving motor milestones.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CPD IV; Cerebelloparenchymal disorder IV; Classic Joubert syndrome; Joubert syndrome type A; Joubert-Boltshauser syndrome; Pure Joubert syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is estimated at approximately 1/100,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset is antenatal, although clinical presentation is typically in the neonatal period with irregular breathing pattern (episodic tachypnea and/or apnea), and nystagmus. During infancy, hypotonia may appear. Cerebellar ataxia (staggering gait and imbalance) may develop later. Delayed acquisition of motor milestones is common. Cognitive abilities are variable, ranging from severe intellectual deficit to normal intelligence. Neuro-ophthalmologic examination may show oculomotor apraxia. In some cases, seizures occur. Careful examination of the face often shows a characteristic appearance: large head, prominent forehead, high rounded eyebrows, epicanthal folds, ptosis (occasionally), an upturned nose with prominent nostrils, an open mouth (which tends to have an oval shape early on, a 'rhomboid' appearance later, and finally can appear triangular with downturned angles), tongue protrusion and rhythmic tongue motions, and occasionally low-set and tilted ears. Other features sometimes present in Joubert syndrome include retinal dystrophy, hepatopathy, nephronophthisis, and polydactyly.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: JS is due to dysfunction of the primary, non-motile cilium found in most cells. The syndrome is genetically heterogeneous with numerous genes and two loci on chromosomes 9q34 (INPP5E) and 11p12-q13 (TMEM216) associated with the disease so far. Most of these genes encode proteins that constitute the primary cilium or the regulatory proteins and transcription factors involved in its development and function.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the main clinical features (hypotonia, ataxia, development delay and oculomotor apraxia), which must be accompanied by the presence of a neuroradiological hallmark, designated as the ''molar tooth sign'' (MTS) on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). MTS results from hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis and midbrain-hindbrain malformations. Moreover the clinical distinct sign is oculomotor apraxia.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Joubert syndrome-related disorders (JSRD), cerebellar vermis malformations without the MTS (which include Dandy-Walker malformation), X-linked cerebellar hypoplasia, ataxia with oculomotor apraxia types 1 and 2 (AOA1, AOA2), congenital disorders of glycosylation (CDG), 3-C syndrome, pontocerebellar hypoplasias/atrophies, orofaciodigital syndromes II and III, and Meckel-Gruber syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is feasible through genetic testing where both disease-causing mutations have been previously identified in an affected family member. Imaging studies can suggest the disease (fetal ultrasonography and MRI) but cannot be use to conduct any antenatal diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling is recommended for families with an affected child; the recurrence risk for future offspring is 25%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is symptomatic and should be multidisciplinary. Education programs, physical, occupational, and speech therapy may improve the hypotonia and reduce the delay in achieving motor milestones. In general, the neurological disability and amaurosis are not progressive. Particularly relevant is the detection of nephronophthisis (NPH) which leads to chronic kidney disease which occurs in about 30% of subjects with all genetic types (with higher risk for mutations in the following genes: CEP290 (12q21.32), RPGRIP1L ( 16q12.2), TMEM216 (11q13.1), TMEM67 (8q22.1), NPHP4 (1p36.31; 1 case), AHI1 (6q23.3). Another aspect that may determine progressivity is the association with a liver disease, and particularly a liver fibrosis that may need liver transplantation.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is favorable for moderate forms of the disease. In patients with nephronophthisis (NPH), end stage renal disease occurs in the second decade of life. Management of patients with more severe forms should be carried out by a specialized reference center. Liver disease does not recur in the transplanted liver.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: X-linked reticulate pigmentary disorder is an extremely rare skin disease described in only four families to date and characterized in males by diffuse reticulate brown hyperpigmented skin lesions developing in early childhood and a variety of systemic manifestations (recurrent pneumonia, corneal opacification, gastrointestinal inflammation, urethral stricture, failure to thrive, hypohidrosis, digital clubbing, and unruly hair and flared eyebrows), while in females, there is only cutaneous involvement with the development in early childhood of localized brown hyperpigmented skin lesions following the lines of Blaschko. This disease was first considered as a cutaneous amyloidosis, but amyloid deposits are an inconstant feature.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Familial cutaneous amyloidosis; PDR; Partington disease; X-linked cutaneous amyloidosis; XLPDR

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Evolution of the skin manifestations of X-linked pigmentary reticulate disorder. [PMC5640471]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: JAK Inhibition in a Patient with X-Linked Reticulate Pigmentary Disorder. [PMC7846528]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Evolution of the skin manifestations of X-linked pigmentary reticulate disorder. [PMC5640471]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A vast group of rare systemic diseases characterized by the presence of insoluble fibrillar protein deposits in tissues. Amyloidoses are classified according to biochemical type of amyloid protein involved.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: AL amyloidosis's estimated global incidence of 1/95,800 people, with males preponderance. Hereditary ATTR amyloidosis (or ATTRv) mid-global prevalence estimate is of 1/450,000 people (range 1/120,000-830,000). In Tuscany, the incidence of ATTR wild type (ATTRwt) and ATTRv is 1/37,500 and 1/370,000, respectively, with male preponderance. AA amyloidosis estimated incidence is 1-2/1,000,000, but is decreasing.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The most frequent forms are AL amyloidosis, involving all organs except the brain, ATTR amyloidosis, ATTRwt involving the heart and ATTRv involving nerves and heart, and AA amyloidosis involving mainly kidneys, thyroid and GI tract. Progression is usually severe, as affected organs' functions are progressively destroyed. Localized amyloidosis usually has a benign course.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: AL amyloidosis is caused by plasma cell clone producing misfolded immunoglobulin LC that deposits as fibrils in vital organs. ATTR amyloidosis is caused by transthyretin, produced mainly by the liver, the retina epithelial cells and choroid plexus. ATTRv is associated with >130 mutations in the transthyretin gene. In the elderly, particularly in men, ATTRwt causes cardiac amyloidosis. AA amyloidosis is caused by persistent high concentration of serum amyloid A (SAA) in chronic inflammatory diseases.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis can be facilitated by clinical red flags. Once the suspicion of amyloidosis is made, the first step is the search for the monoclonal protein. In the presence of a monoclonal protein, a biopsy of abdominal fat, or salivary glands, or target organs is necessary. Typing of amyloid deposits is mandatory, using mass spectrometry, or immunoelectron-microscopy and immunohistochemistry. In the absence of monoclonal protein, scintigraphy with bone tracers can diagnose cardiac ATTR.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The various types of systemic amyloidosis have a similar clinical presentation, and can be misdiagnosed as each other with catastrophic therapeutic consequences. Misdiagnosis with common diseases, such as type 2 diabetes and congestive heart failure, can occur. ATTRv amyloidosis can be misdiagnosed with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is available for severe forms, mainly Portuguese amyloid neuropathies.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling is recommended in patients with hereditary forms of amyloidosis and in their at-risk relatives. Pre-symptomatic genetic testing can be offered in the context of genetic counseling. Clinical monitoring of asymptomatic TTR mutation carriers should start ten years before the predicted age of onset of the disease according to genotype.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Effective therapies are now available for the three major types of amyloidosis. Frontline treatments vary greatly depending on the type of amyloidosis; careful diagnosis must be performed beforehand. For all types of amyloidosis, supportive therapy plays a fundamental role. Appropriate management of the cardiac, renal, liver, gastrointestinal, nutritional, and neurological manifestations requires concerted action with specialists.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The recent development of effective therapies has dramatically improved the outlook of patients with the most common systemic amyloidosis. For AL amyloidosis patients, the median survival is >6 years, with ∼1/3 of patients achieving long-term survival (>10 years) without sign of active disease. The same applies to ATTR amyloidosis. The median survival of patients presenting with polyneuropathy is ∼10 years, and ∼4-5 years for those presenting with cardiac involvement. Disease-modifying therapies recently introduced are expected to significantly improve outcomes. In AA amyloidosis, the prognosis depends on the nature of the underlying disease. Biologic therapies have dramatically improved the prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital heart malformation characterized by an obstruction to flow through the pulmonary valve with a clinical presentation that may vary from critical stenosis presenting in the neonatal period to asymptomatic mild stenosis. The obstruction at the valvular level can be associated with obstruction at the subpulmonary, or supravalvar levels (valvar, subpulmonary, supravalvar pulmonary stenosis (PS).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The birth prevalence of isolated pulmonary valvar stenosis is between 1/2,000-10,000 in Europe and, worldwide, accounts for between 5-8% of children born with a congenital heart defect (CHD).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical presentation varies according to age. In neonates, critical pulmonary stenosis is diagnosed on signs of right heart failure associated with cyanosis due to supra-systemic pressures and right-to-left shunt through the oval foramen, with ductal dependency. In severe untreated forms, dyspnea or syncope on exercise can occur. However, most patients are asymptomatic and diagnosed on presentation of a heart murmur during infancy or childhood. Congenital pulmonary valvar stenosis is most often isolated, with usually thin leaflets, dome-shaped with a central narrow opening. In 6% of children it is associated with a genetic syndrome, with usually thick, dysplastic leaflets. The malformation can also be associated with several complex malformations such as double outlet right ventricle, transposition of the great arteries, and Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology for isolated forms is unknown. Occasionally the malformation is associated with a genetic syndrome (typically the RASopathies) such as Noonan, LEOPARD or Costello syndromes, harboring mutations of gene PTPN11.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Echocardiography is the best diagnostic tool. It establishes the diagnosis, looks for other levels of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction, and usually provides sufficient information to plan the treatment. CT-scan or MRI can be useful to assess the anatomy of the subpulmonary infundibulum and pulmonary branches.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes primary pulmonary causes of cyanosis in neonates, along with other cyanotic heart lesions, such as transposition of the great vessels and tetralogy of Fallot.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Diagnosis on prenatal ultrasound screening is possible but is only detected in approximately 40% of cases; the rate of detection could be improved by the use of color flow Doppler through the outflow tracts.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The risk of recurrence of isolated valvar pulmonary stenosis is low, ranging from 1.7 to 3.7%. Relative risk of recurrence of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction as a whole is high at 48.6%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty is the treatment of choice of isolated valvar pulmonary stenosis. When the valve is dysplastic with thickened leaflets, or when there is an associated subvalvar or supravalvar obstruction, surgical valvulotomy or valvulectomy is indicated.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis of mild forms of valvar pulmonary stenosis is good, with stability or even spontaneous decrease of the gradient with age. The prognosis after balloon valvuloplasty is usually excellent. In rare cases of residual or recurrent pulmonary stenosis, a second balloon valvuloplasty can be attempted with good success rates. If it fails, surgery is indicated. Severe pulmonary regurgitation at late follow-up is rare and may require pulmonary valvar replacement, percutaneous or surgical.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Rheumatoid factor-negative polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare form of polyarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis characterized by childhood-onset chronic arthritis of unknown cause involving five or more joints at disease onset and absence of rheumatoid factor IgM.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Juvenile polyarthritis without rheumatoid factor; Juvenile rheumatoid factor-negative polyarthritis; Rheumatoid factor-negative polyarticular JIA

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Rheumatoid factor-negative juvenile polyarthritis represents around 15-20% of cases of juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). Prevalence has been estimated at between 1 and 13 in 22,200 children, with an annual incidence of 1-26 in 700,000 children. Females are affected more often than males, with a female/male ratio of 3:1.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Rheumatoid factor negative juvenile polyarthritis is clinically heterogeneous with two patient groups distinguished by age of onset and distribution of arthritis. The early onset form typically appears between 2 and 6 years of age with asymmetrical pattern of joint involvement, possible eye inflammation (asymptomatic chronic anterior uveitis), and presence of anti-nuclear antibody. This form resembles oligoarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis. The second group has a later onset around 10 years of age with often symmetrical distribution and distal joint involvement (commonly small joints of the hands, wrist and knees). Patients may be ANA positive or negative. This form closely resembles rheumatoid polyarthritis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology remains unknown but auto-immunity plays a role.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Rheumatoid factor-negative polyarthritis is defined as the presence of arthritis affecting five or more joints at disease onset. Exclusion criteria are the presence of systemic arthritis or psoriasis in the patient, or a family history of psoriasis in one of the parents or a first-degree relative, HLA B27-positivity in males with onset of arthritis after 6 years of age, and detection of rheumatoid factor IgM in two test samples taken three months apart. Other exclusion criteria include: the presence of ankylosing spondylarthritis, enthesitis and arthritis, sacroiliitis with an inflammatory enteropathy or acute anterior uveitis in the patient, or a family history of one of these conditions in a parent or first-degree relative. It is important to note that these diagnostic criteria were established in 2001 (International League of Associations for Rheumatology, Edmonton) and are currently under revision.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include other forms of polyarthritis (associated with inflammatory or haemato-oncologic diseases).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Patients should be managed by a multidisciplinary team, incorporating expertise in pediatric rheumatology, physiotherapy, psychology and infantile orthopedic care. Treatment is based on the association nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents (NSAIDS), and disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs; methotrexate is used as first-line treatment and then in case of inefficacy or intolerance. Biologics such as anti-tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha, tocilizumab (anti IL6 receptor) and abatacept (targeting T lymphocyte activation) could be prescribed. Rehabilitation is necessary in case of limited joint motion. Corticotherapy is used at low doses and as rarely as possible. Intraarticular injection of delayed-action corticoids (triamcinolone hexacetonide) may be recommended in case of localized persistent arthritis.
