There is an increased risk for high myopia, spontaneous retinal detachments and conductive and/or sensorineural hearing loss. All affected individuals have early-onset degenerative joint disease, causing chronic pain and limited mobility. Intelligence is usually normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene (12q13.11-q13.2) encoding type II collagen.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is mainly based on clinical evaluation and radiographic examination. Radiographs show signs of a spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia with initially delayed epiphyseal ossification (especially in the hips) and later on signs of epiphyseal dysplasia. Characteristic findings are moderate rectangular platyspondyly (in contrast to the pear-shaped vertebrae seen in spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita), coronal clefts in the lumbar spine, dumbbell deformity (caused by metaphyseal broadening) of the tubular bones and rather large epiphyses (megaepiphyses). Histological analysis of chondroosseous tissue reveals intracytoplasmic inclusions in chondrocytes with perilacunar ''foaminess'' and sparse, aggregated collagen fibrils, giving a ''Swiss-cheese'' appearance to the cartilage matrix in the growth plate.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Kniest dysplasia should be differentiated from the other type 2 collagenopathies that cause disproportionate short stature, especially the more common spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita. Dumbbell deformity of the tubular bones (especially the femurs) can also be seen in dyssegmental dysplasia, metatropic dysplasia, fibrochondrogenesis and OSMED. Dumbbell deformity of the femurs is also present in Stickler dysplasia but those patients do not have disproportionate short stature
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Short limbs may be detected by ultrasound. Antenatal molecular diagnosis is possible if the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance is autosomal dominant; genetic counseling should be offered to affected individuals informing them that there is a 50% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is supportive only and includes treatment for club feet, cleft palate, hearing loss and visual impairment. Because of increased risk for spontaneous retinal detachments, prophylactic retinopexy may be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the degree of short stature (adult height may range between 110 and 140 cm) and the extent of degenerative joint disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare syndrome with a central nervous system malformation as a major feature characterized by macrocephaly, megalencephaly, bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria, variable degrees of ventriculomegaly/hydrocephalus, developmental delay and intellectual disability, oromotor dysfunction, hypotonia, seizures, and dysmorphic facial features (such as frontal bossing, low-set ears, a flat nasal bridge, and high-arched palate). Postaxial polydactyly of one or more extremities is also common.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Megalencephaly-polymicrogyria-postaxial polydactyly-hydrocephalus (MPPH) syndrome is a rare and recently recognized developmental brain disorder. There is limited experience with this disease, and only a few patients with specific genetic mutations, such as those in CCND2 and PIK3R2, have been reported to date. The phenotypic spectrum associated with variants in genes of the PI3K-AKT pathway is likely to continue to expand as more cases are identified, suggesting ongoing recognition and characterization of the syndrome. [PMC6565554, PMC4989218, PMC3822249, PMC2908594, PMC7051624]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Megalencephaly-polymicrogyria-postaxial polydactyly-hydrocephalus (MPPH) syndrome is a developmental brain disorder characterized by megalencephaly, polymicrogyria (often bilateral perisylvian), and postaxial polydactyly. While hydrocephalus was initially considered a key diagnostic criterion, cases lacking frank hydrocephalus have been reported, though underlying chronic hydrocephalus may still be suggested by other findings. Patients often present with macrocephaly, facial dysmorphism, intellectual disability, and severe developmental delay. Brain malformations can be complex, including mega corpus callosum, hypomyelination, white matter disorganization, and involvement of the brainstem and cerebellum. Seizures, including complex partial seizures, are common. The syndrome is linked to defects in genes of the PI3K-AKT pathway, such as CCND2 and PIK3R2 variants, and its phenotypic spectrum continues to expand. [PMC6565554, PMC4989218, PMC3822249, PMC7051624]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Megalencephaly-polymicrogyria-polydactyly-hydrocephalus (MPPH) syndrome is a developmental brain disorder caused by defects in genes of the PI3K-AKT pathway. Pathogenic causes include de novo variants in CCND2, particularly those clustering in the distal part of the protein, which lead to accumulation of degradation-resistant protein. De novo variants in the PIK3R2 gene, affecting its SH2 domain or the interface with the PI3K catalytic subunit α, are also associated with MPPH. Additionally, an MPPH-like phenotype can result from submicroscopic chromosomal aberrations, such as an unbalanced der(5)t(5;20) translocation involving genes on chromosomes 5q35 and 20q13. High-resolution array analysis is recommended for diagnostic workup. [PMC8725575, PMC6565554, PMC4989218, PMC2908594]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Megalencephaly-polymicrogyria-postaxial polydactyly-hydrocephalus (MPPH) syndrome involves clinical evaluation for features such as macrocephaly, postaxial polydactyly, and facial dysmorphism. Neuroimaging, including head imaging and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), is crucial to identify megalencephaly, polymicrogyria (especially perisylvian), hypomyelination, white matter disorganization, mega corpus callosum, and cortical dysplasia. While hydrocephalus is a classic criterion, it may be absent. Genetic testing is essential, with de novo variants in CCND2 and PIK3R2 identified as pathogenic causes, often detected via whole-exome sequencing. High-resolution array analysis, MLPA, FISH, and SNP-arrays can detect submicroscopic chromosomal aberrations, such as 5q35 deletions, which should be part of the diagnostic workup. [PMC8725575, PMC6565554, PMC4989218, PMC3822249, PMC2908594]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for Megalencephaly-polymicrogyria-postaxial polydactyly-hydrocephalus (MPPH) syndrome includes conditions with overlapping clinical and genetic features. Megalencephaly-capillary malformation-polymicrogyria syndrome (MCAP), caused by somatic PIK3CA mutations, presents with megalencephaly, cutaneous capillary malformations, and postaxial polydactyly. Disorders related to CCND2 variants, particularly distal variants, can cause brain overgrowth and severe cortical malformations, including MPPH. Similarly, PIK3R2 variants are associated with MPPH and bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria (BPP), characterized by megalencephaly, perisylvian polymicrogyria, and corpus callosum anomalies. An MPPH-like phenotype can also be observed with submicroscopic chromosome 5q35 deletions, overlapping with atypical Sotos syndrome, though typical Sotos patients usually lack polymicrogyria. High-resolution array analysis is recommended for diagnostic workup. [PMC8719146, PMC8725575, PMC4989218, PMC2908594]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Megalencephaly-polymicrogyria-postaxial polydactyly-hydrocephalus (MPPH) syndrome is associated with de novo variants in genes such as CCND2 and PIK3R2, which are critical components of the PI3K-AKT pathway. These variants typically lead to brain overgrowth and severe cortical malformations, and the phenotypic spectrum linked to these gene variants is expanding. Additionally, submicroscopic chromosomal aberrations, such as deletions resulting from unbalanced translocations, have been identified in MPPH-like phenotypes. Therefore, diagnostic workup may include whole-exome sequencing for gene variants and high-resolution array analysis to detect chromosomal abnormalities. [PMC8725575, PMC6565554, PMC4989218, PMC2908594]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: A male infant was born by emergent caesarean section at 39 weeks gestational age secondary to maternal and fetal distress. Initial physical examination was notable for macrocephaly (greater than+2SD), postaxial polydactyly of the hands and facial dysmorphism. Head imaging demonstrated diffuse polymicrogyria without hydrocephalus. All findings were consistent with a diagnosis of megalencephaly, polymicrogyria, postaxial polydactyly and hydrocephalus (MPPH) syndrome. At the 4-year follow-up, megalencephaly persisted without evidence of hydrocephalus. The child was severely delayed with a stable seizure disorder controlled with dual antiepileptic therapy. This case meets the classic criteria for MPPH syndrome, adding to the limited experience with this disease. The 4-year follow-up and absence of hydrocephalus, once thought to be a key diagnostic criterion, adds to our understanding of the... [PMC3822249]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The long-term prognosis of Megalencephaly-polymicrogyria-postaxial polydactyly-hydrocephalus syndrome involves persistent megalencephaly and severe developmental delay. A 4-year follow-up of one case showed a stable seizure disorder managed with dual antiepileptic therapy. Hydrocephalus, initially considered a key diagnostic criterion, was not present at the 4-year follow-up in this case, contributing to the understanding of the disease's long-term sequelae. [PMC3822249]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Metatropic dysplasia (MTD) is a rare spondyloepimetaphyseal dysplasia characterized by a long trunk and short limbs in infancy followed by severe and progressive kyphoscoliosis causing a reversal in proportions during childhood (short trunk and long limbs) and a final short stature in adulthood.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown. Approximately 81 cases have been reported in the literature to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The phenotypic spectrum of MTD is variable with severe cases being lethal in utero, or shortly after birth, and others having only milder skeletal changes. Infants present at birth with a long trunk and short limbs. Craniofacial abnormalities can also be noted and include a prominent forehead, midface hypoplasia, and a squared-off jaw. Some are born with an elongation of the coccyx and rarely reported additional findings include sensorineural hearing loss. Rapidly progressive kyphoscoliosis appears during childhood and a reversal in proportions is seen with a shortening of the trunk and relatively long extremities. Kyphoscoliosis can lead to thorax deformities and to a decrease in pulmonary function and respiratory distress that can be fatal. The small joints are usually hypermobile while contractures of the large joints are not uncommon and are usually progressive. Severe kyphoscoliosis and possible atlantoaxial instability can lead to myelopathy. Adults reach an average height of 107-135 cm. Intelligence is normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MTD is due to mutations in the transient receptor potential vanilloid 4 (TRPV4) gene (12q24.1) encoding a polymodal Ca2+ permeable cation channel found in a variety of tissues. Mutations in this gene cause an increase in calcium in the chondrocytes and consequently disrupted endochondral ossification and the clinical manifestations of MTD.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical and radiological findings. Radiological findings include short diaphyses with wide metaphyses, marked platyspondyly, precocious calcification of hyoid and cricoid cartilage, halberd shaped pelvis, severe hypoplasia of the anterior part of the first cervical vertebrae and squared-off, irregular calcaneal bones. Radiological manifestations change at different ages. Molecular genetic testing can identify a mutation in the TRPV4 gene, confirming diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include mucopolysaccharidosis type IV and other types of spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, in particular spondylometaphyseal dysplasia, Kozlowski type, an allelic disorder that shows important overlap with mild MD cases.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible through genetic testing and prenatal assessment (with a 3D computed tomography scan or ultrasound) and should be offered when a mutation in the family is known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: MTD is inherited autosomal dominantly and genetic counseling is possible. Parents with MTD have a 50% risk of passing the disease on to their offspring. Many cases occur de novo, but in families with no history of the disease, germline mosaicism cannot be excluded.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is targeted at possibly avoiding the progression of skeletal deformity and maintaining pulmonary function. Standard practice includes bracing until skeletal maturity is reached. A conservative approach is usually preferred, but surgical procedures (i.e. corrective spine surgery with posterior fusion) can be successful in some cases in halting deformity. Preoperative evaluation of pulmonary function is mandatory before any invasive procedure is considered. Regular follow-up should monitor for any breathing difficulties or signs of myelopathy. A tracheostomy and long-term ventilatory support may be necessary in severe cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis varies on the severity of the disease. Life expectancy is not usually affected unless there are respiratory complications.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Giant axonal neuropathy (GAN) is a severe, slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by progressive motor and sensory peripheral neuropathy, central nervous system involvement (including pyramidal and cerebellar signs), and characteristic kinky hair in most cases.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown, but to date approximately 50 families have been reported. The frequency of this disease however, is likely to be underestimated, due to patients with incomplete phenotypes and high level of consanguinity among some populations. It occurs equally in both sexes.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset of GAN ranges from early infancy to late childhood. Clinical hallmarks include progressive gait disturbance (frequent falls due to muscle weakness, sensory neuropathy and ataxia), everted feet, crouched gait, tightly curled hair, and early-onset central nervous system (CNS) involvement, including pyramidal and cerebellar signs that, when present together almost clinch the diagnosis. Patients usually present with intellectual disability, epilepsy, nystagmus and dysarthria that worsens in the second decade of life, and mortality typically occurs in the third decade. Other clinical signs include facial weakness, optic atrophy, ophthalmoplegia, skeletal deformations (e.g. foot deformities, scoliosis) and tremor. Clinically heterogeneous cases, with GAN presenting with a mild Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT)-like phenotype or manifesting with a later age of onset, absence of kinky hair, and slower progression, have recently been documented.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: GAN is associated with more than 50 different causative mutations in GAN gene (16q24.1), encoding the ubiquitously expressed cytoskeletal protein gigaxonin.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical findings and imaging. Cerebellum abnormalities, demyelination in white matter and glial proliferation in white and gray matter are shown by magnetic resonance imaging. Due to the presence of giant axons in other diseases, peripheral nerve biopsy is not sufficient to diagnose GAN. Genetic molecular testing or immunodetection of gigaxonin confirms diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes CMT-1F, -2E, -4A, -4B, -4C, -4D and -4E, the classic form of infantile neuroaxonal dystrophy, arylsulfatase A deficiency, spinal muscular atrophy, Friedreich ataxia, globoid cell leukodystrophy, n-hexane toxicity, and acrylamide toxicity.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible in families with a known disease-causing mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: GAN is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. Parents of an affected child are obligate heterozygotes and asymptomatic. Genetic counseling can inform parents that the risk of having an affected child is 25%. Carrier testing requires the GAN pathogenic variant to have been identified in an affected member of the family.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic, focusing on stimulating intellectual and physical development, as well as communication skills, through physical, occupational and speech therapy, since the initiation of symptoms. Skeletal deformities and ophthalmoplegia may need surgery. Intrathecal administration of an AAV9-based gene therapy to restore GAN expression is currently being explored.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis varies but is usually poor. Most patients become wheelchair-dependent in the second decade of life and eventually progress to a bedridden state in early adulthood. Secondary complications, such as respiratory failure, may occur. Life expectancy does not exceed the third decade. Lack of curly hair is correlated with milder disease and slower disease progression, which would suggest a less stark prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: X-linked intellectual disability, Wilson type is characterised by severe intellectual deficit with mutism, epilepsy, growth retardation and recurrent infections. It has been described in three males from three generations of one family. The causative gene has been localised to the 11p region of the X chromosome.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Affected males present with severe mental retardation, typically with an IQ between 20 and 30, accompanied by mutism, growth failure, frequent infections, and seizures. Minor anomalies include brachycephaly, a frontal hair whorl, square face, large mouth, thick lips, and prognathism. Despite these features, a characteristic facies is not observed. [PMC1016093]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Wilson type, is a new type of non-specific X-linked mental retardation. Genetic linkage analysis in an affected family identified a maximal two-point lod score with probe DXS255 at chromosomal region Xp11.22. Crossovers were observed with probes mapping to regions Xp22, Xp21, and Xq28. Standard laboratory studies, including karyotype, fragile X screening, and metabolic tests, were normal, suggesting a distinct genetic cause linked to Xp11.22. [PMC1016093]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves a comprehensive workup to exclude other conditions, including karyotyping, fragile X screening, skeletal surveys, and metabolic tests such as blood amino acid, urine organic acid, and HGPRT levels, all of which were normal in affected individuals. Genetic linkage analysis using X chromosome DNA probes, specifically DXS255 at Xp11.22, was instrumental in identifying the genetic locus. Phenotypic comparison with other X-linked intellectual disabilities also aids in differentiation. [PMC1016093]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis for X-linked intellectual disability, Wilson type, involves distinguishing it from other X-linked causes of mental retardation. A comparison with 80 X-linked disorders, including 41 non-specific types, found no other compatible conditions based on phenotypic and linkage data. Furthermore, standard laboratory tests, such as karyotype with fragile X screening, skeletal survey, blood amino acid, urine organic acid, and HGPRT levels, were normal, helping to exclude other known conditions. [PMC1016093]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: This condition is characterized as X-linked mental retardation, observed in affected males across a three-generation family. Genetic linkage analysis identified a locus at chromosomal region Xp11.22. The X-linked inheritance pattern is a critical factor for genetic counseling, informing discussions about familial risk and transmission. [PMC1016093]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: A new type of non-specific X linked mental retardation is described in a three generation family. The three affected males had severe mental retardation (IQ 20 to 30), mutism, growth failure, frequent infections, seizures, and the following minor anomalies: brachycephaly, frontal hair whorl, square face, large mouth, thick lips, and prognathism. There was not a characteristic facies. Normal laboratory studies on the proband included a karyotype with fragile X screening, skeletal survey, blood amino acid, urine organic acid, and HGPRT levels. Linkage analysis was performed with 10 X chromosome DNA probes of which probe DXS255 at chromosomal region Xp11.22 gave a maximal two point lod score of 2.10 if phase was inferred and 1.20 if it was not. Crossovers were shown with probes mapping to regions Xp22, Xp21, and Xq28. Comparison of these patients with 80 X linked causes of mental... [PMC1016093]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Hemolytic anemia due to adenylate kinase deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hemolytic anemia due to adenylate kinase deficiency is a rare hemolytic anemia due to an erythrocyte nucleotide metabolism disorder characterized by moderate to severe chronic nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia that may require regular blood transfusions and/or splenectomy and may be associated with psychomotor impairment.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Hemolytic anemia due to adenylate kinase deficiency is an extremely rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder. Only 14 unrelated families have been reported globally thus far. Cases have been identified in Chinese and Indian families, with one mutation (c.413G > A) speculated to be a high-frequency site. [PMC12031993, PMC9066714, PMC8317388]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hemolytic anemia due to adenylate kinase (AK) deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder characterized by congenital non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia, which can range from moderate to severe. Patients may also present with delays in mental and psychomotor development, though this is noted as occurring in exceptional cases. One patient with severe hemolytic anemia and psychomotor retardation recovered with regular blood transfusion therapy. Interestingly, some individuals with severe enzyme deficiency may not exhibit hemolysis, suggesting variability in clinical expression or interaction with other factors, such as co-occurring thalassemia. [PMC12031993, PMC9066714, PMC8317388, PMC1129224]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hemolytic anemia due to adenylate kinase deficiency is a rare, autosomal recessive genetic disorder caused by mutations in the AK1 gene, located on chromosome 9q. Adenylate kinase (AK) is essential for regulating adenine nucleotide metabolism and maintaining cellular energy homeostasis by catalyzing the ATP + AMP ⇌ 2ADP reaction. Deficiency in red blood cell AK1 leads to a lack of this enzyme's activity, resulting in congenital non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia and, in some cases, psychomotor retardation. Multiple pathogenic variants have been identified in the AK1 gene, including novel homozygous and heterozygous mutations. While profound AK deficiency is linked to hemolysis, some individuals with severe deficiency may not exhibit evidence of hemolysis, possibly due to metabolic compensation or interaction with other erythrocyte defects. Co-occurring conditions like thalassemia can also contribute to severe hemolytic anemia. [PMC12031993, PMC10056885, PMC9066714, PMC8317388, PMC1129224]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of adenylate kinase (AK) deficiency is based on low erythrocyte AK enzymatic activity and the identification of mutations in the AK1 gene. Molecular studies employ whole-exome sequencing or targeted next-generation sequencing to detect genetic variants, which are subsequently confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Bioinformatics tools are utilized to predict the pathogenicity of identified variants. Hematological and biochemical testing may also be performed. Prenatal diagnosis can be achieved through molecular testing of amniotic fluid or chronic villus samples. Next-generation sequencing is also suggested for newborn to early childhood screening. [PMC12031993, PMC9066714, PMC8317388, PMC1129224]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: When evaluating hemolytic anemia, other causes should be considered, even in the presence of adenylate kinase (AK) deficiency. Thalassemia, a common monogenic inherited disease causing hemolytic anemia due to defective hemoglobin synthesis, can co-occur with AK-1 gene variants and contribute to severe anemia. Furthermore, in individuals with severe erythrocyte AK deficiency, the cause of hemolysis may not always be solely attributed to AK deficiency; possibilities include an unrelated enzyme deficiency or other erythrocyte defect, or an interaction of another unidentified defect with AK deficiency. [PMC12031993, PMC1129224]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis for adenylate kinase deficiency is feasible through molecular genetic testing. This involves analyzing samples such as amniotic fluid or chorionic villus, with one case reporting chorionic villus sampling at 11 weeks of gestation. Techniques like whole-exome sequencing or targeted next-generation sequencing, confirmed by Sanger sequencing, are employed to identify pathogenic variants in the AK-1 gene. Such diagnostic approaches provide crucial information for family planning and prenatal counseling, particularly in families with identified AK-1 gene mutations. [PMC12031993, PMC8317388]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Adenylate kinase deficiency is an extremely rare autosomal recessive genetic disorder, making genetic counseling crucial for family planning and antenatal screening. Molecular investigations utilize whole-exome sequencing or targeted next-generation sequencing to identify pathogenic variants in the AK-1 gene, with confirmation by Sanger sequencing. Prenatal diagnosis can be performed through analysis of amniotic fluid during the second pregnancy or by molecular testing of a chorionic villus sample collected at 11 weeks of gestation. This allows for the identification of homozygous mutations in affected individuals and heterozygosity in parents and fetuses, providing valuable information for families, especially in cases with co-occurring conditions like thalassemia. [PMC12031993, PMC8317388]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Regular blood transfusion therapy has been reported as an effective management strategy for patients with hemolytic anemia due to adenylate kinase deficiency. In one case, a patient with severe hemolytic anemia recovered following regular blood transfusion therapy. [PMC9066714]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Hemolytic anemia due to adenylate kinase deficiency is associated with moderate to severe congenital nonspherocytic hemolytic anemia. It can also be linked to mental and psychomotor retardation, though this is noted as occurring in exceptional cases or in a limited number of reported patients. Individuals may present with severe hemolytic anemia and psychomotor retardation, but the anemia component can recover with regular blood transfusion therapy. Notably, some individuals with severe enzyme deficiency may not exhibit hemolysis, indicating variability in clinical presentation. Specific mutations may also be related to the neuropathogenicity observed in some patients. [PMC12031993, PMC9066714, PMC8317388, PMC1129224]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare group of lethal skeletal dysplasias characterized by an endochondral ossification deficiency that leads to dwarfism with extreme micromelia, a small thorax, a prominent abdomen, anasarca and polyhydramnios. There are three types of achondrogenesis that exist and that differ clinically, radiologically, histologically and genetically: achondrogensis type 1a, type 1b and type 2.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Achondrogenesis encompasses lethal skeletal dysplasias. Achondrogenesis type I is a severe, lethal form that appears to be inherited as an autosomal recessive disorder, with death occurring shortly after birth. Achondrogenesis type II is also a lethal skeletal dysplasia, caused by dominant pathogenic variants in COL2A1, which can arise de novo. Achondrogenesis 1B is another lethal phenotype, resulting from pathogenic variants in the SLC26A2/DTDST gene, often involving biallelic mutations. [PMC9843583, PMC8467821, PMC1801144, PMC1715601, PMC1546042]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Pathogenic variants in the SLC26A2/DTDST gene cause the following spectrum of phenotypes: achondrogenesis 1B (ACG1B), atelosteogenesis 2 (AO2), diastrophic dysplasia (DTD), and recessive-multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (rMED), the first 2 being lethal. Here, a cohort and a comprehensive literature review on a genotype-phenotype correlation of SLC26A2/DTDST -related disorders. The local patients were genotyped by Sanger sequencing or next-generation sequencing (NGS). We reviewed data from the literature regarding phenotype, zygosity, and genotype in parallel. The local cohort enrolled 12 patients, including one with a Desbuquois-like phenotype. All but one showed biallelic mutations, however, only one allele mutated in a fetus presenting ACG1B was identified. The literature review identified 42 articles and the analyses of genotype and zygosity included the 12 local patients. Discussion:... [PMC9843583, PMC8467821, PMC1136723, PMC1918434, PMC1715601]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Achondrogenesis encompasses several lethal skeletal dysplasias with distinct genetic etiologies. Achondrogenesis type IB (ACG1B) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by pathogenic variants in the SLC26A2/DTDST gene, leading to a defect in sulfate activation and impaired synthesis of sulfated proteoglycans. Achondrogenesis type II (ACG2) is caused by dominant pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene. These mutations often involve glycine substitutions, such as aspartate for glycine at position 310, or splicing variants like c.1267-2_1269del, which result in abnormal, poorly secreted, or in-frame deleted type II collagen. The Langer-Saldino variant of achondrogenesis, a type I form, is characterized by nonexpression of cartilage type II collagen. Achondrogenesis type I is generally inherited as an autosomal recessive trait. [PMC9843583, PMC8467821, PMC1136723, PMC1918434, PMC1715601]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Achondrogenesis involves a combination of clinical, radiological, and pathological assessments. Genetic testing is a primary method, utilizing techniques such as Sanger sequencing and next-generation sequencing (NGS) of fetal or genomic DNA to identify pathogenic variants in genes like COL2A1 (for type II) and SLC26A2/DTDST (for type IB). PCR amplification, sequence analysis, allele-specific PCR, and heteroduplex analysis are also employed for genetic characterization. Biochemical and cellular analyses contribute to diagnosis, including studies of cartilage extracts for proteoglycan content, analysis of sulfate metabolism in fibroblast cultures (a potential diagnostic tool for type IB), and assessment of collagen alpha-chains and CNBr-peptides. Histological and ultrastructural studies of cartilage, often with electron microscopy and immunohistologic staining for collagen, provide further characterization. [PMC9843583, PMC8467821, PMC1136723, PMC1801144, PMC1918434]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Achondrogenesis requires differentiation from a spectrum of skeletal dysplasias. Achondrogenesis type 1B (ACG1B) is caused by SLC26A2/DTDST gene variants, which also lead to atelosteogenesis 2 (AO2), diastrophic dysplasia (DTD), and recessive-multiple epiphyseal dysplasia (rMED), with ACG1B and AO2 being lethal. Achondrogenesis type II (ACG2) is caused by dominant pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene. COL2A1 defects are also associated with a continuum of chondrodysplasias including hypochondrogenesis (a milder form), spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia congenita (SEDC), Kniest dysplasia, and Stickler syndrome. The severity of COL2A1-related phenotypes, such as ACG2 versus hypochondrogenesis, can correlate with the mutation's location. Specific variants like Langer-Saldino achondrogenesis, characterized by non-expression of type II collagen, may be considered chondrogenesis imperfecta. Familial cases of Achondrogenesis type I with atypical features may represent distinct subvariants. [PMC9843583, PMC8467821, PMC1136723, PMC1801144, PMC1715601]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of achondrogenesis is possible through genetic analysis. For Achondrogenesis type II (ACG2), dominant pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene can be identified in fetal DNA using next-generation sequencing (NGS), with de novo variants confirmed by parental testing. Other like denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis and dideoxynucleotide sequencing can also detect COL2A1 mutations. For Achondrogenesis type IB (ACG1B), pathogenic variants in the SLC26A2/DTDST gene can be identified in a fetus via Sanger sequencing or NGS. Additionally, a sulfation defect, characterized by impaired sulfated proteoglycan synthesis and reduced sulfate activation compounds in cultured fibroblasts, may offer a diagnostic tool for ACG1B. [PMC9843583, PMC8467821, PMC1136723, PMC1918434]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Achondrogenesis is a genetically heterogeneous group of lethal skeletal dysplasias. Achondrogenesis type I, including types IA and IB, is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait, with type IB linked to biallelic pathogenic variants in the SLC26A2/DTDST gene. A sulfation defect in cultured fibroblasts may serve as a diagnostic tool for type IB. In contrast, achondrogenesis type II is caused by dominant pathogenic variants in the COL2A1 gene, with many cases arising de novo. The specific mutation in COL2A1, such as the position of glycine substitutions or the size and location of in-frame deletions, can influence phenotype severity. Genetic testing, including next-generation sequencing, is used to identify these variants, and understanding the inheritance pattern is crucial for family counseling and prenatal diagnosis. [PMC9843583, PMC8467821, PMC1136723, PMC1801144, PMC1918434]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Achondrogenesis is a lethal or perinatally lethal condition. Achondrogenesis type I, type IB, and type II are consistently described as lethal skeletal dysplasias. Specific pathogenic variants, such as those in SLC26A2/DTDST (e.g., V340del, G663R, T512K in homozygosity, or p.R178*, p.K575Sfs*10) and dominant variants in COL2A1, are associated with lethal phenotypes. Death often occurs shortly after birth, frequently due to severe pulmonary hypoplasia. The location of mutations, such as glycine substitutions in the N-terminal region of the type II collagen molecule, can lead to more severe, lethal phenotypes. [PMC9843583, PMC8467821, PMC1136723, PMC1918434, PMC1715601]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare non-syndromic urogenital tract malformation characterized by improper development of the vas deferens leading to male infertility.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Congenital bilateral agenesis of vas deferens; Congenital bilateral aplasia of vas deferens

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Congenital bilateral absence of vas deferens (CBAVD) affects about 1/1,000 males. It is found in 98% of males with cystic fibrosis and accounts for 6-8% of cases of obstructive azoospermia. In about 50% of cases, the CBAVD is associated with the absence of the seminal vesicles. Unilateral renal agenesis is detected in 5-10% of patients with CBAVD, while is present in 5-40% of congenital unilateral absence of vase deferens (ipsilateral).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: CBAVD is usually diagnosed in adult men, either during systematic assessment of cystic fibrosis (CF) or during assessment of isolated infertility (azoospermia). Infertile patients with CBAVD produce small volumes of acidic sperm (< 1 ml with a pH < 7.0). The latter is non-pathognomonic and more common when the seminal vesicles are also absent. CBAVD frequently coexists with kidney anomalies and other comorbidities.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In 1990, mutations in the CFTR gene (the causative gene for cystic fibrosis) were identified in 42% of patients in a population of infertile males with CBAVD, suggesting that CBAVD is a genital form of cystic fibrosis. Since then, an exhaustive analysis of the 27 exons of the CFTR gene has led to the classification of CBAVD patients into four groups: I) patients with two mutations in the CFTR gene (19%), II) patients with one mutation in the CFTR gene and having the IVS8-5T allele in the trans position (33%), III) patients with either a mutation in the CFTR gene or having the IVS8-5T allele (27%) and IV) patients with neither the IVS8-5T allele nor a mutation in the CFTR gene (21%).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of CBAVD is clinical. Traditionally, it was based on the absence of the intrascrotal portion of the vas deferens on palpation. The gold standard for diagnosis is scrotal and transrectal ultrasound, which also allows evaluation of the absence of the seminal vesicles. Abdominal ultrasound should be added to rule out a unilateral renal agenesis. Sperm analysis typically shows azoospermia, hypospermia (<1 ml) and acid pH (<7.0). Genetic testing can confirm the mutation in the CFTR gene.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other causes of azoospermia and obstruction of the seminal tract (e.g. injuries, infections, cysts, etc.).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: CBAVD patients with CFTR mutations should be informed of the increased risk to develop related diseases and transmit CF to their child. The risk is higher in patient without a solitary kidney. If an affected couple (the male partner is a carrier for a severe CFTR mutation) wishes to have a child with assisted reproductive technology (ART; i.e. surgical sperm retrieval and in vitro fertilization techniques), both partners should be offered genetic testing. If the female partner is not a carrier of one of the CFTR mutations, the risks of having a child affected by CF is <1/1000 (2.5 times higher than in the general population). If a mutation is detected in both partners, the risk of having a child with CF is 25%, and 50% if the mutation is on both alleles in one parent.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The diagnosis of CBAVD often has implications that go beyond the problem of infertility because of its potential association with renal anomalies and other clinical conditions related to CFTR mutations. Some patients with a CFTR mutation may later present mild CF symptoms such as recurrent respiratory tract infections and could benefit from referral to a pneumologist or CF center for management and follow-up. In the case of solitary kidney, the patient should be followed a nephrologist.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: CBAVD has no impact on life expectancy. Nevertheless, associated conditions (namely CF or other CFTR-related conditions) can potentially affect quality of life. If a solitary kidney is present, but renal function otherwise normal, quality of life is usually not impacted.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive cataracts, hearing loss, cerebellar ataxia, paranoid psychosis and dementia. Neuropathological features are diffuse atrophy of all parts of the brain, chronic diffuse encephalopathy and the presence of extremely thin and almost completely demyelinated cranial nerves.

Distal trisomy 17q is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome with variable phenotype principally characterized by intellectual disability, developmental delay, short stature, craniofacial dysmorphism (incl. microcephaly, low posterior hairline, frontal bossing, bitemporal narrowing, low-set and malformed ears, flat nasal bridge, long philtrum, wide mouth with downturned corners, thin upper lip) and a short, webbed neck, as well as skeletal anomalies (e.g. brachyrhizomelia, poly-/syndactyly) and joint hyperlaxity. Cardiac, cerebral, and urogenital anomalies are also frequently associated.

A rare, genetic proximal spinal muscular atrophy characterized by degeneration of alpha motor neurons in the anterior horns of the spinal cord and lower brain stem manifesting with onset between 6 to 18 months of age with progressive, proximal muscle weakness, mild to moderate hypotonia and finger polymyoclonour tremor, with areflexia. Motor milestones are classically limited to independent sitting or standing.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Intermediate spinal muscular atrophy; SMA type 2; SMA type II; SMA-II; SMA2

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: In Europe the average prevalence at birth of proximal spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) type 2 is estimated at 1/50,000. Worldwide the prevalence ranges from 1/11,00-175,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset occurs between the ages of 6 and 18 months. Classically, before the advent of the new therapies, affected children achieve sitting independently and may acquire standing but do not acquire independent walking. Progressive proximal muscle weakness is symmetrical and greater in the legs than the arms. Finger trembling is frequent. Scoliosis, joint contractures and ankyloses of the mandible are very common . Progressive respiratory muscle weakness can lead to restrictive lung disease. Cognition is normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is a result of degeneration and loss of the lower motor neurons in the spinal cord and the brain stem nuclei. Causal homozygous mutations/deletions in the SMN1 gene (5q12.2-q13.3) are responsible. SMN1 encodes the survival motor neuron protein (SMN) which is known to participate in critical pathways related to RNA processing and transport, and it is believed that motor neurons are particularly vulnerable to impairments in these processes. Modifier genes include SMN2 (5q13.2), a homologous centromeric copy of SMN1, and NAIP (5q13.1), encoding neuronal apoptosis inhibitory protein. The number of copies of the SMN2 is inversely correlated to disease severity.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The disease is suspected based on clinical history and examination. The gold standard in diagnosis is genetic testing of SMN1 deletion/mutation and, if possible, SMN copy number testing. Muscle biopsy and electromyography should not be performed in patients with typical presentation.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include, congenital muscular dystrophies, congenital myopathies, congenital myasthenic syndromes, neuromuscular junction disease (botulism), and carbohydrate metabolism disorders (glycogen storage disease due to acid maltase deficiency).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible through molecular analysis of amniocytes or chorionic villus cells.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive but around 2% of cases are caused by de novo mutations. Genetic counseling should be offered to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Symptomatic management is multidisciplinary and aims to improve quality of life. Assisted airway clearance and non-invasive ventilations are helpful. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy are recommended to prevent scoliosis, maintain joint mobility and promote function and mobility. Antibiotic therapy is required in case of pulmonary infection. The scoliosis may require a corset/back brace for support, and almost invariably needs surgical correction. In the last few years, nusinersen, an antisense oligonucleotide, has been approved and made available for treatment of all SMA types in Europe and the USA. Clinical trials and real world data have shown that it improves motor function in type 2 patients, with a number of patients achieving walking. The best results are seen following early intervention and in presymptomatic patients. Risdiplam (a small molecule) has a also recently, successfully completed a clinical trials and has become commercially available in US and for compassionate use in Europe. Clinical trials are ongoing to identify other potential drug treatments.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy for affected individuals is variable but, with the new standards of care, particularly for respiratory insufficiency, the majority of patients survive up to adulthood.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Posterior column ataxia - retinitis pigmentosa is characterized by the association of progressive sensory ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Autosomal recessive posterior column ataxia and retinitis pigmentosa; PCARP

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Around 20 cases have been described in the last 50 years.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset of symptoms usually occurs in childhood. The clinical picture is progressive, homogenous and includes severe sensory ataxia, proprioceptive loss (affecting the iliac crest, upper limbs and thorax), generalized areflexia and diffuse pigmentary retinopathy leading to blindness. Scoliosis, camptodactyly, achalasia and/or gastrointestinal motility dysfunction may also be present.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is associated with degeneration of the posterior column of the spinal cord. The causative gene, FLVCR1 (1q32.3), has been identified and localized to the AXPC1 locus (1q32-q31).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive or pseudodominant.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The disease evolves progressively, in some cases leading to a total loss of walking ability and vision after 10 to 30 years of progression.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of posterior column ataxia-retinitis pigmentosa syndrome (PCARP) is associated with homozygous variants in the FLVCR1 gene. Genetic testing for FLVCR1 variants can identify individuals with the syndrome. Specific intronic splice-site variants in FLVCR1 have been linked to the absence of posterior column degeneration, providing valuable prognostic information and helping to differentiate clinical presentations, such as non-syndromic retinitis pigmentosa. [PMC5841564]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Posterior column ataxia-retinitis pigmentosa syndrome (PCARP) is associated with homozygous variants in FLVCR1. However, a specific splice-site variant (c.1092 + 5G>A) in FLVCR1 has been identified that causes non-syndromic retinitis pigmentosa without evidence of posterior column ataxia or cerebellar degeneration. This suggests that not all FLVCR1 variants lead to the full PCARP phenotype, and isolated retinal degeneration can occur, which is a key consideration in differential diagnosis and prognostication. [PMC5841564]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: For patients presenting with retinal degeneration as the sole clinical manifestation due to specific FLVCR1 variants, gene therapy approaches are suggested as a potential therapeutic strategy. Specifically, adeno-associated viral vectors with sub-retinal delivery may represent an approach to halting retinal degeneration in this patient group. [PMC5841564]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cystoid macular dystrophy is an autosomal dominantly inherited cystoid macular edema manifesting with macular atrophy, strabismus and, sometimes, pericentral retinitis pigmentosa. It is associated with a poor visual prognosis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Autosomal dominant cystoid macular edema; DCMD; Familial macular edema

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An intermediate form of lichen myxedematosus (LM) (a form of mucin dermal deposit) which does not meet the criteria for either scleromyxedema or the localized form. Three clinical subtypes have been described and include scleromyxedema without monoclonal gammopathy; localized forms with monoclonal gammopathy and/or systemic symptoms; localized forms with mixed features of the 5 subtypes of localized LM (discrete form, acral persistent papular mucinosis, self-healing papular mucinosis, papular mucinosis of infancy, and a pure nodular form). The course of atypical LM is unpredictable because only a few cases have been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Lichen myxedematosus is classified as a rare group of cutaneous mucinosis. Scleromyxedema, an uncommon, chronic connective tissue disorder and a generalized form of lichen myxedematosus, also exhibits significant rarity. This inherent rarity severely limits the availability of comprehensive epidemiological data, making it challenging to accurately assess its prevalence and incidence. [PMC12318666, PMC7007042]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Scleromyxedema is an uncommon, chronic connective tissue disorder with an obscure etiology. It is distinguished by fibromyxoid skin lesions and elevated serum monoclonal immunoglobulin levels. The condition's rarity limits epidemiological data, making prevalence and incidence assessment difficult. Herein, we detail a clinical case of scleromyxedema, encompassing diagnosis and treatment, to augment medical understanding of this rare entity. The aim of is to delve into the complexities of diagnosing scleromyxedema, encompassing its diverse clinical presentations, with the goal of refining diagnostic acumen and expediting the identification process. This, in turn, mitigates the risks associated with diagnostic delays. DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Atypical lichen myxedematosus is part of the heterogeneous group of cutaneous mucinoses, characterized by excess mucin deposition in the dermis. Differential diagnosis should include other forms of lichen myxedematosus, particularly the generalized form known as scleromyxedema. Scleromyxedema is a chronic connective tissue disorder distinguished by fibromyxoid skin lesions and elevated serum monoclonal immunoglobulin levels, presenting with diverse clinical manifestations. Accurate diagnosis is essential to differentiate these conditions and mitigate risks associated with diagnostic delays. [PMC12318666, PMC7007042]

This, in turn, mitigates the risks associated with diagnostic delays. Moreover, the imperative of instituting pertinent therapeutic measures is highlighted as a fundamental aspect of patient management, underscoring the significance of a... [PMC12318666, PMC7007042]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Cutaneous mucinoses are a heterogeneous group of dermatoses in which excess deposition of mucin in the dermis gives the skin a waxy appearance, with papules and plaques that can vary from self-healing mucinosis to even disrupting the normal shape of a patient's face, conferring a leonine facies, or be part of life threatening diseases like scleromyxedema. will describe the most recent classification on lichen myxedematosus in the generalized (scleromyxedema) and the localized forms, as well as the different organ systems involved in scleromyxedema, diagnostic workup, current management, and prognosis. [PMC7007042]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Schnitzler syndrome is a rare, underdiagnosed disorder in adults characterized by recurrent febrile rash, bone and/or joint pain, enlarged lymph nodes, fatigue, a monoclonal IgM component, leukocytosis and systemic inflammatory response.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Chronic urticaria with gammopathy; Chronic urticaria with macroglobulinemia

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown and about 150 cases have been reported, primarily in Europe.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: There is a slight male predominance and mean age of disease onset is 51 years. Time to diagnosis often exceeds 5 years. The first clinical sign is usually a mildly or non-pruritic skin rash. Elementary lesions are rose or red macules or slightly elevated plaques, which resolve within 24 hours. Lesions can occur on every body part, though involvement of face and extremities is rare. The frequency and duration of flares are variable. Almost all patients develop intermittent fever and body temperature can rise above 40°C. Fever is usually well tolerated and chills are rare. About 80% of patients experience bone and/or joint pain. Bone involvement is common, and 30 to 40% of patients show bone lesions on imaging studies. IgM levels can remain stable or progressively increase at a rate of about 0.5 to 1 g/L/year. Other signs include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), inflammatory anemia sometimes with thrombocytosis (up to 50 % of cases), palpable lymph nodes (45%), and hepatic or splenic enlargement (30%). The monoclonal IgM component is a defining feature of the disease. Inflammatory AA amyloidosis may be a serious complication. The disease follows a chronic course.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Etiology remains unclear but the syndrome is probably an acquired auto-inflammatory disorder. It shares many features with genetically determined auto-inflammatory diseases.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on a combination of clinical, laboratory and radiological findings and on exclusion of another cause. Histopathological skin findings are noteworthy showing a neutrophilic infiltrate of the dermis, without vasculitis and without significant edema, characteristic of neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis. An immediate and marked response to anakinra treatment is supportive of the diagnosis. The initial work-up should include an examination of bone marrow, immunoelectrophoresis of serum and urinary proteins, and determination of immunoglobulin subtypes. The two latter examinations can then be used for follow-up on a biannual basis. Lymph nodes should be biopsied when they are enlarged.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes adult-onset Still's disease, hypocomplementic urticarial vasculitis, cryoglobulinemia, hyper IgD syndrome, and acquired C1 inhibitor deficiency.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Some treatments provide only incomplete and/or transient improvement or control of symptoms (steroids, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, colchicine, dapsone, peflacine, phototherapy) while others are mostly ineffective (anti-histamines, rituximab, intravenous immunoglobulins, TNF-blocking agents, immunosuppressive drugs). In contrast, the IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra relieves all symptoms within hours after the first injection. Injection-site reactions are frequent with anakinra and sometimes severe, and can be a real concern. The neutrophil count must be monitored.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The overall prognosis depends on the development of lymphoproliferative complications such as lymphoma, IgM myeloma or Waldenström's disease. Although these complications have only been reported in about 20% of cases, their incidence may be higher since they generally develop more than 10 to 20 years after the first signs of the syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Schnitzler syndrome is primarily considered an acquired autoinflammatory disorder, generally without a monogenic abnormality. Whole exome sequencing in some patients has not identified causative pathogenic mutations associated with monogenic autoinflammatory diseases. While the syndrome typically lacks evidence of gene divergence causing abnormal inflammasome activation, mutations in MEFV and MYD88 genes, including MYD88 L265P, can be associated with its development. Additionally, novel variants in MEFV and F2 genes have been noted for their potential pathogenic role in some cases. However, the provided abstracts do not offer information regarding inheritance patterns or specific genetic counseling recommendations. [PMC11810973, PMC11765222, PMC10097979, PMC9876706, PMC9065412]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurodegenerative disorder characterized by early-onset cerebellar ataxia, a pyramidal syndrome and peripheral neuropathy.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Autosomal recessive spastic ataxia type 6; ARSACS; SPAX6

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It was initially described in the Charlevoix-Saguenay region of Quebec where incidence of autosomal recessive spastic ataxia of Charlevoix-Saguenay (ARSACS) at birth has been estimated at 1 in 1,932. The incidence and prevalence worldwide remain unknown but ARSACS is now considered one of the more common recessive ataxias worldwide with cases described in several countries including Turkey, Japan, the Netherlands, Italy, Belgium, France, Spain and more than 20 other countries.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: ARSACS is a slowly progressive disease with variable clinical presentation. The age of onset in non-Quebec patients is variable (ranging from late infantile, juvenile to early-adult onset) but in individuals from Quebec, onset occurs between 12 and 18 months of age with gait disturbance and walking difficulties. Other early signs of cerebellar ataxia include upper limbs incoordination, dysarthria and nystagmus. The pyramidal syndrome is characterized by lower limbs spasticity, brisk patellar tendon reflexes and the Babinski sign. Onset of the peripheral neuropathy generally occurs later and leads to absence of the Achilles tendon reflex, distal amyotrophy, pes cavus and deep sensory disturbances (impaired vibration sense). Retinal hypermyelination (without vision loss) is a constant feature in ARSACS patients from Quebec but may be absent in patients from other countries. Cognitive impairments related to cerebellar involvement have been documented. Other manifestations may include spasms, lower limb neuropathic pain and bladder dysfunction.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: ARSACS is caused by autosomal recessive mutations in the SACS gene (13q11), which encodes a large protein of partially known function named sacsin.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of ARSACS is established by molecular genetic testing. Clinical diagnosis relies on the results of neurophysiological data (signs of both axonal and demyelinating neuropathy, with nerve conduction studies revealing loss of sensory nerve conduction and reduced motor conduction velocities). MRI brain revealed superior cerebellar vermian atrophy and T2 linear ''striped'' hypointensities in pons. Retinal examination may also be useful for diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other autosomal recessive ataxias, such as Friedreich ataxia, ataxia with vitamin E deficiency (AVED), Abetalipoproteinemia and hereditary forms of spastic paraplegia, in particular spastic paraplegia type 7, spastic paraplegia type 30 and spastic paraplegia type 20 (SPG20-Troyer syndrome).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible for at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) by genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic aiming towards improving motor control, decreasing spasticity and should include a rehabilitation team approach that includes physiotherapy, occupational therapy and pharmacotherapy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Most patients become wheelchair-dependent by the fifth decade of life. Death generally occurs during the sixth decade but survival into the seventies has been reported.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Sheehan syndrome is a rare, acquired, pituitary hormone deficiency disorder resulting from pituitary necrosis following peri- or postpartum hemorrhage characterized by various symptoms depending on resulting hormone decrease (e.g. failure or difficulty with lactation, oligo- or amenorrhea, hot flashes, decreased libido, weakness, fatigue, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, dizziness, decreased muscle mass, adrenal crisis). Secondary hypothyroidism and secondary adrenal insufficiency may also be presenting signs.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Sheehan syndrome, a rare but potentially serious complication, from ischemic pituitary necrosis following severe postpartum hemorrhage. While its incidence has decreased in developed countries, it remains a prevalent cause of hypopituitarism and a substantial contributor to morbidity and mortality among childbearing women in developing and low-to-middle-income nations. Diagnosis is frequently delayed for many years, often decades, due to the nonspecific, subtle, and gradually progressive nature of symptoms. Although typically diagnosed years postpartum, acute Sheehan syndrome is rare and can present as a life-threatening event with varied manifestations within days to weeks after delivery. [PMC11866701, PMC12228954, PMC11398623, PMC10668181, PMC9411080]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Sheehan syndrome (SS) from pituitary necrosis due to severe postpartum hemorrhage, causing partial or complete anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies. Classic symptoms include agalactorrhea and amenorrhea, but presentations are varied and often delayed for decades due to nonspecific symptoms like fatigue, anhedonia, cold intolerance, hair loss, hypotension, and chronic hyponatremia. Patients may develop central adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, or growth hormone deficiency. Acute manifestations can include adrenal crisis, diabetes insipidus, rhabdomyolysis with acute renal failure, seizures, or coma. Rare complications reported include dilated cardiomyopathy, valvular insufficiency, massive pericardial effusion, and ventricular tachycardia. Imaging often reveals an empty sella or pituitary infarction. [PMC12307206, PMC11866701, PMC11561923, PMC12228954, PMC11398623]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Sheehan syndrome is primarily caused by ischemic pituitary necrosis or infarction, typically resulting from severe postpartum hemorrhage. This extensive bleeding often leads to hypotension during the peripartum period, which reduces blood flow to the physiologically enlarged pituitary gland, causing cell damage and death. While most cases are linked to postpartum hemorrhage, some patients may develop Sheehan syndrome without hemorrhage, suggesting other "various reasons" for avascular necrosis of the anterior pituitary. [PMC12307206, PMC11866701, PMC11561923, PMC12228954, PMC11398623]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Sheehan's syndrome can present with non-specific symptoms such as fatigue, gastrointestinal disturbances, cold intolerance, hair loss, and severe apathy, which may lead to misdiagnosis as psychogenic disorders. It is also a cause of chronic hyponatremia and hypopituitarism, necessitating differentiation from other etiologies of these conditions. Clinicians should maintain a high suspicion for Sheehan's syndrome when evaluating alternative causes of hypoosmolar hyponatremia, especially if unresponsive to rehydration therapy. Furthermore, rapid correction of hyponatremia in Sheehan's patients can precipitate osmotic demyelination syndrome, which requires careful management and distinction from other neurological conditions. [PMC11561923, PMC12228954]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Sheehan syndrome is primarily managed with hormone replacement therapy, including hydrocortisone or methylprednisolone, levothyroxine, and desmopressin for diabetes insipidus, to address pituitary hormone deficiencies. A multidisciplinary approach is essential for comprehensive care, focusing on both underlying hormonal imbalances and acute complications. Symptomatic treatment is a main approach, with specific interventions like MitraClip considered for severe cardiac complications such as mitral valve regurgitation. Meticulous management of chronic hyponatremia is also critical to prevent complications like osmotic demyelination syndrome. Timely and appropriate treatment is vital to improve quality of life and prevent fatal outcomes. [PMC12307206, PMC11866701, PMC11561923, PMC11398623, PMC10668181]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare respiratory malformation characterized by a hamartomatous mass of non-functioning lung tissue of variable extent and with variable degrees of cystic or adenomatoid change. Clinical presentation, prognosis, and presence of associated abnormalities depend on the subtype of the lesion. Based on histopathological findings, five subtypes (types 0 to 4) can be differentiated.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CCAM; CPAM; Congenital cystic adenomatoid malformation of the lung; Congenital cystic adenomatous malformation of the lung; Congenital cystic disease of the lung

DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: The aim was to evaluate the prenatal course, postnatal outcome and diagnostic accuracy of fetuses with a prenatal diagnosis of isolated congenital lung anomalies (iCLA). A retrospective cohort is described from the Amsterdam UMC between January 2007 and January 2022. The CPAM volume ratio (CVR) was calculated. The concordance between prenatal diagnosis and lesion progression was compared to postnatal findings. Postnatal surgical interventions were reported. includes 113 prenatal cases of iCLA. Ten percent (10/100 cases with available CVR) progressed into high-risk lesions (CVR > 1.6), with a negative impact on survival. In total, 108 (95.6%) cases resulted in live birth. Acute respiratory distress was observed in 6.5% (7/108). During postnatal follow-up, the lesion was still detectable in 10/15 (66.7%) cases in which complete regression was seen prenatally. Fifty percent (54/108) of the... [PMC12127225, PMC12233821, PMC11963009, PMC11941308, PMC11379336]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An inherited disorder of angiogenesis characterized by mucocutaneous telangiectases and visceral arteriovenous malformations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is approximately 1/6,000
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The most common clinical signs of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) include recurrent epistaxis (nosebleeds), frequently from childhood, and cutaneous or mucosal telangiectases generally presenting later, and increasing with age, where anemia may become an important part of the disease. Visceral arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) are usually asymptomatic but can lead to complications that produce highly variable manifestations. The age of onset of AVM-related complications is variable, ranging from childhood to geriatric age, with a few cases reported during the neonatal period. Pulmonary AVMs may manifest with brain abscesses, strokes, transient ischemic attacks, signs of chronic hypoxaemia or, rarely, haemorrhagic rupture. AVMs of the central nervous system can be haemorrhagic or, rarely, produce signs of slow compression. Hepatic AVMs, which can remain latent for a long time, in a limited proportion of patients become severe leading to high-output cardiac failure, portal hypertension, pulmonary hypertension or ischemic cholangitis. Hemorrhagic digestive telangiectases increase with age and can worsen chronic anemia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: This genetic disorder is due to pathogenic variants primarily in ENG (9q34.11) or ACVRL1 (12q13.13), encoding proteins involved in vascular development and angiogenic homeostasis of capillaries. Mutations in SMAD4 (18q21.2) occur in rare cases (1-3%) and result in HHT associated with juvenile polyposis. In a small proportion of HHT families, the pathogenic gene variant has not yet been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is clinical and/or molecular. The clinical diagnosis is based on having at least three of the four Curaçao criteria: recurrent epistaxis, cutaneous/mucosal telangiectases, visceral involvement, and a first line family member with HHT. Genetic testing can be used to screen, to confirm a diagnosis, or to rule out the diagnosis if the pathogenic variant is known in the family.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis, digestive angiodysplasias, isolated sporadic AVMs in the lungs, liver and brain, other vascular anomaly syndromes that cause AVMs; benign hereditary telangiectasia; and other causes of recurrent epistaxis (coagulation disorders or other local nasal factors).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal genetic testing is possible in families where the pathogenic variant has been identified in the family, but is not necessary for proper pregnancy and delivery management. Decisions about prenatal genetic testing are the choice of the parents, but discussion of all related issues is appropriate. The usual antenatal scans will be offered, and sonographers aware of the presence of HHT in the family will detect most major AVMs.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant. Penetrance is age dependent, the majority having symptoms before 50 years of age. The phenotype is highly variable, even between members of the same family.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Disease management includes prevention and treatment of epistaxis and anaemia, screening for AVMs, and guidance regarding pregnancy-related issues. The management of pulmonary AVM(s) relies on early detection, occlusion where feasible, and ongoing care in cases of persistent pulmonary AVMs. For severe liver involvement, multidisciplinary patient assessment in a center with expertise in HHT is recommended. Usually, cerebral AVMs that have not bled are not treated, whereas cerebral AVMs that have already bled or have become symptomatic usually require treatment. Gastrointestinal telangiectases may sometimes be the cause of significant anemia, especially in older patients, and need specific management. Awareness of the possibility of AVMs/HHT is important for optimal management of diverse medical states. HHT due to a SMAD4 pathogenic variant requires polyposis screening and aortic follow up.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy is reduced in unscreened patients. In patients assessed and treated for pulmonary AVMs in an HHT Center, life expectancy is comparable to the general population. Pregnancy-related death has been reported, and is a particular risk for women with pulmonary arteriovenous malformations.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, hereditary nephrotic syndrome characterized by proteinuria, hypoalbuminemia, edema, and hyperlipidemia, with an absence of response to an initial trial of corticosteroids (i.e. steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome; SRNS) and a generally complicated course.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Familial idiopathic steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome; Hereditary SRNS; Monogenic SRNS; Isolated SRNS; Genetic SRNS; Genetic FSGS
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset: Adolescent, Adult, Antenatal, Childhood, Infancy, Neonatal

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The annual incidence is 1/ 200,000- 500,000 children.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset may occur anywhere between birth and adulthood but predominantly presents in younger populations. The nephrotic syndrome is defined by severe proteinuria (Urinary Protein/Creatinine ration > 200 mg/mmol) with low serum albumin (<30 g/l) and possible edema. Biopsy shows minimal change disease (MCD), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) or, more rarely, diffuse mesangial sclerosis (DMS), and podocyte foot process effacement by electron microscopy. It is multi-drug resistant and usually progresses to end-stage kidney failure; however, patients have a very low risk of recurrence after kidney transplantation.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Causative pathogenic variants are identified in approximately 10-15% of young adults presenting with SRNS, 30% of children and at least 66% in congenital and infantile cases. Among these genes, NPHS1 (19q13.12) and NPHS2 (1q25.2) are by far the two main autosomal recessive genes implicated in SRNS while INF2 (14q32.33) and WT1 (11p13) are the leading cause of autosomal dominant SRNS. COQ8B (19q13.2) biallelic variants are commonly found in patients of Asian descent. So far, more than 60 single gene causes of SRNS have been reported, however most novel gene variants are rare and involve few families.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Comprehensive gene panels to include all currently known SRNS genes; alternatively cascade testing starting with screening for pathogenic variants in NPHS2 and WT1, the most commonly mutated genes in children, can be performed at the initial stage and if negative expanded to large next generation sequencing based test.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: A number of hereditary renal disorders might present with persistent proteinuria, the hallmark of SRNS. These include defects in ciliary (eg. TTC21B) or tubular (eg. CLCN5, Dent disease) genes or atypical hemolytical syndrome (DGKE). There is also a number of syndromic (i.e. multiorgan) forms associated with defects in WT1, LMX1B, LAMB2, PAX2, etc.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: The decision regarding preimplantation genetic diagnosis and prenatal genetic testing should be discussed with the family in light of the local financial, social, and legal settings.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Recurrence risk counseling should be provided in all cases. Family members who are candidates for living-related kidney donation have to undergo genetic testing as part of evaluation; only heterozygous carriers of a recessive SRNS genetic variant may be considered as a potential donor, while a family member having a variant associated with a dominant inheritance should be dissuaded from kidney donation.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: International Pediatric Nephrology Association 2020 guidelines recommend discontinuing ineffective immunosuppressive therapies, and continuing non -immunosuppressive management, including RAASi and other supportive measures in patients with diagnosis of a hereditary nephrotic syndrome. There is high risk of progression to end-stage kidney disease; however, recurrence of the disease in the grafted kidney after transplantation is exceptional.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy is not dramatically affected in SRNS patients, however individual outcome depends on prompt management and access to specific procedures, i.e. dialysis and kidney transplantation.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal anomaly defined by the presence of three copies of chromosome 8 in some cells of the body, and clinically characterized by facial dysmorphism, typically deep palmar and plantar creases, mild intellectual deficit and joint, urinary, cardiac and skeletal anomalies.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Warkany syndrome; Trisomy 8 mosaicism; Mosaic trisomy chromosome 8

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Historically, the birth prevalence was estimated between 1/25,000-50,000 but supporting epidemiological studies are lacking. Males are more frequently affected than females (sex-ratio 4:1).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Facial dysmorphic features are mild and include elongation of the skull (scaphocephaly), prominent forehead, hypertelorism, deeply set eyes (50%), bulbous upturned nose (60%), micrognathia (with everted lower lips), large dysplastic ears with prominent anthelices and large lobules. Additional features include: agenesis of the corpus callosum, highly arched or cleft palate (8%), short and broad neck, tall stature, elongated narrow chest, shoulders and pelvis. Urinary (hydronephrosis, ureteral reflux), and cardiac and large vessels abnormalities are frequent (40% and 25% respectively). Camptodactyly (70%), arthrogryposis of the joints (aggravating with time), deep palmar (in infants) and plantar furrows (75%), absent or hypoplastic patellae, vertebral malformations (65%: segmentation anomalies, costal anomalies, scoliosis), epilepsy, as well as corneal opacity and strabismus are also commonly observed. Most individuals present a mild-to-moderate intellectual disability (IQ between 50 and 75), with some patients having normal intelligence. Usually speech is more delayed than other developmental domains. There is no correlation between the percentage of trisomic cells and the severity of the intellectual disability.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Mosaic trisomy 8 is the result of a post-zygotic event (error in chromosome segregation during mitosis in a fetus having a normal karyotype or due to spontaneous correction of trisomy 8). Complete trisomy 8 is due to an error in chromosome segregation during meiosis and often results in miscarriage during the first trimester. When, exceptionally, the fetus survives, it presents the same phenotype as mosaic trisomy. Patients with isochromosome 8p (tetrasomy of the short arm (p) of chromosome 8) have the same phenotype as patients with trisomy 8p.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on karyotype analysis or on detection of copy number variation by microarray or whole exome sequencing. In the latter case confirmation by karyotyping is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes non-specific syndromic intellectual disability.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound abnormalities (hydronephrosis, corpus callosum agenesis and increased nuchal fold) are occasionally observed. On the other hand, when mosaic trisomy 8 is detected without ultrasound abnormalities, this should be interpreted with care since confined placental mosaicism frequently occurs. Prenatal diagnosis should be considered in cases where one of the parents has a mosaic trisomy 8.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The origin of the mosaic trisomy 8 is either post-zygotic non-disjunction, i.e. a mitotic error in the fetus, or meiotic non-disjunction resulting in a full trisomy 8 karyotype with subsequently trisomy rescue by mitotic loss of a chromosome 8. Almost all cases occur sporadically, but genetic counseling should be offered to parents and the individuals themselves.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management requires a multidisciplinary approach. In some cases, cardiac surgery may be proposed.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Mosaic trisomy 8 seems to predispose to Wilms tumors, myelodysplasias and myeloid leukemia. Some mosaic trisomy 8 patients have had children. In absence of serious malformations, life expectancy is normal.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal trisomy, characterized by reduced fetal movements and intrauterine growth retardation, low birth weight, and multiple congenital anomalies. The latter include, amongst others, facial dysmorphism (like hypertelorism, cleft lip/palate, micrognathia, low hairline, and small, low-set, and posteriorly rotated ears), head circumference below average, deformities of the hands (camptodactyly) and feet, marked hypertrichosis, and anomalies of the brain, heart, and lungs. Lethality appears to depend on the degree of mosaicism.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: X-linked cone dysfunction syndrome with myopia
