Possible associated health issues (e.g. associated malformations) need to be addressed according to the genetic diagnosis. Hormone substitution is recommended at the time of puberty. Psychological support should also be offered to patients and their families in a specialized DSD-center. Infertility is an important management issue; however, pregnancy may be feasible through zygote egg donation.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With appropriate management, the risk of malignancy is low and the psychological and clinical outcome for patients is good.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hirschsprung disease-deafness-polydactyly syndrome is an extremely rare malformative association, described in only two siblings to date, characterized by Hirschsprung disease (defined by the presence of an aganglionic segment of variable extent in the terminal part of the colon that leads to symptoms of intestinal obstruction, including constipation and abdominal distension), polydactyly of hands and/or feet, unilateral renal agenesis, hypertelorism and congenital deafness. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1988.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Hirschsprung disease-hearing loss-polydactyly syndrome; Santos-Mateus-Leal syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: An association of Hirschsprung disease with polydactyly, unilateral renal agenesis, hypertelorism, and congenital deafness is described in sibs (brother and sister) of consanguineous parents. It is suggested that this might represent a new autosomal recessive syndrome. [PMC1015489]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hirschsprung disease-deafness-polydactyly syndrome is characterized by an association of Hirschsprung disease with polydactyly, unilateral renal agenesis, hypertelorism, and congenital deafness. This combination of features has been observed in siblings from consanguineous parents. [PMC1015489]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The syndrome is suggested to be an autosomal recessive condition. This is based on its occurrence in siblings (a brother and sister) born to consanguineous parents, who presented with Hirschsprung disease, polydactyly, unilateral renal agenesis, hypertelorism, and congenital deafness. This pattern of inheritance indicates that the condition is likely passed down through families in an autosomal recessive manner. [PMC1015489]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The syndrome is described in siblings born to consanguineous parents, suggesting an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. This implies that both parents are carriers of a mutated gene, and each child has a 25% chance of inheriting two copies of the mutated gene and developing the syndrome. [PMC1015489]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A malignant soft tissue tumor which develops from cells of striated muscle. It is the most common form of tumor found in children and adolescents.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The annual incidence is 1/170,000. In children younger than 15 years, the annual incidence is estimated at 1/244,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The median age of diagnosis is 5 years. Rhabdomyosarcoma can develop anywhere in the body, including in sites where striated muscle does not normally occur. The most frequent locations are: the head and neck (40%), including tumors of the orbit and para-meningeal tumors, the genitourinary tract (20%) including tumors in the bladder and/or prostate, in the uterus and vagina, para-testicular tumors, and tumors in the limbs (20%) and trunk (10%). Rhabdomyosarcoma has a high risk of local relapse, a high risk of local extension to lymph nodes and a lower risk of metastases. There are two main histological subtypes of rhabdomyosarcoma: embryonic (80% of cases) and alveolar (15-20% of cases). Clinically there is little difference between the two types. The alveolar form occurs more readily in the limbs, nearly never in the orbits and more frequently affects the lymph nodes.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The cause of rhabdomyosarcoma is unknown, but a translocation t(2;13) is very often associated with the alveolar type.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on positive muscular markers and immunohistochemistry. The evidence of a translocation t(2;13) leads to diagnosis of alveolar forms.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include small round cell tumors (lymphoma, neuroblastoma, Ewing sarcoma). It is possible to distinguish between tumors using immunohistochemistry. Some rhabdomyosarcomas are associated with a genetic predisposition to cancer as part of Li-Fraumeni syndrome or neurofibromatosis type 1.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment should be managed by a multidisciplinary team, expert in the treatment of childhood cancers. Initial surgery should only be considered if it can be completed, and completed without significant consequences. Chemotherapy is indicated in all other cases from diagnosis. Local treatment is carried out by secondary surgery, often complemented by radiotherapy. Alveolar forms require more intensive treatment than embryonic forms. The objective of current protocols is to avoid radiotherapy, if possible, in order to reduce long term sequelae.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Survival depends on the location of the tumor. In localized forms the survival rate is greater than 80% for tumors of the orbit, bladder, vagina and paratesticular region. The survival rate is in the order of 60-70% for other localized tumors. For patients with metastases at diagnosis the survival rate is lower, and adolescents and patients with osteo-medullar metastases have a survival rate of less than 20%.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS) contributes to 3% of all childhood cancers with roughly 400-500 cases diagnosed each year in the United States. The World Health Organization classifies rhabdomyosarcoma into four histological subtypes which include alveolar, embryonal, spindle-cell and pleomorphic. The primary genetic drivers in a subset of alveolar and spindle-cell histological subtypes are gene fusions. explores the fusion oncogenes identified in RMS such as PAX- and NCOA2- based fusions, along with discussing studies defining fusion oncogene biology and tumorigenic mechanisms. Focus areas include data around transformation events and progression along with dysregulated biological processes. Furthermore, we summarize model systems, ranging from cell to animal models, that have been implemented to study fusion oncogenes identified in RMS. With the constant identification of novel fusion... [PMC12209299, PMC11959641]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare acrofacial dysostosis that is characterized by mandibular and malar hypoplasia, small and cup-shaped ears, lower lid ectropion, and symmetrical postaxial limb deficiencies with absence of the fifth digital rays and ulnar hypoplasia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Miller syndrome; POADS; Acrofacial dysostosis, Genee-Wiedemann type; Mandibulofacial dysostosis with postaxial limb anomalies; Postaxial acrodysostosis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Less than 30 cases of Postaxial acrofacial dysostosis (POADS) have been described in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical features further include cholestasis, bilateral inguinal hernia and cleft palate. The patients can develop myopic astigmatism and speech delay can be present. Facial features include sparse eyebrows, almond shaped eyes with up-slanting palpebral fissures, malar hypoplasia, long philtrum, small mouth, and low-set, malformed ears.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease arises from biallelic gene mutations for the enzyme dihydroorotate dehydrogenase (DHODH, 16q22.2), involved in pyrimidine biosynthesis. Nonetheless, despite demonstrated loss of enzyme activity, dihydroorotate (DHO) has not been shown to accumulate.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: DHODH mutations can be determined by PCR and Sanger sequencing. Analysis of DHO and orotic acid (OA) in urine, plasma and blood-spot test can be performed using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The clinical phenotype of Miller syndrome overlaps with mandibulofacial and other acrofacial dysostosis syndromes including Treacher Collins, Guion-Almeida (mandibulofacial dysostosis with microcephaly) and Nager syndromes.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Due to postaxial oligodactyly of fingers and toes, the diagnosis can be established prenatally on clinical grounds and confirmed by molecular testing.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance appears to be autosomal recessive. For parents of an affected individual, there is a 25% risk of having and affected child at each pregnancy. Recurrence risk for children of an affected individual is low if there is no consanguinity.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The patients do not usually need surgical treatment, but sometimes need hearing aids. Logopedic treatment might be helpful.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: There is usually no reduced life expectancy, but intrauterine death has been described.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genodermatosis characterized by a hair shaft dysplasia resulting in hypotrichosis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence and incidence are not known.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Monilethrix has an early onset in infancy. Alopecia, associated with follicular hyperkeratosis and perifollicular erythema, can involve only the occiput and the nape of the neck or, in severe forms, the entire scalp, the eyebrows and eyelashes, and secondary hair. Infants show a characteristic hair shaft dysplasia: dystrophic constrictions regularly separated by elliptical nodes of normal thickness, giving a beaded appearance of affected hair. The thin internodal region shows a high propensity to break. In some cases, nail dystrophy (koilonychia) on fingers and toes has been reported. This symptomatic triad (moniliform hair, follicular hyperkeratosis and nail dystrophy), when associated with other ectodermal defects, such as as neurological, dental, and ophthalmological alterations, constitute the ''moniliform hair syndrome''.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Four genes have been associated with monilethrix: KRT81, KRT83 and KRT86, coding for the type II hair keratins Hb1, Hb3 and Hb6, and are responsible for the autosomal dominant form of the disease. An autosomal recessive form has also been described in a few families, caused by mutations in the DSG4 gene, coding for the desmoglein 4 protein, also involved in hypotrichosis simplex that has clinical overlap with monilethrix.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: A trichogram shows the characteristic moniliform hairs. Trichoscopy is another approach to detect the characteristic hair shaft dysplasia of monilethrix. An electron microscopy-based diagnostic test is available.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes pseudomonilethrix that presents with diffuse alopecia or alopecia limited to the occipital area. However, using trichogram analysis, pseudomoniletrix hair does not present with dystrophic constrictions but with flattened irregular beading.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In severe forms with alopecia and hyperkeratosis on the body, genetic counseling would be necessary.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is disappointing. The best measure is to avoid the mechanical action of combing and brushing. Depilation only achieves repopulation with normal looking hair for a short while. Temporary improvement has been described with daily doses of 125 mg of griseofulvin, zinc-sulfate, X-ray depilation, and topical application of retinoid acid. There have also been improvements with the application of minoxidil and tretinoin, and with the administration of 0.5-1 mg/kg/day of etretinate.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The course of the localized form of monilethrix can be favorable with a reduction of hypotrichosis with time. In general, hypotrichosis improves with age, although remissions have been noted during puberty or pregnancy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) is a severely disabling heritable disorder of connective tissue characterized by congenital malformations of the great toes and progressive heterotopic ossification that forms qualitatively normal bone in characteristic extraskeletal sites.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): FOP; Myositis ossificans progressiva; Stone man syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The worldwide prevalence is approximately 1/2,000,000. There is no ethnic, racial, gender, or geographic predilection to FOP.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Children who have FOP appear normal at birth except for congenital malformations of the great toes (hallux valgus, malformed first metatarsal, and/or monophalangism). During the first decade of life, sporadic episodes of painful soft tissue swellings (flare-ups) occur which are often precipitated by soft tissue injury, intramuscular injections, viral infection, muscular stretching, falls or fatigue. If diagnosis of FOP is suspected, any invasive intervention (such as biopsy), which may lead to flare-ups, is contraindicated. These flare-ups transform skeletal muscles, tendons, ligaments, fascia, and aponeuroses into heterotopic bone, rendering movement impossible. Patients with atypical forms of FOP have been described. They either present with the classic features of FOP plus one or more atypical features (e.g. intercurrent aplastic anemia, craniopharyngioma, childhood glaucoma or growth retardation) (FOP plus), or present major variations in one or both of the two classic defining features of FOP (e.g., normal great toes or severe reduction deficits of digits) (FOP variants).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Classic FOP is caused by a recurrent activating mutation (617G>A; R206H) in the gene ACVR1 (ALK2) encoding Activin A receptor type I/Activin-like kinase 2, a bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) type I receptor. Atypical FOP patients also have heterozygous ACVR1 missense mutations in conserved amino acids.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of FOP is made by clinical evaluation. Plain radiographs can substantiate more subtle great toe abnormalities and the presence of heterotopic ossification. Confirmatory genetic testing is available.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes progressive osseous heteroplasia, osteosarcoma, lymphedema, soft tissue sarcoma, desmoid tumors, aggressive juvenile fibromatosis, and non-hereditary (acquired) heterotopic ossification.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal testing is not yet routinely available.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Although most cases of FOP are sporadic (non-inherited mutations), a small number of inherited FOP cases show germline transmission with an autosomal dominant pattern.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: At present, there is no definitive treatment, but a brief 4-day course of high-dose corticosteroids, started within the first 24 hours of a flare-up, may help reduce the intense inflammation and tissue edema seen in the early stages of the disease. Preventative management is based on prophylactic measures against falls (e.g. improvement in household safety, use of protective headgear), respiratory decline (e.g., incentive spirometry), and viral infections.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The median lifespan is approximately 40 years of age. Most patients are wheelchair-bound by the end of the second decade of life and commonly die of complications of thoracic insufficiency syndrome.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder of the peripheral nervous system characterized by the sudden onset of extreme pain in the upper extremity followed by rapid multifocal motor weakness and atrophy and a slow recovery in months to years. NA includes both an idiopathic (INA, also known as Parsonage-Turner syndrome) and hereditary (HNA) form.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Acute brachial plexus neuritis; Brachial plexus neuritis; Immune brachial plexus neuropathy; Mononeuritis multiplex with brachial predilection; Neuralgic shoulder amyotrophy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The minimum incidence of NA is estimated at 1/50,000-1/30,000 but under recognition and initial misdiagnosis is common. HNA is thought to be 10 times less common than INA.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: NA can occur at any age but is most frequently seen in those between the 3rd-7th decades of life and is more frequent in men. Those with HNA usually present earlier than those with INA but clinically they are virtually indistinguishable. The classic presentation (71% of cases) manifests with sudden onset of aching, burning, or stabbing pains, most often in the shoulders, neck, and/or arm region, showing an upper brachial plexus distribution. Weakness in the periscapular and periglenohumeral muscles follows hours to weeks after the initial onset of pain. These pains are usually relentless, worse at night and last for about 3 weeks. Other manifestations may occur due to the involvement of nerves outside the brachial plexus such as the lumbosacral plexus or phrenic nerves. Certain patients with HNA (with a R88W point mutation) display characteristic physical features (ex. hypotelorism, slanted eyes, epicanthal folds, oval face, cleft palate). Some patients experience a relapsing/remitting course with symptom-free intervals while others have an incomplete recovery with persisting neurologic deficit. Recurrences can occur (75% in HNA and 25% in INA) and persistent musculoskeletal pain develops in 2/3 of patients.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The exact etiology is unknown but genetic, autoimmune and external factors are thought to play a role. The brachial plexus has an underlying predisposition to mechanical injury and attacks caused by an immune-mediated response in this nerve. A viral infection or immunization can precede NA. Bacterial and parasitic infections, surgery, anesthesia, rheumatic disease, trauma, pregnancy and childbirth have all been implicated as possible contributing factors of NA attacks. HNA is associated with a point mutation or duplication of the susceptibility gene SEPT9 on chromosome 17q25.3 in 50% of cases.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the typical clinical features and the exclusion of other disorders (ex. neuroborreliosis, cervical radiculopathy or Pancoast syndrome) using laboratory tests, electromyography and imaging of the cervical spine and brachial plexus. In those where HNA is suspected, a molecular genetic test can be used to identify a SEPT9 mutation, but since HNA is genetically heterogeneous, a negative test does not exclude the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is not routinely offered.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling is possible in families with the HNA susceptibility gene.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment in the acute stage involves pain management, relying mostly on a combination of long-acting opioids and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. Those with chronic pain can be given co-analgesics. Oral prednisone decreases the duration of pain and accelerates recovery in some patients if given in the first weeks of an attack. A daily dose of 1mg/kg for 1 week which is tapered during the 2nd week is recommended. Follow-up is recommended every 6 months. Rehabilitation therapy is now considered important and excessive strain to the affected area should be avoided.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is variable but thought to be good with patients recovering 70-90% of their previous health after 1-2 years. However, many are left with exercise intolerance and poor muscular coordination in the affected and compensating muscles. Quality of life can be affected in those with an incomplete recovery but early diagnosis and proper treatment increase the chances of a full functional recovery.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare epidermal nevus disorder characterized by the association of speckled lentiginous nevi with epidermal sebaceous nevi, and extracutaneous anomalies.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica (PPK) is a rare epidermal nevus syndrome characterized by the co-existence of nonepidermolytic organoid sebaceous nevi and one or more large segmental speckled lentiginous nevi. Within these speckled lentiginous nevi, atypical nevi such as compound Spitz and dysplastic nevi may manifest, and Spitz nevi and melanoma have been documented. Epidermal nevi in PPK are known to give rise to neoplasms including trichoblastoma and basal cell carcinoma. The condition is associated with a postzygotic activating RAS mutation, specifically HRAS G13R. Extracutaneous manifestations can include precocious puberty. Noninvasive imaging techniques like high-frequency ultrasound and optical coherence tomography can help characterize the morphological features of these lesions. [PMC10234170, PMC5961630, PMC5175589]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica is characterized by the co-existence of epidermal nevi and large segmental speckled lentiginous nevi. While previously explained as 'twin spot' mosaicism due to postzygotic crossing-over of two homozygous recessive mutations, it has recently been shown to derive from one postzygotic activating RAS mutation. Specifically, an HRAS mutation, such as HRAS G13R, has been identified in both melanocytic and adnexal components of neoplasms in affected individuals and is associated with the condition. [PMC9207640, PMC5961630, PMC5175589]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica (PPK) is characterized by the co-existence of epidermal nevi, specifically nonepidermolytic organoid sebaceous nevi, with one or more large segmental speckled lentiginous nevi. While patients may undergo numerous biopsies, noninvasive imaging techniques such as high-frequency ultrasound (HFUS) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) are being investigated. These modalities can discriminate morphological features of pigmented lesions and nevus sebaceous, revealing distinct hypoechoic patterns that indicate benign etiology and may help avoid biopsies. HFUS provides deep tissue views, while OCT offers higher resolution. Additionally, genetic analysis using next-generation sequencing can identify postzygotic activating RAS mutations, such as HRAS G13R, which are implicated in PPK. [PMC10234170, PMC5175589]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica (PPK) is a distinct and rare type of epidermal nevus syndrome characterized by coexisting nonepidermolytic organoid sebaceous nevus (SN) with one or more speckled lentiginous nevi (SLN). Atypical nevi including compound Spitz and compound dysplastic may manifest within regions of SLN. Patients with PPK, or similar atypical nevus syndromes, may be subject to a significant lifetime number of biopsies, leading to pain, scarring, anxiety, financial burden, and decreased quality of life. The current literature includes case reports, genetics, and associated extracutaneous symptoms of PPK, but use of noninvasive imaging techniques have not been explored. We investigate the value of high-frequency ultrasound (HFUS) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) in discriminating morphological features of pigmented lesions and nevus sebaceous within one patient with PPK.... [PMC10234170, PMC5175589]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica and precocious puberty associated with HRAS mutation. Phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica (PPK) is characterized by the co-existence of epidermal nevi and large segmental speckled lentiginous nevi of the papulosa type. PPK, previously explained as 'twin spot' mosaicism due to the postzygotic crossing-over of two homozygous recessive mutations, has recently been shown to derive from one postzygotic activating RAS mutation. Epidermal nevi, including those in PPK, are known to give rise to neoplasms such as trichoblastoma and basal cell carcinoma. Within speckled lentiginous nevi, Spitz nevi and melanoma have been well documented. a case of PPK with a combined melanocytic and adnexal neoplasm presenting where the nevi conjoined. Using next-generation sequencing techniques, we were able to identify the same HRAS G13R mutation within both components of the tumor,... [PMC5961630, PMC5175589]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica (PPK) is a distinct and rare type of epidermal nevus syndrome characterized by coexisting nonepidermolytic organoid sebaceous nevus (SN) with one or more speckled lentiginous nevi (SLN). Atypical nevi including compound Spitz and compound dysplastic may manifest within regions of SLN. Patients with PPK, or similar atypical nevus syndromes, may be subject to a significant lifetime number of biopsies, leading to pain, scarring, anxiety, financial burden, and decreased quality of life. The current literature includes case reports, genetics, and associated extracutaneous symptoms of PPK, but use of noninvasive imaging techniques have not been explored. We investigate the value of high-frequency ultrasound (HFUS) and optical coherence tomography (OCT) in discriminating morphological features of pigmented lesions and nevus sebaceous within one patient with PPK.... [PMC10234170, PMC8265418]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica can be associated with severe outcomes, as evidenced by reports of fatal cases. Patients are at risk for developing various neoplasms, including trichoblastoma, basal cell carcinoma, Spitz nevi, and melanoma, which can arise within epidermal nevi and speckled lentiginous nevi. The condition may also be associated with extracutaneous manifestations such as precocious puberty. The presence of atypical nevi often necessitates a significant number of biopsies throughout a patient's lifetime, leading to pain, scarring, and decreased quality of life, although noninvasive imaging may help differentiate benign lesions. [PMC10234170, PMC9207640, PMC5961630, PMC5175589]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) is a large B-cell lymphoma located in the body cavities, characterized by pleural, peritoneal, and pericardial fluid lymphomatous effusions and that is always associated with human herpes virus-8 (HHV-8).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown but it accounts for less than 1% of non-AIDS related lymphomas and approximately 3% of AIDS-related lymphomas.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: PEL is most frequently found in young men that are positive for HIV or have pre-existing AIDS. Very rare non-HIV related cases have been reported but these patients are almost all elderly or immunodeficient due to another cause. Peritoneal, pleural, and pericardial fluid lymphomatous effusions are observed with, in the majority of cases, no mass-like extranodal extension of lymphoma. Symptoms of PEL depend on the body cavity affected and are caused by the accumulation of the malignant effusion. Pleural or pericardial disease has dyspnea as a symptom while abdominal distension is experienced in peritoneal disease. PEL is usually extremely aggressive and dissemination of lymphoma to distant sites, opportunistic infections and HIV-related complications are often fatal. In the rare HIV-negative cases the outcome may be better.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The precise etiology is unknown. PEL is always associated with HHV-8, also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpes (KSHV) and is most frequently found in immunodeficient patients, especially those with advanced AIDS. An infection with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is also present in the majority of PEL cases. The gene products of these viral genomes are thought to inhibit cell apoptosis and promote uncontrolled cell division and subsequent neoplastic transformation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Body cavity fluid is analyzed cytologically and by flow cytometry for the presence of clonal large neoplastic cells (with immunoblastic, anaplastic or plasmablastic appearances) with prominent nucleoli, round to irregular nuclei and occasionally vacuolated cytoplasm. To be given a diagnosis with PEL an infection with HHV-8 must be present. A latency-associated nuclear antigen-1 (LANA-1) assay detects any evidence of HHV-8 in tissue samples. Complete blood counts and positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) scans should also be performed to determine the extent of the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), Burkitt lymphoma, which can present with lymphomatous effusion, anaplastic large cell lymphoma (ALCL) and pyothorax-associated lymphoma (PAL).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: PEL is usually refractory to conventional chemotherapy and treatment guidelines are not well defined. Highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART) should be administered concurrently with chemotherapy in all HIV positive PEL patients. The chemotherapy regimen cyclophosamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisone (CHOP) is most commonly used. Research into molecular targeting therapy for the treatment of PEL is ongoing. There is a single case report of a durable remission for more than 18 months with the use of sobuzoxane.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: PEL has a very poor prognosis with an average life expectancy of 3-4 months after diagnosis. Rare patients with HIV-negative PEL have durable progression free survival after chemotherapy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Clouston syndrome (or hidrotic ectodermal dysplasia) is characterised by the clinical triad of nail dystrophy, alopecia, and palmoplantar hyperkeratosis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The disease was first described in the French-Canadian population (in which it is associated with a founder effect), but has since been identified in several other ethnic groups. The exact prevalence is unknown and the syndrome is likely to be underdiagnosed.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Nail abnormalities are the most consistent feature and frequently manifest at birth or in early infancy. The nails are thickened, slow growing, brittle, often hyperconvex and discoloured with striation. Additional reported features include micronychia, onycholysis and recurrent paronychial infections leading to nail loss. Hair involvement manifests at birth or later during infancy or childhood, and ranges from total to partial, often progressive, alopecia. Residual scalp hair is slow growing, sparse, fine and brittle. Eyebrows and eyelashes are also frequently sparse and axillary, pubic and body hair can be affected. Palmoplantar hyperkeratosis is not a constant finding. When present, it usually begins in childhood and tends to worsen with age; some patients also develop hyperkeratosis and hyperpigmentation over the joints and bony prominences. The teeth are usually unaffected and sweating is normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Clouston syndrome is caused by mutations in the GJB6 gene (13q12), encoding the gap junction protein connexin 30 (Cx30).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis may be suspected on the basis of the clinical triad of nail dystrophy, hypotrichosis and hyperkeratosis of the palms and soles. The diagnosis can be confirmed by molecular analysis of the GJB6 gene.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include pachyonychia congenita and other forms of ectodermal dysplasia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal testing is possible in families where the disease-causing mutation has been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Clouston syndrome is transmitted as an autosomal dominant trait. Disease penetrance is complete, but expression is quite variable even between affected individuals from the same family.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: At present there is no treatment for the disease and management is purely supportive.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The life-span for patients is normal.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Tetrasomy 21 is an extremely rare autosomal anomaly resulting from the presence of 4 copies of chromosome 21, characterized by features of trisomy 21 including developmental delay/intellectual disability, muscular hypotonia, short neck with redundant skin, brachycephaly, microcephaly, flat face, epicanthus, upslanted palpebral fissures, small ears, protruding tongue, single transverse palmar crease, brachydactyly, hypoplastic iliac wings, together with additional features such as prematurity, intrauterine growth retardation, high and broad forehead, hypertelorism. Haematological malignancies are also associated and may occur earlier than in trisomy 21.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Tetrasomy 21 is a very rare aneuploidy, with the complete form being particularly uncommon. The described case represents only the second well-documented instance of complete tetrasomy 21 in the literature. It is more frequently described in its partial form than in its complete form. [PMC6825868]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Tetrasomy 21 is a very rare aneuploidy that can clinically resemble Down syndrome. A fetus with mosaic complete tetrasomy 21 presented with an isolated complete atrioventricular septal defect identified during prenatal ultrasound. Following termination of pregnancy, clinical examination of the fetus further evoked features consistent with trisomy 21 or Down syndrome. [PMC6825868]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Tetrasomy 21 is a very rare aneuploidy that can clinically resemble Down syndrome. It is most often described in its partial form, though complete tetrasomy 21 has also been reported. The condition can present as mosaicism, including very weak or confined tissue-specific forms. This mosaicism poses diagnostic challenges, potentially leading to false-negative test and necessitating careful diagnostic approaches, such as analyzing multiple tissues or using techniques without a culture step. [PMC6825868, PMC1757147]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Prenatal ultrasound may reveal features like an isolated complete atrioventricular septal defect, while clinical examination can evoke Down syndrome. Definitive diagnosis involves genetic analyses such as chromosomal microarray and FISH, which can identify tetrasomy 21. However, diagnosis is complicated by mosaicism, which can lead to false-negative , especially with weak or tissue-specific mosaicism. To mitigate this, diagnostic techniques without a culture step are preferred, and it is recommended to analyze an increased number of cells and tissues. Anomalies detected by microarray should be confirmed by another technique on the same tissue, as microarray alone has limitations in cases of weak mosaicism. [PMC6825868]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Tetrasomy 21 is a very rare aneuploidy that can clinically resemble Down syndrome (trisomy 21). Clinical examination of affected fetuses has been noted to evoke Down syndrome. Attention must be paid to the risk of false-negative test for chromosome 21 aneuploidy, including Down syndrome, due to chromosomal mosaicism, which may involve very weak percentages or different tissue distributions. [PMC6825868]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of tetrasomy 21 can be challenging. Prenatal ultrasound may reveal anomalies such as a complete atrioventricular septal defect, but initial amniotic fluid karyotype might appear normal. This is because tetrasomy 21 can present as a mosaicism, potentially confined to specific tissues, leading to false-negative . Chromosomal microarray analysis and FISH on appropriate tissues can confirm the diagnosis. To improve detection, it is recommended to use diagnostic techniques without a culture step, increase the number of cells and tissues analyzed, and verify microarray findings with another technique on the same tissue, especially when clinical signs suggest Down syndrome. [PMC6825868]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Tetrasomy 21 is a very rare aneuploidy that clinically resembles Down syndrome. Genetic counseling should address the diagnostic challenges, particularly the risk of false-negative due to mosaicism, which can be very weak or confined to specific tissues. For example, a normal karyotype on amniotic fluid may not rule out tetrasomy 21 in the fetus. To improve diagnostic accuracy, it is recommended to privilege diagnostic techniques without a culture step, increase the number of cells and tissues analyzed, and confirm microarray anomalies with another technique on the same tissue. [PMC6825868]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Papillon-Lefèvre syndrome (PLS) is a rare ectodermal dysplasia characterized by palmoplantar keratoderma associated with early-onset periodontitis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is estimated between 1/250,000 and 1/1,000,000 individuals. The male to female ratio is 1:1. PLS is found in all ethnic groups.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Diffuse palmoplantar keratoderma with erythematous plaques develops between the first and fourth years of life, with the soles being usually more severely affected than the palms. Psoriasiform hyperkeratosis can overflow onto the dorsal surfaces of the hands and feet (transgredient spread) and, less frequently, lesions can be seen on the limbs (knees, elbows). Skin lesions are followed by intense gingivitis that rapidly progresses into periodontitis with alveolar bone lysis and early loss of primary dentition. The skin lesions are aggravated by cold and during episodes of severe periodontitis. During childhood, the phenomenon of periodontal disease recurs with rapid loss of permanent dentition. Cases of PLS with mild and/or late-onset periodontal disease have been reported occasionally. PLS is accompanied, in half of the patients, by enhanced susceptibility to cutaneous and systemic infections (furunculosis, skin abscesses, pyoderma, hidradenitis suppurativa, respiratory tract infection...). Patients may also present with malodorous hyperhidrosis, follicular hyperkeratosis, nail dystrophy or dural calcifications. The association of PLS with malignant melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma has been reported in very rare occasions.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: PLS is due to mutations in the CTSC gene (11q14.2) that codes for cathepsin C (also known as dipeptidyl peptidase I), a lysosomal protease playing a role in epidermal differentiation and desquamation and in activation of serine proteases expressed in cells of the immune system. CTSC mutations lead to an almost total loss of cathepsin C activity which seems to result in susceptibility to specific virulent pathogens. It is also suggested that other immune-mediated deficiencies in the host defense mechanism could be involved in the pathogenesis of PLS.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical signs. Dental radiography shows atrophy of the alveolar bone. Neutrophil function tests reveal anomalies of chemotaxis and phagocytosis by polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Skin biopsy shows hyperkeratosis with focal parakeratosis, moderate perivascular infiltration, hypergranulosis, and acanthosis. Biochemical analysis reveals a loss of CTSC activity. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes two rare disorders that are allelic variants of PLS, Haim-Munk syndrome and prepubertal/aggressive periodontitis. Other diseases with similar dermatologic features include localized epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma (Vörner), mal de Meleda, Howel-Evans syndrome, transgrediens et progrediens palmoplantar keratoderma (Greither's disease), and keratosis punctata.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is theoretically possible but has never been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to the parents of an affected individual informing them of the 25% risk their offspring has of inheriting the disease causing mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is based on oral retinoids which attenuate the palmoplantar keratoderma and slow the alveolar bone lysis. Antibiotics, along with oral hygiene and use of mouth rinses, are also recommended for slowing the progression of periodontitis. Ultimately, primary or remaining teeth are extracted and are replaced by dental implants. Antibiotherapy is also used in the treatment of recurrent infections. Etretinate (a synthetic retinoid) shows promising results in the treatment of PLS.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Despite meticulous dental care, all patients eventually become edentulous at the beginning of adulthood. Life expectancy is normal.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare primary organ-specific lymphoma characterized by primary origin in the thyroid gland, sometimes involving cervical lymph nodes, and infrequently more distant sites. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is most common, followed by MALT lymphoma, and follicular lymphoma. More rare types include T-cell lymphomas, Burkitt lymphoma, or classic Hodgkin lymphoma. The condition is usually associated with Hashimoto thyroiditis. Patients typically present with a mass in the thyroid, with or without cervical lymphadenopathy. Hoarseness and dyspnea may occur, while constitutional symptoms are rare. Prognosis is favorable for patients with localized tumors.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Primary thyroid lymphoma (PTL) is a rare extranodal lymphoma, constituting less than 5% of all thyroid malignancies and 2% of extranodal lymphomas. It predominantly affects middle-aged and older adult females, with studies reporting a median age at diagnosis around 65.5-76.2 years. Hashimoto thyroiditis is considered a common risk factor, with many cases showing concomitant thyroiditis. Most PTLs are non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphomas, with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma being the most frequent histotypes. The coexistence of PTL with papillary thyroid carcinoma is exceedingly rare. [PMC11569482, PMC11176462, PMC11107012, PMC10924984, PMC10893725]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Primary thyroid lymphoma is a rare non-Hodgkin B-cell lymphoma, accounting for less than 5% of thyroid malignancies and 2% of extranodal lymphomas. It predominantly affects older adults, particularly women, with a median age at diagnosis often in the mid-60s to mid-70s. Patients typically present with a rapidly enlarging thyroid mass, frequently accompanied by compressive symptoms like dysphagia, dyspnea, and hoarseness. Neck lymphadenopathy and B symptoms may also be observed. The most common histotypes are diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) and mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is a common associated condition, and coexistence with papillary thyroid carcinoma is exceedingly rare. Ultrasound often reveals a goiter or large, solid, very hypoechoic nodules, sometimes with characteristic internal echoes. [PMC11569482, PMC11176462, PMC11107012, PMC10924984, PMC10893725]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Primary thyroid lymphoma is an extranodal lymphoma originating within the thyroid gland, predominantly affecting middle-aged and older adult females. Hashimoto's thyroiditis is considered a common risk factor and frequently coexists with primary thyroid lymphoma, particularly mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma. Most cases are B-cell lymphomas, with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma and MALT lymphoma being the most frequent histotypes. Clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangements are important for diagnosing MALT lymphoma in the context of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Genetic factors, such as an EZH2 gene mutation in primary follicular lymphoma and a pathogenic MEN1 mutation, have been observed in individual cases. [PMC11569482, PMC11107012, PMC10924984, PMC10893725, PMC10080465]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of primary thyroid lymphoma is established through a combination of . Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) or core needle biopsy, often guided by ultrasonography, are key initial steps, with TIRADS categories aiding in FNA recommendations. Histopathological examination, frequently performed on surgical specimens, is crucial for definitive diagnosis. This is complemented by immunohistochemistry, which helps confirm lymphoma subtypes (e.g., CD20 positivity for B-cell lymphomas) and differentiate from other thyroid malignancies. Advanced imaging techniques such as CT scans and scintigraphy may also be utilized. In specific cases, molecular tests like next-generation sequencing for gene mutations or clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangements can aid in diagnosis, particularly for MALT lymphoma coexisting with Hashimoto thyroiditis. Bone marrow biopsy, beta-2 microglobulin, and serum LDH levels may be used for extension evaluation. [PMC11569482, PMC11176462, PMC11107012, PMC10924984, PMC10893725]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Primary thyroid lymphoma (PTL) can be challenging to diagnose, often requiring differentiation from other thyroid malignancies and conditions. It may be initially misdiagnosed as anaplastic thyroid carcinoma or Rosai Dorfman disease, particularly in cases of rapidly enlarging neck masses. Malignant lymphoma is also considered in the differential for papillary carcinoma in lateral aberrant ectopic thyroid tissue. Furthermore, clear large-cell lymphoma is a differential for thyroid lesions exhibiting clear cell change. PTL, including MALT lymphoma and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, frequently coexists with various thyroid carcinomas such as papillary thyroid carcinoma and medullary thyroid carcinoma, particularly in the setting of Hashimoto's thyroiditis. Distinguishing MALT lymphoma from benign lymphoepithelial lesions in Hashimoto's thyroiditis may require clonal immunoglobulin gene rearrangement testing. [PMC11332711, PMC11176462, PMC11107012, PMC10924984, PMC10080465]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Thyroid lymphoma, specifically mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma, has been observed in patients with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1). MEN1 is a familial syndrome associated with a pathogenic MEN1 mutation. Familial genetic screening can identify carriers of this mutation within a kindred. Family members with the MEN1 mutation are then placed under a life-long surveillance program for MEN1 prototypic tumors, highlighting the potential relevance of genetic counseling in such cases. [PMC8663848]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital cardiac malformation that is a variant of an atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD) with an interatrial communication (ostium primum defect) just above the common atrioventricular (AV) valve, no interventricular communication just below the atrioventricular valve, a common atrioventricular junction but separate right and left atrioventricular valvar orifices, and a three-leaflet, left-sided component of the common atrioventricular valve (''cleft''). Shunting is restricted to the atrial level because of fusion of the leaflets of the common AV valve with the crest of the ventricular septum.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): PAVC; Partial atrioventricular canal defect; Partial AVSD

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Partial atrioventricular septum defect (PAVSD) accounts for 1-2% of all congenital heart malformations and its prevalence is estimated to be 1/5,000-1/2,500.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most patients with PAVSD are asymptomatic until late in life. The clinical presentation depends on the degree of mitral regurgitation and on the associated cardiac defects. The two most common clinical manifestations are impaired exercise capacity and exertional dyspnea. Rarely, cardiac failure may occur in infancy. Additional features in adults include palpitations, presyncope or syncope, and sustained atrial arrhythmias. The ventricles may be equal or nearly equal in size (balanced) or one of the ventricles may be significantly larger than the other (unbalanced). Unbalanced ventricles are associated with hypoplasia of the arterial valve above and aortic coarctation if the left ventricle is hypoplastic.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CRELD1 (3p25.3), GATA4 (8p23.1-p22), GATA6 (18q11-q12) and NR2F2 (15q26) have been associated with a small fraction of PAVC cases. These genes encode developmental transcription factors that are critical for normal cardiac morphogenesis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of PAVC is established by means of 2D-echocardiography. Transesophageal echocardiography or cardiac catheterization can be useful in adults (to assess pulmonary vascular resistance and status of the left AV valve and, in patients > 40 years, to exclude coexisting coronary arterial disease). An elevated pulmonary arterial pressure and moderate to severe left atrioventricular valve regurgitation may be observed. First-degree AV block, right bundle branch block, and a superior QRS axis may be noted on electrocardiogram.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes the complete and intermediate forms of atrioventricular septal defects. Intermediate (transitional) atrioventricular septal defect is a variant of complete atrioventricular septal defect with a restrictive ventricular component due to multiple attachments of the bridging leaflets on the crest of the ventricular septum. PAVSD may be associated with syndromes including the RASopathies (particularly Noonan syndrome caused by mutations in PTPN11 and RAF1), Ellis Van Creveld and Down, and CHARGE syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: PAVSD may be detectable prenatally by 4-chamber view screening during obstetric ultrasonography.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The early diagnosis of PAVSD requires cardiology follow-up and elective complete repair between 3 and 5 years of age, which involves closure of a primum atrial septal defect with an appropriately shaped patch through right atriotomy, and partial suture of the ''cleft'' of the left component of the common atrioventricular valve. A pacemaker insertion may be required for complete AV block, which may spontaneously develop after repair. A continuous lifelong follow-up is recommended to avoid late complications. Symptom free patients may be referred for PAVSD repair because of a substantial left-to right atrial shunt (pulmonary to systemic flow ratio 1.8:1) and echocardiographic evidence of right heart volume overload.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Long-term survival after repair of partial AVSD is the rule. The elective age for repair is 3-5 years, but some patients will not present until later in life. The later the repair is made, the greater the loss of ventricular function that occurs. High morbidity and need for reoperation, often related to residual problems of the systemic AV valve such as LAVV regurgitation, may be observed. Furthermore, the prognosis can be severely impaired if the left ventricle and left component of the common atrioventricular valve are hypoplastic or severely malformed. Norwood-type intervention in infancy can be required, as well as prosthetic replacement of the left AV valve.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Congenital megacalycosis is a rare renal malformation, characterized by non-obstructive dilation of the renal calyces as well as an increased calyceal number (12-20), with a normal renal pelvis, ureter, and bladder. It may be unilateral or bilateral and is usually asymptomatic unless complicated by nephrolithiasis and urinary tract infection.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Congenital megacalycosis is a condition that can manifest in the neonatal period. It is characterized by its presentation as neonatal hydronephrosis, indicating a potential for urinary tract dilation or obstruction in newborns. This early presentation suggests that the condition can be identified shortly after birth through findings consistent with hydronephrosis. [PMC2921495]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by a proliferation primarily of granulocytic and monocytic lineages with infiltration of the liver and spleen, among other organs. Blasts and promonocytes account for less than 20% of white blood cells in peripheral blood and bone marrow. Erythroid and megakaryocytic abnormalities are often present. BCR-ABL1 fusion is absent, while somatic mutations in genes of the RAS pathway or monosomy 7 may be found. The condition may also occur in the context of neurofibromatosis type 1 or Noonan syndrome-like disorder. Children of less than three years are predominantly affected, with a clear male preponderance. Most patients present with constitutional symptoms, signs of infection, and hepatosplenomegaly.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) is a rare pediatric myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm overlap disease of infancy and early childhood. It is associated with germline or somatic mutations in RAS pathway genes, including PTPN11, NRAS, KRAS, and CBL, with somatic mutations often behaving more aggressively. JMML is frequently predisposed by RASopathies such as Noonan syndrome, Neurofibromatosis type 1, and CBL syndrome, which are linked to an increased risk of hematological disorders. Karyotype abnormalities and additional epigenetic alterations can also be found. [PMC11431238, PMC11311611, PMC11020124, PMC11475086, PMC10590552]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) is an aggressive pediatric myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm primarily characterized by mutations in the RAS pathway genes, leading to hyperactivation of the Ras/MAPK signaling pathway. These mutations can be germline (e.g., in NRAS, KRAS, PTPN11) or somatic; germline mutations are often associated with a transient myeloproliferative disorder, while somatic RAS mutations tend to behave more aggressively. Specific genetic factors include missense mutations in the PTPN11 gene, often seen in Noonan syndrome, a RASopathy that predisposes individuals to JMML. CBL syndrome, another RASopathy, is known to predispose to CBL-mutated JMML, involving germline CBL loss-of-function variants that can lead to myeloid malignancy through somatic loss of heterozygosity. Karyotype abnormalities and additional epigenetic alterations, including dysregulated microRNA profiles, are also found in JMML, and rarely, other genetic drivers like NUP98-NSD1 fusions can present with features mimicking JMML. [PMC12056752, PMC11970265, PMC11431238, PMC11311611, PMC11020124]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) requires differentiation from various hematological and non-hematological conditions. These include other myeloproliferative disorders and leukemias, such as chronic myeloid leukemia, which is distinguished by the absence of BCR-ABL translocation. Immunodeficiencies, viral infections (including intrauterine infections), and hemophagolymphohistiocytosis are also part of the differential. Transient myeloproliferative disorder (TMD), particularly in patients with germline RAS mutations or Noonan syndrome, can present similarly or sequentially. Leukoerythroblastic reactions, caused by viral infection, osteopetrosis, or hemolysis (e.g., Rh-incompatibility), also need to be considered. Furthermore, other overlapping myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasms, such as those driven by a NUP98-NSD1 fusion, can masquerade as JMML. [PMC11431238, PMC10590552, PMC7889745, PMC8010610]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML) is an aggressive pediatric myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by RAS pathway mutations and significant heterogeneity. Minimal residual disease (MRD) monitoring is crucial for evaluating treatment response and predicting relapse risk. MicroRNA (miRNAs), small non-coding RNAs with pivotal roles in gene regulation, have emerged as promising biomarkers for JMML MRD detection. explores the mechanistic role of miRNAs in JMML pathogenesis, emphasizing their diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic potential. Dysregulated miRNA profiles correlate with distinct JMML subgroups and disease progression, suggesting utility in non-invasive MRD monitoring. Emerging evidence highlights miR-150-5p as a tumor suppressor targeting STAT5b and its therapeutic potential in ameliorating JMML's aberrant signaling pathways. We compare traditional MRD... [PMC12056752, PMC12170293, PMC11311611, PMC11381242, PMC8574163]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans is a rare genodermatosis occurring during infancy or childhood, predominantly affecting males, and characterized by diffuse follicular hyperkeratosis associated with progressive cicatricial alopecia of the scalp, eyebrows and eyelashes. Additional findings can include photophobia, corneal dystrophy, facial erythema, and/or palmoplantar keratoderma.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (KFSD) is a rare, X-linked, hereditary disorder of keratinization. It is characterized by its X-linked inheritance, with male patients typically presenting with prominent features such as follicular hyperkeratosis, scarring alopecia, and corneal dystrophy. Female carriers often exhibit milder manifestations, including dry skin, minimal follicular hyperkeratosis, and sometimes mild corneal dystrophy. [PMC7879284, PMC1015819]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (KFSD) is a rare, X-linked hereditary disorder of keratinization. It is characterized by follicular hyperkeratosis of the skin and progressive scarring alopecia affecting the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes. Corneal dystrophy is a prominent feature, often accompanied by photophobia in male patients. Males may also exhibit hyperkeratosis of the calcaneal regions of the soles and high cuticles on fingernails. Female carriers typically present with milder manifestations, including dry skin, minimal follicular hyperkeratosis, and mild hyperkeratosis of the calcaneal areas of the soles, with some experiencing mild corneal dystrophy without photophobia. Clinical features and trichoscopy aid diagnosis, but pathology is mandatory. [PMC7879284, PMC1015819]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (KFSD) is a rare, X-linked hereditary disorder. It is characterized as a disorder of keratinization, affecting both males and female carriers, though with varying severity. [PMC7879284, PMC1015819]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (KFSD) is aided by particular clinical features. Trichoscopy is described as a very useful tool for diagnosis, with its importance in this hair disease being underlined. However, pathology is mandatory to confirm the diagnosis of KFSD. [PMC7879284]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for Keratosis Follicularis Spinulosa Decalvans include Ichthyosis follicularis, atrichia, and photophobia (IFAP) syndrome, an X-linked recessive disorder caused by MBTPS2 mutations. IFAP presents with ichthyosis, alopecia, spiky follicular hyperkeratotic papules, and photophobia, which may overlap with KFSD. Another condition to consider is Hypotrichosis with Juvenile Macular Dystrophy (HJMD), an autosomal recessive disorder linked to CDH3 mutations. HJMD is characterized by hypotrichosis and progressive macular dystrophy, and has been initially suspected as KFSD before reclassification. [PMC8831308, PMC5219735]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (KFSD) is a rare, X-linked hereditary disorder of keratinization. Due to its X-linked inheritance, male patients typically present with prominent features such as follicular hyperkeratosis, hyperkeratosis of the calcaneal regions, scarring alopecia of the scalp, absence of eyebrows and eyelashes, and corneal dystrophy accompanied by photophobia. Female carriers, however, often exhibit milder manifestations, including dry skin, minimal follicular hyperkeratosis, and mild hyperkeratosis of the calcaneal areas of the soles. Mild corneal dystrophy without photophobia has also been observed in female carriers, highlighting the importance of genetic counseling for affected families. [PMC7879284, PMC1015819]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (KFSD) is a rare, X-linked, hereditary disorder of keratinization, characterized by skin involvement and progressive scarring alopecia of scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes. The diagnosis is helped by the particular clinical features, but pathology is mandatory. We described a case of a female patient referred to the outpatient's hair consultation of our department, in which we performed trichoscopy as a very useful tool for the diagnosis, followed by pathology that confirmed KFSD. In our article, we underlined the importance of trichoscopy for the diagnosis of this hair disease, with also a review of the literature on diagnosis and treatment. Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans (KFSD) is a rare, X-linked, hereditary disorder of keratinization, characterized by skin involvement and progressive scarring alopecia of scalp, eyebrows, and... [PMC7879284]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Keratosis follicularis spinulosa decalvans involves progressive scarring alopecia affecting the scalp, eyebrows, and eyelashes. Male patients typically experience prominent features such as follicular hyperkeratosis, hyperkeratosis of the calcaneal regions, and corneal dystrophy accompanied by photophobia. Female carriers generally have milder manifestations, including dry skin, minimal follicular hyperkeratosis, mild hyperkeratosis of the soles, and sometimes mild corneal dystrophy without photophobia. [PMC7879284, PMC1015819]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) is a bilateral granulomatous anterior uveitis usually occurring within the three months following trauma or a surgical procedure involving one eye.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: SO is reported to affect between 1/1000 and 1/1650 individuals with a history of a penetrating eye wound.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients present with pain, photophobia, paresis of accommodation, metamorphopsia and mild to significant visual loss. The granulomatous anterior uveitis is accompanied by posterior segment findings including moderate to severe vitritis, choroiditis, papillitis, perivasculitis, and yellow-white lesions of the retinal pigment epithelium (Dalen-Fuchs nodules). The inflammation can lead to serous retinal detachment and macular edema. Extraocular symptoms include headache, meningitis or cerebrospinal fluid pleocytosis, hearing loss, poliosis and vitiligo.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of SO is not completely understood. The inflammation is caused by a cell-mediated immune mechanism and autoimmune inflammatory response directed against ocular self-antigens released after the initial injury. The nature of these self-antigens remains controversial. Bacterial infection may potentiate the development of SO and genetic factors may also be implicated as associations with specific major histocompatibility antigens (HLA-DR4, HLA-A11 or HLA-B40) have been reported. SO may occur after ocular trauma (47 to 65 % of patients) or contusions. Wounds involving the ciliary body are associated with the highest risk. Surgical interventions may also trigger SO, with posterior segment surgery carrying a higher risk than anterior segment surgery.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of SO is mainly based on patient history and clinical presentation. Imaging studies (fluorescein or indocyanine green angiography, B-scan ultrasonography and optical coherence tomography) may be useful to confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Laboratory analysis can be performed to eliminate infectious uveitis. When a history of trauma has been confirmed, endophthalmitis and other forms of post-traumatic uveitis (lens-induced uveitis, post-traumatic iridocyclitis) should be included in the differential diagnosis. Other diseases associated with granulomatous uveitis, including sarcoidosis and Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome or uveal effusion syndrome, may also be considered in the absence of a recognized history of ocular trauma.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Prompt and careful closure of all wounds decreases the risk of SO. The primary treatment is high doses of steroids (for a minimum of 3 months), followed by a taper according to the inflammatory response and maintenance therapy for 6-12 months after resolution. Immunomodulators (cyclophosphamide, azathioprine or cyclosporine) may be considered when the inflammation cannot be controlled by steroids alone. Surgical treatment remains controversial and enucleation or evisceration should only be proposed in cases of blindness or pain in the inciting eye as the visual prognosis of the sympathizing eye is variable. Late enucleation has not been shown to be beneficial.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Without treatment, the visual prognosis is poor with SO leading to bilateral blindness. However, prompt wound closure and efficient medical treatment improve the visual prognosis, which may then be relatively good. However, relapses and complications may occur and long-term follow-up is required.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Sympathetic ophthalmia (SO) is a bilateral diffuse uveitis that can arise after ocular trauma or ocular surgery in the inciting eye. Pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) is one of the risk factors for SO. Several reports have described SO developing after 23- and 25-G PPV, but none have described SO occurring after 27-G PPV. herein a case of SO after 27-G PPV for rhegmatogenous retinal detachment. A 42-year-old woman presented with visual disturbance in the right eye. Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/200 in the right eye. Fundus examination revealed off-macula retinal detachment with retinal tears at both ends of retinal lattice degeneration at the temporal-oven peripheral retina of the right eye. We therefore performed 27-G sutureless PPV on the right eye. After 12 days, the retina was reattached, and BCVA improved to 6/30 in the right eye. Fifteen days postoperatively, she experienced... [PMC8091709, PMC3277011]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection is a rare genetic vascular disease characterized by the familial occurrence of thoracic aortic aneurysm, dissection or dilatation affecting one or more aortic segments (aortic root, ascending aorta, arch or descending aorta) in the absence of any other associated disease. Depending on the size, location and progression rate of dilatation/dissection, patients may be asymptomatic or may present dyspnea, cough, jaw, neck, chest or back pain, head, neck or upper limb edema, difficulty swallowing, voice hoarseness, pale skin, faint pulse and/or numbness/tingling in limbs. Patients have increased risk of presenting life threatening aortic rupture.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Familial TAAD; Familial non-syndromic thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection (FTAAD) is primarily driven by genetic factors. Mutations in genes such as MYH11, ACTA2, LOX, and FBN1 are frequently implicated. MYH11 variants, which cause smooth muscle cell dysfunction, are a main cause of TAAD and patent ductus arteriosus, with specific variants leading to exon skipping. ACTA2 mutations are a common cause of non-syndromic familial aortic disease, with some variants demonstrating high penetrance. Loss-of-function LOX variants cause a spectrum of aortic and arterial aneurysmal disease, often with connective tissue findings. FBN1 mutations are the most common genetic cause of Marfan syndrome and annuloaortic ectasia, and polymorphisms in FBN1 and TGF-β signaling genes (TGFB1, TGFB2) are associated with susceptibility. Other genes like PKD1, NOTCH1, ARIH1, SMAD3, and KCNMA1 also contribute. The coexistence of multiple genetic variants, such as LOX and PKD1, may lead to early disease onset. Non-genetic factors, including family history, uncontrolled hypertension, and physically demanding lifestyles, can also play a role. [PMC11212385, PMC11110423, PMC10694883, PMC10671125, PMC10568822]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal presentations of pathogenic mutations linked to familial thoracic aortic aneurysm and aortic dissection have been documented. A de novo KCNMA1 mutation was identified in a 30-week-old fetus with severe growth retardation and duodenal atresia, representing the first antenatal presentation of a pathogenic KCNMA1 mutation. This gene is also associated with early onset aortic root dilatation. Additionally, heart and brain abnormalities were observed during the fetal stage in monozygotic twins carrying a novel MYH11 variant, a gene primarily implicated in thoracic aortic aneurysm/dissection. [PMC11110423, PMC8580096]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked syndromic intellectual disability with neuromuscular involvement characterized by a varying degree of neurodevelopmental delay including hypotonia, hypokinesia, dystonia and spasticity, and a wide range of clinical sequelae secondary to chronic peripheral thyrotoxicosis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): AHDS; MCT8 deficiency; Monocarboxylate transporter 8 deficiency; X-linked intellectual disability-hypotonia syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: At least 371 affected male individuals have been reported in the literature to date. There have been a few female cases reported. In two X-linked intellectual disability cohorts, the prevalence was 0.4% and 1.5%; in another cohort consisting of male and females with unexplained intellectual disability, 2 out of 501 males had SLC16A2 variants. Subsequently, the prevalence has been estimated at 1 in 70,000 male individuals, although there is uncertainty due to the limited data available.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease typically manifests in the first months of life with developmental delay and hypotonia. Key clinical features are hypotonia, hypokinesia, dystonia and spasticity. The majority of patients do not develop speech and are unable to sit or walk. Primitive reflexes are maintained throughout life. Seizures mostly involve generalized, absence-like episodes without a clear motor component. Most patients have a low body weight and feeding problems. Thyrotoxicosis may also lead to other features, such as sweating, tachycardia and elevated systolic blood pressure.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Allan-Herndon-Dudley syndrome (AHDS) or ''MCT8 deficiency'' is caused by variants of the SLC16A2 gene (Xq13.2), which encodes for monocarboxylate transporter (MCT) 8. A wide range of variants has been identified, including truncations, in-frame deletions, nonsense- and missense variants. MCT8 is a specific thyroid hormone transporter, facilitating transport of T3 and T4 into several tissues, including the brain. MCT8 deficiency leads to cerebral hypothyroidism, causing the varying neurodevelopmental features, and a wide range of clinical sequelae secondary to chronic peripheral thyrotoxicosis are caused by elevated serum T3 concentrations.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Developmental delay and other clinical features, combined with abnormal thyroid function tests; elevated (free) 3,3',5'-triiodothyronine (T3), low or low-normal (free) tetraiodothyronine (T4) concentrations, and normal to slightly elevated thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) concentrations should raise suspicion of the diagnosis. Genetic testing of the SLC16A2 gene revealing a pathogenic mutation confirms the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other conditions associated with intellectual disability, such as Pelizaeus-Merzbacher like disease.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: If the mother is a variant carrier, antenatal diagnosis of a male with AHDS is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is X-linked recessive. Affected families should be offered genetic counseling and informed that (if the mother is a carrier) boys have a 50% risk of being affected and girls have a 50% risk of inheriting the SLC16A2 variant. Skewed X inactivation may lead to symptomatic disease in females.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: AHDS management mainly consists of supportive measures. Physical, occupational, and speech therapy may be beneficial. Optimizing nutritional status is crucial. Dystonia may be treated with certain medications, including anticholinergics or baclofen. EEG-proven seizures may be controlled with antiepileptic drugs. The T3 analogue tiratricol (3,5,3'-triiodothyroacetic acid; TRIAC) is able to reduce T3 concentrations and to improve different features (e.g. low body weight, tachycardia) in pediatric and adult male patients with AHDS; marketing authorization has recently been granted by the European Medicine Agency.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Median life expectancy is estimated at 35 years, with 30% of patients dying in childhood. Severity of disease negatively impacts life expectancy, e.g. patients with a low body weight at an early age or the inability to attain head control have a decreased life expectancy. Major causes of mortality are pulmonary infection or aspiration, and sudden death.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Pelizaeus-Merzbacher disease (PMD) is an X-linked leukodystrophy characterized by developmental delay, nystagmus, hypotonia, spasticity, and variable intellectual deficit. It is classified into three sub-forms based on the age of onset and severity: connatal, transitional, and classic PMD.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Diffuse familial brain sclerosis; PMD; Pelizaeus-Merzbacher brain sclerosis; Sudanophilic leukodystrophy, Paelizeus-Merzbacher type

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated prevalence is 1/400,000. PMD affects males but some female heterozygotes presenting with a milder phenotype have also been reported (PMD in female carriers).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease has a broad clinical spectrum. The connatal form is the most severe form presenting, since birth, with hypotonia, nystagmus, respiratory distress, and stridor, with subsequent motor and cognitive delay and spastic quadriparesis. The classic form manifests during the first 2 months of life with nystagmus and hypotonia which is progressively replaced by spasticity. Later signs include ataxia, impaired motor development and intellectual deficit. The transitional form is of intermediate severity between the connatal and classic forms. The mildest presentation of PMD (mild developmental and motor delay beginning at 2-3 years old, later associated with spastic paraplegia, ataxia, and/or mild intellectual deficit) is not clearly distinguishable from PLP1 null syndrome, which consists on mild PMD features associated with peripheral neuropathy, and complicated spastic paraplegia 2 (SPG2), a disorder primarily characterized by spastic gait in its pure form.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: PMD is an X-linked disorder due to mutations or dosage alterations of the PLP1 gene (Xq22) that cause hypomyelination of the central nervous system (CNS). PMD is allelic to SPG2 which is also due to PLP1 mutations. PLP1 encodes the proteolipid protein PLP1, the most abundant protein of the myelin sheath in the CNS, and its alternatively spliced isoform DM20. PLP1 duplications lead to the classic form, missense substitutions from connatal to pure SPG2 forms, and PLP1 null mutations to the null syndrome. Patients without PLP1 mutations but with similar clinical and nearly identical neuroradiologic features as PMD are referred to as having PMD-like disease (PMLD).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical, electrophysiologic, and neuroradiological findings. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals complete (connatal, some transitional forms), partial (mild PMD) or diffuse (null syndrome) hypomyelination. Brainstem auditory evoked potentials (BAEP) may be helpful to differentiate PMD (lack of waves II-V) from PMLD (recordable II-V waves). Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Krabbe disease, Canavan disease, metachromatic leukodystrophy, Alexander disease, familial SPG, PMLD, and cerebral palsy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible when a family's underlying PLP1 mutation has been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is multidisciplinary and involves neurologists, physical therapists, orthopedic doctors, pneumologists, and gastroenterologists. Treatment may include gastrostomy for dysphagia, antiepileptic drugs for seizures, physical therapy with antispasticity drugs (baclofen, diazepam, tizanidine) for spasticity, or corrective surgery for pulmonary compromise in case of severe scoliosis. Regular surveillance is necessary.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: PMD has a progressive course that varies depending on the phenotype. In the most moderate forms, life expectancy is quite long and the disease progresses slowly after adolescence. In the most severe forms, death usually occurs by the second decade.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Pituitary deficiency due to empty sella turcica syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare pituitary deficiency characterized by herniation of the subarachnoid space into the sella turcica, resulting in flattening of the pituitary gland and endocrine dysfunction. Most common endocrine abnormalities are hyperprolactinemia and growth hormone deficit. Clinical symptoms are highly variable and include headaches, irregular menstruation, galactorrhea, obesity, and visual disturbances, among others.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Hypopituitarism due to empty sella turcica syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Turner syndrome is a common sex chromosome disorder characterized by short stature, gonadal dysgenesis, and hypergonadotropic hypogonadism. Empty Sella Syndrome is defined radiologically as the presence of cerebrospinal fluid filling the sella turcica and is associated with hypopituitarism. The association between TS and ESS is rare. a case of Turner syndrome associated with Empty Sella Syndrome, characterized by complete development of secondary sexual characteristics but irregular menstruation. Magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary gland revealed partial empty sella with evidence of pituitary compression. Laboratory investigations indicated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, central hypothyroidism, and an insulin-induced hypoglycemia test suggested insufficient compensatory growth hormone secretion, while cortisol compensation was normal. To ascertain the correlation between Turner... [PMC12170502, PMC11081045, PMC11460033]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Empty Sella Syndrome (ESS) is a radiological finding characterized by cerebrospinal fluid filling the sella turcica, often with pituitary compression, and is associated with hypopituitarism. Clinical presentations vary, encompassing isolated anterior, isolated posterior, or combined pituitary dysfunctions.
