Reported deficiencies include growth hormone deficiency (manifesting as short stature), hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (causing irregular menses or delayed puberty), central hypothyroidism, and ACTH deficiency, which can lead to secondary adrenal insufficiency, hyponatremia, persistent hypotension, or hypoglycemia. Arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) may also occur, presenting with polyuria and increased thirst. Associated symptoms can include headache and dizziness. ESS has been observed in conjunction with conditions such as Turner syndrome and Weiss-Kruszka syndrome. [PMC12170502, PMC11460033, PMC10566049, PMC9987106, PMC10506010]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic factors can contribute to pituitary deficiency due to empty sella turcica syndrome. Weiss-Kruszka syndrome (WSKA), an extremely rare genetic disorder caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in the ZNF462 gene, has been associated with primary empty sella syndrome and growth hormone deficiency, with identified de novo variants. Furthermore, some familial histories of empty sella syndrome, particularly when co-occurring with conditions like Turner syndrome, suggest the presence of an as-yet-undefined genetic-related pathophysiological mechanism that warrants further investigation. [PMC12170502, PMC8111047]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An anthropozoonosis, rare in Europe, clinically characterized by an initial presentation of flu-like symptoms rapidly progressing into life-threatening multisystem failure (notably hepatonephritis) caused by spiral-shaped bacteria belonging to the genus Leptospira. Leptospirosis is a widespread zoonosis with a worldwide distribution and has emerged as a major public health problem in developing countries in South-East Asia and South America.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Estimations from the World Health Organization (WHO) indicate that over 1 million cases of leptospirosis are thought to occur each year, with a mortality rate ranging from 5 to 20% depending on the country. However, the incidence in Europe is much lower with, for example, 600-700 cases in France which is the country with the highest incidence in Europe.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Initial signs of infection include fever associated with shivering and pain (myalgia, headaches and abdominal pain). The disease progresses over several days with severity varying from flu-like symptoms to rapidly life-threatening multisystem failure, with the most characteristic manifestation being hepatonephritis. Marked jaundice, renal insufficiency, neurologic signs, respiratory involvement, myocarditis, painful hepatomegaly with splenomegaly, and bleeding may also occur. Laboratory investigations reveal polynuclear hyperleucocytosis, cholestasis that is in some cases severe and isolated (without or with only limited cytolysis), and occasionally rhabdomyolysis and thrombopenia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Animal hosts (generally rodents) excrete leptospires in their urine. Humans become infected through skin or mucosal contact with contaminated soft water. The incubation period lasts around 10 days.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis relies on PCR results and serology. PCR analysis of blood or urine samples can be used to detect leptospire DNA and allows early diagnosis within the first week following disease onset. Antibodies can become detectable by the 6th to 10th day of the onset of symptoms by IgM ELISA or microscopic agglutination test (MAT). However, leptospirosis is often diagnosed late due to its wide spectrum of symptoms ranging from a flu-like syndrome to renal failure.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The symptoms mimic the clinical presentations of many other diseases, including dengue fever and malaria.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Leptospira remain sensitive to penicillin G and therefore treatment is based on administration of antibiotics. Antibiotic therapy is beneficial but must be administered in the early stage of the disease. Disease prevention revolves around eradication of rodents and the use of proper precautions. In some countries, such as France, a vaccine is also available but is reserved for those in at-risk professions, such as sewerage workers.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Leptospirosis may lead to pulmonary hemorrhages and irreversible multiple organ failure and death in 5 to 20% of cases.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare classic organic aciduria characterized by tissue accumulation and elevation of urinary excretion of 3-hydroxyisobutyric acid. The clinical phenotype ranges from recurrent mild episodes of vomiting with normal cognitive development, to massive acidosis, seizures, and failure to thrive with profound intellectual disability and early death. Dysmorphic craniofacial features (such as microcephaly, triangular face, short, sloping forehead, long, prominent philtrum, and micrognathia) and variable cerebral anomalies have also been described.

DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Primary hyperoxaluria type 2 is a rare monogenic disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. It from the absence of the enzyme glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase (GRHPR). As a consequence of deficient enzyme activity, excessive amounts of oxalate and L-glycerate are excreted in the urine, and are a source for the formation of calcium oxalate stones that result in recurrent nephrolithiasis and less frequently nephrocalcinosis. a case of a 10-month-old patient diagnosed with urolithiasis. Screening of inborn errors of metabolism, including the performance of GC/MS urine organic acid profiling and HPLC amino acid profiling, showed abnormalities, which suggested deficiency of GRHPR enzyme. Additional metabolic disturbances observed in the patient led us to seek other genetic determinants and the elucidation of these findings. Besides the elevated excretion of... [PMC5452357]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Increased urinary excretion of 3-hydroxyisobutyric acid has been observed in patients with Primary hyperoxaluria type 2 (PH2), a monogenic disorder resulting from glyoxylate reductase/hydroxypyruvate reductase (GRHPR) deficiency. In these cases, other metabolites such as 3-aminoisobutyric acid, 3-hydroxypropionic acid, and 2-ethyl-3-hydroxypropionic acids may also be elevated, alongside typical markers of ketosis like 3-OH-butyrate and adipic acid. Some metabolomic changes might be explained by the inhibition of the MMSADH enzyme due to metabolites increasing from GRHPR and AGXT2 enzyme deficiencies. [PMC5452357]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, aggressive and malignant hepatic tumor arising from the hepatocytes. It develops mainly in children over 10 years of age, either in a cirrhotic background, or more commonly in a non-cirrhotic background (70% of cases).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Childhood-onset hepatocellular carcinoma; Pediatric HCC; Childhood-onset HCC

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Primary liver malignancies are rare in children and adolescents. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) constitutes less than 25% of them. Annual incidence is about 1/2,000,000, with higher incidence rates found in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia as a result of endemic hepatitis B (HBV) and aflatoxin exposure. HCC is found more frequently in males (2-3:1). Incidence is higher among adolescents (1/1,250,000).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: HCC mostly develops in pediatric patients with no underlying liver disease, unlike in adults, when it is usually associated with hepatic cirrhosis due to alcohol intake. Pediatric HCC is mostly found in children and adolescents and rarely in children under 5 years of age. The main presenting manifestations are abdominal mass with pain, swelling and discomfort, weight loss, and anorexia. Splenomegaly, nausea, vomiting and jaundice are less commonly observed. Metastases to the mediastinal lymph nodes, lungs, brain and bone marrow are common in advanced disease (25% at presentation). HCC may be associated with congenital diseases, such as biliary atresia, tyrosinemia type 1 (in 50% of cases), alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis, Alagille or Gardner syndrome, Wilson or glycogen storage diseases I-IV, Fanconi anemia, familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), focal nodular hyperplasia and hemochromatosis. A specific HCC variant, fibrolamellar carcinoma (FLC), occurs in older children and young adults, and has an equally dismal prognosis despite a slower growth and less tendency to metastasize.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The pathophysiology of HCC is not well understood. Underlying liver dysfunction is the main predisposing condition (HBV, HCV). Children with neonatal hepatitis, intrahepatic cholestasis, biliary atresia, glycogen-storage diseases and other types of cirrhotic diseases are predisposed to the tumor. The Wnt/beta-catenin pathway is frequently activated via stabilizing mutations in beta-catenin: some patients have been found to harbor mutations in the CTNNB1 (3p21) and MET (7q31) genes. TP53 (17p13.1) gene and the TERT promoter are mutated in 25-30% and 60% of HCC cases, respectively. However, so far, the key genomic alteration in HCC has not yet been identified, and no mutation is used in clinical practice to predict a therapeutic response.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the clinical manifestations, elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) in 50% of cases, histological findings, and on liver imaging. A slowly enlarging mass may be found on physical examination. Abnormal levels of beta human chorionic gonadotropin (b-hCG) may also be detected (rare). Ultrasound typically shows a heterogeneous hyperechoic mass with increased vascularity. Chest CT and abdominal CT/MRI scans with intravenous contrast should be performed for initial staging. Other imaging techniques may also be required to determine possible metastatic spread.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnosis is hepatoblastoma, the most common hepatic tumor in the pediatric population in Western countries. Others include focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH), hepatic adenoma and undifferentiated embryonal sarcoma, as well as other less common liver malignancies.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: At-risk patients should be monitored closely. Screening for HBV and HCV should be performed. Monitoring with ultrasound and AFP every 6 months for all cirrhotic children, those with chronic HBV infection, inherited metabolic diseases or congenital porto-systemic shunts is suggested. The mainstay of curative therapy in non-metastatic patients is primary complete surgical resection (possible in about 25% of presenting children), delayed surgical resection (after neo-adjuvant chemotherapy) or liver transplantation (often across the Milan criteria). Transarterial chemo-embolization (TACE), radio-embolization (TARE) and radiofrequency ablation (RFA) are possible palliative options. Immunotherapies (CAR T cells, PD-1/PD-L1 and CTLA-4 checkpoint inhibitors) are newly emerging field for HCC.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis currently depends on success rates of resection in resectable tumors. 5-year survival rates are moderate in low stage tumors but these rates drop below 20-30% in advanced disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic disease characterized by the association of early onset cataract with persistently raised plasma ferritin concentrations in the absence of iron overload.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Hereditary hyperferritinemia-cataract disease; HHCS; Hereditary hyperferritinemia with cataracts

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact worldwide prevalence of hereditary hyperferritinemia-cataract syndrome (HHCS) remains unknown. It is estimated to be at least 1/200,000 in Australia.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The single clinical presentation of the disease is bilateral cataract that usually manifests after birth, as early as infancy, but also in adolescence or in early adulthood. Age of diagnosis ranges from 6 to 40 years old. Cataracts are described as numerous, pulverulent (dust-like) opacities of the lens causing glare and decreasing visual acuity. HHCS is characterized by variable severity of ocular involvement, and variable serum ferritin levels without iron overload. Ophthalmologic follow-up studies indicate an age-related evolution of lens opacities that might be related to the progressive accumulation of insoluble L-ferritin aggregates. The recognition of HHCS as a distinct disease is important for two main reasons: 1) to enable early detection of cataract even in asymptomatic patients, allowing adequate follow-up and scheduled surgical removal; 2) to avoid misdiagnosis that can lead to useless diagnostic procedures and inadequate treatment.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by a mutation in a translational regulatory element, a stem-loop structure called iron responsive element (IRE), in the 5' non-coding region of the light ferritin (FTL) gene located on 19q13.4-qter. In the absence of iron, the iron regulatory protein (IRP) binds to IRE and represses ferritin synthesis. Mutations affecting the IRE loop, bulge, and two partial deletions affecting either part of the IRE, have been reported. The most widely accepted pathophysiological mechanism is accumulation of insoluble crystalline aggregates of iron-poor L-ferritin protein causing cataract formation, which was demonstrated by immunohistochemical analysis and transmission electron microscopy of HHCS patients' lens aspirate. Age of onset and severity of lens damage vary in patients with the same mutations, even within one family, which suggests that other factors, acquired or genetic, may modulate clinical presentation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected in patients presenting with isolated hyperferritinemia in the absence of other evident cause of hyperferritinemia and iron overload. A personal or family history of early onset cataract should be investigated. Given that the cataract may not immediately be symptomatic, and that cases of de novo mutations have been reported, a comprehensive eye exam including a visual acuity test and a slit lamp examination may be recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Acquired causes of isolated hyperferritinemia should be evaluated and excluded. They include infections and inflammatory diseases, acute and chronic liver diseases, high alcohol intake, metabolic disorders, fatty liver disease, and hypothyroidism. Other inherited diseases may be considered such as genetic hyperferritinemia without iron overload, ferroportin disease, aceruloplasminemia, and Gaucher disease.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is autosomal dominant, with only few reports of spontaneous cases. Genetic counselling should be offered to affected individuals informing them that one of the parents is likely affected and there is a 50% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Patients are treated by cataract surgery when they suffer visual impairment due to cataracts formation. Hyperferritinemia is not associated with iron overload and doesn't require treatment. Thus, venesections should be avoided as they could induce iron deficiency and iron deficient anemia without significant change of ferritin level.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Besides cataracts, there is no other clinical manifestation associated with this disease and the prognosis is good.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cerebral arteriovenous malformation (AVM) is a congenital malformative communication between the veins and the arteries in the brain in the form of a nidus, an anatomical structure composed of dilated and tangled supplying arterioles and drainage veins with no intervening capillary bed, that can be asymptomatic or cause, depending on the location and the size of the AVM, headaches of varying severity, generalized or focal seizures, focalneurological defects (weakness, numbness, speech difficulties, vision loss) or potentially fatal intracranial hemorrhage in case the AVM ruptures.

DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation can be detected in early life, including in fetuses or neonates. Early detection does not inherently indicate a poor prognosis, as outcomes can vary. This highlights the importance of vigilant monitoring and timely intervention to optimize patient outcomes. [PMC11724148]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is an autosomal-dominant vascular disorder characterized by arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) in multiple organs, including the brain. Genetic analysis in affected individuals has revealed novel heterozygous mutations, such as a frameshift mutation in the activin A receptor-like type 1 (ACVRL1) gene. Therefore, genetic counseling should address the autosomal-dominant inheritance pattern of HHT and the potential for specific gene mutations like ACVRL1 in families presenting with cerebral AVMs. [PMC11867738]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Citrullinemia is an autosomal recessively inherited disorder of urea cycle metabolism and ammonia detoxification characterized by elevated concentrations of serum citrulline and ammonia. The disease presents with a large range of manifestations including neonatal hyperammonemic encephalopathy with lethargy, seizures and coma; hepatic dysfunction in all age groups; episodes of hyperammonemia and neuropsychiatric symptoms in children or adults, or, can be asymptomatic in some cases (detected in newborn screening programs). Citrullinemia is divided into two main groups that are encoded by different genes: citrullinemia type I (comprised of acute neonatal citrullinemia type I and adult-onset citrullinemia type I) and citrin deficiency (comprised of adult-onset citrullinemia type II and neonatal intrahepatic cholestasis due to citrin deficiency).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Citrullinemia is a rare autosomal recessive inborn error of the urea cycle due to a deficiency in argininosuccinic acid synthetase. two cases of the infantile form of citrullinemia in which CT revealed bilateral and symmetric corticosubcortical hypoattenuating areas, ulegyric changes, and atrophy in the frontal lobes, as well as atrophy in the gyrus cinguli, insulae, and temporal lobes. [PMC7975255]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Citrullinemia is an inborn error of the urea cycle characterized by markedly increased citrulline values, hyperammonemia, and abnormalities in plasma amino acids and liver functions. Patients may present with coma. In the infantile form, CT scans can reveal bilateral and symmetric corticosubcortical hypoattenuating areas, ulegyric changes, and atrophy in the frontal, gyrus cinguli, insulae, and temporal lobes. [PMC7975255, PMC2977958]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Citrullinemia is an autosomal recessive inborn error of the urea cycle, primarily caused by a deficiency in argininosuccinic acid synthetase. This enzyme deficiency leads to metabolic abnormalities, which can be corrected by orthotopic liver transplantation. The condition can be diagnosed prenatally by assaying argininosuccinic acid synthetase activity in cultured amniotic fluid cells, with increased citrulline concentrations in amniotic fluid providing strong adjunctive evidence. [PMC7975255, PMC2977958, PMC1685476]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of citrullinemia involves several approaches. Biochemical analysis may reveal hyperammonemia and abnormalities in plasma amino acids, with markedly increased citrulline values observed in argininosuccinic acid synthetase deficiency. Enzyme analysis, specifically assaying argininosuccinic acid synthetase activity in cultured amniotic fluid cells or fetal skin fibroblasts, can be used for prenatal diagnosis. An increased concentration of citrulline in amniotic fluid provides strong adjunctive evidence for prenatal diagnosis. In the infantile form, CT scans may show characteristic findings such as bilateral and symmetric corticosubcortical hypoattenuating areas, ulegyric changes, and atrophy in various brain regions. [PMC7975255, PMC2977958, PMC1685476]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Citrullinemia, an inborn metabolic disease, is a urea cycle defect that must be differentiated from other conditions presenting with acute metabolic crisis and hyperammonemia. Other urea cycle defects include carbamyl phosphate synthetase-I deficiency and ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency. Specific biochemical markers aid in differentiation; for example, carbamyl phosphate synthetase-I deficiency is characterized by high plasma glutamine and no measurable citrulline, while argininosuccinic acid synthetase deficiency (Citrullinemia) shows markedly increased citrulline values. Beyond urea cycle disorders, other inborn metabolic diseases such as maple syrup urine disease and methylmalonic acidemia may also be considered in the differential diagnosis. [PMC7080361, PMC2977958]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of citrullinemia can be achieved by monitoring at-risk pregnancies. This involves assaying argininosuccinic acid synthetase activity in cultured amniotic fluid cells, which shows significantly reduced activity in affected fetuses. Additionally, an increased concentration of citrulline in the amniotic fluid provides strong adjunctive evidence for the diagnosis. Confirmation can be made post-termination by assaying ASA synthetase activity in cultured fetal skin fibroblasts and observing citrulline accumulation in fetal tissues. [PMC1685476]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Citrullinemia is an autosomal recessive inborn error of the urea cycle, caused by a deficiency in argininosuccinic acid synthetase. For families at risk, prenatal diagnosis is possible. Successful in utero diagnosis has been demonstrated by microassay of argininosuccinic acid synthetase activity in cultured amniotic fluid cells. Elevated citrulline concentrations in amniotic fluid provide strong adjunctive evidence for this prenatal diagnosis. The infantile form of the disease is associated with significant neurological findings, including bilateral and symmetric corticosubcortical hypoattenuating areas, ulegyric changes, and atrophy in various brain regions. [PMC7975255, PMC1685476]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of citrullinemia involves strategies to remove toxic metabolites and correct underlying enzyme deficiencies. In newborns experiencing acute metabolic crises, continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) can efficiently reduce plasma ammonium levels, improving short and long-term outcomes when combined with early diagnosis, specific medical therapy, and diet. However, some survivors may still develop mental and motor retardation. Orthotopic liver transplantation offers a corrective approach, addressing hyperammonemia and amino acid abnormalities by replacing the deficient enzyme. This procedure has been shown to correct life-threatening metabolic abnormalities, with patients remaining well years after surgery, although post-surgical complications can impact intellectual recovery. [PMC7080361, PMC2977958]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Citrullinemia, as an inborn metabolic disease, can lead to acute metabolic crisis, long-term neurological dysfunction, and death due to the accumulation of toxic metabolites. In newborns with urea cycle defects treated with continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration, the survival rate was 50%, with surviving patients developing mild to severe mental and motor retardation. Orthotopic liver transplantation can correct the life-threatening metabolic abnormalities caused by argininosuccinic acid synthetase deficiency. Patients who underwent liver transplantation were well several years post-surgery, though intellectual recovery may be slightly retarded in some cases due to post-surgical complications. Early diagnosis, specific medical therapy, diet, and extracorporeal support are likely to improve short and long-term outcomes. [PMC7080361, PMC2977958]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: DK1-CDG is characterised by muscular hypotonia and ichthyosis. It has been described in four children from two consanguineous families. All the affected children died during early infancy, two from dilated cardiomyopathy. The syndrome is caused by a deficiency in dolichol kinase 1 (DK1), an enzyme involved in the de novo biosynthesis of dolichol phosphate. The mutations identified in the DK1 gene led to a 96 to 98% reduction in DK activity.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Dolichol kinase deficiency; Hypotonia and ichthyosis due to dolichol phosphate deficiency; CDG syndrome type Im; CDG-Im; CDG1M; Carbohydrate deficient glycoprotein syndrome type Im; Congenital disorder of glycosylation type 1m; Congenital disorder of glycosylation type Im

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: DK1-CDG, also known as DOLK-CDG or CDG-Im, is a congenital disorder of glycosylation with a variable clinical presentation. Previously reported manifestations include dilated cardiomyopathy of variable severity. A severe, fatal case presented with dysmorphic features, genital abnormalities, talipes equinovarus, and severe, refractory generalized seizures. Additional multi-systemic dysfunction included dilated cardiomyopathy, hepatomegaly, severe insulin-resistant hyperglycemia, and renal failure, leading to death at 9 months of age. This expands the known phenotype to include anatomic malformations and multi-systemic involvement. [PMC3909743]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: DK1-CDG, also known as DOLK-CDG or CDG-Im, is a congenital disorder of glycosylation caused by abnormal glycosylation of proteins and lipids. This condition stems from a deficiency in dolichol kinase (DOLK), an enzyme that catalyzes the final step in the biosynthesis of dolichol phosphate (Dol-P), an oligosaccharide carrier required for protein N-glycosylation. Specific cases have identified homozygous DOLK mutations, such as p.Q483K, which lead to severely reduced substrate binding and catalytic activity of the enzyme. [PMC3909743]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of DK1-CDG involves electrospray ionization mass spectrometric (ESI-MS) analysis of transferrin, which can identify a type I congenital disorder of glycosylation. This is followed by next-generation sequencing to demonstrate homozygous DOLK mutations, such as p.Q483K. Confirmation of these mutations in patient fibroblasts can further show severely reduced substrate binding and catalytic activity. [PMC3909743]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The identification of homozygous p.Q483K DOLK mutations in the patient indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern for DK1-CDG. This implies that both parents are likely heterozygous carriers of the mutation. Such genetic information is critical for counseling families regarding the risk of recurrence in future pregnancies. [PMC3909743]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for DK1-CDG can be severe. One reported case described a neonate who presented with dysmorphic features, genital abnormalities, talipes equinovarus, and severe, refractory generalized seizures. Additional multi-systemic manifestations developed, including dilated cardiomyopathy, hepatomegaly, severe insulin-resistant hyperglycemia, and renal failure. These complications were ultimately fatal at 9 months of age. [PMC3909743]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Deafness with labyrinthine aplasia, microtia, and microdontia
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Deafness with labyrinthine aplasia, microtia, and microdontia (LAMM) is a genetic transmission deafness syndrome.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Hearing loss with labyrinthine aplasia, microtia, and microdontia; LAMM syndrome; Microdontia-type I microtia-deafness syndrome; Microdontia-type I microtia-hearing loss syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It has been described in 6 families to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The profound congenital deafness is associated with a complete absence of inner ear structures (Michel aplasia); microtia type I with small auricle and narrow external auditory canal; and microdontia with widely spaced teeth.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Linkage analysis followed by sequencing of candidate genes led to identification of three different homozygous mutations in the FGF3 gene (11q13).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of LAMM syndrome is based on characteristic clinical features, including congenital sensorineural hearing loss, labyrinthine aplasia, type I microtia, and microdontia, with congenital deafness often being the primary presenting feature. Genetic testing is crucial, as the syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in the FGF3 gene. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) is utilized to identify these variants, and further investigations, such as Sanger sequencing, can confirm variant co-segregation with the observed phenotype. [PMC11487696, PMC10178790, PMC6678228]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Over 700 syndromes associated with hearing loss (HL) have been identified. Labyrinthine aplasia, microtia, and microdontia (LAMM syndrome, OMIM: 610706) is a rare HL syndrome characterized by congenital sensorineural HL, labyrinthine aplasia, type I microtia and microdontia, which is caused by biallelic variants in the FGF3 gene. Using Whole-exome sequencing (WES), we identified a novel missense FGF3 variant (c.137G > C, p. Arg46Pro (NM_005247.4) in three unrelated Uyghur ethnic families. This variant is classified as a variant of uncertain significance according to ACMG guidelines, with the applied criteria of PM3, PM2_Supporting, PP3 and PP4. Patients from the three families revealed variable clinical features. We found a novel phenotype, sparse hair, in one of the proband. Our findings expanded the variant and phenotype spectrum of LAMM syndrome and provided new insights to the... [PMC11487696, PMC10178790]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, disease that manifests in childhood or early adolescence with a combination of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and autoimmune adrenal failure.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): APECED syndrome; APS type 1; APS1; Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 1; Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism-chronic candidiasis-Addison disease syndrome; Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1; HAM syndrome; Autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy syndrome; MEDAC syndrome; Hypoparathyroidism-Addison disease-mucocutaneous candidiasis syndrome; Multiple endocrine deficiency-Addison disease-candidiasis syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It is a rare disease that is more common in populations with higher rates of consanguineous marriage and, because of a founder effect, in Finland where the prevalence is estimated at 1/25,000. In the north-west of France the prevalence is estimated at 1/500,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The first manifestation of the disease (usually candidiasis) occurs in childhood with other manifestations appearing progressively. Candidiasis affects particularly the mucosa of the mouth, nails and, more rarely, the genitals, and rarely causes cutaneous effects. The most common autoimmune endocrine involvement is hypoparathyroidism (79-96% of cases). Adrenal failure most often manifests with concurrent mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency (78% of cases). Ovarian failure is possible. Diabetes type 1, autoimmune thyroiditis, and lymphocytic hypophysitis are rarer. Other auto-immune manifestations are common: intestinal malabsorption, atrophic gastritis, autoimmune hepatitis, alopecia, vitiligo, hypoplasia of dental enamel, ungual dystrophy, keratoconjunctivitis, and rheumatologic, bony, muscular, renal, bronchiol and hematologic impairments. Splenic atrophy increases the likelihood for severe infections. There is high phenotypic variability, sometimes within the same family, and the number of manifestations is very variable, ranging from 1 to 10.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is caused by mutations of the AIRE gene (21q22.3) coding for the AIRE transcription factor, which is involved in immune tolerance mechanisms and contributes to the negative selection of autoreactive T lymphocytes in the thymus, lymph nodes and spleen.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the presence of at least two of the three following pathologies: mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and adrenal failure. In cases where one of the patient's siblings is affected, one of the three criteria is sufficient for initial diagnosis, which can then be confirmed by molecular analysis. The presence of a litany of antibodies, specifically organ antibodies (sometimes forewarning of a visceral attack) or more general antibodies (anti-interferon AC) can support the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include IPEX syndrome and, principally, autoimmune polyendocrinopathy type 2.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Although prenatal diagnosis is not recommended, genetic counseling should be offered.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is essentially symptomatic. Hormone replacement is used to treat endocrine disorders. A long course of oral systemic antifungal treatment is effective to treat candidiasis, although some patients remain resistant. Immunosuppressive treatment is recommended for cases with autoimmune hepatitis or with severe malabsorption.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is variable. The more early the manifestations appear, the more numerous the organs involved. The prognosis can be threatened by: oral or esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, sepsis, fulminant hepatitis, renal failure due to interstitial nephritis or bronchial involvement. On average patients live into their forties, but this varies considerably between patients depending on the severity of disorders.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, severe form of mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD) characterized by dysmorphic features, failure to thrive, psychomotor delay, ocular involvement, hypotonia, progressive ataxia, myopathy, and recurrent inflammatory episodes.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact prevalence and incidence of MVA are not known. Fewer than 50 patients have been reported to date. A small proportion of patients with MKD have mevalonic aciduria (MVA), while most cases correspond to the milder phenotype known as Hyperimmunoglobinemia D with periodic fever (HIDS).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset of MVA is usually during infancy and in some severe cases antenatally. The clinical presentation is variable with cases of severe disease with significantly reduced life expectancy to milder cases with no effect on life expectancy. Infants may be born with shortened limbs and dysmorphic features (dolichocephaly, microcephaly, frontal bossing, a triangular-shaped face, down-slanting eyelids, and dysplastic or low-set ears. Affected patients may also present with marked failure to thrive, and recurrent episodes of fever (that may be fatal in infancy) possibly accompanied by hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, arthralgia, myalgia, mouth ulcers, and skin eruptions. During childhood, patients may show failure to thrive, developmental delay and progressive ataxia; in later childhood or adolescence they may develop progressive ocular disorders such as uveitis, blue sclera, retinitis pigmentosa, or cataracts. Short stature and myopathy are reported in older patients.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MVA is caused by mutations in the MVK gene (12q24). MVK encodes mevalonate kinase, which is involved in cholesterol and isoprenoid production. In patients with the severe form of MKD, enzyme deficiency is nearly complete causing the severe manifestations of the disorder. Severity usually depends on the degree of residual enzyme activity.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: MKD follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. Genetic counseling should be proposed to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Inflammatory attacks can often be controlled with interleukin-1 blocking agents such as canakinumab or anakinra. Severely affected patients have been seen to improve significantly upon allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Mevalonic aciduria (MA), a severe phenotype of Mevalonate Kinase Deficiency (MKD), relies on a combination of biochemical and genetic testing. Elevated urinary mevalonic acid and reduced mevalonate enzyme activity are key biochemical markers. Genetic testing, including next-generation sequencing, Sanger sequencing, and whole exome sequencing, is used to identify pathogenic mutations in the mevalonate kinase (MVK) gene. Both homozygous and compound heterozygous MVK gene mutations are associated with the disease, with several novel mutations reported. Early genetic screening is recommended for young children presenting with suggestive clinical features, such as vasculitis, to confirm the diagnosis. [PMC12297814, PMC8987701, PMC8607720, PMC7442240, PMC6708240]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Mevalonic aciduria (MA) is consistently described as the most severe clinical subtype of mevalonate kinase deficiency, often presenting with severe recurrent systemic inflammation and organ deterioration. The prognosis can be poor, with fatalities reported in early infancy due to recurrent septicaemia. Complications, such as acute myeloid leukemia and sepsis following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, have also led to death. Patients may experience growth restriction and developmental delay. Genotype influences disease severity, with homozygous MVK gene mutations frequently associated with MA; specifically, the homozygous A334T mutation may present a milder phenotype, while the I268T homozygous mutation is linked to a more severe presentation. [PMC12297814, PMC8987701, PMC8691729, PMC1721642]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inborn error of amino acid metabolism characterized by elevated blood phenylalanine and low levels or absence of phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme. If not detected early or left untreated, the disorder manifests with mild to severe mental disability.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of phenylketonuria (PKU) shows considerable geographic variation. It is estimated to be 1/10,000 live births in Europe with a higher rate in some countries (Ireland, Italy). Prevalence is particularly high in Turkey: 1/4,000 live births. PKU is far rarer in the Finnish, African and Japanese populations.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In the absence of neonatal diagnosis, symptoms develop within a few months of birth, may be very mild to severe and include gradual developmental delay, stunted growth, microcephaly, seizures, tremors, eczema, vomiting, and musty odor. Untreated patients subsequently develop intellectual disability, behavioral disorders (hyperactivity) and motor disorders. Patients often have fair coloring as a result of tyrosine deficiency. The most common form of the condition is known as classical phenylketonuria and is characterized by severe symptoms. A mild form has also been described (mild PKU), and an even milder form known as mild hyperphenylalaninemia (mild HPA or non-PKU HPA). A subset of patients with milder phenotypes has been found to be responsive to tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4), the cofactor of phenylalanine hydroxylase (BH4-responsive HPA).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: PKU is caused by a wide range of variants in the PAH gene (12q22-q24.2) coding for phenylalanine hydroxylase. Non-PAH variants have been reported to cause a disorder known as hyperphenylalaninemia due to BH4 deficiency. Variant frequency varies among different ethnic groups. Lower levels or absence of the phenylalanine hydroxylase enzyme underlie the clinical manifestations, as a result of toxic accumulation of phenylalanine in the blood and brain.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The disorder is usually diagnosed through neonatal screening programs.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: PKU should be distinguished from BH4 deficiency.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them of the 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The mainstay of treatment is a low-phenylalanine diet and amino acids mixture for the forms that require treatment. According to the European guidelines for the management of PKU, the recommended maintenance level is usually between 120 and 360 micromol/L in newborns, with treatment considered essential in older patients with levels above 600 micromol/L.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable, but favorable if diagnosed early and treated properly.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Mosaic Trisomy 4 is a rare autosomal anomaly, due to the presence of an extra copy of chromosome 4 in a fraction of all cells, with a variable phenotype characterized by intrauterine growth retardation, low birth weight/length/OFC, mild intellectual deficit, congenital heart defects, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, dysmorphic features (asymmetry of the face, eyebrow anomalies, low-set, posteriorally rotated, dysplastic ears, micro-/retrognathia), characteristic thumb abnormalities (aplasia, hypoplasia) and skin abnormalities (hypo/hyperpigmentation). Delayed puberty may be associated.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: A mosaicism is defined by the presence of two or more populations of cells with different genotypes in one individual. Chromosomal germinal mosaicism occurs in germ cells before the onset of meiosis. Previously, few studies have described germinal mosaicism. In , on two siblings who carried identical pure and direct interstitial 4q22.2q32.3 duplication. Procedure investigations included complete clinical description, conventional cytogenetic analysis, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) array experiments and microsatellite study searching for parental origin of the duplication. Microarray CGH and further FISH experiments with BAC clones showed the same 70.8 Mb direct duplication, dup(4)(q22.2q32.3). Molecular studies of the 4q duplication were consistent with maternal origin associated with mitotic or meiotic rearrangements. This structural... [PMC2987392]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Mosaic trisomy 4 syndrome, specifically involving a recurrent 70.8 Mb 4q22.2q32.3 duplication, presents with a range of clinical manifestations. Affected individuals exhibit increased nuchal translucency, growth retardation, and dysmorphy. Cardiopathy and lung malformations have also been observed, though not consistently in all cases. The duplicated region includes genes implicated in neurological development. These features are largely consistent with previously reported pure 4q trisomy of the same region, although thumb and renal abnormalities were not evident in the described cases. [PMC2987392]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: A mosaicism is defined by the presence of two or more populations of cells with different genotypes in one individual. Chromosomal germinal mosaicism occurs in germ cells before the onset of meiosis. Previously, few studies have described germinal mosaicism. In , on two siblings who carried identical pure and direct interstitial 4q22.2q32.3 duplication. Procedure investigations included complete clinical description, conventional cytogenetic analysis, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) array experiments and microsatellite study searching for parental origin of the duplication. Microarray CGH and further FISH experiments with BAC clones showed the same 70.8 Mb direct duplication, dup(4)(q22.2q32.3). Molecular studies of the 4q duplication were consistent with maternal origin associated with mitotic or meiotic rearrangements. This structural... [PMC2987392]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of chromosomal aberrations, including mosaicism and duplications, can be performed using conventional cytogenetic analysis. Further characterization of such structural changes, like a 4q duplication, involves fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), including experiments with BAC clones, and comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) array experiments. Microsatellite studies can also be utilized to investigate the parental origin of these duplications. [PMC2987392]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis should consider conditions with similar chromosomal aberrations. Pure 4q trisomy of the same region presents with similar clinical manifestations, including increased nuchal translucency, growth retardation, and dysmorphy. Cardiopathy and lung malformations may also overlap. However, thumb and renal abnormalities, which were not obvious in cases of 4q22.2q32.3 duplication, might distinguish pure 4q trisomy. [PMC2987392]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: A mosaicism is defined by the presence of two or more populations of cells with different genotypes in one individual. Chromosomal germinal mosaicism occurs in germ cells before the onset of meiosis. Previously, few studies have described germinal mosaicism. In , on two siblings who carried identical pure and direct interstitial 4q22.2q32.3 duplication. Procedure investigations included complete clinical description, conventional cytogenetic analysis, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), comparative genomic hybridization (CGH) array experiments and microsatellite study searching for parental origin of the duplication. Microarray CGH and further FISH experiments with BAC clones showed the same 70.8 Mb direct duplication, dup(4)(q22.2q32.3). Molecular studies of the 4q duplication were consistent with maternal origin associated with mitotic or meiotic rearrangements. This structural... [PMC2987392]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for apparently de novo chromosome aberrations should be undertaken with care. This is highlighted by cases of recurrent chromosomal duplications in siblings, which can be consistent with parental germinal mosaicism, such as maternal ovarian germinal mosaicism. This implies a potential recurrence risk for future pregnancies, even when the aberration appears new in the affected individual. [PMC2987392]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Congenital ectropion uveae is a rare, genetic, non-syndromic developmental defect of the eye characterized by the presence of iris pigment epithelium on the anterior surface of the iris, anterior insertion of the iris, angle dysgenesis and progressive open-angle glaucoma (the latter may present in infancy or may develop later in life). Patients may manifest with headaches, ocular pain, photophobia, and redness, watering and/or swelling of the eye. It can often be associated with neurofibromatosis and less commonly with other ocular abnormalities.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Congenital ectropion uveae (CEU) is described as a rare anomaly. Its rarity contributes to a limited understanding of the condition and challenges in standardizing surgical management for associated complications, such as glaucoma. Ophthalmologists are advised to remain vigilant to avoid missed diagnoses due to its high association with glaucoma. [PMC11749601]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Congenital ectropion uveae (CEU) is a rare, nonprogressive anomaly characterized by the proliferation of the iris pigment epithelium on the anterior surface of the iris. It is often associated with glaucoma, which can present with high intraocular pressure, decreased vision, and mild distending pain. Slit-lamp examination typically reveals 360° ectropion uveae, extending around the pupil to the mid-periphery of the iris. Ophthalmologists should remain vigilant to avoid missed diagnoses due to its high association with glaucoma, which can manifest in adulthood. [PMC11749601]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Congenital ectropion uveae has been observed in association with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). NF1 is an autosomal dominant genetic disease that causes multi-system damage. In a reported case, ectropion uveae was noted in a pediatric patient with NF1 who also presented with unilateral chronic angle-closure glaucoma. [PMC10201525]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Congenital ectropion uveae (CEU) is characterized by the proliferation of the iris pigment epithelium on the anterior surface of the iris. Diagnosis can be challenging and may be initially missed due to its rarity. A definitive diagnosis is made through slit-lamp examination, which reveals 360° ectropion uveae extending around the pupil to the mid-periphery of the iris. The condition is highly associated with glaucoma, which presents with elevated intraocular pressure and an increased cup-to-disc ratio. Ophthalmologists should maintain vigilance to avoid missed diagnoses. [PMC11749601]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The provided abstract describes a case where ectropion uveae was observed in a pediatric patient diagnosed with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) who also presented with unilateral chronic angle-closure glaucoma. This suggests that NF1, particularly when associated with angle-closure glaucoma, should be considered in the differential diagnosis when ectropion uveae is present. [PMC10201525]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Congenital ectropion uveae is frequently associated with glaucoma, for which standardized surgical management is limited. In a reported case, Ahmed glaucoma valve (AGV) implantation with mitomycin C was performed for late-onset glaucoma secondary to CEU in an adult patient. This intervention led to stabilized intraocular pressure without medication for three years and improved visual acuity. AGV implantation with mitomycin C may be considered an effective surgical management option for adult patients with late-onset glaucoma secondary to congenital ectropion uveae. [PMC11749601]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Congenital ectropion uveae (CEU) is described as a nonprogressive anomaly. However, it is highly associated with glaucoma, which can lead to complications such as elevated intraocular pressure and decreased vision. With appropriate surgical management, such as Ahmed glaucoma valve implantation, favorable outcomes can be achieved, including improved visual acuity and stabilization of intraocular pressure without medication over several years. Vigilance for early diagnosis is important due to the strong association with glaucoma. [PMC11749601]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare partial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 12 characterized by variable combinations of developmental delay, intellectual disability, behavioral abnormalities, variable dysmorphic facial features (including microcephalus, coarse face, synophrys, epicanthal folds, large bulbous nose, small ears, low-set and posteriorly rotated ears, or large tongue, among others), and other anomalies such as malformations of the hands and fingers/feet and toes, skin and nail abnormalities, and genitourinary and cardiac abnormalities, among others.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Abnormalities involving the telomere of chromosome 12 are rare, with few reports of deletions involving the 12q24.31 region in the literature. To date, only four cases of deletions in the 12q24.31-q24.33 region have been reported prior to the current case. This suggests that distal deletion 12q syndrome is an exceedingly rare disorder. [PMC7279891]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Distal deletion 12q syndrome is a rare chromosomal abnormality, often involving deletions in the 12q24.31-q24.33 region. Clinical features include global developmental delay and multiple congenital anomalies. The syndrome is also associated with autism spectrum disorder. Diagnosis can be confirmed through genetic testing, such as Human Genome CGH Microarray. [PMC7279891]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal deletion 12q syndrome is caused by chromosomal abnormalities, specifically telomeric or subtelomeric deletions involving the long arm of chromosome 12. Deletions in the 12q24.31 region are rare, with even fewer reported cases involving the 12q24.31-q24.33 bands. These deletions can be interstitial and are confirmed through genetic testing, such as Human Genome CGH Microarray. [PMC7279891]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of distal deletion 12q syndrome, characterized by chromosomal abnormalities such as telomeric/subtelomeric or interstitial deletions in the 12q24.31-q24.33 region, can be confirmed through genetic testing. The Human Genome CGH Microarray 60K has been specifically used to confirm the diagnosis of 12q deletion syndrome. These detailed analyses contribute to the development of genotype/phenotype correlations, which aid in better diagnosis and prognosis of this rare disorder. [PMC7279891]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Detailed analyses of cases with distal 12q deletions, particularly those involving the 12q24.31-q24.33 region, contribute to the development of genotype-phenotype correlations. These correlations are essential for genetic counseling, as they aid in providing a more accurate diagnosis and prognosis for individuals affected by this rare chromosomal abnormality. Understanding these relationships helps families comprehend the implications of the deletion, including associated features such as global developmental delay, multiple congenital anomalies, and autism spectrum disorder. [PMC7279891]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Chromosomal abnormalities are responsible for several congenital malformations in the world, some of these are associated to telomeric/subtelomeric deletions. The abnormalities involving the telomere of chromosome 12 are rare, with few reports of deletions involving 12q24.31 region in the literature, and, to our knowledge, only four of them in the 12q24.31-q24.33 region. a further case of interstitial deletion of bands 12q24.31-q24.33 associated with autism spectrum disorder. A 2-year-old boy with global developmental delay associated with multiple congenital anomalies. The Human Genome CGH Microarray 60K confirmed the diagnosis of 12q deletion syndrome. made a review of the current literature comparing our patient with previously reported cases. These detailed analyses contribute to the development of genotype/phenotype correlations for 12q deletions that will aid in better diagnosis... [PMC7279891]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A respiratory abnormality characterized by respiratory distress due to hyperinflation of one or more affected lobes of the lung.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Congenital lobar hyperinflation; Infantile lobar hyperinflation

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It is a rare disease with the birth prevalence being 1/20,000 to 1/30,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most cases present in the neonatal period or in early infancy. Patients with less severe manifestations may present in early childhood or rarely in adulthood. Clinical picture can range from asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic to severe respiratory impairment requiring immediate intervention. Symptomatic patients present with asymmetric chest wall expansion, respiratory distress, dyspnea, tachycardia, cyanosis, and failure to thrive. The left upper lobe is most commonly affected (41%) followed by the right middle lobe (34%) and the right upper lobe (21%). CLE can occur in association with cardiac malformations in 15 to 20% cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: About 50% of cases have no identifiable etiology; however an abnormality or absence of cartilaginous rings, intrinsic obstruction caused by redundant mucosa, extrinsic obstruction (vascular or bronchial) or hyperinflation alone might explain the CLE. Polyalveolar lobe has also been reported as a cause of CLE.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Chest X ray and CT scan are the key imaging modalities used for diagnosis. Chest X ray shows hyperlucent affected lobes with mediastinal shift and collapse of ipsilateral unaffected segments. CT scan provides details of affected lobes and vascular involvement. Echocardiography to detect concomitant heart disease can also be performed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Respiratory distress and radiolucency in chest X rays can lead to a misdiagnosis of tension pneumothorax. Differential diagnoses also include congenital pulmonary airway malformation, pneumonia, bronchiolitis and foreign body aspiration.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis can be made with ultrasonography by identifying hyperechoic areas in fetal lung and Magnetic Resonance Imaging identify uniform T2 hyperintensity compared to normal lung.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Lobectomy of affected lobes is the widely accepted form of management with a satisfactory outcome. Asymptomatic or mildly symptomatic cases can be managed conservatively but follow up is necessary. Thoracoscopic resection has been attempted and seems to have better post operative outcomes.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Asymptomatic cases may regress spontaneously. Prompt diagnosis and surgical intervention usually provide good long term outcome in symptomatic cases. In some cases, CLE can be lethal.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Isolated lissencephaly type 1 without known genetic defects
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Isolated lissencephaly type 1 without known genetic defects belongs to the genetically heterogeneous group, classic lissencephaly. It is a diagnosis of exclusion, when neither associated malformations nor family history are present, and in the absence of mutations of genes known to be involved in classic lissencephaly. Clinically patients present with the common features of classic lissencephaly such as developmental delay, intellectual disability, and seizures.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Lissencephaly is a rare brain malformation characterized histologically by arrested neuronal migration, resulting in a brain resembling that of a fetus before 23-24 weeks gestation. Diffusion tensor imaging in affected neonates can reveal a dysplastic, densely cellular layer IV visible as a band of anisotropic diffusion. Imaging also shows a lack of connectivity between the cortex and deep white matter, along with an abnormal limbic system. [PMC8149082]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Lissencephaly is recognized as a neuronal migration disorder. In some families, lissencephaly, along with pachygyria and subcortical laminar heterotopia, appears to share an X-linked or autosomal dominant gene. Despite this genetic association, no specific chromosomal abnormalities, particularly involving chromosome 17, were identified in the reported cases. [PMC1073073]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Lissencephaly can be diagnosed using various neuroimaging modalities. Prenatal detection and characterization are possible with multiplanar neuro sonography, anatomical MRI, and advanced MRI techniques. Sonography and conventional MRI allow clear delineation of the condition, with T2-weighted MRI making laminar heterotopia more evident. Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) and DTI tractography are significant for evaluation, revealing dysplastic layers, abnormal connectivity, and dysmorphic connections. MRI can also be used for family screening. [PMC11730443, PMC3997796, PMC7964813, PMC8149082, PMC1073073]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for lissencephaly includes several genetically defined conditions. Miller-Dieker Syndrome (MDS), caused by a heterozygous deletion on chromosome 17 involving genes such as PAFAH1B1, presents with lissencephaly, severe neurological defects, and distinctive facial abnormalities, sometimes with congenital lobar emphysema. Cobblestone lissencephaly (COB) is a severe brain malformation seen in dystroglycanopathies or due to biallelic mutations in TMTC3, often with brainstem and cerebellum hypoplasia. Lissencephaly can also result from TUBA1A mutations. Other considerations include a proximal 14q interstitial deletion, associated with diffuse lissencephaly, agenesis of the corpus callosum, and septo-optic dysplasia. Furthermore, an X-linked or autosomal dominant gene, distinct from chromosome 17 abnormalities, can lead to subcortical laminar heterotopia, pachygyria, or lissencephaly. [PMC12347932, PMC5097947, PMC3997796, PMC4078132, PMC7964813]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Lissencephaly can be recognized through sonographic examination. Prenatal detection and characterization of brain malformations, including lissencephaly, rely on various neuroimaging modalities such as prenatal multiplanar neuro sonography, anatomical MRI, and advanced MRI techniques. A clear understanding of embryology and developmental morphology is essential for improving the prenatal assessment of these structural abnormalities. [PMC11730443, PMC8333626]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Fumaric aciduria (FA), an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder, is most often characterized by early onset but non-specific clinical signs: hypotonia, severe psychomotor impairment, convulsions, respiratory distress, feeding difficulties and frequent cerebral malformations, along with a distinctive facies. Some patients present with only moderate intellectual impairment.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: FA is very rare, fewer than 100 cases have been reported to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Newborns are frequently microcephalic and may present with facial dysmorphisms. Severe encephalopathy manifests with poor feeding, failure to thrive, hypotonia, lethargy and epileptic seizures. In the most severe cases APGAR scores are low immediately following birth, and bradycardia and respiratory failure may follow. Most children do not achieve visual fixation and are unable to speak or walk. Less severely affected individuals survive beyond childhood, most nonetheless displaying moderate cognitive impairment. Some patients have been reported to present with only moderate cognitive deficits. An increased risk of certain tumors has also been reported, in particular familial leiomyomatosis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FA is caused by mutations in the FH gene (1q42.1) encoding fumarate hydratase, an enzyme that catalyzes the transformation of fumarate into malate in the Krebs cycle. Complete deletions of FH have been reported to be fatal, whereas more mildly affected individuals retain some residual enzymatic activity.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Chromatography of organic acids provides evidence of excreted fumaric acid, often associated with succinic acid and alphacetoglutaric acid. Hyperlactacidemia and moderate hyperammonemia are other common findings. Diagnosis can be confirmed by measuring fumarate hydratase activity in leukocytes or cultured fibroblasts. Brain MRI reveals a variety of anomalies including cerebral atrophy, enlarged ventricles and enlarged extra-axial cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) spaces, delayed myelination for age, thinning of the corpus callosum and an abnormally small brain stem. Developmental malformations including bilateral polymicrogyria and absence of the corpus callosum may also be observed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: An elevated level of fumaric acid in urine may be caused by metabolic stress; therefore testing for fumaric aciduria must be repeated after the patient has been stabilized. Differential diagnoses include polymicrogyria and Leigh syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Polyhydramnios, intrauterine growth delay and premature birth occur in over one third of cases. Fetal ultrasound reveals enlarged cerebral ventricles and other brain abnormalities.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: FA is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Only symptomatic treatment is available to FA patients. Gastrostomy may be necessary to facilitate feeding in newborns. Therapies to control seizures should not include a ketogenic diet, which is contraindicated for this family of enzymatic defects. Physical therapy to reduce scoliosis and improve mobility may be helpful in some cases. Special education and occupational therapy are required to attempt to improve motor skills and language development in less severely affected cases. For patients that survive long-term, regular tumor testing is required.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor, except for those patients with only moderate cognitive impairment. Complete losses of enzymatic activity are fatal during childhood with severe psychomotor handicap: verbal communication and independent mobility remain limited. Some milder cases have been reported to survive longer, a diagnosis that is most likely underestimated.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Sideroblastic anemias (SA) are a group of rare heterogeneous inherited or acquired bone marrow disorders, isolated or part of a syndrome, characterized by decreased hemoglobin synthesis, because of defective use of iron (although plasmatic iron levels may be normal or elevated) and the presence of ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow due to the pathologic iron overload in mitochondria as visualized by Perls' staining. The group encompasses (idiopathic) acquired sideroblastic anemia and constitutional sideroblastic anemias. The latter include syndromic sideroblastic anemias such as Pearson syndrome, mitochondrial mypathy and sideroblastic anemias, x-linked sideroblastic anemia-ataxia, thiamine responsive megaloblastic anemia syndrome and nonsyndromic sideroblastic anemias comprising x-linked and autosomal recessive sideroblastic anemias.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Mitochondrial inheritance, Not applicable, X-linked dominant, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: X-linked sideroblastic anemia (XLSA) is a hereditary disorder affecting heme biosynthesis, caused by mutations in the ALAS2 gene, which encodes the erythroid-specific enzyme 5-aminolevulinate synthase. This enzyme, which requires pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) as a cofactor, catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of heme synthesis in erythroid cells. XLSA is characterized by hypochromic microcytic anemia and ring sideroblasts in bone marrow, with most patients showing variable degrees of response to pyridoxine supplementation; however, female carriers of ALAS2 mutations often present a distinct clinical phenotype. A comprehensive review of the literature reveals over 100 distinct ALAS2 mutations linked to XLSA in more than 240 families. Here, seven new patients (four female cases) initially diagnosed with various conditions, later confirmed to have X-linked Sideroblastic Anemia due to... [PMC11977005, PMC12052921, PMC11971136, PMC11847639, PMC10163426]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of X-linked sideroblastic anaemia (XLSA) has been reported in a female fetus presenting with anaemia in the early third trimester. Ultrasound findings at 29 weeks included cardiomegaly, prominent umbilical veins, a small rim of ascites, and an elevated mean cerebral artery peak systolic velocity. Investigations to determine the underlying cause of fetal anaemia involved non-invasive prenatal testing, microarray comparative genomic hybridization, serology to exclude congenital infection, and assessment of maternal and family history. Definitive diagnosis was made through red cell gene sequencing in both the mother and fetus, revealing a heterozygous ALAS2 mutation. [PMC8686580]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare malignant adrenal disease characterized by a tumor that arises from the adrenal cortex. The clinical presentation depends on the hormones secreted; in children virilization is a predominant feature; other manifestations can include symptoms of Cushing syndrome or symptoms related to tumor volume or metastases.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: In childhood, adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) presents typically in the first 5 years of life, with a strong female predominance. The estimated annual incidence is 0.2-0.3 cases per million children and adolescents, but 10-15 times higher in southern Brazil, which is partly attributable to the high frequency of a specific founder tumor protein 53 (TP53) germline mutation in this population (the TP53p.R337H variant). In adults, the estimated incidence is between 0.2 and 2.0 per million per year, with a peak incidence between 40 and 60 years, and with women being more often affected (55-60%).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most ACCs in children and adolescents are hormone-secreting and the clinical presentation reflects the pattern of adrenocortical hormones secreted by the tumor. Signs and symptoms of virilization are present in over 90% of cases, hypertension may also be present. Hirsutism, acne and deepening of the voice may be apparent in both sexes. Girls may also present with clitoromegaly and facial hair, while boys present with phallomegaly and early virilization. Cushing syndrome (CS) occurs in a third of cases with the most common signs being moon facies, centripetal fat distribution and plethora. Most ACCs in adults are hormone-secreting (cortisol +/- sexual steroids) or even manifestations related to tumor volume or metastases, but ACCs account for 2-11% of incidentally discovered adrenal masses.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Germline TP53 mutations (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) have been implicated in 50%-65% of pediatric cases generally, and in 95% of cases in Brazil. Pediatric ACCs have also been associated with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. In adults, the vast majority of ACCs are sporadic; the main somatic genetic alterations occur in genes that encode proteins involved in the WNT-beta-catenin pathway, cell cycle and p53 apoptosis pathway, chromatin remodelling and telomere maintenance pathway, cAMP-protein kinase A (PKA) pathway or DNA transcription and RNA translation pathways. Occasionally, ACCs occur as part of other hereditary syndromes such as Lynch syndrome, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), carney complex and familial adenomatous polyposis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the hormonal evaluation, abdominal imaging (most commonly used first-line modality is an abdominal computed tomography) and 18-fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis should include other adrenal or retroperitoneal tumors and metastasis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal or preimplantation diagnosis may be proposed for those with severe and incurable diseases (e.g. Li Fraumeni, Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome, etc.).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In children and adolescents, referral to a cancer genetics service is recommended. In adults, suspicion of a genetic disease warrants a specialized genetic consultation. Genetic counseling may be proposed to families with a known disease-causing mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Complete, radical surgical resection is the treatment of choice and may be curative, especially for small tumors. Adjuvant therapies with mitotane and/or radiotherapy may be used in an attempt to reduce rates of disease recurrence. In patients with incomplete resection or metastatic spread, treatment options include systemic treatments with mitotane, chemotherapy, immunotherapy, and/or targeted therapies, and locoregional treatments.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: When diagnosed at a local stage, ACC can be cured with radical surgery a surgery, possibly associated with adjuvant mitotane or radiotherapy. At a locally advanced non-resectable or metastatic stage, ACC is a highly aggressive disease with very poor prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare systemic autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of signs and symptoms suggestive of a systemic autoimmune disease that do not fulfil the existing classification criteria. The main clinical manifestations are arthritis with arthralgia, Raynaud's phenomenon, xerostomia, xerophthalmia, and leukopenia, while neurologic or renal involvement are virtually absent.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Based on case reports, undifferentiated connective tissue disease has been diagnosed in adults. Specific instances include a 30-year-old woman and a 51-year-old woman diagnosed with early UCTD. Another case involved a 50-year-old male presenting with complications of UCTD, and a 68-year-old woman who had been diagnosed with the condition several years prior. [PMC8439496, PMC6709088, PMC6319971, PMC5420101]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: A 68-year-old woman was referred for immunological investigation following an episode of meningococcal epiglottitis with associated septicaemia. Several years previously, she had been diagnosed with undifferentiated connective tissue disease. On investigation, alternative pathway complement function was normal; however, classical pathway complement activation was reduced. C1q, C3 and C4 levels were all measured and found to be within their respective normal ranges, but C2 levels were low. Sequencing of the C2 gene was subsequently performed, confirming a diagnosis of type 1 C2 deficiency (C2D). Discussion: C2D is usually hereditary and inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. C2D is often asymptomatic, however, some patients suffer from infections with encapsulated bacteria and/or autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus. Recognition of complement pathway... [PMC8439496, PMC6709088, PMC6319971, PMC5420101, PMC4467005]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD) presents with diverse clinical manifestations. Common onset symptoms include arthralgias, arthritis, Raynaud's phenomenon, mucocutaneous involvement, and sicca symptoms. Various organ systems can be affected, with patients experiencing severe or recurrent infections, such as meningococcal epiglottitis, particularly with C2 deficiency. Renal complications include rhabdomyolysis-induced acute kidney injury and acquired renal glucosuria. Neurological involvement, though rare, can manifest as intracranial lesions, headache, ataxia, or orofacial dyskinesia, or hypertrophic cranial pachymeningitis with scleritis. Pulmonary manifestations include interstitial lung disease, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, and endogenous lipoid pneumonia. Hepatic injury, characterized by fatigue, anorexia, low-grade fever, and skin rashes, can also occur. Immunological findings often include high antinuclear antibody titers and elevated inflammatory markers. [PMC8439496, PMC6709088, PMC6319971, PMC5420101, PMC4840743]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD) has been observed in association with specific underlying conditions and genetic factors. One case reported UCTD in a patient with type 1 C2 deficiency, a hereditary condition typically inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. C2 deficiency is known to predispose individuals to autoimmune diseases, including systemic lupus erythematosus. Additionally, UCTD has been noted in patients carrying the 8.1 ancestral haplotype, suggesting a potential genetic predisposition. It can also co-occur with other autoimmune disorders such as Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. [PMC8439496, PMC1755201]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: When undifferentiated connective tissue disease is associated with C2 deficiency, the condition is typically hereditary and inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. This inheritance pattern implies that affected relatives may also be at risk. Recognition of complement pathway deficiency is important due to the predisposition to severe and/or recurrent infections by encapsulated bacteria. Immunizations are recommended for both the patient and any affected relatives to reduce mortality and morbidity. [PMC8439496]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of undifferentiated connective tissue disease (UCTD) involves targeted therapies based on specific manifestations. Corticosteroids, such as methylprednisolone or prednisone, have been effective in treating rhabdomyolysis-induced acute kidney injury, central nervous system involvement, hypertrophic cranial pachymeningitis, and hepatic injury, often leading to significant improvement in symptoms and laboratory findings. Low-dose corticosteroids are used, sometimes in combination with immunosuppressive drugs like azathioprine for CNS involvement. Hydroxychloroquine has resolved acquired renal glucosuria in a UCTD patient. Additionally, immunisations are important for patients with associated complement deficiencies to reduce infection risk, and supportive care, including intravenous fluids, may be used for complications like rhabdomyolysis. [PMC8439496, PMC6709088, PMC6319971, PMC5420101, PMC2877233]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare respiratory disease characterized by recurrent sinopulmonary infections and bronchiectasis predominantly in the lower lung fields, as well as azoospermia with reduced fertility, due to production of thick, viscous mucus which causes mild airflow obstruction in the respiratory tract and obstruction of sperm transport in the genital tract. Patients commonly present in adulthood. Sweat gland and pancreatic function are normal. The cause of the syndrome is unknown, however mercury exposure had been proposed as a potential cause.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: the case of a 42-year-old man with bronchiectasis who had a history of infertility treatment for obstructive azoospermia. Young's syndrome was suspected based on the triad of obstructive azoospermia, sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. He had normal electron microscopy findings, normal nasal nitric oxide levels (116 nL/min), and no situs inversus. However, we found compound heterozygous variants considered pathogenic in CFAP221. This led to a diagnosis of primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). Distinguishing PCD from Young's syndrome in patients with the triad of obstructive azoospermia, sinusitis, and bronchiectasis is challenging. Young's syndrome may be a phenotype of PCD. [PMC11867755]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Young's syndrome is characterized by a triad of clinical features: obstructive azoospermia, sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. Patients, such as a 42-year-old man described, may present with infertility due to obstructive azoospermia and chronic respiratory issues like bronchiectasis. Distinguishing Young's syndrome from primary ciliary dyskinesia can be challenging, as it may represent a phenotype of the latter, even in cases with normal electron microscopy, nasal nitric oxide levels, and no situs inversus. [PMC11867755]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Young's syndrome may be a phenotype of primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD). In a case where Young's syndrome was suspected based on obstructive azoospermia, sinusitis, and bronchiectasis, compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in CFAP221 were identified, leading to a diagnosis of PCD. Distinguishing between Young's syndrome and PCD can be challenging due to their overlapping clinical presentation. [PMC11867755]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Young's syndrome is suspected based on a clinical triad of obstructive azoospermia, sinusitis, and bronchiectasis.
