Predictors of worse outcomes and frequent surgical intervention are the presence of diffuse lesions compared to discrete stenosis or presence of associated aortic valve disease.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare histiocytic tumor characterized by a malignant proliferation of cells showing morphological and immunophenotypic features of mature tissue histiocytes. Most cases occur in extranodal sites, most commonly the intestinal tract, skin, and soft tissue. Patients may present with a solitary mass, lymphadenopathy, a skin rash or numerous tumors on the trunk and extremities, lytic bone lesions, hepatosplenomegaly with pancytopenia, intestinal obstruction, and/or systemic symptoms. The neoplasm is aggressive with typically poor therapy response.

DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Histiocytic sarcoma as a secondary malignancy following childhood leukemia is extremely uncommon with fewer than 20 cases reported worldwide. They often pose a diagnostic challenge and prognosis is dismal. There is a lack of well-established clinical treatment protocols owing to rarity of disease. Majority were managed with chemotherapy with variable outcomes. Herein a rare case of an 8-year-old girl with secondary BRAF V600 -mutant histiocytic sarcoma following T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. After poor disease control with salvage chemotherapy, she was treated with MAPK-targeted therapy with dabrafenib and trametinib. She demonstrated excellent response and remained in partial remission with no signs of disease progression 3 years later. There is yet to be consensus on the optimal management for this neoplasm. Description of our successful clinical experience highlights that... [PMC11889787, PMC12362440, PMC12279446, PMC12018173, PMC12010022]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Histiocytic sarcoma is an aggressive malignancy generally associated with a dismal and poor prognosis, with reported median overall survival as low as 6 months. Patients often experience disease progression despite multimodal therapies, and conventional chemotherapy may have limited efficacy or variable outcomes. Specific presentations, such as secondary histiocytic sarcoma or those complicated by hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, also carry a poor prognosis. However, certain factors and targeted treatments can influence outcomes. For primary intracranial histiocytic sarcomas, gross total resection, solitary lesions, and radiotherapy are associated with longer overall survival. In cases with specific molecular alterations like BRAF V600, KRAS, MAP2K1 mutations, or high PD-L1 expression, targeted therapies or immune checkpoint inhibitors, sometimes combined with chemotherapy, have demonstrated significant clinical improvement, partial remission, or sustained complete remission for several years in some patients. [PMC11889787, PMC12362440, PMC12279446, PMC12018173, PMC12010022]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cocaine embryofetopathy is a group of clinical signs observed in newborns exposed in utero to cocaine, a short-acting central nervous system stimulant used as a recreational drug through inhalation of the powder or intravenous injection. Cocaine use during pregnancy is associated with intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight, seizures, respiratory distress (decreased apnea density and periodic breathing), feeding difficulties, irritability and lability of state, decreased behavioral and autonomic regulation, poor alertness and orientation and cognitive impairment (impaired auditory information processing , visual-spatial delay and subtle language delay) in the offspring.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Prenatal exposure to cocaine can result in behavioral and neurodevelopmental abnormalities that persist into adulthood. Imaging may reveal focal signal-intensity changes in the substantia nigra, locus ceruleus, and other selected nerve tracts and nuclei. Additionally, affected individuals may present with dilated cardiomyopathy. [PMC7978184]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Cocaine embryofetopathy is associated with in utero exposure to cocaine, which can result in behavioral and neurodevelopmental abnormalities that persist into adulthood. While conventional MR imaging has generally not revealed structural lesions to explain these clinical findings, a case report identified focal MR imaging signal-intensity changes in the substantia nigra, locus ceruleus, and other selected nerve tracts and nuclei in a child with prenatal exposure to cocaine and other drugs. This patient also presented with dilated cardiomyopathy. [PMC7978184]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for cocaine embryofetopathy include MR imaging, which can reveal focal signal-intensity changes in the substantia nigra, locus ceruleus, and other selected nerve tracts and nuclei. Additionally, dilated cardiomyopathy has been observed in cases following prenatal exposure to cocaine and other drugs. [PMC4602417, PMC3573092, PMC7978184]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Prenatal exposure to other substances, such as tramadol, should be considered in the differential diagnosis for neurodevelopmental abnormalities. While prenatal cocaine exposure is associated with behavioral and neurodevelopmental abnormalities, focal MR imaging signal changes in the substantia nigra, locus ceruleus, and other nerve tracts, and dilated cardiomyopathy, prenatal tramadol exposure can also impair neuronal survival and synaptic development. Tramadol exposure may lead to histological and ultrastructural changes in postnatal cortical cerebellar neuronal development, including neurodegenerative signs, demyelination, and defects in cortical size and neuronal development, which could overlap with the neurodevelopmental presentation of cocaine embryofetopathy. [PMC11102883, PMC7978184]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Exposure to levamisole-adulterated cocaine can induce a distinct clinical syndrome characterized by retiform purpura and/or agranulocytosis accompanied by an unusual constellation of serologic abnormalities including antiphospholipid antibodies, lupus anticoagulants, and very high titers of antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies. Two recent case reports suggest that levamisole-adulterated cocaine may also lead to renal disease in the form of pauci-immune glomerulonephritis. To explore this possibility, we reviewed cases of pauci-immune glomerulonephritis between 2010 and 2012 at an inner city safety net hospital where the prevalence of levamisole in the cocaine supply is known to be high. We identified 3 female patients and 1 male patient who had biopsy-proven pauci-immune glomerulonephritis, used cocaine, and had serologic abnormalities characteristic of levamisole-induced autoimmunity.... [PMC4602417]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Prenatal exposure to cocaine can result in behavioral and neurodevelopmental abnormalities that persist into adulthood. These long-term effects may include focal MR imaging signal-intensity changes in specific brain regions, such as the substantia nigra, locus ceruleus, and other selected nerve tracts and nuclei. Additionally, affected individuals may present with conditions like dilated cardiomyopathy. [PMC7978184]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare amyloidosis that complicates chronic inflammatory disorders and is characterized by the aggregation and deposition of amyloid fibrils composed of serum amyloid A protein, an acute phase reactant. The kidney is involved in virtually all patients and dominates the clinical picture. Other frequently involved sites are the liver, the spleen, suprarenal gland, gut and less frequently the heart.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact prevalence is not known. AA amyloidosis occurs in less than 5% of patients with chronic inflammatory disorders. The disease is more frequent in certain countries like Finland, Japan, Turkey and the Middle East.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The predominant feature of AA amyloidosis at diagnosis is renal dysfunction, proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome. AA amyloidosis complicates chronic inflammatory disorders and is typically preceded by many years of active inflammatory disease. These may include chronic inflammatory arthritis, (rheumatoid arthritis, juvenile idiopathic arthritis), chronic infections (bronchiectasis, osteomyelitis, tuberculosis), auto-inflammatory diseases (familial mediterranean fever (FMF), TRAPS syndrome), Crohn's disease and less commonly Castleman's disease, Schnitzler syndrome, vasculitis or neoplasias (lymphoma, mesothelioma). In almost 25% of cases with AA, the cause of inflammation remains unclear (idiopathic AA amyloidosis) and it has been proposed that obesity may have a role in these cases. In the last decades, the progressive improvement of treatment for rheumatic diseases has reduced the number of cases driven by inflammatory arthritis and, in parallel, increased the number of patients with an underlying chronic infectious disease or idiopathic AA amyloidosis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Chronic inflammatory disorders are associated with elevated levels of the acute-phase reactant, serum amyloid A protein (SAA) protein. AA amyloid fibrils are derived from SAA through a process of cleavage, misfolding, and aggregation. Amyloid fibrils associate with other moieties, including glycosaminoglycans and serum amyloid P component (SAP), forming deposits that disrupt structure and function of tissues and organs.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of AA amyloidosis requires the demonstration of amyloid deposits on tissue biopsy revealed by Congo red staining on light microscopy and apple green birefringence on polarized light microscopy and amyloid typing by light microscopy, immunoelectron microscopy or proteomic analysis. Amyloidosis is suspected when signs of renal dysfunction (renal failure and proteinuria) are noted in the background of a chronic inflammatory disease with persistent elevated SAA concentration.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include AL amyloidosis, familial renal amyloidosis and other causes of renal dysfunction like membranous glomerulonephritis and renal vein thrombosis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment of AA amyloidosis relies on treating the underlying inflammatory disease (antimicrobial therapy in chronic infections, colchicine in FMF, immunosuppressive agents in chronic arthritis). The aim of therapy is the reduction of SAA concentration (ideally <10 mg/L) in order to minimize the risk of disease progression and possibly to reverse organ dysfunction. Successful treatment of the underlying inflammatory disorders reduces SAA concentrations. In patients with end stage renal disease and controlled underlying disease, renal transplantation could be considered as a valuable treatment option.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Factors associated with a poor prognosis are older age, a reduced serum albumin concentration, end-stage renal failure at baseline, and the degree by which the SAA concentration is elevated during follow-up. Patients with underlying chronic infectious diseases have a worse outcome. Twenty-four hour proteinuria and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) can identify patients with higher risk of end-stage renal failure at diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: AA amyloidosis can be a complication of hereditary autoinflammatory diseases, such as Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF) and Cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome (CAPS). FMF is a hereditary autoinflammatory disease linked to homozygous mutations, such as M694V/M694V, in the Mediterranean fever protein gene, with familial suspicion noted in relatives. CAPS is caused by NLRP3 mutations, with patients being heterozygous for mutations like p.E304 K. Additionally, AA amyloidosis can occur in VEXAS syndrome, which is caused by somatic mutations in the UBA1 gene. Genetic testing can confirm these underlying conditions. [PMC12234580, PMC5070197, PMC4401971]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by moderate to severe intellectual disability, neurologic signs and symptoms (such as seizures, spasticity, strabismus), characteristic dysmorphic facial features (including broad forehead, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, broad and flat nasal bridge, midline notch of upper lip, lack of upper central incisors, incomplete oral cleft, and prominent mandible), and acne scars. Hearing impairment, pseudo-bulbar palsy, growth retardation, and skeletal anomalies (camptodactyly, clinodactyly, bilateral cubitus valgus, pes cavus/planus) have also been described.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: BACKGROUND Kugelberg-Welander (K-W) syndrome is a type of spinal muscular atrophy that causes weakness of the hip-girdle muscles. If severe enough, this weakness can confine patients to a wheelchair in adult life. Proteinuria, a manifestation of kidney dysfunction, is associated with disorders of many organ systems. The evaluation of kidney function in the context of K-W syndrome is challenging. CASE REPORT A 45-year-old man with K-W syndrome first diagnosed at 5 years of age developed peripheral edema and was found to have proteinuria under 1 g/24 h. His past history was significant for hypertension for 7 years. He was managed conservatively initially, but over the next year the serum creatinine concentration increased from 18 to 32 µmol/L (0.2 to 0.36 mg/dL). A percutaneous kidney biopsy was performed in the fetal position due to an inability of the patient to lay prone or supine.... [PMC6459160]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: BACKGROUND Kugelberg-Welander (K-W) syndrome is a type of spinal muscular atrophy that causes weakness of the hip-girdle muscles. If severe enough, this weakness can confine patients to a wheelchair in adult life. Proteinuria, a manifestation of kidney dysfunction, is associated with disorders of many organ systems. The evaluation of kidney function in the context of K-W syndrome is challenging. CASE REPORT A 45-year-old man with K-W syndrome first diagnosed at 5 years of age developed peripheral edema and was found to have proteinuria under 1 g/24 h. His past history was significant for hypertension for 7 years. He was managed conservatively initially, but over the next year the serum creatinine concentration increased from 18 to 32 µmol/L (0.2 to 0.36 mg/dL). A percutaneous kidney biopsy was performed in the fetal position due to an inability of the patient to lay prone or supine.... [PMC6459160]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare aggressive skin cancer characterized by a rapidly growing nodule with both epithelial and neuroendocrine features, driven in 80% of cases by the oncogenic Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Cutaneous neuroendocrine carcinoma (or Merkel cell carcinoma; MCC) accounts for less than 1% of skin cancers. The annual incidence rates, ranging from 1 out of 1,000,000 to 1 out of 40,000 inhabitants in western countries, has been increasing over the last two decades.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: MCC usually occurs in fair-skinned, elderly people. Overall, 10% of MCC patients are immunosuppressed (transplant recipients, HIV, hematological malignancies). The primary tumor is mostly located on sun-exposed areas and appears as an asymptomatic, rapidly growing, red/violaceous cutaneous nodule. One third of patients already have nodal or distant metastasis at time of diagnosis. A complete work up is necessary at baseline (ultrasonography of the regional lymph nodes and a whole-body imaging with a positron emission tomography scan), allowing to classify the disease according to the 4 stages of the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) system. In less than 10% of cases, MCC is diagnosed in metastatic lymph nodes, with no evidence of skin primary (''occult primary'').
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In 2008, Feng, Chang and Moore discovered that the genome of the Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCPyV) was integrated in the DNA of 80% of MCC samples. Since then, MCPyV has been found to be an ubiquitary resident of skin flora, acquiring oncogenic properties following the occurrence of very rare events (integration of its DNA into the genome of the host cell and mutations of the viral genome). On the other hand, 20% of MCC are related to UV-induced mutations especially on TP53 and pRB oncogenes. In both subsets, the most likely cell of origin is an epithelial cell of the epidermis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of MCC requires a biopsy. Histologically, MCCs appear as a proliferation of basophilic cells with scant cytoplasm, a 'salt and pepper' chromatin pattern and high mitotic rate. The tumor is located in the dermis, frequently extending to the subcutaneous tissue, lacking connection with the epidermis. Immunohistochemistry reveals positivity for neuroendocrine (synaptophysin, chromogranin) and epithelial markers, the hallmark being the paranuclear dot-like pattern of cytokeratin 20 expressed by more than 90% of MCC.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Clinical differential diagnosis includes any disease presenting a skin nodule, ranging from benign cysts or lipomas, to skin malignancies such as carcinomas, lymphomas or skin metastases. On histological sections, the main differential diagnoses include basophilic tumors such as small-cell lung carcinoma, carcinoid tumor, malignant lymphoma, and small-cell melanoma, which can be ruled out by appropriate immunohistochemical panels.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management should be discussed in tumor multidisciplinary boards based on the disease stage and general health status of the patient. Patients with localized disease should have a wide excision of the primary tumor with a sentinel lymph node biopsy in the regional area. In case of regional disease, a complete lymph node dissection is usually indicated. Adjuvant radiation therapy is usually provided on the site of the primary tumor and can be proposed on the regional lymph node area if involved. In patients with advanced disease, first line treatment consists in immunotherapy with a PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitor. Avelumab is approved in several countries worldwide in this setting, retifanlimab is approved in Europe and the USA, while pembrolizumab is only approved in the USA.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: MCC is an aggressive disease with a high propensity to metastasize. Approximately 40% of patients recur within 3 years after initial management, and the overall survival at 5 years is estimated at 60%. The prognosis of patients with advanced disease has improved with the use of immunotherapy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal trisomy 4q is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from the partial duplication of the long arm of chromosome 4, with highly variable phenotype typically characterized by psychomotor delay, intellectual disability, craniofacial dysmorphism (microcephaly, low-set, prominent ears, downslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, epicanthic folds, broad, prominent nasal bridge, high arched and cleft palate, micro-/retrognathia), seizures, as well as tooth and digital anomalies (clinodactyly, polydactyly). Cardiac malformations, renal anomalies, cryptorchidism, hypotonia and hearing impairment have also been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Distal duplication 4q syndrome is associated with mental disability and dysmorphism. Affected individuals may exhibit mental retardation. Endocrine abnormalities have been reported, including end-organ resistance characterized by extreme hyperinsulinaemia, primary hypothyroidism, and hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism. In one fetal case involving both 4q duplication and 7q deletion, ultrasonic multiple malformations were observed. Candidate genes such as SHH and XRCC2 may contribute to the observed abnormalities. [PMC6250448, PMC1049303]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal duplication 4q syndrome is caused by a partial duplication of the long arm of chromosome 4, often involving the distal segment, such as 4q34.1q35.2. This chromosomal abnormality can arise de novo from an unbalanced translocation, where a partial fragment of chromosome 4 is attached to another chromosome. It can also result from the familial segregation of a balanced translocation. Candidate genes like SHH and XRCC2 are considered to potentially explain the observed abnormalities. [PMC6250448, PMC1049303]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of distal duplication 4q syndrome typically involves cytogenetic and molecular . While standard chromosomal karyotype analysis may appear normal, single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array analysis can identify partial duplications of chromosome 4q. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis further clarifies chromosomal rearrangements, showing partial signal fragments. Banding pattern analysis can also reveal the involvement of the distal segment of the long arm of chromosome 4. The combination of SNP array and FISH analysis provides a clear molecular chromosomal diagnosis, and clinical features can support the cytogenetic evidence. [PMC6250448, PMC1049303]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis can be performed via amniocentesis, typically prompted by indications such as increased risk for chromosomal abnormalities or ultrasonic multiple malformations. While standard chromosomal karyotyping may appear normal, single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array analysis can detect partial duplications of chromosome 4q. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis can further confirm these molecular chromosomal findings. The combination of SNP array and FISH provides a clear diagnosis, which is crucial for genetic counseling. [PMC6250448]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for distal duplication 4q syndrome must consider its varied origins. The duplication can arise de novo, as observed in a fetus with a partial duplication of 4q34.1q35.2 and a 16-year-old male with an unbalanced translocation involving distal 4q. Alternatively, it can result from familial segregation of a balanced translocation. Molecular chromosomal diagnosis, utilizing techniques such as SNP array and FISH analysis, is crucial for a clear cytogenetic diagnosis and informing genetic counseling. Such diagnoses can lead to significant decisions, including pregnancy termination in cases of ultrasonic multiple malformations. [PMC6250448, PMC1049303]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Rationale: Chromosome deletion/duplication has been reported to be associated with mental disability and dysmorphism according to the accumulated research evidence. Patient concerns: A 25-year-old woman underwent amniocentesis for cytogenetic and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array analysis at 18 weeks of gestation due to the increased Down syndrome risk of 1/13. Diagnoses: The fetal chromosomal analysis revealed a seemingly "normal" chromosomal karyotype, but the SNP array showed a partial duplication of chromosome 4q34.1q35.2 and a deletion of chromosome 7q34q36.3fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis showed that the couple had normal chromosome 4 and 7, whereas there was a partial signal fragment of chromosome 4 attached on the long arm of chromosome 7 for the fetus. Interventions: The couple finally chose to terminate the pregnancy based on the ultrasonic multiple... [PMC6250448]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Patients with distal duplication 4q syndrome can present with significant challenges. One reported case of a 16-year-old male with partial trisomy 4q showed mental retardation and endocrine abnormalities, including hyperinsulinaemia, primary hypothyroidism, and hypergonadotrophic hypogonadism. Another case involving a fetus with partial duplication of 4q and deletion of 7q presented with multiple malformations, leading to termination of pregnancy. [PMC6250448, PMC1049303]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A type of arthrogryposis characterized by congenital cleft palate, microcephaly, craniostenosis and arthrogryposis (limitation of extension of elbows, flexed adducted thumbs, camptodactyly and clubfeet). Additional features include facial dysmorphism ('myopathic' stiff face, antimongoloid slanting, external ophthalmoplegia, telecanthus, low-set large malrotated ears, open mouth, microgenia and high arched palate). Velopharyngeal insufficiency with difficulties in swallowing, increased secretion of the nose and throat, prominent occiput, generalized muscular hypotonia with mild cyanosis and no spontaneous movements, seizures, torticollis, areflexia, intellectual disability, hypertrichosis of the lower extremities, and scleredema (in the first days of life) are also observed. The disease often leads to early death. Transmission is autosomal recessive. No new cases have been described since 1983.

DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: White-Sutton syndrome (WHSUS), caused by variants in the POGZ gene, should be considered in the differential diagnosis. WHSUS presents with a broad phenotypic spectrum including moderate to severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, variable cerebral malformations, developmental delay, and notably, adducted thumb, which can be a remarkable clinical feature in the first years of life. Other features like peripheral polyneuropathy, short stature, and visual abnormalities are also part of the WHSUS spectrum. [PMC8303405]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: White-Sutton syndrome (WHSUS) is caused by variants in the POGZ gene, located on chromosome 1q21.3. The phenotypic spectrum is broad, encompassing moderate to severe intellectual disability, microcephaly, variable cerebral malformations, short stature, brachydactyly, visual abnormalities, sensorineural hearing loss, hypotonia, sleep difficulties, autistic features, self-injurious behavior, and feeding difficulties. A reported case involved a de novo splicing variant in POGZ, indicating that new mutations can lead to the condition. Genetic testing for POGZ variants can confirm the diagnosis and inform counseling regarding the broad clinical presentation. [PMC8303405]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder/difference of sex development characterized by a primary ovarian defect, either a failure of the gonads to develop or resistance to gonadotrophin stimulation which leads to premature ovarian failure (POF) in otherwise phenotypically female 46,XX individuals.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): 46,XX complete gonadal dysgenesis; 46,XX ovarian dysgenesis; 46,XX pure gonadal dysgenesis; Hypergonadotropic ovarian dysgenesis; XX female gonadal dysgenesis; XX-GD
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients are born with typical female sex characteristics without ambiguity. However, affected individuals present during adolescence or young adulthood with either delayed or absent puberty resulting in primary or sometimes secondary amenorrhea. The internal and external genitalia are typically developed. 46,XX gonadal dysgenesis can occur as part of Perrault syndrome (ovarian dysgenesis and deafness with or without cerebellar ataxia), as well as other rare syndromes such as lung fibrosis-immunodeficiency-gonadal dysgenesis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Ovarian dysgenesis results from genetic defects of ovarian development. Although the underlying etiology remains unknown in most cases, several genes have been implicated including homozygous or compound heterozygous inactivating mutations of the follicle-stimulating hormone receptor gene (FSHR; 2p21-p16), mutations in the BMP15 gene (Xp11.2) and mutations in the NR5A1 gene (9q33), amongst others.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis requires an evaluation of hormonal status (gonadal and adrenal), laboratory investigations to screen for infectious or autoimmune disorders, karyotype analysis, molecular studies and sometimes laparoscopy with biopsy of ovarian tissue.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include other causes of POF, as well as 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis. In addition, secondary ovarian hypoplasia has been described in association with infectious agents (HIV) or autoimmunity (APECED syndrome associated with AIRE gene mutations).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal molecular diagnosis is feasible in cases where a mutation has been identified in the family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling may be offered. Inactivating FSHR mutations are inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, BMP15 mutations are inherited in an X-linked manner and NR5A1 mutations are autosomal dominant in the great majority of cases.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management should include hormone replacement therapy. Calcium and vitamin D supplements may also be proposed. Psychological support should also be offered to patients and their families in a difference/disorder of sexual development-center setting. Infertility is an important management issue; however, pregnancy may be feasible through zygote egg donation.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: With appropriate management, the physiological and clinical outcome for patients is good.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked malformation syndrome characterized by craniofacial abnormalities such as uni- or bicoronal synostosis, hypertelorism and a bifid nose, grooved or split nails, frizzy hair, abnormalities of the shoulder girdle, hands and feet.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It occurs in fewer than 1/100,000 newborns. Detailed phenotypic analysis shows that females are more severely affected than males, a highly unusual characteristic for an X-linked disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Female patients have hypertelorism, and a broad nose with a vertical groove on the top of the nose or a bifid nose, uni or bicoronal craniosynostosis. The following facial abnormalities may be seen: facial asymmetry, downslanting palpebral fissures, dry, curly and frizzy hair, widow's peak, low posterior hairline, webbed neck, highly arched palate, cleft lip and palate, a narrow and V-shaped maxilla. Ophthalmologic abnormalities, abnormal auditory ossicles, and both conductive and sensorineural deafness can be seen. Skeletal deformities may include sloping shoulders with dysplastic clavicles, broad or duplicated thumbs and halluces, short thumbs, brachydactyly, clinodactyly, gaps between the first and second toes, syndactyly, camptodactyly, scoliosis and hyperextensible joints. Longitudinal splits or grooves in the finger- and toe- nails are frequent and characteristic. Diaphragmatic hernia, pectus excavatum or carinatum, breast hypoplasia, cardiac abnormalities, bicornuate uterus, shawl scrotum, hypospadias and agenesis of the corpus callosum occur occasionally. Mild developmental delay can occur. Variable difficulties with speech and language development can be associated. Most of the male patients are mildly affected with hypertelorism only but can occasionally present with a severe female-like phenotype. The cause for this severe phenotype in males is probably mosaic pathogenic variants in EFNB1.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is caused by variants in the EFNB1 gene. This gene encodes ephrin-B1 and maps to Xq13.1. Random X-inactivation explains the more severe outcome in heterozygous females, as this leads to functional mosaicism for cells with differing expression of ephrin-B1, generating abnormal tissue boundaries.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: In case of a low-level of mosaicism for EFNB1 variants, extensive analysis of several types of tissues might be required to detect variants. Variation in EFNB1 is detected from DNA isolated from blood, fibroblast cell lines, saliva and hair roots by a combination of PCR/Sanger sequencing, or by next-generation sequencing and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MPLA; for the detection of deletions in females).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Isolated hypertelorism can mimic the mild presentation of craniofrontonasal syndrome. The disease needs to be distinguished from other syndromes associated with hypertelorism such as SPECC1L-related hypertelorism syndrome and Baraitser-Winter cerebrofrontofacial syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: In case of an established EFNB1 mutation in a parent, prenatal diagnosis is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The risk that an affected female will pass the disease on her daughter or son is 50%. An affected male will pass the disease on to all of his daughters but none of his sons.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Multistage surgery is the general treatment plan for craniosynostosis. The synostotic sutures of the skull are released in the first year of life. The aim of this surgery is decompression of the brain and remodeling of the skull. Correction of the facial anomalies is usually delayed until the age of 5 or later, depending on the severity of hypertelorism, orbital dystopia and shape of the maxilla. Surgical correction of strabismus can be indicated and timing should be discussed within the craniofacial team. Multidisciplinary treatment is mandatory with the input of plastic surgeons, maxillofacial surgeons, ophthalmologists, orthoptists, otolaryngotologists, speech therapists, psychologists and social workers, and orthodontists.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy in general is similar to the normal population. Quality of life may be affected because of a different facial appearance and the consequences of other congenital abnormalities.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare developmental defect during embryogenesis characterized by intellectual deficit, ataxia, postnatal microcephaly, and hyperkinesis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Christianson syndrome (CS) prevalence is estimated to affect 1 in 16,000 to 100,000 males worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Affected males diagnosed with CS typically present with the following core diagnostic features: nonverbal status, intellectual disability (ID), epilepsy, ataxia, postnatal microcephaly, and hyperkinesis. Seizures typically occur prior to the age of three. Secondary symptoms include behaviors associated with autism, Angelman syndrome features, eye movement problems (e.g. strabismus), hypotonia, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), regressions (especially after the 1st decade of life), low height and/weight (progressing with age), and cerebellar vermal atrophy (particularly after the 1st decade). Females with heterozygous NHE6 mutations may present with a wide ranging phenotype ranging from unaffected to more severe neurologic/psychiatric manifestations.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Christianson syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutation of the SLC9A6 gene (Xq26.3), which encodes the endosomal Na+/H+ Exchanger 6 (NHE6) protein.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: CS diagnosis is confirmed by molecular genetic testing. Core diagnostic symptoms include nonverbal status, ID, epilepsy, ataxia, postnatal microcephaly, and hyperkinesis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Angelman syndrome and ID (especially if it appears to follow an X-linked pattern).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal genetic testing is possible if the familial mutation is known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic counseling is advised. Heterozygous females have a 50% risk of transmitting the pathogenic variant in pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management of symptoms associated with seizures, ID/developmental delay, motor deficits, feeding difficulties, and/or eye problems is common. No specific treatment exists.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Progressive symptoms appear to progress as males age, especially after the 1st decade of life. These include regressions (e.g. walking, talking, and fine/gross motor skills), cerebellar atrophy, and low height/weight. Despite reports of premature mortality in CS males (i.e. ranging from approximately 20-50 years), life expectancy is currently unknown.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Congenital muscular dystrophy-infantile cataract-hypogonadism syndrome is characterized by congenital muscular dystrophy, infantile cataract and hypogonadism. It has been described in seven individuals from an isolated Norwegian village and in one unrelated individual. Transmission appears to be autosomal recessive.

An acute arboviral infection caused by a virus of the Flaviviridae family transmitted by an infected mosquito, that is asymptomatic in the majority of cases but that can present in rare occasions with mild flulike symptoms such as low-grade fever, arthralgia, myalgia, and/or rash, or with neurologic manifestations including meningitis, encephalitis with mental confusion or disorientation, tremors and acute flaccid paralysis/poliomyelitis.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: West Nile virus infection can range from asymptomatic to severe neuroinvasive disease. Initial presentations often include mild febrile or flu-like symptoms such as fever, headache, chills, asthenia, vomiting, and myalgias. Neuroinvasive disease can manifest as meningitis, encephalitis, rhombencephalitis, or acute flaccid paralysis, leading to altered mental status, prolonged unresponsiveness (coma), and severe neurological symptoms. Rare cases may involve seizures or strokes. Atypical presentations include gastrointestinal symptoms and persistent high-grade fevers. Ocular involvement, such as chorioretinitis, can cause severe visual loss and characteristic fundus lesions. Other complications include hyponatremia, SIADH, lethargy, and confusion. Immunocompromised and elderly patients, including solid organ transplant recipients, are particularly vulnerable to severe neurological complications and higher mortality. [PMC12035009, PMC12128217, PMC12247393, PMC12297952, PMC11597865]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for West Nile virus infection is primarily supportive. This includes addressing complications such as hyponatremia, which may involve fluid restriction, salt tablets, and 3% saline. For ocular manifestations like intraretinal edema, intravitreal ranibizumab has been administered in a case of chorioretinopathy. In solid organ transplant recipients, treatment strategies have included reducing immunosuppression, and some cases utilized intravenous immunoglobulin, interferon alfa-2b, and ribavirin. However, for general WNV infection, there is no clear role for specific medical treatments such as corticosteroids or IV immunoglobulins. [PMC12035009, PMC12247393, PMC11597865, PMC11446260, PMC11666879]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: West Nile virus infection can be self-resolving, with symptoms typically lasting 3-10 days. However, neuroinvasive disease can lead to severe outcomes, including rapid progression to death, particularly in vulnerable individuals such as the elderly, immunocompromised, or solid organ transplant recipients. In solid organ transplant recipients, WNV infection is associated with a 23.7% mortality rate and severe neurological complications in 43.9% of cases. These complications can include prolonged unresponsiveness, persistent allodynia years after infection, and unique physiological responses. Ocular involvement, such as chorioretinopathy, may result in severe visual loss with partial recovery but potential lasting effects like optic disc pallor. [PMC12035009, PMC12128217, PMC11597865, PMC11952119, PMC11446260]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare lysosomal disease characterized by dysmorphic features and skeletal changes, restricted joint mobility, short stature, and hand deformities (such as claw hands, stiffness of hands, carpal tunnel syndrome, inability to make fists). Most patients have normal intellectual capacity and the clinical progression is less rapid than that of mucolipidosis type II (MLII).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: MLII and mucolipidosis type III (MLIII) represent a spectrum of severity. The estimated combined prevalence at birth of MLII and MLIII is estimated between 1/ 37,000-455,000 worldwide. Whilst data is limited on MLIII, the prevalence at birth has been estimated at 1/1,250,000 in the Netherlands.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In MLIII, symptom onset is often in the first two decades of life and patients typically present with progressive hand deformities and restricted range of joint motion. For these symptoms, patients will often consult specialists such as rheumatologists and orthopedic or plastic surgeons. Progressive hip dysplasia may cause bone pain and leads to waddling gait. Other musculoskeletal problems like dysostosis multiplex, short stature, osteopenia, osteoarthritis, spinal cord compression and carpal tunnel syndrome are common in MLIII. Mild corneal clouding, cardiac valvular disease, mild coarsening of facial features, and mild intellectual disability are also possible.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: There are two subtypes, the MLIII alpha/beta subtype due to pathogenic variants in GNPTAB (12q23.3) and the milder MLIII gamma subtype with pathogenic variants in GNPTG (16p13.3). These two genes encode for the activity of the enzyme N-acetylglucosamine-1-phosphotransferase, which is decreased in MLIII. This enzyme catalyzes the first step of the formation of mannose 6-phosphate (M6P) on specific lysosomal soluble hydrolases. MP6 is an essential targeting signal for the transport to the lysosomes and without this, the enzymes are missorted into the extracellular space and are not broken down within the lysosomes. This all leads to accumulation of the enzymes in connective tissues, cartilage, bones, ligaments, and other tissues.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnostic procedures include clinical/radiographical examination as well measurement of the activity of several lysosomal enzymes in plasma and/or fibroblasts, where these enzymes are elevated in plasma and decreased in fibroblasts. Radiographs reveal increasing osteopenia and dysostosis multiplex. In addition, GlcNAc-1-phophotransferase activity can be measured in fibroblasts. Finally, molecular analysis of GNPTAB (MLII and III α, β) or GNPTG (MLIII γ) can be performed.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes the different types of mucopolysaccharidosis and alpha-mannosidosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible in chorionic villi by molecular testing.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There are currently no curative or disease-modifying treatments available for MLIII. Musculoskeletal problems often requires surgical (orthopedic or plastic) interventions at a young age or pain and or/ anti-inflammatory medications. Bisphosphonate treatment in MLIII patients can decrease pain, increase bone density and improve mobility. However, long-term treatment with bisphosphonates is not to be recommended as this can induce femoral fractures.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The MLIII α/ β subtype has a broad phenotypic range, from severely affected patients that die in childhood to milder affected patients displaying primarily skeletal symptoms, who survive into adulthood. Osteoarthritis is rapidly progressive in all patients (due to dysostosis multiplex and osteopenia) and results in cartilage destruction and bone lesions. All patients clinically suffer from bone and joint pain which has a great impact on the quality of life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Familial pseudohyperkalemia (FP) is an inherited, mild, non-hemolytic subtype of hereditary stomatocytosis that is associated with a temperature-dependent anomaly in red cell membrane permeability to potassium that leads to high in vitro potassium levels in samples stored below 37°C. FP is not associated with additional hematological abnormalities, although affected individuals may show some mild abnormalities like macrocytosis.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown. Less than 15 kindreds have been reported in the literature so far (the majority being from the United Kingdom). The Arg723Gln substitution in ABCB6 leading to FP-Cardiff (a temperature-dependent pattern of cation leak previously recognized in a UK family) may affect 1/500 Europeans.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: FP is an asymptomatic condition that presents through blood tests as unexpectedly high plasma potassium levels, after storage at or below room temperature.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: All families identified so far have mutations in the ABCB6 gene (2q36), leading to an inherited abnormality in the movement of ions across the red cell membrane, such that when the red cells are cooled they lose potassium into the plasma. Mutations in the PIEZO1 gene have been found in a kindred diagnosed as having FP but actually having dehydrated hereditary stomatocytosis (DHS), a condition that can have a similar presentation as FP due to the low number of stomatocytes.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of FP may be suspected in patients with apparent hyperkalemia, but otherwise normal clinical and hematological findings, in whom pseudohyperkalemia due to other causes (cell lysis, extreme leukocytosis or thrombocythemia, or use of EDTA anticoagulant) has been excluded. The presence of red-cell based pseudohyperkalemia can be tested by taking heparinized blood, aliquoting, and storing aliquots at 37, 20 and 0°C over 24 hours. At time points, aliquots are taken and spun and the plasma potassium measured in the sample. In the 'pseudohyperkalemic' sample the plasma potassium will typically be normal at time zero, then rise with time in the samples which are stored at 20 and 0°C. In normal samples there is very little change at any temperature. The affected individuals may show mild abnormalities in the red cells (e.g. macrocytosis).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: FP needs to be differentiated from true hyperkalemia associated with reduced renal function, acidosis, the use of certain medications and rare diseases such as Addison's disease and pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2. Pseudohyperkalemia can also be caused by leukemic and thrombocythemic conditions, lysis during venipuncture and by the use of EDTA anticoagulant.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: FP is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait. Genetic counseling may be provided to patients and their families to explain the autosomal dominant and fully penetrant nature of the disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: No treatment is required. However, correct diagnosis is important so that needless urgent calls to hospital, and occasionally misplaced insulin/glucose and/or fludrocortisone treatment (for supposed true hyperkalemia) can be avoided. Because some FP variants show quite large abnormalities at refrigerator temperatures, affected individuals should not donate blood for transfusion.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis for patients is excellent. Most patients remain asymptomatic.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation disorder characterized by myoclonic seizures, ataxia, generalized epilepsy, muscle weakness and ragged red fibers in the muscle biopsy.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Fukuhara syndrome; Myoclonus epilepsy associated with ragged-red fibres

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence in the general population of Europe ranges between 1/256,000-67,000 in the adult population, and the birth prevalence is reported at 1/202,000 in Sweden.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients usually present during adolescence or early adulthood with myoclonic epilepsy, sometimes with neurosensory deafness, optic atrophy, short stature or peripheral neuropathy. A few cases have been associated with lipomatosis, cardiomyopathy, pigmentary retinopathy, ophthalmoparesis and/or pyramidal signs. The disease is progressive with worsening of the epilepsy and onset of additional symptoms including ataxia, deafness, muscle weakness, and dementia. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain may show cortical atrophy, cerebellar atrophy, basal ganglia calcifications and leucodystrophy. Clinical manifestations may vary greatly between patients from the same family and between families.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MERRF syndrome is caused by mutations in the mitochondrial DNA. Over 80% of individuals with MERRF syndrome carry the m.8344A>G mutation in the lysine transfer RNA (tRNA Lys) gene (MTTK). Other mutations have been found in other transfer RNA genes or in the MTND5 gene. They may be associated with MERRF/MELAS overlap syndrome, in which affected individuals also suffer from stroke-like episodes.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of MERRF syndrome relies on the demonstration of abnormal lactate accumulation in blood or, more often, in the cerebrospinal fluid or MRI brain spectroscopy, and on the muscle biopsy, which reveals the presence of cytochrome c oxidase negative muscle fibers and ragged red fibers. Biochemical analysis of muscle often shows cytochrome c oxidase deficiency or combined respiratory chain defect. Genetic testing usually shows heteroplasmic (coexistence of the mutant form with a residual population of wild type mitochondrial DNA) variant in the mitochondrial DNA. The proportion of the mutation may differ considerably between tissues. However, in MERRF syndrome, this proportion is most often very high (above 90%) in every tissue and the mutation may therefore be easily investigated in blood.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis comprises other syndromes characterized by progressive myoclonic epilepsy and ataxia including Unverricht-Lundborg disease, Lafora disease, neuronal ceroid lipofuscinosis, and sialidosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: The possibility of heterogeneous proportions of the mutation between tissues theoretically hampers prenatal diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The heteroplasmy makes genetic counseling very arduous in MERRF syndrome. Mitochondrial DNA mutations are transmitted through maternal inheritance. An affected man cannot transmit the disease. The mutation will be transmitted along the maternal lineage but its proportion is unpredictable. Although higher proportions of the mutation in the blood of the mother result in a higher risk of having a child with severe phenotype, there are many examples of extreme segregation of the mutation from mother to child, which prevent efficient genetic counseling at an individual level.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: As with other mitochondrial encephalomyopathies, there is no specific treatment for MERRF syndrome. Seizures can be treated with conventional anticonvulsant therapies but valporic acid should be avoided (mainly if the cause of the mitochondrial epilepsy is a patnogenic variant in POLG gene) or administered with care. In the absence of proper clinical trials, it is difficult to evaluate the effect of proposed supportive treatment such as coenzyme Q10 and its analogue idebenone, carnitine, etc.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis for patients with MERRF syndrome is globally poor because of the progressive nature of the disease. However, the severity varies greatly and some patients, mainly those with non-cerebral presenting symptoms, may have a prolonged survival with relatively little handicap.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by aplasia cutis congenita of the scalp, breast anomalies ranging from hypothelia or athelia to amastia, and anomalies of the external ears. Variable clinical characteristics include nail and dental anomalies, syndactyly and camptodactyly of fingers and/or toes, sparse or absent secondary sexual hair, renal malformations, and facial dysmorphism. Cases with severe hypotonia and developmental delay have been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Scalp-ear-nipple (SEN) syndrome is an infrequent congenital disease. Most of the reported cases demonstrate an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, although there is evidence of possible autosomal recessive inheritance. This suggests that SEN syndrome exhibits genetic heterogeneity. [PMC3934383]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Scalp-ear-nipple (SEN) syndrome is an infrequent congenital disease. Its main features include scalp defects, malformed ears, and absence of nipples. While most reported cases demonstrate autosomal dominant inheritance, there is also evidence of possible autosomal recessive inheritance, indicating that SEN syndrome should be recognized as an entity with genetic heterogeneity. [PMC3934383]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Scalp-ear-nipple syndrome is an infrequent congenital disease with a genetic basis. Most reported cases demonstrate an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. However, there is also evidence of possible autosomal recessive inheritance. Therefore, Scalp-ear-nipple syndrome should be recognized as an entity with genetic heterogeneity, given the different genetic manners of inheritance described. [PMC3934383]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Scalp-ear-nipple (SEN) syndrome is primarily based on its main clinical features, which include scalp defects, malformed ears, and the absence of nipples. This infrequent congenital disease is recognized as an entity with genetic heterogeneity. While most reported cases are autosomal dominant, there is evidence of different genetic manners of inheritance, including possible autosomal recessive inheritance, which should be considered in its recognition. [PMC3934383]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Scalp-ear-nipple syndrome is an infrequent congenital disease characterized by scalp defects, malformed ears, and absent nipples. Genetic counseling for this condition should consider its recognized genetic heterogeneity. While most reported cases demonstrate an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, there is also evidence of possible autosomal recessive inheritance. Therefore, a thorough family history and genetic evaluation are crucial to determine the specific inheritance pattern in affected families. [PMC3934383]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare syndrome that belongs to the group of extreme insulin-resistance syndromes (which also includes leprechaunism, the lipodystrophies, and the type A and B insulin resistance syndromes).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It is an extremely rare disorder of unknown prevalence.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Early onset is marked by intrauterine and postnatal growth retardation, hypotrophy of muscle and adipose tissues, acanthosis nigricans (a skin lesion associated with extreme insulin resistance), dental dysplasia, abnormal hair and nails, hirsutism, and acromegaloid facies. A hypertrophic pineal gland has been reported in some cases.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: As in leprechaunism (of which Rabson-Mendenhall syndrome may represent a less severe form); the condition is caused by anomalies in both alleles of the insulin-receptor gene (INSR;19p13.3-p13.2).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Biologically, infants display fasting hypoglycemia, postprandial hyperglycemia and hyperinsulinemia, which progress to permanent hyperglycemia and recurrent diabetic ketoacidosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include early-onset forms of leprechaunism, and moderate and late-onset forms of type A insulin resistance syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The condition is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait and mainly affects children of consanguineous parents.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is problematic and consists of high doses of insulin and/or recombinant insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF1), sometimes associated with IGFBP3 (IGF binding protein).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy may reach a few years.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Donohue syndrome ([DS]; leprechaunism) describes a genetic autosomal recessive disorder that from the presence of homozygous or compound heterozygous mutations in the insulin receptor gene (INSR; 19p13.3-p13.2).Donohue syndrome is associated with a fatal congenital form of dwarfism with features of intrauterine and postnatal growth retardation, exaggerated hyperglycemia with hyperinsulinism and dysmorphic abnormalities. a case of DS owing to the rarity of this syndrome (1 case in every million births). We discuss how the disease presents, its genetic underpinning, and its prevention.The case was encountered in an Arab male born on 1 September, 2014, for consanguineous parents. The delivery was via cesarean section at 37 weeks gestation due to severe intrauterine growth restriction and nonprogress labor term. The patient was admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit due to infection,... [PMC4753905]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare renal tubulopathy secondary to urinary tract infection (UTI) and/or urinary tract malformation (UTM) characterized by renal tubular resistance to aldosterone, characterized by hyponatremia, metabolic acidosis, hyperkalemia and inappropriately high serum aldosterone concentration and clinically manifesting as dehydration, vomiting, and poor oral intake.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: So far, less than 100 cases have been reported worldwide. Because of its association with underlying UTMs, there is a strong male preponderance with more than 80% of affected infants being males. Due to the non-specific manifestations, the true prevalence of transient pseudohypoaldosteronism (TPHA1) is possibly underestimated.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: TPHA1 occurs exclusively during the neonatal or early infantile period (90 % during the first six months of life). The clinical course is transient, typically resolving with treatment of the UTI, and may range from asymptomatic to life-threatening. The clinical features are non-specific and include nausea, vomiting, poor activity and low oral intake. As a consequence, life-threating salt loss, hyperkalemia and hemodynamic compromise may occur.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Risk factors for TPHA1 in infants with UTI include male sex, young age and urinary tract malformation. Young age may contribute to the development of TPHA1 through low renal mineralocorticoid receptor expression and physiological partial aldosterone resistance. Urinary tract malformation has been found to be associated with decreased expression of mineralocorticoid receptor and increase in mineralocorticoid receptor resistance. In addition, bacterial factors including bacterial endotoxins and host factors such as TGF-beta, INF-alpha, IL-1 and -6 have also been speculated to involve the pathogenesis of TPHA1 in infants with UTI.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis can be confirmed by the findings of inappropriately elevated serum aldosterone in the setting of hyponatremia with renal sodium wasting, hyperkalemia with impaired renal potassium excretion, and non-anion gap metabolic acidosis. Infants should be screened for UTI and UTMs.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnoses include patients with impaired renal function (chronic kidney disease stage III to V), pre-existing electrolyte imbalance, medications (Na channel blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor blockers, calcineurin inhibitors, angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors) which may cause pseudohypoaldosteronism. In cases of recurrent or persistent pseudohypoaldosteronism, the differential diagnosis should include pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: TPHA1 is not an inherited condition; however, in the cases of recurrent or persistent pseudohypoaldosteronism after treatment, the genetic analysis for the genes responsible for PHA1 may be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Early recognition and prompt treatment is crucial for affected infants with life-threatening hyperkalemia, salt wasting, and acidosis. The mainstays of treatment include antibiotics for UTI, volume repletion with salt supplementation for hyponatremia and in some cases bicarbonate for correction of metabolic acidosis. The need for additional therapeutic measures, such as loop diuretics, beta2 agonist, ion exchange resins, and calcium gluconate are determined by the severity of hyperkalemia.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The outcome is typically favorable as TPHA1 resolves with treatment of dehydration and urinary tract infection; however, the prognosis for affected infants with life-threatening hyperkalemia, salt wasting, and acidosis depends on early recognition and prompt treatment.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal features that may prompt consideration of conditions mimicking pseudohypoaldosteronism include severe unexplained polyhydramnios. This finding was noted in the antenatal history of a neonate later diagnosed with Bartter syndrome type II, which initially presented with features mimicking pseudohypoaldosteronism. Similarly, antenatal Bartter syndrome, characterized by polyhydramnios, can lead to biochemical findings at birth that mimic primary pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1. [PMC12235412, PMC3055000]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive syndromic cerebellar ataxia characterized by the association of early-onset cerebellar ataxia with hearing loss and blindness. Patients may also present demyelinating peripheral motor neuropathy. Cerebral MRI shows alterations of the cerebellar white matter without cerebellar atrophy.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): SCABD; SCAR3; Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia-blindness-hearing loss syndrome; Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia type 3

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Purpose: NEUROD1 is a tissue-specific basic helix loop helix (bHLH) protein involved in the development and maintenance of the endocrine pancreas and neuronal elements. Loss of NEUROD1 causes ataxia, cerebellar hypoplasia, sensorineural deafness, and severe retinal dystrophy in mice. Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in NEUROD1 have previously been described as a cause of maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) and late-onset diabetes. To date, homozygous loss-of-function NEUROD1 mutations have only been detected in two patients. Both mutations caused permanent neonatal diabetes and severe neurologic defects, including visual impairment. However, a detailed ophthalmological phenotype of this novel syndrome has not yet been reported. Our aim was to characterize the ophthalmological phenotype associated with the previously reported homozygous c.427_428CT mutation in the NEUROD1... [PMC4323689]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia-blindness-deafness syndrome is associated with homozygous null mutations in the NEUROD1 gene. Key clinical features include ataxia, cerebellar hypoplasia, and sensorineural deafness. Patients also experience severe retinal dystrophy, manifesting as nyctalopia, blurry vision, and visual field constriction from early childhood. Ophthalmological examination reveals concentric visual field constriction, total absence of the photoreceptor layer outside the fovea, peripheral chorioretinal atrophy, central RPE mottling, and undetectable retinal electrical responses. Permanent neonatal diabetes and other severe neurologic defects are also observed. [PMC11217631, PMC4323689]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia-blindness-deafness syndrome has multiple genetic etiologies. Wolfram syndrome, a rare autosomal recessive disorder, is most commonly caused by mutations in the WFS1 gene, which encodes the endoplasmic reticulum protein wolframin. This condition is characterized by cerebellar ataxia, sensorineural hearing impairment, and optic atrophy. Additionally, homozygous null mutations in the NEUROD1 gene can cause a similar phenotype. Loss of NEUROD1 is associated with ataxia, cerebellar hypoplasia, sensorineural deafness, and severe retinal dystrophy, with affected patients exhibiting severe neurologic defects and visual impairment. [PMC11217631, PMC4323689]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis involves genetic testing to identify homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the NEUROD1 gene, such as the c.427_428CT mutation. A comprehensive ophthalmological evaluation is essential, including visual acuity testing, automated perimetry to assess visual field constriction, and funduscopy to observe peripheral chorioretinal atrophy and central RPE mottling. Optical coherence tomography can reveal the absence of the photoreceptor layer, while standard full-field electroretinography typically detects no electrical response from the retina. Anterior-segment imaging and fundus-autofluorescence imaging are also part of the diagnostic assessment. [PMC4323689]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses include Wolfram syndrome, an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by optic atrophy, sensorineural hearing impairment, and cerebellar ataxia, alongside diabetes mellitus and other features. Another consideration is homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the NEUROD1 gene, which cause ataxia, cerebellar hypoplasia, sensorineural deafness, and severe retinal dystrophy, often with permanent neonatal diabetes. Both conditions share key features of visual impairment, hearing loss, and ataxia. [PMC11217631, PMC4323689]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Autosomal recessive spinocerebellar ataxia-blindness-deafness syndrome is caused by homozygous mutations in the NEUROD1 gene, indicating an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Affected individuals inherit two copies of the mutated gene, and their parents are typically heterozygous carriers. It is important to note that heterozygous loss-of-function mutations in NEUROD1 have been associated with maturity-onset diabetes of the young (MODY) and late-onset diabetes, providing relevant information for carrier screening and family history assessment. [PMC4323689]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for visual function involves early-onset nyctalopia, blurry vision, and visual field constriction, evident from early childhood. In a patient studied between ages 14 and 19, best corrected visual acuity ranged from 20/25 to 15/25, with concentric visual field constriction sparing only the central 30 degrees. Imaging revealed a total absence of the photoreceptor layer outside the fovea, with only a discoid remnant of cone photoreceptors centrally, and no detectable electrical response from the retina, indicating severe and widespread retinal degeneration. [PMC4323689]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hematologic disease characterized by eosinophilia without evidence of clonality persisting for at least six months, for which no underlying cause can be identified. The condition is associated with signs of organ damage and dysfunction. Clinical manifestations are highly variable, depending on the organ systems involved, and include rapidly developing, life-threatening cardiovascular or neurological complications.

An exceedingly rare, autosomal recessive immune disease characterized by thumb aplasia, short stature with skeletal abnormalities, and combined immunodeficiency described in three sibships from two possibly related families. The skeletal abnormalities included unfused olecranon and the immunodeficiency manifested with severe chickenpox and chronic candidiasis. No new cases have been reported since 1978.

A rare inherited human prion disease characterized by adult onset of slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, with dementia developing relatively late in the disease course (classic ataxic phenotype). Patients may present with gait disturbances and frequent falls, dysarthria, dysphagia, nystagmus, dysmetry, and eventually pancerebellar syndrome, myoclonus, spasticity, severe dementia, and mutism. The disease is invariably fatal after five years on average. Neuropathological hallmark is the presence of numerous multicentric prion protein plaques in the cerebral and cerebellar cortex.

DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) combined with in vitro fertilization (IVF) is a viable option for couples seeking to prevent the transmission of genetic prion diseases, including Gerstmann-Straussler-Scheinker syndrome (GSS), to their offspring. This method allows for the detection and selection of mutation-free embryos. A case demonstrated successful PGD for a woman with a family history of GSS, resulting in the birth of healthy, mutation-free children. Neurologists should be aware of PGD to effectively counsel at-risk families on their reproductive choices. [PMC4349573]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management strategies include symptomatic interventions and reproductive planning. Traditional Chinese Medicine has been reported to decrease walking instability and emotional fluctuations in one case. Swallowing function evaluations, including adjustments to patient posture and food consistency, can facilitate continued oral ingestion. For families at risk, preimplantation genetic diagnosis (PGD) combined with in vitro fertilization (IVF) offers a method to prevent the transmission of the disease to offspring. [PMC9980613, PMC8466103, PMC4349573]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inherited bleeding disorder due to reduced coagulation factor XIII (FXIII) activity level and characterized by hemorrhagic diathesis, frequently associated with spontaneous abortions and defective wound healing. The disease may manifest at any age, but the most severe and life-threatening symptoms such as post-birth umbilical cord bleeding, cephalohematoma, and intracranial hemorrhage, manifest during the neonatal period.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Congenital FXIII deficiency (FXIIID) is one of the rarest coagulation factor deficiencies. Prevalence of the disease is estimated at around 1 in 1 to 3 million individuals. Both sexes are equally affected. In some geographical areas where the practice of consanguineous marriages is common, the occurrence of FXIIID is relatively more frequent.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: FXIIID can manifest at any age, but diagnosis is often made during infancy. Umbilical stump bleeding manifests in up to 80% of patients. Other common signs include intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) (25-30%), soft tissue bleeding, bruising, hemarthroses (20%), and recurrent spontaneous abortions. In most cases, hemorrhages are delayed (12-36hr) after trauma or surgery. Patients may have poor wound healing. Acquired forms of the disease have also been reported in association with hepatic failure, inflammatory bowel disease, and myeloid leukemia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FXIIID is usually caused by mutations in the F13A1 gene (6p24.2-p25) encoding the catalytic A subunit, but mutations could also be found in the F13B gene (1q31-q32.1) encoding the B subunit. Transmission is autosomal recessive. The phenotype is less severe when gene mutations are on the F13B gene.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on quantitative FXIII activity measurement assays. Common clotting assays such as activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT) and Prothrombin Time (PT) are normal and cannot be used for the screening. The most widely used screening test is the clot solubility test. However, this method detects only severe FXIII deficiency (with activity <5%), therefore is not recommended. The FXIII deficiency diagnosis could be performed by the estimation of FXIII activity using photometric or incorporation assays, however, the plasma blanking procedure is mandatory to avoid the activated FXIII-independent ammonia release that could lead to incorrect results in the low-activity range (below 5-10%).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses mainly include the other congenital coagulation factor deficiencies, however, FXIIID is not identified by routine coagulation assays as PT and aPTT, therefore specific FXIII assays have to be performed.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis should be performed in families with severe FXIIID cases; no specific guidelines are available.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Affected families (both parents are carrier of a pathogenic variant) have a 25% chance of having an affected child at each pregnancy. Genetic counseling should be offered to families with high risk of severe cases.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Prophylaxis is necessary in cases with severe and moderate FXIII deficiency showing severe bleedings. pdFXIII concentrate and recombinant FXIII-A2 should be used for prophylaxis.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Patients with high risk of intracranial bleeding could have a low quality of life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Abnormal origin of the pulmonary artery
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:1138
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Abnormal origin of the pulmonary artery can be detected prenatally during mid-trimester anomaly scans, with early detection being crucial for outcomes. Clinical manifestations typically become evident in the newborn period, rather than during infancy, often presenting as respiratory distress or congestive heart failure. Serious symptoms, including congestive heart failure, are commonly observed in the first year of life, with 95% of patients presenting within this timeframe. Microscopic features of pulmonary hypertension can even be present during the first month. While often diagnosed early, cases have also been reported in an 11-year-old child, a 13-year-old girl, and a 22-year-old adult. [PMC11793089, PMC11796241, PMC9713641, PMC6716331, PMC4608209]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Abnormal origin of the pulmonary artery (AOPA) is an exceptionally rare congenital heart disease. Clinical manifestations typically become evident in the newborn period or during the first year of life, often presenting with serious symptoms like congestive heart failure. Historically, the condition carried a poor prognosis with high mortality in the first year of life; however, early diagnosis and prompt surgical repair have significantly improved survival rates, now expected to be at least 95% in some series. The anomalous origin of the right pulmonary artery from the ascending aorta is considerably more common than that of the left, with an approximate 8:1 ratio. While cases are sporadically reported, at least 65 patients were reviewed in the literature by 1987. [PMC11793089, PMC11796241, PMC9713641, PMC6716331, PMC4608209]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Abnormal origin of the pulmonary artery (AOPA) is an exceptionally rare and severe congenital heart malformation, most commonly involving the right pulmonary artery originating from the ascending aorta. Clinical manifestations typically emerge in the newborn period, presenting as respiratory distress, congestive heart failure due to increased pulmonary flow, and poor feeding. Patients may also exhibit low oxygen saturation, cardiomegaly, and differential pulmonary vascularity. The condition is frequently associated with significant pulmonary hypertension and can coexist with other congenital heart lesions, including a right-sided aortic arch, bilateral arterial duct, Tetralogy of Fallot, or aortopulmonary window. Early diagnosis and prompt surgical repair are crucial, as untreated cases have an extremely high mortality rate in the first year of life due to irreversible pulmonary vascular changes. [PMC11793089, PMC11796241, PMC9713641, PMC6716331, PMC4608209]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Anomalous origin of the left pulmonary artery (AOLPA) is an exceptionally rare congenital malformation, requiring particular care to be detected during fetal echocardiography. A 30-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, was referred for a mid-trimester anomaly scan. The three-vessel tracheal view in fetal echocardiographic examination led to the prenatal detection of an AOLPA in the presence of a right-sided aortic arch. Additionally, a bilateral arterial duct and the ductal origin of the left pulmonary artery (LPA) were detected postnatally. Prenatal diagnosis enabled the scheduling of the delivery in a tertiary perinatal center, immediate postnatal treatment with prostaglandin E1 to avoid obstruction of the isolated LPA, as well as surgical repair of the anomaly. The rareness of the disease led to only sporadically published cases of prenatal diagnosis of AOLPA. However, early detection... [PMC11793089, PMC11796241, PMC9713641, PMC6716331, PMC4608209]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of anomalous origin of the pulmonary artery is generally based on clinical information and imaging findings. Prenatal detection is crucial and can be achieved through meticulous fetal echocardiography, particularly by examining the three-vessel tracheal view and the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk. Postnatally, transthoracic echocardiography and pulmonary artery computed tomography angiography (CTA) are key diagnostic tools. While echocardiography can estimate pulmonary artery pressure, CTA provides detailed anatomical information. Historically, cineangiography has also been used to establish an accurate diagnosis. Radiographic and electrocardiographic examinations may reveal associated findings such as cardiomegaly. [PMC11793089, PMC11796241, PMC9713641, PMC1492932]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Abnormal origin of the pulmonary artery can be an isolated finding or coexist with several congenital heart lesions. Direct intrapericardial aortic origin must be distinguished from origin through a persistently patent arterial duct. This rare cardiac anomaly has also been observed in association with Tetralogy of Fallot, which can present with central cyanosis and differential pulmonary vascularity. [PMC6716331, PMC4608209]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of anomalous origin of the pulmonary artery, specifically AOLPA, is exceptionally rare and requires particular care during fetal echocardiography. Detection is possible through a meticulous examination of the bifurcation of the pulmonary trunk, often utilizing the three-vessel tracheal view. While cases of prenatal diagnosis are sporadically published due to the disease's rarity, early detection is considered crucial for the infant's outcome. [PMC11793089]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of anomalous origin of the pulmonary artery primarily involves early diagnosis and prompt surgical repair. Prenatal detection enables planned delivery at a tertiary center and immediate postnatal treatment with prostaglandin E1 to avoid obstruction. Surgical intervention is crucial and should be performed as early as possible, ideally in the neonatal period, to prevent irreversible pulmonary vascular disease. Techniques include translocating the anomalous pulmonary artery to the pulmonary trunk or restoring continuity with grafts. Despite severe pulmonary hypertension, surgical correction can be undertaken following multidisciplinary consultation. Early surgical repair significantly improves survival rates, with reported success rates up to 95%, and can normalize pulmonary arterial pressure and improve long-term outcomes. [PMC11793089, PMC11796241, PMC9713641, PMC6716331, PMC1492932]
