DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Spinal muscular atrophy-progressive myoclonic epilepsy syndrome is characterized by hereditary myoclonus and progressive distal muscular atrophy. Less than 10 cases have been reported. Treatment with clonazepam results in complete and lasting improvement of the myoclonus.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Hereditary myoclonus-progressive distal muscular atrophy syndrome; Jankovic-Rivera syndrome; SMA-PME

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME) is characterized as a rare, autosomal-recessive condition. It is considered a rare form of non-5q spinal muscular atrophy. The available clinical and genomic data, including three new cases, contribute to the understanding of this rare disease. [PMC10246360]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME) is a rare, autosomal-recessive form of non-5q spinal muscular atrophy. This clinically heterogeneous disorder is phenotypically characterized by myoclonic and generalized seizures, accompanied by progressive neurological deterioration. SMA-PME arises from biallelic pathogenic variants in the ASAH1 gene. Specific homozygous missense mutations, such as c.109 C > A (p.Pro37Thr) or c.125 C > T (p.Thr42Met) in exon 2 of the ASAH1 gene, have been identified as causative. [PMC10246360]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME) is a rare, autosomal-recessive condition. It arises from biallelic pathogenic variants in the ASAH1 gene. Specific homozygous missense mutations, such as c.109 C > A (p.Pro37Thr) or c.125 C > T (p.Thr42Met) in exon 2 of the ASAH1 gene, have been identified as causative. Family members can be heterozygous carriers. This condition is classified as a non-5q SMA, as no clinically relevant variants are found in SMN1 or SMN2 genes. [PMC10246360]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Spinal Muscular Atrophy with Progressive Myoclonic Epilepsy (SMA-PME) involves clinical assessment of myoclonic and generalized seizures with progressive neurological deterioration, followed by primary laboratory assessments. Whole-exome sequencing is performed to detect biallelic pathogenic variants in the ASAH1 gene, such as homozygous missense mutations like c.109 C > A (p.Pro37Thr) or c.125 C > T (p.Thr42Met) in exon 2. Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) is used to rule out 5q SMA by assessing SMN1 and SMN2 gene copy numbers. Sanger sequencing can confirm carrier status in family members. [PMC10246360]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is classified into 5q and non-5q forms based on the chromosomal location of causative genes. SMA-PME is a rare, autosomal-recessive, non-5q SMA characterized by myoclonic and generalized seizures with progressive neurological deterioration. It arises from biallelic pathogenic variants in the ASAH1 gene. To differentiate from 5q SMA, Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) is employed to determine SMN1 and SMN2 gene copy numbers, as no clinically relevant variants are identified in SMA-PME patients by MLPA. [PMC10246360]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME) is an autosomal-recessive condition caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the ASAH1 gene. Affected individuals typically present with homozygous missense mutations, such as c.109 C > A or c.125 C > T, in exon 2 of ASAH1. Genetic counseling should inform families that unaffected relatives can be heterozygous carriers, as demonstrated by Sanger sequencing. Whole-exome sequencing is employed to detect disease-causing variants, and multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) can be used to rule out 5q SMA. [PMC10246360]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) could be classified as 5q and non-5q, based on the chromosomal location of causative genes. A rare form of non-5q SMA is an autosomal-recessive condition called spinal muscular atrophy with progressive myoclonic epilepsy (SMA-PME), phenotypically characterized by myoclonic and generalized seizures with progressive neurological deterioration. SMA-PME is a clinically heterogeneous disorder that arises from biallelic pathogenic variants in ASAH1 gene. Following clinical and primary laboratory assessments, whole-exome sequencing was performed to detect the disease-causing variants in three cases of SMA-PME from different families. Also, Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA) was employed for determining the copy numbers of SMN1 and SMN2 genes to rule out 5q SMA. Exome sequencing revealed two different homozygous missense mutations (c.109 C > A... [PMC10246360]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A wide spectrum of malformations involving the distal anus and rectum as well as the urinary and genital tracts, which can affect boys and girls.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: They occur in approximately 1 in 5000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Defects range from mild anal anomalies to complex cloacal malformations. They can therefore be classified into the following groups: imperforated anus without fistula, ARM with rectourinary or rectogenital fistula and complex ARM (cloaca). Associated anomalies include genitourinary defects (in approximately 50% of patients) and spinal anomalies. A cloaca is associated with a urological problem (such as obstructive uropathy) in 90% of babies and with hydrocolpos in 50%. Sacral anomalies (hemisacrum and sacral hemivertebrae) have been described; hemivertebrae may also affect the lumbar and thoracic spine, leading to scoliosis. A tethered spinal cord (in 25% of patients) may result in motor and sensory disturbances of the lower extremities. Syringomyelia and myelomeningocele can occur.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology remains unclear and is likely multifactorial. Familial cases have been described.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The radiological evaluation of a newborn with imperforate anus should include an abdominal and pelvic ultrasound to evaluate for genitourinary defects as they need to be dealt with in the newborn period to avoid serious complications. Spinal ultrasound in the first three months of life and magnetic resonance imaging thereafter are useful radiological modalities for detecting spinal anomalies.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: ARM can occur in association with multisystem syndromes, such as Townes-Brocks syndrome, Currarino syndrome, Pallister-Hall syndrome, and Down syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The risk of ARM for a sibling of a patient with ARM can reach 1%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Patients can either undergo a primary repair procedure (anoplasty) or a protective colostomy and definitive repair at a later date, depending on the malformation. The surgical approach to repairing these defects changed dramatically in 1980 with the introduction of the posterior sagittal approach, which allowed surgeons to view the anatomy of these defects clearly, to repair them under direct vision, and to learn about the complex anatomic arrangement between the rectum and genitourinary tract.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Early diagnosis, management of associated anomalies and efficient meticulous surgical repair can ensure a good functional outcome in terms of bowel and urinary control, and sexual function. However, fecal and urinary incontinence can occur due mainly to associated problems such as a poorly developed sacrum, deficient nerve supply, and spinal cord anomalies. For these patients, an effective bowel management program, including enema and dietary restrictions improves the quality of life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST) is the most common mesenchymal neoplasm of the gastrointestinal (GI) tract, typically presenting in adults over the age of 40 (mean age 63), and only rarely in children, in various regions of the GI tract, most commonly the stomach or small intestine but also less commonly in the esophagus, appendix, rectum and colon. GISTs can be asymptomatic or present with various non-specific signs, depending on the location and size of tumor, such as loss of appetite, anemia, weight loss, fatigue, abdominal discomfort or fullness, nausea, vomiting, as well as an abdominal mass, blood in stool, and intestinal obstruction. GISTs can also be seen in familial syndromes such as Carney triad and neurofibromatosis type 1.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) are rare mesenchymal tumors, accounting for approximately 1% of primary malignant tumors in the digestive system, yet they are the most common mesenchymal tumors of the gastrointestinal tract. Specific subtypes are even rarer, with duodenal GISTs representing 3-5% of all GISTs, and extragastrointestinal stromal tumors (E-GISTs) also being a rare subtype. SDH-deficient GISTs, comprising 5-10% of cases, predominantly affect young people and women. Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is associated with a 5-15% risk of GISTs, which tend to occur earlier and be more aggressive than sporadic cases. The mean age of presentation for E-GISTs is in the sixth decade of life. GISTs generally have a better prognosis than E-GISTs, with factors such as age over 60, male sex, larger tumor size, and higher mitotic rate associated with a worse prognosis in E-GISTs. [PMC12303422, PMC12101094, PMC11934696, PMC11870861, PMC11851347]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) originate from interstitial cells of Cajal or mesenchymal cells within the gastrointestinal tract. The most common driver mutations are in the KIT gene or the platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (PDGFRA) gene, characterizing approximately 85% of cases. Succinate dehydrogenase-deficient (SDH-deficient) GISTs account for 5-10% of cases. Wild-type GISTs, lacking KIT or PDGFRA mutations, can rarely harbor neurotrophic tyrosine receptor kinase (NTRK) fusions. GISTs are also associated with autosomal dominant disorders like Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1). [PMC12282698, PMC12101094, PMC11934696, PMC11851347, PMC11705098]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: The diagnosis of gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) typically employs a multimodal approach. Initial evaluation often involves imaging studies such as contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scans and MRI. Definitive diagnosis requires histopathological examination of biopsy specimens, which can be obtained via CT-guided fine needle aspiration or surgical resection. Immunohistochemical staining is crucial, with CD117 and DOG1 serving as characteristic markers, though other markers like Bcl-2, D2-40, and WT1 may also be used. Genetic analysis for mutations in KIT and PDGFRA genes, along with other genes such as SDH, KRAS, NRAS, BRAF, NF1, and NTRK fusions, is essential for confirming diagnosis, especially for wild-type GISTs, and for guiding treatment. Genetic testing before neoadjuvant therapy is strongly recommended. [PMC12303422, PMC12293881, PMC12102896, PMC12101094, PMC11938173]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic testing is crucial for guiding treatment in gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) and is strongly recommended as a basic examination method. GISTs are often characterized by genetic alterations in genes such as KIT or PDGFRA, and specific mutations like KIT exon 11 deletions influence treatment response. Genetic analysis can also identify NTRK fusions or assess for succinate dehydrogenase deficiency. Furthermore, GISTs can be associated with autosomal dominant disorders like Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1), which carries an increased risk of GISTs, suggesting implications for familial screening and counseling. [PMC12303422, PMC12101094, PMC11934696, PMC11705098, PMC11964538]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Gastrointestinal stromal tumors (GISTs) generally have a better prognosis than extragastrointestinal stromal tumors (EGISTs), with cumulative 5-year survival rates of 85% for GISTs and 38%-60.9% for EGISTs. Factors associated with worse prognosis in EGISTs include age >60 years, male sex, larger tumor size, higher mitotic rate, and nuclear pleomorphism, with omental EGISTs having higher overall survival than mesenteric or retroperitoneal tumors. Specific GIST subtypes, such as those with KIT exon 11 W557_K558 deletion and NF1-related GISTs, are associated with a high risk of recurrence, though NF1-related GISTs respond well to targeted therapy. SDH-deficient GISTs typically exhibit indolent biological behavior, but can have significant manifestations. While some cases show no recurrence after R0 resection or achieve long-term survival (e.g., 8 years for a PHGIST with individualized therapy), disease progression and death can occur despite multiple lines of treatment. Postoperative care, including targeted therapy, is crucial for reducing recurrence risk and improving outcomes. [PMC12303422, PMC12293881, PMC12282698, PMC12314345, PMC12101094]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare congenital myopathy characterized ultrastructurally by the presence of tubular aggregates in the subsarcolemmal region of the muscle fiber. It most commonly presents with slowly progressive proximal muscle weakness predominantly of the lower limbs, periodic paralysis, post-exertion muscle cramps, and muscular pain. Ocular anomalies like ophthalmoplegia or pupillary abnormalities may be associated. The intensity of the symptoms is variable, cases with normal muscle strength but myalgia or fatigue, as well as clinically asymptomatic cases have been described.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Tubular aggregate myopathy is a rare neuromuscular condition. It is frequently associated with genetic variants in STIM1, ORAI1, and CASQ1 genes. Clinical presentation can be congenital, as evidenced by neonatal hypotonia and motor delay. [PMC11978424]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Tubular aggregate myopathy (TAM) is a rare neuromuscular condition characterized by myofiber protein accumulations. Clinically, it presents with progressive muscle weakness, which can be proximal or distal, and may include exercise-induced cramps, myalgia, and muscle stiffness, sometimes following sustained activity or cold exposure. Onset varies, ranging from infancy with neonatal hypotonia and motor delay, to early or late adulthood. Associated features can be multisystemic, including ocular manifestations like ophthalmoplegia, pupillary abnormalities, and miosis. Central nervous system involvement, though rare, has been reported with seizures, intellectual disability, autistic features, and sensorineural hearing loss. Other systemic manifestations include thrombocytopaenia, hyposplenism, ichthyosis, dyslexia, short stature, and immunological involvement with recurrent respiratory infections. Patients may also experience elevated serum creatine kinase, contractures, skeletal deformities, and in severe cases, acute respiratory failure. Histologically, it involves tubular aggregates in muscle fibers, sometimes with vacuolated fibers or fiber-type disproportion. [PMC11978424, PMC11307083, PMC9263075, PMC9539902, PMC6599941]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Tubular aggregate myopathy is primarily associated with genetic mutations, with variants in STIM1 (including gain-of-function mutations), ORAI1, CASQ1, CACNA1S (e.g., p.R528H), RYR1 (e.g., p.Thr2206Met, p.Gly2434Arg), and DPAGT1 (heteroallelic mutations) genes frequently implicated. Some cases are linked to multiple deletions in mitochondrial DNA. Beyond genetic causes, hyperornithinaemia can also lead to myopathy with tubular aggregates. Additionally, pembrolizumab-induced ocular myasthenia gravis with anti-titin antibody has been reported to present with tubular aggregates, suggesting an acquired etiology in some instances. Some cases may not reveal a genetic cause despite extensive analysis. [PMC11978424, PMC11307083, PMC9263075, PMC9539902, PMC6599941]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of tubular aggregate myopathy primarily relies on muscle biopsy, which consistently reveals dense tubular aggregates in myofibers, often in both type I and type II fibers. Biopsy findings can also include atrophic fibers with vacuoles, necrotizing myopathy, hypoplastic endplates, and fiber-type disproportion. Specific staining techniques like modified Gomori's trichrome and nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide-tetrazolium reductase, along with ultrastructural analysis showing 60 nm hexagonal tubules, aid in confirmation. Genetic analyses, including Whole Genome, Exome, and Sanger sequencing, are crucial for identifying causative mutations in genes such as STIM1, ORAI1, CASQ1, CACNA1S, RYR1, and DPAGT1. Further diagnostic investigations may include routine laboratory tests, which can show elevated serum creatine kinase levels, electrophysiologic tests, and muscle magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). [PMC11978424, PMC11307083, PMC9263075, PMC9539902, PMC6599941]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Tubular aggregate myopathy is genetically heterogeneous, associated with mutations in genes such as STIM1, ORAI1, CASQ1, CACNA1S, RYR1, and DPAGT1. Inheritance patterns vary, including autosomal dominant forms (e.g., CACNA1S, STIM1, RYR1) and autosomal recessive forms (e.g., DPAGT1, requiring two heteroallelic mutations). Some cases may also involve multiple deletions in mitochondrial DNA. Genetic counseling should consider the observed incomplete penetrance, as a mutation carrier may not exhibit the full clinical syndrome. Furthermore, identifying a genetic cause can be challenging, with some cases remaining undiagnosed even after whole-genome sequencing. [PMC11978424, PMC11307083, PMC9263075, PMC9539902, PMC4035711]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Tubular aggregate myopathy is characterized by a progressive course, with muscle weakness often beginning in infancy, childhood, or early adulthood. The disease can lead to significant chronic and multisystemic complications, including intellectual disability, chronic respiratory infections, bronchiectasis, and acute hypercapnic respiratory failure. Other manifestations may involve pupillary dysfunction and skeletal deformities. While progression is noted, the severity can vary among affected individuals, and incomplete penetrance of causative mutations has been observed. [PMC11307083, PMC9263075, PMC4035711, PMC2080694, PMC3055001]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare bacterial infectious disease characterized by an affliction of the upper respiratory tract mediated by the toxin of Corynebacterium diphtheriae. Symptoms include formation of an inflammatory pseudomembrane, fever, sore throat, headaches, coughing, dysphagia, dyspnea, and prominently swollen cervical lymph nodes. The disease may lead to respiratory failure and severe toxin-mediated damage of internal organs, including the heart and kidneys. A cutaneous form of diphtheria is more common in tropical climates and usually follows an indolent course.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Rationale: Diphtheria is caused by infection with Corynebacterium diphtheriae and is typically associated with upper respiratory tract involvement, which can manifest with high invasiveness. However, in recent years, non-toxigenic C diphtheriae strains have increasingly emerged as major pathogens responsible for invasive diseases. The uniqueness of this case lies in the challenges of culturing and identifying the bacterial strain, its atypical upper respiratory tract manifestations (which are easily overlooked clinically), and its potential for covert transmission, all of which warrant heightened clinical attention. Patient concerns: A 71-year-old female patient with rheumatoid arthritis presented to the respiratory department of cough with shortness of breath for >2 months. Diagnoses: Pulmonary infections caused by Proteus vulgaris and C diphtheriae biovar Belfanti, and pulmonary... [PMC12091665, PMC11969966, PMC12400019, PMC11378479, PMC10485220]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Diphtheria is caused by infection with *Corynebacterium diphtheriae*, which can produce diphtheria toxin, leading to local and systemic manifestations such as severe respiratory infections and cardiac complications. Increasingly, non-toxigenic *C. diphtheriae* strains are recognized as pathogens, causing invasive diseases like pulmonary infections, cutaneous infections, and fulminant infective endocarditis, even in immunized individuals. These non-toxigenic strains may possess virulence genes for iron uptake and adherence, or have the potential to transform into pathogenic strains. Furthermore, *Corynebacterium ulcerans* is an underestimated zoonosis replacing *C. diphtheriae* infections in industrialized countries, with companion pets being a main source of human infection. Foxes have also been implicated in the transmission of cutaneous diphtheria, though this risk is generally low. [PMC12091665, PMC11969966, PMC12400019, PMC11652731, PMC11199016]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of diphtheria relies on a combination of . Initial identification often involves bacterial culture from relevant sites, such as throat swabs or blood, followed by techniques like Albert stain, biochemical tests, and MALDI-TOF Mass Spectrometry. Genotypic characterization is performed using mPCR, whole-genome sequencing, and Multilocus Sequence Typing (MLST), including ribosomal MLST, which also confirms species and determines sequence types. Toxigenicity testing is crucial and can be done by polymerase chain reaction. Serological assessments, such as ELISA and seroneutralization (Vero Cell TNT), are employed to determine seropositivity. Additionally, histocytology can confirm diphtheria in tissue samples. [PMC12091665, PMC11969966, PMC11890918, PMC11378479, PMC10485220]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Rationale: Diphtheria is caused by infection with Corynebacterium diphtheriae and is typically associated with upper respiratory tract involvement, which can manifest with high invasiveness. However, in recent years, non-toxigenic C diphtheriae strains have increasingly emerged as major pathogens responsible for invasive diseases. The uniqueness of this case lies in the challenges of culturing and identifying the bacterial strain, its atypical upper respiratory tract manifestations (which are easily overlooked clinically), and its potential for covert transmission, all of which warrant heightened clinical attention. Patient concerns: A 71-year-old female patient with rheumatoid arthritis presented to the respiratory department of cough with shortness of breath for >2 months. DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) is a genetic disorder characterized by overgrowth, tumor predisposition and congenital malformations.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients tend to grow at an increased rate during the 2nd half of pregnancy and in the first few years of life; adult heights are typically in the normal range. Abnormal growth may also manifest as hemihyperplasia and/or macroglossia (leading to difficulties in feeding, speech and infrequently, sleep apnea). Hypoglycemia is reported in 30-50% of neonates. A recognizable facial gestalt is common and often normalizes by adulthood. In addition to macrosomia, macroglossia, hemihyperplasia and hypoglycemia, characteristic findings may include omphalocele/umbilical hernia/diastasis recti, embryonal tumor, anterior earlobe crease(s) and posterior helical pit(s), nevus flammeus or other vascular malformations, visceromegaly involving abdominal organs, fetal adrenocortical cytomegaly (pathognomonic), renal abnormalities, positive family history, and rarely cleft palate. Cardiac malformations are found in 9-34% of cases and about half of these have spontaneously-resolving cardiomegaly. Cardiomyopathy is rare. Patients are highly predisposed to embryonal malignancies primarily in the first 8 years of life with a risk estimate of 7.5% (range of 4 - 21%).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: BWS is caused by various epigenetic and/or genetic alterations that dysregulate imprinted genes on chromosome 11p15.5. Molecular subgroups are associated with different recurrence risks and different clinical findings (e.g. tumor risks).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Generally, diagnosis is supported by the presence of at least three characteristic clinical findings, however embryonal tumor development may occur with 'milder' presentations. Positive molecular tests may confirm the diagnosis; however a negative result does not rule out BWS.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Simpson-Golabi-Behmel, Costello, Perlman, and Sotos syndromes, and mucopolysaccharidosis type VI.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal testing by chorionic villus sampling or amniocentesis can be offered, especially if a cytogenetic or genomic abnormality has been identified; methylation alterations are more reliably detected via amniocentesis at present. Amniocentesis may also be indicated for BWS-associated findings detected on fetal ultrasound (e.g. fetal omphalocele). In the absence of a known molecular defect, screening can be undertaken by measurement of maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein and targeted ultrasound screening.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disease occurs sporadically (85%), but familial transmission is reported (15%). Genetic counseling is recommended and recurrence risk estimation and cascade genetic testing should take into account family history and the molecular subgroup of the affected family member.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management typically involves standard supportive medical and surgical strategies. Tumor surveillance should be initiated if BWS is suspected/diagnosed and in a clinically unaffected monozygotic twin of a patient, but should not be guided by genotype/phenotype correlations at this time. Screening for hypoglycemia should be undertaken in the neonatal period if there are suggestive or diagnostic prenatal findings, and even for clinically unaffected newborns at increased risk based on family history.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: At the severe end of the spectrum, patients are at risk of early death due to complications arising from hypoglycemia, prematurity, cardiomyopathy, macroglossia, or tumors. In patients who survive childhood, prognosis is generally good.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic cardiac disease characterized by restrictive ventricular filling due to high ventricular stiffness that results in severe diastolic dysfunction in the absence of dilated or hypertrophied ventricles.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown; however, from a European registry the familial form is reported to account for 30% of restrictive cardiomyopathy.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical presentation of restrictive cardiomyopathy (RCM) is heterogeneous, with onset at any age. Dyspnea is the most common symptom, followed by edema, palpitation, fatigue, orthopnea and chest pain. The typical symptoms upon examination include jugular venous distension, elevated systemic and pulmonary venous pressures, systolic murmur, lower-extremity edema, atrial fibrillation, cardiomegaly, and less frequently atrioventricular block. In advance disease, symptoms include pulmonary congestion, hepatomegaly, ascites and edema. Diastolic volumes are normal or reduced, and whilst initial systolic function is normal or near-normal, it may deteriorate with diseases progression. The ejection fraction is typically above 50%. Mild-to-moderate tricuspid and mitral valve regurgitation is common. Bi-atrial dilatation due chronic elevation of atrial pressure usually develops which along with pulmonary venous congestion and pleural effusions can result in moderate to generalized cardiomegaly. Other changes in cardiac morphology, such as ventricular dilatation, septal and ventricular hypertrophy, typically do not occur in RCM. Myocardial biopsy typically demonstrates interstitial fibrosis, and mild to moderated myocyte hypertrophy, without evidence of amyloid deposition, eosinophil infiltration or other systemic infiltration. Death can occur suddenly or as a result of congestive heart failure, cardiac arrhythmias, or other associated complications.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: RCM is due to increased ventricle stiffness resulting in restricted ventricular filling either unilaterally or bilaterally. Most cases of RCM remain idiopathic; however, an increasing number of disease causing mutations have been identified and include the sarcomere subunits, such as troponin T (TNNT2, 1q32.1), troponin I (TNNI3, 19q13.42), alpha-actin (ACTC, 15q14), beta-myosin heavy chain (MYH7, 14q11.2), myopalladin (MYPN, 10q21.3), and filamin C (FLNC, 7q32.1) as well as kinesin-like protein KIF20A (KIF20A, 5q31.2).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made with cardiac echocardiography supported by electrocardiogram, cardiac catheterization, and endomyocardial biopsy. Typical findings on echography include enlargement of atria, normal or reduced left ventricular end diastolic dimension and/or volume, restrictive left ventricular filling pattern, normal or near normal systolic function, and normal ventricular wall thickness. Thorough hemodynamic evaluation with cardiac catheterization may be required to exclude the differential diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes constrictive pericarditis and infiltrative myocardial disease such as cardiac amyloidosis, and other secondary causes of restrictive myopathy such as storage disease.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: For patients with known mutation, the pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant and, therefore, there is a 50% risk of disease transmission from an affected parent to offspring. Autosomal recessive inheritance has been observed in one family. Genetic counseling should be offered to affected families, with clinical screening of asymptomatic family members.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Cardiac transplant is the sole effective procedure in treating the disease. Pediatric patients should obtain preference on the waiting list due to the high risk of sudden death and to prevent the need for heart-lung transplantation. No single drug improves prognosis of RCM. Whilst diuretics are commonly used to reduce preload, excessive reduction may decrease ventricular filling. Thus, diuretics should be limited to patients presenting with symptomatic pulmonary venous congestion and/or right heart failure. ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitors and vasodilators are considered detrimental for the treatment of RCM. Anti-dysrhythmic therapy or implantable cardioverter defibrillators (AICD) may be an option for patients presenting with atrial fibrillation or ischemia. Pacemaker is considered in the presence of high degree atrioventricular block. Anti-coagulants reduce the risk of thromboembolic events.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is usually poor, especially in pediatric patients, with 50 percent of deaths occurring within 2 years of diagnosis. For patients 10 years of age and above, the 5-year survival rate is 64 percent.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare partial autosomal monosomy characterized by variable combination of craniofacial, developmental, digital, skeletal, and cardiac features: hypotonia, developmental delay, growth deficiency, cleft palate, cardiovascular malformations, abnormalities of the hands and feet and typical dysmorphic features, such as microcephaly, rounded facies, small eyes, broad nasal bridge, upturned nose, full cheeks, small mouth and chin.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Distal deletion 4q syndrome is a well-known rare genetic condition, with terminal deletion of the long arm of chromosome 4 being a rare genetic event. The rarity of this syndrome makes genotype-phenotype correlation difficult due to the broad spectrum of clinical manifestations and variability in deletion size and location. Variable clinical presentations have been reported, and studies often involve reviews of existing literature and databases, with one review encompassing 35 cases. [PMC8536159, PMC4077152, PMC2788106, PMC1803779]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Distal deletion 4q syndrome is a rare genetic condition caused by partial, terminal, or interstitial deletions in the long arm of chromosome 4. The phenotype presents with a broad and highly variable spectrum of clinical manifestations, influenced by the deletion's size, location, and incomplete penetrance. Common features include cardiac, craniofacial, and digital anomalies, intellectual disability, and growth retardation. Specific reported findings encompass congenital hearing impairment, cleft palate, autism spectrum disorder, dysmorphic features, limb defects, renal anomalies (including autoimmune nephropathy), and Pierre Robin sequence. Neurological findings such as developmental delay, mental retardation, and abnormal brain signal intensity have also been noted. However, some individuals with interstitial deletions may present as healthy, highlighting the wide phenotypic range and the difficulty in genotype-phenotype correlation. [PMC8536159, PMC4077152, PMC3010696, PMC2788106, PMC1803779]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal deletion 4q syndrome is a rare genetic condition caused by partial, terminal, or interstitial deletions in the long arm (q) of chromosome 4. These deletions vary significantly in size and location, such as those observed at 4q28, 4q32, 4q33, 4q34.1, and 4q35.1q35.2, ranging from megabases in length. The genetic aberration can arise de novo, as seen with deletions emerging in the maternal germ line or when parental chromosomes are normal, or it can be inherited, sometimes presenting with variable expressivity within families. The syndrome may involve simple deletions, duplications, or complex deletion and duplication events in the distal 4q region, contributing to its broad spectrum of clinical manifestations. [PMC8536159, PMC4077152, PMC3010696, PMC2788106, PMC1803779]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of distal deletion 4q syndrome relies on various cytogenetic and molecular genetic techniques. Initial detection may involve chromosome analysis, including high-resolution metaphase karyotyping. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), particularly subtelomere FISH, is utilized to confirm deletions and identify cryptic translocations. More precise molecular chromosomal diagnoses are achieved through SNP array analysis and comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) or oligonucleotide array comparative genomic hybridization (oaCGH), which can define deletion sizes and breakpoints. These are important for both prenatal diagnosis and genetic counseling. [PMC8536159, PMC6250448, PMC4077152, PMC3010696, PMC2788106]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The 4q deletion syndrome is a well-known rare genetic condition caused by partial, terminal, or interstitial deletion in the long arm (q) of chromosome 4. The phenotype of this syndrome shows a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations due to the great variability in the size and location of the deletion. In the literature, the mostly terminal deletions of chromosome 4q and the relative phenotypes are described, while the interstitial deletions of the long arm of chromosome 4 are rarely cited. Here, on a female fetus presenting no abnormal ultrasound evidence but with multiple chromosome aberrations. Comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH) revealed an interstitial 10.09 Mb deletion at the chromosome at the region of 4q28, arr[hg19] 4q28.1q28.3 (124068262_134158728)x1 combined with a 386.81 Kb microduplication at chromosome 15q11.1, arr[hg19] 15.11 (20249932_20636742)x3. At birth, and... [PMC8536159, PMC6250448, PMC2788106, PMC2584776]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of distal deletion 4q syndrome is possible through various . Amniocentesis, comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH), SNP array, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) have been utilized to identify deletions and duplications in the 4q region. While some fetuses may present with multiple ultrasound malformations, others can show no abnormal ultrasound evidence despite significant chromosomal aberrations. These diagnostic approaches provide molecular chromosomal diagnoses, which are crucial for genetic counseling and informing parental decisions, including termination of pregnancy. Diagnosed aberrations can be de novo or inherited. [PMC8536159, PMC6250448, PMC2788106]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for distal deletion 4q syndrome is challenging due to its broad phenotypic spectrum and variable inheritance. Deletions can be de novo, emerging in the germ line, or inherited from a parent, often demonstrating variable expressivity within families. Recurrent cryptic unbalanced translocations involving 4q have also been identified. Accurate diagnosis and counseling rely on precise molecular characterization using techniques such as array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH), SNP array, and FISH. These provide a clearer cytogenetic diagnosis, which is crucial for prenatal diagnosis and informing patients with similar abnormalities, especially when a normal karyotype is initially observed. Reporting unusual variant chromosomes is important for diagnostic genetic purposes. [PMC8536159, PMC6250448, PMC4077152, PMC3010696, PMC2788106]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Rationale: Chromosome deletion/duplication has been reported to be associated with mental disability and dysmorphism according to the accumulated research evidence. Patient concerns: A 25-year-old woman underwent amniocentesis for cytogenetic and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array analysis at 18 weeks of gestation due to the increased Down syndrome risk of 1/13. Diagnoses: The fetal chromosomal analysis revealed a seemingly "normal" chromosomal karyotype, but the SNP array showed a partial duplication of chromosome 4q34.1q35.2 and a deletion of chromosome 7q34q36.3fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis showed that the couple had normal chromosome 4 and 7, whereas there was a partial signal fragment of chromosome 4 attached on the long arm of chromosome 7 for the fetus. Interventions: The couple finally chose to terminate the pregnancy based on the ultrasonic multiple... [PMC6250448, PMC1803779]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Distal deletion 4q syndrome is highly variable, reflecting a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations influenced by the size and location of the deletion. Some individuals, particularly with interstitial deletions, may exhibit normal development or make good developmental progress with minimal assistance. However, others, especially those with terminal deletions, can experience severe outcomes including global developmental delay, intellectual disability, cardiac and renal anomalies, and chronic renal failure. Variable expressivity is noted even within families, and genotype-phenotype correlation is difficult due to the rarity of the syndrome and incomplete penetrance of symptoms. Long-term challenges can include learning disabilities, neurological issues, and persistent syndromic features. [PMC8536159, PMC4077152, PMC3010696, PMC2788106, PMC1803779]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare lysosomal storage disease characterized by mild to severe spondylo-epiphyso-metaphyseal dysplasia, manifesting with disproportionate short stature (short neck and trunk), joint laxity, pectus carinatum, genum valgum, abnormal gait, tracheal narrowing, spinal abnormalities (kyphosis and scoliosis), respiratory impairment and valvular heart disease.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): MPS4; MPSIV; Morquio disease; Mucopolysaccharidosis type IV

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence at birth varies worldwide between 1/240,000 - 7,600,000, the median worldwide prevalence at birth is approximately 1/1,500,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinically, the two forms of MPS, IVA and IVB, have similar skeletal manifestations; however, MPS IVA has a more severe phenotype. MPS IVA is generally diagnosed during the second year of life. Progressive skeletal and joint deformities lead to impairment in walking and daily activities, and include platyspondyly, kyphosis, scoliosis, pectus carinatum, genu valgum, long bone deformities, and joint hyperlaxity (neck, hands, fingers, hips, knees). A rapidly progressive growth failure, with arrest at around 3-5 years of age in severe cases, results in short stature. Potential nervous complications are secondary to skeletal deformations. From the age of 2 to 5 years, hypoplasia of the odontoid vertebra combined with joint hyperlaxity leads to an instability at the level of the first two cervical vertebrae, with a risk of spinal cord compression. Facial dysmorphism includes prominent forehead, large mandible, and short neck. Respiratory impairment, with heavy restriction of lung capacity, susceptibility to pneumonia, and tracheal obstruction/narrowing, is often indicated by life-threatening sleep apnea, cor pulmonale or anesthetic complications. Extra-skeletal manifestations include hepatomegaly, valvulopathies, hearing loss, corneal clouding and dental hypoplasia. Intelligence is normal. Patients typically have low endurance, debilitating fatigue, and pain. Many patients become wheelchair-dependent in their second decade.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The dysfunction and dysplasia is a result of body-wide accumulation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). MPS IVA is due to deficiency in the enzyme N-acetylgalactosamine-6-sulfate sulfatase (GALNS, 16q24.3) required for degradation of keratin sulfate (KS) and chondroitin 6-sulfate. MPS IVB is due to deficiency in beta-galactosidase (GLB1, 3p22.3) required for KS degradation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Preliminary investigations may include urinary analysis of GAGs; however, total urinary GAG level overlaps between MPS IV patients and age-matched controls. Urine KS and blood KS should be measured. Definitive diagnosis is by demonstration of enzymatic deficiency in plasma, serum, leukocytes or fibroblasts.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes MPS I, II, VI, and VII, spondyloepiphyseal dysplasia, Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, and GM1 gangliosidosis type 3 for MPS IVB.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Where the genetic mutation has previously been identified in a family member, prenatal diagnosis is possible through molecular analysis or enzyme measurements in trophoblasts or amniocytes.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal recessive in both forms and genetic counseling should be offered to affected families. The risk of disease transmission is 25% where both parents are unaffected carriers.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The treatment remains symptomatic (prosthesis, surgery, neck consolidation by vertebral fusion, tracheal vascular reconstruction for near-fatal tracheal obstruction, walking aids or wheelchair). Non-invasive assessment of airway obstruction at an early stage is critical. General anesthesia may be problematic due to intubation difficulties. Imaging of the cervical spine is commonly required. Clinical therapies include hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) and enzyme replacement therapy (ERT), both of which lead to the partial restoration of the clinical phenotype but are not reported to improve skeletal manifestations. ERT with elosulfase alfa is approved for MPS IVA and may be associated with increased endurance and pulmonary function, and reduced urinary excretion of KS. HSCT has been used on over 30 MPS IVA patients, however, further studies are required to evaluate therapeutic efficacy. In MPS IVB, management and treatment remains supportive and surgical.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The common causes of mortality are airway compromise and heart disease. Prognosis depends on disease severity and quality of care. Left untreated, MPS IVA patients do not generally survive beyond the third decade of life; with appropriate management, patients may survive beyond the age of 50 with some surviving over 70 years of age.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare syndromic, genetic cataract characterized by the association of congenital cataract and microcornea without any other systemic anomaly or dysmorphism. Clinical findings include a decreased corneal diameter (inferior to 10 mm) in both meridians in an otherwise normal eye, and an inherited cataract, which is mostly bilateral posterior polar with opacification in the lens periphery that progresses to form a total cataract after visual maturity has been achieved. Association with other ocular manifestations, including myopia, iris coloboma, sclerocornea and Peters anomaly may be observed.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Cataract-microcornea syndrome is a very rare condition, with only a few pedigrees, approximately six, reported in the literature. Transmission is most likely autosomal dominant. One reported family exhibited an unusually high proportion of affected members, leading to speculation about preferential transmission of the gene. [PMC1051708]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Cataract-microcornea syndrome is characterized by a complex ocular phenotype, consistently featuring microcornea, which can be extreme, and congenital cataract, sometimes presenting as dentiform. Associated ocular malformations may include microphthalmia, vitelliform macular dystrophy, uveal colobomas, and persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous. Patients, such as a six-year-old girl, may manifest with photophobia and poor visual behavior. These conditions are often observed bilaterally. [PMC10114320, PMC505470]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiology of cataract-microcornea syndrome involves genetic factors. A complex ocular phenotype comprising microphthalmia, microcornea, and cataract, alongside vitelliform macular dystrophy, has been attributed to variants in both BEST1 and CRYBB2 genes, suggesting that such complex presentations are caused by variations in these two genes. Additionally, microcornea-cataract syndrome has been observed to transmit in an autosomal dominant manner within pedigrees. One family showed an unusually high proportion of affected members, leading to a suspicion of preferential transmission of the chromosome carrying the microcornea-cataract gene. [PMC10114320, PMC1051708]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of cataract-microcornea syndrome involves a thorough ophthalmic examination to identify characteristic features such as bilateral microphthalmia, microcornea, congenital cataract, and Best vitelliform macular dystrophy. Comprehensive genetic testing, including whole exome sequencing, is crucial for identifying pathogenic variants in genes like BEST1 and CRYBB2, which can cause this complex ocular phenotype. A minigene assay may be used to assess the functional impact of identified variants. Overall, a general clinical evaluation combined with comprehensive genetic testing is important for diagnosing complex eye diseases like this syndrome. [PMC10114320]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis includes other complex ocular phenotypes that present with similar features. For instance, Best vitelliform macular dystrophy (BVMD) should be considered when it co-occurs with microphthalmia, microcornea, and congenital cataract, which can be associated with variants in BEST1 and CRYBB2. Additionally, conditions involving uveal colobomas and persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous are relevant, as these have been observed in eyes with bilateral congenital dentiform cataract and extreme microcornea. [PMC10114320, PMC505470]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Cataract-microcornea syndrome is most likely transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner, as observed in pedigrees with a high proportion of affected members. However, complex ocular phenotypes involving microphthalmia, microcornea, and cataract can be caused by variants in multiple genes, such as BEST1 and CRYBB2. These variants can be inherited (e.g., from a father with subclinical disease) or arise de novo. Therefore, comprehensive genetic testing is important for diagnosing these complex eye diseases. [PMC10114320, PMC1051708]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Dopa-responsive dystonia due to sepiapterin reductase deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Dopa-responsive dystonia (DRD) due to sepiapterin reductase deficiency (SRD) is a very rare neurometabolic disorder characterized by dystonia with diurnal fluctuations, axial hypotonia, oculogyric crises, and delays in motor and cognitive development.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Autosomal recessive sepiapterin reductase-deficient DRD; DRD due to SRD; SPR deficiency; Sepiapterin reductase deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown. There have been approximately 43 cases reported to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset usually occurs before the first year of life with manifestations of dystonia, motor and language delays, weakness, axial hypotonia (and hypotonia in a tetraplegic distribution) and oculogyric crises that show diurnal fluctuations (worse at night and better in the morning after sleeping). Sleep disturbances and psychological symptoms (anxiety, irritability) are common later in childhood. Intellectual deficits are frequently noted but some may only experience mild to moderate learning disabilities. Less common features include parkinsonism (tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, masked facies), dysarthria, hyperreflexia, limb hypertonia, and autonomic signs. Frequently, dystonia and obvious diurnal fluctuations only develop during the course of the disease, whereas common presenting symptoms in infancy such as developmental delay and hypotonia are unspecific.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: DRD due to an SRD is due to mutations in the SPR gene (2p14-p12), encoding the enzyme sepiapterin reductase (SR). Various mutations in this gene lead to reduced SR activity and consequently to a reduced production of monoamine neurotransmitters.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Distinctive cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings include low levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic (5-HIAA) and homovanillic acid (HVA), and elevated total biopterin and dihydrobiopterin (BH2). SR activity in fibroblasts is usually reduced or absent. Molecular genetic testing can identify mutations in the SPR gene, confirming the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other forms of DRD such as autosomal recessive DRD and autosomal dominant DRD, infantile dystonia-parkinsonism, infantile-onset spastic paraplegia, some forms of epilepsy and cerebral palsy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible in those with a known SPR mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive and genetic counseling is possible and recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Like other forms of DRD, DRD due to an SRD responds dramatically to levodopa (L-dopa) therapy. L-dopa is often combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor such as carbidopa or benserazide. Treatment should be initiated as early as possible to avoid irreversible neurological damage. The dosage of L-dopa given can range from 0.1 to 16.0 mg/kg/day. Transient dyskinesias frequently occur initially as a result of treatment but are usually resolved by decreasing the dosage. In patients with insufficient improvement of symptoms under L-dopa therapy, 5-hydroxytrytophan (5-HTP) at a dosage of 0.14 to 6 mg/kg/day should be given with carbidopa (to reduce side effects), since combination therapy may result in further improvements of motor and sleep symptoms. Treatment is life-long.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on if treatment is initiated early and on disease severity. Those who receive treatment show significant improvement, but most still experience mild motor and sometimes severe cognitive symptoms if treatment is delayed.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic form of hypertension characterized by hyperkalemia, mild hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, normal or elevated aldosterone, low renin, with normal renal glomerular filtration rate (GFR).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Chloride shunt syndrome; Familial hyperkalemic hypertension; Gordon hyperkalemia-hypertension syndrome; Hypertensive hyperkalemia; Hyperkalemia-hypertension syndrome, Gordon type; Mineralocorticoid resistant hyperkalemia; PHA2; PHAII; Spitzer-Weinstein syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of the disorder is unknown. To date, more than 180 affected individuals and families have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients generally develop hypertension in adulthood. Hyperkalemia, mild hyperchloremic acidosis and low renin are present from a young age and are constant findings. Aldosterone levels may be normal to high. Hypervolemia is frequently observed. Growth failure has been described in some cases. Patients do not present renal failure. Spitzer-Weinstein syndrome is believed to be the early presentation of Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 2 (PHA2) with hypertension associated with other clinical findings such as short stature, muscle weakness, periodic paralysis and dental abnormalities.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: There are five etiological subtypes: PHA type 2A has been mapped to chromosome 1q31-q42, but no specific gene has so far been identified. PHA type 2B is due to mutations in WNK4 (17q21.2), PHA type 2C due to mutations in WNK1 (12p13.33), PHA type 2D due to mutations in KLHL3 (5q31.2), and PHA type 2E due to mutations in CUL3 (2q36.2). WNK1 and WNK4 encode serine/threonine-protein kinase WNK1 and WNK4, respectively, which regulate sodium and potassium reabsorption in the distal renal tubule. Disease-causing mutations in these genes lead to increased sodium reabsorption and decreased potassium secretion. The protein products of CUL3 and KLHL3 function together as part of the cullin-RING-based E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, which has a role in ubiquitin-mediated degradation of the proteins produced by WNK1 and WNK4.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is established by the typical constellation of clinical and biochemical findings including hypertension, hyperkalemia (in the setting of normal GFR) with inappropriately low urinary potassium excretion, hyperchloremia, metabolic acidosis, low or suppressed plasma renin activity, hypercalciuria and family history. The diagnosis can be confirmed by genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes other causes of hyperkalemia, notably chronic kidney disease. If GFR is normal, differential diagnoses include hyperkalemic renal tubular acidosis, as seen with PHA1, hypoaldosteronism, primary adrenal insufficiency, and hyperkalemia secondary to medication (e.g. potassium-sparing diuretics, nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, angiotensin inhibitors, trimethoprim, these forms of hyperkalemic RTA are typically associated with hypovolemia and low blood pressure. An acquired form of PHA2 can be seen with calcineurin inhibitors, especially tacrolimus.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible where the genetic mutation has previously been identified in an affected family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance for PHA2 is typically autosomal dominant; however, PHA2 due to KLHL3 mutations can be inherited in an autosomal recessive or dominant manner. The risk to offspring of inheriting the mutation from an affected parent is 50% for the autosomal dominant forms. Offspring of an individual with autosomal recessive PHA2 are obligate carriers, and typically asymptomatic. Pathogenic variants arising de novo are possible. PHA2 due to CUL3 gene is typically the most severe form. The phenotype of PHA type II due to the WNK1 is typically less severe than PHA2 due to WNK4 or dominant or recessive mutation in the KLHL3 gene.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is based on low-dose thiazide diuretics that are very effective in the correction of hypertension (important to prevent secondary complications), hyperkalemia, and hypercalciuria. Exogenous mineralocorticoids do not improve the biochemical abnormalities and likely worsen the hypertension.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is good with lifelong therapy. Nephrolithiasis can be a complication of the disease if untreated and hypercalciuria persists.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare lichen myxedematosus characterized by a progressive, generalized, papular, sclerodermoid cutaneous eruption usually occurring in association with monoclonal gammopathy, but in the absence of thyroid disease. Histological hallmark is the triad of dermal mucin deposition, fibroblast proliferation, and fibrosis. Patients present with relatively sudden onset of numerous closely spaced, waxy, firm papules and plaques predominantly involving the head, neck, trunk, and dorsal aspects of the extremities, on the background of thickened, edematous, erythematous skin with sclerodermoid appearance. Systemic involvement with cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, pulmonary, musculoskeletal, renal, or nervous system complications is common.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Arndt-Gottron disease; Generalized lichenoid papular eruption; Generalized papular and sclerodermoid lichen myxedematosus

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Scleromyxedema is an uncommon and rare chronic connective tissue disorder. The rarity of the condition significantly limits the available epidemiological data, making it difficult to accurately assess its prevalence and incidence. [PMC12318666]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Scleromyxedema is a rare, chronic, progressive fibromucinous or connective tissue disorder, often considered a generalized and sclerodermic form of lichen myxedematosus. It is characterized by distinctive cutaneous manifestations, including generalized papular and sclerodermoid eruptions, fibromyxoid skin lesions, lichenoid papules, thick disfiguring elephant-like erythematous skin folds, and waxy or shiny papules. Histologically, it involves dermal mucin deposition and fibroblast proliferation. A key feature is the frequent association with elevated serum monoclonal immunoglobulin levels or paraproteinemia. The condition can have severe and potentially lethal extracutaneous manifestations, including neurological involvement (dermato-neuro syndrome with encephalopathy, seizures, coma), renal injury (e.g., C3 glomerulonephritis), pulmonary hypertension, and myopathy. It is also associated with various hematologic disorders, including multiple myeloma and, rarely, acute lymphoblastic leukemia. [PMC12318666, PMC9880447, PMC11216142, PMC9716891, PMC7778741]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Scleromyxedema is a chronic, progressive condition with a propensity for severe and potentially fatal extracutaneous manifestations. These can include life-threatening central nervous system involvement, such as dermato-neuro syndrome progressing to encephalopathy, seizures, and coma, as well as acute renal failure and severe pulmonary hypertension. The disease can be triggered by events like COVID-19 or vaccination, even in patients whose condition was previously controlled. Despite its severity, many complications, including dermato-neuro syndrome and pulmonary hypertension, have been shown to be reversible or significantly improved with treatments like intravenous immunoglobulins, plasmapheresis, or therapies for underlying plasma cell dyscrasia. Accurate diagnosis is essential given the potential for life-threatening outcomes and the positive response to treatment. [PMC9880447, PMC9716891, PMC9811295, PMC8571101, PMC7778741]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic hepatorenal fibrocystic syndrome characterized by cystic dilatation and ectasia of renal collecting tubules, and a ductal plate malformation of the liver resulting in congenital hepatic fibrosis. Clinical presentation, whilst typically in utero or at birth, is variable and in the most severe cases includes Potter-sequence, oligohydramnios, pulmonary hypoplasia, and massively enlarged echogenic kidneys.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is estimated at 1/20,000 live births. Male and female children are equally affected.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical spectrum is broad and may include variable degrees of renal insufficiency, mild to severe life-threating neonatal respiratory distress/failure due to pulmonary hypoplasia, hyponatremia, hypertension and predisposition to urinary tract infections. Patients can progress to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) at varying ages. Congenital hepatic fibrosis (CHF) is invariably presents at birth, although may be clinically undetectable. The progressive manifestations of CHF typically include portal hypertension (pHTN), gastrointestinal varices and associated bleeding, bile duct disease (Caroli syndrome and cholangitis) and hepatosplenomegaly.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: PKHD1 (6p12.2-3) is the most frequently identified causative gene, and encodes the ciliary protein fibrocystin. Mutations in a cilia-related gene, DZIP1L (3q22.3), encoding a zinc finger protein, has also been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The hepatorenal phenotype and a family history consistent with autosomal-recessive inheritance is suggestive of the disease. Ultrasound typically shows hyperechogenic and enlarged kidneys, with retained contour and microcysts. Liver sonography shows biliary duct ectasia, a heterogeneous liver and possibly signs of pHTN and associated varices. Liver function tests typically remain in the normal ranges but thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly may be signs of pHTN. Genetic testing can confirm the causative mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Main differential diagnoses are other hereditary cystic kidney diseases including autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, HNF1beta-associated cystic nephropathies, cystic kidney dysplasia and nephronophthisis, as well as rare metabolic diseases such as glutaric aciduria type II.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Suspicious prenatal ultrasound findings include bilaterally hyperechogenic, enlarged kidneys with poor cortico-medullary differentiation, with or without oligohydramnios and cysts. Prenatal genetic testing is possible where a mutation has been previously identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal recessive. The risk of recurrence in siblings of an affected child is 25%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is supportive with conservative management of chronic kidney disease and hepatic symptoms. In newborns, pulmonary hypoplasia may require mechanical or high frequency ventilation. Hypertension needs aggressive management, often requiring a combination of several drugs, among which angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers (ARB) are the mainstays. Peritoneal dialysis is recommended as first choice renal replacement treatment (RRT) for children with end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Renal transplantation is the best solution in case of ESRD. Depending on the hepatic phenotype, combined liver and kidney transplantation may be necessary. Regular monitoring of the liver disease is required to identify complications. Liver transplantation may be necessary. Multidisciplinary support should be considered for associated neurocognitive and behavioral problems.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The disease is associated with reduced life expectancy, although survival is improving. In the case of neonatal respiratory distress, mortality has been described as high as 30-40%. For patients surviving the neonatal period, about 50% will develop ESRD within the first decade of life. CHF is an important cause of morbidity and mortality.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare isolated nail anomaly characterized by brittle, thin, rough, opaque appearing nails with excessive longitudinal ridging. In a less severe form, the nails retain their luster and present with superficial ridging and multiple small geometric pits. In both varieties, superficial scaling of the nail plate and hyperkeratosis of the cuticles, as well as koilonychia and onychoschizia are observed. Any number of nails may be affected, and fingernails are more often affected than toenails. Spontaneous improvement of the condition may occur.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Idiopathic trachyonychia, also known as twenty-nail dystrophy, is a rare disorder of the nails. It typically occurs as an idiopathic condition in childhood, but it can affect individuals of all ages. [PMC7666700, PMC4735359]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Idiopathic trachyonychia, also known as twenty-nail dystrophy (TND), is a rare condition primarily affecting all 20 nails. It is characterized by nail roughness, longitudinal ridging, fragility, and hyper-pigmentation. While it can occur at all ages, it typically has an early onset in childhood and can be hereditary, sometimes linked to FZD6 gene mutations in isolated recessive nail dysplasia without other systemic findings. The condition is often self-limiting, with cases showing marked improvement and almost full resolution over several years, even with conservative treatment. Histological examination can help rule out other underlying diseases. [PMC7666700, PMC5132090, PMC4735359, PMC1048917]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Idiopathic trachyonychia, often presenting as 20-nail dystrophy, can occur as an idiopathic condition, particularly in childhood, and may be self-limiting. However, it also has a hereditary component, with some cases of isolated recessive nail dysplasia (IRND) linked to mutations in the Frizzled 6 (FZD6) gene. These FZD6 mutations, identified in families with 20-nail dystrophy, highlight the role of Wnt-FZD signaling in nail formation. The condition can be hereditary and idiopathic, sometimes without other associated anomalies or skin signs. [PMC5132090, PMC4735359, PMC1048917]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of idiopathic trachyonychia, also known as 20-nail dystrophy, is based on characteristic clinical features including nail roughness, longitudinal ridging, fragility, and hyper-pigmentation, typically affecting all 20 nails. Histological examination can be performed to discount underlying diseases such as lichen planus. In cases of isolated recessive nail dysplasia presenting as 20-nail dystrophy without other cutaneous or extracutaneous findings, mutations in the Frizzled 6 (FZD6) gene have been identified. The idiopathic form often occurs in childhood without associated diseases or family history. [PMC7666700, PMC5132090, PMC4735359, PMC1048917]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Idiopathic trachyonychia, often manifesting as 20-nail dystrophy, requires differentiation from other causes of diffuse nail changes. While it can be an idiopathic and self-limiting condition in childhood, hereditary forms with early onset and progressive dystrophy without other anomalies are also recognized. Isolated recessive nail dysplasia (IRND), caused by FZD6 mutations, presents as 20-nail dystrophy without other cutaneous or extracutaneous findings. Histological examination can help exclude underlying diseases like lichen planus. Congenital abnormalities of the nail are also frequently associated with congenital ectodermal syndromes, which should be considered in the differential. [PMC5132090, PMC4735359, PMC1048917]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Isolated recessive nail dysplasia (IRND), a condition presenting as 20-nail dystrophy, has been linked to recessive mutations in the Frizzled 6 (FZD6) gene. Mutations in FZD6 have been identified in several families with IRND. Furthermore, hereditary twenty-nail dystrophy has been observed in families across successive generations, underscoring a genetic basis for some forms of the condition. [PMC5132090, PMC1048917]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Idiopathic trachyonychia, particularly in children, is often a self-limiting condition. Conservative treatment is indicated, as cases have demonstrated marked improvement and nearly full resolution of nail dystrophy after several years of follow-up. While trachyonychia can generally respond poorly to treatment, the idiopathic form in children appears to have a more favorable prognosis with a conservative approach. [PMC7666700, PMC4735359]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Idiopathic trachyonychia, particularly when occurring in childhood, is often a self-limiting condition. While trachyonychia in general may respond poorly to treatment, idiopathic forms in children can show a favorable prognosis. Marked improvement and almost full resolution of nail dystrophy have been observed after several years of conservative follow-up, with one case demonstrating significant resolution after six years. This suggests that idiopathic 20-nail dystrophy in children can resolve spontaneously. [PMC7666700, PMC4735359]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A very rare neonatal epileptic encephalopathy disorder characterized clinically by onset of severe seizures within hours of birth that are not responsive to anticonvulsants, but are responsive to treatment with pyridoxal phosphate.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): PNPO-related neonatal epileptic encephalopathy; Pyridoxal phosphate-dependent seizures; Pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate oxidase deficiency; Pyridoxal phosphate-responsive seizures; P5PD-DEE

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Pyridoxamine-5-phosphate oxidase deficiency is a rare inborn error of vitamin B6 metabolism that typically presents with drug-resistant epileptic seizures, including neonatal epileptic encephalopathy. Clinical manifestations can include tic-like movements, unintentional, repetitive, and stereotypic movements of the arms, and facial dimorphism. Seizures observed include habitual hypermotor and generalized tonic-clonic types, with ictal electroencephalography showing generalized background attenuation and biphasic spike-wave complexes. A key feature is that these seizures are resistant to conventional antiepileptic drugs but are responsive to supplementation with pyridoxal 5'-phosphate or pyridoxine. [PMC11566241, PMC11273822]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate deficiency-developmental and epileptic encephalopathy is an inborn error of vitamin B6 metabolism, specifically caused by a deficiency in pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate oxidase (PNPO). This enzyme is a key component of the salvage pathway that metabolizes and supplies pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP), the active cofactor form of vitamin B6. Natural mutations in the PNPO gene lead to null or reduced enzymatic activity, resulting in inadequate PLP levels, particularly in neuronal cells. This PLP deficiency is the underlying cause of drug-resistant epileptic seizures and is known to cause or be implicated in pathologies such as neonatal epileptic encephalopathy. [PMC11566241, PMC11273822]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate oxidase deficiency can be established through whole-genome sequencing, which identifies the underlying genetic cause. This is often supported by biochemical findings, such as a low serum level of pyridoxal 5'-phosphate. Electroencephalography may reveal characteristic patterns, including generalized background attenuation and biphasic spike-wave complexes, in patients presenting with drug-resistant epileptic seizures and other neurological symptoms. [PMC11566241, PMC11536958, PMC12360241]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis for early-onset epileptic encephalopathy should include other inborn errors of vitamin B6 metabolism. Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (PDE), particularly the ALDH7A1-related form, is characterized by early-onset refractory seizures and a dramatic response to pyridoxine, often combined with a lysine-restricted diet and arginine supplementation. Genetic testing for ALDH7A1 can confirm this diagnosis. Another consideration is PNPO-dependent neonatal epileptic encephalopathy (NEE), caused by mutations in the PNPO gene, which in pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) deficiency and seizures that may respond to PLP and/or pyridoxine. Additionally, phosphatase deficiency (hypophosphatasia) due to alkaline phosphatase mutations is known to cause seizures responsive to pyridoxine therapy. [PMC12341594, PMC11536958, PMC12360241, PMC11273822]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Pyridoxine-dependent epilepsy (PDE) due to ALDH7A1 mutations is a genetic disorder, often characterized by early-onset refractory seizures. Genetic testing can identify pathogenic variants in the ALDH7A1 gene, confirming the diagnosis without requiring a pyridoxine trial. This condition is rare, and increased awareness is vital for early diagnosis and appropriate treatment. While newborn screening holds promise for future detection, predicting the long-term outcome for affected individuals remains challenging. The occurrence in consanguineous parents with a homozygous variant suggests an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. [PMC11536958, PMC12360241]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Pyridoxamine 5'-phosphate oxidase (PNPO) deficiency often presents with drug-resistant epileptic seizures that do not respond to conventional antiepileptic drugs. However, the condition is responsive to supplementation with the active vitamin B6 metabolite pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP) and, in some cases, pyridoxine. Pyridoxine supplementation therapy has been shown to resolve seizures, leading to seizure-free outcomes in reported cases. This treatment addresses the underlying PLP deficiency caused by reduced PNPO enzymatic activity. [PMC11566241, PMC11273822]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Pyridoxamine-5-phosphate deficiency, particularly Pyridoxine-Dependent Epilepsy (PDE), is associated with abnormalities of brain development, intellectual, and developmental disability. However, treatment significantly improves outcomes. Pyridoxine monotherapy is highly effective for seizure control, often leading to minimal cognitive decline. Combining pyridoxine with a lysine-restricted diet or arginine supplementation can further enhance cognitive and motor functions and improve seizure management. Early initiation of triple therapy, within the first 6 months of life, shows significant benefits for seizure control and cognitive performance. While immediate seizure cessation is often achieved with pyridoxine, predicting the long-term outcome remains challenging, though there is optimism for continued improvement in clinical outcomes and quality of life. [PMC12341594, PMC11566241, PMC11536958, PMC12360241]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autoinflammatory disease, and form of mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), characterized by periodic attacks of fever and a systemic inflammatory reaction (cervical lymphadenopathy, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, arthralgia and skin manifestations.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): HIDS; Hyper-IgD syndrome; Hyperimmunoglobinemia D with recurrent fever; Hyperimmunoglobulinemia D syndrome; Partial mevalonate kinase deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown but several hundred patients have been reported worldwide. This is unquestionably an under-representation as many patients remain undiagnosed. A founder mutation (p.V377I) may account for the large number of cases reported from the Netherlands.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease usually begins in the first year of life and rarely after 5 years of age, and involves recurrent attacks of fever with abdominal pain, vomiting and diarrhea. Joint involvement (arthralgia/arthritis), swollen lymph nodes, skin lesions (maculopapular rash, vasculitis with purpura or erythema nodosum), early-onset colitis, and headaches may also be observed. Aphthous ulcers may be found and affect the oral mucosa or more rarely the genital and rectal mucosa. Attacks usually last 3 to 7 days and recur every 2 to 8 weeks, but can vary between patients. Frequency of attacks is highest during childhood and usually decreases with age. Severity of attacks also appears to decrease with age. These attacks can occur spontaneously or can be triggered by vaccination, infection and emotional or physical stress. Growth and development is usually not affected, unlike in patients with more severe disease (mevalonic aciduria; MVA). Disease complications are rarely seen in hyperimmunoglobulinemia D with periodic fever (HIDS) patients, but can include AA-amyloidosis, hemophagocytosis, glomerulonephritis, abdominal adhesions, and very rarely joint contractures.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: HIDS is an inherited syndrome caused by mutations in the mevalonate kinase (MVK) gene (12q24). These MVK mutations lead to reduced, but not abolished enzyme activity. This in turn leads to impaired control of the production of inflammatory mediators, which in turn cause inflammatory (fever) attacks.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical manifestations of the disease along with genetic or biochemical evidence of MVK deficiency. Immunoglobulin A (IgA) and IgD levels may be elevated. However, measurement of IgD cannot confirm nor rule out the diagnosis of HIDS. During an attack, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is increased, as well as serum C-reactive protein (CRP), IL-1, IL-6 and TNF-alpha levels. The diagnosis can be made when genetic testing reveals two pathogenic MVK mutations or when a decreased mevalonate kinase activity is found in leukocytes or fibroblasts. Measurement of urinary mevalonic acid might be useful to select patients for MVK gene-analysis or enzyme assay.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Unlike HIDS, the severe form of MKD, MVA, results in nearly complete MVK deficiency. Other autoinflammatory disorders like familial Mediterranean fever (FMF), Tumor necrosis factor receptor 1-associated periodic syndrome (TRAPS) and Muckle-Wells syndrome should be considered. In children, the clinical picture of HIDS can be indistinguishable from PFAPA syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is theoretically possible, but is not usually done.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: HIDS follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. When a couple has an affected child, there is a 25% recurrence risk in a next child. Genetic counselling is therefore recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no curative treatment for HIDS and currently no established standard therapy. Treatment with NSAIDs might relieve symptoms during attacks. Some patients have responded to high-dose prednisone, especially when given at the beginning of an attack. Interleukin-1 blockade with canakinumab or anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist) has also been successful in many cases. Etanercept has also been effective in some patients. Patients should be monitored closely for complications.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis in HIDS is good. Life expectancy is not shortened except in rare cases where severe infections or renal amyloidosis occur. Spontaneous complete disease remission is possible.
