DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An extremely rare and fatal association syndrome, characterized by absence of the mandible, cerebral malformations with facial anomalies related to a defect in cleavage in the embryonic brain (e.g. synophthalmia, malformed and low-set ears fused in midline (otocephaly), agenesis of the olfactory bulbs, microstomia, hypoglossia/aglossia) and situs inversus partialis or totalis.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Agnathia-holoprosencephaly-situs inversus syndrome is a rare condition, with a literature review identifying 30 previously reported cases and presenting two new patients. The majority of these patients are female. Affected individuals typically present with the most severe forms of holoprosencephaly, often including cyclopia, which is observed more frequently than in general holoprosencephaly cohorts. Many patients also exhibit additional clinical findings, particularly situs abnormalities, which are not characteristic of classic holoprosencephaly. [PMC2815073]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Agnathia-holoprosencephaly-situs inversus syndrome presents as a complex constellation of structural cerebral and craniofacial abnormalities. Key features include agnathia, the virtual absence of the mandible, which can manifest as otocephaly with microstomia and synotia, leading to a lethal prognosis due to impossible airway management. Holoprosencephaly, a severe developmental disorder of the forebrain, is frequently observed, often with cyclopia. Many patients, predominantly female, also exhibit additional clinical findings, particularly situs abnormalities. The condition is often diagnosed prenatally, sometimes in the third trimester, with 3D imaging aiding in understanding the disease patterns. [PMC9036374, PMC2815073]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Agnathia, the virtual absence of the mandible, is occasionally associated with holoprosencephaly (HPE), a developmental disorder of the forebrain. This constellation of structural cerebral and craniofacial abnormalities, often including situs abnormalities, is thought to relate to alterations in signaling from forebrain and foregut endoderm organizing centers. These alterations subsequently impact first pharyngeal arch development. However, current models are considered inadequate to fully explain all clinical findings, and further research is required to elucidate the causal and pathogenic basis of this association. [PMC2815073]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Fetal otocephaly, characterized by agnathia, microstomia, and synotia, is typically not recognized until the third trimester. Three-dimensional imaging has been shown to illustrate the complex syndrome and aid in understanding the present disease patterns. The implementation of 3D imaging into routine scans for the assessment of the fetal face and ears is recommended, particularly in situations of unexplained polyhydramnios. [PMC9036374]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The case presented here shows the rare diagnosis of fetal otocephaly with lethal prognosis due to impossible airway management after birth. Otocephaly is characterised by fetal agnathia, microstomia and synotia. As in our case, otocephaly is usually not recognised until the third trimester and leads to challenging clinical situations and decision making.A woman in her 30s presented to our tertiary hospital at 27 weeks of gestation because of an unexplained polyhydramnios. 3D imaging illustrated the complex syndrome of otocephaly and helped understand the present disease patterns. After premature birth, palliative care was agreed on and the newborn was able to pass away peacefully in the arms of his parents.We recommend the implementation of 3D imaging into routine scans for the assessment of the fetal face and ears, especially in situations of unexplained polyhydramnios. [PMC9036374]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of otocephaly, characterized by fetal agnathia, microstomia, and synotia, is often not recognized until the third trimester. Three-dimensional imaging can illustrate the complex syndrome and aid in understanding disease patterns, particularly in cases of unexplained polyhydramnios. The implementation of 3D imaging into routine scans for assessing the fetal face and ears is recommended to improve detection. [PMC9036374]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: The prognosis for otocephaly, which includes agnathia, is lethal due to impossible airway management after birth. In a reported case, after premature birth, palliative care was agreed upon, allowing the newborn to pass away peacefully. There is no mention of other active management or treatment strategies. [PMC9036374]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The case presented here shows the rare diagnosis of fetal otocephaly with lethal prognosis due to impossible airway management after birth. Otocephaly is characterised by fetal agnathia, microstomia and synotia. As in our case, otocephaly is usually not recognised until the third trimester and leads to challenging clinical situations and decision making.A woman in her 30s presented to our tertiary hospital at 27 weeks of gestation because of an unexplained polyhydramnios. 3D imaging illustrated the complex syndrome of otocephaly and helped understand the present disease patterns. After premature birth, palliative care was agreed on and the newborn was able to pass away peacefully in the arms of his parents.We recommend the implementation of 3D imaging into routine scans for the assessment of the fetal face and ears, especially in situations of unexplained polyhydramnios. [PMC9036374]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Non-distal trisomy 10q is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from the partial duplication of the long arm of chromosome 10, characterized by mild to moderate developmental delay, postnatal growth retardation, central hypotonia, craniofacial dysmorphism (incl. microcephaly, prominent forehead, flat, thick ear helices, deep-set, small eyes, epicanthus, upturned nose, bow-shaped mouth, highly arched palate, micrognathia), ocular anomalies (e.g. iris coloboma, retinal dysplasia, strabismus), long, slender limbs and skeletal and digital anomalies (scoliosis, poly/syndactyly). Additional features reported include cardiac defects (e.g. septal ventricular defect), anal atresia, and cryptorchidism.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: The recognition of a specific partial proximal trisomy 10q syndrome is based on a limited number of reported cases. Phenotypic findings from a girl with a partial duplication of the proximal part of the long arm of chromosome 10 were compared to six other published cases with the same karyotype, suggesting the possibility of delineating this syndrome. [PMC1051779]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: The partial proximal trisomy 10q syndrome, a form of non-distal duplication 10q, is characterized by a mild to moderate phenotype. Affected individuals typically present with mild to moderate developmental delay, postnatal growth retardation, and microcephaly. Distinctive craniofacial features include a prominent forehead, small and deep-set eyes, epicanthus, an upturned nose, a bow-shaped mouth, and micrognathia. Thick and flat helices of the ears are also observed, along with long, slender limbs. Severe ocular malformations are considered a possible part of the syndrome. No major phenotypic differences have been noted between patients with duplications of segment 10q11-10q22 and those with 10q21-10q22. [PMC1735480, PMC1050901, PMC1051779, PMC1013478]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Partial trisomy 10q with mild phenotype caused by an unbalanced X;10 translocation. an 11 year old girl with a de novo unbalanced t(X;10) that resulted in a deletion of Xq26-->Xqter and a trisomy of 10q21-->10qter. Her clinical features were of distal trisomy 10q, but she lacked the cardiovascular and renal malformations observed in duplications of 10q24-->10qter and had only moderate mental retardation. X inactivation was assessed on peripheral blood lymphocytes by late replication with BrdU (LR) and the human androgen receptor assay (HAR). By LR the der(X) was inactive without spreading to 10q21-->10qter in all cells. The HAR assay showed skewed methylation of the paternal allele (90%). The correlation of HAR and LR suggests that the der(X) was paternally inherited and is consistent with data from other de novo balanced and unbalanced X;autosome translocations detected in females.... [PMC1735480, PMC1050901, PMC1051779, PMC1013478]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of non-distal duplication 10q syndrome typically involves karyotyping to identify unbalanced translocations, such as t(X;10) or t(2;10), which result in partial trisomy of chromosome 10q. Chromosome painting can confirm partial duplications of the long arm of chromosome 10. Family studies are often crucial for a full evaluation of the patient's karyotype and to determine parental origin. In cases involving the X chromosome, assays like late replication with BrdU and the human androgen receptor assay (HAR) can assess X-inactivation and parental inheritance. Recognition of the syndrome is also aided by characteristic phenotypic findings, including developmental delay, postnatal growth retardation, microcephaly, and specific facial features. [PMC1050901, PMC1051779, PMC1013478]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Partial trisomy 10q can result from unbalanced translocations, such as X;10 or 2;10. The clinical presentation varies, with some cases showing a mild phenotype from an unbalanced X;10 translocation, while others present with moderate or severe mental retardation, particularly when combined with other chromosomal anomalies like partial monosomy 2q. The specific duplicated region influences features; for instance, trisomy of 10q21-10qter may lack cardiovascular and renal malformations observed in duplications of 10q24-10qter. Inheritance can be de novo, with paternal origin identified in some instances, or inherited from a balanced carrier parent, as seen with a t(2;10) translocation present in normal males across generations. Family studies are essential for comprehensive karyotype evaluation. [PMC1735480, PMC1050901, PMC1013478]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Partial trisomy 10q with mild phenotype caused by an unbalanced X;10 translocation. an 11 year old girl with a de novo unbalanced t(X;10) that resulted in a deletion of Xq26-->Xqter and a trisomy of 10q21-->10qter. Her clinical features were of distal trisomy 10q, but she lacked the cardiovascular and renal malformations observed in duplications of 10q24-->10qter and had only moderate mental retardation. X inactivation was assessed on peripheral blood lymphocytes by late replication with BrdU (LR) and the human androgen receptor assay (HAR). By LR the der(X) was inactive without spreading to 10q21-->10qter in all cells. The HAR assay showed skewed methylation of the paternal allele (90%). The correlation of HAR and LR suggests that the der(X) was paternally inherited and is consistent with data from other de novo balanced and unbalanced X;autosome translocations detected in females.... [PMC1735480, PMC1050901, PMC1051779, PMC1013478]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by the association of a typical facial phenotype with microcephaly associated with congenital hypothyroidism, skeletal involvement (polydactyly, long thumb(s) and long first toe(s), and patellar hypoplasia/agenesis), and some degree of global developmental delay, hypotonia and intellectual disability. Facial features include an immobile mask-like face, severe blepharophimosis and ptosis, tear duct abnormalities, a broad nasal bridge, bulbous nasal tip, small mouth, thin upper lip, hypoplastic teeth and small, low set ears. Renal and genital anomalies, usually cryptorchidism, are often present in affected males. Congenital heart defects and growth delay are variably present.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): SBBYS variant of Ohdo syndrome; Hypothyroidism-dysmorphism-postaxial polydactyly-intellectual disability syndrome; SBBYSS; Say-Barber-Biesecker-Young-Simpson syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Although the prevalence of the disorder is unknown, it is thought to be less than 1/1,000,000. To date, 122 individuals with molecularly diagnosed blepharophimosis-intellectual disability syndrome, SBBYS type (SBBYS), have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical diagnosis is typically based on the striking facial gestalt associated with microcephaly. Skeletal anomalies include long thumbs and great toes, patellar hypoplasia/agenesis, polydactyly (both pre and postaxial), camptodactyly, clinodactyly, brachydactyly, syndactyly, club feet , flexion contractures of the knees and/or hips, and anomalies of the spine, and/or ribs. Individuals generally have developmental delay/intellectual disability, which can be mild. Language disorder, autism spectrum features, anxiety, aggressiveness, attention problems, agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, optic nerve hypoplasia and other brain abnormalities have also been reported. Congenital heart malformations (50% of cases), ocular anomalies and bilateral mixed hearing loss are also often present. Renal anomalies (e.g. hydronephrosis or multiple renal cysts), anal and genital anomalies including cryptorchidism, hypospadias, clitoromegaly and/or hypoplasia of the labia minora or majora, are reported in more than 40% of cases. In a minority of cases, thyroid agenesis/hypoplasia, hypothyroidism, intestinal malrotation, dental anomalies, feeding and respiratory difficulties, gastroesophageal reflux, poor growth, short stature, cleft palate, and Pierre Robin sequence are observed. SBBYS is allelic with genitopatellar syndrome and an intermediate phenotype has been described; thus, the disorder may present as part of a spectrum.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is caused by heterozygous variants in KAT6B (10q22) encoding a highly conserved acetyltransferase that is part of the MYST family, and regulates the expression of multiple genes.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical examination, brain imaging and molecular studies (specific gene testing if the specific clinical suspicion has been raised, otherwise broader genomic tests).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis include other genetic syndromes that associates intellectual disability with one or more of the key features of this disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Polyhydramnios, increased nuchal translucency and/or cystic hygroma, renal anomalies can be observed during pregnancy but are non-specific. Genetic diagnosis can be proposed to families in which the pathogenic variant has already been identified in an affected relative.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant. Most of the cases described are de novo, so the empirical risk of recurrence is low, 1-2%. Three families have been described in which the pathogenic variant has been inherited from a parent with a mild phenotype. The recurrence risk in these cases is 50%. To date, no cases of germinal mosaicism have been reported but this cannot be excluded.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management requires a lifelong multidisciplinary approach with specific regular follow-up based on the patient's clinical manifestations (pediatric, neuropsychiatric, cardiological, ophthalmological, audiometric, orpthopedic, and genetic examinations). Occupational, physical, speech (in particular non-verbal methods of communication), feeding and educational therapies must be tailored to the patient's needs. Bowel malrotation is a potentially dangerous medical complication. Particular attention should be paid to monitoring feeding and growth, as feeding problems tend to occur early.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Whilst there is limited data regarding life expectancy, adult patients are reported and there are no known reasons to suspect reduced life expectancy. Autonomy depends on the degree of involvement and the severity of the psychomotor developmental delay.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inherited bleeding disorder with a decreased antigen and/or activity of factor X (FX) and characterized by mild to severe bleeding symptoms.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Congenital Stuart factor deficiency; Stuart-Prower factor deficiency

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence of homozygous forms is estimated at 1/1 000 000. Both sexes are equally affected.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Congenital FX deficiency manifests at any age but in general, severe forms of the disease manifest early in life. Patients may experience severe umbilical cord stump bleeding, recurrent epistaxis, soft-tissue hemorrhages, menorrhagia, easy bruising, intra cranial hemorrhages, hematuria, hemarthroses and excessive bleeding during or following surgery or delivery or trauma.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Inherited congenital FX deficiency is caused by mutations in the F10 gene (13q34) controlling the production of plasma FX. The severity of the bleeding manifestations correlates with the FX level.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on prolonged prothrombin, activated partial thromboplastin, and Russell viper venom times (PT, aPTT, RVVT), and on reduced levels of FX. Molecular testing is available, but unnecessary for diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include deficiencies of factors II, V, VII, VIII, IX, XI, XIII or acquired deficiencies in FX (amyloidosis).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them of the 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy. Heterozygote patients most often remain asymptomatic.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Prothrombin Complex Concentrates (PCCs) or fresh frozen plasma (if PCCs are not available) are usually used to treat hemorrhagic episodes. A plasma-derived FX concentrate is now available.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is good with early diagnosis and adequate treatment.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hereditary continuous muscle fiber activity is a rare, non-dystrophic myopathy characterized by generalized myokymia and increased muscle tone associated with delayed motor milestones, leg stiffness, spastic gait, hyperreflexia and Babinski sign. Symptoms may be worsened by febrile illness or anesthesia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Hereditary continuous muscle fiber activity, associated with recessive loss-of-function mutations in HINT1, involves 24 distinct pathogenic variants reported worldwide. Four confirmed founder variations have been identified in Europe and Asia. The ancient Slavic founder variant c.110G>C (p.Arg37Pro) is the most prevalent, exhibiting a distribution gradient from east to west across Europe. Its geographic distribution has expanded to South America, with a case in Brazil carrying the p.Arg37Pro variant, which originated from the same ancestral founder allele as reported in Europe. [PMC8580089]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: To date, neuromyotonia in the context of an inherited axonal neuropathy has been linked to autosomal recessive mutations in the histidine triad nucleotide binding protein 1 (HINT1) gene. In two unrelated male patients with late-onset, predominantly motor, axonal neuropathy with neuromyotonia, who carried an autosomal dominant c.103G > A mutation in the myelin protein zero (MPZ) gene (NM_000530.8:c.103G > A, p.Asp35Asn), identified by whole-exome sequence analysis (WES). CASE DESCRIPTIONS: The first patient presented progressive leg muscle weakness and stiffness with difficulty in walking, pain and increased creatine kinase levels,during his fifth decade of life. Electrophysiological examination revealed findings of an axonal, length-dependent polyneuropathy with spontaneous activity, mainly neuromyotonia. Over the 20-year disease course since the first reported symptoms, muscle weakness... [PMC12084164, PMC11593638, PMC8580089, PMC7549609, PMC7315896]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hereditary continuous muscle fiber activity can be caused by mutations in several genes. Autosomal recessive pathogenic variants in the HINT1 gene are responsible for an axonal Charcot-Marie-Tooth neuropathy associated with neuromyotonia, with specific biallelic and founder mutations identified. Autosomal dominant mutations in the MPZ gene, such as c.103G > A (p.Asp35Asn), are linked to a novel entity of axonal neuropathy with neuromyotonia. Pathogenic variants in the KCNA1 gene are associated with episodic ataxia type 1 (EA1), characterized by continuous myokymia and ataxia, and can also present with muscle spasms, tetanic crises, or cataplexy, even without ataxia. Additionally, mutations in SCN4A, in combination with KCNA1, have been linked to paramyotonia congenita and episodic ataxia. [PMC12084164, PMC11593638, PMC8580089, PMC7549609, PMC7315896]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: To date, neuromyotonia in the context of an inherited axonal neuropathy has been linked to autosomal recessive mutations in the histidine triad nucleotide binding protein 1 (HINT1) gene. In two unrelated male patients with late-onset, predominantly motor, axonal neuropathy with neuromyotonia, who carried an autosomal dominant c.103G > A mutation in the myelin protein zero (MPZ) gene (NM_000530.8:c.103G > A, p.Asp35Asn), identified by whole-exome sequence analysis (WES). CASE DESCRIPTIONS: The first patient presented progressive leg muscle weakness and stiffness with difficulty in walking, pain and increased creatine kinase levels,during his fifth decade of life. Electrophysiological examination revealed findings of an axonal, length-dependent polyneuropathy with spontaneous activity, mainly neuromyotonia. Over the 20-year disease course since the first reported symptoms, muscle weakness... [PMC12084164, PMC11593638, PMC8580089, PMC7549609, PMC7315896]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Treatment strategies for hereditary continuous muscle fiber activity vary by presentation. For neuromyotonia, symptoms improved with diphenylhydantoin, carbamazepine, and tocainide. In a case linked to a KCNA1 mutation, calcium supplementation offered partial benefit for tetanic episodes but not spasms, and magnesium supplementation worsened symptoms. For Morvan's syndrome and myasthenia gravis, edrophonium was effective for myasthenic symptoms, though high-dose corticosteroids, plasma exchange, and intravenous immunoglobulin provided only transient, limited improvement with frequent relapses. [PMC7315896, PMC4812638, PMC1014391]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for hereditary continuous muscle fiber activity is variable, depending on the specific genetic etiology. Conditions linked to MPZ mutations can manifest as a progressive axonal neuropathy, leading to gradually worsening muscle weakness over decades and eventual loss of ambulation. In contrast, KCNA1-related disorders, such as episodic ataxia type 1, present with a spectrum of symptoms including ataxia, seizures, cognitive impairment, and developmental delay, with symptom severity and presentation influenced by the specific variant. Some cases, including those with certain KCNA1 mutations or Morvan's syndrome associated with MEFV mutations, may experience persistent spasms, tetanic episodes, and weakness, often with only partial or transient improvement despite aggressive therapies and frequent relapses. However, symptoms in other hereditary motor neuropathies with neuromyotonia can be improved with specific medications. [PMC12084164, PMC7549609, PMC7315896, PMC4812638, PMC1014391]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, virus associated tumor due to human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 or human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1 (HTLV-1) and is characterized by the presence of anti-HTLV-1 antibodies, and malignant, mature, medium-sized T cells with condensed chromatin and polylobated nuclei. The malignant cells exhibit a mature CD4+ T cells phenotype and express CD2, CD5, CD25, CD45RO, HLA-DR, and T-cell receptor αβ. Presentation is heterogeneous and is typically of aggressive leukemia or lymphoma, variable skin eruptions, and visceral organ involvement.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is a rare and aggressive CD4+ T-lymphocyte malignancy caused by Human T-lymphotropic virus type-1 (HTLV-1). HTLV-1 is endemic in some countries, including Brazil, where ATLL affects 1-5% of virus carriers. In a study from a tertiary hospital in São Paulo, Brazil, the median age at diagnosis was 59.4 years, with 54.5% of patients being female and 45.5% male. [PMC11842934]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is an aggressive T-cell malignancy primarily associated with human T-lymphotropic virus 1 (HTLV-1) infection, which is considered its etiological agent. This rare and aggressive CD4+ T-lymphocyte malignancy affects 1-5% of HTLV-1 virus carriers. The HTLV-1 Tax oncoprotein plays a crucial role by regulating viral gene expression and persistently activating NF-κB, which is essential for maintaining the viability of HTLV-1-infected T cells. The stability of the Tax oncoprotein is dependent on the activity of the tyrosine kinase KDR, which Tax induces and forms a complex with. [PMC12351232, PMC12328758, PMC12328768, PMC11842934, PMC11199648]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Mogamulizumab, an antibody targeting the CCR4 receptor, is an authorized systemic treatment for adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL), particularly in advanced, relapsed, or refractory stages. Clinical trials and real-world evidence underscore its efficacy, showing significant response rates, disease stability, and extended progression-free survival, with a generally manageable safety profile. Brentuximab vedotin monotherapy has also been considered a viable option for older or frail patients with CD30-positive ATLL who cannot tolerate standard multi-agent chemotherapy, demonstrating partial remission in a case study. Additionally, inhibition of the tyrosine kinase KDR is being investigated as a potential strategy to target HTLV-1-associated diseases by stabilizing the Tax oncoprotein. [PMC12351232, PMC12328768, PMC11199648, PMC10889597]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare ophthalmic disorder characterized by 3 stages: vasculitis, occlusion, and retinal neovascularization, leading to recurrent vitreous hemorrhages and vision loss.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Idiopathic retinal perivasculitis; Idiopathic retinal vasculitis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown. The disorder has been reported worldwide but is more commonly observed in the Indian subcontinent where the estimated annual incidence is 1/135-1/200 ophthalmic patients. Males are predominantly affected. Of late, the disease incidence seems to be reducing.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The predominant age of onset is 20-30 years (earlier in Asians). The disorder can appear in adolescence. Eales disease (ED) is characterized by 3 sequential vascular responses that determine the course of the disease: inflammation (peripheral retinal perivasculitis); occlusion (peripheral retinal capillary non-perfusion); and neovascularisation of the retina or disk, which often leads to vitreous hemorrhage. The first 2 stages are generally asymptomatic while vitreous hemorrhage (often sudden and unilateral) is characterized by small specks, floaters, ''cobwebs'' and a decrease in visual acuity (often remission). The fellow eye is affected in 50-90% of cases after a gap of 3-10 years. Recurrences are common. Recurrent bleeds result in tractional retinal detachments, retinal tears, and epimacular membranes. Others may show a mild reduction of vision associated with retinal vasculitis (without vitreous hemorrhage). In addition, headache, variation in peripheral circulation, dyspepsia, chronic constipation, and epistaxis have also been associated with ED. Saxena and Kumar classification is based on visual outcomes and is as follows: Stage 1: periphlebitis of small (1a) and large (1b) calibre vessels with superficial retinal hemorrhages; Stage 2a: capillary non-perfusion, 2b: neovascularization elsewhere/of the disc; Stage 3a: fibrovascular proliferation, 3b: vitreous hemorrhage; Stage 4a: traction/combined rhegmatogenous retinal detachment and 4b: rubeosis iridis, neovascular glaucoma, complicated cataract and optic atrophy.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of ED remains elusive; Several immunological, molecular biological, and biochemical studies have indicated the roles of human leukocyte antigen, retinal S-antigen autoimmunity, Mycobacterium tuberculosis genome, free radical damage, and hyperhomocysteinemia in the pathogenesis of Eales disease. An increase of peptide growth factors like platelet-derived growth factor, insulin-like growth factor, epidermal growth factor, transforming growth factors alpha and bêta, vascular endothelial growth factor, urokinase, metalloprotease enzymes, and a 88 kDa protein has been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) findings that may show early changes such as periphlebitis, vascular sheathing or peripheral nonperfusion and neovascularization. Wide field angiography is useful for the detection of peripheral lesions in the retina. Ultrasonography is needed to rule out associated retinal detachment and ocular coherence tomography (OCT) offers high-resolution imaging of the retina.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) sequelae, familial exudative vitreoretinopathy, sarcoidosis, Behçet disease, sickle cell anemia, Terson syndrome, posttraumatic vitreous hemorrhage, juvenile diabetes and primary branch retinal vein occlusion.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is symptomatic and depends on the stage of the disease. It includes periodic assessment (in the regressed stage of periphlebitis or fresh vitreous hemorrhage), steroids (periocular injections or systemic) and antitubercular drugs (in the active perivasculitis stage). Laser photocoagulation is used in case of neovascularisation of retina or gross capillary nonperfusion. Vitreous surgery is indicated in non-resolving vitreous hemorrhage (usually > 3 months). Intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy is currently being tested as a definitive therapy for ED.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Isolated episodes of vitreous hemorrhage usually settle down without visual deficit. However, some patients may lose vision significantly due to recurrent episodes of vitreous hemorrhage, macular changes, and tractional or combined retinal detachment involving the macula. Blindness due to ED is rare. There is no known mortality associated with the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Three patients with hemoglobin S-C disease, all with ocular lesions, were studied and contrasted with four other patients who had predominantly either hemoglobin S or C but no ocular lesions. Attention is drawn to the diagnostic value of hemoglobin electrophoresis in such cases. With this technique a diagnosis of hemoglobin S-C disease was made in a patient previously thought to the "Eales' disease"; one sister was found to have asymptomatic hemoglobin S-C disease and unsuspected early ocular lesions. The number of persons in Canada with hemoglobinopathies is increasing. Awareness of an association between abnormal hemoglobins and ocular disease may lead to the recognition of an unsuspected blood disorder or of an unsuspected retinopathy. [PMC1935247]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Sialidosis type 1 (ST-1) is a very rare lysosomal storage disease, and is the normosomatic form of sialidosis, characterized by gait abnormalities, progressive visual loss, bilateral macular cherry red spots and myoclonic epilepsy and ataxia, that usually presents in the second to third decade of life.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Cherry-red spot-myoclonus syndrome; Lipomucopolysaccharidosis; Normomorphic sialidosis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of ST-1 is unknown but it is less frequent than sialidosis type 2 (ST-2). The prevalence of sialidosis (types 1 and 2 combined) has been estimated at approximately 1/5,000,000-1/1,500,000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease usually presents in adolescence (onset usually between 12 and 25 years) with gait disturbance, walking difficulties and/or a loss of visual acuity. Almost all patients display a cherry-red spot on the retina. They may also have generalized myoclonus, in some cases associated with seizures and ataxia. Color vision progressively diminishes while night blindness appears and, in some cases, corneal opacities and nystagmus are present. Intellectual capacity is normal. In contrast to ST-2, patients do not show facial dysmorphism, bone dysplasia or psychomotor retardation.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: ST-1 is due to a mutation of the N-acetyl-alpha-neuraminidase-1 (NEU1) gene (6p21) encoding the lysosomal enzyme neuraminidase, that initiates the degradation of sialoglycoconjugates in lysosomes. Mutations lead to a decrease in enzyme activity and consequently to an accumulation of sialyloligosaccharides in tissues. Disease severity is linked to level of residual neuraminidase activity in vivo and varies between patients.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: An ophthalmological examination (fundoscopy) can visualize bilateral cherry-red spots. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain can reveal diffuse brain atrophy in advanced cases, but is usually normal on first examination. Detection of urinary sialyloligosaccharides can be suggestive of a diagnosis, but excretion levels may be quite low. The diagnosis must be confirmed by the demonstration of deficient neuraminidase activity (in the presence of normal beta-galactosidase activity) in leukocytes or, preferably, in cultured fibroblasts. Diagnosis can be confirmed by molecular genetic testing revealing mutations in the NEU1 gene.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnosis is galactosialidosis, which is characterized by deficiencies in both neuraminidase and beta-galactosidase.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis can be performed by enzyme activity measurement or by molecular genetic analysis if the underlying molecular defect in the family is well established.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: ST-1 is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. Genetic counseling is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for ST-1 and management should be multidisciplinary to allow for adapted symptomatic treatment, which is essential for improving the quality of life of affected patients. In severe cases, patients may require the use of a wheelchair.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: There appears to be no major effect on life expectancy but quality of life can be affected due to myoclonus and resulting mobility issues.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurological disorder comprising fluctuating trunk and limb stiffness, painful muscle spasms, task-specific phobia related to walking, an exaggerated startle response, and often ankylosing deformities such as fixed lumbar hyperlordosis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Stiff man spectrum disorder; Moersch-Woltman syndrome; SMS; SPS

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is estimated at about 1/1,000,000. Approximately 2/3 of patients are female.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The most common form of stiff person spectrum disorders (SPSD) is classic stiff person syndrome (SPS). Age of onset peaks around 45 and symptoms develop over months or years. Progressive muscle stiffness renders the trunk and hips immobile, and the gait becomes stiff and awkward. Superimposed painful spontaneous or reflex-induced muscle spasms may cause serious falls. A specific fear of crossing open spaces (pseudo-agoraphobia) may induce freezing of gait, sudden spasms, and falls. Focal neurological signs are absent. Clinical variants of SPSD include the stiff limb syndrome (SLS) where symptoms affect only one limb, and progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) where stiffness and myoclonic spasms are associated with focal neurological signs. Many patients with SPSD have insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (30%), autoimmune thyroiditis (10%), atrophic gastritis with pernicious anemia (5%), and some have tumors of the breast, lung, colon or thymus.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The presence of antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD-Abs; ~70-80%), glycine receptors (GlyR-Abs; ~10-20%), amphiphysin (~5%) and other, rarer antibodies (e.g. DPPX) in most of cases suggests an autoimmune pathogenesis. The exact immunopathophysiology (idiopathic vs. paraneoplastic; T-cell mediated vs. antibody mediated) varies amongst the different antibody subgroups. In particular for GAD-antibody associated autoimmunity there seems to be a certain genetic predisposition with an association of certain HLA haplotypes (DQA1*03:01-DQB1*03:02-DRB1*04:01HLA haplotype and DRB1*04:01 allele), and genetic variants in genes relevant for immune regulation as risk factors.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis essentially relies on clinical examination, and is substantiated by detection of associated antibodies in serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), and by characteristic electromyographic abnormalities. Scans of the spinal cord can help to exclude mechanical causes such as a cyst or disc compression of the spinal cord.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes an atypical manifestation of a spinal cord disease (e.g. multiple sclerosis; tumors), axial dystonia, tetanus, neuromyotonia, acquired hyperekplexia (startle disease), and functional movement disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Benzodiazepines and baclofen are standard drugs for symptomatic treatment. Immunomodulating therapies (corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, plasmapheresis, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation) have been proposed with variable results. Treatments help to control symptoms in the majority of patients affected by SPSD. PERM is a potentially lethal variant and requires early and consequent immunotherapy. GlyR-antibody mediated disease is often associated with thymomas, which need to be removed. In amphiphysin antibodies-associated SPSD or other paraneoplastic forms, the treatment of the underlying malignancy is of paramount importance.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis varies widely and depends greatly on the immunological and clinical subtype. While there are monophasic forms (e.g. GlyR-antibody related PERM) in which patients may make a good recovery with adequate treatment, the most common GAD-antibody related form is chronic. Many patients lose their ability to walk independently, and stiffness spreads, leading to an overall decline in the functional status and quality of life. In paraneoplastic SPSD, the prognosis is mainly determined by the underlying malignancy.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: To report two pediatric cases of hyperekplexia in a small city of São Paulo state, Brazil. Case description: Two female patients, one aged three years and six months and one aged five months, receiving care from an APAE (Association of Parents and Friends of People with Disabilities) unit, were diagnosed with hyperekplexia 1, a neurological disorder characterized by an excessive startle response. Hyperekplexia cases can be divided into three subgroups: hereditary, sporadic, and symptomatic. Several specialists have examined patient 1 since she was three weeks old, leading to two initial diagnostic hypotheses (childhood chronic non-progressive encephalopathy and spastic cerebral palsy). She was diagnosed with hyperekplexia 1 at eleven months when a genetic test revealed changes in the GLRA1 gene. Patient 2, at birth, presented hyperextension of both legs, low-set ears, cranial asymmetry,... [PMC11940706, PMC10785957]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Immunodeficiency by defective expression of MHC class II
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency characterized by absence of HLA class II molecules on the surface of immune cells, leading to severely impaired cellular and humoral immune response to foreign antigens, severe CD4+ T-cell lymphopenia, and hypogammaglobulinemia. The disease clinically manifests with early onset of severe and recurrent infections mainly of the respiratory and gastrointestinal tract, protracted diarrhea with failure to thrive, and autoimmune disease, and is frequently fatal in childhood.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): MHC class II deficiency; Bare lymphocyte syndrome type 2

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Immunodeficiency by defective expression of MHC class II, also known as bare lymphocyte syndrome type II, is a rare primary immunodeficiency disorder. It is inherited in an autosomal recessive fashion and is characterized by the absence of MHC class II molecules on the surface of immune cells. This deficiency affects cellular and humoral immune responses. [PMC11618159, PMC10570541, PMC9585253, PMC5829618, PMC4720537]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Major Histocompatibility Complex Class II Deficiency is a rare autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency characterized by the absence of MHC class II molecules on immune cells, impairing CD4+ T helper cell development and function, and T cell-dependent antibody production. Patients commonly present in infancy with recurrent fever, progressive respiratory symptoms, diarrhea, and failure to thrive, leading to severe recurrent respiratory, gastrointestinal, and septic infections. Laboratory findings often include pancytopenia, decreased CD4/CD3 ratio, CD4/CD8 inversion, and hypogammaglobulinemia. Complications can include hemophagocytic syndrome, disseminated BCGitis, and severe pneumonia or sepsis. Atypical presentations, such as late and isolated meningoencephalomyelitis or autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, have also been reported. [PMC11618159, PMC10904449, PMC10570541, PMC5829618, PMC4720537]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Immunodeficiency by defective expression of MHC class II, also known as bare lymphocyte syndrome type II, is a rare primary immunodeficiency disorder inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. It is characterized by the absence or deficiency of Major Histocompatibility Complex Class II molecules on the surface of immune cells. This condition stems from defects in MHC class II regulatory genes, leading to a transcriptional defect that affects all class II genes simultaneously. Mutations in genes such as RFXANK, CIITA, RFX5, and RFAXP have been identified as causative. These genetic defects impair the development and function of CD4+ T helper cells, affecting both cellular and humoral T-cell responses to antigens. [PMC11618159, PMC10904449, PMC10570541, PMC9585253, PMC5829618]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of immunodeficiency by defective expression of MHC class II relies on demonstrating the absence or reduced expression of MHC class II molecules on immune cells, such as B cells and monocytes, typically assessed by flow cytometry. Genetic testing, including whole-exon sequencing and Sanger sequencing, is crucial for identifying pathogenic mutations in regulatory genes like RFXANK, RFX5, and CIITA. Further molecular characterization may involve reverse transcription PCR to investigate specific gene expression patterns or immunoblotting for protein detection. Initial clinical and laboratory findings, such as recurrent infections, pancytopenia, altered CD4/CD3 ratios, hypogammaglobulinemia, or hemophagocytic syndrome, often prompt the consideration of immunodeficiency. [PMC11618159, PMC10904449, PMC10570541, PMC9585253, PMC5829618]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Immunodeficiency by defective expression of MHC class II is a combined immunodeficiency that can present with severe recurrent infections, T-cell lymphopenia, and features such as hemophagocytic syndrome or disseminated BCGitis. Other severe combined immunodeficiencies (SCID) should be considered, although MHC class II deficiency may be missed by TREC-based newborn screening for SCID. Conditions causing severe mycobacterial infections, such as gamma interferon receptor 1 deficiency, also warrant consideration. Additionally, immunodeficiency with a defective T-cell response to interleukin 1, characterized by recurrent infections and T-cell dysfunction, could be in the differential. Late and isolated severe infections, like meningoencephalomyelitis, can also be a manifestation of primary immunodeficiency. [PMC11618159, PMC10904449, PMC10570541, PMC10304095, PMC5829618]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: The identification of novel pathogenic splicing mutations, such as compound heterozygous RFX5 variants, provides new insights for genetic counseling and antenatal diagnosis of MHC class II deficiency. Characterization of these mutations, including the investigation of their pathogenicity through like RT-PCR to confirm frameshifts and premature protein truncation, expands the spectrum of known genetic causes. This information is crucial for facilitating prenatal diagnosis and preimplantation genetic testing (PGT) for the disease. [PMC9585253]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Immunodeficiency by defective expression of MHC class II is an inherited autosomal recessive primary immunodeficiency disorder, often linked to mutations in regulatory genes such such as RFXANK, CIITA, RFX5, and RFAXP. Novel pathogenic variants are frequently identified, and genetic diagnosis is typically confirmed through whole-exon sequencing or Sanger sequencing. The identification of these mutations provides new insights for genetic counseling, including the potential for prenatal diagnosis and preimplantation genetic testing for affected families. Consanguineous parentage has been observed in some cases, aligning with its autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. [PMC11618159, PMC10904449, PMC10570541, PMC9585253, PMC5829618]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) is considered the only curative therapy and treatment of choice for Major Histocompatibility Complex Class II Deficiency, with successful outcomes reported in some cases, including from matched sibling donors. However, poor survival outcomes have also been observed. In utero HSCT is a potentially curative approach for severe combined immunodeficiency disorders. Supportive management includes antimicrobial agents for infections, immunoglobulin therapy, and specific treatments for complications such as hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) with IV Dexamethasone, Anakinra, and IVIG, or oral steroids for autoimmune hemolytic anemia. [PMC11618159, PMC10904449, PMC10304095, PMC5829618, PMC4720537]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic proximal spinal muscular atrophy characterized by degeneration of alpha motor neurons in the anterior horns of the spinal cord and lower brain stem manifesting with adult onset, slowly progressive, mild proximal muscle weakness.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): SMA type 4; SMA type IV; SMA-IV; SMA4; Spinal muscular atrophy, adult form

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The average prevalence at birth of proximal spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is estimated at 1/12,000 of which approximately 1% are type 4.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset is typically in the second or third decade of life. The muscle weakness predominantly affects the legs and hip muscles and then progresses to the shoulders and arms. Waddling gait is common. Finger trembling, fasciculation and calf hypertrophy may occur. The clinical picture is similar to that seen in SMA type 3 but the motor weakness is less severe. Cognition is unaffected.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is a result of degeneration and loss of the lower motor neurons in the spinal cord and the brain stem nuclei. Causal homozygous mutations/deletions in the SMN1 gene (5q12.2-q13.3) are responsible. SMN1 encodes the survival motor neuron protein (SMN) which is known to participate in critical pathways related to RNA processing and transport, and it is believed that motor neurons are particularly vulnerable to impairments in these processes. The disease is modified by the gene SMN2 (5q13.2), a homologous centromeric copy of SMN1 (5q13.1), the copy number of which is inversely correlated to disease severity.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on clinical history and examination. In patients with SMN1 anomalies, the diagnosis may be confirmed by genetic testing. Electromyography and muscle biopsy may be necessary.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include the amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, primary lateral sclerosis, Kennedy disease, myasthenia gravis, and carbohydrate metabolism disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible for families in which the mutations in the SMN1 gene have been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The SMN1 gene deletions are transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner. Genetic counseling should be provided.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is symptomatic, involves a multidisciplinary approach, and aims to improve quality of life. Physiotherapy and occupational therapies are recommended. Walking aids may be required as the disease progresses. Documenting functional status in SMA is important, since all patients show limitations in daily functioning. Nusinersen, an antisense oligonucleotide, is now approved for treatment of SMA in Europe and the USA. There is no data currently available concerning treatment in SMA type 4; however, it is believed that nusinersen may be most effective when started as soon as possible after diagnosis. Other clinical trials are ongoing to identify other potential treatments.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Affected individuals have a normal life expectancy. The greatest morbidity is on quality of life, with impairment of daily activities. Some patients may lose the ability to walk.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic, congenital vitamin K-dependant coagulation factor deficiency disorder characterized by decreased levels or absence of coagulation factor VII (FVII), resulting in bleeding diathesis of variable severity.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: European point prevalence appears to be close to 1/300,000, but may be markedly higher in countries where consanguineous marriage is frequent.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Clinical expression of this disorder is highly variable and no consistent relationship has been found between the severity of the hemorrhagic syndrome and the residual levels of FVII activity. The clinical picture can be very severe, with early occurrence of intracerebral hemorrhages or repeated hemarthroses, or, in contrast, may be moderate with cutaneous/mucosal hemorrhages (epistaxis, menorrhagia) or hemorrhages provoked by surgery or trauma. Finally, numerous subjects are completely asymptomatic despite a very low FVII level.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FVII deficiency is caused by mutations in the F7 gene (13q34) coding for FVII. Typically, only homozygotes or compound heterozygotes develop a hemorrhagic syndrome; heterozygotes are usually asymptomatic. More than 250 mutations and six common variants are known to be associated with increased or decreased FVII plasma levels. Large genomic rearrangements have been reported in the literature and in the different locus-specific databases but they are rare. Genetic rearrangements have also been demonstrated, resulting in total or partial deletion of the F7 gene. The proximity and implication with the F10 gene (13q34) might also be the cause of combined deficits.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is suspected with isolated prothrombin time and further confirmed by chronometric assays revealing a FVII activity level below that of pooled normal plasma (with values usually being between 70 and 140%). The deficiency is usually symptomatic only for values below 30%.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include hepatocellular insufficiency, hypoavitaminosis K, acquired FVII deficiency associated with severe sepsis and, more rarely, the presence of autoantibodies against FVII.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Due to the marked heterogeneity of the phenotypes (including asymptomatic individuals), access to prenatal diagnosis depends on the clinical repercussions of the disease in the family being considered. Only the existence of a first child with the very severe form may lead the medical team to propose prenatal diagnosis at the time of a subsequent pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disease is transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner. Due to the wide phenotypic heterogeneity of the disorder, with many asymptomatic patients, genetic counseling tends to differ depending on the clinical features specific to a family.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: At present, the main treatment consists of recombinant activated FVII (eptacog alfa). Concentrated prothrombinic or plasmatic Factor VII may be used as a second choice and frozen plasma as a last resort. However, indications remain difficult to establish prior to surgery in subjects with few or no symptoms. In 2008, recombinant coagulation factor VIIa (rFVIIa) got an Orphan designation in the USA.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Congenital FVII deficiency usually has good prognosis. Nevertheless, disease remains very disabling, or even fatal, in patients who cannot benefit from long-term replacement prophylaxis and which present the most severe forms (intracerebral hemorrhage and repeated hemarthroses).

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Trisomy 5p is a chromosomal abnormality resulting from the duplication of a segment of variable size of the short arm of chromosome 5, which usually involves the distal band 5p15. The clinical presentation is variable but is always associated with severe intellectual deficit.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Duplication 5p; Duplication of the short arm of chromosome 5; Trisomy of the short arm of chromosome 5

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, more than 40 cases have been reported, the majority in association with another chromosomal anomaly.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Duplication of the 5p13 band determines the characteristic phenotype of trisomy 5p (the critical region): dolichocephaly or scaphocephaly with macrocephaly, oval elongated face, epicanthus, absent malar, long philtrum, ogival palate, macroglossia, dysplasic and low-set ears, micrognathia and short neck. Fingers are long. Patients may have microphthalmia or coloboma of the iris. At birth, the fontanelles are wide. Cerebral malformations (hydrocephalus, agenesis of the corpus callosum or Dandy-Walker malformation) are common. Visceral malformations are rare. Hypotonia is severe. There is a marked susceptibility to infections, especially respiratory infections, which can be life-threatening. Intellectual deficit is severe and may be accompanied by epilepsy. Larger duplications (up to the 5p11 band) have similar dysmorphisms, but more often are associated with failure to thrive, visceral and anorectal malformations, diaphragmatic hernia and club feet. Hydramnios may complicate pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The duplication may extend towards the centromere, to the 5p11 band. The majority of reported patients have a large duplication, visible on the standard karyotype. Small subtelomeric duplications are rare. Duplications that extend to the 5p14 band result in variable intellectual deficit, epilepsy and a specific phenotype. There are no established correlations between genes in the critical region and the phenotype observed. In the majority of patients the 5p duplication is associated with the deletion of another chromosome as part of a translocation (familial or de novo). ``Pure'' duplications are rare. Some patients have been reported with interstitial duplication of 5p or an extra chromosome derived from the 5p arm (possibly in the form of a 5p isochromosome); these patients have a phenotype comparable to classical duplication.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on standard karyotyping or molecular determination of the karyotype (FISH, MLPA, CGH array).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In cases of de novo anomalies, the risk of recurrence is low and can be explained by the possibility of a mosaic germline parent.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Disease management does not differ from that of other patients with severe intellectual deficit and includes physical and psychomotor therapy. Respiratory infections should be treated aggressively.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is poor; many patients die in childhood as a result of neurological complications or respiratory infections.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of Trisomy 5p syndrome can be achieved through various . Amniocentesis can detect marker chromosomes, which can then be confirmed as originating from chromosome 5 using fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) with whole chromosome paint 5. Extended cell-free fetal DNA (cffDNA) analysis is also capable of detecting large segmental aneuploidies, including deletions of the short arm of chromosome 5, and may indicate parental chromosomal rearrangements. G-band karyotyping and next-generation sequencing in amniocytes can further confirm chromosomal abnormalities involving chromosome 5. [PMC8243479, PMC7945345]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hereditary disorder of the heme metabolic pathway characterized by accumulation of protoporphyrin in blood, erythrocytes and tissues, with photosensitive skin manifestations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) has been reported worldwide, with prevalence ranging from 1/17,000 to 1/100,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: It usually begins in early childhood, with the first exposure to the sun. EPP manifests as acute painful photosensitivity of the skin with erythema and edema, sometimes petechiae, together with stinging and burning sensations without phlyctens, after exposure to sunlight or illumination in the visible spectrum (particularly in the Soret band [400 - 410 nm]). These episodes have a variable severity depending on the exposure duration and may result in chronic permanent lesions on exposed skin. As protoporphyrin is a lipophilic molecule excreted by the liver, patients with EPP are at risk of cholelithiasis with obstruction of the bile ducts, and chronic liver disease which may progress to acute liver failure.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: In most cases, EPP is due to a partial deficiency of the last enzyme in the heme biosynthesis pathway, ferrochelatase, encoded by the FECH gene (NM_000140.3). The pattern of inheritance of EPP is autosomal dominant where clinical expression is modulated by the presence of the hypomorphic IVS3-48C FECH allele in trans. Autosomal recessive transmission of two mutated alleles of the FECH gene has also been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is established by increased levels of protoporphyrin in plasma and red blood cells, and detection of a plasma fluorescence peak at 635 nm. Further analysis is recommended, including a search for liver damage and measurement of ferrochelatase activity levels. Genetic analysis (mutations in the FECH gene, presence of the hypomorphic IVS3-48C FECH allele in trans) and family screening are also recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes X-linked erythropoietic protoporphyria, phototoxic drug reactions, hydroa vacciniforme, solar urticaria, contact dermatitis, and angioedema.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is theoretically possible, but is not offered.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant. Genetic counseling should be offered to affected individuals informing them that there is a 50 % risk of transmitting the pathogenic variant. Autosomal recessive transmission of two mutated alleles of the FECH gene has also been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is based on preventive measures such as sun avoidance, protection against visible light (especially blue light) using a high UVA index sunscreen with a high critical wavelength (>370 nm), the use of protective filters on windows and the yellow filter on scialytics, short sessions of UVB TL01 before summer, reducing protoporphyrins (by reducing erythropoiesis with transfusions or by administration of cholestyramine, a bile acid chelator, or by careful phlebotomy), preventing the progression of liver damage to liver failure. Conventional analgesics and beta-carotene have limited effectiveness in EPP. Since liver disease is the major risk associated with EPP, regular monitoring of liver function is key. Sequential liver and bone marrow transplant should be considered in the treatment of severe cases presenting with liver damage.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: EPP is a chronic disease, and its prognosis depends on the progression of liver disease. However, photosensitivity can affect patients' quality of life. The latter has been improved by the use of afamelanotide. Two molecules, dersimelagon and bitopertin, are currently under development. Patients with EPP should not be given iron supplements without expert medical advice.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder characterized by chondromatosis, typically involving the clavicles, upper end of the humerus, and lower end of the femur. Lesions are bilateral and symmetrical. The clinical course is benign.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Genochondromatosis type 1 was identified as a new disorder in 1991, initially described in four patients from the same family. The condition is characterized by dominant transmission, indicating a specific genetic inheritance pattern. The existence of previous publications detailing similar cases further supports the recognition of this unique entity. [PMC1016962]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Genochondromatosis is a newly defined disorder characterized by chondromatosis with a specific localization. Affected individuals present with chondromatosis primarily in the clavicle, upper end of the humerus, and lower end of the femur. The condition follows a favorable course and is transmitted in a dominant manner. It is classified among the chondrodysplasias, which involve disorganised development of cartilage. [PMC1016962]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Genochondromatosis is a newly defined disorder characterized by chondromatosis with a specific localization, including the clavicle, upper end of the humerus, and lower end of the femur. It is transmitted in a dominant fashion, as observed in affected families. This condition is classified among the chondrodysplasias, which are characterized by disorganised development of cartilage. [PMC1016962]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Genochondromatosis type 1 is a distinct entity among chondrodysplasias, characterized by specific localization of chondromatosis in the clavicle, upper end of the humerus, and lower end of the femur. Its uniqueness is further supported by a favorable course and dominant transmission. While other chondrodysplasias with disorganized cartilage development, such as metachondromatosis and spondyloenchondroplasia, have been well-defined, genochondromatosis represents a new disorder within this complex group, distinguishing it from numerous other difficult-to-classify clinical subgroups. [PMC1016962]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genochondromatosis type 1 is characterized by dominant transmission. The disorder has a favorable course, and its unique characteristics, including specific localization of chondromatosis, have been confirmed through previous publications of similar cases. [PMC1016962]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Genochondromatosis type 1 is characterized by a favourable course. This observation, along with its dominant transmission and previously reported similar cases, helps confirm the uniqueness of this new entity among chondrodysplasias. [PMC1016962]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Therapy related acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:86846
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Secondary AML; Secondary acute myeloid leukemia; Therapy-related AML and myelodysplastic syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: A population-based nested case-control study in Taiwan revealed that cancer patients who received radiotherapy (RT) or chemotherapy (CT) developed secondary myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) more frequently than those who did not. Specifically, RT increased the risk of MDS for patients with stomach, colorectal, liver, breast, endometrial, prostate, and kidney cancers. CT was more likely to increase the risk of MDS for patients with lung, endometrial, and cervical cancers. A positive interaction between RT and CT was also observed, suggesting a combined effect. [PMC4603069]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Therapy-related acute leukemias, such as acute erythroleukemia (AEL), are increasing in clinical impact. AEL is a rare and unfavorable type of myeloid neoplasia that can develop secondary to cytotoxic therapy. It is characterized by specific genetic alterations, most importantly multi-allelic mutations of the TP53 gene. AEL may appear as part of the therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome/acute myeloid leukemia spectrum, with cases observed following cytotoxic therapy and melphalan-based myeloablation/autologous stem cell transplantation. [PMC11277346]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Therapy-related acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) are increasingly recognized, though their origins remain largely unknown. Radiotherapy and chemotherapy predispose patients to MDS, with a more prominent effect when both modalities are used. Specific cancer sites are associated with increased MDS risk following these treatments. For acute erythroleukemia, a type of myeloid neoplasia, specific genetic alterations like multi-allelic TP53 mutations are featured. Potential mechanisms for leukemic transformation include preexisting preneoplastic hematopoietic stem cells, generation of p53-deficient post-chemotherapy HSCs, reinoculation of mobilized mutated HSCs, and melphalan treatment-related myelodysplasia/leukemia with newly acquired TP53 mutations. [PMC11277346, PMC4603069]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Therapy-related acute erythroleukemia, a type of myeloid neoplasia, is characterized by specific genetic alterations. Most importantly, multi-allelic mutations of the TP53 gene are a feature of this disorder. Pathogenic TP53 variants can be present, distinct from any preexisting conditions, and in parallel with uninvolved or wild-type hemopoiesis. [PMC11277346]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Acute erythroleukemia (AEL), a rare and unfavorable type of myeloid neoplasia, may develop secondary to cytotoxic therapy and can appear as part of the therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome/acute myeloid leukemia (t-MDS/AML) spectrum. AEL is characterized by specific genetic alterations, most importantly multi-allelic mutations of the TP53 gene. Distinguishing AEL within the t-MDS/AML spectrum involves recognizing these genetic features and considering potential origins such as preexisting preneoplastic hematopoietic stem cells or newly acquired TP53 mutations following treatment. [PMC11277346]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The clinical impact of therapy-related acute leukemias is increasing with the extension of cancer-related survival; however, the origins remain largely unknown. Acute erythroleukemia (AEL), a rare unfavorable type of myeloid neoplasia, may also develop secondary to cytotoxic therapy. The disorder is featured by specific genetic alterations, most importantly multi-allelic mutations of the TP53 gene. While AEL might appear as a part of the therapy-related MDS/AML, spectrum information regarding the genetic complexity and progression is largely missing. two AEL cases arising after cytotoxic therapy and melphalan-based myeloablation/autologous peripheral stem cell transplantation due to multiple myeloma (MM). As stated, multiple pathogenic TP53 variants were present unrelated to preexisting MM, in parallel with uninvolved/wild-type hemopoiesis. Potential mechanisms of leukemic... [PMC11277346]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The clinical impact of therapy-related acute leukemias is increasing. Acute erythroleukemia (AEL), which can develop secondary to cytotoxic therapy, is described as a rare and unfavorable type of myeloid neoplasia. This disorder is often characterized by specific genetic alterations, most importantly multi-allelic mutations of the TP53 gene. However, information regarding the genetic complexity and progression of AEL as part of the therapy-related MDS/AML spectrum is largely missing. [PMC11277346]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked syndromic intellectual disability characterized by mild to profound intellectual disability, microcephaly, growth delay, and hypogenitalism. Obesity, early-onset diabetes and epilepsy are more variably present.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, a total of 22 patients from 11 unrelated families, of all origins, have been reported in the literature with pathogenic variants in EIF2S3. Only male patients are affected while carrier females are asymptomatic.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The phenotype is heterogeneous ranging from a severe, complete phenotype, which is associated to a recurrent frameshift variant (p.(Ile465Serfs*4), to a less severe and/or incomplete phenotype associated with various missense variants. Patients with missense variants present with inconstant features including developmental delay (90%), growth retardation (83%), microcephaly (83%), and more variably epilepsy (33%), and obesity (33%). Endocrinopathy including low growth hormone level, hypopituitarism and hypogonadism was described in 66%. Although intellectual disability is common in patients with missense variants, its severity varied from mild to moderate or severe, while all patients with the frameshift variant shared severe to profound intellectual disability. Early-onset diabetes is a recurrent feature found in patients with the recurrent frameshift variant, while hypoglycaemia and glucose dysregulation are not constant in patients with EIF2S3 missense variant.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MEHMO syndrome is caused by pathogenic variants in EIF2S3 (Xp22.11). The gene encodes the gamma subunit of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor-2, eIF2, essential for protein translation. Families with a recurrent frameshift variant p.(Ile465Serfs*4) in EIF2S3 exhibit a severe, full phenotype of MEHMO syndrome. The majority of patients with missense variants exhibit a less severe and/or incomplete phenotype.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is usually found by next generation sequencing (e,g Whole Exome Sequencing).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Wolcott-Rallison syndrome caused by pathogenic variants in EIF2AK3; primary microcephaly-mild intellectual disability-young-onset diabetes syndrome caused by TRMT10A or PPP1R15B; primary microcephaly-epilepsy-permanent neonatal diabetes syndrome caused by IER3IP1 pathogenic variants.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible where the pathogenic variant has previously been identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is X-linked recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (where the mother is a healthy carrier of a disease-causing variant) informing them that there is a 50% risk of having an affected male child at each pregnancy. Intrafamilial phenotypic variation is observed, most particularly concerning EIF2S3 missense variants.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Multidisciplinary care is needed for this multisystemic disorder; initially including neonatal care, and then with regular pediatric, endocrinology and neuropediatric follow-up. Regular glycemic controls are suggested.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis depends on the severity of the syndrome. Patients with missense variants usually have a normal lifespan while severely affected patients (in particular with the recurrent frameshift variant p.(Ile465Serfs*4)) could present a poor life prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A Rickettsial disease characterized by headache, fever and macular or maculopapular rash, with only one-third of patients manifesting all three symptoms. Other common symptoms are chills, malaise, stomach pain, myalgia, loss of appetite, and in some cases confusion and altered level of consciousness. Classical laboratory abnormalities include elevated liver enzymes, lactate dehydrogenase, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and hypoalbuminemia. In children, typical symptoms occur in only half of patients, and abdominal pain, diarrhea, sore throat and anemia are more common.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Murine typhus, caused by Rickettsia typhi, is a global rickettsiosis endemic throughout much of the world, particularly in tropical and subtropical seaboard regions where rats and their fleas (Xenopsylla cheopis) serve as the primary reservoir and vector. Humans are infected when flea feces are rubbed into bite wounds or mucous membranes. The disease is reemerging in areas like Texas, Southern California, and Greece, with an alternate transmission cycle involving opossums and cat fleas noted in the US. While underreported in some regions like the Brazilian Amazon, Taiwan reported an average incidence of 0.11/100,000 person-years. Cases often peak in summer months (May-August) and are more common in males and those in occupations like agriculture. Flea or animal contact is a frequently reported risk factor, and activities like sunbathing with insect bites have been linked to cases in Greece. [PMC10993848, PMC10793017, PMC10660532, PMC7990230, PMC7454102]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for murine typhus include bacterial isolation, real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR), and indirect immunofluorescence assay (IFA). Serology is considered the mainstay of diagnostic testing, with confirmation often requiring demonstration of seroconversion or a fourfold increase in antibody titer between acute- and convalescent-phase sera, as antibodies may not be detectable in the first week of illness. Initial negative serological tests do not rule out the disease, and follow-up serological or molecular tests within 1-2 weeks are recommended. Other include DNA sequencing, nanopore targeted sequencing (e.g., from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or blood microbial cell-free DNA), and immunohistochemistry. IgM and IgG titers are also used for confirmation. [PMC10993848, PMC10793017, PMC10202882, PMC10660532, PMC7982369]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Early empiric treatment with doxycycline, a tetracycline-class antibiotic, is imperative and considered the drug of choice for murine typhus. Timely administration of appropriate antibiotics can reduce patient morbidity and prevent severe complications, including neurological manifestations. Treatment with doxycycline often leads to significant clinical improvement and resolution of symptoms. However, in some severe cases, even with treatment, the disease can be life-threatening or fatal. Specific complications, such as endocarditis, may require additional interventions like valve replacement and prolonged antibiotic therapy. [PMC10793017, PMC10660532, PMC7982369, PMC7748055, PMC7640496]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Murine typhus is typically a mild illness with a good prognosis, but it can be severe or life-threatening in some patients, especially if treatment is delayed or misdiagnosed. Severe manifestations were observed in 43% of cases in Taiwan. Complications can include severe pulmonary issues like adult respiratory distress syndrome and pulmonary embolism, as well as neurological manifestations such as meningoencephalitis, status epilepticus, cerebral infarctions, and abducens nerve palsy. Multi-organ failure, renal failure, and hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis have also been reported, with fatal outcomes occurring. Early and appropriate treatment with doxycycline is imperative to reduce patient morbidity and prevent severe complications. [PMC10993848, PMC10881251, PMC10793017, PMC10202882, PMC10660532]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare systemic autoimmune disease characterized by mass-forming, potentially destructive inflammation and fibrosis in the soft tissues of the retroperitoneum, associated with elevation of serum IgG4 levels and infiltration of IgG4-positive plasma cells in at least one organ or site. Most frequent locations are peripheral to the abdominal aorta, as well as the iliac and renal arteries. Clinical symptoms are unspecific and include abdominal pain, back pain, and edema of the lower extremities. The condition may occur together with IgG4-related disease in other parts of the body.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis (IgG4-RPF) primarily affects middle-aged to elderly males, with a mean age often around 53-62 years. Patients commonly present with localized abdominal pain (61%) and hydronephrosis (96%), which can lead to renal impairment and, in some cases, end-stage renal disease. The condition typically involves the retroperitoneal area, frequently affecting the abdominal aorta, iliac arteries, and ureters, but can also manifest as an isolated perinephric mass or involve other organs like the pancreas and digestive system. IgG4-RPF poses significant diagnostic challenges due to its frequent mimicry of malignancy, often necessitating biopsy for definitive diagnosis and sometimes leading to surgical intervention. It can be associated with various conditions, including autoimmune coagulation factor XIII deficiency, systemic lupus erythematosus, type 2 diabetes mellitus, neurofibromatosis type 1, or occur as an immune-related adverse event from checkpoint inhibitor therapy. [PMC12288730, PMC12146927, PMC11709181, PMC12223607, PMC12365821]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: IgG4-related retroperitoneal fibrosis (IgG4-RPF) is an immune-mediated fibroinflammatory disorder, though its specific etiology is often unclear or idiopathic, accounting for over 75% of cases. While the pathological role of IgG4 antibodies remains largely unknown, they may be involved in autoimmune mechanisms, such as reducing coagulation Factor XIII function. Secondary causes include malignancies (e.g., breast, lung, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, thyroid, carcinoid), infections, medications, and radiotherapy. Other associated conditions include Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, neurofibromatosis type 1, and immune-related adverse events from treatments like immune checkpoint inhibitors or TNF inhibitors.
