In diabetic patients, IgG4-RPF may be linked to chronic inflammation from metabolic syndrome and atherosclerotic plaques. [PMC12288730, PMC12146927, PMC11709181, PMC12223607, PMC11495986]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by facial dysmorphism, hypertrichosis, mild to profound intellectual disability, intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and/or postnatal growth restriction, feeding difficulties, abnormalities of the hands and feet (ranging from severe reductional limb abnormalities, oligodactyly, to brachymetacarpia of the first metacarpus). Variable visceral malformations may be present.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Not applicable, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: In Europe, the prevalence at birth of Cornelia de Lange syndrome (CdLS) is estimated at 1/80,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Distinctive facial features include: well-defined arched eyebrows, synophrys, long eyelashes, short nose, concave nasal ridge, anteverted nares, micrognathia, long smooth philtrum, and downturned corners of the mouth with a thin upper lip. Feeding difficulties and failure to thrive are frequently complicated by gastroesophageal reflux. Global developmental delay, in particular speech delay evolves towards intellectual disability ranging from mild to profound. Various behavioral disorders have been reported (anxiety, autistic traits/autism, shyness, compulsive obsessional disorder, self-injurious behavior, psychiatric disorders). Hearing loss is possible as well as various cardiac, renal, skeletal, gastrointestinal, and genital malformations.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Causative pathogenic variants in six genes involved in structural or regulatory components of the cohesin complex have been identified. NIPBL variants (5p13.2) are the most common cause (70% of patients). Less frequently involved genes include: SMC1A (Xp11.22-p11.21) associated with an X-linked form of CdLS, SMC3 (10q25) missense variants associated with a non-classical phenotype, RAD21 (8q24.11) mainly non-classical phenotype, HDAC8 (Xq13.1) implicated in an X-linked CdLS with some distinctive features, and BRD4 (19p13.12) recently associated with non-classical or mild CdLS. Genotype-phenotype correlations can be made to a certain extent, severe forms are more frequently associated with NIPBL.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is often suspected on clinical presentation and a clinical diagnosis can be confirmed for the classical phenotype if full criteria are met. The diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing for up to 70% of patients presenting a classical phenotype. Gene panels should at least include the causal genes as wells as genes from differential diagnoses (e.g. ANKRD11). Somatic mosaicism occurs quite frequently in CdLS (15%) and saliva or buccal cell swabs should be considered as preferred sample for genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Hypertrichosis is common in other syndromes that affect chromatin/transcription regulation genes such as Coffin Siris Syndrome, Wiedemann Steiner Syndrome, Rubinstein Taybi syndrome, CHOPS syndrome, etc. Other differential diagnoses include mucopolysaccharidosis, fetal alcohol syndrome, and Smith Lemli Opitz syndrome among others. There are overlapping features between KBG syndrome and mild or atypical CdLS.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal ultrasound examination may show IUGR, organ malformations (diaphragmatic hernia, limb defects), increased nuchal thickness, and abnormal facial profile. Prenatal genetic testing can be proposed when the pathogenic variant has been previously identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Most cases are sporadic. Occasionally, familial transmission occurs, following an autosomal dominant pattern. Genetic counseling can be difficult in milder forms given some inter-individual variability. Germline mosaicism explains recurrence cases when the pathogenic variant is not detected in parents. X-linked forms (SMC1A, HDAC8) require specific genetic counseling.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no cure for the disorder but psychoeducational care is necessary. Failure to thrive and gastroesophageal reflux require specific care: tube feeding, gastrotomy and Nissen anti-reflux intervention. Screening for multi-visceral or sensorineural complications helps to improve quality of life.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy with appropriate care is typically unaltered but follow-up data is lacking. Life expectancy can be reduced in case of severe or untreated organ malformations. Quality of life is mostly altered by severe limb defects, behavioral disorders and psychiatric disorders. Hearing impairment can be difficult to diagnose and has been reported to improve with time in some adults.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Familial nasal acilia is a rare genetic otorhinolaryngologic disease characterized by respiratory morbidity due to lack of cilia on the respiratory tract epithelial cells. The disease manifests from birth with respiratory distress, neonatal pneumonia, dyspnea, lobar atelectasis and bronchiectasis. Recurrent infections of the upper and lower respiratory tract, chronic humid coughing, and chronic sinusitis, otitis and rhinitis are typical lifelong presenting conditions.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Familial nasal acilia is characterized by mucociliary dysfunction, which stems from the absence of cilia. This condition leads to respiratory morbidity in affected individuals. The disorder has been observed within families, suggesting a familial pattern of inheritance. [PMC1511659]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Familial nasal acilia is caused by the absence of cilia, leading to mucociliary dysfunction. This condition in respiratory morbidity, as observed in affected family members. The dysfunction can also stem from abnormalities in ciliary ultrastructure. [PMC1511659]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Mucociliary dysfunction can be caused by the absence of cilia or by abnormalities in their ultrastructure. A family in which some members were suffering from respiratory morbidity due to lack of cilia is described. [PMC1511659]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Mucociliary dysfunction can be caused by the absence of cilia or by abnormalities in their ultrastructure. A family in which some members were suffering from respiratory morbidity due to lack of cilia is described. [PMC1511659]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Mucociliary dysfunction can be caused by the absence of cilia or by abnormalities in their ultrastructure. A family in which some members were suffering from respiratory morbidity due to lack of cilia is described. [PMC1511659]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare ophthalmic disorder characterized by mostly unilateral failure of the regression of a fetal ocular vessel component, the tunica vasculosa lentis and/or the hyaloid system, resulting in an anterior (presenting with microphthalmia, leukocoria, cataract, glaucoma, elongated ciliary processes, shallow anterior chamber, and retrolental fibrovascular membranes, among others) or posterior disease subtype (with microphthalmia, leukocoria, presence of a retinal fold or detachment, hypo- or dysplastic optic nerve, and vitreous membranes and stalk), respectively. Most patients present with a combination of the two subtypes.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Non-syndromic congenital retinal non-attachment; PFVS; PHPV; Persistent fetal vasculature syndrome; Congenital retinal detachment; NCRNA disease

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Purpose: was initiated to investigate the causes of childhood blindness and visual impairment in the United States. We also sought a particular etiology--congenital lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV)--which has been considered exceedingly rare, in a fixed target population of children, the severely mentally retarded. We undertook a library-based study of the world literature to shed light on the causes of childhood blindness internationally and to put our data in context. We prospectively examined all consented children (159) at 2 institutions in the United States to determine their ocular status and the etiology of any visual loss present. One of the institutions is a school for the visually impaired (hereafter referred to as Location V), in which most of the students have normal mentation. The other is a home for severely mentally retarded, nonambulatory children (hereafter... [PMC1298279, PMC1298374]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV) is an ocular developmental disorder resulting from incomplete apoptosis of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, potentially caused by somatic mutations. It presents with diverse manifestations, ranging from a trivial remnant of hyaloid vessels to a dense fibrovascular mass causing lens opacity and retinal detachment, affecting either the anterior or posterior eye. Associated clinical findings can include microphthalmus, pronounced retinal folds, nystagmus, falciform retinal detachment, myelinated retinal nerve fibers, congenital dentiform cataract, extreme microcornea, uveal and lens colobomas, Peters' anomaly, maldevelopment of the iris and ciliary body, and goniodysgenesis. Untreated PHPV can lead to severe complications like glaucoma or phthisis. While unilateral PHPV is associated with progressive anisometropic amblyopia, purely anterior presentations may achieve useful vision with treatment. Bilateral PHPV is rare and typically carries a very poor visual prognosis, with no measurable stereopsis or binocularity. [PMC6552573, PMC6114698, PMC4289784, PMC3945809, PMC1723813]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV) is an ocular developmental disorder resulting from incomplete apoptosis of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature. It can be associated with mutations in the KIF11 gene, as seen in Microcephaly with or without chorioretinopathy, lymphedema, or mental retardation. Somatic mutations of a single gene during development are also implicated in causing the range of disease severity. Furthermore, PHPV may arise from migratory disorders of neural crest cells between 4 and 7 weeks of gestation or be an expression of abnormal closure of the embryonic fissure. [PMC11345952, PMC4289784, PMC3945809, PMC1723813, PMC1041847]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV) relies on clinical and imaging findings. Histopathological examination, specifically serial sectioning, has been utilized to diagnose PHPV in complex cases, often alongside other ocular anomalies. MR imaging of the orbits provides characteristic imaging features for both posterior and anterior variants of PHPV. Additionally, optical coherence tomography (OCT) examination is considered useful for predicting visual function in cases of persistent fetal vasculature. [PMC6114698, PMC1723813, PMC8338131]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV) is a cause of childhood blindness and visual loss. The differential diagnosis includes retinoblastoma, particularly when persistent fetal vasculature is present. PHPV is frequently associated with other ocular anomalies such as Peters' anomaly, uveal colobomas, congenital dentiform cataract, extreme microcornea, and Morning glory syndrome, often alongside lens colobomas. Microcephaly with or without chorioretinopathy, lymphedema, or mental retardation (MCLMR) may also present with PHPV. Other conditions causing childhood visual impairment, such as retinopathy of prematurity, optic atrophy, retinitis pigmentosa, optic nerve hypoplasia, and foveal hypoplasia, should also be considered. [PMC11345952, PMC6552584, PMC6114698, PMC5859587, PMC1723813]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV) can be associated with different genetic etiologies. It may present as an additional feature of Microcephaly with or without chorioretinopathy, lymphedema, or mental retardation (MCLMR), an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the KIF11 gene. Alternatively, PHPV can result from somatic mutations of a single gene during development, suggesting a non-heritable cause in some cases. Therefore, the genetic basis for PHPV can vary, influencing genetic counseling. [PMC11345952, PMC3945809]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV) primarily involves early surgical intervention to prevent complications and improve visual outcomes. Surgical procedures include lensectomy, pars plana vitrectomy to remove the fibrovascular stalk, cataract extraction, primary posterior capsulotomy with anterior vitrectomy, intraocular lens implantation, and combined trabeculectomy/trabeculotomy. The main goals are to save the eye from glaucoma or phthisis, achieve a black pupil for cosmetic reasons, and obtain useful vision, especially in cases with anterior involvement. Intensive optometric and orthoptic input is crucial for managing anisometropic amblyopia. While bilateral cases have a poor prognosis, successful outcomes, including 20/40 unaided vision, have been achieved with comprehensive, early, and long-term management. Useful vision (20/70 or better) is attained in a significant proportion of anterior PHPV cases. [PMC4289784, PMC8338131, PMC1298374, PMC1042833]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for useful vision in persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous (PHPV) is generally poor for the majority of patients. However, with treatment, a notable percentage can achieve 20/200 vision or better, particularly in cases of purely anterior involvement, where over 70% may attain this level. Intensive and early surgical intervention, combined with meticulous long-term management, can lead to excellent visual outcomes and prevent complications like glaucoma or phthisis, which are otherwise devastating. Bilateral PHPV carries a very poor visual prognosis. While useful vision can be achieved, stereopsis or binocularity is typically not restored. Physical and mental development are usually normal. [PMC4289784, PMC1298374, PMC1042833]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by short stature, sparse and depigmented scalp hair, typical facial characteristics (broad eyebrows, especially the medial portion, broad nasal ridge and tip, underdeveloped nasal alae, long philtrum, thin upper lip vermilion, and protruding ears), and limb anomalies (brachydactyly, short metacarpals and metatarsals, cone-shaped phalangeal epiphyses, dystrophic nails, and hip dysplasia).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact prevalence is unknown. Around 250 cases have been published in the world literature. The disease is infrequently described as mildly affected individuals may go unnoticed.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease has variable severity and clinical presentation, even between family members. It presents typically with prenatal and postnatal growth delay. The facial characteristics (broad eyebrows, broad nasal ridge and tip, underdeveloped nasal alae, long philtrum, thin upper lip vermilion, and protruding ears) may be noticeable early on but may also remain completely unnoticed, especially as some features such as thin and sparse scalp hair are also common in infants in the general population. As time passes, growth delay, accompanied by increasing hair loss and dental overcrowding, may make the facial features more apparent. The brachydactyly also becomes more visible. Fingers start to deviate due to epiphyseal abnormalities in childhood which continues till adulthood. Increased and/or decreased mobility in the finger joints can occur and may cause pain. Hips abnormalities and associated pain are very common; they may present sometimes in late childhood but almost invariably in adulthood. Radiology typically reveals joint dysplasia, reduced joint space and sclerotic bone. Distal limb mobility problems often develop at a later age. Hip problems can be so severe that hip replacement may be indicated in early adulthood. The term "trichorhinophalangeal syndrome type 3'' has previously been used to refer to a severe form of type 1 with pronounced facial characteristics, short stature and brachydactyly.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: TRP type 1 is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in TRPS1 (8q23.3). Infrequently, inversions and balanced translocation disrupting the function of TRPS1 have been reported. Pathogenic variants are considerably different in type and location, with no clear genotype-phenotype correlation. TRPS1 is a zinc finger transcriptional repressor involved in regulating growth and development of chondrocytes and perichondrium.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is typically suspected on clinical presentation and confirmed by genetic testing with sequencing technology.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other disorders in which ectodermal manifestations are accompanied by distal limb anomalies and/or an unusual shape of the nose such as oculodentodigital dysplasia, cartilage-hair hypoplasia, and Ellis-Van Creveld syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible if a pathogenic variant has been previously identified in a family member. Families should be aware that intra-familial variety in severity can be marked, and the severity of the phenotype cannot be predicted by prenatal testing.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is autosomal dominant with full penetrance. Whilst most cases occur sporadically, genetic counselling should be offered to affected individuals informing them that there is a 50% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy. Germline mosaicism has been detected in rare cases.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The management and treatment are mostly supportive. Ectodermal manifestations of hair, nails and teeth can be managed with esthetic care such as the use of wigs, artificial nails, and extraction of supernumerary teeth. In patients whose growth hormone stimulation tests results are subnornal or abnormal, growth hormone therapy can be considered and may (variably) result in increased growth in height. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy can be beneficial for problems of altered distal limb mobility. Regular simple analgesics (such as NSAID) may be used to treat joint pain. Prosthetic hip implantation should be considered in individuals with severe hip dysplasia, even in early adulthood. If osteopenia is present, bisphosphonates may be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy is normal. The unusual facial morphology and ectodermal manifestations, combined with the reduced mobility, can have a marked impact on the quality of life. Peer support and counseling by a social scientist can be beneficial.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia-cone-rod dystrophy syndrome is characterised by the association of spondylometaphyseal dysplasia (marked by platyspondyly, shortening of the tubular bones and progressive metaphyseal irregularity and cupping), with postnatal growth retardation and progressive visual impairment due to cone-rod dystrophy. So far, it has been described in eight individuals. Transmission appears to be autosomal recessive.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy is characterized as a rare autosomal-recessive disorder. Cases have been identified, including four individuals from two Brazilian families where specific homozygous mutations in PCYT1A were found. [PMC3882913]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy (SMD-CRD) is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder. It is characterized by severe short stature, progressive lower-limb bowing, flattened vertebral bodies, and metaphyseal involvement. Visual impairment is caused by cone-rod dystrophy. Mutations in the PCYT1A gene are responsible for this syndrome. [PMC5392360, PMC3882913]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy is an autosomal-recessive disorder caused by mutations in the PCYT1A gene. This gene encodes the alpha isoform of the phosphate cytidylyltransferase 1 choline enzyme, a key regulator of phosphatidylcholine metabolism. The enzyme is responsible for converting phosphocholine into cytidine diphosphate-choline, a crucial intermediate step in the phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis pathway. Deregulation of this pathway may play a role in the pathogenesis of this and other genetic diseases. [PMC5392360, PMC3882913, PMC3882727]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy is characterized by severe short stature, progressive lower-limb bowing, flattened vertebral bodies, metaphyseal involvement, and visual impairment caused by cone-rod dystrophy. Diagnosis involves identifying mutations in the PCYT1A gene, which are responsible for this disorder. Genetic testing, such as whole-exome sequencing or next-generation sequencing, is used to detect these sequence variants. A thorough clinical evaluation, potentially including whole skeleton X-ray, can aid in the assessment and differentiation of the phenotype. [PMC5392360, PMC3882913]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for spondylometaphyseal dysplasia-cone-rod dystrophy (SMD-CRD), caused by PCYT1A mutations, includes other phenotypes linked to the same gene. These encompass isolated retinal dystrophy without skeletal involvement, and a syndrome of congenital lipodystrophy, severe fatty liver disease, and reduced HDL cholesterol, also lacking retinal or skeletal features. Additionally, a muscular dystrophy with mitochondrial structural abnormalities, resulting from a different enzymatic defect in the phosphatidylcholine pathway, should be considered, as it presents without cartilage, bone, or retinal involvement. [PMC5392360, PMC3882913]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy (SMD-CRD) is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder caused by homozygous mutations in the PCYT1A gene. This gene encodes an enzyme involved in the phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis pathway. Mutations in PCYT1A are also responsible for isolated forms of retinal dystrophy without skeletal involvement, thus expanding the phenotypic spectrum associated with this gene. The deregulation of the phosphatidylcholine pathway may play a role in multiple genetic diseases. [PMC5392360, PMC3882913]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Spondylometaphyseal dysplasia with cone-rod dystrophy is a rare autosomal-recessive disorder characterized by severe short stature, progressive lower-limb bowing, flattened vertebral bodies, metaphyseal involvement, and visual impairment caused by cone-rod dystrophy. Whole-exome sequencing of four individuals affected by this disorder from two Brazilian families identified two previously unreported homozygous mutations in PCYT1A. This gene encodes the alpha isoform of the phosphate cytidylyltransferase 1 choline enzyme, which is responsible for converting phosphocholine into cytidine diphosphate-choline, a key intermediate step in the phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis pathway. A different enzymatic defect in this pathway has been previously associated with a muscular dystrophy with mitochondrial structural abnormalities that does not have cartilage and/or bone or retinal involvement.... [PMC3882913]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Bleeding disorder due to P2Y12 defect
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: P2Y12 defect is a rare hemorrhagic disorder characterized by mild to moderate bleeding diathesis with easy bruising, mucosal bleedings, and excessive post-operative hemorrhage due to defect of the platelet P2Y12 receptor resulting in selective impairment of platelet responses to adenosine diphosphate.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Bleeding disorder due to ADP platelet receptor P2Y12 defect

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date, 14 patients have been described in the world literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: P2Y12 defect is a congenital disorder that manifests by mildly to severely prolonged bleeding time, easy bruising, mucosal bleeding (epistaxis, gastric mucosa bleeding, gum bleeding, etc.), menorrhagia, and bleeding complications after trauma and minor or major surgery.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: P2Y12 defect is caused by mutations in the P2RY12 gene (3q24-q25) which result in the premature truncation of the P2Y12 receptor or in the synthesis of a dysfunctional P2Y12 receptor. ADP activates platelets through its interaction with two G protein-coupled receptors, P2Y1 and P2Y12. The P2Y1 receptor mediates mobilization of ionized calcium and is responsible for ADP-induced shape change andweak and transient aggregation, while the P2Y12 receptor is responsible for the completion and amplification of the response to ADP and to all platelet agonists including thromboxane A2, thrombin, and collagen. P2Y12 receptor thus plays a central role in the formation and stabilization of a thrombus.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission of P2Y12 deficiency is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (where both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them of the 25% risk of having an affected child.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of P2Y12 defect primarily involves assessing impaired platelet responses to adenosine diphosphate (ADP). Characteristic findings include markedly reduced, limited, or absent and rapidly reversible ADP-induced platelet aggregation, which can be detected by such as multiple electrode aggregometry (MEA) showing inadequate ADP response with normal for other agonists like TRAP and ASPI. Further functional tests may reveal impaired inhibition of VASP phosphorylation and PGE1-induced cAMP by ADP, reduced affinity for P2Y12R antagonists/agonists, decreased binding of [3H]2-methylthio-ADP, and lower ADP-induced fibrinogen binding via flow cytometry. Definitive diagnosis often includes genetic analysis of genomic DNA, using techniques such as Southern Blotting or real-time PCR, to identify specific P2Y12 gene mutations. [PMC10573189, PMC7327643, PMC4319231, PMC2663622, PMC295660]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The bleeding disorder due to P2Y12 defect is characterized by limited and rapidly reversible ADP-induced platelet aggregation, a specific receptor defect where ADP fails to lower cAMP levels, and significantly decreased binding of [3H]2-methylthio-ADP. This contrasts with type I Glanzmann's thrombasthenia, where platelets exhibit normal binding of [3H]2-methylthio-ADP and a normal response to ADP in the presence of PGE1. While some activation of GP IIb-IIIa complexes by ADP occurs in P2Y12 defect, the overall capacity of platelets to bind to each other in response to ADP is impaired, resulting in loosely bound aggregates. [PMC295660]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of bleeding disorder due to P2Y12 defect requires a systematic assessment. Intravenous desmopressin (DVVAP) has been administered to manage microvascular bleeding, such as that developed after weaning from cardiopulmonary bypass. DVVAP can be beneficial as a first-line therapy in bleeding patients to improve platelet function. [PMC10573189]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Bleeding disorder due to P2Y12 defect is associated with a lifelong history of abnormal bleeding, which can range from mild to severe. Patients typically experience easy bruising, excessive mucosal bleeding, and increased post-operative bleeding risk. The severity of platelet dysfunction and associated bleeding diathesis can vary, with some individuals presenting with mild symptoms, such as those with P2Y12 haploinsufficiency, while others, particularly with specific genetic defects or combined deficiencies, may experience severe bleeding. [PMC10573189, PMC7327643, PMC4319231, PMC2663622]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare chromosomal abnormality characterized by the presence of an extra chromosome 18 material and manifesting with severe intellectual disability growth delay, and extremely variable multiple congenital anomalies, including minor malformations (cranio-facial dysmorphia, short sternum, overlapping fingers) and major malformations, especially cardiac and cerebral. Neurological involvement may lead to seizures and hypotonia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Incidence is estimated at between 1/6,000 and 1/8,000 births. For unknown reasons, the survival rate is higher in females than in males (with a 3:1 female-to-male prevalence ratio) among live-born trisomy 18 (T18) infants.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The most consistent congenital malformations in individuals with T18 are cardiac defects (ventricular septal defects, atrial septal defects, patent ductus arteriosus, etc.) present in 90% of liveborn infants. Visceral anomalies are present in 60% of patients and encompass urinary tract anomalies (horseshoe kidney, hydronephrosis, agenesis) and gastrointestinal malformations (esophageal atresia, anorectal malformations). Externally, physical features associated with T18 syndrome include low body weight, microcephaly and dolichocephaly with a prominent occiput, micrognathia, low-set, malformed ears with pointed pinnae, clenched fists with overlapping fingers (2nd and 5th digit overriding 3rd and 4th), short sternum with shielded chest, and pes equinovarus and/or rocker-bottom feet. Midline defects, such as cleft lip/palate, omphalocele and myelomeningocele may be present. Radial aplasia and arthrogryposis may be present. T18 is also characterized by a range of brain anomalies, as cerebellar hypoplasia and agenesis of the corpus callosum, and occasionally holoprosencephaly. Trisomy 18 is lethal in utero (95%) or within the first year of life (< 90%) for most affected individuals. Most surviving individuals are non-ambulatory and exhibit severe intellectual disability with limited communication skills.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Free T18 is found in around 95% of cases. Mosaic T18 (in which there is both trisomic and normal cell types) has been reported less than 5% patients with a clinical picture that varies between a normal phenotype and that of classical T18 according to the percentage of trisomic cells present in the tissues. In rare cases, the syndrome is caused by reciprocal translocation between chromosome 18 and another chromosome, hence resulting in a partial T18 (only a part of chromosome 18 is duplicated).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: T18 must be confirmed by conventional karyotyping. Chromosomal microarray will also reveal T18.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The phenotypic appearance of T18 is extremely variable, from children with intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) and minor dysmorphic signs or malformation, to extremely malformed patients. Some may ressemble trisomy 13.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Analysis of fetal DNA in maternal blood (non-invasive prenatal testing; NIPT) has high sensitivity (> 97%). Maternal serum screening based on blood markers and nuchal translucency ultrasound scan may detect a high proportion of T18 fetuses. Many T18 fetuses can be detected by routine fetal ultrasound scan but the extreme phenotypic variability may be a distractor. Small cerebellum and typical position of the clenched hands are good indicators. Invasive prenatal testing like amniocentesis or chorionic villi sampling (CVS) will confirm any suspicion raised by prenatal screening.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The risk of recurrence of trisomy (21, 13 or 18) in families of an index case is around 1%. However, in families in which T18 is associated with a balanced translocation, the risk of recurrence is higher.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is supportive/palliative only. Follow-up is needed for cardiac, respiratory, neurological, genitourinary, abdominal, otolaryngologic, and orthopedic complications.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: In utero death occurs in more than 95% of fetuses. Surgical treatment of the malformations does little to improve the poor prognosis associated with T18: almost 90% of infants die within the first year of life from cardiac, renal or neurological complications, or from repeated infections. Survival rates for T18 are 13.5% at 1 year old and 12.3% at 5 years old. Prolonged survival (in some cases into adulthood) has been reported mainly in cases involving mosaic or partial trisomy (resulting from translocation). The majority of non-mosaic patients develop only limited autonomy (absence of speech and ambulation). The growth delay is significant.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A group of rare genetic peripheral neuropathies characterized by slowly progressive sensory-motor involvement leading to muscle weakness, atrophy and sensory loss, mainly affecting the distal limbs.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CMTX; X-linked hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, including subtypes like CMTX1 and CMTX3, typically presents in childhood or adolescence. CMTX3 is described as a childhood-onset subtype. For CMTX1, reported cases include individuals experiencing initial symptoms such as transient central nervous system symptoms at 7 and 13 years old, or presenting with progressive weakness and atrophies from the age of 17. Other cases describe onset of sudden transient weakness at 11 years old, with recurrence at 13, or transient and recurrent limb weakness at 15 years old. [PMC11415608, PMC10937141, PMC7196464, PMC5728979, PMC4131157]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: X-linked Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1 (CMTX1) represents 5.1-13.8% of all CMT (which have a total pooled prevalence of 1/5,555). CMTX2 was confirmed in 1 family, CMTX3 in 3 large related families in Oceania, CMTX4 and CMTX5 in case/families from the USA, Europe and Asia, and CMTX6 in 5 families from Australia, Brazil, Korea, and Germany.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: CMTX are six progressive sensory-motor neuropathies fully expressed in hemizygous males. In females, disease is usually milder or absent. CMTX1 has adolescence onset and slowly progressive distal muscle wasting and weakness (proximal muscle weakness in severe cases), distal sensory loss, hypo-areflexia, pes cavus and rarely scoliosis. Split hand is frequent. Transient brain dysfunction with white matter abnormalities are rarely described, with dysarthria, dysphagia, motor and/or sensory hemi-syndrome, ataxia, aphasia, or coma. Females show variable disease severity, from asymptomatic to moderate-severe. CMTX2 has early onset and is associated to intellectual disability in some patients. CMTX3 has early onset and rapid course. Males may become wheelchair-bound in the 2nd decade. Females are asymptomatic or rarely mildly affected. Hip dysplasia is reported in some cases. CMTX4 is associated to hearing loss and intellectual disability. Females are asymptomatic. CMTX5 onset occurs in the 1st decade and is associated to sensorineural deafness and optic atrophy. Cognitive impairment and susceptibility to infections are also reported. Occasionally, female carriers may have hearing loss, pes cavus and/or areflexia. CMTX6 onset occurs during the 2nd decade with sensory-motor neuropathy with proximal spreading and a pattern of predominant posterior thigh muscles involvement. Neuropathic pain and upper limbs tremor are possible features. Females may develop mild symptoms like pes cavus, slight hand muscle atrophy and tremor with juvenile or adult onset.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CMTX1 is caused by pathogenic variants (PVs) in GJB1 (Xq13.1). CMTX2 maps to Xp22.2, with no causative gene identified. CMTX3 is caused by a 78-kb insertion from Chr. 8q24.3 to Xq27.1. CMTX4 is caused by AIFM1 (Xq26.1) PVs, CMTX5 by PRPS1 (Xq22.3) PVs and CMTX6 by PDK3 (Xp22.11) PVs.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on family and personal history, clinical examination, nerve conduction studies, and DNA testing. In CMTX1 conduction velocity is usually preserved in females but decreased in males (30-45 m/s in upper limb nerves), often non-homogeneously, with temporal dispersion and sometimes conduction blocks. Nerve biopsy reveals prominent axonal changes. CMTX4-6 patients exhibit an axonal sensory-motor neuropathy. In CMTX3, demyelinating and intermediate patterns are reported. Auditory evoked potentials are often abnormal in CMTX1, CMTX4 and CMTX5.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes other CMT forms and, particularly for CMTX1, chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy. CMTX4-6 must be differentiated from other mitochondrial diseases.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal and preimplantation diagnoses are feasible if the family PV is known.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: CMTX1 and 6 are transmitted as X-linked dominant traits with variable expression in females (from asymptomatic to severe), making genetic counseling difficult. Other CMTX types behave as recessive traits with no or few symptoms in heterozygous females.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no drug treatment available. Rehabilitation therapy and surgical treatment of skeletal deformities are the only options. Hearing aids may be needed for CMTX4-5 patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: CMTXs are generally slowly progressive. CMTX1 male patients often need walking aids; late ambulation loss is rare. Some female patients develop a severe phenotype later in life. Walking aids may be needed in the 3rd-4th decade for CMTX4-5 and after age 50 years in CMTX6. CMTX3 male patients present a rapidly progressive course with possible wheelchair need in the 2nd decade.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, functioning, pituitary adenoma characterized by the presence of a pituitary mass associated with high levels of circulating, free, thyroid hormones in conjunction with normal to high levels of TSH and unresponsiveness of TSH levels to TRH stimulation and T3 suppression tests, typically manifesting with signs and symptoms of mild to moderate hyperthyroidism (e.g. goiter (most frequently observed), palpitation, excessive sweating, arrhythmia, weight loss, tremor) and/or tumor mass effect (such as headache, visual field defects, hypopituitarism). Occasionally, cosecretion of prolactin and/or growth hormone may cause galactorrhea and/or acromegaly.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Pituitary thyrotrophic adenoma; TSH-oma; Thyroid stimulating hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma; Thyrotroph adenoma

DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma (TSHoma) primarily focuses on distinguishing it from Resistance to Thyroid Hormone (RTH), as both present with inappropriate TSH secretion. Differentiating these conditions is critical, with family history, serum SHBG, and THRB gene testing aiding diagnosis. Ectopic TSH-secreting tumors, found outside the sella turcica in locations like the nasopharynx or sphenoid bone, are exceedingly rare but must be considered, particularly with normal pituitary imaging. Diagnosis is further complicated by the potential coexistence of TSHoma with other thyroid conditions, including papillary thyroid carcinoma, autoimmune hypothyroidism, or Graves' disease, which can obscure thyroid function test interpretation. Rarely, pituitary gangliocytoma can also cause inappropriate TSH secretion. [PMC12154014, PMC10955116, PMC10204311, PMC9393506, PMC8718172]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Summary: Thyrotropinomas are an uncommon cause of hyperthyroidism and are exceedingly rarely identified during pregnancy, with limited evidence to guide management. Most commonly they present as macroadenomas and may cause symptoms of mass effect including headache, visual field defects and hypopituitarism. a case of a 35-year-old woman investigated for headaches in whom a 13 mm thyrotropinoma was found. In the lead-up to planned trans-sphenoidal surgery (TSS), she spontaneously conceived and surgery was deferred, as was pharmacotherapy, at her request. The patient was closely monitored through her pregnancy by a multi-disciplinary team and delivered without complication. Pituitary surgery was performed 6 months post-partum. Isolated secondary hypothyroidism was diagnosed postoperatively and replacement thyroxine was commenced. Histopathology showed a double lesion with predominant... [PMC9513668]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Ectopic thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)-secreting tumors are extremely rare, with only 15 reported cases in the literature. Herein, we described a 60-year-old female patient with thyrotoxicosis and elevated or unsuppressed levels of TSH. Family history and laboratory and genetic tests did not support a diagnosis of resistance to thyroid hormone (RTH). Given the unsuppressed TSH, TSH-secreting tumor was suspected, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pituitary gland was performed. Surprisingly, the MRI scans revealed a nodule in the nasopharynx rather than a pituitary tumor in the sella region. Further evaluation using Gallium-68 DOTATATE positron emission tomography/computed tomography ( 68 Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT) demonstrated increased DOTATATE uptake in the nasopharyngeal nodule. Additionally, an octreotide suppression test (OST) revealed an obvious reduction in TSH levels,... [PMC10955116, PMC9393506, PMC8119795]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 is an uniparental disomy of maternal origin that most likely does not have any phenotypic expression except from cases of homozygosity for a recessive disease mutation for which only mother is a carrier.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: a 4-year-old girl with neurodevelopmental abnormalities who has maternal uniparental isodisomy of chromosome 2 leading to homozygosity for a likely pathogenic variant in SPR , and a variant of uncertain significance in ZNF142 . Biallelic pathogenic variants in SPR lead to sepiapterin reductase deficiency (SRD), a dopa-responsive dystonia. Pathogenic variants in ZNF142 are associated with an autosomal recessive neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by impaired speech and hyperkinetic movements, which has significant clinical overlap with SRD. Our patient showed dramatic improvement in motor skills after treatment with levodopa. We also reviewed 67 published reports of uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 (UPD2) associated with various clinical outcomes. These include autosomal recessive disorders associated with loci on chromosome 2, infants with UPD2 whose gestations were associated... [PMC10965300]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 (UPD2) can lead to a diverse range of clinical presentations, primarily when it in homozygosity for pathogenic variants in genes on chromosome 2. Reported features include neurodevelopmental abnormalities such as muscle weakness, neonatal hypotonia, impaired speech, and hyperkinetic movements, with some cases showing dramatic improvement with levodopa. Renal manifestations like hematuria, proteinuria, and kidney impairment (e.g., Alport syndrome, renal dysplasia) are common. Other observed phenotypes encompass skeletal dysplasia, vertebral and limb defects, cardiac defects, immune deficiencies, growth failure, retinal degeneration (including Oguchi disease), ovarian insufficiency, and lethal respiratory failure due to surfactant deficiency. However, maternal UPD2 can also be associated with intrauterine growth restriction followed by good postnatal catch-up growth, or even a normal phenotype, highlighting significant clinical variability. [PMC12126394, PMC10965300, PMC8227568, PMC7057094, PMC3996682]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 (UPD2) is the underlying etiology, which can arise through various mechanisms. This genetic event can lead to autosomal recessive disorders when it in homozygosity for pathogenic variants in genes located on chromosome 2, such as SPR (causing sepiapterin reductase deficiency) and ZNF142. UPD2 has also been associated with confined placental mosaicism for trisomy 2, which may result in intrauterine growth restriction. Notably, some individuals with maternal or paternal UPD2 exhibit normal phenotypes, supporting the that genes on chromosome 2 are not subject to imprinting. [PMC10965300]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 syndrome presents with a diverse clinical spectrum, primarily due to homozygosity for pathogenic variants on chromosome 2. Differential diagnoses encompass various autosomal recessive disorders, including Alport syndrome, congenital myasthenic syndromes (e.g., CMS22), Oguchi disease, sepiapterin reductase deficiency, and Catel-Manzke-Syndrome/VCRL Syndrome. Other associated conditions include a neurodevelopmental disorder with impaired speech and hyperkinetic movements, inherited surfactant deficiency, and complex phenotypes involving skeletal and renal dysplasia, immune deficiencies, growth failure, retinal degeneration, and ovarian insufficiency. Intrauterine growth restriction with good postnatal catchup growth is also noted, and some individuals may even exhibit a normal phenotype. [PMC12126394, PMC10965300, PMC8227568, PMC7057094, PMC3996682]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Non-invasive prenatal testing (NIPT) can indicate rare chromosomal abnormalities, including uniparental disomy. Although NIPT for rare chromosomal abnormalities has a low positive predictive value, it retains clinical significance for risk stratification and pregnancy management. Validation of NIPT-detected anomalies can be performed using karyotyping and/or chromosome microarray analysis, which can enhance the positive predictive value. [PMC12404953]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 (UPD2) can lead to autosomal recessive disorders by causing homozygosity for pathogenic variants, as observed in conditions like sepiapterin reductase deficiency. However, UPD2 can also be an incidental finding with a normal phenotype, supported by evidence that genes on chromosome 2 are not subject to imprinting. Genetic counseling for UPD2-mediated conditions requires comprehensive molecular analysis, including exome sequencing, trio analysis, segregation analysis, and SNP arrays, particularly when Mendelian inheritance is unclear or only one parent is a carrier. This diagnostic approach is crucial for accurate molecular diagnosis and to provide appropriate counseling regarding recurrence risks. Identifying UPD typically implies a very low recurrence risk for future pregnancies, which is a significant implication for families. Confirmation of parental carrier status is vital for precise risk assessment and to anticipate other potential phenotypes. [PMC10965300, PMC9938747, PMC8346044, PMC6687653, PMC7512120]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 syndrome targets the specific autosomal recessive disorders unmasked by the condition. For instance, Alport syndrome, characterized by kidney impairment, has been managed with angiotensin II receptor blockers like candesartan, which decreased urinary protein levels. Sepiapterin reductase deficiency, a dopa-responsive dystonia, showed dramatic improvement in motor skills following treatment with levodopa. In cases of inherited surfactant deficiency, lung transplantation has been performed for affected infants. [PMC12126394, PMC10965300, PMC2794197]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 2 (UPD2) is highly variable, ranging from normal phenotypes to severe, multi-systemic disorders. Prenatally, NIPT-detected UPDs are associated with elevated risks of fetal loss and small-for-gestational-age, although some infants with intrauterine growth restriction show good postnatal catch-up growth. Postnatally, outcomes depend on the specific homozygous recessive genes on chromosome 2. Severe manifestations can include lethal respiratory failure, or a complex phenotype with skeletal and renal dysplasia, immune deficiencies, growth failure, retinal degeneration, and ovarian insufficiency. However, conditions like sepiapterin reductase deficiency may show dramatic improvement with treatment, and Alport syndrome can present as a mild, manageable phenotype. Many individuals with maternal UPD2 are also found to have normal clinical outcomes. [PMC12126394, PMC12404953, PMC10965300, PMC8346044, PMC3996682]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Muscular pseudohypertrophy - hypothyroidism, also known as Kocher-Debre-Semelaigne syndrome is a rare disorder characterized by pseudohypertrophy of muscles due to longstanding hypothyroidism.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The syndrome usually presents between 18 months and 10 years but has been reported at earlier ages including during the neonatal period. Patients present with clinical features of hypothyroidism, including decreased activity and increased sleep, feeding difficulty and constipation, prolonged jaundice, myxedematous facies, large fontanels (especially posterior), macroglossia, a distended abdomen with umbilical hernia, and hypotonia, along with muscle pseudohypertrophy. Pseudohypertrophy involves the muscles of the extremities, limb girdle, trunk, hands and feet but is more prominent in the limbs, resulting in an athletic appearance.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of the muscle pseudohypertrophy is not known but it is thought to be a result of long standing hypothyroidism. Hypothyroidism, or thyroid hormone deficiency, may be congenital and may be permanent or transient.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the presence of clinical features and myopathic changes. In countries with newborn screening programs (with either a primary thyroxine (T4)-follow-up thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) or primary TSH test), infants with congenital hypothyroidism are diagnosed after detection by screening tests.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is based on thyroid supplements. With treatment, reversal of the pseudohypertrophy and clinical symptoms is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Muscular pseudohypertrophy-hypothyroidism syndrome, often referred to as Hoffmann's syndrome, should be considered in the differential diagnosis of myopathic complaints, especially when characterized by muscular weakness and pseudohypertrophy, elevated creatine kinase, and elevated thyroid stimulating hormone. Diagnostic routines, including electromyography and muscle MRI, are useful to differentiate it from other myopathies. A unique triad of hypothyroidism, hypertrophic myopathy, and congenital nystagmus has also been reported, which may require specific differentiation. [PMC10617199, PMC2426415]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The syndrome is associated with mutations in the POU1F1 gene, a pituitary-specific transcription factor. Pathogenic variants, such as c.143-83A>G, disrupt pre-mRNA splicing, leading to morphological and functional abnormalities in the pituitary gland, including hypoplasia and deficiency of thyroxine. Studies in homozygous mice demonstrate postnatal growth failure and pituitary hormone deficiencies, suggesting a recessive inheritance pattern in humans. Genetic counseling should address the implications of POU1F1 mutations and the potential for affected offspring in carriers. [PMC9795478]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for muscular pseudohypertrophy-hypothyroidism syndrome is generally favorable with adequate hormone replacement therapy. Treatment with Levothyroxine or thyroxine can lead to significant clinical and biochemical improvement. In pediatric cases of Kocher-Debré-Semelaigne syndrome, full recovery of myopathy and a significant reversal in the patient's general condition have been observed. For adults with Hoffmann's syndrome, muscle weakness and myalgia typically improve, though this may take several months. Pseudohypertrophy of muscles also regresses with thyroxine treatment. Emphasizing knowledge related to these syndromes can further improve diagnosis and prognosis. [PMC11049470, PMC10617199, PMC4091467, PMC1719134]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare intestinal polyposis syndrome characterized by the development of up to hundreds to thousands of adenomas in the large bowel. It is a multi-system disorder with important extracolonic manifestations.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Colorectal adenomatous polyposis; FAP; Familial polyposis coli

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The birth incidence is ~ 1:5000-30,000. It accounts for <1% of colorectal cancer (CRC) cases.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Familial Adenomatous Polyposis (FAP) patients usually present with symptoms related to the presence of multiple large bowel adenomas, or cancer, (e.g. bleeding, anemia, change in bowel habit). There is a broad phenotypic spectrum, leading to significant variability in clinical presentation and age of onset. It may present in childhood with extracolonic manifestations (ECMs) like osteomas, dental abnormalities, congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), before the large bowel polyposis becomes symptomatic. ECMs also include desmoid tumors, benign cutaneous lesions, adrenal masses and extracolonic cancers (duodenal, gastric, small intestine, and pancreatic cancers, hepatoblastoma, medulloblastoma, and cribriform-morular variant of papillary thyroid cancer). Large bowel adenomas typically start to arise in late childhood but it is uncommon for them to be symptomatic at this age. Gastric Adenocarcinoma and Proximal Polyposis of the Stomach (GAPPS) is caused by pathogenic point mutations in the promoter 1b region of APC. Unlike FAP, it lacks the characteristic large bowel polyposis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: FAP is caused by constitutional pathogenic variants (PV) in the APC gene (5q21-q22). Approximately 25% of cases are de novo, with a relevant proportion caused by postzygotic somatic mosaicism.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: A clinical diagnosis of an adenomatous polyposis syndrome can be made if an individual develops ≥100 large bowel adenomas. An APC PV confirms a genetic diagnosis. Due to overlapping phenotype between FAP and other syndromes, multigene panel testing is recommended. Somatic (post-zygotic) mosaicism is an important cause of unclassified adenomatous polyposis, and its detection may require increasing the sensitivity of the constitutional sequencing data analysis or testing other tissues, such as gastrointestinal tumors or colorectal mucosa.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include: recessive syndromes caused by biallelic PVs in MUTYH, NTHL1, MBD4 and MSH3; dominant syndromes caused by PVs in the exonuclease domain of POLE or POLD1, and AXIN2. Constitutional mismatch repair deficiency (CMMRD) caused by biallelic PVs in the DNA mismatch repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 or PMS2. Lynch syndrome may present with multiple colorectal adenoma, but rarely results in adenomatous polyposis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing (amniocentesis and chorionic villous sampling) are possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance is autosomal dominant (50% risk of transmission of the PV). Predictive genetic testing should be offered to at risk relatives. Asymptomatic children should be offered testing from age 12-14 years (earlier if symptomatic).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Cancer prevention and maintaining a good quality of life are the main goals of management. These patients are best managed in a specialist centre, wherever possible. They require personalized surveillance of the large bowel, and most will need some form of risk-reducing surgery, tailored to individual needs in both type and timing. Upper gastrointestinal tract surveillance should begin at age 25. Gastric and duodenal/ampullary adenomas are common; surveillance, endoscopic therapy and/or risk reducing surgery may be required to manage cancer risk. Desmoid tumors are an important cause of morbidity and mortality in FAP. Most can be managed expectantly and will stabilize without intervention. For progressive cases, surgery (including resection or intestinal transplantation) or systemic therapies may be required. Although there is interest in chemoprevention agents, none are currently recommended in routine clinical practice.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Without intervention, nearly all patients with FAP will develop colorectal cancer. Screening and appropriate intervention significantly reduce this risk and significantly increase life expectancy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Heavy-chain diseases (HCDs) are rare monoclonal lymphoplasma-cell proliferative disorders involving B cells and are characterized by the synthesis of truncated heavy chains without associated light chains.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: HCDs have been described for the three main immunoglobulin classes: alpha-HCD is the most common and has the most uniform presentation whereas gamma- and mu-HCDs have variable clinical presentations and histopathologic features. HCDs can be thought of as variant types of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL), with alpha-HCD presenting as an extranodal marginal-zone lymphoma of mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, gamma-HCD as lymphoplasmacytoid NHL, and mu-HCD as small lymphocytic NHL or chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of these conditions requires documentation of a deleted immunoglobulin heavy chain without a bound light chain in the serum or urine.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable, and no standardized effective treatment programs are available except for alpha-HCD, which in its early stage may respond to antibiotics.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inherited epidermolysis bullosa (EB) characterized by skin fragility and blistering at birth followed by development of photosensitivity and progressive poikilodermatous skin changes.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Kindler syndrome; Poikiloderma of Kindler; Congenital bullous poikiloderma

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Kindler epidermolysis bullosa (KEB) is the fourth major type of EB, after EB simplex, junctional EB and dystrophic EB. The exact prevalence is unknown. More than 250 cases have been reported to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease usually manifests at birth with trauma-induced skin blistering that is more prominent on extremities and tends to regress with age, becoming rare in adulthood. Healing of blisters occurs with minimal scarring. With age, additional skin findings are observed: (i) in most patients, photosensitivity with erythema and photo-induced blisters is obvious since early childhood and often diminishes after adolescence, (ii) progressive skin poikiloderma (atrophy, telangiectases, and reticular pigmentation) manifests from childhood and is predominantly localized to the face and neck, and (iii) skin atrophy is localized to hands and feet in the first years of life but becomes generalized by adolescence. Blisters also affect the mucosae. In the oral cavity, chronic gingivitis and periodontitis are frequent and prominent features in adulthood. Esophageal strictures, causing dysphagia and requiring repeated dilatations, frequently develop in adulthood. Anal (bleeding, stenosis), urogenital (urethral bleeding, meatal stenosis), and ocular (ectropion) involvement has also been described. The frequency of these manifestations increases with age. An additional frequent feature is digit webbing/partial pseudosyndactyly. Laryngeal and intestinal involvement, the latter manifesting with severe colitis, are rare. Other features may include: skin xerosis and fine scaling, palmoplantar hyperkeratosis, milia formation, nail dystrophy, constricting bands of pseudoainhum type, and orogenital leukokeratosis. Finally, KEB patients present an increased susceptibility to the development of squamous cell carcinomas (SCC).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Kindler epidermolysis bullosa is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the kindlin-1 gene (FERMT1; 20p12.3) causing the defective expression of the fermitin family homologue 1 (kindlin-1), a component of cell adhesive focal contacts.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical examination and determination by biopsy of the level within which blisters develop following minor traction. Immunofluorescence antigen mapping and transmission electron microscopy of blistered skin samples show single or multiple cleavage planes at the level of the cutaneous basement membrane zone as well as an extensive reduplication of the lamina densa. Blister formation can occur below the lamina densa, within the lamina lucida or within basal keratinocytes. The diagnosis is confirmed by molecular genetic testing, particularly during the first years of life.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes all forms of inherited EB, in particular dystrophic EB and EB simplex with mottled pigmentation, as well as congenital diseases with photosensitivity and poikiloderma, such as Rothmund-Thomson syndrome, Bloom syndrome, dyskeratosis congenita, poikiloderma with neutropenia or xeroderma pigmentosum.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis can be performed in families at risk of having a child with KEB where the disease-causing genetic variant has been previously identified in an affected family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them of the 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is based on the avoidance of blistering by protective padding of the skin. Skin moisturizers should be applied to reduce xerosis and skin fissures. Preventive measures should also be adopted for photosensitivity. Careful and early care of the oral mucosa is mandatory to preserve dentition. Esophageal strictures can be treated by balloon dilatation with fluoroscopic guidance. Early diagnosis of SCC (skin and mucosal membranes) requires a rigorous and regular follow-up from young adulthood onwards.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: In the majority of cases, life expectancy is normal. However, there are reports of patients with fatal aggressive SCC and, in a case series, skin cancer affected 70% of the patients older than 45 years.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hematological disorder characterized by spontaneous hemorrhage or prolonged bleeding due to factor VIII or IX deficiency.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence in the general population is estimated at 1/12,000. Prevalence at birth is estimated at 1/5,000 in males.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Hemophilia primarily affects males, but female carriers of disease-causing mutations may also manifest generally milder forms of the disease. In general, onset of bleeding anomalies occurs when affected infants start to learn to walk. However, newborns with hemophilia are at risk of intra- or extracranial hemorrhage and other bleeding complications. The severity of clinical manifestations depends on the extent of the coagulation factor deficiency. If the biological activity of the coagulation factor is below 1 IU/dL, hemophilia is severe and manifests as frequent spontaneous hemorrhage and abnormal bleeding as a result of minor injuries or following trauma, surgery or tooth extraction (severe hemophilia A and B). If the biological activity of the coagulation factor is between 1 and 5 IU/dL, hemophilia is moderately severe with abnormal bleeding as a result of minor injuries or following trauma, surgery or tooth extraction but spontaneous hemorrhage is rare (moderately severe hemophilia A and B). If the biological activity of the coagulation factor is between 5 and 40 IU/dL, hemophilia is mild with abnormal bleeding as a result of minor injuries or following trauma, surgery or tooth extraction but spontaneous hemorrhage does not occur (mild hemophilia A and B). In patients with severe hemophilia, bleeding most often occurs in joints (hemarthroses) and muscles (hematomas), but any site may be involved following trauma or injury. Spontaneous hematuria is a frequent and highly characteristic sign of the disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disorder is caused by mutations in the F8 gene (Xq28) encoding coagulation factor VIII, or in the F9 gene (Xq27) encoding coagulation factor IX, which are implicated in hemophilia types A and B, respectively.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is made on the basis of coagulation tests revealing prolonged coagulation times (activated partial thromboplastin time, aPTT). Type and severity of hemophilia are determined through specific measurements of factor VIII and IX activity and antigen levels.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes von Willebrand disease, combined factor VIII and factor V deficiency and other coagulation anomalies leading to prolonged coagulation times.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis performed on chorionic villi or amniocytes is rapid and informative when the familial, causative mutation is known. Knowing the familial mutation status in the fetus allows for preparation of delivery and early newborn medical management.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance is X-linked recessive and genetic counseling is recommended for affected families. For female carriers, there is a 50% risk that male offspring will be affected and a 50% risk that female offspring will be carriers. Overall, there is a 25% risk for each pregnancy that the baby will be a male offspring with hemophilia and a 25% risk that the baby will be a heterozygous female offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is provided by multidisciplinary comprehensive hemophilia care centers. Replacement therapy consisting of administration of the missing factor VIII (hemophilia A) or factor IX (hemophilia B) is the most straightforward treatment approach. Plasma-derived and recombinant factor VIII and factor IX concentrates are available. Non-factor therapies also exist for hemophilia A and new therapeutical approaches including gene therapy are under development. Treatment may be administered after a hemorrhage or prophylactically, to prevent bleeding. The most frequent complication is the production of inhibitory antibodies against the administered coagulation factor. Surgical interventions, most notably orthopedic surgery, may be carried out but should be conducted in specialized centers.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Left untreated, the disease course is severe and, in severe hemophilia, is generally fatal. Insufficient or incorrect treatment of recurrent hemarthroses and hematomas leads to physical impairment with severe disability associated with stiffness, joint deformation and physical disability. However, current treatment approaches (early prophylaxis) prevent these complications and the prognosis is favorable. Hemorrhage, HIV and HCV infections, and hepatic disease are the leading causes of death.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare syndromic craniosynostosis characterized by craniosynostosis with midface hypoplasia, radiohumeral synostosis, femoral bowing and joint contractures.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Antley-Bixler syndrome (ABS) has been described in more than 100 patients. The relative prevalence of the two main etiologies is unknown but cases due to FGFR2 variants seem rarer than those due to POR variants.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Children present with characteristic facial features, including a large domed forehead, flat nose, and midface hypoplasia with proptosis and dysplastic ears. The types of craniosynostosis may include trigonocephaly (due to early metopic synostosis) or brachycephhaly but also severe pansynostosis with cloverleaf skull. Characteristic skeletal features include the radio-humeral synostosis, femora bowing (with possible fractures). Arachnodactyly and/or camptodactyly, choanal atresia and cleft palate have also been reported. A diverse range of malformations (cardiac, renal, anal or vertebral) are often associated. Urogenital anomalies with sexual ambiguity due to impaired steroidogenesis can occur. Intellectual development is variable.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Two genetically distinct forms are observed: type 1 Antley-Bixler syndrome is associated with heterozygous mutations in the FGFR2 gene (10q26) without impairment of steroidogenesis, whereas type 2 Antley-Bixler is associated with homozygous mutations in the POR gene (7q11.2), encoding cytochrome P450 oxidoreductase (POR), which plays a direct role in steroidogenesis. Type 2 Antley-Bixler can thus be accompanied by sexual ambiguity, but this is not a compulsory finding.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is usually suspected by imaging features and confirmed by molecular screening: next generation sequencing panels, whole exome sequencing and whole genome sequencing.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: A similar clinical picture is observed due to in utero environmental exposure to 1) fluconazole, a lanosterol 14 alpha-demethylase inhibitor and 2) methotrexate. A similar phenotype has been reported associated with biallelic CYP26B1 variants.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: ABS may be evoked in case of syndromic craniosynostosis including radio-humeral synostosis, femora bowing, choanal atresia and other visceral malformations.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Inheritance depends on the gene involved. ABS due to FGFR2 is autosomal dominant, and most cases are de novo. Affected families should be informed that it is associated with a low recurrence risk (the residual risk is due to germinal mosaicism risk, estimated to approximately 1%). ABS due to POR variants is an autosomal recessive disorder. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them of the 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic, and includes early neurosurgical as well as pulmonary and orthopedic management. This disorder is associated with a high risk of pediatric complications.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is poor with the majority of reported patients dying during infancy due to respiratory and medullary complications.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia is the most common form of autoimmune hemolytic anemia defined by the presence of warm autoantibodies against red blood cells (autoantibodies that are active at temperatures between 37-40°C).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Warm auto-antibodies are responsible for 60/70% of AIHA, whose annual incidence is estimated to be between 1/35,000-1/80,000 in North America and Western Europe.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Warm AIHA is more common in women (female to male ratio approximately 2:1 in adults). The disease is characterized by symptoms due to the anemia including fatigue, exertional dyspnea, and, more rarely, jaundice and dark urine in case of severe hemolysis. If the disease is severe, fever, chest pain, syncope or heart failure may occur. Hemolysis occurs mainly in the spleen, so mild splenomegaly is relatively common.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Approximately half of cases of warm AIHA are primary (idiopathic) while the other half are secondary to an underlying condition, frequently chronic lymphocytic leukemia or an autoimmune systemic disease such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical and laboratory evidence of hemolytic anemia and the detection of autoantibodies with the direct anti-globulin test (DAT). Typically in warm AIHA, the DAT pattern is IgG alone or IgG with complement C3.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis of warm AIHA includes a post-transfusional alloimmune hemolytic anemia and, when the DAT is negative (less than 5% of all warm AIHAs), every other cause of either hereditary or acquired hemolytic anemia.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The most common therapy and the cornerstone of treatment for warm AIHA are corticosteroids. If these are ineffective, splenectomy can be considered. Rituximab has become an option in refractory disease and the use of immunosuppressors can be helpful in chronic severe refractory cases.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Warm AIHA is often severe but death is usually a rare outcome, except in elderly patients who have a higher risk of cardiovascular manifestations (in cases with severe anemia) and also of severe treatment-induced infections. Prognosis depends on the underlying condition.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare familial cardiomyopathy characterized by the dilation of left ventricle and progressively impairing of systolic ventricular function, in the absence of abnormal loading conditions or coronary artery disease sufficient to cause global systolic impairment. The disease may cause heart failure or arrhythmia. The disease is isolated when no additional atypical cardiac or extracardiac manifestations are present.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Mitochondrial inheritance, X-linked recessive

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence and incidence of Familial isolated dilated cardiomyopathy (FDC) is unknown; however, the incidence of dilated cardiomyopathy (DCM) is estimated between 1/12,000-28,000 worldwide; the prevalence of dilated cardiomyopathy is estimated at 1/2500; FDC is reported to make up about 20-30% of DCM case (range 2-65%).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The disease is defined by the presence of two major clinical criteria: left ventricular (LV) fractional shortening less than 25% and/or LV ejection fraction less than 45% with LV end diastolic diameter greater than 117% of the predicted value (corrected for age and body surface area based on Henry's formula), in the absence of abnormal loading conditions or coronary artery disease sufficient to cause global systolic impairment. The disease can develop at any age, in either sex. LV mass is often greatly increased in this disorder but LV wall thickness is normal. Symptoms of heart failure may be present as well as arrhythmias. Other presentations include the incidental detection of asymptomatic cardiomegaly and symptoms related to coexisting conduction disturbance or thromboembolic complications. Typically, there is a history of DCM in the family.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Around 30-40% of FDC has an identified genetic origin attributed to over 50 genes, a number that is constantly increasing as new genes are discovered. Most mutations include titin (TTN; 15-27%), lamins A/C (LMNA; 6%), Beta-myosin heavy chain (MYH7; 4.20%), myopalladin (MYPN; 3.50%) and cardiac troponin T (TNNC1, TNNI3 and TNNT2; 2.90%).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Clinical screening of relatives, in particular first degree relatives, of primary DCM cases using electrocardiogram (ECG) and echocardiography allow the identification of familial FDC. Two or more affected relatives with dilated cardiomyopathy meet the above major criteria for the disease. Cardiac catheterization and CT or MRI scan are used also. Genetic screening of the family is also possible.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis include the various non-genetic causes of dilated cardiomayopathy, such as cardiac AL amyloidosis or senile amyloidosis, peripartum cardiomyopathy, sarcoidosis, myocarditis, autoimmune cardiomyopathy.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Fetal echocardiography, B and M-mode, is the main diagnostic tool to determine the neonatal outcome. A hemodynamic evaluation can be performed by Doppler mode. Antenatal diagnosis is very rare due to the manifestation of the pathology later on during adult life. Fetal echocardiography is therefore not widely recommended unless there is a family history of neonatal case. Prenatal genetic testing may be considered on a case-by-case basis in the context of a pathogenic variant identified in the family.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Familial dilated cardiomyopathy is primarily an autosomal dominant disease, but autosomal recessive, X-linked and mitochondrial forms have also been described. Genetic counseling is therefore possible. The transmission outcome is 50% in an autosomal dominant case and 25% for a recessive transmission.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The pathology is treated with a combination of medications, depending on the symptoms. Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors, angiotensin II receptor blockers, beta-blockers, diuretics, digoxin, blood-thinning medications are used. The management of alimentation is important in affected families, and exercise and healthy habits are essential.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis of dilated cardiomyopathy is very poor in the absence of therapeutic management but mortality is largely reduced by medical and non-medical treatments. The prognosis may be influenced by the associated mutations.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A teratogenic embryofetopathy that results from maternal exposition to methimazole (MMI; or the parent compound carbimazole) in the first trimester of pregnancy. MMI is an antithyroid thionamide drug used for the treatment of Graves' disease. In the infant, MMI may result in choanal atresia, esophageal atresia, omphalocele, omphalomesenteric duct anomalies, congenital heart disease (such as ventricular septal defect), renal system malformations and aplasia cutis. Additional features that may be observed include facial dysmorphism (short upslanting palpebral fissures, a broad nasal bridge with a small nose and a broad forehead) and athelia/hypothelia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Methimazole/carbimazole embryofetopathy; Methimazole/carbimazole embryopathy; MMI/CMZ embryopathy; MMI/CMZ embryofetopathy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: BACKGROUND Methimazole embryopathy is caused by maternal methimazole intake during early pregnancy. It causes fetal malformations such as choanal atresia, esophageal atresia, aplasia cutis, omphalomesenteric duct remnants, urachal remnants, and omphalocele. Gallbladder agenesis is sometimes complicated with other malformations, but there have been no reports of gallbladder agenesis due to methimazole or concomitant methimazole embryopathy with gallbladder agenesis. CASE REPORT The mother of a male neonate had taken methimazole for hyperthyroidism until pregnancy was recognized at 7 weeks of gestation. Ultrasonography at 12 weeks and 4 days of gestation showed the fetus had a cystic lesion in the umbilical region. The child was born at the gestational age of 38 weeks and 5 days. At birth there was omphalocele, omphalomesenteric fistula, and a scalp defect, and the child was diagnosed... [PMC7491944]
