DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Methimazole embryopathy is characterized by fetal malformations caused by maternal methimazole intake during early pregnancy. These malformations include choanal atresia, esophageal atresia, aplasia cutis, omphalomesenteric duct remnants, urachal remnants, and omphalocele. A specific case presented with omphalocele, omphalomesenteric fistula, a scalp defect, and gallbladder agenesis, which was associated with dilatation of the biliary duct. Postnatal hypothyroidism requiring levothyroxine administration was also observed. Long-term follow-up for gallbladder agenesis is recommended due to potential complications like choledocholithiasis or biliary malignant tumors. [PMC7491944]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Methimazole embryopathy is caused by maternal methimazole intake during early pregnancy. This exposure can lead to various fetal malformations, including choanal atresia, esophageal atresia, aplasia cutis, omphalomesenteric duct remnants, urachal remnants, and omphalocele. A specific case involved maternal methimazole intake until 7 weeks of gestation, resulting in a neonate with omphalocele, omphalomesenteric fistula, a scalp defect, and gallbladder agenesis. [PMC7491944]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of methimazole embryofetopathy is based on a maternal history of methimazole intake during early pregnancy. Characteristic fetal malformations, including choanal atresia, esophageal atresia, aplasia cutis, omphalomesenteric duct remnants, urachal remnants, and omphalocele, are key indicators. These malformations can be detected prenatally via ultrasonography, such as a cystic lesion in the umbilical region. Postnatally, physical examination confirms defects like omphalocele and scalp defects. Further imaging with ultrasonography or MRI can identify specific anomalies such as gallbladder agenesis or biliary duct dilatation. Blood testing may also reveal associated conditions like hypothyroidism. [PMC7491944]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of methimazole embryofetopathy can involve ultrasonography. In one reported case, fetal ultrasonography performed at 12 weeks and 4 days of gestation identified a cystic lesion in the umbilical region. This finding was observed in a neonate subsequently diagnosed with methimazole embryopathy, which included omphalocele and omphalomesenteric fistula at birth. [PMC7491944]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management focuses on addressing specific malformations and complications. Emergency surgery may be required for conditions such as omphalocele with omphalomesenteric fistula. Hypothyroidism, if present, is treated with levothyroxine. Long-term outpatient follow-up is recommended for certain malformations, such as gallbladder agenesis with a dilated common bile duct, due to the potential for future complications like choledocholithiasis or biliary malignant tumors. [PMC7491944]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for methimazole embryopathy can vary depending on the specific malformations. In one reported case, a neonate with omphalocele, omphalomesenteric fistula, scalp defect, and gallbladder agenesis underwent surgery. Hypothyroidism was well controlled with levothyroxine, and the patient was asymptomatic at six months post-discharge. However, gallbladder agenesis, especially with a dilated common bile duct, demands long-term follow-up due to the potential for choledocholithiasis or biliary malignant tumors, even if asymptomatic in the neonatal period. [PMC7491944]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by neonatal hypotonia, global developmental delay, normal to accelerated growth, absent to severely delayed speech, and minor dysmorphic features.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Due to the non-specific clinical phenotype and often insufficient laboratory testing, the syndrome is underdiagnosed, and its true incidence remains unknown. Phelan-McDermid syndrome occurs with equal frequency in males and females and has been reported in mosaic and non-mosaic forms.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The severity of the developmental delay tends to vary with deletion size, with most individual functioning in the severe to profound range. Behavior is autistic-like with decreased perception of pain and habitual chewing or mouthing. Major milestones are delayed, receptive language skills typically exceed expressive skills, and many individuals are nonverbal. Other neurological features include seizures, ataxic gait, sleep disturbance, abnormal brain imaging, and regression or loss of skills. Common physical traits include long eye lashes, large or unusual ears, relatively large hands, dysplastic toenails, full brow, dolicocephaly, full cheeks, bulbous nose, and pointed chin. Between 10 to 25% of individuals have gastrointestinal reflux, cardiac abnormalities, renal anomalies, lymphedema, or visual defects.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The majority of cases result from the loss of 22q13.3 due to a simple deletion, translocation, ring chromosome or other structural chromosome changes involving the SHANK3 gene (PMS-SHANK3 related). About 15% of people have a heterozygous pathogenic variant in the SHANK3 gene. Less frequently, an individual may have an interstitial deletion of 22q13 that does not involve the SHANK3 gene (PMS-SHANK3 unrelated).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of monosomy 22q13.3 syndrome should be considered in all cases of hypotonia of unknown etiology and in individuals with absent speech. Chromosomal microarray is recommended as the first tier of testing. Detection of pathogenic variants of SHANK3 requires gene testing (genome sequencing, exome sequencing).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes syndromes associated with hypotonia, developmental delay, speech delay and/or autistic-like behavior (Prader-Willi, Angelman, Williams, Smith-Magenis, fragile X, Sotos, FG, and velocardiofacial syndromes, autism spectrum disorders and cerebral palsy).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible where a parental chromosome rearrangement or pathogenic variant has previously been identified. Because of the difficulty in detecting parental mosaicism, antenatal diagnosis may also be offered to parents of children with apparently de novo deletions or pathogenic variants.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal dominant; while most cases occur sporadically, genetic counseling should be offered to affected individuals informing them that there is a 50% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy. The risk of affected offspring is also increased for parents who carry balanced structural abnormalities of chromosome 22. The risk estimate to a translocation carrier depends on the type of chromosome abnormality, the size of the chromosome segments involved, the mode of ascertainment, the sex of the transmitting parent, and other factors. Most risk estimates will fall below 30%.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Individuals with monosomy 22q13.3 should have routine examinations by the primary care physician, as well as genetic evaluations with referral to specialists if neurological, gastrointestinal, renal, or other systemic problems are suspected. Affected individuals benefit from early intervention programs, intense occupational and communication therapies, adaptive exercise and sport programs, and other therapies to strengthen their muscles and increase their communication skills. Because ring chromosome 22 is associated with a specific risk of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), individuals ring 22 must undergo increased surveillance for symptoms of NF2.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: No apparent life-threatening organic abnormalities accompany the diagnosis of monosomy 22q13.3.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 16 syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 16 is a uniparental disomy of maternal origin which might be associated with intrauterine growth retardation and an elevated risk of congenital malformations. Healthy carriers have also been reported. In addition, cases of homozygosity for a recessive disease mutation for which the mother was a carrier have been described, and specific phenotype depends on the inherited disorder.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR) with or without additional abnormalities is recognised as a common feature of maternal uniparental disomy for chromosome 16 (mUPD 16) and is usually associated with confined placental mosaicism (CPM). Although it is likely that the CPM largely contributes to the IUGR, postnatal growth retardation and other common abnormalities may also be attributed to the mUPD. Five cases with mUPD 16 and CPM were analysed for common regions of isodisomy using polymorphic markers distributed along the length of the chromosome. In each case the aberration was consistent with a maternal meiosis I error. Complete isodisomy was not detected in any of the patients although two patients were found to be mixed with both iso- and heterodisomy. Interestingly, the patient with the greater region of isodisomy was the most severely affected. The fact that there were no common... [PMC1734327]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 16 (mUPD16) is commonly associated with intrauterine and postnatal growth retardation, sometimes with additional abnormalities. Specific features can include prenatal growth restriction, macrocephaly at birth, forehead protrusion, and clinodactyly of the fifth finger, showing phenotypic overlap with Silver-Russell syndrome. Other manifestations may involve hemimegalencephaly, characterized by enlargement of one cerebral hemisphere. Some cases present with a constellation of retinal, renal, and skeletal findings, consistent with ciliopathies like Mainzer-Saldino syndrome. Lethal respiratory failure due to surfactant deficiency has also been reported in newborns. The severity of the condition may correlate with the extent of isodisomy. [PMC8142457, PMC5593155, PMC5517791, PMC2794197, PMC1734327]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Maternal uniparental disomy (mUPD) of chromosome 16 occurs when both chromosomes of a homologous pair are inherited from the mother. This typically arises from chromosomal rescue events, such as trisomy rescue (which can be incomplete) or monosomy rescue. Maternal meiosis I errors are consistently implicated in the generation of mUPD 16, leading to maternal heterodisomy, often with segmental isodisomy. The resulting disomy can be complete, segmental, or a mixture of iso- and heterodisomy. This mechanism can unmask deleterious biallelic mutations or involve imprinted genes. [PMC11907602, PMC5517791, PMC1734327]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 16 (UPD(16)mat) and related conditions involves a range of molecular and genetic . Noninvasive prenatal screening (NIPS) may indicate a need for further investigation. Definitive diagnosis often utilizes trio whole exome sequencing (trio-WES), genome-wide genotyping arrays, oligo-SNP microarrays, and sequencing of protein-coding regions. Microsatellite analysis and polymorphic markers are employed to identify regions of isodisomy or heterodisomy. Methylation analyses are crucial for detecting epigenetic alterations, such as hypomethylation of specific imprinted domains. ddPCR analysis can verify mosaicism, while Sanger sequencing and gene resequencing confirm specific mutations. These can be applied to DNA from various tissues, including leukocytes, buccal swabs, and brain tissue. [PMC11907602, PMC8142457, PMC5593155, PMC5517791, PMC2794197]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses for maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 16 (UPD(16)mat) include conditions with overlapping phenotypes or related genetic mechanisms. Silver-Russell syndrome (SRS) and isolated imprinting defects of the ZNF597 gene, located on 16p13.3, can present with features similar to UPD(16)mat, as overexpression of ZNF597 may contribute to some associated phenotypes. Additionally, ciliopathies like Mainzer-Saldino syndrome (MZSDS) should be considered, particularly when partial uniparental isodisomy of chromosome 16 unmasks deleterious biallelic mutations in genes such as IFT140, leading to shared retinal, renal, and skeletal findings. Trisomy 16 mosaicism can also be relevant, as it may co-occur with maternal segmental UPD 16 due to incomplete trisomy rescue, explaining discrepancies in prenatal screening. [PMC11907602, PMC8142457, PMC5517791]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis can involve noninvasive prenatal screening (NIPS), which may yield a positive result. However, discordance can occur between a positive NIPS and a negative prenatal diagnosis. In such instances, further investigation using techniques like trio whole exome sequencing (trio-WES) and ddPCR can identify maternal segmental uniparental disomy (UPD) on chromosome 16, often characterized by isodisomic and heterodisomic genomic segments. This can be combined with low-level trisomy 16 mosaicism, which together explain the mismatch between screening and diagnostic findings. [PMC11907602]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 16 (mUPD 16) from inheriting both copies of chromosome 16 from the mother, often through mechanisms like incomplete trisomy rescue, which can explain discordance between noninvasive prenatal screening and prenatal diagnosis. This condition is associated with intrauterine growth retardation and other abnormalities, potentially due to confined placental mosaicism and the involvement of imprinted genes. mUPD 16 can unmask deleterious biallelic mutations (e.g., in IFT140 or TBC1D24) if the mother is a heterozygous carrier, leading to specific recessive disorders. The presence of segmental isodisomy, often resulting from a maternal meiosis I error, facilitates the expression of such mutations. Phenotypes may also overlap with conditions like Silver-Russell syndrome, possibly due to overexpression of imprinted genes like ZNF597 or isolated imprinting defects. Therefore, comprehensive genetic evaluation is crucial for diagnosis and counseling. [PMC11907602, PMC8142457, PMC5517791, PMC1734327]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: evaluate the etiology and pregnancy outcomes of fetuses underwent invasive prenatal diagnosis for fetal growth restriction (FGR) accompanied by structural malformations. Data from 130 pregnancies referred for prenatal diagnosis for FGR accompanied by structural malformations were obtained between July 2011 and July 2023. Traditional karyotyping was conducted for all the subjects. A total of 37 (28.5%) cases of chromosomal abnormalities were detected by karyotyping, including 30 cases of numerical anomalies and seven cases of unbalanced structural anomalies. Trisomy 18 was the most common abnormalities, accounting for 51.4%, significantly higher than any other chromosomal abnormality. The cohort was predominantly comprised of early-onset FGR (88.5%) compared to late-onset FGR (11.5%). The incidences of chromosomal abnormalities in this two groups were 29.6% (34/115) and 20.0% (3/15),... [PMC11035600, PMC7899829, PMC2794197]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Maternal uniparental disomy for chromosome 16 (mUPD 16) is commonly associated with intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR), which may occur with or without additional abnormalities. Postnatal growth retardation and other common abnormalities can also be attributed to mUPD. The severity of the condition appears to correlate with the extent of isodisomy, with patients having a greater region of isodisomy being more severely affected. [PMC1734327]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic isolated chorioretinal dystrophy characterized by distinctive slowly progressing chorioretinal atrophic lesions inducing significant visual impairment. There are three clinical stages. Atrophic macular lesion and nasal subretinal deposits are evident soon after birth (stage 1), the macular lesions progress beyond the retinal vascular arcades, and the foci of nasal atrophy coalesce into a confluent white lesion (stage 2), and marked expansion of both the macular and the nasal atrophic lesions toward the optic disc is observed (stage 3). Patients may also present with photophobia, nystagmus and myopia.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Progressive bifocal chorioretinal atrophy, characterized by patchy chorioretinal atrophy (PCA), can manifest with symptoms like metamorphopsia and blurred vision, leading to decreased best-corrected visual acuity over time. Fundus examination may reveal a white, well-defined patchy lesion with hypofluorescence. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) shows features such as a posteriorly curved sclera, thickened choroid, and disrupted ellipsoid zone, with eventual disappearance of the RPE-Bruch's membrane complex. The condition can progress to macular intrachoroidal cavitation (ICC), where a hyporeflective space forms beneath the retinal pigment epithelium, and the sensory retina becomes thinner and displaced posteriorly. The white patchy lesion and hypofluorescence region gradually expand, indicating progressive atrophy of the outer retina and RPE. [PMC8677981]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Progressive bifocal chorioretinal atrophy is associated with pathologic myopia. It is characterized by patchy chorioretinal atrophy (PCA) which can progress over time to macular intrachoroidal cavitation (ICC). This progression involves the atrophy of the outer retina and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), leading to the disappearance of the RPE-Bruch's membrane complex and disruption of the ellipsoid zone. The condition can lead to expansion of lesions and decreased visual acuity. [PMC8677981]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic involve fundus examination, which reveals a white, well-defined patchy chorioretinal atrophy (PCA) that shows hypofluorescence on autofluorescence. Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) is crucial, initially demonstrating a posteriorly curved sclera, thickened choroid, and disrupted ellipsoid zone. OCT also identifies the disappearance of the RPE-Bruch's membrane complex and connections of blood vessels from the sclera to the choroid. Over time, OCT can track the progression of PCA to macular intrachoroidal cavitation (ICC), showing expansion of the disorganized ellipsoid zone, thinning of the sensory retina, and persistent absence of the RPE-Bruch's membrane complex. [PMC8677981]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Patchy chorioretinal atrophy (PCA) and macular intrachoroidal cavitation (ICC), particularly in the context of pathologic myopia, represent conditions involving focal chorioretinal atrophy. PCA has been observed to progress to ICC over time, characterized by a hyporeflective space beneath the retinal pigment epithelium. These entities should be considered in the differential diagnosis of other chorioretinal atrophies. [PMC8677981]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Rationale: Macular intrachoroidal cavitation (ICC) is characterized by presence of a hyporeflective space beneath the unaltered retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and is noted around the region of focal chorioretinal atrophy in eyes with pathologic myopia. The findings suggest that the patchy chorioretinal atrophy (PCA) progresses to ICC with time. However, there have been no reports describing long-term observational studies using OCT. We collected a case of PCA progression to macular ICC using OCT during a 4-year follow-up. Patient concerns: A 65-year-old woman presented with metamorphopsia and blurred vision in her left eye. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/20 and spherical equivalent refraction was -14.0 diopters in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed a white, well-defined PCA at the superonasal to the fovea which showed hypofluorescence determined by... [PMC8677981]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Progressive bifocal chorioretinal atrophy, as observed in a case of patchy chorioretinal atrophy with macular intrachoroidal cavitation, shows a worsening prognosis over time. Over a four-year follow-up, the chorioretinal lesion and hypofluorescence region gradually expanded, leading to a decrease in best-corrected visual acuity from 20/20 to 20/100. Ocular changes include the expansion of a disorganized ellipsoid zone, thinning of the sensory retina, and the disappearance of the RPE-Bruch's membrane complex. The sensory retina also becomes prominently displaced posteriorly, indicating progressive structural deterioration. [PMC8677981]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare non-syndromic central nervous system malformation characterized by complete or near-complete absence of the cerebellum with a normal sized posterior fossa, possibly accompanied by hypoplasia of the brainstem. The clinical picture is highly variable, but typically includes ataxia, dysarthria, tremor, dysmetria, dysdiadochokinesia, and oculomotor abnormalities, in addition to impaired mental, motor, and language development and intellectual disability.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Near total absence of cerebellum; Subtotal absence of cerebellum

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Variants in the CASK gene result in a wide range of observed phenotypes in humans, such as FG Syndrome 4 and intellectual disabilities. Intellectual developmental disorder with microcephaly and pontine and cerebellar hypoplasia (MICPCH) is an X-linked disorder that affects females and is characterized by severely impaired intellectual development and variable degrees of pontocerebellar hypoplasia. Variants in CASK are the main genetic cause of MICPCH. Variants in CASK can explain most patients with MICPCH, but there are still some patients whose disease aetiology cannot be explained. An 11-month-old female diagnosed with MICPCH exhibited general developmental delays, microcephaly, and cerebellar hypoplasia. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was used to find a novel heterozygous missense variant (NM_003688.3: c.638T>G) of CASK in this patient. Strikingly, this variant reduced the expression... [PMC9169347, PMC8440675, PMC6553355, PMC5567146, PMC3415795]

Intellectual developmental disorder with microcephaly and pontine and cerebellar hypoplasia (MICPCH) is an X-linked disorder that affects females and is characterized by severely impaired intellectual development and variable degrees of pontocerebellar hypoplasia. Variants in CASK are the main genetic cause of MICPCH. Variants in CASK can explain most patients with MICPCH, but there are still some patients whose disease aetiology cannot be explained. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was used to find a novel heterozygous missense variant (NM_003688.3: c.638T>G) of CASK in this patient. Strikingly, this variant reduced the expression... [PMC9169347, PMC8440675, PMC6553355, PMC5567146, PMC3863087]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Variants in the CASK gene result in a wide range of observed phenotypes in humans, such as FG Syndrome 4 and intellectual disabilities. Intellectual developmental disorder with microcephaly and pontine and cerebellar hypoplasia (MICPCH) is an X-linked disorder that affects females and is characterized by severely impaired intellectual development and variable degrees of pontocerebellar hypoplasia. Variants in CASK are the main genetic cause of MICPCH. Variants in CASK can explain most patients with MICPCH, but there are still some patients whose disease aetiology cannot be explained. An 11-month-old female diagnosed with MICPCH exhibited general developmental delays, microcephaly, and cerebellar hypoplasia. Whole-exome sequencing (WES) was used to find a novel heterozygous missense variant (NM_003688.3: c.638T>G) of CASK in this patient. Strikingly, this variant reduced the expression... [PMC9169347, PMC8440675, PMC6553355, PMC5567146, PMC4133931]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis often involves neuroimaging studies to identify structural abnormalities such as cerebellar hypoplasia, underdevelopment, atrophy, or an enlarged cisterna magna. Genetic investigations are crucial, with whole-exome sequencing (WES) and exome reanalysis frequently employed to identify pathogenic variants in genes like CASK or TRIP4. Molecular diagnostic testing can detect specific gene mutations or deletions, such as those in EP300 or POLR3B, or microdeletions identified by SNP array analysis. Cytogenetic analysis may reveal translocations, for example, involving PTK2 and THOC2. Proteomic profiling and protein structure prediction analysis can further support the pathogenicity of identified genetic variants. [PMC9169347, PMC8440675, PMC7539513, PMC6553355, PMC5567146]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Cerebellar hypoplasia can be a feature of numerous conditions, requiring a broad differential diagnosis. These include intellectual developmental disorder with microcephaly and pontine and cerebellar hypoplasia (MICPCH) caused by CASK gene variants, and cerebellar hypoplasia with spinal muscular atrophy (PCH1) linked to TRIP4 gene variants. Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome 2 (RSTS2) with EP300 mutations can present with cerebellar underdevelopment and neural tube defects. Other considerations are cerebellar hypoplasia with endosteal sclerosis (CHES syndrome) due to POLR3B variants, and a novel recessive syndrome characterized by microcephaly, cerebellar hypoplasia, and congenital heart conduction defect. Cerebellar hypoplasia has also been reported in association with Neurofibromatosis type 1, Moebius' syndrome, and a de novo X;8 translocation creating a PTK2-THOC2 gene fusion. Additionally, a new multiple congenital anomaly-mental retardation syndrome with Pierre Robin sequence and cerebellar hypoplasia, and SUNCT syndrome or trigeminal neuralgia associated with cerebellar hypoplasia, should be considered. [PMC9169347, PMC8440675, PMC6553355, PMC5567146, PMC3863087]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for isolated cerebellar agenesis must consider a diverse range of genetic etiologies and inheritance patterns. X-linked disorders, such as those caused by CASK gene variants, are characterized by pontocerebellar hypoplasia and can be identified through genetic diagnosis. Autosomal recessive inheritance is observed with variants in genes like TRIP4, associated with cerebellar hypoplasia and spinal muscular atrophy, and POLR3B, linked to CHES syndrome. Dominant inheritance, as seen with EP300 gene mutations in Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome 2, can also include cerebellar underdevelopment. Furthermore, de novo events, including microdeletions (e.g., 13q12.3) and translocations (e.g., PTK2-THOC2 gene fusion), contribute to the condition. Genetic testing, including whole-exome sequencing and SNP array analysis, is crucial for identifying specific pathogenic variants and informing families about recurrence risks and phenotypic spectrum. [PMC9169347, PMC8440675, PMC7539513, PMC6553355, PMC5567146]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: on the similar phenotypes and clinical course of two sisters. Both patients had an enlarged cisterna magna suggestive of cerebellar hypoplasia, agenesis/hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, Pierre Robin sequence requiring tracheostomy, camptodactyly, microphthalmia, colobomas, seizures, a distinctive facial appearance, global developmental delay, and mental retardation. that the distinct pattern in these sisters constitutes a previously undescribed syndrome of likely autosomal recessive inheritance. [PMC3241992]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Conditions involving cerebellar hypoplasia are often associated with a severe prognosis, typically presenting with neonatal or congenital onset. Patients commonly experience severe psychomotor delay, global developmental delay, and moderate to severe intellectual disability or mental retardation. While some forms may be non-progressive, associated complications can include congenital ataxia, constitutive growth delay, microcephaly, second-degree heart block, childhood-onset insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, seizures, and Pierre Robin sequence, sometimes requiring tracheostomy. [PMC5567146, PMC4133931, PMC3415795, PMC3241992]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive lysosomal disease characterized by accumulation of GM2 gangliosides in the nervous system due to hexosaminidase A and hexosaminidase B deficiency as a consequence of biallelic pathogenic variants in the HEXB gene.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of the disease is 1/380,000 live births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical picture is almost identical to that of Tay-Sachs disease: three forms have been described according to age of onset. The infantile form begins at 3-6 months of age for the early infantile (< 12 months) and 12-24 months for the late infantile. The earliest signs are an incessant startle response to noise, and a progressive loss of vision. Psychomotor regression appears during the second semester of life with hypotonia, amaurosis, rapidly pharmacoresistant epilepsy and progressive macrocephaly. A cherry-red macular spot is nearly always present and is strongly evocative even if not specific. Light visceromegaly or cardiomyopathy may be present in infantile Sandhoff disease, contrary to infantile Tay-Sachs disease. Muscular weakness progresses and leads to paralysis. The disorder degenerates into a state of decerebration and is fatal during childhood. Onset of the juvenile form is at 2-10 years of age, with progressive cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, behavioral disorders, and cognitive regression. Death occurs during the second decade. The adult form begins around the age of 10 or later, and is often not diagnosed until adulthood. The onset is insidious with a progressive course. Two initial clinical presentations are described: i) proximal lower limbs weakness with amyotrophy due to a motor neuropathy (mimicking progressive spinal amyotrophy; first complaint: difficulty to climb stairs) that eventually extends to upper limbs and distal parts of the limbs; ii) generalized cerebellar ataxia (more rarely dystonia). In the course of the disease the motor neuropathy almost always occurs, other motor symptoms may occur (dysarthria, swallowing disorder). Cognition is usually preserved.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The causative gene HEXB encodes the beta subunit of hexosaminidase A and hexosaminidase B and is located on chromosome 5 (5q13.3).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Hexosaminidase A and hexosaminidase B enzymatic activities on blood leukocytes is always very low compared to normal values (around 0% for severe infantile form, around 10-15% for adult form). Diagnosis should be confirmed by HEXB gene sequencing. The diagnosis may be firstly suggested by pathogenic variants findings from a panel of genes, or exome or genome sequencing, and should be confirmed by hexosaminidase A and hexosaminidase B enzymatic activities measurement. Abnormal oligosaccharides urinary excretion may be detected in Sandhoff disease.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: GM2 gangliosidosis, AB variant (GM2A gene variant), may perfectly mimic Sandhoff or Tay-Sachs diseases, but with normal hexosaminidase A and B enzymatic activities. In adults the differential diagnoses include proximal spinal muscular atrophy and autosomal recessive diseases causing cerebellar ataxia (e.g. Niemann Pick disease type C).
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is available: a complete study of hexosaminidases A and B activities, and HEXB gene sequencing for the propositus and both parents is requested before prenatal diagnosis may be done for the fetus.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive; at-risk couples (both parents are carriers of a pathogenic variant) have a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no specific and efficient treatment for Sandhoff disease. Treatment is symptomatic.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: For the pediatric forms: the severity is correlated to age of onset, with a more rapid regression in the early infantile form leading to death around 2-4 years of age, whereas death occurs in the second decade in the juvenile form. All patients will have pharmacoresistant epilepsy in the advanced stages of the disease. For the adult form: the disease is usually very slow progressive and may last decades. Patients are progressively disabled, may lose the ability to walk and have difficulties for upper limbs utilization, speech, swallowing, and may more rarely have cognitive symptoms.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Hereditary breast and/or ovarian cancer syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A genetic condition characterized by hereditary susceptibility to breast and/or ovarian cancer. It can be defined using family history criteria, or through identification of germline pathogenic variants (GPVs) in clinically validated HBOC genes. However, the genetic basis of about half of clinical HBOC is currently unknown or unexplained by single-gene variants, and approximately half of individuals who harbour PVs in HBOC genes do not have a suggestive family history.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of any germline HBOC-related pathogenic variant has been estimated to be about 1:70 women in the general population.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: HBOC is not associated with specific phenotypic features. Individuals with breast cancer may have any histological subtypes, the most common being ductal adenocarcinoma. Early-onset of cancer, bilateral breast cancer, familial occurrence of cancer over several generations, male breast cancer, multiple tumors in a same individual, multifocality and triple negative cancer are features suggestive of hereditary HBOC.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Genes associated with HBOC are classified as 1) high-risk genes, increasing breast and/or tubo-ovarian cancer risk by at least fourfold, and 2) moderate-risk genes, increasing risk by two- to fourfold. However, there is considerable overlap between these two groups. Autosomal dominant alterations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 are likely to account for most HBOC cases. Other genes linked to hereditary breast or ovarian cancer are PALB2, ATM, CHEK2, BARD1 (only breast), RAD51C, RAD51D (breast and ovary) and BRIP1 (only ovary). TP53, PTEN, CDH1, and STK11 are linked to increased breast cancer susceptibility and also to other specific syndromes. Disease severity and age at onset may show variability within and between families harboring the same pathogenic variant, suggesting the involvement of other genetic as well as non-genetic factors. These PVs may also increase susceptibility to other cancer types such as prostate cancer and pancreatic cancer.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on suggestive clinical features associated with significant family history. Individuals should be offered genetic testing with multigene panels of clinically validated HBOC genes. Analysis of single nucleotide variants and large rearrangements are needed for comprehensive genetic testing. If a pathogenic variant is identified through tumor testing, germline testing can be considered to confirm the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes familial breast cancer not associated with known genetic susceptibility.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Once the PV in HBOC-related genes has been identified in the family, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing for known highly penetrant high cancer risk PV are possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: HBOC-related genes are inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. The vast majority of probands inherited it from a parent, with very few being de novo. Offsprings of affected individuals have a 50% chance of inheriting the PV, but the penetrance of the disease is currently unknown. Molecular genetic testing should be offered to both parents and their at-risk relatives who should be counseled regarding their cancer risk, the risk of transmission, and recommendations for cancer screening and prophylactic surgery. Counseling should also mention possible rare autosomal recessive conditions, such as Fanconi anemia, when biallelic PVs in some genes are inherited (i.e. BRCA2, BRCA1, PALB2) and if the partner's family history is also suggestive of HBOC. Testing of asymptomatic individuals < 18 years of age is not recommended and should be deferred until they reach adulthood and can make independent decisions.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The management strategies in healthy carriers include yearly surveillance and surgical risk-reduction options. For patients with a BRCA1/2-associated cancer, there are personalized approaches based on DNA-damaging agents or targeted therapies such as poly-ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitors. Secondary preventive measures might be considered, such as contralateral risk reducing mastectomy or prophylactic bilateral salpingoophorectomy.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Breast and/or ovarian cancers in carriers of a BRCA1 or BRCA2 pathogenic variant may have increased chemosensitivity which might be linked to a slight survival advantage in the first few years after diagnosis compared to other patients.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, biliary tract disease characterized by progressive obliterative cholangiopathy of the intra- and extrahepatic bile ducts, occuring in the embryonic/ perinatal period, leading to severe and persistent neonatal jaundice and acholic stool.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Non-syndromic biliary atresia; Isolated atresia of bile ducts

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Biliary atresia (BA) prevalence at birth is 1/ 15,000-19,000 in Europe and North America.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Diagnosis is mostly made at 2-6 weeks of age, presenting with cholestasis, jaundice, acholia and possibly choluria and hepatomegaly, and sometimes vitamin K deficiency induced bleedings. Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia associated with an increase in γ-glutamyltransferase (GGT) are biochemical signs of the disease. The pathology is characterized by an ongoing inflammatory process of the entire biliary tree, although the disease is defined as an irreversible closure/ atresia of the extrahepatic bile ducts. In 10-20% of cases, biliary atresia is associated with other malformations (syndromic biliary atresia).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology is yet to be explained, but it is believed that it can be the result of the interaction of genetic, environmental, immune, and infectious factors, individually or in combination.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Preoperative evaluation may include abdominal ultrasound, hepatobiliary scintigraphy, percutaneous liver biopsy, endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography, and magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP). However, the definitive diagnosis is confirmed only by cholangiography.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis include other causes of neonatal cholestasis, for example infections, Alagille syndrome, alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, progressive familiar intrahepatic cholestasis (PFIC) and hormonal deficiencies.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Signs of biliary atresia on prenatal ultrasonography has rarely been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disease is not yet identified to be hereditary. The genetic counseling is therefore not possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Kasai portoenterostomy is the gold standard treatment, consisting in total extraction of the hilar fibrosis and subsequent biliary-enteric anastomosis, with favorable results in a maximum of 50% of cases, in which there is total restitution of the biliary drainage and normalization of total bilirubin levels.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The main prognostic factors to short- and long-term survival after surgery include age at surgery, type of biliary atresia, and experience of the center. Out of the possible complications, the most common are cholangitis, portal hypertension, and ongoing deterioration of the liver function with cirrhosis, leading to end-stage failure. Early liver transplantation is required in about 50% of the cases. Very long term survival with native liver decreases to about 25%.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Kennedy's disease, also known as bulbospinal muscular atrophy (BSMA), is a rare X-linked recessive motor neuron disease characterized by proximal and bulbar muscle wasting.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): SBMA; X-linked BSMA; X-linked bulbospinal amyotrophy; X-linked bulbospinal muscular atrophy; X-linked spinal and bulbar muscular atrophy; SMAX1

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of BSMA is 1/30,000 male births. The incidence is 1/526,315 males/year.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset occurs between 30-60 years of age. Initial clinical manifestations include tremor, muscle cramps, muscle twitching, fatigue and slurred speech. With disease progression patients additionally develop weakness and wasting of the limb and bulbar muscles, manifesting as dysarthria, dysphonia, hanging jaw, tongue wasting, chewing difficulty and impaired mobility. Intellectual decline is minimal to none. In the terminal stages of the disease some patients may be unable to swallow or breathe. Non-neurological manifestations include gynecomastia, hypogonadism (leading to infertility and impotence) and in rare cases Dupuytren's contracture, or groin hernia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: BSMA is caused by an unstable expansion of a CAG triplet repeat (40-62 repeats) in exon 1 of the androgen receptor (AR) gene on chromosome Xq11-12. The abnormally increased repetition of this CAG triplet leads to an expanded stretch of glutamines within the androgen-receptor (AR). Polyglutamine-expansion results in misfolding and proteolysis of the mutated AR, rendering it insensitive to androgen hormones. In the nucleus AR fragments are produced, which aggregate and these aggregates are believed to cause dysregulation of the transcription of various other proteins and consecutively lead to motor neuron degeneration. Without a sufficient number of motor neurons, initiation and maintenance of muscle contractions can no longer occur, leading to progressive muscle wasting. Recently, a BSMA phenotype with distal predominance of limb weakness and wasting has been reported, caused by mutations in a subunit of the dynactin 1 DCTN1 gene.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is established upon medical history, clinical examination, elevated creatine-kinase, testosterone, progesterone, follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinizing hormone, reduced nerve conduction velocities or reduced nerve action potential amplitudes, acute or chronic denervation and re-innervation on electromyography and documentation of the mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include hereditary spastic paraplegia, spinocerebellar ataxia, other motor neuron diseases, myopathies, neuropathies, lead or aluminum poisoning, and cervical spondylosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible for mothers carrying the mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Female mutation carriers usually do not manifest clinically but have a 50% risk to transmit the mutation to their male and female offspring. Affected males do not transmit the disease but 100% of their daughters become mutation carriers.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Symptomatic treatment includes physiotherapy and rehabilitation, agents against tremor and muscle cramps and hormone therapy or surgical treatment of gynecomastia. Recently, treatment of patients with the anti-testosterone leuprorelin was found to be beneficial. In advanced stages of the disease, tube feeding or ventilatory support may be indicated.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Disease progression is slow with only one third of patients requiring a wheelchair 20 years after diagnosis. Prognosis of BSMA is usually fair with only a small decrease in life expectancy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 21 syndrome
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A uniparental disomy of maternal origin that does not seem to have an adverse impact on the phenotype of an individual. There is a possibility of homozygosity for a recessive disease mutation for which the mother is a carrier and specific phenotype depends on the inherited disorder.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Uniparental disomy (UPD) occurs when both homologous chromosomes are inherited from a single parent. To date, the UPD of all autosomes and the X chromosome has been recorded. A few cases of UPD of chromosome 21 have been documented. At 15 weeks of gestation, a 25-year-old pregnant woman's non-invasive prenatal screening revealed a high risk of trisomy 21. Although no anomalies were detected in the fetal ultrasonography, amniocentesis was performed, and the fetal karyotype analysis was found normal. A single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array revealed that the fetus had the copy-neutral region of homozygosity (ROH) in the long arm of chromosome 21. Subsequently, single whole-exome sequencing was performed due to the risk of recessive gene variants in ROH, and no homozygous like pathogenic or pathogenic variants were found on the long arm of chromosome 21. After genetic counseling, the... [PMC11920191, PMC1049975, PMC1682298]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Uniparental disomy (UPD) occurs when both homologous chromosomes are inherited from a single parent, and UPD of chromosome 21 has been documented. In some cases, isodisomy of chromosome 21, where two identical chromosomes are inherited from the mother, can arise as a compensatory mechanism. This mechanism involves the duplication of a chromosome in mitosis following the loss of an abnormal homologous chromosome, such as in instances of monosomy 21 or deletion of chromosome 21. The associated phenotypes, including growth failure, microcephaly, facial dysmorphism, muscular hypertonia, and severe psychomotor retardation, are attributed to the cells with monosomy or deletion of chromosome 21. [PMC11920191, PMC1049975]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic approaches for maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 21 syndrome involve several genetic . Initial non-invasive prenatal screening may indicate a high risk of trisomy 21, even when subsequent fetal karyotype analysis appears normal. In such instances, a single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array can identify copy-neutral regions of homozygosity on chromosome 21, suggesting uniparental disomy. Definitive confirmation of maternal origin is achieved through DNA polymorphism analysis. Additionally, cytogenetic mosaicism, such as monosomy 21 or deletions, may be detected in tissues like fibroblasts, although lymphocyte karyotypes can normalize over time. Copy number variation sequencing can also reveal placental mosaicism. [PMC11920191, PMC1049975, PMC1682298]

Subsequently, single whole-exome sequencing was performed due to the risk of recessive gene variants in ROH, and no homozygous like pathogenic or pathogenic variants were found on the long arm of chromosome 21. After genetic counseling, the... [PMC11920191, PMC7847594, PMC1049975, PMC1682298]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis may be prompted by non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS) indicating a high risk of trisomy 21. Even with normal fetal ultrasonography and a normal fetal karyotype from amniocentesis, further investigation can be pursued. A single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) array may reveal a copy-neutral region of homozygosity (ROH) on the long arm of chromosome 21. Whole-exome sequencing can then be performed to assess for recessive gene variants within the ROH. Additionally, copy number variation sequencing of placental tissue might show mosaic trisomy 21. [PMC11920191]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for maternal uniparental disomy of chromosome 21 (mUPD21) should address its potential for prenatal detection, often following high-risk non-invasive prenatal screening. While isolated mUPD21, particularly isodisomy, can be associated with a normal phenotype, complex cases involving compensatory isodisomy may present with severe features like growth failure and psychomotor retardation. These severe phenotypes are attributed to co-existing abnormal cell lines, such as monosomy 21 or deletions, rather than the isodisomy itself. Paternal uniparental isodisomy for chromosome 21 is also linked to a normal phenotype, suggesting no imprinted genes. Counseling should also consider the possibility of placental mosaicism and the dynamic nature of cytogenetic findings, which can sometimes appear falsely normal. [PMC11920191, PMC1049975, PMC1682298]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare lysosomal disease characterized by accumulation of sulfatides in the central and peripheral nervous system due to deficiency of the enzyme arylsulfatase A, leading to demyelination. Three clinical subtypes can be distinguished based on the age of onset: late infantile, juvenile, and adult. Lead symptoms are deterioration in motor or cognitive function or behavioral problems, depending on the subtype, all eventually culminating in a decerebrated state and death after a highly variable disease course and duration. Mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive.

DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD) is a progressive, demyelinating neuro-metabolic disorder, classically recognized as fatal, particularly in young children, though it can affect all ages with varying neurological trajectories. The disease leads to progressive degeneration of white matter, encephalopathy, and impairments in motor control, reflexes, and muscle tone, ultimately resulting in chronic respiratory insufficiency. While hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) can offer symptomatic and survival benefits by stabilizing central nervous system disease and halting progression in pre-symptomatic and early symptomatic patients, outcomes depend on the disease stage at transplantation. HCT can also be associated with severely progressive polyneuropathy, leading to loss of mobility and, in some cases, death due to respiratory failure. Intrathecal baclofen may improve comfort but does not alter the progressive course. [PMC12361609, PMC11781823, PMC11233286, PMC11320896, PMC11348663]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inflammatory/autoimmune disorder of unknown origin characterized by interstitial keratitis (IK) and audiovestibular dysfunctions.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Cogan syndrome (CS) prevalence is unknown. To date, approximately 300 cases have been reported. The disease is primarily described in causasians patients with no gender predilection.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: CS mainly affects young adults, with a median age at onset between 20 and 30 years, and occasionally affects children. The syndrome shows a large spectrum of clinical features. Non-syphilitic IK and cochleovestibular symptoms with unilateral or bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo and tinnitus are typical CS manifestations. The interval between the onset of ocular and audio-vestibular involvement is usually less than 2 years. CS presentation is considered atypical in presence of unusual ocular involvement (such as uveitis, chronic or recurrent conjunctivitis, scleritis, optic disc edema, and retinal vasculitis, with or without IK), audiovestibular symptoms that do not resemble Menière disease, or when the latency between the two organ involvement is more than 2 years A systemic disease expression is reported in at least 1/3 of the patients, especially in atypical cases, with general symptoms such as fever, headaches, weight loss, and/or in presence of signs of organ involvement, mostly cardiovascular (aortitis, aortic insufficiency, congestive heart failure, Raynaud's phenomenon), neurological (peripheral neuropathy, meningitis, hemiparesis or hemiplegia due to a cerebral vascular accident and aphasia due to a transient ischaemic event) and gastrointestinal systems (diarrhea, melena and abdominal pains).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CS is supposed to have an autoimmune etiology, and autoantibodies to inner ear antigens and corneal structures, such as the Cogan peptide are usually present, even if they cannot be considered specific CS serological biomarkers.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is mainly clinical of exclusion of infections (in primis syphilis and Lyme disease) on the good response to corticosteroid treatment. There are no confirmatory diagnostic tests, even if laboratory tests, audiogram, and imaging may be useful for supporting the diagnosis and excluding other potential etiologies.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include syphilis, Menière disease, Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, tuberculosis, polyarteritis nodosa, granulomatosis with polyangiitis and Takayasu arteritis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Corticosteroids are the cornerstone of CS therapy. Topical glucocorticoids in association with cycloplegics may be considered for the management of isolated, mild eye involvement, while systemic corticosteroids should be considered for more severe eye involvement, hearing impairment, and systemic manifestations. Treatment with high doses of systemic corticosteroids (1-1.5 mg/kg of prednisone daily) are expected to prevent deafness, with a beneficial response usually within 2-3 weeks. However corticosteroids have proven to be of short-term benefit, and they carry a risk of serious side effects, therefore in patients with refractory or steroid-dependent disease, a second line treatment with immunosuppressants should be considered, although conventional immunosuppressive drugs such as methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, azathioprine, or cyclosporin A seem to have a limited efficacy. There are increasing reports of successful response to Infliximab, a tumor necrosis alpha (TNFalpha) blocker. Infliximab showed cochleovestibular symptoms improvement and allowed corticosteroid tapering, with a significantly difference when compared to patients treated with steroids alone or conventional DMARDs. The early use of infliximab as first line therapy in severe cases seems to be even more effective. Cochlear implantation is a valuable rescue surgical strategy in cases of severe sensorineural hearing loss unresponsive to intensive immunosuppressive regimens.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is mainly related to the risk of permanent deafness and cardiovascular complications, especially aortic insufficiency. Severe internal organ involvement and cardiovascular complications-related deaths are rare.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Cogan syndrome is described as a disorder without a hereditary pattern. This suggests that the condition is not typically passed down through families, which is a key consideration for genetic counseling. [PMC10436999]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal trisomy 19q is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome characterized by low birth weight, developmental delay, intellectual disability, short stature, craniofacial dysmorphism (incl. microcephaly, midface hypoplasia, hypertelorism, flat nasal bridge, ear anomalies, short philtrum, downturned corners of the mouth, micrognathia) and a short neck with redundant skin folds. Additional features may include hypotonia, skeletal anomalies (e.g. clino/camptodactyly), seizures and congenital cardiac, urogenital and gastrointestinal malformations.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Distal duplication 19q syndrome is a rare condition. Only six patients with partial trisomy of the long arm of chromosome 19 (19q) caused by direct interstitial duplications have been reported to date. Few other cases of proven distal trisomy 19q are available for comparison, with one abstract describing a new case of partial trisomy 19q and another noting the first Asian case report for a specific interstitial duplication. [PMC5653492, PMC1734984, PMC1050740, PMC1016504]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Distal duplication 19q syndrome is characterized by developmental delay, growth retardation, and various dysmorphic features. Reported clinical findings include microcephaly, short stature, high bossed forehead, pointed short ear lobes, small nose, bilateral convergent strabismus, left simian crease, a gap between the first and second toes, mild clinodactyly, and a broad, barrel-shaped thorax. More severe manifestations can involve facial dysmorphism, bilateral coloboma, narrow and hypoplastic nails, cardiac malformations such as Fallot's tetralogy, genitourinary and gastrointestinal anomalies, and agenesis of the corpus callosum. However, the phenotype can range from mild to severe, with some cases presenting with only minor dysmorphic features. [PMC5653492, PMC1734984, PMC1050740, PMC1016504, PMC1016348]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal duplication 19q syndrome is caused by partial trisomy of the long arm of chromosome 19 (19q). This can result from direct interstitial duplications, such as a 1.13 Mb segment within 19q13.32, or an intercalary duplication of 19q (e.g., 19q13.13-13.2). The duplication can be de novo in origin, as seen in cases of dup(19q) or unbalanced translocations like 46,XX,-10,+der(10)t(10;19)(q26.3; q13.3) leading to distal trisomy 19q. It can also be inherited, for example, from a maternal balanced translocation such as t(13;19)(p13;q13.2), resulting in trisomy 19q13.2-->qter. Some cases involve a pure duplication of 19q as a sole chromosomal abnormality, while others may present with additional chromosomal changes like a simultaneous deletion of 16q. [PMC5653492, PMC1734984, PMC1050740, PMC1016504, PMC1016348]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of distal duplication 19q syndrome involves cytogenetic investigations. Initial G-banded chromosome analysis may reveal an unbalanced karyotype, such as an additional segment on another chromosome, which can then be further defined by Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to confirm distal trisomy 19q. However, G-banded chromosome analysis may appear normal for smaller duplications. In such cases, array comparative genomic hybridization (array-CGH) is effective, capable of detecting interstitial duplications as small as 1.13 Mb within 19q13.32. [PMC5653492, PMC2986486, PMC1050740]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: In a 2 and a half-year-old girl with onset of puberty before the age of 5 months, short stature, hand anomalies and severe mental retardation, an 8.9 Mb interstitial 19p13 duplication containing 215 predicted genes was detected. It was initially assumed that the duplication involved the kisspeptin receptor gene, GPR54, known to stimulate induction of puberty, but more refined duplication mapping excluded this possibility. In an attempt to further understand the genotype-phenotype correlation, global gene expression was measured in skin fibroblasts. The overall expression pattern was quite similar to controls, and only about 25% of the duplicated genes had an expression level that was increased by more than 1.3-fold, with no obvious changes that could explain the precocious puberty. The proband's mother carried a balanced between-arm insertion of the duplicated segment that resembled a... [PMC2986486]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Distal duplication 19q syndrome can arise de novo, as observed in several reported cases, or be inherited from a parent carrying a balanced chromosomal rearrangement, such as a translocation or insertion. When a parent is a balanced carrier, there is a risk of transmitting an unbalanced duplication to offspring. The clinical presentation can vary, with some de novo duplications associated with a mild phenotype. Genotype-phenotype correlation is complex, but smaller duplication segments may correlate with milder clinical features. Further identification of critical regions is needed to better understand these correlations. [PMC5653492, PMC2986486, PMC1734984, PMC1050740, PMC1016504]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Only 6 patients with partial trisomy of the long arm of chromosome 19 (19q), caused by direct interstitial duplications, have been reported until today. Herein, a pediatric patient with a novel 1.13 Mb direct interstitial duplication within 19q13.32, which is the smallest fragment affected so far. A five-year old Korean boy of healthy parents presented with microcephaly, growth retardation, developmental delay, and craniofacial dysmorphism. Even though G-banded chromosome analysis at resolution of 550-band revealed normal karyotype, duplication of 1.13 Mb fragment within 19q13.32 was detected by array comparative genomic hybridization. Comparing with previously reported patients with pure duplication involving 19q as a sole chromosomal abnormality, our case showed the smallest duplication segment with relatively mild degree of clinical features. Our present case might serve as the... [PMC5653492, PMC1734984]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A neurodevelopmental teratologic syndrome due to prenatal exposure to toluene. The disease is characterized by prematurity, low birth weight, dysmorphic features (short palpebral fissures, deep set eyes, low set ears, mid-facial hypoplasia, flat nasal bridge, thin upper lip, micrognathia, spatulate fingertips and small fingernails), central nervous system dysfunctions (intellectual disability, microcephaly, language impairment, hyperactivity, visual dysfunction) and postnatal growth delay. Prenatal exposure to toluene occurs as a result of incidental occupational exposure or solvent abuse during pregnancy. The features of toluene embryopathy often overlap with those seen in fetal alcohol syndrome.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Toluene embryopathy is a rare condition, with only a limited number of cases reported in the literature. Prior to 1989, three affected children had been described. This abstract adds two more cases, bringing the total reported to five. These cases emphasize the importance of toluene as a potential human teratogen. [PMC1015602]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Toluene embryopathy is characterized by a range of features including microcephaly, central nervous system dysfunction, and variable growth deficiency. Affected individuals typically exhibit attentional deficits, hyperactivity, and developmental delay, with language deficits being more pronounced. Minor craniofacial and limb anomalies are also part of the clinical presentation. These characteristics are observed in children born to women who regularly inhaled toluene throughout pregnancy. [PMC1015602]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Toluene embryopathy is caused by maternal exposure to toluene during pregnancy. Affected children have been reported whose mothers regularly inhaled toluene throughout pregnancy. Toluene is considered a potential human teratogen, leading to the characteristic features of the embryopathy. [PMC1015602]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Toluene embryopathy is characterised by microcephaly, central nervous system dysfunction, attentional deficits and hyperactivity, developmental delay with greater language deficits, minor craniofacial and limb anomalies, and variable growth deficiency. Previously, three affected children, born to women who inhaled toluene regularly throughout pregnancy, have been reported. Two more cases are described emphasising the importance of toluene as a potential human teratogen. [PMC1015602]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Toluene embryopathy is characterised by microcephaly, central nervous system dysfunction, attentional deficits and hyperactivity, developmental delay with greater language deficits, minor craniofacial and limb anomalies, and variable growth deficiency. Previously, three affected children, born to women who inhaled toluene regularly throughout pregnancy, have been reported. Two more cases are described emphasising the importance of toluene as a potential human teratogen. [PMC1015602]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare X-linked intellectual disability characterized by marked neonatal hypotonia, progressive quadriparesia, severely delayed developmental milestones (walking at 3 years of age), gastroesophageal reflux, stereotypic movements of the hands, esotropia and infantile autism.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Cantagrel type, is characterized by severe mental retardation in affected males. Female carriers of the genetic alteration are not affected. This condition is associated with the disruption of the KIAA2022 gene, which is highly expressed in the brain, suggesting a role in brain development and/or cognitive function. [PMC1735597]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Cantagrel type, has been linked to a pericentric inversion of the X chromosome, inv(X)(p22.3;q13.2), which disrupts two genes: KIAA2022 and P2RY8. The severe intellectual disability in affected males is attributed to the absence of the KIAA2022 gene product. KIAA2022 is highly expressed in the brain, suggesting a role in brain development or cognitive function. While P2RY8 is also disrupted, it is not expressed in the brain and its haploinsufficiency in female carriers has no phenotypic consequence. However, mutations in KIAA2022 were not found in other X-linked intellectual disability families. [PMC1735597]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: X-linked intellectual disability, Cantagrel type, is associated with an X-linked inheritance pattern. In affected families, a pericentric inversion of the X chromosome, inv(X)(p22.3;q13.2), disrupts the KIAA2022 gene. Male carriers of this inversion exhibit severe intellectual disability, while female carriers are not affected. The severe phenotype in males is attributed to the absence of the KIAA2022 gene product. While KIAA2022 is highly expressed in the brain, mutations in this gene were not found in other X-linked intellectual disability families, suggesting the specific inversion is a key factor in this type. [PMC1735597]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: IgG4-related dacryoadenitis and sialoadenitis (Mikulicz disease) is an IgG4-related sclerosing disease characterized by persistent, usually painless, bilateral enlargement of the lacrimal, parotid, and submandibular glands associated with elevated levels of serum immunoglobulin (Ig) G4 and with lymphocyte and IgG4-positive plasmacyte infiltration. It predominantly causes mouth and eye dryness but can also affect other organs such as the lungs, liver, and kidneys, and be accompanied by complications such as autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP), retroperitoneal fibrosis, and tubulointerstitial nephritis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Chronic dacryoadenitis and sialadenitis; Mikulicz disease

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: IgG4-related dacryoadenitis and sialadenitis (Mikulicz's disease) is described as a rare and very uncommon chronic condition. It can affect a broad age range, including pediatric patients (e.g., an 11-year-old female), middle-aged individuals (e.g., a 51-year-old female), and elderly women (e.g., a 77-year-old patient). The condition is noted to be more common in middle-aged and elderly females. [PMC11603467, PMC11181676, PMC10375769, PMC5743147]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: IgG4-related dacryoadenitis and sialadenitis, also known as Mikulicz's disease, is characterized by abnormal enlargement of glandular tissue in the head and neck, typically involving bilateral lacrimal, parotid, submandibular, and sublingual glands. Patients may present with palpable mass lesions, swelling of the upper eyelids, and neck areas, sometimes accompanied by dry eyes or mouth. Imaging often reveals enlarged glands, which can show irregular hypoechoic parenchyma or homogeneous enlargement. Elevated serum IgG4 levels are a key laboratory finding, and histopathology shows lympho-plasmacytic infiltration with numerous IgG4-positive plasma cells. The disease can affect pediatric to elderly populations and may overlap with other IgG4-related conditions like hypophysitis, lymphadenitis, or autoimmune pancreatitis, and rarely, acquired hemophilia A. Differential diagnoses include Sjögren's Syndrome and malignant lymphomas. [PMC11603467, PMC11181676, PMC10375769, PMC9803436, PMC7864275]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiopathobiology of IgG4-related disease, including chronic sclerosing sialadenitis, is not fully understood. It is hypothesized that the inflammatory and fibrotic processes, along with increased serum IgG4 levels, result from an interaction between B cells and T helper cells, suggesting a key role for T cells in pathogenesis. In IgG4-related ophthalmic disease, CD4+ naive T-cells are highly likely to differentiate into regulatory T-cells. General immune dysregulation, potentially involving permissive genetic backgrounds, epithelial barrier damage, and changes in the microbiome, are considered common risk factors for autoimmune disorders, which may contribute to the disease's development. The condition is characterized by lymphoplasmacytic infiltration and fibrosis. [PMC11814061, PMC11897659, PMC9236833]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: IgG4-related dacryoadenitis and sialadenitis, often referred to as Mikulicz's disease, requires careful differentiation from several conditions. Primary Sjögren's syndrome (SS) presents diagnostic challenges due to shared clinical features like dry eyes, dry mouth, and bilateral lacrimal and salivary gland enlargement, especially in early stages. Distinguishing factors include SS-related antibodies (anti-SSA, anti-SSB) and normal serum IgG4 levels in SS, contrasting with elevated IgG4 in Mikulicz's disease. Malignant lymphomas, such as ocular adnexal mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma and mantle cell lymphoma, can mimic IgG4-related disease, necessitating histopathological examination and IgG4 testing for differentiation. Sarcoidosis is also mentioned as a potential underlying etiology for Mikulicz Syndrome. [PMC11897659, PMC10375769, PMC9803436, PMC7864275, PMC5743147]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Corticosteroid therapy, including oral prednisolone or prednisone, is the primary treatment for IgG4-related dacryoadenitis and sialadenitis. This treatment leads to marked relief of symptoms, significant improvement in associated manifestations like nausea and vomiting, and a reduction in the size of enlarged lacrimal, submandibular, and parotid glands. For instance, a regimen of 30 mg/d of prednisone for three weeks, followed by a 10 mg/d maintenance dose for six months, has been shown to normalize gland size and prevent recurrence. The condition is clinically characterized by its responsiveness to glucocorticoid treatment. [PMC11603467, PMC11181676, PMC9803436, PMC7864275, PMC3882427]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: IgG4-related dacryoadenitis and sialadenitis, also known as Mikulicz's disease, generally has a favorable prognosis, particularly with corticosteroid therapy. Symptoms such as gland swelling, nausea, vomiting, and hearing impairment often show marked relief following treatment. While some cases may be benign and self-limiting, steroid administration typically leads to significant recovery, with affected glands returning to normal size. With maintenance therapy, recurrence may not be observed within a 6-month follow-up period. [PMC11603467, PMC11181676, PMC9803436, PMC7864275, PMC5743147]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare viral disease characterized by invasive and/or disseminated adenovirus infection in immunocompromised patients, either acquired de novo or arising from reactivation of persistent latent infection. The clinical picture comprises a wide range of manifestations including pneumonia, colitis, hepatitis, hemorrhagic cystitis, tubulointerstitial nephritis, encephalitis, and disseminated disease, among others. Severity varies with age and immune status, and life-threatening courses may occur.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Adenovirus infection in immunocompromised patients, including kidney and liver transplant recipients, hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, and those with primary immunodeficiencies, presents with diverse and often nonspecific clinical manifestations. The spectrum ranges from asymptomatic or flu-like illness to severe, disseminated, and life-threatening multi-organ failure. Common symptoms include fever, dysuria, diarrhea, and general malaise. Organ involvement can include nephritis, characterized by interstitial nephritis, acute tubular necrosis, and granulomas, often leading to reversible graft dysfunction. Hepatic manifestations range from granulomatous hepatitis and abscesses to fulminant liver failure, which carries a high fatality rate. Respiratory involvement can manifest as pneumonia and severe acute respiratory distress syndrome. Disseminated infections can involve the upper respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, and blood, potentially leading to septic shock and death. [PMC11825578, PMC12233852, PMC11103978, PMC10151298, PMC10733164]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis of adenovirus infection in immunocompromised patients is variable, ranging from favorable outcomes to high mortality. In kidney transplant recipients, adenovirus nephritis often leads to reversible graft dysfunction, with most cases showing favorable evolution and recovery of kidney function, though mortality has been reported. However, disseminated adenovirus infection, particularly with multi-organ involvement such as fulminant liver failure or severe acute respiratory distress syndrome, carries a high fatality rate, especially in immunocompromised patients, despite aggressive treatment. While most children with adenovirus-associated acute hepatitis recover without complications, liver transplantation may be required in some instances. For hematopoietic stem cell transplant recipients, disseminated adenovirus infection is associated with a relatively high mortality, though successful viral clearance and cure have been achieved with advanced therapies. [PMC11825578, PMC12233852, PMC11103978, PMC11051986, PMC10151298]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal dominant skeletal disorder, characterized by progressive bone resorption in the distal phalanges (acro-osteolysis), progressive osteoporosis, distinct craniofacial changes, dental anomalies, and occasional association with renal abnormalities.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Acroosteolysis dominant type; Acroosteolysis with osteoporosis and changes in skull and mandible; Arthrodentoosteodysplasia; Cheney syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Less than 100 cases are confirmed to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Whilst affected individuals may appear normal at birth and during infancy, minor facial abnormalities, such as a small mandible, may come to clinical attention in half of affected infants. With age, affected children develop facial dysmorphism (dolicho-bathrocephaly, coarse hair, synophrys, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, low set ears, midface flattening, long philtrum, and micrognathia). The fontanels are delayed in closure. Short stature manifests in early childhood and is progressive, presumably due to vertebral compression. Acroosteolysis becomes manifest between preschool age and mid-childhood and clinically presents as short finger tips and nails with pseudoclubbing. Osteoporosis is evident even in childhood, but is conspicuously progressive in late adolescent to adulthood, leading to biconcave codfish vertebrae and kyphoscoliosis. Bone weakness at the craniovertebral junction causes platybasia and basilar invagination, resulting in syringomyelia, hydrocephalus and neurologic deficits. Dental anomalies include severe crowding, periodontitis, and premature loss of teeth. Some patients are at potential risk of renal failure due to multiple renal cysts. Serpentine fibula-polycystic kidney syndrome (SFPKS) is the most severe manifestation of Hajdu-Cheney syndrome, which manifests with bent (serpentine) fibulae and radii as well as congenital renal cysts.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disorder is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants in the NOTCH2 gene mapped on 1p12 and encoding the neurogenic locus notch homolog protein 2 (Notch2). All known disease-causing variants are located in exon 34, and cause abnormally increased Notch2 signaling (gain-of-function). Of note, pathogenic variants in NOTCH2 also cause a different malformation syndrome, Alagille syndrome type 2.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is made on clinical and radiological grounds, and is confirmed by molecular detection of pathogenic variants in the NOTCH2 gene.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The facial abnormalities are commonly misdiagnosed with Noonan syndrome in infancy and early childhood. The differential diagnosis includes genetic syndromes with pediatric acroosteolysis, such as pyknodysostosis, mandibuloacral dysplasia, as well as congenital insensitivity to pain.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is theoretically possible in affected families in which the causal NOTCH2 variant has been previously identified. The fetal manifestation of SFPKS can be detected on prenatal ultrasonography.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant. The offspring of an affected individual is at a 50% risk of having the pathogenic variant in NOTCH2. However, most cases are sporadic in occurrence.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Only symptomatic treatment is available for the specific symptoms. Bisphosphonate therapy is beneficial for osteoporosis, though it is not helpful for acroosteolysis. Individuals with renal failure require the standard medical intervention. Regular dental examinations are important.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The life expectancy of patients is not severely impaired. Osteoporosis and associated fractures cause significant morbidity. Basilar invagination occasionally leads to syringomyelia and seldom hydrocephalus. Dental management is important for the quality of life.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genodermatosis disease with great phenotypic variation and characterized most commonly by ichthyosis following the lines of Blaschko, chondrodysplasia punctata (CDP), asymmetric shortening of the limbs, cataracts and short stature.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CDPX2; CDPXD; CPXD; Chondrodystrophia calcificans congenita; Conradi-Hünermann-Happle syndrome; X-linked chondrodysplasia punctata type 2

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence of X-linked dominant chondrodysplasia punctata (CDPX2) has been estimated to be at least 1/400,000 births with 95% of patients being female.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Congenital ichthyosiform erythroderma is the typical neonatal manifestation. Erythema is usually generalized while hyperkeratotic scales generally follow Blaschko's lines and tend to fade during a period of weeks to months. In older children, ichthyosis following Blaschko's lines is the most frequent clinical finding (95% of cases) and it improves with age. Hyperkeratosis, especially involving hair follicles, and late atrophy appear at sites of previous scaling, typically in a follicular pattern (atrophoderma vermiculata). Follicular atrophoderma is particularly common on the trunk, forearms and dorsal aspect of the hands. Patchy areas of cicatricial alopecia are common.
