Asymmetric shortening of the limbs, usually affecting the humerus and femur, together with CDP, are the most common skeletal abnormalities. Facial dysmorphism (low nasal bridge, frontal bossing, hypertelorism, high arched palate) is common. Joint contractures affecting the hips, hands and feet are frequent. Talus valgus and other deformities may be seen. The vertebral column exhibits moderate to severe scoliosis and short stature is common. Most patients (60%) suffer from cataracts (mainly unilateral), which may be congenital or appear early in life. Microphthalmia, microcornea and epicanthus have been reported. Intelligence is normal.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CDPX2 is due to mutations in the EBP gene (Xp11.23-p11.22) encoding the emopamil binding protein (EBP), which acts as a delta8-delta7-sterol isomerase that catalyzes the conversion of 8(9)-cholestenol to lathosterol in the distal cholesterol biosynthesis pathway. A deficiency in EBP leads to the accumulation of 8-dehydrocholesterol (8DHC) and 8(9)-cholestenol in the skin, plasma and other body tissues.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of CDPX2 relies on clinical, biochemical and genetic tests. CDP, usually consisting of epiphyseal stippling, is the fundamental radiological finding. Biochemical analyses show increased levels of 8(9) cholestenol and 8-dehydrocholesterol. Molecular testing for EBP mutations confirms diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include CDPX1; RCDP; chondrodysplasia punctata, tibia-metacarpal type; CHILD syndrome; systemic lupus erythematosus; MEND syndrome, and vitamin K deficiencies.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis and preimplantation genetic diagnosis may be an option for families with a known disease-causing mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: CDPX2 is inherited in an X-linked dominant manner and genetic counseling is possible. Somatic mosaicism in the father or de novo mutations can explain the occurrence of offspring with CDPX2 when no mutations are found in the mother. Germline mosaicism and anticipation has also been reported in families with CDPX2. In most cases it is lethal in males.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is multidisciplinary. Treatment of skin lesions includes the use of emollients and keratolytics (i.e. ammonium lactate 12%, petrolatum ointment). Topical administration of lovastatin and cholesterol may be beneficial for ichthyosis. Orthopedic management and surgery may be necessary in those with bone deformities. Cataracts should be extracted and vision correction devices provided. Physical, occupational and speech therapies may be necessary. Regular follow-up with dermatologists and ophthalmologists and orthopedic evaluations are recommended. Hearing aids may be needed.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: There is usually no effect on life-expectancy (rarely scoliosis can compromise cardiac and pulmonary function) but quality of life may be severely affected.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, cardiac condition characterized by severely decreased cardiac output, hypoperfusion and end-organ dysfunction, in the presence of adequate intravascular volume. The clinical presentation is variable and may range from subtle hemodynamic alterations to overt cardiovascular collapse. Commonly reported features include dyspnea, crackles, elevated jugular venous pressure, altered mental state, abnormal pulse pressure, oliguria, cold extremities, and increased serum lactate levels.

DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (CPVT) is an inherited ion channelopathy characterized by a structurally normal heart sensitive to catecholamines. It primarily presents as Bidirectional ventricular tachycardia (BiVT) and is a significant cause of sudden cardiac death in children. our experience with central Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation (ECMO) therapy in a 4-year-old boy with CPVT. Despite these measures, his CPVT was refractory to standard medical treatment and mechanical ventilatory support, with symptom progression. Consequently, ECMO support was initiated in addition to existing treatment. The patient was successfully weaned off ECMO on the 10th day of therapy and was discharged in a good condition. Follow-up after discharge showed favorable outcomes. The successful outcome in this case was attributed to the application of ECMO, which helped maintain the... [PMC11705711, PMC12265929]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Cerebro-costo-mandibular syndrome (CCMS) is characterized at birth by posterior rib gaps and orofacial anomalies reminiscent of Pierre Robin syndrome that include palatal defects (short hard palate, absent soft palate, absent uvula), micrognathia and glossoptosis.
DiseaseInfo.Inheritance: Autosomal dominant, Autosomal recessive, Not applicable

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: More than 80 cases have been reported to date; both males and females are equally affected.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: CCMS is characterized by orofacial and costovertebral developmental anomalies. Severity is highly variable. Intrauterine growth retardation and low birth weights are common. Orofacial anomalies may include absent soft palate and a short hard palate with posterior notching, micrognathia and glossoptosis. Characteristic dorsal rib defects are sine qua non of the syndrome and often result in a bell-shaped thorax. Posterior rib gaps and rib defects are revealed by X-ray; there is no apparent continuity between the ossiﬁed ribs which are usually divided into two portions. This may lead to ''flail chest,'' a paradoxical movement of a segment of the thoracic wall due to broken ribs, which may further hamper respiration. Respiratory difficulties lead to generalized cyanosis and potential hypoxic brain injuries that may be responsible for intellectual deficit that may be observed later. Associated malformations were described in rare cases: microcephaly, absence of external ear canals and spina bifida. Those patients who survive infancy may suffer from growth retardation, scoliosis, reduced lung capacity, dental anomalies, feeding disturbances, conductive hearing loss and language disturbances. Patients who survive the first year of life are reported to survive to adulthood and to harbor a less severe form. These patients may suffer from growth retardation, scoliosis, reduced lung capacity, dentition anomalies, feeding disturbances, intellectual deficit, conductive hearing loss and language disturbance.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: No causative gene has been identified to date. It has been proposed, however, that defects in the sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling cascade may be responsible for these developmental anomalies.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Clinical presentation, along with typical chest X-ray findings, confirms the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include trisomies 13 and 18, and Pierre Robin syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Although most cases are spontaneous, both autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant patterns of inheritance have been observed in familial cases.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Orofacial anomalies responsible for breathing and feeding difficulties must be immediately addressed and severe cases must be transferred to intensive care units. Affected infants require feeding assistance and should lie in the prone position to help bring the tongue forward and liberate the trachea. Intubation or placement of a nasopharyngeal airway may be necessary. As tracheal intubation may prove impossible, a neonatal laryngeal mask airway, intermittently replaced by nasal prongs and continuous positive airway pressure, may be required. In these most severe cases, tongue-lip adhesion surgical intervention may provide a long term solution. A Haberman feeder may be of use in infants with cleft palate and nasogastric tube supplementation may be required to provide supplementary caloric intake.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends upon the severity of anomalies. The most severe forms are often fatal within the first hours after birth and 25% of all reported cases are fatal during the first month of life. This correlates significantly with greater numbers of missing ribs or gaps.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Cerebrocostomandibular syndrome (CCMS) is consistent with Mendelian autosomal recessive inheritance with high penetrance. This is based on observations of the syndrome in four siblings, including two pairs of twins, despite a negative family history in previous generations. This pattern suggests that parents of affected individuals are likely carriers, and there is a recurrence risk for subsequent offspring. [PMC1017059]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare chromosomal anomaly comprising variable parts of chromosome 8. The phenotype of mosaic or non-mosaic supernumerary r(8)/mar(8) ranges from almost normal to variable degrees of minor abnormalities, and growth and mental retardation overlapping with the well-known mosaic trisomy 8 syndrome.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Ring chromosome 8 (r(8)) is considered one of the least frequent types of ring chromosomes. While the estimated newborn incidence for all human ring chromosomes is 1/50,000, with an annual occurrence of 2,800 patients globally, specific epidemiological data for r(8) syndrome are not detailed. The literature suggests that reported clinical cases for ring chromosomes in general are significantly under-represented, implying a challenge in understanding their true occurrence. [PMC9519620, PMC7763634]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Ring chromosome 8 syndrome is characterized by multiple congenital abnormalities and developmental delay, including mental retardation. Affected individuals often present with microcephaly and dysmorphic features. Specific findings can include a prominent nose, highly arched palate, and low-set ears. Other clinical manifestations may involve diffuse muscle hypotonia, feeding problems, and motor alalia. [PMC7763634, PMC1015827, PMC1013644]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Ring chromosome 8 is a rare chromosomal abnormality, often originating from maternal chromosome 8. Its formation can lead to mosaicism, such as 46,XY,r(8)/45,XY,-8 or 46,XY/46,XY,8r patterns, due to mitotic instability and subsequent loss of the ring chromosome in some somatic cells. This loss may be an etiological mechanism for mosaic imprinting disorders. In some instances, the ring chromosome has shown duplication of the most distal bands of both arms. Maternal anesthesia and surgery during early pregnancy were considered a possible cause in one reported case. [PMC7763634, PMC1682354, PMC1013644]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for ring chromosome 8 syndrome have evolved from traditional banding cytogenetics, including R-banding, to advanced molecular techniques. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), including chromosome painting, is used to identify and characterize ring chromosomes. More recently, chromosome microarray analysis (CMA), such as aCGH + SNP array, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) or targeted massive parallel sequencing are employed to detect and characterize genomic alterations. Real-time PCR can further confirm identified aberrations. While routine banding analysis may sometimes be insufficient, these collectively enable the detection and detailed characterization of ring chromosome 8, though standardized laboratory practices are still evolving. [PMC9519620, PMC7763634, PMC1682354, PMC1013644]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Ring chromosome 8 syndrome can present with a phenotype that partially overlaps with Birk-Barel syndrome, an imprinting disorder associated with KCNK9 gene mutations. Although KCNK9 mutations may not be found in r(8) cases, the loss of a ring chromosome in some somatic cells, leading to autosomal monosomy with an inactive allele of an imprinted gene, is considered a possible etiological mechanism for mosaic imprinting disorders that could share features. [PMC7763634]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Detection of human ring chromosomes, including ring chromosome 8, can be achieved using such as banding cytogenetics, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), chromosome microarray analysis (CMA), and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) to characterize genomic alterations. Prenatal screening and diagnosis are considered to be of great significance in preventing dysplasia in children, which can be caused by chromosomal abnormalities. While current diagnostic practices for ring chromosomes face challenges in evaluating compound effects, advancements in genomic technologies aim for standardized cytogenomic diagnosis. [PMC9519620, PMC9055171]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Ring chromosomes, including ring chromosome 8, are rare, with an estimated newborn incidence of 1/50,000. They are associated with diverse clinical presentations, including intellectual disability, dysmorphology, congenital malformations, and short stature. Genetic counseling should consider the heterogeneity of clinical features, which can encompass chromosome-specific deletion/duplication syndromes and gene-related defects. Diagnostic such as banding cytogenetics, FISH, CMA, and WGS are employed for detection. Prenatal screening and diagnosis are significant for preventing dysplasia in children, and retrospective analysis of rare cases is valuable for clinical diagnosis and recurrence risk assessment. Challenges persist in evidence-based interpretation due to under-representation of clinical cases and a lack of comprehensive diagnostic analysis. [PMC9519620, PMC9055171]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Human ring chromosomes (RCs) are rare diseases with an estimated newborn incidence of 1/50,000 and an annual occurrence of 2,800 patients globally. Over the past 60 years, banding cytogenetics, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), chromosome microarray analysis (CMA), and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) has been used to detect an RC and further characterize its genomic alterations. Ring syndrome featuring sever growth retardation and variable intellectual disability has been considered as general clinical presentations for all RCs due to the cellular losses from the dynamic mosaicism of RC instability through mitosis. Cytogenomic heterogeneity ranging from simple complete RCs to complex rearranged RCs and variable RC intolerance with different relative frequencies have been observed. Clinical heterogeneity, including chromosome-specific deletion and duplication syndromes,... [PMC9519620, PMC9055171]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Ring chromosome 8 syndrome is associated with severe growth retardation and variable intellectual disability, which are considered general clinical presentations for ring chromosomes. Clinical outcomes are heterogeneous, encompassing chromosome-specific deletion and duplication syndromes, gene-related organ and tissue defects, cancer predisposition to different types of tumors, and reproductive failure. Reported cases often present with congenital microcephaly, developmental delay, dysmorphic features, muscle hypotonia, feeding problems, motor alalia, and mental retardation. However, establishing evidence-based clinico-cytogenomic correlations and recommending follow-up management is challenging due to the under-representation of clinical cases and a lack of comprehensive diagnostic analysis. [PMC9519620, PMC7763634, PMC1015827, PMC1013644]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, acquired, self-limiting, infectious disease due to the mite-borne bacteria Rickettsia akari characterized by an asymptomatic, 0.5 to 2 cm in diameter papulovesicle that typically ulcerates and forms an eschar, followed by a generalized papulovesicular rash associating variable constitutional symptoms, such as localized lymphadenopathy, fever, malaise, and headaches. Additonal symptoms may include diaphoresis, myalgia and, less frequently, rhinorrhea, pharyngitis, nausea, vomiting, splenomegaly, conjunctival hyperemia, and abdominal pain. Systemic symptoms resolve within 6-10 days.

DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Scrub typhus (ST), caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, is typically transmitted through mite bites, but vertical transmission from mother to infant remains poorly understood. This case presents a 13-day-old female neonate diagnosed with congenital ST. The infant developed severe systemic involvement, including fever, jaundice, respiratory distress, and signs of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH). Despite broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, her condition worsened. PCR and serological tests confirmed the diagnosis of ST in both the neonate and the mother, with IgM positivity indicating congenital infection. Following treatment with doxycycline, the patient's condition improved. This case adds to the growing body of evidence supporting the vertical transmission of ST and highlights the need for increased awareness of congenital ST. [PMC12337731]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, syndromic nail anomaly disease characterized by the variable triad of characteristic yellow nails, chronic respiratory manifestations, and primary lymphedema.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence and incidence rates are not known, but Yellow nail syndrome (YNS) is considered a rare condition. To date, approximately 400 cases have been reported, mainly as single case reports. The disorder affects males and females equally.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Most cases of YNS are of late onset, after 50 years of age, but the disease has also occasionally been observed in neonates and children. Patients generally complain of slowed or arrested nail growth: the nails become thickened and opaque, with yellowish or green discoloration. The cuticles are absent and the proximal nail fold swollen. Increased transverse curvature is another feature, which may lead to nail plate shedding. Both fingernails and toenails are affected, but severity may vary. Only 1/3 of the patients with nail changes have associated lymphedema and respiratory tract involvement. Nail changes may precede the development of lymphedema or respiratory manifestations by years. Lymphedema is the most consistent associated finding and usually affects the lower limbs. Respiratory conditions include cough, bronchitis, tracheobronchitis, bronchiectasis, chronic sinusitis, chronic respiratory infections, and pleural effusions. YNS may exceptionally be a paraneoplastic disorder (lung cancer).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of YNS has not been elucidated. Impaired lymphatic drainage not due to anatomical abnormalities, but rather to a functional disorder, appears to have a central role.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Nail changes in YNS are pathognomonic and the presence of typical nail alterations is an absolute requirement for the diagnosis. This is because the three main signs (i.e. nail changes, respiratory disorders, and lymphedema) may not be present all at once in the patient.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The most important nail differential diagnoses include chronic paronychia, which shares absence of the cuticle and nail thickening and discoloration, and onychomycosis of the toenails, which produces thickening and onycholysis. Onychogryphosis and acquired pachyonychia should also be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Spontaneous improvement in nail signs is reported in up to 30% of cases. Oral α‐tocopherol (vitamin E) at high doses, 600 to 1200 international units (IU) daily has been reported to be effective in about half of patients.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Some patients recover fully, but the respiratory condition and the associated symptoms are often chronic. Serious lymphedema and respiratory complications may affect quality of life and periodic follow-up is mandatory. Patients with YNS present several comorbidities other than the respiratory ones, possibly due to their older age, therefore they tipically have a lower life expectancy when compared to the general population.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The genetic basis of yellow nail syndrome is considered controversial, with its etiology remaining unknown, although familial cases suggest a genetic component. For primary lymphatic dysplasia, which can present with lower limb edema, pathogenic variants in the PIEZO1 gene have been identified. These mutations follow an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern and are associated with lymphatic malformation type 6 (LMPHM6). [PMC10238584, PMC8734484]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, multisystemic inherited metabolic disease characterized clinically, by a variable spectrum of severity, primarily comprised of psychomotor delay, myopathy and liver dysfunction. Most patients present in infancy, but the onset can be already in utero or in adult age. Hypermethioninemia is frequent, but often absent in infancy. Creatine kinase is elevated in most patients.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset: Adolescent, Adult, Antenatal, Childhood, Infancy, Neonatal

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Approximately 15 cases of S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase (SAHH) deficiency have been described to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset is typically in infancy, but may occur in utero or in adult age. In infancy, the clinical picture is typically comprised of developmental delay and hypotonia due to myopathy with markedly increased creatine kinase (CK) plasma levels, and more variably with cerebral hypomyelination, coagulation abnormalities and hepatopathy. Microcephaly, strabismus and behavioral changes are frequent. Severe cases may present in utero with fetal hydrops, congenital brain anomalies (pontine and cerebellar hypoplasia, hypoplastic corpus callosum), synthetic liver failure, respiratory insufficiency due to severe muscle weakness and death in early infancy. Specific biochemical findings include markedly increased plasma S-adenosylhomocysteine (AdoHyc) and S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet) in combination with normal or near normal total homocysteine (tHcy) and hypermethioninemia which is not always present, particularly not in early infancy. Whilst the disease is typically severe with poor developmental outcomes, the phenotype can vary from mild to asymptomatic (one report). The milder phenotype includes later disease onset and milder weakness and developmental delay. Hepatocellular carcinoma was reported in one patient and was possibly present in another.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is due to mutations in the gene encoding S-adenosylhomocysteine hydrolase, AHCY (20q11.22), an enzyme involved in methionine metabolism.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis should be suspected in patients with any combination of the clinical symptoms and in all patients with unexplained hypermethioninemia. Marked elevations of AdoMet and AdoHcy, in combination with normal or near normal tHcy are characteristic for the disease, thus plasma AdoMet and AdoHcy should be measured where there is clinical suspicion for the disease. Since these biochemical assays are poorly available, gene analysis could be a better choice. The latter , as well as enzyme assay of AdoHcy hydrolase, serves also for confirmation of the diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Based on the multiorgan clinical presentation, SAHH deficiency has a very wide differential diagnosis, with chronic myopathies, muscular dystrophies, floppy infant syndrome and group of isolated persistent hypermethioninemias being the most important.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal testing is possible if a genetic mutation has been previously identified in a family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal recessive. Where both parents are unaffected carriers of the disease, the risk of transmission to offspring is 25%. There is variable disease severity between different families. Intrafamilial variability is also possible.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Whilst there is little evidence to support specific treatment strategies, the current consensus is on a methionine-restricted diet (with methionine-free amino acid mixture supplementation), which can decrease and sometimes even normalize plasma AdoMet and AdoHcy. Subsequent close clinical and biochemical monitoring seem mandatory. Phosphatidylcholine, creatine and cysteine supplementation may be beneficial. Liver transplantation has resulted in clinical and biochemical improvement in a single case.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the severity of the disease and ranges from death during the neonatal period to survival into adulthood and possibly normal life span. Functional outcomes in surviving patients are frequently severe, with the most common impact on neurodevelopment and mobility. Long term follow-up is missing in most patients and accurate and precise prognosis is not possible. Whilst dietary management is promising in some cases, it is not effective in all (improving metabolic parameters but not functional outcomes). Evidence on liver graft is limited.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A multiple congenital anomaly characterized by a broad phenotype with Coloboma, Choanal atresia/stenosis, Cranial nerve dysfunction, and Characteristic external and inner ears (known as the major 4 C's).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CHARGE association; Coloboma-heart defects-atresia choanae-retardation of growth and development-genitourinary problems-ear abnormalities syndrome; Hall-Hittner syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Incidence is estimated to be around 1:8500 - 1:17.000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: This syndrome has high clinical variability. In the neonatal period, it can present with cyanosis due to choanal atresia or cyanotic heart disease (e.g., conotruncal malformations). Dysmorphic features include a square face, prominent forehead, nasal bridge, and facial asymmetry. Coloboma can cause vision loss, affecting the iris (including microphthalmia) but more commonly the retina. Ear anomalies, such as low-set cupped ears, triangular concha, and inner ear defects, often result in sensorineural hearing loss. Some patients have cleft lip and/or palate. Cranial nerve abnormalities commonly affect olfactory, facial, auditory, vestibular, and swallowing-related nerves (IX, X, XI). Global developmental delay, often due to sensory deficits, can lead to underestimated intellect. A distinct behavioral profile includes ADHD and anxiety, often linked to sensory processing issues. Pharyngeal/laryngeal malformations, severe GERD, and bowel dysmotility are frequent. Orthopedic issues include scoliosis and protracted shoulders. Genital anomalies (e.g., micropenis, undescended testes) result in delayed puberty. Endocrine dysfunction includes growth hormone deficiency and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, leading to arrested or absent puberty.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: CHARGE syndrome is due to heterozygous pathogenic variants (PVs) in CHD7 (8q12.2), encoding the chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is initially clinical; any of the major 4 C's criteria should prompt screening for additional anomalies. MRI of the temporal lobe may reveal absent or hypoplastic semi-circular canals. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic testing, which can include gene-targeted testing (CHD7 single-gene testing, multigene panel) and/or comprehensive genomic testing (chromosomal microarray, exome sequencing, exome array, genome sequencing) depending on the phenotype. Epigenetic signature analysis/methylation array from peripheral blood leukocytes is useful when no PV or a variant of uncertain clinical significance has been identified.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: 22q11.2 deletion/duplication syndromes, 1q21.1 and, 5q11.2 microdeletion, VACTERL/VATER association, Kabuki syndrome, renal coloboma syndrome, cat-eye, and Joubert, BOR, Pallister-Hall, Mowat-Wilson, Feingold, Abruzzo-Erickson, Kallmann, TRRAP-related disorder, Mullegama-Klein-Martinez and isotretinoin syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Once a CHD7 PV has been identified in an affected family member, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is autosomal dominant and typically caused by a de novo PV. The empiric recurrence risk to siblings of a proband is approximately 1-2%, considering potential parental germline mosaicism. Many affected individuals cannot reproduce, but in rare cases, the PV is inherited from a heterozygous parent; in which case, the recurrence risk is 50%. There is no phenotype-genotype correlation and the severity can vary widely within a family. Molecular genetic testing is recommended for the parents of a proband to confirm their genetic status and provide reliable counseling.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management requires a multi-disciplinary coordinated approach as this condition affects most organ systems. Collaboration between medical, surgical and anesthesia teams, therapists and deaf blindness specialists is essential. If feasible, multiple procedures should be performed under one anesthesia to reduce risks.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Mortality is highest during the neonatal period due to the combination of cyanotic heart disease, TEF choanal atresia. apnea, and/or aspiration. Beyond this neonatal period, morbidity is often associated with post-operative airway events.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Malignant atrophic papulosis (MAP) is a rare, chronic, thrombo-obliterative vasculopathy characterized by papular skin lesions with central porcelain-white atrophy and a surrounding teleangiectatic rim. Systemic lesions may affect the gastrointestinal tract and the central nervous system (CNS) and are potentially lethal.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): MAP; Cutaneo-muco-intestinal syndrome; Papulosis atrophicans maligna

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Less than 200 cases have been described in the literature.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: MAP onset occurs in adults aged 20-50 with skin lesions that appear initially as small erythematous papules, predominantly on the trunk and the upper extremities. Over several days, the center of the lesions sinks and develops a characteristic morphology: 0.5-1 cm wide papules with an atrophic porcelain-white center and an erythematous, teleangiectatic rim. This condition is chronic and lesions persist over years, often throughout life. Face, scalp, palms of hands and soles of feet are rarely involved. In the systemic variant, which may develop simultaneously or even years after cutaneous symptoms, patients may present with multiple limited infarcts of the intestine, with abdominal pain, bleeding and diarrhea, and/or of the CNS, with cerebrovascular accidents (in rare cases, medullary). It may more rarely manifest as pericarditis or in other organs such as the lungs, presenting as pleuritis. Ocular involvement, which affects the eyelids, conjuctiva, retina, sclera and the choroid plexus, as well as the development of diplopia and ophthalmoplegia (as secondary side effects of the neurologic involvement), has also been described.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiopathogenesis of the disease remains unknown. Hypotheses implicating vasculitis, coagulopathy or a primary dysfunction of endothelial cells have been proposed. Many patients have been reported to have defects in blood coagulation.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based primarily on the cutaneous clinical picture that is nearly pathognomonic. In early stages, histology of lesions may reveal a superficial and deep perivascular lymphocytic infiltration with distinct mucin deposition. Later a wedge-shaped connective tissue necrosis in the deep dermis, due to a thrombotic occlusion of the small arteries and sparse lymphocytes, occurs. More developed lesions show prominent changes in the dermoepidermal junction, with atrophy of the epidermis and an area of sclerosis in the papillary dermis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The histology of early lesions resembles cutaneous lupus erythematosus. More developed lesions can imitate lichen sclerosus.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: A genetic predisposition with an autosomal dominant trait has been suggested.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Therapeutic efforts with anticoagulants and compounds that facilitate blood perfusion, such as acetylosalicylic acid, pentoxifylline, dipyridamole, ticlodipine and heparin have achieved a partial regression of skin lesions in some individual cases. As all patients may potentially develop the systemic, life-threatening variant, an annual follow-up is mandatory. A clinical inspection of the skin should be combined with additional examinations including brain magnetic resonance tomography, gastroscopy, colonoscopy, X-ray of the chest and abdominal ultrasound, in order to assess the long-term prognosis. No effective treatment for the systemic manifestations has been established, however, subcutaneous treprostinil has been tested successfully in one case with intestinal and CNS manifestations.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Idiopathic, monosymptomatic, cutaneous presentations are benign, however, systemic manifestations can develop years after the occurrence of skin lesions. Systemic manifestations are progressive and may lead to serious complications: bowel perforation and peritonitis as well as thrombosis of the cerebral arteries or massive cerebral hemorrhage, meningitis, encephalitis, radiculopathy and myelitis which have been reported to be lethal in around 50% of patients within 2-3 years.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis (HGF) is a rare benign, slowly progressive, non-inflammatory fibrous hyperplasia of the maxillary and mandibular gingivae that generally occurs with the eruption of the permanent (or more rarely the primary) dentition or even at birth. It presents as a localized or generalized, smooth or nodular overgrowth of the gingival tissues of varying severity. It can be isolated, with autosomal dominant inheritance, or as part of a syndrome.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Autosomal dominant gingival fibromatosis; Autosomal dominant gingival hyperplasia; Hereditary gingival hyperplasia

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Hereditary gingival fibromatosis (HGF) is consistently described as a rare or uncommon genetic condition in clinical practice. It is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern and is known for its considerable genetic diversity. Multiple genes and loci have been associated with HGF, including SOS1, REST, ZNF862, TBC1D2B, KREMEN2, and KCNQ1. The condition is considered a heterogeneous group of disorders, with variants in different genes contributing to its pathogenesis. [PMC11354241, PMC11403129, PMC8856651, PMC8474844, PMC6347941]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Spinocerebellar ataxia with axonal neuropathy type 1
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Spinocerebellar ataxia with axonal neuropathy type 1 is a rare, genetic neurological disorder characterized by a late childhood onset of slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia. Initial manifestations include weakness and atrophy of distal limb muscles, areflexia and loss of pain, vibration and touch sensations in upper and lower extremities. Gaze nystagmus, cerebellar dysarthria, peripheral neuropathy, stepagge gait and pes cavus develop as disease progresses. Cerebellar atrophy (especially of the vermis) is present in all affected individuals. Additional reported manifestations include seizures, mild brain atrophy, mild hypercholesterolemia and borderline hypoalbuminemia.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Spinocerebellar ataxia with axonal neuropathy type 1 (SCAN1) is an extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder. Previously, only a single missense variant (p.His493Arg) in the TDP1 gene had been reported, found in three Arab families with a possible common founder effect. A recent study identified a novel missense variant (p.His478Tyr) in a consanguineous Pakistani family, further expanding the known genetic and clinical spectrum of this condition. [PMC11584435]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Spinocerebellar ataxia with axonal neuropathy type 1 (SCAN1) is an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by cerebellar ataxia and axonal neuropathy. One reported patient presented with additional clinical features, notably a congenital onset of the disease, which was distinct from those previously described in other families. The condition is classified among cerebellar ataxias with peripheral neuropathy. [PMC11584435]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Spinocerebellar ataxia with axonal neuropathy type 1 (SCAN1) is an extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder. It is caused by mutations in the tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase 1 (TDP1) gene. A previously reported missense variant (p.His493Arg) was found in three Arab families. A novel missense variant (p.His478Tyr) in exon 13 of the TDP1 gene has also been identified in a Pakistani family, expanding the known mutation spectrum associated with SCAN1. [PMC11584435]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Spinocerebellar ataxia with axonal neuropathy type 1 (SCAN1) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase 1 (TDP1) gene. Diagnostic involve genetic testing, such as whole exome sequencing, to identify pathogenic variants in the TDP1 gene. For example, a novel missense variant (p.His478Tyr) was identified using whole exome sequencing. Sanger sequencing is subsequently performed to verify the autosomal recessive segregation of identified variants within affected families. [PMC11584435]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Ataxia with oculomotor apraxia type 1 (AOA1) should be considered in the differential diagnosis. This autosomal-recessive neurodegenerative disorder typically presents in childhood with slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia, followed by oculomotor apraxia and a severe primary motor peripheral axonal motor neuropathy. AOA1 is caused by bi-allelic mutations in the APTX gene. [PMC4593195]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Spinocerebellar ataxia with axonal neuropathy type 1 (SCAN1) is an extremely rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the TDP1 gene. Genetic counseling should emphasize the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, meaning affected individuals inherit a mutated gene from each carrier parent. Previously, a p.His493Arg missense variant was identified, with a possible founder effect in Arab families. A novel p.His478Tyr missense variant has also been reported in a consanguineous Pakistani family, highlighting the increased risk in such unions. Genetic testing, including whole exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing for variant verification, can confirm the diagnosis and aid in family planning. [PMC11584435]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal trisomy 7p is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from the partial duplication of the short arm of chromosome 7, with highly variable phenotype typically characterized by severe to profound psychomotor delay, intellectual disability, dysmorphic features (incl. dolichocephaly, microbrachycephaly, high and/or broad forehead, large anterior fontanel, hypertelorism, downslanting palpebral fissures, low-set, dysplastic ears, low, broad and prominent nasal bridge, abnormal palate, micro-/retrognathia), and hypotonia. Cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, skeletal and urogenital anomalies have commonly been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Distal duplication 7p syndrome, characterized by a partial trisomy of the short arm of chromosome 7, was initially described in a single family. The unbalanced translocation was identified in one family member, with five others carrying the balanced form. This familial translocation is considered a rare telomeric attachment, previously undescribed in humans, suggesting the condition is exceptionally rare. [PMC1013579]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Prominent clinical features of distal duplication 7p syndrome include general mental and motor retardation. Affected individuals may also present with microbrachycephaly, along with cardiac and oral abnormalities. [PMC1013579]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal duplication 7p syndrome is characterized by a partial trisomy of the short arm of chromosome 7. This chromosomal abnormality has been observed in association with a familial translocation between chromosome 7 and chromosome 22. The unbalanced form of this translocation, resulting in the partial trisomy, was found in affected individuals, while other family members carried the balanced form. [PMC1013579]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Subchromosomal deletions and duplications could currently be detected by noninvasive preliminary screening (NIPS). However, NIPS is a screening test that requires further diagnosis. Here a fetus with an autosomal abnormality revealed by NIPS and conventional karyotype combined with copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq) confirmed the fetus with an unbalanced translocation. Patient concern: This was the fourth pregnancy of a 30-year-old woman who underwent 2 spontaneous abortions and gave birth to a child with a normal phenotype. The woman and her husband were healthy and nonconsanguineous. NIPS indicated a repeat of about 19-Mb fragment at the region of 16q22.1-q22.4 at 17-week gestation. Diagnoses: The combination of traditional karyotype and CNV-seq could better locate the abnormal chromosomal region and further identify the source of fetal chromosomal abnormalities.... [PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Subchromosomal deletions and duplications could currently be detected by noninvasive preliminary screening (NIPS). However, NIPS is a screening test that requires further diagnosis. Here a fetus with an autosomal abnormality revealed by NIPS and conventional karyotype combined with copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq) confirmed the fetus with an unbalanced translocation. Patient concern: This was the fourth pregnancy of a 30-year-old woman who underwent 2 spontaneous abortions and gave birth to a child with a normal phenotype. The woman and her husband were healthy and nonconsanguineous. NIPS indicated a repeat of about 19-Mb fragment at the region of 16q22.1-q22.4 at 17-week gestation. Diagnoses: The combination of traditional karyotype and CNV-seq could better locate the abnormal chromosomal region and further identify the source of fetal chromosomal abnormalities.... [PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Distal duplication 7p syndrome can be associated with familial translocations, such as a 7p;22q translocation, where a balanced form may be present in multiple family members. An unbalanced translocation, leading to the duplication, can be inherited from a parent carrying such a balanced rearrangement. Prenatal screening like noninvasive preliminary screening (NIPS) can indicate chromosomal abnormalities, which then require further diagnostic confirmation using conventional karyotype and copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq). [PMC7899829, PMC1013579]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare primary bone dysplasia characterized by global developmental delay, hypotonia, ossification anomalies of the cranial vault, abnormalities of the long bones due to defective remodeling, thoracic deformity, and progressive osteopenia. Dysmorphic craniofacial features include microcephaly, hypertelorism, narrow mouth, cleft palate, and micrognathia.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Aim of this case report is to describe oro-facial abnormalities in a patient affected by Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome, a rare autism syndrome, with not well described dental and cranial malformations. Helsmoortel-Van der Aa Syndrome is a rare autosomal genetic syndrome causing mental impairment and autism, craniofacial dysmorphism, chest deformity and multiple organs dysfunction. Oro-facial involvement in Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome has not been thoroughly described yet. The present article reports a case of a 9 years old male patient affected by Helsmoortel-Van der Aa Syndrome, presenting with oral breathing typical facies, high arched palate, II class and dental crowding. The patient teething was adequate to his age. The enamel of incisors and molars showed demineralization areas and dark spots, a clinical picture consistent with molar incisor hypomineralization syndrome. These... [PMC8430785]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Helsmoortel-Van der Aa syndrome, an autosomal genetic syndrome, presents with mental impairment, autism, craniofacial dysmorphism, chest deformity, and multiple organ dysfunction, along with oro-dental manifestations including enamel demineralization and hypomineralization. Congenital insensitivity to pain with anhidrosis (CIPA), caused by NTRK1 mutations, also involves mental retardation, nasal malformation, submucous cleft palate, and dental abnormalities such as hypomineralization and dentin hypoplasia. Both conditions share features of psychomotor developmental delay and craniofacial/dental anomalies, which may be relevant for differential diagnosis. [PMC8430785, PMC3682965]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Poliomyelitis is a viral infection caused by any of three serotypes of human poliovirus, which is part of the family of enteroviruses.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Progress in global poliomyelitis eradication, since its beginning in 1988, has been remarkable. In 1988, 125 countries were endemic for poliomyelitis and an estimated 1000 children were being paralyzed every day by wild poliovirus. By the end of 2003, six polio-endemic countries remained (Afghanistan, Egypt, India, Niger, Nigeria, Pakistan), and less than 3 children per day were being paralyzed by the poliovirus. The Global Poliomyelitis Eradication Initiative is ongoing. There remain only 4 endemic countries (Pakistan, Afghanistan, India, and Nigeria) and just 2000 reported cases globally in 2006.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: It primarily affects children under the age of 5. Generally the infection is limited to the grastrointestinal tract and nasopharynx and is often asymptomatic. The central nervous system, primarily the spinal cord, may be affected, leading to rapidly progressive paralysis. Motor neurons are mainly affected. Encephalitis may also occur.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Transmission is mainly person-to-person, principally through the fecal-oral route. The virus replicates in the nervous system and particularly affects motor neurons in the anterior horn of the spinal cord (`polio' means `gray').
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Poliomyelitis must be distinguished from other paralytic conditions by isolation of virus from stool.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Prevention is the only cure for paralytic poliomyelitis. Two vaccines against poliomyelitis are available: an inactive injectable vaccine and a live attenuated vaccine that is taken orally. Europe was certified as polio-free in June 2002 and immunization and disease surveillance continue to ensure the region remains polio-free

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare form of localised hypertrichosis characterized by hair growth near the laryngeal prominence during childhood.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Isolated anterior cervical hypertrichosis is a very rare form of primary localized hypertrichosis. As of 2016, a total of 33 patients with this condition had been reported in the literature. The condition frequently presents as an isolated defect, accounting for 70% of reported cases. Sporadic cases have been observed, with some patients having no familial history of similar cases. [PMC4829167]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Isolated anterior cervical hypertrichosis is a very rare form of primary localized hypertrichosis, characterized by a tuft of terminal hair on the anterior neck, specifically just above the laryngeal prominence. While its etiology remains unknown, it frequently presents as an isolated defect in 70% of reported cases. Although it can be associated with other abnormalities, specific common associations are not detailed. One reported case involved a 15-year-old female who developed the condition five years prior. [PMC4829167]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Anterior cervical hypertrichosis is a very rare form of primary localized hypertrichosis. It consists of a tuft of terminal hair on the anterior neck just above the laryngeal prominence. The etiology is still unknown. In this article, we reported a 15-year-old female patient who presented to our clinic with a complaint of hypertrichosis on the anterior aspect of the neck for the last five years. Her past medical history revealed no pathology except for vesicoureteral reflux. On the basis of clinical presentation, our patient was diagnosed with anterior cervical hypertrichosis and she was considered to be a sporadic case due to lack of other similar cases in familial history. To date, 33 patients with anterior cervical hypertrichosis have been reported. Anterior cervical hypertrichosis can be associated with other abnormalities, but it frequently presents as an isolated defect (70%). The... [PMC4829167]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of anterior cervical hypertrichosis is primarily based on clinical presentation. The condition is characterized by the presence of a tuft of terminal hair on the anterior neck, situated just above the laryngeal prominence. It is considered a very rare form of primary localized hypertrichosis, and frequently presents as an isolated defect. [PMC4829167]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Anterior cervical hypertrichosis is a very rare form of primary localized hypertrichosis. It consists of a tuft of terminal hair on the anterior neck just above the laryngeal prominence. The etiology is still unknown. In this article, we reported a 15-year-old female patient who presented to our clinic with a complaint of hypertrichosis on the anterior aspect of the neck for the last five years. Her past medical history revealed no pathology except for vesicoureteral reflux. On the basis of clinical presentation, our patient was diagnosed with anterior cervical hypertrichosis and she was considered to be a sporadic case due to lack of other similar cases in familial history. To date, 33 patients with anterior cervical hypertrichosis have been reported. Anterior cervical hypertrichosis can be associated with other abnormalities, but it frequently presents as an isolated defect (70%). The... [PMC4829167]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The etiology of anterior cervical hypertrichosis is currently unknown. Cases are often considered sporadic, as observed in patients without a familial history of the condition. While it can be associated with other abnormalities, it frequently presents as an isolated defect. Due to the unknown etiology and sporadic nature, specific genetic counseling regarding inheritance patterns is not available. [PMC4829167]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic disease characterized by generalized joint laxity leading to recurrent dislocation of major joints, such as the hip (often with congenital hip dislocation), shoulder, elbow, or patella. Patients often experience muscle and joint pain (sometimes with effusion) and may develop degenerative joint changes at a relatively early age. Skin abnormalities are absent.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Familial joint instability syndrome; Familial joint laxity; Joint instability syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Familial articular hypermobility syndrome, often linked to the hypermobility type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (hEDS), is considered the most common type of EDS and the most common heritable connective tissue disorder. An EDS diagnosis is most prevalent in white females aged 0-30 years old, with a prevalence of 259.6 per 100,000. Joint hyperlaxity is prevalent in hand clinics, accounting for 6% of new patients, which is twice the expected rate, suggesting it is likely underdiagnosed. Patients presenting with hyperlaxity in hand clinics are typically younger, with an average age of 37.1 years, and often receive their first musculoskeletal specialist evaluation in this setting. [PMC12209458, PMC12146307, PMC7021119]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic syndrome with limb duplication, polydactyly, syndactyly, and/or hyperphalangy characterized by duplication anomalies such as triphalangeal thumbs, phalangeal duplication of other digits, and polydactyly, associated with highly variable combinations of ectrodactyly, brachydactyly, and syndactyly of hands and/or feet. Severe nail dysplasia or absence of nails is also observed.

DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Tibial hemimelia is a rare congenital limb deficiency which is characterised by a hypoplastic/aplastic tibia. It actually represents a spectrum of anomalies, ranging from mild hypoplasia of the tibia to total absence of the tibia. Several classifications based on radiological description exist in the literature. The tibial hemimelia is usually described with preaxial mirror polydactyly, split hand/foot syndrome-ectrodactyly, polydactyly-triphalangeal thumb syndrome (Werner syndrome) and micromelia-trigonal brachycephaly syndrome. a child with unclassified tibial hemimelia. The child had right incomplete tibial hemimelia with bifid tibia, left complete tibial hemimelia, bilateral split hands and left split foot. This is the first report of the bifid tibia in the literature. [PMC5015155]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by intrauterine growth retardation (IUGR), postnatal failure to thrive, severe feeding difficulties, microcephaly/trigonocephaly, facial dysmorphism, a recognizable upper limb posture and severe developmental delay. The upper limb posture consists of internal rotation of the shoulders, flexion of the elbows, ulnar deviation of wrists and/or metacarpophalangeal joints.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): BOS syndrome; Bohring syndrome; C-like syndrome; Oberklaid-Danks syndrome; Opitz trigonocephaly-like syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date 46 cases have been described, less than half of which were molecularly confirmed as carrying a heterozygous pathogenic variation in ASXL1.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Bohring-Opitz syndrome (BOS) is characterized by IUGR, severe neonatal feeding difficulties, and microcephaly/trigonocephaly, cleft lip/palate and hirsutism. Facial dysmorphism is characterized by glabellar/frontal nevus flammeus, synophrys, proptosis, hypertelorism, depressed wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares, full cheeks, and micrognathia. The posture of upper limbs, common in all patients at birth, is characterized by internal rotation of the shoulders, flexion of the elbows, ulnar deviation of wrists and/or metacarpophalangeal joints. Most patients exhibit truncal hypotonia and hypertonic extremities at birth. Seizures and obstructive sleep apnea/sleep disturbances can occur during infancy. Other abnormalities can involve the following organs: brain (corpus callosum defects), eyes (retinal and optic nerve abnormalities, high myopia), heart (bradycardia, septal defect), gastrointestinal tract (cycling emesis, gastroesophageal reflux disease) as well as the joints (contractures, congenital hip/radial head dislocations).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: BOS is due to a heterozygous pathogenic variation in ASXL1 (20q11.21), which acts as a chromatin modulator.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Clinical diagnosis can be confirmed by sequencing of ASXL1 or by intellectual disability-related next generation sequencing panel including the gene. If sequencing is negative, multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification may be used.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: A BOS-like phenotype related to KLHL7 has been described which has several features in common with BOS (including a similar upper limb posture) but is clinically distinguished by the absence of trigonocephaly, synophrys, high myopia and cycling emesis. Other diseases sharing several features with BOS but lacking the BOS posture include C syndrome, Shashi-Pena syndrome, Bainbridge-Ropers syndrome and Cornelia de Lange syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible on chorionic villi or amniotic fluid where the pathogenic variant has been previously identified in the family. Prenatal genetic counseling should therefore be offered to parents of patients with ASXL1 variants to discuss the genetic risks and reproductive options.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is autosomal dominant; however, most cases are de novo. Genetic counseling should be offered to all at-risk couples since germinal mosaicism may occur.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management requires an early multidisciplinary approach. Seizures are drug-responsive. An increased risk of Wilms tumor is reported. An abdominal ultrasound every 3-4 months is suggested in the first 8 years of life.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The rate of infant mortality is high. In patients who survive infancy, feeding difficulties and recurrent infections become less severe. Older patients may have some purposeful limb movements, however, their resting state returns to BOS posture. Intellectual disability ranges from severe to profound.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Familial developmental dysphasia is a severe form of developmental verbal apraxia characterized by a deficit in spontaneous speech, writing, grammatical judgment and repetition, defective articulation, moderate to severe degree of dyspraxia, a reduced use of consonant clusters, and comprehension delay. Hearing and intelligence are normal.

Mazabraud syndrome is a rare primary bone dysplasia characterized by the association of fibrous dysplasia with intramuscular myxomas. Fibrous dysplasia (usually polyostotic, sometimes monostotic) occurs during the growth period and can be asymptomatic or can present with pain, skeletal deformities or fractures while intramuscular myxoma, associated with polyostotic fibrous dysplasia is usually multifocal, typically occuring in the vicinity of skeletal lesions, and presents in adulthood as a painless soft-tissue mass (most commonly in the thigh). Although it is a benign condition, local recurrences of myxomas after incomplete excision and malignant transformation of a fibrous dysplastic lesion into osteogenic sarcoma have been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Mazabraud syndrome is a rare to extremely rare condition, with less than 100 cases reported worldwide to date. A review of the international literature in 2009 referred to 67 cases. The syndrome mostly occurs in women, with females twice as likely to be affected as males. It is characterized by fibrous dysplasia, most commonly in the femur and pelvis, and intramuscular myxomas, often multiple (in over 70% of cases) and frequently found in the quadriceps muscle, with lower limbs being the most affected. [PMC12256957, PMC6166146, PMC4527122, PMC4294916, PMC2903125]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Mazabraud syndrome is characterized by the coexistence of fibrous dysplasia and intramuscular myxomas, with accurate diagnosis relying on imaging and histopathological evaluation. Radiologic imaging, including MRI and ultrasound, plays a crucial role in identifying and assessing both the bone lesions and intramuscular myxomas, as well as monitoring disease progression. Histopathological confirmation, often obtained through percutaneous or bone biopsy, is critical for confirming the diagnosis of intramuscular myxoma and fibrous dysplasia. Differential diagnosis may involve other tests, such as electrophoresis of proteins, to exclude conditions like multiple myeloma. Long-term follow-up with imaging is also essential to monitor changes in lesions and detect potential malignant transformation. [PMC12256957, PMC12064253, PMC4527122, PMC4294916]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Mazabraud syndrome, defined by fibrous dysplasia and intramuscular myxomas, requires careful differential diagnosis. The bone lesions of fibrous dysplasia, especially when polyostotic or locally aggressive with cortical destruction and soft tissue extension, can mimic malignant conditions such as multiple myeloma or bone metastases from primary cancers like thyroid carcinoma. McCune-Albright syndrome, which also features polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, must be considered, though it is distinguished by additional features like café-au-lait skin pigmentations and endocrine dysfunction. Isolated intramuscular myxomas, without associated fibrous dysplasia, also represent a distinct entity. [PMC12064253, PMC6166146, PMC4527122, PMC4294916]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of Mazabraud syndrome typically involves conservative approaches for symptomatic fibrous dysplasia. Intramuscular myxomas are often treated with surgical excision, with early wide excision suggested due to potential late recurrences, though some patients may opt against surgery. For locally aggressive fibrous dysplasia, surgical treatment, zoledronic acid, or observation have been reported. Crucially, close and long-term follow-up, including radiologic imaging, is essential to monitor disease progression, assess changes in lesions, and detect any potential malignant transformation. [PMC12256957, PMC12064253, PMC6166146, PMC4527122, PMC4294916]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Mazabraud syndrome involves generally benign fibrous dysplasia (FD) and intramuscular myxomas, but long-term prognosis requires careful monitoring. Patients can develop additional myxomas over decades, which may recur locally or symmetrically and reach significant size. While myxomas typically remain benign, malignant transformation of fibrous dysplasia into osteosarcoma or fibrosarcoma has been reported, especially in cases associated with McCune-Albright syndrome. Therefore, close and long-term follow-up is essential to monitor the progression of lesions and detect any potential malignant transformation. [PMC12256957, PMC6166146, PMC12201371]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare ectodermal dysplasia syndrome with bone abnormalities characterized by onychodystrophy; anomalies of the lower jaw, oral vestibule and dentition; post-axialpolydactyly; moderately restricted growth with short limbs; and normal intelligence. Although it closely resembles Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, an allelic disorder and another type of ciliopathy, WAD is usually a milder disease without the presence of heart abnormalities and is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Curry-Hall syndrome; Weyers acrodental dysostosis; Weyers acrofacial dysostosis

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: We have studied a four-generation family with features of Weyers acrofacial dysostosis, in which the proband has a more severe phenotype, resembling Ellis-van Creveld syndrome. Weyers acrofacial dysostosis is an autosomal dominant condition with dental anomalies, nail dystrophy, postaxial polydactyly, and mild short stature. Ellis-van Creveld syndrome is a similar condition, with autosomal recessive inheritance and the additional features of disproportionate dwarfism, thoracic dysplasia, and congenital heart disease. Linkage and haplotype analysis determined that the disease locus in this pedigree resides on chromosome 4p16, distal to the genetic marker D4S3007 and within a 17-cM region flanking the genetic locus D4S2366. This region includes the Ellis-van Creveld syndrome locus, which previously was reported to map within a 3-cM region between genetic markers D4S2957 and D4S827. Either... [PMC1716089]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Weyers acrofacial dysostosis is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by a specific set of features. These include dental anomalies, nail dystrophy, and postaxial polydactyly. Individuals with this condition also typically present with mild short stature. In some cases, a more severe phenotype resembling Ellis-van Creveld syndrome has been observed. [PMC1716089]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Weyers acrofacial dysostosis is an autosomal dominant condition. The disease locus has been mapped to chromosome 4p16, residing within a 17-cM region flanking the genetic locus D4S2366, distal to D4S3007. This region also encompasses the locus for Ellis-van Creveld syndrome. It is hypothesized that Weyers acrofacial dysostosis and Ellis-van Creveld syndrome may be allelic conditions, with mutations in the same gene, or that their genes are closely located. This raises the possibility that Weyers acrofacial dysostosis is the heterozygous expression of a mutation that, in homozygous form, causes the autosomal recessive Ellis-van Creveld syndrome. [PMC1716089]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Weyers acrofacial dysostosis is based on characteristic clinical features including dental anomalies, nail dystrophy, postaxial polydactyly, and mild short stature. Genetic studies have linked the disease locus to chromosome 4p16, specifically distal to the genetic marker D4S3007 and within a 17-cM region flanking D4S2366. This region also contains the Ellis-van Creveld syndrome locus, suggesting that these conditions may be allelic or caused by mutations in closely located genes. [PMC1716089]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Ellis-van Creveld syndrome (EvC) is a key differential diagnosis for Weyers acrofacial dysostosis. Both conditions share features such as dental anomalies, nail dystrophy, and postaxial polydactyly. However, EvC is an autosomal recessive condition characterized by additional features including disproportionate dwarfism, thoracic dysplasia, and congenital heart disease, whereas Weyers acrofacial dysostosis is autosomal dominant with mild short stature. Genetic analysis suggests that both conditions map to chromosome 4p16, raising the possibility that they are allelic or that Weyers acrofacial dysostosis represents the heterozygous expression of a mutation that, in homozygous form, causes EvC. [PMC1716089]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Weyers acrofacial dysostosis is an autosomal dominant condition, implying a 50% chance of transmission to offspring from an affected parent. Research suggests the possibility that Weyers acrofacial dysostosis may be the heterozygous expression of a mutation that, in homozygous form, causes the autosomal recessive Ellis-van Creveld syndrome. [PMC1716089]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare multisystem disorder characterized by congenital cataracts, glaucoma, intellectual disabilities, seizures, postnatal growth retardation and renal tubular dysfunction with chronic renal failure.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Lowe disease; Lowe oculo-cerebro-renal syndrome; Lowe syndrome; OCRL; Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-biphosphate 5-phosphatase deficiency; Lowe oculo-cerebro-renal dystrophy; Lowe oculocerebrorenal dystrophy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated prevalence is 1/500,000 and males are almost exclusively affected.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Oculocerebrorenal syndrome of Lowe (OCRL) is a congenital disorder characterized by ocular abnormalities (bilateral congenital discoid cataracts, glaucoma with or without buphthalmos, strabismus, hypermetropia and corneal and conjunctival cheloids), neurological involvement (developmental delay, seizures, hypotonia present at birth typically with absence of deep tendon reflexes), stereotypic behavior (temper tantrums, aggressiveness and obsessive compulsive behavior), postnatal growth retardation, mild to severe intellectual disability (mean IQ 40-50), stereotypic hand movements, renal dysfunction of the Fanconi type (proximal tubular acidosis; phosphate wasting leading to renal rickets, osteomalacia and pathological fractures) and progressive decline in kidney function leading to end-stage renal failure in adulthood. Subtle cataracts are obligate findings in female carriers after puberty. Other clinical manifestations include facial dysmorphism (frontal bossing, deep-set eyes, chubby cheeks, fair complexion), destructive teno-synovitis in older patients, short stature, mucocutaneous anomalies (eruptive vellus hair cysts, tricoepithiloma, excess skin folds and eruption cysts in oral cavity), dental malformations, cryptorchidism and bleeding tendency due to platelet dysfunction.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: OCRL results from mutations in OCRL (Xq25), leading to phosphatidylinositol (4,5) bisphosphate accumulation, defective membrane trafficking and disturbed actin cytoskeleton remodeling. In the kidney, disturbed endosomal trafficking impairs protein reabsorption and digestion in the proximal tubules. In the eye, abnormal actin remodeling leads to disorganization of embryonic lens epithelium and abnormal development of the trabecular meshwork that regulates aqueous humor outflow from the eye.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of OCRL is based on specific ophthalmologic, neurologic and renal abnormalities. Laboratory findings reveal features of renal Fanconi syndrome and elevations in plasma creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase and transaminases levels. The presence of low-molecular weight proteinuria is the first renal abnormality and is invariably present after birth. Brain imaging reveals brain atrophy, delayed myelination, pachygyrias, hydrocephalus as well as white matter lesions suggestive of periventricular leukomalacia. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic screening of OCRL.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Dent disease type 2 (an allelic disease with a milder phenotype), congenital infections (such as congenital rubella syndrome), Nance-Horan syndrome, Smith-Lemli-Opitz syndrome, muscle-eye-brain disease, cystinosis and peroxisomal disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal testing is possible and unless the mutation in the family has been defined previously, assay of enzyme activity is preferred. Elevated maternal serum and amniotic fluid alpha-fetoprotein or presence of cataract on ultrasound may be used for prenatal screening.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is X-linked and genetic counseling is recommended for affected families. If the mother is a carrier, 50% of her sons will inherit the disease whereas 50% of her daughters will be carriers. De novo mutations are reported in 30% of affected males.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment of OCRL includes early cataract extraction to avoid amblyopia, glaucoma control by either medications or surgery and postoperatively, eye glasses. Contact lenses are contraindicated. Nasogastric tube feedings or feeding gastrostomy may be required. Treatment also includes physical and speech therapy, use of drugs (clomipramine, paroxetine and risperidone) for behavioral problems, correction of tubular dysfunction by alkali supplements, phosphate, potassium and water. Potassium citrate may be useful to prevent nephrocalcinosis.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Quality of life depends on extent of neurological and renal manifestations. Life span rarely exceeds 40 years and death occurs between 20-40 years, as a consequence of renal disease, hypotonia, increased susceptibility to infectious disease, seizures and sudden death. Glaucoma is often difficult to control.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare vaginal malformation characterized by congenital uterovaginal outflow tract obstruction due to failure of the urogenital sinus to form the caudal aspect of the vagina, which is then replaced by fibrous tissue. The malformation may occur as an isolated developmental defect or in association with other anomalies, such as cervical agenesis, imperforate hymen, and bicornuate bicervical uterus. Presenting signs and symptoms include primary amenorrhea, cyclic pelvic pain, abdominal pain, dyspareunia, pelvic mass, menstrual disorder, and periodic fever.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Vaginal atresia is a rare congenital obstructive disease of the female reproductive tract, characterized by the absence or underdevelopment of the vaginal canal due to a failure of canalization. It presents with various clinical manifestations, most commonly primary amenorrhea and cyclical lower abdominal or pelvic pain in adolescent girls. Other signs can include a pelvic mass, difficulty with bowel movements, or inability to perform intercourse. The condition can be distal, complete, or involve a transverse vaginal septum, and may be complicated by hematometrocolpus, hematosalpinx, or hydrometrocolpos. It is frequently associated with other congenital anomalies, including cervical dysplasia or agenesis, megacolon, caudal regression syndrome, VACTERL association, Winter syndrome (renal hypoplasia, hearing loss), persistent urogenital sinus, and septate uterus. Diagnosis relies on clinical examination, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Secondary vaginal atresia, though rare, can occur following events like caesarean section due to postpartum genital tract adhesions. [PMC12303453, PMC11350548, PMC10896708, PMC8360086, PMC7907872]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Vaginal atresia can be congenital, resulting from a failure of canalization in the urogenital sinus. It is also associated with several syndromes and conditions, including Caudal Regression Syndrome, Winter syndrome (an autosomal recessive condition involving renal and middle ear anomalies), VACTERL association (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb defects), and McKusick-Kaufmann syndrome (characterized by hydrocolpos, polydactyly, imperforate anus, and heart defects). Persistent urogenital sinus and cloaca can also lead to distal vaginal atresia. Secondary vaginal atresia is a rare postpartum complication, potentially caused by trauma, adhesions, or events such as severe dystocia, obstructed labor, frequent pelvic examinations, or caesarean section. [PMC10896708, PMC7907872, PMC7680234, PMC7175489, PMC6250493]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of vaginal atresia typically involves clinical examination, which may reveal the absence of a vaginal opening, a vaginal cup, or a pelvic bulge. Imaging techniques are crucial, with ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) commonly employed to assess the extent of atresia, identify associated anomalies like hematometrocolpus, and guide surgical planning. Ultrasound can confirm the pelvic origin and cystic nature of masses, while MRI helps delineate uterine cavity expansion and atresia sites. In complex or misdiagnosed cases, diagnostic laparoscopy, hysteroscopy, or intraoperative confirmation may be necessary. Antenatal ultrasound can also detect signs such as fetal ascites or hydrometrocolpos. [PMC12303453, PMC10896708, PMC8360086, PMC7907872, PMC7680234]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Vaginal atresia can be a feature of several congenital anomalies and syndromes. It is associated with Caudal Regression Syndrome, which involves maldevelopment of the caudal body half and genitourinary system. Winter syndrome is characterized by distal vaginal atresia, renal hypoplasia, and conductive hearing loss, typically presenting with primary amenorrhea and cyclic pelvic pain. The VACTERL association, encompassing vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb defects, can also co-occur with distal vaginal atresia. Other differential considerations include cervical agenesis combined with septate uterus, persistent urogenital sinus and cloaca leading to hydrometrocolpos, and transverse vaginal septum with cervical dysgenesis. McKusick-Kaufmann syndrome is characterized by hydrocolpos due to vaginal atresia, postaxial polydactyly, imperforate anus, and congenital heart defects, with some overlap with Pallister-Hall syndrome. [PMC10896708, PMC7175489, PMC6250493, PMC5779782, PMC3931976]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of conditions involving vaginal atresia can be made via ultrasonography. In one case, a primigravida at 32 weeks of gestation showed ultrasonographic evidence of fetal ascites, a cystic pelvic mass, hydronephrosis, and oligohydramnios. These findings were attributed to fetal urine draining into the abdomen due to vesicovaginal fistula and distal vaginal atresia. Antenatal ultrasound findings, along with autopsy , were discussed in this case. A persistent urogenital sinus, which can be associated with vaginal atresia, should be suspected in cases of isolated fetal ascites when viral tests are negative and there are no cardiac anomalies, as early diagnosis allows for treatment. [PMC3931976]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Vaginal atresia can be a component of various syndromes. Winter syndrome, which includes distal vaginal atresia along with renal and middle ear anomalies, is characterized by autosomal recessive transmission. Hydrocolpos due to vaginal atresia is also a hallmark of McKusick-Kaufmann syndrome, which is associated with postaxial polydactyly, imperforate anus, and congenital heart defects. Understanding the specific syndrome is important for etiological considerations. [PMC7175489, PMC1050234]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of vaginal atresia primarily involves surgical interventions to restore the utero-vaginal tract, relieve pain, preserve fertility, and enable sexual intercourse. Common procedures include perineal vaginoplasty, pull-through vaginoplasty, and cervicovaginal anastomosis. Neovagina creation can be achieved through adhesiolysis or techniques like the Vecchietti procedure, and fallopian tube transplantation has been innovated for cervicovaginal reconstruction. Diagnostic laparoscopy with drainage of hematocolpus, colpotomy, and hysteroscopy may also be performed. Postoperatively, vaginal stents or moulds, with soft silicone materials preferred for patient compliance, are crucial, and postoperative dilation may be necessary. Multidisciplinary collaborative care, often utilizing telemedicine for remote guidance and follow-up, is emphasized, alongside supportive measures like analgesia and continuous oral contraception for symptom management. [PMC12303453, PMC11350548, PMC10896708, PMC11559355, PMC8360086]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Surgical interventions for vaginal atresia generally yield satisfactory outcomes, aiming to restore the integrity of the uterovaginal tract, alleviate symptoms like pelvic pain, and enable regular menstrual cycles. Successful cases report menarche within weeks, asymptomatic status with regular withdrawal bleeding at one year, and improved pain with regular cycles at three years post-surgery. Fertility preservation is possible, particularly for complete vaginal atresia with cervical external os obstruction, though re-stenosis and pelvic inflammation rates vary depending on the specific type of cervical aplasia. Early diagnosis and appropriate surgical intervention are crucial for averting complications and decreasing long-term morbidity. Patient compliance with postoperative management, such as stent use, is critical for treatment success. Minimally invasive procedures can also create a neovagina while preserving continence. [PMC11350548, PMC10896708, PMC11559355, PMC8360086, PMC7680234]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Vitamin K antagonist embryofetopathy is characterized by a group of symptoms that may be observed in a fetus or newborn when the mother has taken oral vitamin K antagonists, such as warfarin during pregnancy.
