Vitamin K antagonists are anticoagulant drugs that provide efficient thromboprophylaxis and that can cross the placenta. 5-12 % of infants exposed to warfarin between 6-9 weeks gestation present nasal hypoplasia and skeletal abnormalities, including short limbs and digits (brachydactyly), and stippled epiphyses. Warfarin fetopathy with central nervous system abnormalities (hydrocephalus, intellectual disability, spasticity, and hypotonia) or ocular abnormalities (microphthalmia, cataract, optic atrophy), fetal loss, and stillbirth, occurs in infants exposed at later gestations. Additional features that have been reported after in utero warfarin exposure include facial dysmorphism (cleft lip and/or palate, malformed ears), choanal atresia or stenosis, aorta coarctation, situs inversus totalis, bilobed lungs, and ventral midline dysplasia.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Vitamin K antagonist embryopathy; di Sala syndrome; Warfarin embryofetopathy; Warfarin embryopathy

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Vitamin K antagonist embryofetopathy, also known as fetal warfarin syndrome, occurs in fetuses exposed to warfarin during pregnancy. Fetuses are at an increased risk of developing this embryopathy. While low-dose warfarin (≤5 mg/day) is associated with a lower risk of general warfarin-related fetopathy, the risk of the specific embryopathy itself appears to remain unchanged. [PMC5893982]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Vitamin K antagonist embryofetopathy presents with characteristic congenital abnormalities. The most consistent features include nasal hypoplasia and stippling of vertebrae or bony epiphyses, often manifesting as chondrodysplasia punctata. Skeletal abnormalities, such as distal digital hypoplasia, pectus excavatum, dolichocephaly, brachydactyly, polydactyly, short neck, and growth retardation, are also reported. Fetal intracranial hemorrhage, subdural hematoma, and severe coagulopathy, leading to profound anemia and excessive bleeding, are significant complications, typically occurring in the second or third trimester. Other findings include facial dysmorphism, dentofacial manifestations, ventricular septal defects, and ocular abnormalities. [PMC10423455, PMC8768003, PMC5893982, PMC3624665, PMC3316846]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The phenotype of vitamin K antagonist embryofetopathy, characterized by features such as nasal hypoplasia, distal digital hypoplasia, and epiphyseal stippling (chondrodysplasia punctata), can be mimicked by other conditions. An inborn deficiency of vitamin K epoxide reductase, leading to a congenital deficiency of multiple vitamin K-dependent coagulation factors, presents with virtually identical features. Therefore, other causes of chondrodysplasia punctata should also be considered in the differential diagnosis. [PMC1684308, PMC1607783]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis primarily relies on imaging techniques. Fetal ultrasonography can reveal signs such as an intracranial mass, subdural hematoma, or intracerebral hemorrhage, observed as early as 24 weeks and up to 35 weeks of gestation. Fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can also demonstrate subdural hematoma. Intensive ultrasonic monitoring and regular MRI are suggested strategies for surveillance in pregnancies exposed to warfarin. While direct monitoring of fetal coagulation parameters is difficult, these imaging modalities help in suspecting and identifying warfarin-associated fetal complications. [PMC10423455, PMC3624665, PMC3055110]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Vitamin K antagonist embryofetopathy can lead to severe outcomes, including fatal intracranial hemorrhage, particularly in the second or third trimester. Cases of fetal intracranial hemorrhage have been reported, with one resulting in pregnancy termination and another showing multiple bleeding sites and low Apgar scores at birth. However, some infants with antenatal intracerebral hemorrhage and severe coagulopathy have been discharged in good condition with no clinically overt neurological deficit after correction of coagulopathy and anemia. Other manifestations, such as skeletal abnormalities and ventricular septal defects, may not require specific treatment during the first year of life. [PMC10423455, PMC5893982, PMC3624665, PMC3055110]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia type I that is characterized by papulosquamous, ichthyosiform plaques on the limbs appearing shortly after birth and later manifestations including progressive ataxia, dysarthria, nystagmus and decreased reflexes.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Erythrokeratodermia with ataxia; SCA34; Spinocerebellar ataxia and erythrokeratodermia

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: To date the disorder has been reported in 45 patients including 4 asymptomatic carriers, from one French-Canadian family and three Japanese families.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset occurs from shortly after birth to adolescence with the appearance of papulosquamous, ichthyosiform plaques on the limbs, which are often only present in the winter. After the age of 25 years they tend to disappear completely. Progressive ataxia, dysarthria, decreased reflexes, and nystagmus are further clinical signs of the disease that occur after the onset of skin manifestations, generally from the third to fifth decade of life. Patients occasionally present with autonomic dysfunction and pyramidal signs. Cerebellar and pontine atrophy is visible with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in individuals who develop cerebellar ataxia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disorder is due to a mutation in the ELOVL4 gene (6q14).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on characteristic clinical findings (skin lesions occurring shortly after birth and adult-onset slowly progressive cerebellar ataxia), and on the molecular genetic testing. Mutations in the ELOVL4 gene confirms diagnosis of SCA34. Magnetic resonance imaging usually shows marked atrophy of the cerebellum and pontine which is sometimes accompanied by Hot Cross Bun sign that is common in cerebellar type of multiple system atrophy.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other forms of autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia. From the view point of radiological findings, multiple system atrophy is important in differential diagnosis, especially in patients who also develop autonomic dysfunction.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible in families with a known ELOVL4 mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disorder is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and genetic counseling is possible. Genetic counseling should be proposed to individuals having the disease-causing mutation informing them that there is 50% risk of passing the mutation to offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is only supportive. Physical activity should be maintained as much as possible with the help of prosthetic devices. Motorized chairs/scooters are eventually necessary. Speech therapy and communication devices should be offered to those with severe dysarthria.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Disease progression is slow; the patients require cane or walker in their late 60s, and wheelchair in their 70s.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A severe congenital cardiac malformation characterized by both atria related entirely or almost entirely to one functionally single ventricular chamber. The clinical manifestations include congestive heart failure, failure to thrive, cyanosis, hypoxemia and neurodevelopmental disabilities.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Univentricular heart is a rare or uncommon congenital heart disease, with specific forms like univentricular dextrocardia and uniatrial biventricular connection also described as rare. While typically presenting with cyanotic manifestations from childhood, late-onset symptoms can occur, allowing for long-term asymptomatic periods. In a study of adult patients with single ventricle without Fontan palliation, the most common defect was double inlet left ventricle (34%), with 69% having left ventricular morphology. Age-adjusted survival for these adults was 73% at 40 years and 53% at 50 years. For complex congenital heart disease patients with single-ventricle physiology, the age of onset for clinical supraventricular tachycardia was 6.7 years, observed in a cohort of 17 males and 13 females. [PMC11657621, PMC7337453, PMC7161119, PMC6280275, PMC5210343]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Conditions that may present similarly to a univentricular heart include uniatrial biventricular connection (UBC), which is characterized by the absence of one atrioventricular connection and drainage of the other atrium into both ventricles. While UBC hearts are often classified as functionally univentricular and require Fontan palliation, some cases, particularly those representing a variant of atrioventricular septal defects with extreme ventriculoatrial malalignment, may be amenable to biventricular repair. Additionally, severe neonatal Ebstein's anomaly, especially with circular shunting, can necessitate a univentricular repair strategy. [PMC7161119, PMC3352727]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Fetal diagnosis represents a key innovation in the management of univentricular heart physiology, contributing to improved diagnostic techniques over the past 40 years. These advancements, including fetal diagnosis and interventions, are particularly aimed at preventing or reducing brain damage. For example, a prenatal diagnosis of Ebstein's anomaly, which can present with univentricular physiology, was made at 30 weeks of gestation, leading to a planned delivery and subsequent palliative operations. [PMC9986776, PMC3352727]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal trisomy 3p is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from the partial duplication of the short arm of chromosome 3, with highly variable phenotype principally characterized by craniofacial dysmorphism (incl. brachy-/microcephaly, square facies, frontal bossing, bitemporal indentation, hypertelorism/telecanthus, low-set and/or dysmorphic ears, short nose with broad, flat nasal bridge, prominent cheeks and philtrum, downturned corners of mouth, micrognathia/retrognathia, short neck) associated with psychomotor delay, moderate to severe intellectual disability, cardiac (e.g. patent ductus arteriosus) and urogenital (e.g. renal hypoplasia, hypogenitalism) abnormalities, as well as seizures and presence of whorls on fingers.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: A mother with a translocation rcp (1;3) (q32;p25) gave birth to a son with duplication of 1q32 leads to qter and deletion of 3p25 leads to pter. At 17 1/2 years of age, the proband was severely mentally retarded and presented a pattern of multiple minor dysmorphic stigmata and anomalies, including hypertrichosis, synophrys, ocular hypertelorism, ptosis, convergent squint, cleft uvula nad narrow palate, poorly modelled auricles, funnel chest, kyphoscoliosis, umbilical and inguinal hernias, and cubitus valgus. He had normal stature and did not have any apparent malformations. [PMC1048662]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Terminal 7q deletion is a rare chromosomal anomaly resulting from partial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7. 7q terminal deletion syndrome in variable clinical phenotypes, such as microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, craniofacial abnormalities, sacral hypoplasia, etc. a case of prenatal diagnosis of this syndrome with multiple abnormalities including holoprosencephaly and other craniofacial anomalies seen on ultrasound seen at NT scan. Pregnancy was terminated and chromosomal microarray showed ∼5.5 MB deletion in chromosome 7 spanning the 7q36.2-36.3 region. In addition, a literature review was done to enlist the various prenatal ultrasound features of this rare syndrome. We described a unique case of near-negative chromosome mosaicism in chorionic villi but complete monosomy X in amniotic fluid. Chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis were performed separately in the first and... [PMC11609106, PMC10277675, PMC5427656]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Other chromosomal anomalies that may present with overlapping features or require distinction include terminal 7q deletion syndrome, characterized by microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, and craniofacial abnormalities. Pure partial trisomy of 16q, specifically 16q12.2q24.3, is associated with intrauterine growth retardation, facial dysmorphism, hypotonia, congenital heart defects, and distal contractures. Additionally, complex rearrangements such as duplication of 1q and partial monosomy 3p, resulting from parental translocations, can lead to severe mental retardation and multiple dysmorphic stigmata. [PMC11609106, PMC9082733, PMC1048662]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Terminal 7q deletion is a rare chromosomal anomaly resulting from partial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 7. 7q terminal deletion syndrome in variable clinical phenotypes, such as microcephaly, holoprosencephaly, craniofacial abnormalities, sacral hypoplasia, etc. a case of prenatal diagnosis of this syndrome with multiple abnormalities including holoprosencephaly and other craniofacial anomalies seen on ultrasound seen at NT scan. Pregnancy was terminated and chromosomal microarray showed ∼5.5 MB deletion in chromosome 7 spanning the 7q36.2-36.3 region. In addition, a literature review was done to enlist the various prenatal ultrasound features of this rare syndrome. We described a unique case of near-negative chromosome mosaicism in chorionic villi but complete monosomy X in amniotic fluid. Chorionic villus sampling and amniocentesis were performed separately in the first and... [PMC11609106, PMC10277675]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, autosomal recessive, organic aciduria that is characterized by variable clinical presentation ranging from acute neonatal onset of metabolic decompensation to later onset of chronic, non-specific manifestations including failure to thrive and/or developmental delay. All patients are prone to intermittent, acute metabolic decompensation. During metabolic episodes, urine analysis demonstrates elevated isovaleric acid derivatives.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Accurate data on the prevalence is not readily available. Best estimates come from newborn screening studies that estimate prevalence at birth between 1/50,000-150,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Patients present along a spectrum. Acute, neonatal presentation is characterized by onset in the first two weeks of life with vomiting, seizures, and lethargy, progressing to coma. Metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap is apparent on laboratory evaluation. Hyperammonemia may occur. Later onset is relatively non-specific with failure to thrive and/or developmental delay. Patients who survived an early acute presentation are subsequently indistinguishable from those with the chronic phenotype. All patients are prone to intermittent acute episodes of decompensation with minor illnesses. Childhood onset metabolic acidosis is typically brought on by prolonged fasting, increased intake of protein-rich food or infections, and can be fatal if not treated immediately. The characteristic smell of isovaleric acid may be present, and is likened to sweaty feet/body sweat. Though severe developmental delay and neurologic sequelae are present in some patients, they are likely related to severe biochemical presentations.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Isovaleric acidemia (IVA) is caused by mutations in the IVD gene (15q15.1) encoding the enzyme isovaleryl-CoA dehydrogenase (IVDH) resulting in accumulation of isovaleric acid and its derivatives. Asymptomatic patients with specific mutations have been reported, especially when identified through newborn screening.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Where implemented, diagnosis is through newborn blood spot screening. Otherwise, in symptomatic individuals diagnosis is suspected based on the clinical presentation. Metabolite or molecular genetic testing confirms diagnosis. Characteristic urine metabolites includes elevated N‐isovalerylglycine, N‐isovalerylcarnitine and 3‐hydroxyisovaleric acid. Isovalerylcarnitine (''C5 carnitine'') is elevated in blood. The urine organic acids may normalize when a patient is well.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: In acutely decompensating patients, the differential diagnosis includes other organic acidemias (including lactic acidosis), urea cycle defects, and sepsis. On newborn screening, ''C5-carnitine'' may also indicate 2-methylbutyryl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency; urine organic acids and molecular testing readily differenciate the two disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal genetic testing is possible when the mutation of a proband has previously been determined.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal recessive; genetic counseling is recommended for affected families. The risk of disease transmission at each pregnancy is 25% when the parents are proven or obligate carriers.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Lifelong management is with a low protein diet. Children diagnosed with IVA should be referred to a metabolic dietician who can tailor the diet to support normal growth and development. Supplementing with artificial protein restricted in leucine may be required. L-carnitine and glycine may be prescribed to clear excess isovaleric acid. Emergency treatment in times of metabolic stress (including illness and fasting) is with an anabolic diet. Reducing, but not eliminating, natural protein in the diet for 12-24 hours may help, but only if additional other calories can be given to promote anabolism.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis for patients diagnosed by newborn screening is excellent with the potential for normal neurodevelopmental outcome with appropriate metabolic management. Patients who present symptomatically can have significant neurologic sequelae including neurodevelopmental delay, especially if acidosis and hyperammonemia are severe.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (FCOD) is a rare fibro-osseous lesion in the jaw that predominantly affects middle-aged women of African descent. It is generally asymptomatic or may manifest with pain and gingival swelling. Radiologically, it is characterized by multiple dense lobulated bone lesions, often symmetrically located in various regions of the jaw.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Florid osseous dysplasia; Focal cemento-osseous dysplasia

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (FCOD) is a rare, benign fibro-osseous lesion primarily involving the mandible and maxilla, with the mandible being the most affected site. It predominantly affects middle-aged women, particularly those of African or Asian descent, with a reported female-to-male ratio of 21:1 and a mean age of affected individuals around 57.4 years. While genetic inheritance is unusual, familial cases have been reported, affecting multiple family members. [PMC11692410, PMC11452594, PMC8134641, PMC7780834, PMC7021850]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (FCOD) relies on a thorough history check, multiple clinical examinations, and imaging studies. Radiographic findings, including panoramic radiographs and cone beam computed tomography (CBCT), are crucial, revealing unique features that evolve through radiolucent, mixed, and radiopaque stages. However, these features can mimic periapical inflammatory conditions or other jaw lesions, necessitating careful differential diagnosis. Pulp vitality tests are essential to distinguish FCOD from endodontic pathologies. While histological analysis (biopsy) can confirm diagnosis, it is generally avoided for FCOD itself due to the risk of infection, though it may be important for diagnosing complications or co-occurring conditions like osteosarcoma or actinomycosis. Radiological-based diagnostic algorithms are proposed to aid clinicians. [PMC11692410, PMC11452594, PMC11534625, PMC8134641, PMC7780834]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Familial forms of florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (FLCOD), also known as familial florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (FFLCOD) or familial florid osseous dysplasia (FOD), are recognized, though considered unusual or rare. These familial cases have been reported in multiple family members, including mother-daughter pairs. Genetic features are suggested as important parameters for classifying hereditary forms of FLCOD. Additionally, florid osseous dysplasia of the jaws is a characteristic feature of Gnathodiaphyseal dysplasia (GDD), an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutations in the ANO5 gene, which has been identified in affected families. In rare instances, FLCOD has been observed in patients with Li-Fraumeni Syndrome, linked to a germline TP53 mutation, suggesting that in individuals with tumor predisposition syndromes, even benign lesions like COD may warrant close monitoring. [PMC11452594, PMC8134641, PMC7780834, PMC6617922, PMC4830924]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (FCOD) is primarily conservative, with long-term follow-up consistently recommended, often annually or radiologically, especially for symptomatic cases or those with associated cysts. Surgical treatment for FCOD itself is generally discouraged as it may predispose to infection. However, if complications arise, such as secondary infection, conservative management includes infection control and surgical debridement or removal of necrotic bone. Accurate diagnosis through clinical examination, imaging, and pulp vitality tests is crucial to prevent misdiagnosis and avoid unnecessary interventions like root canal therapy. In cases with co-occurring lesions like simple bone cysts or peripheral giant cell granulomas, these may require specific surgical exploration or treatment. Multidisciplinary team management is also noted. [PMC11692410, PMC11452594, PMC11534625, PMC8134641, PMC8010010]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Florid cemento-osseous dysplasia (FCOD) is generally considered a benign, non-neoplastic, and self-limited fibro-osseous lesion, often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally. Despite its benign nature, it can be a chronic and disfiguring condition. The most frequent and challenging complication is secondary infection, often associated with tooth extraction or surgical intervention, which may necessitate debridement. Long-term, consistent follow-up, including radiological monitoring, is crucial to prevent complications and observe lesion stability or transformation. Surgical treatment is generally discouraged due to the risk of infection. [PMC11692410, PMC11452594, PMC11534625, PMC8134641, PMC8010010]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic neuromuscular disease characterized by permanent myotonia, mask-like facies (with blepharospasm, narrow palpebral fissures, small mouth with pursed lips and puckered chin) , and chondrodysplasia (variably manifesting with short stature, pectus carinatum, kyphoscoliosis, bowing of long bones, epiphyseal, metaphyseal, and hip dysplasia).
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Aberfeld syndrome; Burton skeletal dysplasia; Burton syndrome; Catel-Hempel syndrome; Dysostosis enchondralis metaepiphysaria, Catel-Hempel type; Myotonic chondrodystrophy; Myotonic myopathy, dwarfism, chondrodystrophy, ocular and facial anomalies; Osteochondromuscular dystrophy; SJS; SJS1; Schwartz-Jampel syndrome type 1; Schwartz-Jampel-Aberfeld syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Approximately, 130 cases have been described in the literature to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Presentation is typically by 1 year to 2 years of age, but may occur earlier, with myotonia, maske-like facies, short stature, non-progressive muscle weakness, muscle hypertrophy, progressive restriction of range of motion and paucity of subcutaneous tissue. Facial features consist of blepharospasm, progressive blepharophimosis, pursed lips and a puckered chin. Micrognathia, low-set ears with folded helices and dystopia canthorum have also been reported. The myotonia is characterized by continuous muscle activity recorded on electroneuromyography. Limited joint mobility leads to an unsteady gait. Joint stiffness is progressive, reaching its peak during adolescence The severity of chondrodysplasia is variable and may consist of flattening of the vertebral bodies, hip dysplasia, metaphyseal widening, slender diaphyses, kypho-scoliosis, multiple joint contractures and bowing of long bones. Rarely, myopia, inguinal and umbilical hernias and micro-orchidism have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Loss of function mutations in HSPG2 (1p36) are causative. HSPG2 encodes perlecan, a major component of the cellular matrix that plays an important role in maintaining cartilaginous tissue integrity and regulating muscle excitability. The exact pathogenesis is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is established by demonstration of both myotonia via electromyography and chondrodysplasia via radiographs. Genetic testing may confirm diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Schwartz-Jampel syndrome (SJS) is non-allelic with Stuve-Wiedemann syndrome, a severe skeletal dysplasia that is typically fatal during the neonatal period and was formerly described as SJS type 2. Other differential diagnosis should include Freeman Sheldon and Marden Walker syndrome and, in cases with minimal skeletal abnormalities, myotonic disorders ( including myotonia congenita, myotonia permamens, and myotonic dystrophy).
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to affected families, informing them that the risk of disease transmission is 25% where both parents are unaffected carriers.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The management of patients with SJS is primarily supportive and best offered by a team comprising a neurologist, a geneticist, a physical therapist, an orthopedic surgeon, an ophthalmologist and a psychologist. Medical treatment with muscle relaxants and antiepileptic drugs, such as carbamazepine, phenytoin, or procainamide, aimed to alleviate myotonia has limited usage, although early initiation of treatment may limit the extent of disability. Physical therapy is important to prevent contracture formation and fixed skeletal deformity. Botulinum toxin A injections for blepharospasm has been reported with limited and variable results Rarely, surgical intervention is considered for blepharospasm including orbicularis oculi myectomy or levator aponeurosis resection improve functional and cosmetic outcome. Malignant hyperthermia is a potentially lethal complication of anesthesia.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Progressively worsening blepharospasm is an important morbidity that can interfere with vision. The disease appears to stabilize after adolescence and does not affect life span.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder due to poisoning caused by the ingestion of unripe Blighia sapida fruits, clinically characterized by toxic hypoglycaemia and inhibition of neoglucogenesis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Acute intoxication by Blighia sapida; Jamaican vomiting sickness; Jamaican vomiting syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The true incidence is unknown and most likely underreported. It is relatively frequent in the Caribbean and Western Africa where the fruit is consumed. In contrast, it is rare in France and other Western countries.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical manifestations are severe and rapidly progressing (delirium, toxic hepatitis, acute dehydration and a state of shock, convulsions, coma) and may lead to death.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The hypoglycaemia is caused by the effect of hypoglycin A, which is found in the arils of the Blighia sapida fruit. When ingested, hypoglycin A is metabolized into (methylenecyclopropyl)acetyl-CoA, which inhibits several enzymes required for beta oxidation of fatty acids and gluconeogenesis.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical presentation following consumption of ackee fruit.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Other acute poisonings and acute gastritis are among the differential diagnoses.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic (administration of glucose, IV or per os)
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Although the intoxication is generally benign or has a favourable outcome, ingestion of large doses may lead to death: ackee fruit intoxication lead to 29 deaths in 1998 and more than 50 in 2001.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Distal trisomy 16q is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from the partial trisomy of the long arm of chromosome 16, with variable phenotype principally characterized by developmental delay, severe intellectual disability, hypotonia, facial dysmorphism (incl. high, prominent forehead, epicanthic folds, dysplastic ears, broad/depressed nasal bridge, malar hypoplasia, narrow and arched palate, thin upper lip vermilion, micrognathia) and hand/feet anomalies (e.g. arachnodactyly, talipes equinovarus). Cardiac defects, genitourinary malformations and vertebral anomalies are also associated. Thrombocytopenia and recurrent infections have also been reported.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Pure partial trisomy 16q12.1q22.1 is a rare chromosome copy number variant (CNV). The primary clinical phenotypes associated with this syndrome include abnormal facial morphology, global developmental delay (GDD), short stature, and reported predisposing factors for atypical behavior, autism, the development of learning disabilities, and neuropsychiatric disorders. The dosage-sensitive genes associated with partial trisomy are not disclosed preventing to establish a genotype-phenotype correlation. a case of a Chinese patient diagnosed with GDD and an abnormal facial shape, who was found to have partial trisomy 16 through karyotyping and high-throughput sequencing analysis. Karyotype and CNV tracing analyses were also conducted on the biological parents of the patient to assess for any chromosomal structural abnormalities. Additionally, we included 29 patients with pure partial trisomy... [PMC11667835, PMC9082733]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Distal duplication 16q syndrome is associated with severe congenital defects, growth retardation, and early lethality. Primary clinical phenotypes include abnormal facial morphology or dysmorphism, global developmental delay, and short stature or intrauterine growth retardation. Patients may also present with hypotonia, micrognathia, congenital heart defects, distal contractures, urogenital abnormalities, and hearing loss. Some individuals develop atypical behavior, autism, learning disabilities, or neuropsychiatric disorders. More severe symptoms may be observed when the duplicated region is located at the distal part of 16q, and complications like pulmonary hypertension and chronic lung disease have been reported. [PMC11667835, PMC7899829, PMC9082733]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Distal duplication 16q syndrome is caused by a partial trisomy of the long arm of chromosome 16 (16q), which is a rare chromosome copy number variant. This can occur as a pure partial trisomy 16q, often a de novo duplication, such as a 21.96 Mb duplication in regions like 16q12.1q22.1. More commonly, segmental trisomy of 16q is described concomitantly with partial monosomy of another chromosome, frequently resulting from a parental balanced translocation. For instance, a duplication in 16q22.1-q24.3 may be observed alongside a deletion in 7p22.3-p22.2 due to an inherited paternal translocation. While partial trisomy 16q is speculated to be associated with continuous gene duplication, functional studies are still needed to identify the specific causative gene or critical region. [PMC11667835, PMC7899829, PMC9082733]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of distal duplication 16q syndrome can involve noninvasive preliminary screening (NIPS), which requires further confirmation. Definitive diagnosis is achieved through conventional karyotyping combined with molecular genetic tests such as high-throughput sequencing analysis, including CNV-seq and whole exome sequencing (WES). Parental karyotyping and CNV tracing analyses are conducted to assess for chromosomal structural abnormalities or balanced translocations. Ultrasound examination can also reveal associated fetal morphological abnormalities. Genotype-phenotype correlation analysis is performed to understand the clinical implications of the duplicated region. [PMC11667835, PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Distal duplication 16q syndrome should be differentiated from other chromosomal abnormalities, particularly those involving partial monosomy of another chromosome. Such complex imbalances often result from parental balanced translocations, as seen in cases with concomitant partial trisomy 16q and partial monosomy 7p. Pure partial trisomy of chromosome 16q is exceedingly rare, suggesting that co-occurring chromosomal deletions are a common feature to consider. [PMC7899829, PMC9082733]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis can be initiated by noninvasive preliminary screening (NIPS), which is capable of detecting subchromosomal duplications, such as a 19-Mb fragment repeat at 16q22.1-q22.4. However, NIPS is a screening test requiring further diagnosis. Conventional karyotype combined with copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq) is a useful tool to confirm and precisely locate the abnormal chromosomal region, and to identify the source of fetal chromosomal abnormalities. Prenatal ultrasound examination may also reveal associated findings, such as fetal micrognathia. [PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for distal duplication 16q syndrome is complex due to its rarity and variable origins. The duplication can occur de novo or result from a parental balanced translocation, which may lead to concomitant partial monosomy of another chromosome in the offspring. Therefore, parental karyotyping and CNV tracing are crucial to identify the source of the chromosomal abnormality. While non-invasive prenatal screening (NIPS) can indicate potential issues, definitive diagnosis requires further tests such as conventional karyotype combined with CNV-seq. Genetic counseling is particularly challenging given the potential for severe, life-limiting congenital anomalies. Although distal duplications may be associated with more severe symptoms, a clear genotype-phenotype correlation with the size of the duplicated segment has not been established, and causative genes require further functional studies. [PMC11667835, PMC7899829, PMC9082733]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Distal duplication 16q syndrome is often associated with severe congenital defects, growth retardation, and early lethality, though it is occasionally compatible with life. Pure partial distal 16q duplication is exceedingly rare, with very few long-term survivors reported, often experiencing life-limiting congenital anomalies. Patients with distal duplications may exhibit more severe symptoms. Infants can have continued morbidity, such as pulmonary hypertension and chronic lung disease. Survivors typically present with global developmental delay, short stature, atypical behavior, autism, learning disabilities, and neuropsychiatric disorders. [PMC11667835, PMC9082733]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, fatal multiple congenital anomalies/dysmorphic syndrome characterized by facial dysmorphism (incl. dolichocephaly/scaphocephaly, high frontal hairline, laterally overlapping upper eyelids, hypertelorism, prominent eyelashes, deep-set eyes, macrocornea, nystagmus, dysplastic ears, abnormal auricles, prominent nasal bridge, dental dysplasia), visual impairment, deafness, seizures, generalized skeletal dysplasia, high fingerprint ridge count, cryptorchidism, hypospadias, spasticity and severe intellectual disability. An increased chromosome breakage and a fatal lymphoid malignancy have been reported. There has been no further description in the literature since 1974.

Tropical endomyocardial fibrosis is a restrictive cardiopathy, occuring almost exclusively in children and young adults in tropical and subtropical regions, characterized by endocardial fibrosis, affecting the apices and the inflow tract of the right or left ventricle (or both) and manifesting with a restrictive cardiomyopathy and atrioventricular regurgitation leading to severe pulmonary hypertension, very high systemic venous pressure and congestive cardiac failure. Suspected etiologies include helminth and protozoal infestation and malnutrition.
ORPHA:3451

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: West syndrome, also known as infantile spasms syndrome (ISS) or infantile epileptic spasm syndrome (IESS), is an early-onset epileptic encephalopathy characterized by uncontrollable or drug-resistant epileptic spasms. Patients typically present with severe electroencephalogram abnormalities, often a hypsarrhythmic pattern, which can be symmetric or asymmetric. Common clinical features include severe hypotonia, spasticity, and significant developmental delay, affecting cognitive and behavioral development. Brain magnetic resonance imaging may show structural abnormalities, such as tumors, or no significant findings. Associated features can include abnormal facial features, sparse hair, and short neck. Genetic factors are critical, with variants in genes like CCDC82, CHD3, CSNK1A1, and WWOX identified in affected individuals. [PMC12369191, PMC12173265, PMC12056308, PMC12282255, PMC11298992]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A very rare autosomal recessive, slowly progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the triad of cerebellar ataxia (that generally manifests at adolescence or early adulthood), chorioretinal dystrophy, which may have a later onset (up to the fifth-sixth decade) leading to variable degrees of visual impairment, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (delayed puberty and lack of secondary sex characteristics). Ataxia-hypogonadism-choroidal dystrophy syndrome belongs to a clinical continuum of neurodegenerative disorders along with the clinically overlapping cerebellar ataxia-hypogonadism syndrome.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome (BNS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the PNPLA6 gene. Few cases have been reported, and the syndrome is considered poorly recognized, suggesting under-identification. It is a distinct pleiotropic single gene disorder, with cases identified in consanguineous families, such as a large Zoroastrian (Parsi) kindred. [PMC8859865, PMC5243903, PMC4245359, PMC1051065]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome (BNS) is characterized by chorioretinal dystrophy, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and cerebellar dysfunction and atrophy. Patients often present with progressive night blindness, impaired vision, primary amenorrhea, and non-development of secondary sexual characteristics. Cerebellar ataxia, including gait ataxia, typically manifests before early adulthood, though late-onset in the third or fourth decade has been reported, accompanied by neurological deterioration and progressive cerebellar atrophy. Chorioretinal abnormalities can be subtle, including foveal stippling and hypopigmentation. The phenotype is variable; some individuals may present with hypogonadism and visual impairment without initial ataxia, or even pure cerebellar ataxia without other features. Neuropsychiatric symptoms, short stature, and hypersegmented neutrophils have also been noted. While primarily associated with biallelic pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 gene, de novo variants in the HK1 gene have also been identified. [PMC12176038, PMC8859865, PMC6330241, PMC5970027, PMC5243903]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome (BNS) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder primarily caused by pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 gene. These mutations can be biallelic, compound heterozygous, or homozygous, with many clustering in the phospholipase esterase domain. PNPLA6 mutations are associated with a spectrum of phenotypes, including complex ataxia with retinal and endocrine manifestations, and pure cerebellar ataxia. Genetic heterogeneity is suggested by the identification of a de novo variant in the hexokinase 1 (HK1) gene in an individual presenting with a BNS-consistent phenotype, which expands the known HK1 genotypic and phenotypic spectrum. [PMC12176038, PMC8859865, PMC6330241, PMC5970027, PMC5243903]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Ataxia-hypogonadism-choroidal dystrophy syndrome (Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome) is primarily based on clinical characteristics, including chorioretinal dystrophy, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and cerebellar dysfunction or atrophy. Patients may present with progressive night blindness, impaired vision, primary amenorrhea, or non-development of secondary sexual characteristics. Gene sequencing is currently the primary diagnostic method, with whole-exome sequencing and Sanger sequencing used to identify pathogenic variants in genes such as PNPLA6 and HK1. Homozygosity mapping, RNA-sequencing, and qRT-PCR can also be employed. Ophthalmic evaluation, including clinical examination and multimodal imaging, is crucial to detect often subtle chorioretinal abnormalities, and neuroophthalmologic evaluation is advocated in suspected cases. Endocrine and neurological evaluations are also important components of the diagnostic process. [PMC12176038, PMC8859865, PMC6330241, PMC5970027, PMC5243903]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for ataxia-hypogonadism-choroidal dystrophy syndrome primarily includes Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome (BNHS), characterized by chorioretinal dystrophy, hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, and cerebellar dysfunction and atrophy. BNHS is associated with biallelic pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 gene, and genetic heterogeneity is suggested by a de novo HK1 variant. Gordon Holmes syndrome (GHS) is another related condition presenting with early-onset cerebellar ataxia and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, but it is distinguished by pyramidal signs and lacks chorioretinal dystrophy, also being linked to PNPLA6 mutations. A novel disorder or variant of BNHS has been described, including features such as short stature and hypersegmented neutrophils in addition to the core symptoms. Furthermore, a specific PNPLA6 mutation found in a BNHS patient was previously related to Oliver-McFarlane syndrome. [PMC12176038, PMC5970027, PMC1735249, PMC1051065]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Boucher-Neuhäuser syndrome is a rare, distinct pleiotropic single gene disorder with an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. It is primarily caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in the PNPLA6 gene, which can be compound heterozygous or homozygous. Genetic heterogeneity has also been observed, with a de novo variant in the HK1 gene identified in one case. Gene sequencing is the primary diagnostic method for this syndrome, which is often poorly recognized. Genetic counseling should address the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern and the implications of identified PNPLA6 or HK1 variants, including evaluation for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism in HK1-related cases. [PMC12176038, PMC8859865, PMC5970027, PMC5243903, PMC4245359]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for Ataxia-hypogonadism-choroidal dystrophy syndrome is not extensively detailed in the provided abstract. However, individuals with variants in hexokinase 1 (HK1), which can present with this syndrome, should undergo evaluation for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, as this specific symptom is potentially amenable to treatment. [PMC12176038]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Ataxia-hypogonadism-choroidal dystrophy syndrome involves progressive neurological deterioration. Longitudinal follow-up has indicated the development of neuropsychiatric symptoms and progressive cerebellar atrophy, particularly in individuals with HK1 variants. While gait ataxia typically manifests before early adulthood, onset can occur later, in the third or fourth decade. The severity of retinal changes can also vary, with some cases presenting with relatively milder changes. [PMC12176038, PMC4245359]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, genetic metabolic disorder characterized by reduced activity of unfractionated serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and various symptoms from life-threatening, severely impaired mineralization at birth to musculo-skeletal pain in adulthood.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Exact prevalence and incidence data for hypophosphatasia (HPP) are not available. In North and West Europe, the birth prevalence of severe forms of the disease (perinatal lethal and infantile forms) has been estimated to be 1/300 000. Because of possible dominant autosomal inheritance, moderate forms of HPP are expected to be more frequent and are estimated to have a prevalence of 1/6300.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Six different clinical forms of HPP have been described, although there is a continuum of severity. Perinatal lethal HPP involves significant hypomineralization and leads to hypercalcemia and respiratory insufficiency. Prenatal benign HPP involves prenatal skeletal manifestations that slowly resolve to become non-lethal. Infantile HPP is characterized by rickets developing between birth and six months of age. Childhood HPP ranges from low bone mineral density with unexplained fractures to rickets. Adult HPP involves early loss of adult dentition and stress fractures of the lower extremities in middle age. In the mildest form, adults may present with only unspecific signs like musculo-skeletal pain or osteoporosis. Lastly, odontoHPP includes premature exfoliation of primary teeth and/or severe dental caries.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: More than 400 different mutations in the ALPL gene (1p36.12) are known to cause hypophosphatasia. The gene encodes alkaline phosphatase, tissue-nonspecific isozyme (TNSALP) involved in skeletal mineralization.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is based on laboratory testing and molecular genetic testing of the ALPL gene to detect causative mutations. Serum alkaline phosphatase (AP) activity is markedly reduced while 5'pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) in blood and urinary phosphoethanolamine (PEA) are increased but the latter is not pathognomonic. Ultrasound is used in prenatal and perinatal forms. Clinical examinations and radiographs help to establish the diagnosis in infantile, childhood and adult forms.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: In the prenatal context, the differential diagnosis includes osteogenesis imperfecta, campomelic dysplasia, hypophosphatemic rickets and achondrogenesis. The main differential diagnosis in other forms is osteogenesis imperfecta.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis can be performed through mutation analysis following chorionic villus sampling.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Perinatal and severe infantile HPP are typically inherited as autosomal recessive traits. Prenatal benign, moderate infantile, childhood HPP, adult HPP and odontohypophosphatasia can be inherited in an autosomal recessive or autosomal dominant manner, depending on the specific effect the gene mutation has on TNSALP activity. The less severe the disease, the more likely it is dominantly inherited. The range of inheritance patterns partially explains the clinical heterogeneity. In both autosomal recessive and dominant hypophosphatasia, de novo mutations are exceptional. In autosomal dominant hypophosphatasia, affected patients may have an affected parent but penetrance appears to be low. HPP displays highly variable expressivity. Genetic counseling is complicated by these factors but should be offered to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Supportive symptomatic treatment in childhood and adult forms includes non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (children), teriparatide (adults) and orthopedic management. Dental monitoring and care are essential. Since its availability, enzyme replacement therapy plays an increasing role, especially in pediatric severe forms.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The perinatal form is almost always fatal within days or weeks. Respiratory complications lead to high mortality rates in the infantile form. Life expectancy is not thought to be affected in childhood and adult forms or in odontohypophosphatasia.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Mixed autoimmune hemolytic anemia is a type of autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) defined by the presence of both warm and cold autoantibodies, which have a deleterious effect on red blood cells at either body temperature or at lower temperatures.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Mixed AIHA occurs in less than 10% of cases of AIHA, whose annual incidence is between 1/35,000-1/80,000 in North America and Western Europe.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Mixed AIHA can occur at any age but is rare in children. Patients with mixed AIHA usually present with abrupt onset severe hemolysis and anemia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Mixed AIHA can be idiopathic or secondary, mainly associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and lymphoma.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical or laboratory evidence of hemolytic anemia and the detection of autoantibodies, usually both IgG and IgM, with the direct anti-globulin test (DAT) showing a pattern of IgG with complement C3, and the presence of cold agglutinins (IgM) in the serum at a significant titer.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Erroneous diagnosis of mixed AIHA is sometimes made on the basis of inadequate serologic studies as a large proportion of patients with warm AIHA also have cold autoantibodies that are measured but are clinically insignificant. Unless a cold autoantibody with a high thermal amplitude (>30 degrees C) is observed in association with a warm autoantibody, a diagnosis of mixed AIHA is not warranted.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The principles of management are comparable to that of warm AIHA, including corticosteroids and, if these are ineffective, splenectomy, but avoidance of cold must also be considered. Cautious transfusion is possible in cases with severe anemia. However, the best compatible or ``least incompatible'' packed red blood cell units must be identified by the blood centre to avoid post-transfusional hemolysis.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The disease responds to corticosteroids, and may be followed by remission, but usually runs a chronic course with intermittent exacerbations.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: The Monocyte Monolayer Assay (MMA) is an in vitro simulation of red blood cell (RBC) alloantibody behavior. It has been classically applied to predict the risks of post-transfusion hemolytic reactions when transfusing incompatible RBC units. Quantifying erythrophagocytosis by MMA may be an interesting option for situations where there is doubt whether a RBC autoantibody is mediating significant hemolysis. Here, three situations involving RBC autoantibodies in which the MMA was decisive for clarifying the diagnosis and choosing the best clinical treatment. Case 1. Pregnant patient with severely anemic fetus exhibited warm autoantibody without signs of hemolysis. MMA revealed 30% of monocyte index (MI) highlighting that fetal hemolysis was caused by maternal autoantibody. Prednisone was prescribed with fetal clinical improvement. Cases 2 and 3. Two patients with the diagnosis of mixed... [PMC6817274]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare inherited human prion disease characterized by adult onset of progressive disturbance and loss of circadian rhythms, dysautonomia with increased sympathetic activity, and cognitive impairment with fluctuating vigilance, impaired long-term memory, disorientation, and oneiric states. Motor disturbances include myoclonus, cerebellar ataxia, and pyramidal signs. The disease rapidly leads to a somnolent or comatose state and is typically fatal after 9 or 30 months on average (bimodal course). Neuropathologic examination shows marked neuronal loss and gliosis predominantly in thalamic nuclei and inferior olives, while deposition of abnormal prion protein may be relatively sparse.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Fatal familial insomnia (FFI) is a rare, rapidly progressive neurodegenerative prion disease with an insidious onset, making early diagnosis challenging. The typical clinical presentation includes persistent insomnia and other sleep disorders, autonomic dysfunction, and cognitive impairment, often progressing to rapidly progressive dementia. Patients may also experience psychobehavioral abnormalities, abnormal movements such as parkinsonism, ataxia, tremor, myoclonus, and gait disturbances. While insomnia is a frequent and essential symptom, atypical presentations without prominent insomnia or mimicking other conditions like Alzheimer's disease have been reported. The methionine-valine polymorphism at codon 129 of the PRNP gene can influence the clinical phenotype. The disease course is rapid, leading to severe functional decline and death, often within months to a few years. [PMC12305898, PMC11665128, PMC11722714, PMC11654706, PMC8519249]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Fatal familial insomnia is an incurable, rapidly progressive, and fatal prion disease for which no effective treatment is currently available. Management focuses on best supportive care, timely palliation, and emotional support. Various interventions, including anti-infection agents, immunotherapies, amantadine, doxycycline, Risperidone, Olanzapine, Alprazolam, Clonazepam, and Deanxit, have shown no obvious or lasting effects. However, one patient responded temporarily to drugs strengthening mitochondrial function, and nocturnal noninvasive ventilation improved arterial blood gases and subjective sleep quality in another case, though its impact on survival is unknown. Research continues into potential antiprion strategies like vaccination and targeting cell surface receptors. [PMC11722714, PMC11654706, PMC8519249, PMC8220472, PMC6392909]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 6
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare axonal hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy disease characterized by progressive, peripheral, axonal sensorimotor neuropathy (of variable severity), affecting predominantly the distal lower limbs, associated with progressive, variably severe, optic atrophy, which frequently leads to visual loss. Patients typically present distal limb muscle weakness and atrophy, hypo/areflexia, foot deformities, poor visual acuity (often with a central scotoma), nystagmus, and reduced peripheral and nocturnal vision. Additional reported manifestations include sensorineural hearing loss, major joint contractures, anosmia, scoliosis/lumbar hyperlordosis, cognitive impairment and vocal cord paresis.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): CMT6; Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 6; Peripheral neuropathy and optic atrophy; Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type VI; HMSN 6; HMSN VI

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type VI (HMSN type VI) is defined by the association of hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy with optic atrophy. This syndrome has been reported with both autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant inheritance patterns. Autosomal recessive inheritance has been described in at least two families, with electrophysiological studies reported in one. Autosomal dominant inheritance has also been observed, affecting individuals across three generations. [PMC10631856, PMC1074097, PMC1073804]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type VI (HMSN VI) is characterized by a combination of neuropathy and optic atrophy. The neuropathy is typically axonal, manifesting as distal motor weakness, muscle atrophy, and sometimes loss of small fibers, though an asymptomatic, mainly sensory neuropathy has also been reported. Optic atrophy is a consistent feature, with onset ranging from childhood to adulthood, and can lead to visual impairment, although visual acuity improvement has been observed. Additional clinical features may include borderline intellectual disability, cerebellar ataxia, sensorineural hearing loss, and diffuse cerebral and cerebellar atrophy. HMSN VI can be inherited in an autosomal dominant or autosomal recessive manner, with pathogenic variants identified in genes such as NDUFS6, MFN2, and C12orf65. [PMC10977349, PMC10808857, PMC5282685, PMC3155637, PMC1074097]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 6 (HMSN VI) is a genetically heterogeneous disorder associated with optic atrophy and neuropathy, exhibiting both autosomal dominant and autosomal recessive inheritance patterns. Pathogenic variants in the MFN2 gene are a known cause, with a specific c.1090C→T mutation linked to HMSN VI, and other MFN2 variants causing Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A and phenotypes including optic atrophy. A novel homozygous MFN2 variant (D414V) has been characterized in a patient with ataxia, deafness, and blindness. Additionally, a homozygous NDUFS6 variant (c.309 + 5 G > A) has been identified in a patient with axonal neuropathy, optic atrophy, and intellectual disability, expanding the clinical spectrum of NDUFS6-associated phenotypes. Compound heterozygote mutations of C12orf65 also cause distal motor neuropathy and optic atrophy. [PMC10977349, PMC10808857, PMC5282685, PMC3155637, PMC1074097]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 6 (HMSN type VI), characterized by neuropathy and optic atrophy, can exhibit both autosomal recessive and autosomal dominant inheritance patterns. Autosomal recessive inheritance has been observed in families with childhood-onset neuropathy and adult-onset optic atrophy. Conversely, autosomal dominant inheritance has also been reported, affecting multiple generations. Specific genetic causes include homozygous or bi-allelic variants in genes such as NDUFS6 and MFN2, and compound heterozygote mutations in C12orf65, which are associated with recessive forms. The availability of specific DNA-based genetic testing is crucial for diagnosis, particularly given the variable ages of onset observed in genetic diseases. [PMC10977349, PMC10631856, PMC10808857, PMC5282685, PMC2671886]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Advances in the care of patients with hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy, also known as Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease, include better supportive treatments, encompassing both clinical and surgical interventions. Furthermore, new treatment perspectives are emerging from discoveries in the field of genetics, such as RNA interference and gene editing techniques. [PMC10631856]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 6 can vary. Bi-allelic NDUFS6 variants have been linked to severe outcomes, including lethal infantile mitochondrial disease or Leigh syndrome. However, improvement in visual function has been observed in some patients; one individual with HMSN type VI demonstrated significant improvement in visual acuity and resolution of visual field defects over a 7-year period, despite persistent inner retinal abnormalities. The condition can manifest with childhood-onset neuropathy and adult-onset optic atrophy. [PMC10977349, PMC3155637, PMC1074097, PMC1073804]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis characterized at birth by the presence of large, thick, plate-like shell over the whole body associated with severe ectropion, eclabium, and flattened ears, that later develops into a severe scaling erythroderma. Harlequin ichthyosis is the most severe disorder of this group.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): HI; Ichthyosis congenita, Harlequin type; Autosomal congenital ichthyosis, Harlequin type

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence is estimated to be less than 1/300,000 births.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Affected infants born encased in a collodion membrane (taut, shiny, translucent membrane appearing as an extra skin layer) with armorlike white-grayish scales, distributed throughout the body, and divided into irregular and quadrangular plates by deep fissures, with severe restriction of movements. Facial features are distorted due to extreme ectropion, conjunctival edema, eclabium and broadened nose. Infants also present with contractures, synechiae of auricles and/or toes with a possible risk of autoamputation. The risk of death is high during the neonatal period, babies being susceptible to severe temperature dysregulation, feeding difficulties, infections and respiratory problems. When they survive, the collodion membrane sheds after a few weeks and transforms into severe erythroderma with severe scaling and persistent ectropion. Other clinical features are often associated such as palmoplantar keratoderma, failure to thrive, short stature, malformed ears and digits, nail deformities and alopecia.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: HI is due to recessive mutations in the ABCA12 gene encoding the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter, involved in lipid transport from lamellar granules to the apical surface of granular layer keratinocytes. Homozygous mutations in this gene cause protein function loss and affect important nucleotide-binding fold domains and transmembrane domains resulting in impaired lipid barrier function.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical examination. Biopsy is not useful but reveals massive compact orthohyperkeratosis. Skin ultrastructure shows vesicular lamellar bodies ghosts and a paucity of secreted lamellar granules in the stratum corneum. Molecular analysis reveals homozygous ABCA12 mutations.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: HI may be confused with less severe forms of ichthyosis. Later in life, the differential diagnosis includes other disorders from the autosomal recessive congenital ichthyosis (ARCI) group, restrictive dermopathy, infantile systemic hyalinosis, and Neu-Laxova syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is mandatory and consists in DNA analysis of amniocentesis and chorion villus sampling materials, rather than fetal skin biopsies. Ultrasonography shows diffuse scaling, digital contractures, flattened rudimentary external ear, nasal hypoplasia, everted eyelids, typical fish mouth, open fetal mouth, and macroglossia.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The disease is transmitted as an autosomal recessive trait. Genetic counseling should be offered to the affected families informing them of the 25% risk of recurrence in each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: In the neonatal period, management requires a multidisciplinary approach (dermatologists, neonatologists, ophthalmologists, surgeons, dieticians, and psychologists for family support). Gastrostomy may be necessary. Emollients and oral retinoids (1-2mg/kg/day) are recommended. It is important to keep invasive procedures to a minimum in order to avoid skin infections. Management of survivors is similar for all severe ARCIs and includes the use of emollients, keratolytics, and retinoids.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: HI is associated with substantial (50%) morbidity and mortality soon after birth and throughout childhood due to sepsis and/or respiratory failure (75% of cases). Survivors can have a normal life expectancy but may develop severe skin disease with eye complications related to persistent ectropion, delayed developmental and motor milestones, and social difficulties. Current medical treatments achieved a significant improvement in quality and expectancy of life, however the severity of the disease might still affect life duration. The prognosis of the disease with actual treatments is still under evaluation.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Hemolytic anemia due to diphosphoglycerate mutase deficiency
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: ORPHA:714

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Erythrocytosis is associated with increased red blood cell mass and can be either congenital or acquired. Congenital secondary causes are rare and include germline variants increasing haemoglobin (Hb)-oxygen affinity (e.g., Hb or bisphosphoglycerate mutase (BPGM) variants) or affecting oxygen-sensing pathway proteins. Here, five adults from three kindreds with erythrocytosis associated with heterozygosity for BPGM variants, including one novel. Functional analyses showed partial BPGM deficiency, reduced 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate levels and/or increased Hb-oxygen affinity. We also review currently known BPGM variants. contributes to raising awareness of BPGM variants, and in particular that heterozygosity for BPGM deficiency may already manifest clinically. An inherited and complete deficiency of diphosphoglycerate mutase was discovered in the erythrocytes of a 42-yr-old man of French... [PMC10092417, PMC371847]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Erythrocytosis is associated with increased red blood cell mass and can be either congenital or acquired. Congenital secondary causes are rare and include germline variants increasing haemoglobin (Hb)-oxygen affinity (e.g., Hb or bisphosphoglycerate mutase (BPGM) variants) or affecting oxygen-sensing pathway proteins. Here, five adults from three kindreds with erythrocytosis associated with heterozygosity for BPGM variants, including one novel. Functional analyses showed partial BPGM deficiency, reduced 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate levels and/or increased Hb-oxygen affinity. We also review currently known BPGM variants. contributes to raising awareness of BPGM variants, and in particular that heterozygosity for BPGM deficiency may already manifest clinically. An inherited and complete deficiency of diphosphoglycerate mutase was discovered in the erythrocytes of a 42-yr-old man of French... [PMC10092417, PMC371847]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of diphosphoglycerate mutase (BPGM) deficiency involves several approaches. Genetic testing, such as targeted NGS panels, can identify germline BPGM variants. Functional analyses are crucial, demonstrating partial BPGM deficiency, reduced 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate levels, and/or increased hemoglobin-oxygen affinity. An enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) system is available to determine BPGM protein content in human erythrocytes, which can detect BPGM enzymopathy. Furthermore, direct measurement of diphosphoglycerate mutase activity in erythrocytes can reveal undetectable levels, often accompanied by significantly reduced 2,3-diphosphoglycerate levels. [PMC10927185, PMC10092417, PMC6807899, PMC371847]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling should address that BPGM deficiency is associated with germline variants. Heterozygosity for BPGM variants can lead to clinical manifestations, such as congenital erythrocytosis, due to partial BPGM deficiency, reduced 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate levels, or increased hemoglobin-oxygen affinity. This highlights that carriers may be symptomatic and should be considered in family planning and risk assessment. [PMC10092417]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare condition associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and characterized by unwanted weight loss (involving both fat and muscle) of more than ten percent of body weight, with either diarrhea or weakness and fever which have lasted at least 30 days and are not related to an infection.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: AIDS wasting syndrome is characterized by severe wasting, often presenting with hyporexia and proximal limb weakness. It is a prominent feature of advanced HIV/AIDS and end-stage disease, frequently observed alongside opportunistic infections like esophageal actinomycosis, disseminated cryptococcosis, recurrent sepsis, and Kaposi sarcoma. Wasting can also manifest as subcutaneous fat loss in HIV/HAART-associated lipodystrophy syndrome. Cachexia, including cardiac cachexia, is a related public health challenge, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where it is linked to HIV, malaria, tuberculosis, and end-stage heart disease. Myopathies with vesicular changes, sometimes associated with zidovudine treatment, may also involve wasting. [PMC10347741, PMC11307658, PMC6794836, PMC5717311, PMC4769467]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hereditary vascular malformation characterized by the presence of small, multifocal, venous lesions involving the skin and mucosa.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Cutaneous and mucosal venous malformation; VMCM

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Prevalence is unknown but 18 families have been identified so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Multifocal venous lesions are usually small (<2 cm), involving skin and mucosa with cervicofacial distribution in ~50% of cases and extremities in ~40%. They are soft, compressible and grow proportionally with age. Some are present at birth and new ones appear over time. Small lesions are usually asymptomatic, whereas larger lesions can invade subcutaneous muscle, causing pain, bleeding and/or functional limitation. About 90% of carriers develop symptoms by age 20. There is significant clinical variation in size, location and number of lesions, even among affected individuals from the same family. Patients with VMCMs have normal mental and physical development.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: VMCMs are caused by germline TEK (TIE2) variant—commonly R849W, R897S, or R897C—that lead to ligand-independent receptor activation. Lesion formation requires a somatic second-hit variant in the same gene, consistent with a two-hit model.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on clinical evaluation, supported by Doppler ultrasound showing slow-flow and MRI to assess lesion extent. Ultrasound typically reveals compressible venous cavities. Diagnostic genetic testing for TEK mutations is available.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis includes: glomuvenous malformations (GVMs) which are inherited, multifocal, darker lesions that are painful and superficial, without mucosal involvement; blue rubber bleb nevus syndrome (BRBN) caused by somatic TEK variants, marked by cutaneous and mucosal lesions with distinctive gastrointestinal involvement; and multifocal venous malformations (MVMs) which are clinically similar to VMCMs but sporadic, due to somatic mosaicism and lacking familial inheritance.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is feasible for affected families in which the disease-causing mutation has been identified, but is not widely available.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: VMCMs are transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner with incomplete penetrance, likely explained by the paradominant inheritance (germline variant plus second-hit somatic variant). Genetic counseling should inform affected families about the 50% transmission risk and variability in clinical expression. Anticipation has not been observed, meaning that symptoms do not usually appear earlier or become more severe in the subsequent generations.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Sclerotherapy, alone or with surgery, remains standard for local symptom management, though this is less effective in multifocal disease. In patients with elevated D-dimers (suggesting localized intravascular coagulopathy), low-molecular-weight heparin may reduce pain. Estrogen-containing oral contraceptives should be avoided due to thrombosis risk. Activating TEK variants drive constitutive PI3K-AKT-mTOR activation, supporting the benefit of sirolimus in symptoms control, as demonstrated across different studies.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis for patients is good, malignant transformation has not been reported and the life expectancy is not reduced.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare lysosomal disease characterized by a clinical phenotype that combines the features of different sulfatase deficiencies (whether lysosomal or not). Clinical manifestations can include developmental delay, progressive neurologic deterioration, hydrocephalus, hypotonia, coarse facial features, retinopathy, skeletal anomalies, hepatomegaly and ichthyosis to a variable degree. Multiple sulfatase deficiency (MSD) comprises severe to attenuated forms historically classified as neonatal (most severe form), infantile (most common form) or juvenile (rarest form).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated prevalence is 1/500,000. So far, there are approximately 150 reported cases without apparent ethnological and sexual distribution.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: This disease begins between birth and the juvenile period. Patients with an early neonatal form can present with intrauterine growth retardation and respiratory distress at birth. They may also have facial dysmorphism, skeletal abnormalities, splenomegaly, congenital heart defects, ichthyosis and muscle hypotonia. Failure to thrive is a common clinical sign inherent to the different clinical MSD presentations. The infantile form often presents with developmental delay preventing the child from reaching developmental milestones, mildly coarse facial features, ichthyosis, organomegaly, dysostosis multiplex, and ichthyosis of variable degree. Attenuated forms differ from severe forms in that the disease progresses more slowly and not all clinical signs need to be present. Patients often achieve independent ambulation and speech before neurocognitive decline begins. Retinopathy, gallbladder sludge, hydrocephalus, hypertrichosis, dysostosis multiplex, and neuropathy can occur at all stages and in every form of MSD.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: An autosomal recessive mutation in the SUMF1 gene on chromosome 3p26 causes MSD. The mutation alters the function of the sulfatase-activating enzyme FGE (Formylglycine-generating enzyme). There exist over 50 pathogenic mutations of SUMF1 most of which are missense mutations allowing residual FGE function towards sulfatase activation that result in reduced (to a variable degree) or completely absent activity sulfatases (lysosomal or not).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Clinical manifestations associated with a detection of glycosaminoglycans and sulfatides in the urine is indicative of MSD. The diagnosis is confirmed if there is loss of activity of at least two sulfatases in leukocytes or if a genetic test reveals a pathogenic mutation in the SUMF1 gene.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes all single sulfatase deficiencies like metachromatic leukodystrophy (arylsulfatase A deficiency), Hunter syndrome, Maroteaux-Lamy syndrome, or Sanfilippo syndrome type A and D among others. X-linked ichthyosis, saposin B deficiency, mucolipidosis and other lysosomal diseases are additional differential diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Preimplantation and prenatal genetic testing can be performed if pathogenic SUMF1 variants have been identified in an affected family member.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The transmission is autosomal recessive. With each pregnancy, there is a 25% chance that the child will be affected and a 50% chance that the child will be a carrier.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Currently, no specific treatment exists. A multidisciplinary approach is essential to increase quality of life and includes physiotherapy, skin treatment, neurological examinations, and monitoring of bone fragility, hearing, vision, gastrointestinal and respiratory disorders.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: MSD has multiple clinical expressions and a prognosis can be hard to establish. However there exist different categories of MSD which may help evaluate its severity. The 50% survival rate has been estimated to be approximately 13 years. High motor function, achievement of speech, low number of clinical signs at a given age and high residual functionality of the FGE variant correlate with an attenuated course of MSD, and vice versa.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare gastroenterologic disease characterized by recurrent acute pancreatitis and/or chronic pancreatitis in at least 2 first-degree relatives, or 3 or more second-degree relatives in 2 or more generations, for which no predisposing factors are identified. This rare inherited form of pancreatitis leads to irreversible damage to both exocrine and endocrine components of the pancreas.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The estimated prevalence of hereditary chronic pancreatitis (HCP) is approximately 1/300,000 people in Europe (1/800,000 in Germany, approximately 1/333,000 in France and approximately 1/175,000 in Denmark).
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Onset of HCP is typically early in life, during childhood and adolescence. The clinical presentation is highly variable and includes chronic or intermittent mild to severe abdominal pain associated with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency, leading to maldigestion and/or pancreatic endocrine insufficiency (glucose intolerance progressing to diabetes mellitus type 3c) in some cases. The disease is slowly progressive. The risk of developing pancreatic carcinoma after the age of 50 is elevated in patients with HCP. However, the exact risk increase is difficult to assess.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Mutations in the PRSS1 (7q34) gene, encoding cationic trypsinogen, play a causative role in chronic pancreatitis. It has been shown that the PRSS1 mutations increase autocatalytic conversion of trypsinogen to active trypsin and thus probably cause premature, intrapancreatic trypsinogen activation disturbing the intrapancreatic balance of proteases and their inhibitors. Other genes, such as the anionic trypsinogen (PRSS2; 7q34), the serine protease inhibitor, Kazal type 1 (SPINK1; 5q32) and the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR; 7q31.2) have been found to be associated with chronic pancreatitis (idiopathic and hereditary). Recently, mutations in carboxypeptidase A1 (CPA1; 7q32.2), carboxylesterlipase (CEL; 9q34.13) and pancreatic lipase (PNLIP; 10q25.3) have been found to be associated with HCP and idiopathic chronic pancreatitis with early onset.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis of HCP is based on clinical features along with family history of chronic pancreatitis, absence of precipitating factors and a negative workup for known causes of chronic pancreatitis. Imaging (abdominal ultrasound, endoscopic ultrasound, exceptionally with endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) reveals morphological changes like pancreatic calcifications, pancreatic duct changes, pseudocysts, bile duct and duodenal obstruction. The diagnosis might be substantiated by variants in the genes mentioned above.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other forms of chronic pancreatitis mainly alcoholic chronic pancreatitis, idiopathic chronic pancreatitis, autoimmune pancreatitis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is not encouraged.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Genetic testing should only be performed in carefully selected patients by direct DNA sequencing. Mutation in the PRSS1 gene is transmitted in an autosomal dominant manner with incomplete penetrance.
