DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Rationale: Bohring-Opitz syndrome is a severe congenital disorder associated with a de novo mutation in the additional sex combs-like 1 (ASXL1) gene, and it is characterized by symptoms that include developmental delay and musculoskeletal and neurological features. Patient concerns: The patient was a girl, an in vitro fertilization (IVF) baby, with delayed motor development, drooling, short stature, slow growth, low muscle tone, image diagnosis of hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, delayed tooth eruption, high palatal arch, adduction of the thumb, drooling, not chewing, excessive joint activity, and ligament relaxation. Diagnosis: Whole-exome sequencing analysis detected 1 novel disruptive frameshift mutation in ASXL1 in the proband but wild-type ASXL1 in both parents. Interventions: Approximately 1 year of rehabilitation training, which included exercise therapy, toy imitation... [PMC8812699, PMC7933106, PMC6770791, PMC4000731, PMC1013640]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal complications were observed during the pregnancy of a patient who later presented with features consistent with trigonocephaly-short stature-developmental delay syndrome, including craniosynostosis, short stature, and significant developmental delays. These complications included fetal ascites, echogenic bowel, polyhydramnios, and an incompetent cervix, leading to a premature birth at 29 weeks gestation. [PMC7933106]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for syndromes characterized by trigonocephaly, short stature, and developmental delay involves considering various inheritance patterns. Some conditions demonstrate autosomal dominant transmission, with affected individuals appearing in successive generations, though expression can be variable, making clinical recognition of carrier status challenging in some parents. Autosomal recessive inheritance is also observed, where unaffected parents carry mutations that lead to disease in their offspring, often identified as homozygous or compound heterozygous variants. Additionally, de novo mutations, detectable through whole-exome sequencing, can cause severe congenital disorders, highlighting the importance of molecular diagnosis for accurate recurrence risk assessment and family planning, especially in contexts like in vitro fertilization. [PMC8812699, PMC6770791, PMC4000731, PMC1013640, PMC1013359]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management involves multidisciplinary support tailored to specific symptoms. Rehabilitation training, including exercise therapy, toy imitation, cognitive and daily living skills training, gesture language, oral muscle training, and hand movement training, has shown improvements in motor development, feeding, and object manipulation. For severe neonatal complications, interventions have included tracheostomy for respiratory issues, a peritoneovenous shunt for ascites, and a gastrostomy tube for feeding difficulties. [PMC8812699, PMC7933106]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for conditions presenting with trigonocephaly, short stature, and developmental delay can vary significantly. Some forms are associated with severe complications, such as hepatic fibrosis leading to liver failure and early death. Other cases involve significant medical challenges, including severe respiratory issues and feeding difficulties, alongside profound developmental delays, requiring extensive interventions. However, with rehabilitation, some patients can achieve developmental milestones like crawling, standing, and walking with assistance, though delays may persist. For specific presentations of trigonocephaly with minor anomalies, a good prognosis is emphasized, although untreated cases can result in disfiguring oxycephaly. [PMC8812699, PMC7933106, PMC4000731, PMC1013359]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder characterized by multiple congenital anomalies. The name is a mneumonic for the common features observed in SHORT syndrome that include; short stature, hyperextensibility of joints, ocular depression, Rieger anomaly and teething delay. Other common manifestations of SHORT syndrome are mild intrauterine growth restriction, partial lipodystrophy, delayed bone age, hernias and a recognizable facial gestalt.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Lipodystrophy-Rieger anomaly-diabetes syndrome; Rieger anomaly-partial lipodystrophy syndrome

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of SHORT syndrome is unknown. Less than 50 cases have been reported in the literature to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Individuals with SHORT syndrome often display mild intrauterine growth restriction. Feeding difficulties and/or failure to thrive present in early childhood and final adult height is shorter than average (155-163 cm in males and 143-160 cm in females). Most patients have a characteristic facial gestalt, often described as progeroid, with triangular face shape, prominent forehead, ocular depression, hypoplastic alae nasi, low-hanging columella, downturned corners of the mouth, micrognathia and prominent (but not typically low-set or posteriorly located) ears. Partial lipodystrophy may be evident in the face at birth and later in the chest and upper extremities (including the hands), but it is usually not reported in the buttocks and legs. Delayed dentition, hypodontia, enamel hypoplasia, malocclusion and multiple dental caries are frequently reported. Ophthalmic anomalies (e.g. Rieger anomaly, Axenfeld anomaly, glaucoma) are also characteristic of the disease. Diabetes is seen in approximately 2/3 of individuals with SHORT syndrome after the age of 15 years. Other less common manifestations include hyperextensibility of joints and/or hernias, sensorineural hearing loss and ovarian cysts in females. Intellectual development and cognition are usually unaffected although mild impairment with speech delay has been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: SHORT syndrome is due to mutations in the PIK3R1 gene (5q13.1), encoding phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase regulatory subunit alpha. Mutations are thought to impair the PI3K/AKT/mTOR pathway, which plays an important role in cellular proliferation and growth.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the presence of the characteristic features and confirmed by molecular genetic testing identifying a PIK3R1 mutation. The presence of all 5 features of the acronym is not necessary for a positive diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include Silver-Russell syndrome, Alagille syndrome, Floating-Harbor syndrome, growth delay due to insulin-like growth factor I resistance, Berardinelli-Seip congenital lipodystrophy and Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis is possible in families with a known disease-causing mutation.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: SHORT syndrome is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. Genetic counseling is recommended for at-risk families. De novo cases have also been described. Genetic counseling should be proposed to individuals having the disease-causing mutation informing them that there is 50% risk of passing the mutation to offspring.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment is symptomatic and requires a multidisciplinary team. Screening for insulin resistance is recommended starting in mid-late childhood. Glucose intolerance and diabetes mellitus can be treated with diet, lifestyle, oral medication and insulin, while growth hormone therapy is contraindicated. Ophthalmological management and follow-up (i.e. regular eye examinations) are necessary to reduce and stabilize ocular pressures and to preserve vision. Dental anomalies can be treated using standard methods (e.g. crowns and dental prostheses).
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Individuals with SHORT syndrome are considered to have a normal life-expectancy.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Humero-radio-ulnar synostosis is an extremely rare, genetic, congenital joint formation defect disorder characterized by uni- or bilateral fusion of the humerus, radius and ulnar bones, leading to loss of elbow motion and, in most, functional arm incapacity. It may appear as distal humeral bifurcation with absent elbow joint and shortened arm length on imaging. Hand abnormalities, namely oligoectrosyndactyly, may be associated.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Further report of a patient with humeroradioulnar synostosis and hydronephrosis. on a patient with humeroradioulnar synostosis and lambdoid synostosis. The case differs from three previously described cases in minor details, but the upper limb abnormalities are strikingly similar. [PMC1050195, PMC1016243]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic, potentially fatal form of dilated cardiomyopathy that develops during the final month of pregnancy or within five months after delivery.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a rare, life-threatening cardiac condition characterized by heart failure due to left ventricular systolic dysfunction (ejection fraction <45%) that typically develops in late pregnancy or the early postpartum period, often without an identifiable cause. It is a leading cause of maternal morbidity and mortality, associated with a high mortality rate. The condition's clinical presentation frequently overlaps with normal pregnancy-related physiological changes, leading to diagnostic delays. While often idiopathic, PPCM is particularly prone to develop in individuals with a history of preeclampsia and hypertension. Genetic variants (e.g., TTN, BAG3, LMNA) are implicated, and it can be associated with infections like influenza A virus or, exceedingly rarely, with sickle cell disease. [PMC12126653, PMC11901409, PMC12046153, PMC10977545, PMC10860229]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) has a complex genetic landscape, with notable genes such as titin (TTN), Bcl2-associated athanogene 3 (BAG3), lamin A/C (LMNA), and filamin C (FLNC) implicated. Genetic analysis is recommended, particularly in patients with a positive family history, as it can provide insights into the pathogenesis of heart failure, including PPCM. Integrating genetic profiling into personalized medicine approaches holds promise for enhancing diagnostic precision and tailoring therapeutic outcomes for individual patient profiles. FLNC pathogenic variants, including biallelic forms, are associated with PPCM and arrhythmias. [PMC12046153, PMC11179814, PMC11305805]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for peripartum cardiomyopathy varies, with some patients achieving full recovery of left ventricular function within months. Others demonstrate partial recovery or significant improvement in symptoms and cardiac function, transitioning to lower NYHA classes. While amelioration of heart function can occur over several years, full recovery is not always observed. Early diagnosis and precise management are essential for achieving favorable patient outcomes, and interventions like ablation can lead to improvement. Hemodynamic stabilization can also be achieved with appropriate treatment. [PMC12126653, PMC12046153, PMC11577443, PMC10977545, PMC10311228]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare bone disease and a form of microcephalic primordial dwarfism characterized by severe pre- and postnatal growth retardation, with marked microcephaly in proportion to body size, skeletal dysplasia, abnormal dentition, insulin resistance, and increased risk for cerebrovascular disease.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): MOPD type II; Majewski osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Microcephalic osteodysplastic primordial dwarfism type II (MOPDII) is one of the most common forms of microcephalic primordial dwarfism (MPD) and accounts for more than 150 cases worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: MOPDII is congenital, with a perinatal and infancy onset. It is characterized by severe pre- and postnatal growth retardation, with proportionate severe microcephaly, skeletal dysplasia, abnormal dentition, an increased risk for cerebrovascular disease (aneurysms and Moya Moya disease in 19%-52% of cases) and insulin resistance. Intrauterine growth restriction (IUGR) is common. The average length, weight, and head occipitofrontal circumference (OFC) at birth are respectively 7.0, 3.9, and 4.6 SDs below the population mean (after correcting for gestational age <37 weeks). Head growth appears to stop by 18 months of age giving rise to the appearance of progressive microcephaly. At maturity, the average height, weight, and OFC are respectively 10.3, 14.3, and 8.5 SDs below the population mean. Skeletal dysplasia with progressive scoliosis, radial head dislocation and coxa vara may be seen. Distinct craniofacial features include prominent, small pinnae with attached lobes; small, dysplastic and poorly rooted, opalescent dentition and sparse hair. Further hallmarks of MOPD II include high-pitched nasal voice, areas of hypo- and hyperpigmentation (with café-au-lait spots), poikiloderma, acanthosis nigricans, and truncal obesity in adolescence and adulthood. A disorder initially named primordial short stature-microdontia-opalescent and rootless teeth was originally and mistakenly reported to have distinct MOPD, but it is now recognized to be the same entity as MOPD II.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MOPD II is caused by mutations in PCNT (21q22.3), encoding pericentrin, which anchors a wide range of centrosomal proteins and protein complexes during cell division. Disruption of pericentrin is thought to cause mitotic spindle defects, and impaired cell proliferation. A role in ATR DNA damage dependent signaling has also been proposed.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on clinical features, radiographic examinations of bone age that usually show disharmonic maturation of centers and a retarded bone age. Diagnosis is confirmed by genetic screening of PCNT. Some individuals have elevated platelet counts.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes Meier-Gorlin syndrome, LIG4 syndrome, XRCC4 deficiency, Seckel syndrome, MOPD types I and III, SHORT syndrome, Schimke immuno-osseous dysplasia, and Dubowitz syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Pregnancies with affected children are often complicated by the observation of IUGR. Early age of delivery is noted. C-sections may be performed at earlier ages due to the IUGR. Prenatal diagnosis is possible if the causative mutation(s) in PCNT have been identified in the carrier parents.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive. Genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them that there is a 25% risk of having an affected child at each pregnancy.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management is mainly symptomatic. Screening for CNS vascular abnormalities with brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) is recommended at diagnosis and every 12 to 18 months. Yearly screening for signs of insulin resistance including a lipid profile should be performed (beginning at grade school age), as well as monitoring for anemia, platelet counts, and hip and spine anomalies.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Life expectancy is generally decreased, but individuals live into their 30s. Many complications arise, but most can be handled by adapting modern medical techniques to the diminutive size. Vascular anomalies are a common complication. They may involve neurovasculature in childhood, and renal and coronary arteries in adulthood, the latter of which may be life-threatening.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare autosomal recessive retinal disorder characterized by color blindness, nystagmus, photophobia, and severely reduced visual acuity due to the absence or impairment of cone function.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): ACHM; Complete or incomplete color blindness; Pingelapese blindness; Rod monochromacy; Rod monochromatism; Total color blindness

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence is estimated to be 1/30,000-1/50,000 worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: ACHM is characterized by reduced visual acuity, pendular nystagmus, increased sensitivity to light (photophobia), a small central scotoma, and reduced or complete loss of color discrimination. Most individuals have complete ACHM, with total lack of function in all three types of cones. Rarely, individuals have incomplete ACHM, with similar, but generally less severe symptoms.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Five genes (GNAT2 (1p13), PDE6C (10q24), PDE6H (12p13), CNGA3 (2q11.2), and CNGB3 (8q21.3)) have been associated with ACHM, all encoding key components of the cone phototransduction cascade (G-protein GNAT2 > phosphodiesterase PDE6C/PDE6H > cyclic nucleotide gated channel CNGA3/CNGB3). Mutations in CNGB3 are the most prevalent, followed by CNGA3, while the others are rare causes of ACHM.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis of ACHM is based on clinical ophthalmological examination, psychophysical testing (i.e. color vision) and electrophysiological testing (electroretinography - ERG) where a loss of photopic but normal scotopic responses is observed. Optical coherence tomography shows progressive disruption and/or loss of the inner/outer segment junction of the photoreceptors and an attenuation of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) within the macular region. The diagnosis is verified by molecular genetic analysis of the causative genes.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes blue cone monochromatism (BCM), Leber congenital amaurosis, other cone dystrophies, and cerebral achromatopsia
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis may be offered by specialized laboratories to at-risk couples.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: ACHM is transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner. Carrier testing for family members at risk of mutations is possible once the disease-causing mutations have been identified in the family. Furthermore, genetic counseling should be offered to at-risk couples (both individuals are carriers of a disease-causing mutation) informing them of the 25% risk of having an affected child.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: There is no specific therapy available. Management is symptomatic and includes regular ophthalmological follow-up examination. Patients should be informed about the possibility of using filtering glasses or contact lenses (red tinted or brown) to reduce photophobia and to improve contrast sensitivity. Low-vision aids include high-powered magnifiers for reading.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: ACHM is usually a stationary disease, yet macular degeneration can occur.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare deafness characterized by the association of bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and white hair with scattered black tufts, as well as skin areas of hyper- and hypopigmentation. Additional reported features include global developmental delay and moderate intellectual disability, growth retardation, microcephaly, hypotonia, mild dysmorphic facial features (deeply set eyes, broad nasal bridge, slight bowing of the upper lip), retinal depigmentation, anomalies of the fingers and toes, and white matter abnormalities on brain imaging.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): O'Doherty syndrome; Pigmentary disorder with hearing loss; Pigmentary disorder with deafness

DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Ermine phenotype, also known as H syndrome, is an autosomal recessive genodermatosis caused by mutations in the SLC29A3 gene. Genetic counseling should inform families about the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, indicating that both parents are typically carriers and each child has a 25% chance of being affected. Clinical suspicion for H syndrome arises with features such as short stature, hyperglycemia, and other endocrine and cutaneous abnormalities, guiding diagnostic considerations. [PMC11457316, PMC10720192, PMC6681376, PMC6473230, PMC6503064]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The term congenital hypopigmentary disorders refers to a wide group of heterogeneous hereditary diseases, clinically characterized by inborn pigmentary defects of the iris, hair, and/or skin. They include Gray Hair Syndromes (GHSs), a rare group of autosomal recessive genodermatosis hallmarked by inborn silvery gray hair. GHSs encompass Griscelli, Chediak⁻Higashi, Elejalde, and Cross syndromes, which are all characterized by a broad spectrum of severe multisystem disorders, including neurological, ocular, skeletal, and immune system impairment. In this manuscript, in detail the clinical, trichoscopic, and genetic features of a rare case of Griscelli syndrome; moreover, we provide an overview of all the GHSs known to date. Our report highlights how an accurate clinical examination with noninvasive , like trichoscopy, may play a crucial rule in diagnosis of rare and potentially lethal... [PMC6473230, PMC6503064]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder characterized by the association of mullerian duct and distal limb anomalies. Females present with anomalies ranging from a vaginal septum to complete duplication of uterus and vagina, and males present with micropenis. The limb anomalies varied from postaxial polydactyly to severe upper limb hypoplasia with split hand.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Müllerian duct anomalies-limb anomalies syndrome encompasses several rare conditions, including Hand-Foot-Genital Syndrome (HFGS) and limb/pelvis-hypoplasia/aplasia syndrome. HFGS has been observed in families, while limb/pelvis-hypoplasia/aplasia syndrome is a newly recognized condition reported in single cases. The co-occurrence of VACTERL association with Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome is also rare, with a limited number of published cases identified in the literature. While often appearing isolated, familial recurrence in some forms suggests genetic factors are involved. [PMC11063329, PMC5178070, PMC2889242, PMC1016237]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Müllerian duct anomalies-limb anomalies syndrome encompasses a range of Müllerian and limb defects. Müllerian anomalies can include agenesis or aplasia of the uterus, vagina, fallopian tubes, and sometimes ovaries, as observed in Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome. Other presentations include unicornuate uterus with rudimentary horns, which may lead to severe dysmenorrhea, hematometra, endometriosis, or ectopic pregnancy, and uterovaginal septa. Limb anomalies manifest as hand and foot symptoms or more generalized limb/pelvis hypoplasia/aplasia. The syndrome frequently co-occurs with VACTERL association, characterized by vertebral defects, anal atresia (often with rectovestibular fistula), cardiac defects, tracheoesophageal fistula/esophageal atresia, and renal defects. Anal atresia and renal defects are particularly common in these co-occurrences. [PMC6543654, PMC5178070, PMC4447938, PMC2889242, PMC1016237]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Müllerian duct anomalies-limb anomalies syndrome encompasses conditions with heterogeneous genetic etiologies. Hand-Foot-Genital Syndrome (HFGS), characterized by uterovaginal septa and limb anomalies, is caused by mutations in HOXA13, specifically an expansion of its third polyalanine tract. Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome, involving agenesis or aplasia of the uterus and upper vagina, is associated with genetic variants including deletions in 17q12 (LHX1, HNF1B) and 16p11.2 (TBX6), and sequence variations in GREB1L and PAX8. The limb/pelvis-hypoplasia/aplasia syndrome with Müllerian aplasia has also been observed in a consanguineous family, suggesting a genetic basis. The co-occurrence of MRKH syndrome with VACTERL association (vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb defects) further highlights complex embryopathogenesis. [PMC11063329, PMC5178070, PMC2889242, PMC1016237]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for Müllerian duct anomalies vary based on presentation. For conditions like Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome, characterized by uterine and upper vaginal agenesis, diagnosis typically occurs during adolescence with primary amenorrhea, supported by a normal 46,XX karyotype. Genomic investigations, including chromosomal microarray and genome-wide sequencing, can identify associated genetic variants. In cases of unicornuate uterus, often presenting with secondary dysmenorrhea, pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and laparotomy can reveal the anomaly and associated complications. For Müllerian agenesis in newborns with anorectal malformations, examination under anesthesia, imaging studies, and diagnostic laparoscopy may be necessary. Hand-foot-genital syndrome, involving Müllerian fusion anomalies, can be diagnosed by sequence analysis of HOXA13, though this is typically reserved for patients with other characteristic sequelae. [PMC11063329, PMC6543654, PMC4447938, PMC2889242]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnoses include VACTERL association, which can present with Müllerian anomalies such as unicornuate uterus or Müllerian agenesis, alongside vertebral, anal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, and limb defects. Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome, characterized by uterovaginal agenesis, may co-occur with VACTERL. Hand-Foot-Genital Syndrome (HFGS), caused by HOXA13 mutations, is another consideration, presenting with uterovaginal septa and hand/foot symptoms. Additionally, the limb/pelvis-hypoplasia/aplasia syndrome, featuring Müllerian aplasia and limb/pelvis defects, should be considered. [PMC6543654, PMC5178070, PMC4447938, PMC2889242, PMC1016237]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling is increasingly relevant due to the identified genetic etiologies and familial recurrence of Müllerian duct anomalies. For conditions like Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome, a heterogeneous genetic basis is suggested, with variants in genes such as LHX1, HNF1B, TBX6, GREB1L, and PAX8 implicated. In cases presenting with both Müllerian duct and limb anomalies, characteristic of Hand-Foot-Genital Syndrome, a novel expansion of the HOXA13 polyalanine tract has been identified as a genetic cause. Therefore, genetic counseling should address recurrence risk, particularly with emerging fertility treatments, and guide appropriate genetic testing based on the specific clinical presentation, such as HOXA13 sequencing for true HFGS. [PMC11063329, PMC2889242]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management for Müllerian duct anomalies, which can be a component of this syndrome, includes surgical resection for symptomatic conditions such as functioning non-communicating rudimentary horns to prevent complications like hematometra and endometriosis. For coexisting anorectal malformations in patients with Müllerian agenesis, definitive anorectoplasty is a key management component. Uterus transplantation is an emerging fertility treatment option for individuals with Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome. Additionally, genetic counseling is important to discuss the recurrence risk associated with identified genetic etiologies. [PMC11063329, PMC6543654, PMC4447938]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Patients with Müllerian duct anomalies, such as Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser syndrome, face significant implications including absolute infertility. Other anomalies, like unicornuate uteri with functioning non-communicating rudimentary horns, are susceptible to gynecologic and obstetric complications such as hematometra, endometriosis, and ectopic pregnancy. Surgical resection of these horns is usually recommended and can lead to resolution of symptoms, with patients experiencing regular periods and pain subsidence. Given the increasing evidence for genetic etiologies, genetic counseling concerning recurrence risk in offspring will likely increase. [PMC11063329, PMC6543654]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Neuroblastoma is a malignant tumor of neural crest cells, the cells that give rise to the sympathetic nervous system, which is observed in children.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: It represents about 10% of solid tumors in infants and children under the age of 15, with an annual incidence of about 1/70,000 in children in this class of age.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In 90% of cases the neuroblastoma is diagnosed before the age of five. The clinical presentation of neuroblastoma is very variable and depends on the stage and location of the tumor, which can develop at any site in the sympathetic nervous system (around 80% of cases develop in the abdomen). Localized forms are discovered fortuitously or are revealed by the presence of an abdominal or thoracic mass that can be associated with pain. At the time of diagnosis, metastatic forms represent about 50% of cases. The most frequent metastatic sites are bone marrow, bone, liver and skin. Symptoms of metastasis including bone pain, limp, paralysis, hepatomegaly (Pepper's syndrome), and exophthalmia (Hutchinson's syndrome), indicate metastatic neuroblastoma. The disease can also be associated with arterial hypertension, fever, and an altered general state (weight loss, pain, irritability, and anemia).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Neuroblastoma has been linked to numerous genetic anomalies which affect prognosis: amplification of the oncogene MYCN (2p24.3) is a factor for poor prognosis; triploidy, numerical anomalies of chromosomes are associated with a good prognosis, while di- or tetraploidy and segmental chromosomal anomalies (including loss from 1p, from 11q, or gains of 17q) are associated with poor prognosis. Recently, a mutation of the ALK gene has been described in about 12% of cases.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on evidence of an elevated level of metabolites of urinary catecholamines (VMA, HVA, and dopamine) and on an image of the initial tumor by ultrasound and brain scan or by MRI. MIBG (iodine-131-meta-iodobenzylguanidine) scintigraphy and medullary analysis are useful for finding metastases. Tumor biopsy confirms the diagnosis, allows histological classification and helps find amplification of MYCN.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include nephroblastoma, which makes it necessary to systematically check urinary catecholamines in case of an abdominal tumor. Bone pain and limp can be interpreted as synovitis of the hip. Possible bilateral peri-orbital hematomas, caused by orbital metastases, should not lead to a diagnosis of maltreatment.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Neuroblastoma can be identified using antenatal ultrasound and therefore adequate management after the birth can be provided.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Localized forms of neuroblastoma are treated by surgical resection, sometimes preceded by chemotherapy. Treatment of metastatic forms in children of more than one year and forms with amplification of MYCN is by: conventional chemotherapy, surgery of the initial tumor, high dose chemotherapy with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, local radiotherapy and maintenance therapy with retinoic acid.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The majority of localized tumors have an excellent prognosis after surgery. Children under one year have a better prognosis than older children. Some tumors may even show spontaneous regression. In contrast, approximately 60% of children older than one year with neuroblastoma present metastatic disease at diagnosis with poor outcome, even with intensive treatment. In children older than one year, the five-year survival rate varies between 95% for some localized tumors to 30% in cases of metastatic neuroblastoma.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RSTS) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by severe global developmental delay (GDD) and distinctive facial grimacing. The loss of function of the CREBBP and EP300 genes is recognized as a genetic etiology of RSTS. However, the association between CREBBP variants and an increased risk of tumors remains unknown, despite multiple reports of tumor comorbidities related to RSTS. The aim of is to elucidate the tumors associated with CREBBP variants in the context of RSTS by presenting a case of ganglioneuroblastoma (GNB) in a patient diagnosed with RSTS. a 9-month-old male patient exhibiting distinctive facial features, enorchia, and GDD. Whole exome sequencing (WES) revealed a de novo pathogenic variant in NM_004380 (CREBBP): c.1068del (p.Gln356Hisfs*33). At one year of age, the patient experienced an unexplained fever lasting for two months, and the... [PMC11956269]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare, congenital, non-syndromic heart malformation characterized by a single fibrous annulus with two orifices opening into the left ventricle. Clinical presentation is variable and related to the degree of resulting mitral insufficiency and/or stenosis, and depending on the associated heart disease, most commonly atrioventricular septal defect, obstructive left-sided lesions, and cyanotic heart disease. Rare cases of isolated disease have been reported.
DiseaseInfo.Age of onset_G: Double-orifice mitral valve (DOMV) can be diagnosed across a broad age spectrum. While severe cases, especially those with concomitant cardiac anomalies or valve malfunction, often lead to early diagnosis in childhood, such as in a 4-year-old male or a 5-year-old girl, the condition can also be discovered in young adults (e.g., a 24-year-old woman) or middle-aged individuals (e.g., a 40-year-old woman). Furthermore, DOMV has been identified in elderly patients, including a 63-year-old, a 64-year-old, a 70-year-old, and a 75-year-old, sometimes as an incidental finding without clinical symptoms. [PMC9152849, PMC8617400, PMC8336376, PMC8086644, PMC4907761]

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Double-orifice mitral valve (DOMV) is described as a rare to extremely rare congenital cardiac anomaly. It is frequently associated with other cardiac defects, such as atrial septal defect or bicuspid aortic valve, and can rarely present in isolation. Severe concomitant cardiac anomalies or valve malfunction usually lead to an early diagnosis in childhood. However, DOMV can also be an incidental finding in adulthood, with valve function preserved for long periods, and the prevalence of isolated DOMV in adulthood is not known. While DOMV can be detected in some genetic syndromes, its simultaneous appearance with bicuspid aortic valve in Turner syndrome is considered rare. [PMC8617400, PMC8336376, PMC4683737]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Double-orifice mitral valve (DOMV) is a rare congenital anomaly, possibly originating from insufficient endocardial fusion during embryogenesis. It may also be caused by a developmental arrest of the left ventricular myocardium, particularly when coexisting with left ventricular noncompaction. DOMV is frequently associated with other cardiac defects, including bicuspid aortic valve, aortic coarctation, atrial septal defect, ventricular septal defect, atrioventricular canal defects, and components of Atypical Shone's complex or Tetralogy of Fallot. It can also be detected in genetic syndromes such as Turner syndrome and Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease. [PMC10307588, PMC9152849, PMC8617400, PMC8336376, PMC8086644]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Double-orifice mitral valve is primarily diagnosed using echocardiography. Both two-dimensional (2DE) and three-dimensional (3DE) transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) are suitable modalities to assess the anomaly's anatomical and functional properties. Three-dimensional transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) also plays a significant role, especially for detailed visualization. Advanced 3DE technologies, such as TrueVue, TouchVue, and TrueVue Glass, can supplement 2DE by providing clear spatial structures and realistic light-shadow effects, improving diagnostic performance. Color Doppler echocardiography can reveal associated conditions like mitral regurgitation. In some cases, the condition may be discovered or confirmed during open heart surgery. [PMC8617400, PMC8336376, PMC4907761, PMC4683737, PMC3128372]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Rheumatic mitral stenosis is an important consideration in the differential diagnosis, as it can simulate a double-orifice mitral valve. Cases of rheumatic heart disease have been reported where severe mitral stenosis presents with a deformed, double orifice-like mitral valve, making it a condition that can be confused with or mimic a true double-orifice mitral valve. [PMC3794150, PMC3128372]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Double-orifice mitral valve (DOMV) can be associated with various genetic syndromes. It has been reported in patients with Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease. Furthermore, DOMV, especially when co-occurring with bicuspid aortic valve malformation, has been observed in Turner syndrome. The literature also indicates that DOMV or bicuspid aortic valve can be detected in other genetic syndromes, suggesting a broader association with underlying genetic conditions. [PMC10307588, PMC8336376]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of double-orifice mitral valve (DOMV) depends on its functional status and associated anomalies. Surgical repair, such as mitral repair for central bridge DOMV or excision of associated defects like supramitral ring, subaortic membrane, and ventricular septal defects, may be performed. Percutaneous transluminal mitral commissurotomy (PTMC) is an option for stenotic DOMV. For DOMV with mitral regurgitation, medical management with angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors and diuretics can alleviate symptoms, with long-term follow-up recommended. However, if DOMV is isolated and without functional abnormalities, no further follow-up may be necessary. Perioperative complications, such as refractory pulmonary hypertensive crisis, can occur. [PMC11184660, PMC6489406, PMC4907761, PMC4683737, PMC3128372]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An extremely rare mostly lethal congenital disorder characterized by absence of all four limbs and frequent associated major malformations involving the head, face, eyes, skeleton, heart, lungs, anus, urogenital, and central nervous systems. The syndrome has been described in fewer than 20 patients mainly of middle Eastern descent.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: A male child with tetra-amelia, hypotrichosis, upward slanting palpebral fissures, lack of lacrimal openings, hypoplastic lacrimal ducts and sacs opening towards the exterior, prominent and bulbous nose, large downturned mouth, high narrow palate, bilateral preauricular pits, sacral dimple, bilateral undescended testes, and developmental retardation is reported. The parents were second cousins. His karyotype on cultured blood lymphocytes was normal. Since the next fetus conceived by the mother was found on prenatal ultrasonography to have no limbs, abortion was induced. The face of the abortus closely resembled that of the proband. It is postulated that this malformation syndrome was due to the homozygous state of a rare autosomal recessive mutation. [PMC1050288]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Tetra-amelia-multiple malformations syndrome is characterized by the absence of all four limbs (tetra-amelia). Associated features include hypotrichosis, upward slanting palpebral fissures, lack of lacrimal openings, and hypoplastic lacrimal ducts and sacs opening towards the exterior. Patients present with a peculiar face, including a prominent and bulbous nose, large downturned mouth, and high narrow palate. Other findings may include bilateral preauricular pits, a sacral dimple, bilateral undescended testes, and developmental retardation. [PMC1050288]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The syndrome is postulated to be caused by the homozygous state of a rare autosomal recessive mutation. This is supported by the observation that the parents of an affected child were second cousins, and a subsequent fetus from the same parents also presented with the condition. Karyotype analysis on cultured blood lymphocytes of the proband was normal, ruling out chromosomal abnormalities as the cause. [PMC1050288]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis can involve karyotyping, which in one reported case was normal on cultured blood lymphocytes. Prenatal ultrasonography has also been utilized, revealing the absence of limbs in a fetus, which led to induced abortion. The facial features of the abortus closely resembled those of the proband, suggesting a consistent phenotype detectable prenatally. [PMC1050288]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Prenatal ultrasonography has been used to detect the absence of limbs in a fetus, leading to induced abortion. In one case, a subsequent fetus of parents with an affected child was found to have no limbs via prenatal ultrasonography, and the abortus's facial features closely resembled those of the proband. [PMC1050288]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The syndrome is postulated to be due to the homozygous state of a rare autosomal recessive mutation, supported by the parents being second cousins. The proband's karyotype was normal. Recurrence in a subsequent pregnancy, detected by prenatal ultrasonography showing no limbs and a facial resemblance to the proband, further supports this genetic basis. This information is critical for counseling families on recurrence risk and prenatal diagnostic possibilities. [PMC1050288]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: A male child with tetra-amelia, hypotrichosis, upward slanting palpebral fissures, lack of lacrimal openings, hypoplastic lacrimal ducts and sacs opening towards the exterior, prominent and bulbous nose, large downturned mouth, high narrow palate, bilateral preauricular pits, sacral dimple, bilateral undescended testes, and developmental retardation is reported. The parents were second cousins. His karyotype on cultured blood lymphocytes was normal. Since the next fetus conceived by the mother was found on prenatal ultrasonography to have no limbs, abortion was induced. The face of the abortus closely resembled that of the proband. It is postulated that this malformation syndrome was due to the homozygous state of a rare autosomal recessive mutation. [PMC1050288]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neuropsychiatric syndrome associated with administration of antipsychotic or other central dopamine (D2) receptor antagonists, and characterized by hyperthermia, muscular rigidity, autonomic dysfunction and altered consciousness.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) occurs in 1/5,000 to 10,000 patients treated with antipsychotics or other central dopamine (D2) receptor antagonists (all age groups; male:female ratio 2:1 in some studies; higher incidence rates have been reported in the past). The incidence may be lower with newer less potent antipsychotics and with reduced severity of symptoms, particularly for clozapine.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: In about 16% of patients, the syndrome occurs within 24 hours after the initiation of the antipsychotic treatment, 66% within the first week, and less commonly within or after 30 days on stable medication regimens. Manifestations include hyperthermia, muscular rigidity and tremor, mental status alteration and autonomic dysfunction. Other signs may include profuse diaphoresis, tachycardia, tachypnea, labile blood pressure, acidosis, incontinence, and elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) and transaminases from rhabdomyolysis with risk of subsequent renal failure. Once symptoms develop, they last on average 7-10 days after discontinuation of oral triggering drugs, with peak intensity within the first 72 hours. Risk factors include prior NMS episodes, physical exhaustion, agitation, dehydration, pre-existing catatonia, use of restraints, use of high doses, high potency drugs, acute parenteral forms of antipsychotics, and rapid antipsychotic dosage increase.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The syndrome is thought to result from acute central dopamine receptor blockade. All antipsychotic agents, typical or atypical, may trigger the syndrome, although potent antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) are more frequently associated. Dopamine blocking agents used in non-psychiatric settings (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, droperidol) and dopamine depleting agents (tetrabenazine) have also been implicated.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical signs of the syndrome in the context of treatment with dopamine blocking agents, and the exclusion of alternative etiologies via thorough investigation with laboratory and imaging tests. Although elevated CK is a frequent correlate of muscle dysfunction in NMS, it is nonspecific. The likelihood of an NMS diagnosis can be assessed using the International Expert Consensus (IEC) criteria which are based on priority scores assigned to major clinical features (antipsychotic exposure, hyperthermia, rigidity, mental status changes, CK elevation, etc.). A total cut-off threshold score of ≥74 on the IEC criteria offers 69.6% sensitivity and 90.7% specificity in diagnosing NMS.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis is of prime importance. It includes malignant hyperthermia of anesthesia, serotonin syndrome, parkinsonism hyperpyrexia syndrome, heat stroke, idiopathic malignant catatonia, infections (sepsis, meningitis, encephalitis), autoimmune disorders (limbic encephalitis with NMDA receptor antibodies, lupus cerebritis) delirium tremens, status epilepticus, salicylate poisoning, endocrinopathies, stroke, and brain trauma.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Immediate cessation of the antipsychotic medication and supportive measures (volume resuscitation, physical cooling) are essential in management. Specific treatments are unproven. Benefits in cases treated empirically based on phenomenology, severity and duration of symptoms with benzodiazepines, dopaminergic agents (bromocriptine, amantadine), dantrolene (in cases with extreme hyperthermia, rigidity and rhabdomyolysis) and electroconvulsive therapy have been reported. Careful monitoring for cardiorespiratory failure, renal failure, aspiration pneumonia and coagulopathies is required. Ventilatory assistance and dialysis may be required.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: After discontinuation of oral psychotropic agents, resolution usually occurs within 1-2 weeks in most uncomplicated cases. However, the syndrome is still potentially lethal. Death may result from sudden cardiorespiratory arrest, aspiration pneumonia, pulmonary emboli, myoglobinuric renal failure, or disseminated intravascular coagulation. Mortality rate is estimated at 5-10% with adverse outcomes more likely with potent antipsychotics, older age and pre-existing cardiorespiratory disease. Most patients recover completely but amnestic syndromes, extrapyramidal and cerebellar disorders, peripheral neuropathy, myopathy and contractures have been reported in rare cases.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genomic exploration has identified genetic associations with neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS), with pathogenic variants in genes like EIF2B2 correlating with the NMS phenotype. Genetic studies can aid in the diagnosis of NMS, particularly in pediatric neurological disorders. While NMS is observed in contexts where other conditions, such as malignant hyperthermia, are inherited pharmacogenomic diseases, the abstracts do not explicitly detail the inheritance pattern or specific genetic counseling recommendations for NMS itself. However, genetic information can be crucial for diagnostic clarity in cases presenting with rhabdomyolysis and may inform discussions on potential preventive measures. [PMC11786458, PMC11660009]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare disorder characterised by hemolytic anemia, associated with metabolic acidosis and 5-oxoprolinuria in moderate forms, and with progressive neurological symptoms and recurrent bacterial infections in the most severe forms.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: This disease has been detected in at least 70 patients in more than 50 families worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Several mutations have been identified in the gene encoding glutathione synthetase, localized to chromosome 20q11.2. Glutathione synthetase catalyses the last step in the synthesis of glutathione and a deficiency results in low levels of glutathione. Acidosis is due to reduced feedback inhibition of gamma-glutamyl cysteine synthetase in the gamma-glutamyl cycle, which ultimately leads to overproduction and accumulation of 5-oxoproline.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis usually involves the following: clinical findings, the finding of 5-oxoprolinuria, low levels of glutathione, low activity of glutathione synthetase, and mutation analysis of the glutathione synthetase gene.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Other causes of 5-oxoprolinuria include 5-oxoprolinase deficiency, diet (certain infant formulas and tomato juice), severe burns, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, inborn errors of metabolism not involving the gamma-glutamyl cycle, e.g. X-linked ornithine trancarbamylase deficiency, urea cycle defects, tyrosinemia, as well as homocystinuria, drug metabolism (paracetamol, vigabatrin, flucloxacillin, netimicin), prematurity, malnutrition, pregnancy and nephropatic cystinosis.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Antenatal diagnosis is possible.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Transmission is autosomal recessive.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Management includes correction of the acidosis, supplementation with antioxidants and avoidance of drugs known to precipitate hemolytic crises in patients with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, e.g. phenobarbital, acetylsalicylic acid and sulfonamides.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: A long-term follow up study of 28 patients with glutathione synthetase deficiency has showed that the factors most predictive of survival and long-term outcome are early diagnosis, correction of acidosis and early supplementation with vitamin C and vitamin E.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Glutathione synthetase deficiency (GSD) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder. The severe form typically presents in the neonatal period with acute metabolic acidosis, hemolytic anemia, and progressive neurological symptoms, often accompanied by 5-oxoprolinuria. Other features can include hyperbilirubinemia, recurrent bacterial infections, and febrile convulsions. Neurological impairment can range from mild neurodevelopmental delay to severe progressive encephalopathy, with some patients achieving normal intellectual development with long-term treatment. A less severe form may manifest primarily with hemolytic anemia, without neurological findings or 5-oxoprolinuria, and can be associated with a concurrent deficiency of glutathione-S-transferase. [PMC10106969, PMC5769757, PMC4961564, PMC1294405, PMC423305]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Hemoglobin D disease(HbD) is a hemoglobinopathy characterized by production of abnormal variant hemoglobin known as hemoglobin D, with no or mild clinical manifestations (splenomegaly, very mild anemia).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Hemoglobin D disease, specifically the Hb D-Punjab variant, is a rare hemoglobinopathy. A population-based genetic screening program in Guangxi, China, identified Hb D-Punjab in two unrelated families. The frequency of this variant was extremely low, reported as 0.0045% in the screened population of 11,019 participants. This finding enriches the spectrum of hemoglobin variants in the Chinese population. [PMC12390978]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Hemoglobin D disease, an autosomal recessive disorder, presents with varied clinical features. Hemoglobin D-Punjab, for example, often has minimal manifestations and can be asymptomatic. However, when combined with other conditions, such as in sickle cell/hemoglobin D-Punjab disease, clinical features can resemble sickle cell anemia. Such cases may involve complications like hypersplenism, necessitating regular transfusions and potentially splenectomy, which can lead to splenic sinusoidal iron overload. Additionally, patients with Hemoglobin D are susceptible to hemolytic crises, particularly when exposed to certain medications. [PMC12390978, PMC7394553, PMC1770290]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hemoglobin D disease, specifically the Hb D-Punjab variant, is categorized within the hemoglobinopathies, which are a group of autosomal recessive genetic disorders. These conditions are characterized by a high degree of clinical and genetic heterogeneity. The Hb D-Punjab variant is a rare hemoglobin variant identified at a specific genetic locus. Analyzing its origin and genotype-phenotype correlation is crucial for clinical management and genetic counseling. [PMC12390978]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for hemoglobin D disease include comprehensive genetic screening and high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). Single-molecule real-time (SMRT) sequencing is an efficient and reliable genetic screening tool that has identified rare variants like Hb D-Punjab. While HPLC is used to estimate variant hemoglobins, it can sometimes misidentify Hb D. In such cases, sample dilution experiments can resolve the mistaken identification, allowing for the correct elution of the Hb D peak on HPLC. [PMC12390978, PMC500653]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Hemoglobin D can be mistakenly identified as Hemoglobin E, particularly by high performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), as seen in cases of Hb S/D misdiagnosed as Hb S/E. This misidentification can be resolved through sample dilution. Additionally, rare hemoglobin variants such as Hemoglobin D-Punjab and Hemoglobin O-Arab, found at the same genetic locus, require differentiation due to their distinct clinical presentations, with Hb O-Arab typically showing more obvious manifestations. [PMC12390978, PMC500653]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Hemoglobinopathies, including Hemoglobin D, are autosomal recessive disorders with significant clinical and genetic heterogeneity. Comprehensive genetic screening for hemoglobin variants is crucial for prevention and and treatment. Genetic counseling for hemoglobinopathies involves analyzing the frequency, origin, and genotype-phenotype correlation of these variants. For instance, Hb D-Punjab has been shown to have a minimal impact on hemoglobin structure, consistent with relatively mild manifestations, which informs counseling for affected individuals. [PMC12390978]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management strategies can include regular transfusions, though the dangers of iron overload should be remembered. Splenectomy may be performed for hypersplenism. Additionally, certain therapies, such as hydroxychloroquine, can induce hemolytic crises in patients with underlying hemoglobinopathies and should be avoided or closely monitored, especially if co-existing conditions like G6PD deficiency are present. [PMC7394553, PMC1770290]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: The prognosis for Hemoglobin D disease varies depending on the specific genetic combination. Hemoglobin D-Punjab, for instance, has a minimal impact on hemoglobin structure and is associated with less obvious manifestations, with some individuals with Hemoglobin D thalassemia being asymptomatic. Even in the presence of co-morbidities like COVID-19 and G6PD deficiency, a mild drop in hemoglobin may occur without requiring transfusion. However, sickle cell/Hemoglobin D-Punjab disease presents with clinical features similar to sickle cell anemia, a severe disorder. This form may necessitate regular transfusions from infancy and interventions such as splenectomy for complications like hypersplenism, with iron overload being a potential danger. [PMC12390978, PMC7394553, PMC1770290]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Mosaic trisomy 16 is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome with a highly variable phenotype ranging from minor anomalies with normal development to intrauterine growth retardation, abnormal skin pigmentation, craniofacial and body asymmetry, cardiac (e.g. ventricular septal defect) and genital (e.g. hypospadias, cryptorchidism) anomalies, scoliosis and hearing loss to neonatal death. Additional features observed include skeletal malformations (e.g. clino/polydactyly, talipes), mild facial dysmorphism, and developmental delay.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Mosaic trisomy 16 is an exceptionally rare condition, as full trisomy 16 is generally considered incompatible with fetal survival. A liveborn infant with mosaic trisomy 16, who survived for 11 weeks, was reported in 1990. This particular case was believed to be the first instance of mosaic trisomy 16 confirmed by cytogenetic banding in a live newborn. [PMC1590154]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Trisomy 16 is thought to be incompatible with fetal survival. A boy with mosaic trisomy 16 who lived for 11 weeks is reported. Chromosome analysis was carried out on skin fibroblasts grown during life and confirmed on samples taken at necropsy. We believe that this is the first report of mosaic trisomy 16 that has been confirmed by cytogenetic banding. [PMC1590154]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Mosaic trisomy 16 syndrome is characterized by trisomy 16 mosaicism. This condition can occur in combination with maternal segmental uniparental disomy (UPD) 16, where both chromosomes of a homologous pair are inherited from the same parent. The etiology of this combination is attributed to incomplete trisomy rescue, a process that is one of the main hypotheses for UPD generation. A low level of trisomy 16 mosaicism, such as 3%, has been quantitatively verified in conjunction with maternal segmental UPD 16. [PMC11907602]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnostic for mosaic trisomy 16 syndrome often begin with noninvasive prenatal screening (NIPS), which can indicate chromosomal abnormalities but requires further confirmation. Confirmatory prenatal diagnoses utilize conventional karyotype analysis, frequently combined with techniques such as copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq) or ddPCR to verify mosaic levels. Trio whole exome sequencing (trio-WES) can also identify segmental uniparental disomy and suggest low-level mosaicism. Postnatally, chromosome analysis on skin fibroblasts, confirmed by cytogenetic banding, has been used to diagnose mosaic trisomy 16. Additionally, prenatal ultrasound can evaluate fetal morphology for associated findings. [PMC11907602, PMC7899829, PMC1590154]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Uniparental disomy (UPD) is a specific type of chromosomal variation in which both chromosomes of a homologous pair are inherited from the same parent. It is responsible for a wide range of disorders. Monosomy rescue and trisomy rescue are the two main hypotheses of UPD generation. An older parturient woman with a positive noninvasive prenatal screening (NIPS) test but a negative prenatal diagnosis was referred to the hospital. Trio whole exome sequencing (trio-WES) and ddPCR were further performed. Utilizing Trio-WES analysis, our research identified a maternal segmental UPD on chromosome 16, characterized by isodisomic genomic segments at the ends of the chromosome arms and heterodisomic genomic segments near the centromere. Moreover, several nuanced signs pointing to the paternal chromosome 16 were discovered, suggesting a low level of trisomy 16 mosaicism. A homozygous missense... [PMC11907602]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis for mosaic trisomy 16 syndrome often begins with noninvasive prenatal screening (NIPS), which can indicate chromosomal abnormalities. However, NIPS is a screening test that requires further diagnostic confirmation. Discrepancies between positive NIPS and negative prenatal diagnoses can occur, as seen in a case where a low level (3%) of trisomy 16 mosaicism was later verified by trio whole exome sequencing (trio-WES) and ddPCR. Conventional karyotype, copy number variations sequencing (CNV-seq), and prenatal ultrasound are also utilized. CNV-seq combined with karyotype is a useful tool for confirming and precisely locating chromosomal abnormalities indicated by NIPS. [PMC11907602, PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for mosaic trisomy 16 syndrome is complex due to its varied presentations and severe outcomes. Partial trisomy 16, often associated with severe congenital defects, growth retardation, and early lethality, underscores the challenges in counseling, especially concerning life-limiting anomalies. Segmental trisomy 16q can occur purely or concomitantly with partial monosomy of another chromosome, frequently resulting from a parental balanced translocation. Noninvasive prenatal screening (NIPS) may indicate abnormalities, but it is a screening test requiring further diagnostic confirmation. Cases with positive NIPS but negative prenatal diagnosis have revealed trisomy 16 mosaicism and maternal segmental uniparental disomy 16, attributed to incomplete trisomy rescue, highlighting the need for comprehensive evaluation. [PMC11907602, PMC9082733, PMC7899829]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Trisomy 16 is generally considered embryonic lethal or incompatible with fetal survival. However, mosaic trisomy 16 can allow for limited postnatal survival, as evidenced by a reported case living for 11 weeks. Partial trisomy 16, while occasionally compatible with life, is associated with severe congenital defects, growth retardation, and early lethality, with very few long-term survivors and life-limiting congenital anomalies. [PMC9082733, PMC1590154]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Lyme disease (named after the towns in the USA where the disease was first identified) is a bacterial infection caused by Borrelia burgdorferi.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Incidence is variable and is estimated at 1-70/20,000 in Europe.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical manifestations can be divided into three stages. Onset of the initial stage occurs between three days and one month after being bitten by an infected tick (generally the patient is aware of the bite) and is marked by erythema migrans, a characteristic cutaneous lesion that appears over time at various sites of the body. The second stage is characterized by dissemination to the central nervous system (resulting in facial paralysis, encephalitis etc.), joints, skin, heart and eye. The third (chronic) stage of the disease is characterized by joint, neurologic and cutaneous manifestations.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The disease is transmitted to humans by bites from contaminated ticks (Ixodes) but rodents, birds and lizards are the main hosts.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis relies on recognition of the clinical picture during the initial stage of the disease, detection of Borrelia burgdorferi through analysis of cultures, PCR and detection of Borrelia burgdorferi DNA, or through elevations in antibody levels in patients in the second and third stages of the disease.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Treatment revolves around administration of antibiotics (amoxicillin and cyclines); with the treatment being more effective the earlier the antibiotics are administered. Prevention revolves around eradication of the ticks and on individuals taking protective measures against tick bites when visiting at-risk zones.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: In , a 23-year-old female who, while pregnant, was exposed to Borrelia burgdorferi but did not develop significant signs or symptoms (joint pain, arthritis) of Lyme disease until shortly after delivering a healthy child at term. Serologic testing confirmed infection with B. burgdorferi . A 3-week course of treatment with doxycycline was completely curative. There was no evidence for congenital or perinatal transmission of this pathogen at any point pre-term or postnatally. The key reasons that could account for this unique clinical scenario are discussed in the context of previously published related reports. [PMC10976031]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Monosomy 13q34 is a rare chromosomal anomaly syndrome, resulting from the partial deletion of the long arm of chromosome 13, principally characterized by global developmental delay, mild intellectual disability, obesity and mild craniofacial dysmorphism (microcephaly, wide rectangular forehead, downslanting palpebral fissures, mild ptosis, prominent nose with long nasal bridge and broad tip, small chin). Other variable reported features include congenital heart defects, hand and foot anomalies (e.g. polydactyly) and agenesis of the corpus callosum.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Monosomy 13q34 syndrome presents with variable clinical features, with a severely malformed phenotype linked to deletions in 13q32. Reported findings include fetal growth restriction, cerebellar hypoplasia (e.g., Dandy-Walker malformation), and eye malformations such as microphthalmia and coloboma. Other features include overlapping fingers, hearing loss, pleurocentrum in thoracic vertebrae, and reduced anogenital distance. Esophageal atresia (Gross type A) has been observed, potentially as part of VATER/VACTER association, which encompasses vertebral defects, anorectal malformations, cardiac defects, tracheoesophageal fistula, renal malformations, and limb defects. Hirschsprung's disease has also been reported. [PMC9793530, PMC1015558]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Monosomy 13q34 syndrome is caused by deletions on chromosome 13q, with variable clinical features related to different potential breakpoints. Reported deletions include segments such as 13q32.1-qter, 13q31.3-qter, and 13q22.1-q32.1. Haploinsufficiency of genes like ZIC2/ZIC5 is implicated in Dandy-Walker malformation, while EFBN2 haploinsufficiency is associated with eye malformation and hearing loss. The possible involvement of IRS2, COLA1, and COLA2 in eye malformation has also been identified. [PMC9793530, PMC1015558]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Monosomy 13q34 syndrome involves genetic testing. Prenatal diagnosis can be achieved through karyotyping, as demonstrated by amniocentesis identifying a 46,XX,del(13)(q32.1-qter) karyotype. Postnatal confirmation or more precise characterization of the deletion can be performed using array comparative genomic hybridization (aCGH), which revealed a deletion of 13q31.3-qter in one reported case. [PMC9793530]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Differential diagnosis for Monosomy 13q34 syndrome may include conditions presenting with overlapping features. For instance, chromosome 15q26 deletion syndrome is associated with short stature, intrauterine growth restriction, failure to thrive, congenital heart disease, microcephaly, and dysmorphic features. Furthermore, specific manifestations like esophageal atresia, which can occur in distal 13q deletion syndrome, may prompt consideration of VATER/VACTER association, a spectrum of anomalies including vertebral defects, anorectal malformations, cardiac defects, tracheoesophageal fistula, renal malformations, and limb defects. [PMC11729826, PMC9793530]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal diagnosis of distal 13q deletion syndrome can be indicated by various fetal anomalies. In one reported case, findings at 31 weeks gestation included fetal growth restriction, absence of a gastric bubble, cerebellar hypoplasia, overlapping fingers, and polyhydramnios. The diagnosis was subsequently established antenatally through amniocentesis, revealing a karyotype of 46,XX,del(13)(q32.1-qter). [PMC9793530]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling for Monosomy 13q deletion syndrome should address the variable clinical features, which are related to different potential breakpoints in chromosome 13q. Determining the association between accurate breakpoints and specific clinical features is essential for prognosis. Prenatal diagnosis is possible, as demonstrated by a case diagnosed via amniocentesis and confirmed by array comparative genomic hybridization, which can identify deletions such as 13q31.3-qter. [PMC9793530]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Chromosome 13q deletion syndrome shows variable clinical features related to the different potential breakpoints in chromosome 13q. The severely malformed phenotype is known to be associated with the deletion of a critical region in 13q32. However, esophageal atresia is a rare symptom and the relevant region is unknown. Thus, determining the association between accurate breakpoints and new clinical features is essential. A 28-year-old Japanese primigravid woman was referred for fetal growth restriction, absence of a gastric bubble, cerebellar hypoplasia, overlapping fingers, and polyhydramnios at 31 weeks gestation. At 38 + 0 weeks, she delivered a 1774 g female infant. The infant presented with isolated esophageal atresia (Gross type A), Dandy-Walker malformation, right microphthalmia, left coloboma, overlapping fingers, pleurocentrum in the thoracic vertebrae, reduced anogenital... [PMC9793530]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Chromosome 13q deletion syndrome shows variable clinical features related to the different potential breakpoints in chromosome 13q. The severely malformed phenotype is known to be associated with the deletion of a critical region in 13q32. However, esophageal atresia is a rare symptom and the relevant region is unknown. Thus, determining the association between accurate breakpoints and new clinical features is essential. A 28-year-old Japanese primigravid woman was referred for fetal growth restriction, absence of a gastric bubble, cerebellar hypoplasia, overlapping fingers, and polyhydramnios at 31 weeks gestation. At 38 + 0 weeks, she delivered a 1774 g female infant. The infant presented with isolated esophageal atresia (Gross type A), Dandy-Walker malformation, right microphthalmia, left coloboma, overlapping fingers, pleurocentrum in the thoracic vertebrae, reduced anogenital... [PMC9793530]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: An acute arboviral infection caused by a Coltivirus transmitted by an infected tick and characterized by a biphasic fever with headache, myalgias, arthralgias, and fatigue that can last 3 weeks or more. In some cases, macular, maculopapular, or petechial rash and/or stiff neck, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and sore throat may also occur.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): American mountain fever; Colorado tick encephalitis; Colorado tick-borne disease; Mountain fever; Mountain tick fever

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Colorado tick fever virus is transmitted by Dermacentor andersoni ticks. In Canada, these ticks are found in the southern regions of British Columbia, including the Rocky Mountains, Alberta, and southwestern Saskatchewan. Human cases of Colorado tick fever have been reported in southern Alberta. Clinical suspicion for the disease should be considered in patients presenting with a biphasic febrile illness and leukopenia following tick exposure in these appropriate geographic areas. [PMC5930916, PMC1267986]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Colorado tick fever should be clinically suspected in patients presenting with a biphasic febrile illness and leukopenia. This condition is transmitted by Dermacentor andersoni ticks. Clinical suspicion is warranted following tick exposure in appropriate geographic areas, which in Canada include the southern regions of British Columbia, Alberta, and southwestern Saskatchewan. [PMC5930916]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Colorado tick fever is caused by the Colorado tick fever virus. This virus is transmitted to humans through the bite of Dermacentor andersoni ticks. In Canada, these ticks are found in specific geographic areas, including the southern regions of British Columbia (Rocky Mountains) and Alberta, as well as southwestern Saskatchewan. [PMC5930916]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Colorado tick fever should be clinically suspected in patients presenting with a biphasic febrile illness and leukopenia. This suspicion is further supported by a history of tick exposure in the appropriate geographic area where Dermacentor andersoni ticks are found, such as southern British Columbia, Alberta, and southwestern Saskatchewan. [PMC5930916]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Heartland virus (HRTV) is a tick-borne phlebovirus recently described in Missouri that is associated with fever, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia. The virus has also been detected in Ambylomma americanum ticks. Here the first fatal case of HRTV disease in an 80-year-old Tennessee resident. He was hospitalized with fever, confusion, leukopenia, and thrombocytopenia and developed multiorgan failure and hemorrhage. A tick-borne illness was suspected and testing for ehrlichiosis was negative. He died on hospital day 15, and autopsy specimens were tested for various pathogens as part of an unexplained death evaluation. HRTV antigens were detected in postmortem spleen and lymph nodes by immunohistochemistry, and HRTV was detected in premortem blood by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction and by isolation in cell culture. This case demonstrates that HRTV infection can cause severe... [PMC4608028]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Peters anomaly (PA) is a congenital corneal opacity disorder characterized by a central corneal leukoma that obstructs the pupil leading to visual loss as well as absence of the posterior corneal stroma and Descemet membrane.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Peters anomaly (PA) is a rare congenital disorder characterized by anterior segment dysgenesis during fetal development, leading to corneal opacity and iridocorneal adhesions. The genetic basis is complex and incompletely understood, with both isolated and syndromic forms. Numerous genes have been implicated, including FOXC1, PEX2, ZFHX4, CENPF, PITX3, SOX11, B3GLCT, BMP4, COL4A1, FOXE3, PAX6, and WFS1, often involving de novo or heterozygous variants, deletions, or bi-allelic mutations. These genetic factors can result in haploinsufficiency or contribute to various syndromic presentations like Strømme, Coffin-Siris, Peters plus, and Wolfram-like syndromes. Beyond genetics, other factors such as hydroxychloroquine exposure during pregnancy and epigenetic influences have been suggested. Histopathological findings, including immature or absent Descemet's membrane, also point to developmental anomalies. [PMC12250460, PMC10671177, PMC10270777, PMC10798386, PMC9509590]
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis_G: Antenatal imaging of Peters anomaly has been reported, with sonographic images exhibiting the condition. Ultrasound can detect opacity of the fetal eyeballs, which may initially lead to a suspicion of congenital cataract. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can also be arranged to assess for other anomalies, such as those in the central nervous system. The opacity of the fetal eyeballs may persist on follow-up scans. [PMC7513296]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Dubowitz syndrome (DS) is a rare multiple congenital syndrome characterized primarly by growth retardation, microcephaly, distinctive facial dysmorphism, cutaneous eczema, a mild to severe intellectual deficit and genital abnormalities.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The total birth prevalence in Europe has been estimated at 1/500,000. Over 150 cases have been described to date.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Newborns often have a low birth weight with a small head and body size. Facial appearance is characteristic with narrow or triangular shaped head and high or sloping forehead, flat supraorbital ridge, scanty lateral eyebrows, short palpebral fissures, blepharophimosis, ptosis, abnormally modeled ears, broad and flat nasal bridge, micrognathia and unusual configuration of the mouth. Sumucous cleft palate is common. Other findings include cutaneous ezema, high-pitched or hoarse voice, hypospadias and cryptorchidism. Skeletal abnormalities in DS include sacral dimple, and clinodactyly (5th fingers), with cutaneous syndactyly of toes or fingers. Intellectual deficit is mostly mild to moderate. Furthermore a variety of ocular and dental abnormalities, such as hyperopia, cataracts, tapetoretinal degeneration, strabismus and taurodontia, anodontia/hypodontia or hyperdontia have been reported. Behavioral characteristics may include hyperactivity with short attention span, impulsivity and shyness. The spectrum of manifestations of Dubowitz syndrome may also comprise: hematological (aplastic anemia) and congenital heart defects, frequent infections, chromosomal instability and developement of malignancies (acute lymphoblastic leukemia or neuroblastoma).
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The etiology of Dubowitz syndrome has not been evidently elucidated. Two causal genes have been put forward in separate isolated cases and include NSUN2 and LIG4. However due to the large phenotypic overlap of Dubowitz syndrome with other clinical entities, there remains uncertainty on the etiology.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the multiple clinical manifestations and is commonly made in early childhood.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnosis includes fetal alcohol syndrome, Bloom syndrome, LIG4 syndrome and Fanconi anemia.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal growth retardation may be observed on ultrasound but does not lead to a reliable prenatal diagnosis.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: In some families, Dubowitz syndrome appears to have an autosomal recessive transmission. However, it has been suggested recently that Dubowitz syndrome is a microdeletion/microduplication syndrome rather than an autosomal disorder.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Growth, dental speech, behavioral and intellectual development and a general health status check should be monitored regularly and treated appropriately. Eczema and recurrent infections require conservative treatment. Surgical intervention might be necessary for certain cardiovascular, urogenital, craniofacial or limb anomalies. Surveillance of hematological and malignant disorders is recommended.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: The prognosis is very variable depending on the severity and types of congenital anomalies present and the long-term outcome still remains elusive, as no data is available after puberty.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Infantile-onset spinocerebellar ataxia (IOSCA) is a hereditary neurological disorder with early and severe involvement of both the peripheral and central nervous systems. It has only been described in Finnish families.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: So far, 24 cases have been reported. In Finland, IOSCA has a population carrier frequency of more than 1:230.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: IOSCA is characterized by very early ataxia, athetosis and reduced tendon reflexes (between 9 and 18 months of age). Ophthalmoplegia and sensorineural hearing loss are diagnosed in childhood. Other features, such as optic atrophy and sensory neuropathy with progressive loss of myelinated fibers in the sural nerve, appear later in the disease course. Hypogonadism may occur in females. Some patients show intellectual deficit. Epilepsy is a late manifestation and seizures may be life-threatening.
