Even with no obvious predisposing disorder, it may still be prudent to evaluate close kin for the presence of aortic root dilatation, since some genetic disorders have no manifestation other than acute aortic dissection secondary to aortic medial pathology. Close monitoring for at-risk family members, including the index patient, may need to be a life-long process. [PMC6654457]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Given the heritable nature of conditions predisposing to acute aortic dissection, it is crucial to identify any underlying disorders. This allows for screening of close relatives for inherited traits that could put them at risk for similar catastrophic events. Even without an obvious predisposing disorder, evaluating close kin for aortic root dilatation is prudent, as some genetic conditions may present solely with acute aortic dissection due to aortic medial pathology. Lifelong monitoring for at-risk family members, including the index patient, may be necessary. [PMC6654457]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management following acute aortic dissection involves determining the presence of any predisposing disorders, particularly heritable ones. This is crucial for screening close relatives for inherited traits that may put them at risk for similar catastrophic events, including aortic root dilatation. Lifelong close monitoring is recommended for at-risk family members, as well as the index patient, to manage the condition. [PMC6654457]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Acute aortic dissection, a significant manifestation of the syndrome, is a rare but life-threatening condition in children and adolescents. It is described as a catastrophic event. Due to its severe nature, close and potentially lifelong monitoring is essential for affected individuals and at-risk family members to manage the ongoing risk. [PMC6654457]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A chronic autoimmune subepidermal bullous disease characterized by grouped pruritic lesions such as papules, urticarial plaques, erythema, and herpetiform vesiculae, with a predominantly symmetrical distribution on extensor surfaces of the elbows (90%), knees (30%), shoulders, buttocks, sacral region, and face of children and adults. Erosions, excoriations and hyperpigmentation usually follow. It may also appear as a consequence of gluten intolerance.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is a rare autoimmune disease, considered the specific cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease, occurring in gluten-sensitive individuals with shared HLA haplotypes (DQ2 and DQ8). Some studies have reported a reduced incidence of DH, possibly due to earlier recognition of celiac disease. While diagnosis can be challenging in low prevalence, resource-limited populations, atypical presentations have been noted, including in Japanese patients who may lack intestinal involvement or typical celiac serological markers, with similar cases potentially occurring in Caucasian patients. A case has also been reported in an African woman. [PMC6579917, PMC6195247, PMC4435051]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Dermatitis herpetiformis (DH) is an autoimmune, inflammatory skin disease considered the specific cutaneous manifestation of celiac disease (CD). It from hypersensitivity to dietary gluten in gluten-sensitive individuals, sharing Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) haplotypes DQ2 and DQ8 with CD. Almost all DH patients exhibit typical small bowel alterations seen in CD and generate circulating autoantibodies against tissue transglutaminase (tTG). The supposed autoantigen in DH is epidermal transglutaminase (eTG), and a key immunopathological finding is granular IgA deposits at the dermal-epidermal junction. [PMC6579917, PMC6195247, PMC4435051]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Glioblastomas are malignant astrocytic tumors (grade IV according to the WHO classification).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Glioblastomas represent the most frequent brain tumors in adults, with an annual incidence of around 1/33,330. Prevalence is estimated at 1/100,000.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: They may occur at any age, but 70% of cases are seen in patients between 45 and 70 years of age. The tumors are usually located in the brain hemispheres, but can be found anywhere in the central nervous system. The disease often progresses rapidly (over 2 to 3 months), except when the glioblastoma develops within a pre-existing low grade astrocytoma (secondary glioblastoma). Neurological signs are nonspecific as they result from intracranial hypertension and include headaches and vomiting, often associated with behavioral changes or focal neurological deficits. Histological variants (gliosarcoma and giant cell glioblastoma) have been described for which the treatment protocols and prognosis are similar to those of glioblastoma.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The cause of the disease is unknown, except when it occurs after therapeutic irradiation of the brain for another disease. The genetic abnormalities detected (amplification of the EGFR gene (7p12), mutations in the TP53 gene (17p13.1), loss of chromosome 10) vary depending on the nature of the tumor: primary glioblastoma (de novo) or a secondary glioblastoma (developing from a benign astrocytic tumor).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Radiologic studies, computerized tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrate characteristic features such as an infiltrating tumor associated with heterogeneous contrast enhancement and areas of necrosis.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The differential diagnosis should include infectious and parasitic diseases with central nervous system involvement. Familial forms of glioblastoma are very rare but the tumor may occur as part of a syndrome such as Turcot syndrome, neurofibromatosis type 1 or Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: The first-line treatment is usually surgery, either to confirm the diagnosis with a biopsy or to remove as much of the tumor as possible. Complete resection is rarely feasible, since tumor cells usually infiltrate the surrounding brain. Treatment is then completed with radiotherapy targeted at the tumor bed, combined with chemotherapy (nitrosoureas and temozolomide). In terms of survival, the benefits from adjuvant treatments after surgery are significant, although they remain modest. In case of relapse, second-line chemotherapy or reoperation may be performed. Due to the relative rarity of this tumor, management of glioblastoma patients should be carried out by multidisciplinary teams with expertise in neuro-oncology within prospective studies aiming to improve patient survival and quality of life.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is poor, especially in the absence of gross total resection, in older patients and in case of severe neurological deficits.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Glioblastoma can be associated with specific genetic syndromes. For instance, glioblastoma in patients with NF1 germline mutations (NF1-associated GBM) represents a unique entity, potentially linked to better treatment response and overall survival. Additionally, glioblastoma has been reported in individuals with Lynch-like syndrome, characterized by a significant family history of cancer and decreased mismatch repair protein expression, even when no pathogenic variant in related genes is detected. While brain tumors are known in Lynch syndrome, this association with Lynch-like syndrome suggests a need for further investigation into brain tumor surveillance in these patients. [PMC12025599, PMC12097828]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: PPoma is a type of pancreatic endocrine tumor that hypersecretes pancreatic polypeptide (PP) but that does not cause a hypersecretion syndrome (is non-functioning) and instead presents with only non-specific symptoms such as weight loss, abdominal pain, jaundice, diarrhea and/or an abdominal mass, hence leading to a late diagnosis. PPoma can be associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia 1 (MEN-1).

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology_G: PPomas are ultra-rare pancreatic tumors, occurring in less than 2% of all pancreatic neoplasms. They are typically nonfunctional or silent, often discovered incidentally. Approximately two dozen reports of PP-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors exist in the literature. While generally nonfunctional, some cases have shown associations. One case report suggests a link with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 (MEN1). Additionally, several reports indicate an association between PP-secreting tumors and diabetes mellitus, with hypersecretion of pancreatic polypeptide potentially contributing to its development. Pancreatic polypeptide hyperplasia, a related condition, is also rarely reported. [PMC6780158, PMC4268541, PMC3788883]
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: PPomas are rare pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, often silent and usually non-functional. When symptoms arise, they can be due to compression of surrounding tissues, such as obstruction of the main pancreatic and common bile duct, potentially causing acute hemorrhagic pancreatitis or severe pain on eating. Hypersecretion of pancreatic polypeptide may lead to watery diarrhea syndrome or be associated with diabetes mellitus, which can improve postoperatively. Elevated plasma pancreatic polypeptide concentrations are typically observed. PPomas can be malignant and metastatic at presentation, and an association with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1 has been suggested. [PMC6780158, PMC4268541, PMC3788883, PMC2443035, PMC1916378]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: A single case report has suggested a possible association between pancreatic polypeptide-secreting tumors (PPomas) and multiple endocrine neoplasm type 1 (MEN1). This observation stemmed from an autopsy of a 68-year-old male diagnosed with MEN1, where a PPoma was incidentally discovered in the head of the pancreas. This represents the first reported instance linking PPomas with MEN1. [PMC6780158]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of PPoma often involves detecting elevated plasma pancreatic polypeptide (PP) concentrations, which can be basal or protein-meal-stimulated, as PP secretion is used as a marker for neuroendocrine tumors. Histopathologically, tumors exhibit a glandular structure with a tubuloacinar arrangement and strong intracytoplasmic PP activity by immunohistochemistry, typically negative for glucagon. Radioimmunoassay of tumor tissue extracts reveals PP content significantly exceeding that of normal pancreas. While often silent, PPomas may be suspected in cases of watery diarrhea syndrome, diabetes mellitus, or when symptoms arise from tissue compression. [PMC6780158, PMC4268541, PMC3788883, PMC1916378, PMC2417429]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: The differential diagnosis for PPoma, a pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor, includes pancreatic polypeptide hyperplasia, which can also cause symptoms like watery diarrhea syndrome. Other pancreatic islet cell tumors should be considered, as PP-secreting tumors may co-secrete insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin, or have elevated levels of these hormones. Additionally, some pancreatic tumors may present with elevated pancreatic polypeptide and calcitonin. Beyond the pancreas, non-argentaffin rectal carcinoids can also exhibit pancreatic polypeptide-like immunoreactivity, often alongside glucagon or glicentin, linking them to non-argentaffin endocrine cells of the human rectum. [PMC3788883, PMC1916378, PMC2417429, PMC1903769]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Background and Here a rare case of a pancreatic polypeptide-secreting tumour (PPoma) discovered by accident during an autopsy. These PPomas occur in less than 2% of all pancreatic neoplasms and are almost exclusively silent, i.e., they are non-functional. Symptoms arising from PPoma are due to its compression of surrounding tissue. The autopsy was performed on a 68-year-old male diagnosed with multiple endocrine neoplasm type 1 (MEN1) due to the patient's sudden death. A solitary, densely fibrotic, pink-brown tumour, 18 mm in size tumorous mass, was localised in the head of the pancreas. Microscopically, the tumour had a glandular structure with a tubuloacinar arrangement of the cells. Immunohistochemically, we detected strong PP (pancreatic polypeptide) intracytoplasmic activity and negative glucagon activity. The PPoma was located in the head of the pancreas, likely resulting in the... [PMC6780158]
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management often involves surgical resection or excision, which has shown to improve or resolve associated conditions like diabetes mellitus and successfully treat symptoms such as watery diarrhea syndrome. For malignant or metastatic tumors, surgical excision is performed, and aggressive palliative surgery, such as pancreatico-jejunostomy, can effectively manage severe symptoms, even in cases with long-term survival. Additionally, therapeutic hepatic artery embolization has been noted to improve general health in patients with hepatic metastases. The overall approach emphasizes aggressive management of symptoms. [PMC4268541, PMC3788883, PMC2443035, PMC2417429]
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis_G: Prognosis for PPoma can vary. For malignant pancreatic polypeptide-secreting tumors, long-term survival is possible even with metastatic disease, with one reported case surviving over six years after original excision following aggressive surgical palliation. Surgical resection of PP-secreting pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors can lead to improvement or resolution of associated diabetes mellitus. In cases of pancreatic polypeptide hyperplasia, surgical resection has been successfully performed with a 2-year follow-up. Therapeutic interventions like hepatic artery embolization can also improve the general health of patients with PP-secreting tumors. [PMC7811659, PMC4268541, PMC3788883, PMC2443035, PMC2417429]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Ewing's sarcoma is a malignant small round cell bone tumor with strong metastatic potential.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Annual incidence is estimated at 1/312,500 in children under the age of 15.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: It occurs between the ages of 5 and 30 with a peak of incidence between ages 12 and 18. The most frequent symptom is pain. Other symptoms depend on the organs closest to the tumor: motor, sphincteric disorders caused by nervous compression or mechanical disorders are associated with pelvic tumors; respiratory disorders or pleural effusion are associated with costal tumors; medullar or radicular compression are associated with vertebral tumors. The tumor initially develops most frequently in bone, particularly in the pelvis (30%), thorax (rib, clavicle, scapula) (20%), femur (16%), tibia (9%), vertebrae (8%) and humerus (5%). The disease has a high potential for metastases (lung, bone, bone marrow). Neuroepithelioma is a highly differentiated neural variant. Askin's tumor is a thoracic variant which can be slightly or well differentiated.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Although no specific cause has been identified, a specific translocation involving the EWSR1 gene (22q12.2) is present in 90% of tumors of this type, most often a translocation t(11;22)(q24;q29). Many variants of this translocation have been described (involving the ERG, ETV1, FLI1 and NR4A3 genes).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: The diagnosis is suggested after the identification, by PCR (polymerase chain reaction), of these translocations.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include other small round cell tumors: neuroblastoma, embryonal or alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and mesenchymatous chondrosarcomas. The existence of a translocation involving the EWSR1 gene allows these diseases to be ruled out.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Treatment should be managed by a multidisciplinary team with expertise in treating childhood cancers. Treatment starts systematically with chemotherapy to reduce the size of the primary tumor and to eradicate or prevent metastases. Surgery is recommended whenever the location of the tumor allows. Local radiotherapy is sometimes necessary, either in addition to surgery or alone for inoperable tumors. For more severe forms of the disease (limited response to initial chemotherapy or metastases already present at diagnosis), high dose chemotherapy with stem cell transplantation can be suggested as a last resort treatment. Targeted therapies, for example with anti-IGF-R (insulin-like growth factor receptor), are currently being studied.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Survival without recurrence of localized forms is around 70%. For forms with lung metastases the survival rate is around 50%. Forms with metastases of the bones or bone marrow have a more severe prognosis.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare retinal vasoproliferative disease affecting preterm infants characterized initially by a delay in physiologic retinal vascular development and compromised physiologic vascularity, and subsequently by aberrant angiogenesis in the form of intravitreal neovascularization.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The incidence of Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is increasing as higher numbers of premature neonates survive into infancy, particularly in developing countries. Some estimates among preterm birth infants are over 30%. In some countries, ROP accounts for up to 10% of childhood blindness. Higher prevalence has been reported in South East Asia, Latin America, and subSaharan Africa. Incidence rates are similar in Caucasian and Black populations, but progression to severe forms may be more frequent in Caucasians.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The degree of prematurity generally correlates with the severity of the clinical manifestations, with the smallest neonates having the highest risks. In affected infants, normal retinal development is incomplete at the time of preterm birth. Subsequently, aberrant angiogenesis in the form of intravitreal neovascularization occurs leading to later cicatricial fibrosis causing partial or complete retinal detachment and possible loss of vision. Patients may also develop ametropia, anisometropia, amblyopia or strabismus. Glaucoma has also been reported in affected individuals.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: The pathophysiological mechanisms underlying ROP remain poorly understood. Associations with severe ROP include high oxygen at birth and oxygenation fluctuations during the neonatal course, low birth weight and young gestational age, and poor postnatal growth. In candidate gene studies, gene mutations associated with severe ROP have been reported, including NDP (Xp11.4-p11.3), FZD4 (11q14-q21), and LRP5 (11q13.4).
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Neonates born before 30 weeks of gestation or with a birth weight below 1,500 g should be screened for ROP, but specific guidelines may vary based on regional statistics and characteristics of affected preterm infants world-wide. Diagnosis is based on characterization of ROP severity in preterm infants usually determined by dilated fundus examination with scleral depression but increasingly more with review of photographic images. ROP is categorized into 3 zones and severity in 5 stages (stages 1 to 5, from mild disease to total retinal detachment).
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: The main differential diagnostic considerations for early ROP are conditions associated with peripheral avascular retina and intravitreal neovascularization, including familial exudative vitreoretinopathy (FEVR) or incontinentia pigmenti. For stage 5 ROP, other conditions causing leukocoria are included (e.g. retinoblastoma, persistent fetal vasculature, toxocariasis, etc.).
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Close work with neonatologists is recommended. All attempts are made to avoid high oxygen at birth (100% oxygen). Optimal monitoring and regulation of oxygen saturation is recommended and is chosen based on gestational age and overall health of the infant. However, the optimum saturation level is not known. Following screening of at-risk infants, monitoring is recommended based on retinal findings. Treatment options include transpupillary or sometimes transscleral laser photocoagulation of the peripheral avascular retina. For the most severe forms of ROP like zone I severe ROP and aggressive posterior ROP, intravitreal treatment with agents that interfere with the bioactivity of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) are being studied and considered. Visual rehabilitation is critical because of the association with myopia and refractive errors. Anisometropia should be corrected and associated amblyopia or strabismus treated. Protective eyewear and low-vision aids may be required.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Gestational age and birth weight are the main prognostic factors in ROP. Also associated is poor postnatal weight gain. ROP often resolves but if it develops severe characteristics, it can lead to blindness.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Genetic counseling is relevant for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) when it co-occurs with hereditary disorders or presents with atypical features. For instance, ROP co-occurring with oculocutaneous albinism (OCA), an autosomal recessive condition, involves genetic testing for OCA2 variants to confirm diagnosis and predict laser treatment effectiveness. Additionally, ROP-like extraretinal fibrovascular proliferation may be associated with bi-allelic variants in genes like ESAM, leading to a neurodevelopmental disease. In such cases, family history is crucial, and newborn siblings of affected children should undergo early ophthalmic examination to prevent severe outcomes. Genetic analysis can thus inform diagnosis, prognosis, and guide management strategies for these complex presentations. [PMC11163733, PMC10750092]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare primary glomerulopathy of unknown cause characterized by edema, nephrotic-range proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia that responds to standard prednisone treatment within 4-6 weeks.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The annual incidence of idiopathic nephrotic syndrome varies by ethnicity and region ranging from 1/5,900-85,000 children, of which 70-98% are steroid sensitive. The disease is less frequently reported in adults. It has a male predominance (approximately 2:1) in young children.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Disease onset can occur at any age, but mostly between 2 - 6 years, frequently preceded by an upper respiratory tract infection. Patients typically present with edema, mainly periorbital and of lower extremities. Anasarca may develop with pleural and pericardial effusion, ascites, abdominal pain (due to hypoperfusion) and cold extremities with hypotension. Intravascular volume depletion and oliguria are present, and concomitant factors, (sepsis, diarrhea, diuretic use) can lead to acute kidney injury. Proteinuria typically has a relapsing and remitting course of varying frequency, and can be steroid-dependent in certain cases (relapsing during steroid therapy or within 15 days of its discontinuation). Urinalysis reveals nephrotic-range proteinuria and blood chemistry results show reduced serum albumin and total protein, reduced total calcium with ionized calcium usually normal, markedly decreased IgG levels, and hyperlipidemia. Hemoconcentration leads to increased hematocrit levels and thrombocytosis. A state of hypercoagulability (due to hypovolemia, hyperdyslipidemia, thrombocytosis) leads to an increased risk of, usually venous, thrombosis.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Etiology is thought to be immune-mediated, although exact mechanism leading to disruption of the glomerular filtration barrier and proteinuria is unknown.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical manifestations, laboratory findings, and response to prednisone. Although renal biopsy is usually not performed, it may be advisable in the presence of atypical features (e.g. onset age < 1 or > 12 years, gross hematuria, low serum complement C3, marked hypertension, renal failure without severe hypovolemia), if prolonged therapy with calcineurin inhibitors is required or if the patient's clinical course is particularly difficult. Renal biopsy will most frequently show minimal changes with a negative immunofluorescence (so-called minimal change disease), though occasionally it may show other pictures.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include membranous nephropathy, IgA nephropathy, renal vasculitis, C3 glomerulopathy and post-infectious glomerulonephritis.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: At onset, management includes symptomatic care with, in severe cases, albumin infusions. In children, prednisone (60mg/m2/day) is the mainstay of therapy. If the patient presents frequent relapses or steroid-dependent disease, second-line steroid-sparing immunosuppression with various agents, including antiproliferatives, levamisole, calcineurin inhibitors, mycophenolate mofetil and, more recently, rituximab, is prescribed.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is variable. After remission of the first episode, the risk of relapse is negligible in 30% of patients. Approximately 20%-30% progress to infrequent relapses (rarely more than 3-4 episodes in total) with prednisone alone. The remaining 40%-50%, mostly children < 5 years of age, have a frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent course. Rarely, patients with initially steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome develop secondary steroid resistance, leading to progressive renal failure. In forms that remain steroid-responsive, renal function is typically preserved. Long-term outcome is heavily influenced by side effects of protracted administration of steroids and second-line steroid-sparing agents. The disease tends to resolve following puberty, but a significant percentage, around 10-15% of patients, will continue to present this disease in adulthood.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The aim of is to provide clinicians with characteristics of children with nephrotic syndrome and cerebral sinovenous thrombosis (CSVT). We have reviewed 37 articles of pediatric cases and provided 1 new case. PRISMA guidelines were followed. Sixty-two patients were included in the review. CSVT was more common in males, usually occurred within 6 months of nephrotic syndrome onset and was found more often in outpatients. The superior sagittal sinus was the most common sinus affected. Non-contrast computed tomography was the most frequent radiologic study performed, with 30% of negative for CSVT. Headache and vomiting were the most common symptoms while neurologic symptoms were less frequent. Anticoagulation treatment was strongly inconsistent throughout the literature. Thrombosis outcomes were favorable. The most common possible risk factors were corticosteroid treatment, proteinuria and... [PMC10484110]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: Baraitser-Winter syndrome (BWS) is a malformation syndrome, characterized by facial dysmorphism (hypertelorism with ptosis, broad bulbous nose, ridged metopic suture, arched eyebrows, progressive coarsening of the face), ocular coloboma, pachygyria and/or band heterotopias with antero-posterior gradient, progressive joint stiffening, and intellectual deficit of variable severity, often with severe epilepsy. Pachygyria - epilepsy - intellectual disability - dysmorphism (Fryns-Aftimos syndrome (FA)) corresponds to the appearance of BWS in elderly patients.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: BWS and FA were initially considered separate entities. They were reported collectively in approximatively 30 unrelated patients so far.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: The clinical picture includes striking dysmorphism, hypertelorism, metopic ridging giving a trigonocephalic appearance to the skull, wide palpebral fissures, long downslanted palpebral fissures, congenital ptosis, broad nose with large bulbous or flat tip, prominent nasal root, long philtrum, mild micrognathia and highly arched eyebrows. Facial characteristics get coarser in late infancy and adolescence, with marked nasogenian folds. Cleft lip and palate may be present. Ocular anomalies such as iris and/or retinal coloboma with or without microphthalmos are frequent. Most patients present with some degree of cortical dysplasia, pachygyria (often more marked in the frontal area) and subcortical band heterotopias. In most severe cases, the brain has a lissencephalic aspect, but some patients have a normal MRI. Head circumference tends to evolve to microcephaly during infancy. Growth is mildly delayed, and final stature is below normal. Patients have been reported with hydronephrosis, but, visceral malformations are rare. Intellectual deficiency ranges from mild to profound and correlates with the severity of brain anomalies and the presence of seizures which may be drug-resistant. Limitation of movement in large joints (knee, shoulder, elbow) become apparent in adolescence, and affect walking abilities in adulthood. Kyphoscoliosis may also develop. In infancy, neurological problems are prominent and facial dysmorphism less obvious.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: BWS is a genetically heterogeneous disorder, caused by a heterozygous mutation in one of the 2 genes coding for ubiquitously expressed actins: ACTB, located to 7p22-p12 (BRWS1) and ACTG1 on 17q25.3 (BRWS2). All mutations are missense and probably act by a gain of function mechanism, as deletions of the same genes do not result in BWS phenotype.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is confirmed by DNA sequencing of ACTG1 and ACTB.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: In infancy, BWS may resemble Noonan syndrome. Teebi Type Hypertelorism has similar palpebral appearance. CHARGE syndrome, Norman-Roberts type lissencephaly syndrome and other syndromes with lissencephaly/pachygyria as a major feature are partially overlapping.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Abnormal gyration pattern may be detected prenatally. Recurrence risk is probably < 1%. Antenatal diagnosis is possible, but the low recurrence risk and the risk of induced miscarriage have to be discussed.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: All molecularly confirmed cases are sporadic, with, in theory, an autosomal dominant transmission, but effective transmission has never been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Developmental delay is managed by appropriate educative measures. Epilepsy management is difficult, as in other forms of pachygyria, some patients are drug resistant, even with polytherapies. Orthopedic monitoring is mandatory, considering progressive joint limitations that could lead to loss of autonomous ambulation.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Early prognosis may be poor in those with severe brain anomalies, but most patients with milder CNS anomalies can reach adulthood, although most patients will never be autonomous.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Name: Moderate and severe traumatic brain injury
DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare neurologic condition characterized by brain damage caused by an external mechanical force, with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9 to 12 in moderate traumatic brain injury (TBI), or 3 to 8 in severe TBI, respectively. TBI can be closed (with the dura mater remaining intact) or open (with penetration of the dura mater) and may lead to focal damage, such as cerebral contusion and hemorrhage, as well as diffuse axonal injury and secondary damage due to increased intracranial pressure. Signs and symptoms are highly variable, depending on the nature, severity, localization, and extent of the trauma.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Moderate and severe traumatic brain injury can arise from diverse causes. Motor vehicle crashes and road traffic accidents are frequently reported etiologies. Falls, including severe falls and those sustained during activities like mountain trips, also contribute significantly. Equestrian sports are associated with a high risk of TBI. Penetrating trauma, such as stab wounds or knife penetration, can lead to severe intracranial injuries. Furthermore, caregiver shaking of infants is strongly associated with unexplained intellectual disability, indicating it as a cause of TBI in early childhood. [PMC11922699, PMC11569656, PMC11833521, PMC12036360, PMC12220057]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Lhermitte-Duclos disease is a rare subtype of gangliocytoma, a benign tumor growth in the cerebellum often associated with Cowden syndrome, a sporadic genetic pleomorphic disorder that is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner and caused by a harmful mutation in the PTEN gene. Such a mutation can originate malignant and benign tumors, including dysplastic gangliocytoma of the posterior cranial fossa. two illustrative cases of Lhermitte-Duclos disease that we encountered and surgically treated during the last few years. We also performed a systematic literature review concerned with the surgical management of Lhermitte-Duclos disease and Cowden syndrome. Both patients were young females complaining of occipital headaches and underwent brain MRIs that revealed unilateral discrete cerebellar atrophy and expansive lesions of the posterior cranial fossa with characteristic striate T-2... [PMC12136761]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare chromosomal anomaly characterized by variable developmental delay with intellectual disability, epilepsy, pigmentary skin anomalies and characteristic facial features usually caused by mosaic tetrasomy of the short arm of chromosome 12. A wide range of pulmonary, cardiac, renal, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, ophtalmologic and auditory features are also associated.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The exact prevalence at birth is uncertain but was estimated to be around 1/20,000. The frequency of Pallister-Killian syndrome (PKS) is likely underestimated due to the difficulty in identifying tissue-limited mosaicism, especially in peripheral blood cells.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: A number of cases are prenatally diagnosed because of abnormal ultrasonic findings. The most common signs include abnormal facial shape, rhizomelic limb shortening, small hands and feet with nail hypoplasia. Hypotonia is usually present at birth and may cause feeding difficulties. Neurologic involvement with brain malformation, severe/moderate intellectual disability, and seizures are frequent. Craniofacial features include a ''coarse'' face with flat profile, high forehead with high anterior hairline, characteristic frontotemporal pattern of alopecia, sparseness of eyebrows and eyelashes, upslanting palpebral fissures, hypertelorism, epicanthic folds, flat and broad nasal bridge, short nose with anteverted nares, long philtrum, large mouth with a Cupid's bow appearance, thick upper lip vermilion and invasion of vermilion of the upper lip by philtral skin (called ''Pallister lip''), macroglossia and low-set, posteriorly rotated ears. A wide range of congenital malformations may be present, including abnormality of skin pigmentation, deafness, congenital heart defects, diaphragmatic hernia, omphalocele, anal atresia, sacral appendages and polydactyly.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: Patients with this syndrome have mosaicism for a supernumerary isochromosome 12p, resulting in four copies of the short arm of chromosome 12 instead of the normal two. On rare occasions mosaic hexasomy with two isochromosomes have been described. The isochromosome is mostly of maternal origin. Karyotype is 47, XX or XY, i(12)(p10)/ 46,XX or XY. The degree of mosaicism is highly variable. Complete or partial 12p duplications (with trisomy 12p) can also cause a PKS phenotype.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Clinical recognition is very important because the additional chromosome is usually absent from routine blood lymphocyte examination. Interphase fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) on a buccal smear with DNA probes specific for chromosome 12 may allow for a rapid and non-invasive preliminary diagnosis. CGH and SNP-arrays from peripheral blood sample can also be useful diagnosis tools. However, cytogenetic diagnosis may require a skin biopsy and examination of fibroblast chromosomes due to the variable quality of other sampling methods. The isochromosome is usually present in 30-100% of fibroblast metaphases. Cytogenetic discrimination between mosaic i(12)p and 12p duplication, which may result from an unbalanced translocation, is essential in genetic counseling.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include trisomy 12p syndrome and Fryns syndrome.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: The syndrome can be suspected by non-invasive prenatal testing from the distinctive ultrasound findings such as diaphragmatic hernia, polydactyly, cardiac and brain malformations, thickened nuchal fold, hydrops fetalis and polyhydramnios. Amniocentesis can be performed for prenatal genetic testing.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: All reported cases of PKS have been sporadic. Theoretically, there could be a risk of recurrence should a parent present with iso12p germline mosaicism. A PKS phenotype may be caused by chromosomal duplications including 12p; in such cases, the possibility of a parent being a carrier of a balanced translocation should be excluded.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: Diaphragmatic hernia may require early surgery during the first days or months of life. Seizures are common and require standard therapy. Rehabilitation (physical therapy, psychomotor and speech therapy) should be started as soon as possible.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis depends on the degree of mosaicism, on the presence of diaphragmatic hernias and other congenital anomalies and epilepsy. Intellectual disability can be severe, but in 27% of the reported cases it was found to range from mild to moderate.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic retinal disorder characterized by childhood-onset of markedly delayed visual adaptation to both dark and light conditions, marked difficulties tracking moving objects, and mild photophobia. Visual acuity is variably reduced, while color vision is unaffected.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: Purpose: To characterize photoreceptor structure and mosaic integrity in subjects with ​RGS9- and R9AP-associated retinal dysfunction (bradyopsia) and compare to previous observations in other cone dysfunction disorders such as oligocone trichromacy. Design: Observational case series. setting: Moorfields Eye Hospital (United Kingdom) and Medical College Wisconsin (USA). Study population: Six eyes of 3 subjects with disease-causing variants in ​RGS9 or R9AP. Main outcome measures: Detailed retinal imaging using spectral-domain optical coherence tomography and confocal adaptive-optics scanning light ophthalmoscopy. Cone density at 100 μm from foveal center ranged from 123 132 cones/mm(2) to 140 013 cones/mm(2). Cone density ranged from 30 573 to 34 876 cones/mm(2) by 600 μm from center and from 15 987 to 16,253 cones/mm(2) by 1400 μm from center, in keeping with data from normal subjects.... [PMC4653116]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Bradyopsia is a retinal dysfunction associated with disease-causing variants in the RGS9 or R9AP genes. Subjects with molecularly confirmed bradyopsia exhibit a relatively intact and structurally normal photoreceptor mosaic. This cellular phenotype allows for distinction from other cone dysfunction disorders, such as oligocone trichromacy, and suggests different underlying pathomechanisms. [PMC4653116]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of bradyopsia involves detailed retinal imaging, utilizing spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) and confocal adaptive-optics scanning light ophthalmoscopy. These characterize photoreceptor structure and mosaic integrity. While standard clinical findings are insufficient to distinguish bradyopsia from other cone dysfunction disorders, advanced imaging can reveal a relatively intact and structurally normal photoreceptor mosaic, which helps differentiate it. A small, focal hyporeflective lesion at the foveal center may be observed in RGS9-associated disease. Molecular confirmation is also noted as a diagnostic element. [PMC4653116]
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis_G: Bradyopsia shares common clinical symptoms with oligocone trichromacy, making differentiation challenging based on standard clinical findings alone. However, adaptive-optics imaging can distinguish these disorders. In oligocone trichromacy, imaging reveals a sparse mosaic of normal wave-guiding cones at the fovea with no visible structure outside the central fovea. In contrast, molecularly confirmed bradyopsia presents with a relatively intact and structurally normal photoreceptor mosaic, allowing for distinction based on the cellular phenotype and suggesting different pathomechanisms. [PMC4653116]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A lysosomal storage disease with multisystemic involvement leading to a massive accumulation of glycosaminoglycans and a wide variety of symptoms including distinctive coarse facial features, short stature, cardio-respiratory involvement and skeletal abnormalities. It manifests as a continuum varying from a severe form with neurodegeneration to an attenuated form without neuronal involvement.
DiseaseInfo.Synonyme(s): Hunter syndrome; Iduronate 2-sulfatase deficiency; MPS2; MPSII; Mucopolysaccharidosis type II

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: Mucopolysaccharidosis type 2 (MPS2) prevalence at birth in Europe is 1/166,000. It is an X-linked recessive disorder; very rare cases of female presentation have been reported.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: MPS2 patients appear healthy at birth, with initial symptoms appearing between 18 months and 4 years of age. Macrocephaly develops during infancy and infants initially grow at normal or above average rates. Initial manifestations include: frequent respiratory tract infections (in particular otitis media); umbilical and inguinal hernia; intractable diarrhea; hepatosplenomegaly; and skin lesions resembling an orange peel (on the shoulder, back and thighs). A distinctive facies with thickening of lips and nostrils as well as an enlarged and protruding tongue forms slowly and may become evident between 2-4 years of age, later in attenuated cases. Progression varies from a severe form (MPS2, severe form) with early psychomotor regression to an attenuated form (MPS2, attenuated form) which manifests without cognitive involvement.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: MPS2 results from iduronate-2-sulfatase (I2S) deficiency, which leads lysosomal accumulation of two specific mucopolysaccharides, dermatan sulfate (DS) and heparan sulfate (HS). The causative gene, IDS, is located on Xq28, approximately 320 mutations have been reported to cause MPS2.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on clinical signs followed by the detection of increased levels of DS and HS in the urine and confirmed by the demonstration of the enzyme deficiency in the serum, leukocytes or fibroblasts, or in dried blood spot samples. Enzymatic activity of another sulfatase should also be assessed. Genetic testing requires searching for exonic or whole-gene deletions, for point mutations in IDS and its promoter region, and for recombination with the nearby pseudogene IDS2.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Differential diagnoses include mucopolysaccharidosis type 1, 6, 7; sialidosis type 2; mucolipidosis type 2 and 3; and multiple sulfatase deficiency.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: Prenatal diagnosis by measuring IDS activity or by mutation analysis in chorionic villi or amniocytes is only performed for male fetuses.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: Women at risk of being a carrier should undergo genetic testing as MPS2 is X-linked recessive. Female carriers transmit the disorder to 50% of their sons; only 12 cases of affected girls have been described due to skewed X-inactivation.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: All patients should be considered for weekly intravenous enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) which has been shown to alleviate somatic symptoms. Cranial shunting should be performed to relieve cases of hydrocephalus. Hernia repair, tonsillectomy and adenoidectomy (to liberate the upper respiratory tract) and in some cases positive pressure ventilation or tracheostomy may be required. Cardiac valve or hip replacement and carpal tunnel release may be necessary over time. Extensive palliative care is required, patients must be regularly evaluated by echocardiogram, respiratory function, full radiologic examination to identify dysostosis multiplex, cranial and cervical MRI with or without lumbar puncture to assess cerebrospinal fluid pressure, hearing tests, eye exams and nerve conduction velocity tests.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable. In the severe form (60-80% of cases) life expectancy is markedly reduced, death generally occurring before the age of 25 often as a result of cardio-respiratory complications. In the attenuated form, patients may survive into adulthood, sometimes even beyond the age of 60, and intellectual deficits are most often absent in these cases.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic neurologic syndrome characterized by the triad of ichthyosis, hepatosplenomegaly and late-onset cerebellar ataxia that presents with progressive dysarthria, unsteadiness of gait. Ichthyosis usually manifests with marked hyperkeratosis, affecting the hands, arms and legs, primarily on the extensor surfaces of the limbs. The severity of ataxia and limb and disability of limb movements are variable. Upward vertical gaze palsy, sluggish reflexes and impaired memory may also be present. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1979.

DiseaseSummary.Clinical description_G: This unique disorder has been described in a sibship, affecting at least two brothers. It is characterized by a distinct triad of clinical features: ichthyosis, hepatosplenomegaly, and cerebellar ataxia, with the latter presenting as late-onset. While clinical features and investigations have been described, no specific metabolic abnormality has been identified so far. [PMC1048549]
DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: The etiology of ichthyosis-hepatosplenomegaly-cerebellar degeneration syndrome remains largely unknown. The disorder has been observed in a sibship, indicating a potential familial or genetic basis for its occurrence. However, despite investigations, no specific metabolic abnormality has been identified as the underlying cause to date. [PMC1048549]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: A sibship is described in which at least two brothers suffer from a unique disorder characterised by ichthyosis, hepatosplenomegaly, and late onset cerebellar ataxia. The clinical features and investigations are described. No metabolic abnormality has been found so far. [PMC1048549]
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: The disorder has been observed in a sibship, affecting at least two brothers, which strongly suggests an inherited basis. While the specific mode of inheritance is not explicitly stated, the occurrence in siblings points towards a recessive pattern. At the time of the report, no metabolic abnormality had been identified, indicating the underlying genetic cause was not yet elucidated. [PMC1048549]

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare genetic, multiple congenital anomalies syndrome characterized by cleft lip, with or without cleft palate, pits in the lower lip, contractures of the lower extremities, abnormal external genitalia, syndactyly of fingers and/or toes, and a pyramidal skin fold over the hallux nail.

DiseaseSummary.Epidemiology: The prevalence of autosomal-dominant-popliteal pterygium syndrome (AD-PPS) is unknown. However, based on the occurence of cleft lip/palate in the general population, the prevalence at birth of popliteal pterygium syndrome (PPS) has been suggested at 1/300,000 with more than 200 cases of AD-PPS being reported worldwide.
DiseaseSummary.Clinical description: Presentation may be as early as the first trimester, with detection of cleft lip and/or palate on ultrasound. In addition to facial clefts (91%-97%), patients may have lower lip pits or sinuses (45%), webbing of the skin extending from the ischial tuberosities to the heels (popliteal pterygium with contractures possibly impairing mobility) (58%), bifid scrotum and cryptorchidism in affected males and hypoplasia of the labia majora in females, finger and/or toe syndactyly, and skin abnormalities around the nails. Almost all patients have a pyramidal fold of skin overlying the nail of the hallux. Some may have missing teeth. Other occasional features include filiform synechiae connecting the upper and lower jaws (syngnathia) or the upper and lower eyelids (ankyloblepharon), spina bifida occulta, retrognathia, accessory medial meniscus, and talipes. Growth and intellectual development are normal in patients with AD-PPS although there are some reports of delayed language acquisition and learning disabilities.
DiseaseSummary.Etiology: AD-PPS is associated with mutations in the IRF6 gene (1q32.2-q32.3), involved in the formation of epithelial tissues, especially the periderm. Almost all affected patients harbor mutations in IRF6.
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods: Diagnosis is based on the presence of the characteristic range of clinical findings (cleft lip with or without cleft palate, popliteal pterygium, genital and nail anomalies), and can be confirmed by molecular genetic testing. AD-PPS is highly associated with missense mutations in the DNA Binding Domain of IRF6(encoded in exons 3 and 4) that alter residues that are predicted to interact directly with DNA.
DiseaseSummary.Differential diagnosis: Mildly affected AD-PPS patients have significant clinical overlap with Van der Woude syndrome (VWS), a disorder caused by deletions and mutations in the same gene (IRF6). In fact, affected individuals in the same family, having the same mutation in IRF6, have been diagnosed with AD-PPS and with VWS. The cause of this variable expressivity is not known. Bartsocas-Papas syndrome, CHAND syndrome and multiple pterygium syndrome should also be considered.
DiseaseSummary.Antenatal diagnosis: If the disease-causing mutation has been identified in the family, prenatal diagnosis for at-risk pregnancies is possible through molecular analysis following amniocentesis or chorionic villus sampling.
DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling: The pattern of inheritance is autosomal dominant with a 50% risk of disease transmission to offspring. However, penetrance is incomplete and expressivity is variable. De novo mutations have also been reported. Genetic counseling should be provided to affected families.
DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment: In infants, nutritional intake and weight gain should be monitored. Cleft lip and/or palate should be treated surgically at an early stage and orthodontically by a specialized multidisciplinary team. Speech therapy as well as audiological and dental assessments should also be provided. Surgery may also be required for lip pits, popliteal pterygium, syndactyly and ankyloblepharon. Rarely, surgical correction of abnormal genitalia may be considered. Management of the other manifestations of AD-PPS is generally supportive and symptomatic.
DiseaseSummary.Prognosis: Overall prognosis is good. Growth and intelligence are expected to be normal, and corrective surgeries are available, especially for orofacial clefts. However, the prognosis for physical activity depends on the severity of the pterygium and the success of corrective surgery. Genital anomalies may cause infertility.

DiseaseInfo.Disease Definition: A rare hereditary poikiloderma characterized by infantile onset of vesicopustule formation on hands and feet and widespread eczematoid dermatitis (both spontaneously resolving during childhood), as well as gradually developing diffuse poikiloderma with striate and reticulate atrophy (excluding the face, scalp, and ears), and development of keratotic papules on hands, feet, elbows, and knees, beginning in early childhood. There have been no further descriptions in the literature since 1981.

DiseaseSummary.Etiology_G: Hereditary acrokeratotic poikiloderma, also known as Kindler syndrome, is a rare autosomal recessive genodermatosis caused by mutations in the FERMT1 gene. This gene encodes kindlin-1, and its mutations lead to a reduction or complete absence of kindlin-1 in keratinocytes. This deficiency in defective integrin activation, cell adhesion, and migration. Kindlin-1 also plays a role in regulating epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) signaling and protecting EGFR from lysosomal-mediated degradation. Various types of FERMT1 mutations have been identified, including single nucleotide substitutions (missense, nonsense), frameshift, duplication, and large deletion mutations, with patients often being homozygous or compound heterozygous for these mutations. Revertant mosaicism, through mechanisms like slipped mispairing or mitotic recombination, can lead to localized restoration of kindlin-1 expression. [PMC12117226, PMC11099494, PMC7506884, PMC6345584, PMC4642877]
DiseaseSummary.Diagnostic methods_G: Diagnosis of Kindler Syndrome (KS) relies on clinical evaluation, noting characteristic features such as blistering, photosensitivity, and progressive poikiloderma. Dermoscopy serves as a useful tool, aiding in the identification of poikiloderma, adermatoglyphia, and cigarette paper scarring. Genetic analysis is crucial for confirmation, typically involving multi-gene panel tests, direct sequencing of the FERMT1 gene, and Sanger sequencing to identify pathogenic mutations. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) and PCR can further characterize gene deletions. Additionally, reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) on gingival fibroblasts can confirm the lack of kindlin-1 mRNA expression. Differential diagnosis, including the exclusion of conditions like porphyria cutanea tarda, is performed using specific laboratory findings. DiseaseSummary.Genetic counseling_G: Kindler Syndrome is an autosomal recessive genodermatosis caused by mutations in the FERMT1 gene, making genetic counseling essential. This is particularly important in populations with consanguineous marriages, as affected individuals often have healthy parents who are carriers of FERMT1 mutations. Genetic analysis, including multi-gene panel tests and Sanger sequencing, is crucial for confirming the diagnosis by identifying pathogenic mutations. Clinical evaluation and heightened awareness of both typical and atypical manifestations are also vital, especially in settings where genetic testing may be unavailable. DiseaseSummary.Management and treatment_G: Management of hereditary acrokeratotic poikiloderma, a form of Kindler syndrome, primarily focuses on supportive care and symptomatic relief. This includes antibiotics for infections, iron supplementation for anemia, and nonadhesive wound care products with emollients for skin fragility. Ocular manifestations are treated with topical lubricants, low-potency steroids, and immunomodulators. Oral health requires interdisciplinary care, encompassing orthodontic treatment, maintenance therapy for periodontal disease, and surgical intervention for mucosal stenoses. Guidelines exist for dental care, including anesthesia. While new genetic and cellular therapies show promise, further research is needed for their full therapeutic realization, emphasizing the current importance of a multidisciplinary approach and regular follow-up.
